additional_notes: Used as a proper noun for the continent; usually takes the preposition "na" (= em + a) when saying someone lives/is there: "morar na América do Sul", "estar na América do Sul".
target_language_example: Eu quero viajar pela América do Sul no ano que vem.
native_language_example: I want to travel around South America next year.

meaning: the World Cup (usually the FIFA soccer tournament).
additional_notes: A fixed name for an international championship. In everyday Portuguese, “a Copa do Mundo” most often refers to the FIFA men’s soccer World Cup, but it can also be specified (e.g., “Copa do Mundo da FIFA”, “Copa do Mundo feminina”). Usually used with the definite article: “a Copa do Mundo”.
target_language_example: A Copa do Mundo acontece a cada quatro anos.
native_language_example: The World Cup happens every four years.

meaning: “God forgive me.” (said to apologize, show remorse, or soften what you’re about to say)
additional_notes: Used as an expression of guilt/remorse or as a polite hedge before saying something harsh, sensitive, or disloyal (similar to “God forgive me” / “forgive me for saying this” / “I hate to say it”). It can appear as a stand-alone sentence (“Deus me perdoe.”) or inserted with commas: “Deus me perdoe, mas…”. A common variant is “Que Deus me perdoe” (“May God forgive me”).
target_language_example: Deus me perdoe, mas eu acho que ele está mentindo.
native_language_example: God forgive me, but I think he’s lying.

additional_notes: Often used on its own (“Deus sabe.”) or as “Só Deus sabe…” (“Only God knows…”) to mean nobody really knows, or the speaker doesn’t know. It can also hint that the outcome depends on fate/unknown circumstances.
target_language_example: Deus sabe quando ele vai voltar.
native_language_example: God knows when he’ll be back.

additional_notes: A common religious well-wish used to express care, gratitude, or goodwill (often when saying goodbye or after someone helps you). You’ll also often hear it as “Que Deus te abençoe” (“May God bless you”), which is slightly more formal/explicitly wish-like. In Brazil, “te” is common; you may also hear “Deus o/a abençoe” in more formal speech.
target_language_example: Muito obrigado pela ajuda. Deus te abençoe.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for the help. God bless you.

additional_notes: Used to refer to two people named João and Maria. In examples, it’s a couple (they loved each other, broke up, went on a date). Can also be said as a surprised question (“João e Maria?”) meaning “João and Maria? / You mean João and Maria?”
target_language_example: Você viu João e Maria juntos ontem?
native_language_example: Did you see João and Maria together yesterday?

meaning: Your Majesty (a very formal way to address a king or queen).
additional_notes: Used in royal or ceremonial contexts when speaking directly to a monarch. In Portuguese it’s a respectful third-person form: you typically use third-person verbs and pronouns with it (e.g., “Vossa Majestade quer...”, “se Vossa Majestade o conhece”). You may also see it abbreviated as “V. M.” in writing.
target_language_example: Vossa Majestade deseja que eu espere aqui?
native_language_example: Does Your Majesty want me to wait here?

additional_notes: Used after verbs of movement (like ir, levar, voltar) when the exact destination is unknown, not specified, or not important. It can be used in questions (“Ela foi a algum lugar?”) or statements (“Quero levar você a algum lugar romântico.”). In expressions like “Você vai a algum lugar com isso?”, it can mean “Are you getting anywhere with that?” (making progress), not literally going somewhere.
target_language_example: Vamos a algum lugar tranquilo para conversar.
native_language_example: Let’s go somewhere quiet to talk.

meaning: to ride a bicycle; to learn how to ride a bike.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like "aprender" (to learn), "ensinar" (to teach), "querer" (to want) to express the activity/skill of riding a bicycle. Here, "a" introduces the action in European Portuguese (roughly like the English infinitive "to" in this context), and "andar de bicicleta" literally refers to going/riding by bicycle.
target_language_example: Aprendi a andar de bicicleta quando tinha seis anos de idade.
native_language_example: I learned to ride a bicycle when I was six years old.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is already inside and traveling on a ship, plane, train, bus, etc. Common in announcements and questions about whether everyone has gotten on. With verbs like “estar/ficar a bordo” (to be/remain on board) and “trazer/levar a bordo” (to bring/take on board).
target_language_example: O voo só vai partir quando todos estiverem a bordo.
native_language_example: The flight will only depart when everyone is on board.

additional_notes: Used with time periods and quantities to express frequency/regular intervals: a cada semana (every week), a cada três horas (every three hours), a cada ano (every year), a cada três meses (every three months). It can also mean "to each" when referring to visiting/doing something for each item in a set (e.g., ir a cada monumento = go to each monument).
target_language_example: Tomo água a cada duas horas.
native_language_example: I drink water every two hours.

meaning: every day; day by day (as time goes by).
additional_notes: Often used to show gradual change or progress over time (“more and more … a cada dia”, “ficar + comparative + a cada dia”). It can mean a routine frequency (“every day”) or emphasize that something is increasing/decreasing little by little (“day by day”).
target_language_example: A cada dia, eu entendo um pouco mais de português.
native_language_example: Day by day, I understand a little more Portuguese.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is currently traveling toward a destination or will arrive soon. Often used with forms of “estar”: “está a caminho”, “estamos a caminho”. It can also refer to help or an order/shipment that is coming (“Não há ajuda a caminho”).
target_language_example: O táxi já está a caminho.
native_language_example: The taxi is already on the way.

additional_notes: Used to say you are in transit or going toward a destination (a place or event). Often used with the verb "estar": "Estou a caminho de..." It’s similar to "indo para", but emphasizes that you’re already en route.
target_language_example: Já estou a caminho de casa.
native_language_example: I’m already on my way home.

meaning: on the way home; heading home.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is traveling/going back to their home at that moment. Often appears at the start of a sentence as a time phrase: "A caminho de casa, ...". You can also say "estar a caminho de casa" (to be on the way home).
target_language_example: Estou a caminho de casa, chego em dez minutos.
native_language_example: I'm on my way home; I'll be there in ten minutes.

meaning: “to sing” (as an infinitive after a verb); also “singing” (ongoing action, esp. in European Portuguese).
additional_notes: Used with many verbs to express the action that follows: e.g., "começar a cantar" (to start singing), "ensinar a cantar" (to teach to sing), "persuadir a cantar" (to persuade to sing). In European Portuguese, "estar a + infinitive" expresses an action in progress: "estais a cantar" = "you are singing". In Brazilian Portuguese, the ongoing form is more often "estar cantando".
target_language_example: Eles estão a cantar no coro hoje.
native_language_example: They are singing in the choir today.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "estar" (to be) or "ficar" to express an action in progress in European Portuguese: "estar a chorar" = "to be crying". It can also follow another verb to show the manner/state while doing something: "telefonou ... a chorar" = "called ... while crying". With "começar", it means "to start crying": "começar a chorar".
target_language_example: Ela está a chorar porque perdeu o telemóvel.
native_language_example: She is crying because she lost her phone.

meaning: to dance; dancing (used with another verb).
additional_notes: Common in European Portuguese after another verb, especially with verbs like aprender/ensinar/tentar/ver: “aprender a dançar” = “to learn to dance”, “ensinou o Tom a dançar” = “taught Tom to dance”, “viste-o a dançar?” = “did you see him dancing?”. It’s also used in the progressive with estar: “estou a dançar” = “I’m dancing.”
target_language_example: Eles ficaram a olhar para nós a dançar.
native_language_example: They stood there watching us dance.

additional_notes: “A + infinitive” is very common in Portuguese after verbs like ensinar (to teach), aprender (to learn), ajudar (to help), começar (to start), and others. Here, “a dirigir” refers to the action of driving. Note: “dirigir” can also mean “to manage/run/lead” (e.g., dirigir uma empresa = to run a company), but with aprender/ensinar it usually means driving a vehicle.
target_language_example: Ela está a aprender a dirigir.
native_language_example: She is learning to drive.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a female person as the recipient or target of an action, especially after verbs like dar, dizer, explicar, or mostrar. It is the explicit form with the preposition a; Portuguese may also use lhe in many of these contexts, while a ela can sound clearer or more emphatic.
target_language_example: Mostrei a foto a ela.
native_language_example: I showed her the photo.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition a + the stressed pronoun ele. It often appears after verbs or expressions that take a, and can also be used for clarity or emphasis instead of lhe.
target_language_example: Eu expliquei tudo a ele ontem.
native_language_example: I explained everything to him yesterday.

meaning: 'to him that…' (introduces what you told/said/reported to him).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like dizer (to say/tell), contar (to tell), pedir (to ask), explicar (to explain) to mark the person receiving the information: "disse/contou/pediu a ele que + clause". Very common alternative: "disse-lhe/contou-lhe/pediu-lhe que…" (lhe = to him/to her).
target_language_example: Eu expliquei a ele que não posso ir hoje.
native_language_example: I explained to him that I can’t go today.

additional_notes: Used with verbs that take an indirect object (often verbs of saying, giving, showing, telling): dizer a eles (tell them), dar a eles (give them), mostrar a eles (show them). For an all-female group, use "a elas". In everyday speech, "para eles" is also common and often interchangeable depending on the verb/region.
target_language_example: Vou enviar a eles a mensagem hoje.
native_language_example: I'm going to send them the message today.

additional_notes: Used after a verb that takes an indirect object (like dizer, pedir, prometer) to introduce what you’re telling/asking/promise them. "a eles" = "to them" (masculine or mixed group); for feminine-only group: "a elas que". Often you’ll see the same pattern with nouns: "a ele/ela que" (to him/her that).
target_language_example: Expliquei a eles que não posso ir hoje.
native_language_example: I explained to them that I can’t go today.

meaning: writing; to write (often in an ongoing/continuous sense).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like “continuar” or “passar” to mean “to keep/start doing” something (continuar a escrever = keep writing; passar a escrever = start writing). In European Portuguese, “estar a escrever” is the common way to say “to be writing” (right now). In Brazilian Portuguese, you’ll more often hear “estar escrevendo”. Also appears in pairs like “a ler e a escrever” = “to read and write.”
target_language_example: Estou a escrever um e-mail, já te respondo.
native_language_example: I’m writing an email; I’ll reply to you in a moment.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the current time, often implying it’s late, inconvenient, unexpected, or unusual (“at this hour”). Common in questions/scolding and apologies for calling/being out. Can be expanded: “a essa hora da noite” = “at this hour of the night”.
target_language_example: Por que você está me ligando a essa hora?
native_language_example: Why are you calling me at this hour?

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a topic already mentioned: “regarding that matter/issue.” Common after verbs like falar (to talk), saber (to know), ter informação (to have information), sentir-se culpado (to feel guilty). Also appears as “a este respeito” (about this) or “a respeito disso/daquilo.”
target_language_example: Não tenho nada a declarar a esse respeito.
native_language_example: I have nothing to say about that.

meaning: at this time; at this hour (of the day/night).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the current time, often with surprise or judgment about what someone is doing ("still awake at this hour?"). Very common with "da noite" (at this time of night) and "do dia" (at this time of day).
target_language_example: Você ainda está trabalhando a esta hora?
native_language_example: Are you still working at this hour?

additional_notes: Used with another verb to mean “speaking/talking” as an activity. Very common in European Portuguese in the pattern “estar a + infinitive” (e.g., “estou a falar” = “I’m speaking / I’m talking”). It can also come after other verbs like “continuar” (continue), “aprender” (learn), and “divertir-se” (have fun) to mean “to speak/talking”.
target_language_example: Ele está a falar ao telefone agora.
native_language_example: He is talking on the phone right now.

additional_notes: Used to show support for someone/something ("a favor de" + noun/pronoun). Common with "votar a favor" (to vote in favor) and "ser/estar a favor" (to be in favor). In legal contexts, "a favor de" can mean “in favor of” as in a decision granted to one side.
target_language_example: Eu sou a favor de mudar o horário da reunião.
native_language_example: I’m in favor of changing the time of the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to express support or approval of an idea, person, plan, or action. Often used with a verb in the infinitive: “a favor de + infinitive” (e.g., a favor de ir, a favor de abortar a missão). The opposite is “contra” (against).
target_language_example: Você é a favor de mudar o plano?
native_language_example: Are you in favor of changing the plan?

additional_notes: Common in European Portuguese. After estar, it often corresponds to English "-ing": estou a fazer = "I am doing/making". After another verb, it can also mean "to do/make": ajudar a fazer = "help to do/make".
target_language_example: Estou a fazer o jantar.
native_language_example: I'm making dinner.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like convencer (to convince), forçar (to force), ajudar (to help), prometer (to promise) to talk about someone doing a specific action. Here, "a" introduces the infinitive ("fazer"), and "aquilo" means "that" (a specific thing/action, often something already mentioned).
target_language_example: Eu não vou te obrigar a fazer aquilo.
native_language_example: I’m not going to force you to do that.

additional_notes: Often appears as "estar a fazer isso" in European Portuguese, meaning "to be doing that" (an action in progress). It can also be used after certain verbs with "a" + infinitive, like "acostumar-se a" (to get used to) and "ajudar a" (to help to). In Brazilian Portuguese, the continuous idea is more commonly "estar fazendo isso".
target_language_example: Estou a fazer isso agora.
native_language_example: I'm doing that now.

meaning: (1) in order to (in “a fim de”); (2) feel like / be up for (in “estar a fim”).
additional_notes:
Two very common patterns:
1) **a fim de + infinitive** = purpose/goal: *Estou estudando a fim de poder falar...* (“I’m studying in order to be able to speak...”).
2) **estar (não) a fim (de + infinitive / de + noun)** = desire or willingness (often informal): *Não estou a fim* (“I don’t feel like it / I’m not up for it”), *Está a fim de comer?* (“Do you feel like eating?”). In questions, **O que você está a fim de…?** means “What do you feel like…?”.
target_language_example: Hoje eu não estou a fim de sair; quero ficar em casa.
native_language_example: Today I don’t feel like going out; I want to stay home.

meaning: “in order to” / “so as to”; also (estar) “up for; feel like; want to”.
additional_notes:
Two common uses:
1) Purpose: “a fim de + infinitive” = “in order to …” (more formal/written than “para”).
2) Desire/willingness: “estar a fim de + infinitive/noun” = “to feel like / be up for …”. This is common in speech and can be used jokingly or accusingly depending on tone (e.g., “Você está a fim de me sacanear!”).
target_language_example: Estou a fim de sair mais cedo a fim de pegar o ônibus.
native_language_example: I feel like leaving early in order to catch the bus.

meaning: 'to read'; also used in European Portuguese for the ongoing action 'reading' (estar a ler).
additional_notes: Used after some verbs + infinitive: ensinar/aprender a ler = 'to teach/learn to read'. In European Portuguese, "estar a + infinitive" expresses an action in progress: "Estou a ler" = "I am reading" (Brazilian Portuguese more often uses "estar + gerund": "Estou lendo").
target_language_example: Desculpa, não posso falar agora — estou a ler.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't talk right now — I'm reading.

additional_notes: Used mainly with verbs of movement (ir, sair, levar, mandar) to mean that someone isn’t going/heading anywhere. It commonly appears with "não" (double negative in Portuguese is normal): "Não vou a lugar nenhum" = “I’m not going anywhere.”
target_language_example: Hoje eu não vou a lugar nenhum; vou ficar em casa.
native_language_example: Today I’m not going anywhere; I’m staying home.

additional_notes: Introduces a condition that is the exception to what was just said: something is true or will happen *except if* the condition after "a menos que" happens. It’s commonly followed by the subjunctive (e.g., "a menos que chova", "a menos que seja"). You can place it mid-sentence or at the end.
target_language_example: Eu vou, a menos que você diga que é perigoso.
native_language_example: I’ll go, unless you say it’s dangerous.

additional_notes: Used after a preposition (like a, para, de, com) when the pronoun is the object of that preposition: para mim (for me), com mim (with me), de mim (from me). Very common in phrases like “conte a mim” (tell me) and “leve ... a mim” (take ... to me). With emphasis you may see “a mim” at the end: “Não contei a ninguém, só a mim.” In reflexive/emphatic contexts, it can appear with “mesmo(a)”: “a mim mesmo” = “to myself.”
target_language_example: Por favor, explique isso a mim.
native_language_example: Please explain that to me.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is going/coming/visiting somewhere for work reasons, not tourism. Common with verbs like ir, vir, viajar, visitar: "viajar a negócios". Often implies a business trip.
target_language_example: Estou em Lisboa a negócios esta semana.
native_language_example: I’m in Lisbon on business this week.

additional_notes: Common in two patterns: (1) "não ... a não ser ..." = "not ... except ..." / "nothing/no one ... except ..." (e.g., "Ninguém sabia disso a não ser o Tom."). (2) "não ter escolha a não ser + infinitive" = "to have no choice but to + verb" (e.g., "não tive escolha a não ser pegar..."). It can also introduce an exception/condition similar to "unless".
target_language_example: Não vou sair hoje, a não ser que você precise de mim.
native_language_example: I’m not going out today, unless you need me.

additional_notes: Often followed by **que**: **a não ser que + subjunctive** (“unless …”). Also used with a time/case: **a não ser quando…** (“except when…”). Commonly comes after a negative statement to add an exception: **não… a não ser que…**.
target_language_example: Não vou sair hoje, a não ser que você precise de ajuda.
native_language_example: I’m not going out today unless you need help.

additional_notes: Used before a verb (often in the subjunctive) to give an exception or condition: something is true/will happen, unless this other thing happens. Common in warnings, rules, and plans. Often followed by the present subjunctive: “a não ser que eu/ele/você faça…”.
target_language_example: Eu vou, a não ser que chova.
native_language_example: I’ll go unless it rains.

meaning: aware; informed; up to date (on something).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like “estar”, “ficar” (to become), “manter” (to keep), or “colocar” (to bring someone) + “a par” + “de” + topic: “estar a par de…” = to be aware of/about; “ficar/ser colocado a par de…” = to be brought up to speed; “manter-me a par” = keep me informed.
target_language_example: Não estou a par das mudanças no horário.
native_language_example: I’m not aware of the schedule changes.

meaning: from; starting from (a point in time, place, or source).
additional_notes: Used to mark the starting point of something in time ("a partir de amanhã" = starting tomorrow), in distance/location ("a partir daqui" = from here), or in origin/source ("a partir do latim" = from Latin; "a partir destas observações" = from these observations). Very often appears as "a partir de" + noun/pronoun.
target_language_example: A partir de amanhã, vou estudar português todos os dias.
native_language_example: Starting tomorrow, I'm going to study Portuguese every day.

meaning: 'from' (starting at a time/point) or 'based on' (using something as a source).
additional_notes: Used to mark a starting point in time, place, or a situation: "a partir de segunda-feira" = starting Monday; "a partir de então" = from then on. It can also mean "from/out of" in the sense of origin or source: "fazer dinheiro a partir de um negócio" = make money from a business; "ir para o servidor a partir de seu computador" = go to the server from your computer. Often interchangeable with "desde" for time (starting from), but "a partir de" emphasizes the start point.
target_language_example: O curso começa a partir de amanhã.
native_language_example: The course starts tomorrow (starting from tomorrow).

additional_notes: Used to mark a change starting at this moment and continuing into the future (new rule, decision, or situation). Often followed by a verb in the future or near future: “A partir de agora, vamos… / você vai… / faremos…”. You can place it at the beginning (common with a comma) or later in the sentence.
target_language_example: A partir de agora, eu vou estudar português todos os dias.
native_language_example: From now on, I’m going to study Portuguese every day.

additional_notes:
Used with verbs like:
- "ter ... a perder" = "to have ... to lose" (often in questions: "O que você tem a perder?" = "What do you have to lose?")
- "(não) ter tempo/minuto a perder" = "(not) have time/a minute to waste" (means you must hurry)
- "deixar ... a perder" = "to let ... go to waste/ruin" (to fail to use something valuable, like love or an opportunity).
target_language_example: Vamos embora — não temos um segundo a perder.
native_language_example: Let's go—we don't have a second to waste.

meaning: about to; to the point of (doing something).
additional_notes: Commonly used in two patterns: (1) with estar/ficar + a ponto de + infinitive to mean something is imminent: "estava a ponto de se queimar" (she was about to burn herself). (2) after intensifiers like "tão" to show an extreme degree/result: "tão estúpido a ponto de acreditar" (so stupid as to believe). Often matches English "so ... that" / "so ... as to". With "a ponto de" you typically use an infinitive verb after it.
target_language_example: Eu estava a ponto de sair quando você ligou.
native_language_example: I was about to leave when you called.

additional_notes: Common in commands/announcements (military, police, inspections, sports) meaning everyone should be ready and in position. Can also mean someone is on duty/standing watch (“ficar/estar a postos”). Often used alone as a short response: “A postos.” = “Ready.”
target_language_example: Fiquem a postos — o chefe está a chegar.
native_language_example: Stay ready — the boss is about to arrive.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an initial situation/feeling/opinion that may change later. Common at the start of a sentence (“A princípio, …”) or at the end (“… a princípio”). Often implies “in the beginning, but not necessarily later.”
target_language_example: A princípio, achei a ideia ruim, mas depois gostei.
native_language_example: At first, I thought the idea was bad, but later I liked it.

meaning: 'by the way' (to introduce an extra comment or new topic).
additional_notes: Used to add something you just remembered or to shift the conversation: “A propósito, ...”. It can also mean “on purpose/intentional” in other contexts (e.g., “Ele fez isso a propósito.”), but in the examples here it’s the conversational “by the way.”
target_language_example: A propósito, você tem um carregador que eu possa usar?
native_language_example: By the way, do you have a charger I can use?

additional_notes: Used to say you are walking rather than using a vehicle. It can describe how you travel (viajamos a pé) or that you’re currently without transportation/stranded (Estou a pé).
target_language_example: O hotel é perto, então vamos a pé.
native_language_example: The hotel is close, so we’ll go on foot.

additional_notes: Used to say there is no specific time restriction (now, later, day or night). Often used to give permission or indicate something can happen unexpectedly: "a qualquer hora" = "whenever"/"at any moment". Common with verbs like "vir" (come), "ligar/chamar" (call), "acontecer" (happen).
target_language_example: Você pode ligar a qualquer hora, se precisar de ajuda.
native_language_example: You can call anytime if you need help.

additional_notes: Used to say something can happen (or someone can arrive) at an unspecified time, possibly very soon. Common with future or near-future situations: “vai chegar a qualquer momento” = “could arrive any minute now / any time.” It can also mean “whenever you want” with permission: “Você pode vir a qualquer momento.”
target_language_example: A entrega pode chegar a qualquer momento.
native_language_example: The delivery could arrive any moment now.

additional_notes: Used in questions to ask the distance from one place to another. Often followed by “de” + a reference point: “A que distância de aqui/daqui…?” You can answer with a distance: “A 2 km daqui.”
target_language_example: A que distância do hotel fica o aeroporto?
native_language_example: How far is the airport from the hotel?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a specific time on the clock. Common in questions about schedules (buses, meetings, meals). Often followed by a verb: "A que horas (você) sai?" You can also hear the shorter "Que horas...?" in everyday speech.
target_language_example: A que horas começa a aula?
native_language_example: What time does class start?

additional_notes: Used to ask about a specific time. "Vocês" is the common way to say "you" (plural) in Brazil (it uses 3rd-person plural verbs: vocês chegaram). Often followed by a verb: a que horas vocês chegaram/saíram/vão/fecham?
target_language_example: A que horas vocês vão sair hoje?
native_language_example: What time are you (all) going to leave today?

additional_notes: Used when the person is the object of a verb or the complement of a preposition, especially in more formal Portuguese. Common in questions (A quem você disse? = To whom did you say it?) and in relative clauses (o amigo a quem convidei = the friend whom I invited). In everyday speech, many people replace it with "para quem" or "pra quem" depending on the verb/preposition.
target_language_example: A quem você entregou a chave?
native_language_example: To whom did you give the key?

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic you’re talking about: falar a respeito de algo (“to talk about something”), confusão a respeito de… (“confusion about…”), dizer algo a respeito (“to say something about it”). Often appears with "de" + noun/pronoun (a respeito de você, a respeito disso).
target_language_example: Queria te perguntar uma coisa a respeito do trabalho.
native_language_example: I wanted to ask you something about work.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic of a conversation, question, or information: falar/perguntar a respeito de algo (“talk/ask about something”), ler livros a respeito de X (“read books about X”). It can also appear in expressions like não ter ideia a respeito de... (“to have no idea about...”). Often interchangeable with sobre in many contexts, though a respeito de can sound a bit more formal.
target_language_example: Preciso falar com você a respeito de um problema.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you about a problem.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a specific topic or situation already mentioned (“that”). Very common after verbs like falar (to talk), saber (to know), pensar (to think), and in questions like “O que vamos fazer a respeito disso?” (= “What are we going to do about that?”). Similar to “sobre isso” and “quanto a isso” (slightly more formal).
target_language_example: Ainda não decidimos nada a respeito disso.
native_language_example: We still haven't decided anything about that.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic you’re talking or thinking about. It’s a bit more formal than "sobre". It contracts with articles: a respeito do (de + o), a respeito da (de + a), a respeito dos, a respeito das; before a name you often see "a respeito de" (e.g., "a respeito do Tom" is also common in speech).
target_language_example: Ainda não decidimos nada a respeito do projeto.
native_language_example: We still haven't decided anything about the project.

meaning: 'namely' (to specify); also used with other verbs meaning 'to find out/come to know'.
additional_notes:
Common uses:
1) As a set phrase meaning “namely / that is to say”, introducing a specification or list: “A saber, …”.
2) As “a” + infinitive “saber” after certain verbs (e.g., “vir a saber”, “ajudar a saber”), meaning “to find out / come to know / learn”. Example: “Como ela veio a saber...?” = “How did she come to know...?”
target_language_example: Trouxe três coisas, a saber: pão, queijo e frutas.
native_language_example: I brought three things, namely: bread, cheese, and fruit.

additional_notes: “A” + infinitive is commonly used after verbs like “preferir” to mean “rather than (do something)”: “prefiro ficar em casa a sair” = “I prefer staying home to going out.” With “obrigar (alguém) a …”, it means “to force (someone) to …”: “obrigou-nos a sair” = “forced us to leave.”
target_language_example: Preferimos ficar aqui a sair agora.
native_language_example: We prefer to stay here rather than go out now.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" (e.g., "estar a salvo") to say someone/something is safe or protected from harm. Common in situations involving danger, emergencies, or reassurance.
target_language_example: Quando chegámos ao hotel, soube que as crianças estavam a salvo.
native_language_example: When we arrived at the hotel, I knew the children were safe.

additional_notes: Used mainly with verbs like “estar” or “ficar” to say someone/something is safe or has been brought to safety. Common in contexts like accidents, emergencies, or protecting something valuable (e.g., “Estamos a salvo”, “O documento ficou a salvo”).
target_language_example: Depois do incêndio, todos ficaram a salvo.
native_language_example: After the fire, everyone was safe.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the next step or the following thing in a sequence. Common with verbs like "fazer" (o que fazer a seguir = what to do next) and in instructions ("A seguir," = Next,/In the following,).
target_language_example: Não sei o que dizer a seguir.
native_language_example: I don't know what to say next.

meaning: 'to be' (infinitive), often in passive-style phrases like 'to be + past participle'.
additional_notes: Used as the infinitive of the verb **ser** with the preposition **a**, commonly after other verbs: **passar a ser** (to become), **continuar a ser** (to continue to be), **voltar a ser** (to be again). It’s also very common in passive constructions: **o primeiro a ser punido/demitido** (“the first to be punished/fired”) and **a ser encontrado(a)** (“to be found”).
target_language_example: Ela foi a última a ser chamada.
native_language_example: She was the last to be called.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to the subject (the same person), often for emphasis or contrast (e.g., “more than himself”). It commonly appears after verbs like ajudar, culpar, perdoar, amar, and can vary by gender/number: a si mesmo (masc. sing.), a si mesma (fem. sing.), a si mesmos/a si mesmas (plural). In informal speech, many people use “a você mesmo/a ti mesmo” instead.
target_language_example: Por favor, ajude a si mesmo.
native_language_example: Please help yourself.

additional_notes: Used to talk about taking something seriously (often with verbs like "levar" or "tomar": "levar/tomar a sério" = "to take seriously"). It can also be a short reply meaning "seriously" or "for real?" depending on tone/context (e.g., "Muito a sério.").
target_language_example: Você está falando a sério?
native_language_example: Are you serious? / Are you for real?

meaning: alone; in private (with no one else around).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is by themselves, or that two (or more) people are together privately, without other people present. Common with verbs like “ficar” (to stay), “deixar” (to leave/let), “conversar/falar” (to talk), and with time expressions like “um momento/algum tempo a sós”.
target_language_example: Preciso ficar um pouco a sós para pensar.
native_language_example: I need to be alone for a bit to think.

meaning: alone; in private (just the two of us).
additional_notes: Used after a verb (often “falar”, “ver”, “deixar”) to say someone is alone or that you want to be with someone privately, without other people present. Common in requests like “Posso falar com você a sós?” (“Can I speak to you in private?”).
target_language_example: Podemos conversar a sós por um minuto?
native_language_example: Can we talk in private for a minute?

meaning: on time; in time (before it’s too late).
additional_notes: Used to say you arrive/finish before a deadline or before something happens. Very common with verbs like chegar (to arrive), conseguir (to manage), and correr (to run). You can add “de + infinitive” to say in time to do something: “a tempo de ajudar” = “in time to help.”
target_language_example: Chegamos a tempo de pegar o trem.
native_language_example: We arrived in time to catch the train.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something must be done or avoided regardless of difficulties, risks, or consequences. Often goes with commands or strong statements of necessity (e.g., "tem que", "deve", "precisa").
target_language_example: Temos que proteger as crianças a todo custo.
native_language_example: We have to protect the children at all costs.

additional_notes: Used to address or refer to a whole group of people. Common in greetings ("Olá/Boa noite a todos") and after verbs like "dizer" (to tell) or "contar" (to tell). Often appears as "a todos" (masculine/mixed group) or "a todas" (all women).
target_language_example: Quero agradecer a todos pela ajuda.
native_language_example: I want to thank everyone for the help.

meaning: working; to be working (in the middle of working).
additional_notes: "A" + infinitive is a common way (especially in Portugal) to express an action in progress: "estar a trabalhar" = "to be working." It’s also often used after verbs like "voltar" (to return) to mean "to go back to doing something": "voltar a trabalhar" = "to go back to work."
target_language_example: Estou a trabalhar agora; posso falar mais tarde.
native_language_example: I’m working right now; can I talk later?

additional_notes: Combination of the preposition a with the indefinite article um. The exact English translation depends on the verb and context: it often means movement or direction ('to a'), but can also be 'at a' or similar in natural English.
target_language_example: Eu dei o livro a um amigo.
native_language_example: I gave the book to a friend.

additional_notes: In European Portuguese, it commonly appears in the continuous form "estar a ver" = "to be watching/looking" and also "to get/understand" ("Está a ver?" = "Do you see/understand?"). In the expression "ter a ver (com)", it means "to have (something) to do with" (e.g., "Não tem a ver com..." = "It has nothing to do with...").
target_language_example: Desculpa, não estou a ver o que queres dizer.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t see/understand what you mean.

additional_notes: In sentences like “ele a ama”, **a** is a clitic direct-object pronoun meaning **“her”**. It comes before the verb (**ama** = “(he) loves”). This is common in more formal/standard Portuguese; in everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people often use **ele ama ela** instead.
target_language_example: Ele a ama de verdade.
native_language_example: He truly loves her.

meaning: “(he/she/I) loved her” / “(he/she/I) used to love her.”
additional_notes: “a” is an unstressed object pronoun meaning “her” (or “it” for a feminine noun) and it usually comes before the verb: eu a amava = I loved her. “amava” is the imperfect past of amar, often used for ongoing feelings in the past or a habitual/unfinished past situation (so it can sound like “loved” or “used to love,” depending on context).
target_language_example: Naquela época, eu a amava muito, mas ela não sabia.
native_language_example: Back then, I loved her a lot, but she didn’t know.

meaning: 'knows her' / 'knows it' (referring to a feminine person or thing).
additional_notes: “a” is an unstressed object pronoun meaning “her/it” (feminine) placed before the verb: conhecer (to know/meet). It refers back to a woman or a feminine noun already mentioned. Common in European Portuguese and in more formal Brazilian Portuguese; in everyday Brazilian Portuguese people often say “conhece ela” (less formal) instead.
target_language_example: Você a conhece bem, não é?
native_language_example: You know her well, don't you?

additional_notes: “A” is an unstressed object pronoun meaning “her” (direct object). It can come before the verb (e.g., “Ele a matou.” = “He killed her.”). “Matou” is the past (simple past) form of “matar” (to kill). In speech, “a” may sound very short and attach to the verb.
target_language_example: Ele a matou sem dizer uma palavra.
native_language_example: He killed her without saying a word.

additional_notes: From the verb "ver" (to see): "vi" = "I saw" (simple past). "a" is the direct-object pronoun meaning "her" (or "you" feminine in some contexts). In Portuguese, object pronouns often come before the verb ("eu a vi"), but they can also come after it ("vi-a"), especially in more formal writing. You’ll also see "o vi" (I saw him/it) and "os/as vi" (I saw them).
target_language_example: Eu a vi ontem no supermercado.
native_language_example: I saw her yesterday at the supermarket.

meaning: "saw her" / "saw it" (referring to a feminine object).
additional_notes: "a" is a direct-object pronoun meaning "her" or "it" (for feminine nouns). It usually goes before the verb in Brazilian Portuguese ("Você a viu" = "You saw her"), but in European Portuguese you’ll often see it attached after the verb ("Viu-a").
target_language_example: Você a viu na festa ontem?
native_language_example: Did you see her at the party yesterday?

meaning: the soul; (figuratively) the heart/essence of something.
additional_notes: Means a person’s soul/spirit (often in religious or philosophical contexts). It can also be used figuratively to mean the central part, driving force, or essence of something (similar to “the heart of the matter”). Gender: feminine (a alma). Plural: as almas.
target_language_example: Ela colocou a alma no projeto.
native_language_example: She put her heart and soul into the project.

additional_notes: Means “the weapon” in general; in many everyday contexts it refers specifically to a firearm (“gun”), depending on situation. Used with verbs like abaixar (lower), pegar (pick up), carregar (carry), colocar (put/place).
target_language_example: A polícia apreendeu a arma.
native_language_example: The police seized the weapon.

meaning: the flag (of a country, place, or organization).
additional_notes: Most commonly refers to a national flag (e.g., the French flag), but can also mean a flag/icon in an app, website, or settings—something you can “change” or “switch” (mudar/trocar a bandeira). Gender: feminine (a bandeira).
target_language_example: Você pode trocar a bandeira do idioma nas configurações.
native_language_example: You can switch the language flag in the settings.

additional_notes: Usually refers to facial hair on the chin/cheeks. Common related expression: "fazer a barba" = "to shave" (literally, "to do the beard"). You can also use it with verbs like "deixar crescer" (to grow) or "cortar" (to cut/trim).
target_language_example: Ele deixou crescer a barba durante as férias.
native_language_example: He grew his beard out during the vacation.

meaning: to grow (out) a beard; to let your beard grow.
additional_notes: Commonly used with the verb "deixar": "deixar a barba crescer" = "to let your beard grow / to grow out your beard". In the present continuous, it’s often "estar deixando a barba crescer" (I’m/he’s letting it grow).
target_language_example: No inverno, vou deixar a barba crescer.
native_language_example: In the winter, I’m going to grow out my beard.

meaning: the battle; a fight/struggle (literal or figurative).
additional_notes: Used for a military battle (often followed by "por/pelo" = "battle for" or "de" = "battle of"), and also for a figurative rivalry or ongoing conflict between people/companies/ideas ("a batalha entre..."). Gender: feminine ("a"). Plural: "as batalhas".
target_language_example: A batalha entre os dois times foi intensa.
native_language_example: The battle between the two teams was intense.

additional_notes: Common noun meaning “beauty,” either in general (an abstract quality) or the beauty of a specific person/thing. Often used with “de/da” to specify what is beautiful: “a beleza da cena” (the beauty of the scene), “a beleza de um anjo” (the beauty of an angel). Can also be used more generally: “Para que serve a beleza?” (What is beauty for?).
target_language_example: A beleza do pôr do sol me deixou sem palavras.
native_language_example: The beauty of the sunset left me speechless.

additional_notes: Literally “the mouth.” Common in expressions: “fechar a boca” (shut your mouth / close your mouth), “manter a boca fechada” (keep your mouth shut), “molhar a boca” (to wet your whistle / have a little drink), and “até a boca” meaning “up to the brim” (filled to the top).
target_language_example: Ele ficou com a boca cheia de água só de pensar no jantar.
native_language_example: His mouth watered just thinking about dinner.

additional_notes: Usually refers to a sports/toy ball. It can also mean a round object in general (e.g., "uma bola de ferro" = "an iron ball"). Often used with verbs like "chutar" (to kick) and "pegar" (to catch/pick up).
target_language_example: Onde está a bola?
native_language_example: Where is the ball?

additional_notes: Usually refers to a woman’s handbag/purse that you carry by hand or on your shoulder. Common with verbs like colocar (put), deixar (leave), pegar (grab), and roubar (steal). Not the same as bolsa de valores (“stock exchange”) or bolsa de estudo (“scholarship”).
target_language_example: Esqueci a bolsa no carro.
native_language_example: I forgot my purse in the car.

additional_notes: Literally means “the head.” In context, “algo para a cabeça dele/dela” often means something to help with a headache (e.g., painkillers). Common with head-movement verbs: “balançar a cabeça” can mean to shake your head (no/disagreement) or nod your head depending on context.
target_language_example: Estou com dor de cabeça; preciso de algo para a cabeça.
native_language_example: I have a headache; I need something for it.

additional_notes: Means “the head of him” (a + cabeça + dele). Used both literally (someone’s head, head injury) and in dramatic/threatening contexts (“cut off his head”, “bring me his head”). In everyday speech, Portuguese often uses just “a cabeça” (or “a cabeça dele”) instead of “a sua cabeça” when it’s clear whose head it is.
target_language_example: Ele bateu a cabeça dele na porta e ficou tonto.
native_language_example: He hit his head on the door and got dizzy.

additional_notes: Feminine singular noun with the definite article: a (the). Used for a piece of furniture to sit on. Common in basic descriptions (material, size) and in commands/requests (mover, derrubar). The plural is as cadeiras (the chairs).
target_language_example: Pode colocar a cadeira perto da mesa?
native_language_example: Can you put the chair near the table?

additional_notes: Commonly refers to a physical box/container. In stores, "caixa" can also mean the checkout/cash register or the cashier, depending on context.
target_language_example: Guardei os documentos na caixa.
native_language_example: I kept the documents in the box.

additional_notes: Literally “the bed” (definite article + noun). In everyday Portuguese, “ir para a cama” means “to go to bed” (go to sleep/lie down), and “vá para a cama” is a common way to tell someone to go to bed.
target_language_example: Estou com sono — vou para a cama.
native_language_example: I’m sleepy — I’m going to bed.

additional_notes: Commonly used with clothing verbs like tirar (to take off), colocar/vestir (to put on/wear), abotoar/desabotoar (to button/unbutton). It can also refer to a blouse or jersey depending on context, but it often means a (usually men’s) shirt.
target_language_example: Ele esqueceu a camisa no carro.
native_language_example: He forgot the shirt in the car.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a doorbell at a house/apartment. You’ll often see it with verbs like "tocar" (to ring) or "tocar a campainha" (to ring the doorbell). It can also refer to other bells (e.g., a school bell), depending on context.
target_language_example: A campainha está quebrada, então me liga quando você chegar.
native_language_example: The doorbell is broken, so call me when you arrive.

additional_notes: Used to name the capital city of a state/country/region: “A capital da Bahia é Salvador.” Often comes before a place name (a capital da França) or as an apposition between commas (“Madrid, a capital da Espanha, ...”). Note the contraction: de + a = da (feminine), because capital is feminine (a capital).
target_language_example: Qual é a capital da Itália?
native_language_example: What is the capital of Italy?

additional_notes: Used to name the main/official city of a place. The pattern is: **A capital do + [masculine noun]** (e.g., *do Brasil*) and **A capital da + [feminine noun]** (e.g., *da França*). You can also say **capital de** with names (often cities/places) without an article: *A capital de Portugal é Lisboa.*
target_language_example: A capital do Canadá é Ottawa.
native_language_example: The capital of Canada is Ottawa.

meaning: the meat; meat (as a general food item).
additional_notes: Definite-article form used when referring to meat as a specific item or as a category in context (e.g., the meat you bought, the meat being discussed). Common in shopping/cooking: “A carne estava em promoção” (on sale), “A carne estragou-se” (went bad), “A carne não deve ser consumida crua” (shouldn’t be eaten raw). It can also mean “flesh” in other contexts, but this entry focuses on food.
target_language_example: A carne estava em promoção hoje.
native_language_example: The meat was on sale today.

additional_notes: Usually means a written letter/message (sent or kept). It can also mean a card (e.g., a playing card), depending on context. Note: "a" is the feminine singular definite article “the”.
target_language_example: Eu recebi a carta ontem.
native_language_example: I received the letter yesterday.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “wallet” (where you keep money/cards/ID). In some contexts, especially at school or in offices, “carteira” can also mean a desk (often a student desk). The meaning is usually clear from context (e.g., “perdi a carteira” = lost my wallet; “uma maçã sobre a carteira” could be a desk).
target_language_example: Esqueci a carteira em casa, então não posso pagar agora.
native_language_example: I forgot my wallet at home, so I can’t pay right now.

additional_notes: A straightforward combination of a + casa. a is the feminine singular definite article ('the'), and casa means 'house' or sometimes 'home', depending on context.
target_language_example: A casa é muito antiga.
native_language_example: The house is very old.

meaning: “the house of … / …’s house”; also “a …house” (made for/for use by something).
additional_notes: Used with a person/owner to mean someone’s home: "a casa de seu irmão" = "your brother’s house". It’s also used to form compound nouns: "casa de passarinho" (birdhouse), "casa de bonecas" (dollhouse). In some contexts, "de" can describe a characteristic like color/material (e.g., "casa de verde" = house painted green), but that’s a broader use of "de" rather than a fixed meaning of the whole phrase.
target_language_example: Vamos jantar na casa de Maria hoje?
native_language_example: Are we going to have dinner at Maria’s house today?

additional_notes: "A" = "the" (feminine singular). "Casa" = "house/home". "Dela" means "of hers" (refers to a woman), so "a casa dela" is literally "the house of hers". Often used when giving directions or asking where someone’s home is: "Onde fica a casa dela?".
target_language_example: Vou até a casa dela depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: I’m going to her house after work.

additional_notes: Means literally “the house/home of him.” Used to refer to a house that belongs to him or the place where he lives. “Dele” = “of him / his” (male owner). For a female owner, say “a casa dela” (“her house”).
target_language_example: A casa dele está à venda.
native_language_example: His house is for sale.

meaning: the scene (a part of a story, film, play, or an event being described).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific moment or segment in a narrative (film/theater/book) or to an event/situation being described: "descrever a cena" = "describe the scene"; "a cena com..." = "the scene with...". In some contexts (especially in Portugal), it can also be used informally to mean "the thing / that situation", but the core meaning is "scene".
target_language_example: A cena final do filme é emocionante.
native_language_example: The final scene of the movie is moving.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive verb to talk about having (or giving someone) an opportunity to do something. Common with verbs like "ter" (to have), "dar" (to give), and in negative forms like "nunca teve a chance de" (never had the chance to).
target_language_example: Você vai ter a chance de conhecer meus pais amanhã.
native_language_example: You’ll have the chance to meet my parents tomorrow.

additional_notes: Refers to a physical key. The article a means "the" and is used with feminine singular nouns, so chave is a feminine noun. In everyday Portuguese, this phrase is very common in expressions like a chave da casa or a chave do carro.
target_language_example: Não encontro a chave do carro.
native_language_example: I can't find the car key.

additional_notes: Means the key (or key fob) that belongs to the car. Very common with verbs like procurar (to look for), colocar/pôr (to put/place), and in questions with onde (where): “Onde (eu) coloquei/pus a chave do carro?” You can also hear “as chaves do carro” (the car keys).
target_language_example: Não acho a chave do carro; você viu onde eu deixei?
native_language_example: I can’t find the car key; did you see where I left it?

additional_notes: Used with the definite article “a” (feminine singular) to talk about rain in a specific situation/time (“A chuva parou.” = “The rain stopped.”). Without the article, “chuva” can be more general (e.g., “Gosto de chuva.” = “I like rain.”). Common verbs: cair (to fall), parar (to stop), ouvir/escutar (to hear/listen to).
target_language_example: A chuva começou de repente, mas parou rápido.
native_language_example: The rain started suddenly, but it stopped quickly.

additional_notes: Means “the city/town” in general, or a specific city already known from context. It can also be used more broadly to mean “everyone in town” (e.g., "a cidade toda" = "the whole town"). Often followed by "em que/onde" to specify which city: "a cidade em que eu nasci" = "the city where I was born".
target_language_example: Eu quero conhecer melhor a cidade.
native_language_example: I want to get to know the city better.

meaning: the whole city; the entire city.
additional_notes: Means all of the city/all the people in the city. Used to emphasize that something affects or is known/visible throughout the entire city. Often used with verbs like "cobrir" (cover), "saber" (know), "ver" (see), and with expressions like "a cidade inteira vai saber" (“the whole city will know”).
target_language_example: O desfile parou a cidade inteira por duas horas.
native_language_example: The parade brought the whole city to a stop for two hours.

additional_notes: “Cobra” is a feminine noun, so it usually takes feminine articles/pronouns (a, uma; ela). In Portuguese, “cobra” commonly means “snake” in general (not only the specific animal called a “cobra” in English). Plural: “as cobras” (the snakes).
target_language_example: Cuidado: a cobra está perto da trilha.
native_language_example: Careful: the snake is near the trail.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the morally correct or appropriate action in a situation. Very common with verbs like fazer (“to do”) and with certainty/opinion phrases: fazer a coisa certa, achar que fez a coisa certa, ter certeza de que está fazendo a coisa certa. You can also use it as advice: Faça a coisa certa.
target_language_example: Mesmo sendo difícil, ele decidiu fazer a coisa certa.
native_language_example: Even though it was hard, he decided to do the right thing.

additional_notes: "A" is the feminine singular definite article ("the"). "Comida" can mean food in general or a prepared meal, depending on context: "A comida deste hotel" = the hotel’s food; "preparar a comida" = to prepare the meal. Often used alone in conversation to refer to the food/meal that’s being talked about or is present (e.g., "A comida." = "The food.").
target_language_example: A comida está pronta; vamos comer.
native_language_example: The food is ready; let’s eat.

additional_notes: Used in restaurants/cafés to ask for the bill. You can say it by itself, or add a waiter call like “Garçom,”. “A conta” = “the bill/check”; “por favor” = “please”. Common polite variants include “Pode me trazer a conta, por favor?” (can you bring me the check?) and the more formal “Poderia trazer a conta, por favor?” (could you bring the check?). In Brazil, “conta” is the usual word for the restaurant bill.
target_language_example: Garçom, a conta, por favor.
native_language_example: Waiter, the check please.

additional_notes: Usually refers to the color of an object (a cor do carro, a cor da parede). In some contexts it can refer to a person’s skin color (a cor da pele), especially when discussing race or discrimination. Gender: feminine (a cor, as cores).
target_language_example: Qual é a cor favorita dela?
native_language_example: What is her favorite color?

additional_notes: Used for a physical rope or string you can pull, cut, or that can break. It’s the feminine singular form, so it often appears with feminine articles and adjectives (a corda, esta corda, a corda longa).
target_language_example: Segure bem a corda para não cair.
native_language_example: Hold the rope tightly so you don’t fall.

meaning: the race; the run (as an event).
additional_notes: Used for a race/competition (running, car race, etc.) and for the act/event of running (not just one quick run to the store). In sports contexts you’ll often see verbs like terminar (finish), recomeçar (restart), vencer/ganhar (win), perder (lose), and abandonar (drop out).
target_language_example: Ele está treinando para a corrida de 10 km.
native_language_example: He is training for the 10 km race.

additional_notes: Most commonly means "the kitchen" (the room), especially with verbs of movement like "levar" (to take). It can also mean "cooking/cuisine" (the style of food), e.g., "A cozinha portuguesa" = "Portuguese cuisine". Feminine noun: "a cozinha".
target_language_example: A cozinha fica ao lado da sala.
native_language_example: The kitchen is next to the living room.

additional_notes: Criança is grammatically feminine, so it takes a in the singular, but it can refer to either a boy or a girl. The plural is as crianças, meaning 'the children'.
target_language_example: A criança está no parque.
native_language_example: The child is in the park.

additional_notes: Usually used with "ser" to ask who is responsible ("De quem é a culpa?" = "Whose fault is it?") and with "ter" for feeling guilty ("Tenho culpa" / "Tenho um sentimento de culpa" = "I feel guilty"). Common collocation: "jogar a culpa em" someone = "to blame" someone.
target_language_example: Não foi minha intenção, mas eu sinto muita culpa.
native_language_example: It wasn’t my intention, but I feel very guilty.

additional_notes: Definite article + noun. Used for a photo/video camera; in some contexts it can also mean a surveillance camera or a phone’s camera. Gender: feminine (a/uma câmera). Plural: as câmeras.
target_language_example: Você pode pegar a câmera para mim?
native_language_example: Can you grab the camera for me?

additional_notes: A common noun phrase used to talk about a choice/judgment that is made. Often appears with verbs like tomar (to make) and with expressions like estar em mãos de alguém (“to be in someone’s hands”). In Portuguese, decisão is feminine, so it takes a: a decisão; plural: as decisões.
target_language_example: Preciso tomar a decisão hoje.
native_language_example: I need to make the decision today.

additional_notes: Most often means “the difference” between two things: Qual é a diferença? = “What’s the difference?” It also appears in common expressions like fazer a diferença (“to make a difference,” i.e., have a positive impact) and fazer toda a diferença (“to make all the difference,” i.e., be crucial).
target_language_example: Esse detalhe fez toda a diferença.
native_language_example: That detail made all the difference.

additional_notes: Used to compare two (or more) things/people/ideas. Common in questions: "Qual é a diferença entre A e B?" It can be followed by nouns, pronouns, or clauses (e.g., "a diferença entre fazer e não fazer").
target_language_example: Não sei qual é a diferença entre esses dois modelos.
native_language_example: I don't know what the difference is between these two models.

additional_notes: Used with numbers and units to say how far something is, often in patterns like “a distância de X até Y” or “a distância de X a Y” (“the distance from X to Y”). In questions: “Qual a distância?” = “How far is it?” It can also be used more generally for “distance” (e.g., in sports, the race distance).
target_language_example: Qual é a distância do hotel até a praia?
native_language_example: How far is it from the hotel to the beach?

additional_notes: Used with two things/places/groups to talk about how far apart they are. Can be physical (locations) or figurative (social/economic gap, differences). Common patterns: "A distância entre X e Y é..." and "Qual é a distância entre X e Y?".
target_language_example: A distância entre a minha casa e a estação é de dez minutos a pé.
native_language_example: The distance between my house and the station is a ten-minute walk.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: definite article + noun. Often used with verbs like "sentir" (to feel), "estar" (to be), and with "para a dor" meaning "for the pain" (e.g., medicine). You may also hear "dor de" + body part ("dor de cabeça" = headache).
target_language_example: Eu posso te dar remédio para a dor.
native_language_example: I can give you medicine for the pain.

additional_notes: Often refers to electricity in everyday situations (power goes out/comes back: "A energia acabou/caiu"). It can also mean energy in general (solar energy, saving energy) or a more abstract sense (inner energy, positive energy, life force).
target_language_example: Hoje faltou a energia no meu bairro.
native_language_example: Today the power went out in my neighborhood.

additional_notes: Refers to a way in (door/gate/access point): "a entrada principal" = "the main entrance". It can also mean something entering a place, especially in the pattern "a entrada de/do/da + noun" (e.g., "a entrada do ar" = "the entry of air"). Feminine noun: "a entrada", "as entradas".
target_language_example: A entrada do metrô é logo ali.
native_language_example: The subway entrance is right there.

meaning: the team; the crew/staff (group working together).
additional_notes: Used for a group of people working together toward a goal (sports team, work team, staff). It’s feminine: "a equipe"; plural "as equipes". Often appears with sports verbs like "marcar" (score) and "sofrer" (concede) a goal.
target_language_example: A equipe está pronta para começar o jogo.
native_language_example: The team is ready to start the game.

additional_notes: Means "the school" (definite article + noun). Used for a specific school already known from context, or to talk about school as an institution in general (e.g., "A escola é importante" = "School is important").
target_language_example: A escola fica perto da minha casa.
native_language_example: The school is near my house.

additional_notes: Uses the feminine singular definite article "a" (= "the") with the noun "espada" (sword). Common when talking about a specific sword already known in the context (e.g., a particular weapon that was stolen).
target_language_example: Onde está a espada?
native_language_example: Where is the sword?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a man’s wife. It’s a possessive structure: a esposa (the wife) + dele (of him = his). Often used when the husband has already been mentioned: "E a esposa dele?" = "And his wife?". Variants: "a esposa dela" (her wife), "a mulher dele" (his wife, more common in everyday speech).
target_language_example: Eu conheci a esposa dele ontem.
native_language_example: I met his wife yesterday.

additional_notes: "A estação" most often means a transit station (train/bus/subway): "A estação fica a dois quilômetros" (The station is two kilometers away). It can also mean a season of the year, usually with a clarifying phrase or context: "Verão é a estação mais quente do ano" (Summer is the hottest season of the year).
target_language_example: Podemos nos encontrar na estação às oito?
native_language_example: Can we meet at the station at eight?

additional_notes: Used for a road that connects places, often outside cities (more like a main road than a small street). Common with verbs like cruzar (to cross), pegar (to take), and with descriptions of condition: cheia (busy), coberta de gelo (icy), danificada (damaged), estreita (narrow).
target_language_example: A estrada para a praia está fechada hoje.
native_language_example: The road to the beach is closed today.

additional_notes: Definite article + noun: "a" = "the" (feminine singular), so "a faca" means "the knife". Used for everyday knives (kitchen knife, table knife, etc.). Common with prepositions/locations: "na gaveta" (in the drawer), "em cima da mesa" (on top of the table).
target_language_example: Cadê a faca?
native_language_example: Where’s the knife?

additional_notes: Used before a noun to talk about something that isn’t there or isn’t enough of: "a falta de exercícios" (lack of exercise), "a falta de resposta" (no response). It can also be used as a complaint/exclamation: "Olha a falta de respeito!" (“Look at the disrespect!”). Note: "a falta de" is not related to English "fault" here; it’s about missing/absence.
target_language_example: A falta de tempo me impede de viajar agora.
native_language_example: Lack of time keeps me from traveling right now.

additional_notes: Means “the family” in general, or a specific family depending on context. It’s feminine singular; often used with verbs in the singular (e.g., “a família é…”). You can also use it after some prepositions like “com a família” (“with the family”).
target_language_example: No domingo, a família se reúne para almoçar.
native_language_example: On Sunday, the family gets together for lunch.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a male person's family. It’s a noun phrase made of: "a" (the) + "família" (family) + "dele" (his/of him). Often used to avoid ambiguity compared to "sua família" (which can mean his/her/your family depending on context).
target_language_example: Ele vai viajar com a família dele no fim de semana.
native_language_example: He’s going to travel with his family this weekend.

additional_notes: Literally “the happiness.” Often used to talk about happiness as an abstract idea or life goal (e.g., wanting, seeking, finding happiness).
target_language_example: Ela procura a felicidade na vida simples.
native_language_example: She looks for happiness in a simple life.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an event where people gather to celebrate or have fun (a birthday party, a celebration, a social gathering). In Portuguese, "a" means "the" (feminine singular), so you’ll often see it in questions like "Foi boa a festa?" (= "Was the party good?") or after prepositions like "sobre a festa" (= "about the party").
target_language_example: A festa começou às oito, mas só terminou de madrugada.
native_language_example: The party started at eight, but it only ended in the early morning.

additional_notes: "A" is the feminine singular definite article (“the”). "Filha" means “daughter” (female child) and is often used with possessives: "minha filha" (my daughter), "sua filha" (your/his/her daughter). In questions like "A filha?", it can mean “The daughter?” (confirming who someone is talking about).
target_language_example: Onde está a filha?
native_language_example: Where is the daughter?

additional_notes: Used to identify a woman as someone’s daughter. "do" is the contraction of "de" + "o" (“of the”), used with masculine singular nouns (e.g., "do João", "do líder"). For a woman, you typically use "a filha da" ("da" = "de" + "a").
target_language_example: Ela é a filha do professor.
native_language_example: She is the professor’s daughter.

additional_notes: A common noun for a large area covered with trees. Uses the feminine definite article “a” (“the”): “a floresta”. Often used with prepositions like “na floresta” (in the forest) and “pela floresta” (through the forest).
target_language_example: Há muitos animais na floresta.
native_language_example: There are many animals in the forest.

additional_notes: Used for physical strength (e.g., "com toda a força" = "with all my strength"), someone’s power/ability (especially in fights or rankings), or a natural/scientific force (e.g., gravity). In Portuguese, "força" is feminine, so it usually comes with "a" ("a força").
target_language_example: Ele empurrou a porta com toda a força.
native_language_example: He pushed the door with all his strength.

additional_notes: Means “the photo/picture.” It’s the feminine singular form with the definite article: a = “the” (feminine singular) + foto = “photo.” Used when referring to a specific photo that’s known from context.
target_language_example: Você tem a foto no seu celular?
native_language_example: Do you have the photo on your phone?

additional_notes: Means “the girl” (definite article + noun). Used to refer to a specific girl already known or mentioned in context. In some places (especially Brazil), "garota" can also mean a young woman (like “girl” in English).
target_language_example: A garota está esperando o ônibus.
native_language_example: The girl is waiting for the bus.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause describing which girl you mean. "que" is the most common relative pronoun in Portuguese and often corresponds to “who/that” in English. The verb in the relative clause is conjugated normally (e.g., "a garota que trabalha..." = “the girl who works...”); for a male person you’d say "o garoto que".
target_language_example: A garota que mora aqui ao lado é minha colega de trabalho.
native_language_example: The girl who lives next door is my coworker.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese as a more conversational alternative to nós. Even though it means "we," it usually takes a third-person singular verb: a gente vai, a gente gosta. In other contexts, it can literally mean "the people," but that is not the meaning in these examples.
target_language_example: A gente vai sair mais tarde.
native_language_example: We're going out later.

additional_notes: “A gente” is a very common informal way to say “we” in Brazilian Portuguese (often equivalent to “nós”). It usually takes 3rd-person singular verbs: “a gente não terminou” (not “terminamos”). “Não” comes before the verb to negate it; in speech you may also hear double negation like “a gente não viu nada” (“we didn’t see anything”).
target_language_example: A gente não pode sair agora.
native_language_example: We can’t leave now.

meaning: "we can" / "we could" (it’s possible; we’re allowed; we’re able to).
additional_notes: "A gente" is very common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese and means "we" in a casual way, but it takes singular verb forms: "a gente pode" (not *podemos*). It can express (1) ability/possibility ("We can hear the ocean from here"), (2) permission ("Can we play now?"), or (3) something that can happen/typically happens ("We can get sick"). In questions it often works like "Can we…?" / "Where can we…?"
target_language_example: A gente pode ir de ônibus ou a pé.
native_language_example: We can go by bus or on foot.

additional_notes: Common, informal way to say goodbye or to confirm you’ll meet again. "A gente" often means "we" in everyday Brazilian Portuguese (even though it’s grammatically singular), and "se vê" means "see each other". You can add a time/place: "a gente se vê amanhã" (tomorrow), "a gente se vê em casa" (at home).
target_language_example: Tá bom, a gente se vê amanhã!
native_language_example: Alright, see you tomorrow!

additional_notes: Very common in Brazilian Portuguese. "A gente" literally means "the people," but in everyday speech it means "we". Even though it means "we," it takes singular verb forms: "a gente vai" (not *a gente vamos*). Often followed by an infinitive: "a gente vai resolver" = "we’re going to solve (it)".
target_language_example: A gente vai chegar cedo amanhã.
native_language_example: We’re going to arrive early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese meaning “we/us,” often more informal than “nós.” Even though it refers to multiple people, it usually takes singular verb forms (e.g., “a gente vai,” not “a gente vamos”). It can also mean “people” in general depending on context.
target_language_example: A gente vai chegar mais cedo amanhã.
native_language_example: We’re going to arrive earlier tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used as a polite way to describe someone doing you a favor. Usually followed by an infinitive: "fazer/ter a gentileza de + infinitive" (e.g., "fez a gentileza de ajudar").
target_language_example: Você teria a gentileza de repetir, por favor?
native_language_example: Would you be kind enough to repeat, please?

additional_notes: Very common slang in Brazil for "money" (like "cash" or "bucks"). Often used with verbs like pegar/levar (to take), conseguir (to get), roubar (to steal), and dar (to give): "Me dê a grana" = "Give me the money." In more formal contexts, use "o dinheiro".
target_language_example: Não tenho a grana agora, posso pagar amanhã.
native_language_example: I don’t have the cash right now; I can pay tomorrow.

additional_notes: Means “war” in general, or “the war” when talking about a specific conflict already known from context (e.g., a country “won the war”). Often appears in set phrases like “sobre a guerra” (about the war) and “entre X e a guerra” (between X and war).
target_language_example: Ele escreveu um artigo sobre a guerra.
native_language_example: He wrote an article about the war.

additional_notes: Used with the feminine singular definite article a (“the”). Depending on context, história can mean (1) a narrative or account of events (“story”), including something made up (Ele inventou a história inteira. = “He made up the whole story.”), or (2) the past of a person/place/thing (“history”), as in História do Brasil (“History of Brazil”). In the expression contar a história, it means “to tell the story” (often implying someone survived to tell it).
target_language_example: Eu não acredito nessa história.
native_language_example: I don’t believe that story.

meaning: “the time” / “the hour” (the current time, or the appropriate moment).
additional_notes: Most commonly refers to the current time: “Olha a hora!” = “Look at the time!” It can also mean “the right moment/appropriate time” depending on context: “A hora não é boa” = “It’s not a good time,” and “Era a hora dela” = “It was her time/moment.” Often appears with relative clauses: “a hora que…” = “the time that…/the time when…,” e.g., “até a hora que eu quiser” = “until whatever time I want.”
target_language_example: Que horas são? Eu não sei a hora.
native_language_example: What time is it? I don’t know the time.

meaning: "(can’t) wait to" (be eager for something to happen).
additional_notes: Used most often in the expression (não) ver a hora de + infinitive to say you’re really looking forward to doing something, or impatient for it to happen: Não vejo a hora de viajar. In the examples, it expresses excitement/anticipation, not the literal time on a clock.
target_language_example: Não vejo a hora de te ver de novo.
native_language_example: I can’t wait to see you again.

additional_notes: Refers to people as a whole (the entire human species), often in general or philosophical statements. It can also mean “humanity” in the sense of human nature/qualities (e.g., compassion), but in many contexts it simply means “all humans.” Feminine noun: a humanidade.
target_language_example: Precisamos proteger a humanidade e o planeta.
native_language_example: We need to protect humanity and the planet.

additional_notes: Most often used with a possessive to ask or talk about someone’s age: “a idade dele/dela/vocês”. It can also mean age as a concept, especially in phrases like “com a idade” (“with age/as you get older”). Often appears with “ter”: “Quantos anos você tem?” is more common than “Qual é a sua idade?” in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Com a idade, ele ficou mais paciente.
native_language_example: With age, he became more patient.

meaning: the idea; a plan or thought.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a thought, concept, suggestion, or plan. Very common in expressions like “A ideia é…” (“The idea is…”), “a ideia de + infinitive/noun” (“the idea of…”), and “passar pela cabeça” (“to come to mind”).
target_language_example: A ideia de viajar amanhã me anima.
native_language_example: The idea of traveling tomorrow excites me.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a plan, possibility, or concept. Most often followed by an infinitive ("a ideia de + verb": a ideia de comprar, viver, tornar-se). It can also be followed by "que" to introduce a clause: "a ideia de que ..." (the idea that ...). Common with verbs like "ter" (to have) and "abandonar" (to abandon/give up).
target_language_example: Ela desistiu da ideia de viajar este ano.
native_language_example: She gave up the idea of traveling this year.

additional_notes: Refers to a church building or, more generally, the institution/community. Note that in the very common phrase “ir à igreja” (“to go to church”), the preposition “a” + the article “a” contract to “à”, so you won’t see the exact string “a igreja” in that specific construction.
target_language_example: Os pais dele vão todos os domingos para a igreja.
native_language_example: His parents go to church every Sunday.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you believe or perceive based on clues, not certainty. Often appears with verbs like ter (to have) or ficar com (to be left with) in phrases such as “ter a impressão de que…” / “ficar com a impressão de que…”.
target_language_example: Tive a impressão de que ele não queria conversar.
native_language_example: I had the impression that he didn’t want to talk.

additional_notes: A common tech term meaning computer systems that can learn, recognize patterns, or make decisions. Usually used with the definite article: “a inteligência artificial”. Often shortened to “IA” (e.g., “a IA”).
target_language_example: Muitas empresas já usam a inteligência artificial para melhorar o atendimento ao cliente.
native_language_example: Many companies already use artificial intelligence to improve customer service.

meaning: her sister (the sister of a woman/girl).
additional_notes: “dela” means “of hers/of her” and refers to a female person (ela). It’s a common way to express possession after the noun: “a irmã dela” = “her sister.” You can also say “a sua irmã,” but “a irmã dela” is often clearer (since “sua” can mean “your” or “his/her” depending on context).
target_language_example: Eu vou falar com a irmã dela amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m going to talk to her sister tomorrow.

additional_notes: Means “his sister” (a female sibling of a man/boy). Used when the sister has been mentioned or is clear from context. "dele" refers to “of him/his” and agrees with the owner (a male person), not with "irmã". You can also use it after the noun: "a irmã do Tom" = “Tom’s sister.”
target_language_example: Você conhece a irmã dele?
native_language_example: Do you know his sister?

additional_notes: "A" is the feminine singular definite article in Portuguese ("the"). You use "a janela" to talk about a specific window that’s clear from context.
target_language_example: Abre a janela, por favor.
native_language_example: Open the window, please.

additional_notes: Usually refers to an official law/rule: "A lei foi alterada" (the law was changed), "violar a lei" (break the law), "obedecer a lei" (obey the law). It can also be used more generally for a principle or 'law of nature' ("a lei da natureza"). The dramatic phrase "Eu sou a lei!" means 'I am the law!' (said by someone claiming authority).
target_language_example: Ninguém está acima da lei.
native_language_example: No one is above the law.

additional_notes: Used for freedom as a general concept (e.g., speech, rights) or personal freedom. Often followed by "de" + noun/verb to specify the kind of freedom: "a liberdade de fala" (freedom of speech), "a liberdade de escolher" (freedom to choose). It can also appear in slogans/toasts like "Para a liberdade!" (To freedom!) and in phrases like "pela liberdade" (for freedom / in favor of freedom).
target_language_example: A liberdade de escolher é importante.
