native_language_example: Freedom to choose is important.

additional_notes: Common in school contexts to mean homework assigned by a teacher. Usually used with the verb fazer: fazer a lição de casa = “to do homework.” It’s typically treated as a singular task/set of work (even if it includes many exercises).
target_language_example: Ainda não fiz a lição de casa.
native_language_example: I still haven’t done my homework.

meaning: the dishes; the dishwashing (as a chore).
additional_notes: "Louça" refers to tableware like plates, cups, glasses, and other items used for eating/drinking. In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, "lavar a louça" means to wash the dishes (do the dishwashing), and it can refer to the whole chore (washing and sometimes drying/putting away).
target_language_example: Hoje é sua vez de lavar a louça.
native_language_example: Today it’s your turn to do the dishes.

additional_notes: A feminine singular noun phrase (a + lua). Used for the Moon in general (usually lowercase in Portuguese). With names of celestial bodies, Portuguese commonly uses the definite article (o sol, a lua).
target_language_example: Hoje a lua está muito bonita.
native_language_example: The moon looks very beautiful tonight.

additional_notes: Means “the light” in a literal sense (light in a room, daylight, etc.) and also figuratively (“guidance,” “clarity,” “hope,” etc.). Common in everyday speech: “acender a luz” = “to turn on the light.”
target_language_example: Pode apagar a luz, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you turn off the light, please?

additional_notes: Often means a spoken language, especially in phrases like "falar a língua" (to speak the language) and "a língua de X" (the language of X), e.g. "a língua da diplomacia". It can also mean the physical tongue (in your mouth). In some contexts, expressions with "língua" can be idiomatic (e.g. telling someone to hold back what they’re saying).
target_language_example: Eu estou a aprender a língua, mas ainda não falo bem.
native_language_example: I’m learning the language, but I still don’t speak well.

additional_notes: Feminine form of the comparative/superlative of "grande" (big/great). It’s used with feminine nouns: "a maior riqueza" (the greatest wealth), "a maior indústria" (the biggest industry). Often appears in patterns like "a maior de todas" (the greatest of all) or "a maior das ..." (the greatest of the ...). For masculine nouns, use "o maior". Note: "maior" can look like English "major," but it usually means bigger/greater, not "major" (as in a college major).
target_language_example: Esta é a maior cidade do país.
native_language_example: This is the biggest city in the country.

meaning: most of the time; the majority of the time.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens during most moments in a period (often meaning “usually”). It can go at the end of the sentence or after the verb: “Ele fica em casa a maior parte do tempo.” / “Ele passa a maior parte do tempo em casa.”
target_language_example: Eu trabalho em casa a maior parte do tempo.
native_language_example: I work from home most of the time.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what is true for most members of a group. It can be followed by a relative clause ("a maioria das pessoas que...") or an aside like "se não todas" (“if not all”). Verb agreement is often plural in everyday speech ("a maioria das pessoas gostam"), though singular is also possible ("a maioria... gosta") because the subject is "a maioria".
target_language_example: A maioria das pessoas aqui trabalha de segunda a sexta.
native_language_example: Most people here work Monday to Friday.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to mean “more than half” or, more generally, “most.” It agrees in gender/number with the noun: most common is "a maioria dos" (before masculine plural or mixed groups), and "a maioria das" (before feminine plural). Often followed by a singular verb in Portuguese ("A maioria dos alunos é..."), though plural is also sometimes used.
target_language_example: A maioria dos clientes prefere pagar com cartão.
native_language_example: Most of the customers prefer to pay by card.

meaning: "mom" / "mommy" (affectionate way to refer to the mother).
additional_notes: "Mamãe" is a warm, familiar term often used by children or when speaking affectionately about someone’s mother. It usually refers to one specific person (the mother), so it often appears with the definite article: "a mamãe" = "Mom" / "Mommy". In direct address you can also just say "Mamãe!"
target_language_example: A mamãe já chegou em casa.
native_language_example: Mom is already home.

additional_notes: Used to say something lasted for the entire morning. Often follows a verb (e.g., esperar/ficar/passar) and can come after it: “esperei a manhã inteira”.
target_language_example: Fiquei estudando a manhã inteira.
native_language_example: I studied all morning.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happened during the entire morning (from morning start until around lunchtime). Often comes after the verb ("esperei a manhã toda") or after what you were doing ("passei a manhã toda ajudando..."). You can make similar phrases with other times: "a tarde toda" (all afternoon), "a noite toda" (all night), "o dia todo" (all day).
target_language_example: Fiquei a manhã toda estudando para a prova.
native_language_example: I spent all morning studying for the test.

additional_notes: A definite noun phrase: "a" = "the" (feminine singular) + "maçã" = "apple". Used when referring to a specific apple or to apples in general in a generic statement (e.g., "A maçã é vermelha" = "The apple is red"). Often appears with food-prep verbs like cortar (to cut) and descascar (to peel).
target_language_example: Vou comer a maçã depois do almoço.
native_language_example: I'm going to eat the apple after lunch.

additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns (stated or implied): "a melhor aluna" = "the best student". It can also stand alone when the noun is understood: "Você é a melhor" = "You’re the best." Masculine is "o melhor"; plural is "as melhores".
target_language_example: Para mim, ela é a melhor professora da escola.
native_language_example: To me, she’s the best teacher at the school.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the most recommended method for an action. It’s usually followed by an infinitive verb: “a melhor maneira de + verb” (e.g., “a melhor maneira de fazer isso…”). You can change “melhor” to other adjectives: “a pior maneira de…” (the worst way to), “uma boa maneira de…” (a good way to).
target_language_example: A melhor maneira de aprender português é praticar um pouco todos os dias.
native_language_example: The best way to learn Portuguese is to practice a little every day.

additional_notes: "a" is the feminine singular definite article ("the"). "menina" means "girl" (a female child/young girl). Used with "que" to form descriptions like "the girl who...". In Brazil, "menina" can also be used informally to refer to a young woman (similar to "girl" in English), depending on context.
target_language_example: A menina mora aqui perto.
native_language_example: The girl lives nearby.

additional_notes: Means “the table” (definite article + noun). Used for a physical table (dining table, desk-like table, etc.). Often appears with actions like limpar (to clean), pôr/tirar (to put on/remove), and with estar + adjective/covered expressions (e.g., “a mesa estava coberta de...” = “the table was covered with...”).
target_language_example: Pode colocar os pratos na mesa?
native_language_example: Can you put the plates on the table?

additional_notes: Used to say two things are identical or equal. Often appears with the verb “ser” (e.g., “X e Y são a mesma coisa” = “X and Y are the same thing”). It can also mean people have/choose identical items (like clothes): “vestir a mesma coisa” = “to wear the same thing.”
target_language_example: Acho que isso e aquilo são a mesma coisa.
native_language_example: I think this and that are the same thing.

additional_notes: Used to compare two actions, choices, or things and say they are identical. It’s often followed by a person or clause: “a mesma coisa que o Tom…”, “a mesma coisa que eu pedi”. Common pattern: fazer/comer/pedir a mesma coisa que + someone + verb.
target_language_example: Vou pedir a mesma coisa que você pediu.
native_language_example: I’m going to order the same thing you ordered.

additional_notes: used with feminine singular nouns to mean "my". Portuguese often uses the definite article before possessives, so a minha literally includes "the" even though English usually just says "my". When the noun is omitted, a minha can also mean "mine".
target_language_example: A minha casa fica perto daqui.
native_language_example: My house is near here.

additional_notes: Uses the feminine singular form of "friend" (amiga), so it refers to a woman/girl. "A" is the definite article ("the"), and in Portuguese it’s common to say "a minha" (literally "the my"). For a male friend, say "o meu amigo". Can also mean "my girlfriend" in some contexts, but usually it just means "my friend".
target_language_example: A minha amiga mora perto daqui.
native_language_example: My (female) friend lives near here.

additional_notes: Literally “the my grandmother” (a + minha + avó). In Portuguese it’s common to use the definite article (a/o) before possessives, especially in European Portuguese, though it can also appear in Brazilian Portuguese. You can also say “minha avó” without the article in many contexts.
target_language_example: A minha avó faz um bolo ótimo aos domingos.
native_language_example: My grandmother makes a great cake on Sundays.

additional_notes: A possessive noun phrase: "a" (the, feminine singular) + "minha" (my, feminine singular) + "bicicleta" (bicycle). Use it when the bicycle is a specific one the listener can identify (often your own). Portuguese also allows "minha bicicleta" without the article, but "a minha bicicleta" is very common in European Portuguese and also used in Brazil for emphasis or clarity.
target_language_example: Onde está a minha bicicleta?
native_language_example: Where is my bike?

additional_notes: Means “the/my pen” (feminine singular). It’s formed by the definite article + possessive: a (the, feminine) + minha (my, feminine) + caneta (pen). In Portuguese, it’s very common to use the article with possessives (a minha caneta), though you may also hear just “minha caneta” in some contexts.
target_language_example: Desculpa, esta é a minha caneta.
native_language_example: Sorry, this is my pen.

additional_notes: Commonly used when talking about losing, finding, returning, or asking who has your wallet. In Portuguese, the possessive usually comes after the article: a minha (feminine singular) + carteira. "Carteira" can also mean "handbag" or "briefcase" depending on context, but in these examples it means the wallet/purse with your money and cards.
target_language_example: Você viu a minha carteira?
native_language_example: Have you seen my wallet?

additional_notes: Uses the feminine singular definite article “a” because “casa” is feminine. Often means “home” (the place you live), not only a physical house. You can also say “minha casa” without the article in some contexts, but “a minha casa” is common for emphasis/contrast (e.g., “a minha casa, não a sua”).
target_language_example: A minha casa está suja.
native_language_example: My house/home is dirty.

additional_notes: Used when the speaker is talking about their own wife. Often shortened to just “minha esposa” (without “a”), especially after a verb: “Amo minha esposa.” “Esposa” is feminine; the masculine is “o meu marido” (“my husband”). In Portugal, you may also hear “mulher” used to mean “wife” in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Vou jantar com a minha esposa hoje.
native_language_example: I’m going to have dinner with my wife today.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your own family. "A" is the definite article (“the”), and it stays when you add a possessive like "minha". You may also see "minha família" without the article, especially in more general statements (e.g., "Minha família é pequena").
target_language_example: Hoje vou jantar com a minha família.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to have dinner with my family.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the speaker’s daughter. "a" is the definite article (“the”), often used before possessives in Portuguese: "a minha filha" = literally “the my daughter” (natural in Portuguese). You can also hear "minha filha" without "a" in some contexts. "filha" is feminine; for a son, use "o meu filho".
target_language_example: A minha filha tem sete anos.
native_language_example: My daughter is seven years old.

additional_notes: Means “my sister,” with the definite article “a” (“the”) commonly used before possessives in Portuguese. Use it when talking about your sister as a specific person. In European Portuguese, “a minha irmã” is very common; in Brazilian Portuguese you may also hear “minha irmã” without the article.
target_language_example: A minha irmã mora em Lisboa.
native_language_example: My sister lives in Lisbon.

additional_notes: In everyday Portuguese, "mulher" can mean "woman" in general, but "a minha mulher" commonly means "my wife". It uses the feminine singular possessive "minha"; in speech and informal writing you’ll often see it without the article: "minha mulher". A more explicitly formal word for "wife" is "esposa".
target_language_example: Vou sair com a minha mulher hoje à noite.
native_language_example: I’m going out with my wife tonight.

additional_notes: Means “my mother.” Often used when talking about your mother as the object of a verb (e.g., "Eu chamei a minha mãe" = "I called my mother"). In everyday speech, it’s also very common to say simply "minha mãe" (without "a"), especially as the subject: "Minha mãe está em casa."
target_language_example: Vou ligar para a minha mãe mais tarde.
native_language_example: I'm going to call my mom later.

additional_notes: Used with the feminine singular definite article (a) + possessive (minha) + noun (mão). In Portuguese, body parts are often said with an article and/or possessive depending on emphasis; here it clearly means the speaker’s hand (often in requests like "Hold my hand" or "Squeeze my hand").
target_language_example: Você pode lavar a minha mão?
native_language_example: Can you wash my hand?

additional_notes: Used to refer to your girlfriend. "a" and "minha" are feminine to match "namorada". For a male partner, say "o meu namorado" (my boyfriend). In European Portuguese you may also hear "a minha namorada" shortened to "a minha" when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Vou sair com a minha namorada hoje à noite.
native_language_example: I’m going out with my girlfriend tonight.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your personal point of view. Often appears with verbs like dar (to give), pedir (to ask for), dizer (to say), and ouvir/escutar (to hear/listen to): "Pediram a minha opinião" = "They asked for my opinion." You can also swap the possessive for other people: a tua opinião (your), a opinião dele/dela (his/her).
target_language_example: Na minha opinião, isto não vai funcionar.
native_language_example: In my opinion, this isn't going to work.

additional_notes: Used when you give someone your promise or guarantee that something is true or that you will do something. Very common with the verb “dar” (dar a minha palavra = to give my word) and also with “ter” (tens/têm a minha palavra = you have my word). You can add “de que …” to introduce what you’re promising (e.g., “Dou a minha palavra de que…”).
target_language_example: Dou a minha palavra de que vou chegar a horas.
native_language_example: I give you my word that I’ll arrive on time.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase used to talk about your life in general (experiences, time, or existence). Often appears in set phrases like “a minha vida inteira” (“my whole life”) and with verbs like “mudar” (to change) or “custar” (to cost, e.g., “cost me my life”). Usually “minha vida” also works without the article, but with the article (“a”) it can sound more specific/emphatic in context.
target_language_example: A minha vida mudou muito desde que me mudei para cá.
native_language_example: My life has changed a lot since I moved here.

meaning: “mine” (feminine), referring to something that belongs to me.
additional_notes: Used instead of repeating a feminine noun already mentioned (e.g., bicicleta, caneta). It agrees with the noun it replaces: a minha (feminine singular); as minhas (feminine plural). Often appears after comparisons ("melhor do que a minha") or as a standalone choice/command ("Pegue a minha"). Contrast: o meu / a minha = “my …” before a noun; o meu / a minha = “mine” when the noun is implied.
target_language_example: Não gosto dessa cadeira; prefiro a minha.
native_language_example: I don’t like that chair; I prefer mine.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: "montanha" = mountain, and "a" is the feminine singular definite article ("the"). Used to talk about a specific mountain in context; for mountains in general you might see "uma montanha" (a mountain).
target_language_example: A montanha é muito alta.
native_language_example: The mountain is very tall.

additional_notes: Means “death,” usually with the definite article a (“the”). Common in expressions like desde a morte de… (“since the death of…”), lutar contra a morte (“fight against death”), and morte certa (“certain death”). In Portuguese, you often keep the article where English may or may not use “the.”
target_language_example: Depois da morte do avô, a família ficou muito triste.
native_language_example: After the grandfather’s death, the family was very sad.

additional_notes: Used with a person’s name or relationship (e.g., "a morte de minha mãe") to talk about someone’s passing. Very common in more formal or neutral contexts (news, stories, serious conversations). Often appears in phrases like "desde a morte de..." (since the death of...).
target_language_example: A morte de seu pai mudou tudo na família.
native_language_example: The death of his father changed everything in the family.

additional_notes: A noun phrase meaning “the death of him.” Used to talk about a man’s death; for a woman you’d say “a morte dela” (her death). Often appears after verbs like “lamentar” (to mourn/regret) or in explanations like “se deve a…” (is due to…).
target_language_example: Ainda estou tentando aceitar a morte dele.
native_language_example: I’m still trying to accept his death.

meaning: “the death of (a man / a masculine noun)”
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s death. "do" = "de" + "o" (“of the”, masculine singular). For a woman/feminine noun: "a morte da"; plural: "a morte dos" (masc/mixed) / "a morte das" (fem).
target_language_example: Ainda estamos tristes com a morte do nosso amigo.
native_language_example: We’re still sad about the death of our friend.

additional_notes: Used to make statements/definitions about death. Portuguese often uses the definite article with abstract nouns: "a morte" = "death" (lit. "the death"). Pattern: "A + noun + é + adjective/noun" (e.g., "A morte é inevitável.").
target_language_example: A morte é inevitável.
native_language_example: Death is inevitable.

additional_notes: Compositional phrase: a is the feminine singular definite article ('the') and mulher means 'woman'. Depending on context, mulher can sometimes also mean 'wife', but in these examples it means 'the woman'.
target_language_example: A mulher está esperando na porta.
native_language_example: The woman is waiting at the door.

additional_notes: Literally “the woman of him.” In everyday Portuguese, “a mulher dele” commonly means “his wife.” It uses a common possession pattern: noun + “dele” (= his/of him). For “her wife,” you’d say “a mulher dela.”
target_language_example: Você já conheceu a mulher dele?
native_language_example: Have you met his wife yet?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause with **que** describing which woman you mean. **Que** can refer to the subject ("the woman who called") or the object depending on the sentence, but in English it usually translates as **who/that**.
target_language_example: A mulher que mora aqui trabalha no hospital.
native_language_example: The woman who lives here works at the hospital.

meaning: the crowd; a large group of people (in one place).
additional_notes: Used for a big group of people gathered together (at a concert, in the street, etc.). It’s singular in Portuguese (“a multidão”), but it refers to many people. Common with verbs showing the group’s reaction: “A multidão adorou...”, “caiu na gargalhada”, “entrou em pânico”.
target_language_example: Havia uma multidão na porta do estádio.
native_language_example: There was a crowd at the stadium entrance.

additional_notes: Used for the household appliance that washes clothes. Often followed by the thing being washed: “máquina de lavar roupa” (washing machine) or “máquina de lavar louça” (dishwasher). Common with verbs like “usar” (to use), “consertar” (to fix), “ligar/desligar” (to turn on/off), and “fazer barulho” (to make noise).
target_language_example: A máquina de lavar quebrou, então vou lavar a roupa à mão.
native_language_example: The washing machine broke, so I'm going to wash the clothes by hand.

additional_notes: Means “the mother of her” (dela = de + ela). Used to refer to a female person’s mother when talking about her. It’s definite (“the”), but in English it’s usually just “her mother.”
target_language_example: A mãe dela mora aqui perto.
native_language_example: Her mother lives nearby.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a male person’s mother. Literally “the mother of him” (a + mãe + dele). In Portuguese you commonly use this structure (noun + dele/dela) instead of saying “his/her” before the noun. With a female owner, you’d say “a mãe dela” (“her mother”).
target_language_example: Eu falei com a mãe dele ontem à noite.
native_language_example: I spoke with his mother last night.

additional_notes: Used to identify someone as the mother of a specific person: “a mãe do + [name]”. The “do” is a contraction of “de + o” (“of the”). If the person is female, you usually say “a mãe da” (“de + a”).
target_language_example: Você é a mãe do João?
native_language_example: Are you João’s mother?

additional_notes: Often used with body-part expressions. Portuguese commonly uses the definite article where English may use a possessive: for example, apertar a mão dele = "shake his hand." In expressions like passar a mão, the exact meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: Ela levantou a mão para perguntar.
native_language_example: She raised her hand to ask a question.

additional_notes: "A" is the feminine singular definite article ("the"). "A música" can mean music in general (an art form) or a specific song, depending on context. In Portuguese, "música" is often used where English would say "song" (e.g., "cantar uma música" = "to sing a song").
target_language_example: Você pode colocar a música mais baixa, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you turn the music down, please?

meaning: 'music is…' (used to define or describe music).
additional_notes: Common sentence starter: "A música" = "music" (feminine singular), and "é" = "is" (from "ser"). Used to give a definition/opinion or say what music means to someone. Often followed by adjectives (boa, maravilhosa) or a noun phrase (a língua universal, a sua paixão).
target_language_example: A música é importante para mim.
native_language_example: Music is important to me.

additional_notes: Means “the girlfriend of him” (referring to a specific male person already known in the conversation). In Portuguese, possession is often shown with "de" + pronoun after the noun: "a namorada dele" = "his girlfriend" ("dele" = of him). You may also hear "a sua namorada" (his girlfriend), but "sua" can sometimes be ambiguous (his/her/your depending on context).
target_language_example: Eu conheci a namorada dele ontem.
native_language_example: I met his girlfriend yesterday.

additional_notes: Used with the definite article “a” to refer to nature in general (the environment, plants, landscapes, etc.). It can also mean “nature” in a more abstract sense (e.g., the nature/character of something), but in everyday beginner contexts it most often means the natural world.
target_language_example: Vamos caminhar na natureza neste fim de semana.
native_language_example: Let's go for a walk in nature this weekend.

additional_notes: Feminine singular noun with the definite article “a” (= “the”). Used when talking about snow in general or specific snow already known in context. Common related phrases: “Está nevando” (It’s snowing), “Tem neve na rua” (There’s snow on the street).
target_language_example: A neve cobriu a cidade durante a noite.
native_language_example: The snow covered the city overnight.

additional_notes: Used to say something lasted for the entire night. Often follows the verb: “chorar a noite inteira” (cry all night), “ficar acordado a noite inteira” (stay awake all night). You can also say “a noite toda” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Eu trabalhei a noite inteira e agora estou exausto.
native_language_example: I worked all night and now I’m exhausted.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the previous night (yesterday night). Very common with the past tense to say what happened. You may also see the equivalent word order “na noite passada” (= “on/during last night”).
target_language_example: A noite passada eu fiquei em casa e vi um filme.
native_language_example: Last night I stayed home and watched a movie.

additional_notes: Used to say something lasted throughout the entire night. Often placed after the verb: "trabalhamos a noite toda". You can also use it with "ficar" to describe a state for the whole night (e.g., "ficou quieto a noite toda").
target_language_example: Eu fiquei acordado a noite toda estudando para a prova.
native_language_example: I stayed awake all night studying for the test.

additional_notes: Means “our” with the feminine singular possessive (nossa). The article “a” often appears before possessives in Portuguese (especially in Portugal): a nossa família = “our family”. It agrees with a feminine singular noun (a nossa casa, a nossa empresa). You may also hear it without the article: nossa família. It can also stand alone as “ours” when the noun is understood: A culpa foi a nossa. = “The blame was ours.”
target_language_example: A nossa casa fica perto do centro.
native_language_example: Our house is near downtown.

additional_notes: Literal phrase: "a" (the) + "nossa" (our) + "casa" (house/home). Often used to mean “our home” in a general sense, not just the physical building. Note: in the idiom "A nossa casa caiu!" it means “We’re in trouble!” / “We’ve been found out!” (slangy).
target_language_example: Hoje vamos ficar na nossa casa e descansar.
native_language_example: Today we’re going to stay at our place and rest.

meaning: 'the offer' (a proposal or deal), often a job offer.
additional_notes: Used for something offered to someone (a proposal, deal, invitation, or opportunity). Very common in work contexts: "oferta de emprego" / "oferta de trabalho" = "job offer". Often appears with verbs like "aceitar" (accept), "recusar" (refuse), and "considerar" (consider).
target_language_example: Recebi uma oferta melhor e decidi aceitar.
native_language_example: I received a better offer and decided to accept it.

additional_notes: Commonly used for (1) an instruction/command: "dar a ordem" (give the order), "seguir a ordem" (follow the order), "mandar a ordem" (send the order), including legal orders like "a ordem do Tribunal" (the court order); and (2) the sequence or correct arrangement of things: "a ordem dos números" (the order of the numbers), "a ordem correta" (the correct order).
target_language_example: Por favor, siga a ordem das instruções.
native_language_example: Please follow the order of the instructions.

additional_notes: Used when choosing or referring to the other item/person in a pair or set. It’s feminine: you use it with feminine nouns (e.g., “a cadeira” → “a outra”). The masculine form is “o outro”. Common in phrases like “Agora a outra.” (“Now the other one.”) and in contrasts like “uma coisa com a outra” (“one thing with the other”).
target_language_example: Eu não quero esta; quero a outra.
native_language_example: I don’t want this one; I want the other one.

additional_notes: Means "the word" ("palavra" = "word"; "a" = "the" for a feminine singular noun). Used when talking about spelling, meaning, translating, or looking up a word. It can also mean "promise/word" in expressions like "manter a palavra" = "keep your word".
target_language_example: Não entendi a palavra; você pode explicar o significado?
native_language_example: I didn’t understand the word; can you explain the meaning?

additional_notes: Usually refers to a wall inside a building or a wall as a barrier/structure. Common with verbs like pintar (to paint), decorar (to decorate), consertar (to fix), atravessar (to go through), derrubar (to knock down). In the expression "falar com a parede", it means "to talk to a wall" (talking to someone who doesn’t listen).
target_language_example: Não fure a parede.
native_language_example: Don’t drill into the wall.

additional_notes: Used with "de" to mean "the part of" something: "a parte do telhado" = "the part of the roof". It’s also common with adjectives or superlatives to specify which part: "a parte mais difícil" = "the hardest part".
target_language_example: Qual é a parte mais importante do trabalho?
native_language_example: What is the most important part of the job?

additional_notes: Most commonly refers to a sports game: "a partida de futebol" = "the soccer match." In other contexts, "a partida" can mean someone’s departure: "concordou com a partida" = "agreed with the departure/leaving." Note the common expression "dar a partida" (or "dê a partida!") meaning "to start" an engine/vehicle (car, ship, etc.).
target_language_example: A partida começa às oito.
native_language_example: The match starts at eight.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a travel ticket: *comprar a passagem* = “to buy the ticket” (often you can specify *passagem do metrô*, *passagem de ônibus*, etc.). It can also mean a passage/corridor or crossing/way through, especially in contexts like evacuations or moving through a narrow place.
target_language_example: Preciso comprar a passagem do ônibus para amanhã.
native_language_example: I need to buy the bus ticket for tomorrow.

meaning: peace (calm; absence of war or conflict).
additional_notes: Usually used with the definite article: “a paz” = “peace.” It can mean peace between people/countries (“a paz no mundo”) or inner peace (“encontrar a paz”). Common in blessings/wishes: “Que a paz esteja com você” (“May peace be with you”).
target_language_example: Depois de falar com ela, senti a paz voltar ao meu coração.
native_language_example: After talking to her, I felt peace return to my heart.

additional_notes: Feminine noun: a pedra (the stone), uma pedra (a stone). Often used for an actual rock/stone, but it can also mean a gemstone set in jewelry (e.g., uma pedra verde = a green stone/gem).
target_language_example: Você pode guardar a pedra no bolso, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you put the stone in your pocket, please?

meaning: 'the penalty/sentence' (legal punishment); also 'the feather'. In 'valer a pena': 'worth it'.
additional_notes: “Pena” has multiple common meanings. In legal contexts (crime, confession, infraction), “a pena” means the punishment/penalty or prison sentence (e.g., reduzir a pena = reduce the sentence). In everyday contexts about birds, “uma pena” means a feather. Very common fixed expression: “valer a pena” = to be worth it (often said alone as “Valeu a pena.”).
target_language_example: A pena foi reduzida depois da confissão.
native_language_example: The sentence was reduced after the confession.

additional_notes: Means the leg (body part), usually from the hip down to the foot. Often used with injury verbs like "machucar a perna" (hurt your leg) and "quebrar a perna" (break your leg). "Perna" is feminine, so it takes "a" (singular) and "as" (plural: "as pernas").
target_language_example: Eu machuquei a perna ontem.
native_language_example: I hurt my leg yesterday.

meaning: 'the person who' (introduces a description of someone).
additional_notes: Used to refer to someone and add a defining clause after que (who/that). Very common in statements and questions when you don’t know the person’s name or you want to describe them: “a pessoa que + verb…”.
target_language_example: A pessoa que me ajudou ontem trabalha aqui.
native_language_example: The person who helped me yesterday works here.

additional_notes: Refers to the police force or institution. In Portuguese, polícia is usually treated as a singular feminine noun: a polícia chegou. To talk about one police officer, use um policial or uma policial.
target_language_example: A polícia chegou logo depois do acidente.
native_language_example: The police arrived right after the accident.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of prender, used for a completed action: the police arrested/detained someone. The person arrested is usually introduced with a direct object: “A polícia prendeu o homem.” In everyday English, “arrest” is the most common translation when it’s official police action.
target_language_example: A polícia prendeu o suspeito ontem à noite.
native_language_example: The police arrested the suspect last night.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific bridge already known from context. "Ponte" is feminine, so it goes with "a" (the) and adjectives often agree: "a ponte alta" (the tall/high bridge). Common with directions and travel: "ir para a ponte" (go to the bridge), "levar até a ponte" (take/drive me to the bridge).
target_language_example: A ponte fica perto da estação.
native_language_example: The bridge is near the station.

meaning: “the fucking …” (a very vulgar intensifier before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to add anger, impatience, or strong emphasis before a noun, typically in the pattern “a porra da + [feminine noun]” (e.g., a porra da água). With masculine nouns it usually becomes “a porra do + [masculine noun]”. It’s highly offensive/profane (from “porra,” literally “semen,” used as a swear word), so avoid in polite situations; even among friends it can sound aggressive.
target_language_example: Onde está a porra da água?
native_language_example: Where’s the fucking water?

meaning: “the fucking …” (a very vulgar, angry intensifier before a noun).
additional_notes: Used to show strong annoyance, impatience, or emphasis before a noun: “a porra do X”. It’s profanity and can sound aggressive/hostile—avoid in polite situations. It agrees with the noun’s gender/number via the article after “porra”: “a porra do carro” (masc. sg.), “a porra da chave” (fem. sg.), “a porra dos carros” (masc. pl.), “a porra das chaves” (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Onde está a porra do meu carro?
native_language_example: Where is my fucking car?

additional_notes: Includes the feminine singular definite article a ('the'). porta refers to a physical door, and you’ll often see it with verbs like abrir (open), fechar (close), trancar (lock), and bater (slam/shut).
target_language_example: A porta está aberta.
native_language_example: The door is open.

additional_notes: Used to describe a door that is currently open or that someone left open. Common with the verb deixar (“to leave”): Deixa/Deixe a porta aberta (“Leave the door open”). Note agreement: porta (feminine) + aberta (feminine).
target_language_example: Não deixa a porta aberta, está frio.
native_language_example: Don’t leave the door open; it’s cold.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the main entrance door of a house or building. Often appears with verbs like estar (A porta da frente estava aberta.) and usar (Usa/Use a porta da frente.). In instructions, “Usa” is informal (tu) and “Use” is more formal/polite (você).
target_language_example: Por favor, bate na porta da frente.
native_language_example: Please knock on the front door.

additional_notes: Used to describe the state of a door being closed. Common after verbs like deixar/manter (“leave/keep”) and encontrar (“find”): “Deixe/Mantenha a porta fechada” = “Leave/Keep the door closed”; “Encontrou a porta fechada” = “He found the door closed.”
target_language_example: Quando cheguei, encontrei a porta fechada.
native_language_example: When I arrived, I found the door closed.

meaning: the possibility of; the chance/opportunity to.
additional_notes: Used to talk about whether something might happen (often with risk/likelihood) or whether someone has the opportunity/ability to do something. It’s usually followed by a noun or an infinitive ("a possibilidade de viajar"), and it can also introduce a clause with "de que" ("a possibilidade de que isso aconteça").
target_language_example: Existe a possibilidade de chover amanhã.
native_language_example: There’s a possibility it will rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Feminine noun: praia. It usually appears with the definite article: a praia (“the beach”). Common with the verb ficar to talk about location/distance: “A praia fica perto/longe daqui?” You can also use it with ir para to mean “to go to the beach”: “ir para a praia”.
target_language_example: Vamos para a praia no fim de semana.
native_language_example: We're going to the beach on the weekend.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what meteorologists/apps say the weather will be like (today, tomorrow, this weekend, etc.). Common patterns: “Qual é a previsão do tempo para amanhã?” (What’s the forecast for tomorrow?) and “A previsão do tempo é que…” (The forecast is that…). You may also hear “previsão meteorológica” as a more formal synonym.
target_language_example: Segundo a previsão do tempo, vai fazer frio no fim de semana.
native_language_example: According to the weather forecast, it’s going to be cold this weekend.

additional_notes: Used with the feminine definite article “a” (“the”). Common with verbs like “chegar”/“vir” to talk about the season approaching: “A primavera vai chegar logo.”
target_language_example: Na primavera, o tempo fica mais agradável.
native_language_example: In spring, the weather becomes more pleasant.

additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns (explicit or implied). It’s the feminine form of the ordinal number: a primeira página (“the first page”). You can also use it on its own to mean “the first one” when the noun is understood from context. Masculine: o primeiro; plural: as primeiras / os primeiros.
target_language_example: A primeira vez é sempre difícil.
native_language_example: The first time is always difficult.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the first action, thought, or item in a sequence: "A primeira coisa que eu fiz/vi/disse foi..." It’s often followed by a verb phrase, and you can change it for gender/number (e.g., "O primeiro" / "A primeira"; "As primeiras coisas").
target_language_example: A primeira coisa que eu vou fazer é ligar para você.
native_language_example: The first thing I’m going to do is call you.

additional_notes: Uses the feminine definite article “a” (= “the”) with “princesa” (princess). Often refers to a specific princess known from the story/context (e.g., in fairy tales or games: “save the princess”). Capitalize as part of a name/title: “a princesa Buttercup”.
target_language_example: Onde está a princesa?
native_language_example: Where is the princess?

additional_notes: Feminine form of the noun (professor/a). Used with the definite article a (“the”). You’ll see it for school teachers and also for female university instructors in Portuguese. If you know the teacher’s name, you can say: a professora Rosa. Plural: as professoras.
target_language_example: A professora vai explicar a lição agora.
native_language_example: The teacher is going to explain the lesson now.

additional_notes: “Prova” is a feminine noun. In many contexts it means “proof/evidence” (as in showing something is true). It can also mean “test/exam” depending on context (e.g., “Tenho uma prova amanhã.” = “I have a test tomorrow.”).
target_language_example: Você tem alguma prova disso?
native_language_example: Do you have any proof of that?

additional_notes: Used to refer to the next item in a sequence when the noun is understood from context (e.g., a próxima música = the next song). It’s feminine because it agrees with an implied feminine noun (música, história, etc.). For a masculine implied noun, use "o próximo" (e.g., o próximo trem = the next train).
target_language_example: Vamos para a próxima pergunta.
native_language_example: Let’s go to the next question.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the main point or the real problem, often followed by "que" ("a questão é que..."). Common in explanations and arguments, similar to English "The thing is, ...".
target_language_example: A questão é que eu não tenho tempo hoje.
native_language_example: The thing is, I don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used for a female monarch or, more generally, for a woman seen as the most important/best in a group (“queen of…”). Often paired with "o rei" (the king).
target_language_example: A rainha vai visitar a cidade amanhã.
native_language_example: The queen is going to visit the city tomorrow.

additional_notes: Means “the answer” to a question/problem, or “the response” to a message/situation. Uses the feminine singular definite article “a” (= “the”), so you’ll often see it after verbs like saber (to know), dar (to give), and ser (to be): “saber a resposta” = “to know the answer”, “dar a resposta” = “to give the answer”.
target_language_example: Você já sabe a resposta?
native_language_example: Do you already know the answer?

additional_notes: Means “his answer/response,” referring to something said or decided by a male person. It’s formed with the noun + possessive: a resposta (the answer) + dele (of him / his). Often used with verbs like esperar/aguardar (to wait for) and with adjectives like positiva/negativa (positive/negative).
target_language_example: Ainda estou esperando a resposta dele.
native_language_example: I'm still waiting for his answer.

additional_notes: Common noun used for scheduled meetings (work, school, organizations). Often appears with verbs like "ser" (to be held), "acontecer" (to happen), and "terminar" (to end). You can ask about time/place with "Quando/onde será a reunião?"
target_language_example: A reunião começa às nove, na sala 3.
native_language_example: The meeting starts at nine, in room 3.

additional_notes: "A" is the feminine singular definite article ("the"). "Rua" usually means a street (typically in a town/city). It’s used for the street itself (e.g., crossing it) and in addresses/locations (e.g., the street where someone lives).
target_language_example: O café fica na rua de cima.
native_language_example: The café is on the street up there.

meaning: the exit; the way out; (on roads) the exit/off-ramp.
additional_notes: Used for the place where you leave a building ("A saída é pela esquerda"), for leading someone to the door/exit ("até a saída"), and for a highway exit you might miss ("Perdemos a saída"). It comes from the verb "sair" (to leave/go out).
target_language_example: Desculpe, onde fica a saída?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the exit?

additional_notes: Means “health” as a general concept or someone’s physical condition. It’s commonly used with the definite article “a” (“the”) in Portuguese, especially for abstract ideas (e.g., a saúde, a felicidade). It also appears in phrases like “recuperar a saúde” (to recover one’s health) and “fazer bem à saúde” (to be good for your health) — note that with the verb phrase “fazer bem a”, “a + a saúde” typically contracts to “à saúde.”
target_language_example: A maior riqueza é a saúde.
native_language_example: The greatest wealth is health.

additional_notes: Means throughout the entire week. Often used with verbs like ficar, chover, estar, trabalhar, etc. Word order: article + time period + toda (e.g., o dia todo, o ano todo).
target_language_example: Vou trabalhar a semana toda.
native_language_example: I'm going to work all week.

additional_notes: A respectful way to address or refer to a woman, especially in formal situations or when speaking to an older woman. In direct address, it usually takes third-person verb forms. Depending on context, it can also mean "the lady."
target_language_example: A senhora precisa de ajuda?
native_language_example: Do you need help, ma'am?

additional_notes: Used to address a woman politely (often older, a customer, or someone you don’t know well). It’s “a senhora” (the lady/ma’am) + “está” (is/are), typically followed by a temporary state, location, or an action in progress: “com fome” (hungry), “de volta” (back), “ligando” (calling), “visitando” (visiting). In Brazil, “a senhora” is more formal than “você.”
target_language_example: A senhora está esperando alguém?
native_language_example: Are you waiting for someone, ma’am?

additional_notes: Used to politely address an adult woman (“a senhora” = ma’am/you, formal). Often heard in customer service, with older people, or when you want to be extra respectful. The verb “quer” is from “querer” (to want), and in questions it can mean “want” or “would like.” Object pronouns may appear in formal phrasing: “A senhora quer que eu a ajude…?” = “Would you like me to help you…?”
target_language_example: A senhora quer pagar em dinheiro ou no cartão?
native_language_example: Would you like to pay in cash or by card?

meaning: formal/polite way to ask a woman “do you have…?”
additional_notes: Used when speaking politely to an older woman or in formal situations. Although it literally means “the lady has,” in conversation it functions like “do you have…?” Portuguese uses 3rd-person verbs with titles like “a senhora” (so you say “a senhora tem,” not “a senhora tens”). Common in questions about possessions, money, availability, or quantities (e.g., “Quantos a senhora tem?” = “How many do you have?”).
target_language_example: A senhora tem um documento com foto?
native_language_example: Do you have a photo ID?

meaning: 'you are' (polite/formal, addressing a woman) / 'the lady is'.
additional_notes: "A senhora" is a respectful way to address an adult/older woman (like "ma’am"). With "é" (from "ser"), it’s used to describe identity or characteristics: e.g., asking about allergies, saying someone is confident, or identifying someone as a mother. It can mean either directly addressing the woman ("you are") or talking about her in the third person ("the lady is"), depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: A senhora é médica?
native_language_example: Are you a doctor, ma’am?

meaning: “Miss” / “young lady” (polite way to refer to or address a woman).
additional_notes: Used as a respectful form of address or reference, often for an unmarried/young woman (similar to “Miss” in names: “a senhorita Green”). It can also mean “the young lady” when talking about someone (“a senhorita do piano?” = “the piano young lady?”). In some contexts it can sound old-fashioned or overly formal.
target_language_example: Com licença, a senhorita pode me ajudar?
native_language_example: Excuse me, miss, can you help me?

additional_notes: Means “the situation” (a state of affairs or set of circumstances). Very common in news and everyday speech: e.g. economic, political, or personal situations. Often used with verbs like “estar” (A situação está difícil.) and expressions like “fugir do controle” (A situação fugiu do controle.).
target_language_example: A situação aqui melhorou um pouco, mas ainda está complicada.
native_language_example: The situation here has improved a bit, but it’s still complicated.

additional_notes: “Sopa” is a feminine noun, so it commonly appears with the feminine singular article “a” (= “the”). Used to talk about soup as a dish (“A sopa está boa.” = “The soup tastes good.”). With “cheirar a”, it means “to smell like” something: “cheirar a sopa” = “to smell like soup.” Sentence 2 (“A sopa!”) can be an exclamation (e.g., calling attention to the soup, announcing it’s ready, or ordering it in context).
target_language_example: A sopa está quente.
native_language_example: The soup is hot.

additional_notes: Possessive used with a feminine singular noun: a sua moto = "your motorcycle." Depending on context, sua can also mean "his," "her," or "its." The article a is common in Portuguese before possessives and is usually not translated into English.
target_language_example: A sua bolsa está aqui.
native_language_example: Your bag is here.

additional_notes: Means help provided by the person you’re talking to. Uses the possessive “sua” with the definite article “a.” Common in polite contexts (thanks, requests). In Brazil, “sua” can sometimes sound more formal than “sua” used in very casual speech; you may also hear “a tua ajuda” (more informal/European Portuguese and some regions) or “sua ajuda” without the article in some contexts.
target_language_example: Obrigado pela sua ajuda.
native_language_example: Thank you for your help.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a letter belonging to the person you’re addressing, using the possessive "sua". Often sounds more formal/polite than "a tua carta" (common in Portugal and informal contexts). In Brazil, "sua" is widely used because people often address someone as "você".
target_language_example: Obrigado por enviar a sua carta; vou responder amanhã.
native_language_example: Thank you for sending your letter; I’ll reply tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive "sua" to mean "your" (formal "you" = você) or "his/her/its" depending on context; adding "a" makes it "the your house" → "your house." Often said as "sua casa" without the article, and in Brazilian Portuguese you may also hear "a casa de você" to avoid ambiguity.
target_language_example: Posso visitar a sua casa amanhã?
native_language_example: Can I visit your house tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to refer to the wife of the person you’re speaking to. "Sua" agrees with the noun (esposa = feminine), and it can also mean "his/her/your" depending on context, but in direct questions to someone it often means "your". Often used with the article: "a sua esposa".
target_language_example: A sua esposa está em casa agora?
native_language_example: Is your wife at home now?

meaning: your wife (or his/her wife, depending on context).
additional_notes: Uses the possessive “sua” (feminine singular) + “esposa” (wife). In Brazilian Portuguese, “a sua esposa” is often used to mean “your wife” when speaking to “você,” but it can also mean “his wife” or “her wife” because “seu/sua” can refer to him/her/you—context usually makes it clear. You can also say “a esposa dele/dela” to be unambiguous (“his/her wife”).
target_language_example: A sua esposa trabalha aqui?
native_language_example: Does your wife work here?

meaning: your absence (in “sentir a sua falta” = “to miss you”).
additional_notes: Used as the object in the very common expression “sentir falta de (alguém)” (“to miss (someone)”). “Sua” can mean “your” (often more formal, or in Brazil also for “his/her/their/your” depending on context). Don’t confuse “falta” with English “fault”: here it means “absence/lack”.
target_language_example: Vou sentir muito a sua falta quando você viajar.
native_language_example: I’m going to miss you a lot when you travel.

meaning: “your family” (formal), or “his/her family” depending on context.
additional_notes: “Sua” can mean “your” (formal singular, like to a customer/stranger) or “his/her/its/their,” so the meaning depends on who is being talked to/about. In Brazil, many people say “a família dele/dela” to be clearer. Often used when asking how someone’s relatives are or when talking about supporting/providing for one’s family.
target_language_example: Você conhece a sua família aqui na cidade?
native_language_example: Do you know your family here in the city?

additional_notes: “Sua” is a possessive that can mean “your” (formal), but also “his/her/their” in some contexts—Portuguese often relies on context to know whose daughter it is. To be clearer, people may say “a filha dele” (his daughter) or “a filha dela” (her daughter).
target_language_example: A sua filha já chegou em casa?
native_language_example: Has your daughter arrived home yet?

additional_notes: Literally “your age.” Common in comparisons and time expressions like “quando eu tinha a sua idade” (“when I was your age”). Also used in advice about maturity/behavior: “de acordo com a sua idade” (“according to/appropriate for your age”). Uses the formal/neutral possessive “sua” (also used with “você”); with “tu,” you’ll often see “a tua idade.”
target_language_example: Quando eu tinha a sua idade, eu estudava e trabalhava ao mesmo tempo.
native_language_example: When I was your age, I studied and worked at the same time.

additional_notes: Literally “the your sister.” In Portuguese, possessives often come with an article (a/o): a sua irmã, o seu irmão. In many contexts, “sua” can also mean “his/her/their,” so speakers may use “a irmã dele/dela” to be more specific.
target_language_example: A sua irmã fala inglês?
native_language_example: Does your sister speak English?

meaning: your wife (or your woman, depending on context).
additional_notes: Most commonly means “your wife” when talking to a man about his spouse. In some contexts, especially informal speech, it can also mean “your girlfriend/partner” (“your woman”). Uses the formal possessive “sua” (your); in everyday Brazilian Portuguese people often say “a sua esposa” (more formal) or “a sua namorada” (girlfriend) when they want to be specific.
target_language_example: A sua mulher trabalha aqui?
native_language_example: Does your wife work here?

meaning: your hand; (also) your help/support; (also) a woman's hand in marriage (formal).
additional_notes: Literally “your hand” (feminine singular). Used in physical contexts (shake, hold, move, take away your hand). In expressions like “Dê-me a sua mão!” it means “Give me your hand!” (e.g., to help someone). In “pedir a sua mão”, it’s a traditional/formal way to ask to marry someone (“ask for your hand in marriage”).
target_language_example: Pode me dar a sua mão para atravessar a rua?
native_language_example: Can you give me your hand to cross the street?

additional_notes: "a" is the feminine singular definite article (“the”), and "sua" means “your” (feminine singular noun). "namorada" is “girlfriend.” Used when speaking to someone about their girlfriend. In Brazil, "sua" is often interchangeable with "a sua" (e.g., "Conheci sua namorada"); in Portugal, "a sua" is common and can sound more formal/clear. It can also be used in the sense of “your date/partner” depending on context.
target_language_example: A sua namorada vem à festa hoje?
native_language_example: Is your girlfriend coming to the party today?

additional_notes: Uses the possessive "sua" to refer to the person you’re addressing as "você" (you). Common in polite/formal contexts, but it can also sound sharp or sarcastic depending on tone (e.g., "Quem pediu a sua opinião?" = "Who asked for your opinion?"). Often appears with verbs like "dar" (to give), "pedir" (to ask for), "ter" (to have), "respeitar" (to respect).
target_language_example: Gostaria de saber a sua opinião sobre este assunto.
native_language_example: I’d like to know your opinion about this matter.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun to emphasize that something belongs to the person you’re talking about (or to “you” in a general sense): a sua própria língua = your own language. It adds emphasis, like “your very own.” In other contexts it can also mean “his/her/its own” depending on who “sua” refers to.
target_language_example: Você tem a sua própria opinião.
native_language_example: You have your own opinion.

additional_notes: Usually means “your health” when talking about someone’s wellbeing (often with você/o senhor/a senhora; e.g., "melhorar a sua saúde"). It can also be used alone as a toast before drinking, equivalent to “Cheers!/To your health!” (often written with an exclamation point).
target_language_example: Vou fazer um exame porque estou preocupado com a sua saúde.
native_language_example: I’m going to get a check-up because I’m worried about your health.

additional_notes: Used for taking turns or waiting in a sequence. Common patterns: "É a sua vez" (It’s your turn), "É a sua vez de + infinitive" (It’s your turn to + verb), and "Espere a sua vez" (Wait your turn). You can change the possessive: "a minha vez" (my turn), "a nossa vez" (our turn), etc.
target_language_example: É a sua vez de falar.
native_language_example: It’s your turn to speak.

additional_notes: "Sua" is a possessive meaning “your,” and "viagem" means “trip/journey.” It’s common in polite conversation, especially with "você". In Brazil, "sua" can sometimes be ambiguous (your vs. his/her/their), but in questions like "Como foi a sua viagem?" it usually clearly means “your trip.”
target_language_example: Espero que a sua viagem tenha sido tranquila.
native_language_example: I hope your trip was smooth.

additional_notes: Used to address someone with the polite/formal possessive “sua” (especially with você/o senhor/a senhora). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people often say “a sua vida” in polite contexts, and “a tua vida” in more informal contexts (common in Portugal and some regions). In formal writing, “sua” can sometimes also mean “his/her/their,” so context matters.
target_language_example: Você está arriscando a sua vida.
native_language_example: You’re risking your life.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a feminine noun that’s understood from context, often avoiding repeating it: e.g., “a sua (mãe/bolsa/casa)”. It agrees with the implied noun (a sua = feminine singular). Common in comparisons (“mais … do que a sua” = “than yours”) and in set expressions like “Sorte a sua” (“Lucky you/That’s your luck”).
target_language_example: Eu trouxe a minha garrafa; cadê a sua?
native_language_example: I brought my bottle; where’s yours?

additional_notes: Used to say an action lasted for the entire afternoon. It often comes after the verb ("Esperei a tarde toda"), and it can also appear with a gerund phrase to emphasize duration ("passaram a tarde toda conversando" = spent all afternoon talking).
target_language_example: Fiquei trabalhando a tarde toda.
native_language_example: I kept working all afternoon.

meaning: the temperature (how hot or cold something is).
additional_notes: Used with the definite article “a” (“the”). Common in weather (“a temperatura de hoje…”) and health contexts (“a temperatura dele/dela está normal” = their body temperature is normal). You can specify whose/what temperature with “de” (e.g., “a temperatura do quarto”, “a temperatura dele”).
target_language_example: Qual é a temperatura agora?
native_language_example: What is the temperature right now?

meaning: the storm; (figuratively) a crisis or difficult time.
additional_notes: Literally a strong storm (wind/rain, etc.). It can also be used figuratively for a tough period: esperar a tempestade passar = “wait for things to calm down.” Common proverb: “Quem semeia o vento colhe a tempestade” = “You reap what you sow” (bad actions bring bad consequences).
target_language_example: Vamos ficar em casa até a tempestade passar.
native_language_example: Let’s stay home until the storm passes.

meaning: the Earth; the land/ground; soil; (also) a people’s land/territory.
additional_notes: Meaning depends on context: (1) "a Terra" (often capitalized) refers to the planet Earth. (2) "a terra" can mean land/ground/soil (what you walk on or plant in). (3) With "de" + people/group ("a terra de vocês", "a terra dos nossos ancestrais"), it can mean someone’s homeland or territory.
target_language_example: Depois da chuva, a terra ficou muito molhada.
native_language_example: After the rain, the ground/soil got very wet.

additional_notes: Feminine singular noun. Used for a tower or tall structure (e.g., a building tower, watchtower, or control tower). Often refers to a specific tower known from the context; plural: as torres.
target_language_example: A torre é muito alta.
native_language_example: The tower is very tall.

additional_notes: Feminine singular form used with feminine nouns (e.g., "a tua mesa" = "your table"). It can also stand alone as a possessive pronoun meaning "yours" when the noun is understood from context (e.g., "A minha é azul, e a tua é vermelha." = "Mine is blue, and yours is red."). Typically used when speaking to one person informally (tu).
target_language_example: Posso pegar a tua caneta por um minuto?
native_language_example: Can I borrow your pen for a minute?

additional_notes: Used to talk to one person about their sister. "Tua" is an informal/neutral way to say "your" (singular) in European Portuguese; in Brazilian Portuguese, "sua" is often used instead (especially with "você"), while "tua" is common in some regions and contexts. "A" is the feminine singular definite article (“the”).
target_language_example: A tua irmã vem conosco hoje?
native_language_example: Is your sister coming with us today?

additional_notes: Literally “the your mother” (Portuguese commonly uses the definite article with family members). Uses **tu** (informal “you”), so it’s common with friends, family, or when insulting/arguing. In more formal contexts you’d usually say **a sua mãe** (“your mother,” formal/neutral).
target_language_example: A tua mãe já chegou a casa?
native_language_example: Has your mother already gotten home?

additional_notes: A common noun phrase used for what is real or factual. Very often used after verbs like dizer, contar, or saber: dizer a verdade = to tell the truth.
target_language_example: Ele finalmente disse a verdade.
native_language_example: He finally told the truth.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an honest statement, often to correct a misunderstanding or admit something. It can add emphasis, like “to be honest,” and is commonly followed by a full clause (sometimes with “que,” sometimes omitted in casual speech).
target_language_example: A verdade é que eu não tenho tempo hoje.
native_language_example: The truth is I don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Feminine singular noun with the definite article a. Used for a specific trip/journey: A viagem foi interessante? (“Was the trip interesting?”). Common with verbs like ser/estar (foi), ir (vai), and with cost questions: Quanto a viagem vai custar? / A viagem vai custar quanto?
target_language_example: A viagem começa amanhã de manhã.
native_language_example: The trip starts tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Literally includes the definite article ('the'), but Portuguese often uses the article where English would simply say 'life' in a general sense.
target_language_example: A vida nem sempre é fácil.
native_language_example: Life is not always easy.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s life/story: "A vida de Sméagol" = "Sméagol’s life." Very common in expressions like "salvar a vida de [alguém]" (to save [someone]’s life) and "custar a vida de [alguém]" (to cost [someone]’s life). Note the contraction: "de" + "o/um/uma" → "do/dum/duma" (e.g., "a vida de um animal" is often said as "a vida dum animal").
target_language_example: Ele arriscou a própria vida para salvar a vida de uma criança.
native_language_example: He risked his own life to save a child's life.

additional_notes: Literally “the life of hers.” Portuguese often expresses possession with the pattern: noun + dela/dela(s)/dele/dele(s) (“of her/of him/of them”), especially for emphasis or clarity. Here, “dela” = “de + ela” (of + she/her) and refers to a female person.
target_language_example: Eu me preocupo com a vida dela.
native_language_example: I worry about her life.

meaning: (for) one’s whole life; all one’s life.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize duration across an entire lifetime. Common with verbs like passar (“to spend”) or expressions like ter ... pela frente (“to have ... ahead of you”). In “Você tem a vida inteira pela frente”, it means you still have your whole life ahead of you.
target_language_example: Ela esperou a vida inteira por esse momento.
native_language_example: She waited her whole life for that moment.

additional_notes: Used to correct an unrealistic idea or expectation about life, often followed by a comparison (como...) or by saying what life is/isn't (não é só..., não é um...). Common in sayings and advice; it can sound emphatic depending on context.
target_language_example: A vida não é fácil, mas vale a pena.
native_language_example: Life isn’t easy, but it’s worth it.

meaning: (for) one’s whole life; all one’s life.
additional_notes: Used as an adverbial time expression to emphasize duration from early life up to now, or for an entire lifetime. Often comes after the verb (e.g., trabalhou a vida toda), and can refer to someone’s life in general or up to a specific moment (e.g., treinou a vida toda para isto).
target_language_example: Eu esperei a vida toda por este momento.
native_language_example: I’ve waited my whole life for this moment.

additional_notes: Used to make general statements or opinions about life. Often followed by an adjective (A vida é dura. = Life is hard.) or a noun phrase (A vida é um sonho. = Life is a dream.).
target_language_example: Às vezes, a vida é complicada.
native_language_example: Sometimes, life is complicated.

additional_notes: Refers to someone’s voice (the sound they make when speaking or singing). It can also mean a voice you hear (e.g., in your head) or figuratively “a voice/message” that reaches people (e.g., news/word spreading). Common pattern: "a voz de + person" (a voice of someone).
target_language_example: Eu reconheci a voz dele imediatamente.
native_language_example: I recognized his voice immediately.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the person (or sometimes an animal) who was harmed, attacked, or affected by a crime, accident, or bad situation. It can also be used figuratively to mean someone being treated unfairly or blaming others (e.g., “You’re the victim here.”). Feminine noun: a vítima (o/a vítima).
target_language_example: A vítima ainda está no hospital, mas vai se recuperar.
native_language_example: The victim is still in the hospital, but will recover.

additional_notes: Means “the water” (definite article + noun). Often used when talking about water in general in a specific context (e.g., the water in the pool, shower, tap, etc.).
target_language_example: A água está quente agora.
native_language_example: The water is hot now.

additional_notes: Definite noun phrase: **a** = “the” (feminine singular) + **árvore** = “tree”. Used when referring to a specific tree already known from context. Plural is **as árvores** (“the trees”).
target_language_example: A árvore está no jardim.
native_language_example: The tree is in the garden.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is the least desired, least needed, or least expected option. Common with verbs like "querer" (want), "precisar" (need), and "esperar" (expect): "A última coisa que eu quero/preciso/esperava…".
target_language_example: A última coisa que eu preciso agora é de mais problemas.
native_language_example: The last thing I need right now is more problems.

a última pessoa que eu esperava

target_language_multi_word_term: a última pessoa que eu esperava
additional_notes: Used to express surprise: someone shows up or does something, and they were the least expected. Literally “the last person that I expected.” You can change the verb to match the situation: “a última pessoa que eu queria ver” (the last person I wanted to see).
target_language_example: Ele foi a última pessoa que eu esperava ver na festa.
native_language_example: He was the last person I expected to see at the party.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (“a única coisa”, “a única saída”, “a única mulher”, “a única testemunha”). It can also stand alone when the noun is understood: “Ela foi a única” = “She was the only one.” Masculine form: “o único”. Plural: “os/as únicos/únicas”.
target_language_example: Ela é a única pessoa que sabe a verdade.
native_language_example: She is the only person who knows the truth.

additional_notes: Used to point out the single option/action/thing that is possible or remains. It’s often followed by a verb phrase (a única coisa que posso fazer…) or by a clause explaining what that “only thing” is (A única coisa que se pode fazer é…).
target_language_example: A única coisa que eu quero agora é descansar.
native_language_example: The only thing I want right now is to rest.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a lower position (physical or figurative) or a value under a limit. Common with measurements and numbers: “abaixo de 10 euros” (under 10 euros). It can also be used in writing to refer to what comes later: “abaixo, segue…” (“below, it follows…”).
target_language_example: A temperatura ficou abaixo de zero ontem.
native_language_example: The temperature stayed below zero yesterday.

additional_notes: Used for a pregnancy loss that happens naturally (not induced). In everyday conversation, people often say just “aborto” when context is clear, but “aborto espontâneo” is more specific and can sound more clinical. Common verbs: “ter/sofrer um aborto espontâneo” (to have/suffer a miscarriage).
target_language_example: Sinto muito, ela sofreu um aborto espontâneo no mês passado.
native_language_example: I’m so sorry, she had a miscarriage last month.

additional_notes: Uses the imperative of the verb abrir (“to open”) in the você form. It’s a common way to ask someone to open a door, often with por favor (“please”). In casual speech you may also hear abre a porta (more informal/less polite) and pra mim instead of para mim (“for me”).
target_language_example: Por favor, abra a porta que está trancada.
native_language_example: Please open the door that’s locked.

additional_notes: Imperative (command) form of "abrir" directed at "você" (often used without saying "você"). Can be literal (telling someone to physically open their eyes, e.g., after sleeping or during an exam) or figurative, meaning "wake up / pay attention / realize what’s going on."
target_language_example: Abra os olhos e preste atenção no que o médico vai dizer.
native_language_example: Open your eyes and pay attention to what the doctor is going to say.

additional_notes: Common command/request. Literally “(you) open the door,” using the verb abrir (“to open”) + a porta (“the door”). In polite requests, you’ll often hear it with “por favor” or in the formal form “A senhora / O senhor abre a porta…?”.
target_language_example: Por favor, abre a porta para eu entrar.
native_language_example: Please, open the door so I can come in.

meaning: “open it” (referring to a feminine noun, e.g. a door/window).
additional_notes: Formed by the verb "abrir" (to open) + the object pronoun "a" (“it/her”), written with a hyphen as an enclitic pronoun. Use it when the thing you’re opening is grammatically feminine (e.g. "a porta", "a janela"). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, many speakers also say "abrir ela" in casual speech, but "abri-la" is the standard written form.
target_language_example: Você pode abri-la, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you open it, please?

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "abrir" in the 1st person singular: "eu abri" = "I opened". Used for a completed action in the past. You can add details like how/with what ("com minha chave" = "with my key"), which door ("a porta da garagem" = "the garage door"), or for whom ("para Tom" = "for Tom"). In writing, it’s commonly spelled with an accent: "abri" (not *"abrí" in Brazilian Portuguese; "abri" has no accent).
target_language_example: Ouvi alguém bater e abri a porta devagar.
native_language_example: I heard someone knock and I opened the door slowly.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase: "abrir" = "to open" and "a caixa" = "the box". Used for physically opening a box, often with tools (e.g., "com um pé de cabra" = "with a crowbar") or a key ("Você precisa de uma chave..."). You can use it in questions ("Posso abrir a caixa?") and with verbs like "conseguir" (manage to), "tentar" (try), and "forçar" (force someone to).
target_language_example: Não consigo abrir a caixa; você pode me ajudar?
native_language_example: I can't open the box; can you help me?

additional_notes: Used for physically opening a window. Very common in polite requests: "Você se importa se eu abrir a janela?" / "Você se incomoda se eu abrir a janela?" = "Do you mind if I open the window?". With "estar a" + infinitive it means an action in progress (European Portuguese): "Ela está a abrir a janela" = "She is opening the window."
target_language_example: Está calor aqui; você se importa se eu abrir a janela?
native_language_example: It’s hot in here; do you mind if I open the window?

additional_notes: Used to ask or talk about opening a door. Common in polite requests with the conditional: “Poderia… abrir a porta?” = “Could you… open the door?” Also appears after modal verbs like “poder” (can) and “ser capaz de” (be able to), and after “tentar” (try).
target_language_example: Você pode abrir a porta, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you open the door, please?

meaning: to make way; to clear/open a path (also: to pave the way).
additional_notes: Used both literally (clearing a physical route) and figuratively (creating an opportunity or making progress possible). Often appears as an imperative: "Abram caminho!" = "Make way!"
target_language_example: Com licença, preciso abrir caminho para passar.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I need to make way to get through.

additional_notes: Usually used as **abrir mão de** + noun/infinitive: **abrir mão de um direito** (give up a right), **abrir mão do dinheiro** (give up the money), **abrir mão de fazer algo** (give up doing something). Common when talking about concessions, negotiations, or sacrifices.
target_language_example: Não vou abrir mão dos meus princípios.
native_language_example: I won’t give up my principles.

additional_notes: "Abriu" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "abrir" (to open). Used to describe a completed action in the past. Often followed by details about how/why the door was opened (e.g., "com um chute" = with a kick; "lentamente" = slowly; "para" + infinitive = in order to).
target_language_example: Quando cheguei, ele já abriu a porta.
native_language_example: When I arrived, he had already opened the door.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize zero amount/knowledge/possession. Common with negation (não tem/sabe absolutamente nada), and can also appear as de absolutamente nada (“about nothing at all”).
target_language_example: Eu não vi absolutamente nada na rua ontem à noite.
native_language_example: I didn’t see absolutely anything on the street last night.

meaning: 'just' (did something); indicates the very recent past.
additional_notes: Used as **acabar de + infinitive** to say something happened moments ago. With **ele/ela/você** the form is **acaba de**: *Ele acaba de chegar* = “He just arrived.” Other persons: *eu acabo de*, *nós acabamos de*, *eles acabam de*. In the past you can use *acabou de* (“just did”). Not the same as *acabar* meaning “to finish/end” in general.
target_language_example: Ele acaba de concluir a faculdade.
native_language_example: He just finished college.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb to say something happened moments ago/recently: "acabamos de + infinitive". It’s the 1st person plural present of "acabar" used as a time expression (e.g., "acabamos de chegar" = "we just arrived").
target_language_example: Acabamos de chegar em casa.
native_language_example: We just got home.

meaning: to put an end to; to destroy/finish off (sometimes: to kill).
additional_notes: Used with a direct object: acabar com + noun/pronoun. It can be practical/neutral (“end this problem”) or very strong (“destroy/kill”), especially in threats like “Vou acabar com você/ele” (“I’ll finish you/him off”). Often translates as “end,” “get rid of,” “ruin,” or “wipe out,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Precisamos acabar com esse barulho agora.
native_language_example: We need to put an end to this noise now.

meaning: to put an end to this; to finish this (once and for all).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "acabar com" (“to end/stop/get rid of”) + "isso" (“this/that”). Common when you want to end a situation/problem or finally get something done. Often appears with emphasis like "de uma vez por todas" (“once and for all”) or "logo" (“quickly/right away”).
target_language_example: Vamos acabar com isso hoje.
native_language_example: Let’s put an end to this today.

meaning: to have just; to have done something a moment ago
additional_notes: Usually used as acabar de + infinitive. Most often it indicates that something happened very recently: acabar de chegar = “to have just arrived.” In other contexts, acabar can mean “to finish,” so the precise meaning depends on the structure and context.
target_language_example: Acabar de chegar e já ter de sair de novo é frustrante.
native_language_example: To have just arrived and already have to leave again is frustrating.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened very recently. It’s formed with the present tense of "acabar" + de + infinitive: (eu) acabei de..., (você/ele/ela) acabou de..., (nós) acabamos de..., (eles/elas) acabaram de.... In everyday Portuguese it often corresponds to English "I just..." / "I’ve just...".
target_language_example: Acabei de chegar em casa.
native_language_example: I just got home.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb to say you did something moments ago: "Acabo de + infinitive". It’s the present tense of "acabar" used this way; you can also change the subject: "Eu acabo de...", "Ela acaba de...", "Nós acabamos de...".
target_language_example: Acabo de chegar em casa.
native_language_example: I just got home.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened very recently (just now). Formed with the verb "acabar" + "de" + infinitive: "acabei de chegar" (I just arrived), "ela acabou de sair" (she just left). The verb "acabar" conjugates to match the subject (acabei/acabou/acabaram, etc.).
target_language_example: Um mosquito acabou de me picar.
native_language_example: A mosquito just bit me.

additional_notes: Uses the structure **acabar de + infinitive** to say something happened **very recently**. The verb **acabar** is conjugated for the subject: **eu acabei de chegar**, **você/ele acabou de chegar**, **nós acabamos de chegar**, **eles acabaram de chegar**. Often used with surprise or emphasis: *Mas você acabou de chegar!*
target_language_example: Ela acabou de chegar em casa.
native_language_example: She just got home.

meaning: (He/She/It) just left; has just gone out.
additional_notes: Uses the structure **acabar de + infinitive** to say something happened very recently. Change the subject as needed: **Eu acabei de sair** (I just left), **Ela acabou de sair** (She just left).
