additional_notes: Used with a time span meaning “from X until someone dies” (até a morte dele/dela) or with a verb to mean something happened “to the point of death” (sangrar/espancar até a morte). Often appears in serious or violent contexts.
target_language_example: Ele trabalhou até a morte, sem descanso.
native_language_example: He worked himself to death, without any rest.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (e.g., andar, ir, caminhar) to show the endpoint/destination: you go/walk as far as the door. Often implies stopping there (or reaching it) before doing something else.
target_language_example: Ela correu até a porta e bateu.
native_language_example: She ran to the door and knocked.

additional_notes: Used to talk about everything that has happened (or hasn’t happened) from the past until the present moment. Very common in questions about someone’s experience: "Como você está gostando ... até agora?"
target_language_example: Até agora, está tudo bem.
native_language_example: So far, everything is fine.

additional_notes: Used in two common ways: (1) as a farewell meaning “see you tomorrow” (often on its own: “Até amanhã!”), and (2) to set a deadline meaning “by/until tomorrow” (e.g., “até amanhã de manhã” = “by tomorrow morning”).
target_language_example: Te ligo até amanhã de manhã.
native_language_example: I’ll call you by tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used to talk about reaching this place (physical) or this point (in time/progress). Very common with verbs of movement like vir (to come), chegar (to arrive), trazer (to bring), and can imply effort or distance (“all the way here”).
target_language_example: Obrigado por vir até aqui para me ajudar.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming all the way here to help me.

meaning: (all the way) home; up to (someone’s) home.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement/support like acompanhar (to walk/escort), levar (to take), and dar uma carona (to give a ride). It means the person goes with you or takes you as far as your home (often for safety or convenience). Usually appears with a possessive or pronoun implied by context: até em casa (to my/your home), até a tua casa/até a sua casa.
target_language_example: Posso te acompanhar até em casa depois do jantar.
native_language_example: I can walk you home after dinner.

additional_notes: A common goodbye used when you expect to see the person again (often later the same day or fairly soon). It can be used on its own or with a name/term of endearment (e.g., "querido", "mãe"). "Até logo mais!" adds emphasis: "see you later (then)!"
target_language_example: Estou indo agora — até logo!
native_language_example: I'm leaving now — see you soon!

meaning: "until then" / "until that time"; or "up to there" (to that place).
additional_notes: Used in two common ways: (1) time: "Até lá" = "See you/Until then" (often as a short goodbye). (2) place: "ir/caminhar até lá" = "go/walk over there" or "as far as that place". Meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: Te ligo amanhã; até lá, bom trabalho.
native_language_example: I'll call you tomorrow; until then, good work.

additional_notes: A common, friendly goodbye said when you expect to see the person again. Often used on its own or after something like "tá"/"está bem" ("OK"), and can be followed by a name.
target_language_example: Então tá, até mais!
native_language_example: Alright then, see you later!

additional_notes: Used to mark an endpoint in space or time. It is até + the masculine singular article o, so it appears before masculine nouns. In some varieties, especially European Portuguese, you may also see até ao instead.
target_language_example: Caminhei até o mercado.
native_language_example: I walked to the market.

meaning: until the end; all the way (to the end).
additional_notes: Used for going/continuing something up to the final point in time or space: a struggle or activity ("lutar/cantar até o fim"), a time period ("até o fim do mês" = until the end of the month), or a route ("até o fim da estrada" = to the end of the road). Often implies persistence/continuing without stopping.
target_language_example: Eu vou ficar com você até o fim.
native_language_example: I’ll stay with you until the end.

meaning: "until the end" / "all the way" (to the end point).
additional_notes: Used for time (stay/watch until something finishes) or for completing an action to its limit (pull/press/turn all the way). Often implies not stopping early.
target_language_example: Assista ao vídeo até o final.
native_language_example: Watch the video until the end.

meaning: “to the very last” (to the last one/bit).
additional_notes: Used for emphasis to mean leaving nothing out—often in set phrases like “até o último centavo” (“every last penny”) or “até o último homem” (“to the last man”). It can imply persistence or totality, sometimes with a threatening tone depending on context.
target_language_example: Ela procurou até o último minuto para encontrar o documento.
native_language_example: She searched until the very last minute to find the document.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “until” before a verb: "Espere até que eu volte" = “Wait until I come back.” It often follows commands and shows a condition that must happen before stopping: "Não parem até que..." / "Vamos trabalhar até que...". It can also introduce a change in the story/time: "até que um dia..." = “until one day...”. In casual speech, "até que" can mean “actually / not bad (considering...)”: "Até que não foi um dia ruim" = “It actually wasn’t a bad day.”
target_language_example: Fique aqui até que eu volte.
native_language_example: Stay here until I come back.

meaning: “finally / at last” (often after a long wait).
additional_notes: Used to express relief, impatience, or mild annoyance that something happened only after taking longer than expected. Common in spoken Portuguese and can be followed by a statement or used on its own (“Até que enfim!”).
target_language_example: Até que enfim terminou a reunião!
native_language_example: The meeting finally ended!

additional_notes: Used to talk about a deadline or end time that lasts up to Monday ("ficar até segunda-feira" = "stay until Monday"). As a goodbye, "Até segunda-feira!" means "See you on Monday!" Similar patterns: "até amanhã" (see you tomorrow / until tomorrow), "até mais" (see you later).
target_language_example: Então tá, até segunda-feira!
native_language_example: Alright then, see you on Monday!

additional_notes: Used to say something continues late into the evening or night (e.g., working, staying out, staying awake). Often appears with verbs like trabalhar (to work), ficar acordado (to stay awake), and ficar fora (to stay out).
target_language_example: Não fique acordado até tarde.
native_language_example: Don't stay up late.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize something surprising or extreme: “even…” / “even as much as…”. Often appears before the word or phrase being highlighted (e.g., “até mesmo anos” = “even years”). Similar to “até” (up to/until), but “até mesmo” adds emphasis like English “even”.
target_language_example: Ela ajudou todo mundo, até mesmo quem não agradeceu.
native_language_example: She helped everyone, even those who didn’t say thank you.

meaning: "Yeah, right!" / "As if!" (sarcastic); sometimes "it even seems/looks like".
additional_notes: Very common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese. Said alone (“Até parece!” / “Até parece.”) it’s usually sarcastic disbelief, like you don’t believe what was said. In regular sentences, it can be literal: “até” = “even” + “parecer” = “to seem/look,” meaning “it even seems/looks (like)…”.
target_language_example: —Ele disse que vai pagar tudo hoje. —Até parece!
native_language_example: —He said he’s going to pay for everything today. —Yeah, right!

additional_notes: Used to mock or reject what was said or implied, often meaning you don’t believe it or think it’s unlikely. Common in casual speech and frequently said with an ironic tone. Often appears as the standalone interjection “Até parece!” and with “que” it introduces a clause: “Até parece que ele vai ajudar…”
target_language_example: Até parece que ele vai pagar tudo sozinho.
native_language_example: Yeah right—as if he’s going to pay for everything by himself.

additional_notes: Imperative of the verb avisar (“to let someone know, to warn, to notify”) + me (“to me”). Used to ask someone to inform you when something happens or before they do something: “Avise-me quando…” (“Let me know when…”), “Avise-me com antecedência” (“Let me know in advance”). In everyday speech, people often say “Me avise” too.
target_language_example: Avise-me se você se atrasar.
native_language_example: Let me know if you’re going to be late.

additional_notes: Very informal. "cara" is a casual way to address a male friend (like "dude"). "aí" here works like an interjection (roughly "hey"), and it can also show emphasis in requests: "Relaxa aí, cara" = "Relax, man."
target_language_example: Calma aí, cara, já tô indo.
native_language_example: Calm down, dude, I'm coming.

meaning: in there; inside (where you are / that place).
additional_notes: Used to refer to something or someone located inside a place near the listener (or a place just mentioned). Common in questions like “Tem alguém aí dentro?” (“Is anyone in there?”). It can also be figurative, meaning something “inside you” (feelings, fire, etc.).
target_language_example: Tem alguém aí dentro?
native_language_example: Is anyone in there?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a place that is higher (upstairs, on the roof, on top of something) and relatively close to the listener. Often contrasts with aqui em cima (“up here”) and lá em cima (“up there/farther away”).
target_language_example: Espera aí em cima que eu já subo.
native_language_example: Wait up there; I’m coming up in a moment.

meaning: “There it is/there you are” (here it is; that’s it).
additional_notes: Used to point something/someone out when it appears or is found (“There he is!”), to hand something over (“Here you go.”), or as an exclamation meaning “That’s it!” / “Exactly!” Often followed by a noun/pronoun: “Aí está ele.”
target_language_example: —Você achou meu celular? —Aí está, em cima da mesa.
native_language_example: —Did you find my phone? —There it is, on the table.

meaning: 'does (someone) there have…?' / 'then/in that case there is/are…' / 'that one has…' (context-dependent)
additional_notes: "Aí" is very flexible in Brazilian Portuguese. With "tem", it can mean (1) "there" (location / addressing people): "Alguém aí tem…?" = "Does anyone there have…?"; (2) "in that case/then" (logical consequence): "Mas aí tem que…" = "But then you have to…"; or (3) referring to a person/thing like "that one": "Essa aí tem…" = "That one has…". In exclamations, "Aí tem coisa!" often means "Something’s going on / that’s suspicious."
target_language_example: Alguém aí tem carregador de celular?
native_language_example: Does anyone there have a phone charger?

additional_notes: Used for the formal dance tied to a school graduation (often high school). You’ll commonly see it with the verb "ir" (ir ao baile de formatura) and with "convidar" (convidar alguém para o baile de formatura).
target_language_example: Você já tem par para o baile de formatura?
native_language_example: Do you already have a date for prom?

meaning: a group/band/bunch of (often insulting: “you bunch of …”).
additional_notes: Means “a group of” in a neutral/descriptive way (often with criminals/animals/creatures), but it’s very commonly used to insult people directly: “bando de + insult” (“you bunch of idiots!”). In insults, it’s informal and aggressive.
target_language_example: O que vocês estão fazendo, bando de idiotas?
native_language_example: What are you doing, you bunch of idiots?

additional_notes: Used to describe a bar mainly aimed at gay people / the LGBTQ+ community. Gender agreement: "um bar gay" (a gay bar). It’s common and neutral in Portuguese; you’ll also see "bar LGBT" / "bar LGBTQIA+".
target_language_example: Vamos a um bar gay hoje à noite?
native_language_example: Shall we go to a gay bar tonight?

meaning: a lot of time; quite a while.
additional_notes: Means there is plenty of time available, or that something has lasted for a long time. Common with verbs like ter (to have time), passar (to spend time), and conhecer (to have known someone) + há: "há bastante tempo" = "for quite a while."
target_language_example: Ainda temos bastante tempo antes do voo.
native_language_example: We still have plenty of time before the flight.

additional_notes: Literally “fried potato.” Very often you’ll also see the plural “batatas fritas” when referring to a portion of fries, especially on menus. The phrase “a cavalo” is a common add-on meaning it comes topped with a fried egg (e.g., “batata frita a cavalo”).
target_language_example: Quero batata frita a cavalo.
native_language_example: I want French fries topped with a fried egg.

additional_notes: Literally “fried potatoes.” In Portugal, this usually means French fries; in the UK context it can also correspond to “chips” (as in “fish and chips”). Common when ordering food: “um hambúrguer com batatas fritas” (a burger with fries) or “um saco de batatas fritas” (a bag of chips/fries).
target_language_example: Para acompanhar, pode ser uma dose de batatas fritas?
native_language_example: As a side, can it be a portion of fries?

additional_notes: Used for the action of knocking (often repeatedly) to get someone’s attention so they open the door. Commonly appears with verbs like "começar a" (to start to) and "vir" (to come).
target_language_example: Antes de entrar, você precisa bater na porta.
native_language_example: Before coming in, you need to knock on the door.

additional_notes: Very informal and often considered crude. Most commonly used about a man (similar to “jerk off”), though it can be used more generally depending on context. Not appropriate in polite conversation; in more neutral language you can say “se masturbar”.
target_language_example: Ele disse que ia bater uma antes de dormir.
native_language_example: He said he was going to jerk off before going to sleep.

additional_notes: Used when someone knocks to be let in (often with "alguém" as the subject: "Alguém está batendo à porta"). It can also be used figuratively to mean something is about to happen: "A oportunidade está batendo à porta" (“Opportunity is knocking”).
target_language_example: Ouvi alguém bater à porta; você pode atender?
native_language_example: I heard someone knock at the door; can you answer it?

meaning: to have a drink (usually alcohol, often a beer).
additional_notes: Common in Brazil as an informal, friendly way to suggest going out for a drink. Literally "to drink one", but it usually implies an alcoholic drink and can mean just one drink or casually drinking together.
target_language_example: Depois do trabalho, vamos beber uma?
native_language_example: After work, shall we go have a drink?

additional_notes: Verb + object pronoun: "beijar" (to kiss) + "-la" (her) attached with a hyphen. The accent in "beijá-" shows the stress when the pronoun is attached (common with infinitives). You can use the same pattern with other pronouns: beijá-lo (kiss him), beijá-las (kiss them, feminine), beijá-los (kiss them, masculine/mixed).
target_language_example: Eu queria beijá-la, mas fiquei com vergonha.
native_language_example: I wanted to kiss her, but I felt shy.

additional_notes: Used as a noun or adjective to refer to the area right next to the ocean (the seafront). Common in place names and descriptions like “avenida beira-mar” (seafront avenue) or “hotel beira-mar” (seaside hotel). Literally means “edge of the sea.”
target_language_example: Vamos caminhar na beira-mar no fim da tarde.
native_language_example: Let’s take a walk along the seafront in the late afternoon.

additional_notes: Used when you accept something up to a point and then add a limitation, disagreement, or exception. Common patterns: "Estou bem, mas…" (I’m fine, but…), "Tudo bem, mas…" (Okay/Fair enough, but…). "Bem" can mean "well" (doing something well) or "fine/okay" (state/approval); the comma signals a pause before the contrast with "mas" (but).
target_language_example: Tudo bem, mas eu preciso ir agora.
native_language_example: Okay, but I need to go now.

additional_notes: A noun used to talk about how well someone feels physically and mentally, or their general quality of life (often in contexts like health, work, and lifestyle). Common in phrases like “bem-estar físico/mental” (physical/mental well-being) and “bem-estar social” (social well-being).
target_language_example: Exercício regular melhora o bem-estar.
native_language_example: Regular exercise improves well-being.

meaning: successful; doing well (having achieved good results).
additional_notes: An adjective meaning someone/something has had success. Often used with "ser" ("Ele é bem-sucedido") or with "em" to specify the area: "bem-sucedido em negócios" (successful in business). It agrees with the noun: bem-sucedido (masc. sing.), bem-sucedida (fem. sing.), bem-sucedidos/bem-sucedidas (plural).
target_language_example: Eu sei que posso ser bem-sucedido.
native_language_example: I know I can be successful.

meaning: 'welcome' (addressed to a woman); also 'welcome/very appreciated' (for help, money, etc.).
additional_notes: Feminine form of "bem-vindo". Use it to welcome a female guest/person ("Bem-vinda, Adèle!") or to say something would be appreciated: "Qualquer quantia será bem-vinda" (= any amount will be welcome). For a man, use "bem-vindo"; for a group or mixed group, "bem-vindos".
target_language_example: Sua sugestão será muito bem-vinda.
native_language_example: Your suggestion will be very welcome.

additional_notes: Used when greeting someone arriving/being introduced to a place, group, or situation. "Bem-vinda" is feminine; for a man, use "bem-vindo ao". "Ao" = "a" + "o" and is used before masculine singular nouns (ao clube, ao mundo); with feminine nouns you use "à" (bem-vinda à festa). Often said with an implied "Seja": (Seja) bem-vinda ao nosso restaurante!
target_language_example: Bem-vinda ao time!
native_language_example: Welcome to the team!

additional_notes: Used to welcome a female person to a place, country, event, or group. Agree it with the person: bem-vindo à (male), bem-vindos/as à (plural). It’s often followed by “à” because it commonly comes before a feminine noun (à = a + a), e.g., “à França”, “à nossa casa”. With masculine nouns, you’ll usually see “bem-vinda ao …” (ao = a + o), e.g., “Bem-vinda ao Brasil”.
target_language_example: Bem-vinda à minha cidade!
native_language_example: Welcome to my city!

additional_notes: Feminine plural of "bem-vinda". Used to greet a group of women/girls (or a mixed group when referring specifically to women) arriving somewhere: "Bem-vindas a/ao...". It can also mean "welcome" in the sense of "appreciated/accepted": "Sugestões serão bem-vindas" = "Suggestions are welcome." Common greeting: "Sejam bem-vindas!" = "Welcome!"
target_language_example: Bem-vindas ao nosso hotel!
native_language_example: Welcome to our hotel!

additional_notes: Used to greet someone arriving or being introduced: “Bem-vindo, Maria.” It agrees with the person: bem-vindo (male), bem-vinda (female), bem-vindos/bem-vindas (plural). In “Ele não é bem-vindo”, it means “he is not welcome” (not accepted). It can also describe something that would be appreciated: “Um abraço seria muito bem-vindo.” (= a hug would be very welcome).
target_language_example: Seja bem-vindo à nossa casa!
native_language_example: Welcome to our home!

meaning: "welcome to" (addressing a man or mixed group).
additional_notes: Used to welcome someone to a place, group, home, event, etc. It agrees with who you’re welcoming: use "bem-vinda à" for a woman, "bem-vindos ao" for a group of men/mixed, and "bem-vindas à" for a group of women. "Ao" = "a" + "o" (to the + masculine noun); with feminine nouns use "à" = "a" + "a" (to the + feminine noun): "Bem-vindo ao grupo" / "Bem-vinda à festa".
target_language_example: Bem-vindo ao nosso time!
native_language_example: Welcome to our team!

additional_notes: Used to greet someone arriving at a place, event, or situation. 'à' = 'a' + 'a' (to the, feminine singular), so it’s used before feminine nouns (à Austrália, à China, à Wikipédia, à máquina, à primeira aula). With masculine nouns, use 'bem-vindo ao' (ao Brasil). You can also use the more formal invitation 'Seja bem-vindo(a) à…'.
target_language_example: Bem-vindo à nossa casa!
native_language_example: Welcome to our house!

additional_notes: Used to greet someone arriving at a place or joining something. Agree it with the person: bem-vindo (male), bem-vinda (female), bem-vindos/bem-vindas (plural). Often followed by a city, country, organization, event, or home. You may also see “Bem-vindo(a)!” by itself.
target_language_example: Bem-vindo a São Francisco!
native_language_example: Welcome to San Francisco!

meaning: “welcome to” (addressing a man or a mixed/unspecified group).
additional_notes: Used to greet someone arriving or being introduced to a place, group, situation, or experience. It agrees with who you’re welcoming: bem-vinda (woman), bem-vindos (group of men/mixed), bem-vindas (group of women). Often appears with contractions: ao = a + o (“to the”, masculine singular), à = a + a (feminine singular), aos = a + os, às = a + as. Can also be used ironically or humorously depending on tone (e.g., “Bem-vindo ao inferno!”).
target_language_example: Bem-vindo ao clube.
native_language_example: Welcome to the club.

meaning: “Welcome” (to more than one person, or to a mixed group).
additional_notes: Adjective meaning “well-received.” It agrees with the people being welcomed: bem-vindo (one man), bem-vinda (one woman), bem-vindos (men/mixed group), bem-vindas (women). Often used alone as a greeting (“Bem-vindos!”) or in phrases like “Vocês são (muito) bem-vindos aqui” = “You’re (very) welcome here.” The negative “não ser bem-vindo” means “not to be welcome.”
target_language_example: Sejam bem-vindos à nossa casa!
native_language_example: Welcome to our home!

meaning: “welcome to” (addressing a group; masculine or mixed group).
additional_notes: Used to greet people arriving/starting something. It’s the plural form of "bem-vindo" + "a" + "o" (ao = "to the" for masculine singular nouns). For an all-female group, use "bem-vindas à" (à = "to the" for feminine singular nouns).
target_language_example: Pessoal, bem-vindos ao nosso curso de português!
native_language_example: Guys, welcome to our Portuguese course!

additional_notes: Used to greet people arriving at a place, group, or situation. "Bem-vindos" is plural (mixed group or all men). For all women, say "Bem-vindas". For one person, use "bem-vindo" (man) / "bem-vinda" (woman). Use "à" before feminine singular nouns (a + a), e.g., "à cidade", "à família"; use "ao" before masculine singular nouns (a + o), e.g., "ao Brasil".
target_language_example: Bem-vindos à nossa empresa!
native_language_example: Welcome to our company!

additional_notes: Used to add another item in a list or to connect two related phrases, similar to “as well as” in English. It’s common in more formal speech and especially in writing. It can usually be replaced by “e também” in everyday conversation.
target_language_example: Precisamos comprar pão, leite, bem como frutas para o jantar.
native_language_example: We need to buy bread, milk, as well as fruit for dinner.

additional_notes: Can be sincere praise (“Bem feito, mestre!” / “Muito bem feito.”) meaning something was done well. It can also be said on its own or with “para você” as a sarcastic/commenting phrase meaning “you deserved that” (“Morreu, bem feito.” / “Isso é bem feito para você.”). Tone depends heavily on context.
target_language_example: Você perdeu o ônibus? Bem feito por ter saído tão tarde.
native_language_example: You missed the bus? Serves you right for leaving so late.

meaning: the greater good; a higher/most important good.
additional_notes: Often used to talk about something considered more important than personal interests (commonly in the phrase “pelo bem maior” = “for the greater good”). It can also mean someone’s most valuable “asset,” especially in expressions like “A saúde é o nosso bem maior” (“Health is our greatest good/asset”).
target_language_example: A saúde é o nosso bem maior.
native_language_example: Health is our greatest asset.

additional_notes: This combination is uncommon in modern everyday Portuguese. When it appears, it’s typically in more formal or older-style writing as a comparison, similar to **tanto quanto** (“as much as / as … as”). In conversation, you’ll almost always hear **tanto quanto** instead.
target_language_example: Eu te respeito bem quanto a qualquer outra pessoa aqui.
native_language_example: I respect you as much as anyone else here.

additional_notes: Used before a verb to add emphasis, often with a tone like “I really did / I sure do,” sometimes implying “I told you so” or “you can’t say I didn’t warn you” (e.g., “Eu bem que te avisei.”). It can also emphasize a possibility or wish (“Eu bem que poderia…” = “I really could…” / “I sure could…”), and in reactions it can sound like “yeah, you wish!” (“Você bem que gostaria!”).
target_language_example: Eu bem que tentei te ligar ontem, mas você não atendeu.
native_language_example: I really did try to call you yesterday, but you didn’t answer.

meaning: "Well, then…" / "Well, so…" (used to move the conversation forward or draw a conclusion).
additional_notes: A common spoken/discourse phrase. You can use it to: (1) react and conclude from what was said (“Well then, I must have imagined it”), (2) give the next instruction (“Well then, don’t move”), (3) suggest starting/continuing (“Well then, let’s go”). On its own (“Bem, então?”) it can mean “Well, then?” / “So?” to prompt someone to continue or to ask what happens next.
target_language_example: Bem, então vamos embora.
native_language_example: Well then, let’s leave.

meaning: “Well, I’m…” / “Okay, I’m…” (used to start a reply).
additional_notes: "Bem," is a common conversational filler meaning “well/so/okay,” often used to introduce what you’re about to say. "Estou" means “I am” (or “I’m,” sometimes “I’m doing”). It’s typically followed by a place, a feeling/state, or what you’re doing: "Bem, estou indo" (“Well, I’m going/leaving”), "Bem, estou preocupada" (“Well, I’m worried”).
target_language_example: Bem, estou com um pouco de pressa.
native_language_example: Well, I’m in a bit of a hurry.

meaning: 'Well, I...' (used to start a reply, often to give your opinion or explain yourself).
additional_notes: Common conversational opener. "Bem" works like English "well" to pause, soften what you’re about to say, or signal you’re thinking; then "eu" introduces what *you* think/know/do. Often followed by a statement: "Bem, eu acho..." (Well, I think...), "Bem, eu não sei..." (Well, I don’t know...).
target_language_example: Bem, eu acho melhor irmos agora.
native_language_example: Well, I think it’s better if we go now.

additional_notes: Used as a discourse marker before disagreeing, correcting someone, or backing off what was just said. "Bem" here is like English "well" to soften the response; "não" can also be repeated at the end of the sentence in Portuguese for emphasis (e.g., "..., não?").
target_language_example: Bem, não. Acho melhor a gente ir amanhã.
native_language_example: Well, no. I think it’s better if we go tomorrow.

meaning: “Well, what…?” (used to start a question or response).
additional_notes: A common conversational opener. It often signals you’re about to ask a question (“Well, what do you want?”) or react to what someone said (“Well, whatever you say.”). You’ll also see it without a comma in writing: “Bem, o que você quer?”
target_language_example: Bem, o que você vai fazer agora?
native_language_example: Well, what are you going to do now?

meaning: “Well, maybe/perhaps…” (hesitating or softening what you say).
additional_notes: Used as a conversational opener to show you’re thinking, unsure, or giving a tentative answer/suggestion. Often followed by a comma: “Bem, talvez…”. You can also hear it without a pause (“Bem talvez…”), but the meaning is the same: it introduces a possibility rather than a certainty.
target_language_example: Bem, talvez eu possa tentar amanhã.
native_language_example: Well, maybe I can try tomorrow.

meaning: "Well, you..." (used to react, introduce a point, or push back in conversation).
additional_notes: Common spoken setup at the start of a sentence, often when responding to someone or shifting to a new point. It can sound hesitant (“Well, you see...”) or slightly confrontational (“Well, you did...”), depending on tone and context. Usually followed by a statement or question directed at the other person.
target_language_example: Bem, você sabe que isso não vai funcionar.
native_language_example: Well, you know this isn’t going to work.

additional_notes: Common, friendly/colloquial way to say someone (or a group) is nice, decent, and pleasant. Often used with "ser": "Ele/ela é boa gente" = "He/She is a nice person." Although it contains feminine "boa", the expression is typically used the same way regardless of the person’s gender, and it can refer to one person or to people in general depending on context.
target_language_example: O João é boa gente, sempre ajuda quando alguém precisa.
native_language_example: João is a nice person; he always helps when someone needs it.

additional_notes: Used as a greeting in the evening and as a way to say good night when leaving or before going to sleep. It can also describe an evening/night: "Foi uma boa noite" = "It was a good night."
target_language_example: Boa noite! Até amanhã.
native_language_example: Good night! See you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or ask for positive information (often after bad news). Common patterns: “Tenho uma boa notícia” (I have good news), “Você tem alguma boa notícia?” (Do you have any good news?), “A boa notícia é que...” (The good news is that...). Note: “Nenhuma notícia é uma boa notícia” is a set saying meaning “no news is good news.”
target_language_example: Tenho uma boa notícia: conseguimos resolver o problema.
native_language_example: I have good news: we managed to solve the problem.

additional_notes: Used to acknowledge that a question is valid or interesting, often when you don’t know the answer yet or need to think. It can be said alone (“Boa pergunta.”) or with a verb (“Essa/Esta é uma boa pergunta.”).
target_language_example: Boa pergunta — deixa eu pensar um pouco.
native_language_example: Good question—let me think for a moment.

additional_notes: Used to wish someone luck before an exam, trip, interview, competition, etc. Often said on its own ("Boa sorte!") or with "para" ("Boa sorte para você!"). With verbs like "desejar" (to wish), it appears as "desejar boa sorte (a alguém)" or with an object pronoun: "Desejo-lhe boa sorte."
target_language_example: Boa sorte na prova amanhã!
native_language_example: Good luck on the test tomorrow!

meaning: 'Good afternoon' (a polite greeting used in the afternoon).
additional_notes: Used as a greeting from around midday until early evening. Often said on its own or followed by the person’s name or a polite form of address (e.g., "Boa tarde, senhora"). It can also start a conversation: "Boa tarde, como vai?"
target_language_example: Boa tarde, tudo bem?
native_language_example: Good afternoon, how are you?

additional_notes: Used to wish someone well before they travel. It can also be used when asking how the trip went: "Fez boa viagem?" = "Did you have a good trip?". Often said with "Até logo" (see you soon) or with "de volta" to mean “have a good trip back.”
target_language_example: Boa viagem! Manda mensagem quando chegar.
native_language_example: Have a good trip! Text me when you arrive.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a friendly, helpful attitude (“goodwill”) or someone being ready/able to do something (“willingness”). Common in phrases like “ter boa vontade” (to be willing / to show goodwill) and “com boa vontade” (with goodwill / if you’re willing).
target_language_example: Obrigado pela sua boa vontade em me ajudar.
native_language_example: Thank you for your willingness to help me.

additional_notes: Used to greet someone who has arrived or is joining a group/event. Common in set phrases like “Boas-vindas a/ao/à…” (“Welcome to…”) and “Dar boas-vindas (a alguém)” (“to welcome (someone)”). Often appears in plural and with a hyphen.
target_language_example: Sejam todos bem-vindos e recebam as nossas boas-vindas!
native_language_example: Everyone is welcome—please accept our warm welcome!

additional_notes: Used to announce or ask about something positive. Very common with verbs like ter (tenho/temos/tens boas notícias) and with the preposition com (ficar feliz com as boas notícias = to be happy about the good news). Often appears with the definite article: as boas notícias (“the good news”).
target_language_example: Tenho boas notícias: o seu pedido foi aprovado.
native_language_example: I have good news: your request was approved.

additional_notes: Used when someone is unfairly or conveniently blamed so others avoid responsibility. Very common in politics, workplaces, and conflicts. Typically appears with verbs like "ser" (to be) and "precisar de" (to need): "Ele é o bode expiatório" / "Precisam de um bode expiatório".
target_language_example: Não coloquem a culpa nela — ela não é o bode expiatório.
native_language_example: Don’t blame her—she’s not the scapegoat.

additional_notes: Literally “golf ball” (a ball used in the sport of golf). Often used with the indefinite article: "uma bola de golfe" (“a golf ball”). In passive/accident contexts you may see "ser atingido por uma bola de golfe" (“to be hit by a golf ball”).
target_language_example: Cuidado: você pode ser atingido por uma bola de golfe.
native_language_example: Careful: you could be hit by a golf ball.

additional_notes: Used for the cake made for a birthday celebration, often with candles on top. You can say "meu/minha" before it (e.g., "meu bolo de aniversário") to mean "my birthday cake."
target_language_example: Vamos comprar um bolo de aniversário para ela.
native_language_example: Let’s buy a birthday cake for her.

additional_notes: Used for money or funding awarded to a student to pay for studies (tuition, living costs, etc.), often based on merit or need. Common with verbs like conseguir/ganhar (to get/win) and with destinations: “uma bolsa de estudos na Alemanha” (a scholarship to study in Germany).
target_language_example: Ela conseguiu uma bolsa de estudos para fazer mestrado em Portugal.
native_language_example: She got a scholarship to do a master’s degree in Portugal.

meaning: “Enjoy your meal!” / “Bon appétit!”; also “a good appetite.”
additional_notes: Used as a fixed phrase said before eating to wish someone an enjoyable meal: Bom apetite! It can also be used more literally with verbs like ter/estar com to mean “(to have) a good appetite” (e.g., Ele tem um bom apetite; A caminhada deixou-o com bom apetite).
target_language_example: O jantar está pronto — bom apetite!
native_language_example: Dinner is ready — enjoy your meal!

additional_notes: Most commonly used as a greeting meaning “good morning,” often said from early morning until around noon (e.g., in person or when answering the phone: “... bom dia!”). With an article, it can also literally mean “a good day” (e.g., “Ontem foi um bom dia.” = “Yesterday was a good day.”).
target_language_example: Bom dia! Tudo bem?
native_language_example: Good morning! How are you?

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s ability/skill in a subject. Pattern: (ser) bom/boa em + [subject]. It agrees with the person: bom (male), boa (female). You can intensify it with muito (“very”): muito bom/boa em matemática.
target_language_example: Eu sou bom em matemática.
native_language_example: I’m good at math.

additional_notes: Used to talk about practical, reasonable thinking (often contrasted with emotion or impulse). Common in advice or warnings: "Tenha bom senso" = "Use common sense." Also in phrases like "ter bom senso" (to have common sense).
target_language_example: Antes de decidir, tenha bom senso e pense nas consequências.
native_language_example: Before you decide, use common sense and think about the consequences.

additional_notes: A common greeting when you meet someone (“Bom te ver, Tom.”). In the past it becomes a goodbye-style phrase: “Foi bom te ver” = “It was nice seeing you.” You can intensify it with “muito” and add “de novo” for “again”: “Foi muito bom te ver de novo.”
target_language_example: Bom te ver de novo!
native_language_example: Nice to see you again!

additional_notes: Often used as a compliment after someone does something well: "Bom trabalho!" You can also use it literally to describe employment or work quality: "um bom trabalho" (a good job), "por seu bom trabalho" (for his/her good work).
target_language_example: Bom trabalho! Você resolveu o problema bem rápido.
native_language_example: Good job! You solved the problem really quickly.

additional_notes: A serious, formal term used in historical, political, or military contexts. Often appears with the article ("uma/a bomba atômica") and verbs like "usar" (to use), "utilizar" (to utilize), and "ser destruído por" (to be destroyed by). In everyday conversation, people may also say "bomba nuclear".
target_language_example: Nunca deveríamos usar uma bomba atômica de novo.
native_language_example: We should never use an atomic bomb again.

additional_notes: Used for a snow figure made from snow (usually a body and head). Very common with the verb "fazer" (to make): "fazer um boneco de neve" = "to make a snowman". Plural: "bonecos de neve".
target_language_example: As crianças fizeram um boneco de neve no jardim.
native_language_example: The kids made a snowman in the yard.

meaning: angry with me; mad at me.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" or "ficar" (to be / to get) to say someone is angry at you: "Ele está bravo comigo" (He’s mad at me) or "Ele ficou bravo comigo" (He got mad at me). "Bravo" can also mean “fierce” (e.g., an animal), but in everyday conversation it often means “angry.”
target_language_example: Desculpa — eu não queria te deixar bravo comigo.
native_language_example: Sorry — I didn’t mean to make you mad at me.

additional_notes: Most commonly it means the physical right arm (often with body/health or movement verbs like quebrar, levantar, mostrar). It can also be used figuratively to mean someone’s most trusted helper: “Ele é meu braço direito” = “He’s my right-hand man/person.”
target_language_example: A Júlia é meu braço direito no trabalho.
native_language_example: Júlia is my right-hand person at work.

additional_notes: Often means “to play with” (especially with kids, pets, toys, games). In more serious contexts, it can mean “to joke about” or “make light of” something (sometimes implying it’s not appropriate). Don’t confuse with “brincar de” (“to play at / pretend to be”).
target_language_example: As crianças adoram brincar com o Tom.
native_language_example: The kids love to play with Tom.

meaning: to play with fire; to take a dangerous risk.
additional_notes: Often used literally (being careless with real fire) or figuratively to warn that someone is doing something risky that could have bad consequences. Common pattern: “É (como) brincar com fogo” / “Você está brincando com fogo”.
target_language_example: Mentir para ela de novo é brincar com fogo.
native_language_example: Lying to her again is playing with fire.

additional_notes: Used literally in science/space contexts to mean a region in space with extremely strong gravity from which not even light can escape. It’s a common noun phrase: "um buraco negro" (a black hole), "o buraco negro" (the black hole).
target_language_example: Os cientistas observaram um buraco negro no centro da galáxia.
native_language_example: Scientists observed a black hole at the center of the galaxy.

meaning: to pick him/it up; to go get him/it.
additional_notes: From "buscar" (to get/pick up) + the object pronoun "-lo" (him/it). The accent (buscá-) appears because in Brazilian Portuguese the final -r of the infinitive is dropped before attaching the pronoun: "buscar + o" → "buscá-lo". Very common with verbs of movement: "ir buscá-lo" (go pick him/it up), "vir buscá-lo" (come pick him/it up), often for picking someone up at places like a station or airport. "-lo" can refer to a male person (him) or to a thing (it), depending on context.
target_language_example: Posso passar às oito para buscá-lo no trabalho?
native_language_example: Can I stop by at eight to pick him up at work?

additional_notes: Common name for the food item (a sausage in a bun, often with toppings). It’s masculine: “um/ o cachorro-quente”; plural “cachorros-quentes”. Even though it literally looks like “hot dog,” it refers to the sandwich/food, not an actual dog.
target_language_example: Vamos comer um cachorro-quente depois do jogo.
native_language_example: Let’s eat a hot dog after the game.

meaning: "each day" / "every day" (also: "more and more" in comparisons).
additional_notes: Literal meaning is “each day.” It can mean (1) “every day” in general statements (Cada dia conta. = Every day counts.), and (2) “more and more / increasingly” when used with comparatives like melhor/pior/maior (A situação fica cada dia pior. = The situation gets worse and worse.).
target_language_example: Estou me sentindo cada dia melhor.
native_language_example: I’m feeling better and better every day.

additional_notes: Used to talk about individuals in a group one by one: “Cada um tem a sua opinião.” It’s often followed by “de +” (cada um de nós = each of us). For females, you can also say “cada uma”.
target_language_example: Cada um faz a sua parte.
native_language_example: Each person does their part.

additional_notes: Used to talk about individual people within the group that includes the speaker (“nós” = “we/us”). Common in statements of responsibility, ability, or giving something to everyone in the group (one per person). You can change “nós” to another pronoun: “cada um de vocês” (each of you), “cada um deles” (each of them).
target_language_example: Cada um de nós tem um papel importante neste projeto.
native_language_example: Each of us has an important role in this project.

additional_notes: Used to refer to each individual item/person in a feminine group, often with: **cada uma de + plural noun** ("each of the...") or **cada uma delas** ("each of them"). It agrees in gender: **cada um** (masc.) / **cada uma** (fem.). Common in instructions and descriptions: "Descreva cada uma...". Informal spoken Portuguese also uses the exclamation **"É cada uma!"** meaning something like "Unbelievable!/What a thing!" (varies by context).
target_language_example: Quero ver cada uma delas antes de escolher.
native_language_example: I want to see each one of them before choosing.

meaning: each time; increasingly (in patterns like “cada vez mais/menos/pior”).
additional_notes: Used in comparisons to show a change that keeps progressing: “cada vez mais” (more and more), “cada vez menos” (less and less), “cada vez pior/melhor” (worse and worse / better and better). It also appears in time expressions like “cada vez que…” (“every time that…”) and in “um pouco de cada vez” (“a little at a time”).
target_language_example: A cidade está cada vez mais cara.
native_language_example: The city is getting more and more expensive.

additional_notes: Used to show a gradual increase or intensification over time. It often modifies an adjective/adverb ("cada vez mais popular", "cada vez mais sem esperança") or a whole situation (becoming increasingly withdrawn).
target_language_example: Estou cada vez mais cansado ultimamente.
native_language_example: I’ve been getting more and more tired lately.

additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about accessibility (“acesso para cadeira de rodas?”) or to say someone uses a wheelchair (“usar cadeira de rodas”). You may also hear “numa cadeira de rodas” (“in a wheelchair”).
target_language_example: Este edifício tem entrada acessível para cadeira de rodas.
native_language_example: This building has a wheelchair-accessible entrance.

meaning: “Where is the…?” (asking where a specific feminine person/thing is).
additional_notes: “Cadê” is a very common, informal way to say “onde está…?” or “onde está a…?”. Use “cadê a” before feminine nouns (a mochila, a mulher, a licença). For masculine nouns, you’ll hear “cadê o…?”.
target_language_example: Cadê a chave do carro?
native_language_example: Where’s the car key?

additional_notes: Common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese to ask where something/someone is. Used with a masculine singular noun because of “o” (= “the”). For feminine/plural: “cadê a…?”, “cadê os…?”, “cadê as…?”. “Cadê?” can also be used alone when the missing thing is clear from context.
target_language_example: Cadê o meu celular?
native_language_example: Where’s my phone?

additional_notes: “Cadê” is a very common, informal way to ask where someone/something is (roughly “where is/are…?”). You can use it by itself (“Cadê você?”) or with a name (“João, cadê você?”). In more formal speech, you might say “Onde você está?” instead.
target_language_example: Ei, cadê você? Estou te esperando na entrada.
native_language_example: Hey, where are you? I’m waiting for you at the entrance.

additional_notes: Common, polite phrase when ordering at a café/restaurant or asking someone to serve/make coffee. You can add details after it, like "com creme e açúcar" (with cream and sugar) or use "Um café, por favor" (a coffee, please) and "Mais café, por favor" (more coffee, please).
target_language_example: Um café, por favor, sem açúcar.
native_language_example: A coffee, please, without sugar.

additional_notes: A very common drink order. You can use it after verbs like beber/tomar (“to drink/have”) or by itself when ordering: “Quero café com leite.” In Brazil, it usually means coffee mixed with milk (more like “café au lait” than a latte).
target_language_example: Para mim, um café com leite, por favor.
native_language_example: For me, a coffee with milk, please.

additional_notes: The standard way to say “breakfast” in Brazilian Portuguese. Often used with verbs like “tomar” (to have/eat/drink): “tomar café da manhã” = “to have breakfast.” You can also say “fazer café da manhã” when you prepare/make breakfast.
target_language_example: Eu tomo café da manhã às oito todos os dias.
native_language_example: I have breakfast at eight every day.

additional_notes: Very common in Brazilian Portuguese as an informal (often rude/forceful) way to tell someone to go away or leave a place. It comes from the verb phrase “cair fora” (“to leave/get out”), and “cai fora” is the command form used with “você” (even if “você” isn’t said). You can add places with “daqui” (from here) or “de + lugar” (out of/from a place): “Cai fora daqui!”, “Cai fora do meu quarto!”.
target_language_example: Cai fora do meu quarto agora!
native_language_example: Get out of my room now!

meaning: to leave / get out (often: to bail, quickly).
additional_notes: Common, informal way to say you should leave a place or situation, often because it’s uncomfortable, unsafe, or you just don’t want to stay. Frequently used with a location: “cair fora daqui” (get out of here), “cair fora deste lugar” (get out of this place). Can be used as advice or a suggestion: “Tem que cair fora.” / “Vamos cair fora.”
target_language_example: Eu preciso cair fora daqui agora.
native_language_example: I need to get out of here now.

additional_notes: Used for the moment you drift off to sleep (often unintentionally). Very common with "não" (não cair no sono = not fall asleep) and after "até" (até cair no sono = until you fall asleep).
target_language_example: Eu estava tão cansado que acabei por cair no sono no sofá.
native_language_example: I was so tired that I ended up falling asleep on the couch.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of cair: caiu = “fell.” Used for people or objects that drop/fall down. “No chão” means “on the ground/on the floor” (chão = ground/floor). You can change the subject: “Eu caí no chão” = “I fell on the ground.”
target_language_example: O copo caiu no chão e quebrou.
native_language_example: The glass fell on the floor and broke.

additional_notes: Literally “box of sand.” Used for a children’s sandpit (play area) or, very commonly, for a cat’s litter box (“caixa de areia do gato”). With pets you’ll often hear verbs like limpar (to clean) and esvaziar (to empty).
target_language_example: Preciso limpar a caixa de areia do gato hoje.
native_language_example: I need to clean the cat’s litter box today.

additional_notes: Used for the box where letters are delivered (at a house/building) or collected for sending. Very common with verbs like verificar (to check), esvaziar (to empty), and abrir/estar aberta (to open/be open). Also used in expressions like "não vai chegar mais nenhuma carta" (no more letters will arrive) referring to that mailbox/address.
target_language_example: Vou verificar a caixa de correio depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: I’m going to check the mailbox after work.

additional_notes: Used for the place where incoming messages arrive in an email app, messaging app, or social media. Often appears with verbs like "abrir" (open), "acessar" (access), and "estar cheia" (be full).
target_language_example: Vou limpar minha caixa de entrada hoje.
native_language_example: I’m going to clean out my inbox today.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the machine you use to withdraw cash, check your balance, etc. In Brazil, people often just say "caixa" when the context is clear, and you may also hear "terminal". Common collocations: "ir ao caixa eletrônico" (go to the ATM), "sacar dinheiro" (withdraw cash), "o caixa eletrônico engoliu o cartão" (the ATM kept/swallowed the card).
target_language_example: Preciso sacar dinheiro; tem um caixa eletrônico perto daqui?
native_language_example: I need to withdraw cash; is there an ATM near here?

additional_notes: A very rude/hostile way to tell someone to be quiet. Common in arguments and can sound aggressive; avoid in polite situations. You may also hear it as an order to one person ("Cala a boca!") or to a group ("Calem a boca!").
target_language_example: Cala a boca e me escuta por um minuto.
native_language_example: Shut up and listen to me for a minute.

meaning: to shut up; to be quiet (often as a command).
additional_notes: Commonly used in orders, arguments, or threats telling someone to stop talking. It’s rude/harsh in most situations; softer alternatives include “fica quieto(a)” or “pode falar mais baixo?”. Conjugates like a normal verb phrase: “cala a boca!” (you—informal), “calem a boca!” (you all), “cale a boca!” (formal), “calar a boca” (infinitive).
target_language_example: Dá pra calar a boca, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you shut up, please?

additional_notes: Imperative + reflexive pronoun from "calar-se" (to be quiet). Used as a direct order; often rude/hostile, especially with insults or vocatives after it (e.g., "Cale-se, ..."). A more polite alternative is "Por favor, fique em silêncio" or "Pode falar mais baixo?".
target_language_example: Cale-se e me deixe falar.
native_language_example: Shut up and let me speak.

additional_notes: A very direct command; often rude/hostile depending on tone and context. Literally "shut/close the mouth" (from the verb *calar*). Used to tell someone to stop talking; in polite situations prefer *"por favor, fique quieto(a)"* or *"pode falar mais baixo?"*.
target_language_example: Cale a boca e me escute por um minuto.
native_language_example: Shut up and listen to me for a minute.

additional_notes: Very common informal expression used to stop someone, slow things down, or ask for a moment. Often said at the start of a sentence when you disagree, need clarification, or think the other person is going too fast or doing something extreme. The tone can range from friendly to annoyed depending on context.
target_language_example: Calma aí — deixa eu entender o que aconteceu.
native_language_example: Hold on—let me understand what happened.

additional_notes: A common clothing item. Often appears with formal wear, especially in the phrase “camisa branca e gravata” (“white shirt and tie”). In Portuguese, colors usually agree in gender/number with the noun: camisa branca (feminine singular), camisas brancas (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Vou usar uma camisa branca para a reunião.
native_language_example: I’m going to wear a white shirt to the meeting.

additional_notes: Refers to a colorful, usually short-sleeved, tropical-pattern shirt. In speech you may hear it used to identify someone by what they’re wearing: “o da camisa havaiana” = “the guy in the Hawaiian shirt.”
target_language_example: O cara da camisa havaiana está ali no bar.
native_language_example: The guy in the Hawaiian shirt is over there at the bar.

additional_notes: Means the place/area where people play golf. "Campo" = field/grounds; "de golfe" specifies the sport. Often used with articles and possessives: "um/este/o/meu/seu campo de golfe".
target_language_example: Vamos jogar amanhã no campo de golfe?
native_language_example: Shall we play tomorrow at the golf course?

meaning: A minefield; a situation full of hidden dangers or sensitive issues.
additional_notes: Literal meaning: an area with land mines. Very commonly used figuratively to mean a tricky or risky situation where one wrong move can cause serious problems (e.g., a difficult conversation, politics at work). Often used as a warning: “É um campo minado!”
target_language_example: Falar de dinheiro com eles é um campo minado.
native_language_example: Talking about money with them is a minefield.

additional_notes: Used for a pen that writes with a small ball at the tip (as opposed to a pencil or fountain pen). Often shortened in everyday speech to just "caneta" when the type doesn’t matter. You’ll commonly see it with colors: "caneta esferográfica azul/vermelha/preta".
target_language_example: Você tem uma caneta esferográfica azul para eu assinar?
native_language_example: Do you have a blue ballpoint pen for me to sign?

additional_notes: Refers to a piece of outerwear worn to protect you from rain. Often used with verbs like vestir/estar vestindo (to wear), colocar (to put on), and tirar (to take off).
target_language_example: Leve uma capa de chuva porque vai chover.
native_language_example: Bring a raincoat because it's going to rain.

additional_notes: Often used with the verb ser: ser capaz de + infinitive ("to be able to / capable of doing something"). It can describe ability/skill, or whether someone has the courage/nerve to do something. Also common in phrases like "capaz de tudo" = "capable of anything".
target_language_example: Você é capaz de resolver isso sozinho?
native_language_example: Are you able to solve this on your own?

additional_notes: Used to express ability, capacity, or possibility, typically with forms of the verb "ser": "(ser) capazes de" + infinitive. Often plural to agree with a plural subject (e.g., "Eles são capazes de..."). The negative form ("não ser capazes de") means “not able to / unable to.” In some contexts it can imply extreme behavior or willingness (e.g., "capazes de tudo" = “capable of anything / will do anything”).
target_language_example: Esses soldados são capazes de lutar e apreciar música.
native_language_example: Those soldiers are able to fight and appreciate music.

additional_notes: Used to say two people are physically facing each other, or that something is said/done directly in person (not by phone, message, etc.). Often follows verbs like "falar" (to speak), "dizer" (to say), "encontrar" (to meet), and "sentar" (to sit).
target_language_example: Prefiro conversar cara a cara.
native_language_example: I prefer to talk face to face.

additional_notes: Used to specify the type of meat ("carne") you’re talking about. In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people more often say "carne bovina" (more formal/technical) or simply "carne" when the context already makes it clear it’s beef. You can use it in preferences and questions: "gostar de" (to like) and "preferir X a Y" (to prefer X to Y).
target_language_example: No churrasco, vamos comprar carne de boi e frango.
native_language_example: For the barbecue, we’re going to buy beef and chicken.

additional_notes: Used to talk about pork as a type of meat/food. Often appears in menu or shopping contexts. You can also say simply "porco" for "pig" (the animal), but "carne de porco" is specifically the meat.
target_language_example: Hoje vou cozinhar carne de porco com batatas.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to cook pork with potatoes.

additional_notes: A noun phrase meaning a sporty, high-performance car. It’s typically used with the indefinite article (um/uma) and can be modified by color or other adjectives: “um carro esportivo vermelho”.
target_language_example: Eu nunca dirigi um carro esportivo.
native_language_example: I’ve never driven a sports car.

meaning: a new car (a car that is brand-new or recently bought).
additional_notes: "Carro" means "car" and "novo" means "new"; the adjective usually comes after the noun in Portuguese ("carro novo"). It can mean either brand-new (never used) or simply newly purchased, depending on context.
target_language_example: Eles chegaram no trabalho com um carro novo.
native_language_example: They arrived at work in a new car.

additional_notes: Used for a letter (often romantic) written to someone you love. Also used more broadly for a very affectionate written message. Plural: "cartas de amor".
target_language_example: Ele escreveu uma carta de amor para ela.
native_language_example: He wrote a love letter to her.

additional_notes: Used for the official document/card that gives you permission to drive. You’ll often see it with verbs like "mostrar" (to show) and "obter" (to get), or in phrases like "sem carteira de motorista" (without a driver’s license).
target_language_example: Esqueci minha carteira de motorista em casa.
native_language_example: I forgot my driver’s license at home.

additional_notes: A noun for a picture card you write a short message on and send by mail, often from a trip. Common with verbs like mandar/enviar (to send) and with de/da to say where it’s from: "um cartão-postal da Austrália" (a postcard from Australia).
target_language_example: Comprei um cartão-postal e vou mandar para minha família.
native_language_example: I bought a postcard and I’m going to send it to my family.

additional_notes: Used for paying by card and talking about credit limits. Often appears with verbs like "aceitar" (to accept): "Você aceita cartão de crédito?" and "ter" (to have): "Você tem um cartão de crédito?". In sentence 2, "Passei a mão no..." means "I stole/ grabbed" (informal), not a normal way to talk about using a card.
target_language_example: Posso pagar com cartão de crédito?
native_language_example: Can I pay with a credit card?

additional_notes: A card you write a short message on and send by mail. With verbs like "enviar" (to send), "mandar" (to send), and "entregar" (to hand/deliver): "enviar/mandar um cartão postal". You can also add the place it’s from with "de": "um cartão postal de Boston".
target_language_example: Comprei um cartão postal para mandar para minha família.
native_language_example: I bought a postcard to send to my family.

additional_notes: Common in European Portuguese for the room with a toilet (and often a shower/bath). Used after verbs like ir à casa de banho (“to go to the bathroom”). In Brazil, people more often say banheiro.
target_language_example: Desculpe, onde fica a casa de banho?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the bathroom?

additional_notes: A house in a rural area, often used as a weekend/holiday place (a “second home”). It can range from a simple cottage to a larger property. Not necessarily a working farm, but it may be near gardens/land.
target_language_example: No feriado, vamos passar alguns dias na nossa casa de campo.
native_language_example: On the holiday, we’re going to spend a few days at our country house.

meaning: nursing home; retirement home (a place where elderly people live and receive care).
additional_notes: Commonly refers to a residential facility for older adults, often with medical or daily-living assistance. In Brazil it can also be called "asilo" (can sound old-fashioned/negative) or "instituição de longa permanência para idosos (ILPI)" (formal). Usually used with "em/numa": "Ele está em uma casa de repouso."
target_language_example: Minha avó mora em uma casa de repouso perto do hospital.
native_language_example: My grandmother lives in a nursing home near the hospital.

additional_notes: Reflexive verb: casar-se (to get married) + com (with/to). You can also hear the non-reflexive form casar com, especially in casual speech, but casar-se com is common in writing and careful speech. The pronoun agrees with the subject: eu caso-me com…, ele/ela casa-se com…, nós casamo-nos com… (often simplified in Brazilian Portuguese to eu me caso com…, ele/ela se casa com…, a gente se casa com…).
target_language_example: Você quer casar-se com ela algum dia?
native_language_example: Do you want to marry her someday?

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "com" to say who someone marries: "casar com alguém" = "to marry someone". Very commonly used in the reflexive form "se casar com" (especially meaning "to get married to"): "Ela vai se casar com o João." In the examples, "casar com ele" = "marry him".
target_language_example: Ela não quer se casar com ele.
native_language_example: She doesn’t want to marry him.

additional_notes: Used when talking about marriage with the speaker as the partner. Very common in proposals and relationship talk: “Quer casar comigo?” = “Do you want to marry me?” / “Will you marry me?” The verb is “casar” (to marry), and “comigo” means “with me” (com + mim). It can appear in different tenses: “vai se casar comigo” (are you going to marry me?), “querendo casar comigo” (wanting to marry me).
target_language_example: Você quer casar comigo um dia?
native_language_example: Do you want to marry me someday?

meaning: a doghouse (small house/shelter for a dog).
additional_notes: "Casinha" is the diminutive of "casa" (house), so it often sounds like “little house” and can feel cute/affectionate. Commonly used with "construir" (to build) or "fazer" (to make): "construir/fazer uma casinha de cachorro".
target_language_example: Vamos comprar uma casinha de cachorro para o nosso cão.
native_language_example: Let’s buy a doghouse for our dog.

additional_notes: Used to warn about a consequence or to say what will happen if a condition is not met. Often follows an instruction or condition: "Faça X; caso contrário, Y." It’s close in meaning to "senão" in many contexts.
target_language_example: Leve um guarda-chuva; caso contrário, você vai se molhar.
native_language_example: Take an umbrella; otherwise, you’ll get wet.

additional_notes: Used to warn about what will happen if a condition isn’t met or if you do the opposite of what was said. Often comes at the start of a sentence followed by a comma: “Caso contrário, …”. You can think of it as “if not / in the opposite case”.
target_language_example: Temos que sair agora; caso contrário, vamos perder o ônibus.
native_language_example: We have to leave now; otherwise, we’ll miss the bus.

additional_notes: Simple past (pretérito perfeito) of **casar com** = “to marry (someone)”. Used to say who a person married. The preposition **com** (“with”) is required: **casou com ele/ela**, **casou com o João**. In questions, it often means “Did (he/she) marry …?”
target_language_example: Ela casou com o namorado da faculdade.
native_language_example: She married her college boyfriend.

additional_notes: Literally “castle of sand.” Used for a castle-shaped structure made with sand, usually on the beach. Common with the verb “fazer” or “construir” (to make/build).
target_language_example: Vamos fazer um castelo de areia perto do mar.
native_language_example: Let’s make a sandcastle near the sea.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened earlier than it should have. Often used with verbs like chegar (to arrive), começar (to start), or desistir (to give up): "Cheguei cedo demais" (I arrived too early), "Desistimos cedo demais" (We gave up too early).
target_language_example: Acho que liguei cedo demais.
native_language_example: I think I called too early.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen at some point in the future, even if you don’t know when. Often at the beginning of a sentence for emphasis ("Cedo ou tarde, ..."), or at the end ("..., cedo ou tarde.").
target_language_example: Cedo ou tarde, vamos encontrar uma solução.
native_language_example: Sooner or later, we’ll find a solution.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a time span (duration) or someone/something’s age. Often appears with expressions like “há cem anos” (a hundred years ago), “mais de cem anos” (more than a hundred years), and “quase cem anos” (almost a hundred years).
target_language_example: Meu bisavô viveu até os cem anos.
native_language_example: My great-grandfather lived to be 100 years old.

additional_notes: Used for emphasis to mean “fully/entirely” or “with complete certainty/agreement.” Common with verbs like concordar (“agree”) and expressions like estar certo / ter certeza (“be sure / be certain”). In questions (“Cem por cento?”) it can mean “100%, really?” or “Are you sure?”
target_language_example: Eu não estou cem por cento preparado para a prova.
native_language_example: I’m not 100% ready for the test.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun (or another quantity phrase) to indicate a large approximate number. Common patterns: "centenas de pessoas" (hundreds of people), "centenas de livros" (hundreds of books), and with bigger numbers: "centenas de milhares" (hundreds of thousands), "centenas de milhões" (hundreds of millions).
target_language_example: Havia centenas de pessoas na fila.
native_language_example: There were hundreds of people in line.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to express a very large approximate quantity (100,000–999,999). Often followed by "de" + plural noun: "centenas de milhares de pessoas/soldados/dólares". You can also drop the second "de" in some contexts: "centenas de milhares morreram" (hundreds of thousands died).
target_language_example: Centenas de milhares de pessoas participaram do evento.
native_language_example: Hundreds of thousands of people took part in the event.

additional_notes: Used before a number, amount, time, or distance to show it’s an estimate (not exact): cerca de uma hora (about an hour), cerca de trinta anos (about thirty years). It can also refer to time ago: cerca de um ano atrás (about a year ago).
target_language_example: A reunião começa em cerca de dez minutos.
native_language_example: The meeting starts in about ten minutes.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you’re 100% sure about something. Common with “ter” (to have) as in “Tenho certeza absoluta (de que...)” = “I’m absolutely sure (that...)”. It can also be used alone as an emphatic answer: “Tenho certeza absoluta!”
target_language_example: Você tem certeza absoluta de que fechou a porta?
native_language_example: Are you absolutely sure you locked the door?

additional_notes: Used to name/identify something or someone. It’s the reflexive form of the verb “chamar” (to call) and is very common in definitions and explanations: “X chama-se Y” = “X is called Y.” You can also use it alone when pointing something out: “Chama-se Jackson.” = “(His name) is Jackson.”
target_language_example: Isto chama-se pão de queijo.
native_language_example: This is called pão de queijo.

meaning: to attract attention; to draw attention (often on purpose).
additional_notes: Used when someone wants others to notice something or someone, or when you want to avoid being noticed. It can be neutral (e.g., to highlight an idea) or slightly negative (e.g., someone seeking attention).
target_language_example: Não faça barulho; não queremos chamar a atenção.
native_language_example: Don’t make noise; we don’t want to draw attention.

additional_notes: Used when you want to contact law enforcement (typically by phone) to report an emergency, crime, or problem. Common patterns: "Vou chamar a polícia" (I’m going to call the police), "Temos que chamar a polícia" (We have to call the police), "Pode chamar a polícia" (You can call the police).
target_language_example: Se ele voltar, eu vou chamar a polícia.
native_language_example: If he comes back, I’m going to call the police.

meaning: to attract attention; to draw attention.
additional_notes: Often appears as "chamar a atenção" (with the article "a"). You can specify who you want to notice you with "chamar a atenção de alguém" (e.g., "chamar a atenção do professor"). In some contexts, "chamar a atenção de alguém" can also mean to tell someone off/reprimand them, but it frequently just means to get noticed.
target_language_example: Tom faz tudo para chamar atenção.
native_language_example: Tom does everything to attract attention.

meaning: to call someone names; to insult someone (name-calling).
additional_notes: Used when someone insults another person by using offensive labels or mocking words, often in an argument. In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, it’s often phrased as "chamar [alguém] de [algo]" (e.g., "Ele me chamou de idiota" = "He called me an idiot"), but "chamar nomes" is also used to refer to the act of name-calling in general.
target_language_example: Não fique me chamando nomes!
native_language_example: Stop calling me names!

additional_notes: Used when you want someone to contact a doctor and have them come to help (at home, at work, or in an emergency). In Portuguese, “chamar” can mean both “call (on the phone)” and “send for / summon.” You can also say “chamar o médico” when it’s a specific doctor.
target_language_example: Ele está com muita dor; vou chamar um médico agora.
native_language_example: He’s in a lot of pain; I’m going to call a doctor now.

additional_notes: An urgent command using the formal imperative of "chamar" (to call). Used in emergencies or when threatening to involve law enforcement. With pronouns it can appear as: "Quer que eu chame a polícia?" (Do you want me to call the police?).
target_language_example: Se ele não parar, chame a polícia.
native_language_example: If he doesn’t stop, call the police.

additional_notes: Used to introduce yourself with your name. It comes from the verb "chamar-se" (to be called) in the present tense: (eu) chamo-me + name. In everyday Portuguese, especially in Brazil, you’ll also hear "me chamo" or simply "sou" (e.g., "Sou a Laura").
target_language_example: Olá, chamo-me Daniel.
native_language_example: Hi, my name is Daniel.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "chamar a polícia". Used to say someone contacted the police (usually by phone) in a specific completed event. You can change the subject (eu/ele/ela/você) and the tense: "Eu chamei a polícia" (I called the police), "Você vai chamar a polícia?" (Are you going to call the police?).
target_language_example: Ela chamou a polícia porque ouviu barulhos estranhos.
native_language_example: She called the police because she heard strange noises.

meaning: to call him (something); to refer to him as (a name/title).
additional_notes: Used with the object pronoun “-lo” (= “him”) attached to the verb chamar: chamar + o → chamá-lo. It’s often followed by a name, nickname, or description: “chamá-lo de Tom” (“call him Tom”), “chamá-lo de gênio” (“call him a genius”). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese you may also hear “chamar ele de…”.
target_language_example: Podemos chamá-lo de João?
native_language_example: Can we call him João?

meaning: "a chance to" / "a chance of" (opportunity or possibility of something happening).
additional_notes: Used before a verb in the infinitive (chance de + infinitive) or before a noun to talk about the possibility/opportunity of an action or result: "chance de ganhar" (chance to win), "chance de fuga" (chance of escape). Often appears with "ter" (to have) and "existe" (there is): "tem uma chance de...", "existe alguma chance de...?". In negative form, "sem chance de..." means "no chance of...".
target_language_example: Você tem alguma chance de chegar a tempo?
native_language_example: Do you have any chance of arriving on time?

additional_notes: Literally “slot/key,” it’s the common name for a flathead screwdriver (used with slotted screws). In everyday speech, many people also say “chave de fenda” loosely to mean “screwdriver” in general; for a Phillips screwdriver you may also hear “chave Phillips” or “chave de cruz.”
target_language_example: Você tem uma chave de fenda para eu apertar esse parafuso?
native_language_example: Do you have a screwdriver so I can tighten that screw?

additional_notes: Used for the tool with an adjustable jaw, common in toolkits and for plumbing/mechanical tasks. In Brazil, “chave” is often used for different kinds of wrenches (e.g., chave de fenda = screwdriver), so “chave inglesa” specifically means the adjustable one.
target_language_example: Você pode me emprestar a chave inglesa por um minuto?
native_language_example: Can you lend me the adjustable wrench for a minute?

additional_notes: Used to say you’ve had enough and want something to stop. Often followed by a noun or an infinitive: “Chega de conversa!” (Enough talk!), “Chega de discutir!” (No more arguing!). It’s a firm, sometimes impatient command. Also used with “por hoje” = “for today.”
target_language_example: Chega de desculpas — vamos resolver isso agora.
native_language_example: Enough excuses — let’s fix this now.

meaning: to arrive on time; to make it in time.
additional_notes: Used when talking about arriving before a deadline or before something starts (e.g., class, a train/metro). Often followed by "para" + event ("chegar a tempo para a escola") or "a/ao" + place/transport ("chegar a tempo ao metro"). You can also use it in questions about whether you’ll make it: "Vamos chegar a tempo?"
target_language_example: Se sairmos agora, ainda dá para chegar a tempo para o filme.
native_language_example: If we leave now, we can still make it to the movie on time.

meaning: to arrive at; to reach (a place or level).
additional_notes: "Chegar a" means "to arrive at / to reach" and it combines with the masculine singular article "o" to form "ao" (a + o = ao). Used for physical destinations (chegar ao estádio) and also figuratively for goals, limits, or extremes (chegar ao topo, chegar ao fundo do poço).
target_language_example: Como é que você fez para chegar ao estádio?
native_language_example: How did you manage to get to the stadium?

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone arriving at the place where the speaker is ("here"). Often appears with time expressions (e.g., "a que horas" = "at what time") or with "até" ("wait until..."). In the past, "cheguei aqui" = "I arrived here"; with the present, "chega aqui" can mean "(he/she) arrives here".
target_language_example: Me avisa quando você chegar aqui.
native_language_example: Let me know when you get here.

additional_notes: Means to arrive at your home. In Brazil, "chegar em casa" is very common in everyday speech. You may also see "chegar a casa" (more common in Portugal and sometimes considered more formal/prescriptive).
target_language_example: Eu vou te ligar quando chegar em casa.
native_language_example: I’ll call you when I get home.

additional_notes: Used for reaching a place (“there”), often with time or urgency: “chegar lá a tempo” (get there on time), “chegar lá cedo” (get there early), “chegar lá o mais rápido possível” (get there as fast as possible). It can be followed by a means of transport with “de”: “chegar lá de ônibus/trem” (get there by bus/train).
target_language_example: Se sairmos agora, vamos chegar lá antes das oito.
native_language_example: If we leave now, we’ll get there before eight.

meaning: to arrive at / to get to (a feminine destination)
additional_notes: Used with a destination: "chegar" + "a" (to) + the place. The preposition "a" often contracts with the feminine singular article "a" to form "à" (e.g., "chegar à escola", "chegar à ilha"). With masculine singular, it’s usually "chegar ao" (e.g., "chegar ao aeroporto"). Very common in directions: "Como chegar à/ao...?".
target_language_example: Você sabe como chegar à estação de trem?
native_language_example: Do you know how to get to the train station?

additional_notes: Past tense of chegar (“to arrive/get”) in the 3rd person singular (ele/ela/você). Used for people or things: “Ele chegou aqui.” = “He got here.” In context it can also sound like an order or exclamation (e.g., “Agora, chegou aqui!” = “Now, come here!” / “Get over here now!”).
target_language_example: Ela chegou aqui bem cedo.
native_language_example: She got here very early.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "chegar em casa" = "to get/arrive home." It’s used to say when someone got home (depois da meia-noite), in what condition (encharcado), or what was happening then (quando ela chegou em casa). You can change the subject: "eu cheguei em casa" (I got home), "eles chegaram em casa" (they got home).
target_language_example: Tom chegou em casa depois da meia-noite.
native_language_example: Tom arrived home after midnight.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of chegar: eu cheguei = “I arrived.” Used to say you got home, often followed by what happened next (e.g., “assim que…” = “as soon as…”). In Brazil, you’ll also hear “cheguei em casa”; in Portugal, “cheguei a casa” is common too.
target_language_example: Cheguei em casa e tomei um banho.
native_language_example: I got home and took a shower.

additional_notes: Used to say something contains a lot of something else. It agrees with what is “full”: cheia (feminine singular), cheio (masculine singular), cheias (feminine plural), cheios (masculine plural). Common with both literal things (cheia de fotos, cheia de maçãs) and abstract ideas (cheia de energia, cheia de riscos, cheia de altos e baixos).
target_language_example: A rua estava cheia de gente.
native_language_example: The street was full of people.

additional_notes: Means “full of” in both literal and figurative senses (e.g., cheio de energia = full of energy; cheio de esperança = full of hope; cheio de coisas para fazer = lots of things to do). “Cheio” agrees with the subject: cheio (m.sg.), cheia (f.sg.), cheios (m.pl.), cheias (f.pl.).
target_language_example: Estou cheio de energia hoje.
native_language_example: I’m full of energy today.

additional_notes: Used to say that something contains a lot of something, literally (e.g., bags full of sand) or figuratively (e.g., full of energy/tears). It agrees with the noun it describes: cheio de (masc. sing.), cheia de (fem. sing.), cheios de (masc. pl.), cheias de (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Os copos estão cheios de água.
