native_language_example: The glasses are full of water.

additional_notes: Used to say what something smells like. Common patterns: "com cheiro de + noun" (having a smell of…), "estar com cheiro de…" (to smell like…), "ter cheiro de…" (to have a smell of…), and "sentir cheiro de…" (to smell/notice a smell of…). Can also be used in questions: "tem cheiro de quê?" (what does it smell like?).
target_language_example: Esse casaco está com cheiro de cigarro.
native_language_example: This coat smells like cigarettes.

additional_notes: A common drink; often ordered or offered (e.g., at a café or at home). Literally means “hot chocolate.”
target_language_example: Está frio hoje; vou tomar um chocolate quente.
native_language_example: It’s cold today; I’m going to have a hot chocolate.

meaning: afternoon tea; a late-afternoon tea/snack (sometimes a formal tradition).
additional_notes: Literally “tea of the afternoon.” It can mean a light meal in the late afternoon (tea + something to eat), or the more formal British-style “afternoon tea” (often in hotels/cafés, with sandwiches and sweets). You’ll often see it with verbs like “tomar/fazer o chá da tarde” (to have afternoon tea) and with “na hora do chá da tarde” (at afternoon-tea time).
target_language_example: Vamos tomar um chá da tarde às cinco?
native_language_example: Shall we have afternoon tea at five?

additional_notes: A common beverage. Used after verbs like beber (to drink) and gostar de (to like), and when ordering: Um chá verde, por favor. Note: in Portuguese you can contrast teas with colors, e.g., chá verde (green tea) vs. chá preto (black tea).
target_language_example: De manhã, eu tomo chá verde sem açúcar.
native_language_example: In the morning, I drink green tea without sugar.

meaning: five years (a duration), or at five years old.
additional_notes: Used either to talk about a length of time (e.g., "por cinco anos" = for five years) or age ("com cinco anos" / "quando eu tinha cinco anos" = at five years old / when I was five). With time in the past, Portuguese often uses "há cinco anos" or "cinco anos atrás" (= five years ago).
target_language_example: Trabalhei nessa empresa por cinco anos.
native_language_example: I worked at that company for five years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (for five days), frequency (five days a week), or how long something has been happening (for the past five days). Often appears with "por" (for) and "há" (ago/for—depending on context, e.g., "há cinco dias" = five days ago / for five days).
target_language_example: Vou ficar na cidade por cinco dias.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay in the city for five days.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an amount of money. With verbs like pagar/dar, it often appears with: **dar** (to give) + amount (Eu vou te dar cinco dólares.), **pagar** (to pay) + amount (Paguei cinco dólares.), and **pagar** + amount + **a mais** (to pay extra/more than expected: Paguei cinco dólares a mais.). In Brazil, you’re more likely to hear *cinco reais* in everyday life, but *dólares* is common when referring to US currency.
target_language_example: Você tem cinco dólares trocados?
native_language_example: Do you have five dollars in change?

additional_notes: Used to say something happened five minutes ago ("há cinco minutos") or to ask for a short amount of time ("só cinco minutos"). In conversation it can also mean "just a moment" even if it’s not exactly five minutes.
target_language_example: Espera cinco minutos, por favor.
native_language_example: Wait five minutes, please.

additional_notes: The number 55. Used for ages with "aos" (e.g., "aos cinquenta e cinco anos" = "at 55 years old") and in larger numbers like "quinhentos e cinquenta e cinco" (555).
target_language_example: Ela fez cinquenta e cinco anos em janeiro.
native_language_example: She turned fifty-five in January.

additional_notes: Used for the safety belt in a car (and sometimes other vehicles). Often appears with verbs like usar/estar usando (“to wear/be wearing”) and can take an article: o cinto de segurança (“the seat belt”), um cinto de segurança (“a seat belt”).
target_language_example: Por favor, coloque o cinto de segurança antes de sair.
native_language_example: Please put on your seat belt before leaving.

additional_notes: Used to talk about surgeries done to change or repair appearance (face, body, skin), for cosmetic reasons or after injuries/medical issues. Often used with verbs like fazer (to have/get) and ser submetido(a) a (to undergo), and with the indefinite article: uma cirurgia plástica.
target_language_example: Ela quer fazer cirurgia plástica no nariz.
native_language_example: She wants to get plastic surgery on her nose.

additional_notes: Used to strongly confirm something or say it’s obvious/expected. Common in answers and emphatic statements: “Claro que sim!” (“Of course!”). Often followed by a verb: “Claro que fizeram.” = “Of course they did.”
target_language_example: Claro que eu posso te ajudar.
native_language_example: Of course I can help you.

additional_notes: Used to answer a question or deny something emphatically. Often comes at the start of a reply (“Claro que não!”). In speech it can be followed by a reason (“Claro que não, estou ocupado.”).
target_language_example: — Você vai hoje? — Claro que não, estou cansado.
native_language_example: — Are you going today? — Of course not, I’m tired.

additional_notes: A strong, friendly way to say “yes” or to confirm what someone asked. Often used as a full reply, sometimes followed by a term of address (e.g., “querido”) or a short explanation (“Claro que sim, me lembro.”).
target_language_example: —Você pode me ajudar amanhã? —Claro que sim!
native_language_example: —Can you help me tomorrow? —Of course!

additional_notes: Used to describe a social/economic group between the working class and the wealthy. Common after verbs like “ser”/“vir de” (to be/come from) and with places/people: “bairro de classe média” (a middle-class neighborhood), “jovens de classe média” (middle-class young people).
target_language_example: Ela trabalha muito, mas ainda se considera da classe média.
native_language_example: She works a lot, but she still considers herself middle class.

additional_notes: A common way to talk generally about unusual events, behavior, or topics. It’s plural and often used with verbs like acontecer (“to happen”): Coisas estranhas aconteceram… You can also use it to describe someone’s interests: pensar a respeito de coisas estranhas (“think about strange things”).
target_language_example: Ultimamente, coisas estranhas estão acontecendo no bairro.
native_language_example: Lately, strange things have been happening in the neighborhood.

meaning: 'things to do' (tasks/activities you need or want to do).
additional_notes: Very common everyday phrase. Often used to talk about being busy ("tenho muitas coisas para fazer", "estou cheio de coisas para fazer"). With "melhores coisas para fazer", it means you'd rather do something else ("I have better things to do").
target_language_example: Desculpa, não posso sair agora — tenho coisas para fazer.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go out now—I have things to do.

meaning: classmate (someone you study in the same class as).
additional_notes: Used for a person in the same class/course at school or university. Use "colega" for a male classmate and "colega" for a female classmate; what changes is the article/possessive: "o meu colega" (male) vs. "a minha colega" (female). You can add "antigo/antiga" to mean "former" (e.g., an old classmate).
target_language_example: Vou almoçar com um colega de classe depois da aula.
native_language_example: I'm going to have lunch with a classmate after class.

meaning: roommate (someone you share a room or place to live with).
additional_notes: Used for a person you live with, especially in shared housing (apartment/house) or a dorm. Gender changes with the person: "meu colega de quarto" (male) / "minha colega de quarto" (female). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people also say "roommate" or "companheiro(a) de quarto" depending on context.
target_language_example: Meu colega de quarto chega tarde quase todos os dias.
native_language_example: My roommate gets home late almost every day.

additional_notes: Used for people who are in the same class (at school, university, or a course). You can also say "colega de classe" (singular). Similar options: "colegas" (classmates/colleagues, depending on context) and "colegas de turma" (same group/class).
target_language_example: Eu vou estudar com meus colegas de classe depois da aula.
native_language_example: I'm going to study with my classmates after class.

additional_notes: "colocou" is the simple past of "colocar" and means "put" or "placed." "o" means "the" before a masculine singular noun. This phrase is used when someone put something somewhere, and it can also be used more figuratively, as in causing a situation or state.
target_language_example: Ela colocou o prato na mesa.
native_language_example: She put the plate on the table.

additional_notes: Infinitive form of colocar + the clitic pronoun -la (“her/it,” referring to a feminine noun). Often used after another verb (e.g., Basta/Vamos/Devo/Queria colocá-la...) and commonly with a location or purpose: colocá-la no elevador (in the elevator), num manicômio (in an asylum), para adoção (up for adoption), em posição (into position), para dormir (to sleep/bed).
target_language_example: Você pode colocá-la na mesa, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you put it on the table, please?

meaning: “to put/place it” or “to put him” (depending on context).
additional_notes: Colocá-lo = colocar (“to put/place”) + -lo (“it/him”). It’s the infinitive form used after expressions like “precisa”, “vamos”, “temos que”, “pode”, etc. In everyday speech, many people also say “colocar ele” instead of “colocá-lo”, but “colocá-lo” is more standard/written.
target_language_example: Você pode colocá-lo aqui na mesa.
native_language_example: You can put it here on the table.

additional_notes: Imperative of colocar (“to put/place”) + object pronoun -o (“it,” for a masculine object). Used to tell someone to put something somewhere: coloque-o ali/na mesa/na prateleira/sobre a mesa. In everyday speech, many people also say “coloca ele” or “coloca-o” depending on region and formality. With “de volta”, it means “put it back.”
target_language_example: Por favor, coloque-o aqui na bancada.
native_language_example: Please put it here on the counter.

additional_notes: A common combination of com ('with') + a ('the'). It is used before feminine singular nouns. With women's names, the article may be used or omitted depending on region and style.
target_language_example: Vou ao cinema com a minha irmã.
native_language_example: I'm going to the movies with my sister.

meaning: “with (your/the) head”; also in idioms like “Onde você está com a cabeça?” = “What are you thinking?/What’s wrong with you?”
additional_notes: Used literally to describe doing something using the head (e.g., acenar com a cabeça = to nod/shake your head; bater com a cabeça = to hit/bump your head). In expressions like “Onde você está com a cabeça?” or “Não sei onde ele está com a cabeça”, it means someone is being careless, distracted, or making bad decisions.
target_language_example: Ela disse que ia dirigir depois de beber, e eu perguntei: “Onde você está com a cabeça?”
native_language_example: She said she was going to drive after drinking, and I asked, “What are you thinking?”

meaning: with the family; with one’s family.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is together/doing something with their family. In some contexts it can also imply “messing with someone’s family” (a threat/strong warning), like in “mexeu com a família errada.”
target_language_example: Hoje vou almoçar com a família.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to have lunch with my family.

additional_notes: Often used instead of the more formal "conosco" in everyday Brazilian Portuguese. It refers to being together (staying/coming) or agreeing "with us" (sharing the same opinion).
target_language_example: Você quer almoçar com a gente hoje?
native_language_example: Do you want to have lunch with us today?

additional_notes: Very common, informal way to say "with us." Uses "a gente" (literally "the people") as an everyday substitute for "nós" (we/us). More formal equivalent: "conosco" or "com nós" (less common). Often used in invitations: "Vem com a gente" = "Come with us."
target_language_example: Você quer almoçar com a gente?
native_language_example: Do you want to have lunch with us?

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together with your mother (in the same place, living together, leaving someone in her care) or that you learned/did something alongside her. In Portuguese, “com” often means “with,” including living with someone (“moro com...”).
target_language_example: Vou jantar com a minha mãe hoje.
native_language_example: I’m going to have dinner with my mother today.

additional_notes: Used to say you do an action using your left hand (e.g., writing, holding something). You can also hear the variant “com a esquerda”.
target_language_example: Eu abro a porta com a mão esquerda.
native_language_example: I open the door with my left hand.

meaning: "with the news" / "upon hearing the news" (showing a reaction).
additional_notes: Often used after a feeling/reaction to show what caused it, especially with "ficar" + adjective: "ficar surpreso(a)/triste/atordoado(a) com a notícia". In English this is often more natural as "at the news" or "upon hearing the news." Note: "notícia" means "news" (not "notice").
target_language_example: Ele ficou preocupado com a notícia.
native_language_example: He got worried at the news.

meaning: with the police; to/with the police (speaking or dealing with them).
additional_notes: "Com" means "with," and "a" is "the" (feminine singular), so it literally means "with the police." Often used with verbs like "falar" (to talk) or "trabalhar" (to work): "falar com a polícia" = "to talk to the police." In questions like "Está contando com a polícia?", it means "Are you counting on the police?"
target_language_example: Se acontecer alguma coisa, ligue e fale com a polícia.
native_language_example: If anything happens, call and talk to the police.

additional_notes: "Alguém" means “someone” (an unspecified person). "Com alguém" is very common after verbs like: estar com alguém (be with someone / sometimes “be seeing someone” depending on context), sair com alguém (go out with/date someone), falar com alguém (talk to someone), falhar com alguém (let someone down / fail someone), casar com alguém (marry someone).
target_language_example: Você pode falar com alguém da recepção?
native_language_example: Can you talk to someone at the front desk?

additional_notes: This is the preposition "com" (with) + the plural feminine definite article "as" (the). It’s used before plural feminine nouns: "com as minhas mãos" (with my hands), "com as crianças" (with the children). In phrases like "para com as", it can mean "toward/regarding the" (showing attitude toward the laws, rules, etc.).
target_language_example: Vou sair com as minhas amigas hoje.
native_language_example: I’m going out with my (female) friends today.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with children or doing something alongside them. Also common after adjectives/commands to describe how you should behave toward them (e.g., "Seja paciente com as crianças" = "Be patient with the children"). "As" is the plural feminine form of "a" ("the") used with "crianças".
target_language_example: Eu trabalho com as crianças todas as tardes.
native_language_example: I work with the children every afternoon.

additional_notes: Literally means being together/along with a group of women. Very common after verbs like ir/vir (to go/come), ficar (to stay), dormir (to sleep), gastar (to spend), and funcionar (to work) to say something happens “with women” (e.g., works with women, spend money with women).
target_language_example: Ele foi com as mulheres para a reunião.
native_language_example: He went with the women to the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to say you do something using your hands (instead of a tool), or to describe what your hands are doing/where they are: “com as mãos nos bolsos” (with hands in pockets), “com as mãos pra cima” (with hands up). Often followed by a phrase describing position.
target_language_example: Ele abriu a porta com as mãos ocupadas.
native_language_example: He opened the door with his hands full.

additional_notes: Used after many verbs/adjectives to talk about how someone interacts with people in general (e.g., discutir com as pessoas = argue with people, ser rude com as pessoas = be rude to people, lidar com as pessoas = deal with people, habilidades com as pessoas = people skills). It can also refer to a specific group mentioned in context (e.g., “com as pessoas já mortas” = “with the people who are already dead?”).
target_language_example: Ele é muito paciente com as pessoas.
native_language_example: He is very patient with people.

additional_notes: Used to suggest doing something in a calm, patient way, often to avoid stress or conflict. Very common as advice/command: "Vai com calma" = "Take it easy" / "Slow down". Also used for reviewing/checking something carefully: "Já viu com calma?" = "Have you looked at it carefully (without rushing)?"
target_language_example: Vamos conversar com calma depois.
native_language_example: Let’s talk calmly later.

additional_notes: Means you’re certain about what you’re saying. Often used as an emphatic adverb, and it can be placed at the start of the sentence ("Com certeza, ...") or inserted as a parenthetical (", com certeza,"). With negation, it commonly appears as "com certeza não" (= "definitely not").
target_language_example: Com certeza eu vou amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m definitely going tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar/ficar to talk about someone being in a jealous mood/state. It can be followed by “de” to say who/what the jealousy is about: “com ciúmes de alguém” (jealous of someone). Very common in questions like “Está com ciúmes?”
target_language_example: Ele ficou com ciúmes do meu amigo.
native_language_example: He got jealous of my friend.

additional_notes: Used to describe doing an action in a careful, cautious way (often for safety or to avoid damage). It can modify physical actions (Abra a porta com cuidado.) or more abstract actions like considering/analysing something (considerou a oferta com cuidado).
target_language_example: Pise com cuidado, o chão está molhado.
native_language_example: Step carefully; the floor is wet.

meaning: with a headache; having a headache.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" (or "ficar") to describe someone’s current condition: "Estou com dor de cabeça" = "I have a headache." Also common with "acordar" to say you woke up with one: "Acordei com dor de cabeça." Often paired with other symptoms: "com dor de cabeça e garganta inflamada".
target_language_example: Estou com dor de cabeça, acho que vou deitar cedo.
native_language_example: I have a headache; I think I’m going to go to bed early.

additional_notes: Used when talking about being together with, comparing to, or doing something involving a female person. After the preposition com, Portuguese uses ela.
target_language_example: Eu quero falar com ela amanhã.
native_language_example: I want to talk with her tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with a group of women/girls or feminine nouns. Means “with them” in the sense of being together/alongside them, or doing something toward them (e.g., be nice to them). Compare: com eles = with them (masculine or mixed group).
target_language_example: Você pode ir com elas até a loja?
native_language_example: Can you go with them (the girls) to the store?

additional_notes: Basic prepositional phrase with a male person. It is used after com in many contexts: going somewhere with him, living with him, being careful with him, etc. In some fixed expressions, English may translate it less literally, such as contar com ele = 'count on him'.
target_language_example: Vou ao cinema com ele.
native_language_example: I'm going to the movies with him.

additional_notes: Means “with them” when talking about being together (going somewhere, staying/spending time), or doing something together. It’s also used with certain verbs that naturally take “com” in Portuguese, like falar com (“talk to”), concordar com (“agree with”), and ser rígido com (“be strict with”). Pronoun: eles = “them” (masculine or mixed group).
target_language_example: Posso ir com eles amanhã.
native_language_example: Can I go with them tomorrow?

meaning: "with that" / "because of that" (referring to a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Uses the preposition "com" (with) + "essa" (that/this, feminine). It usually refers back to a feminine thing already mentioned: "com essa velocidade" (with that speed), "com essa notícia" (because of that news). It also appears in the common expression "Para com essa...", meaning "Stop it/Cut it out with that...".
target_language_example: Para com essa ideia e vamos embora.
native_language_example: Cut it out with that idea and let’s go.

additional_notes: Used with the demonstrative pronoun/adjective "esse" (masculine singular) to mean “with that/with this one,” usually referring to something near the listener or something just mentioned. It agrees with a masculine singular noun: "com esse nome" (with that name), "com esse dinheiro" (with that money). In commands, it can sound like “stop with that…”: "Parem com esse barulho!"
target_language_example: Não mexa com esse botão.
native_language_example: Don’t mess with that button.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens or can be done without much effort. It can describe actions (resolver, encontrar, fazer) or someone’s tendency to react quickly (se assusta/se cansa com facilidade = gets scared/tired easily).
target_language_example: Ela aprende línguas com facilidade.
native_language_example: She learns languages easily.

meaning: with a fever; having a fever.
additional_notes: Used with "estar" (or sometimes "ficar") to talk about someone’s current condition: "estar com febre" = "to have a fever" (temporary state). In Portuguese you commonly say "com" + symptom/condition (e.g., "com dor", "com gripe").
target_language_example: Acho que estou com febre desde ontem.
native_language_example: I think I’ve had a fever since yesterday.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar": "estar com fome" = "to be hungry". Literally "with hunger", but the natural translation is just "hungry".
target_language_example: Estou com fome, vamos comer alguma coisa.
native_language_example: I’m hungry, let’s eat something.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens regularly or many times. Common with verbs to describe habits or repeated actions (e.g., "penso com frequência", "acontece com frequência").
target_language_example: Ele viaja a trabalho com frequência.
native_language_example: He travels for work often.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" (or sometimes "ficar") to say you feel cold: "Estou com frio" = "I'm cold". You can add a body part with "em/no/na" (often contracted): "com frio nos pés" = "cold feet" (literally, cold in the feet).
target_language_example: Estou com frio, pode fechar a janela?
native_language_example: I'm cold—can you close the window?

additional_notes: A common, literal phrase used to refer to something already mentioned or something physically present. The exact English choice can be 'with that' or 'with it' depending on context. In the fixed expression 'para com isso', the whole phrase means 'stop that' or 'stop it'.
target_language_example: Não sei o que fazer com isso.
native_language_example: I don't know what to do with that.

additional_notes: Polite phrase used to get someone’s attention, ask a question, pass by, interrupt briefly, or request permission (often like “may I…?”). Common at the start of a sentence: “Com licença, posso entrar?” You may also hear “Com licença.” alone meaning “Excuse me.”
target_language_example: Com licença, você pode me ajudar?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you help me?

additional_notes: Used to say you are together with your father, doing something with him, or interacting with him (e.g., talking, arguing). In some contexts, “com” can also imply learning/receiving help or influence from him (similar to “from” in English), as in “Aprendi muito com meu pai.”
target_language_example: Vou ao mercado com meu pai hoje.
native_language_example: I’m going to the market with my father today.

additional_notes: Used to say you are together/doing something in the company of your friends. Often follows a verb (e.g., sair, ir, comer, encontrar-se). You may also hear variations like "com as minhas amigas" (with my [female] friends) or simply "com amigos" (with friends).
target_language_example: No sábado, vou ao cinema com meus amigos.
native_language_example: On Saturday, I'm going to the movies with my friends.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" to describe how someone feels at that moment: "estar com (muita) fome" = "to be (very) hungry." "Com" here is part of the expression (literally "with hunger"), not something you translate word-for-word in English.
target_language_example: Depois do treino, eu estava com muita fome.
native_language_example: After the workout, I was very hungry.

additional_notes: Used to describe doing an action in a cautious, gentle way to avoid mistakes or accidents. It commonly follows the verb (e.g., "fale/ande/segure/abra com muito cuidado").
target_language_example: Por favor, dirija com muito cuidado na chuva.
native_language_example: Please drive very carefully in the rain.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" (or "ficar") to describe someone’s current emotional state. Often followed by "de" + infinitive to say what you’re afraid of: "estar com muito medo de + verb".
target_language_example: Estou com muito medo de voar.
native_language_example: I’m very afraid of flying.

additional_notes: Composed of com + o. Use it before a masculine singular noun. Besides physical accompaniment ('with the son'), it can also appear in expressions about communication, means, relationship, or purpose, so English may sometimes sound more natural as 'to the', 'by', or 'for the purpose of' depending on context.
target_language_example: Eu vou ao cinema com o meu irmão.
native_language_example: I'm going to the movies with my brother.

additional_notes: Used to express deep sadness, often after a breakup, loss, or disappointing news. It commonly follows verbs like "estar" (to be) or appears after a clause explaining what happened.
target_language_example: Depois do término, ela ficou com o coração partido.
native_language_example: After the breakup, she was heartbroken.

meaning: 'with the money' (carrying it, using it, or referring to it).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition "com" to indicate (1) having/carrying the money ("fugiu com o dinheiro" = ran away with the money), (2) what someone does using the money ("o que você fez com o dinheiro?"), or (3) living/surviving on money that comes from somewhere ("vive com o dinheiro que..." = lives on the money that...).
target_language_example: Vou pagar a conta com o dinheiro que trouxe.
native_language_example: I’m going to pay the bill with the money I brought.

additional_notes: Used with "com" (with) + "o pai" (the father). It can mean being together with the father (doing something with him) or living with him ("morar com o pai"). In context it often means “his/her father,” even though Portuguese uses the definite article (o) instead of a possessive.
target_language_example: Ela vai viajar com o pai neste fim de semana.
native_language_example: She’s going to travel with her dad this weekend.

additional_notes: Used after verbs that normally take the preposition “com” (“with”), especially in questions or relative clauses. Common patterns: “com o que…?” = “with what…?” (Com o que estamos lidando?); “com o que [alguém] disse” = “with what [someone] said” (concordar com o que…); “viver com o que [você] ganha” = “live on what you earn.” Literally “com” + “o que” (“what/that which”).
target_language_example: Com o que você está preocupado?
native_language_example: What are you worried about?

meaning: "with the result" / "about the outcome" (showing how someone feels about what happened).
additional_notes: Used after adjectives (e.g., feliz, satisfeito, desapontado, perplexo) to say someone’s reaction to the outcome of something. You’ll also see it with possessives: com o resultado do exame/da eleição/do jogo.
target_language_example: Não estou contente com o resultado do jogo.
native_language_example: I’m not happy with the result of the game.

meaning: with time; over time; as time goes by.
additional_notes: Used to talk about gradual change or something that happens eventually. Often at the start of a sentence (“Com o tempo, …”) meaning “Over time/As time goes by, …”. It can also mean “with the amount of time (that)” in phrases like “com o tempo que…”, referring to a length of time someone had/used.
target_language_example: Com o tempo, a gente aprende a ter paciência.
native_language_example: Over time, we learn to be patient.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun: com os cardeais (“with the cardinals”), com os próprios erros (“from/with your own mistakes”). It’s simply the preposition com (“with”) + the plural masculine article os (“the”). (Feminine plural is com as.)
target_language_example: Vou sair com os meus amigos depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: I’m going out with my friends after work.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is doing an activity together with friends. Often refers to the subject’s own friends (e.g., “Tom sai com os amigos” = “Tom goes out with his friends”), though it can also mean “with the friends” in context. You’ll also hear the feminine form “com as amigas” (with the female friends) and the mixed/generic plural “com os amigos” (with friends).
target_language_example: Hoje vou jantar com os amigos.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to have dinner with my friends.

meaning: "with the (his/her) children"; also "toward the children" (after an adjective).
additional_notes: Literally means “with the children.” In context it often implies “with his/her children,” since Portuguese can leave out the possessive (e.g., “com os filhos” = “with his children”). After adjectives like "severo", "duro", or "rígido", "com" can mean “toward” or “in dealing with” (e.g., "severo com os filhos" = “strict with/toward the children”).
target_language_example: Ela é muito paciente com os filhos.
native_language_example: She is very patient with her children.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how you interact with other people. Common after adjectives and verbs like “ser” (be), “falar” (talk), “interromper” (interrupt), “brigar” (fight), “ser gentil” (be kind). In sentence 1, the natural phrasing is: “Não interrompa os outros quando estão falando” (“Don’t interrupt others when they’re talking”).
target_language_example: Ela é muito paciente com os outros.
native_language_example: She is very patient with others.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together with their parents (e.g., going somewhere, spending time). With verbs like “morar” (to live), it means living in the same home as their parents. “os pais” is “the parents”; in context it often means “his/her parents.”
target_language_example: Hoje vou almoçar com os pais.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to have lunch with my parents.

meaning: with someone else; with another person.
additional_notes: Often used when talking about confusing one person for another ("confundir alguém com outra pessoa" = "to mistake someone for someone else"). It can also mean being together with someone else in a situation (e.g., "na cama com outra pessoa" = "in bed with someone else").
target_language_example: Desculpe, você me confundiu com outra pessoa.
native_language_example: Sorry, you mistook me for someone else.

additional_notes: Used to accept a request or offer politely (often as a standalone reply: “Com prazer.”). Also used with verbs like ajudar/aceitar (“gladly”) or lembrar (“to remember fondly”): “Lembro com prazer…” = “I remember … with pleasure.”
target_language_example: Eu te ajudo com prazer.
native_language_example: I’ll help you gladly.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" (or "ficar") to mean you’re in a hurry: "Estou com pressa" = "I’m in a hurry." It can also describe how something was done: "Fiz com pressa" = "I did it in a rush." Often followed by "de" + infinitive to say what you’re rushing to do: "com pressa de ver" = "in a hurry to see."
target_language_example: Desculpa, estou com pressa de pegar o ônibus.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm in a hurry to catch the bus.

meaning: "with how much" / "for how much" (asking about amount or price).
additional_notes: Used in questions to ask the amount of money or quantity involved in something, often meaning "for how much?" when talking about buying/selling (price). It’s usually followed by a verb (e.g., comprar, vender, ficar) or by a noun (e.g., com quanto dinheiro). In everyday speech, people also commonly use "por quanto?" to ask the price.
target_language_example: Com quanto você comprou esse celular?
native_language_example: How much did you buy this phone for?

additional_notes: Used to ask about how frequently someone does an action. It’s typically followed by a verb (e.g., "com que frequência você vai...?"). In everyday speech, people also say "Com que frequência você..." or simply "Com que frequência...".
target_language_example: Com que frequência você vai à academia?
native_language_example: How often do you go to the gym?

additional_notes: Used to ask or say which person someone is with, talks to, works with, spends time with, etc. Common in questions and relative clauses. Portuguese normally keeps the preposition before quem: com quem.
target_language_example: Com quem você mora?
native_language_example: Who do you live with?

additional_notes: Used to ask or state the person someone is with. Common in questions like “Com quem você estava falando?” (“Who were you talking to?”). In everyday speech, it often comes at the start of a question; you can also hear “Você estava falando com quem?” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Com quem você vai ao cinema?
native_language_example: Who are you going to the movies with?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like estar/ficar to say someone is (or becomes) angry: "estar com raiva" = to be angry, "ficar com raiva" = to get angry. Often followed by "de" or "com" to say who/what you’re angry at: "com raiva do Tom" = angry at Tom, "com raiva de mim" = angry at me.
target_language_example: Ele ficou com raiva porque perdeu o ônibus.
native_language_example: He got angry because he missed the bus.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" (or "ficar") to say you feel nostalgia/longing for home. "Saudade" is a common Portuguese word for a deep feeling of missing someone/something; in English you’ll usually translate it as "to miss" or "to feel nostalgic."
target_language_example: Estou com saudades de casa desde que me mudei.
native_language_example: I've been homesick since I moved.

additional_notes: Most commonly, **estar com sede** means “to be thirsty” (literally “to be with thirst”): *Estou com sede.* In more formal/news/business contexts, **com sede em + place** means “based in” / “headquartered in”: *uma empresa com sede em São Paulo*.
target_language_example: Depois da caminhada, estou com sede.
native_language_example: After the walk, I'm thirsty.

additional_notes: A compositional phrase: com means "with" and seu is a possessive that can mean "your" (especially with você) or "his/her/their" depending on context. In Brazilian Portuguese, seu can be ambiguous, so speakers may use dele/dela/deles/delas for clarity.
target_language_example: Eu falei com seu professor ontem.
native_language_example: I spoke with your teacher yesterday.

additional_notes: "Com" means "with". "Seu" can mean "your" (informal singular) or "his/her" depending on context, so "com seu pai" can mean "with your father" or "with his/her father." If you need to be crystal clear, you can also hear/see: "com o pai dele" (with his father) / "com o pai dela" (with her father).
target_language_example: Ela mora com seu pai.
native_language_example: She lives with her father.

meaning: with your friends / with his friends (depending on context).
additional_notes: Means “with + someone’s friends.” In Brazilian Portuguese, "seu/seus" can refer to "your" (formal) or "his" (and sometimes "her"), so the exact meaning depends on who is being talked to/about. If you want to be clear, you can say "com os amigos dele" (with his friends) or "com os amigos dela" (with her friends).
target_language_example: Ela foi ao cinema com seus amigos.
native_language_example: She went to the movies with her friends.

additional_notes: Means being together/doing something in the company of one’s children. "Com" = "with". "Seus" agrees with "filhos" (masculine plural) and can mean "your" (especially in Brazil) or "his/her/their" depending on context; often clarified with "dele/dela/deles/delas" if needed.
target_language_example: Eu gosto de cozinhar com seus filhos aos domingos.
native_language_example: I like to cook with your children on Sundays.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is together with their parents. In Portuguese, "seus" can mean "your" (formal) or "his/her/their" depending on context. In casual speech, Brazilians often use "com os pais" (with the parents) or "com os seus pais" for clarity; you may also see "com seus pais" after a question like "Você...".
target_language_example: Você vai viajar com seus pais neste fim de semana?
native_language_example: Are you going to travel with your parents this weekend?

meaning: sleepy; feeling like you want to sleep.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" (or "ficar") to describe a temporary state: "estar com sono" = to be sleepy; "ficar com sono" = to get sleepy. Often used in everyday situations (at night, after lunch, after a long day).
target_language_example: Estou com sono, vou dormir cedo.
native_language_example: I'm sleepy, I'm going to sleep early.

additional_notes: Literally “with your mother,” but **sua mãe** can mean “your mother” (very common in Brazil) or “her mother,” depending on context. Used for accompanying someone (ir/viajar/sair com sua mãe), living with someone (morar com sua mãe), interacting/behavior (ser gentil com sua mãe), or conflict (brigar com sua mãe). If you want to be unambiguous in Brazilian Portuguese, you can also say **com a mãe dela** (“with her mother”) or **com a sua mãe** (“with your mother”).
target_language_example: Mary mora em Boston com sua mãe.
native_language_example: Mary lives in Boston with her mother.

additional_notes: Used with feminine plural nouns: com suas amigas (with her/your friends), com suas cortinas (with her/your curtains). Note that "suas" can mean "your", "his", "her", or "their" depending on context (it agrees with the thing owned, not the owner). For masculine plural, use "com seus"; for singular, "com sua" / "com seu".
target_language_example: Ele chegou com suas malas e entrou no hotel.
native_language_example: He arrived with his bags and went into the hotel.

additional_notes: Used to say something involves all people in a group or in general. Common after verbs like "se dar bem" (get along), "ser" (be), "falar" (talk), etc. Contrast: "com alguém" (with someone) vs. "com ninguém" (with nobody).
target_language_example: Ela fala com todo mundo na festa.
native_language_example: She talks to everyone at the party.

meaning: "with everything" / "with all (that one has)"; also "all out" (with full force/effort).
additional_notes: Often literal: "com tudo" = "with everything" (sometimes followed by a clarification: "com tudo, com as crianças"). It can also be used more idiomatically to mean doing something with maximum effort or intensity, especially with verbs like "ir"/"vir" ("vai com tudo", "virão com tudo") or in encouragement ("Vamos com tudo!").
target_language_example: Vamos com tudo e terminamos isso hoje.
native_language_example: Let’s go all out and finish this today.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: com um lápis = 'with a pencil'. Here, um is the masculine form of the indefinite article ('a/an'), though it can also mean 'one' in other contexts.
target_language_example: Eu escrevo com um lápis azul.
native_language_example: I write with a blue pencil.

additional_notes: Used to describe doing something while smiling (often to show friendliness, politeness, or good humor). Common with verbs like cumprimentar (to greet), falar (to speak), dizer (to say), and desejar (to wish). You may also hear close variations like “com um sorriso no rosto” or “com um sorriso nos lábios” (“with a smile on his/her face/lips”).
target_language_example: Ele respondeu com um sorriso.
native_language_example: He answered with a smile.

additional_notes: "com" usually means "with". "uma" means "a/an" for feminine singular nouns (uma blusa, uma xícara, uma dor). Used for accompaniment/association (casado com uma canadense), tools or means (com uma calculadora; com uma rede; com uma mão), and a condition/state (estar com uma dor de cabeça = to have a headache).
target_language_example: Vou sair com uma amiga depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: I'm going out with a (female) friend after work.

meaning: with a knife; using a knife.
additional_notes: Uses "com" (with) to indicate the tool/instrument used to do something. Often follows a verb: "cortar ... com uma faca" (to cut ... with a knife), "gravar ... com uma faca" (to carve ... with a knife). In descriptions, it can also mean someone is carrying/holding a knife: "com uma faca nas mãos" (with a knife in (his) hands).
target_language_example: Não mexa nisso com uma faca; é perigoso.
native_language_example: Don’t mess with that using a knife; it’s dangerous.

additional_notes: Used after verbs to show association/companionship or who something involves (e.g., casar com uma mulher = marry a woman; negociar com uma mulher = negotiate with a woman). With verbs like dormir/estar, it can imply having sex with a woman depending on context.
target_language_example: Ele saiu com uma mulher que conheceu no trabalho.
native_language_example: He went out with a woman he met at work.

additional_notes: A very common phrase used for being together with someone, taking something along with someone, or referring to someone's situation depending on context, as in Está tudo bem com você? ('Is everything okay with you?').
target_language_example: Posso ir com você?
native_language_example: Can I go with you?

additional_notes: Used to say you’re with a group of people you address as "vocês" (= you all / you plural). It’s "com" (with) + "vocês". Common with verbs like "ir" (to go) and with the expression "estar com" (to be with): "Ele está com vocês" = "He is with you (all)".
target_language_example: Posso ir com vocês?
native_language_example: Can I go with you (all)?

additional_notes: From the verb “comer” (to eat) + “carne” (meat). Used to say that someone eats meat (i.e., is not vegetarian), or to ask if someone eats meat. You can add a type of meat: “come carne branca” (eats white meat), “come carne de cavalo” (eats horse meat).
target_language_example: Você come carne ou é vegetariano?
native_language_example: Do you eat meat or are you vegetarian?

additional_notes: Imperative of **começar a** + infinitive, used to tell someone to start doing something. It’s the more general/neutral command form often used with **você** (e.g., *Comece a falar*, *Comece a fazer as malas*).
target_language_example: Comece a estudar agora, por favor.
native_language_example: Start studying now, please.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "começar" + "a" + infinitive. Used to say you started doing something at a specific moment in the past: "comecei a falar" (I started to speak), "comecei a escrever" (I started writing). You can add time expressions like "aos trinta anos" (at 30) or "quando eu tinha cinco anos" (when I was five). Other persons: "começou a" (he/she started to), "começamos a" (we started to).
target_language_example: Quando ouvi a música, comecei a dançar.
native_language_example: When I heard the music, I started to dance.

additional_notes: "Comendo" is the gerund ("-ing" form) of the verb "comer" (to eat). It’s commonly used with "estar" to talk about something happening right now: "estou/está/estão comendo..." It can also describe someone while they do another action: "Ele o viu comendo um sanduíche" = "He saw him eating a sandwich."
target_language_example: Estou comendo um sanduíche agora.
native_language_example: I’m eating a sandwich now.

additional_notes: Used when you don’t want to specify exactly what will be eaten (any food will do). Very common in offers and suggestions (e.g., before going out) and can also mean “at least eat a little” when someone hasn’t eaten.
target_language_example: Estou com fome; vou comer alguma coisa antes da reunião.
native_language_example: I’m hungry; I’m going to eat something before the meeting.

meaning: refreshments; food and drinks (at a party/event).
additional_notes: Common in European Portuguese as a fixed expression, usually plural, referring to snacks and drinks provided at a gathering (e.g., a meeting, party, reception). It’s slightly informal and often used like a noun: “Há comes e bebes” / “Vai haver comes e bebes”.
target_language_example: Na festa vai haver comes e bebes para toda a gente.
native_language_example: At the party there will be refreshments for everyone.

additional_notes: Past tense (ele/ela/você cometeu) of the verb "cometer" + "suicídio". This is a serious, formal expression; in everyday conversation you may also hear "tirou a própria vida" (“took their own life”), which can sound a bit less blunt.
target_language_example: A polícia disse que ele cometeu suicídio.
native_language_example: The police said he committed suicide.

additional_notes: Pretérito perfeito (simple past) of "cometer um erro" = "to make/commit a mistake." "Cometeu" agrees with ele/ela and also with "você" (common in Brazilian Portuguese). For "eu": "cometi um erro"; for "nós": "cometemos um erro." Used when pointing out or admitting a specific mistake.
target_language_example: Eu acho que você cometeu um erro.
native_language_example: I think you made a mistake.

additional_notes: Past tense of "cometer um erro" (to make/commit a mistake). "Cometi" is first-person singular in the simple past (pretérito perfeito), used to admit or explain a mistake. Often followed by details with "ao" + infinitive ("cometi um erro ao enviar...") or with "de" to specify the type ("erro de digitação" = typo).
target_language_example: Desculpa, cometi um erro ao preencher o formulário.
native_language_example: Sorry, I made a mistake when filling out the form.

additional_notes: Form of the verb "começar" (to start) followed by "a" + infinitive. Used to say someone starts doing something: "Ele começa a esquecer..." (He starts to forget...). It can also be an imperative giving a command or encouragement: "Começa a largar" = "Start letting go" / "Start dropping it" (context-dependent).
target_language_example: Ela começa a estudar mais cedo este ano.
native_language_example: She starts studying earlier this year.

additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive to say that “we” began to do something. Often appears as “começamos a + infinitive” (e.g., começar a ver, começar a falar). The reflexive pronoun can come after it (e.g., “começamos a nos beijar” = “we started kissing”).
target_language_example: Começamos a entender melhor depois da conversa.
native_language_example: We started to understand better after the conversation.

meaning: to start to; to begin to
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive verb to express the beginning of an action or process, e.g. começar a fazer, começar a pagar, começar a nevar. This entry is given in the infinitive, though in real sentences the verb often appears conjugated.
target_language_example: Quero começar a fazer isso imediatamente.
native_language_example: I want to start doing that immediately.

meaning: to start again; to begin again (from scratch).
additional_notes: Used when you repeat an attempt or restart a process after a mistake, interruption, or failure. You can use it as a question (“Posso começar de novo?”) or with obligation/advice (“Temos que…”, “Você deve…”). Often implies resetting and trying again, similar to “start over.”
target_language_example: Se der errado, a gente pode começar de novo.
native_language_example: If it goes wrong, we can start again.

meaning: "they started/began to" (followed by a verb in the infinitive).
additional_notes: This is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "começar" for "eles/elas/vocês". It’s commonly used with "a" + infinitive to say someone began doing something: "começaram a trabalhar" = "they started to work".
target_language_example: Depois do sinal, eles começaram a correr.
native_language_example: After the signal, they started to run.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of “começar a” + infinitive: “(someone) started to (do something).” Used to describe the beginning of an action in the past, often as a reaction to something. The subject can vary: “Eu comecei a chorar”, “Ela começou a chorar”, “Ele começou a chorar”.
target_language_example: O Tom começou a chorar quando caiu.
native_language_example: Tom started to cry when he fell.

additional_notes: Used to say that rain began at a specific moment. It’s the past tense of “começar a + infinitive” (“to start to + verb”): começou (he/she/it started) + a + chover (to rain). Often appears with time words like assim que (as soon as), quando (when), pouco depois (shortly after).
target_language_example: A gente ia fazer um piquenique, mas começou a chover.
native_language_example: We were going to have a picnic, but it started to rain.

additional_notes: Past tense: "começar a" + infinitive means "to start/begin to (do something)." Here, "começou" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "começar" and is used for a completed event in the past. "Correr" means "to run," but it can also mean "to rush" depending on context.
target_language_example: Quando ouviu o barulho, ela começou a correr.
native_language_example: When she heard the noise, she started running.

additional_notes: Uses the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of **começar** (“to start”) + **a** + infinitive (**estudar**). The form **começou** is 3rd person singular (ele/ela/você). You can swap the language: *começou a estudar português/inglês*. In questions, it commonly appears with **já** (“already/yet”): *Você já começou a estudar francês?*
target_language_example: O Tom começou a estudar francês no ano passado.
native_language_example: Tom started studying French last year.

additional_notes: Past tense: “começou” is the preterite of *começar* (“to start”), and *a falar* means “to speak/talk.” Used when someone begins speaking, often after a moment or at a specific time (e.g., *assim que...* = “as soon as...”). You can change the subject: *eu comecei a falar* (I started), *eles começaram a falar* (they started).
target_language_example: Ela começou a falar quando o professor chegou.
native_language_example: She started talking when the teacher arrived.

additional_notes: Past tense (3rd person singular) of the phrase “começar a trabalhar.” Used to say when someone entered the workforce or began a specific job. Often followed by details like place (em Boston), time (em junho / ontem / há três anos), job role (como carpinteiro), or employer (para o tio).
target_language_example: Ela começou a trabalhar em uma loja quando tinha 18 anos.
native_language_example: She started working in a store when she was 18.

additional_notes: Used to talk about food/cooking from China or Chinese-style dishes, often in preferences (gostar de) or when saying what someone cooks (fazer). In Portuguese, the adjective usually comes after the noun: comida (food) + chinesa (Chinese, feminine to match comida).
target_language_example: Vamos pedir comida chinesa hoje à noite.
native_language_example: Let’s order Chinese food tonight.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the type of food (cuisine) from Japan. Often appears after verbs like gostar de (to like), comer (to eat), or acostumar-se com/a (to get used to). You can also say culinária japonesa for a more formal “Japanese cuisine.”
target_language_example: Hoje vamos comer comida japonesa no centro.
native_language_example: Today we’re going to eat Japanese food downtown.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens the same way it normally does (often with a hint of “no surprise”). It can go at the start of the sentence (Como de costume, …) or at the end (, como de costume).
target_language_example: Como de costume, ela chegou cedo ao trabalho.
native_language_example: As usual, she arrived early to work.

meaning: “like this” / “such as this” (referring to this thing/place/event).
additional_notes: Used to compare something to the one you’re pointing to or talking about right now. It agrees in gender/number with the noun: como este (masc. sing.), como esta (fem. sing.), como estes (masc. pl.), como estas (fem. pl.). Often appears after a noun: “um lugar como este” = “a place like this.”
target_language_example: Nunca vi um restaurante como este.
native_language_example: I’ve never seen a restaurant like this.

additional_notes: used before a singular masculine noun. It often makes comparisons ('like a') or shows a role, function, or job ('as a'). With a feminine noun, you would use 'como uma'.
target_language_example: Ele canta como um profissional.
native_language_example: He sings like a professional.

meaning: like a baby (very soundly; or crying/acting childishly).
additional_notes: Used after a verb to compare someone’s behavior to a baby’s. With dormir, it usually means “sleep very soundly/peacefully” (“sleep like a baby”). With chorar or agir, it often suggests crying a lot or acting immature/childish.
target_language_example: Depois da caminhada, eu dormi como um bebê.
native_language_example: After the walk, I slept like a baby.

additional_notes: Used with verbs to compare someone’s behavior or manner to what is considered (often stereotypically) manly: e.g., “se comportar como um homem” (“behave like a man”). It can also mean “as a (young) man” when talking about someone’s life stage (e.g., “Como um homem jovem…”).
target_language_example: Ele enfrentou o problema como um homem.
native_language_example: He faced the problem like a man.

meaning: like a fish (very well/easily; especially about swimming).
additional_notes: Used mainly in comparisons, especially with verbs like "nadar" (to swim): "nadar como um peixe" = to swim very well. It can also appear in other expressions, e.g., "beber como um peixe" = to drink a lot (alcohol). Related fixed phrase: "como um peixe fora d'água" means "like a fish out of water" (feeling out of place).
target_language_example: Ela nada como um peixe desde criança.
native_language_example: She’s been swimming like a fish since she was a child.

meaning: 'like a' / 'as a' (used to compare something to a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used in comparisons (similes): **como** = 'like/as' + **uma** = 'a/one' (feminine). It agrees with the noun that follows: **como um** (masculine) vs **como uma** (feminine). Often followed by a noun phrase: *como uma barata tonta* ('like a headless chicken'), *como uma luz deslumbrante* ('like a dazzling light').
target_language_example: Ele estava pálido como uma parede.
native_language_example: He was as pale as a wall.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like agir (to act), tratar (to treat), chorar (to cry), dormir (to sleep) to compare someone’s behavior to a child’s. It can be negative (immature: “Stop acting like a child”) or neutral/positive depending on context (e.g., “dormir como uma criança” = to sleep very soundly).
target_language_example: Ele respondeu como uma criança e depois pediu desculpa.
native_language_example: He replied like a child and then apologized.

additional_notes: Used to compare someone/something to the person you’re talking to. Very common after nouns like "alguém" (someone), "gente" (people), "uma pessoa" (a person): "alguém como você" = "someone like you." Depending on context it can also mean "as you" (in comparisons of how someone does something), but in these examples it means "like you."
target_language_example: Não conheço ninguém como você.
native_language_example: I don’t know anyone like you.

meaning: 'What do you mean?' / 'How so?' (often expressing surprise or disbelief).
additional_notes: Used as a reaction when you don’t understand, or when what someone said sounds wrong or surprising. It can be said alone as a question (“Como assim?”) or followed by what you’re questioning (“Como assim não vai…?”). Tone can range from genuinely confused to mildly confrontational depending on context.
target_language_example: —Vou cancelar a viagem. —Como assim? A gente já comprou as passagens!
native_language_example: —I’m going to cancel the trip. —What do you mean? We already bought the tickets!

additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s condition or how something is going (health, a situation, progress, etc.). It can be followed by a person or thing: "Como está o seu pai?" (How is your father?), "Como está sua tosse?" (How is your cough?). With a name or form of address, it works like a greeting: "Como está, Leon?" (How are you, Leon?). It can also appear after verbs like "ver" to mean “check how it is”: "Ver como está o almoço" (Check how lunch is).
target_language_example: Como está o trabalho hoje?
native_language_example: How’s work today?

additional_notes: Used to ask or express that something is impossible, unlikely, or unthinkable. Often rhetorical (e.g., expressing disbelief or insisting you wouldn’t do something). In questions, it can also mean “how would I be able to…?” depending on context.
target_language_example: Como eu poderia ajudá-lo sem saber o endereço?
native_language_example: How could I help you without knowing the address?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the way to do something or what is possible for you to do. Often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., ajudar, baixar, pular, resistir, saber, superar). In speech, it may be shortened to “Como posso…?”.
target_language_example: Como eu posso chegar ao centro de ônibus?
native_language_example: How can I get to the bus station?

meaning: "How did (it happen that)…?" / "How come…?" (asking how something happened).
additional_notes: Used to ask for an explanation of how something happened or how someone did something. It often sounds a bit more emphatic/curious than plain "como". Common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese before a past action (e.g., "Como foi que você…?").
target_language_example: Como foi que você aprendeu português tão rápido?
native_language_example: How did you learn Portuguese so fast?

additional_notes: Used to ask for an explanation of the cause or sequence of events (“How did this happen?”). It can also introduce an indirect question after verbs like dizer/explicar/contar/saber: “Ele explicou como isso aconteceu” (“He explained how that happened”). Often expanded with “exatamente” for emphasis: “Como isso aconteceu exatamente?”
target_language_example: Ainda não entendo como isso aconteceu.
native_language_example: I still don’t understand how that happened.

additional_notes: Used to express strong indignation or offense at what someone did or is doing. It’s a confrontational, rhetorical question and is followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., falar, cozinhar, ignorar) or sometimes a clause with "você" implied.
target_language_example: Como ousa me acusar sem provas?
native_language_example: How dare you accuse me without proof?

additional_notes: Used to question possibility, ability, or explanation. Often expresses disbelief or surprise ("How can you say that?") and is also used in indirect questions after verbs like querer saber (“to want to know”): “Ela quer saber como pode perder peso.” It can refer to a person or to “it,” depending on context; “Como pode isto ter acontecido?” = “How could this have happened?”
target_language_example: Como pode você achar isso normal?
native_language_example: How can you think that’s normal?

additional_notes: Used to ask how to do something or whether something is possible for the speaker. It is usually followed by an infinitive verb: como posso entrar, como posso ajudar. In some contexts, especially rhetorical ones, it can mean "how could I".
target_language_example: Como posso ajudar?
native_language_example: How can I help?

additional_notes: Uses the simple past of poder (pôde = “could/was able to”), often to criticize what someone did: “Como pôde fazer isso?” = “How could you do that?” It can also refer to things (not just people): “Como pôde durar tanto tempo?” = “How could it last so long?” Subject pronouns are often omitted; context tells whether it means “you/he/she/it.”
target_language_example: Como pôde dizer isso para ela?
native_language_example: How could you say that to her?

additional_notes: Used to ask how someone is sure about a fact or claim. Often followed by a full clause (subject + verb): "Como sabe que ele está lá?" You can change the subject and verb: "Como você sabe que..." (more explicit), "Como sabem que..." (you all/they know).
target_language_example: Como sabe que ela está dizendo a verdade?
native_language_example: How do you know she’s telling the truth?

additional_notes: Used in questions with the particle “se” to talk about how something is done in general, without saying who does it. Common with verbs like abrir, escrever, chamar, explicar, trancar, etc. Often translates as “How do you…?”, “How does one…?”, or “How is … done?” (not the same as “como se” meaning “as if/like if” in other contexts).
target_language_example: Como se usa isto?
native_language_example: How do you use this?

meaning: "what is it called?" / "what’s the name of…?"
additional_notes: Used to ask for the name of something. Literally “how is it called,” but in English it’s “what is it called?” Often followed by a noun or pronoun: Como se chama este/esse…? You can also add a language: Como se chama … em inglês/japonês?
target_language_example: Como se chama isso em português?
native_language_example: What is that called in Portuguese?

additional_notes: Used to ask for instructions or the method for doing something. Very common with an object (“Como se faz esta coisa?”) or with “para” + infinitive to ask how to do a specific action (“Como se faz para ligar esse computador?”). Often appears alone (“Como se faz?”) or as “Mostre-me como se faz!” (“Show me how it’s done!”). The “se” makes it an impersonal/passive-like expression (“how it is done”).
target_language_example: Você pode me explicar como se faz para abrir essa conta?
native_language_example: Can you explain to me how to open that account?

additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s emotional or physical state. Often appears alone as a question ("Como se sente?") or followed by context: "Como se sente agora?" / "Como se sente com..." / "Como se sente sendo...?". You may also hear the slightly more explicit version "Como você se sente?".
target_language_example: Como se sente depois da cirurgia?
native_language_example: How do you feel after the surgery?

additional_notes: Informal/colloquial way of saying “como estás?” In writing you may also see “como tás?” (with an accent) or, especially in Brazil, “como tá?” It’s used to ask how someone is doing (usually with friends, family, or in casual situations).
target_language_example: Ei, como tas? Tudo bem?
native_language_example: Hey, how are you? All good?

additional_notes: Common greeting/question asking about someone’s well-being. Often used as a standalone question (“Como vai?” = “How are you?”). You can add a person after it: “Como vai ele?” (How is he doing?), “Como vai a sua mãe?” (How is your mother doing?).
target_language_example: Olá, como vai você?
native_language_example: Hi, how are you?

additional_notes: A compositional phrase made of como + você. It often starts questions about manner or method: in natural English, this is usually rendered as "how do you..." or "how did you...," depending on the tense of the following verb. It can also appear in exclamations such as "Como você é...!" = "How ... you are!"
target_language_example: Como você fez isso?
native_language_example: How did you do that?

meaning: “How did you manage (to)?” / “How did you do it?”
additional_notes: Used to ask how someone was able to do something (often something difficult, surprising, or impressive). It’s usually followed by an infinitive verb (como você conseguiu fugir? = “how did you manage to escape?”) or by “isso” (como você conseguiu isso? = “how did you do that?”). In conversation, you can also just ask “Como você conseguiu?” when the action is clear from context. Note: in Brazil, “você” is common; in Portugal you may hear “Como conseguiste?” (informal) or “Como conseguiu?” (more formal).
target_language_example: Como você conseguiu terminar tão rápido?
native_language_example: How did you manage to finish so fast?

additional_notes: Most commonly used as a question to ask someone’s condition: “Como você está?” (“How are you?”). It can also appear inside a longer question (“Por que está perguntando como você está?” = “Why are you asking how I am?”). With an adjective, it can be an exclamation showing surprise/admiration: “Como você está bonita!” = “You look so beautiful!”
target_language_example: Oi! Como você está hoje?
native_language_example: Hi! How are you today?

additional_notes: Used to ask how someone is able/allowed to do something (“How can you contribute?”). It’s also very common to show surprise, disbelief, or criticism (“How can you not know?”, “How can you think such a thing?”). Often followed by an infinitive verb (contribuir, saber, pensar, permitir, etc.).
target_language_example: Como você pode dizer isso?
native_language_example: How can you say that?

additional_notes: Used to express shock, anger, or disappointment about something the other person did (often rhetorical). Literally "how you could"; *pôde* is the past of *poder* ("to be able to"). Commonly followed by an infinitive: *Como você pôde fazer/falar/ser...?* You can also use *como você pode...?* for present/ongoing situations.
target_language_example: Como você pôde mentir para mim?
native_language_example: How could you lie to me?

additional_notes: Used to ask what evidence or reason someone has for a statement. It’s usually followed by a clause (subject + verb): “Como você sabe que o Tom está lá?” In everyday conversation, you’ll also hear “Como você sabe disso?” (“How do you know that?” / “How do you know?”).
target_language_example: Como você sabe que ele está dizendo a verdade?
native_language_example: How do you know that he’s telling the truth?

additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s emotional or physical state (question) or to say you understand/know someone’s feelings (statement). Often followed by time/place words (agora, hoje, aqui) or by “sobre + topic” (“about + topic”). In writing, questions take a question mark: “Como você se sente…?”; as a statement it appears without one: “Sei como você se sente.”
target_language_example: Depois da notícia, como você se sente?
native_language_example: After the news, how do you feel?

meaning: 'how are you going to…?' / 'how will you…?'.
additional_notes: Used to ask about the way/plan/method someone will do something. It’s often followed by a verb in the infinitive (ajudar, contar, cozinhar, impedir, etc.). Not the same as 'Como você vai?' meaning 'How are you?' (greeting).
target_language_example: Como você vai chegar lá tão cedo?
native_language_example: How are you going to get there so early?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the way or method a group of people did something. It often starts a question: "Como vocês + verb...?" (e.g., chegaram = arrived, conseguiram = managed/got). "Vocês" is the common way to say "you" (plural) in Brazil.
target_language_example: Como vocês vão para o trabalho todos os dias?
native_language_example: How do you all get to work every day?

additional_notes: A common, friendly check-in question about someone’s situation in general. Often followed by “com + person” (Como vão as coisas com a Ana?), or “em + place” (…em casa, …em Boston). You can also use it alone as a general greeting.
target_language_example: Oi! Como vão as coisas por aí?
native_language_example: Hi! How are things going over there?

meaning: "how is it possible?" / "how can that be?"
additional_notes: Used to question how something can happen or be true; often rhetorical and shows surprise, disbelief, or complaint. You can also add "isso": "Como é possível isso?" (“How is that possible?”).
target_language_example: Como é possível que ele ainda não tenha chegado?
native_language_example: How is it possible that he still hasn't arrived?

additional_notes: Used in questions to add emphasis, very similar to simply using "como". It often doesn’t change the basic meaning, just makes the question sound more natural/insistent (like “how on earth…?” depending on tone). Common in both European and Brazilian Portuguese. Usually followed by the verb: "Como é que você fez isso?"
target_language_example: Como é que eu faço para pagar com cartão?
native_language_example: How do I pay by card?

additional_notes: Used to start questions, often with emphasis or surprise. You’ll commonly see it followed by a verb: “Como é que você faz…?”, “Como é que você se sentiu…?”, “Como é que você vai…?”. In casual speech it’s sometimes shortened to “como você…?”.
target_language_example: Como é que você aprendeu português tão rápido?
native_language_example: How did you learn Portuguese so fast?

meaning: "how is it...?" / "what's it like...?"; also "what did you say?"
additional_notes: Very common (and fairly informal) way to start a question, often equivalent to just “como...?” but more emphatic in speech: “Como é que é teu nome?” = “What’s your name?” It can also be used alone as “Como é que é?” to mean “Come again?” / “What did you say?” when you didn’t hear or you’re surprised.
target_language_example: Como é que é morar aqui no inverno?
native_language_example: What’s it like to live here in the winter?

additional_notes: Used after verbs like mostrar (to show), ensinar (to teach), saber (to know), and pedir (to ask) to talk about the method or steps for doing something. The pronoun isso usually refers to something not physically close or already mentioned ("that"), but many speakers also use it broadly like "this/that" in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Você sabe como fazer isso sozinho?
native_language_example: Do you know how to do that by yourself?

additional_notes: Used with negation after **como**. Common patterns: **Viu como não...** / **Eu sabia como não...** = “(You saw/I knew) that ... wouldn’t/didn’t ...”. It can also introduce an example or comparison: **..., como não me deixou...** = “..., like when you didn’t let me...”. Very often appears in **não tem como não + infinitive** = “there’s no way not to … / you can’t not …” (e.g., **Não tem como não rir**).
target_language_example: Não tem como não notar que ele está nervoso.
native_language_example: There’s no way not to notice that he’s nervous.

additional_notes: Used to agree to someone’s preference or instruction, often in a polite, formal way (e.g., with “senhor/senhora”). Depending on tone, it can also sound resigned or slightly sarcastic, like “fine, have it your way.” Often used as a short standalone reply.
target_language_example: —Posso sentar aqui? —Como queira.
native_language_example: —Can I sit here? —As you wish.

meaning: 'how do you say…?' (used to ask for a word or phrase).
additional_notes: Used when you want to know how to say something in Portuguese (or in another language). Often followed by the word/idea you want to translate, e.g., “Como se diz ‘thank you’ em português?” It can also be used to ask for the correct wording: “Como se diz isso de forma educada?”
target_language_example: Como se diz "receipt" em português?
native_language_example: How do you say “receipt” in Portuguese?

meaning: “how it’s done / how to do it.”
additional_notes: Used when explaining or demonstrating a process. Literally “how one does (it)”; "se" makes it impersonal (like “you/one”). Often appears after verbs like mostrar (to show), ensinar (to teach), and aprender (to learn): "mostrar/ensinar como se faz".
target_language_example: Você pode me mostrar como se faz esse bolo?
native_language_example: Can you show me how to make this cake?

additional_notes: Used to compare something to a hypothetical, imagined, or unreal situation. It often introduces a clause with the imperfect subjunctive: como se fosse, como se tivesse, como se quisesse. In negative expressions like não é como se..., it means 'it’s not like...'.
target_language_example: Ela me olhou como se me conhecesse.
native_language_example: She looked at me as if she knew me.

additional_notes: Used to describe an unreal or hypothetical situation, or to compare something to an imagined scenario. It’s commonly followed by a verb in the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., estivesse, fosse, tivesse). You can change the verb to match the subject and meaning: como se eu estivesse… / como se ela estivesse….
target_language_example: Ele falava baixo, como se estivesse com medo de acordar alguém.
native_language_example: He spoke quietly, as if he were afraid of waking someone up.

meaning: as if (it) were; like if (it) were.
additional_notes: Used to compare something to an imagined or unreal situation: “as if it were…”. Very common after verbs like falar (to speak), agir (to act), parecer/soar (to seem/sound), chorar (to cry). Often implies exaggeration, make-believe, or that something isn’t really true. It uses the past subjunctive of ser: fosse (from ser = to be). You can follow it with a noun (“como se fosse meu pai” = as if he were my dad) or a clause (“como se fosse verdade” = as if it were true).
target_language_example: Ela me olhou como se fosse a primeira vez que me visse.
native_language_example: She looked at me as if it were the first time she had seen me.

additional_notes: Used to say something is typical, expected, or happens every time. It can introduce a whole sentence ("Como sempre, ...") or come after what it describes ("... , como sempre"). Often carries a tone of mild criticism, admiration, or resignation depending on context.
target_language_example: Ele esqueceu as chaves, como sempre.
native_language_example: He forgot his keys, as usual.

additional_notes: Used for someone you share a bedroom or room with (e.g., in a dorm, shared house, or apartment). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people also often say “colega de quarto” or simply “meu roommate” in some contexts.
target_language_example: Meu companheiro de quarto chega tarde quase todos os dias.
native_language_example: My roommate gets home late almost every day.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that something/someone is very different from another thing/person, often with "de" ("diferente de mim" = "different from me"). It can describe a comparison (different from X) or a change ("as if he became a completely different person").
target_language_example: Depois da reforma, a casa ficou completamente diferente.
native_language_example: After the renovation, the house looked completely different.

additional_notes: "Comprar" means "to buy". "Alguma coisa" means "something" (an unspecified thing). You can add what it’s for with "para": "comprar alguma coisa para o Tom" = "buy something for Tom". In questions, it often means "anything": "Você precisa comprar alguma coisa?" = "Do you need to buy anything?"
target_language_example: Vamos comprar alguma coisa para o jantar.
native_language_example: Let’s buy something for dinner.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "comprar" (to buy) + the article "um" (a) + "carro" (car) + adjective "novo" (new). "Novo" agrees with "carro" (masculine singular). You can swap in other nouns/adjectives: "comprar uma casa nova" (buy a new house).
target_language_example: Estou economizando para comprar um carro novo no ano que vem.
native_language_example: I’m saving up to buy a new car next year.

additional_notes: Used when the noun is understood from context (e.g., a phone, computer, carpet). It agrees with the gender of the thing being replaced: comprar um novo (masc.), comprar uma nova (fem.). You can also say comprar um novo + noun: comprar um novo computador.
target_language_example: Meu celular quebrou, então vou comprar um novo.
native_language_example: My phone broke, so I'm going to buy a new one.

additional_notes: A common everyday phrase: "comprar" = to buy, "uma" = a, "casa" = house/home. Often used when talking about plans, wishes, or the real-estate market. You can swap in other things to buy: "comprar um carro" (buy a car), "comprar um apartamento" (buy an apartment).
target_language_example: Estamos pensando em comprar uma casa no próximo ano.
native_language_example: We’re thinking about buying a house next year.

additional_notes: Used to say you purchased one item (masculine singular) in the past. "Comprei" is the past tense of "comprar" (to buy) for "I". "Um" matches masculine nouns; with feminine nouns you usually use "uma" (e.g., "Comprei uma bicicleta"). Often followed by the item bought and possible descriptions: "Comprei um carro vermelho".
target_language_example: Comprei um presente para minha mãe.
native_language_example: I bought a present for my mom.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of comprar: comprei = “I bought.” Used to say you purchased a book, often followed by details like what kind of book (comprei um livro de piadas) or when (comprei um livro ontem). You can swap the object: comprei um café, comprei um presente.
target_language_example: Comprei um livro novo para estudar português.
native_language_example: I bought a new book to study Portuguese.

additional_notes: Past tense of "comprar" (to buy). "Comprou" usually means "he/she/you (formal) bought"—the subject comes from context (e.g., "Ela comprou...", "Tom comprou..."). You can add details with adjectives ("um carro vermelho" = a red car) or indicate who it’s for with "para" ("comprou um carro para Maria" = bought a car for Maria).
target_language_example: Ela comprou um carro usado ontem.
native_language_example: She bought a used car yesterday.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "comprar" for "he/she/you (formal) bought" + "uma casa" (a house). Used to talk about a completed purchase in the past; the subject is often a name or pronoun: "Ele comprou uma casa".
target_language_example: Ela comprou uma casa no ano passado.
native_language_example: She bought a house last year.
