additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "comprar" (to buy): "comprou" = "bought" (3rd person singular: he/she/you formal). Often used with a subject like "O Tom" or "Papai". "câmera" can mean a photo/video camera; in Brazil people also commonly say "câmera" for a phone’s camera.
target_language_example: Ela comprou uma câmera nova ontem.
native_language_example: She bought a new camera yesterday.

meaning: “to buy it / to buy him” (comprar + object pronoun lo).
additional_notes: “-lo” is a clitic pronoun attached to the verb meaning “it” or “him” (masculine object). It often attaches with a hyphen: comprá-lo = comprar + o. The accent (comprá-) keeps the stress when the pronoun is attached. You may also see future forms like “comprá-lo-ei” (“I will buy it/him”).
target_language_example: Eu vou comprá-lo amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m going to buy it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express agreement with someone. You can soften or qualify it with phrases like “em parte” (in part) or specify the topic with “sobre isso” (about that) / “nesta questão” (on this issue). Negative form: “não concordo com você” = “I don’t agree with you.”
target_language_example: Concordo com você, mas acho que podemos tentar de outro jeito.
native_language_example: I agree with you, but I think we can try a different way.

additional_notes: Past tense (ele/ela/você) of **concordar em + infinitive** to say someone agreed to do something: *concordou em pagar / ajudar / assinar*. In the present, you’ll often see **concorda em** (“agrees to”).
target_language_example: Ele concordou em esperar mais um pouco.
native_language_example: He agreed to wait a little longer.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or encourage trust. It can be a statement (Confia em mim.) or a question (Confia em mim?). It uses the verb confiar (“to trust”) with the preposition em (“in/on”): confiar em alguém = to trust someone. Also appears as “confie em mim” (more formal/polite) and “confia em mim, [name]” when addressing someone directly.
target_language_example: Confia em mim, vai dar tudo certo.
native_language_example: Trust me, everything will be fine.

additional_notes: Used to say you trust someone/something, or that you can count on them. Very common pattern: confiar em + person/thing (e.g., confiar em você). You can also use it with “poder”: Você pode confiar em mim. (“You can trust me.”).
target_language_example: Posso confiar em você com esse segredo?
native_language_example: Can I trust you with this secret?

meaning: to trust me; to rely on me.
additional_notes: Used when you want to reassure someone that you are reliable or honest. The verb is "confiar em" (to trust in), and you can swap the pronoun: confiar em você (trust you), confiar nele/nela (trust him/her), confiar na gente (trust us).
target_language_example: Pode confiar em mim: eu vou resolver isso hoje.
native_language_example: You can trust me: I’ll sort this out today.

meaning: to trust him; to rely on him.
additional_notes: Used when talking about trusting a specific man or relying on him to do something. In Portuguese, "confiar" commonly takes the preposition "em" (confiar em alguém), and "nele" = "em" + "ele" (literally “in him”). Often used in questions and advice, e.g., "Como posso confiar nele?" / "Você não deveria confiar nele."
target_language_example: Você não deveria confiar nele.
native_language_example: You shouldn't trust him.

additional_notes: Imperative form of "confiar" (to trust), used to ask someone to rely on you or believe what you’re saying. You can say it alone ("Confie em mim.") or followed by a name; it can sound reassuring, but also suspicious depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: Confie em mim — eu vou cuidar de tudo.
native_language_example: Trust me — I’ll take care of everything.

meaning: "(he/she/you) knows the" / "do you know the …?" (masculine singular object).
additional_notes: From the verb "conhecer" (to know, to be familiar with, to meet) + "o" (= "the", masculine singular). "Conhece o ...?" is a very common way to ask if someone knows/is familiar with someone or something. It can also be used in general statements and sayings (e.g., "se conhece o amigo" = "you get to know who your friend is").
target_language_example: Você conhece o caminho para a estação?
native_language_example: Do you know the way to the station?

meaning: to meet her; to get to know her.
additional_notes: "Conhecê-la" = "conhecer" (to meet / to know someone) + "-la" (her). It’s the infinitive "conhecer" with an accent (conhecê-) because a pronoun is attached. Used when you want to meet someone for the first time or get acquainted with them (not just recognize them).
target_language_example: Estou animado para conhecê-la amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m excited to meet her tomorrow.

meaning: to meet him; to get to know him.
additional_notes: Infinitive of "conhecer" + the object pronoun "o" (= him / it / you [formal]) attached at the end. When a pronoun is attached to an infinitive, the final "-r" drops and an accent is added: conhecer + o → conhecê-lo. Often used for meeting someone for the first time ("to meet"), not just already knowing them.
target_language_example: Tenho vontade de conhecê-lo pessoalmente.
native_language_example: I’d like to meet him in person.

meaning: “can do that / is able to do that.”
additional_notes: Uses the verb "conseguir" (to manage to, to be able to) + infinitive. "Consegue" is the he/she/you (formal) form in the present tense. Common in questions like "Você consegue...?" to ask if someone is capable of doing something or can manage it.
target_language_example: Você consegue fazer isso hoje?
native_language_example: Can you do that today?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "conseguir" to mean managing to obtain something. "Conseguir um emprego" focuses on successfully getting hired (not just looking). Often used with time expressions like "assim que eu puder" (as soon as I can) or "tão logo quanto eu puder" (as soon as I can).
target_language_example: Ela está tentando conseguir um emprego na área de tecnologia.
native_language_example: She is trying to get a job in the tech field.

additional_notes: Used when referring to fixing a specific issue or object already known from context. “Isso” usually means “that/this” (something not in your hands right now). Can be used for repairing objects, solving problems, or correcting mistakes. Common patterns: “Você pode consertar isso?” (Can you fix this/that?) and “Vou consertar isso.” (I’ll fix it.)
target_language_example: Calma, eu vou consertar isso amanhã.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll fix it tomorrow.

meaning: to fix it; to repair it.
additional_notes: "Consertá-lo" = "consertar" (to fix/repair) + "-lo" ("it/him," masculine direct object). In everyday use, it most often means “fix it” (a computer, car, phone, etc.). In Brazil you’ll also commonly hear the pronoun before the verb: "Vou consertá-lo" or "Vou consertar isso" (more common).
target_language_example: Meu celular parou de funcionar, mas o técnico vai consertá-lo amanhã.
native_language_example: My phone stopped working, but the technician will fix it tomorrow.

meaning: "I can do that/this"; "I’m able to do it".
additional_notes: Uses the verb "conseguir" (eu consigo) to express ability or managing to do something (often after effort). It’s similar to "posso fazer isso" (“can I do this?”) but "consigo" focuses more on capability/success. "isso" usually means “that/it” (sometimes “this” depending on context). In questions, you typically just use rising intonation: "Consigo fazer isso?"
target_language_example: Não se preocupa, eu consigo fazer isso.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I can do it.

additional_notes: Refers to an account you have at a bank for holding money and making transfers/payments. Common with verbs like abrir (open), fechar (close), acessar (access), and with prepositions like na/para a minha conta bancária (to/into my bank account).
target_language_example: Você pode depositar o pagamento na minha conta bancária?
native_language_example: Can you deposit the payment into my bank account?

meaning: 'of/for (someone/something)' in expressions about responsibility, care, or noticing.
additional_notes:
Usually appears with a verb and then "do" (or "da/dos/das"):
- **tomar conta do + noun** = to take care of / look after ("Tome conta do escritório.")
- **dar conta do + noun** = to manage/handle; sometimes to notice/be aware of ("Não deu conta do desaparecimento...")
- **dar-se conta do + clause/noun** = to realize ("Se deu conta do que falou?")
- **pôr na conta do + person/thing** = to blame/attribute to ("Põe na conta do Papa.")
target_language_example: Eu tomo conta do meu irmão hoje à noite.
native_language_example: I’m looking after my brother tonight.

additional_notes: Past participle form of the verb **contar** (“to tell”) + **a verdade** (“the truth”). It’s commonly used with auxiliary verbs like **ter/haver** (e.g., *ter contado a verdade* = “to have told the truth”) and especially in sentences about what someone should/shouldn’t have said (*devia/deveria ter contado a verdade*).
target_language_example: Você devia ter contado a verdade desde o começo.
native_language_example: You should have told the truth from the beginning.

additional_notes: Used when counting backwards (e.g., 10, 9, 8...) to a start time or event (a launch, the beginning of a game, etc.). Often said as an announcement: “Começa a contagem regressiva” (“The countdown starts”).
target_language_example: Preparados? Vou começar a contagem regressiva: dez, nove, oito…
native_language_example: Ready? I’m going to start the countdown: ten, nine, eight…

additional_notes: Used to introduce a requirement or condition that must be met for something to be acceptable or true. It’s often followed by the subjunctive (e.g., “contanto que seja…”, “contanto que não haja…”). You can place it at the start of the sentence or in the middle.
target_language_example: Você pode usar meu carro, contanto que devolva com o tanque cheio.
native_language_example: You can use my car, as long as you return it with a full tank.

meaning: to tell him; to inform him.
additional_notes: Uses the verb "contar" (to tell) with the indirect object pronoun "a ele" (= to him). Very common when you’re revealing news or information: "Não vou contar a ele" (I’m not going to tell him). In everyday speech, many people also say "contar pra ele" (more informal).
target_language_example: Eu preciso contar a ele a verdade hoje.
native_language_example: I need to tell him the truth today.

additional_notes: Used when someone reveals what really happened or speaks honestly. Common with verbs like "dever" (should) and often followed by "para" + person: "contar a verdade para alguém". You can also say "contar toda a verdade" (tell the whole truth).
target_language_example: Prometo contar a verdade para você.
native_language_example: I promise to tell you the truth.

additional_notes: Used with the verb contar (“to tell”) plus the contraction ao = a + o (“to the” + masculine singular noun/person). It introduces who you’re telling: contar ao Tom = “tell Tom.” For feminine names/nouns, use contar à (a + a): contar à Maria. You can also use contar a alguém (“tell someone”) when there’s no article, especially with pronouns: contar a mim/ele/ela.
target_language_example: Nós temos de contar ao Tom imediatamente.
native_language_example: We have to tell Tom immediately.

meaning: to count to ten; (also) to take a moment to calm down.
additional_notes: Literal meaning is counting from 1 to 10 (often used when asking about language ability: “Can you count to ten in…?”). It can also be used as a way to manage anger or stress (“count to ten before you react”). In threats or games it can introduce a countdown: “I’m going to count to ten and then…”
target_language_example: Quando eu fico com raiva, eu paro e vou contar até dez.
native_language_example: When I get angry, I stop and I’m going to count to ten.

meaning: to tell everything; to tell it all.
additional_notes: Used when you’ll reveal all the details/information (often about what happened). With people, you’ll commonly see: “contar tudo pra/pro alguém” (“tell someone everything”). Note: “contar” can also mean “to count,” so “contar tudo” usually means “tell it all” from context, not “count everything.”
target_language_example: Vou contar tudo sobre isso para o professor.
native_language_example: I'm going to tell the teacher everything about it.

additional_notes: Usually used with verbs like manter (keep), ter (have), perder (lose), and entrar em contato com (get in touch with). It can mean staying in communication with a person, or being connected/in touch with something (e.g., a plane, reality, a situation).
target_language_example: Eu perdi contato com meus amigos da escola.
native_language_example: I lost contact with my school friends.

additional_notes: Used for looking into someone’s eyes while interacting. Common with verbs like: fazer contato visual (make eye contact), manter contato visual (keep/maintain eye contact), evitar (fazer) contato visual (avoid eye contact), perder contato visual (lose eye contact). You can add "com" to specify the person: "contato visual com Maria".
target_language_example: Durante a entrevista, tente manter contato visual com o recrutador.
native_language_example: During the interview, try to maintain eye contact with the recruiter.

additional_notes: Imperative form of the verb **contar** (“to tell” / “to count”) + **me** (“to me”). Used to ask someone to give you information: **Conte-me a história** (“Tell me the story”), **Conte-me imediatamente se algo acontecer** (“Let me know immediately if something happens”). In Brazilian Portuguese, you’ll also commonly hear **me conte** with the pronoun before the verb, especially in everyday speech. Don’t confuse with **conte comigo** (“count on me”).
target_language_example: Conte-me quando você chegar em casa.
native_language_example: Let me know when you get home.

additional_notes: Imperative form of the verb "contar" (“to tell/to recount”) + "nos" (“to us”). Used to ask someone to tell or explain something to a group (the speaker included). Often followed by a direct object ("Conte-nos a história"), a clause ("Conte-nos o que sabe"), or "sobre" + topic ("Conte-nos sobre..." / more commonly "Conte-nos..." without repeating "sobre").
target_language_example: Conte-nos como foi a viagem.
native_language_example: Tell us how the trip was.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say someone kept doing an action: **continuar a + infinitive**. Here it’s **continuou** (he/she/it continued) + **a** + verb (e.g., *continuou a sair, a caminhar, a vencer, a gritar*). In Brazilian Portuguese you may also hear **continuou + gerund** (e.g., *continuou caminhando*), with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Mesmo cansado, ele continuou a trabalhar.
native_language_example: Even though he was tired, he kept working.

additional_notes: A common phrase for traditional children’s stories involving magic, fairies, princes/princesses, etc. Used like a normal noun; plural: "contos de fadas". You can also use it figuratively to mean something unrealistically perfect or unrealistic: "Isso é conto de fadas" (That’s a fairy tale / That’s unrealistic).
target_language_example: O autor traduziu o conto de fadas para nossa língua materna.
native_language_example: The author translated the fairy tale into our native language.

additional_notes: Used to show opposition to an idea, law, person, or action (ser/estar/votar contra a…; manifestar-se contra a…). It can also mean moving in the opposite direction of something (contra a correnteza = against the current) or going against a principle/expectation (ir contra a lógica = go against logic). Changes with the noun’s gender/number: contra o, contra os, contra as.
target_language_example: Sou contra a decisão, mas vou respeitá-la.
native_language_example: I'm against the decision, but I'll respect it.

additional_notes: Used to express opposition or being in conflict with something masculine singular. Common with verbs like lutar (to fight), ser (to be), estar (to be), bater (to hit). With rules or norms: “é contra o regulamento” = “it’s against the rules/regulations.” For voting/opinions: “estar contra o tratado” = “to be against the treaty.” It’s “contra o” because “o” = “the” (masculine singular); compare “contra a” (feminine), “contra os/as” (plural).
target_language_example: Eles estão contra o plano.
native_language_example: They are against the plan.

additional_notes: Used for the handheld device you use to control a TV, air conditioner, etc. Commonly shortened in speech to "o controle" when context is clear. You can specify the device with "da TV" / "da televisão" ("the TV remote").
target_language_example: Você viu o controle remoto?
native_language_example: Have you seen the remote control?

meaning: to convince him (to do something / of something).
additional_notes: "Convencê-lo" = convencer + "-lo" (him). The "-lo" is an object pronoun attached to the verb (common with infinitives), and it refers to a male person. Often used with: (1) "convencê-lo a" + infinitive (to convince him to do something), or (2) "convencê-lo de que" + clause (to convince him that...). In speech, many speakers also use "convencer ele" (more informal/colloquial), but "convencê-lo" is the more standard written form.
target_language_example: Preciso convencê-lo a vir comigo.
native_language_example: I need to convince him to come with me.

additional_notes: Used to dismiss what someone is saying as not serious, not true, or just wasting time ("Enough talk", "Stop with the BS"). Often appears with phrases like "chega de..." (enough of...), "para com..." (stop with...), or "sem..." (without...).
target_language_example: Chega de conversa fiada — vamos direto ao assunto.
native_language_example: Enough nonsense—let’s get straight to the point.

additional_notes: Means “to have a conversation with” someone. It’s followed by a person (or pronoun): conversar com alguém (to talk to someone), conversar com meus pais (to talk with my parents). Often implies a friendly or longer talk than just “speak to” (falar com), but they can overlap in everyday use.
target_language_example: Posso conversar com você depois do trabalho?
native_language_example: Can I talk to you after work?

meaning: to talk with you; to have a conversation with you.
additional_notes: Used when you want to speak directly with someone, often implying a longer or more serious chat than just saying a quick thing. You can add the topic with “sobre” (about): “conversar com você sobre...”
target_language_example: Preciso conversar com você depois da reunião.
native_language_example: I need to talk with you after the meeting.

additional_notes: "Conversou" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "conversar" (to talk/chat). It’s followed by "com" to introduce the person you talked with: "conversou com a Maria" (talked to Maria). In everyday English, this is often just "talked to" rather than the more formal "conversed with".
target_language_example: Tom conversou com Maria ontem.
native_language_example: Tom talked to Maria yesterday.

additional_notes: Used as a color adjective and usually stays invariable (no feminine/plural change): "um chapéu cor-de-rosa", "duas camisas cor-de-rosa". Often hyphenated (cor-de-rosa). Literally “color of a rose.”
target_language_example: Comprei uma blusa cor-de-rosa.
native_language_example: I bought a pink blouse.

meaning: “broken heart” (heartbroken; very sad because of love).
additional_notes: Often used with the preposition **de**: **estar/ficar de coração partido** = “to be/become heartbroken.” It can describe someone after a breakup, rejection, or unrequited love. Literally “broken heart,” and it matches English usage closely.
target_language_example: Ela terminou comigo e eu fiquei de coração partido.
native_language_example: She broke up with me and I was heartbroken.

additional_notes: Often used as “correr atrás de + noun/pronoun” (e.g., correr atrás do cachorro, correr atrás de um sonho). It can be literal (physically running after someone/something) or figurative (making an effort, taking initiative to achieve something). On its own (“Você precisa correr atrás.”), it implies “you need to take action / make it happen.”
target_language_example: Se você quer esse emprego, tem que correr atrás.
native_language_example: If you want that job, you have to go after it.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of **correr para** (“to run to/toward”), used to show quick movement in the direction of a person or place. It’s usually followed by a destination: **correu para a mãe** (to the mother), **correu para o quarto** (to the room). With a pronoun, it can be **correu para ela/ele** (“ran to her/him”).
target_language_example: Quando ouviu o barulho, ele correu para a porta.
native_language_example: When he heard the noise, he ran to the door.

additional_notes: Used for a machine that cuts grass (for a lawn/garden). Often comes with verbs like "funcionar" (to run/work), "precisar de" (to need), and "emprestar" (to lend/borrow). Also commonly said as "cortador de relva" in European Portuguese.
target_language_example: Vou usar o cortador de grama para cortar a grama do quintal.
native_language_example: I’m going to use the lawn mower to cut the grass in the backyard.

meaning: to cut your hair; to get a haircut.
additional_notes: Used for both cutting hair yourself and going to a barber/salon. Very commonly said as "cortar o cabelo" (generic), or "cortar o meu/seu cabelo". In requests/commands you’ll often hear "Preciso cortar o cabelo" (I need a haircut) or "Vai cortar o cabelo" (Go get a haircut).
target_language_example: Eu vou cortar o cabelo amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m going to get a haircut tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the style/result (“Esse corte de cabelo ficou ótimo”) or the act of getting a haircut (“precisar de um corte de cabelo”). Very common in salons and everyday conversation. Often appears with verbs like fazer (to get/do), precisar de (to need), and ficar (to look/turn out).
target_language_example: Vou fazer um corte de cabelo amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m getting a haircut tomorrow.

additional_notes: "Costumava" is the imperfect of "costumar" and expresses a past habit or a previous, regular state. It’s commonly used to contrast the past with the present (often with "como" / "não mais").
target_language_example: Este bairro costumava ser mais tranquilo.
native_language_example: This neighborhood used to be quieter.

meaning: “I believe/think that …” (expressing an opinion or uncertainty).
additional_notes: Common, slightly formal way to introduce what you think is true. Often used with negation: “não creio que …” = “I don’t think/believe that …”. In Portuguese, what follows frequently uses the subjunctive when it’s uncertain or denied (e.g., “Não creio que seja …”, “Não creio que tenhamos …”). Similar to “acho que”, but “creio que” can sound a bit more careful or formal.
target_language_example: Creio que ele vai chegar mais tarde.
native_language_example: I think he’ll arrive later.

additional_notes: Often a slightly more formal/literary alternative to “acreditar que”. Very common in the fixed pattern “fazer (alguém) crer que…” = “to make (someone) believe that…”. It’s followed by a clause introduced by “que”.
target_language_example: Temos motivos para crer que ambos estão perto.
native_language_example: We have reasons to believe that both are nearby.

additional_notes: Used mainly in legal, historical, and political contexts for extremely serious acts (e.g., slavery, torture, genocide) considered offenses against all humankind. Usually appears with the verb “ser” (é/foi) or “cometer” (cometer um crime contra a humanidade). Plural: “crimes contra a humanidade”.
target_language_example: O genocídio foi considerado um crime contra a humanidade.
native_language_example: Genocide was considered a crime against humanity.

additional_notes: Used to warn someone about something that could be dangerous, fragile, or cause problems. It’s often said as a standalone warning ("Cuidado com o cachorro!") or as advice ("Cuidado com seu orgulho"). Followed by a noun or pronoun (com + o/a/os/as, meu/minha, seu/sua, etc.).
target_language_example: Cuidado com essa escada; ela está molhada.
native_language_example: Be careful with those stairs; they’re wet.

meaning: 'Watch out for the' / 'Be careful with the' (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used as a warning. "Cuidado" means "care" and "com" means "with"; "a" is "the" for feminine singular nouns (e.g., a mala, a profundidade). With masculine nouns, it’s "cuidado com o".
target_language_example: Cuidado com a estrada molhada!
native_language_example: Watch out for the wet road!

meaning: "Be careful not to…" / "Watch out so you don’t…"
additional_notes: Used to warn someone to avoid a possible negative outcome. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb (often with a reflexive pronoun): "Cuidado para não se cortar" (Be careful not to cut yourself). You can also hear the shorter version "Cuidado para não + verb" in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Cuidado para não esquecer as chaves.
native_language_example: Be careful not to forget your keys.

meaning: to take care of; to look after; to see to (something)
additional_notes: Used for taking care of a person, animal, or thing, or being responsible for it. Also commonly used in the sense of handling/dealing with something: "Eu cuido disso" = "I’ll take care of that". With pronouns it often means taking care of oneself or someone else: "cuidar de mim" (take care of me), "cuidar de si mesmo" (take care of yourself/themselves).
target_language_example: Ouça, não precisa cuidar de mim o tempo todo.
native_language_example: Listen, you don’t need to take care of me all the time.

meaning: to take care of it/that; to handle it.
additional_notes: Used when you’re saying you will deal with a task, problem, or responsibility. "Disso" literally means "of that" and often corresponds to English "it" or "that" in context. Common in offers/assurances: "Deixa comigo, eu cuido disso" (Leave it to me, I’ll handle it).
target_language_example: Não se preocupe, eu vou cuidar disso amanhã.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll take care of it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Imperative form of "cuidar-se" used to tell someone to look after themselves, often when saying goodbye or as a warning to be careful. It can be polite ("Cuide-se, por favor") or sharp/insulting depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Está muito frio hoje—cuide-se!
native_language_example: It’s very cold today—take care!

additional_notes: Used to talk about how expensive it is to live in a place (prices of rent, food, transportation, etc.). Common in comparisons and discussions about salaries and inflation: “o custo de vida é alto/baixo”, “aumentou”, “subiu”.
target_language_example: O custo de vida nesta cidade é muito alto.
native_language_example: The cost of living in this city is very high.

additional_notes: Used to share a candid opinion or comment as if it were private or off the record. Often comes at the start of a sentence ("Cá entre nós,") to soften or introduce criticism, gossip, or a frank assessment. Tone can be friendly but may also sound judgmental depending on what follows.
target_language_example: Cá entre nós, eu não gostei muito desse filme.
native_language_example: Between you and me, I didn’t really like that movie.

additional_notes: A medical term meaning cancer in the lungs. Often appears with health topics like smoking (fumar / o fumo) and with the structure “morrer de …” (“to die of …”): “morreu de câncer de pulmão”.
target_language_example: Ele está em tratamento para câncer de pulmão.
native_language_example: He is being treated for lung cancer.

additional_notes: Very common in casual Brazilian Portuguese as a contraction of “você é louco”. It can be a real question (showing disbelief) or an exclamation reacting to something surprising, risky, or unbelievable. Often said to a friend, and it can sound rude depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Cê é louco? Não faz isso!
native_language_example: Are you crazy? Don’t do that!

meaning: a vicious circle (a self-reinforcing problem cycle).
additional_notes: Used to describe a situation where one problem causes another, which then makes the first problem worse, repeating in a loop. Often used figuratively in everyday speech; you may also hear the near-synonym “ciclo vicioso.”
target_language_example: Se eu durmo pouco, fico cansado e não consigo trabalhar bem; aí fico estressado e durmo ainda menos — é um círculo vicioso.
native_language_example: If I sleep little, I get tired and can’t work well; then I get stressed and sleep even less—it’s a vicious circle.

additional_notes: Used for a scannable square code (usually scanned with a phone camera) to open a link, check in, or identify someone. In Brazil and Portugal you’ll often see it in signs and forms like “Escaneie o código QR” (Scan the QR code). Pronounced like the letters “quê-erre” in Portuguese.
target_language_example: Você pode me mostrar o código QR no seu telefone?
native_language_example: Can you show me the QR code on your phone?

meaning: from class / of the class (de + a aula).
additional_notes: “Da” is the contraction of “de” + “a” (from/of + the). With “aula” (class/lesson), it often appears in common phrases like “antes da aula” (before class), “no meio da aula” (in the middle of class), “ausente da aula” (absent from class), and “expulsar da aula” (to kick/expel from class). In English you usually just say “class” (without “the”).
target_language_example: Cheguei atrasado e perdi o começo da aula.
native_language_example: I arrived late and missed the beginning of class.

meaning: "from the bed" / "off the bed" (from the bed’s surface).
additional_notes: "da" = "de" + "a" (“from/of” + “the”, feminine). Used to show movement away from the bed (cair/rolar da cama = fall/roll off the bed) or to mean “of the bed” when talking about parts/things that belong to it (lençóis da cama = the bed sheets). Contrast: "na cama" = in/on the bed; "na beira da cama" = on the edge of the bed.
target_language_example: Ela levantou-se da cama às sete.
native_language_example: She got out of bed at seven.

additional_notes: Contraction of **de + a casa**. Most commonly it means **“from the house”** (movement out of a house) or **“of the house”** (showing a relation to the house/home), depending on context. It also appears in the fixed expression **por conta da casa** = **“on the house”** (paid for by the restaurant/bar/store).
target_language_example: Ele saiu da casa bem cedo hoje.
native_language_example: He left the house very early today.

additional_notes: "Da" = "de" + "a". Use it with feminine singular nouns like "chuva" to express source/cause ("molhado da chuva" = wet from the rain) or belonging ("água da chuva" = rainwater).
target_language_example: O barulho da chuva me ajuda a dormir.
native_language_example: The sound of the rain helps me sleep.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de + a" (= "of/from the" for feminine singular nouns). Common in expressions like superlatives ("a mais ... da cidade" = "the most ... in the city") and to specify something belonging to or associated with the city ("o centro da cidade" = "the city center").
target_language_example: Esse é o melhor restaurante da cidade.
native_language_example: This is the best restaurant in town.

additional_notes: "Da" = "de" + "a". Most often it links something to the kitchen: "o chão da cozinha" (the kitchen floor), "o armário da cozinha" (the kitchen cabinet), "a mesa da cozinha" (the kitchen table). With foods, "cozinha" can mean "cuisine" (style of cooking): "cozinha chinesa" = Chinese cuisine.
target_language_example: As chaves estão em cima do balcão da cozinha.
native_language_example: The keys are on top of the kitchen counter.

additional_notes: “da” is a contraction of “de” + “a” (“of/from” + “the” feminine singular). So “da escola” can mean “of the school” (e.g., “o jornal da escola” = “the school newspaper”) or “from the school” depending on context.
target_language_example: Vou sair da escola às três.
native_language_example: I’m going to leave school at three.

meaning: from the station; (sometimes) of the station.
additional_notes: Contraction of "de + a". With movement verbs, it commonly means "from the station" (leaving/starting there): "sair da estação", "vim da estação". It can also mean "of the station" when describing something that belongs to or is related to a station, often clarified by context (e.g., "da estação de trem" = "of/from the train station").
target_language_example: Saí da estação e fui direto para o hotel.
native_language_example: I left the station and went straight to the hotel.

additional_notes: Contraction of **de + a** → **da**, used with the feminine noun **estrada** (“road”). It can mean **near/by the road** (*ao lado da estrada*), **on the road** (*do lado direito da estrada*), or **off the road** when used with verbs like **sair** (*sair da estrada* = to leave/go off the road). The exact meaning depends on the verb or preposition around it.
target_language_example: O carro saiu da estrada por causa da chuva forte.
native_language_example: The car went off the road because of the heavy rain.

meaning: “of the family” / “from the family” (family’s; one of the family).
additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "a" = "da". Most often marks something that belongs to the family ("o negócio da família" = the family business) or someone who is part of the family/household ("Ele é da família" = he’s one of the family). With feelings like "saudade", it can mean missing one’s family ("saudade da família").
target_language_example: Sinto saudade da família quando viajo.
native_language_example: I miss my family when I travel.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "a". Used to show possession/origin or association with the forest: "guardião da floresta" (guardian of the forest), "menino da floresta" (boy from the forest), "fronteira ... da floresta" (the forest’s border/edge).
target_language_example: Ele é o protetor da floresta.
native_language_example: He is the protector of the forest.

additional_notes: Used mainly in two common ways: (1) with nouns to mean the front one (e.g., "porta da frente" = "front door", "banco da frente" = "front seat"); (2) in expressions like "sair da frente" meaning "move out of the way". In the second use it often comes with "da minha frente" ("out of my way").
target_language_example: Pode sair da frente, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you move out of the way, please?

meaning: “of the war” / “about the war” (de + a guerra).
additional_notes: It’s the contraction of **de + a** before the feminine noun **guerra** (“war”): **da**. Used to link something to the war (e.g., *after the war*, *fear of the war*, *war effort*). With masculine nouns you’ll often see **do** (= de + o).
target_language_example: Eles falaram muito da guerra na aula de história.
native_language_example: They talked a lot about the war in history class.

additional_notes: Means “de + a história” (“of the story/history”). Used after a noun to specify what story/history you mean: versão da história (“version of the story”), fio da história (“thread/plot of the story”), crime da história (“crime in history”), período da história (“period of history”). Also appears in expressions like os dois lados da história (“both sides of the story”).
target_language_example: Antes de tirar conclusões, ouça o outro lado da história.
native_language_example: Before jumping to conclusions, hear the other side of the story.

meaning: “cool/awesome” (informal); or literally “of the time/hour” in phrases with hora.
additional_notes: Common slang in Brazilian Portuguese meaning “cool/awesome,” often used alone as a reaction: “Da hora!” You’ll also see the literal meaning in expressions like “perder a noção da hora” (to lose track of time), “passou da hora de…” (it’s past time to…), “me lembrar da hora” (to remind me of the time), and “ciente da hora” (aware of the time).
target_language_example: Esse lugar é da hora!
native_language_example: This place is awesome!

additional_notes: Contraction of **de + a**. Use **da igreja** to show possession/association (**o telhado da igreja** = the church’s roof) or origin/movement (**sair da igreja** = to leave the church). It can also appear in location phrases (**a oeste da igreja** = west of the church).
target_language_example: Depois da missa, eles saíram da igreja.
native_language_example: After mass, they left the church.

additional_notes: "Da" = "de" + "a". With "janela" (feminine singular), it can mean origin/source ("from the window": Ele pulou da janela.) or possession/association ("of the window": o vidro da janela = the window glass).
target_language_example: O barulho vinha da janela.
native_language_example: The noise was coming from the window.

additional_notes: Used mainly after clock times to specify that the time is in the morning: "às oito da manhã" = "at eight in the morning" (8:00 a.m.). It’s also used in ranges: "da manhã até a noite" = "from morning until night". Related: "de manhã" often means "in the morning" in a general sense (not tied to a specific time).
target_language_example: A reunião é às nove da manhã.
native_language_example: The meeting is at nine in the morning.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "a" = "da" (“from the” or sometimes “of the,” feminine). Used with "mesa" to show origin/removal or where something fell from: "caiu da mesa" (fell off the table), "tirou ... da mesa" (took ... from the table). Often contrasts with location phrases like "na mesa" (on the table) and "perto da mesa" (near the table).
target_language_example: Tirei o prato da mesa para limpar.
native_language_example: I took the plate off the table to clean.

meaning: in the same way; the same way.
additional_notes: Used to compare actions, feelings, or perspectives. Often appears with “que” to mean “in the same way as …” (e.g., “da mesma maneira que nós”). You can also use it on its own to mean “the same way” (e.g., “saio da mesma maneira” = “I leave the same way (I came in)”).
target_language_example: Eu penso da mesma maneira que você.
native_language_example: I think the same way as you.

additional_notes: Contraction of de + a minha, used before a feminine singular noun. It shows possession with a preceding preposition, so the exact English translation depends on context and the verb: it can be "of my," "from my," or simply "my" in natural English (for example, preciso da minha ajuda = "I need my help").
target_language_example: Tire as mãos da minha bolsa.
native_language_example: Take your hands off my bag.

additional_notes: Used to mean “of my house/home” or “from my house/home,” depending on the verb or expression. It’s the contraction of “de + a” (da) + “minha casa” (“my house/home”). Common in location phrases like “em frente da minha casa” (in front of my house) or “perto da minha casa” (near my house).
target_language_example: Tem um parque perto da minha casa.
native_language_example: There’s a park near my house.

additional_notes: "Da" is the contraction of "de" + "a". Use it to indicate possession or association (a photo *of* my family), or separation/origin (I got separated *from* my family; someone *from* my family). If the noun is masculine, it’s "do" (de + o): "do meu irmão".
target_language_example: Recebi uma mensagem da minha família ontem.
native_language_example: I got a message from my family yesterday.

additional_notes: "Da" is a contraction of "de" + "a" and can mean either possession/origin ("of") or source ("from"), depending on context. Used to identify something that belongs to your daughter ("o carro da minha filha" = "my daughter's car") or something that comes from her ("ganhei ... da minha filha" = "I got ... from my daughter").
target_language_example: Este brinquedo é da minha filha.
native_language_example: This toy is my daughter's.

additional_notes: "Da" = "de" + "a". It’s used mainly to show possession/origin ("a photo of my sister") or source ("a letter from my sister"). With verbs like "gostar", Portuguese uses "de": "gostam mais da minha irmã" = "like my sister more" (literally "like more of my sister"). "Da minha irmã" refers to something feminine singular ("a minha irmã").
target_language_example: Tenho saudades da minha irmã.
native_language_example: I miss my sister.

additional_notes: This is the contraction of "de" + "a" + "minha mãe" → "da minha mãe". Use it to show possession or origin: something that belongs to your mother ("É da minha mãe" = "It’s my mom’s") or something that comes from her ("uma carta da minha mãe" = "a letter from my mom"). In sentence 1, it appears inside a profanity/insulting outburst ("da porra da minha mãe"), which is very rude; the phrase "da minha mãe" itself is neutral.
target_language_example: Esse casaco é da minha mãe, mas eu posso pegar emprestado.
native_language_example: This coat is my mom’s, but I can borrow it.

additional_notes: Used after a superlative or strong statement to mean something is the biggest/best/worst, etc., you’ve ever experienced (e.g., “a melhor noite da minha vida” = “the best night of my life”). It can also be used more generally with “vida” in expressions about your personal life (“tomar conta da minha vida” = “take care of my own life”) and in commands like “Saiam da minha vida!” (“Get out of my life!”).
target_language_example: Foi o dia mais importante da minha vida.
native_language_example: It was the most important day of my life.

additional_notes: “da” is a contraction of “de + a” (of/from + the, feminine singular). Use it to indicate something that belongs to the mountain or is associated with it (e.g., o pico da montanha = the mountain’s peak; o ar da montanha = the mountain air).
target_language_example: Gosto do silêncio da montanha.
native_language_example: I like the quiet of the mountains.

additional_notes: “Da” is the contraction of “de + a” (“of/from + the” feminine singular). With “morte” (death), it’s used to talk about death in general (“vida depois da morte”) or a specific death (“a notícia da morte dele”, “depois da morte do autor”).
target_language_example: Tenho medo de falar da morte com as crianças.
native_language_example: I’m afraid to talk about death with the kids.

meaning: "of the mother" / "mom’s" (feminine singular: de + a mãe).
additional_notes: Used to show possession or origin with the noun "mãe" (mom): "a comida da mãe" = "mom’s food". It can also appear in the insult "filho(s) da mãe" (informal/strong), similar to "son(s) of a bitch" depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: O conselho da mãe foi muito bom.
native_language_example: Mom’s advice was very good.

meaning: "of the night" / "evening (one)" (as in “nightly news”, “this time of night”).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify “at night” or a “nighttime/evening” version of something: a esta hora da noite (“at this time of night”), o jornal da noite (“the evening news”). Often appears in fixed expressions like antes da noite (“before nightfall”) and da noite para o dia (“overnight; suddenly”).
target_language_example: Não gosto de sair sozinho a esta hora da noite.
native_language_example: I don’t like going out alone at this time of night.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "a nossa". Used before a feminine singular noun to mean "of our" or "from our" (e.g., "da nossa missão" = "of our mission"; "da nossa classe" = "from our class"). For masculine singular, use "do nosso".
target_language_example: Você se lembra da nossa primeira viagem?
native_language_example: Do you remember our first trip?

meaning: “of the pool” / “from the pool” / “out of the pool.”
additional_notes: "Da" is the contraction of "de + a" and changes meaning based on the verb/context: location/possession ("o fundo da piscina" = the bottom of the pool) or movement away ("sair da piscina" = to get out of the pool). It can also mean "from the swimming pool" as a place/setting (e.g., someone or something "da piscina").
target_language_example: As crianças saíram da piscina porque estava frio.
native_language_example: The kids got out of the pool because it was cold.

additional_notes: "Da" is the contraction of "de" + "a". Use "da polícia" to show that something belongs to, is associated with, or comes from the police (e.g., "arma da polícia" = police weapon). It’s also used in titles/roles and specific branches: "inspetor da polícia", "da polícia federal".
target_language_example: Ele recebeu uma ligação da polícia.
native_language_example: He got a call from the police.

additional_notes: *Da* is the contraction of *de* (“of/from”) + *a* (“the”, feminine). So *da porta* is used to talk about something belonging to the door (*a maçaneta da porta* = “the door handle”) or location/movement related to it (*de trás da porta* = “from behind the door”; *mais perto da porta* = “closer to the door”).
target_language_example: A chave caiu da porta.
native_language_example: The key fell from the door.

additional_notes: “Da” is a contraction of “de + a” (“from/of” + “the” feminine singular). So “da prisão” can mean “from the prison/jail” or, more generally, “of the prison,” depending on context (e.g., “da prisão da sua mente” = “from the prison of your mind”).
target_language_example: Ele saiu da prisão ontem.
native_language_example: He got out of prison yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the next occasion something happens. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis ("Da próxima vez, ...") or after the verb ("... da próxima vez"). Common with reminders, requests, or hopes for improvement.
target_language_example: Da próxima vez, a gente conversa com mais calma.
native_language_example: Next time, we’ll talk more calmly.

meaning: “of the street” / “from the street” (used in phrases like “the other side of the street,” “end of the street”).
additional_notes: It’s the contraction of **de + a** (feminine singular) → **da**. In these examples, it commonly appears in fixed location phrases: **do outro lado da rua** (“across the street”), **dos/dois lados da rua** (“on both sides of the street”), **ao longo da rua** (“along the street”), **no fim da rua** (“at the end of the street”).
target_language_example: A farmácia fica do outro lado da rua.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is across the street.

meaning: “from the room” / “of the room” (de + a sala).
additional_notes: Contraction of **de + a**. Use **da sala** mainly in two common ways: (1) **movement out of a room**: *sair da sala* = “to leave the room”; (2) **something belonging to/located in the room**: *o canto da sala* = “the corner of the room”, *a luz da sala* = “the room light.” Often contrasts with **na sala** (“in the room”) and **para a sala** (“to the room”).
target_language_example: Pode tirar essas cadeiras da sala, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you take these chairs out of the room, please?

additional_notes: Contraction of de + a + sua, used before a singular feminine noun. Depending on the verb or expression, it can mean 'of your' or 'from your'; in many sentences, English will translate it simply as 'your' because Portuguese often uses an article before possessives.
target_language_example: Preciso da sua ajuda.
native_language_example: I need your help.

meaning: "of your help" / "your help" (typically after verbs like "precisar de").
additional_notes: "da" = "de" + "a". It commonly appears after expressions that take "de", especially "precisar de" (to need). So "Eu preciso da sua ajuda" is literally "I need of your help," but natural English is "I need your help." With verbs that don’t take "de", you’d usually say "a sua ajuda" (e.g., "Quero a sua ajuda" = "I want your help"). "Sua" is a polite/common way to say "your"; depending on context/region, it can sometimes also mean "his/her".
target_language_example: Eu preciso muito da sua ajuda para resolver isso.
native_language_example: I really need your help to solve this.

meaning: of your family; from your family.
additional_notes: "Da" = "de" + "a" and often means "of the" or "from the". Use it to talk about something belonging to your family (e.g., "a vida da sua família" = "your family’s life") or someone who is a member of your family (e.g., "alguém da sua família" = "someone in/from your family").
target_language_example: Você recebeu notícias da sua família?
native_language_example: Have you heard from your family?

additional_notes: Used to refer to something belonging to or related to the person you’re speaking to (formal/polite “you”). It’s a contraction: de + a = da, so it literally means “of the your daughter (feminine)”. For “of your son,” use “do seu filho.”
target_language_example: Gosto muito da sua filha.
native_language_example: I like your daughter a lot.

additional_notes: "Da" is the contraction of "de" + "a" (feminine singular): "da" = "of the / from the". With a person, it often corresponds to English possessive: "a carta da sua mãe" = "your mother’s letter". It can also mean origin/source: "Eu apanhei mais da sua mãe" = "I got hit more by your mother" (i.e., by/from her).
target_language_example: Eu não achei o telefone da sua mãe.
native_language_example: I couldn’t find your mother’s phone.

meaning: of you / on your part (used to say it’s kind/nice of someone to do something).
additional_notes: Common in polite comments, often after an adjective like "gentil", "simpático", "legal": "É muito gentil da sua parte + infinitive" (e.g., ajudar, emprestar, oferecer-se). It highlights the other person’s action as considerate.
target_language_example: Foi muito atencioso da sua parte me avisar.
native_language_example: It was very thoughtful of you to let me know.

meaning: "of your life" (your personal life; your own life).
additional_notes: Literally "from/of your life" = de + a + sua + vida. Used to refer to someone’s life in general, often in phrases like "desistir da sua vida" (give up your life) or "cuidar da sua vida" (mind your own business). In the example, it suggests giving up your own life/routine to be with someone.
target_language_example: Você não precisa abrir mão da sua vida por causa de ninguém.
native_language_example: You don’t need to give up your life for anyone.

meaning: 'in the afternoon' / 'of the afternoon' (time period after midday).
additional_notes: Used after a clock time to specify that it’s in the afternoon (e.g., "às cinco da tarde" = 5 PM). It can also describe something related to the afternoon in general (e.g., "o sol da tarde" = the afternoon sun).
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar às três da tarde.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at 3 PM.

meaning: “in life”; in “O que você faz da vida?”, “what do you do (for a living / with your life)?”
additional_notes: “Da” is the contraction of “de + a” (“of/from + the” feminine singular), so literally it’s “of the life,” but in common phrases it often means “in life” or “in your life.” Very common in set expressions like “faz parte da vida” (“it’s part of life”) and as a casual way to ask someone’s job: “O que você faz da vida?” / “O que vocês fazem da vida?”
target_language_example: Ele mudou de cidade e começou uma nova fase da vida.
native_language_example: He moved to another city and started a new phase in his life.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "a" + "árvore". Used to express origin or movement away from a tree (e.g., cair/descer da árvore = to fall/come down from the tree), or possession/association (e.g., galhos da árvore = the tree’s branches).
target_language_example: As folhas caíram da árvore ontem à noite.
native_language_example: The leaves fell from the tree last night.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the most recent prior occasion something happened. Common patterns: “da última vez que…” = “the last time (that)…”, and “como da última vez?” = “like last time?”
target_language_example: Da última vez que fomos lá, estava fechado.
native_language_example: The last time we went there, it was closed.

additional_notes: “da” is the contraction of “de + a” and can mean “of the”, “from the”, or sometimes “in the”. With “vida” (life), it commonly appears in phrases like “a coisa mais importante da vida” (the most important thing in life) or “a canção da vida” (the song of life).
target_language_example: Ela é a pessoa mais importante da vida dele.
native_language_example: She is the most important person in his life.

additional_notes: Used for a woman who supports the bride during a wedding (part of the wedding party). In everyday Portuguese it usually means “bridesmaid”; “maid of honor” can be expressed as “a madrinha” or “a dama de honra principal,” depending on the region. Often appears with wedding-related words like “vestido de dama de honra” (bridesmaid dress).
target_language_example: Ela vai ser dama de honra no casamento da irmã.
native_language_example: She’s going to be a bridesmaid at her sister’s wedding.

additional_notes: Very informal and often rude/angry. Used as an exclamation to show you don’t care anymore (“Dane-se, vamos tentar!” = “Fuck it, let’s try!”). It can also be aimed at someone as an insult (roughly “fuck you”), especially with vocatives like “cara” or stronger insults; avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Dane-se, eu vou embora.
native_language_example: Fuck it, I’m leaving.

meaning: “in … (time) / … from now” (a time from the present).
additional_notes: Used to say how long from now something will happen: "daqui a duas semanas" = "two weeks from now". It’s commonly followed by a time expression (minutos, horas, dias, semanas, anos, etc.). You may also hear it in farewells like "Até daqui a duas semanas" (“See you in two weeks”).
target_language_example: Volto daqui a cinco minutos.
native_language_example: I’ll be back in five minutes.

meaning: in a little while; soon (a short time from now).
additional_notes: Used to say something will happen shortly after now. Common in spoken Portuguese to delay an action politely (e.g., calling back, coming back). It can stand alone as a brief reply (“Daqui a pouco.” = “In a bit / Soon.”). Often used with future tense or near-future context.
target_language_example: Espera um pouco — eu já falo com você daqui a pouco.
native_language_example: Wait a bit—I’ll talk to you in a little while.

additional_notes: Standard spelling is “dar à luz” (with a grave accent marking contraction: a + a = à). You requested the exact term “dar a luz” in the example, so the sentence below keeps that exact spelling even though it is nonstandard. Neutral/formal expression commonly used in news, medical, or written contexts. Less commonly, in a figurative/literary sense, it can mean “to bring to light” (reveal).
target_language_example: Ela vai dar a luz uma menina amanhã.
native_language_example: She is going to give birth to a girl tomorrow.

meaning: to hold hands; to give someone your hand (also: to help).
additional_notes: Often used literally for holding hands: “dar a mão a alguém” = to give someone your hand / to hold hands with someone. It can also be used figuratively to mean helping or supporting someone, similar to “lend a hand”.
target_language_example: Quer dar a mão comigo?
native_language_example: Do you want to hold hands with me?

meaning: to give someone the floor (let them speak); to give one’s word (promise).
additional_notes: Common in meetings, debates, and classrooms: "dar a palavra a alguém" = to allow that person to speak ("I’ll give the floor to Ana"). It can also mean to promise/commit to something: "dar a palavra" or "dar a sua palavra" = to give your word. Meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: Vou dar a palavra ao João para ele explicar.
native_language_example: I’ll give João the floor so he can explain.

additional_notes: Literally “to give a class/lesson,” but it’s the normal way to say “to teach” in many contexts. Often followed by the subject with “de” (dar aula de música = teach music) and/or the student(s) with “para” (dar aula para ele = teach him / give him lessons). Can be used generally (Eu gosto de dar aula. = I like teaching.) or for a specific lesson (Não posso te dar aula amanhã. = I can’t teach you / give you a lesson tomorrow.)
target_language_example: Eu gosto de dar aula.
native_language_example: I like teaching.

meaning: To pay attention to; to show interest (often romantic).
additional_notes: Common in Brazil and usually informal. Often used in the negative to say you’re ignoring someone: “não dar bola (para alguém)” = “not to pay attention to someone / not to care.” It can also mean showing interest or “giving someone a chance,” especially in flirting contexts.
target_language_example: Eu vou dar bola pra ele na festa, mas espero que ele perceba.
native_language_example: I’m going to show interest in him at the party, but I hope he notices.

meaning: to call the shots; to be the one in control.
additional_notes: Common idiom meaning someone is the decision-maker or dominates a situation (in a group, a business, politics, a game, etc.). Often used with an explicit subject: "Quem dá cartas aqui sou eu" ("I'm the one in charge here"). Not usually understood literally as "give cards".
target_language_example: Naquela empresa, é o diretor financeiro que dá cartas.
native_language_example: In that company, the CFO is the one who calls the shots.

meaning: to work out; to succeed; to turn out well.
additional_notes: Commonly used to say a plan/idea/relationship will succeed or that things will be okay ("vai dar certo"). You can also use it with "fazer" to mean "make it work" (e.g., "fazer dar certo").
target_language_example: Calma — vai dar certo.
native_language_example: Relax — it’ll work out.

meaning: to manage/cope with (something); (dar-se conta) to realize/notice.
additional_notes: Very common in Brazil. With a direct object, it often means “to handle/deal with”: "Não dou conta do trabalho." = “I can’t handle the work.” In questions like "Vai dar conta?", it means “Can you handle it / Will you manage?” In the reflexive form "dar-se conta (de)", it means “to realize/notice”: "Nem me dei conta." = “I didn’t even realize.” Depending on context, it can also imply being able to “take on/defeat” someone (e.g., "dar conta dele").
target_language_example: Você acha que vai dar conta de fazer isso hoje?
native_language_example: Do you think you’ll be able to manage to do this today?

meaning: to work hard; to put in a lot of effort.
additional_notes: Common in Brazil (and understood elsewhere) to talk about working/studying intensely or making a big effort toward a goal. It can refer to a job, school, training, or any situation where you’re really trying. It’s fairly colloquial.
target_language_example: Eu preciso dar duro para passar no concurso.
native_language_example: I need to work hard to pass the exam (for a public job).

meaning: to hit on (someone); to flirt with (someone).
additional_notes: Usually used as “dar em cima de alguém”. It’s a common, informal way to say someone is flirting aggressively or making romantic/sexual advances.
target_language_example: Ele estava tentando dar em cima dela na festa.
native_language_example: He was trying to hit on her at the party.

meaning: to get on someone’s nerves; to really annoy/irritate.
additional_notes: Common, conversational expression. Usually used with an indirect object: “dar-me nos nervos” (get on my nerves), “dar-te nos nervos” (get on your nerves), “dar-lhe nos nervos” (get on his/her nerves). You can also say “isso dá-me nos nervos” (“that gets on my nerves”).
target_language_example: Esse barulho dá-me nos nervos.
native_language_example: That noise gets on my nerves.

meaning: to leave/get out (quickly); to take off; to get out of there.
additional_notes: Very common, informal Brazilian Portuguese expression meaning to go away/leave a place, often suddenly or because it’s better to go (e.g., danger, awkward situation). Can also imply walking out on someone/ending things abruptly depending on context. Used as a verb phrase with normal conjugation (e.g., "vou dar o fora", "vamos dar o fora").
target_language_example: Quando a polícia chegou, resolvemos dar o fora.
native_language_example: When the police arrived, we decided to get out of there.

meaning: to listen to; to pay attention to (someone’s advice/warnings).
additional_notes: Used when someone chooses (or refuses) to take what another person says seriously. Commonly used with “a”: “dar ouvidos a alguém” (to listen to someone). In the negative, it means to ignore: “não dar ouvidos”.
target_language_example: Você deveria dar ouvidos a Tom.
native_language_example: You should listen to Tom.

additional_notes: Used with a direct object (the thing) + "para" + the recipient, or with "para" + recipient + the thing: "dar [algo] para [alguém]" / "dar para [alguém] [algo]". In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, "para" is often shortened to "pra": "dar pra".
target_language_example: O Tom decidiu dar para a Mary tudo o que ela pediu.
native_language_example: Tom decided to give Mary everything she asked for.

meaning: to find a way; to fix/handle something (often by improvising).
additional_notes: Used when you need to make something work, solve a problem, or arrange a workaround—often with the sense of “we’ll manage somehow.” Common patterns: “dar um jeito de + infinitive” (find a way to do something) and “dar um jeito em/na + noun” (fix/straighten out something: a problem, your life, a situation). In some contexts it can also suggest “pulling strings” or making an arrangement.
target_language_example: Nós precisamos dar um jeito de resolver este problema.
native_language_example: We need to find a way to solve this problem.

meaning: to go for a walk; to take a stroll.
additional_notes: A very common, neutral way to suggest a short, leisurely walk (often for pleasure, to get some air, or to look around). Often used in invitations: “Quer/Vamos dar um passeio?” You can also say where: “dar um passeio no parque / pela cidade”.
target_language_example: Depois do jantar, vamos dar um passeio no parque.
native_language_example: After dinner, let’s go for a walk in the park.

meaning: to go for a walk; to take a walk.
additional_notes: A very common, natural way to talk about going for a walk (often for leisure or light exercise). It’s often used with “sair para” (to go out to) or “ir” (to go): “sair para dar uma caminhada”, “fui dar uma caminhada”. You can add details like time/place: “de manhã cedo” (early in the morning), “no parque” (in the park).
target_language_example: Vamos dar uma caminhada depois do jantar?
native_language_example: Shall we go for a walk after dinner?

meaning: to give someone a hand; to help.
additional_notes: Common everyday expression for offering or asking for help (often with a specific task). It can be used alone ("Você vai me dar uma mão?") or with a preposition to specify the area/task: "dar uma mão na cozinha" (help in the kitchen) / "dar uma mão com isso" (help with this). Usually takes an indirect object: "me/te/lhe/nos dar uma mão".
target_language_example: Você pode me dar uma mão com essas caixas?
native_language_example: Can you give me a hand with these boxes?

additional_notes: Common, polite way to say you will look at something briefly or check it. Often used with invitations/requests: "Você quer dar uma olhada?" (Do you want to take a look?). You can add context with prepositions: "dar uma olhada em" (take a look at something) and "dar uma olhada ao redor" (look around).
target_language_example: Posso dar uma olhada no documento rapidinho?
native_language_example: Can I take a quick look at the document?

meaning: to go for a walk/drive; to take a stroll/ride.
additional_notes: Common way to say you’re going out briefly just to walk around, get some fresh air, or drive around with no specific destination. Often used with "sair" (e.g., "saí para dar uma volta") and as an invitation ("Vamos dar uma volta?"). Depending on context, it can be on foot or by car/bike.
target_language_example: Depois do jantar, vamos dar uma volta no bairro.
native_language_example: After dinner, let’s go for a walk around the neighborhood.

meaning: to act like / to pretend to be (often in an annoying, ironic, or critical way)
additional_notes: Common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese. Use it before a noun or adjective to say someone is “playing at being” something: "dar uma de esperto" (act all smart), "dar uma de vítima" (play the victim), "dar uma de chefe" (act like the boss). It often implies disapproval or sarcasm.
target_language_example: Ele vive dando uma de esperto, mas não sabe de nada.
native_language_example: He’s always acting all smart, but he doesn’t know anything.

additional_notes: Often used with "a": "dar valor a (algo/alguém)" = to value/appreciate (something/someone). It can mean recognizing importance or being grateful (sometimes after not appreciating it before). You may also hear it as advice/criticism: "Você tem que dar valor!" = "You need to appreciate it!"
target_language_example: Você precisa dar valor ao que tem.
native_language_example: You need to appreciate what you have.

meaning: to take a turn / go around; to take a walk or short ride (often: “dar uma volta”).
additional_notes: Often appears with an article: **dar uma volta** (“to take a walk/short ride” or “go around the block”) and in the plural **dar voltas** (“to go around in circles”). You can specify what you go around with **dar a volta em/no/na**: *dar a volta no quarteirão* (“go around the block”). It’s built from **dar** (“to give”) + **volta** (“turn/return/lap”), but the idiomatic meaning is not literally “give a turn.”
target_language_example: Vamos dar volta no quarteirão depois do jantar?
native_language_example: Shall we go around the block after dinner?

additional_notes: Common, neutral expression used mainly for humans (and sometimes animals). Often used without mentioning the baby (e.g., "estar prestes a dar à luz" = to be about to give birth), or with an object ("dar à luz um/uma..." = to give birth to a...). Although the literal words are “give to the light,” the idiomatic meaning is “give birth.”
target_language_example: Maria está prestes a dar à luz.
native_language_example: Maria is about to give birth.

meaning: old-school; from back in the day.
additional_notes: Informal Brazilian Portuguese expression used to describe something from earlier times (music, clothes, habits, jokes, etc.), often with a nostalgic or “classic” feel. Common patterns: “coisa das antigas” (old-school stuff) and “(ser) das antigas” (to be old-school, to like things the old way).
target_language_example: Essa música é das antigas, mas eu ainda adoro.
native_language_example: This song is old-school, but I still love it.

additional_notes: “Das” = “de + as” (of/about/from + the, feminine plural). Use it with verbs/adjectives that take “de” to mean “about” or “of”: e.g., “cuidar das coisas” (take care of things), “esquecer das coisas” (forget things), “saber das coisas” (know about things). In “uma das coisas…”, it means “one of the things…”.
target_language_example: Não se preocupe com isso; eu cuido das coisas.
native_language_example: Don’t worry about it; I’ll take care of things.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a description or clause about specific things. It’s the contraction of "de" + "as" (“of” + “the” feminine plural) + "coisas" (“things”) + "que" (“that/which”). Common after verbs/nouns like "lembrar-se de" (to remember), "falar de" (to talk about), or "natureza/gênero de" (the nature/type of).
target_language_example: Ela se esqueceu das coisas que eu disse ontem.
native_language_example: She forgot the things that I said yesterday.

meaning: “of the children” / “the children” (after certain verbs and prepositions).
additional_notes: Contraction of **de + as** (“of/from/about” + “the” feminine plural) → **das**. Used before **crianças** (“children”), a feminine plural noun. Common after verbs/prepositions like **cuidar de** (to take care of), **perto de** (near), and in phrases like **a educação das crianças** (“the children’s education”).
target_language_example: Não fale assim na frente das crianças.
native_language_example: Don’t talk like that in front of the children.

meaning: “of my” / “from my” (feminine plural); often “of mine” or “one of my …” depending on context.
additional_notes: Contraction of **de + as minhas**. Used with feminine plural nouns: **das minhas piadas** (“of my jokes”), **das minhas filhas** (“of my daughters”). After words like **uma** (“one”), it commonly means **“one of my …”**: **uma das minhas citações** (“one of my quotes”). With verbs that take **de** (like **precisar de** = “to need”), it can mean “(some) of my …”: **Preciso das minhas ferramentas** (“I need my tools / I need some of my tools”).
target_language_example: Esta é uma das minhas fotos favoritas.
native_language_example: This is one of my favorite photos.

meaning: 'of the clouds' / 'from the clouds' (de + as nuvens).
additional_notes: "Das" is the contraction of "de + as" ("of/from the" + feminine plural). The exact meaning depends on the verb/preposition before it: e.g., "atrás das nuvens" = "behind the clouds" (atrás de), "acima das nuvens" = "above the clouds" (acima de), "sombras das nuvens" = "shadows of the clouds". In "sai das nuvens", it’s literally "come out of the clouds" and can be used like telling someone to stop daydreaming.
target_language_example: O sol apareceu depois das nuvens.
native_language_example: The sun appeared after the clouds.

meaning: “of the people” / “from the people”; also used like “(some) of the people” after a quantity or superlative.
additional_notes: Contraction of **de + as** (“of/from” + “the” feminine plural) → **das**, used with the plural noun **pessoas** (“people”). Common after expressions like **a menor** (“the smallest”), **muitas** (“many”), **algumas** (“some”), etc.: **a menor das pessoas** = “the smallest/least among people,” **muitas das pessoas** = “many of the people.” Also appears with relative clauses: **das pessoas que...** = “of the people who...”.
target_language_example: Algumas das pessoas na fila estavam com pressa.
native_language_example: Some of the people in the line were in a hurry.

meaning: “of/from your” (feminine plural), i.e., “of/from yours” depending on context.
additional_notes: Contraction of **de + as suas**. It’s used before a **feminine plural** noun: *das suas coisas* (“from your things”), *das suas fotos* (“of your photos”). It can refer to **your / his / her / their** depending on the form of address and context (e.g., *Você* uses *suas*).
target_language_example: Eu preciso de algumas das suas respostas até amanhã.
native_language_example: I need some of your answers by tomorrow.

meaning: "of Jesus"; also a common part of Portuguese names (surname element).
additional_notes: Literally "of Jesus" (de + Jesus). It can refer to Jesus Christ in phrases like "histórias sobre a infância de Jesus" (stories about Jesus’ childhood) or "um quadro de Jesus" (a painting of Jesus). It’s also very common in full names as a family-name element (e.g., "Alexandre de Jesus..."), and in that case it usually isn’t translated—it's just part of the person’s name. "Jesus" is typically capitalized when referring to Jesus Christ.
target_language_example: Ela tem uma foto de Jesus na sala.
native_language_example: She has a photo of Jesus in the living room.

meaning: "Christmas" (used to describe something related to Christmas).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean “Christmas + noun” / “for Christmas,” especially with things like cartões de Natal (Christmas cards), enfeites de Natal (Christmas decorations), presente de Natal (Christmas present). Often corresponds to English “Christmas” used as an adjective.
target_language_example: Comprei um suéter de Natal para a festa.
native_language_example: I bought a Christmas sweater for the party.

meaning: "of such-and-such" / "so-and-so" (used when the person or thing isn’t specified).
additional_notes: Used after a name or noun to mean “so-and-so,” especially when you don’t know, don’t remember, or don’t want to mention the exact name. Very common in the fixed expression "Fulano de Tal" (“so-and-so”).
target_language_example: Ele disse que falou com o Fulano de Tal, mas não explicou quem era.
native_language_example: He said he talked to so-and-so, but he didn’t explain who it was.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar/ficar to say you agree with someone: “Estou (totalmente/parcialmente) de acordo com você.” It can also be used alone as a short reply meaning “OK / agreed” (“De acordo?” = “Agreed?”). “Nunca estaremos de acordo” means “We’ll never agree / be on the same page.”
target_language_example: De acordo — vamos fazer assim.
native_language_example: OK—let’s do it that way.

additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is based on a source (a newspaper, a person, a report) or follows a rule/standard (a situation, instructions, your age). Common in formal and neutral contexts. Often placed at the start of a sentence when citing a source: “De acordo com o jornal, …”.
target_language_example: De acordo com as regras, não é permitido fumar aqui.
native_language_example: According to the rules, smoking isn’t allowed here.

additional_notes: Used to mark a change starting at the present moment and continuing into the future. Often appears at the beginning of the sentence, followed by a comma, but can also be placed later in the sentence. Common in promises, rules, decisions, or new habits.
target_language_example: De agora em diante, vou estudar português todos os dias.
native_language_example: From now on, I'm going to study Portuguese every day.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened or is true in an unclear, unspecified, or not fully explained way. Often used when the method isn’t known (“somehow”) or when there’s a partial similarity/difference (“in some way”). Can appear at the start of the sentence or after the subject, often set off by commas.
target_language_example: De algum modo, vamos dar um jeito.
native_language_example: Somehow, we’ll make it work.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition "de" + "alguma coisa" (“something”). Common after verbs/expressions that require "de", such as: "saber de" (to know about), "precisar de" (to need), "brincar de" (to play at/pretend), and "esquecer-se de" (to forget). It refers to an unspecified thing and often implies “anything” in offers ("precisar de alguma coisa?").
target_language_example: Se você souber de alguma coisa, me avise.
native_language_example: If you know about something, let me know.

meaning: 'somehow' / 'in some way' (often: 'in some way or another').
additional_notes: Used to say something happens or is possible, but you don’t know exactly how, or you’re speaking generally about a way/method. Common in questions offering help: “Posso ajudar de alguma forma?” = “Can I help in any way?” Often appears at the beginning or between commas for emphasis: “De alguma forma, …”.
target_language_example: De alguma forma, vamos resolver isso hoje.
native_language_example: Somehow, we’re going to sort this out today.

meaning: "of love" / "about love" (used to describe something related to love).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify that it has to do with love: carta de amor (love letter), história de amor (love story), falar de amor (to talk about love). In phrases like só de amor, it means “only on love” (i.e., love alone isn’t enough to live on).
target_language_example: Ele escreveu uma canção de amor para ela.
native_language_example: He wrote a love song for her.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say it’s for someone’s birthday or related to a birthday: jantar de aniversário (birthday dinner), presente(s) de aniversário (birthday present(s)), cartão de aniversário (birthday card).
target_language_example: Vamos fazer um bolo de aniversário para ela.
native_language_example: Let’s make a birthday cake for her.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something known, done, or said before an event happens. Very common with thanks or apologies: “Obrigado(a) de antemão” = “Thanks in advance.” It can go at the beginning or end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Peço desculpa de antemão por qualquer atraso.
native_language_example: I apologize in advance for any delay.

meaning: "to learn new things" (used after verbs like gostar).
additional_notes: Most commonly appears after verbs that take the preposition "de", especially "gostar de" (to like/enjoy). So "gostar de aprender coisas novas" = "to like learning new things." You can change the person/tense of the surrounding verb (e.g., "pensei que você gostasse...").
target_language_example: Ela gosta de aprender coisas novas todos os dias.
native_language_example: She likes learning new things every day.

meaning: “of art”; used to describe something related to art.
additional_notes: Often used after a noun to specify a type/category: museu de arte (“art museum”), comerciante de arte (“art dealer”), obra de arte (“work of art”).
target_language_example: Ela trabalha em um museu de arte.
native_language_example: She works at an art museum.

meaning: by plane; on a plane (traveling by air).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like "ir", "viajar", and "andar" to say the means of transportation (how you travel). Common patterns: "ir de avião" (go by plane), "viajar de avião" (travel by plane), "andar de avião" (fly / travel by plane). Also appears in nouns like "passagem de avião" (plane ticket).
target_language_example: Vamos de avião para Lisboa amanhã.
native_language_example: We’re going to Lisbon by plane tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say the color something is (especially after verbs like pintar, tingir, colorir). It often comes after the past participle: "pintado de azul" = "painted blue." You can add shades: "de azul claro" (light blue).
target_language_example: Eles pintaram a parede de azul.
native_language_example: They painted the wall blue.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean that something is meant for drinking: "água de beber" (drinking water), "algo/alguma coisa de beber" (something to drink). It’s often used when offering or asking for a beverage.
target_language_example: Tem alguma coisa de beber?
native_language_example: Is there anything to drink?

meaning: “of baseball” / “baseball” (used to describe something related to baseball).
additional_notes: Uses the preposition "de" to say that something is related to baseball: "taco de beisebol" (baseball bat), "campo de beisebol" (baseball field), "jogo de beisebol" (baseball game), "equipe de beisebol" (baseball team). "Beisebol" is the Portuguese word for "baseball".
target_language_example: Ele comprou uma luva de beisebol.
native_language_example: He bought a baseball glove.

meaning: on good terms; at peace (with someone).
additional_notes: Common in the pattern “ficar de bem com (alguém)” = “to make up with / be on good terms with (someone)”.
