As a standalone reply (“De bem!”), it can mean “All good!” or “No hard feelings!” In some contexts “de bem + adv/adj” is an intensifier meaning “really/quite” (e.g., “de bem longe” = “from really far away”, “de bem mais” = “quite a bit more”).
target_language_example: Depois da discussão, a gente ficou de bem.
native_language_example: After the argument, we made up / we were on good terms.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of going/traveling (ir, andar, chegar, voltar) to say the means of transportation: ir de bicicleta = to go by bike. You can contrast it with other transport using "de" (de carro, de ônibus, etc.).
target_language_example: Hoje vou de bicicleta para o trabalho.
native_language_example: Today I'm going to work by bike.

additional_notes: Common in informal Brazilian Portuguese, especially in replies like “Tô de boa” / “Não, tô de boa” meaning “I’m good” (often: “No thanks, I’m fine”). It can also mean “calmly/peacefully” (“vai de boa” = “go easy”). Note: “de boa fé” is a different fixed expression meaning “in good faith,” and “de boa aparência/família” means “of good appearance/family,” not the same slang use.
target_language_example: Hoje eu tô de boa, prefiro ficar em casa.
native_language_example: Today I’m good—I’d rather stay home.

additional_notes: Used to show that someone does something freely, without pressure or reluctance. It can also imply a friendly attitude or intention (“good will”), especially in expressions like “um gesto de boa vontade” (a goodwill gesture).
target_language_example: Eu assinei o acordo de boa vontade, sem ninguém me obrigar.
native_language_example: I signed the agreement willingly, without anyone forcing me.

additional_notes: Used to say you do something voluntarily and with a good attitude (not reluctantly). Common with verbs like aceitar (accept), cumprir (fulfill), fazer (do), dizer (say), ajudar (help). It can appear before or after the verb: “aceitou de bom grado” / “de bom grado aceitou”.
target_language_example: Eu ajudaria de bom grado, se você precisar.
native_language_example: I’d gladly help if you need it.

meaning: in white; dressed/wearing white; painted white.
additional_notes: Used with "(estar/ir) de + color" to say someone is wearing that color: "Ela foi de branco" (She went dressed in white). Also used with verbs like "pintar" to say something was painted that color: "pintar as paredes de branco".
target_language_example: No casamento, todos foram de branco.
native_language_example: At the wedding, everyone went dressed in white.

meaning: face down; lying on your stomach (prone).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like deitar (to lie down), dormir (to sleep), estar/deitar-se (to be lying down) to describe the position with your belly on the surface and your face toward the ground/bed. Common in instructions: “Deite de bruços.”
target_language_example: Ele caiu e ficou de bruços no chão.
native_language_example: He fell and ended up face down on the floor.

meaning: “headfirst”; also used in set phrases like “dor de cabeça” (headache) and “de cabeça pra cima/baixo” (right-side up/upside down).
additional_notes:
Literal idea is “with/by the head,” but in everyday Portuguese it appears in common expressions: 
- "dor(es) de cabeça" = headache(s) (very common, fixed phrase)
- "saltar/pular/mergulhar de cabeça" = to jump/dive headfirst (also figuratively: to jump into something fully)
- "de cabeça pra cima" / "de cabeça pra baixo" = right-side up / upside down.
target_language_example: Ele mergulhou de cabeça na piscina.
native_language_example: He dove headfirst into the pool.

additional_notes: Used for objects that are physically inverted (a book, a picture, etc.) and also figuratively for situations/life being completely disrupted or changed ("virar a vida de cabeça para baixo"). Often used with "estar" for a state ("está de cabeça para baixo") and with verbs like "virar"/"ficar" to indicate something was turned or became upside down.
target_language_example: Deixei o celular cair e agora a tela está de cabeça para baixo.
native_language_example: I dropped my phone and now the screen is upside down.

meaning: from start to finish; completely; through and through.
additional_notes: Used to say someone knows something very well (a city, a neighborhood, a subject) or that something is done/read/seen in full. Commonly appears with verbs like “conhecer” (to know) and “ler” (to read). Literally “from end to end,” similar to “from top to bottom.”
target_language_example: Eu li o relatório de cabo a rabo.
native_language_example: I read the report from start to finish.

additional_notes: Used after a number/quantity to say how many should be taken or done per turn (um de cada vez = one at a time; três de cada vez = three at a time). Common in instructions and procedures, often with verbs like entrar (to enter), pegar/tirar (to take/remove), fazer (to do).
target_language_example: Vamos resolver um problema de cada vez.
native_language_example: Let’s solve one problem at a time.

additional_notes: Literally “of coffee.” Very common after verbs that require the preposition “de,” like gostar de (to like), precisar de (to need), and also in expressions of quantity: um copo de café (a cup of coffee), um pouquinho de café (a little bit of coffee).
target_language_example: Você quer um pouco de café?
native_language_example: Do you want some coffee?

additional_notes:
Common in two patterns:
- **roupa(s) de cama** = bedding/bed linen (sheets, pillowcases, etc.).
- **estar/ficar de cama** = to be stuck in bed, usually because you’re ill.
Also appears in fixed contrasts like **de mesa e de cama** (“table and bed”), meaning someone only talks about eating/food and sex/relationships (depending on context).
target_language_example: Estou de cama desde ontem, então vou faltar ao trabalho.
native_language_example: I’ve been in bed since yesterday, so I’m going to miss work.

additional_notes: In Portuguese, *gostar* is normally followed by **de + infinitive**: *gostar de cantar* = “to like singing / to like to sing.” Here, **de** doesn’t translate word-for-word into English; it’s required by the grammar.
target_language_example: Ela gosta de cantar no carro.
native_language_example: She likes to sing in the car.

additional_notes: Very common in Brazilian Portuguese (often informal). Used to say something happens instantly: “(logo) de cara”. It also appears in fixed expressions: “dar de cara com (alguém/alguma coisa)” = “to run into/come across”, and “ficar de cara amarrada” = “to be sulky / have a long face.”
target_language_example: Eu não entendi de cara, mas depois fez sentido.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand right away, but later it made sense.

meaning: made of meat; meat (as a type/flavor).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify that something is made with meat or is a meat version: "sopa de carne" (meat soup), "molho de carne" (meat sauce). In "um pouco de carne", it means “some meat” (the substance/food).
target_language_example: Eu quero um sanduíche de carne.
native_language_example: I want a meat sandwich.

additional_notes: Used to say you travel/arrive/go somewhere using a car as transportation (similar to “by car”). It often contrasts with other transport: de ônibus (by bus), de bicicleta (by bike), a pé (on foot). In phrases like “acidente de carro”, it means “car accident” (an accident involving a car), not “by car.”
target_language_example: A gente vai de carro ou de ônibus?
native_language_example: Are we going by car or by bus?

additional_notes: Often used without an article when talking about home in a general sense: sair de casa = leave home, longe de casa = far from home. After some nouns, it can also mean 'home/house' as a modifier, as in chaves de casa ('house keys') and deveres de casa ('homework').
target_language_example: Ela saiu de casa muito cedo.
native_language_example: She left home very early.

additional_notes: Used to soften a statement or show it’s only partly/approximately true. Often comes at the beginning of a sentence (with a comma) or after the verb: "Ele ficou, de certa forma, desapontado". Can also be used alone as a short, hesitant answer meaning "in a way".
target_language_example: De certa forma, eu entendo o que você quer dizer.
native_language_example: In a way, I understand what you mean.

additional_notes: Used to express certainty about something (often in European Portuguese). It can also appear in the pattern “de certo que …” = “I’m sure/certain that …”.
target_language_example: De certo, ele já chegou a casa.
native_language_example: Surely, he has already arrived home.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify that it contains beer or is related to beer: garrafa de cerveja (beer bottle), copo de cerveja (glass of beer), lata de cerveja (can of beer), fardo de cerveja (case/pack of beer). It literally means “of beer.”
target_language_example: Você quer uma garrafa de cerveja ou uma lata de cerveja?
native_language_example: Do you want a bottle of beer or a can of beer?

additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify what it is made of or what flavor/type it is. Common in foods: "barra de chocolate" (chocolate bar), "sorvete de chocolate" (chocolate ice cream). Often translates as "chocolate" before the noun in English.
target_language_example: Eu quero um bolo de chocolate.
native_language_example: I want a chocolate cake.

meaning: to cry (used with verbs that take “de” + infinitive).
additional_notes: “De chorar” is the infinitive phrase “to cry” after certain verbs that require the preposition “de”, such as: gostar de (to like / would like to), parar de (to stop), deixar de (to stop / to not do anymore), não conseguir parar de (to not be able to stop). Example patterns: “Pára de chorar” = “Stop crying”; “Não pude deixar de chorar” = “I couldn’t stop myself from crying.”
target_language_example: Eu não consigo parar de chorar.
native_language_example: I can’t stop crying.

meaning: 'of tea' (used to describe something that contains/serves tea).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify the type/content, especially in phrases like "xícara de chá" (a cup of tea) or "colher de chá" (teaspoon). With drinks, Portuguese often uses "de" to mean "of" (content/type): "uma xícara de chá", "um copo de água". On its own, "de chá" usually sounds incomplete—you typically say the full phrase (e.g., "xícara de chá").
target_language_example: Vou fazer uma xícara de chá para você.
native_language_example: I’m going to make a cup of tea for you.

additional_notes: Used to talk about position or perspective: visto/olhado de cima = “seen from above.” With nouns it often means “upper/top”: a prateleira de cima = “the top shelf.” Common extension: de cima a baixo = “from top to bottom.”
target_language_example: Olha a cidade de cima: é linda à noite.
native_language_example: Look at the city from above: it’s beautiful at night.

additional_notes: Literally “of eating.” Common after expressions like “a fim de” (in the mood to / wanting to) and in phrases like “algo de comer” = “something to eat.” In many cases it points to food as an option/need (something to eat) rather than the general action of eating.
target_language_example: Tem algo de comer aqui?
native_language_example: Is there something to eat here?

additional_notes: Used after a noun: "pessoas de cor", "garoto de cor", "filhos de cor". In modern Portuguese this phrasing can sound dated and may be considered offensive depending on context; you may hear alternatives like "pessoas negras" (Black people) or "pessoas não brancas" (non‑white people), depending on what is meant.
target_language_example: Na turma, havia muitos alunos de cor.
native_language_example: In the class, there were many students of color.

additional_notes: Commonly used to talk about what normally happens. Very frequent in comparisons with "mais/menos ... do que de costume" (= "more/less ... than usual"). Often placed after the verb or at the end of the clause: "acordou mais cedo do que de costume".
target_language_example: Hoje cheguei mais tarde do que de costume.
native_language_example: Today I arrived later than usual.

meaning: made of leather; leather (as a material).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to say what it’s made from: "um cinto de couro" (a leather belt), "luvas de couro" (leather gloves). It describes the material (couro = leather/hide) and is very common in shopping/product descriptions.
target_language_example: Você tem uma carteira de couro?
native_language_example: Do you have a leather wallet?

additional_notes: Used to say when something happens (daytime), often contrasted with “à noite” (at night). You can use it with routines and habits (e.g., sleep/work) or to describe how something looks/changes depending on the time of day.
target_language_example: Eu prefiro estudar de dia e descansar à noite.
native_language_example: I prefer to study during the day and rest at night.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify that it relates to money (e.g., "quantia de dinheiro" = "an amount of money", "fonte de dinheiro" = "a source of money", "desperdício de dinheiro" = "a waste of money"). Very common with "precisar de" → "precisar de dinheiro" = "to need money".
target_language_example: Precisamos de dinheiro para pagar o aluguel.
native_language_example: We need money to pay the rent.

meaning: emergency; for emergencies; in an emergency situation.
additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something intended for emergencies or done because of an emergency (e.g., "pouso/aterrissagem de emergência" = emergency landing, "procedimentos/equipamento de emergência" = emergency procedures/equipment). Also used in set phrases like "Em caso de emergência" (in case of emergency).
target_language_example: Onde fica a saída de emergência?
native_language_example: Where is the emergency exit?

meaning: 'of energy' / 'energy' (used to describe the type/purpose of something).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify that it relates to energy, similar to English noun modifiers like “energy source” or “power outage.” Common combinations: “fonte de energia” (energy source), “campos de energia” (energy fields), “corte de energia” (power outage), “vara de energia” (energy/power rod).
target_language_example: Precisamos de uma nova fonte de energia para a cidade.
native_language_example: We need a new energy source for the city.

meaning: to enter; to get into (used after certain verbs/adjectives).
additional_notes: Portuguese often uses the preposition “de” before an infinitive after some verbs and adjectives. Common patterns include: “difícil de entrar” (hard to get into), “impedir [alguém] de entrar” (to stop/prevent someone from entering), and “proibido de entrar” (forbidden to enter). In English you usually just say “to enter / from entering,” without an equivalent of “de.”
target_language_example: É difícil de entrar nessa universidade.
native_language_example: It’s hard to get into that university.

additional_notes: Used after words like algo/nada (something/nothing) to mean “something/nothing wrong”: algo de errado = “something wrong,” nada de errado = “nothing wrong.” It often refers to a mistake or a problem.
target_language_example: Não há nada de errado com isso.
native_language_example: There’s nothing wrong with that.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean it’s someone’s pet/kept for companionship: “animal de estimação” (pet) and also “meu cachorro de estimação” (my pet dog). By extension it can describe a favorite/cherished personal item (“meu violão de estimação”), meaning one you’re fond of.
target_language_example: Você tem algum animal de estimação?
native_language_example: Do you have any pets?

meaning: 'to study' (used after verbs/expressions like 'precisar de', 'ter de', or 'com o propósito de').
additional_notes: Portuguese often uses **de + infinitive** after certain expressions. Common ones in the examples are **ter de estudar** = “to have to study” and **precisar de estudar** = “to need to study”. With **com o propósito de estudar**, it means “with the purpose of studying / in order to study.” In English this is usually translated with **to + verb** (not “of studying”).
target_language_example: Eu preciso de estudar hoje à noite.
native_language_example: I need to study tonight.

additional_notes: Used to confirm or emphasize that something is true. Often appears at the start of a sentence as a connector (“De fato, ...”) or after a statement for emphasis (“..., de fato.”). Similar to “na verdade”, but “de fato” tends to sound a bit more formal.
target_language_example: Ele parecia calmo, mas estava nervoso, de fato.
native_language_example: He seemed calm, but he was actually nervous, in fact.

meaning: 'to do that' / 'from doing that' (de + infinitive, depending on the verb).
additional_notes: Used after certain verbs that require **de + infinitive**. With **impedir/proibir** it usually means **“from doing that”** (blocking an action): *impedir alguém de fazer aquilo*. With **convencer** it usually means **“to do that”** (persuading someone to do something): *convencer alguém de fazer aquilo*. **Aquilo** means “that (thing/that action)” (something more distant or already known from context).
target_language_example: Ela me convenceu de fazer aquilo, mas depois me arrependi.
native_language_example: She convinced me to do that, but later I regretted it.

additional_notes: Used when a verb in the infinitive (fazer) comes after certain words/structures that require the preposition “de”. Common patterns include: “chance de fazer isso” (chance to do it), “envergonhado(a) de fazer isso” (embarrassed to do it / embarrassed about doing it), “precisar de fazer isso” (to need to do it), and “ser dispensado(a) de fazer isso” (to be excused from doing it). Also appears with obligation expressions like “ter de fazer isso” = “have to do it” (often written “tens de / têm de”).
target_language_example: Não tenho vontade de fazer isso hoje.
native_language_example: I don’t feel like doing it today.

additional_notes: Used with estar/ficar (“to be”) to say someone isn’t working that day/shift: Estou de folga hoje. It also appears in phrases like dias de folga (“days off”) and tirar X de folga (“to take X off / take time off”), often referring to work or school.
target_language_example: Estou de folga amanhã, então posso te ajudar à tarde.
native_language_example: I’m off tomorrow, so I can help you in the afternoon.

additional_notes: Used after verbs/adjectives to say something happens because of hunger: e.g. "morrer de fome" (to starve), "desmaiar de fome" (to faint from hunger), "estar/ficar com fome" vs. "dar fome" (to make you feel hungry). In the fixed phrase "morto(s) de fome", it can literally mean "starving", but it’s also commonly used as a pejorative insult meaning "poor/dirty/low-life" depending on context.
target_language_example: Estou tremendo de fome porque não comi nada hoje.
native_language_example: I'm shaking from hunger because I haven't eaten anything today.

meaning: in a … way; in a … manner.
additional_notes: Used to describe how something is done, usually followed by an adjective (e.g., de forma misteriosa, de forma magnífica). Similar to “de maneira”. It can also introduce a more specific clarification, often with an adverb like “particular” (“in particular”).
target_language_example: Ele falou comigo de forma educada.
native_language_example: He spoke to me in a polite way.

additional_notes: Used to strongly negate or emphasize that something is not true or should not happen. Common in formal or neutral contexts. Often placed near the verb or after "não" for extra emphasis (e.g., "não ... de forma alguma").
target_language_example: Eu não concordo de forma alguma com essa decisão.
native_language_example: I don't agree with that decision at all.

additional_notes: Uses "de" to link something to the French language. Common with things like classes, tests, books, and dictionaries: "aula de francês" (French class), "teste de francês" (French test), "dicionário de francês" (French dictionary). With "gostar de" (to like), it means liking the language: "gosto de francês".
target_language_example: Tenho aula de francês às segundas-feiras.
native_language_example: I have French class on Mondays.

meaning: of soccer; soccer (as an adjective phrase).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify it’s related to soccer: partida de futebol (soccer match), clube de futebol (soccer club), time/equipe de futebol (soccer team), bola de futebol (soccer ball), torneio de futebol (soccer tournament). It’s the preposition de (“of”) + futebol (“soccer/football”), so it works like “soccer” in English (a soccer match). In Brazil, futebol usually means soccer; in Portugal it can also mean football (soccer) in general.
target_language_example: A gente vai assistir a um jogo de futebol hoje à noite.
native_language_example: We’re going to watch a soccer match tonight.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like estar/ficar to say someone is currently on vacation or has time off: "Estou de férias". Also appears with sair ("sair de férias" = to go on vacation) and with a time period: "estavam de férias em julho passado". Note: "férias" can also mean vacation days/leave ("dias de férias").
target_language_example: Estou de férias na semana que vem.
native_language_example: I’m on vacation next week.

additional_notes: Used to say something costs nothing (often with verbs like "ser" or "sair": "É de graça", "Sai de graça"). It can also mean "gratis" in offers and promotions ("Você pode levar de graça"). In some contexts, it can also mean "for nothing / without reason" (e.g., "apanhar de graça"), but the examples here are about price.
target_language_example: A entrada do museu é de graça aos domingos.
native_language_example: Museum entry is free on Sundays.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something related to war (similar to an adjective in English). Common patterns: “esforço de guerra” (war effort), “crimes de guerra” (war crimes), “tempo de guerra” (wartime), “ferida/ferimentos de guerra” (war wound(s)).
target_language_example: Durante o tempo de guerra, havia racionamento de comida.
native_language_example: During wartime, there was food rationing.

additional_notes: Used to say a rule, habit, or situation will change and apply starting now and continuing into the future. Commonly placed at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis, but it can also appear mid-sentence.
target_language_example: De hoje em diante, vou chegar mais cedo ao trabalho.
native_language_example: From now on, I’m going to arrive earlier at work.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to mark something connected to honor or given special respect. Very common in set phrases: “código de honra” (honor code), “palavra de honra” (word of honor), “lugar de honra” (place of honor), “guarda de honra” (honor guard).
target_language_example: Eles fizeram uma cerimónia de honra para o professor.
native_language_example: They held an honorary ceremony for the professor.

additional_notes: Used after an age (usually with "anos") to specify someone's age: "oito anos de idade" = "eight years old". It commonly appears with "ter" ("Ele tem 10 anos (de idade)") or "ter" in the past ("quando tinha 10 anos (de idade)"). "De idade" is often optional and can be omitted in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ela tem vinte e cinco anos de idade.
native_language_example: She is twenty-five years old.

meaning: of English; in English (as a subject).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify that something is related to the English language, especially as a school subject or course: "curso de inglês" (English course), "aulas de inglês" (English classes), "professor(a) de inglês" (English teacher). Also used in questions like "Você gosta de inglês?" meaning "Do you like English?" (the language/subject).
target_language_example: Eu tenho prova de inglês amanhã.
native_language_example: I have an English test tomorrow.

additional_notes: de is a preposition used before the infinitive ir. It often depends on the word before it, as in medo de ir, decisão de ir, or cansado de ir. In English, it may be translated literally as 'of going' or more naturally as 'to go,' depending on the expression.
target_language_example: Ela está cansada de ir ao escritório todos os dias.
native_language_example: She is tired of going to the office every day.

meaning: 'in a way' / 'properly' (often used with another word, like 'de outro jeito' or 'de jeito nenhum').
additional_notes: Literally 'of (a) way/manner'. By itself it's uncommon; it usually appears in fixed expressions or with modifiers: (1) 'de outro jeito' = 'another way', (2) 'de qualquer jeito' = 'any old way / carelessly', (3) 'de jeito nenhum' = 'no way / not at all'. Also related: 'dar um jeito' = 'to find a way / fix it' (informal, very common).
target_language_example: De jeito nenhum eu vou falar com ele hoje.
native_language_example: No way am I going to talk to him today.

additional_notes: Used for strong refusal or emphasis, often as a stand-alone answer: “De jeito nenhum!” It can also reinforce a negation inside a sentence (“não ... de jeito nenhum” = “not ... at all / no way”). Common in both spoken and written Portuguese; tone can sound firm or blunt depending on context.
target_language_example: De jeito nenhum eu vou mentir para você.
native_language_example: No way am I going to lie to you.

meaning: 'of milk' / 'made with milk' (used to describe something milk-related).
additional_notes: Uses "de" + a noun to describe the type/material/flavor of something. Common in phrases like "chá de leite" (milk tea), "café de leite" (coffee with milk), "produtor de leite" (milk producer/dairy farmer), or to identify containers/products: "jarra de leite" (milk jug).
target_language_example: Quero um café de leite, por favor.
native_language_example: I’d like a coffee with milk, please.

meaning: to read the book (used after verbs that take “de” + infinitive).
additional_notes: In Portuguese, some verbs are followed by **de + infinitive**. So **de ler o livro** is the action “to read the book,” attached to another verb: **terminar de ler o livro** (to finish reading the book), **estar terminando de ler o livro** (to be finishing reading the book), **esquecer-se de ler o livro** (to forget to read the book). In English we usually don’t translate the “de” as “of.”
target_language_example: Eu me esqueci de ler o livro ontem.
native_language_example: I forgot to read the book yesterday.

meaning: in mourning; grieving (especially after a death).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar/ficar" ("estar de luto", "ficar de luto") to say someone is mourning. It can also describe wearing mourning clothes (often black) or a place/period connected to mourning (e.g., "sala de luto"). Often refers to mourning after someone dies, including collective mourning ("o país ficou de luto").
target_language_example: Depois da morte da avó, a família ficou de luto por uma semana.
native_language_example: After Grandma’s death, the family was in mourning for a week.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say what material something is made of: "X é de madeira" (X is wooden / made of wood) or "um/uma X de madeira" (a wooden X).
target_language_example: Preciso de uma estante de madeira para o meu quarto.
native_language_example: I need a wooden bookshelf for my bedroom.

meaning: of legal age; an adult (18+ in Brazil).
additional_notes: Common in Brazil, especially in everyday conversation and in contexts like clubs, alcohol, or legal responsibility. Often contrasted with "de menor" (a minor). It’s usually used after a linking verb: "ser/estar de maior".
target_language_example: Você é de maior?
native_language_example: Are you an adult (of legal age)?

meaning: bad/evil; wrong. (Also in “ficar de mal com”: to be mad at / on bad terms with.)
additional_notes: Very common after words like nada/ninguém/algo to mean “nothing/anyone/anything bad”: “Nada de mal vai acontecer.” It can also describe a person: “ninguém de mal” = “no bad people / nobody evil.” In questions like “O que ele fez de mal?”, it means “what (bad thing) did he do?” A separate fixed expression is “ficar de mal com (alguém)” = to be upset with someone / not speaking / on bad terms.
target_language_example: Não quero que aconteça nada de mal com você.
native_language_example: I don’t want anything bad to happen to you.

additional_notes: Used to strongly deny or reject something, often as a standalone answer: “De maneira alguma!” It can also intensify a negation in longer sentences, similar to “by no means” or “in no way”: “Não é de maneira alguma raro…” = “It’s by no means rare…”. Often appears with “não” (e.g., “Não, de maneira alguma.”).
target_language_example: Você vai desistir? De maneira alguma!
native_language_example: Are you going to give up? No way!

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens during the morning (often as part of a routine). It can refer to one specific morning (e.g., hoje de manhã = this morning) or mornings in general (often with words like sempre/todo dia).
target_language_example: Eu trabalho de manhã e estudo à noite.
native_language_example: I work in the morning and study at night.

additional_notes: Used with nouns to say something is related to the school subject math: teste de matemática (math test), livro de matemática (math book), aula de matemática (math class). Often translates naturally as “math” in English rather than “of mathematics.”
target_language_example: Hoje tenho prova de matemática.
native_language_example: Today I have a math exam.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" (or "ficar") to describe someone’s current mood/temporary state: "Estou/Ele está de mau humor". You can add time expressions: "hoje", "de manhã", "nessa manhã".
target_language_example: Hoje eu estou de mau humor porque dormi pouco.
native_language_example: Today I’m in a bad mood because I slept poorly.

additional_notes: Most commonly used after a noun to specify that it’s about memory: problemas de memória (memory problems), perda de memória (memory loss), falhas de memória (memory lapses). It can also mean “from memory” in phrases like recitar/decorar de memória (“to recite/know by heart,” literally “from memory”).
target_language_example: Ela está com falhas de memória ultimamente.
native_language_example: She’s been having memory lapses lately.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say something is not genuine (e.g., a toy, a fake story): "uma arma de mentira" = a fake gun / toy gun. It can also describe actions that are only for show: "chorar de mentira" = to pretend to cry.
target_language_example: Ele comprou um relógio de mentira.
native_language_example: He bought a fake watch.

additional_notes: Very vulgar. Often comes after a noun to insult it or show strong disgust: "equipe de merda" = “shitty team,” "decisões de merda" = “shitty decisions.” It can also intensify an insult when used with a person/thing (“um X de merda” ≈ “a fucking/shitty X”). Avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Esse serviço de merda não funciona nunca.
native_language_example: This shitty service never works.

additional_notes: uses the stressed pronoun mim after the preposition de, not eu. Depending on the expression, it can mean 'of me', 'about me', and sometimes 'from me'. Common in phrases like parte de mim ('part of me') and falar de mim ('talk about me').
target_language_example: Ela sempre cuida de mim.
native_language_example: She always takes care of me.

additional_notes: Used with verbs and expressions that take the preposition “de” to mean “from/of me,” with extra emphasis from “mesmo” (= “self / even”). Common with: rir de mim mesmo (“laugh at myself”), esperar isso de mim mesmo (“expect that of myself”), esquecer de mim mesmo (“forget about myself”), fugir de mim mesmo (“run away from myself”).
target_language_example: Às vezes eu rio de mim mesmo quando cometo um erro bobo.
native_language_example: Sometimes I laugh at myself when I make a silly mistake.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize a negation. Often appears after "não" to reinforce it ("não ... de modo algum" = "not ... at all"), but it can also be said alone as a firm refusal/denial ("De modo algum!").
target_language_example: Eu não vou aceitar isso de modo algum.
native_language_example: I will not accept that at all / by any means.

meaning: with sauce; soaking; (figuratively) laid up / out of action.
additional_notes: Common uses: (1) Food: "com/de molho" = served with sauce or dressing ("Um pouco de molho também."). (2) Soaking: "deixar X de molho" = leave something soaking (often clothes or beans); "ficar de molho" can also mean staying in water (e.g., in a bathtub). (3) Figurative: "estar/ficar de molho" = be stuck resting because you’re sick/injured or can’t go out (often a casual expression).
target_language_example: Estou de molho desde ontem por causa da gripe.
native_language_example: I’ve been laid up since yesterday because of the flu.

meaning: “of dying / to die”; also used to mean “extremely” (like “to death”).
additional_notes:
Often follows feelings or reactions: 
- medo de morrer = “fear of dying” (literal)
- um susto de morrer, rir de morrer = “scared to death”, “laugh to death” (intensifier meaning “very/so much”).
With this intensifier use, English usually doesn’t translate it word-for-word.
target_language_example: Aquele filme é de morrer de medo.
native_language_example: That movie is terrifying (scary as hell).

additional_notes: Used mainly for people physically holding hands (often couples, parents and children, etc.). It can also be used figuratively to mean that two things go together closely or happen together (e.g., “walks hand in hand with doubt”). Often appears with verbs like andar/caminhar/estar/ir (“to walk/be/go”) + de mãos dadas.
target_language_example: Eles foram para casa de mãos dadas.
native_language_example: They went home holding hands.

meaning: empty-handed; without bringing anything (especially a gift, money, or results).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like chegar/voltar/sair/retornar (“to arrive/come back/leave/return”) to say someone came back with nothing. It can be literal (not carrying anything) or figurative (no gift, no money, no success/results). Often implies disappointment or that you expected to bring something.
target_language_example: Eu não quero chegar na festa de mãos vazias, então vou levar um vinho.
native_language_example: I don’t want to arrive at the party empty-handed, so I’ll bring a wine.

additional_notes: Very common with verbs that take **de + noun**, such as **gostar de** (to like), **entender de** (to know about / be knowledgeable about), and **falar de** (to talk about). In these cases, **de música** usually means “about music,” not literally “of music.”
target_language_example: A gente estava falando de música no almoço.
native_language_example: We were talking about music at lunch.

additional_notes: Common after negatives (não, ninguém) to mean “of anything/anything at all”: "não sei de nada" = “I don’t know anything.” It can also mean “you’re welcome” as a fixed reply to “obrigado/obrigada,” but in your examples it’s the literal sense “of nothing/anything.”
target_language_example: Eu não desconfio de nada.
native_language_example: I don’t suspect anything.

additional_notes: Used after an adjective (often a medical/physical condition) to say someone has had it since they were born: "cego de nascença" (blind from birth). It can also be used alone as a short answer: "É de nascença." = "It’s congenital / from birth."
target_language_example: Ela tem surdez de nascença.
native_language_example: She has congenital deafness (deaf from birth).

additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean “business (related)” (e.g., parceiro de negócios = business partner, reunião de negócios = business meeting, viagem de negócios = business trip). It can also describe someone’s “business sense” (noção de negócios).
target_language_example: Ela está em São Paulo numa viagem de negócios.
native_language_example: She is in São Paulo on a business trip.

meaning: “of snow”; “snow-” (used to describe something made of/covered with snow).
additional_notes: Usually follows a noun to specify snow as the material or type: bola de neve (“snowball”), queda de neve (“snowfall”), coberto de neve (“covered in snow”). It’s the preposition de + neve (“snow”).
target_language_example: As montanhas estavam cobertas de neve.
native_language_example: The mountains were covered in snow.

additional_notes: Used to say when something happens during the night-time period. Very common in Brazilian Portuguese; you may also see/hear "à noite" with the same meaning. With a time word like "ontem", it means "last night" (e.g., "ontem de noite").
target_language_example: A gente pode conversar de noite.
native_language_example: We can talk tonight/in the evening.

additional_notes: A very common everyday way to say that something happens another time. It is less formal than novamente. Depending on context, it can sometimes suggest doing something from the beginning, but most often it simply means again.
target_language_example: Eu esqueci a chave de novo.
native_language_example: I forgot the key again.

additional_notes: Used to talk about doing something another time or repeating an action. Common in commands/suggestions like “Pense de novo” (“Think again”). Often goes near the verb: “ver de novo” (see again), “fazer de novo” (do again). In Brazilian Portuguese it’s also used for “back” (e.g., “Estou de novo em casa” = “I’m back home / home again”).
target_language_example: Pode explicar de novo, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you explain again, please?

additional_notes: Means “of us” in expressions like “a maioria de nós” (most of us) or “alguns de nós” (some of us). It can also mean “about us” after certain verbs that take “de”, e.g. “tomar conta de nós” (take care of us) and “pensar de nós” (think about us / what someone thinks of us).
target_language_example: Metade de nós não sabia da reunião.
native_language_example: Half of us didn’t know about the meeting.

meaning: keeping an eye on; watching out for; eyeing (wanting/being interested in).
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like estar/ficar: "estar de olho" (to be watching), "ficar de olho (em...)" (to keep an eye on / watch out for). It often takes "em" or contractions like "no/na/nuns/nas": "de olho nele", "de olho na história". Depending on context it can mean either (1) monitoring/supervising someone or something, or (2) having your eye on something you want ("Estou de olho num livro...").
target_language_example: Fica de olho na bolsa enquanto eu pago.
native_language_example: Keep an eye on the bag while I pay.

additional_notes: Used to ask about origin or starting point. Common in direct questions ("De onde você é?" = "Where are you from?") and in indirect questions after verbs like saber/imaginar/lembrar ("Não sei de onde ele veio." = "I don’t know where he came from."). Often followed by a verb ("de onde você veio") or used with "ser" to ask someone’s origin ("de onde você é").
target_language_example: Você sabe de onde ela é?
native_language_example: Do you know where she’s from?

additional_notes: Literally “from where (it) came.” Used either as a direct question (“De onde veio isso?”) or inside a longer sentence (“o lugar de onde veio” = “the place where (you) came from”). “Veio” is the past of “vir” (to come) for ele/ela/você; for “you all” it’s “de onde vieram?”.
target_language_example: De onde veio essa informação?
native_language_example: Where did this information come from?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the origin or source of something (a person, sound, idea, problem, etc.). Often appears inside a longer question: “Você sabe de onde vem…?” (= “Do you know where … comes from?”). If the subject is plural, use “de onde vêm” (with an accent): “De onde vêm eles?”.
target_language_example: Você sabe de onde vem esse barulho?
native_language_example: Do you know where that noise is coming from?

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe the material something is made of: moedas de ouro (gold coins), cruz de ouro (gold cross), selo de ouro (gold seal). Often equivalent to English “gold” as an adjective, even though Portuguese uses “de + material”.
target_language_example: Ela usa um anel de ouro todos os dias.
native_language_example: She wears a gold ring every day.

additional_notes: Used to show that something belongs to, comes from, or is related to a different person (not you). Common after verbs like pegar (to take/get), emprestar (to lend), and with nouns like problemas, cabelo, coisas. It can imply you shouldn’t be taking/using something that isn’t yours.
target_language_example: Não use as coisas de outra pessoa sem pedir.
native_language_example: Don’t use someone else’s things without asking.

meaning: made of paper; paper (as the material).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to say what something is made from: "aviões de papel" (paper airplanes), "saco de papel" (paper bag). It’s a literal, compositional use of "de" (of/from) + "papel" (paper).
target_language_example: Você tem um saco de papel?
native_language_example: Do you have a paper bag?

additional_notes: Used to say you should look/observe carefully or at close range. Often appears with verbs like “olhar” (to look) or “ver” (to see): “olhar de perto” = “look closely / up close”. It can also indicate moving something away from someone/something: “tirar X de perto de mim” = “take/remove X from near me / away from me.”
target_language_example: Quero ver de perto como funciona.
native_language_example: I want to see up close how it works.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say what material it’s made of: "copo de plástico" (plastic cup), "garrafa de plástico" (plastic bottle). It contrasts with other materials like "de vidro" (glass) or "de papel" (paper).
target_language_example: Você tem uma garrafa de plástico?
native_language_example: Do you have a plastic bottle?

additional_notes: Common in phrases like “tecnologia de ponta” / “equipamentos de ponta” (advanced, state-of-the-art). With objects, it can describe the type of tip: “caneta de ponta fina” (fine-tip pen). In “de ponta a ponta,” it means “from end to end / from start to finish.”
target_language_example: O hospital investiu em equipamentos de ponta.
native_language_example: The hospital invested in state-of-the-art equipment.

additional_notes: Used literally for something physically inverted (e.g., a book, a table), often with verbs like "virar" (to turn/flip): "Vire-o de ponta-cabeça." It’s also common figuratively to mean things are disorganized or chaotic: "Está tudo de ponta-cabeça."
target_language_example: A sala ficou de ponta-cabeça depois da festa.
native_language_example: The living room was a mess after the party.

meaning: not talkative; a person of few words.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone who speaks little and is usually quiet or concise. Commonly appears after a noun with ser/estar: “Ele é um homem de poucas palavras.” It can be neutral or slightly approving (someone who doesn’t talk much but does what they say).
target_language_example: Ela é de poucas palavras, mas muito atenciosa.
native_language_example: She’s a woman of few words, but very thoughtful.

meaning: first-rate; top-quality. Also: right away/on the first try.
additional_notes: With nouns, it often describes high quality: “madeira de primeira” (top-quality wood), “serviço de primeira” (first-rate service). In some contexts (especially with verbs like acreditar, entender, acertar), it can mean doing something immediately or on the first attempt: “acreditou de primeira” = “believed it right away.”
target_language_example: O atendimento aqui é de primeira.
native_language_example: The service here is first-rate.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is alert and prepared to respond quickly if needed (common in work, emergency, military/police contexts). Often with verbs like “ficar/estar de prontidão” (to be on standby) or “colocar de prontidão” (to put/keep on standby).
target_language_example: Fique de prontidão: podemos precisar de você a qualquer momento.
native_language_example: Stay on standby: we may need you at any moment.

additional_notes: Used to say something was done intentionally (not by accident), often with everyday verbs like fazer, deixar, colocar, dizer. Common contrast: "sem querer" = "by accident" / "unintentionally".
target_language_example: Eu fiz isso de propósito.
native_language_example: I did that on purpose.

additional_notes: Used after a noun with "de" to specify what something is made of or what type it is. Common in food-related phrases like "migalhas de pão" (breadcrumbs) or "rastro de migalhas de pão" (trail of breadcrumbs).
target_language_example: Preciso de migalhas de pão para empanar o frango.
native_language_example: I need breadcrumbs to bread the chicken.

additional_notes: Most commonly used with the verb estar/ficar: estar de pé = to be standing; ficar de pé = to stand up. Can also mean something is still standing/in place or still happening as planned (e.g., O almoço está de pé? = Is lunch still on?). Often used in commands: De pé! = Stand up!
target_language_example: Ficamos de pé durante o hino.
native_language_example: We stayed standing during the anthem.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe it: "produtos de qualidade" = "quality products" / "high-quality products." It can also appear in the expression "tempo de qualidade" meaning "quality time" (time spent in a meaningful, attentive way).
target_language_example: Estamos procurando um hotel de qualidade, mas com preço justo.
native_language_example: We’re looking for a good-quality hotel, but at a fair price.

additional_notes: Used to move the conversation along, to return to the main point, or to say that something is true regardless of other factors (often at the start of a sentence). Similar to “de qualquer maneira”.
target_language_example: De qualquer forma, vamos embora agora.
native_language_example: Anyway, let's leave now.

meaning: "anyway" / "in any case"; also "in any way" (sometimes: "sloppily/without care").
additional_notes: Often means something will happen or be done regardless of circumstances ("I was going to do it anyway"). In some contexts it describes the manner: doing something carelessly or looking messy/unkempt ("um cara velho, de qualquer jeito" = an old guy, kind of shabby).
target_language_example: Eu não queria sair, mas fui de qualquer jeito.
native_language_example: I didn’t want to go out, but I went anyway.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen regardless of circumstances, or to move on in the conversation (like English “anyway”). It can appear at the start of a sentence (“De qualquer maneira, ...”) or after the main idea (“... de qualquer maneira”).
target_language_example: De qualquer maneira, eu vou terminar isso hoje.
native_language_example: Anyway, I’m going to finish this today.

additional_notes: Used to move the conversation along, add a conclusion, or say that something is true regardless of other details (often followed by a comma: “De qualquer modo, …”). Similar in meaning to “de qualquer forma”.
target_language_example: De qualquer modo, vamos sair agora.
native_language_example: Anyway, we’re leaving now.

meaning: “of four / four (in number)”; also “on all fours” (with ficar/estar).
additional_notes: Very common to indicate quantity, age, duration, etc.: “grávida de quatro meses” (four months pregnant), “o segundo de quatro” (the second of four), “uma viagem de quatro horas” (a four-hour trip), “submarino de quatro pás” (with four propeller blades). With posture verbs, it means being on hands and knees: “ficar/estar de quatro”. Depending on context, “ficar de quatro” can also be used with a sexual meaning.
target_language_example: O meu cachorro ficou de quatro quando viu o gato.
native_language_example: My dog got down on all fours when it saw the cat.

additional_notes: Used to ask about the method, manner, or way something should be done. Common in more formal or careful speech; in everyday conversation, people often also say simply "como?". It can appear at the start of the question ("De que forma eu posso te ajudar?") or later ("Vai tirar fotos de que forma?").
target_language_example: De que forma você prefere receber o pagamento?
native_language_example: How would you prefer to receive the payment?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the manner, method, or style of doing something. It often comes before a verb (De que jeito devo pedir?) or after a noun/verb phrase to ask for a preference (Ovos feitos de que jeito? Você os quer de que jeito?). Similar to "como?", but "de que jeito" can sound more like "what kind of way" or "which way".
target_language_example: De que jeito você prefere o café, com leite ou sem?
native_language_example: How do you prefer your coffee, with milk or without?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the method, way, or manner something happens or will be done. It’s a bit more formal/explicit than just "como?" and can appear in full questions or alone as a follow-up: "De que maneira?" = "How so?/In what way?".
target_language_example: De que maneira podemos resolver esse problema?
native_language_example: How can we solve this problem?/In what way can we solve this problem?

additional_notes: Used with "quem" after the preposition "de". Most commonly it asks/indicates possession or authorship: "De quem é...?" = "Whose is it? / Whose ... is this?" It can also mean "about whom" after verbs like "falar" (to talk): "de quem eu falei" = "(the person) I talked about". In relative clauses it can refer to the person something belongs to: "o dinheiro de quem" = "the money of the person whose (money it is)".
target_language_example: De quem é esse casaco?
native_language_example: Whose coat is this?

meaning: “Whose is that?” / “Whose ... is that?” (asking who something belongs to).
additional_notes: Used to ask about ownership. You normally add the noun right after it: “De quem é essa bicicleta?” = “Whose bike is that?” Here “essa” refers to something near the listener or being pointed at. You can also change the demonstrative and gender: “de quem é este/esta/esse/essa/aquele/aquela …?”. Often you’ll just say “De quem é?” when the thing is obvious.
target_language_example: De quem é essa mala?
native_language_example: Whose suitcase is that?

meaning: “whose is this?” / “who does this belong to?” (masculine: esse).
additional_notes: Used to ask who an object/thing belongs to. It’s made of de (“of”) + quem (“who”) + é (“is”) + esse (“this,” masculine). For feminine nouns, use “De quem é essa…?” (ex.: essa bolsa). For plural, use “De quem são esses/essas…?” (ex.: esses livros / essas chaves). In Portuguese you often add the noun after it: “De quem é esse celular?”
target_language_example: De quem é esse casaco aqui?
native_language_example: Whose coat is this here?

meaning: “Whose is this?” (asking who something belongs to).
additional_notes: Used to ask who an object belongs to. It agrees with what you’re talking about: “esta” for feminine singular things (ex.: camisa, comida, pizza). For masculine, use “de quem é este...?” (ex.: este livro). You can also omit the demonstrative: “De quem é a camisa?”
target_language_example: De quem é esta chave?
native_language_example: Whose key is this?

meaning: “Whose is this?” / “Who does this belong to?”
additional_notes: Used to ask who the owner is. Often followed by a noun: “De quem é este telemóvel?” = “Whose phone is this?” Agreement matters: este (masc. singular), esta (fem. singular), estes/estas (plural). You can also say “De quem é isso/isto?” (“Whose is that/this?”).
target_language_example: De quem é este telemóvel?
native_language_example: Whose phone is this?

additional_notes: Used in questions after the preposition de. The exact English translation depends on the verb or noun: falando de quê? = 'talking about what?', piloto de quê? = 'pilot of what?'. In Brazilian Portuguese, quê is the stressed form used at the end of a question or before punctuation.
target_language_example: Você está reclamando de quê?
native_language_example: What are you complaining about?

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens unexpectedly and quickly. Very common in storytelling and everyday speech. It can go at the start of the sentence ("De repente, ..."), in the middle (", de repente,"), or at the end ("... de repente"). It can also be used loosely to mean "out of nowhere" / "for no reason" depending on context.
target_language_example: Eu estava andando na rua e, de repente, começou a chover.
native_language_example: I was walking down the street and, all of a sudden, it started to rain.

additional_notes: Used to add an extra comment or to move on from the main point (“anyway / in any case”). Often appears at the beginning of a sentence, like: “De resto, …” = “Besides that, … / Otherwise, …”. Depending on context it can also mean “as for the rest”.
target_language_example: De resto, está tudo bem.
native_language_example: Besides that, everything is fine.

meaning: routine; routinely; as a matter of habit.
additional_notes: Used to describe something done regularly/automatically, without special reason or excitement. Common in phrases like “exame de rotina” (routine check-up), “visita de rotina” (routine visit), and “coisa de rotina” (just a routine thing). It can also describe doing/saying something out of habit (e.g., “falou de rotina”).
target_language_example: Vou ao dentista de rotina uma vez por ano.
native_language_example: I go to the dentist for a routine visit once a year.

meaning: “of clothes / of laundry”; in some expressions, “(with) clothes on.”
additional_notes: Common after nouns to mean a quantity/type of clothes: **carga de roupa** (“a load of laundry”), **fábrica de roupa** (“clothing factory”). Very common in the fixed expression **trocar de roupa** = “to change clothes.” In casual speech you may also hear it to mean doing something **with your clothes on** (e.g., jumping in the water).
target_language_example: Vou trocar de roupa antes de sair.
native_language_example: I’m going to change clothes before going out.

meaning: fed up; sick and tired (of something).
additional_notes: Very common informal Brazilian Portuguese expression to say you’ve had enough and are annoyed/frustrated. Often followed by "de" + noun/infinitive: "de saco cheio de + [something]" (fed up with ...). You can also say it alone as an exclamation: "Tô de saco cheio!"
target_language_example: Tô de saco cheio de esperar; vamos embora.
native_language_example: I'm fed up with waiting; let's go.

additional_notes: Usually used after the verb "ter" (to have): "ter de + infinitive" expresses obligation/necessity, like "have to" in English. So "tenho/temos/têm de sair" = "I/we/they have to leave". By itself, "de sair" is incomplete and normally needs a verb before it.
target_language_example: Tenho de sair agora.
native_language_example: I have to leave now.

meaning: "of blood" / "blood" (used to describe something related to blood).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify that it involves blood, especially in medical contexts: "transfusão de sangue" (blood transfusion), "doação de sangue" (blood donation). It also appears in common expressions like "homem de sangue frio" (a cold-blooded man).
target_language_example: Ele precisa de uma transfusão de sangue urgente.
native_language_example: He needs an urgent blood transfusion.

meaning: 'from Monday' / 'on Monday' (often used in time ranges or deadlines).
additional_notes: Used mainly with time expressions. Most commonly it appears in ranges like “de segunda a sábado” = “from Monday to Saturday.” It can also mark a deadline: “antes de segunda” = “before Monday.” Here, “segunda” is short for “segunda-feira” (Monday).
target_language_example: A academia abre de segunda a sexta.
native_language_example: The gym is open from Monday to Friday.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say something was previously owned/used (e.g., roupa de segunda mão, carro de segunda mão, loja/livraria de segunda mão). It can also mean information you heard from someone else ("ouvir de segunda mão" = hear secondhand).
target_language_example: Comprei uma bicicleta de segunda mão para economizar dinheiro.
native_language_example: I bought a secondhand bike to save money.

meaning: 'of safety/security'; used to describe something meant to protect people or property.
additional_notes: Often follows a noun to form common phrases like "guarda de segurança" (security guard), "óculos de segurança" (safety goggles), "câmera de segurança" (security camera), "chefe de segurança" (head of security), and "portas de segurança" (security doors). "Segurança" can mean both 'security' and 'safety', so the best translation depends on context.
target_language_example: Temos protocolos de segurança para emergências.
native_language_example: We have safety/security protocols for emergencies.

additional_notes:
Literally “of (the) week.” On its own it’s not very common; you’ll most often see it inside set phrases like:
- "fim de semana" = weekend
- "dia(s) de semana" = weekday(s) (i.e., Monday–Friday)
It links the noun before it to “week,” similar to English “week-” or “of the week,” depending on the expression.
target_language_example: No fim de semana, a gente costuma sair.
native_language_example: On the weekend, we usually go out.

meaning: the usual; the same as always.
additional_notes: Used after a noun or pronoun to mean the familiar/typical one(s) from always (the regular choice, routine things, the same old). Common in phrases like “o mesmo de sempre” (the same as always), “as coisas de sempre” (the usual things), and “a [X] de sempre” (the usual [X]).
target_language_example: Vou pedir o de sempre.
native_language_example: I’m going to order the usual.

additional_notes: Used before the infinitive ser (“to be”) after many nouns/adjectives/expressions that require the preposition de, like orgulho de… (proud of…), vergonha de… (ashamed of…), cansado(a) de… (tired of…). Often translates naturally as “of being” in English: orgulho de ser = “proud of being.”
target_language_example: Ela tem medo de ser rejeitada.
native_language_example: She is afraid of being rejected.

additional_notes: "De" shows a relationship like possession, origin, or association (often like English "of" or "from"). "Seu" can mean "your" (formal) or "his/her" in many contexts, so it may be ambiguous; sometimes people use "do teu pai" (your, informal) or "do pai dele/dela" (his/her) to be clearer. Often contracts to "do seu pai" (= de + o).
target_language_example: Eu ouvi isso de seu pai ontem.
native_language_example: I heard that from your/his/her father yesterday.

meaning: of your parents / of his parents / of her parents / of their parents.
additional_notes: Uses the possessive "seus" (plural of "seu") + "pais" (parents). In Portuguese, "seu/seus" can mean "your" (especially with "você"), "his", "her", or "their"—the context shows which. The preposition "de" often translates as "of" (or sometimes "from").
target_language_example: Ele mora perto de seus pais.
native_language_example: He lives near his parents.

meaning: "of yourself/himself/themself" (reflexive: referring back to the same person).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to the subject (reflexive), often after nouns/adjectives and in set phrases. It agrees in gender/number: de si mesma (fem. singular), de si mesmos (masc./mixed plural), de si mesmas (fem. plural). Common collocations: sentir pena de si mesmo (feel sorry for yourself), rir de si mesmo (laugh at yourself), orgulhoso de si mesmo (proud of yourself), tirar uma foto de si mesmo (take a photo of yourself).
target_language_example: Tom nunca sentiu pena de si mesmo.
native_language_example: Tom never felt sorry for himself.

meaning: more than enough; extra; to spare.
additional_notes: Used after a noun to say there is an excess/abundance of something (time, space, money, reasons, etc.). Common patterns: "tempo de sobra" (plenty of time), "espaço de sobra" (plenty of space), "dinheiro de sobra" (money to spare), "motivos de sobra" (more than enough reasons).
target_language_example: Ainda tenho comida de sobra para o jantar.
native_language_example: I still have extra food for dinner.

additional_notes: A compositional phrase: de + sua. Sua is a possessive used with a feminine singular noun, so this often means 'of your' or simply 'your' in natural English. In context, sua can also sometimes mean 'his', 'her', or 'their'. In expressions like de sua parte, it means 'on your part' or 'of you'.
target_language_example: Preciso de sua ajuda.
native_language_example: I need your help.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition “de” (“of/from”) + “sua mãe” (“your/his/her mother”). “Sua” can mean “your” (often in more formal/polite contexts) or “his/her,” so the exact meaning depends on context. Common after nouns (ex: “o telefone de sua mãe” = “your/his/her mother’s phone number”).
target_language_example: Você sabe o endereço de sua mãe?
native_language_example: Do you know your mother’s address?

meaning: "of you" / "on your part" (used to comment on someone’s action or attitude).
additional_notes: Often used after an adjective to evaluate someone’s behavior: "É/foi + adjective + de sua parte (+ infinitive)". It can praise ("muito nobre de sua parte") or criticize ("insensato de sua parte"). You’ll also see variations like "da sua parte" and with other possessives: "da minha parte", "da parte dele/dela".
target_language_example: Foi muito gentil de sua parte me ajudar.
native_language_example: It was very kind of you to help me.

meaning: “of your/his/her life” (referring to someone’s lifetime, or a part/rest of it).
additional_notes: Uses the possessive "sua" (“your / his / her / their,” depending on context). Very common in phrases like "a maior parte de sua vida" (most of his/her life), "grande parte de sua vida" (a large part of your life), and "para o resto de sua vida" (for the rest of your life). In "cuide de sua vida," it means “mind your own business.”
target_language_example: Ela trabalhou a maior parte de sua vida como professora.
native_language_example: She worked most of her life as a teacher.

additional_notes: Used to show possession after a noun, usually meaning “of his/her/your/their” depending on context. It’s the combination of the preposition “de” + the possessive “suas” (feminine plural: “your/his/her/their”). Common after words like “uma/algumas/umas” + noun: “uma de suas fotos” = “one of your (his/her/their) photos.”
target_language_example: Preciso de algumas de suas respostas para terminar o relatório.
native_language_example: I need some of your answers to finish the report.

meaning: from time to time; every now and then.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens occasionally, not regularly. It can describe habits (someone visits, writes) or events that occur once in a while (Acontece de tempos em tempos.). It often goes at the end of the sentence, but it can also come earlier for emphasis.
target_language_example: Eu gosto de sair sozinho de tempos em tempos.
native_language_example: I like to go out alone from time to time.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition "de" + "ti" (stressed form of "tu") and appears after verbs/adjectives that take "de" (e.g., "precisar de" = to need; "rir de" = to laugh at). Often expresses "from you" (e.g., "esconder nada de ti" = hide nothing from you) or is part of fixed expressions like "depois de" (after) and "antes de" (before): "depois de ti" = after you; "antes de ti" = before you. Common in Portugal; in Brazil many speakers use "de você" instead.
target_language_example: Não vou falar mal de ti.
native_language_example: I’m not going to talk badly about you.

additional_notes: Used to say something belongs to, includes, or applies to every item in a group of feminine plural nouns (as). Common in general statements: "a base de todas as ciências" (the basis of all sciences), "pessoas de todas as idades" (people of all ages), "de todas as maneiras" (in all the ways). With masculine plural nouns, use "de todos os"; with singular, "de toda a" / "de todo o".
target_language_example: Este livro é útil para alunos de todas as áreas.
native_language_example: This book is useful for students from all areas.

additional_notes: Used to move the conversation along or to say something is true despite what was just mentioned. It often appears at the start of a sentence (“De todo modo, …”) or at the end (“…, de todo modo.”). Similar in meaning to “de qualquer forma”.
target_language_example: De todo modo, vamos ter que decidir hoje.
native_language_example: Anyway, we’ll have to decide today.

additional_notes: Often used with negation to soften what you’re saying: “não … de todo” = “not entirely / not completely.” In some contexts (especially in Portugal), it can also mean “at all,” usually in negative sentences (similar to “não … nada”). It’s a bit formal compared to alternatives like “completamente” or “de jeito nenhum” (for “not at all”).
target_language_example: Não estou de todo convencido.
native_language_example: I’m not entirely convinced.

additional_notes: Used to mean “out of everyone/everything in a group” or “belonging to everyone/everything” when the following noun is masculine plural (os sonhos, os povos, os prazeres). For feminine plural, use “de todas as”. Often appears in superlatives or emphasis: “o primeiro de todos os…” = “the first of all…”.
target_language_example: Este é o melhor de todos os restaurantes da cidade.
native_language_example: This is the best of all the restaurants in the city.

meaning: “to have to work” / “to need to work” (after a form of "ter de").
additional_notes: Most often appears as part of the structure "ter de + infinitive" (e.g., "tem de trabalhar", "terá de trabalhar"), which expresses obligation/necessity (“have to”). "De trabalhar" by itself is incomplete without the verb that comes before it (usually "ter"). Not the same as "de + working" in English.
target_language_example: Amanhã eu tenho de trabalhar cedo.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have to work early.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something related to work (e.g., "dia de trabalho" = workday, "horário de trabalho" = working hours, "roupa de trabalho" = work clothes). With "falar de trabalho", it means “to talk about work” (the topic). Often contrasts with "de folga" (off work).
target_language_example: Hoje eu tenho reunião de trabalho às nove.
native_language_example: Today I have a work meeting at nine.

meaning: 'to lock the door' (usually after forgetting/remembering to do it).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like esquecer (to forget), lembrar (to remember), or pedir/mandar (to ask/tell) to express the action you forgot/remember/should do: esquecer de trancar a porta = 'to forget to lock the door'. You can specify which door: trancar a porta da frente = 'lock the front door'.
target_language_example: Lembre-se de trancar a porta antes de dormir.
native_language_example: Remember to lock the door before going to sleep.

additional_notes: Used to say the means of transport (how you travel): ir/chegar/voltar/viajar **de trem**. Common in Brazil; in Portugal you’ll often hear **de comboio** for “by train.” Also appears in phrases like **estação de trem** (“train station”).
target_language_example: Prefiro ir ao centro de trem porque é mais rápido.
native_language_example: I prefer to go downtown by train because it’s faster.

additional_notes: Used to indicate something coming or appearing from a position behind something/someone (e.g., "de trás da porta" = "from behind the door"). It also shows location when combined with "lá/aí/aqui": "lá de trás" = "back there". In set phrases like "banco de trás", it means "the back seat".
target_language_example: O cachorro saiu de trás do carro.
native_language_example: The dog came out from behind the car.

meaning: traffic-related; road/vehicle traffic (as in rules, laws, accidents).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify it’s about road traffic: regras/leis de trânsito (traffic rules/laws), acidentes de trânsito (traffic accidents). Often contrasts with other meanings of "trânsito" like "passage" or "movement," but in everyday contexts it usually refers to vehicles on roads.
target_language_example: Hoje houve muito trânsito e também um acidente de trânsito na avenida.
native_language_example: Today there was a lot of traffic and also a traffic accident on the avenue.

additional_notes: Often means “of everything” after certain verbs/nouns: compartilhar de tudo (share everything), fazer uma piada de tudo (make a joke out of everything), comer de tudo (eat almost anything). Very common fixed expression: fazer de tudo = “do everything/anything possible” (make every effort), usually followed by para + infinitive (e.g., fiz de tudo para te ajudar).
target_language_example: Eu vou fazer de tudo para chegar a tempo.
native_language_example: I’ll do everything I can to arrive on time.

meaning: “tennis” (the sport); also “tennis” as a modifier (e.g., tennis shoes/racket).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like gostar de to talk about liking the sport: Eu gosto de tênis = “I like tennis.” It also describes things related to the sport in noun phrases like calçados de tênis (“tennis shoes”) or raquete de tênis (“tennis racket”).
target_language_example: Ela está de tênis e com uma raquete de tênis.
native_language_example: She’s wearing tennis shoes and has a tennis racket.

additional_notes: A common combination of the preposition de with the masculine singular article um. It often means "of a," but depending on context de can also be translated other ways, such as "from a." It is used before singular masculine nouns.
target_language_example: Ele precisava de um minuto para pensar.
native_language_example: He needed a minute to think.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition “de” + “um amigo” (“a friend”). It often marks a source/origin (“from a friend”), as in “pegar/receber … de um amigo.” It can also mean “of a friend” in relationships like “um amigo de um amigo” (“a friend of a friend”). Some verbs require “de”, like “precisar de” (“to need”), e.g., “O que eu preciso é de um amigo.”
target_language_example: Eu ouvi isso de um amigo.
native_language_example: I heard that from a friend.

de um dia para o outro

target_language_multi_word_term: de um dia para o outro
meaning: suddenly; overnight (from one day to the next).
additional_notes: Used to say something happened very quickly and unexpectedly, as if it changed from one day to the next. It can describe events, feelings, relationships, or situations. Often used with commas in the middle of a sentence for emphasis: "tornou-se, de um dia para o outro, ...".
target_language_example: Ele ficou famoso de um dia para o outro.
native_language_example: He became famous overnight.

meaning: “of a man” (belonging to, about, or from a man).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to show possession or relationship: “a vida de um homem” (a man’s life), “a reputação de um homem” (a man’s reputation). Also used to mean “about a man” depending on context: “a história de um homem” (the story of a man). Common with masculine nouns; with feminine it becomes “de uma mulher” (of a woman).
target_language_example: Eu ouvi a história de um homem que morava aqui.
native_language_example: I heard the story of a man who lived here.

additional_notes: Combination of the preposition “de” + “uma” (“a/an”, feminine). It’s used before a feminine singular noun. Common translations depend on context: “of a” (possession/description/part of) and “from a” (origin). Very common in phrases like “de uma maneira/forma” = “in a way / in a manner” (literally “of a way”).
target_language_example: Ele falou de uma maneira muito calma.
native_language_example: He spoke in a very calm way.

meaning: about something; (in “Sabe/Quer saber de uma coisa?”) “you know what?”
additional_notes: Common after verbs like falar (“to talk”): “Preciso falar de uma coisa com você” = “I need to talk to you about something.” It’s also used to emphasize certainty: “Tenho certeza de uma coisa” = “I’m sure of one thing.” In questions like “Sabe de uma coisa?” / “Quer saber de uma coisa?”, it’s a conversational lead-in to get attention before saying something.
target_language_example: Quer saber de uma coisa? Acho melhor a gente ir embora.
native_language_example: You know what? I think we’d better leave.

additional_notes: Used to describe how something is done or how something is true, often followed by an adjective or adverb: "de uma forma diferente" (in a different way), "de uma forma incrível" (in an incredible way), "de uma forma mais discreta" (more discreetly). It can also be used to soften a statement, similar to "in a way" in English: "Isso seria irônico de uma forma" (That would be ironic in a way). Common set phrase: "de uma forma geral" = "generally / in general".
target_language_example: Podemos resolver isso de uma forma mais simples.
native_language_example: We can solve this in a simpler way.

additional_notes: Used to describe how something is done or expressed, often followed by an adjective (e.g., de uma maneira especial, de uma maneira bela). Common set phrase: "de uma maneira geral" = "in general / generally speaking".
target_language_example: Você pode explicar isso de uma maneira mais simples?
native_language_example: Can you explain that in a simpler way?

additional_notes: Used to show possession or association with a woman (e.g., “the hands of a woman” = “a woman’s hands”). It’s formed with the preposition “de” + the indefinite article “uma” (a) + “mulher” (woman). In English it often becomes ’s (a woman’s) or “of a woman,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ele falou sobre a vida de uma mulher corajosa.
native_language_example: He talked about the life of a brave woman.

meaning: 'once and for all' / 'already' (do it now, stop delaying).
additional_notes: Often used to show impatience or urgency, pushing someone to do something immediately or make a decision: "Decidam de uma vez!" (Decide already!). It can also mean doing something all at the same time/in one go: "pegar tudo de uma vez" (take everything at once). The tone depends on context and can sound a bit forceful in commands.
target_language_example: Diz logo de uma vez o que você quer.
native_language_example: Just say already what you want.

meaning: once and for all; for good (finally).
additional_notes: Used to say you want something settled definitively, so it won’t happen again or won’t need to be discussed anymore. Common with verbs like resolver, decidir, acabar com, parar, and often adds a strong, impatient or determined tone.
target_language_example: Vamos resolver isso de uma vez por todas.
native_language_example: Let’s settle this once and for all.

meaning: all at once; once and for all (already!).
additional_notes: Often used to add emphasis/urgency, like “already!” or “just do it now” (e.g., "Vamos terminar de uma vez."). It can also mean doing something in a single go or simultaneously ("tudo de uma vez", "dois... de uma vez").
target_language_example: Fala logo de uma vez o que aconteceu.
native_language_example: Just say already what happened.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is authentic or true. After a noun, it often means “real/true” (e.g., "meu pai de verdade" = "my real/biological dad"; "um herói de verdade" = "a real hero"). After a verb or in questions, it often means “really / genuinely” ("Você me ama de verdade?" = "Do you really love me?").
target_language_example: Ele é meu amigo de verdade.
native_language_example: He’s my real (true) friend.

meaning: summer; summertime (used to describe something as 'summer' or 'for summer').
additional_notes: Used after a noun to say it is associated with summer or typical of summer: e.g., "sol de verão" (summer sun), "brisa de verão" (summer breeze), "vestido de verão" (summer dress). Often corresponds to English “summer” used as an adjective.
target_language_example: Gosto de tomar limonada nas tardes de verão.
native_language_example: I like having lemonade on summer afternoons.

additional_notes: Used after a verb to emphasize that something happens definitively/irreversibly (often like “for good” or “once and for all”): “começou de vez” = “started for good.” It can also be used in short exclamations/complaints (“De vez!”) meaning “come on already!” / “enough already!” Depending on context, it can add intensity, especially with mental-state verbs: “pirou de vez” = “completely lost it.”
target_language_example: Ele decidiu parar de fumar de vez.
native_language_example: He decided to quit smoking for good.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens occasionally (not often, not regularly). It can go at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence: “De vez em quando, ...” / “..., de vez em quando.” Common with verbs like acontecer (to happen), ocorrer (to occur), cometer (to make/commit), encontrar-se (to meet).
target_language_example: De vez em quando, eu saio para jantar com meus amigos.
native_language_example: From time to time, I go out to dinner with my friends.

additional_notes: Portuguese often uses "de" before an infinitive after certain verbs, especially "gostar de" (to like). So "gostar de viajar" = "to like traveling / to like to travel." Here, "de viajar" is the infinitive phrase that names the activity.
target_language_example: Ela não gosta de viajar sozinha.
native_language_example: She doesn't like traveling alone.

additional_notes: Literally "of life." Common after nouns to describe something related to life (e.g., "disposição de vida" = zest/attitude for life) and especially after amounts of time to mean someone has that much life left ("meia hora de vida", "seis meses de vida").
target_language_example: O médico disse que ele tem poucos dias de vida.
native_language_example: The doctor said he has only a few days to live.

meaning: 'from sight'; used in phrases like 'perder de vista' (lose sight of) and 'sair de vista' (go out of sight).
additional_notes:
Most common in set expressions about seeing/not seeing someone or something: 
- "perder (alguém/algo) de vista" = to lose sight of (someone/something), often in a crowd or when distracted.
- "sair de vista" = to disappear/go out of sight.
Different meaning in "ponto de vista" = point of view/opinion (not about physical sight).
target_language_example: Não perde ela de vista — ela já vai entrar no ônibus.
native_language_example: Don’t lose sight of her—she’s about to get on the bus.

meaning: back; back again (to its original place/state).
additional_notes: Often used after verbs to mean returning something/someone to where it was (levar/colocar/pôr X de volta). It can also mean getting something back (pegar X de volta). In some contexts it’s like “back on/attached again” (e.g., costurar o dedo de volta).
target_language_example: Você pode colocar o livro de volta na estante, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you put the book back on the shelf, please?

additional_notes: Used to talk about returning to a previous place, state, or owner. Very common in phrases like estar de volta ('to be back'), trazer de volta ('to bring back'), and pegar de volta ('to get/take back').
