target_language_example: Quando você estiver de volta, me avisa.
native_language_example: When you're back, let me know.

additional_notes: Used to show a return to a specific masculine place or context. It often follows verbs like voltar, colocar, mandar, levar (e.g., “colocar … de volta ao armário” = “put … back in the cupboard”). With feminine nouns, it becomes “de volta à” (à escola).
target_language_example: Depois do almoço, voltamos de volta ao trabalho.
native_language_example: After lunch, we went back to work.

additional_notes: Used to express returning to a destination: "voltar" (to return) + "para" (to/toward). Very common with movement verbs like "correr" (run), "mandar" (send), "mudar" (move), or with tickets/trips: "passagem de volta" = a return ticket. Note: "de volta" can also be used without "para" ("Estou de volta" = "I'm back").
target_language_example: Depois do almoço, voltamos de volta para o trabalho.
native_language_example: After lunch, we went back to work.

meaning: of chess; chess (as an adjective phrase).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify it’s related to the game of chess (xadrez). Common with words like jogo (jogo de xadrez = chess game) and jogador/jogadora (jogador de xadrez = chess player).
target_language_example: Comprei um livro de xadrez para aprender aberturas.
native_language_example: I bought a chess book to learn openings.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify that something is made for/with/contains water, or is a quantity/type of water: “copo de água” (a glass of water), “aquecedor de água” (water heater). Often translates literally as “of water,” but in English you may also say “water” as an adjective (“water heater”).
target_language_example: Você quer uma garrafa de água?
native_language_example: Do you want a bottle of water?

additional_notes: Used to say how you travel (means of transportation), especially with verbs like ir, vir, chegar: “Eu vim de ônibus” = “I came by bus.” In English you usually say “by bus,” while Portuguese commonly uses “de + [transport]” (de carro, de trem, de metrô, etc.).
target_language_example: A gente vai de ônibus porque é mais barato.
native_language_example: We’re going by bus because it’s cheaper.

additional_notes: Used to say something (or someone) is in the space below the bed. Often appears after verbs like estar (to be), esconder (to hide), encontrar (to find), olhar (to look), or correr/fugir (to run away). You’ll also hear the shorter form “debaixo da cama” without any extra words; it can also be said as “embaixo da cama” in everyday speech.
target_language_example: O cachorro dorme debaixo da cama quando está com medo.
native_language_example: The dog sleeps under the bed when it’s scared.

additional_notes: Used to describe something located or happening beneath a table. Often appears after a verb like estar (to be), esconder-se (to hide), deitar-se (to lie down), or haver/ter (there is/there are). You can swap in other nouns: debaixo da cama (under the bed), debaixo da cadeira (under the chair).
target_language_example: As chaves estão debaixo da mesa.
native_language_example: The keys are under the table.

additional_notes: Used to say something is physically underneath something else. It’s a contraction: debaixo de + o = debaixo do (masc. singular). Variations: debaixo da (de + a), debaixo dos (de + os), debaixo das (de + as). Common in set phrases like debaixo do braço (“under the arm”) and questions like Você olhou debaixo do...? (“Did you look under the...?”).
target_language_example: O gato está debaixo do carro.
native_language_example: The cat is under the car.

meaning: toe (a toe; literally “finger of the foot”).
additional_notes: Used to refer to any toe. The plural is usually “dedos do pé” (toes). Common in everyday contexts like injuries, shoes, and body parts.
target_language_example: Bati o dedo do pé na quina da cama.
native_language_example: I banged my toe on the corner of the bed.

additional_notes: Imperative form of the reflexive verb “deitar-se” (“to lie down”). It’s commonly used as an instruction (e.g., by a doctor, therapist, or in service situations): “Deite-se na cama/no sofá” = “Lie down on the bed/on the sofa.”
target_language_example: Por favor, deite-se e tente relaxar.
native_language_example: Please lie down and try to relax.

additional_notes: Used to ask for permission or to request that someone allows you to do something: "Deixa-me + infinitive" (deixa-me ajudar, deixa-me sair, deixa-me dormir). It can sound polite with "por favor". In European Portuguese you’ll often see object pronouns attached with a hyphen (deixa-me, ajudar-te, falar-te). In Brazilian Portuguese you may hear "deixa eu" more often.
target_language_example: Deixa-me explicar uma coisa.
native_language_example: Let me explain something.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese; it’s a colloquial form of the more formal "deixe-me". It’s usually followed by a verb in the infinitive: "deixa eu ir", "deixa eu falar", "deixa eu ver". You can also add an object pronoun: "deixa eu te ajudar" (let me help you).
target_language_example: Deixa eu ver o cardápio, por favor.
native_language_example: Let me see the menu, please.

meaning: “Let me see.” / “Let me have a look.”
additional_notes: Used to ask permission to look at something (e.g., a phone), or to ask someone to move so you can see. It’s also used as a thinking filler (“Let me see…”). Very common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese; more formal alternatives include “deixe-me ver” or “deixa eu olhar”. Adding swear words (e.g., “porra”) makes it rude/strong.
target_language_example: Deixa eu ver o que você escreveu.
native_language_example: Let me see what you wrote.

additional_notes: Used to stop talking about something, to dismiss a mistake/question, or to say it’s no longer important (e.g., you found it, changed your mind, or don’t want to discuss it). Often said as a quick standalone phrase. "Pra" is the informal spoken form of "para".
target_language_example: Eu ia te pedir um favor, mas deixa pra lá.
native_language_example: I was going to ask you a favor, but never mind.

additional_notes: Often followed by an infinitive verb. (1) "deixar de" + infinitive = to stop doing something: "deixar de tentar" = stop trying. Common in commands: "Deixa(r) de me perturbar" = Stop bothering me. (2) With a negative + "poder" ("não posso/pôde/podia deixar de" + infinitive) it means "can’t/couldn’t help (doing)": "não pude deixar de rir" = I couldn’t help laughing. Note: "deixar de lado" is a fixed variation meaning "to set aside" (e.g., details, worries).
target_language_example: Não consegui deixar de pensar nisso.
native_language_example: I couldn’t help thinking about it.

meaning: to leave (someone) alone; to let (someone) be.
additional_notes: Used when asking someone to stop bothering you or to respect your privacy/quiet. The object pronoun can change: me deixar em paz (leave me alone), te deixar em paz (leave you alone), deixar ela/ele em paz or deixá-la/deixá-lo em paz (leave her/him alone). You can also add time: por alguns minutos (for a few minutes).
target_language_example: Pode me deixar em paz, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you leave me alone, please?

meaning: to let slip; to let escape.
additional_notes: Used when someone unintentionally reveals information ("let something slip") or fails to keep/hold something and it escapes. Common patterns: “deixar escapar + informação/segredo/comentário” (let slip information/a secret/a comment) and “deixar escapar + oportunidade/detalhe” (miss an opportunity/a detail).
target_language_example: Ele acabou por deixar escapar o segredo sem querer.
native_language_example: He ended up letting the secret slip unintentionally.

additional_notes: Usually means "let/allow" when followed by another verb: deixar o Tom ir = let Tom go. In other contexts it means "leave": deixar o país = leave the country. Here, o is the masculine singular article "the"; in some varieties of Portuguese it can also appear before men's names.
target_language_example: Você não deve deixar o cachorro entrar.
native_language_example: You shouldn't let the dog come in.

meaning: to let it go; never mind; drop it.
additional_notes: Used when you decide not to worry about something, not argue, or not continue a topic. It can also suggest giving up on an idea or stopping a complaint. Common in everyday speech, often as “Deixa pra lá.”
target_language_example: Ah, vamos deixar para lá — não vale a pena discutir.
native_language_example: Ah, let’s let it go — it’s not worth arguing.

meaning: to let (someone/something) pass; to allow through.
additional_notes: Used when asking or telling someone to make space or give permission to go by/through (a doorway, crowd, checkpoint, etc.). It can take a direct object: “deixar passar alguém” (let someone through). In other contexts it can also mean “to let something go/overlook,” but the examples here are about allowing passage.
target_language_example: Com licença, você pode me deixar passar?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you let me through?

meaning: to leave it alone; to let it be.
additional_notes: Used when you want someone (or yourself) to stop touching, bothering, or arguing about something and stop interfering. Common in advice or mild warnings. Often implies “don’t bring it up” or “don’t mess with it.”
target_language_example: É melhor deixar quieto e ir embora.
native_language_example: It’s better to leave it alone and go away.

additional_notes: Imperative form of **deixar** + the object pronoun **-a** (“her”). Used to tell someone to allow her to do something (**Deixe-a dormir.** = “Let her sleep.”) or to leave her somewhere/alone or stop involving her (**Deixe-a fora disto.** = “Leave her out of this.”). Often followed by an infinitive (deixe-a + verb) or by a place/adverb (deixe-a lá, deixe-a comigo).
target_language_example: Deixe-a em paz, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave her alone, please.

additional_notes: Used to ask for a moment to explain something, often before giving details or justifying an action. It can sound polite or firm depending on tone; with an exclamation mark (“Deixe-me explicar!”) it can sound more insistent. Commonly followed by what you want to explain (a situação, as regras, o que precisa ser feito, por que/porque...).
target_language_example: Deixe-me explicar melhor antes de você decidir.
native_language_example: Let me explain better before you decide.

meaning: “let me go” / “let me (do it)” (allow me to go).
additional_notes: From **deixar** (“to let/allow”) + **me** (“me”) + **ir** (“to go”). Used to ask permission or request that someone allow you to leave or accompany them: *Deixe-me ir com você/contigo.* It can also be used more generally as “let me…” before an action or shift in the conversation (often followed by an infinitive or a direction like *direto ao ponto*).
target_language_example: Deixe-me ir embora, por favor.
native_language_example: Please let me go / let me leave.

additional_notes: Used to ask for a moment to check/think (“Let me see if I can find it”), or to ask someone to show you something (“Let me see your hands”). In speech it can be a polite request or a firm command depending on tone. Also appears as “deixa eu ver” (more informal, common in Brazil).
target_language_example: Deixe-me ver se entendi direito.
native_language_example: Let me see if I understood correctly.

additional_notes: Formed by the command form of **deixar** (“to let/allow/leave”) + **nos** (“us”). Common in polite requests: **Por favor, deixe-nos + infinitive** (“Please let us + verb”). With adjectives it can mean “leave us [alone/quiet/etc.]”: **Deixe-nos sozinhas/sozinhos**. You may also hear **deixa a gente…** in informal Brazilian Portuguese for “let us…”.
target_language_example: Por favor, deixe-nos explicar tudo com calma.
native_language_example: Please let us explain everything calmly.

additional_notes: Imperative form of "deixar" for "você" + the object pronoun "-o" (= "him" or "it"). Common in instructions: "Deixe-o esfriar" (let it cool), "Deixe-o aqui/aí" (leave it here/there). Depending on context it can also mean "leave him alone / stop it" (e.g., "Deixe-o, rapaz.").
target_language_example: Deixe-o na mesa, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave it on the table, please.

additional_notes: Imperative (você form) of "deixar" + the object pronoun "-os" (= "them", masculine/mixed group). Often used to give permission or not interfere: "Deixe-os fazer" = "Let them do it." In some contexts it can mean "leave them (alone)". With "pra lá" ("Deixe-os pra lá"), it means "leave them be / ignore them / forget it."
target_language_example: Deixe-os em paz; eles estão cansados.
native_language_example: Leave them alone; they’re tired.

additional_notes: From the verb "deixar" (to leave/let) + "em paz" (in peace). Very common as a request or command. You can add or change the object pronoun: "me deixe em paz" (leave me alone), "nos deixe em paz" (leave us alone), "deixe-a em paz" (leave her alone). Often used firmly; adding "por favor" makes it more polite.
target_language_example: Por favor, me deixe em paz — eu só quero descansar.
native_language_example: Please leave me alone — I just want to rest.

additional_notes: Imperative of "deixar" (to let/allow) + "-me" (me). Used to ask permission or request that others allow you to do something. "Deixem" is plural (speaking to you all); to one person, use "deixe-me". Often followed by an infinitive: "deixem-me explicar / ir / lavar".
target_language_example: Deixem-me terminar, por favor.
native_language_example: Let me finish, please.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of “deixar cair” (to drop/let fall). Used when something accidentally falls from someone’s hand or they cause it to fall. Often followed by the object: “deixou cair o lápis.” Can also be used alone when the object is obvious: “Ei, você deixou cair.”
target_language_example: Você deixou cair o seu lenço.
native_language_example: You dropped your handkerchief.

additional_notes: This is the verb **deixar** + the object pronoun **-la** (= “her”). It often appears with a hyphen when the pronoun is attached to the verb (common with infinitives): **deixar + a → deixá-la** (accent added for pronunciation). Meaning depends on context: **deixá-la em paz** = “leave her alone”; **deixá-la fazer** = “let her do (it)”.
target_language_example: Pode deixá-la aqui por um minuto?
native_language_example: Can you leave her here for a minute?

meaning: to leave him/it; to let him/it (do something).
additional_notes: This is the verb "deixar" + the object pronoun "o" (= "him" or "it"), written with a hyphen: deixá-lo. It’s common after an infinitive ("deixar") and often means either (1) "leave him/it" (stop taking him/it with you) or (2) "let him/it" (allow something to happen), depending on context. The accent (deixá-) appears when the pronoun is attached, to keep the stress/pronunciation consistent.
target_language_example: Não vou deixá-lo sozinho em casa.
native_language_example: I’m not going to leave him alone at home.

meaning: “to leave them” / “to let them” (leave/allow them to do something).
additional_notes: This is the verb **deixar** + the object pronoun **-los** (“them,” masculine or mixed group). In Portuguese, object pronouns are often attached to the end of the verb with a hyphen (**deixá-los**). The accent (á) appears because **deixar** loses its final **r** before adding **-los**. It’s used both for physically leaving someone (“leave them”) and for allowing/permitting (“let them”).
target_language_example: Vou deixá-los entrar, mas só por cinco minutos.
native_language_example: I’ll let them come in, but only for five minutes.

additional_notes: Used to say something belongs to (or is associated with) a male person ("of him" → "his"). In Portuguese, possession is often expressed with "de" + pronoun: "dele" (of him / his), "dela" (of her / hers), "deles" (of them, masc./mixed), "delas" (of them, fem.). In sentences like "O cinto dele é preto", it means "His belt is black" (literally: "The belt of him is black").
target_language_example: O carro dele é novo, mas o meu é velho.
native_language_example: His car is new, but mine is old.

additional_notes: Place where police work and where you go to report a crime, file a complaint (fazer um boletim de ocorrência), or speak to an officer. Common with verbs like ir à (go to), entrar em (enter), and with estar/ficar na (be at). Often shortened in speech to “delegacia”.
target_language_example: Você pode me acompanhar até a delegacia de polícia para registrar a ocorrência?
native_language_example: Can you come with me to the police station to file a report?

additional_notes: Used to say something is excessive to the point that it prevents an action or isn’t suitable: usually **adjective/adverb + demais + para**. Common patterns: **(1) adj + demais para + infinitive** (e.g., *nervoso demais para falar* = too nervous to speak). **(2) adj + demais para + person + infinitive** (e.g., *pequenos demais para eu calçar* = too small for me to put on).
target_language_example: Estou cansado demais para sair hoje.
native_language_example: I'm too tired to go out today.

additional_notes: Used to say something is excessive to the point that another action/state is not possible or not appropriate. Pattern: "[adjective/adverb] demais para ser + past participle" (e.g., descrita, rejeitada, usada, tratada) or sometimes "demais para ser + adjective/noun". "Demais" means "too" here (not "the others").
target_language_example: Este lugar é longe demais para ser alcançado a pé.
native_language_example: This place is too far to be reached on foot.

additional_notes: Used to indicate something located within a specific feminine noun (da = de + a). With masculine nouns, use "dentro do" (do = de + o). It can be literal (inside a box/house) or figurative (inside my head; divisions within an organization). Often appears with verbs like "estar", "haver", "olhar" and questions like "O que há dentro da...?"
target_language_example: Tem alguém dentro da sala.
native_language_example: There is someone inside the room.

additional_notes: Used to indicate something located in the interior of a place or container (dentro de casa, dentro de um envelope). It can also be figurative, meaning 'within' someone (dentro de mim = inside me). Often followed by a noun; with pronouns you’ll commonly see forms like dentro de mim/ti/si/nós/vocês. In speech and writing it frequently contracts with the definite article: dentro de + a/o/as/os → dentro da/do/das/dos (e.g., dentro de a bolsa = dentro da bolsa).
target_language_example: Deixei as chaves dentro de uma bolsa.
native_language_example: I left the keys inside a bag.

additional_notes: Used to indicate something is located or happens inside a specific (masculine singular) place, object, or space. It’s a contraction of "dentro de" + "o" (the). For feminine singular, use "dentro da"; for plural, "dentro dos/das".
target_language_example: Há um gato dentro do armário.
native_language_example: There is a cat inside the closet.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is in the interior of a car. Often follows verbs like esperar (to wait), estar (to be), deixar (to leave), manter (to keep). You can also hear variations like dentro do carro trancado (“inside the locked car”) or just dentro do carro (“inside the car”) when context is clear.
target_language_example: Deixe a mochila dentro do carro, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the backpack inside the car, please.

additional_notes: Common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese to postpone doing something or deciding something. "A gente" is an informal way to say "we" (it takes 3rd-person singular verbs: a gente vai, a gente vê). Often followed by a verb: "Depois a gente vê/combina/marca/arruma".
target_language_example: Depois a gente conversa com calma.
native_language_example: We’ll talk later, calmly.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen following a lesson/class period. Often used when making plans: "depois da aula" (after class), "depois das aulas" (after classes). Also common with time add-ons like "hoje" (today) or "hoje à noite" (tonight).
target_language_example: Vamos tomar um café depois da aula.
native_language_example: Let’s have a coffee after class.

additional_notes: Used to talk about time after the school day ends. Common when making plans or asking what someone does after classes. Often follows an activity: "Vou estudar depois da escola". The structure is "depois de" + a noun; before a feminine noun like "escola," it becomes "depois da" (de + a).
target_language_example: Vamos sair depois da escola?
native_language_example: Shall we go out after school?

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than 12:00 a.m. The structure is common: depois de/da + a time or event (e.g., depois do almoço = after lunch). Here, da = de + a because meia-noite is feminine (a meia-noite).
target_language_example: A festa só terminou depois da meia-noite.
native_language_example: The party only ended after midnight.

additional_notes: Used before a noun or an infinitive verb to say that one thing happens after another. Compare with depois on its own, which often means "afterward" or "later."
target_language_example: Depois de jantar, fomos passear.
native_language_example: After dinner, we went for a walk.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the day two days from now. Common in planning (appointments, trips). It’s a fixed expression: "depois" (after) + "de" (of) + "amanhã" (tomorrow).
target_language_example: A reunião é depois de amanhã às dez.
native_language_example: The meeting is the day after tomorrow at ten.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a date two days from today. It’s a fixed time phrase: depois (after) + de (of) + amanhã (tomorrow). Often used with future plans, deadlines, or appointments (e.g., “até/no máximo depois de amanhã” = “by/at the latest, the day after tomorrow”).
target_language_example: Tenho uma reunião depois de amanhã às nove.
native_language_example: I have a meeting the day after tomorrow at nine.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later than the action of eating. Common pattern: "depois de" + infinitive (verb), e.g., "depois de comer" (after eating), "depois de trabalhar" (after working). Often placed at the start or end of a sentence; a comma is common when it comes first.
target_language_example: Depois de comer, vou escovar os dentes.
native_language_example: After eating, I'm going to brush my teeth.

additional_notes: Used to say that one action happens after another. It’s followed by a past participle: depois de ter + conhecido/encontrado/passado/tomado, etc. Often interchangeable with the personal infinitive form: depois de eu/ele/ela ter + past participle (when you want to specify who did it).
target_language_example: Depois de ter terminado o trabalho, fui para casa.
native_language_example: After having finished work, I went home.

additional_notes: Used when something happens despite doubts, expectations, or difficulties—often with a sense of surprise or “despite everything.” It can refer to a final outcome ("in the end") or emphasize that, considering everything, the result is different than expected ("after all").
target_language_example: Ele decidiu me ajudar depois de tudo.
native_language_example: He decided to help me after all.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to something just mentioned (an event or situation) and say what happens next or how someone feels afterward. Common at the start of a sentence (“Depois disso, …”) or at the end (“… depois disso.”).
target_language_example: Depois disso, fomos direto para o hotel.
native_language_example: After that, we went straight to the hotel.

additional_notes: Used to indicate that something happens later in time than a specific event or time period. It’s the contraction of "depois de" + "o" (masculine singular). For feminine singular, you’ll often see "depois da" (de + a). Often followed by a noun ("depois do café da manhã") or by an infinitive when it stays as "depois de" (e.g., "depois de comer" = after eating).
target_language_example: Depois do trabalho, vou para casa.
native_language_example: After work, I’m going home.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later in the day, following the lunch meal. Often refers to the early afternoon. You can also say it with "logo" for emphasis: "logo depois do almoço" = "right after lunch."
target_language_example: Tenho uma reunião depois do almoço.
native_language_example: I have a meeting after lunch.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens later than the dinner meal. "Depois de" + a noun often becomes "depois do" (de + o) before a masculine singular noun like "jantar".
target_language_example: Vamos dar um passeio depois do jantar.
native_language_example: Let's go for a walk after dinner.

additional_notes: Used to talk about plans that happen when the workday ends. You can also hear similar phrases like "depois da escola" (after school). Often used with verbs like "fazer" (to do), "ir" (to go), and "sair" (to go out).
target_language_example: A gente pode tomar um café depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: We can have a coffee after work.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause (with a verb) meaning that one event happens later than another: “after + subject + verb”. Often followed by past tense in stories: “depois que parou de chover…” = “after it stopped raining…”. For a single word meaning “afterwards/then,” you usually use “depois” (without “que”).
target_language_example: Depois que terminei o trabalho, fui para casa.
native_language_example: After I finished work, I went home.

meaning: bloodshed; spilling of blood (violence causing injuries/deaths).
additional_notes: Used when talking about violent conflict (crime, riots, war) where people may be hurt or killed. Very common with verbs like “evitar” (to avoid) or “haver” (to be/occur): “evitar um derramamento de sangue” = “avoid bloodshed.” It’s a serious, formal expression.
target_language_example: Os líderes chegaram a um acordo para evitar um derramamento de sangue.
native_language_example: The leaders reached an agreement to avoid bloodshed.

meaning: “to rest in peace” (said about someone who has died).
additional_notes: Used in condolences or memorial contexts, often as a wish or prayer for a deceased person. Commonly appears conjugated as “(que ele/ela) descanse em paz” (“may he/she rest in peace”). The base form “descansar em paz” may appear in dictionaries, explanations, or as an infinitive phrase (e.g., “desejo que ele possa descansar em paz”).
target_language_example: Depois de tanto sofrimento, espero que ele possa descansar em paz.
native_language_example: After so much suffering, I hope he can rest in peace.

meaning: to rest a little; to take a short break.
additional_notes: Used to suggest or ask for a brief rest (physically or mentally). Common with "podemos/precisamos" (we can/we need), "tudo bem se eu..." (is it okay if I...), and "você deveria" (you should).
target_language_example: Depois do almoço, vamos descansar um pouco.
native_language_example: After lunch, let's rest a little.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "descer" (to go down) with "de" + a vehicle to mean getting off/out of it: "descer do ônibus", "descer do trem", "descer do carro". Very common in Brazil; you can also hear "sair do ônibus" (to get out of the bus).
target_language_example: Você pode me avisar quando for hora de descer do ônibus?
native_language_example: Can you let me know when it's time to get off the bus?

meaning: "Sorry, but…" (a polite way to introduce a disagreement, correction, or complaint).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to soften what comes next (often something negative or contradictory). You can also hear/see "me desculpe, mas" (same meaning). Common in both spoken and written Portuguese.
target_language_example: Desculpe, mas eu não concordo com isso.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I don’t agree with that.

additional_notes: Used to apologize (“Sorry”), to politely get someone’s attention (“Excuse me”), or to introduce a request/question, often with “mas” (“Excuse me, but…”). It’s the formal/polite imperative of "desculpar" + object pronoun "me" (“me”); you may also hear the shorter “desculpe”.
target_language_example: Desculpe-me, mas você pode repetir a pergunta?
native_language_example: Excuse me, but can you repeat the question?

meaning: “forgive me for …” / “sorry for …” (followed by a reason).
additional_notes: Used to apologize for something you did or didn’t do. After por, you typically use an infinitive (por incomodar, por ser, por não ter respondido) or a noun (por isso). desculpe-me is polite/formal; in casual speech you’ll also hear desculpa por …
target_language_example: Desculpe-me por chegar atrasado.
native_language_example: Sorry for arriving late.

additional_notes: Used to apologize for an action, situation, or time period. Typically followed by a noun (desculpe por isso/ontem) or by a verb in the infinitive (desculpe por incomodar; desculpe por não poder…). In Brazil you can also hear the less formal variant “desculpa por …”.
target_language_example: Desculpe por ter chegado atrasado.
native_language_example: Sorry for arriving late.

meaning: “Sorry, I…” / “Excuse me, I…” (to apologize before explaining what you did or didn’t do).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to apologize and then give a reason, explanation, or correction. Common in everyday situations (e.g., being distracted, making a mistake). You can also say “Desculpa, eu…” in more informal settings.
target_language_example: Desculpe, eu me enganei.
native_language_example: Sorry, I made a mistake.

meaning: “Sorry, no…” / “Excuse me, no…” (a polite way to refuse or say you can’t).
additional_notes: Used to politely disagree, refuse, or say you didn’t understand or can’t do something. Often followed by a verb: “Desculpe, não entendi” (I didn’t understand), “Desculpe, não posso” (I can’t). You can also say “Desculpa” (more informal) instead of “Desculpe”.
target_language_example: Desculpe, não posso ir hoje.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go today.

meaning: 'since then' (from that time until now/another reference point).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something started at a particular moment in the past and has continued up to the present (or up to another time you’re talking about). Often follows a past event mentioned just before: "Aconteceu X. Desde então..."
target_language_example: Conheci a Ana em 2018, e desde então falamos quase todos os dias.
native_language_example: I met Ana in 2018, and since then we’ve talked almost every day.

meaning: from the beginning; from the start.
additional_notes: Used to say something is true or should happen starting at the very first moment. Common with verbs like ser/estar ("it was"), pensar ("to think"), and contar ("to tell").
target_language_example: Eu sabia desde o começo que ia dar errado.
native_language_example: I knew from the beginning that it was going to go wrong.

additional_notes: Used to say something has been true starting at the beginning of a period/event and continuing afterward. Also used for instructions meaning to start reading/doing something from the first part (e.g., from the start of a page).
target_language_example: Desde o início da reunião, ele parecia nervoso.
native_language_example: From the start of the meeting, he seemed nervous.

additional_notes: Used in two main ways: (1) As a question meaning “since when?”, often expressing surprise, doubt, or challenge: “Desde quando isso é crime?” ≈ “Since when is that a crime?” (2) To mark the starting point of a situation (usually with a verb in the past): “Desde quando parei de fumar...” = “Ever since I stopped smoking...”.
target_language_example: Desde quando você sabe dirigir?
native_language_example: Since when do you know how to drive?

meaning: “Since when have you…?” (asking from what time; often also expressing surprise/challenge).
additional_notes: Used to ask when a situation started: “Desde quando você está…?” = “How long have you been…/Since when have you been…?” In many contexts it can sound skeptical or surprised (like “Since when do you care about…?”). It’s also used in a challenging way to question someone’s authority: “Desde quando você tem o direito…?” = “Since when do you have the right…?”
target_language_example: Desde quando você sabe falar português tão bem?
native_language_example: Since when have you been able to speak Portuguese so well?

additional_notes: Two common uses: (1) time: "since" (from a point in the past until now), often with a past event: "Passaram-se seis anos desde que eu comecei..."; (2) condition: "as long as / provided that", commonly followed by the subjunctive: "desde que eu esteja com uma calculadora" (= as long as I have a calculator). Context usually makes it clear which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Eu moro aqui desde que consegui esse emprego.
native_language_example: I’ve lived here since I got this job.

additional_notes: Used to express good wishes to someone you address with “você/o senhor/a senhora.” “Lhe” is an object pronoun meaning “to you” (or “to him/her,” depending on context), so this is a polite/formal way to say you wish someone luck, success, etc. Common with phrases like “boa sorte,” “tudo de bom,” “todo o sucesso.”
target_language_example: Desejo-lhe um ótimo dia.
native_language_example: I wish you a great day.

additional_notes: Used for animated TV shows, movies, or cartoon characters. Very common with verbs like "assistir" (to watch): "assistir a um desenho animado". It can also describe something that comes from a cartoon: "É de um desenho animado."
target_language_example: As crianças gostam de ver desenho animado antes de dormir.
native_language_example: The kids like to watch cartoons before going to sleep.

additional_notes: Used to describe the way something is done or the way someone behaves (often meaning “like this/that,” depending on context). It commonly follows verbs like fazer (to do/make), falar (to speak), tratar (to treat), preferir (to prefer). In speech you may also hear the equivalent forms “deste jeito” / “desse jeito.”
target_language_example: Não faça isso dessa maneira; tente de outra forma.
native_language_example: Don’t do it this way; try another way.

meaning: this time (as opposed to other times).
additional_notes: Used to contrast the current attempt/occasion with previous ones (“not like last time”). Often carries emphasis like “for once” or “this time, for real,” especially in threats, promises, or complaints. You can also say “não dessa vez” = “not this time.”
target_language_example: Dessa vez, eu vou chegar na hora.
native_language_example: This time, I’m going to arrive on time.

meaning: like that; that way (in that manner).
additional_notes: Used to describe how something is done or how someone/something is. It often points to a way you can see or that was just shown/mentioned (e.g., giving instructions: “Do it like this/that”). Can also describe someone’s typical behavior or personality: “Ele é desse jeito.”
target_language_example: Não fala comigo desse jeito.
native_language_example: Don’t talk to me like that.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the current attempt/occasion, often contrasting with other times (past tries or what usually happens). It can sound hopeful (“this time it’ll work”) or annoyed/surprised (“what did he do this time?”).
target_language_example: Desta vez, vou chegar cedo.
native_language_example: This time, I’m going to arrive early.

meaning: "of/from this city" (meaning the city being talked about).
additional_notes: "Desta" = "de" + "esta" ("of/from" + "this"). It’s used to refer back to a specific city that’s already known in the conversation or context. Common with things that belong to the city ("a rua principal desta cidade" = "the main street of this city") or movement/connection ("sair desta cidade" = "leave this city").
target_language_example: Os problemas desta cidade são parecidos com os da minha.
native_language_example: The problems of this city are similar to those of mine.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the present/most recent attempt or occasion (often contrasting with previous times). Common in promises, warnings, or emphasis: "but this time...". Equivalent to "esta vez"; "desta" is a contraction of "de" + "esta".
target_language_example: Desta vez, vou chegar cedo.
native_language_example: This time, I’m going to arrive early.

meaning: to stop her; to detain/hold her (back).
additional_notes: "Detê-la" = "deter" (to stop, detain, hold back) + "-la" (her/it, feminine direct object). It’s used when you’re talking about stopping a woman (or a feminine thing like "a bola", "a máquina") from moving, acting, escaping, etc. In everyday Portuguese you may also hear "pará-la" (“to stop her/it”) when it’s more about stopping motion rather than detaining.
target_language_example: A polícia tentou detê-la, mas ela correu.
native_language_example: The police tried to stop/detain her, but she ran.

meaning: to stop him; to detain/arrest him.
additional_notes: "Detê-lo" = "deter" (to stop, prevent, detain) + "-lo" (him). It often means physically stopping someone, but in police/legal contexts it commonly means "to detain/arrest him." In European Portuguese you may also see "detê-lo" where Brazilian Portuguese often uses "detê-lo" too (formal/written) or "deter ele" (less standard).
target_language_example: A polícia conseguiu detê-lo antes que ele fugisse.
native_language_example: The police managed to arrest him before he escaped.

meaning: “gave him/her” (or “gave to you” in formal address).
additional_notes: Past tense of **dar** (“to give”) + the indirect object pronoun **lhe** (“to him/her/to you” formal). It typically appears before a thing being given: **Deu-lhe um bolo** (“She gave him a cake”). **Lhe** refers to the person receiving something (not the thing itself).
target_language_example: O professor deu-lhe um livro.
native_language_example: The teacher gave him/her a book.

meaning: "gave a" / "did a" (past tense of dar + feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine noun to mean someone "gave" something (an object) or "gave/did" an action/event: deu uma cesta (gave a basket), deu uma descrição (gave a description), deu uma mão (gave a hand/helped), deu uma aula (gave/taught a class), deu uma tapa (gave a slap), deu uma folha (gave a sheet), deu uma risada (gave a laugh), deu uma ideia (gave an idea/overview). The noun that follows determines the natural English translation.
target_language_example: Ele deu uma resposta rápida.
native_language_example: He gave a quick answer.

additional_notes: Used literally for gods from Greek mythology (often followed by “do/da” + what they are the god of: “o deus grego do amor”). It can also be used figuratively to describe someone as extremely attractive or with an idealized, muscular body (“como se fosse um deus grego”).
target_language_example: Ele chegou na praia se achando um deus grego.
native_language_example: He showed up at the beach acting like he was a Greek god.

meaning: 'one should' / 'you should' (impersonal; general advice or obligation).
additional_notes: Impersonal construction: **deve-se + infinitive** is used to give general rules, recommendations, or obligations without saying who exactly (like English “one should…” or “you should…” meaning people in general). Often seen in instructions, manuals, and formal writing. Example pattern: **Deve-se ter cuidado** = “One should be careful.”
target_language_example: Em lugares públicos, deve-se falar baixo.
native_language_example: In public places, one should speak quietly.

additional_notes: Formed from dever + estar. Often used to make a guess or deduction about a current state or situation ('must be'), but in some contexts it can also express expectation or advisability ('should be'). It is commonly followed by an adjective, participle, or location.
target_language_example: Ela deve estar em casa agora.
native_language_example: She must be at home now.

meaning: "must be" / "is probably" (used to make a strong guess).
additional_notes: Used when you infer someone/something’s location or condition from clues (not certainty). It’s the present-tense form of "dever" + "estar" and commonly translates as "must be" or "is probably". It can refer to places ("deve estar no carro") or states/conditions ("deve estar cansado", "deve estar certo").
target_language_example: Ela deve estar em casa, porque as luzes estão acesas.
native_language_example: She must be at home, because the lights are on.

additional_notes: Used to express a logical guess or strong assumption that something exists or is true. It’s the verb haver (“to exist/there is/are”) with deve (“must/should”), usually followed by a noun: deve haver uma razão (“there must be a reason”).
target_language_example: Deve haver uma maneira melhor de fazer isso.
native_language_example: There must be a better way to do this.

additional_notes: Used both for deduction and for expectation. In many contexts it means 'must be' or 'is probably' when the speaker is guessing based on clues: Ela deve ser médica. It can also mean 'should be' when talking about what is right, expected, or appropriate: Um professor deve ser justo.
target_language_example: Ela deve ser médica.
native_language_example: She must be a doctor.

additional_notes: Used to make a guess or deduction about someone or something. It comes from the verb **dever** (“must/should”) + **ser** (“to be”) + **um** (“a/an”). Often implies “I’m pretty sure,” based on evidence, but can also be a softer “probably.” (Feminine: **deve ser uma**.)
target_language_example: Pelo jeito, deve ser um erro.
native_language_example: Looks like it must be a mistake.

additional_notes: Used to make a deduction or guess about something (high probability), like “I bet it’s…” or “It must be…”. It can also express what something is likely like: “isso deve ser…” = “that must be…/that’s probably…”. Negative: “não deve ser…” = “it probably isn’t/it must not be.”
target_language_example: Está muito quieto aqui; deve ser feriado.
native_language_example: It’s very quiet here; it must be a holiday.

additional_notes: Often used to make a deduction or guess about something, especially in the past: deve ter + past participle = 'must have done' or 'probably did'. In everyday English, it is often translated with 'must have' rather than obligation.
target_language_example: Ele deve ter esquecido a chave em casa.
native_language_example: He must have forgotten the key at home.

additional_notes: Used to make a logical guess about something in the past based on evidence or context. From dever (must/should) + ter sido (to have been). Commonly followed by an adjective or description: "Deve ter sido difícil/divertido." You can soften it further with "acho que": "Acho que deve ter sido..."
target_language_example: Você está com cara de cansado; deve ter sido um dia longo.
native_language_example: You look tired; it must have been a long day.

additional_notes: Used to express a logical conclusion or strong assumption about something that happened in the past (not certainty). It’s formed with "dever" + "ter" + past participle: "deve ter tido" = "must have had" (for ele/ela/você). Other persons: "devem ter tido" (they/you all), "devo ter tido" (I).
target_language_example: Ele deve ter tido um problema no caminho.
native_language_example: He must have had a problem on the way.

additional_notes: Used to make a confident guess or logical conclusion about something (often based on evidence), not to talk about an obligation. It’s the verb **dever** (“must/should”) + infinitive **ter** (“to have”), and can mean either that someone/something probably *has* something (**Ele deve ter raiva.**) or that something probably *exists/there is* (**Deve ter alguém aí.**).
target_language_example: Deve ter um jeito de resolver isso.
native_language_example: There must be a way to solve this.

meaning: 'must be' / 'are probably' (they should be; likely state).
additional_notes: Combination of dever (in the 3rd-person plural: devem) + estar. It’s used to make a guess or strong assumption about someone’s current state or situation (often translated as “must be” or “are probably”). It can also express obligation (“they should be”), but with situations like "devem estar mortos/preocupados" it usually means likelihood, not a rule.
target_language_example: Eles devem estar em casa agora.
native_language_example: They must be at home now.

additional_notes: Form of the verb phrase “dever + ser” for “they/you (plural)”: devem = must/should/ought to (or likely), ser = to be. Use it to express obligation/recommendation (“should/must be”) or a logical guess (“must be/probably are”), depending on context.
target_language_example: Eles devem ser novos aqui.
native_language_example: They must be new here.

meaning: "must have" / "should have" (probably did something in the past).
additional_notes: This is the verb "dever" (they/you-plural must/should) + "ter" + past participle, used to make a guess/inference about a past action: "Eles devem ter entrado" = "They must have gone in". It can also express expectation rather than certainty, depending on context.
target_language_example: Eles devem ter saído mais cedo para evitar o trânsito.
native_language_example: They must have left earlier to avoid traffic.

additional_notes: From the verb "dever" (to should/ought to/must) + an infinitive. It’s used to express advice, a recommendation, or an obligation: "Devemos fazer isso" = "We should do this" (often a suggestion), and in some contexts it can feel stronger, like "We must do this." You can swap in another infinitive: "devemos ir" (we should go), "devemos esperar" (we should wait).
target_language_example: Acho que devemos fazer isso hoje.
native_language_example: I think we should do it today.

additional_notes: Used for school assignments students do at home. It’s often used without an article (e.g., “tenho dever de casa”) or with a possessive (e.g., “meu/seu dever de casa”). Also commonly said as “lição de casa” in Brazil, with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Preciso terminar meu dever de casa antes de sair.
native_language_example: I need to finish my homework before going out.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of dever (deveria) + estar to express what is expected, advisable, or morally necessary in a situation. It’s very common before a gerund to mean “should be doing”: deveria estar fazendo = “should be doing.” In context it can sound like regret or criticism ("I know I should be doing this now").
target_language_example: Você deveria estar estudando agora, não jogando.
native_language_example: You should be studying now, not playing.

meaning: “should be” / “ought to be” (should be in a place or state).
additional_notes: Formed by the conditional of "dever" (deveria = should/ought to) + "estar" (to be, temporary/state/location). Used to express expectation, obligation, or what is considered correct: "Ele deveria estar na escola" (he’s supposed to be at school). It can also be used to guess where someone is: "Tom deveria estar na biblioteca" (Tom is probably/should be at the library). With "ali" it can mean "shouldn’t be there" (something isn’t supposed to be in that place).
target_language_example: Você deveria estar descansando agora.
native_language_example: You should be resting now.

meaning: 'should be here' / 'was supposed to be here'.
additional_notes: Uses the conditional form of dever (deveria) to express expectation, obligation, or what would be appropriate. Often implies that someone is expected to be in this place now (or by a specified time): 'Ele deveria estar aqui ao meio-dia' = 'He was supposed to be here at noon.' With negation, 'não deveria estar aqui' means 'shouldn't be here' (not allowed / not appropriate / not expected).
target_language_example: Ela já deveria estar aqui.
native_language_example: She should already be here.

meaning: “should do that/this” (was supposed to do that/this).
additional_notes: Uses the conditional form of dever (deveria) to express advice, obligation, or what someone is expected/supposed to do. Often translates as “should” in English; depending on context it can also mean “was supposed to” (especially when talking about a past plan or expectation). Subject can change: eu/ele/a gente/nós deveria(m) fazer isso.
target_language_example: Você deveria fazer isso agora, antes que fique tarde.
native_language_example: You should do that now, before it gets late.

additional_notes: “Deveria” is the conditional form of “dever” (“should/ought to”). With an infinitive like “ir” (“to go”), it’s used to talk about what someone should do (advice, expectation, or obligation) in a somewhat softer/less direct way than “deve ir.” It can also be used in questions like “Por que ele deveria ir?” = “Why should he go?”
target_language_example: Acho que você deveria ir agora.
native_language_example: I think you should go now.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of dever (deveria) to express what is expected, recommended, or morally/rightfully the case. Common in opinions and suggestions (e.g., "Isso deveria ser..."), and can also express criticism or a judgment about what should happen.
target_language_example: Isso deveria ser mais simples.
native_language_example: That should be simpler.

meaning: “should have been” / “was supposed to have been”.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a past situation that was expected, intended, or ideal, often implying regret or criticism. Grammar: conditional of dever (deveria = should) + ter + past participle (sido = been). Also common with other participles: deveria ter feito (should have done), deveria ter dito (should have said).
target_language_example: A reunião deveria ter sido ontem, mas foi adiada.
native_language_example: The meeting should have been yesterday, but it was postponed.

meaning: "should have" (something that was advisable/expected in the past, but didn’t happen—or shouldn’t have happened).
additional_notes: Used to talk about past actions in a judgmental/reflective way: what someone was expected to do, or what would have been better (or wrong) to do. It’s usually followed by a past participle: "deveriam ter escutado" (should have listened), "deveriam ter passado" (should have passed). "Deveriam" agrees with the subject (they/you all).
target_language_example: Vocês deveriam ter chegado mais cedo.
native_language_example: You (all) should have arrived earlier.

additional_notes: Used to make a suggestion or talk about what would be the right thing to do. "Deveríamos" is the conditional of "dever" (to have to/should) and often sounds a bit softer/more tentative than "devemos" (we must/should). You can add a place after "ir" (e.g., "deveríamos ir para casa") or use it as a question: "Deveríamos ir?" = "Should we go?"
target_language_example: Está ficando tarde; deveríamos ir para casa.
native_language_example: It’s getting late; we should go home.

meaning: “we should have” (we ought to have, in the past).
additional_notes: Used to talk about what would have been the right thing to do in the past, often expressing regret or mild criticism. It’s typically followed by a past participle to form the Portuguese equivalent of “should have + past participle”: deveríamos ter contado (should have told), deveríamos ter ligado (should have called), deveríamos ter desistido (should have given up). In negatives, it becomes não deveríamos ter (“we shouldn’t have”).
target_language_example: Deveríamos ter saído mais cedo.
native_language_example: We should have left earlier.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone/something is expected to be (duty, obligation, or logical expectation). It’s the imperfect of **dever** + infinitive (**estar**), often implying “was supposed to be” in a past/ongoing situation. Common in questions and negatives: **Não devia estar...** (“Shouldn’t he/she be...?” / “He/she wasn’t supposed to be...”).
target_language_example: Ele devia estar em casa a esta hora.
native_language_example: He should be at home at this time.

meaning: "must have been / was probably" (guess) or "should be" (expectation).
additional_notes: Imperfect of "dever" + "ser". Very common for making a guess about something (often about the past): "Devia ser..." = "It must have been / it was probably..." It can also express what would be expected or appropriate: "Você devia ser..." = "You should be..." (sometimes sounding like a suggestion).
target_language_example: Devia ser muito tarde, porque já não havia ninguém na rua.
native_language_example: It must have been very late, because there was no one on the street anymore.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of "dever" + infinitive "ter" to talk about what was advisable/expected in the past but didn’t happen (often with regret). Very common in the negative: "não devia ter..." = "I/you shouldn’t have...". The subject can change: "Eu devia ter..." (I should have), "Você devia ter..." (you should have), "Ele/ela devia ter..." (he/she should have).
target_language_example: Eu devia ter te avisado antes.
native_language_example: I should have warned you earlier.

additional_notes: Used to give the cause/reason for something, especially in more formal or written Portuguese. It’s followed by a noun or noun phrase ("devido a um acidente", "devido ao trânsito"), and it often appears at the beginning of the sentence or after the main clause. Agreement is common: devido (masc. sing.), devida (fem. sing.), devidos/devidas (plural), though many learners will also hear the invariable form "devido a" in practice.
target_language_example: O voo atrasou devido ao mau tempo.
native_language_example: The flight was delayed due to bad weather.

additional_notes: Used to give the cause/reason for something, usually with a noun or noun phrase: devido à chuva (due to the rain), devido à nossa situação (due to our situation). It’s relatively formal and common in writing. The base form is devido a; it changes with the noun: devido ao (masc. singular), devido à (fem. singular), devido aos (masc. plural), devido às (fem. plural).
target_language_example: O voo atrasou devido à neblina.
native_language_example: The flight was delayed due to fog.

meaning: “I should do” / “I must do” (I have an obligation).
additional_notes: Used to talk about duty, obligation, or what you feel is the right thing to do. It’s the 1st-person singular present of the verb “dever” (to have to / should) + an infinitive: “devo fazer”, “devo dizer”, “devo ir”. In questions, it often means “Should I…?”; depending on context it can be softer (“should”) or stronger (“must”).
target_language_example: Eu devo fazer isso hoje ou posso deixar para amanhã?
native_language_example: Should I do this today, or can I leave it for tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to infer or suppose something happened in the past, often when you’re not 100% sure (e.g., based on evidence or a realization). It’s the present of "dever" + infinitive "ter" and typically comes before a past participle: "devo ter esquecido" = "I must have forgotten."
target_language_example: Estou cansado hoje; devo ter dormido pouco.
native_language_example: I’m tired today; I must have slept little.

additional_notes: Means a period of ten years ("por mais dez anos" = "for ten more years") or someone’s age. For age, Portuguese commonly uses "ter" (to have): "eu tinha dez anos" = "I was ten (years old)". You may also see "com dez anos" = "at age ten/when (someone) was ten".
target_language_example: Eu me mudei para cá há dez anos.
native_language_example: I moved here ten years ago.

additional_notes: Used to state a price, value, amount spent, or money you want to borrow/lend. Typically used with verbs like pagar (to pay), gastar (to spend), valer (to be worth), and emprestar (to lend/borrow, depending on context).
target_language_example: Quanto custa? — Custa dez dólares.
native_language_example: How much does it cost? — It costs ten dollars.

additional_notes: Used to state the exact number 10,000, or approximately when combined with words like "cerca de" (about) or "mais de" (more than). Common with counts (palavras, conexões) and measurements (metros).
target_language_example: O estádio tem capacidade para dez mil pessoas.
native_language_example: The stadium has a capacity for ten thousand people.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (Esperou dez minutos. = “He/She waited ten minutes.”), time remaining (Faltam dez minutos. = “Ten minutes left.”), or a delay when followed by “de” (com dez minutos de atraso = “ten minutes late / with a ten-minute delay”).
target_language_example: A reunião começa em dez minutos.
native_language_example: The meeting starts in ten minutes.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an age or a time period of 16 years. With ages, Portuguese often uses "ter" (to have): "Tenho dezesseis anos" = "I am sixteen (years old)." You may also see it with time expressions like "dezesseis anos depois" (sixteen years later) or with "fazer" for birthdays: "vai fazer dezesseis anos" (will turn sixteen).
target_language_example: Meu irmão tem dezesseis anos.
native_language_example: My brother is sixteen years old.

additional_notes: Used to state age (“Tenho dezoito anos.” = “I’m eighteen.”) or to talk about a time starting at age 18 (“desde os dezoito anos” = “since (I/they was/were) eighteen”). Often appears with “ter” (to be [a certain age]) and with “pelo menos” to indicate a minimum age requirement.
target_language_example: Ele fez dezoito anos na semana passada.
native_language_example: He turned eighteen last week.

meaning: everyday life; day-to-day (routine) / day by day.
additional_notes: Often used with a preposition: "no dia a dia" = "in (my/your) everyday life" or "in day-to-day life" (your routine, daily reality). Without an article it can also mean gradual change over time: "dia a dia" = "day by day".
target_language_example: No dia a dia, eu tento comer melhor e dormir cedo.
native_language_example: In everyday life, I try to eat better and go to bed early.

additional_notes: Refers to the holiday called “Thanksgiving.” In Portuguese it’s often used when talking about the US/Canadian holiday; in Brazil it exists on the calendar (as “Dia Nacional de Ação de Graças”) but isn’t as widely celebrated as in the US. Often written with capitals as a holiday name: “Dia de Ação de Graças.”
target_language_example: Nos Estados Unidos, o Dia de Ação de Graças é comemorado em novembro.
native_language_example: In the United States, Thanksgiving is celebrated in November.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happens all the time or without stopping (often implying effort, exhaustion, or urgency). Common with verbs like trabalhar (work), estudar (study), procurar (look for), and continuar (continue).
target_language_example: Ela estudou dia e noite para a prova.
native_language_example: She studied day and night for the test.

additional_notes: Usually used with an article or possessive: "o dia todo" (all day / the whole day), "um dia todo" (a whole day), "meu dia todo" (my whole day). Very close in meaning to "o dia inteiro".
target_language_example: Fiquei em casa o dia todo.
native_language_example: I stayed home all day.

additional_notes: Used with a noun/pronoun to show physical position (in front of something/someone) or a figurative situation (facing a choice/problem; in the face of evidence, rules, etc.). Common in more formal writing when meaning “facing/in the face of.”
target_language_example: Diante de tantas opções, não sei o que escolher.
native_language_example: With so many options, I don’t know what to choose.

meaning: difficulty (in) doing something; trouble (with) doing something.
additional_notes: Used with the verb ter (“to have”): ter dificuldade em + infinitive (often with se + verb for reflexive actions), meaning you struggle to do something. In the negative, não ter/tive dificuldade em means it was easy for you to do it (no trouble).
target_language_example: Ela tem dificuldade em acordar cedo.
native_language_example: She has trouble waking up early.

additional_notes: Used to say something is difficult to do: difícil de + infinitive (difícil de entender, difícil de explicar). It can also describe people/things that are hard to deal with in a certain way (e.g., difícil de contentar = hard to please). Often appears as "é/foi/será difícil de..." or after a noun: "uma teoria difícil de explicar".
target_language_example: Este texto é difícil de ler sem um dicionário.
native_language_example: This text is hard to read without a dictionary.

additional_notes: Used to instruct someone (often politely/formally) to pass a message on to a third person. The pronoun “-lhe” means “to him/her” (indirect object), attached to the imperative form “diga” (from dizer, “to say/tell”). Common in requests like “Diga-lhe que espere” (“Tell him/her to wait”).
target_language_example: Por favor, diga-lhe que eu chego às oito.
native_language_example: Please tell him/her that I’ll arrive at eight.

additional_notes: Formal/polite way to say “tell me,” using the imperative of "dizer" + the object pronoun "-me" (“me”). Common when addressing someone as "você" (or in formal writing/speech). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese you’ll also hear "me diga"; in European Portuguese, "diz-me" is common in informal contexts.
target_language_example: Diga-me onde fica a estação, por favor.
native_language_example: Tell me where the station is, please.

meaning: “let it be said” / “it should be noted” (parenthetical aside).
additional_notes: Used as a fixed, formal-sounding expression to add a remark or emphasize a point, often between commas. Very common in the patterns “diga-se de passagem” (“by the way”) and “diga-se a propósito” (“incidentally”). It’s the verb “dizer” in the imperative (“diga”) + the particle “se”, used impersonally.
target_language_example: Ele aceitou o trabalho e, diga-se de passagem, fez um ótimo serviço.
native_language_example: He accepted the job and, by the way, did an excellent job.

additional_notes: "Diga" is the formal (você / o senhor, a senhora) imperative of "dizer" (“to say/tell”). It’s commonly followed by "a" before an indirect object (the person you’re telling): "diga a ele" (tell him), "diga a ela" (tell her), "diga ao professor" (tell the teacher). Often used with "que" to introduce what you’re telling: "Diga a ele que…".
target_language_example: Diga a ela que eu chego às oito.
native_language_example: Tell her that I’ll arrive at eight.

additional_notes: Used to give an instruction/request to pass a message to a woman/girl (“ela” = her). The verb is in the imperative (formal ‘you’): diga. Informal equivalents are often “diz pra ela que…” / “fala pra ela que…”.
target_language_example: Por favor, diga a ela que eu vou ligar mais tarde.
native_language_example: Please tell her that I’ll call later.

additional_notes: Used to instruct someone (you) to pass a message to a man: "Tell him that...". It’s in the imperative form (diga) and sounds polite/formal; in everyday speech you’ll also hear "Diz pra ele que..." (informal). Often followed by a full clause: "diga a ele que" + [sentence].
target_language_example: Diga a ele que estou a caminho.
native_language_example: Tell him that I'm on my way.

additional_notes: Imperative form (formal) of "dizer" + "a verdade". Used to ask/tell someone to be honest: "Diga a verdade!" You can make it more polite with "por favor" or use "me/nos/lhe" to say who should be told: "Diga-me a verdade" (tell me the truth), "Diga-nos a verdade" (tell us the truth). In informal speech, you’ll often hear "diz a verdade" (to one person) or "digam a verdade" (to multiple people).
target_language_example: Por favor, diga a verdade: você quebrou o celular?
native_language_example: Please tell the truth: did you break the phone?

additional_notes: Used to give an instruction: diga (formal imperative of "dizer") + ao (= a + o). It means "tell/say to [someone]" where the person is masculine singular and usually introduced by a name/title: "Diga ao Tom...". For feminine singular, use "diga à" (a + a). Often followed by "que..." (tell him that...) or "para..." (tell him to...).
target_language_example: Diga ao João que eu ligo mais tarde.
native_language_example: Tell João that I’ll call later.

additional_notes: Used with the formal you (você) to give an instruction to report information or introduce what you want someone to say. It’s often followed by a full clause: “Diga que + [sentence]”. To address a friend informally, you’d usually use “diz que”.
target_language_example: Por favor, diga que eu chego mais tarde.
native_language_example: Please tell them that I’ll arrive later.

meaning: "let's say" / "so to speak" (used to soften or qualify what you’re saying).
additional_notes: Used as a conversational hedge when you want to be less direct, give an approximate description, or signal that your wording isn’t exact. It can appear at the beginning, in the middle (set off by commas), or at the end of a sentence.
target_language_example: Ele é, digamos assim, o líder do grupo.
native_language_example: He is, so to speak, the leader of the group.

additional_notes: Used with "para" to show either (1) the recipient of the money ("dar/entregar dinheiro para alguém" = give/hand money to someone) or (2) the purpose ("dinheiro para + infinitive" = money to do something, e.g., "dinheiro para comprar"). In everyday speech, many speakers also use "dinheiro pra" (a common contraction of "para").
target_language_example: Eu preciso de dinheiro para pagar o aluguel.
native_language_example: I need money to pay the rent.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has the necessary amount of money to purchase something. Often followed by the item (e.g., “uma casa”, “tudo que precisa”). Word-by-word it’s dinheiro (money) + suficiente (enough) + para comprar (to buy).
target_language_example: Não tenho dinheiro suficiente para comprar esse computador agora.
native_language_example: I don’t have enough money to buy that computer right now.

meaning: human right (a basic right everyone should have).
additional_notes: Usually used in the singular to talk about one specific right (um direito humano), or in the plural to talk about the topic in general (direitos humanos). Common in news, politics, and law contexts.
target_language_example: A liberdade de expressão é um direito humano.
native_language_example: Freedom of speech is a human right.

additional_notes: Used to say you go home without stopping anywhere else (no detours). It often comes after a verb of going/moving (ir, voltar, levar) and can be used with different tenses (vou/fui).
target_language_example: Depois da aula, vou direto para casa.
native_language_example: After class, I'm going straight home.

meaning: "I’d say (that)…" / "I would say (that)…" (to give an opinion or guess).
additional_notes: Uses the conditional form of dizer ("to say") to sound more tentative or polite—like making a careful statement, estimate, or suggestion. Often used when you’re not 100% sure or when softening an opinion.
target_language_example: Diria que isso é uma boa ideia.
native_language_example: I’d say that this is a good idea.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase. "Dirigir" means "to drive"; "um carro" means "a car." You’ll often hear it with ability ("Eu consigo dirigir um carro"), permission/age ("muito jovem/novo para dirigir"), and requirements ("precisa de uma licença"). In Brazil, "carteira de motorista" / "CNH" is the driver’s license; in Portugal, "carta de condução."
target_language_example: Eu não posso dirigir um carro sem carteira de motorista.
native_language_example: I can't drive a car without a driver's license.

additional_notes: Used for the internal storage device in a computer (HDD) and also for external hard drives (disco rígido externo). Common with verbs like encher (fill up), copiar (copy), remover (remove), substituir (replace), and with security phrases like proteção por senha (password protection).
target_language_example: Preciso fazer backup porque o disco rígido está dando problema.
native_language_example: I need to back up (my files) because the hard drive is having problems.

additional_notes: Past tense of dizer ('to say/tell'). Used to report what someone told you: [Someone] disse-me que + clause. In Brazilian Portuguese, this is often phrased as "me disse que"; in Portugal, "disse-me que" is common. You can replace the person: "Ele/ela disse-me que..."
target_language_example: O meu chefe disse-me que a reunião foi cancelada.
native_language_example: My boss told me that the meeting was canceled.

additional_notes: "Disse" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "dizer" (to say/to tell). "Disse a" introduces the person you spoke to: "disse a + name" (often with an article: "disse ao/à"). After that you can add what was said: "disse a Maria o que..." (told Maria what...), "disse a Maria para..." (told Maria to...), "disse a Maria que..." (told Maria that...). With male names it commonly becomes "disse ao": "Ele disse ao Tony."
target_language_example: Eu disse ao João que estava atrasado.
native_language_example: I told João that I was late.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of **dizer a verdade** (“to tell the truth”). Used to report that someone was truthful about something in a completed situation. Often appears with a subject: **Eu/Ele/Ela/Tom disse a verdade**. In English, “tell the truth” is more common than the literal “say the truth.”
target_language_example: Ela disse a verdade sobre o que aconteceu.
native_language_example: She told the truth about what happened.

additional_notes: From the verb "dizer" (to say) in the past (ele/ela/você disse = he/she/you said) + "alguma coisa" (something/anything). In questions like "Ele disse alguma coisa?", it often means "Did he say anything?". You can add "para" + a person ("disse alguma coisa para a Maria") or "sobre" + a topic ("disse alguma coisa sobre isso").
target_language_example: Você disse alguma coisa para o médico?
native_language_example: Did you say anything to the doctor?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "dizer" (to say) in the simple past ("disse" = "I/you/he/she said") plus "isso" (that/it). Very common when denying, confirming, or asking about something someone said: "Eu não disse isso" (I didn’t say that), "Por que disse isso?" (Why did you say that?). Often you’ll hear it with a subject ("Eu/Você/O senhor") or without it when it’s clear from context.
target_language_example: Eu nunca disse isso para você.
native_language_example: I never said that to you.

additional_notes: "disse" is the past form of dizer. With para + a person, it means saying something to someone. It can be followed by an infinitive to mean "told someone to do something" (disse para ele esperar) or by que to report what was said (disse para ela que...).
target_language_example: Ela disse para mim esperar aqui.
native_language_example: She told me to wait here.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said. "disse" is the past form of dizer ("to say"), and "que" introduces the reported statement.
target_language_example: Ela disse que vai chegar tarde.
native_language_example: She said that she is going to arrive late.

additional_notes: Used to report what a woman/girl said. **disse** is the simple past of *dizer* (“to say”), **que** means “that” and introduces the reported clause, and **ela** means “she.” In Portuguese, the subject pronoun (**ela**) is sometimes optional (you may also hear/see *disse que…* without *ela*).
target_language_example: O João disse que ela vai chegar mais tarde.
native_language_example: João said that she’s going to arrive later.

additional_notes: Used to report what a man/boy said. "disse" is the past tense of "dizer" (to say), followed by "que" (that) and "ele" (he). In context, you’ll often replace "ele" with another subject ("disse que eu…" = said that I…, "disse que ela…" = said that she…).
target_language_example: Ela disse que ele estava cansado.
native_language_example: She said that he was tired.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about a man’s identity/state/characteristic (era = “was”). It’s common in storytelling or when repeating information. Often followed by an adjective or noun: “disse que ele era solteiro” (said he was single), “disse que ele era forte” (said he was strong). In everyday speech you may also hear/see the shorter version “disse que ele…” without repeating “era” if the next part uses a different verb.
target_language_example: Ela disse que ele era professor, mas na verdade ele trabalhava em outra área.
native_language_example: She said that he was a teacher, but actually he worked in another field.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about a man/boy’s state or condition. **disse** is the past of *dizer* (“said/told”), **que** = “that,” and **ele estava** is the imperfect past of *estar* (“he was/was feeling/was located”). Very common in indirect speech: *Ela disse que ele estava cansado.*
target_language_example: Ela disse que ele estava cansado demais para sair.
native_language_example: She said that he was too tired to go out.

additional_notes: Used to report what a man said he wanted. Common in indirect/reported speech: **disse que** (“said that”) + **ele queria** (“he wanted”). In Portuguese, **que** (“that”) is usually kept (more than in English), and **queria** is the imperfect past, often used for what someone wanted at that time.
target_language_example: Ela disse que ele queria sair mais cedo.
native_language_example: She said he wanted to leave earlier.

additional_notes: Used in reported/indirect speech: someone "said that...". "disse" is the past of dizer (to say/tell). "que" = "that". "era" is the imperfect of ser (to be), often meaning "was" in descriptions/background info. The subject of "era" is understood from context (he/she/it/that situation).
target_language_example: Ele disse que era tarde demais para ligar.
native_language_example: He said it was too late to call.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said in the past (indirect/reported speech). "disse" = "said" and "que" = "that". "estava" is the past form of "estar" and often translates as "was" (a temporary state). The subject after "que" is often omitted when it’s the same as the previous subject (e.g., "Tom disse que estava..." = "Tom said that he was...").
target_language_example: Ela disse que estava cansada, mas foi trabalhar mesmo assim.
native_language_example: She said that she was tired, but she went to work anyway.

additional_notes: Used in reported speech to say what someone said they were going to do. The verb "ir" in the imperfect ("ia") commonly expresses a planned/expected future from a past point of view (similar to English “was going to”). The subject changes with context ("eu disse que ia...", "ele disse que ia..."). Often "que" can be omitted in casual speech ("disse que ia" → "disse que ia"/"disse que ia"), but it’s standard to include it.
target_language_example: Ela disse que ia chegar mais cedo, mas se atrasou.
native_language_example: She said she was going to arrive earlier, but she got delayed.

additional_notes: Used in reported/indirect speech: someone said something, and you report it with "disse que..." (= "said that..."). "Queria" is the imperfect of "querer" and often translates as "wanted" in this context. The subject is usually understood from context (e.g., "O Tom disse que queria..." = "Tom said he wanted..."). You can follow it with a verb in the infinitive: "disse que queria ajudar" (wanted to help).
target_language_example: Ela disse que queria falar com você.
native_language_example: She said she wanted to talk to you.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about their own feelings or physical/emotional state. In Portuguese, "se sentia" agrees with the subject (e.g., "ele disse que se sentia..." / "ela disse que se sentia...") and the adjective that follows usually agrees too ("cansado" for a man, "cansada" for a woman). It’s common in indirect/reported speech after verbs like "disse" (said).
target_language_example: Ela disse que se sentia nervosa antes da entrevista.
native_language_example: She said that she felt nervous before the interview.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said (reported speech). "disse" = "(he/she) said"; "que" = "that"; "tinha" is the imperfect of "ter" (to have), often used after "disse que" to express past information or obligations: "disse que tinha algo" = "said (she) had something"; "disse que tinha que" + verb = "said (she) had to" (meaning "said she needed to/was supposed to"). The subject is usually understood from context (e.g., "Ela disse...", "Tom disse...").
target_language_example: Ele disse que tinha que sair mais cedo.
native_language_example: He said he had to leave early.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about “you” in the past. It’s a common pattern: [name] disse que você estava + adjective/verb phrase (e.g., ocupado/irritado/dirigindo). Note: “disse” can refer to “he said” or “she said” (Portuguese doesn’t specify gender here).
target_language_example: Ela disse que você estava cansado.
native_language_example: She said that you were tired.

meaning: 'they told me that…' / 'I was told that…'.
additional_notes: Used to report information you heard from other people. Literally 'they told me that', with the indirect object pronoun -me ('to me') attached to the verb. Often followed by a full clause in the past or present. Can also introduce advice/instructions: "Disseram-me que eu devia…" (they told me I should…) or a command in the subjunctive: "Disseram-me que voltasse…" (they told me to come back…).
target_language_example: Disseram-me que a reunião foi cancelada.
native_language_example: They told me that the meeting was canceled.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "dizer": "eles/elas disseram" + "que" to introduce what someone reported. Used to relay information or repeat what other people claimed. Often followed by another verb in the past (e.g., "disseram que precisavam...") or present (e.g., "disseram que o pai está...").
target_language_example: Eles disseram que iam chegar cedo.
native_language_example: They said they were going to arrive early.

meaning: “(they) said that they …” (reporting what someone said about them).
additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech: "disseram" = “(they) said” (past tense), "que" = “that,” and "eles" = “they” (the group being talked about). You can replace "eles" with another subject (e.g., "disseram que eu...", "disseram que ela...").
target_language_example: Eles disseram que eles vão chegar mais tarde.
native_language_example: They said that they will arrive later.

additional_notes: Used to report what people said (reported speech). "Disseram" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "dizer" for "they" (3rd person plural). "Estavam" is the imperfect past of "estar" (they were), often used to describe a situation/state in progress at that time (e.g., being afraid, being in a hurry).
