It’s commonly followed by an expression like "com medo" (afraid), "com pressa" (in a hurry), or another verb phrase ("voltando" = coming back/returning).
target_language_example: Eles disseram que estavam cansados, então foram embora cedo.
native_language_example: They said they were tired, so they left early.

additional_notes: Imperative form of the reflexive verb "divertir-se" (to have fun). It’s the polite/standard command used with "você"; for "tu" you often hear "diverte-te" (more common in Portugal) or "se diverte" (common in Brazil). Often followed by "com" (with), "na/no" (at/in), or "enquanto" (while).
target_language_example: Divirta-se no passeio e me conte depois!
native_language_example: Have fun on the outing and tell me about it afterward!

additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech or someone’s opinion/information. It’s made of "diz" ("says"—present tense, 3rd person singular of "dizer") + "que" ("that"). Common pattern: [person] diz que + clause (e.g., "Ela diz que..." / "O Tom diz que...").
target_language_example: Ela diz que vai chegar tarde.
native_language_example: She says that she’s going to arrive late.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone (or something like a letter/legend) says about a man. In everyday speech, you can omit the repeated subject and just say “diz que…” if it’s clear who “he” is (e.g., “O Tom diz que está melhor hoje.”).
target_language_example: O médico diz que ele precisa descansar mais.
native_language_example: The doctor says that he needs to rest more.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone claims or states they want. "diz" is the present tense of "dizer" (to say) for ele/ela/você. "que" means "that" and introduces the next clause. Portuguese often omits the subject in the second clause when it’s the same person (so "diz que quer" = "diz que ele/ela quer"). You can change the subject/tense: "eu digo que quero" (I say I want), "eles dizem que querem" (they say they want).
target_language_example: Ela diz que quer aprender português.
native_language_example: She says she wants to learn Portuguese.

additional_notes: Used to report what people say, believe, or claim. Often used for general/unspecified sources (like “they say…”), but it can also literally mean “(they) say that” when the subject is clear from context. The verb is the 3rd person plural of dizer (to say).
target_language_example: Dizem que vai chover amanhã.
native_language_example: They say it’s going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report something you’ve heard (rumors, general talk, or information from unspecified people). "Dizem" is the 3rd-person plural of "dizer" (“to say”) and often works like English “they say…”. You can also use it without "ele": "Dizem que…" = “They say that…” / “It’s said that…”.
target_language_example: Dizem que ele vai voltar amanhã.
native_language_example: They say he’s coming back tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses the gerund ("dizendo") to describe the ongoing act of telling the truth, often in questions or statements about whether someone is being honest. Common patterns: "estar dizendo a verdade" (to be telling the truth), "acabar dizendo a verdade" (to end up telling the truth), "me/te/lhe dizendo a verdade" (telling me/you/him/her the truth).
target_language_example: Você está dizendo a verdade ou está brincando comigo?
native_language_example: Are you telling the truth or are you kidding with me?

additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech or the content of what someone says. Often follows verbs like estar/fazer/receber/responder/ligar: e.g., “recebi um telegrama dizendo que…” = “I got a telegram saying that…”. It can mean either (1) someone is literally speaking (“ela estava me dizendo que…”) or (2) a message/report contains information (“estão dizendo que…”, “um telegrama dizendo que…”).
target_language_example: Ele me mandou uma mensagem dizendo que ia se atrasar.
native_language_example: He sent me a message saying that he was going to be late.

meaning: to tell him/her (or to tell you, formal).
additional_notes: “Lhe” is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to him/to her” (and in some contexts, especially formal speech, “to you”). With the infinitive “dizer”, Portuguese often attaches the pronoun with a hyphen: “dizer-lhe” = literally “say to him/her”. In many sentences it’s equivalent to “tell + person” in English.
target_language_example: Preciso dizer-lhe uma coisa importante.
native_language_example: I need to tell him/her something important.

additional_notes: Formed by the verb "dizer" + the object pronoun "me" (“me”), joined with a hyphen when the pronoun comes after the verb (common in European Portuguese), especially with infinitives in polite questions: "Pode/Poderia dizer-me...". You’ll also see the same idea with other verb forms, e.g. "Diga-me..." (“Tell me...”).
target_language_example: Pode dizer-me a que horas começa a reunião?
native_language_example: Can you tell me what time the meeting starts?

additional_notes: Used before the person who receives the information: dizer a alguém. In English, this often translates as tell someone rather than say to someone. The preposition a may contract with articles: dizer ao professor, dizer à Maria. With pronouns, you commonly see forms like dizer a ele / a ela.
target_language_example: Vou dizer a ela a verdade.
native_language_example: I'm going to tell her the truth.

additional_notes: Used to indicate the male person you’re speaking to or about receives the message. In everyday Portuguese, it’s also common to say "dizer para ele" (especially in Brazil). The pronoun "ele" = "him"; for "her" you use "dizer a ela".
target_language_example: Vou dizer a ele que chego mais tarde.
native_language_example: I'll tell him that I'll arrive later.

additional_notes: Means to speak honestly (not lie). Common with verbs like "ter que" / "tive de" (to have to) and "prometer" (to promise): "prometer dizer a verdade" = "to promise to tell the truth."
target_language_example: Preciso dizer a verdade, mesmo que doa.
native_language_example: I need to tell the truth, even if it hurts.

meaning: to say goodbye; to bid farewell.
additional_notes: Used for the act of saying goodbye, often when leaving or when something is ending. You can also use it more figuratively (e.g., saying goodbye to a phase, habit, or situation).
target_language_example: Tenho que ir agora — preciso dizer adeus.
native_language_example: I have to go now — I need to say goodbye.

additional_notes: Used with a direct object (algo = “something”) to indicate you speak or state an unspecified thing. It often appears with prepositions like “a/para” to show who you’re speaking to: “dizer algo a/para alguém” (to say something to someone). The verb “dizer” changes with the subject (eu digo, você/ele diz, nós dizemos, vocês/eles dizem).
target_language_example: Quero dizer algo importante para você.
native_language_example: I want to say something important to you.

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object introduced by the preposition “a”. “ao” = “a” + “o” (to the / to him). Common variants: “dizer à” (to the / to her), “dizer aos” (to the / to them masc.), “dizer às” (to the / to them fem.). In everyday English, it often translates as “tell” rather than “say to”: “dizer ao Tom” = “tell Tom”.
target_language_example: Preciso dizer ao meu chefe que vou chegar atrasado.
native_language_example: I need to tell my boss that I’m going to be late.

additional_notes: Used for referring to a specific statement or comment. Isso usually points to something already mentioned or understood from context, and in English it is often translated as either 'that' or 'it' depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Não acredito que ele foi capaz de dizer isso.
native_language_example: I can't believe he was able to say that.

additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech, an opinion, or a statement, followed by a full clause. Because the entry is given in the infinitive, example sentences may use the exact infinitive phrase "dizer que" rather than a conjugated form. With an indirect object such as me, lhe, or lhes, it can often mean "tell someone that".
target_language_example: É mais seguro dizer que a popularidade é ruim.
native_language_example: It is safer to say that popularity is bad.

meaning: to say/tell something (often to introduce a point).
additional_notes: Often used to preface what you’re about to say, like “I have to say something” or “Let me tell you something.” The something can be stated next ("Dizer uma coisa: ...") or left implied ("Vou te dizer uma coisa." can mean “Let me tell you something” with suspense). Common variants: "querer dizer uma coisa" (to want to say something), "ter que dizer uma coisa" (to have to say something).
target_language_example: Tenho que dizer uma coisa: não concordo com isso.
native_language_example: I have to say something: I don’t agree with that.

meaning: “(he/she/it) said that…” / “(he/she/it) used to say that…”
additional_notes: “Dizia” is the imperfect past of *dizer* (“to say/tell”), often used for repeated/habitual things in the past (“used to say”). It can also set the background for a past situation (“was saying”). “Que” introduces what was said (a clause), like English “that.”
target_language_example: Ele dizia que ia ligar mais tarde.
native_language_example: He said (that) he would call later.

additional_notes: A scientific/technical term for the gas made of carbon and oxygen. Commonly used when talking about plants (they absorb CO₂ and release oxygen), air pollution, and climate change. Often appears with the verb "absorver" (to absorb) or "emitir/liberar" (to emit/release).
target_language_example: Os carros emitem muito dióxido de carbono.
native_language_example: Cars emit a lot of carbon dioxide.

additional_notes: Used after comparative words like "mais" (more), "menos" (less), "melhor" (better), "pior" (worse), "maior" (bigger/older), and "menor" (smaller/younger): "mais/menos … do que" = "more/less … than". It’s a contraction of "de" + "o que" (literally “of what/that which”), but in modern Portuguese it functions like "than" in comparisons.
target_language_example: Ela fala mais devagar do que eu.
native_language_example: She speaks more slowly than I do.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de + o". Use it to mean origin ("from the sky/heaven") or possession/association ("of Heaven"). Often written with capital "C" ("Céu") in religious contexts to mean "Heaven". Common in exclamations like "Meu Deus do Céu!" (strong surprise/shock: "My God in heaven!").
target_language_example: Uma luz caiu do Céu.
native_language_example: A light fell from the sky.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "o" = "do". Used to link something to a specific accident (e.g., "a cena do acidente" = "the scene of the accident"), or after certain verbs to mean "about the accident" (e.g., "me contou do acidente" = "told me about the accident").
target_language_example: Ainda não sabemos a causa do acidente.
native_language_example: We still don't know the cause of the accident.

additional_notes: “Do” is the contraction of “de + o” and usually means “of the” (or sometimes just “of,” depending on English phrasing). “Do amor” is common in phrases like “poção do amor” (love potion) or “deus do amor” (god of love), meaning something related to love. It can refer to love in general or a more specific, known idea of love, depending on context.
target_language_example: Ela escreveu um poema do amor.
native_language_example: She wrote a poem about love.

meaning: “of the year” (also used in expressions like “this time of year”).
additional_notes: It’s the contraction of “de + o” → “do”, so it literally means “of the year.” Common in superlatives and descriptions (e.g., “a estação mais quente do ano” = “the hottest season of the year”) and in time expressions like “nesta altura do ano” = “at this time of year.”
target_language_example: Dezembro é uma das épocas mais movimentadas do ano.
native_language_example: December is one of the busiest times of the year.

meaning: inside out; (figuratively) turned upside down / completely upset.
additional_notes: Literally refers to the wrong side of clothing facing outward: "a camisa do avesso" (shirt inside out). Very common with verbs like "estar/ficar" (to be/end up) and "virar" (to turn): "virar do avesso" can also mean to turn something over completely, rummage through it, or disrupt everything ("turn it upside down").
target_language_example: A jaqueta está do avesso — deixa eu arrumar.
native_language_example: The jacket is inside out — let me fix it.

meaning: 'of the bathroom' or 'from/out of the bathroom.'
additional_notes: "Do" = "de + o". Its meaning depends on context: it can show possession/association ("a cortina do banheiro" = "the bathroom curtain") or movement from a place with verbs like "sair" ("sair do banheiro" = "to leave/come out of the bathroom").
target_language_example: Ele saiu do banheiro e voltou para a sala.
native_language_example: He left the bathroom and went back to the living room.

meaning: 'out of the way' / 'off the path' (literally 'from the path/way').
additional_notes: Common in set phrases like **sair do caminho** (“get out of the way”) and **desviar-se do caminho** (“to stray/deviate from the path,” literal or figurative). **do** = **de + o** (“from the/the”).
target_language_example: Por favor, saia do caminho para eu passar.
native_language_example: Please, get out of the way so I can get through.

meaning: a very vulgar intensifier meaning “fucking / damn” (often insulting) or “really/very”.
additional_notes: Literally “of the dick,” but used idiomatically as a strong, rude intensifier. It commonly follows a noun or insult (“idiota do caralho”, “vadia do caralho”) to make it much harsher, similar to “fucking idiot/bitch.” It can also intensify neutral nouns (“um prazer do caralho” = “a fucking amazing/huge pleasure”), but it’s still highly offensive and not appropriate in polite company.
target_language_example: Esse filme é bom pra caralho, mas a galera do cinema estava chata do caralho.
native_language_example: That movie is really fucking good, but the people at the theater were fucking annoying.

additional_notes: "Do" is the contraction of "de" + "o" (= "of/from" + "the"). It’s very common and can mean: possession/association ("o pneu do carro" = "the car’s tire"), topic ("reclamar do carro" = "complain about the car"), or movement from inside ("sair do carro" = "get out of the car").
target_language_example: Tirei as malas do carro.
native_language_example: I took the bags out of the car.

meaning: "of the crime" / "of crime" (related to a crime or criminal activity).
additional_notes: Contraction of "de + o" (= "do"). Used to link something to a specific crime (e.g., "arma do crime" = the weapon used in the crime) or to crime in general (e.g., "mundo do crime" = the criminal underworld). It can also appear after some verbs/adjectives that take "de" (e.g., "absolvido do crime" = acquitted of the crime).
target_language_example: A polícia recolheu as provas do crime.
native_language_example: The police collected the evidence from the crime.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "o". Used literally for something coming from above ("descer do céu") or figuratively/religiously to mean "from heaven" ("o Senhor do céu"). In descriptions, it can mean "from above" ("vista do céu" = seen from the sky/air).
target_language_example: Caiu uma chuva forte do céu de repente.
native_language_example: A heavy rain suddenly fell from the sky.

meaning: of the day; today’s; (depending on context) during the day.
additional_notes: "Do" = "de + o" ("of the"). Used after a noun to talk about something that belongs to that day or is typical/available that day: "compromissos do dia" (the day’s appointments), "prato especial do dia" (today’s special), "boa ação do dia" (good deed of the day), "questões do dia" (current issues / issues of the day). It also appears in time expressions like "a esta hora do dia" (at this time of day) and "pelo resto do dia" (for the rest of the day).
target_language_example: Ainda tenho duas reuniões do dia e depois vou descansar.
native_language_example: I still have two meetings for today and then I’m going to rest.

meaning: 'of the day when' (used to introduce the event that happened on that day).
additional_notes: Used when you mention a specific day and then add a clause explaining what happened on that day. It often follows verbs like lembrar (to remember): "(Eu) lembro/me lembro do dia em que...". The full structure is "de + o dia" → "do dia" + "em que" (when/that).
target_language_example: Nunca vou me esquecer do dia em que a gente se mudou para esta cidade.
native_language_example: I’ll never forget the day when we moved to this city.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to say something/someone is from, in, or related to high school: "estudantes do ensino médio" (high school students), "time ... do ensino médio" (high school team). It’s the contraction of "de + o" ("do") + "ensino médio". In Brazil, "ensino médio" is the stage after "ensino fundamental" (roughly grades 10–12).
target_language_example: Ela é professora do ensino médio.
native_language_example: She is a high school teacher.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de + o" → "do", used before a masculine singular noun. With verbs like "gostar" (to like) and "achar" (to think/find), "do filme" means "the movie" in the sense of "about the movie" (your opinion of it).
target_language_example: O que você achou do filme?
native_language_example: What did you think of the movie?

meaning: of the government; from the government.
additional_notes: "Do" is the contraction of "de + o" and often means "of the" or "from the". Use "do governo" to describe something that belongs to the government (e.g., "selo do governo" = government seal) or that comes from the government (e.g., a message or announcement).
target_language_example: Recebi um e-mail do governo sobre os impostos.
native_language_example: I received an email from the government about taxes.

additional_notes: "Do" is the contraction of "de + o". It can mean (1) origin/coming from a place: "sair do hospital" (leave the hospital), or (2) belonging/relationship: "perto do hospital" (near the hospital), "médico do hospital" (a hospital doctor).
target_language_example: Ela saiu do hospital ontem à noite.
native_language_example: She left the hospital last night.

meaning: of the hotel; from the hotel.
additional_notes: "Do" = "de" + "o" ("of/from the"). It’s used to link something to the hotel (e.g., "o quarto do hotel" = "the hotel room") or to show movement/source (e.g., "saindo do hotel" = "leaving the hotel").
target_language_example: Vou pegar a chave do hotel na recepção.
native_language_example: I’m going to get the hotel key at the front desk.

meaning: 'the way (that)' / 'how' (something is done or how someone is).
additional_notes: Used to describe manner or style: how someone does something or how something should be done. Often follows verbs like gostar de (to like), amar (to love), fazer (to do), and should/ought expressions: do jeito que deveria (“the way it should”). It can introduce a clause: do jeito que + subject + verb.
target_language_example: Quero que você faça isso do jeito que eu expliquei.
native_language_example: I want you to do it the way I explained.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is outdoors or not inside a building/room. Often used with verbs like esperar (to wait), assistir (to watch), ficar/estar (to be), and trabalhar (to work).
target_language_example: Vamos esperar do lado de fora.
native_language_example: Let’s wait outside.

meaning: "of the sea" / "from the sea" (contraction of "de + o mar").
additional_notes: Used to link something to the sea (origin, type, location, etc.). It’s the contraction of "de" + "o" + "mar". Common in phrases like "água do mar" (sea water), "ondas do mar" (sea waves), "perto do mar" (near the sea), and "no fundo do mar" (at the bottom of the sea).
target_language_example: O som do mar me acalma.
native_language_example: The sound of the sea calms me.

meaning: the same way; just the same.
additional_notes: Used to say something is done or happens in an identical or very similar way. Often appears with comparisons: "do mesmo jeito que..." (the same way as...). It can also mean "anyway / regardless" in phrases like "...do mesmo jeito" (I’ll do it/it’ll happen just the same).
target_language_example: A gente pode ir a pé ou de ônibus; vamos chegar lá do mesmo jeito.
native_language_example: We can go on foot or by bus; we’ll get there either way.

additional_notes: Contraction of de + o + meu, used before a masculine singular noun. The exact English translation depends on context: de can mean 'of', 'from', and with some verbs it may be part of the verb pattern, as in gostar de or achar de.
target_language_example: O carro do meu vizinho é azul.
native_language_example: My neighbor's car is blue.

meaning: “of my car” / “from my car” (also “in/on/under my car,” depending on context).
additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "o" (= "do"), followed by "meu" (my) + "carro" (car). Portuguese uses "de" in many place/possession expressions, so "do meu carro" can mean possession (something belonging to your car: "a bateria do meu carro"), origin (taken from your car), or location when combined with another word: "na mala do meu carro" (in the trunk of my car), "debaixo do banco do meu carro" (under the seat of my car).
target_language_example: Esqueci a carteira no porta-luvas do meu carro.
native_language_example: I forgot my wallet in my car’s glove compartment.

meaning: “of my son” / “about my son” (depends on the verb/context).
additional_notes: “Do” = “de” + “o” (of/from/about + the). With possession, it often means something belongs to your son: “São do meu filho.” (“They’re my son’s.”). With verbs like “falar de”, it means the topic is your son: “Não quero falar do meu filho.” (“I don’t want to talk about my son.”).
target_language_example: Isso é do meu filho, não mexa.
native_language_example: That’s my son’s—don’t touch it.

additional_notes: Used to show possession or association with your husband. It’s the contraction of "de + o" → "do", so it can mean "of the" or indicate ownership: "o advogado do meu marido" = "my husband’s lawyer". Often comes after the noun it refers to (ternos do meu marido = my husband’s suits).
target_language_example: Você viu as chaves do meu marido?
native_language_example: Have you seen my husband’s keys?

additional_notes: “Do” is the contraction of “de + o” and often means “of” (possession/relationship: “a casa do meu pai” = “my father’s house”) or “from” (origin/source: “ganhei isso do meu pai” = “I got this from my father”). The exact meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: Peguei o carro do meu pai para ir ao trabalho.
native_language_example: I took my father’s car to go to work.

additional_notes: Most commonly used after a superlative ("o/a mais…", "o melhor", "o maior") to mean "in the world": "o maior do mundo" = "the biggest in the world". Literally it’s "de" (of/from) + "o" (the) + "mundo" (world) → "of the world". In phrases like "toda a razão do mundo", it means "all the reason in the world" (i.e., plenty of reason).
target_language_example: Esse é o restaurante mais barato do mundo aqui perto.
native_language_example: This is the cheapest restaurant in the world around here.

meaning: out of nowhere; suddenly (with no warning or apparent reason).
additional_notes: Used when something happens unexpectedly or without explanation: alguém aparece/chega do nada (“someone shows up out of nowhere”), decidir/fazer algo do nada (“decide/do something suddenly”). It can also mean “from nothing / from scratch” in contexts like começar do nada (“start from nothing”). Common in spoken Portuguese; often paired with de repente (“suddenly”).
target_language_example: A gente estava conversando e ele começou a gritar do nada.
native_language_example: We were talking and he suddenly started yelling out of nowhere.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "o" + "nosso" (= "de" + "o nosso"). It’s used to show possession/association with something masculine singular: "do nosso clube" = "of our club". For feminine singular, use "da nossa"; for plural, "dos nossos" / "das nossas".
target_language_example: O gerente do nosso hotel não está aqui hoje.
native_language_example: The manager of our hotel isn’t here today.

meaning: across the street (on the other side of the street).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located on the opposite side of the street from where you are (often implying it’s nearby). Common with verbs like morar (to live) and ficar/estar (to be located). You can add bem for emphasis: bem do outro lado da rua = right across the street.
target_language_example: A farmácia fica bem do outro lado da rua.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is right across the street.

additional_notes: Contraction of **de + o** (“of/from the”) + **outro** (“other”). Common in patterns like **um ... do outro** (“one ... the other”), e.g. **um atrás do outro** (“one after the other”) and **um do lado do outro** (“next to each other”). Also used with verbs like **cuidar do outro** (“to take care of others/someone else”).
target_language_example: Eles sempre cuidam do outro quando um está doente.
native_language_example: They always take care of each other when one is sick.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "o" + "país". Most often means "of the country" (e.g., "a capital do país" = "the capital of the country"). It can also mean "from the country" depending on the verb/context (e.g., "fora do país" = "outside the country").
target_language_example: O presidente do país falou na televisão.
native_language_example: The country's president spoke on TV.

meaning: "of the people" / "from the people"; (also) "ordinary, common (not elite)".
additional_notes: Used to show belonging to a group of people (e.g., "do povo do rio" = "from the river people"). It can also describe someone as a regular person ("uma pessoa do povo"), and in some contexts it can mean "from the crowd/populace" (e.g., protecting someone "do povo" = from the people/crowd).
target_language_example: Ela é do povo e entende os problemas do dia a dia.
native_language_example: She’s one of the people and understands everyday problems.

additional_notes: "do" is a contraction of "de" + "o" and usually means "of the" or "from the". "prédio" means "building" (often an apartment or office building). Used to show possession/origin or to locate something relative to the building (e.g., "atrás do prédio" = "behind the building").
target_language_example: A entrada do prédio fica à direita.
native_language_example: The building’s entrance is on the right.

additional_notes: “Do” is the contraction of “de” + “o” (“of/from the”). So “do quarto” can mean (1) coming from a room: “sair do quarto” = “leave the room,” or (2) belonging to/related to a room: “as janelas do quarto” = “the room’s windows.” “Quarto” often means a bedroom or a hotel room.
target_language_example: Você pode trazer as malas do quarto?
native_language_example: Can you bring the suitcases from the room?

additional_notes: Usually appears when the verb or expression uses the preposition de, such as precisar de, falar de, or ter ideia de. It is the contraction of de + o + que, and in English it is often translated simply as 'what'.
target_language_example: Ela sabe do que está falando.
native_language_example: She knows what she's talking about.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like saber, lembrar-se, falar, ter ideia to refer back to an event. It’s the contraction de + o (“do”) + que aconteceu (“what happened”), so it often translates as “about what happened” or “of what happened,” depending on the verb: falar do que aconteceu (talk about what happened), lembrar-se do que aconteceu (remember what happened), não ter ideia do que aconteceu (have no idea what happened).
target_language_example: Ela ainda está chateada por causa do que aconteceu ontem.
native_language_example: She’s still upset because of what happened yesterday.

additional_notes: used in comparisons, usually after words like mais, menos, melhor, or pior, to compare two things or people. In many cases, Portuguese can also use just que with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Ela fala mais devagar do que eu.
native_language_example: She speaks more slowly than I do.

meaning: "than the" (used after a comparison with mais/menos).
additional_notes: Used in comparisons to introduce the second item being compared. "Do que" means "than"; "a" is the feminine singular definite article "the" (used before feminine nouns like "a riqueza", "a sua mãe"). It can also appear as "do que o" (masculine), "do que os/as" (plural), or just "do que" if no article is needed.
target_language_example: Este livro é mais interessante do que a revista.
native_language_example: This book is more interesting than the magazine.

additional_notes: Used to compare yourself with someone/something, especially after comparatives like “mais/menos … do que” (more/less … than). Often the verb is understood: “Ele é mais alto do que eu (sou)” = “He is taller than I (am).” Also appears in the preference structure “antes X do que eu” = “rather X than me.” In careful Portuguese it’s “do que eu” (not *do que mim*), though *do que mim* can be heard in informal speech.
target_language_example: Ela sabe mais sobre isso do que eu.
native_language_example: She knows more about that than I do.

additional_notes: Used after comparatives with mais/menos/melhor/pior/etc. to compare a reality with your expectation: “more/less/better/worse … than I expected.” It’s very common in the pattern “(um pouco/muito) mais/menos … do que eu esperava.”
target_language_example: O voo foi bem mais longo do que eu esperava.
native_language_example: The flight was much longer than I expected.

additional_notes: Used after a comparison (usually with mais/menos: “more/less”) to say reality is different from your expectation: “more/less … than I thought.” Often follows adjectives (mais caro do que eu pensava) or time/quantity expressions (mais tempo do que eu pensava).
target_language_example: A viagem foi mais longa do que eu pensava.
native_language_example: The trip was longer than I thought.

additional_notes: Used in comparisons with "mais/menos... do que" (“more/less... than”), before a masculine singular noun that takes the definite article "o": e.g., "mais importante do que o ouro" (“more important than gold”). Variants: "do que a" (feminine singular), "do que os/as" (plural). Often the article is omitted when speaking generally (e.g., "mais importante do que ouro").
target_language_example: Este livro é mais interessante do que o filme.
native_language_example: This book is more interesting than the movie.

additional_notes: Used after a comparison (often with "mais" or "menos") to say something is more/less true than the listener expects: "mais … do que você pensa" = "more … than you think." It can also appear as "do que você imagina" (same idea).
target_language_example: Isso é mais importante do que você pensa.
native_language_example: This is more important than you think.

additional_notes: It’s the contraction of "de" + "o" + "quê" and is used after a verb or adjective that takes "de" (e.g., "ter medo de" = to be afraid of). Very common as an echo/clarification question: repeating what someone said and asking “of what?” or “what (are you talking about)?"
target_language_example: Você está falando do quê?
native_language_example: What are you talking about?

meaning: “of the king” / “the king’s” (belonging to the king).
additional_notes: "Do" is a contraction of "de" + "o" and often means possession or association. Use it before a masculine singular noun like "rei" (king): "a mesa do rei" = "the king’s table". It can also mean someone connected to the king, like "os soldados do rei" (the king’s soldiers).
target_language_example: Esse castelo é do rei.
native_language_example: That castle belongs to the king.

meaning: “of the river” / “from the river” (de + o rio).
additional_notes: “Do” is the contraction of **de + o** (“of/from the”). So **do rio** literally means “of/from the river” and is very common in location phrases like **ao longo do rio** (along the river), **na beira do rio** (on the riverbank), **na margem do rio** (on the river’s edge), and **do lado (leste/oeste) do rio** (on the east/west side of the river).
target_language_example: O hotel fica do outro lado do rio.
native_language_example: The hotel is on the other side of the river.

additional_notes: Contraction of de + o + seu. Used before a masculine singular noun. Depending on context, seu can mean 'your' (with você) or 'his/her'. In English, this phrase is often translated simply as 'your' or 'his/her' rather than literally 'of your'.
target_language_example: Precisamos do seu apoio agora.
native_language_example: We need your support now.

meaning: “of your car” (sometimes “from your car,” depending on the verb).
additional_notes: This is the contraction of **de + o** → **do**, plus **seu carro** (“your car”). It’s used to show possession or relation: **as chaves do seu carro** = “the keys of your car / your car keys.” With some verbs, **de** can mean “from,” so context matters (e.g., “take [something] from your car”).
target_language_example: Tire tudo do seu carro antes de vender.
native_language_example: Take everything out of your car before selling it.

meaning: on your side; by your side (next to you).
additional_notes: Literally “of your side.” Used mainly in two ways: (1) physical position: sitting/standing next to someone (“sentar/ficar do seu lado”); (2) support/loyalty: being on someone’s side in a disagreement or situation (“estou do seu lado” = “I’m on your side”). The possessive can change: do meu lado (my), do teu lado (your—Portugal/informal), do lado dele/dela (his/her), do nosso lado (our).
target_language_example: Eu estou do seu lado, aconteça o que acontecer.
native_language_example: I’m on your side, no matter what happens.

additional_notes: Used to show possession or relationship with “pai” (father): “do” = “de” (of/from) + “o” (the), and “seu” = “your” (also can mean “his/her/their” depending on context). Common in phrases like “a jaqueta do seu pai” (your father’s jacket) and “a idade do seu pai” (your father’s age).
target_language_example: Eu me lembro do seu pai quando ouço essa música.
native_language_example: I remember your father when I hear that song.

meaning: “of the sofa” or “from the sofa” (de + o).
additional_notes: Do is the contraction of de + o (“of/from the”). It commonly appears inside location phrases like embaixo do sofá (“under the sofa”) and atrás do sofá (“behind the sofa”), and with verbs like sair do sofá (“get off the sofa / leave the sofa”).
target_language_example: Tire as moedas debaixo do sofá.
native_language_example: Take the coins from under the sofa.

meaning: “of the sun” / “from the sun” (and sometimes just “the sun”).
additional_notes: “Do” = “de + o” and it commonly links something to the sun: origin (“luz do sol” = sunlight), relationship (“planetas… do sol” = planets of the sun/solar system), or proximity (“mais próximo do sol” = closest to the sun). With verbs like “gostar de”, “do sol” can mean “the sun” as the object (“Gosto do sol.”).
target_language_example: A energia do sol é muito forte hoje.
native_language_example: The sun’s energy is very strong today.

meaning: 'from the roof' / 'off the roof' (from a roof).
additional_notes: Contraction of "de + o" → "do". Used after verbs that express coming/falling/jumping from somewhere (e.g., "cair do telhado", "pular do telhado"). Not the same as "no telhado" (= on the roof) or "no telhado" with "em cima do telhado" (= up on the roof).
target_language_example: O gato caiu do telhado e eu corri para ajudar.
native_language_example: The cat fell off the roof and I ran to help.

meaning: 'of the time' / 'about the time' (sometimes: 'about the weather').
additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "o" (= "of/from/about the"). Used with the masculine singular noun "tempo". Common in fixed phrases about time (e.g., "a roda do tempo" = "the wheel of time") and in time comparisons like "um terço do tempo" ("a third of the time"). With verbs like "falar"/"reclamar", "do tempo" often means talking/complaining about the weather.
target_language_example: Não tenho muito do tempo hoje, mas posso te ajudar amanhã.
native_language_example: I don’t have much time today, but I can help you tomorrow.

meaning: “of yours / of your (masculine singular)” or “from your (masculine singular)” (de + o teu).
additional_notes: Used with masculine singular nouns to show possession or origin after the preposition “de” (“of/from”). It’s a contraction: de + o teu → do teu. Example: “Eu preciso do teu carro” = “I need your car” (literally “I need of your car”). For feminine singular, you’d use “da tua”; for plural, “dos teus / das tuas”.
target_language_example: Não me lembro do teu nome.
native_language_example: I don’t remember your name.

meaning: “from work” / “from the job/workplace”; sometimes “of the work” depending on context.
additional_notes: Contraction of "de + o" → "do". Most often used with verbs of leaving/coming back to indicate origin: "sair do trabalho" (leave work), "voltar do trabalho" (come back from work). It can also mean "of the work" in phrases like "cansado do trabalho duro" (tired of hard work) or "gosta do trabalho dele" (likes his work).
target_language_example: Chego do trabalho às seis e meia.
native_language_example: I get home from work at six thirty.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "o" ("do"). Used for possession/location ("a traseira do trem" = the back of the train) and for movement away from something ("descer/saltar do trem" = to get off/jump off the train). Note: "trem" means "train" (not "tram").
target_language_example: Vou descer do trem na próxima estação.
native_language_example: I’m going to get off the train at the next station.

meaning: from scratch; starting over from the beginning.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like "começar" (to start) and "fazer" (to make/do) to mean there’s nothing prepared yet and you’re beginning at step one. Often implies restarting or building something entirely yourself (not using a template or previous work).
target_language_example: Não se preocupe: se der errado, a gente começa do zero.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: if it goes wrong, we’ll start over from scratch.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de + o" → "do". Used with verbs like "descer" (to get off) or "ser expulso" (to be kicked out) to show movement away from the bus or leaving it.
target_language_example: Ele desceu do ônibus na próxima parada.
native_language_example: He got off the bus at the next stop.

meaning: “two brothers”; also a common place name (e.g., Morro/Ilha/Praia dos Dois Irmãos).
additional_notes: Literally it’s the number dois (“two”) + irmãos (“brothers”). You’ll often see it capitalized (Dois Irmãos) as a proper noun for places in Brazil; in place names it may appear with a preposition/article, e.g., dos Dois Irmãos (“of the Two Brothers”).
target_language_example: Vamos encontrar a trilha do Morro dos Dois Irmãos amanhã.
native_language_example: Let’s find the trail to Morro dos Dois Irmãos tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an age (“aos dois anos” = “at age two”), a time period (“por um/dois anos” = “for one/two years”), time from now (“daqui a dois anos” = “in two years”), and age difference (“dois anos mais velha” / “dois anos a mais” = “two years older”).
target_language_example: Eu morei lá por dois anos.
native_language_example: I lived there for two years.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened two years before now (or before the time being talked about). It often goes at the beginning or end of the sentence: “Dois anos atrás, ...” / “... dois anos atrás.” You can swap the number: “um ano atrás”, “três anos atrás”, etc.
target_language_example: Nós nos mudamos para cá dois anos atrás.
native_language_example: We moved here two years ago.

additional_notes: Used to say there are exactly two cars. Often appears after verbs like “ter” (to have) or with an article: “os dois carros” = “the two cars.”
target_language_example: Eu só tenho dois carros, não três.
native_language_example: I only have two cars, not three.

additional_notes: Used to say an amount of time (duration) or a time difference (e.g., late/early by two days). You can place it after a verb or after the time word you’re describing (e.g., “dois dias atrasado” = “two days late”).
target_language_example: Vamos ficar aqui por dois dias.
native_language_example: We’re going to stay here for two days.

additional_notes: Literally “two sons” (filho = son; plural filhos). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, “filhos” is also often used generically to mean “children” when the gender isn’t important or is mixed. If you want to be explicitly gender-neutral you can say “dois filhos/duas filhas” as appropriate, or “duas crianças” (“two kids/children”).
target_language_example: Nós temos dois filhos e moramos em São Paulo.
native_language_example: We have two children and we live in São Paulo.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a group of two male people. "Dois" agrees with a masculine plural noun like "homens" (singular: "um homem"; plural: "dois/três homens"). Often used with the definite article: "os dois homens" = "the two men".
target_language_example: Vi dois homens na entrada do prédio.
native_language_example: I saw two men at the entrance of the building.

meaning: two brothers (or, depending on context, two siblings).
additional_notes: Most often means “two brothers” (irmãos = male siblings). In mixed/unspecified groups, Portuguese often uses the masculine plural “irmãos” to mean “siblings” in general. If you mean specifically “two sisters,” say “duas irmãs.” If you mean “two siblings” clearly, you can also say “dois irmãos(ãs)” or “dois irmãos, um menino e uma menina,” but in everyday speech “dois irmãos” is often used when the gender is understood from context.
target_language_example: Ela tem dois irmãos e mora com a mãe.
native_language_example: She has two brothers and lives with her mother.

additional_notes:
Used to express a duration or time reference of two months. Common with:
- "durante/por dois meses" = for two months (length of time)
- "há dois meses" = two months ago
- "faz/já faz dois meses" = it’s been two months (since something happened)
Also used in contexts like pregnancy to indicate how far along someone is: "grávida de dois meses" (two months pregnant).
target_language_example: Estou trabalhando aqui há dois meses.
native_language_example: I’ve been working here for two months.

additional_notes: Used literally to say something takes/needs two minutes, and very commonly as a quick request meaning “just a moment / give me a second.” You’ll often see it in requests ("me dê dois minutos") or asking someone to wait ("esperar dois minutos").
target_language_example: Só dois minutos e eu já volto.
native_language_example: Just two minutes and I'll be right back.

additional_notes: Used for scores, rankings, grades, or point differences. Common patterns: "por dois pontos" = "by two points" (margin of victory/defeat), and "valer dois pontos" = "to be worth two points" (e.g., an assignment/exam question). Also used in punctuation to mean “colon” (:), but the examples here are about scoring.
target_language_example: O time ganhou por dois pontos.
native_language_example: The team won by two points.

meaning: housewife; homemaker (woman who manages the home).
additional_notes: Refers to a woman whose main work is taking care of the household (cleaning, cooking, managing the home), usually not in paid employment. Often used with articles/possessives: "uma/a dona de casa", "minha dona de casa" (less common). Can be neutral but may feel old-fashioned or stereotyped depending on context.
target_language_example: Ela é dona de casa e cuida dos filhos durante o dia.
native_language_example: She’s a homemaker and takes care of the kids during the day.

additional_notes: A very common everyday phrase for pain in your head. Often used with: (1) "estar com dor de cabeça" (to have a headache right now) and (2) "ter dor de cabeça" (to have a headache). It can also be used figuratively to mean a "headache/problem" (something that causes trouble), depending on context.
target_language_example: Acho que estou com dor de cabeça; vou descansar um pouco.
native_language_example: I think I have a headache; I’m going to rest a bit.

additional_notes: Commonly used with the verb/structure “estar com” to mean you currently have a toothache: “Estou com dor de dente.” You can add intensity with adjectives like “forte” (strong) or “uma bela” (a nasty/big, often ironic way to say it’s bad).
target_language_example: Estou com dor de dente desde ontem.
native_language_example: I’ve had a toothache since yesterday.

additional_notes: A common way to say you have pain in your stomach. Often used with "estar com" (temporary condition) or "ter" (to have): "Estou com dor de estômago" / "Tenho dor de estômago".
target_language_example: Acho que comi demais e estou com dor de estômago.
native_language_example: I think I ate too much and I have a stomachache.

meaning: back pain; pain in the back.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like "estar com" or "ter" to say someone has back pain. Often appears as "com dor nas costas" (without an article) or "com uma dor nas costas" (emphasizing one particular pain/episode).
target_language_example: Depois de carregar as caixas, fiquei com dor nas costas.
native_language_example: After carrying the boxes, I ended up with back pain.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone who is in a very deep sleep and hard to wake up. It’s built from the gerund/continuous form "dormindo" (sleeping) + the adverb "profundamente" (deeply), often used with "estar": "está dormindo profundamente".
target_language_example: Fala baixo: ele está dormindo profundamente.
native_language_example: Speak quietly: he’s fast asleep.

meaning: to sleep a little / to get some sleep.
additional_notes: Used to say you need (or could use) some rest, often because you’re tired. It can mean literally sleeping for a short time (a nap) or more generally “get some sleep.” In Brazil, it’s common to say “precisar dormir um pouco”; in Portugal you may also hear “precisar de dormir um pouco.”
target_language_example: Estou muito cansado(a); vou dormir um pouco.
native_language_example: I’m very tired; I’m going to get some sleep.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de + os" → "dos". Used to link something to "reis" (kings), often in names (e.g., surnames like "Silva dos Reis" or place names). You may also see it in cultural/religious contexts like "Dia de Reis" (Epiphany/Three Kings’ Day) or "Festa dos Reis".
target_language_example: Ela se chama Ana dos Reis.
native_language_example: Her name is Ana dos Reis.

additional_notes: Used to compare or choose between two people/things: superlatives like "o mais... dos dois" (the ...-est of the two), and also with "nenhum dos dois" (neither of the two). It’s the contraction of "de + os" ("dos") + "dois".
target_language_example: Eu prefiro este dos dois.
native_language_example: I prefer this one out of the two.

additional_notes: Contraction of **de + os** (“of/from” + “the”): **dos**. Used to show possession or association (“the lives of men”), or to mean humans/mankind in general (“the world of men”). In comparisons, it can mean “one of the (men)” (e.g., *um dos homens mais inteligentes* = “one of the smartest men”).
target_language_example: A história dos homens é cheia de mudanças.
native_language_example: The history of mankind is full of changes.

meaning: “of the limits” (and in phrases like passar dos limites: “beyond the limits / too far”).
additional_notes: Dos = de + os (“of/from the”). You’ll often see it with passar: passar dos limites = to overstep/go too far (behavior, comments, smells, etc.). With dentro: dentro dos limites = within the limits. It can also be literal, as in “the limits of human knowledge” (os limites do conhecimento humano).
target_language_example: Você passou dos limites com esse comentário.
native_language_example: You went too far with that comment.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de + os meus". Used to link something to "my" masculine plural nouns (e.g., "meus móveis", "meus colegas"). It often appears after verbs/expressions that take "de" like "precisar de" (to need), "separar-se de" (to get rid of / separate from), or phrases like "em nome de" (on behalf of).
target_language_example: Estou com saudade dos meus amigos.
native_language_example: I miss my friends.

additional_notes: "Dos" is a contraction of "de + os" ("of/from + the"). Use "dos meus amigos" to say something is part of your friends ("some of my friends" = "alguns dos meus amigos"), belongs to them/comes from them ("favores dos meus amigos" = "favors from my friends"), or to talk about something related to them ("falar dos meus amigos" = "talk about my friends").
target_language_example: Vou falar dos meus amigos para você mais tarde.
native_language_example: I’ll talk about my friends to you later.

additional_notes: Contraction of **de + os** → **dos** (“of the” / “from the”) + **meus filhos** (“my children”). Used to show possession or relation: **a mãe dos meus filhos** (“the mother of my children”), **a língua materna dos meus filhos** (“my children’s mother tongue”), **longe dos meus filhos** (“far from my children”).
target_language_example: Preciso falar com a professora dos meus filhos.
native_language_example: I need to talk to my children’s teacher.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "os" + "meus pais". Used to show possession or relation ("something of/from my parents") and commonly follows verbs and nouns that take "de" (e.g., "cuidar de" = "to take care of").
target_language_example: Sinto saudades dos meus pais.
native_language_example: I miss my parents.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say it’s your ideal version of that thing (a dream place, dream job, dream girl/guy, etc.). Very common in romantic contexts: “a garota/o garoto dos meus sonhos” = “the girl/guy of my dreams.” Literally “from the my dreams” (de + os).
target_language_example: Este é o emprego dos meus sonhos.
native_language_example: This is the job of my dreams.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de" + "os" + "nossos". Used to talk about something that belongs to you/your group: "alguns dos nossos colegas" = "some of our colleagues". It can also stand alone when the noun is understood: "um dos nossos" = "one of ours". It agrees with gender/number: "das nossas" (feminine plural), "do nosso" (masc. singular), "da nossa" (fem. singular).
target_language_example: Alguns dos nossos amigos não podem vir hoje.
native_language_example: Some of our friends can’t come today.

additional_notes: Contraction of "de + os" → "dos". Used to show possession or relation: "a vida dos outros" = “other people’s lives,” "os erros dos outros" = “other people’s mistakes.” It can also appear with verbs that take "de" to mean “(different) from others”: "diferente dos outros" = “different from the others.”
target_language_example: Não gosto de falar dos outros.
native_language_example: I don’t like talking about other people.

meaning: “of your” / “of his/her/its” / “of their” (plural masculine), used before a plural noun.
additional_notes: "Dos" = "de" + "os" (“of the”). "Seus" is the possessive (your/his/her/their) agreeing with a masculine plural noun (e.g., pecados, trabalhos, cachorros). So "dos seus + noun" means “of your/his/her/their + noun.” Note: "seu(s)/sua(s)" can be ambiguous (your vs his/her/their); context usually clarifies.
target_language_example: Preciso de alguns dos seus documentos para fazer o cadastro.
native_language_example: I need some of your documents to register you.

additional_notes: Contraction of de + os: dos. Use it to mean belonging to your parents (e.g., a casa dos seus pais = your parents’ house) or referring to something involving them (depender dos seus pais = depend on your parents; sentir falta dos seus pais = miss your parents). You can swap in their/your/his/her by changing seus: dos meus pais (my), dos pais dele (his), dos pais dela (her).
target_language_example: Vou jantar na casa dos seus pais amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m going to have dinner at your parents’ house tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an amount of time ("for twelve years") or someone’s age ("twelve years old"). With age, Portuguese often says "ter X anos" (to be X years old), and you can add "de idade" for emphasis: "doze anos (de idade)". With duration, you often use "há" or "faz": "Moro aqui há doze anos."
target_language_example: Ela tem doze anos.
native_language_example: She is twelve years old.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has two female children. Agreement matters: "duas" is feminine plural to match "filhas" (daughter). Compare: "duas filhas" (two daughters) vs. "dois filhos" (two sons) and "dois filhos" can also mean "two children" in general (mixed gender). Often appears with "ter": "Ele tem duas filhas."
target_language_example: Minha irmã tem duas filhas e um filho.
native_language_example: My sister has two daughters and one son.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (por duas horas = for two hours), how long something took (demorou duas horas para... = it took two hours to...), and time relative to now or another event (duas horas depois = two hours later; duas horas atrás = two hours ago).
target_language_example: A reunião vai durar duas horas.
native_language_example: The meeting will last two hours.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has exactly two sisters. "irmãs" is the plural of "irmã" (sister), and "duas" agrees with the feminine noun (you’d say "dois irmãos" for "two brothers"). In "(as) duas irmãs", it means "the two sisters" (a specific pair).
target_language_example: Ela tem duas irmãs e um irmão.
native_language_example: She has two sisters and one brother.

additional_notes: Literally the feminine form of “two” (duas) + “people” (pessoas). Used to say there are two individuals involved, present, or mentioned (e.g., witnesses, people at home, a relationship, an agreement between two people).
target_language_example: Só há duas pessoas na sala.
native_language_example: There are only two people in the room.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a 2-week length of time or a point in time relative to now. Common patterns: "daqui a duas semanas" = "in two weeks" (from now); "faz duas semanas" = "two weeks ago" / "it’s been two weeks"; "duas semanas atrás" = "two weeks ago." Note: "duas" (feminine) agrees with "semanas" (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Vou ficar em Portugal por duas semanas.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay in Portugal for two weeks.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens 2 times (often placed after the verb): "eu fui duas vezes" = "I went twice." It’s also common in comparisons with "mais" to mean "twice as …": "duas vezes mais velho/forte/comprida" = "twice as old/strong/long."
target_language_example: Vou conferir o endereço duas vezes para ter certeza.
native_language_example: I’m going to check the address twice to be sure.

additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens in a typical week. The order is: number + "vezes" (times) + "por" (per) + time period ("semana" = week). You can swap the number: "uma vez por semana" (once a week), "três vezes por semana" (three times a week).
target_language_example: Eu vou à academia duas vezes por semana.
native_language_example: I go to the gym twice a week.

additional_notes: Used to place an event or situation in the time period when a war was happening. Often appears after the main verb or at the end of the sentence. You can swap in another time period: "durante a noite" (during the night), "durante o dia" (during the day).
target_language_example: Muitas famílias se mudaram durante a guerra.
native_language_example: Many families moved during the war.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened at some point in the nighttime period (not necessarily all night). Common in weather updates and describing things that occurred while people were sleeping. Often equivalent to “overnight” in English.
target_language_example: A temperatura caiu durante a noite.
native_language_example: The temperature dropped overnight.

meaning: during the vacation(s) / during the holidays.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens in the time period when you’re on vacation or when a school/work break is happening. "Férias" is often plural in Portuguese even when English would say "vacation." You can also specify which break: "durante as férias de primavera" (during spring break).
target_language_example: Durante as férias, eu gosto de viajar e descansar.
native_language_example: During vacation, I like to travel and rest.

meaning: during the day; in the daytime.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens at some point within the daytime period (not at night). Common with routines or time-limited actions: trabalhar/dormir/cuidar de alguém durante o dia.
target_language_example: Eu estudo durante o dia e trabalho à noite.
native_language_example: I study during the day and work at night.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens within the summer period. Often comes at the beginning of a sentence (“Durante o verão, …”) or after the verb (“… durante o verão”).
target_language_example: Durante o verão, a cidade fica muito cheia de turistas.
native_language_example: During the summer, the city gets very crowded with tourists.

additional_notes: Used to express doubt about a statement. It’s typically followed by a clause with a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., “Duvido que ele esteja…”, “Duvido que ele vá…”). You can also use it in other persons: “Duvidamos que…” (we doubt that), “Você duvida que…?” (Do you doubt that…?).
target_language_example: Duvido que ela chegue a tempo.
native_language_example: I doubt that she’ll arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used to express doubt about a statement or situation. It’s the start of a clause with “duvidar que…”, which typically takes the subjunctive (e.g., esteja, vá). “o” is the masculine singular definite article (“the”) and can change depending on the noun: duvido que a… / duvido que os… / duvido que as….
target_language_example: Duvido que o ônibus chegue a tempo.
native_language_example: I doubt that the bus will arrive on time.

additional_notes: Contraction of “dá” (tu imperative of dar, “to give”) + “me” (“to me”). Used to ask/order someone you address as tu to hand you something. In European Portuguese it’s common to use this with family/close people; with strangers you’d usually say “dê-me …” (formal). Often add “por favor” to be polite.
target_language_example: Dá-me a caneta, por favor.
native_language_example: Give me the pen, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about possibility or feasibility, usually followed by an infinitive: “Dá para + verb” = “You can / It’s possible to + verb.” In questions it often means “Can you…?” (e.g., asking if someone can notice/sense something). In casual speech it’s very common to hear the contracted form “dá pra”.
target_language_example: Dá para me ajudar com isso?
native_language_example: Can you help me with this?

meaning: "you can see" / "it's possible to see"; also "you can tell" (it’s obvious).
additional_notes: Common way to say something is visible or noticeable. Often followed by a place/way of seeing ("Dá para ver de longe" = you can see it from far away) or by "que" + clause to mean "you can tell that..." ("Dá para ver que..." = it’s obvious that...). Can also be used alone as a comment ("Dá para ver." = You can see / It shows) or as a question ("Dá para ver?" = Can you see it?).
target_language_example: Daqui dá para ver a montanha.
native_language_example: From here you can see the mountain.

additional_notes: Informal form of "dá para". Used to say something is possible: "Dá pra fazer" = "You can do it / It’s possible to do it." In questions/requests it can sound impatient or annoyed: "Dá pra parar?" = "Can you stop?" Also, "dar pra alguém" can be slang meaning "to sleep with someone" (sexual), depending on context.
target_language_example: Não dá pra sair hoje; está chovendo muito.
native_language_example: We can’t go out today; it’s raining a lot.

meaning: “you can see” / “it’s possible to see” (also: “you can tell…”).
additional_notes: Common spoken way of saying “dá para ver” (“pra” = informal “para”). Used to talk about visibility or possibility: “Dá pra ver aqui dentro?” = “Can you see in here?” With “que”, it means “you can tell/see that…”: “Dá pra ver que está…” = “You can tell that it is…”.
target_language_example: Daqui dá pra ver o mar.
native_language_example: From here you can see the sea.

meaning: "Give it a break" / "Cut it out" (stop what you’re doing/saying).
additional_notes: Very common in Brazilian Portuguese and informal. Used to tell someone to stop bothering you, calm down, or stop insisting/arguing—often said with annoyance. Depending on context, it can also mean “take a break,” but in phrases like the examples it’s more like “come on, give it a rest.”
target_language_example: Dá um tempo, você não para de reclamar!
native_language_example: Give it a break, you won’t stop complaining!

meaning: (informal) “give/take/have a …” used with a noun to mean “do a quick …”
additional_notes: Used as a very common light-verb pattern: **dar + uma + [noun]**. The exact meaning depends on the noun that follows, e.g. **dá uma olhada** = “take a look,” **dá uma pancada** = “give a hit/knock,” **dá uma surra** = “give a beating,” **dá uma palavrinha** = “have a quick word/chat,” **dar uma saída** = “go out for a bit / step out.” In casual speech you may hear **dá** where standard grammar would be **dê** (imperative) or **dá/va(i) dar** depending on the context.
target_language_example: Dá uma olhada aqui rapidinho.
native_language_example: Take a quick look here.

additional_notes: From the verb dar (to give): dê = formal command (você) meaning “give”; -lhe = indirect object pronoun meaning “to him/to her/to you (formal)”. Used to say “Give him/her …” or “Send/offer him/her …” depending on context (e.g., dê-lhe meus cumprimentos = “give/send him my regards”). Often followed by what you’re giving: dê-lhe isto / dê-lhe um presente.
target_language_example: Se você o encontrar, dê-lhe este recado.
native_language_example: If you run into him, give him this message.

additional_notes: Formal/neutral command meaning “give me…”. It’s the imperative of dar used with você/o senhor/a senhora, plus the object pronoun me (“to me”). The hyphen connects the verb to the pronoun in writing. In the negative, the pronoun usually comes before the verb: não me dê (don’t give me).
target_language_example: Por favor, dê-me um copo de água.
native_language_example: Please, give me a glass of water.

additional_notes: Polite, common way to ask someone to look at something briefly. It’s the imperative form of “dar uma olhada” (literally “to give a look”). Often followed by em/na/no/nas/nesse/nisto + the thing/place you want someone to look at: “Dê uma olhada nessa foto.”
target_language_example: Dê uma olhada no documento e me diga o que você acha.
native_language_example: Take a look at the document and tell me what you think.

additional_notes: A combination of e ('and') + a ('the'). It is used before a feminine singular noun. Before some female names, Portuguese may use a even though English usually just says 'and Mary,' not 'and the Mary.'
target_language_example: Eu encontrei o João e a Ana ontem.
native_language_example: I met João and Ana yesterday.

meaning: “and the other (one)” / “what about the other one?”
additional_notes: Used to refer to the second of two people/things already mentioned (“one… and the other…”). With a question intonation (“E a outra?”) it means “And the other one?” / “What about the other one?”. Often implies you’re comparing two options or asking about the remaining item/person.
target_language_example: Eu já falei com uma delas; e a outra, já chegou?
native_language_example: I already talked to one of them; what about the other one—has she arrived yet?

additional_notes: Often used at the start of a sentence to move the story forward or to ask what happens next. In questions ("Bem, e agora?" / "E agora, onde está...?"), it can mean “so, what now?” or “so, where is it now?” In statements, it simply means “and now” in the sense of “from now on / at this point” (e.g., "Nunca ajudou... e agora quer...").
target_language_example: Perdi o ônibus... e agora?
native_language_example: I missed the bus... what now?

additional_notes: Used to add “the children” as an extra item/person in a list or to include them in an activity ("X e as crianças"). "E" = “and”; "as" is the plural feminine form of “the” (used with "crianças"). Often corresponds to English “and the kids/children.”
target_language_example: Vamos ao parque eu, você e as crianças.
native_language_example: You, me, and the children are going to the park.

additional_notes: Used at the end of a list to mean there are more similar items, but you won’t name them all. It can also be said alone (“E assim por diante.”) to mean “and so on,” implying the same pattern continues. Often corresponds to “etc.” in writing.
target_language_example: Precisamos de cadeiras, mesas, toalhas e assim por diante.
native_language_example: We need chairs, tables, tablecloths, and so on.

additional_notes: Common informal greeting in Brazilian Portuguese, similar to “hey” / “what’s up?”. Often followed by a name ("E aí, Pompeu?"). It can also be used to move a conversation forward (“so…?” / “and then?”) depending on context.
target_language_example: E aí, tudo bem?
native_language_example: What's up, everything good?

additional_notes: Used to link actions in a story: first one thing happens, and then someone starts doing another action. After "começou a" you use an infinitive verb (e.g., "ler", "conversar"). The subject is understood from context; you can also say "e eu comecei a…", "e ela começou a…".
target_language_example: Ele abriu a porta e começou a explicar o problema.
native_language_example: He opened the door and started to explain the problem.

meaning: "and how...?" (a follow-up question asking for the way/manner).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question to continue a conversation: it links to what was just said and asks for details about the process, method, or explanation. Often translates naturally as “So how…?” or “And how…?” in English.
target_language_example: E como você fez isso tão rápido?
native_language_example: And how did you do that so quickly?

additional_notes:
Very common in conversation. 
- As a reaction, it can mean “So what?” (often challenging or dismissive): "Sou, e daí?" (“I am—so what?”).
- In a sequence of events, it can mean “And then?” / “So then what?”: "E daí o que você fez?" (“And then what did you do?”).
- It can also be used as a casual check-in after greeting someone: "Oi, e daí?" (“Hi, what’s up?”).
target_language_example: Ele reclamou do trabalho, e daí eu perguntei: "E daí, o que você vai fazer?"
native_language_example: He complained about work, and then I asked: “So, what are you going to do?”

additional_notes: Used to add the next step in a sequence of actions or events. Very common in spoken instructions and storytelling. It can also introduce something that happens later after a longer time gap: "E depois de tudo..." = "And after everything...".
target_language_example: A gente janta e depois assiste a um filme.
native_language_example: We have dinner and then we watch a movie.

additional_notes: Used to move a conversation forward or prompt a response (often like “so, …?”), and also to show what happens next as a consequence (“…and then…”). In writing it may appear after a comma: “E então, …”.
target_language_example: E então, o que vamos fazer agora?
native_language_example: So, what are we going to do now?

additional_notes: Used to join the speaker to another person or to add a new clause about yourself. Common in subjects like "Tom e eu" = "Tom and I." In standard Portuguese, "eu" is used here as the subject form.
target_language_example: Maria e eu vamos sair mais tarde.
native_language_example: Maria and I are going out later.

meaning: “and I are” (used after another subject, to make “X and I are …”).
additional_notes: Used in the subject of a sentence: “(Name) e eu estamos …” = “(Name) and I are …”. The verb is plural (estamos) because it refers to two or more people. Common with names and family terms (Tom e eu; meu irmão e eu).
target_language_example: Maria e eu estamos cansados hoje.
native_language_example: Maria and I are tired today.

meaning: 'and I don't / didn't' (often: 'and I didn't' or 'and I wasn't').
additional_notes: Used to continue a sentence and contrast your action/state with someone else’s, or to add a negative statement after mentioning something. It’s followed by a verb or verb phrase, and the tense depends on context (e.g., e eu não queria = and I didn’t want; e eu não poderei = and I won’t be able). Sometimes the main verb is repeated for clarity ("e eu não fui"), and sometimes it’s understood from context.
target_language_example: Ela aceitou o convite, e eu não aceitei.
native_language_example: She accepted the invitation, and I didn’t.

meaning: "and I want" / "and I we want" (used in "X and I want...").
additional_notes: Used after naming another person to form the subject “X e eu” (“X and I”). Because the subject is plural (“X + me”), the verb is in the 1st person plural: queremos (“we want”). Common patterns: “Ela e eu queremos…” / “Tom e eu queremos…”.
target_language_example: Minha irmã e eu queremos ir ao cinema hoje.
native_language_example: My sister and I want to go to the movies today.

meaning: “and I are” (used to say you and another person are something).
additional_notes: Used after another subject: “(Name/Person) e eu somos …” = “(Name/Person) and I are …”. With “eu” (I), Portuguese uses the verb form “somos” (we are). You can also use it with “você e eu somos …” = “you and I are …”.
target_language_example: Minha irmã e eu somos brasileiras.
native_language_example: My sister and I are Brazilian.

additional_notes: Used to add that the speaker is the same as the person just mentioned (they also like/do/are the same thing). Often comes at the end of the sentence after a comma: "..., e eu também." The subject pronoun "eu" is emphasized here; in casual speech you may also hear just "eu também". With verbs, Portuguese often drops the second verb because it’s understood from context ("Ela gosta..., e eu também" = "...and I do too").
target_language_example: Ele vai ao cinema amanhã, e eu também.
native_language_example: He’s going to the movies tomorrow, and I am too.

meaning: "and I have" (as part of a plural subject: "X and I have").
additional_notes: Used when the subject is two or more people including you: "Tom e eu" = "Tom and I". In Portuguese, the verb must agree with the plural subject, so you use "temos" (we have), not "tenho" (I have). Common patterns: "[Pessoa] e eu temos ..." (something in common / the same age / the same problem).
target_language_example: Minha irmã e eu temos a mesma opinião.
native_language_example: My sister and I have the same opinion.

meaning: "and I'm going to / and I will".
additional_notes: Used to link what came before with what the speaker intends to do next. It’s "e" (and) + "eu" (I) + "vou" (I go), but in Portuguese "ir" + infinitive is a very common way to talk about the near future (plans/intentions): "e eu vou" + verb (usually in the infinitive) → "and I’m going to" (e.g., "e eu vou ficar", "e eu vou nadar"). It can also sound like a firm promise or threat depending on context.
target_language_example: Termina o trabalho, e eu vou te buscar.
native_language_example: Finish the work, and I’ll come pick you up.

meaning: “and I were …” (imperfect past, 1st-person plural of ser).
additional_notes: Used after another subject to form a compound subject: “X e eu éramos …” = “X and I were …”. Because the subject is “X + I”, Portuguese uses the verb in the plural (nós): éramos. Common with descriptions in the past (age, relationship, situation): “éramos amigos”, “éramos do mesmo time”. You can also say “eu e X éramos …” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: A Ana e eu éramos colegas de trabalho.
native_language_example: Ana and I were coworkers.

meaning: 'and a half' (used with time and durations).
additional_notes: Used after an hour or time to mean “:30” or “half an hour more.” Examples: “duas e meia” = 2:30; “uma hora e meia” = 1.5 hours (one hour and a half). You can also say “meia-noite e meia” = 12:30 a.m.
target_language_example: A reunião é às três e meia.
native_language_example: The meeting is at 3:30.

additional_notes: Used after a number/quantity to mean “+ 1/2”: três e meio (3.5), um mês e meio (1.5 months), um quilo e meio (1.5 kg), um dólar e meio ($1.50). It agrees in gender/number with the noun: use e meia with feminine nouns (e.g., uma hora e meia = 1.5 hours).
target_language_example: Quero dois cafés e meio, por favor.
native_language_example: I’d like two and a half coffees, please.

additional_notes: Used to add "my mother" to a sentence with the conjunction "e" ("and"). It can connect two subjects ("meu pai e minha mãe" = "my father and my mother") or continue a story by adding what your mother did/said (often at the start of a sentence: "E minha mãe..." = "And my mother...").
target_language_example: Eu fui ao mercado e minha mãe ficou em casa.
native_language_example: I went to the market and my mother stayed at home.

meaning: “and never again / and never anymore” (from then on, it never happens again).
additional_notes: Used after an action to say something did not happen again after that point. Very common with the past ("... e nunca mais voltou") and in commands/warnings ("... e nunca mais volte!"). Often implies “never again” or “never heard/seen/found again.”
target_language_example: Ele saiu de casa e nunca mais voltou.
native_language_example: He left home and never came back.

additional_notes: A very common combination: e links ideas ('and') and não negates what follows. It can be translated literally as 'and not', but in natural English it often becomes 'and don't', 'and didn't', etc., depending on the verb tense and context.
target_language_example: Ele chegou cedo e não falou com ninguém.
native_language_example: He arrived early and didn't speak to anyone.

additional_notes: Usually just combines e + o, meaning "and the" before a masculine singular noun. In short questions like "E o Frank?", it often means "what about Frank?".
target_language_example: E o João, já chegou?
native_language_example: What about João, has he arrived yet?

additional_notes: Used in questions to add a follow-up or continue a topic: “And what (about it)?” / “So what should I do/expect?” Often comes after another point or question, and can be followed by a verb phrase (e.g., “e o que você faz?” = “and what do you do?”).
target_language_example: A gente já tentou de tudo... e o que fazemos agora?
native_language_example: We’ve tried everything... so what do we do now?

additional_notes: Used after mentioning something to include everything else not listed. It can refer to remaining people/things (often followed by “de …”: “E o resto da família?” = “And the rest of the family?”) or mean “and so on” in a casual way (“ir ao Marrocos e o resto” = “go to Morocco and all that”).
target_language_example: Vou comprar pão, leite e o resto.
native_language_example: I’m going to buy bread, milk, and the rest.

meaning: "and the" (masculine plural), often also "what about the…?"
additional_notes: Used to join ideas: "… e os …" = "… and the …". In questions, starting with "E os …?" is a common way to ask "And the …? / What about the …?" when continuing a topic. "os" is the masculine plural form of "the" (used with plural masculine or mixed-gender groups).
target_language_example: E os documentos? Você trouxe?
native_language_example: And the documents? Did you bring them?

additional_notes: Used after a person or group to include the remaining people/things not named (e.g., “Tom e os outros” = “Tom and the others”). It can refer to other people (“everyone else”) or other items in a set (though with things you’ll often see “e os outros/as outras” depending on gender/number).
target_language_example: A Ana e os outros já chegaram.
native_language_example: Ana and the others have already arrived.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or continue a question asking for an explanation, often reacting to something just said (sometimes with a challenging tone). It’s literally “e” (and) + “por que” (why). Often followed by a verb: “E por que você fez isso?”
target_language_example: Você quer ir embora? E por que agora?
native_language_example: You want to leave? And why now?

additional_notes: Used to bring up another topic/person/thing, often to ask for an update or to make sure it’s considered. Typically followed by a noun with the correct contraction: ao (a + o, masculine singular), à (a + a, feminine singular), aos (plural masculine), às (plural feminine).
target_language_example: E quanto ao pagamento, você pode fazer hoje?
native_language_example: And what about the payment—can you do it today?

meaning: “How about…?” / “What about…?” (to suggest something or ask for an opinion).
additional_notes: Often used to make a suggestion: “E que tal + noun/verb?” (e.g., “E que tal um café?” / “E que tal sair mais cedo?”). On its own (“E que tal?”) it means “How about it?” or “So, what do you think?”. It can also switch the topic to another option: “Ok, e que tal o Eddie?” = “OK, what about Eddie?”.
target_language_example: E que tal irmos ao cinema hoje à noite?
native_language_example: How about we go to the movies tonight?

additional_notes: Often used to introduce a hypothetical possibility, worry, or suggestion: e se...? = 'what if...?' Literally it is 'and if', so in some contexts it can also simply connect clauses with that more literal meaning.
target_language_example: E se chover amanhã?
native_language_example: What if it rains tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a hypothetical situation, suggestion, worry, or challenge, followed by a verb (often in the subjunctive): e se eu for…? e se eu fizer…? It can sound neutral (planning) or confrontational depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: E se eu chegar mais cedo amanhã?
native_language_example: What if I arrive earlier tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a concern or alternative possibility, often when something might not happen or might not work: “E se não der certo?” (“What if it doesn’t work?”). It can also be followed by a consequence: “E se não chover, vamos à praia.” (“And if it doesn’t rain, we’ll go to the beach.”).
target_language_example: E se não tivermos tempo, podemos ir amanhã.
native_language_example: What if we don’t have time? We can go tomorrow.
