additional_notes: "Eles" = "they" (masculine or mixed group). "Querem" is the present tense of "querer" (to want). It’s followed by an infinitive (Eles querem ajudar = They want to help) or by a noun/pronoun (Eles querem isso = They want that).
target_language_example: Eles querem falar com você agora.
native_language_example: They want to talk to you now.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past (queriam, from querer) to talk about what “they” wanted or intended over a period of time, in the background, or repeatedly in the past. Often followed by an infinitive (queriam saber, queriam ter) or by “que” + verb to express what they wanted.
target_language_example: Eles queriam comprar uma casa, mas era muito caro.
native_language_example: They wanted to buy a house, but it was too expensive.

meaning: "they know" (sometimes: "they can," for a learned skill).
additional_notes: From the verb "saber" (to know). Use it for facts/information (Eles sabem que...), for knowing how to do something (Eles sabem nadar.), and often for learned skills/languages (Eles sabem inglês.). For knowing a person/place (being acquainted/familiar), Portuguese usually uses "conhecer" instead (Eles conhecem o Tom.).
target_language_example: Eles sabem a resposta.
native_language_example: They know the answer.

additional_notes: "Eles" = "they" (for a group of men or a mixed group). "têm" is the present-tense form of "ter" with "eles/elas/vocês". Used for possession (Eles têm dois gatos.), having something available (Eles têm bastante tempo.), or being right (Eles têm razão!). With "ter que" + infinitive, it means obligation: "Eles têm que se comportar" = "They have to behave."
target_language_example: Eles têm que sair agora, mas têm tempo amanhã.
native_language_example: They have to leave now, but they have time tomorrow.

meaning: “they have a” (for a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "ter" (to have). "têm" is the present tense for "eles/elas/vocês" (they/you all). "um" means "a/an" for a masculine singular noun; for feminine you’d use "uma".
target_language_example: Eles têm um carro novo.
native_language_example: They have a new car.

meaning: “they go” or “they are going to” (talking about what they will do).
additional_notes: From the verb **ir** (“to go”) in the present: **eles vão** = “they go/they’re going.” Very often it’s used with another verb in the infinitive (**vão + infinitive**) to express a near future or intention: **eles vão alugar** = “they’re going to rent.” In warnings/threats it can sound like “they will”: **Eles vão te pegar** = “They’ll get you.” The pattern **vão é + infinitive** adds emphasis/contrast, like “what they’re really going to do is…” / “they’re going to (actually) …”.
target_language_example: Calma—eles vão chegar daqui a pouco.
native_language_example: Relax—they’re going to arrive in a little while.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is written, spoken, or done using French. Common after verbs like falar (to speak), escrever (to write), dizer (to say), colocar (to put), and aprender (to learn). Portuguese also uses similar patterns with other languages: em inglês, em espanhol, em português.
target_language_example: Você pode repetir isso em Francês, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you repeat that in French, please?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a place that isn’t known, isn’t important to specify, or hasn’t been decided yet. Very common with verbs like estar (to be), ir (to go), encontrar-se (to meet), and with questions like "Você viu...?".
target_language_example: Acho que deixei meu celular em algum lugar aqui em casa.
native_language_example: I think I left my phone somewhere here at home.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen or has happened at an unspecified time—either in the future ("at some point") or in the past ("at some time"). Often used when you don’t know exactly when, or it’s not important. Similar to "alguma vez" when talking about past experience, but "em algum momento" can also point to the future.
target_language_example: A gente precisa conversar em algum momento desta semana.
native_language_example: We need to talk at some point this week.

meaning: in/on/at something; into something (depending on the verb).
additional_notes: This is the preposition **em** + **alguma coisa** (“something”). Many Portuguese verbs require **em** before their object, where English often uses a different preposition or none at all. Examples: **agarrar-se em alguma coisa** = “hold on to something,” **bater em alguma coisa** = “hit/bump into something,” **atirar em alguma coisa** = “shoot at something.”
target_language_example: Eu pensei em alguma coisa para o jantar.
native_language_example: I thought of something for dinner.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like “estar/ficar” to say something has started and is continuing (not finished yet). Common with discussions, projects, reforms, investigations, work, etc. Similar to “em curso,” and often placed after the noun: “projetos em andamento.”
target_language_example: A investigação está em andamento, então ainda não temos respostas.
native_language_example: The investigation is ongoing, so we still don’t have answers.

meaning: in trouble; in a difficult situation.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" (e.g., "estar em apuros") to say someone is in trouble or has a serious problem (often needing help). It can refer to legal trouble, financial trouble, or just being in a bad situation.
target_language_example: Se você não pagar a tempo, vai ficar em apuros.
native_language_example: If you don’t pay on time, you’ll be in trouble.

additional_notes: Often used with location words like “lá” or “aqui”: “lá em baixo” = “down there/below.” With objects like tires, “(estar/ter) em baixo” commonly means “to be low/flat” (pressure is low).
target_language_example: O elevador está lá em baixo.
native_language_example: The elevator is down there.

meaning: in good hands; safe and well cared for.
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone that a person/thing is being looked after by someone competent or trustworthy (e.g., a doctor, a professional, a friend). Often said directly to someone as reassurance: “Você está em boas mãos.”
target_language_example: Pode ficar tranquilo(a): seu filho está em boas mãos.
native_language_example: You can relax: your child is in good hands.

meaning: blank; (figuratively) without anything happening / with nothing to say or write.
additional_notes: Used literally for an empty space/page ("um espaço/página em branco"). Figuratively, it can mean a date/event "went by without anything" ("passou em branco") or that you’ll leave an answer empty ("deixar em branco").
target_language_example: Na prova, deixei a última pergunta em branco.
native_language_example: On the test, I left the last question blank.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen in the near future. Common with future or near-future expressions (e.g., "vou", "devo", "provavelmente"). It can also mean "in short" in some contexts, but the most common beginner meaning is time-related: "soon".
target_language_example: Eu volto em breve.
native_language_example: I'll be back soon.

additional_notes: Common time expression meaning something will happen in the near future. Often used when leaving/ending a conversation: "Volto em breve" = "I’ll be back soon." Literally "in brief," but it does NOT usually mean "briefly" in English.
target_language_example: A médica disse que teremos os resultados em breve.
native_language_example: The doctor said we’ll have the results soon.

additional_notes: Used with nouns to express that someone is trying to find something or going somewhere with the goal of finding it (often a solution, adventure, evidence, a place to live, etc.). Common after verbs like ir/andar/viajar/procurar (e.g., "foi em busca de...").
target_language_example: Ela veio à cidade em busca de trabalho.
native_language_example: She came to the city in search of work.

additional_notes: Used with numbers to mean a rate or proportion (e.g., "um em cada quatro" = "one in four"). Also used with repeated situations to mean "at each" occurrence ("em cada estação", "em cada refeição", "em cada momento"). Often followed by a noun or "um/uma" + noun.
target_language_example: Eu bebo um copo de água em cada aula.
native_language_example: I drink a glass of water in each class.

additional_notes: Used for being at one's home or place where one lives. After some verbs of movement, English often just says "home" while Portuguese still uses em casa, as in chegar em casa = "arrive home."
target_language_example: Hoje vou ficar em casa.
native_language_example: Today I'm going to stay at home.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is at home (not out/at work/school) specifically today. Common with the verb "estar" (temporary state): "estou/está/estão em casa hoje". You can also use "ficar" to mean 'stay'/'remain': "vou ficar em casa hoje".
target_language_example: Não posso sair; vou ficar em casa hoje.
native_language_example: I can’t go out; I’m going to stay home today.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" to describe something burning (often strongly): "está em chamas". It can describe objects, vehicles, buildings, or places. With verbs like "entrar" it means "to catch fire" (e.g., "entrou em chamas").
target_language_example: O prédio está em chamas; chame os bombeiros!
native_language_example: The building is on fire; call the firefighters!

additional_notes: Often used with **de**: **em cima de** = “on top of / on” (in contact with something): *O livro está em cima da mesa.* It can also describe movement/impact onto someone/something: *cair em cima de alguém* = “fall on/onto someone.” In casual contexts it can mean “on (someone)” as in *mijar em cima* = “pee on.”
target_language_example: Deixei o celular em cima da mesa.
native_language_example: I left my phone on top of the table.

meaning: at the last minute; on short notice.
additional_notes: Used when something is done or decided very close to the deadline/starting time, often implying it was rushed or inconvenient. Common with verbs like avisar (to let someone know), marcar (to schedule), decidir/cancelar (to decide/cancel), and aceitar (to accept).
target_language_example: Eles mudaram o horário da reunião em cima da hora.
native_language_example: They changed the meeting time at the last minute.

meaning: on top of the table; on the table.
additional_notes: Literally “on top of the table.” Used to say an object is resting on the surface of the table (books, plates, mail, etc.). Very common with verbs like colocar/pôr (to put/place), deixar (to leave), and estar/ter/haver (to be/there is).
target_language_example: Deixa as chaves em cima da mesa, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the keys on the table, please.

meaning: on top of the table; on the table (resting on its surface).
additional_notes: Used to indicate something is placed on the table’s surface (not inside/under it). Very common with verbs like colocar/botar/deixar (“to put/leave”).
target_language_example: O celular está em cima da mesa.
native_language_example: The phone is on the table.

meaning: on top of; above; right over/very close to.
additional_notes: Often used literally for location/position: "em cima de uma cadeira" = "on top of a chair." It can also indicate closeness or being right over someone: "bem em cima de você" = "right over you/very close to you." In set expressions, the meaning depends on the verb: "ficar em cima de alguém" = to stay on someone/keep a close eye on someone; "dar em cima de alguém" = to hit on/flirt with someone (informal).
target_language_example: Tom tirou o casaco e o colocou em cima de uma cadeira.
native_language_example: Tom took off his coat and put it on top of a chair.

meaning: in five minutes; five minutes from now.
additional_notes: Used to say something will start/happen after a 5-minute wait (relative to now or another reference point). Common with future tense ("começará", "chegarei"), commands ("Saia em cinco minutos!"), and announcements/status updates ("Carregamento final em cinco minutos"). You can swap the number: "em dois minutos", "em dez minutos", etc.
target_language_example: Posso te ligar em cinco minutos?
native_language_example: Can I call you in five minutes?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" (or "ficar") to say someone is/was in a coma (unconscious for a long time, usually for medical reasons). Often followed by a duration: "por três anos" (for three years).
target_language_example: Ele ficou em coma depois do acidente.
native_language_example: He was in a coma after the accident.

meaning: in common; shared (by two or more people/things).
additional_notes: Used to talk about something shared (a friend, interests, features, experiences). Common patterns: “ter algo/muito em comum” = “to have something/a lot in common”; “um(a) … em comum” = “a shared …” (e.g., “um amigo em comum” = “a mutual friend”). Often comes after the noun it describes: “interesses em comum” (shared interests).
target_language_example: Nós temos os mesmos objetivos em comum.
native_language_example: We have the same goals in common.

additional_notes: Commonly used in set phrases with verbs like **levar em conta** / **ter em conta** (“to take into account, to consider”). Also appears in fixed expressions like **levando tudo em conta** (“all things considered”) and **tendo em conta que...** (“considering that..., given that...”).
target_language_example: Temos de ter isso em conta antes de decidir.
native_language_example: We have to take that into account before deciding.

meaning: in detail; in a detailed way.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like descrever, explicar, contar, falar to say something is described/explained thoroughly, with many specifics. Similar to “com detalhes.”
target_language_example: Você pode explicar isso em detalhes, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you explain that in detail, please?

meaning: in ten minutes; within ten minutes (after 10 minutes).
additional_notes: Used to talk about how long something takes (duration) or when something will happen (in 10 minutes from now). In schedules, you’ll also see the pattern “de X em X” meaning “every X” (e.g., “de dez em dez minutos” = “every ten minutes”).
target_language_example: A reunião começa em dez minutos.
native_language_example: The meeting starts in ten minutes.

meaning: up to date; on time (not overdue).
additional_notes: Used for keeping something current or properly maintained (e.g., language skills, tasks). With payments/bills, it means paying on time and not being behind: "pagar as contas em dia" = to keep bills paid up / not overdue. Common with verbs like "manter" (keep) and "pôr/colocar" (bring) + something + "em dia".
target_language_example: Estou tentando deixar meus e-mails em dia.
native_language_example: I'm trying to get my emails up to date.

additional_notes: Used to mark a starting point and say that something will happen from that moment onward. Very common with time or reference words like “daqui em diante” (from now on/from here on out) and “de hoje/esta noite em diante” (from today/tonight on). Often followed by a plan, rule, or change: “Daqui em diante, nós cuidamos de tudo.”
target_language_example: Daqui em diante, vou estudar português todos os dias.
native_language_example: From now on, I'm going to study Portuguese every day.

meaning: toward; in the direction of (to the).
additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or orientation toward a specific masculine singular place/person/thing introduced by "o" (ao = a + o). With feminine nouns, use "em direção à" (à = a + a): "em direção à praia". Common with verbs of motion like "ir", "correr", "caminhar".
target_language_example: O ônibus vai em direção ao centro.
native_language_example: The bus goes toward downtown.

meaning: in two days (within two days; two days from now).
additional_notes: Used to express a time limit or deadline (“within two days”) or that something will happen after a two-day wait (“two days from now”). With a present/future context it often means two days from now; with tasks it often means within two days.
target_language_example: Eu te ligo em dois dias.
native_language_example: I’ll call you in two days.

additional_notes: Used to single out one person/thing/situation from others. Very common in questions like "Algum ... em especial?" (= "Any ... in particular?"). It can also modify a clause: "Em especial quando..." (= "Especially when..."). In negative phrases, "ninguém/nada ... em especial" means "no one/nothing in particular."
target_language_example: Você quer alguma sobremesa em especial?
native_language_example: Do you want any dessert in particular?

additional_notes: Used after many verbs/adjectives that take the preposition **em** before an infinitive, like **concordar em** (agree to), **sonhar em** (dream of/about), **hesitante em** (hesitant to/about), **melhor em** (better at). In English it often becomes “to do that” or “doing that,” depending on the context.
target_language_example: Ela insistiu em fazer isso sozinha.
native_language_example: She insisted on doing that alone.

additional_notes: Used mainly with verbs like "pegar" or "ser pego" (to catch / to be caught) to say someone was caught while committing something (often a crime) or immediately after, with clear evidence. Common patterns: "pegar alguém em flagrante" and "ser pego em flagrante".
target_language_example: Ele foi pego em flagrante roubando no supermercado.
native_language_example: He was caught red-handed stealing at the supermarket.

additional_notes: Used to indicate that something is spoken, written, read, or studied in the French language: for example conversar em francês, um livro em francês, or estudar/especializar-se em francês.
target_language_example: Ela escreveu a carta em francês.
native_language_example: She wrote the letter in French.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs of movement or progress. With "seguir/ir" it can mean literally "forward" (moving ahead) or figuratively "move on" (continue with your life/plans). In imperatives like "Vão em frente!" / "Sigam em frente!", it commonly means "go ahead!" / "carry on!" (permission or encouragement). It can also mean "in front (of)" in location phrases, often as "em frente a" or "em frente de" (Brazilian Portuguese): "estacionado em frente do prédio" = "parked in front of the building."
target_language_example: Pode começar; vá em frente.
native_language_example: You can start; go ahead.

additional_notes: Used to say something is directly before something else, often on the other side facing it (e.g., buildings across the street). Commonly followed by a noun: "em frente a + lugar/coisa". In everyday Portuguese you may also hear "em frente de" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: A farmácia fica em frente ao supermercado.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is in front of the supermarket.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a position directly before a place/thing, often outside it (e.g., in front of a building) or facing it (e.g., in front of a mirror). It contracts with masculine singular nouns: em + frente + a + o = em frente ao. With feminine singular: em frente à; plural: em frente aos / em frente às.
target_language_example: O café fica em frente ao banco.
native_language_example: The café is in front of the bank.

additional_notes: Used to locate something directly in front of another place/object (often a building): *em frente à casa/loja*. It can also mean “opposite” in the sense of facing across a street or space. It’s the contraction of *a + a* after the preposition *em frente a*; with other articles you’ll also see *em frente ao* (*a + o*), *em frente aos/às*.
target_language_example: Encontrei Tom em frente à loja.
native_language_example: I met Tom in front of the store.

additional_notes: Used to make a general statement or describe what is true most of the time (a typical tendency), not necessarily in every single case. It can go at the beginning of the sentence (often followed by a comma) or after the subject ("X em geral..."). Also appears in the phrase "o público em geral" = "the general public".
target_language_example: Em geral, eu prefiro viajar de manhã.
native_language_example: In general, I prefer to travel in the morning.

additional_notes: Used to mean staying alert and ready for danger or action (“ficar em guarda” = to stay on guard). It can also be a command meaning “On guard!” (common in fencing/duels or as a sharp warning). With “estar em guarda”, it can mean being posted on guard duty or positioned on watch.
target_language_example: Fica em guarda — alguém pode aparecer a qualquer momento.
native_language_example: Stay on guard—someone might show up at any moment.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is written, spoken, read, etc. in the English language. Often follows the verb: falar em inglês (to speak in English), escrever em inglês (to write in English), ler em inglês (to read in English).
target_language_example: Você pode me explicar isso em inglês?
native_language_example: Can you explain that to me in English?

additional_notes: Used to say something important could be gained or lost, or could be affected by the situation (e.g., life, honor, money, future). Very common with the verb “estar”: “está/estavam em jogo” (“is/was at stake”). Note: “jogo” can also mean “gambling” in phrases like “viciado em jogo” (“addicted to gambling”), but “em jogo” in your examples is the “at stake” meaning.
target_language_example: Com tanta coisa em jogo, precisamos decidir com calma.
native_language_example: With so much at stake, we need to decide calmly.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happened during the month of June. "em" is the common preposition for months in Portuguese (em janeiro, em fevereiro, etc.).
target_language_example: Vamos viajar em junho.
native_language_example: We’re going to travel in June.

additional_notes: Used to specify the language something is written/spoken in. Often appears with verbs like "estar" (to be), "escrever" (to write), "dizer" (to say), or "servir" (to work/be useful). Can also be used alone as a clarifying question: "Em latim?" = "In Latin?"
target_language_example: Está escrito em latim.
native_language_example: It’s written in Latin.

meaning: in math; at math (as a subject/skill).
additional_notes: Used after adjectives or expressions to say someone is good/bad/first in the school subject or skill area of mathematics (e.g., bom/ruim/péssimo/primeiro em matemática, notas em matemática). Often interchangeable with “na matemática” in casual speech, but “em matemática” is very common when talking about ability or performance.
target_language_example: Eu sou melhor em matemática do que em história.
native_language_example: I’m better at math than at history.

meaning: in half an hour; in 30 minutes.
additional_notes: Used to say something will happen after 30 minutes from now (or from a reference time). Common with future actions: "Em meia hora eu volto" (I’ll be back in half an hour). It can also mean that something can be done within that time span, depending on context.
target_language_example: Te ligo em meia hora.
native_language_example: I’ll call you in half an hour.

meaning: in less than (a period of time).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens within a shorter time than the amount mentioned. It’s followed by a time expression (e.g., um minuto, uma semana, dois anos, três meses). Often answers “How long did it take?” or “When will it happen?”
target_language_example: Eu termino o trabalho em menos de uma hora.
native_language_example: I’ll finish the work in less than an hour.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "ter" (to have) or "manter" (to keep) to talk about an idea, plan, intention, or something you should remember/consider. Common patterns: "O que você tem em mente?" = "What do you have in mind?" and "Tenha em mente que..." = "Keep in mind that...".
target_language_example: Eu tenho uma viagem em mente para o fim do ano.
native_language_example: I have a trip in mind for the end of the year.

meaning: in my heart (in my feelings; deeply cared about).
additional_notes: Used to express strong affection, love, or emotional importance. Common in romantic, family, or heartfelt contexts (e.g., remembering someone, saying they matter to you). You can change the possessive: em seu coração (in your heart), em nosso coração (in our hearts).
target_language_example: Mesmo longe, você está em meu coração todos os dias.
native_language_example: Even far away, you’re in my heart every day.

meaning: in my place; instead of me.
additional_notes: Used to say someone does something as a substitute for you (“go in my place”), or to ask someone to imagine being you (“if you were in my place”). Common variants: “no meu lugar” and (formal) “em meu lugar”; you can also change the possessive: “em seu lugar” (in your place), “em nosso lugar” (in our place).
target_language_example: Você pode ir ao médico em meu lugar hoje?
native_language_example: Can you go to the doctor in my place today?

additional_notes: Literally means 'in me' and is built from em + mim. It is used with the pronoun mim after the preposition em. In English, the preposition often changes or disappears depending on the verb: confiar em mim = 'trust me,' pensar em mim = 'think about me,' ficar apertado em mim = 'be tight on me.'
target_language_example: Você acredita em mim?
native_language_example: Do you believe in me?

meaning: at my house; in my home.
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens at your place (your home). In everyday speech you’ll often also hear “na minha casa” (= em + a) and “em casa” (without “minha”) depending on context.
target_language_example: Podemos nos encontrar em minha casa às oito.
native_language_example: We can meet at my house at eight.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your personal view (similar to “I think” or “as far as I’m concerned”). It can come at the start of the sentence or be inserted in the middle, often set off by commas. Also commonly said as “na minha opinião” and, more formally, “em minha opinião”.
target_language_example: Em minha opinião, este filme é bom, mas é muito longo.
native_language_example: In my opinion, this movie is good, but it’s too long.

meaning: in hand; on hand (physically with you/in your possession).
additional_notes: Used when something is physically with someone, ready to use, or under someone’s control/possession. Common with verbs like "ter" (to have) and "manter" (to keep): "ter/manter ... em mãos" = to have/keep something on hand. With "entregar ... em mãos" it means handing it directly to someone (in person). It can also be used figuratively: "cair em mãos inimigas" = to fall into enemy hands.
target_language_example: Já estou no aeroporto com o passaporte em mãos.
native_language_example: I’m already at the airport with my passport in hand.

meaning: in the name of; on behalf of.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is acting/speaking with the authority of a person, group, institution, or principle (e.g., the company, the family, the law, the police). It’s common in formal announcements, requests, speeches, and legal/official contexts. The preposition changes with the noun: em nome de + a = em nome da (feminine singular), em nome de + o = em nome do (masculine singular), em nome de + os/as = em nome dos/das (plural).
target_language_example: Estou aqui em nome da empresa para resolver o problema.
native_language_example: I’m here on behalf of the company to solve the problem.

meaning: 'in the name of' (for/under someone’s authority) or 'in the name of' (registered under).
additional_notes: Used in two very common ways: (1) Registration/ownership: "estar/ficar em nome de alguém" = to be in someone’s name (on the documents), e.g., property, car, insurance. (2) Authority/appeal/exclamation: "Em nome de Deus!" or "Em nome de X" = invoking someone/something for emphasis, authority, or pleading (similar to "for God’s sake" / "in the name of..." in English).
target_language_example: O contrato está em nome de meu irmão.
native_language_example: The contract is in my brother’s name.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located or happens within something that belongs to or is associated with “us,” before a feminine noun (e.g., área, loja, vizinhança). It’s the combination of "em" (in/on/at) + "nossa" (our, feminine singular). For masculine nouns, use "em nosso" (e.g., em nosso bairro).
target_language_example: Tem um parque novo em nossa cidade.
native_language_example: There’s a new park in our city.

additional_notes: Used to say things are organized, correct, or properly arranged: "Os documentos estão em ordem." It’s also a brief confirmation meaning "OK/All right!/All set!" (often as "Em ordem!"), similar to "Tudo em ordem" = "Everything’s in order/Everything’s fine."
target_language_example: Está tudo em ordem por aqui.
native_language_example: Everything is in order here.

meaning: "in other words"; used to rephrase or explain something more clearly.
additional_notes: Used to restate what you just said in a different way (often simpler, clearer, or more direct). It can appear at the start of a sentence or in the middle, set off by commas. Common in both speech and writing.
target_language_example: Não tenho tempo hoje; em outras palavras, não posso ir.
native_language_example: I don’t have time today; in other words, I can’t go.

additional_notes: Used to say a person/thing is in a different location, or to suggest moving the conversation/activity to a different place. Often used with verbs like estar/ficar (to be/stay), ir (to go), or conversar (to talk).
target_language_example: Vamos comer em outro lugar.
native_language_example: Let’s eat somewhere else.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happened (or will happen) during the month of October. Common with past and future events: "aconteceu em outubro" (happened in October), "vai acontecer em outubro" (will happen in October).
target_language_example: As aulas começam em outubro.
native_language_example: Classes start in October.

meaning: partly; in part; to some extent.
additional_notes: Used to say something is only partially true/valid, or that only some responsibility/cause/inspiration comes from something. Common patterns: “em parte é verdade” (it’s partly true), “concordo em parte” (I partly agree), “foi em parte minha culpa” (it was partly my fault), “inspirou-se em parte em/por…” (was inspired in part by…).
target_language_example: Eu entendo o que você quer dizer, mas só concordo em parte.
native_language_example: I understand what you mean, but I only partly agree.

additional_notes: Used when you want to speak away from other people, often to discuss something personal, sensitive, or confidential. It commonly follows verbs like falar (to speak) and conversar (to talk): “falar com alguém em particular”.
target_language_example: Depois da reunião, posso falar com você em particular?
native_language_example: After the meeting, can I speak with you in private?

additional_notes: Used to say someone is peaceful/non-violent or that a situation is calm (no fighting, no conflict). Common in contexts like arriving without hostile intentions ("viemos em paz" = "we come in peace") or living without war/arguments ("viver em paz com alguém" = "to live in peace with someone").
target_language_example: Quero viver em paz com meus vizinhos.
native_language_example: I want to live in peace with my neighbors.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar (e.g., "estar em perigo") to say someone is in a dangerous situation or at risk of harm. Common in warnings and emergencies ("Você está em perigo!").
target_language_example: Não te aproximes do fogo — estás em perigo.
native_language_example: Don’t go near the fire—you’re in danger.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is physically present rather than calling/writing/sending someone else. It can add emphasis/surprise: "Ele veio em pessoa" (“He came in person!”). It’s also used in expressions like "a simpatia em pessoa" meaning “friendliness itself / the very personification of friendliness.”
target_language_example: Prefiro falar com você em pessoa.
native_language_example: I’d rather talk to you in person.

meaning: in broad daylight; in the middle of the day (when it’s fully light outside).
additional_notes: Used to stress that something happens openly and surprisingly (or shamelessly) during daytime, when you’d expect people to see it. Often appears with events like crimes ("attacked/robbed in broad daylight") or with behavior that seems inappropriate for the time ("drinking in broad daylight").
target_language_example: Eles foram roubados em plena luz do dia, na rua principal.
native_language_example: They were robbed in broad daylight, on the main street.

meaning: exactly (at an exact time); “on the dot.”
additional_notes: Used after a clock time to emphasize punctuality/precision: “às seis em ponto” = “at six o’clock exactly.” Literally “in/at point,” but in English you normally translate it as “exactly/on the dot,” not “in point.”
target_language_example: A reunião começa às nove em ponto.
native_language_example: The meeting starts at nine o’clock sharp.

meaning: "in a few words"; briefly; in short.
additional_notes: Used to introduce a summary or simplified explanation of something. Often set off by commas at the start of a sentence ("Em poucas palavras, ..."). It can also come after what you’re summarizing to indicate a condensed version (similar to "... in a nutshell").
target_language_example: Em poucas palavras, não posso ir hoje.
native_language_example: In short, I can’t go today.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens quickly or within a short period of time. It can come at the beginning of a sentence for emphasis ("Em pouco tempo, ...") or after the verb ("aprender em pouco tempo"). In questions ("Em pouco tempo?") it expresses surprise or doubt about how fast something will happen.
target_language_example: Vou terminar este trabalho em pouco tempo.
native_language_example: I'll finish this work in a short time.

meaning: first; first of all; in the first place.
additional_notes: Used to (1) introduce the first point in a list or explanation (often at the start of a sentence), (2) mean “in the first place” (= to begin with/initially, especially in questions like “why… in the first place?”), and (3) talk about priority or ranking: “se colocar em primeiro lugar” = “put yourself first,” and “ficar em primeiro lugar” = “come in first place.”
target_language_example: Em primeiro lugar, vamos entender o que aconteceu.
native_language_example: First of all, let’s understand what happened.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "estar" (to be) or "entrar" (to go into) to describe a sudden state of fear/anxiety and loss of calm. Common in warnings/advice: "Não entre em pânico" = "Don’t panic."
target_language_example: Quando ouvi o alarme, fiquei em pânico.
native_language_example: When I heard the alarm, I panicked.

additional_notes: Used mainly with the verb "estar" ("estar em pé") to describe a person who is standing rather than sitting/lying down. It can also describe something that is still upright/standing or still functioning after trouble (e.g., a neighborhood/building still "standing"). Common opposite: "sentado/a" (seated).
target_language_example: Pode esperar ali em pé, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you wait there standing up, please?

additional_notes: Used to say something happens where other people can see/hear it (not in private). Often used with actions you might do on a stage or in front of others (cantar em público) or things that may be inappropriate/embarrassing when others are watching (beijar, insultar em público).
target_language_example: Ela não gosta de falar em público.
native_language_example: She doesn't like speaking in public.

meaning: "in which" (asking which place/option something is in).
additional_notes: Used in questions with the preposition "em" + "qual" to ask which specific location/container/option (city, office, hotel, shelf, etc.) something is in. It agrees with the noun: "em qual" (singular) / "em quais" (plural). Often interchangeable with "em que" in everyday speech (e.g., "Em que cidade mora?").
target_language_example: Em qual rua fica o restaurante?
native_language_example: On which street is the restaurant?

additional_notes: Used to say there is no specific location (it doesn’t matter where). Often appears with relative phrases like “em qualquer lugar onde...” (“anywhere where...”) or “em qualquer lugar que...” (“wherever...”). In questions it can sound like “wherever you are?”.
target_language_example: Você pode me ligar em qualquer lugar, eu atendo.
native_language_example: You can call me anywhere, I’ll answer.

meaning: "in how much" (usually in questions about an amount or length of time).
additional_notes: Most commonly seen in expressions like "em quanto tempo...?" = "in how long...?". Note: Portuguese more often uses the single word "enquanto" to mean "while", which is different from "em quanto".
target_language_example: Em quanto tempo você chega lá?
native_language_example: How long will it take you to get there?

meaning: 'in which' / 'on which' / 'at which' (asking which place, time, situation, etc.).
additional_notes: Used in questions to ask which specific place, time, circumstance, topic, etc. something is in/at/on. Often followed by a noun: "Em que rua?" (On what street?), "Em que parte da cidade?" (In what part of the city?). The exact English preposition varies with context.
target_language_example: Em que dia vocês chegam?
native_language_example: On what day do you arrive?

additional_notes: Used to connect a noun to a clause that gives more information about it. Often appears after places, situations, or times. With places, it is often translated as "where"; in more literal or formal English, "in which." It is common in writing and slightly more formal than "onde" in some contexts.
target_language_example: Esse foi o momento em que tudo mudou.
native_language_example: That was the moment when everything changed.

additional_notes: Used after adjectives like rico/pobre/abundante (or phrases like sem igual) to specify what the country is rich/poor/abundant in. Common pattern: “ser + adjective + em + [noun]” (e.g., “rico em…”, “pobre em…”).
target_language_example: O Brasil é muito rico em recursos naturais.
native_language_example: Brazil is very rich in natural resources.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic or reference point you’re talking about. Common after nouns/adjectives that express feelings or opinions: "preocupado em relação a..." (worried about...), "nervoso em relação a..." (nervous about...). Can also be used for comparisons/positions: "à esquerda em relação a X" (to the left relative to X). Followed by a noun, pronoun, or clause.
target_language_example: Tenho uma dúvida em relação a este exercício.
native_language_example: I have a question about this exercise.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic you’re talking about or the thing something refers to. It’s a common, fairly formal way to say “about/regarding.” It agrees with the noun: em relação ao (to the, masculine), em relação à (to the, feminine), em relação aos (plural masculine), em relação às (plural feminine).
target_language_example: Tenho uma pergunta em relação ao seu pedido.
native_language_example: I have a question regarding your order.

additional_notes: Used to show sequence: something happens immediately after another event or as the next step. Often placed at the start of a sentence ("Em seguida, ...") or after the verb ("logo em seguida" = "right afterwards"). Similar to "depois" and "a seguir", but "em seguida" often feels a bit more immediate/step-by-step.
target_language_example: Terminei o trabalho e, em seguida, fui para casa.
native_language_example: I finished the work and then I went home.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: em seu quintal, em seu tempo livre, em seu elo. The exact possessor depends on context; seu can also mean 'your' in some contexts, but beginners will often also see dele/dela used for clarity.
target_language_example: Ela guardou o celular em seu bolso.
native_language_example: She put her phone in her pocket.

additional_notes: "Em" = "in" and "escritório" = "office". "Seu" is a possessive that can mean "his", "her", "your" (formal), or sometimes "their" depending on context. To be more specific, people often say "no escritório dele" (in his office) or "no escritório dela" (in her office).
target_language_example: Vou deixar os documentos em seu escritório.
native_language_example: I’m going to leave the documents in your office.

additional_notes: Literally “in your room,” but in Portuguese the possessive "seu" can mean "his," "her," "your" (formal), or "their". Context usually makes it clear; if needed, speakers may use "no quarto dele/dela" to be specific.
target_language_example: Ela ficou em seu quarto o dia todo.
native_language_example: She stayed in her room all day.

additional_notes: Used to describe something visible on someone’s face (a smile, an expression) or something applied to the face (e.g., water). It agrees with the person: em meu rosto (on my face), em seu rosto (on your face / on his/her face), em nosso rosto (on our face), em seus rostos (on your/their faces).
target_language_example: Havia preocupação em seu rosto.
native_language_example: There was worry on his/her face.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like pegar, tomar, carregar, segurar to mean holding or carrying someone in one’s arms (often romantic or protective). "Seus" agrees with the person who is doing the holding; it can mean "his," "her," "your" (formal), or "their" depending on context. You may also see "em meus braços" (in my arms) or "em seus próprios braços" (in their own arms).
target_language_example: Ela adormeceu em seus braços.
native_language_example: She fell asleep in his arms.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like ficar, estar, permanecer, ouvir, and trabalhar to say someone is quiet or something happens with no talking/noise. Often describes a temporary state: "ficar em silêncio" = "to fall/go quiet."
target_language_example: Por favor, fiquem em silêncio durante o filme.
native_language_example: Please stay quiet during the movie.

meaning: in/on/at his, her, or your (formal) (feminine noun).
additional_notes: "Em" is a preposition meaning "in/on/at" depending on context. "Sua" means "his/her/your (formal)" and agrees with a feminine noun (e.g., "sua mesa", "sua casa"). It can refer to "his" or "her"; if you need to be clearer, Portuguese often uses "dele" (his) / "dela" (hers).
target_language_example: Ela deixou o celular em sua bolsa.
native_language_example: She left her phone in her bag.

meaning: at your/his/her/their home; in your/his/her/their house.
additional_notes: Means “at someone’s place/home.” The possessive “sua” can refer to you (formal) or to him/her/them, so context matters. Often used with verbs like estar (to be), chegar (to arrive), morar (to live), and convidar (to invite): “em sua casa” = “at your place.”
target_language_example: Posso te ligar quando eu estiver em sua casa?
native_language_example: Can I call you when I’m at your place?

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening/being present during someone’s lifetime or personal life. Often with verbs like haver/ter (to have/there to be): “Há… em sua vida?” = “Is there/Has there been … in your life?” Can also mean “in your private life” depending on context. Common variation: “na sua vida” (same meaning).
target_language_example: Você já teve um cachorro em sua vida?
native_language_example: Have you ever had a dog in your life?

additional_notes: Literally means something is physically being held (e.g., a book, a drink). It’s also used figuratively to say someone controls or is responsible for something ("My future is in your hands") or to blame someone for harm ("You have their blood on your hands"). The possessive (suas) can mean your, his, her, or their depending on context; in Brazil people often use "nas suas mãos" or "em suas mãos" with the same idea.
target_language_example: Agora a decisão está em suas mãos.
native_language_example: Now the decision is in your hands.

meaning: in time; still in time (not too late); full-time (em tempo integral).
additional_notes: Common uses: (1) "estar/ficar em tempo de + infinitive" = still in time to do something (there’s still time; it’s not too late): "Ainda está em tempo de mudar de ideia." (2) "em tempo integral" = full-time (job/activity). (3) At the start of a sentence, "Em tempo," can mean "by the way / just a quick note" to add something important (often in writing).
target_language_example: Você ainda está em tempo de ligar para ela antes de sair.
native_language_example: You’re still in time to call her before you leave.

meaning: 'in you' / 'in you (singular, informal)' after certain verbs (e.g., believe, trust, be interested).
additional_notes: "Em ti" is used with verbs that take the preposition "em" + a person, especially "confiar em" (to trust), "acreditar em" (to believe in), and "estar interessado/a em" (to be interested in). "Ti" is the object form used with "tu" (you, informal singular).
target_language_example: Eu confio em ti.
native_language_example: I trust you.

additional_notes: Used to say something is in many places or throughout an area. Very common with verbs like estar (to be), encontrar (to find), procurar (to look for), aparecer (to appear). You can also say "por toda parte" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Deixei meus óculos em casa e procurei em toda a parte.
native_language_example: I left my glasses at home and looked everywhere.

additional_notes: Used to say something is present/seen in many places or all around. It’s equivalent to “por toda parte” and often follows a verb like estar/haver/ter (e.g., “há ... em toda parte”).
target_language_example: Tem turistas em toda parte no verão.
native_language_example: There are tourists everywhere in the summer.

meaning: in all the / in every (plural feminine).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens or exists in every case/place/item within a group. It’s the preposition “em” (in/on/at) + “todas as” (all the, feminine plural). It must be followed by a feminine plural noun (e.g., línguas, redes sociais, estações, direções). For masculine plural, use “em todos os”.
target_language_example: Ele para em todas as cidades pequenas no caminho.
native_language_example: It stops in every small town along the way.

meaning: "anyway" / "in any case" (used to move on or conclude).
additional_notes: Used to shift the conversation, return to the main point, or conclude after a side comment or uncertainty. Often appears at the beginning of a sentence, similar to English “Anyway, ...”.
target_language_example: Em todo caso, vamos continuar amanhã.
native_language_example: Anyway, let’s continue tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say something/someone is in all places or that you looked in all places. Common with verbs like procurar (to look for), estar/ter (to be/there is/are), and encontrar (to find). Also appears as “por todo lugar” with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Eu vejo placas em todo lugar nesta cidade.
native_language_example: I see signs everywhere in this city.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens or is true globally/in many countries. Often with verbs like "ser conhecido" (to be known), "ser falado" (to be spoken), "ser estudado" (to be studied), etc.
target_language_example: Esse filme fez sucesso em todo o mundo.
native_language_example: That movie was a hit all over the world.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens or can be found in many places, with no specific location. Common with verbs like estar/ir/andar/olhar/encontrar (to be/go/walk or ride/look/find). It can emphasize thoroughness ("They looked everywhere") or general presence ("People like us are everywhere").
target_language_example: Eu vejo essas placas em todos os lugares.
native_language_example: I see those signs everywhere.

additional_notes: Used when something is given or done as compensation for something else. Often followed by "de" + the thing you receive/give: "em troca de" (in exchange for). It can also start a sentence to mean "in return": "Em troca, eu lhe dei...".
target_language_example: Eu te ajudo com a mudança em troca de um almoço.
native_language_example: I’ll help you move in exchange for lunch.

additional_notes: A common combination of em + um, used before a singular masculine noun. Depending on context, em can mean in, on, or at: em um foguete = in a rocket, em um prato = on a plate, em um hotel = at/in a hotel. It is often contracted to num in everyday Portuguese.
target_language_example: Ela mora em um apartamento pequeno.
native_language_example: She lives in a small apartment.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened as a result of a car crash/traffic accident. Common after verbs like morrer/falecer (“to die”) and ser morto (“to be killed”). Also appears as em + um/uma + acidente de + [vehicle]: em um acidente de moto, em um acidente de ônibus. In Portugal, you’ll often hear num acidente de carro (em + um = num).
target_language_example: Ela ficou ferida em um acidente de carro ontem à noite.
native_language_example: She was injured in a car accident last night.

additional_notes: Used for location: someone is seated on a bench. In Portugal you’ll often see the contraction “num banco” (= em um banco). Don’t confuse with “um banco” meaning “a bank” (financial institution); context like “sentado” usually makes it clear it’s a bench.
target_language_example: Ela estava sentada em um banco no parque.
native_language_example: She was sitting on a bench in the park.

meaning: in one day; (sometimes) one day / someday.
additional_notes: Most often used for a time limit or duration: doing something within 24 hours ("finish it in one day"). In some contexts (especially with verbs like "sonhar", "esperar"), it can mean "one day" in the sense of "someday" ("Sonho em um dia..." = "I dream that one day..."). Also appears as "em um só dia" for extra emphasis.
target_language_example: Acho que consigo resolver isso em um dia.
native_language_example: I think I can solve this in one day.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is located at a hotel, staying there, working there, or doing something there. Often appears with verbs like ficar/estar hospedado (to stay), trabalhar (to work), and fazer uma reserva (to make a reservation). In Portugal you’ll also commonly hear "num hotel" (short for "em um hotel").
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar em um hotel perto do aeroporto.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at a hotel near the airport.

additional_notes: Used to say where something happens. "em" = in/at, "um" = a (masculine singular), "restaurante" = restaurant. In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, you’ll also often hear "num restaurante" (contraction of "em um").
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar em um restaurante perto do hotel.
native_language_example: Let’s meet in a restaurant near the hotel.

additional_notes: Means “em” (in/on/at) + “uma” (a/an, feminine singular). Used before feminine singular nouns: em uma fazenda (in a farm), em uma queda (in a fall), em uma agência (at a travel agency). Common spoken/written contraction: “numa”. Masculine equivalent: “em um” (often “num”).
target_language_example: Eles ficaram em uma casa pequena perto da praia.
native_language_example: They stayed in a small house near the beach.

meaning: in one hour; in an hour (from now).
additional_notes: Used to say something will happen one hour from the present moment (a future time). Very common with the future tense or near-future expressions. Also appears as "em 1 hora" or "em uma hora"; in casual speech you may hear "numa hora" (= em + uma).
target_language_example: A reunião começa em uma hora.
native_language_example: The meeting starts in an hour.

meaning: in a week; within one week; in one week’s time.
additional_notes: Used with different time meanings depending on context: (1) duration to complete something (“I got there in a week” = it took one week), (2) deadline/within (“I can’t finish it in a week” = within one week), or (3) time from now (“He’ll be back in a week” = one week from now). Often interchangeable with “em 1 semana”.
target_language_example: Eu termino o relatório em uma semana.
native_language_example: I’ll finish the report in a week.

additional_notes: Used to show a replacement/alternative choice: X happens/you choose X em vez de Y (instead of Y). Very common after verbs like "preferir" (prefiro X em vez de Y). It’s typically followed by a noun/pronoun or an infinitive verb: "em vez de ir" (instead of going).
target_language_example: Vamos de ônibus em vez de ir de carro.
native_language_example: Let’s take the bus instead of going by car.

additional_notes: Used to say you choose a different option or something happens as an alternative to what was expected, suggested, or mentioned before. Often comes at the beginning or end of a sentence. It can also be used in questions to ask for an alternative (e.g., "O que você quer em vez disso?").
target_language_example: Não vou sair hoje; vou ficar em casa em vez disso.
native_language_example: I’m not going out today; I’m staying home instead.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a reason or circumstance that influences a decision or situation. Often appears in more formal contexts (emails, announcements, official writing). Similar in meaning to "por causa de" (because of) or "diante de" (faced with), but "em vista de" sounds more formal. Commonly followed by a noun phrase (e.g., "em vista de problemas técnicos").
target_language_example: Em vista de o voo estar atrasado, vamos remarcar a reunião.
native_language_example: Given that the flight is delayed, we're going to reschedule the meeting.

additional_notes: Used for (1) movement or position around something (“girar em volta de”, “em volta do pescoço”), (2) being gathered around something (“em volta da fogueira”), and (3) looking around your surroundings (“olhar em volta”). Often appears as: “em volta de” + noun/pronoun, or as the adverb “em volta” on its own (similar to “around”).
target_language_example: Tem muita gente em volta do palco.
native_language_example: There are a lot of people around the stage.

additional_notes: Used to indicate (1) something surrounding a place/person (physical sense), or (2) an approximate number/time/amount. Common with quantities and time expressions: “em volta de 10 minutos” = “about 10 minutes”, “em volta de 50 euros” = “around 50 euros”. Often followed by numbers/amounts; with time you may also see the variant “em volta das oito” (“around eight o’clock”).
target_language_example: Chegamos lá em volta de oito horas.
native_language_example: We got there around eight o’clock.

additional_notes: Used to say something is spoken (not just thought or read silently). Common with verbs like ler (to read), falar (to speak), repetir (to repeat). It can also mean that something sounds a certain way when said out loud (e.g., Em voz alta, parece estúpido. = Said out loud, it sounds stupid.).
target_language_example: Pode ler isso em voz alta, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you read that out loud, please?

additional_notes: Used to say an effort, wait, attempt, or hope had no result. Common with verbs like esperar (to wait), tentar (to try), procurar (to look for), and pedir (to ask).
target_language_example: Tentamos ligar várias vezes, mas foi em vão.
native_language_example: We tried calling several times, but it was in vain.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a location directly beneath a table. Very common with verbs like estar/ficar (to be), colocar/pôr (to put), esconder-se (to hide), and olhar/procurar (to look/search). Often interchangeable with “debaixo da mesa” in everyday speech.
target_language_example: O cachorro está embaixo da mesa.
native_language_example: The dog is under the table.

additional_notes: Used to indicate something is physically beneath something else (location/position). Often interchangeable with "debaixo de" in everyday speech. Contracts with definite articles: "embaixo do/da/dos/das".
target_language_example: Encontrei isso embaixo de sua cama.
native_language_example: I found this under your bed.

additional_notes: Very informal and often rude (like “to bug someone” / “to be a pain”). Common in commands: “Para de encher o saco!” = “Stop bothering me!” Literally it’s “to fill the bag,” and in slang “saco” can also be a crude reference, so avoid in formal/polite situations.
target_language_example: Para de encher o saco e me deixa trabalhar.
native_language_example: Stop bothering me and let me work.

meaning: to find a job (to get a job).
additional_notes: Used when talking about getting employment (job-hunting). Often appears with verbs like precisar de / ter de (need to) and with adjectives like novo (new) or permanente (permanent). You can also say “arrumar um emprego” (common in Brazil) with a very similar meaning.
target_language_example: Ela está tentando encontrar um emprego desde o mês passado.
native_language_example: She has been trying to find a job since last month.

meaning: to find her / to find it (feminine).
additional_notes: This is the infinitive verb "encontrar" (to find) + the direct object pronoun "-la" (= her/it, for a feminine person or thing). The pronoun is attached with a hyphen; the accent (encontrá-) shows the stress when the pronoun is attached. It can refer to a woman/girl ("her") or to a feminine noun ("it"), e.g., "a chave" (the key).
target_language_example: Preciso encontrá-la antes que seja tarde.
native_language_example: I need to find her/it before it's too late.

additional_notes: "Encontrá-las" is "encontrar" (to find) + "-las" (them, feminine plural). The accent in "encontrá-" appears when the pronoun is attached to the end of the verb (enclisis). Used for objects that are feminine plural (e.g., "as chaves" = the keys, "as meninas" = the girls). In everyday speech, many people also say "encontrar elas", but in careful/standard writing you’ll see "encontrá-las".
target_language_example: Temos que encontrá-las antes que escureça.
native_language_example: We have to find them before it gets dark.

additional_notes: This is the infinitive verb encontrar (“to find/meet”) + the object pronoun -lo (“him/it”), attached with a hyphen (enclisis). The accent (encontrá-) marks the stressed syllable when the pronoun is added. Common after infinitives: "Vou encontrá-lo" = “I’m going to find/meet him.” In context it can mean either “find” (locate) or “meet” (run into/meet up), depending on the situation.
target_language_example: Preciso encontrá-lo antes da reunião.
native_language_example: I need to find him before the meeting.

meaning: to find them; to meet them.
additional_notes: "Encontrá-los" = "encontrar" (to find/meet) + "-los" (them, masculine or mixed group). It’s an infinitive with the object pronoun attached, common in Brazilian Portuguese (often after another verb like "tentar" or "poder"). In everyday speech you may also hear "encontrar eles", but "encontrá-los" is more standard/written.
target_language_example: Se você vir meus amigos, me avise: eu preciso encontrá-los.
native_language_example: If you see my friends, let me know: I need to find them.

additional_notes: Common in discussions about electricity generation, technology, and politics. In everyday Portuguese, people also say “energia nuclear”; both refer to energy released from reactions in an atom’s nucleus (especially nuclear power).
target_language_example: A energia atômica pode gerar eletricidade, mas exige muitos cuidados com segurança.
native_language_example: Nuclear energy can generate electricity, but it requires a lot of safety precautions.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the electrical power supply in general (what powers lights and appliances) and in everyday situations like a power outage (ficar sem energia elétrica) or the electricity bill (conta de energia elétrica). Often interchangeable with just "energia" or "luz" in casual speech, depending on the region.
target_language_example: Se faltar energia elétrica hoje, a gente liga para a companhia.
native_language_example: If the power goes out today, we’ll call the utility company.

additional_notes: Used to talk about electricity/power produced using nuclear reactions, or the general idea/industry of nuclear power. Common in debates about safety, the environment, and energy policy (e.g., ser contra / ser a favor de).
target_language_example: Muitas pessoas discutem se a energia nuclear deve ser usada.
native_language_example: Many people discuss whether nuclear energy should be used.

additional_notes: Used to describe an action or situation in progress in the past that forms the background for another event. Often followed by a verb in the gerund (e.g., "lendo") or another ongoing past action; "estava" is the imperfect past of "estar".
target_language_example: Eu vi um acidente enquanto eu estava dirigindo para casa.
native_language_example: I saw an accident while I was driving home.

additional_notes: Used to switch to something happening at the same time as another event, or during the waiting period between two moments. Often placed at the start of a sentence, followed by a comma: "Enquanto isso, ...".
target_language_example: Eu preparo o jantar; enquanto isso, você pode pôr a mesa.
native_language_example: I’ll make dinner; meanwhile, you can set the table.

additional_notes: Used with a subject (who teaches) + "ensina francês" + optional details like where ("em Boston"), to whom ("para crianças"), to you ("me"), and how often ("duas vezes por semana"). "Ensinar" is the verb "to teach"; "francês" is the language "French".
target_language_example: Ela ensina francês online.
native_language_example: She teaches French online.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "ensinar" (to teach) + the subject/language being taught (here, "francês"). You can add the person you teach with "ensinar francês a alguém" (to teach French to someone). In everyday speech, many people also say "dar aulas de francês" (to give/teach French classes).
target_language_example: Tom gosta de ensinar francês.
native_language_example: Tom likes to teach French.

additional_notes: Used with the verb “ensinar” (to teach) plus the subject “inglês” (English). You can use it to talk about your job/profession (“Ensinar inglês é minha profissão.”) or to ask someone for lessons (“Você pode/poderia me ensinar inglês?”). “Pode” is more direct; “poderia” is more polite.
target_language_example: Ela começou a ensinar inglês online este ano.
native_language_example: She started teaching English online this year.

meaning: elementary/middle school (basic education before high school).
additional_notes: In Brazil, "ensino fundamental" is the main stage of basic education that typically comes after preschool and before "ensino médio" (high school). It covers the early school years (often grades 1–9), so in English it can map to “elementary school” and/or “middle school” depending on the context. Common uses: "no ensino fundamental" (in elementary/middle school), "desde o ensino fundamental" (since elementary/middle school).
target_language_example: Eu mudei de escola no ensino fundamental.
native_language_example: I changed schools in elementary/middle school.

additional_notes: Refers to the stage of schooling after “ensino fundamental” and before university/college. Commonly used in phrases like “no ensino médio” (in high school) or “quando eu estava no ensino médio” (when I was in high school). In Brazil it typically covers three years; in Portugal you’ll also hear “ensino secundário.”
target_language_example: Eu conheci meus melhores amigos no ensino médio.
native_language_example: I met my best friends in high school.

meaning: to enter (into); to get into; to enter into (an agreement/state)
additional_notes: Used with a destination/place/institution/organization: entrar em casa (enter the house), entrar em Harvard (get into Harvard). Also used in abstract expressions: entrar em acordo (“come to an agreement” / “enter into an agreement”). In everyday Portuguese it is very often contracted with the article: entrar em + a/o/as/os → entrar na/no/nas/nos (e.g., entrar na sala, entrar no carro).
target_language_example: Espero que o Tom consiga entrar em Harvard.
native_language_example: I hope Tom manages to get into Harvard.

meaning: to contact; to get in touch with.
additional_notes: Used to talk about reaching someone by phone, email, message, etc. Very common in polite questions and requests: “Como posso/posso entrar em contato com…?” Also often used with verbs like tentar (“try”) and ir (“will”): “tentei entrar em contato…”, “vou/irá entrar em contato…”.
target_language_example: Vou entrar em contato com você amanhã.
native_language_example: I’ll get in touch with you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "entrar" (to enter) to mean suddenly beginning to feel panic (often in stressful or scary situations). Common in advice/commands like "Não entre em pânico" (Don’t panic).
target_language_example: Quando vi que tinha perdido o passaporte, comecei a entrar em pânico.
native_language_example: When I saw I had lost my passport, I started to panic.

additional_notes: Most commonly means "among us" (within our group): "Há um médico entre nós?" It can also mean "between us" in the sense of sharing or dividing something: "Há um pouco de dinheiro entre nós" (= we have some money among us / between us). Context usually makes the meaning clear.
target_language_example: Entre nós, ninguém quer sair hoje.
native_language_example: Between us, nobody wants to go out today.

additional_notes: Used with plural masculine nouns (os) to mean (1) “among the” in the sense of being in a group or within a set of people/things: "popular entre os garotos" (popular among the boys); and (2) “between the” when talking about a relationship or comparison involving two sides/groups: "entre os Estados Unidos e a Grã-Bretanha" (between the U.S. and Great Britain). For feminine plural, use "entre as".
target_language_example: Há muita competição entre os candidatos.
native_language_example: There’s a lot of competition among the candidates.

additional_notes: Used to refer to something involving two people/things, or a middle point between two extremes. Common in expressions like “A verdade está entre os dois” (“The truth is somewhere in between”). Can also mean “between the two of us/them” in the sense of shared responsibility (“Damos um jeito entre os dois”).
target_language_example: Podemos dividir a conta entre os dois.
native_language_example: We can split the bill between the two of us.

meaning: among themselves; with each other (within a group).
additional_notes: Used when the action happens mutually inside a group (two or more people/animals/things) and doesn’t involve outsiders. Often follows the verb: falar entre si, sorrir entre si, trocar algo entre si, comunicar-se entre si.
target_language_example: Depois da reunião, os colegas combinaram tudo entre si.
native_language_example: After the meeting, the coworkers agreed on everything among themselves.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of **entrar**: **ele/ela entrou** = “he/she entered.” **na** is a contraction of **em + a** (“in/into + the”), so **entrou na sala** is literally “entered in the room,” but in English you normally say “entered the room” or “came into the room.” You can swap the subject: **Eu entrei na sala** (I entered), **eles entraram na sala** (they entered).
target_language_example: Quando ela entrou na sala, todo mundo ficou em silêncio.
native_language_example: When she entered the room, everyone went quiet.

additional_notes: Used at the beginning of a question to transition to a new topic or ask for an update, often after some prior context. It can sound like English “So, how was it?” / “So, how can we…?” and is common in conversation. "Então" here works like a connector (“so/then”), and "como" introduces the “how” question.
target_language_example: Então, como foi a viagem?
native_language_example: So, how was the trip?

meaning: "So, I..." / "Then, I..." (used to continue a story or explain what you did next).
additional_notes: Common at the start of a sentence to link to what was said before and introduce your next action or conclusion. Often used in storytelling: "Então, eu..." = "So/Then, I...". In speech it can also work like a filler meaning "well..." depending on tone.
target_language_example: Então, eu decidi ligar para ela.
native_language_example: So, I decided to call her.

meaning: "So, what…?" / "Well then, what…?" (used to start a question).
additional_notes: Used at the beginning of a question to move a conversation forward, ask for an opinion, or ask what happens next. It can sound slightly impatient or challenging depending on tone (like English “So, what now?”). Often followed by a verb: “Então, o que fazemos agora?”
target_language_example: Então, o que você quer fazer hoje?
native_language_example: So, what do you want to do today?

meaning: “So, why…?” (asking for a reason, often with a challenging or impatient tone).
additional_notes: Used to question someone’s motives or logic: “So then, why…?” It often comes after something said or implied, as a follow-up that pushes for an explanation. In speech it can sound confrontational depending on intonation. You’ll also see it without the comma: “Então por que…”.
target_language_example: Então, por que você não me contou antes?
native_language_example: So, why didn’t you tell me earlier?

meaning: So, let’s… (used to move on or get started).
additional_notes: Often used at the start of a sentence to signal the next step, a decision, or to encourage action (like “Alright then, let’s…”). You can follow it with an infinitive: “Então, vamos continuar” (let’s continue), “Então, vamos entrar” (let’s go in).
target_language_example: Então, vamos embora antes que chova.
native_language_example: So, let’s leave before it rains.

meaning: “So, you…?” / “So, you…” (used to lead into a question or conclusion).
additional_notes: Used as a discourse starter to transition to a point, follow up on what was just said, or draw a conclusion about the other person. Often introduces a question (“Então, você está pronto?”) or a firm conclusion (“Então, você nega.”). Tone depends on context: it can be neutral (“So, are you ready?”) or confrontational (“So you deny it.”).
target_language_example: Então, você vai mesmo embora agora?
native_language_example: So, are you really leaving now?

meaning: "then why...?" (asking for a reason, based on what was just said).
additional_notes: Used to follow up on previous information and question it or point out a seeming contradiction: “If that’s true, then why…?” Often sounds challenging or insistent, depending on tone. Commonly followed by a negative question like “Então por que não…?” (“Then why don’t…?”).
target_language_example: Então por que você não me avisou antes?
native_language_example: Then why didn't you tell me earlier?

additional_notes: Used after a condition (often introduced by “Se…”) to mean “in that case, prepare yourself” or “be ready for what comes next.” In standard Portuguese you’d more commonly hear “então se prepara” or “então se apronte.” This exact wording (“se pronto”) sounds nonstandard/colloquial and may appear as a shortened or mistaken form.
target_language_example: Se você vai mesmo falar com ela hoje, então se pronto: ela pode ficar chateada.
native_language_example: If you’re really going to talk to her today, then get ready: she might get upset.

meaning: "So, let’s…" / "Well then, let’s…" (to suggest starting an action).
additional_notes: Used to move a conversation forward into action or a decision, often as an introduction before a verb: “Então vamos fazer…?” = “So shall we do…?” It can sound like encouragement, impatience, or simply transitioning (“OK then”).
target_language_example: Então vamos começar agora?
native_language_example: So, shall we start now?

additional_notes: Used in dating years in a neutral, non-religious way, equivalent to “d.C.” (depois de Cristo / AD). Often appears with the abbreviation “EC” (e.g., 2024 EC). The opposite is “antes da Era Comum” (AEC) = BCE.
target_language_example: O ano 476 é frequentemente citado como o fim do Império Romano do Ocidente, na Era Comum (EC).
native_language_example: The year 476 is often cited as the end of the Western Roman Empire, in the Common Era (CE).

additional_notes: Used to say that one female person/thing was the only one in a group or situation. It’s the imperfect past of "ser" (era = was). Change for gender/number: "era o único" (masc.), "eram os/as únicos(as)" (plural). Often followed by "a" + infinitive ("a usar") or "que" + verb ("que conseguia ver").
target_language_example: Ela era a única que sabia a resposta.
native_language_example: She was the only one who knew the answer.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past of **ser** (*era*) + an adjective/nationality (*canadense*). Common for describing someone’s identity/background in the past (e.g., nationality): **Eu era canadense** = “I was Canadian,” **Ele era canadense** = “He was Canadian.”
target_language_example: Quando eu morava no Brasil, muita gente achava que eu era canadense.
native_language_example: When I lived in Brazil, many people thought I was Canadian.

meaning: (someone) was a child / when (someone) was a child.
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of "ser" (era) to describe an ongoing past state: being a child. Often appears after "quando" (when): "quando eu/ele/ela era criança". With plural subjects it becomes "eram crianças" (they were children). You can also say "quando eu era pequeno/a" as a similar idea.
target_language_example: Quando eu era criança, eu brincava na rua todos os dias.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I played in the street every day.

additional_notes: Imperfect past of **ser** (“to be”) + **mais** (“more”). Used to compare in the past (**era mais… (do que)…** = “was more… (than)…”). Very common in the negative: **não era mais** = “was no longer / wasn’t anymore”.
target_language_example: Naquela época, eu era mais tímido do que hoje.
native_language_example: Back then, I was shyer than I am today.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past of **ser** (**era**) to describe a past state/characteristic, often as background description (not a one-time event). **muito** intensifies an adjective: *era muito diferente/pequena/maduro*.
target_language_example: Quando eu era criança, a escola era muito longe.
native_language_example: When I was a child, the school was very far away.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past of "ser" (era) to describe an ongoing state in the past (age/background), often with "quando" (“when”). It can refer to “I was very young” or “he/she was very young,” depending on context; Portuguese often drops the subject pronoun.
target_language_example: Eu era muito jovem quando comecei a trabalhar.
native_language_example: I was very young when I started working.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past of the verb "ser" (to be): "ele era" = "he was" / "it was". "Era o" is used before a masculine singular noun: "era o lugar" (it was the place), "era o Sami" (it was Sami). For feminine, use "era a"; for plural, "eram os/as". Note: Portuguese "era" here means "was" and is not the English noun "era" (a time period).
target_language_example: Eu achava que era o Paulo, mas era o Pedro.
native_language_example: I thought it was Paulo, but it was Pedro.

additional_notes: Used to say that one male person (or a masculine noun) was the only one with a certain ability, knowledge, or situation in the past. It’s the past (imperfect) of “é o único que” (“is the only one who”). The verb after “que” is often in the imperfect (e.g., sabia, estava, podia) to describe a state or ongoing situation in the past. For a female subject, use “era a única que”.
target_language_example: Tom era o único que estava acordado.
native_language_example: Tom was the only one who was awake.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of "ser" ("era" = "was") + "tão" ("so/that") to intensify an adjective or adverb: "Ele era tão amável" (He was so kind). It often appears in the structure "tão ... que" ("so ... that"). With comparisons, Portuguese uses "tão ... quanto" ("as ... as").
target_language_example: Ela era tão cansada que foi dormir cedo.
native_language_example: She was so tired that she went to bed early.

additional_notes: "era" is the imperfect past of "ser" (to be) for "he/she/it/you (formal)". Use it for descriptions/background or situations that were true in the past (not a one-time action). It’s usually followed by a noun with an article: "era um" (masculine) / "era uma" (feminine). For plural, use "eram": "eram uns/umas" (or just "eram" + noun).
target_language_example: Quando eu era criança, meu pai era um professor.
native_language_example: When I was a child, my dad was a teacher.

meaning: “was a man” (used to describe a man in the past).
additional_notes: "Era" is the imperfect past of "ser" (to be), often used for descriptions/background information (age, personality, reputation, appearance). It’s commonly followed by adjectives or descriptions: "era um homem forte", "era um homem de má reputação". Often corresponds to English “used to be” or “was” for ongoing past descriptions.
target_language_example: Ele era um homem muito gentil quando era jovem.
native_language_example: He was a very kind man when he was young.

meaning: "(he) was a boy" / "when (he) was a boy."
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past of **ser** (*era*) to describe someone’s age or situation in the past. Often appears with **quando** or **ainda** (*when / still*): *quando ainda era um menino* = “when he was still a boy.” You can change the article for gender/number: *era uma menina* (was a girl), *era um homem* (was a man).
target_language_example: Quando eu era um menino, eu morava no interior.
native_language_example: When I was a boy, I lived in the countryside.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **ser** in the imperfect (**era**) + **uma** (“a/an” feminine) to describe what someone/something was, or to set the scene in the past (background details like time, weather, a typical morning). For masculine nouns, use **era um**.
target_language_example: Quando eu era criança, era uma escola pequena.
native_language_example: When I was a child, it was a small school.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of "ser" (era) to describe someone as a child in the past, often giving background or describing what someone was like back then. You can add adjectives after "criança" (e.g., normal, delicada, extraordinária).
target_language_example: Quando eu era uma criança, eu gostava muito de desenhar.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I really liked drawing.

additional_notes: Used at the beginning of fairy tales or stories to set the scene in an unspecified past. Literally “it was one time,” but it functions like the fixed English phrase “once upon a time.”
