target_language_example: Eu estava tentando ligar para você quando a bateria acabou.
native_language_example: I was trying to call you when the battery died.

meaning: “was working” / “were working” (an ongoing action in the past).
additional_notes: Uses the past form of **estar** (estava) + gerund (**trabalhando**) to describe something that was in progress at a specific time in the past. Change **estava** to match the subject: **eu estava**, **você/ele/ela estava**, **nós estávamos**, **vocês/eles/elas estavam** trabalhando.
target_language_example: Eu estava trabalhando quando você ligou.
native_language_example: I was working when you called.

meaning: “was so…” (describing a past state or condition).
additional_notes: Used with the imperfect of “estar” (estava) + “tão” to intensify an adjective/adverb in the past: “estava tão frio” = “it was so cold.” It often appears in patterns like “estava tão … que …” (“was so … that …”) and comparisons like “estava tão … quanto …” (“was as … as …”).
target_language_example: Eu estava tão cansado que fui dormir cedo.
native_language_example: I was so tired that I went to sleep early.

additional_notes: Used to describe a mild state or feeling in the past. Common pattern: "estava um pouco" + adjective (surpreso/a, preocupado/a, confuso/a). You can change the person/tense: "estou um pouco" (I am a little), "estavam um pouco" (they were a little).
target_language_example: Eu estava um pouco cansado, então fui para casa mais cedo.
native_language_example: I was a little tired, so I went home early.

additional_notes: Past continuous with **estar** (imperfect) + gerund: **estar usando** = “to be using/wearing” at that time. With objects/clothes/accessories, **usar** often means **“to wear”** (óculos, máscara, cinto de segurança, sandálias).
target_language_example: Eu estava usando uma jaqueta quando começou a chover.
native_language_example: I was wearing a jacket when it started to rain.

additional_notes: Used to describe what someone had on at a specific moment in the past. It’s the imperfect of “estar” (estava) + the gerund of “vestir” (vestindo). Common when asking/describing clothing in past situations (e.g., “What was he wearing?”).
target_language_example: Ela estava vestindo um vestido vermelho quando eu a vi.
native_language_example: She was wearing a red dress when I saw her.

additional_notes: "Estava" is the imperfect past of "estar" (to be/to be located), used for states and ongoing situations in the past. "Estava aqui" means someone/something was here at that time (present/located here), often as background information: "quando Tom estava aqui" = "when Tom was here." It can also be used in expressions like "estava aqui na ponta da língua" (literally “it was here on the tip of my tongue,” meaning you almost remembered).
target_language_example: Achei que você estava aqui ontem à noite.
native_language_example: I thought you were here last night.

additional_notes: Imperfect past of "estar com". Common uses: (1) being with someone: "Eu estava com ele" = "I was with him"; (2) having something on you or in a certain physical state: "estava com a boca aberta" = "my mouth was open"; (3) having a temporary condition/illness/feeling: "estava com um resfriado" = "I had a cold", "estava com receio" = "I was afraid". Often followed by a person (com ele/ela/eles) or a noun (com febre, com medo, com pressa).
target_language_example: Eu estava com medo de me perder.
native_language_example: I was afraid of getting lost.

additional_notes: Past tense (imperfect) of "estar" + "em casa". Used to say someone was at home during a period of time or at a certain moment in the past. Often implies an ongoing situation in the past ("was at home"), not a single completed event. In questions: "Você estava em casa?" = "Were you at home?"
target_language_example: Eu estava em casa quando você ligou.
native_language_example: I was at home when you called.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of estar (estava) + lá (“there”) to say someone/something was in a place at that time. Often used when telling a story or setting a scene: Entrei, e quem estava lá? (“I walked in, and who was there?”).
target_language_example: Quando cheguei, ela já estava lá.
native_language_example: When I arrived, she was already there.

meaning: “was in/on/at the” (past location; feminine singular place).
additional_notes: Used to say where someone/something was in the past. It’s the imperfect past of “estar” (estava = was) + “na” (em + a), meaning “in/on/at the” for feminine singular nouns (na China, na montanha). For masculine places, use “estava no” (no Brasil). For plural, “estava nas/nos”.
target_language_example: Ontem eu estava na escola até às cinco.
native_language_example: Yesterday I was at school until five.

additional_notes: Imperfect past of **estar + gerúndio** (estavam + falando) to show an action in progress in the past, often giving background or setting the scene. Used with a subject like **eles/elas/vocês** (“they/you all”) and commonly followed by **com** (talking with), **sobre** (talking about), or a language: **em francês/português** (“in French/Portuguese”).
target_language_example: Quando eu cheguei, eles já estavam falando sobre o trabalho.
native_language_example: When I arrived, they were already talking about work.

additional_notes: Imperfect past of **estar** (3rd person plural) + **lá** (“there”). Used to say that multiple people were present in a place at that time, often as background/description. (Contrast: **estiveram lá** = “they were there” as a completed event.)
target_language_example: Quando eu cheguei, eles já estavam lá.
native_language_example: When I arrived, they were already there.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the place where you enter/exit the metro (subway). Very common with location phrases like "perto de" (near), "próximo a" (close to), and questions like "Onde fica...?" (Where is...?). In Brazil, "metrô" is common; in some places you may also hear "estação de metro" (without the accent) or "estação do metrô".
target_language_example: Desculpe, onde fica a estação de metrô mais próxima?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the nearest метро/subway station?

additional_notes: Used to refer to the place where you catch or arrive by train. Often used with prepositions like “até a” (to/until the), “na” (in/at the), and “em frente da” (in front of the). Also commonly appears in questions asking for directions: “Como chegar à estação de trem?”
target_language_example: A estação de trem fica longe daqui?
native_language_example: Is the train station far from here?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the current year (the year we are in now). Often placed at the end of the sentence, but it can also come first for emphasis: “Este ano, ...”.
target_language_example: Este ano vou estudar mais português.
native_language_example: This year I’m going to study more Portuguese.

additional_notes: "Este" means "this" (masculine singular) and is used for something close to the speaker or the one being pointed out/mentioned right now. "Artigo" usually refers to an article in a newspaper, magazine, blog, or website, and can also mean a specific section of a law ("artigo 5º"). Often used when talking about a specific text you’re reading, writing, correcting, or rating.
target_language_example: Você pode me enviar este artigo por e-mail?
native_language_example: Can you email me this article?

meaning: “this car” (a car near the speaker / the one being pointed out).
additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative "este" (“this”) with the masculine singular noun "carro". Use it to refer to a specific car that’s close to you (physically or in the current situation). For a car farther away, you’ll often hear "esse carro" or "aquele carro" depending on context/region.
target_language_example: Este carro é muito confortável.
native_language_example: This car is very comfortable.

additional_notes:
Used to describe a car (price, size, comfort, etc.) or to say who it belongs to. You can follow it with:
- an adjective: “Este carro é espaçoso.” (This car is spacious.)
- a noun/name with de/do/da/dos/das to show ownership: “Este carro é do Tom.” (This car is Tom’s.)
- a possessive (teu/seu/etc.): “Este carro é teu?” (Is this car yours?)
target_language_example: Este carro é muito rápido, mas é caro.
native_language_example: This car is very fast, but it’s expensive.

additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative "este" (“this”) to point to a specific dictionary that is near the speaker, in the speaker’s hands, or being referred to right now (often contrasted with "esse dicionário" / "aquele dicionário"). "Dicionário" is masculine, so it takes "este" (not "esta").
target_language_example: Você pode me emprestar este dicionário por um minuto?
native_language_example: Can you lend me this dictionary for a minute?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific document that is near the speaker or being shown/handled. "Este" agrees with a masculine noun (documento). Often used with requests (e.g., to translate or send it).
target_language_example: Você pode assinar este documento, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you sign this document, please?

meaning: "this movie/film" (one that’s near you, just mentioned, or the one you’re pointing to).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific movie in the current context. "Este" agrees with masculine singular nouns like "filme" (this = este; movie = filme). Often used when recommending, asking about, or describing a particular movie: "Você viu este filme?"
target_language_example: Eu gostei muito deste filme.
native_language_example: I really liked this movie.

meaning: 'this movie/film is…' (used to describe a movie).
additional_notes: Used before an adjective or description: “Este filme é horrível/maravilhoso/ruim”, or “Este filme é para adultos”. You can also hear “Esse filme é…” (very common, especially in Brazil) with a similar meaning. Adjectives agree with the noun; since “filme” is masculine, you typically use masculine forms (bom, ruim, maravilhoso).
target_language_example: Este filme é muito bom, mas é para adultos.
native_language_example: This movie is very good, but it’s for adults.

meaning: "this man" (a man near the speaker or being pointed out/identified).
additional_notes: Uses the demonstrative "este" to refer to a specific man that is close by, present, or just mentioned/being shown (often like “this man here”). In many situations, people may also use "esse homem" with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Eu não confio neste homem.
native_language_example: I don’t trust this man.

additional_notes: A demonstrative phrase used to point out a specific book. "este" means "this" and agrees with the masculine singular noun "livro." In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, "este" and "esse" are often used less strictly than in formal grammar.
target_language_example: Este livro é muito interessante.
native_language_example: This book is very interesting.

meaning: 'this book is' (used to describe the book or say what it is like/whose it is).
additional_notes: "Este" means "this" (masculine singular), and "livro" is masculine, so you use "este livro". Use "é" (from "ser") to give a description ("é excelente"), identify or classify ("é básico"), express possession with "de" ("é dela" / "é do João"), or say what it’s about ("é sobre..."). For location or temporary state you’d usually use "está" instead (e.g., "Este livro está na mesa.").
target_language_example: Este livro é muito interessante, mas é longo.
native_language_example: This book is very interesting, but it’s long.

meaning: "this place" (a place near you or the one you’re talking about).
additional_notes: Used to point out a specific location that feels close in space or in the conversation. Often contrasts with "esse lugar" (that place near the listener / just mentioned) and "aquele lugar" (that place over there / farther away). "Lugar" can mean a physical spot (a room, restaurant, city) or a more general place.
target_language_example: Não gosto deste lugar à noite.
native_language_example: I don’t like this place at night.

additional_notes: Used to describe a place you’re in or talking about. "Este" agrees with the masculine noun "lugar" (for a feminine noun you’d use "esta": "Esta cidade é…"). You usually follow it with an adjective (e.g., aberto, esquisito, feio, magnífico) or another description.
target_language_example: Este lugar é muito tranquilo à noite.
native_language_example: This place is very calm at night.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a particular problem that is near in context (the one you’re talking about now) or sometimes physically near. "Este" agrees with the masculine noun "problema"; for a feminine noun you’d use "esta" (e.g., "esta situação").
target_language_example: Precisamos resolver este problema hoje.
native_language_example: We need to solve this problem today.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a category or style of something close to the speaker’s context. It’s commonly followed by a noun (este tipo de comida) and often pairs with adjectives like pensamento, concreto, comida, problema, etc. You can also see plural: estes tipos de.
target_language_example: Não gosto deste tipo de música.
native_language_example: I don't like this kind of music.

meaning: 'this work' / 'this job' (the specific work/task being talked about).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a particular job, task, assignment, or piece of work that’s understood from context (often something you’re currently doing or discussing). In Portuguese, "trabalho" can mean both "work" and "job"; the meaning depends on the situation.
target_language_example: Não aguento mais este trabalho.
native_language_example: I can't take this job anymore.

additional_notes: Used to point out a specific dress that is near the speaker or that the speaker is referring to in the moment. Common in shopping or when giving opinions about clothes. You’ll often see it with verbs like "ficar bem" / "cair bem" (to look good/suit someone), "custar" (to cost), and "comprar" (to buy).
target_language_example: Você acha que este vestido fica bem em mim?
native_language_example: Do you think this dress looks good on me?

additional_notes: Used to negate or correct what someone might be assuming, followed by a masculine singular noun (e.g., caso, ponto, problema). For feminine nouns, you’ll usually see: "esta não é a". For plurals: "estes não são os" / "estas não são as".
target_language_example: Este não é o momento para discutir isso.
native_language_example: This is not the time to discuss that.

additional_notes: Used to identify, point out, or introduce someone or something. With o, it normally comes before a masculine singular noun: este é o capitão = this is the captain. Before some names, Portuguese may use o even when English would just say 'this is Bob.'
target_language_example: Este é o meu professor de português.
native_language_example: This is my Portuguese teacher.

meaning: “This is your …” (used to identify something that belongs to you).
additional_notes: Used when pointing out or confirming an item is someone’s (e.g., food, flight). The possessive “seu” agrees with the thing owned: “seu” (masc. singular), “sua” (fem. singular), “seus” (masc. plural), “suas” (fem. plural). “Seu/sua” can mean “your” (often for “you” in more formal contexts, or when addressing someone as “o senhor / a senhora”) and can also mean “his/her/their” depending on context.
target_language_example: Com licença, este é o seu bilhete?
native_language_example: Excuse me, is this your ticket?

additional_notes: Used to introduce/identify something: “this is a …”. It agrees with gender/number: for feminine use “esta é uma” (this is a [fem.]), and for plural “estes são” / “estas são” (these are). In Portuguese, “um/uma” can mean “a/an” or “one” depending on context.
target_language_example: Este é um bom restaurante.
native_language_example: This is a good restaurant.

meaning: 'this is a good' (used to describe a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Use it to say something is good: "Este" = "this" (near the speaker), "é" = "is", "um" = "a", "bom" = "good" (masculine). It’s normally followed by a masculine noun: "Este é um bom lugar." For feminine nouns, use "Esta é uma boa..." (e.g., "Esta é uma boa ideia.").
target_language_example: Este é um bom restaurante.
native_language_example: This is a good restaurant.

additional_notes: Used to identify or introduce something you’re pointing to or talking about. "Este" = “this” (masculine singular, for something near the speaker), "é" = “is”, "um livro" = “a book”. You can swap in another noun: "Este é um carro" (“This is a car”).
target_language_example: Este é um livro interessante.
native_language_example: This is an interesting book.

additional_notes: “Estes” is a demonstrative meaning “these” for masculine plural nouns (plural of “este”). Use it to point out shoes that are near the speaker or in the current situation. You’ll also see “esses sapatos” (“those shoes,” often closer to the listener) and “aqueles sapatos” (“those shoes over there/far away”).
target_language_example: Vou comprar estes sapatos hoje.
native_language_example: I’m going to buy these shoes today.

additional_notes: Used to identify or point out a group of items/people that are close to the speaker. "Estes" is the masculine plural of "este" (this/these), and it agrees with masculine plural nouns (e.g., CDs, livros, filhos). For feminine plural, use "estas são".
target_language_example: Estes são os meus amigos.
native_language_example: These are my friends.

additional_notes: Uses the verb **estar** in the **pretérito perfeito** (**esteve**) to say someone was in this place at some point in the past (often a completed visit). Common in statements (**Alguém esteve aqui.**), questions (**Ele esteve aqui?**), and negatives (**nunca esteve aqui**). You can add time expressions like **na semana passada** (last week) or **o dia todo** (all day).
target_language_example: O médico esteve aqui esta manhã, mas já foi embora.
native_language_example: The doctor was here this morning, but has already left.

meaning: “was in” / “was at” (simple past of estar + em; 3rd person singular).
additional_notes: Used to say someone (he/she/you formal/it) was in a place at a specific time in the past: “Quando esteve em Londres…” = “When he was in London…”. It can also mean “has ever been to” (or “has never been to”) with adverbs like “jamais/nunca”: “Tom jamais esteve em Boston” = “Tom has never been to Boston.” It can be used figuratively too: “Você sempre esteve em meus pensamentos” = “You’ve always been in my thoughts.”
target_language_example: Quando esteve em Londres, ele visitou o Museu Britânico.
native_language_example: When he was in London, he visited the British Museum.

meaning: "was in" / "has been to" (simple past of "estar" + "in the").
additional_notes: "Esteve" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "estar" (he/she/you-formal was). Use "esteve na" before feminine singular places ("na" = "em" + "a"), e.g., "na Alemanha", "na Austrália", "na praia". Depending on context, it can mean (1) being in a place for a period of time in the past ("was in"), or (2) having visited a place at least once (often translated as "has been to").
target_language_example: Nossa professora de alemão esteve na Alemanha?
native_language_example: Was our German teacher in Germany?

meaning: lifestyle; the way someone lives (habits, routine, and living conditions).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a person’s or group’s typical way of living, including daily habits, work-life, spending, diet, and social behavior. Common with adjectives like "saudável" (healthy), "extravagante" (extravagant), "simples" (simple). Often appears with verbs like "viver" (to live), "ter" (to have), "invejar" (to envy), and "adaptar" (to adapt) as in "adaptar o estilo de vida".
target_language_example: Depois que começou a trabalhar de casa, ela mudou o estilo de vida.
native_language_example: After she started working from home, she changed her lifestyle.

meaning: “were here / was here” (subjunctive: expressing a wish, doubt, or an unreal situation).
additional_notes: “Estivesse” is the imperfect subjunctive of estar (“to be”). It’s commonly used after expressions like achei que… (“I thought that…”), eu queria que… (“I wanted/wish that…”), and como se… (“as if…”). It often implies uncertainty, desire, or something not true at the moment. With different subjects: eu estivesse, você/ele estivesse, nós estivéssemos, vocês/eles estivessem.
target_language_example: Eu queria que você estivesse aqui hoje.
native_language_example: I wish you were here today.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "aprender" in the present continuous to talk about what you’re currently in the process of learning (a language, a skill, a subject). Often followed by a noun ("Estou aprendendo inglês") or by "a" + infinitive ("Estou aprendendo a dirigir" = I’m learning to drive). In Portuguese, the simple present "Aprendo" can also sometimes mean "I learn/I’m learning," but "estou aprendendo" emphasizes that it’s happening now/these days.
target_language_example: Estou aprendendo português para viajar.
native_language_example: I’m learning Portuguese to travel.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive verb to explain why you are here / what you intend to do: “Estou aqui para ajudar / falar / propor…”. You can change the verb “estou” for other people or tenses (e.g., “estamos aqui para…” = “we’re here to…”).
target_language_example: Estou aqui para falar com o gerente.
native_language_example: I’m here to speak with the manager.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re doing well, especially about your health or how you feel. It can also mean you’re OK with a situation (“I’m fine like this / I’m good here”). For more emphasis you can say “Estou bem, obrigado(a).”
target_language_example: Não se preocupe — estou bem.
native_language_example: Don’t worry — I’m fine.

additional_notes: Used to show you’re not being serious, often after saying something that could be taken literally or as a threat. Very common in speech (also: "tô brincando"). You can add "com você" to mean "I’m messing with you / I’m teasing you." In the negative ("não estou brincando"), it means "I’m not kidding" (I’m serious).
target_language_example: Calma, eu estou brincando!
native_language_example: Relax, I'm kidding!

additional_notes: Used to say you’re tired, annoyed, or fed up with a repeated action or ongoing situation. It’s usually followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., fazer, fingir, perder) or a noun (e.g., seus insultos). Change for gender/number: estou cansada de (female speaker), estamos cansados/cansadas de (we).
target_language_example: Estou cansado de esperar; vamos embora.
native_language_example: I'm tired of waiting; let's go.

additional_notes: Used to express strong confidence about a statement. It’s the 1st-person singular present of estar + certo (“to be certain”) + de que (“that”). You can change the subject: estou/está/estamos certos de que… (e.g., Ela está certa de que…, Estamos certos de que…).
target_language_example: Estou certo de que tudo vai dar certo.
native_language_example: I’m sure that everything will work out.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a temporary state/condition you’re experiencing or “with you” at the moment (problems, symptoms, feelings, cravings, hunger, etc.): "estou com fome" = "i’m hungry", "estou com dor de cabeça" = "i have a headache". It can also mean “i’m with (someone)” in the literal sense: "estou com a Ana" = "i’m with Ana". Often overlaps with "tenho" (“i have”), but "estou com" tends to sound more like a current/temporary condition.
target_language_example: Estou com dor de cabeça hoje.
native_language_example: I have a headache today.

additional_notes: Used to say you feel hunger. Literally “I am with hunger,” but it’s the normal everyday way to say “I’m hungry.” You can change the subject/person: “está com fome” (you/he/she is hungry), “estamos com fome” (we’re hungry), “estão com fome” (they’re hungry).
target_language_example: Estou com fome; vamos comer alguma coisa.
native_language_example: I’m hungry; let’s eat something.

additional_notes: Used to politely (or firmly) say you don’t have much time. It’s very common in conversation; you can add emphasis with “realmente” (really) or soften it with “desculpe” (sorry). You can also change the subject: “está com pressa?” (are you in a hurry?), “tô com pressa” is a more informal spoken version.
target_language_example: Desculpe, estou com pressa — podemos falar depois?
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m in a hurry—can we talk later?

additional_notes: Present continuous form: **estar** (estou) + gerund (**comendo**) to describe what you’re eating right now. Often followed by the food: *Estou comendo arroz.* You can also add *com* to say who you’re eating with: *Estou comendo com meu irmão* (“I’m eating with my brother”).
target_language_example: Agora não posso falar; estou comendo.
native_language_example: I can’t talk right now; I’m eating.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or emphasize what you mean, often to clarify or correct a misunderstanding. It’s the present continuous of "dizer" (to say): "eu estou dizendo" = "I’m saying". Common in contrasts like: "Não estou dizendo que X, estou dizendo que Y" (I’m not saying X, I’m saying Y).
target_language_example: Estou dizendo que precisamos sair agora.
native_language_example: I’m saying that we need to leave now.

additional_notes: From **estar** (to be) + **esperando** (waiting). Commonly followed by **por** + person/thing (**Estou esperando por você**) or directly by the thing/person (**Estou esperando o encanador**). Depending on context, **esperar** can also mean “to expect” or “to hope,” but **estou esperando** is most often used for “I’m waiting.”
target_language_example: Estou esperando o ônibus há dez minutos.
native_language_example: I’ve been waiting for the bus for ten minutes.

additional_notes: Present continuous idea with estar + gerund: estar + falando. Commonly followed by de (about): "Estou falando de..." = "I’m talking about...". You can also use it to emphasize your point: "É disso que estou falando!" = "That’s what I’m talking about!". Often used with adverbs: "muito sério" (very seriously), "rápido demais" (too fast).
target_language_example: Estou falando do meu trabalho agora.
native_language_example: I’m talking about my job right now.

meaning: "I’m tired of / fed up with" (something or someone).
additional_notes: Used to express annoyance or that you’ve had enough of a person, situation, or repeated action. It’s often stronger than simply being tired. It agrees with the speaker: "estou farto de" (male speaker) / "estou farta de" (female speaker). You can follow it with a noun/pronoun ("de tudo", "de você") or an infinitive verb ("de esperar", "de cantar").
target_language_example: Estou farto de esperar aqui.
native_language_example: I’m fed up with waiting here.

additional_notes: Present continuous with **estar + gerund**. Used for actions happening now or around now: **estou fazendo** + object (estou fazendo o dever de casa = I’m doing homework; estou fazendo o Ratatouille = I’m making Ratatouille). Often used in questions like **O que estou fazendo?** (What am I doing?) and **Por que estou fazendo isso?** (Why am I doing this?).
target_language_example: Agora estou fazendo o jantar, depois eu ligo para você.
native_language_example: I’m making dinner now; then I’ll call you.

additional_notes: Used to express how you feel right now (a current/temporary state). It’s the verb “estar” (to be) + “feliz” (happy). You can add what you’re happy about with: “estou feliz de…” / “estou feliz em…” / “estou feliz por…” (roughly “I’m happy to…” / “I’m happy about…”).
target_language_example: Estou feliz por você ter vindo hoje.
native_language_example: I’m happy you came today.

meaning: 'I'm going' / 'I'm on my way' (or 'I'm doing' in the sense of 'I'm doing (well/badly)').
additional_notes: From the verb ir (to go): eu estou indo = literally “I am going.” It’s used for movement/direction (often with a + place or para + destination): “Estou indo ao cinema.” / “Estou indo para casa.” It’s also common as an answer to “Como você está indo?” meaning “How are you doing/How’s it going?” (e.g., “Estou indo muito bem.”).
target_language_example: Tchau, estou indo!
native_language_example: Bye, I'm leaving / I'm on my way.

additional_notes: Used with a destination (place) to say you’re on your way or planning to go. Very common in Brazilian Portuguese; in more formal contexts you may also hear “estou a ir para” (Portugal) or simply “vou para”.
target_language_example: Estou indo para o trabalho agora.
native_language_example: I’m going to work now.

meaning: “I’m feeling” (talking about how you feel physically or emotionally).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective (or sometimes an adverb) to describe your current state: Estou me sentindo bem/mal, melhor, estranho(a), cansado(a). It’s the present progressive of sentir-se (“to feel”), and is slightly more explicit than just “me sinto” (“I feel”).
target_language_example: Hoje estou me sentindo cansado, então vou dormir cedo.
native_language_example: Today I’m feeling tired, so I’m going to sleep early.

additional_notes: Used to express how you feel right now. It’s the verb estar (temporary state) + muito (very) + feliz (happy). Often followed by de + infinitive or em + infinitive to say what you’re happy about: "Estou muito feliz de te encontrar" (happy to see you) / "Estou muito feliz em conhecê-la" (happy to meet you).
target_language_example: Estou muito feliz por você estar aqui.
native_language_example: I'm very happy you’re here.

additional_notes: Used with "em" + a noun/pronoun (thinking about someone/something) or "em" + infinitive verb (considering doing something). It often expresses a plan or possibility: "Estou pensando em viajar" = "I’m considering traveling."
target_language_example: Estou pensando em mudar de emprego.
native_language_example: I’m thinking about changing jobs.

additional_notes: Used to express worry/concern about a person or situation. It agrees with the speaker’s gender/number: a man says "estou preocupado com"; a woman says "estou preocupada com"; plural: "estamos preocupados/preocupadas com". The preposition "com" means "about" here and is followed by a noun or pronoun (e.g., "ela", "isso", "o trabalho").
target_language_example: Estou preocupado com o exame de amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m worried about tomorrow’s exam.

additional_notes: From the verb "procurar" (to look for). "Estou procurando" is the present continuous form used to say you’re currently trying to find someone or something. It’s commonly followed by a noun ("Estou procurando meu irmão") or by "alguém que..." (someone who...).
target_language_example: Estou procurando um bom restaurante perto daqui.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a good restaurant near here.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb to say you are in the process of making an effort right now: “Estou tentando + verb” (e.g., estou tentando ajudar = I’m trying to help). In speech it’s common to drop “eu” (subject pronoun), and you can also use other forms like “tô tentando” (more casual).
target_language_example: Estou tentando aprender português, mas ainda é difícil.
native_language_example: I’m trying to learn Portuguese, but it’s still hard.

additional_notes: Present continuous with **estar + gerund** (*estou + trabalhando*) to say what you’re doing right now. Often used as a short reply to explain you’re busy (e.g., “Estou trabalhando!”). You can add **para** / **para que** to express purpose: *Estou trabalhando para…* (“I’m working to… / so that…”).
target_language_example: Não posso falar agora; estou trabalhando.
native_language_example: I can’t talk right now; I’m working.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective (or sometimes an adverb) to intensify what you’re saying: "Estou tão preocupado/a" = "I’m so worried." The adjective agrees with the speaker (worried: preocupado = male, preocupada = female). It’s often followed by a result clause with "que": "Estou tão cansado que…" = "I’m so tired that…". In questions, it stays the same: "Por que estou tão nervoso?" = "Why am I so nervous?".
target_language_example: Estou tão cansado que vou dormir cedo.
native_language_example: I’m so tired that I’m going to sleep early.

additional_notes:
Used to express strong happiness. Often followed by:
- “por + [reason/person]” = happy about/for (e.g., “Estou tão feliz por você.”)
- “que + [result]” = so happy that… (e.g., “Estou tão feliz que não consigo me conter.”)
You can swap the subject: “ele/ela está tão feliz” (he/she is so happy), “estamos tão felizes” (we’re so happy).
target_language_example: Estou tão feliz por finalmente ter terminado o trabalho.
native_language_example: I’m so happy I finally finished the work.

additional_notes: Used to say you are in a place (your location) or to emphasize your presence/arrival (e.g., answering when someone is looking for you: “Eu estou aqui!”). Often appears with time expressions: “Estou aqui há uma semana” = “I’ve been here for a week.”
target_language_example: Calma, eu estou aqui para ajudar.
native_language_example: Relax, I’m here to help.

additional_notes:
"Estar com" is very common and has a few everyday uses:
1) Possession/holding: "Estou com sua chave" = I have your key (it’s with me).
2) Being together/with someone: "Estou com você" = I’m with you.
3) A temporary condition/symptom: "Estou com dores..." = I have pains / I’m having pain.
4) Being 'with' something scheduled/filled: "Estou com a agenda lotada" = My schedule is full.
It’s usually temporary (different from "tenho", which often sounds more general/permanent).
target_language_example: Desculpa, não posso sair hoje: estou com a agenda lotada.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go out today: my schedule is full.

additional_notes: Used to point out something you see in the sky (“Look, a shooting star!”). Literally “falling star,” but it refers to a meteor streaking across the sky. Common with verbs like ver (“to see”) and olha/olhe (“look!”).
target_language_example: Pedi um desejo quando vi uma estrela cadente.
native_language_example: I made a wish when I saw a shooting star.

additional_notes: "estuda" is the present-tense form of "estudar" for ele/ela/você (he/she/you formal). Use it to say someone studies French. For "I study French": "Eu estudo francês"; for "Do you study French?": "Você estuda francês?"
target_language_example: Ela estuda francês na universidade.
native_language_example: She studies French at the university.

additional_notes: Uses the gerund "estudando" (from "estudar", to study) to describe an ongoing activity. Often used after expressions like "passar tempo"/"passar X horas" (to spend time) or with "estar" to emphasize that the action is currently in progress ("está estudando francês" = is studying French right now/these days).
target_language_example: Ela está estudando francês para viajar para Paris.
native_language_example: She’s studying French to travel to Paris.

additional_notes: Means learning the French language (for school, work, or personal interest). You can use it with or without "de" depending on the verb before it (e.g., "precisar de estudar francês" / "precisar estudar francês").
target_language_example: Eu quero estudar francês este ano.
native_language_example: I want to study French this year.

additional_notes: A common phrase for learning foreign languages (e.g., English, Spanish, French). You can pair it with intensity words like "muito" (a lot) and "demais" (really/so much) to emphasize how much you like it.
target_language_example: Eu quero estudar idiomas para viajar.
native_language_example: I want to study languages to travel.

additional_notes: Used to talk about learning English as a subject (at school, in a course, or on your own). You conjugate only the verb: eu estudo inglês, eles estudam inglês, comecei a estudar inglês. With modal verbs like dever (“should”) it often appears in the infinitive: devemos estudar inglês.
target_language_example: Devemos estudar inglês.
native_language_example: We should study English.

additional_notes: Used when someone studies in a foreign country, often for a semester/year exchange program, university, or with a scholarship (bolsa de estudos). Also common: “fazer intercâmbio” (to do an exchange).
target_language_example: Ela vai estudar no exterior no próximo semestre.
native_language_example: She’s going to study abroad next semester.

meaning: is on the way (to); is heading to.
additional_notes: Used with places to say someone/something is traveling toward a destination. Very common with "de" (from) and "para" (to): "Está a caminho de casa" (on the way home), "Está a caminho de Boston" (heading to Boston).
target_language_example: O autocarro está a caminho do aeroporto.
native_language_example: The bus is on the way to the airport.

additional_notes: Used with estar to describe a current state. “Aberta” agrees with a feminine noun (e.g., a porta, a janela). For masculine nouns, use “está aberto” (e.g., o restaurante está aberto). Often used in questions like “(A porta) está aberta?”
target_language_example: A loja está aberta agora.
native_language_example: The store is open now.

additional_notes: Used with **estar** to describe a temporary/current state: something is open right now (a door, trunk, museum, zipper, etc.). **Aberto** agrees with the noun: **está aberto** (masc. singular), **está aberta** (fem. singular), **estão abertos/abertas** (plural). Common in questions about hours/availability: **O museu está aberto hoje?**
target_language_example: O museu está aberto hoje?
native_language_example: Is the museum open today?

additional_notes: Present tense of the verb phrase "estar" + gerund ("acontecendo" from "acontecer"). Used to describe something that is happening right now or currently unfolding: "Algo estranho está acontecendo" = "Something strange is happening." Very common in questions like "O que está acontecendo?" ("What’s happening?/What’s going on?").
target_language_example: O que está acontecendo aqui?
native_language_example: What’s going on here?

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar (temporary state) to say someone is awake. Agree with the person: acordado (male) / acordada (female). Common in questions: “Você está acordado?” = “Are you awake?”
target_language_example: Ele ainda está acordado?
native_language_example: Is he still awake?

meaning: is used to; is accustomed to; is used to doing (something).
additional_notes: Used with a following verb in the infinitive (introduced by “a”): “estar acostumado a + infinitive” = ‘to be used to doing something’ (habit/familiarity). The subject can change: “Estou/Ele/Ela/Estamos… acostumado(a)(s) a…”. In writing and many regions you may also see “estar habituado a” with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Tom está acostumado a falar em público.
native_language_example: Tom is used to speaking in public.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has romantic feelings for a person. It’s built from estar (temporary state) + apaixonado (in love) + por (for/with). You can change it for gender and number: está apaixonada por (female), estão apaixonados/apaixonadas por (plural). Common with names or pronouns: por você, por ele, por ela.
target_language_example: Ele está apaixonado por você há meses.
native_language_example: He’s been in love with you for months.

meaning: "is learning to" (is in the process of learning how to do something).
additional_notes: Used with the present progressive in Portuguese (estar + gerund) to show an ongoing learning process. It’s followed by a verb in the infinitive: está aprendendo a + verb (e.g., fazer, programar, tocar). You can change the subject and verb form: estou aprendendo a (I am learning to), está aprendendo a (he/she/you are learning to), estamos aprendendo a (we are learning to).
target_language_example: O Tom está aprendendo a programar.
native_language_example: Tom is learning to program.

meaning: is here / (he, she, you formal) is here
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is present in this place right now. It’s the 3rd-person singular of "estar" (temporary state/location): "ele/ela/você está aqui" = "he/she/you are here". Other common forms: "estou aqui" (I’m here), "estamos aqui" (we’re here), "estão aqui" (they’re here). Often used to reassure, to point out someone’s presence, or in questions: "Sua mãe está aqui?" = "Is your mom here?".
target_language_example: Ela está aqui, Norick.
native_language_example: She’s here, Norick.

additional_notes: Used with people and transport (bus/train/flight) to say someone/something is late. With clocks/watches it usually means the clock is slow (showing an earlier time than it should), i.e., it’s running behind. Also common: “estou atrasado” (I’m late), “estamos atrasados” (we’re late).
target_language_example: Desculpe, cheguei tarde porque o metrô está atrasado.
native_language_example: Sorry, I arrived late because the subway is delayed.

meaning: is increasing; is getting bigger (is going up).
additional_notes: Present continuous: "estar" + gerund (aumentando) describes something that is currently happening or developing. Used for quantities (prices, debt, numbers), distance/gaps, and also intensity/strength of things like waves or storms. Often translated as “is increasing/going up” or “is getting stronger.”
target_language_example: O preço do aluguel está aumentando este ano.
native_language_example: Rent prices are increasing this year.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is (or stays) “there” at a place (often near the listener). Common in questions like “Mas, quem está aí?” (= “Who’s there?”). With você/tu it can mean “are you there?” (also on the phone or online). Can also sound like “standing/remaining there” when followed by a posture/adjective: “está aí parado/parada” (= “(you’re) just standing there”).
target_language_example: Você está aí na porta ainda?
native_language_example: Are you still there at the door?

additional_notes: Present continuous: estar (está) + gerund (bebendo) to talk about an action happening at the moment. Often followed by what someone is drinking: “está bebendo chá/café/água”. Can also be used more generally as “is drinking (alcohol)”, depending on context (e.g., “Por que você está bebendo a esta hora?”).
target_language_example: Ela está bebendo água porque está com sede.
native_language_example: She is drinking water because she is thirsty.

additional_notes: Can be used to agree or accept something ('okay', 'all right', 'fine'), or to say that a person or thing is in a good condition ('is well', 'is fine'). In expressions like 'está bem assim', it means 'it's fine like that'.
target_language_example: Está bem, podemos sair agora.
native_language_example: Okay, we can leave now.

additional_notes: Literally “it is good.” Commonly used to say something is acceptable or satisfactory (“That’s fine for me.”). It can also describe conditions like weather/time (“The weather is good.”). In conversation, it can function like “okay, that’s fine,” and sometimes contrasts with a suggestion for improvement (e.g., “It’s good, but you can do better.”).
target_language_example: Se for às oito, está bom para mim.
native_language_example: If it’s at eight, that works for me / that’s fine for me.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "brincar" + "com" to talk about playing together or interacting playfully with someone or something (kids, pets, toys). The form "está brincando" is present continuous (something happening right now). You can change the subject: "Estou brincando com..." (I’m playing with...), "Ele/Ela está brincando com..." (He/She is playing with...).
target_language_example: Maria está brincando com as suas bonecas.
native_language_example: Maria is playing with her dolls.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" to describe a temporary state (being drunk right now). It agrees with the person's gender/number: "está bêbada" (woman), "estão bêbados/bêbadas" (plural). You can add words like "ainda" (still) or "de novo" (again).
target_language_example: Ele está bêbado, então vou chamar um táxi.
native_language_example: He’s drunk, so I’m going to call a taxi.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective (or adverb) to show a gradual change over time: cada vez mais + adjective/adverb. It often translates as “increasingly” or “more and more.” You can change the verb to match the subject/tense (e.g., está/estão/ficou/vai ficar cada vez mais…).
target_language_example: O trânsito está cada vez mais complicado aqui.
native_language_example: Traffic is getting more and more complicated here.

additional_notes: Means someone is tired right now (present state). Often used with “de” + verb/noun to mean “is tired of” doing something: “está cansado de ler” = “is tired of reading.” You can add “demais” for “too”: “está cansado demais para…” = “is too tired to…”. Feminine form: “está cansada.” Plural: “estão cansados/cansadas.”
target_language_example: Ele está cansado demais para sair hoje.
native_language_example: He is too tired to go out today.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone is correct or that something is right/correct. On its own, Está certo. can also mean 'okay' or 'all right' as a response or agreement. In negative sentences, it often means something is not right, fair, or acceptable.
target_language_example: Acho que você está certo.
native_language_example: I think you're right.

additional_notes: Used with **estar + gerund** to talk about something in progress or about to happen soon. With places/people/transport it usually means “is arriving/coming” (*O irmão está chegando*). With time, seasons, ages, or an ending it often means “is approaching” (*O inverno está chegando*; *está chegando aos trinta* = “is nearing thirty”; *está chegando ao fim* = “is coming to an end”).
target_language_example: O ônibus está chegando.
native_language_example: The bus is coming/arriving soon.

additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns (e.g., a cidade, a maleta, a piscina, a caixa) to say something is full of something. It agrees in gender/number: está cheio de (masc. sing.), estão cheias de (fem. plural), estão cheios de (masc. plural).
target_language_example: A sala está cheia de gente.
native_language_example: The room is full of people.

additional_notes: Used to say something contains a lot of something (objects, people, substances, or even abstract things like "lies"). It agrees with the thing that is full: está cheio de (masculine singular), está cheia de (feminine singular), estão cheios de / estão cheias de (plural). Often sounds natural in English as “is full of,” and sometimes as “is covered in” (e.g., a keyboard full of dirt).
target_language_example: Esse livro está cheio de mentiras.
native_language_example: This book is full of lies.

meaning: 'is crying' (is in the act of crying).
additional_notes: "Está" is the present tense of "estar" and is used with a gerund (-ando/-endo/-indo) to talk about something happening right now (estar + gerund = present continuous). You can use it in statements (Ele está chorando.) and questions (Por que ele está chorando?). Negation: "não está chorando" = "isn't crying."
target_language_example: Ela está chorando porque perdeu o brinquedo.
native_language_example: She is crying because she lost the toy.

additional_notes: Uses the verb estar + gerund (chovendo) to describe what’s happening right now. You can add time words like agora (now), ainda (still), novamente (again), and intensity words like forte (hard/heavily). Often used by itself as a weather statement: “Está chovendo.”
target_language_example: Está chovendo muito hoje, melhor levar um guarda-chuva.
native_language_example: It’s raining a lot today; better bring an umbrella.

additional_notes: Form of **estar com** + noun. Very common to express a **current/temporary condition** or what someone/something currently has: *está com pouca tinta* (has little ink), *está com escassez* (is facing a shortage), *está com mau humor* (is in a bad mood). It can also mean **being with someone** (accompanied): *está com você*. The verb **estar** signals something seen as current/temporary (not a permanent characteristic).
target_language_example: Minha impressora está com pouca tinta.
native_language_example: My printer has little ink.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" + "com" to describe a temporary condition or symptom (being sick). Often used in questions about someone’s health: "Você está com febre?".
target_language_example: A criança está com febre desde ontem.
native_language_example: The child has had a fever since yesterday.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" to talk about a temporary physical state. The pattern is "estar com" + a noun: "Ele/ela está com fome" (He/she is hungry), "Você está com sede" (You’re thirsty). You can also ask: "Você está com fome?"
target_language_example: Tom sabe que Maria está com fome.
native_language_example: Tom knows that Maria is hungry.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar (temporary state) + com medo (fear) + de + a noun or a verb in the infinitive. After de, you can say what someone fears: a thing/person (de cães, de médicos) or an action/situation (de cometer erros, de ficar doente). You can change the subject and tense: estou com medo de..., ele/ela está com medo de..., estavam com medo de...
target_language_example: Tom está com medo de cometer erros.
native_language_example: Tom is afraid of making mistakes.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar + com to describe a temporary emotional state. You can add who/what the anger is directed at with "com raiva de" + person/thing (e.g., "com raiva de mim", "com raiva da gente").
target_language_example: Ela está com raiva de mim por causa do atraso.
native_language_example: She’s angry at me because of the delay.

additional_notes: Portuguese commonly uses "estar com" + a noun to describe temporary physical states/needs (e.g., thirst, hunger): "estar com sede" = to be thirsty. It agrees with the subject: eu estou com sede, você está com sede, ele/ela está com sede, nós estamos com sede. In polite/formal speech, "O senhor/A senhora está com sede?"
target_language_example: Depois da caminhada, ele está com sede.
native_language_example: After the walk, he is thirsty.

additional_notes: Present continuous in Portuguese: estar (conjugated) + gerund (-ando/-endo/-indo). Used for an action happening right now. Changes with the subject (e.g., eu estou comendo, você/ele/ela está comendo, nós estamos comendo, eles/elas estão comendo).
target_language_example: Ela está comendo uma maçã agora.
native_language_example: She is eating an apple now.

meaning: “is starting to / is beginning to” (happening now).
additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive (often with changes like “a + ficar/ter/derreter/afetar”). It emphasizes that a change or process has just started and is in progress. Conjugates with the subject: “estou começando a…”, “ele/ela está começando a…”, “estamos começando a…”.
target_language_example: Está começando a chover.
native_language_example: It’s starting to rain.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective to emphasize the state or condition someone/something is in. It’s the verb estar (for a temporary state) + the adverb completamente. Often followed by an adjective like errado (wrong), certo (right), pronto (ready), etc.
target_language_example: Ele está completamente cansado hoje.
native_language_example: He is completely tired today.

additional_notes: Used to say someone strongly believes something is true. It’s built from estar (state) + convencido (convinced) + de que (that). Typically followed by a full clause: “Ele está convencido de que…”. Note gender agreement changes the form: convencido (male) / convencida (female). This entry uses the masculine form exactly as written.
target_language_example: O Tom está convencido de que a Mary está errada.
native_language_example: Tom is convinced that Mary is wrong.

additional_notes: Used with the verb phrase "estar + conversando" to describe an action happening now (present continuous idea). It’s often followed by a person or group introduced with "com" (with): "com Maria", "com os amigos". You can also say "estou/está/estamos/estão conversando com" depending on who is doing the talking.
target_language_example: Ele está conversando com o professor agora.
native_language_example: He’s talking with the teacher right now.

additional_notes: Used with **estar + gerúndio** to talk about an action happening right now: **estar correndo** = “to be running.” Often followed by **para** + infinitive to show purpose (e.g., *está correndo para pegar o trem* = “is running to catch the train”). It can also be used more figuratively to mean “running around / rushing around.”
target_language_example: Ela está correndo para não se atrasar.
native_language_example: She’s running so she won’t be late.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine noun (e.g., resposta, tradução, bandeira) to say it is correct/right. It’s the verb estar (temporary/state) + the adjective correta; for masculine nouns, use “está correto”. Common in checking answers, translations, or whether something is right.
target_language_example: A data está correta no formulário?
native_language_example: Is the date correct on the form?

additional_notes: Present continuous form of “crescer” (to grow): “estar” + gerund (“-ndo”) describes something happening now or developing over time. Used for physical growth (children, plants) and for trends/amounts (population, discrimination, power).
target_language_example: O interesse por esse assunto está crescendo rapidamente.
native_language_example: Interest in this topic is growing quickly.

meaning: “is giving / is doing” (present continuous of dar).
additional_notes: Used with a following noun/phrase to describe an ongoing action. It can mean: giving/providing (dar banho = give a bath), producing (dar flores = produce flowers/bloom), holding/throwing (dar uma festa = throw a party), or doing an idiomatic action (dar uma volta = take a walk/drive). The exact translation depends on what comes after “dando”.
target_language_example: O professor está dando aula agora.
native_language_example: The teacher is teaching (giving class) now.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something has returned (to a place, situation, or activity). You can add a destination with "a/à" (e.g., "de volta a/à" + place). Often used in announcements: "X está de volta!"
target_language_example: O ônibus já está de volta ao centro.
native_language_example: The bus is already back downtown.

additional_notes: Used to say that something can be accessed, used, bought, or chosen at the moment. Common with things like videos/content (“na sua região” = in your region), domain names, appointments, rooms, products, or seats. It’s the verb "estar" (temporary state) + "disponível"; often appears in questions like "Está disponível?"
target_language_example: Desculpe, este produto ainda está disponível?
native_language_example: Sorry, is this product still available?

additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive after "a": "estar disposto a + infinitive". It expresses willingness or readiness to do something, often implying agreement or openness to act. Conjugates by person/tense and can vary for gender/number: "estou disposto(a) a...", "estamos dispostos(as) a...", "não está disposto(a) a...".
target_language_example: Ele está disposto a ajudar você amanhã.
native_language_example: He is willing to help you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Present progressive of "dizer" (to say): "estar" + "dizendo". Used for something being said right now or for reported speech in structures like "Se você está dizendo que..." = "If you're saying that...". Changes with the subject: "estou dizendo" (I’m saying), "está dizendo" (you/he/she is saying), "estão dizendo" (they are saying).
target_language_example: O que você está dizendo? Eu não entendi.
native_language_example: What are you saying? I didn’t understand.

additional_notes: Used to report or question what someone claims or implies. Very common in conversation when you want to confirm, challenge, or clarify what the other person means. Often followed by a complete clause: “Está dizendo que + [statement]?”
target_language_example: Você está dizendo que não quer ir?
native_language_example: Are you saying you don’t want to go?

additional_notes: Used with a body part (often with a possessive) to say it’s currently causing pain. It’s the verb "doer" (“to hurt, ache”) in the present continuous: "(algo) está doendo". You can also ask "Ainda está doendo?" = "Does it still hurt?"
target_language_example: Minha cabeça está doendo desde ontem.
native_language_example: My head has been hurting since yesterday.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "estar" because it describes a condition/state (usually temporary). "Doente" is an adjective meaning sick/ill. Often used with time expressions like "desde" (since): "está doente desde quinta-feira" = has been sick since Thursday. For a more general/ongoing meaning, Portuguese may use "ser doente" (to be a sickly person).
target_language_example: A mãe dele está doente desde quinta-feira.
native_language_example: His mother has been sick since Thursday.

additional_notes: Present continuous: estar (conjugated) + gerund (-ndo) to describe an action happening now. Here, "está" can change with the subject (estou/está/estamos/estão). Often used with a location: "está dormindo no quarto" = "is sleeping in the bedroom."
target_language_example: Ele está dormindo agora; fala mais baixo.
native_language_example: He’s sleeping right now; speak more quietly.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" to say someone is physically at home (location/temporary situation). Often appears in questions and negatives: "Você está em casa?" / "Não estou em casa." You can swap the subject: "Ele/Ela está em casa".
target_language_example: Você está em casa agora?
native_language_example: Are you at home now?

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar to describe something currently burning or in flames (a building, forest, city, etc.). Often a serious/emergency description.
target_language_example: O prédio está em chamas; chame os bombeiros!
native_language_example: The building is on fire; call the firefighters!

meaning: is in danger; is at risk.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" to say someone/something is in danger (often immediate or serious). You can also use it in questions: "Você está em perigo?". Common with "vida": "A vida dele está em perigo" = "His life is in danger."
target_language_example: Se você ficar aqui, você está em perigo.
native_language_example: If you stay here, you're in danger.

meaning: “is wrong” / “is incorrect” (for a person, idea, or situation).
additional_notes: Used with the verb “estar” to say something/someone is wrong in the current situation. With “com” it often means “something is wrong with …”: “Algo está errado com meu computador.” For general/moral “wrong,” Portuguese often uses “errado” too, depending on context.
target_language_example: Desculpe, acho que você está errado sobre o horário.
native_language_example: Sorry, I think you’re wrong about the time.

additional_notes: Used to suggest or ask if someone is keeping a secret or not telling the full truth. Often appears in questions ("Está escondendo algo?") or tag questions ("..., não está?"). You can add "de mim/nós" to say who it’s being hidden from: "está escondendo algo de nós".
target_language_example: Você está escondendo algo de mim?
native_language_example: Are you hiding something from me?

additional_notes: Present continuous: "estar" (conjugated) + gerund ("escrevendo") to describe an action in progress at the moment. Changes with the subject: "estou escrevendo" (I’m writing), "está escrevendo" (you/he/she/it is writing), "estamos escrevendo" (we’re writing), etc. You can add where/what language/what you’re writing: "está escrevendo no escritório", "está escrevendo em irlandês", "está escrevendo as respostas".
target_language_example: Ela está escrevendo um e-mail agora.
native_language_example: She is writing an email now.

additional_notes: This is estar + gerund, used for an action happening right now. It usually means someone is waiting, often with an object or implied for someone/something. With um filho, it means is expecting a baby.
target_language_example: Ele está esperando o ônibus.
native_language_example: He is waiting for the bus.

additional_notes: Present continuous with "estar" + gerund (-ando/-endo/-indo). Used for an action happening now or around the current period. It changes with the subject (eu estou estudando, você/ele/ela está estudando, nós estamos estudando, eles/elas estão estudando). Often followed by what is being studied ("está estudando inglês") or where ("está estudando na biblioteca").
target_language_example: Ela está estudando para a prova agora.
native_language_example: She is studying for the test now.

additional_notes: Present continuous (estar + gerund) used to talk about an action happening now or around the current period. Subject can change: ele/ela/você está estudando francês; eu estou estudando francês; nós estamos estudando francês.
target_language_example: Ela está estudando francês para a viagem.
native_language_example: She is studying French for the trip.

additional_notes: Present continuous form of falar: estar + falando. It describes something happening right now. Because está is also used with você, it can also mean 'you are talking/speaking' depending on context.
target_language_example: Ela está falando com o professor agora.
native_language_example: She is talking to the teacher now.

additional_notes: Used with a person (or group) after com: está falando com Maria / com estranhos / com alguém. It can mean talking in general or having a conversation. Common negative form: não está falando com... (“isn’t talking to/with...”, sometimes implying they’re not on speaking terms).
target_language_example: Ela está falando com o médico agora.
native_language_example: She’s talking with the doctor now.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "faltar" to say something/someone isn’t there, hasn’t shown up, or isn’t included. Common patterns: "Está faltando + noun" (Something is missing), "Alguém está faltando?" (Is someone absent/missing?), and "Está faltando + item" when you need one more (e.g., a fork, a period at the end of a sentence).
target_language_example: Está faltando uma cadeira aqui.
native_language_example: A chair is missing here.

meaning: 'are (you/he/she) doing here' (often in “O que está fazendo aqui?” = 'What are you doing here?').
additional_notes: Uses **estar + fazendo** (present continuous) to talk about what someone is doing right now. In questions like **“O que está fazendo aqui?”**, the subject is often implied (usually **você**), and the tone can sound surprised, suspicious, or confrontational depending on context. You can also add a place word: **aqui fora** = 'out here'.
target_language_example: O que você está fazendo aqui tão cedo?
native_language_example: What are you doing here so early?

additional_notes: Present continuous in Portuguese: **estar** (conjugated) + **fazendo** (gerund of *fazer*) + **isso** (“this/that”). Used to say someone is doing something right now or around the current time. Often appears with a subject (e.g., *Tom está fazendo isso*) or implied subject (e.g., *Por que está fazendo isso?*).
target_language_example: Por que você está fazendo isso?
native_language_example: Why are you doing this/that?

additional_notes: Uses the verb phrase **estar + gerund** (*está fazendo*) to talk about an action in progress (happening now). **Isto** means “this” (often something close to the speaker or the situation at hand). Commonly appears in questions like **Por que está fazendo isto?** (“Why are you doing this?”).
target_language_example: Por que você está fazendo isto comigo?
native_language_example: Why are you doing this to me?

additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns (e.g., agência, janela, ponte, pista). It’s the verb estar + adjective fechada, often implying a current/temporary state (closed right now). Depending on context it can mean a place isn’t open (a business is closed), something is shut (a window/door), or access is blocked (a road/bridge/lane is closed). In some contexts it can imply “locked” (e.g., fechada por dentro = locked from the inside).
target_language_example: A loja está fechada agora.
native_language_example: The store is closed right now.

additional_notes: Used to say a place/service is currently closed (temporary state): *O banco está fechado.* It can also mean something is shut/locked (*O depósito já está fechado.*). In conversation, *Ok, está fechado* can mean “OK, it’s settled / deal.”
target_language_example: Desculpe, o banco está fechado agora.
native_language_example: Sorry, the bank is closed right now.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a change in progress (something is gradually changing). It’s the present continuous of "ficar" (to become/get), often followed by an adjective: "está ficando triste" (is getting sad), "está ficando excitante" (is getting exciting).
target_language_example: O tempo está ficando frio.
native_language_example: The weather is getting cold.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a temporary condition (the weather, a place, or something that feels cold). Often appears as an exclamation: “Como está frio!” = “It’s so cold!” You can add details like “do lado de fora” (outside) or intensify with “demais” (too): “Não está frio demais?” = “Isn’t it too cold?”
target_language_example: Aqui dentro está frio, mas lá fora está pior.
native_language_example: It’s cold in here, but outside it’s worse.

meaning: “is working / is functioning” (it works; it’s operating).
additional_notes: Used with the verb estar + gerund (funcionando) to talk about something that is working/operating right now or currently. Common for machines, devices, services, connections, systems, and also plans/treatments (“working” = having the desired effect). In questions, it often means “Is it working?”
target_language_example: O Wi‑Fi está funcionando agora?
native_language_example: Is the Wi‑Fi working now?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" to describe a temporary state/condition. You can add time with "de": "Ela está grávida de oito meses" (eight months pregnant). Common in questions: "Está grávida?" / "Está grávida de quanto tempo?".
target_language_example: Ela está grávida de três meses.
native_language_example: She is three months pregnant.

additional_notes: A common present progressive form in Brazilian Portuguese: estar + gerund. It describes someone or something in the process of going somewhere now or around now. It can also be used figuratively, as in está indo longe demais ('is going too far').
target_language_example: Ela está indo para casa agora.
native_language_example: She's going home now.

meaning: is going well / is doing well.
additional_notes: Used to say that a situation, activity, trip, project, transition, etc. is progressing in a good way. It can be a full statement ("Está indo bem.") or a question ("Está indo bem?"). You’ll also hear the plural: "estão indo bem" (they are going well).
target_language_example: O trabalho está indo bem, mas ainda falta muito.
native_language_example: Work is going well, but there's still a lot to do.

additional_notes: Present continuous of “ir embora” (“to leave/go away”). Used when someone is in the process of leaving or about to leave. Can be a statement (“Ele está indo embora.”), an exclamation (“Está indo embora!”), or a question (“Está indo embora?”). Often followed by a time phrase: “por pouco tempo” = “for a short time.”
target_language_example: Ele está indo embora agora.
native_language_example: He’s leaving now.

meaning: “is going to / is heading to” (a destination).
additional_notes: Used with a destination after para. It describes someone/something currently on the way or with a planned movement toward a place. Very common in the present continuous: estar + indo + para + place. The subject can be a person, vehicle, etc.
target_language_example: O ônibus está indo para o centro agora.
native_language_example: The bus is going downtown now.

meaning: is interested in; is interested in doing.
additional_notes: Used with the verb estar + interessado (must agree with the subject: interessado/interessada/interessados/interessadas) + em + noun or infinitive verb. Common for stating or asking interest in a topic (em química, em matemática) or in doing something (em aprender, em estudar, em fazer).
target_language_example: Alguém aqui está interessado em estudar francês?
native_language_example: Is anyone here interested in studying French?

additional_notes: Uses the pattern **estar + gerund** to talk about something happening right now. **Jogar** often means “to play” (soccer, video games, cards, etc.). Depending on context, **jogar** can also mean “to throw,” but with no object it commonly means “to play.”
target_language_example: Ela está jogando futebol agora.
native_language_example: She is playing soccer now.

additional_notes: Uses the present progressive in Portuguese: **estar (present tense) + gerund**. With **você/ele/ela/o senhor/a senhora**, you often say **está lendo**; with other subjects it changes (e.g., **estou lendo** = I’m reading, **estão lendo** = they/you all are reading). Often implies an action happening now or around the current time. It can also be used figuratively in **Você está lendo meus pensamentos** (“You’re reading my mind”).
target_language_example: O que você está lendo agora?
native_language_example: What are you reading right now?

meaning: 'is free' / 'is available'; also 'is free from' (not affected by something).
additional_notes: Used with a noun/pronoun as the subject + "estar" (temporary state). Meanings depend on context: (1) availability/open/unoccupied: "Aquilo/isto está livre" = "That/this is free/available." Common with "de" to mean "free from" (no longer affected): "estar livre de poluição" / "estar livre de dívidas". With people it can mean "free" in the sense of released/not imprisoned: "Ela está livre!"
target_language_example: A cadeira está livre, pode sentar aqui.
native_language_example: The chair is free/available; you can sit here.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is outside the building/room or outdoors nearby. It can also mean “out there” (not here, at another location), but in these examples it’s mainly literal: outside. Often answers “Where is (someone)?” or is used to ask who is outside (Quem está lá fora?).
target_language_example: O João está lá fora esperando você.
native_language_example: João is outside waiting for you.

additional_notes: A common Brazilian Portuguese pattern: está + me + gerund. It means that someone is doing something to or toward me right now, as in está me escutando = 'is listening to me'. The pronoun me means 'me', and the verb that follows completes the meaning.
target_language_example: Ela está me chamando agora.
native_language_example: She is calling me now.

additional_notes: From "estar" (to be, temporary/current) + "olhar" (to look). Used for an action in progress: someone is watching/looking at you at the moment. Very common in questions like "Por que está me olhando?" (Why are you looking at me?). In Brazil you may also hear the more formal/standard order "está olhando para mim".
target_language_example: Por que você está me olhando assim?
native_language_example: Why are you looking at me like that?

meaning: “Are you listening to me?” / “Can you hear me?”
additional_notes: Used to check if someone is paying attention or can hear you (often with an impatient or insistent tone). It commonly implies “you” even when “você” isn’t said (e.g., “(Você) está me ouvindo?”). In casual Brazilian Portuguese you may also hear “tá me ouvindo?” (short for “está…”).
target_language_example: Ei, está me ouvindo? Eu falei com você.
native_language_example: Hey, are you listening to me? I spoke to you.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something is following you (physically, right now). It’s the present continuous: estar + gerund (seguindo). Often used in questions like “Por que (você) está me seguindo?” = “Why are you following me?” The object pronoun “me” (“me”) can also come after the verb in Brazil: “está seguindo-me” (less common in everyday speech).
target_language_example: Por que você está me seguindo?
native_language_example: Why are you following me?

additional_notes: Progressive form: estar (present) + gerund (mentindo) = “is lying” (lying right now / in this situation). Changes with the subject: eu estou mentindo (I’m lying), você está mentindo (you’re lying), ele/ela está mentindo (he/she is lying), nós estamos mentindo (we’re lying), vocês estão mentindo (you all are lying), eles/elas estão mentindo (they’re lying). Often used in questions or accusations.
target_language_example: Acho que ele está mentindo para nós.
native_language_example: I think he’s lying to us.

meaning: “is living in” (currently living in a place).
additional_notes: Used with estar + morando (gerund of morar) to talk about a temporary or current living situation (where someone is living these days). Often appears with time words like agora (“now”) and ainda (“still”). For a more permanent sense, Portuguese often uses morar in the present (e.g., “Ele mora em Boston” = “He lives in Boston”).
target_language_example: Ela está morando em São Paulo este ano.
native_language_example: She’s living in São Paulo this year.

meaning: “is dying” / “is on the verge of dying.”
additional_notes: Present continuous of *morrer* (“to die”) with *estar* + gerund. Used for someone literally dying (*Arwen está morrendo*) or for things in decline or disappearing (*O jazz está morrendo*). You can also say *está a morrer* (common in Portugal).
target_language_example: Sem água, a planta está morrendo.
native_language_example: Without water, the plant is dying.

additional_notes: Uses estar + adjective to describe a current state. Morta is the feminine form (morto = masculine). Often literal (“she’s dead”), but in casual speech it can also be used figuratively to mean “she’s exhausted/knocked out” depending on context.
target_language_example: Depois da corrida, ela está morta de cansaço.
native_language_example: After the run, she’s dead tired.

additional_notes: Used to say someone (or an animal) is dead. It uses the verb "estar" (temporary state/condition) + "morto" (dead). Often used with "já" to mean "already" ("Já está morto." = "He/It’s already dead."). You can negate it with "não" ("Ele não está morto." = "He isn’t dead.").
target_language_example: Sinto muito, mas o seu gato está morto.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but your cat is dead.

meaning: “That’s very good / fine.” or “(he/she/it) is doing very well.”
additional_notes: Used to express approval or agreement (“That’s fine/very good”) or to comment on someone’s condition/state, often health (“He’s doing very well”). It agrees in person: e.g., “Está muito bem” (it’s fine / you’re fine), “Ele/Ela está muito bem” (he/she is doing very well).
target_language_example: Não se preocupe, a sua mãe está muito bem.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, your mother is doing very well.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" (temporary state) + "muito" (very) + "doente" (sick/ill) to describe someone’s current condition. You can change the subject and the verb form (e.g., "estou muito doente" = I’m very sick; "eles estão muito doentes" = they’re very sick).
target_language_example: Eu acho que o Tom está muito doente.
native_language_example: I think Tom is very sick.

additional_notes: Uses estar to describe a temporary condition, especially the weather. Common patterns: “Está muito quente aqui/hoje” (It’s very hot here/today) and “Está muito quente para + infinitive” (It’s too hot to…).
target_language_example: Aqui está muito quente hoje.
native_language_example: It’s very hot here today.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is located in the kitchen right now. It’s the verb estar (temporary state/location) + na (= em + a, “in the”) + cozinha (“kitchen”). You can change the subject: Ele/Ela está na cozinha; O bolo está na cozinha.
target_language_example: O João está na cozinha fazendo café.
native_language_example: João is in the kitchen making coffee.

additional_notes: Used to say that the appropriate/expected moment has arrived to do an action. Very common in everyday speech. Conjugates for person/tense (e.g., "estou na hora de...", "era/chegou a hora de..."). Often followed by an infinitive verb (comer, ir, sair).
target_language_example: Está na hora de sair.
native_language_example: It's time to leave.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something appears on an actual list (guest list, attendance list, waitlist, checklist, etc.). Often used in questions to check whether someone is included/registered (e.g., at an event entrance). You can swap the subject: “Meu nome está na lista.” / “Ela está na lista.”
target_language_example: Desculpe, seu nome não está na lista.
native_language_example: Sorry, your name isn’t on the list.

additional_notes: Used for location or position. está comes from estar, and no is the contraction of em + o (“in/on/at” + “the”) before a masculine singular noun. With você, está translates as “are,” as in Você está no banco? = “Are you at the bank?”
target_language_example: O livro está no carro.
native_language_example: The book is in the car.

meaning: “is in the hospital” (is hospitalized / currently at the hospital).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is currently at the hospital, often because they’re receiving medical care. With durations, use “há”: “está no hospital há três semanas” = “has been in the hospital for three weeks.” (In European Portuguese you may also hear “está no hospital” for “is at the hospital,” even without implying hospitalization; context helps.)
target_language_example: Meu pai está no hospital desde ontem.
native_language_example: My dad has been in the hospital since yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is busy (not available) at the moment. Uses "estar" (temporary state) + the adjective "ocupado". It changes for gender/number: "está ocupada" (she), "estão ocupados/ocupadas" (they). Very often used in questions like "Você está ocupado?" (= Are you busy?).
target_language_example: Você está ocupado agora?
native_language_example: Are you busy now?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "olhar" with the preposition "para" to say someone is directing their eyes/attention toward something: "estar + olhando" expresses an action happening right now. With people it can sound like 'staring at' depending on tone/context. You can change the subject/person: "estou olhando para" (I’m looking at), "ele/ela está olhando para" (he/she is looking at), "você está olhando para" (you’re looking at).
target_language_example: O cachorro está olhando para o gato.
native_language_example: The dog is looking at the cat.

additional_notes: Uses the present continuous (estar + gerund) to describe an action happening at the moment: está olhando.
