additional_notes: Used to say you like something/someone. It’s “eu gosto de” + “do” (= de + o) before a masculine singular noun or name treated as masculine. For feminine singular, use “eu gosto da” (de + a). With plural, “dos/das”. In Portuguese, “gostar” uses “de” (gostar de algo).
target_language_example: Eu gosto do café.
native_language_example: I like coffee.

additional_notes: Used to express preference. Often appears in comparisons with **do que** (“than”): *Eu gosto mais de X do que de Y* (“I like X more than Y / I prefer X to Y”). You can also use it without a comparison to mean you generally prefer that thing.
target_language_example: Eu gosto mais de chá do que de café.
native_language_example: I like tea more than coffee.

additional_notes: Used to say you like something/someone a lot. It’s: eu (I) + gosto (I like) + muito (a lot) + da (= de + a), which is used before feminine singular nouns (a Austrália, a culinária, a língua, a minha avó). For masculine singular, you usually use “eu gosto muito do …” (do = de + o).
target_language_example: Eu gosto muito da sua cidade.
native_language_example: I really like your city.

additional_notes: Used to express a strong liking for a person, thing, or activity. After "de" you can use: (1) a noun: "Eu gosto muito de morangos" (I really like strawberries); (2) an infinitive verb: "Eu gosto muito de ajudar" (I really like helping). With people you also use "de": "Eu gosto muito de você" (I like you a lot / I’m very fond of you).
target_language_example: Eu gosto muito de aprender português.
native_language_example: I really like learning Portuguese.

meaning: “I was going to…” / “I would…” (past intention or planned future-from-the-past).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of ir ("to go") to talk about an intention/plan in the past: “I was going to call…”. It’s often followed by an infinitive (eu ia fazer, eu ia chamar). It can also mean something that was about to happen (“I was going to be late”) or what someone expected you would do (“Você achou que eu ia…?”).
target_language_example: Eu ia te ligar, mas meu celular ficou sem bateria.
native_language_example: I was going to call you, but my phone ran out of battery.

additional_notes: Used to strongly insist that what you’re saying is true, or to promise something. Often said at the end for emphasis (“..., eu juro.”). You can also add what you’re swearing by: “Eu juro pelos meus pais...” (“I swear on my parents...”). Common in emotional speech; can also be used as reassurance when someone doubts you.
target_language_example: Eu juro que não fui eu.
native_language_example: I swear it wasn’t me.

meaning: "I swear (that)…" (to strongly insist something is true, or to make a solemn promise).
additional_notes: Used before a clause introduced by "que". It can emphasize truthfulness ("I swear I heard a noise") or a serious commitment ("I swear I'll never..."). In everyday speech it can simply add emphasis, similar to "I swear" in English.
target_language_example: Eu juro que não fui eu.
native_language_example: I swear it wasn't me.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression: it is just eu + já, usually before the verb. Most often it means 'already'; in English this is often translated with the present perfect: eu já li = 'I've already read'. In superlative phrases it can mean 'ever' (a mais cara que eu já comprei), and with near-future verbs it can mean 'now/right away' (eu já vou).
target_language_example: Eu já vi esse filme.
native_language_example: I've already seen that movie.

additional_notes: Used to remind someone that you’ve said something before. Often expresses emphasis or impatience/annoyance, especially when used alone at the end of a sentence (e.g., “... eu já disse.”). It can also introduce something you mentioned earlier (“Eu já disse como/que...” = “I already said how/that...”).
target_language_example: Para de perguntar; eu já disse que não.
native_language_example: Stop asking; I already said no.

additional_notes: Used to say you read in general or habitually, or that you are reading something (depending on context). Often followed by what you read: *eu leio um livro / eu leio o poema*. In comparisons like *quanto mais eu leio...*, it means “the more I read...”.
target_language_example: Eu leio notícias todos os dias.
native_language_example: I read the news every day.

additional_notes: Used when the speaker (eu = “I”) is doing something *to/for* someone, with **lhe** as an indirect object pronoun. **lhe** most commonly means “to you” (formal, like *você/o senhor/a senhora*) or “to him/her,” depending on context. It often comes right before the verb: *eu lhe deixei* (“I left you/him/her”), *eu lhe mandei* (“I sent you/him/her”).
target_language_example: Eu lhe contei a verdade ontem.
native_language_example: I told you/him/her the truth yesterday.

additional_notes: "Lhe" is an object pronoun meaning "to you" (formal) or "to him/her". This uses the verb "dar" (to give) in the simple past (pretérito perfeito): "dei" = "I gave". In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people often say "eu te dei" (to you, informal) or "eu dei para você" instead of "eu lhe dei".
target_language_example: Eu lhe dei minha palavra.
native_language_example: I gave you my word.

additional_notes: "eu me" is "eu" + the reflexive pronoun "me." It is used when the action refers back to the speaker, especially with reflexive or pronominal verbs: "eu me levanto" = "I get up," "eu me machuquei" = "I hurt myself." In English, "me" is often not translated separately, so the whole expression may sound like just "I" depending on the verb.
target_language_example: Eu me sinto cansado hoje.
native_language_example: I feel tired today.

additional_notes: Past tense of the reflexive verb "casar-se" (to get married). Often followed by "com" + the person you married: "Eu me casei com um canadense." You can also say it without naming the person: "Eu me casei ontem."
target_language_example: Eu me casei com a minha namorada no ano passado.
native_language_example: I got married to my girlfriend last year.

additional_notes: Very common and neutral in Brazilian Portuguese. It literally means “I call myself” (chamar = to call), and it’s followed by your name: “Eu me chamo Ana.” Often shortened in speech to “Me chamo Ana.” Alternatives you may also hear: “Meu nome é…” (more direct: “My name is…”).
target_language_example: Oi, eu me chamo Laura. Prazer!
native_language_example: Hi, my name is Laura. Nice to meet you!

additional_notes: Used to say you met someone, either on purpose (meeting up) or by chance (running into). Very common in Brazilian Portuguese with people: “Eu me encontrei com a Ana.” You can also hear the non-reflexive version with the same meaning: “Eu encontrei a Ana.”
target_language_example: Eu me encontrei com o João depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: I met up with João after work.

additional_notes: Uses the reflexive pronoun “me” with the verb “esconder-se” (to hide oneself). It’s the pretérito perfeito (completed past action): “eu me escondi” = I hid (at a specific time). Common with place phrases like “atrás de…” (behind) or “em/no/na…” (in/on + the).
target_language_example: Quando ouvi um barulho, eu me escondi atrás da porta.
native_language_example: When I heard a noise, I hid behind the door.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **(se) lembrar (de)** = “to remember.” It often comes with **de**: *Eu me lembro de você* (“I remember you”). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, many people also say **Eu lembro** (without *me*), with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Eu me lembro de quando a gente se conheceu.
native_language_example: I remember when we met.

additional_notes: Used to say you remember a person/thing (“Eu me lembro de vocês dois.”) or to remember doing something in the past (“Eu me lembro de ter ouvido…”, “Eu me lembro de tê-lo encontrado…”). The pattern is usually: eu me lembro de + noun/pronoun, or eu me lembro de + verb in the infinitive (often ter + past participle to mean “having done”). In everyday speech, many people also say “eu lembro de” (without “me”).
target_language_example: Eu me lembro de ter visto esse filme quando era criança.
native_language_example: I remember seeing that movie when I was a kid.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of **levantar-se** (“to get up / to stand up”). It can mean standing up from a seat (**da cadeira**) or getting out of bed / starting your day, often with a time (**muito cedo**, **trinta minutos atrás**, **às seis**). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people also say **eu levantei** (without **me**) with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Eu me levantei do sofá quando a campainha tocou.
native_language_example: I got up from the sofa when the doorbell rang.

additional_notes: From the verb "perder-se" (to get lost). Used when you lose your way physically (in a city, a forest, etc.). It can also be used figuratively to mean you felt confused/overwhelmed or "lost" in someone’s world/universe. Common variants: "Me perdi" (I got lost) and "Eu me perdi" (more emphasis).
target_language_example: Desculpe o atraso, eu me perdi no caminho.
native_language_example: Sorry I'm late, I got lost on the way.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a question you’re thinking about (often with curiosity or uncertainty). It’s followed by a clause, like a question embedded in a sentence: “Eu me pergunto como ele fez isso” (“I wonder how he did that”). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people also often say “Eu me pergunto como…” or simply “Me pergunto como…”.
target_language_example: Eu me pergunto como isso vai terminar.
native_language_example: I wonder how this will end.

additional_notes: Used to express curiosity or uncertainty about something (often followed by a full clause: eu me pergunto o que + subject + verb). Very common in conversation and writing. You may also hear the shorter form “me pergunto o que …” when the subject “eu” is implied.
target_language_example: Eu me pergunto o que vai acontecer amanhã.
native_language_example: I wonder what will happen tomorrow.

eu me pergunto por que o

target_language_multi_word_term: eu me pergunto por que o
additional_notes: Used to express curiosity or puzzlement about a reason. It’s typically followed by a masculine noun (o) or a male name/title (o Tom, o professor). For feminine nouns, you’ll usually see: "eu me pergunto por que a...". "por que" here means "why" in an indirect question.
target_language_example: Eu me pergunto por que o ônibus está atrasado.
native_language_example: I wonder why the bus is late.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a question you’re thinking about (you don’t know the answer). It often continues with a person or thing: “Eu me pergunto se o Tom...” = “I wonder if Tom...”. Note: Portuguese also uses “se” for “if/whether” (not just “if” in conditions). “o” is the masculine singular article (“the”); in other sentences you may see “a” (fem.), “os” (masc. plural), or “as” (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Eu me pergunto se o professor vai chegar cedo.
native_language_example: I wonder if the teacher is going to arrive early.

additional_notes: Used to describe your emotional or physical state in the past. It’s the past tense of "eu me sinto" (“I feel”), with the reflexive pronoun "me". You typically follow it with an adjective: "Eu me senti cansado(a), culpado(a), envergonhado(a), impotente." Adjectives often change for gender (cansado/cansada, culpado/culpada, envergonhado/envergonhada).
target_language_example: Eu me senti melhor depois de descansar.
native_language_example: I felt better after resting.

additional_notes: Common way to talk about how you feel (emotionally or physically). It uses the reflexive verb "sentir-se" ("to feel"), so Portuguese says "I feel myself" even though English usually just says "I feel". The adjective that follows often agrees with the speaker (e.g., "cansado" for a man, "cansada" for a woman). You can also drop "eu" and just say "me sinto" in many contexts.
target_language_example: Eu me sinto melhor hoje.
native_language_example: I feel better today.

additional_notes: Often refers to feeling physically sick (“I don’t feel well”) or emotionally bad/guilty (“I feel bad about…”). Common patterns: “Eu me sinto mal.” (I feel bad/unwell.) / “Eu me sinto mal em + infinitive” (I feel bad about doing something: “...em mentir” = about lying) / “Eu me sinto mal por/pelo/pela + person/thing” (I feel sorry for someone: “...pelo Tom”).
target_language_example: Hoje eu me sinto mal, então vou ficar em casa.
native_language_example: Today I feel unwell, so I’m going to stay home.

additional_notes: Used to say that you think you should receive something (a rest, a chance, respect, etc.) because it’s fair or you’ve worked for it. The verb is "merecer" (to deserve); "eu" is often optional in Portuguese ("Mereço um descanso").
target_language_example: Depois de tanta correria, eu mereço férias.
native_language_example: After so much rushing around, I deserve a vacation.

additional_notes: "Eu" means "I" and "moro" is the present tense of "morar" (to live/reside). Use it to say where you live (a town, neighborhood, house, country, etc.). Common patterns: "Eu moro em + city/country" (Eu moro em Lisboa.) and "Eu moro na/no + place" (Eu moro na rua X; Eu moro no centro.).
target_language_example: Eu moro em São Paulo, mas trabalho em outra cidade.
native_language_example: I live in São Paulo, but I work in another city.

additional_notes: Use this to say where you live (city, state, country, etc.). The verb is **morar** (“to live/reside”), and **em** means “in.” The place name usually comes right after: *Eu moro em Boston.*
target_language_example: Eu moro em São Paulo, mas trabalho no Rio.
native_language_example: I live in São Paulo, but I work in Rio.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of the verb "nascer" (to be born). Often followed by where or when you were born: "eu nasci em..." (in), "eu nasci no/na..." (in the + masc./fem. place), or "eu nasci em [year/decade]". In relative clauses you’ll often see "onde eu nasci" (where I was born) or "em que eu nasci" (in which I was born).
target_language_example: Eu nasci no Brasil, mas cresci nos Estados Unidos.
native_language_example: I was born in Brazil, but I grew up in the United States.

additional_notes: Used to say your birthplace. It’s the past tense of “nascer” (to be born): “eu nasci” = “I was born,” followed by “em” + a city/country (often without an article with city names). You can add more info with “mas cresci em …” (“but I grew up in …”).
target_language_example: Eu nasci em Lisboa, mas moro em Londres agora.
native_language_example: I was born in Lisbon, but I live in London now.

additional_notes: Used when the speaker says something has not happened at any time or that they have never done/felt something. It normally comes before the verb or verb phrase. The exact English tense depends on the verb that follows.
target_language_example: Eu nunca vou esquecer este dia.
native_language_example: I'll never forget this day.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize a decision or promise not to do something again. Often followed by a verb in the present or future (e.g., "eu nunca mais volto", "eu nunca mais voltarei"). In everyday speech, "eu" is often omitted: "Nunca mais volto."
target_language_example: Eu nunca mais falo com ele.
native_language_example: I'll never talk to him again.

additional_notes: Used to say that at no time in the past (up to now) you had something or experienced something. Very common with nouns (uma oportunidade, uma famdlia, esse problema) and also with structures like "eu nunca tive a inteno de..." (I never meant/intended to...) and "eu nunca tive que..." (I never had to...). In Portuguese it often corresponds to English present perfect: "I've never had...".
target_language_example: Eu nunca tive tempo para aprender portugu�eas antes.
native_language_example: I've never had time to learn Portuguese before.

additional_notes: Used to negate a statement about yourself. It is usually followed by a verb: eu não tenho = "I don't have", eu não estou = "I'm not". Depending on the verb tense, it can also mean things like "I didn't" or "I won't". In Portuguese, não comes before the verb. The subject pronoun eu is often optional, but it may be included for emphasis or clarity.
target_language_example: Eu não gosto de café.
native_language_example: I don't like coffee.

additional_notes: Used to express doubt or disagreement with an idea. It introduces what you believe is unlikely or not true. In Brazilian Portuguese, it’s very common to use the subjunctive after it (eu não acho que ele venha), though in everyday speech you may also hear the indicative (eu não acho que ele vem). Often the “eu” is dropped: “não acho que …”.
target_language_example: Eu não acho que ela tenha tempo hoje.
native_language_example: I don’t think she has time today.

meaning: "I don’t believe it" / "I can’t believe it."
additional_notes:
Used to express disbelief. It can stand alone as an exclamation (Eu não acredito!) or be followed by:
- em + noun/pronoun: Eu não acredito nisso. (I don’t believe in that / I don’t believe that.)
- que + clause: Eu não acredito que ela fez isso. (I can’t believe she did that.)
Adding "mais" often means "anymore": Eu não acredito mais. (I don’t believe it anymore / I’m not buying it anymore.)
target_language_example: Eu não acredito que isso está acontecendo!
native_language_example: I can’t believe this is happening!

additional_notes: Used to say you’re unable to do something (because of difficulty, inability, lack of means, etc.). Often followed by an infinitive: "eu não consigo + verb" (eu não consigo dormir, eu não consigo ler). It can also express “I can’t manage to” or “I can’t bring myself to,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu não consigo entender isso agora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t understand this right now.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t understand something (a situation, an explanation, what someone means). Often followed by a clause with “como” (how) or “o que” (what): “Eu não entendo como…” / “Eu não entendo o que…”. You can also say it alone (“Eu não entendo.”) to ask for clarification. In everyday speech, people also shorten it to “Não entendo.”
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu não entendo o que você quer dizer.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don't understand what you mean.

meaning: “I didn’t do anything / I did nothing.”
additional_notes: Used to say you didn’t do anything (often in self-defense: “It wasn’t me / I didn’t do it”). In Portuguese, “não… nada” is a common double negative and is normal/standard. You can add time details (e.g., “o dia todo” = all day) or explanations (“…que não quisesse fazer” = …that I didn’t want to do).
target_language_example: Calma, eu não fiz nada de errado.
native_language_example: Calm down, I didn’t do anything wrong.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t like something or someone. It’s the verb gostar (to like) in the present tense: eu gosto = I like, eu não gosto = I don’t like. It normally takes de before what you like/dislike: eu não gosto de café. With pronouns it stays the same: eu não gosto de você = I don’t like you. You can also use it before a verb in the infinitive: eu não gosto de estudar = I don’t like studying.
target_language_example: Eu não gosto de acordar cedo.
native_language_example: I don’t like waking up early.

meaning: "I don't / I won’t" (used before a verb with the pronoun "me").
additional_notes: This is a very common sequence: subject (eu) + negation (não) + object/reflexive pronoun (me) + verb. It often appears with reflexive verbs (verbs ending in -se), like "formar-se" → "eu não me formo" (“I don’t graduate”), or with verbs that take "me" as an object, like "importar" in "eu não me importo" (“I don’t mind”). Word order is fixed here: "não" comes before "me", and both come before the verb.
target_language_example: Eu não me lembro do nome dele.
native_language_example: I don’t remember his name.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past of poder (podia) to describe an ongoing inability, restriction, or impossibility in the past (often due to rules, circumstances, or physical inability). It can also express "there was no way I could" in context. For a single, completed event, you may also hear "eu não pude" (I couldn't/wasn't able to at that moment).
target_language_example: Eu não podia dormir por causa do barulho.
native_language_example: I couldn't sleep because of the noise.

additional_notes: Used to say you are unable to do something or it’s not possible for you (because of time, rules, money, etc.). It can also be a polite way to refuse a request: "Eu não posso" = "I can’t". Often followed by an infinitive: "eu não posso ir" (I can’t go), "eu não posso pagar" (I can’t pay).
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu não posso falar agora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t talk right now.

additional_notes: Past tense of "não posso" (“I can’t”). Uses the verb "poder" in the pretérito perfeito (pude) to say you were unable to do something at a specific time or in a specific situation. Often followed by an infinitive: "eu não pude dormir/falar/lembrar". With "mais" it can mean “I couldn’t anymore” (no longer able to).
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu não pude ir ontem.
native_language_example: Sorry, I couldn’t go yesterday.

meaning: “I didn’t want to.” / “I wasn’t trying to.”
additional_notes: Literally “I not wanted” (imperfect of querer). Used to express that you didn’t want to do something or didn’t intend for something to happen; often implies regret or a soft apology (e.g., “I didn’t mean to ruin it”). You can add an object: “Eu não queria isso” (I didn’t want that) or an infinitive: “Eu não queria voltar” (I didn’t want to go back). In speech you may hear: “Eu não queria, não.” for emphasis.
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu não queria te magoar.
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t mean to hurt you.

additional_notes: Used to refuse something or say you don’t want to do something. It’s often followed by an infinitive verb (eu não quero incomodar = “I don’t want to bother”) or a noun/pronoun (eu não quero nenhuma banana = “I don’t want any banana”; eu não quero ninguém = “I don’t want anyone”). You can also use it alone as a short, firm answer: porque eu não quero (“because I don’t want to”).
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu não quero sair hoje.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don't want to go out today.

additional_notes: First-person singular, imperfect past of "saber" (to know). Used to say you lacked knowledge at that time, often as an explanation or apology: "Eu não sabia que..." = "I didn't know that...".
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu não sabia que era proibido estacionar aqui.
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn't know it was forbidden to park here.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t have the information/answer. In conversation it’s often said alone (“Eu não sei.”) or added as a parenthetical comment (“Para onde exatamente, eu não sei.” = “Where exactly, I don’t know.”). You can also follow it with a clause introduced by “que” (“Eu não sei que…”) to mean “I don’t know what/that…”.
target_language_example: Eu não sei onde ele mora.
native_language_example: I don’t know where he lives.

additional_notes: Used to start a sentence when you’re unsure about something and the next part specifies what you don’t know (what someone said, wants, is thinking, what something is, etc.). Often followed by a verb clause: “eu não sei o que eles estão dizendo” (what they’re saying).
target_language_example: Eu não sei o que aconteceu ontem à noite.
native_language_example: I don’t know what happened last night.

additional_notes: Means “I am not” using the verb ser (sou = “I am”, 1st person singular, present). It’s used for identity, inherent characteristics, professions, and more permanent states (Eu não sou um herói. / Eu não sou ambicioso.). For temporary states/conditions, Portuguese often uses estar instead: Eu não estou bem (“I’m not well”).
target_language_example: Eu não sou a pessoa certa para isso.
native_language_example: I'm not the right person for that.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past of ter (tinha) to say you didn’t have something in the past, often describing a situation/state over a period of time. It can be followed by a noun (eu não tinha amigos) or by a phrase like certeza de/que (eu não tinha certeza se/que...).
target_language_example: Quando eu era criança, eu não tinha tempo para brincar.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I didn’t have time to play.

additional_notes: Used to say you refuse to do something or that you don’t intend to do it (often about the near future). It’s made of “eu” (I) + “não” (not) + “vou” (I go), where “vou” is the present tense of the verb “ir” (to go) and is commonly used like English “going to” for planned actions.
target_language_example: Eu não vou esperar mais.
native_language_example: I’m not going to wait anymore.

additional_notes: Used to refuse or say you won’t go somewhere or won’t do something. "Vou" is the present tense of "ir" (to go) and often expresses a near future (“I’m going to…”). It can be followed by a destination with prepositions like "para" (to), "até" (up to/as far as), or "a" (to), or it can stand alone: "Eu não vou."
target_language_example: Eu não vou com vocês hoje.
native_language_example: I’m not going with you (all) today.

additional_notes: Here, `o` is not the article `o` ("the"). It is a masculine singular direct-object pronoun meaning "him" or "it." In Portuguese, this pronoun often comes before the verb: `eu o vejo` = "I see him / it." In everyday spoken Brazilian Portuguese, many speakers often use `ele` after the verb instead (`eu vejo ele`).
target_language_example: Eu o encontrei ontem.
native_language_example: I met him yesterday.

meaning: “I met him.” / “I got to know him.”
additional_notes: Uses the verb **conhecer** (to meet / to know a person or place). **Conheci** is the simple past (pretérito perfeito): a completed event in the past. **O** is the object pronoun “him” placed before the verb in Portuguese (common in writing and more formal speech); in everyday Brazilian Portuguese you’ll often hear **“eu conheci ele”** instead. (Don’t confuse **conhecer** with **saber**, which is “to know (facts/how to)”.)
target_language_example: Eu o conheci no trabalho no ano passado.
native_language_example: I met him at work last year.

meaning: "I know him" / "I know it" (sometimes "I know you" in formal speech).
additional_notes: This uses the object pronoun "o" (= him/it; also "you" in very formal Brazilian Portuguese) before the verb: "conheço" = "(I) know". It typically means knowing a person (being acquainted), not knowing a fact (for facts, Portuguese often uses "saber"). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, many people would say "Eu conheço ele" instead of "Eu o conheço".
target_language_example: Pode deixar, eu o conheço bem.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I know him well.

additional_notes: "Eu" = I. "o" is an object pronoun meaning “him” (formal/written style in Brazilian Portuguese; in speech many people say "eu encontrei ele"). "Encontrei" is the past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "encontrar" (to find/meet). It can mean you discovered someone/something (“found him unconscious”) or you ran into/met someone (“met him in the street”).
target_language_example: Eu o encontrei na rua ontem à noite.
native_language_example: I ran into him on the street last night.

additional_notes: "O" is the direct-object pronoun (“him/it”) placed before the verb. "Vi" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "ver" (“to see”). Used for a completed action in the past; for a woman/thing referred to as feminine, use "eu a vi" (“I saw her/it”). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, many speakers more often say "eu vi ele" / "eu vi isso" instead of "eu o vi".
target_language_example: Eu o vi na rua mais cedo.
native_language_example: I saw him on the street earlier.

additional_notes: "Eu odeio" is "I hate" with the verb *odiar* in the present tense (1st person singular). It’s followed by a noun ("Eu odeio química.") or by a clause, often with **quando**: "Eu odeio quando..." = "I hate it when...".
target_language_example: Eu odeio quando chove no fim de semana.
native_language_example: I hate it when it rains on the weekend.

additional_notes: “Os” is a direct object pronoun meaning “them” (for a group of men, or a mixed-gender group). It goes with a verb: “Eu os vejo” = “I see them,” “Eu os conheci” = “I met them.” In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, many speakers often use “eles/elas” instead (“Eu vi eles”), but “eu os + verb” is the standard/grammar-book form.
target_language_example: Eu os vi ontem no centro.
native_language_example: I saw them yesterday downtown.

additional_notes: "Os" is the direct-object pronoun “them” (usually masculine or mixed group) and "vi" is the past tense of "ver" (to see): “I saw.” In Portuguese, object pronouns like "o/os/a/as" can come before the verb ("eu os vi") in more formal/written style. In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, many speakers prefer "Eu vi eles/elas" instead. You can also follow it with another verb to mean “I saw them [do something]”: "Eu os vi entrar" (I saw them enter).
target_language_example: Eu os vi chegando tarde na reunião.
native_language_example: I saw them arriving late to the meeting.

additional_notes: "Eu ouvi" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "ouvir" (to hear). It’s used when you heard something at a specific moment in the past: "Eu ouvi um barulho" (I heard a noise). With people, it can mean you listened to them: "Eu ouvi o Tom cuidadosamente" (I listened to Tom carefully). Common pattern: "ouvir alguém + gerund" = heard someone doing something ("Eu ouvi você chorando" = I heard you crying). Also: "ouvi falar (de...)" = I heard (about...)/I’ve heard (of...).
target_language_example: Eu ouvi você chamando meu nome ontem.
native_language_example: I heard you calling my name yesterday.

meaning: “I heard that…” / “I’ve heard that…” (reporting information you heard from someone else).
additional_notes: Used to introduce second-hand information or a rumor. It often implies you’re not fully sure it’s true (similar to “I hear that…”). The verb is the past of ouvir (“to hear”): eu ouvi = “I heard.” You can also use it without “eu”: “Ouvi dizer que…”
target_language_example: Eu ouvi dizer que vai chover amanhã.
native_language_example: I heard it’s going to rain tomorrow.

meaning: I stopped smoking / I quit smoking.
additional_notes: "Parar de" + infinitive means "to stop doing" something. "Eu parei de fumar" is in the past (pretérito perfeito) and refers to a completed action: you stopped smoking. In conversation, people may also say "Parei de fumar" (dropping "eu").
target_language_example: Eu parei de fumar no ano passado.
native_language_example: I quit smoking last year.

additional_notes:
Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of **passar** for “I”. Meaning depends on what comes next:
- **passar por (aqui/lá)** = to pass by, stop by briefly: *Eu passei por aqui.*
- **passar + time period** (a manhã, o dia, a semana) = to spend time: *Eu passei a semana inteira em Boston.*
- **passar em/na (prova)** = to pass an exam/test: *Eu passei na prova.*
- **passar por cima de** (figurative) = to disregard/step over others to get what you want.
target_language_example: Eu passei a tarde toda estudando para a prova.
native_language_example: I spent the whole afternoon studying for the test.

additional_notes: Past tense of "pedir" (to ask for / request / order): "eu pedi" = "I asked" or "I ordered" depending on context. Common patterns: (1) pedir + noun: "Eu pedi ajuda" (I asked for help), "Eu pedi o almoço" (I ordered lunch). (2) pedir para + person + infinitive: "Eu pedi para o Tom assinar..." (I asked Tom to sign...). (3) pedir para que + subjunctive (more formal): "Eu pedi para que ele nos enviasse..." (I asked him to send us...). You can also say "pedir permissão a/alguém" = "ask someone for permission."
target_language_example: Eu pedi uma água e pedi para a garçonete trazer a conta.
native_language_example: I ordered a water and asked the waitress to bring the bill.

meaning: 'I took' / 'I got' / 'I caught' (past tense of pegar).
additional_notes: "Eu peguei" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "pegar" and its meaning depends on what comes next. Common beginner uses: **pegar + transport** = “to take” (Eu peguei o elevador / um ônibus / um táxi); **pegar + something** = “to catch/get” (Eu peguei um peixe!); **pegar no sono** = “to fall asleep” (Eu peguei no sono enquanto lia).
target_language_example: Eu peguei um táxi para casa.
native_language_example: I took a taxi home.

meaning: "I thought that" / "I used to think that."
additional_notes: Used to introduce a belief or expectation you had (often in the past), sometimes implying it turned out to be wrong or different than expected. The verb is in the imperfect tense (pensava), which often suggests an ongoing or habitual thought in the past. Often followed by another verb in the past (e.g., conhecia) or conditional (e.g., seria).
target_language_example: Eu pensava que ele já tinha chegado.
native_language_example: I thought he had already arrived.

meaning: “I thought that the …” (about a man/masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to introduce something you believed in the past (often something that turns out not to be true). It’s the imperfect tense of pensar (“to think”), common for past beliefs/assumptions. Use “que a” with feminine nouns (Eu pensava que a Maria era canadense) and just “que” before names/pronouns (Eu pensava que ele era canadense).
target_language_example: Eu pensava que o seu irmão morava aqui.
native_language_example: I thought that your brother lived here.

meaning: "I thought you..." / "I used to think you..."
additional_notes: Used to introduce a belief or assumption you had (often that turned out to be wrong). "Pensava" is the imperfect tense of "pensar" (to think), so it often implies an ongoing or repeated thought in the past. It’s commonly followed by a verb in the past (e.g., "conhecia", "gostava", "tinha"). In everyday speech, "que" is sometimes omitted: "Eu pensava você..." (less formal).
target_language_example: Eu pensava que você já sabia disso.
native_language_example: I thought you already knew that.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you believed/assumed in the past (often something that turned out to be wrong or surprising). Very common before a full clause: “eu pensei que + [sentence]”. In Portuguese, this often triggers the subjunctive in the following clause when it expresses uncertainty/assumption (e.g., “eu pensei que ele fosse…”), but you’ll also see the indicative when it’s treated more like a fact or reported belief (e.g., “eu pensei que isso era…”).
target_language_example: Eu pensei que você já tinha saído.
native_language_example: I thought you had already left.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you believed in the past (often something that turned out to be different). Common before an adjective or noun phrase: “Eu pensei que era óbvio” (I thought it was obvious), “Eu pensei que era pouco demais” (I thought it was too little). Often implies a mistaken assumption depending on context.
target_language_example: Eu pensei que era hoje, mas é amanhã.
native_language_example: I thought it was today, but it’s tomorrow.

meaning: “I thought that the …” (I believed the … was/ would be …).
additional_notes: Used to introduce what you believed in the past. After "pensei que", Portuguese often uses the subjunctive in the following clause (e.g., "estivesse", "fosse", "falasse"), especially when expressing uncertainty, a mistaken assumption, or reported expectation. In everyday speech, many people also use the indicative (e.g., "estava"). "o" is the masculine singular article (“the”); it can change to "a/os/as" depending on the noun (e.g., "eu pensei que a Maria...").
target_language_example: Eu pensei que o ônibus chegaria mais cedo.
native_language_example: I thought the bus would arrive earlier.

meaning: “I thought you…” (introducing what you believed, often in the past).
additional_notes: Used when you assumed something about the other person. "Pensei" is the simple past of "pensar" (to think), and "que" introduces the clause that follows. In speech you can change "você" to another subject (e.g., "eu pensei que ele/ela…", "eu pensei que vocês…").
target_language_example: Eu pensei que você estava em casa.
native_language_example: I thought you were at home.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you became aware of or understood (often suddenly or after observing something). In everyday Portuguese, "perceber" can mean both "to realize" (understand a fact) and "to notice" (observe something). After "percebi que", you use a clause with a verb: "eu percebi que estava...", "eu percebi que era...".
target_language_example: Eu percebi que tinha esquecido a carteira em casa.
native_language_example: I realized I had forgotten my wallet at home.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **perguntar** (“to ask”). **Eu perguntei a + person** means “I asked + person” (the **a** introduces the person you asked). You can then add what you asked using **se** (“if/whether”), a question word (**o que**, **onde**, etc.), or the topic with **sobre** (“about”). Common pattern: **Eu perguntei ao/à + person …** (a + o = **ao**; a + a = **à**).
target_language_example: Eu perguntei ao professor se a prova era hoje.
native_language_example: I asked the teacher if the test was today.

additional_notes: "Eu poderia" is the conditional form of "poder" (to be able to / can). It’s used for polite requests (like "Could I…?" / "Could you…?") and for hypothetical situations (often in "if" sentences: "Se..., eu poderia..." = "If..., I could/would be able to..."). It’s typically followed by an infinitive: "eu poderia ver" (I could see).
target_language_example: Eu poderia te ajudar amanhã, se você quiser.
native_language_example: I could help you tomorrow, if you want.

meaning: “I could have” (a past possibility/ability that didn’t happen).
additional_notes: Used with a past participle (e.g., comprado, evitado, visitado) to talk about something you were able/likely to do in the past, but didn’t. Often appears with a condition (Se eu soubesse..., Se eu tivesse...) to mean “I could have (done it) if…”.
target_language_example: Eu poderia ter chegado mais cedo, mas perdi o ônibus.
native_language_example: I could have arrived earlier, but I missed the bus.

additional_notes: First-person singular of poder. It can express ability, permission, or possibility depending on context. In questions, it often means 'can I...?' or 'may I...?' You will also often hear just posso without eu.
target_language_example: Eu posso te ajudar agora.
native_language_example: I can help you now.

meaning: “Can I talk/speak with …?” / “I can talk/speak with …”
additional_notes: Used to ask permission or request to speak to someone (often on the phone or in a formal situation): “Eu posso falar com o gerente?” You can also use it as a statement about ability/possibility (“Eu posso falar com Tom por horas.” = “I can talk to Tom for hours”). In polite requests, add “por favor” or use a question tone.
target_language_example: Eu posso falar com você um minuto, por favor?
native_language_example: Can I talk with you for a minute, please?

meaning: "I can do that." / "Can I do that?"
additional_notes: Used to say you have the ability or permission to do something. In questions ("Eu posso fazer isso?"), it often means "May I do that?" depending on context and tone. In statements ("Eu posso fazer isso."), it means "I can do this/that." The pronoun "isso" = "that/this" (referring to an action or idea just mentioned).
target_language_example: Calma — eu posso fazer isso sozinho.
native_language_example: Relax — I can do this on my own.

additional_notes: Used to ask for permission or check if it’s possible for you to go somewhere. Often followed by a time (amanhã), a companion (com você), a place (ao cinema / na sua casa), or a means of transport (de trem). In conversation, “Eu posso ir?” commonly means “May I go?”
target_language_example: Eu posso ir agora ou você prefere mais tarde?
native_language_example: Can I go now, or would you prefer later?

meaning: “I can give you …” / “Can I give you …?”
additional_notes: Used to offer or ask permission to give something to someone. Literally: eu (I) + posso (can) + te (you, informal singular) + dar (to give). Very common in service/medical contexts (offering medicine, information, help). In more formal situations, you may hear “eu posso lhe dar …” (to you) instead of “te”.
target_language_example: Eu posso te dar um copo d’água?
native_language_example: Can I give you a glass of water?

additional_notes: First-person singular of precisar. Use eu preciso + infinitive for actions (eu preciso sair = I need to leave) and eu preciso de + noun/pronoun for things (eu preciso da sua ajuda = I need your help). In everyday Portuguese, eu is often dropped: preciso. Note that preciso can also mean "precise/exact" as an adjective in other contexts.
target_language_example: Eu preciso descansar um pouco.
native_language_example: I need to rest a little.

additional_notes: Used to say you have to purchase something. You can add the item right after comprar (e.g., “Eu preciso comprar ovos”) or use “alguma coisa” (something) if you’re not specific. Often followed by “para + infinitive” to say the purpose: “Eu preciso comprar … para comer” (to eat). In everyday speech, people also say “Preciso comprar…” without “Eu.”
target_language_example: Eu preciso comprar leite e pão hoje.
native_language_example: I need to buy milk and bread today.

additional_notes: Used to say you need something or someone. It’s typically followed by a noun/pronoun (eu preciso de um táxi; eu preciso de você/vocês). In Brazilian Portuguese, you often hear the short form “preciso de…” when the subject “eu” is implied.
target_language_example: Eu preciso de ajuda agora.
native_language_example: I need help now.

additional_notes: Used to say you need a greater amount of something. Usually followed by a noun: "Eu preciso de mais água." You can also use "mais" + a number/quantifier: "mais alguns minutos" (a few more minutes), "mais um" (one more).
target_language_example: Desculpe, eu preciso de mais tempo para terminar.
native_language_example: Sorry, I need more time to finish.

additional_notes: Used to say you need one item (singular). Use before a masculine noun: "Eu preciso de um envelope." For feminine nouns, use "eu preciso de uma" (e.g., "uma caneta"). To be less specific, you can add "...aqui/agora" (here/now) or say what it’s for.
target_language_example: Eu preciso de um táxi agora.
native_language_example: I need a taxi now.

meaning: "I need a..." / "I need one..." (before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to say you need something, when the thing is a feminine noun (uma). In Portuguese you normally say "precisar de" + noun/article: "Eu preciso de uma + [noun]". For masculine nouns, use "eu preciso de um".
target_language_example: Eu preciso de uma garrafa de água.
native_language_example: I need a bottle of water.

additional_notes: Used to say you need someone’s presence, help, or support. Often followed by more details: agora (“now”), aqui (“here”), or para isso (“for this”). In questions (“Eu preciso de você?”) it can mean “Do I need you?” or “Do I need your help?” depending on context. In Portuguese it literally uses “precisar de” (“to need”) + “você” (“you”).
target_language_example: Eu preciso de você para terminar esse trabalho.
native_language_example: I need you to finish this work.

meaning: I need to talk to you.
additional_notes: Use this to say you need to speak with someone, often because something is important or needs attention. You can add timing words like agora (now), depois (later), hoje (today), imediatamente (immediately), or add a topic with sobre (about): “Eu preciso falar com você sobre…” (I need to talk to you about…). In casual speech, “eu” is often dropped (“Preciso falar com você”), but the full form is clear and neutral.
target_language_example: Eu preciso falar com você agora.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you now.

additional_notes: Used to ask/request that someone do an action. It’s typically followed by a verb (often in the present subjunctive): “Eu preciso que você compre/ajude/ouça…”. For a noun/thing instead of an action, Portuguese usually uses “Eu preciso de …” (e.g., “Eu preciso de ajuda.”).
target_language_example: Eu preciso que você chegue cedo amanhã.
native_language_example: I need you to arrive early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say you require information, often because it’s important or urgent. It can be followed by a clause with "o que" (what), "onde" (where), "quando" (when), etc., or used on its own: "Há algo que eu preciso saber" (There’s something I need to know).
target_language_example: Eu preciso saber se você vem hoje.
native_language_example: I need to know if you're coming today.

additional_notes: “Eu prefiro” is the 1st-person singular of the verb “preferir” (“to prefer”). It’s often followed by an infinitive (“eu prefiro ficar…”) or by nouns (“eu prefiro vinho…”). For comparisons, common patterns are: “eu prefiro X a Y” (“I prefer X to Y”) and “eu prefiro X do que Y” (“I prefer X rather than Y”).
target_language_example: Hoje eu prefiro tomar um chá em vez de café.
native_language_example: Today I’d rather have tea instead of coffee.

meaning: “I intend to / I plan to / I mean to.”
additional_notes: Used to state an intention or plan, usually for the near or medium future. It’s followed by a verb in the infinitive (pretendo comprar, pretendo dizer, pretendo fazer). It sounds fairly formal/neutral—more deliberate than just “vou…” (“I’m going to…”).
target_language_example: Eu pretendo estudar mais este semestre.
native_language_example: I intend to study more this semester.

additional_notes: Used with a verb to say something nearly happened but didn’t (or almost didn’t happen): “Eu quase esqueci…” = “I almost forgot…”. With “quase não”, it means “hardly / almost not”: “eu quase não o reconheço” = “I hardly recognize you.” Often used for close calls (“Eu quase morri” = “I almost died”).
target_language_example: Eu quase perdi o ônibus hoje.
native_language_example: I almost missed the bus today.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something you do very rarely. It’s the subject pronoun “eu” (“I”) plus the adverb phrase “quase nunca” (“almost never”). You can replace “eu” with other subjects (e.g., “ele quase nunca…”, “a gente quase nunca…”, “nós quase nunca…”).
target_language_example: Eu quase nunca como fora durante a semana.
native_language_example: I almost never eat out during the week.

additional_notes: Literally the imperfect form of querer with eu. It often means 'I wanted' in past statements, but it is also commonly used to sound softer or more polite, similar to 'I'd like'. It is usually followed by an infinitive verb or a clause.
target_language_example: Eu queria te ver hoje.
native_language_example: I wanted to see you today.

meaning: “I wish I could” / “I would like to be able to.”
additional_notes: Used to express a desire to have the ability or opportunity to do something. It’s a polite, slightly softer way to say what you want, often implying you currently can’t (or aren’t able to). Typically followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., falar, te dar, ir, ajudar).
target_language_example: Eu queria poder ajudar mais, mas estou trabalhando hoje.
native_language_example: I wish I could help more, but I’m working today.

additional_notes: Used to express a wish or desire about another action or situation, usually followed by a new clause with the subjunctive. In English it often becomes "I wanted someone to..." or "I wished that..." rather than a word-for-word translation.
target_language_example: Eu queria que você viesse comigo.
native_language_example: I wanted you to come with me.

meaning: “I wanted him/it to…” / “I’d like him/it to…” (introduces a request or desire).
additional_notes: Used before another clause, typically with the subjunctive, to say what you wanted/would like someone (masculine) or something to do: “Eu queria que o Tom saísse.” The “o” is the masculine definite article (“the”) and often comes before a man’s name or a masculine noun (“o Tom”, “o carro”). “Queria” (imperfect) can sound softer/more polite than “quero”.
target_language_example: Eu queria que o João me ajudasse com isso.
native_language_example: I wanted João to help me with that.

meaning: “I wanted you to…” / “I wish you would…” (followed by the subjunctive).
additional_notes: Used to express a desire or wish about what someone else does/did. It’s typically followed by the subjunctive: present subjunctive for a current/general wish (ex.: Eu queria que você gostasse de mim.), and past subjunctive (tivesse/estivesse) for a wish/regret about the past (ex.: Eu queria que você tivesse me contado a verdade.). Often translates naturally as “I wish you would…” or “I wish you had…”.
target_language_example: Eu queria que você me ajudasse hoje.
native_language_example: I wanted you to help me today. / I wish you would help me today.

meaning: “I wanted to know / I was wondering.”
additional_notes: Common polite way to introduce a question or express curiosity. It uses the imperfect past (queria) and often sounds softer/more tentative than directly asking (e.g., “Eu quero saber…”). Frequently followed by “se…” (if/whether) or “o que…” (what).
target_language_example: Eu queria saber se você pode me ajudar.
native_language_example: I was wondering if you could help me.

meaning: “I wanted to be …” / “I would like to be …”.
additional_notes: Literally “I wanted to be.” With a job/role (policial, professor), it usually means a past desire (“I wanted to be…”). In polite conversation, imperfect tense like this can also soften the request and sound like “I would like to be…”. Often followed by a noun (eu queria ser médico) or an adjective (eu queria ser o melhor).
target_language_example: Quando eu era criança, eu queria ser veterinário.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I wanted to be a vet.

meaning: “I wish I had” / “I wanted to have”.
additional_notes: Used to express a desire or wish to possess something or to have a quality (time, courage, caution, etc.). Often sounds like a wistful wish (“If only I had…”), especially when the speaker doesn’t have it right now. In everyday speech, “queria” can also be a polite/soft way to say “I’d like…”, but with “ter” it commonly expresses wanting to have something.
target_language_example: Eu queria ter mais tempo para descansar.
native_language_example: I wish I had more time to rest.

meaning: “I wanted to see” / “I’d like to see.”
additional_notes: Literally “I wanted to see.” In conversation, it can also be a polite/soft way to say what you would like (similar to “I’d like to…”), especially when followed by an infinitive or a clause (e.g., “eu queria ver se…” = “I wanted to see if…”). Often used to express a wish or intention that may not happen or is hypothetical.
target_language_example: Eu queria ver se você pode me ajudar com isso.
native_language_example: I wanted to see if you can help me with this.

additional_notes: A straightforward way to say what you want. It can be followed by a noun (eu quero este celular) or an infinitive verb (eu quero comprar). In Portuguese, the subject pronoun is often omitted, so quero by itself can also mean "I want" when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Eu quero aprender português.
native_language_example: I want to learn Portuguese.

additional_notes: Used to say you want to eat in general, or that you want to eat a specific thing. Often followed by a food/item (e.g., “eu quero comer pizza”) or by “isso/aquilo” (“this/that”). You can change the subject to be polite: “Eu queria comer…” (“I’d like to eat…”) or “Eu quero…” + infinitive for other wants (e.g., “Eu quero beber” = “I want to drink”).
target_language_example: Eu quero comer pizza hoje à noite.
native_language_example: I want to eat pizza tonight.

meaning: “I want to stay” / “I want to remain.”
additional_notes: Used to say you want to stay somewhere or remain in a situation. With a time expression, it often means “stay longer” (e.g., mais tempo, o máximo que puder). With “com + pessoa” (ficar com você), it can mean “stay with you” in the sense of spending time together; depending on context, “ficar com alguém” can also mean “to hook up/date,” but “Eu quero ficar com você” can be either romantic or simply staying together.
target_language_example: Eu quero ficar aqui até amanhã.
native_language_example: I want to stay here until tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say you want someone/something (masculine singular: o = “the”) to do something, followed by a verb in the subjunctive: “Eu quero que o Tom faça/fique/traga/ajude.” With feminine singular use “eu quero que a…”, and with plural “eu quero que os/as…”. In English you often translate it as “I want Tom to…”.
target_language_example: Eu quero que o meu filho durma cedo hoje.
native_language_example: I want my son to go to sleep early today.

additional_notes: Used to say what you want someone to do. In Portuguese, after "quero que" the next verb is often in the present subjunctive: "Eu quero que você vá", "...cante", "...volte" (not *"você vai", *"você canta"). You can also add an object pronoun: "Eu quero que você me ajude" (I want you to help me).
target_language_example: Eu quero que você me ajude amanhã.
native_language_example: I want you to help me tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express what you want someone to be or become, followed by a verb in the subjunctive (seja, from ser = “to be”). It commonly introduces a quality (honesta/o), a state (amada), or a role/position (meu técnico, o meu gerente). Word order is fixed: eu quero que + você + seja + complement.
target_language_example: Eu quero que você seja feliz aqui.
native_language_example: I want you to be happy here.

additional_notes: Used to state a desire/request directed at more than one person. After "quero que", Portuguese typically uses the present subjunctive (e.g., "vocês façam", "vocês fiquem", "vocês sejam"). "Vocês" is the common way to say "you" (plural) in Brazil; in Portugal you may also hear "vós" in limited contexts, but "vocês" is widely understood.
target_language_example: Eu quero que vocês me ajudem amanhã.
native_language_example: I want you all to help me tomorrow.

meaning: “I want to know” / “I’d like to know.”
additional_notes: Used to introduce a question or request for information, often followed by a question word (quem, com quem, como, o que, por que, quando, onde) or by a noun phrase (ex.: o teu nome). It can sound direct/insistent depending on tone; for a softer/politer version you can use “Eu queria saber…” (“I was wondering…”).
target_language_example: Eu quero saber onde fica a estação de metrô.
native_language_example: I want to know where the subway station is.

additional_notes: Used to say what you want to become or what you want to be like (a job, role, or a lasting characteristic): "Eu quero ser médico", "Eu quero ser rico". Uses the verb "ser" (to be) for identities/professions and more permanent traits; for temporary states you often use "estar" instead ("eu quero estar bem" = I want to be well). You can change the subject: "ele quer ser", "a gente quer ser", etc.
target_language_example: Eu quero ser melhor em português.
native_language_example: I want to be better at Portuguese.

meaning: 'I want to have' (I want to possess/own; or I want to have in the sense of having children/pets).
additional_notes: "Eu quero" = "I want" + "ter" = "to have". Used to say you want to own something (a car, a cat) or want to have something in life (children, a job). If you’re talking about wanting to do an activity, Portuguese usually uses "eu quero" + infinitive (e.g., "eu quero comer" = "I want to eat").
target_language_example: Eu quero ter uma casa grande um dia.
native_language_example: I want to have a big house someday.

meaning: "I want a" (for a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say you want something: eu quero + um + [masculine singular noun]. Often used when ordering or requesting. For feminine nouns, use "eu quero uma" (e.g., "Eu quero uma água"). You can also drop the article in some cases ("Eu quero água" = "I want water").
target_language_example: Eu quero um café, por favor.
native_language_example: I want a coffee, please.

meaning: "I want to see" / "I want to watch".
additional_notes: Used to express a desire to look at something (photos, flowers), watch something (a movie), meet someone (often in contexts like asking to speak to someone: "Eu quero ver seu chefe"), or find out how something turns out ("Eu quero ver como isso acaba" = "I want to see how this ends"). With another verb, it can mean "I want to see (someone) do something": "Eu quero ver você rir".
target_language_example: Eu quero ver o que aconteceu.
native_language_example: I want to see what happened.

additional_notes: Used to say you do something infrequently. In Portuguese, the adverb "raramente" often comes right after the subject "eu" and before the verb: "Eu raramente + verb". It can also work with other subjects (e.g., "Ela raramente...").
target_language_example: Eu raramente saio à noite durante a semana.
native_language_example: I rarely go out at night during the week.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize what you’re saying about yourself. Often followed by a verb in the past/present ("eu realmente detesto...", "eu realmente detestava..."). You can also place "realmente" later for emphasis: "eu detestava realmente..." (less common) or use it alone: "realmente" = "really" / "indeed".
target_language_example: Eu realmente não entendo isso.
native_language_example: I really don’t understand that.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you like or enjoy something (a thing, an activity, or doing something with someone). It’s built from: eu (I) + realmente (really) + gosto de (I like). After "gosto de", you typically use a noun ("gosto de basquete") or a verb in the infinitive ("gosto de beber", "gosto de sair"). To mention a person, you often use "gosto de" + person or "gosto de" + infinitive + "com" (e.g., "gosto de sair com o Tom").
target_language_example: Eu realmente gosto de aprender português.
native_language_example: I really like learning Portuguese.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize your desire or intention. Often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., “eu realmente quero ir”, “eu realmente quero fazer”). In speech you may also hear “eu quero muito…” with a similar meaning (“I really want to…”).
target_language_example: Eu realmente quero aprender português este ano.
native_language_example: I really want to learn Portuguese this year.

additional_notes: Used to say you already knew something (often based on ongoing knowledge or expectation in the past). It’s followed by a clause (eu sabia que + [sentence]). In Portuguese, the imperfect sabia often implies a continuing state of knowing; contrast with eu soube que (“i found out / i learned that”).
target_language_example: Eu sabia que você ia chegar cedo.
native_language_example: I knew that you were going to arrive early.

additional_notes: Used to say you already knew a fact about a specific masculine noun/person. After "que", Portuguese often uses the article "o" before a masculine name or noun (e.g., "o Tom" = "Tom"). For feminine nouns/names, use "a": "Eu sabia que a Maria…". The verb is in the imperfect ("sabia"), often implying you knew it at that time (in the past).
target_language_example: Eu sabia que o João ia chegar cedo.
native_language_example: I knew that João was going to arrive early.

additional_notes:
Used to say you already knew something about the other person. 

Grammar: 
- "eu" = I 
- "sabia" = knew / used to know (imperfect past of "saber") 
- "que" = that 
- "você" = you (informal/neutral in Brazil; in Portugal "você" can sound more formal or even a bit rude depending on context—"tu" is common instead).

Often followed by a verb in the past (e.g., "estava"), conditional ("entenderia"), or future-in-the-past ("iria").
target_language_example: Eu sabia que você ia chegar cedo.
native_language_example: I knew you were going to arrive early.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of the verb “sair” for “I”. It’s used when you left a place or went out (e.g., left home, left a building, exited an elevator). Often followed by “de” + place: “eu saí de casa” (I left the house). With an action word it can mean leaving in a certain way: “eu saí correndo” (I ran out / I left running).
target_language_example: Eu saí do trabalho cedo ontem.
native_language_example: I left work early yesterday.

additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive to say you know how to do something: "Eu sei + infinitive" (eu sei dirigir = I can drive). By itself, it often means "I know" (e.g., as a response to information). The verb is "saber" (eu sei, você sabe, ele/ela sabe).
target_language_example: Eu sei cozinhar, mas não sei fazer bolo.
native_language_example: I can cook, but I can’t make cake.

meaning: “I can speak / I know how to speak.”
additional_notes: Used to say you have the ability to speak a language. It’s often followed directly by the language name ("Eu sei falar chinês") or by "em" + language ("Eu sei falar em Interlíngua"). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, many people also say "Eu falo..." or "Eu sei..." to express the same idea.
target_language_example: Eu sei falar português e espanhol.
native_language_example: I can speak Portuguese and Spanish.

additional_notes: Literally 'I know.' It is the first-person singular of saber. It is used for knowing facts or information, and can also be used by itself as a reply meaning 'I know.' In a rhetorical question like 'E eu sei?', it means 'How would I know?'
target_language_example: Eu sei que você está cansado.
native_language_example: I know that you're tired.

meaning: “I know, but …” (acknowledging something, then giving an objection/exception).
additional_notes: Used in conversation to show you understand or agree with what was said, but you still have a concern, different opinion, or practical problem. Often introduces a contrasting point after “mas” (“but”). You can also hear it as “eu sei, mas…” with a pause to soften disagreement.
target_language_example: Eu sei, mas não posso hoje; podemos amanhã?
native_language_example: I know, but I can’t today; can we do it tomorrow?

meaning: "I know how" / "I know what ... is like".
additional_notes: Used to say you have the knowledge/ability to do something (often followed by an infinitive: "eu sei como fazer...") or that you understand someone’s experience/feelings ("eu sei como isso deve ser..."). You can also use it with a clause to mean you know the way something is/was ("eu sei como ele era").
target_language_example: Eu sei como chegar lá, mas hoje estou sem carro.
native_language_example: I know how to get there, but today I don’t have a car.

additional_notes: Used to say you already have that information. "Disso" = "of that / about that" (referring back to something previously mentioned). Often used with emphasis ("Eu sei disso!") or with modifiers like "muito bem" (very well), "agora" (now), "bem o suficiente" (well enough), or "de cor" (by heart).
target_language_example: Eu sei disso, não precisa repetir.
native_language_example: I know that—you don’t need to repeat it.

additional_notes: Used to say you know the location or the right place to do something. It’s typically followed by a verb in the infinitive (e.g., “onde procurar”, “onde se esconder”) or by a full clause (e.g., “onde fica o banco”). In conversation, “Eu” is often omitted: “Sei onde…”.
target_language_example: Eu sei onde fica a estação de metrô.
native_language_example: I know where the subway station is.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something the speaker knows or is sure about. In English, "that" is often optional, so it can also be translated naturally as "I know" plus a clause.
target_language_example: Eu sei que você está cansado.
native_language_example: I know that you're tired.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you know: “Eu sei que…” = “I know that…”. The final “o” is the masculine singular definite article (“the”), often used before masculine names in Brazilian Portuguese (e.g., “o Tom”, “o João”). If the next word is feminine, you’ll usually see “eu sei que a …” instead.
target_language_example: Eu sei que o meu irmão vai chegar tarde.
native_language_example: I know that my brother is going to arrive late.

additional_notes: Used to state that you know something about the other person. It’s often followed by a verb describing what the person does/did/is (e.g., “eu sei que você fala...”, “eu sei que você fez...”). In polite speech, you may also hear “eu sei que o senhor / a senhora...” for “I know that you...” (formal).
target_language_example: Eu sei que você está preocupado, mas vai dar tudo certo.
native_language_example: I know that you’re worried, but everything will be fine.

additional_notes: Used to state that you understand someone’s desire/intention, usually followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., ajudar, fazer, ir). Often introduces empathy or a lead-in to a suggestion, limit, or next point (e.g., “Eu sei que você quer ajudar, mas…”). In Brazil, você is common; in Portugal, you’ll often hear “Eu sei que tu queres…”.
target_language_example: Eu sei que você quer sair, mas ainda não terminou o trabalho.
native_language_example: I know you want to go out, but you haven’t finished the work yet.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something you do every time / as a habit. In Portuguese, "sempre" often comes right before the main verb: "Eu sempre escovo..." You can also omit "eu" when it’s clear from context: "Sempre escovo os dentes..."
target_language_example: Eu sempre chego cedo ao trabalho.
native_language_example: I always arrive early at work.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a long-standing desire. "Quis" is the past form of "querer" (to want). In English it’s often translated as "I’ve always wanted..." even though Portuguese uses a simple past form here. Commonly followed by an infinitive: "eu sempre quis + verb" (e.g., "viajar", "aprender", "ter").
target_language_example: Eu sempre quis aprender português.
native_language_example: I've always wanted to learn Portuguese.

additional_notes: Often used alone as an apology (“I’m sorry”). When followed by “a falta (de alguém)” or “a sua falta,” it means “I miss (someone) a lot” (literally, “I feel the absence a lot”). You can intensify it with “muito” (“so much”), e.g., “Eu sinto muito (mesmo).”
target_language_example: Eu sinto muito a sua falta desde que você foi embora.
native_language_example: I’ve missed you a lot since you left.

additional_notes: First-person singular of ser. Used for identity, profession, origin, and more permanent characteristics. In Portuguese, eu is often omitted when the subject is clear, so sou is also very common. Compare with eu estou for temporary states or location.
target_language_example: Eu sou estudante.
native_language_example: I am a student.

meaning: 'I am the…' (used before a feminine noun/title/name).
additional_notes: Used to identify yourself as someone/something feminine, often followed by a job, role, nickname, or description. The article changes with grammatical gender: **eu sou o** + masculine noun (e.g., *eu sou o professor*), **eu sou a** + feminine noun (e.g., *eu sou a professora*). With many names you can also say **eu sou a/o + name** for emphasis/identification, though **eu sou + name** is also common.
target_language_example: Eu sou a professora nova.
native_language_example: I am the new (female) teacher.

additional_notes: Used to identify yourself as a specific person/role/thing, usually followed by a noun ("eu sou o goleiro") or a superlative ("eu sou o mais alto"). "o" is the masculine singular definite article ("the"); use "eu sou a" for feminine ("I am the"), and "eu sou os/as" for plural ("I am the [plural]").
target_language_example: Eu sou o responsável por isso.
native_language_example: I am the one responsible for this.

additional_notes: Used to identify yourself as a person/thing (profession, role, type of person, nationality, group, etc.). It’s the verb “ser” (to be) in the present: “eu sou” = “I am”, followed by “um” (masculine “a/an”). For feminine nouns, you usually use “eu sou uma” (e.g., “eu sou uma professora”). Before a plural group noun, you use “eu sou um deles/umas delas” = “I’m one of them.”
target_language_example: Eu sou um estudante, mas também sou um músico.
native_language_example: I'm a student, but I'm also a musician.

meaning: "I am a" (used before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: This is the verb "ser" (to be) in the present: "eu sou" = "I am" + the feminine indefinite article "uma" = "a/an". Use it before feminine nouns/adjectives used as nouns: "Eu sou uma professora" (I’m a teacher). For masculine nouns, use "eu sou um".
target_language_example: Eu sou uma estudante de português.
native_language_example: I am a Portuguese student.

meaning: “I found out that / I learned that.”
additional_notes: Used to report that you got some information or news in the past (often newly discovered). It’s the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of *saber* (“to know”), followed by **que** + a full clause.
target_language_example: Eu soube que a reunião foi cancelada.
native_language_example: I found out that the meeting was canceled.

additional_notes: Used to make a recommendation or give advice. In Portuguese, after “sugiro que…”, it’s very common to use the present subjunctive (e.g., coma, cozinhe, descanse, vá). Often corresponds to English “I suggest you…” or “I recommend that you…”.
target_language_example: Eu sugiro que você chegue mais cedo amanhã.
native_language_example: I suggest you arrive earlier tomorrow.

meaning: "I suspect that..." (I have a feeling/guess that...).
additional_notes: Used to express suspicion or an educated guess about a situation. It’s often followed by a clause in the subjunctive when the speaker is uncertain (e.g., "Eu suspeito que o Tom esteja..."). In your examples, "o" is just the masculine definite article (“the”) starting the next noun phrase (e.g., "o Tom"), so you can also say "Eu suspeito que a..." (feminine) or simply "Eu suspeito que...".
target_language_example: Eu suspeito que o professor não vai aceitar essa resposta.
native_language_example: I suspect the teacher won’t accept that answer.

additional_notes: Used to limit or soften what the speaker says: eu só + verb means the speaker only did that action, did it a small number of times, or simply wanted/needed something. In natural English, it often translates as either "I just" or "I only," depending on context.
target_language_example: Eu só queria ajudar.
native_language_example: I just wanted to help.

additional_notes: Used to soften what you’re saying, explain your intention, or show it was a simple/limited goal. Often followed by an infinitive (eu só queria ajudar, ir, checar) or by “que” + subjunctive to say what you wanted someone else to do (eu só queria que você a visse). In everyday speech it can also imply a mild complaint or disappointment (like “I only wanted to…”).
target_language_example: Eu só queria falar com você por um minuto.
native_language_example: I just wanted to talk to you for a minute.

additional_notes: Used to say your intention in a soft/limited way. "só" often means "just/only" to reassure someone or to show you're not asking for much: "Eu só quero verificar" (I just want to check) / "Eu só quero ajudar" (I only want to help).
target_language_example: Eu só quero fazer uma pergunta.
native_language_example: I just want to ask a question.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you want to happen, often followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., "eu só quero que ele venha" = "I just want him to come"). In English you often drop “that,” but in Portuguese "que" is normally required here.
target_language_example: Eu só quero que você seja feliz.
native_language_example: I just want you to be happy.

additional_notes:
Used to emphasize a limitation or small amount of something you have. 
- With numbers: highlights a small quantity ("Eu só tenho dois filhos" = I only have two children).
- With time/amount left: often means "I have only" ("Eu só tenho mais uma pergunta" = I have only one more question).
- With "para + verb" or "para culpar": can mean "all I have (left) is..." / "the only ..." ("Eu só tenho a mim mesmo para culpar" = I only have myself to blame).
Word order: "só" usually comes right before "tenho" in this pattern.
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu só tenho dez reais comigo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I only have ten reais on me.

additional_notes: Used to say that the same thing is true for you. As a short reply, it often means "me too"; in a full sentence, it usually means "I also" or "I too."
target_language_example: Eu também quero ir.
native_language_example: I want to go too.

additional_notes: Used when the speaker (“eu”) does something to “you” (“te”). In Brazilian Portuguese it commonly appears right before a verb: “eu te digo” (I tell you), “eu te mostro” (I show you), “eu te falei” (I told you). “Te” is an unstressed object pronoun; in more formal writing you may see “eu lhe …” or “eu o/a …” depending on meaning/region.
target_language_example: Eu te ajudo amanhã.
native_language_example: I’ll help you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression by itself. It is the common pattern eu + te: eu means "I" and te means "you" as the object of the verb, so the full meaning depends on the verb that follows, as in eu te amo ("I love you") or eu te dei a chave ("I gave you the key"). In Brazilian Portuguese, te usually comes before the verb.
target_language_example: Eu te espero aqui.
native_language_example: I'll wait for you here.

additional_notes: A direct, personal way to say you love someone. Uses the object pronoun "te" (you, informal/singular). In Brazil, "eu te amo" is often felt as stronger/more serious than "eu te adoro" or "eu gosto de você". In Portugal you may also hear "amo-te" with the pronoun after the verb.
target_language_example: Eu te amo de verdade.
native_language_example: I really love you.

additional_notes: Used to remind someone of something you already said (sometimes with emphasis or mild frustration). Often followed by a clause with a verb (e.g., "eu te disse que era...", "eu te disse que ele..."), or with the subjunctive/imperative idea after "que" to report a command/request (e.g., "Eu te disse que saísse" = "I told you to leave"). In Brazil, you’ll also hear "eu disse pra você que..." with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Eu te disse que ia chegar cedo.
native_language_example: I told you I was going to arrive early.

additional_notes: "Eu" = I, "te" = you (informal singular object pronoun), "dou" = I give (from "dar"). Used to offer or promise to give something to someone: "Eu te dou X" = I’ll give you X. In more formal speech, you may hear "Eu lhe dou" (I give you) instead.
target_language_example: Eu te dou um desconto se você pagar hoje.
native_language_example: I’ll give you a discount if you pay today.

additional_notes: Uses the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of **ver**: **vi** = “I saw.” **Te** is an object pronoun meaning “you” (common in Brazil, especially in informal speech). You may also hear **Eu vi você** with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Eu te vi ontem no metrô.
native_language_example: I saw you yesterday on the subway.

additional_notes: First-person singular of ter. Used for possession and also for things like relationships, jobs, difficulties, and experiences. In Portuguese, the subject pronoun is often omitted, so you'll also frequently hear just tenho.
target_language_example: Eu tenho uma irmã.
native_language_example: I have a sister.

additional_notes: Used to express obligation/necessity. Pattern: "ter de" + infinitive (e.g., "tenho de fazer" = "I have to do"). In everyday speech, people also say "eu tenho que" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Eu tenho de trabalhar amanhã cedo.
native_language_example: I have to work early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used before another verb in the infinitive to express obligation or necessity: eu tenho que fazer = I have to do. This is a very common everyday pattern; you may also see ter de with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Eu tenho que sair agora.
native_language_example: I have to leave now.

meaning: "I have to go" / "I need to leave."
additional_notes: Used to say you must leave (because of time, an obligation, or a plan). Often followed by a place with "para" (e.g., "ir para a aula") or by another verb to show purpose (e.g., "ir dizer"). In speech, "para" is often shortened to "pra" ("ir pra casa").
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu tenho que ir agora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go now.

meaning: "I have three" (I possess/there are three of something I have).
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to say you have three of something: "Eu tenho três + [plural noun]". The verb "ter" means "to have". In Brazilian Portuguese, "tenho" is often pronounced like "TEN-yo."
target_language_example: Eu tenho três irmãos.
native_language_example: I have three brothers.

additional_notes: Used to say that you possess, have, or need to deal with something. Here, um is the masculine singular indefinite article ('a/an') before a masculine noun, and it can also mean 'one' when the noun is omitted. For feminine nouns, use uma instead.
target_language_example: Eu tenho um cachorro muito brincalhão.
native_language_example: I have a very playful dog.

meaning: "I have a friend who..." (introducing what a friend does/is).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a friend and then add a relative clause with que (“who/that”) describing them (job, identity, or actions). You can swap amigo for amiga, and change tenho to tinha/terei, etc., depending on tense.
target_language_example: Eu tenho um amigo que mora em Lisboa.
native_language_example: I have a friend who lives in Lisbon.

additional_notes: Used before a singular feminine noun: eu tenho uma irmã (I have a sister), eu tenho uma entrega (I have a delivery). With feminine phrases like "uma dor de cabeça" (a headache) or "uma bexiga fraca" (a weak bladder). For a masculine noun, use "eu tenho um".
target_language_example: Eu tenho uma consulta amanhã.
native_language_example: I have an appointment tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to get someone’s attention politely before asking something. Often followed by "para você" / "pra você" (“for you”) or "para te fazer" (“to ask you”). "Pra" is an informal contraction of "para".
target_language_example: Oi, eu tenho uma pergunta: onde fica o banheiro?
native_language_example: Hi, I have a question: where is the bathroom?
