additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "tentar" with "eu". Used to say you made an attempt at something, often followed by an infinitive: "Eu tentei + verb" (e.g., "Eu tentei ligar"). You can also add duration with "por": "Eu tentei por quase uma hora" = "I tried for almost an hour."
target_language_example: Eu tentei falar com ela ontem, mas não consegui.
native_language_example: I tried to talk to her yesterday, but I couldn’t.

meaning: "I would have" (past conditional; used for unreal/ hypothetical past situations).
additional_notes: Used to talk about something you would have done in the past, often in regrets, missed opportunities, or imagined scenarios. Very common with an if-clause: "Se eu soubesse..., eu teria + participle" (If I had known..., I would have...). It’s the conditional of "ter" (to have): eu teria, você/ele teria, nós teríamos, vocês/eles teriam, usually followed by a past participle (e.g., "dito", "feito", "enviado").
target_language_example: Se eu tivesse mais tempo, eu teria terminado o trabalho ontem.
native_language_example: If I had had more time, I would have finished the work yesterday.

additional_notes: Imperfect past of "ter" (to have). Use it for past situations/states that were ongoing or habitual ("Quando eu tinha 10 anos..." = "When I was 10..."). With "tinha de" or "tinha que", it commonly means obligation: "I had to".
target_language_example: Quando eu tinha a sua idade, eu tinha um emprego.
native_language_example: When I was your age, I had a job.

meaning: "I had to" / "I needed to" (I was obligated to do something).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past of "ter" (tinha) + "que" + infinitive to express obligation/necessity in the past: "Eu tinha que fazer..." = "I had to do...". Often implies a requirement, duty, or something you felt was necessary. In casual speech, "Eu" is sometimes dropped: "Tinha que ir" = "(I) had to go."
target_language_example: Eu tinha que estudar, mas acabei dormindo.
native_language_example: I had to study, but I ended up falling asleep.

additional_notes: Used with **fotos** to mean “I took (pictures)” (eu tirei uma foto). It can also be used with **grades** to mean “I got (a grade)” (eu tirei um D). In other contexts, *tirar* can also mean “to remove/take off,” but the examples here are about photos/grades.
target_language_example: Eu tirei uma nota boa na prova.
native_language_example: I got a good grade on the test.

additional_notes: Used to talk about having/experiencing something in the past: help (Eu tive ajuda…), a dream (Eu tive aquele sonho…), good times (Eu tive bons momentos…), difficulty (Eu tive dificuldade…), a teacher (Eu tive um ótimo professor…), an appointment/commitment (Eu tive outro compromisso…). Often followed by a noun or noun phrase. You can add a time word like *ontem* (yesterday) or *essa noite* (tonight/last night).
target_language_example: Eu tive um dia difícil no trabalho.
native_language_example: I had a difficult day at work.

meaning: I had to (I was obliged to).
additional_notes: Past tense of "ter de" (to have to / must). Use it to say you were required to do something: "Eu tive de + infinitive" (Eu tive de esperar / fazer / dizer). Often interchangeable with "eu precisei" (I needed to), but "tive de" emphasizes obligation/necessity.
target_language_example: Eu tive de sair cedo por causa do trabalho.
native_language_example: I had to leave early because of work.

meaning: "I had to" / "I needed to" (I was obliged to).
additional_notes: Used to say you were required to do something in the past. It comes from the verb *ter* (to have): *tive* = "I had" (past), plus *que* introducing the action that was necessary. Often followed by an infinitive verb: *Eu tive que + verbo* (e.g., *fazer, ir, pagar*). In everyday speech, you may also hear *eu tive de* with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Eu tive que ir ao médico ontem.
native_language_example: I had to go to the doctor yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a dream you experienced while sleeping. Often followed by details with "com" (about/with): "tive um sonho com..." or by a description: "um sonho engraçado/horrível". In storytelling, it can also be followed by a clause introduced with "em que" (“in which”). In everyday conversation, you’ll often also hear "eu sonhei" (“I dreamed”), which is a shorter equivalent.
target_language_example: Eu tive um sonho com você ontem à noite.
native_language_example: I had a dream about you last night.

additional_notes: Uses **ter** (“to have”) in the **pretérito perfeito** (simple past): **eu tive** = “I had.” **uma** is the feminine singular article (“a”), so it’s followed by a feminine noun (e.g., *uma conversa*, *uma infância*). With a masculine noun, use **eu tive um** (e.g., *eu tive um problema*).
target_language_example: Eu tive uma ideia ontem.
native_language_example: I had an idea yesterday.

additional_notes: Most commonly used with musical instruments: **Eu toco piano/violão/violino** (“I play the piano/guitar/violin”). You can also hear **tocar em + instrument** (especially in Brazilian Portuguese), meaning the same thing: **tocar na gaita** (“play the harmonica”). In other contexts, **tocar (em)** can mean “to touch.”
target_language_example: Eu toco piano, mas não toco violão.
native_language_example: I play the piano, but I don’t play the guitar.

additional_notes: Uses the verb “trabalhar” in the pretérito perfeito to say you worked or you used to work in a specific, completed time period. Often followed by muito (a lot) or by na/numa/nesta/nessa + place to say where you worked.
target_language_example: Eu trabalhei lá no ano passado.
native_language_example: I worked there last year.

additional_notes: Basic present-tense statement with the subject pronoun for emphasis/clarity. In Portuguese, the subject pronoun is often optional, so you’ll also hear just “trabalho” = “I work.” You can add details after it: “eu trabalho aqui” (I work here), “eu trabalho demais” (I work too much), “eu trabalho por conta (própria)” (I’m self-employed / I work for myself).
target_language_example: Eu trabalho em casa hoje.
native_language_example: I work from home today.

additional_notes: Used to say you brought someone or something to a place. It’s the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of the verb “trazer” for “eu” (I): eu trago (I bring) → eu trouxe (I brought). Often followed by what/whom you brought: “eu trouxe uma coisa”, “eu trouxe você”, “eu trouxe as crianças”.
target_language_example: Eu trouxe meu guarda-chuva porque estava chovendo.
native_language_example: I brought my umbrella because it was raining.

additional_notes: Very common in Brazilian Portuguese conversation. It’s the informal contraction of “eu estou” and is used to talk about how you are/feel (“eu tô bem”), your current situation (“eu tô em casa”), or what you’re doing right now with a verb in -ndo (“eu tô estudando” = “I’m studying”). In more formal writing/speech, use “eu estou”.
target_language_example: Eu tô cansado, então vou dormir cedo.
native_language_example: I’m tired, so I’m going to sleep early.

additional_notes: "Eu" = "I" and "uso" is the present tense of "usar" (to use; to wear). Use it for using tools/methods ("Eu uso flashcards") and for wearing items like clothes or accessories ("Eu uso luvas"). Often you’ll also hear the more natural phrasing with "estar" for clothing: "Estou usando luvas" = "I’m wearing gloves (right now)".
target_language_example: Eu uso este aplicativo todos os dias.
native_language_example: I use this app every day.

meaning: "I see" (I notice/understand; or I literally see with my eyes).
additional_notes: Present tense of the verb "ver" (to see), used both for physical sight (seeing a dog, tears) and for realizing/recognizing something ("I see how good you are"). Often followed by a direct object: "Eu vejo + [thing/person]" or a clause: "Eu vejo como...".
target_language_example: Eu vejo o que você quer dizer.
native_language_example: I see what you mean.

additional_notes: Present tense of "vir" (to come) with "eu" (I). Very common with **de + place** to say where you’re from: *Eu venho do Brasil* (“I come from Brazil”). It can also describe a planned/near-future action in conversational Portuguese: *Amanhã eu venho aí* (“Tomorrow I’ll come over / I’m coming there”).
target_language_example: Eu venho te buscar às oito.
native_language_example: I’ll come pick you up at eight.

additional_notes: First-person singular preterite of ver ("to see"). It refers to something you saw in the past. In Portuguese, eu is often omitted because vi already means "I saw."
target_language_example: Eu vi um filme muito bom ontem.
native_language_example: I saw a very good movie yesterday.

meaning: “I saw the …” (with a masculine noun/name after it).
additional_notes: Used to say you saw someone or something. "vi" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "ver" (to see). "o" is the masculine singular definite article (“the”) and is used before masculine nouns (o carro, o rapaz). In Brazilian Portuguese, it’s also common in many regions to use "o" before male first names ("o Tom"), though this varies by region and formality.
target_language_example: Eu vi o João no supermercado ontem.
native_language_example: I saw João at the supermarket yesterday.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of the verb "vir" (to come): "eu vim" = "I came/I arrived". Often followed by details like where/from where ("eu vim de..." = "I came by...") or how you came ("eu vim sozinho/sozinha" = "I came alone"; the adjective agrees with the speaker’s gender: sozinho = male, sozinha = female).
target_language_example: Eu vim do trabalho.
native_language_example: I came from work.

meaning: “I came to / I came here to” (to do something).
additional_notes: Used to say your purpose for coming: **Eu vim para + infinitive** (verb in the infinitive), e.g. *eu vim para dizer*, *eu vim para te dar*. With a place/noun, it can mean “I came to (this place)”: *Eu vim para esse país...*. Often followed by **te** (“you”) before the infinitive: *vim para te ajudar* (“I came to help you”).
target_language_example: Eu vim para ajudar você com a mudança.
native_language_example: I came to help you with the move.

additional_notes: Used with places to say where you live (Eu vivo em/na…). It can also be figurative: eu vivo na confiança/na esperança… (“I live in/with the confidence/hope…”), or to mean how you live or what you focus on (Eu vivo só o presente = “I live only in the present”).
target_language_example: Eu vivo no Brasil, mas trabalho online.
native_language_example: I live in Brazil, but I work online.

additional_notes: Usually followed by an infinitive to talk about a future action: eu vou ajudar = 'I'm going to help' or 'I'll help'. On its own, eu vou can also mean 'I'm going' or 'I go'. In everyday Portuguese, eu is often omitted when clear from the verb: vou ajudar.
target_language_example: Eu vou ligar para você amanhã.
native_language_example: I'm going to call you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses **ir + infinitive** (**vou fazer**) to talk about a plan or near-future action (“I’m going to do”). Depending on context it can also sound like a firm decision or promise (“I will do it”). Often used alone as an answer: **Eu vou fazer.**
target_language_example: Calma, eu vou fazer isso hoje.
native_language_example: Relax, I’m going to do that today.

meaning: “I’m going to stay” / “I’m going to be (become)” (with a state/feeling).
additional_notes: Uses the near future: eu vou + infinitive. With ficar, it often means (1) staying/remaining somewhere: “Eu vou ficar lá” = “I’m going to stay there”; (2) becoming a state or emotion: “Eu vou ficar nervoso” = “I’m going to get nervous”; (3) ending up/being located: “É onde eu vou ficar?” = “Is that where I’m going to stay (end up)?”
target_language_example: Eu vou ficar em casa hoje.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay at home today.

additional_notes: Literal future with "vou" (ir + infinitive): "vou morrer" = "I’m going to die" / "I will die" (often when something bad is about to happen). Can be used seriously (danger, illness) or dramatically/exaggerated in speech ("I’m dying!"), depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: Se eu não tomar esse remédio, eu vou morrer.
native_language_example: If I don’t take this medicine, I’m going to die.

meaning: “I’m going to (do something) to/for you” (talking to ‘you’).
additional_notes: Common start of a near-future promise, plan, or threat. It’s built from: eu (I) + vou (I’m going) + te (you, informal singular object pronoun). Use with a verb right after it: eu vou te ligar (I’ll call you), eu vou te levar (I’ll take you), eu vou te processar (I’m going to sue you). In many places, people also use “vou lhe” (more formal) or “vou te” mainly with someone you address as “você/tu”.
target_language_example: Eu vou te ajudar com isso amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m going to help you with that tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **ir** (“to go”). In Portuguese, **eu vou** can mean “I’m going” (now/soon) or “I’ll go” (near future), depending on context. Common with destinations: **eu vou lá** (“I’ll go there”), **eu vou pra lá** (“I’m going over there”), **eu vou para casa** (“I’m going home”). It’s also used to accept/agree: **Tá bem, eu vou!** (“Okay, I’ll go!”).
target_language_example: Calma, eu vou com você.
native_language_example: Relax, I’ll go with you.

additional_notes: Used to say you are going to a place (now, soon, or at a stated time). Often followed by a city/country name (Eu vou para Istambul) or by a place with an article: para o (masc. singular), para a (fem. singular), para os (masc. plural), para as (fem. plural). In everyday speech, "para" is often shortened to "pra": "Eu vou pra casa".
target_language_example: Eu vou para casa depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: I'm going home after work.

additional_notes: Used to refer to someone you used to date (a past romantic partner). The prefix “ex-” means “former” and can be used with other relationship words too (e.g., ex-namorado = ex-boyfriend, ex-marido = ex-husband, ex-mulher = ex-wife).
target_language_example: Eu vi minha ex-namorada ontem no shopping.
native_language_example: I saw my ex-girlfriend yesterday at the mall.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone you used to date but are no longer in a relationship with. It’s often used with possessives like "meu/minha" (my) or "seu/sua" (your): "meu ex-namorado", "seu ex-namorado". Feminine form: "ex-namorada" (ex-girlfriend).
target_language_example: Ela encontrou o ex-namorado na festa.
native_language_example: She ran into her ex-boyfriend at the party.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something matches in the same way you thought, expected, remembered, or wanted. Often followed by a verb phrase (“exatamente como fazer…”) or a full clause (“exatamente como eu esperava”). It can refer to manner (“how to do it”) or similarity (“just like he is”).
target_language_example: Fiz exatamente como você me disse.
native_language_example: I did exactly as you told me.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize precision about an action or information: “exactly what (I said / you heard / you did)”. Common after verbs like fazer (to do), dizer (to say), ouvir (to hear), and pedir (to ask for). Often followed by a clause with a verb (e.g., “exatamente o que você fez”).
target_language_example: Eu quero saber exatamente o que aconteceu.
native_language_example: I want to know exactly what happened.

additional_notes: Used for the portable device used to put out a fire. In emergencies you might ask where it is: “Onde fica o extintor de incêndio?” You may also hear just “extintor” when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Em caso de incêndio, use o extintor de incêndio e chame os bombeiros.
native_language_example: In case of fire, use the fire extinguisher and call the firefighters.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "falar" (to speak) + a language. "Fala" is the present tense for você/ele/ela and also for formal address (o senhor/a senhora). For informal "you", you often hear "Você fala alemão?"; for "I speak", use "Eu falo alemão."
target_language_example: Você fala alemão?
native_language_example: Do you speak German?

additional_notes: Very common in Brazilian Portuguese as a casual way to greet someone or prompt them to speak. Depending on tone and context, it can mean “hey!” (as a greeting), “tell me” (asking for information), or “say something” / “go ahead.” Often used with someone’s name or nickname: “Fala aí, João.”
target_language_example: Fala aí, o que foi que aconteceu?
native_language_example: Hey, what happened?

meaning: (he/she/you formal) speaks Spanish; also used in questions: “Do you speak Spanish?”
additional_notes: "Falar" means "to speak" and "espanhol" means "Spanish". The form "fala" is used with ele/ela/você and with polite forms like "o senhor/a senhora". For "I speak Spanish," say "Eu falo espanhol." For "Do you (informal tu) speak Spanish?" you may hear "Tu falas espanhol?" (more common in Portugal).
target_language_example: Você fala espanhol?
native_language_example: Do you speak Spanish?

additional_notes: Uses the verb **falar** (to speak) + the language name. It usually appears with a subject: **Ele fala francês.** You can change the person: **Eu falo francês** (I speak French), **Você fala francês?** (Do you speak French?). For emphasis you can add adverbs like **fluentemente** (fluently) or **só** (only).
target_language_example: Você fala francês?
native_language_example: Do you speak French?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "falar" (to speak) + the language "inglês". "fala" is the 3rd-person singular present (he/she/you formal speaks). Common in questions like "Você fala inglês?" (Do you speak English?) and statements like "Ele/Ela fala inglês."
target_language_example: Desculpe, você fala inglês?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you speak English?

additional_notes: Used to say that someone can speak the Japanese language. It’s the verb "falar" (to speak) conjugated for "he/she/you (formal)/it" in the present tense: "(ele/ela/você) fala". In questions you’ll often see it as "Você fala japonês?" (Do you speak Japanese?) or "Alguém aqui fala japonês?" (Does anyone here speak Japanese?).
target_language_example: Ela fala japonês e inglês.
native_language_example: She speaks Japanese and English.

additional_notes: Very common in Brazilian Portuguese, usually said to react to something you think is absurd, exaggerated, or hard to believe. It can be used as an exclamation by itself ("Fala sério!") or as a question ("Você fala sério?"). It can also be used to criticize someone for not being serious: "Você não fala sério!" ≈ "You can't be serious."
target_language_example: Fala sério, você esqueceu o aniversário dela de novo?
native_language_example: Seriously, you forgot her birthday again?

additional_notes: Present tense of the verb "falar" (to speak) with "eles/elas/vocês": "(they/you all) speak". Used to say that a group knows/speaks the French language. For a singular person: "fala francês" (he/she/you speak French).
target_language_example: Eles falam francês muito bem.
native_language_example: They speak French very well.

additional_notes: “Falando com” is the gerund (present participle) of “falar” + “com” (“to talk/speak with”). It describes an ongoing action: someone is in the middle of talking with someone else. In many situations it translates as “talking to” in English, even though Portuguese uses “com” (“with”). It often appears after verbs like “estar/ficar/passar (tempo)” to emphasize duration or that the action is happening right now.
target_language_example: Estou falando com a minha mãe agora; posso te ligar depois?
native_language_example: I'm talking to my mom now; can I call you later?

additional_notes: Used to show you mean what you're saying or to check if someone is joking. Often appears with verbs like “estar” (estou falando sério) or on its own in conversation: “Tá falando sério?” / “Tô falando sério.”.
target_language_example: Falando sério, eu preciso ir embora agora.
native_language_example: Seriously, I need to leave now.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone who learned a language from childhood as their first language (L1). It agrees with the person: common forms are "falante nativo" (masc.) and "falante nativa" (fem.). You can also say "falante nativo de + idioma" (e.g., "de francês").
target_language_example: Eu queria saber falar francês como um falante nativo.
native_language_example: I wish I could speak French like a native speaker.

additional_notes: Used when saying who you want to talk to or speak with. The person comes after com: falar com alguém. If you want to mention the topic, Portuguese often adds sobre, as in falar com alguém sobre algo.
target_language_example: Quero falar com você depois da aula.
native_language_example: I want to talk to you after class.

meaning: to talk to her; to speak with her.
additional_notes: Used when you want (or managed) to have a conversation with a woman/girl. "Falar" = to speak/talk, "com" = with/to (in this context), "ela" = she/her. In questions, it often means "Did you manage to reach her and talk?"
target_language_example: Preciso falar com ela hoje à tarde.
native_language_example: I need to talk to her this afternoon.

additional_notes: Common pattern: **falar com + person** = “to talk to/speak with (someone)”. **ele** means “him” (literally “he”), and you can swap it: *falar com ela* (talk to her), *falar com você* (talk to you), *falar com eles/elas* (talk to them). Often used after requests/commands: *deixa-me falar com ele* (let me talk to him), *vá falar com ele* (go talk to him).
target_language_example: Preciso falar com ele agora.
native_language_example: I need to talk to him now.

meaning: to talk to them; to speak with them.
additional_notes: "Falar com" is the common way to say “talk to / speak with.” "Eles" means “they/them” (masculine or mixed group). Often used with verbs like "querer" (to want), "dever" (should), "ter que" / "precisar" (have to/need), and "tentar" (to try): e.g., "Eu tenho que falar com eles" = “I have to talk to them.”
target_language_example: Depois do almoço, vou falar com eles sobre o trabalho.
native_language_example: After lunch, I’m going to talk to them about work.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun. In Brazilian Portuguese, o can also appear before some men's names, so falar com o Tom means 'talk to Tom,' not 'talk to the Tom.'
target_language_example: Preciso falar com o professor depois da aula.
native_language_example: I need to talk to the teacher after class.

additional_notes: Used when someone wants or needs to have a conversation with you (often about something important): e.g. “Preciso falar com você” = “I need to talk to you.” Literally “to speak/talk with you.” You may also hear “falar contigo” (more informal/region-dependent).
target_language_example: Posso falar com você um minuto?
native_language_example: Can I talk to you for a minute?

meaning: to talk to you (plural) / to speak with you (plural).
additional_notes: Used when addressing two or more people. In Brazil, "vocês" is the common plural "you" in both formal and informal situations; in Portugal you may also hear "falar convosco". Often used for requests or urgency: "Preciso falar com vocês" = "I need to talk to you all."
target_language_example: Depois da reunião, eu quero falar com vocês por cinco minutos.
native_language_example: After the meeting, I want to talk to you all for five minutes.

additional_notes: Means “to talk/speak with me.” It’s the verb "falar" + "com" (with) + "migo" (me). Often used to ask when someone will talk to you, or to invite someone to contact you (sometimes implying something important or private). Common variants: "pode falar comigo" (you can talk to me), "preciso falar com você" (I need to talk to you).
target_language_example: Você pode falar comigo depois da aula?
native_language_example: Can you talk to me after class?

additional_notes: Used to address one person with the informal pronoun “tu” (“contigo” = “with you”). Common in Portugal and in some regions of Brazil; in many Brazilian contexts you’ll also hear “falar com você”. Often used when you want to speak to someone about something or in private: “falar contigo sobre/a respeito de…”; “falar contigo em particular”.
target_language_example: Quando tiver um minuto, queria falar contigo.
native_language_example: When you have a minute, I’d like to talk to you.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition “em” to say what language you’re speaking: “falar em + idioma” (also common: “falar francês” without “em”). It can describe ability (“Ele sabe falar em francês”) or what you’ll use in a situation (“Você vai falar em francês com o Tom?”).
target_language_example: No trabalho, eu preciso falar em francês com alguns clientes.
native_language_example: At work, I need to speak in French with some clients.

meaning: to speak in public; to speak in front of an audience.
additional_notes: Used for giving a speech or talking to a group (e.g., a presentation, a class, a crowd). Often appears with verbs like detestar/gostar de (to hate/like) and estar acostumado(a) a (to be used to).
target_language_example: Eu fico nervoso(a) quando tenho que falar em público.
native_language_example: I get nervous when I have to speak in public.

additional_notes: Refers to using the French language. After falar, francês means the language, not a French person. Common with verbs like querer, poder, and gostar de.
target_language_example: Meu irmão está aprendendo a falar francês.
native_language_example: My brother is learning to speak French.

additional_notes: "Falar" means "to speak" (a language). Use it with the language name: falar português, falar espanhol, etc. Common in questions about ability with "poder": "Você pode falar inglês?" You can also use "saber" to mean "to know how to" in general: "Não sei falar inglês" = "I don't know how to speak English."
target_language_example: Você pode falar inglês?
native_language_example: Can you speak English?

meaning: to speak badly of (someone/something); to badmouth.
additional_notes: Often used with "de": "falar mal de alguém" = to speak ill of someone (criticize them, often behind their back). It can also literally mean "to speak badly" (e.g., not expressing yourself well), but the most common everyday meaning is "to badmouth/criticize."
target_language_example: Por favor, não comece a falar mal dela.
native_language_example: Please don’t start badmouthing her.

meaning: to talk about it; to discuss it.
additional_notes: Common way to bring up (or avoid) a topic. "Isso" = "it/that" (something known from context). Often used with "com" + person: "falar sobre isso com você" (talk about it with you). You can soften or strengthen it with phrases like "em privado" (in private) or "já não quero" (I don't want to anymore).
target_language_example: Podemos falar sobre isso depois do jantar?
native_language_example: Can we talk about it after dinner?

meaning: to be serious; to speak seriously.
additional_notes: Often appears in the expression/imperative “Fala sério!” meaning “Seriously?” / “Come on, be serious.” It can also be used more literally: “Estou falando sério.” = “I’m being serious.” As an infinitive, “falar sério” can describe someone’s intention or habit of speaking seriously.
target_language_example: Você precisa falar sério comigo sobre isso.
native_language_example: You need to be serious with me about this.

meaning: "you speak Portuguese" (often used as "Do you speak Portuguese?")
additional_notes: Uses the verb form "falas" for "tu" (you, informal/singular). It’s commonly heard in Portugal and in some regions/contexts elsewhere. As a question, it’s usually just intonation: "Falas português?" A more universal/polite alternative is "Você fala português?"
target_language_example: Falas português?
native_language_example: Do you speak Portuguese?

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to speak to a specific man/person/thing: **fale** is the polite/neutral command form (as in *você fale*), and **com o** is the contraction of **com + o** (“with/to the”). For a feminine noun, use **fale com a**; for plural, **fale com os/as**. In everyday English it’s usually translated as “talk to …” rather than the literal “talk with …”.
target_language_example: Por favor, fale com o gerente.
native_language_example: Please talk to the manager.

meaning: Talk to me / speak to me.
additional_notes: Imperative form of **falar** (“to speak/talk”), used to ask or demand that someone talk to you. Often sounds firm or direct, especially in arguments. You can soften it with **por favor** (“Fale comigo, por favor.”). In the negative: **não fale comigo** (“don’t talk to me”).
target_language_example: Por favor, fale comigo quando tiver um minuto.
native_language_example: Please talk to me when you have a minute.

additional_notes: Imperative form of **falar** used to give a polite/formal instruction (addressing “you” as **você**). **para o** = “to the” (masculine singular), so it’s used before a male person/title (e.g., *o Tom*, *o coronel*). Common patterns: **Fale para o + [person] + infinitive** (*Fale para o Tom fechar...* = “Tell Tom to close...”) or **Fale para o + [person] + que + clause** (*Fale para o coronel que...* = “Tell the colonel that...”).
target_language_example: Fale para o João me ligar quando chegar.
native_language_example: Tell João to call me when he arrives.

additional_notes: Past of "falar" used to say you talked to someone. Very common in conversation; often followed by a person ("falei com o Tom", "falei com ela") or with "sobre" to say what you talked about ("falei com ele sobre..." or "falei sobre... com ele").
target_language_example: Já falei com o médico, e está tudo certo.
native_language_example: I already spoke with the doctor, and everything is fine.

additional_notes: Past tense of falar (to speak/talk): falei = “I spoke/I talked.” Used with com (“to/with”) and the masculine definite article o (“the”) before a man’s name or a masculine noun: “Falei com o Tom” = “I spoke to/with Tom.” For a woman’s name, you typically use “falei com a …” (e.g., “Falei com a Ana”). Also common with a role/title: “Falei com o médico” = “I spoke to the doctor.”
target_language_example: Já falei com o gerente sobre o problema.
native_language_example: I already spoke to the manager about the problem.

additional_notes: Used to say you (the speaker) speak French. It’s the present tense of *falar* (“to speak”): *eu falo* = “I speak / I am speaking.” You can add frequency or context: *todos os dias* (every day), *em casa* (at home), *no trabalho* (at work), *com os meus pais* (with my parents).
target_language_example: Desculpe, não falo francês muito bem.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t speak French very well.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of the verb phrase “falar com” = “to talk to/with.” It’s used to say someone had a conversation with or addressed another person: “falou com ele” (spoke to him), “falou com a gente” (spoke with us). In Portuguese, “com” is required after “falar” when you mention the person you spoke to.
target_language_example: Você realmente falou com o Tom?
native_language_example: Did you really talk to Tom?

additional_notes: Past tense of falar com + ele. Often means “talked to him” (a conversation), but can also be “spoke to him” (briefly). In questions it’s commonly used as “Did you talk to him?”: Você falou com ele? With você, the verb stays in 3rd person (falou).
target_language_example: Você falou com ele ontem à noite?
native_language_example: Did you talk to him last night?

meaning: “(he/she/you) spoke/talked with the …” (to a male person/thing).
additional_notes: “Falou” is the simple past of falar (“to speak/talk”) and is also commonly used in conversation as “you spoke” (você) in Brazilian Portuguese. “Com” means “with/to”. “O” is “the” (masculine singular), so it’s followed by a masculine noun or a man’s name/title: “falou com o Tom”, “falou com o pai”, “falou com o garçom”. For feminine, use “falou com a …”.
target_language_example: Você já falou com o gerente?
native_language_example: Have you talked to the manager?

additional_notes: Uses the conditional form of the verb (here, fazer → faria) to talk about what someone would do in a hypothetical situation, or to ask if someone would do something. Often appears with a subject pronoun: eu faria isso (I would do that), você faria isso? (Would you do that?), ele/ela faria isso (He/She would do that).
target_language_example: Eu não faria isso no seu lugar.
native_language_example: I wouldn’t do that in your place.

meaning: "would do something like that" (often showing shock/disapproval).
additional_notes: Uses the conditional of fazer (faria = would do) to talk about a hypothetical action. Common in questions like “Quem faria uma coisa dessas?” to express disbelief, suspicion, or moral judgment about an act. “dessas” means “like that/like those,” referring back to something just mentioned or understood.
target_language_example: Eu jamais faria uma coisa dessas com você.
native_language_example: I would never do something like that to you.

meaning: “please” (used to ask someone to do or not do something).
additional_notes: Common in Portugal (often as “faz favor” or “faça favor”). Used at the end of a request (“…, faz favor.”) or in the pattern “faz/faça favor de + infinitive” (“faz favor de não me irritar” = “please don’t irritate me”). Depending on tone, it can sound polite or, in a reprimand, more like “just don’t…, please.”
target_language_example: Fecha a porta, faz favor.
native_language_example: Close the door, please.

additional_notes: "faz" is the present tense (ele/ela/você) of "fazer" (to do/make). "isso" means "that/it". Often used when talking about someone’s repeated behavior: "Ele faz isso" = "He does that." In questions, Portuguese may drop the subject: "Por que faz isso?" usually means "Why do you do that?" (speaking to "você").
target_language_example: Por que você faz isso?
native_language_example: Why do you do that?

meaning: “is part of” / “belongs to” (a group, organization, team, etc.).
additional_notes: Used with the verb phrase **fazer parte de** (“to be part of”). **Faz parte da** is used before a **feminine** noun because **de + a = da** (e.g., *da associação*, *da equipe*). With a masculine noun you use **do** (*de + o*): *faz parte do time*. You can also use it in a broader sense of being included in something (*faz parte da cultura* = “it’s part of the culture”).
target_language_example: Meu irmão faz parte da equipe de futebol da escola.
native_language_example: My brother is part of the school's soccer team.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "fazer parte de" (to be part of). It’s used to say something belongs to a group, activity, job, plan, etc., or that something is a normal/expected element of it. "do" is the contraction of "de" + "o" (of the + masculine singular). Other common forms: "faz parte da" (de + a), "faz parte dos" (de + os), "faz parte das" (de + as).
target_language_example: Isso faz parte do acordo.
native_language_example: That’s part of the agreement.

additional_notes: Used to say something is logical/understandable. Often appears as a question (Faz sentido?) meaning “Does it make sense?” or as an answer (Faz sentido.) meaning “That makes sense.” You can also use it with a subject: Isso faz sentido. / Esta frase faz sentido?
target_language_example: Isso faz sentido para você?
native_language_example: Does that make sense to you?

meaning: "It’s been a long time since" (I/we/you last did something).
additional_notes: Used to say you haven’t done/seen something for a long time. Structure: "Faz tempo que não" + present tense (e.g., "vejo", "aparece", "fazemos", "consigo") even though it refers to time up to now. You can add the person/object after the verb: "Faz tempo que não vejo você" = It’s been a long time since I last saw you.
target_language_example: Faz tempo que não falo com a minha irmã.
native_language_example: It’s been a long time since I last talked to my sister.

meaning: "three years ago" / "it’s been three years" (talking about time elapsed).
additional_notes: Uses the impersonal verb "fazer" to say how much time has passed. Very common in patterns like "Faz três anos que..." (It’s been three years since...) or at the end of a sentence: "Eu moro aqui faz três anos." In this use, "faz" stays in the 3rd-person singular (not *faço*).
target_language_example: A gente se mudou para cá faz três anos.
native_language_example: We moved here three years ago.

additional_notes: Literally “does everything” (from the verb fazer, “to do/make”). Used to say someone does all the tasks or takes care of everything. Common variations: “faz tudo por você” = “does everything for you”; “faz tudo do seu jeito” = “does everything your way”; “faz tudo ele mesmo” = “does everything himself.”
target_language_example: Aqui no escritório, a Ana faz tudo sozinha.
native_language_example: Here in the office, Ana does everything by herself.

meaning: "(they/you all) do that" / "(they/you all) do it".
additional_notes: "Fazem" is the present tense (they / you all) form of "fazer" (to do, to make). "Isso" means "that" or "it" (referring to an action or thing already understood). Often appears in questions like "Como é que vocês fazem isso?" (How do you do that?).
target_language_example: Por que tantas pessoas fazem isso?
native_language_example: Why do so many people do that?

additional_notes: “Fazendo” is the gerund of **fazer** (“to do/make”), used to talk about an action in progress or repeated. **Isso** usually means “that/this/it” (often “that/it” in English). Common in questions and descriptions: *estava fazendo isso* (“was doing that”), *continuei fazendo isso* (“I kept doing it”).
target_language_example: Eu estava fazendo isso sem perceber.
native_language_example: I was doing it without realizing it.

meaning: “as a favor” / “please” (asking someone to do something).
additional_notes: Used mainly in polite requests, often at the end of the sentence, similar to “would you… please?” or “if you don’t mind.” Literally “doing a favor,” from the verb phrase “fazer um favor” (to do someone a favor). It can also appear inside a sentence meaning “doing us/me a favor.”
target_language_example: Você pode fechar a janela, fazendo um favor?
native_language_example: Could you close the window, please?

additional_notes: Used for shaving facial hair (usually with a razor). Often appears with a frequency/time expression: “fazer a barba todo dia” (shave every day). You can also specify whose beard with a possessive: “fazer a minha/sua barba”.
target_language_example: Eu preciso fazer a barba antes de sair.
native_language_example: I need to shave before going out.

additional_notes: A common daily routine phrase. Literally “to do the bed,” but the natural meaning is “to make the bed” (arrange the sheets/blankets and pillows). Often used with a subject: “Eu vou fazer a cama” (I’m going to make the bed).
target_language_example: Eu vou fazer a cama todas as manhãs.
native_language_example: I’m going to make the bed every morning.

additional_notes: A very common pattern: **fazer** + **algo** (“something”). Use it when the action isn’t specified or doesn’t matter. Often appears with modal verbs like **querer** (want), **poder** (can), **ter de** (have to), or with time words like **primeiro** (first) and **depois** (after/later). In everyday English it’s usually “do something,” even though the literal translation is “make something.”
target_language_example: Vamos fazer algo este fim de semana?
native_language_example: Shall we do something this weekend?

additional_notes: Common way to say you need to take action (often when there’s a problem): "Temos de fazer alguma coisa" = "We have to do something." You can add what it’s about with "a respeito" (about it) or "sobre" (about), or specify the action after "fazer". Also used with modal/need verbs like "precisar", "ter de", "dever", and "tentar".
target_language_example: Vamos fazer alguma coisa para ajudar.
native_language_example: Let’s do something to help.

meaning: to have sex; to make love.
additional_notes: Common euphemism for having sex, often with a romantic tone. It’s used with or without “com” (with): “fazer amor (com alguém)”. In questions, it can sound forward or intimate: “Quer fazer amor?”
target_language_example: Eles começaram a namorar e, depois de um tempo, decidiram fazer amor.
native_language_example: They started dating and, after a while, they decided to make love.

meaning: to have a birthday; to celebrate one’s birthday (to turn another year older).
additional_notes: Used to say it’s someone’s birthday or that they turn a certain age. Very common with time expressions: “Eu vou fazer aniversário amanhã.” (I’m going to have my birthday tomorrow.) / “Ela vai fazer aniversário em maio.” (She will have her birthday in May.) / “Ele vai fazer aniversário de 30 anos.” (He’s going to turn 30.) You can also ask: “Quando você vai fazer aniversário?” (When is your birthday?).
target_language_example: Eu vou fazer aniversário amanhã.
native_language_example: My birthday is tomorrow.

meaning: to have a birthday; to turn (an age).
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s birthday or the age they are turning. Common patterns: “Hoje eu faço anos” = “It’s my birthday today.” and “Eu faço anos amanhã” = “My birthday is tomorrow.” If you want to specify the age, Portuguese usually says “fazer X anos” (e.g., “Eu faço 30 anos amanhã” = “I turn 30 tomorrow”), but the fixed multi-word term here is “fazer anos”.
target_language_example: Eu faço anos amanhã.
native_language_example: My birthday is tomorrow.

additional_notes: Means “to do that (thing)”, referring to a specific action already known from context. Very common with modal/auxiliary verbs: “poderia fazer aquilo?” (could you do that?), “querer fazer aquilo” (want to do that), “capaz de fazer aquilo” (able to do that), “começou a fazer aquilo” (started to do that), “prestes a fazer aquilo” (about to do that). Often interchangeable with “fazer isso”, but “aquilo” tends to point to something more distant/less immediate (in time, space, or in the conversation).
target_language_example: Eu não vou fazer aquilo de novo.
native_language_example: I’m not going to do that again.

meaning: to do things; to handle things (in a certain way).
additional_notes: A very common, general phrase used to talk about someone’s way/method of doing something (often followed by phrases like “de uma certa maneira”, “do jeito dela”, “assim/desta maneira”). It can refer to routines, decisions, or how you approach tasks, not necessarily physical “making” of objects.
target_language_example: Podemos fazer as coisas com calma.
native_language_example: We can do things calmly.

meaning: to pack (your bags) / to pack up.
additional_notes: Used when you’re preparing to leave (for a trip, moving out, being sent somewhere, etc.). Very common with "ter que" or "precisar" (Ter que fazer as malas = I have to pack). You can also say "começar a fazer as malas" (to start packing).
target_language_example: A gente sai amanhã cedo, então vou fazer as malas hoje à noite.
native_language_example: We leave early tomorrow, so I’m going to pack tonight.

meaning: to make up; to reconcile (after a conflict).
additional_notes: Used when people (or groups) stop being angry at each other and restore a good relationship after a fight or disagreement. It can also be used more generally, e.g., "fazer as pazes com o passado" = to come to terms with the past. Often used with "com": "fazer as pazes com alguém".
target_language_example: Depois da discussão, eles vão fazer as pazes.
native_language_example: After the argument, they’re going to make up.

additional_notes:
Common in two patterns:
1) fazer algo bem = “to do something well” (talking about skill or quality): Você sabe fazer isso bem.
2) fazer bem (a alguém) = “to do (someone) good / be good for (someone)”: Isso vai te fazer bem (“That will do you good”). The “a alguém” is often implied (fazer bem a mim/ele/ela/nós/vocês/eles).
target_language_example: Tenho certeza de que você vai fazer bem a apresentação.
native_language_example: I’m sure you’ll do the presentation well.

meaning: to make a face; to grimace.
additional_notes: Used when someone twists their face to show dislike, disgust, pain, or to tease/joke. You can use it about yourself or others (often with children: “Não faça careta!” / “Não faz careta!”).
target_language_example: Ela fez fazer careta quando provou o remédio.
native_language_example: She made a face when she tasted the medicine.

meaning: to keep someone company; to accompany someone (so they’re not alone).
additional_notes: Used when you stay with someone or go with them to be together (often to be supportive or so they don’t feel lonely). Common patterns: “fazer companhia a alguém” (to keep someone company) and with an object pronoun: “te/lhe fazer companhia”.
target_language_example: Eu vou fazer companhia ao meu avô no hospital.
native_language_example: I’m going to keep my grandpa company at the hospital.

meaning: to go shopping; to do the shopping (buy things).
additional_notes: Literally “to make purchases.” Very common with places: “fazer compras no supermercado/no shopping.” It can mean shopping in general (“Eu gosto de fazer compras”) or doing necessary errands/groceries (“Tenho que fazer compras”).
target_language_example: Vamos fazer compras amanhã de manhã.
native_language_example: Let’s go shopping tomorrow morning.

meaning: to pretend; to make believe; to act as if.
additional_notes: Used when someone is imagining something, playing make-believe (often with kids), or behaving as if something were true when it isn’t. Common patterns: “fazer de conta que + clause” (pretend that…), and “vamos fazer de conta (que…)” (let’s pretend (that…)).
target_language_example: Vamos fazer de conta que está tudo bem.
native_language_example: Let’s pretend everything is fine.

meaning: to do everything / to do anything (to achieve something).
additional_notes: Often used with “para” + infinitive to mean “to do everything (possible) to…”: “Vou fazer de tudo para ajudar.” It can mean literally “do everything” (complete all tasks) or, more commonly, “do everything I can / do whatever it takes,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Vou fazer de tudo para chegar a tempo.
native_language_example: I’ll do everything I can to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Usually needs a noun or an implied object: "fazer esse trabalho" (do this/that job), "fazer esse pedido" (make this/that request). "Esse" commonly refers to something near the listener or something already mentioned (roughly “that”/“this” depending on context). You’ll also see other demonstratives: "fazer este" (this, near me) and "fazer aquele" (that over there).
target_language_example: Você pode fazer esse relatório hoje?
native_language_example: Can you do that report today?

meaning: to be missed; to be needed (to be lacking).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something is absent and you miss them, or that something is necessary and isn’t available. Common patterns: “Você faz falta.” (You’re missed.) / “Você me faz falta.” (I miss you.) / “Faz falta dinheiro.” (Money is needed.) / “Faz falta ter tempo.” (Having time is necessary.) Note: the subject is what is missed/needed; the person who misses can appear as an indirect object (me/te/lhe/nos/lhes).
target_language_example: Você vai fazer falta.
native_language_example: You’ll be missed.

meaning: to border; to share a border (with).
additional_notes: Usually used with "com": "fazer fronteira com" + place/country/region. Common in geography and travel contexts to say two places are neighboring and have a land border.
target_language_example: Portugal e Espanha fazem fronteira.
native_language_example: Portugal and Spain share a border.

meaning: to kill time; to hang around (waiting).
additional_notes: Used when you’re waiting and passing time without a specific task. It can also mean deliberately stalling or making someone wait (e.g., “fazer hora para ele” = to keep him waiting). Don’t confuse with “fazer horas extras” (to work overtime).
target_language_example: Cheguei cedo, então fiquei no café para fazer hora até a loja abrir.
native_language_example: I arrived early, so I stayed at the café to kill time until the store opened.

meaning: to have an idea; (usually) to have no idea.
additional_notes: Most often used with negation: "não faço ideia" = "I have no idea" / "I don’t know at all." You can also hear it as a question to express surprise: "Faz ideia?" = "Can you imagine?" (In Portugal you may also hear "Não faço a mínima ideia" = "I have absolutely no idea.")
target_language_example: Eu não consigo fazer ideia de onde está o meu telemóvel.
native_language_example: I can't imagine / I have no idea where my phone is.

additional_notes: A common way to refer back to an action that was already mentioned or is clear from context. In natural English, it can sometimes also be translated as "do it," depending on the situation.
target_language_example: Eu não posso fazer isso agora.
native_language_example: I can't do that now.

meaning: to do that now / to do it now.
additional_notes: Used to talk about doing a specific thing immediately. Often appears with obligation/necessity verbs like “dever” (should), “ter que” (have to), “precisar” (need to), or permission like “poder” (can). Word order is flexible in speech (e.g., “fazer isso agora” / “agora fazer isso”), but “fazer isso agora” is the most common.
target_language_example: Eu não posso fazer isso agora; faço mais tarde.
native_language_example: I can’t do that now; I’ll do it later.

meaning: to do that again; to do it again.
additional_notes: Used to talk about repeating an action. "Fazer" = "to do/make", "isso" = "that/it" (refers to something just mentioned or understood), and "de novo" = "again". Very common in questions and plans: "Você quer fazer isso de novo?" (Do you want to do it again?).
target_language_example: Não vou fazer isso de novo.
native_language_example: I’m not going to do that again.

additional_notes: Common, flexible phrase built from: fazer (to do/make) + isso (that/it) + hoje (today). Use it to talk about completing a task today. You can swap the time word: fazer isso amanhã (tomorrow), fazer isso agora (now). In questions, it often becomes: Você/Vocês quer(em) fazer isso hoje? (“Do you want to do that today?”).
target_language_example: Eu posso fazer isso hoje, mas não amanhã.
native_language_example: I can do that today, but not tomorrow.

meaning: to do that again; to do it again.
additional_notes: Use this to say someone will repeat an action. It’s built from: fazer (to do/make) + isso (that/it) + novamente (again). In everyday speech, you’ll often also hear "fazer isso de novo" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Não vou fazer isso novamente.
native_language_example: I’m not going to do that again.

meaning: to do that again (to repeat it).
additional_notes: Used to ask or say that an action should be repeated. Very common with polite add-ons like “por favor” (“please”). You can swap “isso” for “isto” (“this”) depending on variety/context, and “outra vez” can also be said as “de novo”. Often appears with “ter que / ter de” (“have to”): “Você tem que fazer isso outra vez.”
target_language_example: Desculpa, não ouvi bem — podes fazer isso outra vez?
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t hear well — can you do that again?

additional_notes: Used when someone offers, agrees, or is willing to do something on another person’s behalf. You can change the pronoun: fazer isso por mim (for me), por ele/ela (for him/her), por nós (for us), por vocês (for you all). In questions: Você pode fazer isso por mim?
target_language_example: Posso fazer isso por você hoje.
native_language_example: I can do that for you today.

meaning: to do this alone / by yourself.
additional_notes: Used when someone will do a task without help. It often implies independence or that help is needed (especially in negatives like “não posso fazer isso sozinho”). You can swap in another object: “fazer isso” (do it) + “sozinho/sozinha” (alone), matching the person’s gender. In Portuguese, “sozinho” can mean both “alone” and “on your own” (without help).
target_language_example: Você consegue fazer isso sozinho ou quer ajuda?
native_language_example: Can you do this on your own, or do you want help?

additional_notes: Common, neutral way to talk about performing an action (“do this”). It often appears after verbs that take an infinitive, especially with the preposition “a”: aprender a fazer isto (learn to do this), começar a fazer isto (start to do this). In everyday speech, “isso” is frequently used instead of “isto,” but both mean “this” in this kind of sentence.
target_language_example: Não sei como fazer isto sozinho.
native_language_example: I don’t know how to do this by myself.

meaning: to harm; to be bad for; to make (someone) feel sick.
additional_notes: Used to say something is harmful or unhealthy (often with an indirect object introduced by “a/ao/à”: “faz mal a alguém” = it harms someone) or that it makes you feel unwell (“Isso me faz mal” = That makes me feel sick / doesn’t agree with me). Common with foods, habits, weather, etc.: “fazer mal à saúde” (to be bad for your health).
target_language_example: Leite pode fazer mal para algumas pessoas, então elas evitam.
native_language_example: Milk can be bad for some people, so they avoid it.

meaning: to screw up; to do something really stupid (vulgar).
additional_notes: Informal and crude: literally “to do shit,” but it’s used to mean making a mess of something, making a bad mistake, or causing trouble. Common in warnings (“Não vai fazer merda”) or to admit fault (“Eu fui fazer merda e…”).
target_language_example: Eu fui fazer merda e apaguei o arquivo errado.
native_language_example: I went and screwed up and deleted the wrong file.

additional_notes: Means “to do nothing / not do anything,” often used after words like “sem” (without) or “não” (not). Common patterns: “sem fazer nada” = “without doing anything”; “não fazer nada” = “to not do anything.” In negative sentences, it can also imply “there’s nothing (we) can do” (e.g., “não podíamos fazer nada”). In “não vou te fazer nada,” it means “I’m not going to do anything to you” (i.e., harm you).
target_language_example: Hoje eu só quero ficar em casa sem fazer nada.
native_language_example: Today I just want to stay home and do nothing.

additional_notes: Used to say someone repeats an action or behaves in the same way as someone else, or that they’re able/allowed to do an identical action. Often followed by “que + [person/clause]”: “fazer o mesmo que eu” = “do the same as me.”
target_language_example: Se você pedir sem gelo, eu posso fazer o mesmo.
native_language_example: If you ask for it without ice, I can do the same.

additional_notes: Used before a verb (often 'querer') to mean doing whatever someone wants or doing what is necessary/appropriate in context. Very common in patterns like: 'fazer o que eu quero' (do what I want), 'fazer o que você quiser' (do whatever you want), 'deixar alguém fazer o que…' (let someone do what…).
target_language_example: Você pode fazer o que quiser, mas tem que avisar antes.
native_language_example: You can do whatever you want, but you have to let me know first.

additional_notes: Used in questions about what someone wants, plans, or is going to do. Very common after another verb, as in quer fazer o quê? In pra fazer o quê?, it can mean 'what for?'. Literally, it is 'do what'.
target_language_example: Depois do trabalho, você vai fazer o quê?
native_language_example: After work, what are you going to do?

meaning: to do the work; to get the job done.
additional_notes: Used for completing a task or piece of work. Often appears with modifiers like "direito" (properly) or "pela metade" (halfway), and with objects like "o trabalho sujo" (the dirty work). It can also be used in questions about someone’s ability: "Ele consegue fazer o trabalho?"
target_language_example: Se você começar, eu te ajudo a fazer o trabalho.
native_language_example: If you start, I’ll help you do the work.

meaning: to be part of; to belong to.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is included in a group, family, project, or situation. Common pattern: "fazer parte de + noun" (fazer parte da família; fazer parte deste projeto). You can also use it alone as an invitation: "Venha fazer parte" (“Come join us / come be part of it”).
target_language_example: Estou orgulhoso de fazer parte deste projeto.
native_language_example: I am proud to be part of this project.

meaning: to make light of; to mock; to downplay.
additional_notes: Very commonly used as **fazer pouco de (alguém/alguma coisa)**. It can mean (1) **to mock/tease** someone or (2) **to downplay/underestimate** something (treat it as unimportant).
target_language_example: Você está a fazer pouco de mim?
native_language_example: Are you making fun of me?

meaning: to do anything; to do whatever (someone wants).
additional_notes: Common with the idea of having no limits or being free/able to choose: Você pode fazer qualquer coisa! (“You can do anything!”). In questions it often means “anything at all”: Se você pudesse fazer qualquer coisa… (“If you could do anything…”). With fear/hesitation it means being afraid to take any action: medo de fazer qualquer coisa (“afraid to do anything”). You’ll also see it followed by a clause: qualquer coisa que (eu/ele) quisesse = “whatever (I/he) wanted.”
target_language_example: Hoje eu posso fazer qualquer coisa que eu quiser.
native_language_example: Today I can do whatever I want.

meaning: to insist (on); to make a point of; to really want to (as something matters to you).
additional_notes: Commonly used as "fazer questão de" + infinitive or noun to emphasize that something is important to you and you are determined to do it or have it done. Often implies polite insistence or emphasis: "Eu vou fazer questão de..." (I’ll make a point of / I’ll insist on...). Conjugates like a normal verb phrase (e.g., "faço", "fez", "vai fazer").
target_language_example: Eu vou fazer questão de pagar a conta.
native_language_example: I’m going to insist on paying the bill.

meaning: to make sense; to be logical/meaningful.
additional_notes: Used to say something is understandable or logical (or not). Very common with negation: “não faz sentido” = “it doesn’t make sense.” You can also use it about something being meaningful: “Isso faz sentido para mim” = “That makes sense to me.”
target_language_example: Isso pode fazer sentido para você?
native_language_example: Can that make sense to you?

meaning: to have sex; to have sexual intercourse.
additional_notes: Common and fairly direct way to talk about having sex. Conjugates like a normal verb phrase: fazer (present) / fez (past) / fazendo (gerund). Often used with "com" + a person ("fazer sexo com alguém" = have sex with someone) and in the negative ("não fazer sexo" = not have sex).
target_language_example: Eles não querem fazer sexo agora.
native_language_example: They don't want to have sex right now.

meaning: to pretend; to act like (put on an act).
additional_notes: Informal (very common in Brazil). Used when someone is deliberately acting a certain way—often to look cool, impress someone, or hide what they really feel. It can also appear as “fazer tipo que …” = “to pretend that …”.
target_language_example: Ele fez tipo que não ouviu e continuou andando.
native_language_example: He pretended he didn’t hear and kept walking.

additional_notes: Used when you need to call someone, usually by phone. You can specify the type: "fazer uma ligação telefônica" (make a phone call), or the destination: "fazer uma ligação para o Japão" (make a call to Japan). Very common with "precisar" and "ter que/ter de" to say you need to call.
target_language_example: Vou fazer uma ligação rapidinho e já volto.
native_language_example: I’m going to make a quick call and I’ll be right back.

meaning: to take a break; to pause.
additional_notes: Used when you stop an activity for a short rest. Common at work or while studying: "Preciso fazer uma pausa" (I need a break). Often used with "precisar", "querer", "poder", or "dever" + infinitive. It can also mean pausing a conversation or task briefly, depending on context.
target_language_example: Vamos fazer uma pausa de cinco minutos.
native_language_example: Let’s take a five-minute break.

additional_notes: Used when you want to ask someone some questions (often in a polite or low-pressure way). Very common with "preciso" (I need to) or "quero" (I want to): "Preciso fazer umas perguntas." You can add an indirect object: "te" (to you, informal), "lhe" (to you, formal), or "a você".
target_language_example: Posso fazer umas perguntas sobre o seu trabalho?
native_language_example: Can I ask a few questions about your job?

additional_notes: A very common, child-friendly/euphemistic way to say “to urinate.” Used with ter que (“have to”): "Tenho que fazer xixi" = “I have to pee.” You can also hear "fazer cocô" for “to poop.”
target_language_example: Espera um minutinho — eu preciso fazer xixi.
native_language_example: Wait a minute — I need to pee.

additional_notes: "fazê-lo" is "fazer" + the object pronoun "-lo" (= "him/it"). It’s often used after an infinitive (or certain verb forms) where Portuguese attaches the pronoun to the end with a hyphen. Depending on context, it can mean "do it" (with "-lo" = "it") or "make him do..." / "make it happen" (with "-lo" = "him" or "it"), especially when followed by another verb: "fazê-lo mudar" = "make him change".
target_language_example: Eu não consigo fazê-lo funcionar.
native_language_example: I can’t make it work.

additional_notes: Imperative (command) form of **fazer** + the object pronoun **o** (“it” or “him”), written with a hyphen. Often used as a direct command: **Faça-o agora mesmo.** It can also be followed by an infinitive to mean “make him/it (do something)”: **Faça-o entrar** (“Make him/it come in”), **Faça-o parar** (“Make him/it stop”).
target_language_example: Se você acha melhor, faça-o hoje.
native_language_example: If you think it’s best, do it today.

additional_notes: Uses the formal command form (imperative) of fazer: faça (“do/make”). Often said to give someone permission, show indifference, or end an argument: “Go ahead—do whatever you want.” You can also say “faça o que você quiser” (same meaning, with você).
target_language_example: Se você não quer ouvir meu conselho, faça o que quiser.
native_language_example: If you don’t want to listen to my advice, do whatever you want.

additional_notes: From the verb "fazer" (to do/make): "faço" = "I do/make" (present tense). "Isso" means "that/it" (often something just mentioned or understood from context). Used to talk about doing an action or habit: "Eu faço isso" = "I do that", but Portuguese can drop "eu" and just say "Faço isso".
target_language_example: Não faço isso com frequência.
native_language_example: I don’t do that often.

additional_notes: Used when asking for permission or offering to close a window (e.g., because of cold, noise, or rain). In Portuguese, you can use "Devo..." (Should I...?) or "Posso..." (May/Can I...?) before it. The verb is "fechar" (to close) + "a janela" (the window).
target_language_example: Está frio aqui — vou fechar a janela.
native_language_example: It’s cold in here — I’m going to close the window.

additional_notes: Used when asking or reminding someone to shut the door. Common in polite requests with "pode/poderia" (can/could), "por favor" (please), or "você se importaria em..." (would you mind...). Often followed by "ao sair" = "when you leave/on your way out."
target_language_example: Você poderia fechar a porta, por favor?
native_language_example: Could you close the door, please?

additional_notes: Imperative form of the verb “fechar” (to close) used to give an instruction. Commonly said to one person; to be more polite you can add “por favor” (“Feche a porta, por favor.”). “Feche a porta atrás de você” means “Close the door behind you.”
target_language_example: Feche a porta, por favor, está fazendo frio.
native_language_example: Close the door, please—it's cold.

additional_notes: Imperative (command/request) form of "fechar" (to close) + "os olhos" (the eyes). It’s typically used when giving instructions (e.g., during a test, exercise, meditation, or to help someone remember something). You can soften it with "por favor" ("Feche os olhos, por favor.").
target_language_example: Feche os olhos por um momento e respire fundo.
native_language_example: Close your eyes for a moment and take a deep breath.

additional_notes: "Fechou" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "fechar" (to close). It’s used for a completed action in the past. Often appears with "a porta" (the door) or with a specific door: "fechou a porta do escritório" (closed the office door). You can also use it as a question: "Quem fechou a porta?" (Who closed the door?).
target_language_example: Antes de sair, ele fechou a porta.
native_language_example: Before leaving, he closed the door.

additional_notes: Usually appears with a helper verb like ter/haver to form the past (“ter feito isso” = “to have done that/it”). It refers back to something already mentioned (isso = “that/it”). You’ll often see it in different tenses/moods: “já tinha feito isso” (had already done it), “nunca tenha feito isso” (have never done it), “pode ter feito isso” (may have done it).
target_language_example: Eu nunca tinha feito isso antes.
native_language_example: I had never done that before.

additional_notes: Used as a Christmas greeting, either on its own ("Feliz Natal!") or as part of a longer wish like "Desejo um feliz Natal" (I wish you a Merry Christmas). "Natal" is the holiday; "feliz" means happy. You can add who you’re greeting (e.g., "pessoal" = folks/everyone) or who you’re wishing it to ("pra todo mundo" = for everyone).
target_language_example: Feliz Natal, família!
native_language_example: Merry Christmas, family!

additional_notes: Standard birthday greeting. Often followed by the person’s name ("Feliz aniversário, Tom!") or a form of address like "vovó" (grandma). You can also say "Feliz aniversário para você!" (Happy birthday to you!).
target_language_example: Feliz aniversário, mãe! Espero que você tenha um dia lindo.
native_language_example: Happy birthday, Mom! I hope you have a lovely day.

additional_notes: A common greeting said around New Year’s (before and after midnight on December 31 / January 1). Often used on its own or followed by wishes like "Feliz Ano Novo e muita saúde!" Capitalization varies; you’ll often see it written as "Feliz Ano Novo" in messages and cards.
target_language_example: Feliz Ano Novo! Que seja um ano cheio de paz e saúde.
native_language_example: Happy New Year! May it be a year full of peace and health.

additional_notes: Used for the household appliance that you use to remove wrinkles from clothes. Often said as “ferro de passar roupa(s)” to make it extra clear it’s for clothes. In Brazil, “ferro” alone can also mean an ironing iron when the context is obvious.
target_language_example: Você pode desligar o ferro de passar quando terminar?
native_language_example: Can you turn off the iron when you’re done?

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of fazer (“to do/make”) in the 3rd person singular: fez. It’s commonly used with você (which takes 3rd-person verb forms) as well as ele/ela. Often used to say someone took some action (“at least you did something”) or in questions implying suspicion/curiosity (“Did you do something…?”).
target_language_example: Você fez alguma coisa para ajudar?
native_language_example: Did you do anything to help?

additional_notes: "Fez" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "fazer" (to do/to make) for ele/ela/você. "Aquilo" means "that" (often something more distant, previously mentioned, or a specific thing/situation). The phrase is often used to point to or take responsibility for an action: "Quem fez aquilo?" = "Who did that?"
target_language_example: Ele fez aquilo de propósito.
native_language_example: He did that on purpose.

additional_notes: Past (simple past / pretérito perfeito) of "fazer" (to do/make) + "isso" (that/it). It usually refers to a specific action someone completed in the past. Changes with the subject: "eu fiz isso" (I did that), "ela fez isso" (she did that), "eles fizeram isso" (they did that).
target_language_example: Por que você fez isso?
native_language_example: Why did you do that?

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of **fazer** (“to do/make”) with **isto** (“this”). Used to say that someone did something in the past, often in questions or accusations (e.g., “Quem fez isto?”). **Isto** usually refers to something close to the speaker or something happening right now; in everyday speech, **isso** is also very common depending on context.
target_language_example: Quem fez isto?
native_language_example: Who did this?

additional_notes: Past tense of fazer (“to do/make”) + o que (“what/that which”). Used to say someone did what another person said/asked, or did what was necessary (often followed by a clause: “fez o que + [someone said/was needed]”).
target_language_example: Ela fez o que eu pedi.
native_language_example: She did what I asked.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "fazer" used to praise someone for a completed action. You can change the subject (e.g., eu fiz, você fez, ela fez, nós fizemos) and add emphasis like "realmente" (really). Often used with "Você" (informal) or "O senhor/A senhora" (formal).
target_language_example: Parabéns, você fez um bom trabalho no relatório.
native_language_example: Congratulations, you did a good job on the report.

meaning: 'made a' / 'did a' (past tense of fazer + a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun to say someone created, prepared, built, or carried out something: fez uma salada (made a salad), fez uma doação (made a donation), fez uma lista (made a list). It’s the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of fazer for ele/ela/você: ele fez uma…. For a masculine noun, you usually see fez um….
target_language_example: Ela fez uma reserva para amanhã.
native_language_example: She made a reservation for tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say that a place is located far away from where you are now. It’s built with: ficar (to be/ to be located) + longe (far) + daqui (from here). Very common in questions and negatives: "Fica longe daqui?" (Is it far from here?), "Não fica longe daqui." (It’s not far from here.).
target_language_example: O supermercado fica longe daqui?
native_language_example: Is the supermarket far from here?

additional_notes: Used to say where a place/thing is situated. It’s the verb "ficar" (to be located) + "no" (= "em" + "o", meaning "in/on the"). Very common for giving addresses/locations: "O restaurante fica no centro." The exact English preposition depends on the place: often "in" (in Portugal, in the city) or "on" (on the third floor, on the east side).
target_language_example: A farmácia fica no centro da cidade.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is located in the city center.

additional_notes: A compositional phrase meaning to remain in this place. It can be used for people staying somewhere or for things that should remain where they are, as in 'isso deve ficar aqui' = 'this should stay here.'
target_language_example: Vou ficar aqui até você voltar.
native_language_example: I'll stay here until you come back.

meaning: to be okay / to be fine; (also) to look good (on someone)
additional_notes: Commonly used to reassure someone that a person or situation will turn out okay, especially about the future (e.g., “vai ficar bem” = “you’ll be okay / it’ll be fine”). Although it can be understood literally as “to remain well,” English usually renders it as “be okay/fine.” In another frequent sense, it means “to look good (on someone)” (e.g., “Essa camisa fica bem em você.”).
target_language_example: Escute, você vai ficar bem.
native_language_example: Listen, you’ll be okay.

meaning: to stay with him; to keep/have him (and often: to hook up with him).
additional_notes: "Ficar com" is a very common phrase. Literally it’s "to stay with," but depending on context it can mean (1) to keep/hold onto something or someone (e.g., "You can keep him/it"), or (2) to get romantically involved in a casual way ("hook up"/"make out"), especially in Brazilian Portuguese. The surrounding context usually makes the meaning clear.
target_language_example: Você quer ficar com ele hoje à noite?
native_language_example: Do you want to hook up with him tonight?

additional_notes: Used to say someone stays/keeps staying at home instead of going out (often by choice or because they have to, e.g., illness). With a time expression it can imply duration: "ficar em casa a semana inteira" = "stay home the whole week".
target_language_example: Hoje eu vou ficar em casa e descansar.
native_language_example: Today I'm going to stay at home and rest.

meaning: to stand up; to remain standing (on your feet).
additional_notes: Used when someone moves into a standing position or stays standing instead of sitting/lying down. Common in rules/instructions (e.g., “Não é pra ficar em pé” = “You’re not supposed to stand up/be standing”). With places like buses, it often means “to stand (not sit)” during the ride.
target_language_example: Se você estiver cansado, pode sentar; não precisa ficar em pé.
native_language_example: If you’re tired, you can sit down; you don’t need to stand.

meaning: to wise up; to be alert/watch out.
additional_notes: Often used as a warning or advice to pay attention and not be fooled (similar to “be careful” or “stay sharp”). Literally “to become smart/clever,” but in everyday speech it commonly means to be on your guard. Note: in the imperative you’ll often hear “fica esperto” (without the final -r), but the dictionary form is “ficar esperto.”
target_language_example: Você precisa ficar esperto com esse golpe na internet.
native_language_example: You need to watch out for that online scam.

meaning: to fall behind; to be left behind.
additional_notes: Used when someone/something doesn’t keep up (in a race, a group, progress at work/school, etc.). It can be literal (not moving forward with others) or figurative (lagging in progress). Also common in the sense of “leave the past behind” (deixar algo para trás).
target_language_example: Se você não estudar, vai ficar para trás na turma.
native_language_example: If you don’t study, you’ll fall behind in the class.

meaning: 'to be alone' / 'to stay by yourself' (said by a woman).
additional_notes: Used to say you want to be alone for a while (not with other people). With a man, you’d say "ficar sozinho". "Ficar" often means "to stay/remain" or "to end up"; here it’s about staying in that state (alone).
target_language_example: Depois do trabalho, eu só quero ficar sozinha um pouco.
native_language_example: After work, I just want to be alone for a bit.

meaning: to be alone; to stay alone (by yourself).
additional_notes: "Ficar" often means "to stay" or "to end up" in a situation. "Ficar sozinho" is commonly used to say you want some time by yourself (often to rest, think, or have privacy). You can add a reason with "para": "ficar sozinho para pensar".
target_language_example: Vou ficar sozinho um pouco para descansar.
native_language_example: I’m going to be alone for a bit to rest.

meaning: 'will be fine/OK' or 'will look good (on someone)'.
additional_notes: Future tense of "ficar" + "bem". Most commonly used to reassure someone: "Tudo ficará bem" = "Everything will be fine." With people, it often means someone’s health/situation will turn out OK: "Ele ficará bem." With clothes or appearance, it means something will suit/look good on someone: "Este chapéu ficará bem nela."
target_language_example: Não se preocupe, tudo ficará bem amanhã.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything will be fine tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express pleasure or willingness about doing something. Typically followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., ajudar, ouvir, saber, conhecer). In speech, you may also hear it as “Fico feliz em…” (“I’m happy to…”), or with other subjects: “Ele/Ela fica feliz em…” (“He/She is happy to…”).
target_language_example: Fico feliz em ajudar você com isso.
native_language_example: I’m happy to help you with that.

additional_notes: Used to express happiness/relief about a situation or fact. After “que”, Portuguese typically uses the subjunctive (“esteja”, “tenha”, “não foi nada” can also appear) to talk about how you feel about something rather than stating it neutrally.
target_language_example: Fico feliz que você tenha chegado bem.
native_language_example: I’m glad you arrived safely.

additional_notes: "Ficou" is the past (pretérito perfeito) of "ficar" and often means "to become" in these contexts. "Ficou doente" indicates a change of state (someone wasn’t sick before, then became sick). You can add time expressions like "neste final de semana" (this weekend) or "há alguns dias" (a few days ago).
target_language_example: Ela ficou doente neste final de semana.
native_language_example: She got sick this weekend.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **ficar** in the past tense (**ficou**) to say someone remained at home instead of going out/going to work/going to school. The subject is usually clear from context or stated explicitly (e.g., **Maria ficou em casa**). Often appears with time expressions (**ontem**, **o dia todo**, **a semana inteira**) or reasons (**porque estava doente**).
target_language_example: Ontem, Maria ficou em casa o dia todo.
native_language_example: Yesterday, Maria stayed at home all day.

additional_notes: "Ficou" is the past tense of "ficar" and often means "to become" or "to remain." "Em silêncio" means "in silence." Used to describe a person or a place that suddenly becomes quiet, or someone who stops talking for a moment.
target_language_example: Quando ouviu a notícia, ela ficou em silêncio.
native_language_example: When she heard the news, she fell silent.

additional_notes: From **ficar** (“to become/to end up”) + **louco** (“crazy”). Often used as an exclamation or rhetorical question to show surprise, disbelief, or criticism: **Você ficou louco?** can mean “Are you crazy?” (not necessarily a literal mental-health statement). You can change the person: **eu fiquei louco**, **ela ficou louca**, **eles ficaram loucos**.
target_language_example: Você ficou louco? Isso é muito perigoso.
native_language_example: Are you crazy? That’s very dangerous.

additional_notes: Used with ficar in the past tense (ele/ela/você ficou) to describe a change of state or how someone ended up feeling/being, usually followed by an adjective: ficou muito impressionada, ficou muito preocupado, ficou muito cético, ficou muito rico. Other forms: eu fiquei, nós ficamos, eles/elas ficaram.
target_language_example: Ela disse que ficou muito impressionada.
native_language_example: She said she became very impressed.
