additional_notes: A noun phrase for the genre in books, movies, and TV. Often used after verbs like gostar de (to like) and ler/assistir (to read/watch): "gosto de ficção científica", "leio ficção científica". You can also shorten it in casual speech to "sci-fi" (pronounced like in English).
target_language_example: Você prefere comédia ou ficção científica?
native_language_example: Do you prefer comedy or science fiction?

meaning: a very strong insult: “son of a bitch” / “motherf***er”.
additional_notes: Extremely offensive and vulgar; avoid in polite conversation. Literally “daughter of a prostitute/whore,” but it’s used like English “son of a bitch/motherf***er” to insult someone, express rage, or emphasize something negative (e.g., “Guerra filha da puta!” = “F***ing war!”). Often appears with gender/number variants: “filho da puta” (male), “filhos da puta” (plural).
target_language_example: Cale a boca, filha da puta!
native_language_example: Shut up, you motherf***er!

additional_notes: Extremely vulgar/insulting; used to curse at someone or call them a disgusting person. Often used alone as an exclamation (“Filho-da-puta!”) or directed at someone with “seu” (“Seu filho-da-puta!” = “You son of a bitch!”). Avoid in polite settings.
target_language_example: Seu filho-da-puta, sai daqui agora!
native_language_example: You son of a bitch, get out of here now!

additional_notes: A common Brazilian Portuguese insult used to show anger, contempt, or frustration. It can sometimes be said jokingly among close friends, but it’s still rude/offensive and not appropriate in polite situations. Often used alone as an exclamation (“Filho da mãe!”) or to refer to someone (“Aquele filho da mãe…”).
target_language_example: Aquele filho da mãe me enganou e ainda riu da minha cara.
native_language_example: That bastard tricked me and still laughed in my face.

additional_notes: Very strong, vulgar insult. Used to refer to someone (“Ele é um filho da puta.” = “He’s a motherfucker/son of a bitch.”) or to address them directly (“Anda, filho da puta!”). Extremely offensive—avoid in polite or everyday situations. Can also be intensified with adjectives before it (e.g., “seu … filho da puta”).
target_language_example: Esse filho da puta mentiu pra mim.
native_language_example: That motherfucker lied to me.

meaning: only child (a son with no siblings).
additional_notes: Used to say someone has no brothers or sisters. For a girl, you usually say “filha única”. In religious contexts, “o Filho único de Deus” means “the only begotten Son of God” (Jesus).
target_language_example: Ele é filho único, então cresceu sem irmãos.
native_language_example: He’s an only child, so he grew up without siblings.

additional_notes: Strong profanity used to insult or express anger, often shouted as an exclamation (“Filhos da puta!”). It’s plural; singular is “filho da puta”. Avoid in polite conversation—can easily start a fight.
target_language_example: Saiam daqui, seus filhos da puta!
native_language_example: Get out of here, you motherfuckers!

additional_notes: Commonly used with the preposition "no" ("on/at the weekend"): "no fim-de-semana". In greetings/well-wishes, you can say "Bom fim-de-semana" (“Have a good weekend”). In European Portuguese this is the standard spelling; in Brazilian Portuguese you often see "fim de semana" (without hyphens).
target_language_example: Vamos descansar no fim-de-semana.
native_language_example: We’re going to rest on the weekend.

additional_notes: Informal and often emphatic; used to shut down a conversation, argument, or topic (can be said alone: “Fim de papo!”). Literally “end of chat/talk,” but it functions like “No more discussion.” Note: a related phrase is “não estou a fim de papo” = “I’m not in the mood to talk.”
target_language_example: Eu já decidi: vamos embora, fim de papo.
native_language_example: I’ve already decided: we’re leaving, end of discussion.

additional_notes: Common everyday term for Saturday and Sunday. Often used with prepositions like “no fim de semana” (on/over the weekend) and “antes do fim de semana” (before the weekend). You can also say “bom fim de semana!” as a friendly send-off.
target_language_example: Vamos à praia no fim de semana.
native_language_example: Let's go to the beach this weekend.

meaning: “end of the world”; also “the middle of nowhere” (very far away).
additional_notes: Literally “end of the world.” It can be used (1) in the literal/apocalyptic sense, or (2) hyperbolically to mean something very distant/remote (“no fim do mundo”). In questions like “É o fim do mundo?”, it often means “Is it the end of the world?” / “Is it really that terrible?” (sometimes implying “It’s not the end of the world.”).
target_language_example: A casa deles fica no fim do mundo, mas é linda.
native_language_example: Their house is in the middle of nowhere, but it’s beautiful.

additional_notes: Common way to refer to Saturday and Sunday (or the period from Friday night through Sunday). Often used with demonstratives/prepositions: "neste/este final de semana" (this weekend), "no próximo final de semana" (next weekend), "passar o final de semana" (to spend the weekend).
target_language_example: Vamos viajar no próximo final de semana.
native_language_example: We’re going to travel next weekend.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the ending of a story, movie, book, or situation that turns out well. Very common with "com" (e.g., "um filme com final feliz") and in questions like "Tem/Existe um final feliz...?".
target_language_example: Tomara que este livro tenha um final feliz.
native_language_example: I hope this book has a happy ending.

additional_notes: A common everyday noun for the thin string used to clean between teeth. Often used with verbs like “usar” (to use) and “passar” (to floss): “passar fio dental” = “to floss.” You can also say “um fio dental” when referring to a piece/container of floss.
target_language_example: Você tem fio dental? Eu preciso passar fio dental depois de comer.
native_language_example: Do you have dental floss? I need to floss after eating.

additional_notes: Imperative (command/request) using the você form of the verb ficar (“to stay”). Used to tell someone to remain in the same place, often temporarily (e.g., while you do something).
target_language_example: Fique aqui, por favor, e espere um minuto.
native_language_example: Stay here, please, and wait a minute.

additional_notes: Imperative form of the verb ficar (“to stay”) + calmo (“calm”), used to tell someone to remain calm. Often said in tense situations; you can soften it with “por favor” (Por favor, fique calmo.) or use “fique calma” when speaking to a woman.
target_language_example: Por favor, fique calmo e me escute um minuto.
native_language_example: Please stay calm and listen to me for a minute.

additional_notes: Imperative form (você) of "ficar" + "longe": a command/request telling someone not to come near something/someone, often for safety or to set a boundary. Common patterns: "Fique longe de + [thing/person]" (Stay away from...), "Fique longe daqui" (Stay away from here). Can also be used alone: "Fique longe!".
target_language_example: Fique longe da janela, por favor.
native_language_example: Stay away from the window, please.

additional_notes: Imperative in the você form (formal or neutral), from ficar (“to stay”) + quieto (“quiet/still”). Used to tell someone to stop talking or stop moving, often as a warning (e.g., so someone won’t hear you). You can also hear: “Fique quieta” (to a woman) and “Fiquem quietos/quietas” (plural).
target_language_example: Fique quieto por um minuto, por favor.
native_language_example: Be quiet for a minute, please.

meaning: "I suddenly got/ended up with" (a feeling, condition, or situation).
additional_notes: Past tense of "ficar com" (eu fico com → eu fiquei com). Very common for emotions/conditions that come on suddenly: "fiquei com inveja" (I got jealous), "fiquei com medo" (I got scared), "fiquei com sono" (I got sleepy). With "sorte", it means "to get lucky" (not literally "to stay with luck").
target_language_example: Quando vi o preço, fiquei com medo de comprar.
native_language_example: When I saw the price, I got scared to buy it.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "ficar" + "em casa". Use it to say you remained at home (often because of weather, being sick, or choosing not to go out). You can also say "não fui a/ao/à + place; fiquei em casa" (“I didn’t go to…; I stayed home”).
target_language_example: Hoje eu não saí: fiquei em casa e descansei.
native_language_example: Today I didn’t go out: I stayed at home and rested.

additional_notes: Commonly refers to sticky tape used for sealing, fixing, or holding things together (similar to Scotch tape). You may also hear it with a specific type, e.g., “fita adesiva transparente” (clear tape) or “rolo de fita adesiva” (a roll of tape).
target_language_example: Preciso de fita adesiva para fechar essa caixa.
native_language_example: I need tape to seal this box.

additional_notes: "Fiz" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "fazer" (to do/make) for "eu" (I). "Isso" means "that/it" (something not close to the speaker, or just a general "it"), and can refer back to an action already mentioned: "Nunca fiz isso" = "I’ve never done that." Often used to explain a reason with "porque" or "pelo/pela" (because of/for): "Fiz isso pelo Sami" = "I did it for Sami."
target_language_example: Desculpa — fiz isso sem pensar.
native_language_example: Sorry — I did it without thinking.

additional_notes: "Fizeram" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "fazer" for "eles/elas" (they) or "vocês" (you all). "isso" means "that/it" (a specific action or thing already known from context). Often used in questions ("Como fizeram isso?" = "How did you do that?") or statements ("Eles fizeram isso" = "They did it").
target_language_example: Por que vocês fizeram isso?
native_language_example: Why did you (all) do that?

meaning: "(if someone) did that" / "were to do that" (imperfect subjunctive of fazer + isso).
additional_notes: Used with the imperfect subjunctive (fizesse) to talk about a hypothetical or uncertain action in the past or future. Common after "se" (if) and after verbs/expressions that trigger the subjunctive, like "querer que" (to want someone to…), "pedir que" (to ask that…), and "permitir que" (to allow that…). Often implies something imagined or not yet real: "Se eu fizesse isso, ..." = "If I did that / If I were to do that, ...".
target_language_example: Se eu fizesse isso agora, eu teria problemas.
native_language_example: If I did that now, I would have problems.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase for a forest in hot, humid regions with lots of rainfall. Often used in environmental contexts (e.g., protecting nature). You’ll also hear it with an article: “a floresta tropical” (the tropical rainforest).
target_language_example: Muitos animais vivem na floresta tropical.
native_language_example: Many animals live in the tropical rainforest.

meaning: “Fuck it.” / “Screw it.” (expression of anger, frustration, or not caring).
additional_notes: Very vulgar and informal. Often used alone as an outburst (“Foda-se!”). It can also start a sentence meaning “whatever / I don’t care, let’s do it,” like “Foda-se, vamos nessa.” Literally comes from the verb “foder” (“to fuck”) + “-se,” but it’s used idiomatically as an exclamation and is not appropriate in polite situations.
target_language_example: Foda-se, não vou discutir mais.
native_language_example: Fuck it, I’m not going to argue anymore.

additional_notes: In Portuguese it’s very often used in the plural: “fogos de artifício” (fireworks, as a display). Singular “fogo de artifício” refers to one firework.
target_language_example: Comprámos um fogo de artifício para celebrar a passagem de ano.
native_language_example: We bought a firework to celebrate New Year’s Eve.

additional_notes: Plural phrase. Used for public displays or individual fireworks (the show or the items). Often appears with verbs like ver/assistir (to watch), fazer/soltar (to set off), detestar (to hate).
target_language_example: Vamos ver os fogos de artifício na praia hoje à noite.
native_language_example: Let's watch the fireworks on the beach tonight.

additional_notes: "Foi" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "ir" (to go) for ele/ela/você. Use "foi a" before a destination (city/country/event) when the destination takes the preposition "a". Often contracts: "foi a" + "o" → "foi ao"; "foi a" + "os" → "foi aos"; "foi a" + "a" → "foi à"; "foi a" + "as" → "foi às". Example: "Ele foi ao cinema" / "Ele foi à escola".
target_language_example: Ela foi a Lisboa no ano passado.
native_language_example: She went to Lisbon last year.

additional_notes: Used to say someone went to a masculine singular place/event. It’s the past tense of ir (“to go”) in the ele/ela/você form: foi. ao is the contraction of a + o (“to the” + masculine singular). For feminine singular, you use foi à (a + a).
target_language_example: Ele foi ao mercado depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: He went to the market after work.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "ir embora" = "to leave/go away." It often implies leaving a place or departing (sometimes “leave for good,” depending on context). Used with many subjects: "Eu fui embora" (I left), "Eles foram embora" (They left).
target_language_example: Quando terminou a reunião, ele foi embora sem dizer nada.
native_language_example: When the meeting ended, he left without saying anything.

meaning: “went too far” (crossed a line; overdid it).
additional_notes: Used to say someone’s action, comment, or behavior was excessive or unacceptable. Common with “você” (você foi longe demais) or with names (Tom foi longe demais). Often refers to a social/moral boundary, not physical distance.
target_language_example: Eu acho que você foi longe demais.
native_language_example: I think you went too far.

meaning: “went to / went to the” (he/she/it went to).
additional_notes: Past tense of *ir* (“to go”): *ele/ela foi* = “he/she went.” Used with destinations or places. *para* can mean “to” or “toward,” often with the sense of purpose/destination. Use *para a* before feminine singular nouns (*para a Austrália, para a França, para a universidade*) and *para o* before masculine singular nouns (*para o Brasil, para o trabalho*). It can also be used for outcomes like punishments (*foi para a detenção* = “got sent to detention”).
target_language_example: Ela foi para a praia depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: She went to the beach after work.

additional_notes: Past tense (ele/ela/você) of **ir para a cama** (“to go to bed”). Often used for the moment someone goes to bed (not necessarily that they fell asleep). You can add time words like **logo após/depois** (“right after/after”) or actions before it (e.g., **tomou um banho e foi para a cama**).
target_language_example: Ela estava cansada e foi para a cama cedo.
native_language_example: She was tired and went to bed early.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of **ir** (to go): **foi** = “went” for **ele/ela/você**. Used when someone leaves and goes to their home. Often followed by how they got home: **de ônibus** (by bus), **a pé** (on foot). You can change the subject: **Eu fui para casa** (I went home), **Nós fomos para casa** (we went home).
target_language_example: Depois do trabalho, Fadil foi para casa.
native_language_example: After work, Fadil went home.

meaning: "went to" (he/she/it went to + a feminine noun/place).
additional_notes: "Foi" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "ir" (to go), used for a completed action. "À" = "a" (to) + "a" (the), so it’s used before feminine singular places/nouns (e.g., "à praia", "à biblioteca", "à prisão"). With masculine nouns you use "ao" (e.g., "foi ao mercado"), and with most countries you use "a" without the article (e.g., "foi a Portugal"), though some take an article (e.g., "foi à Itália").
target_language_example: Ela foi à farmácia comprar remédio.
native_language_example: She went to the pharmacy to buy medicine.

additional_notes: "Foi" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "ir" (to go) for ele/ela/você. "À" = "a" (to) + "a" (the, feminine), because "escola" is feminine: "a escola". Used to say that he/she went to school on a particular day/occasion; it can also imply attending school that day (as opposed to staying home).
target_language_example: A menina foi à escola apesar de estar doente.
native_language_example: The girl went to school despite being sick.

additional_notes: Used to say something was the first one in a sequence or ranking. It’s the past tense of "ser" (foi = was) + the feminine form "a primeira"; use "foi o primeiro" for masculine. Often followed by a noun (e.g., "a primeira escolha", "a primeira palavra") or used when the noun is understood from context.
target_language_example: Ela foi a primeira a chegar.
native_language_example: She was the first to arrive.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened for the first time in the past. The verb after "que" is commonly in the simple past (pretérito perfeito) to describe what happened: "Foi a primeira vez que vi...", "Foi a primeira vez que nós viemos...". You can change the tense to match the situation (e.g., "É a primeira vez que..." = "It’s the first time that...").
target_language_example: Foi a primeira vez que eu viajei sozinho.
native_language_example: It was the first time that I traveled alone.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has been accused/charged with a crime or wrongdoing. It’s the past tense passive of "acusar": "ele foi acusado de...". Commonly followed by a verb in the infinitive ("de + infinitive": "de desperdiçar") or by a noun ("de lavagem de dinheiro", "de assassinato", "de sequestro").
target_language_example: Ele foi acusado de lavagem de dinheiro.
native_language_example: He was accused of money laundering.

additional_notes: Passive voice in the past: "foi" (was) + "assassinado" (killed intentionally, usually with planning). It can refer to any murder, but "assassinated" is especially natural for famous or political figures (e.g., Júlio César). You can add the agent with "por": "foi assassinado por Maria" (was murdered by Maria), or the place/time: "foi assassinado ali" / "na noite passada".
target_language_example: O jornalista foi assassinado perto de casa.
native_language_example: The journalist was murdered near his house.

meaning: “that’s how (it happened)” / “that’s how it was that …”
additional_notes: Used to introduce an explanation of how something happened or how someone achieved something. It’s in the past tense (foi = “was”), so it’s common in storytelling or recounting events. Often followed by a verb phrase: “Foi assim que eu aprendi…” = “That’s how I learned…”.
target_language_example: Foi assim que eu consegui o emprego.
native_language_example: That’s how I got the job.

additional_notes: Uses the passive voice: ser + past participle (foi + atropelado) to say someone was struck/run over by a vehicle. The past participle agrees with the subject: atropelado (masculine singular) / atropelada (feminine singular). You can also change the agent: “foi atropelado por um ônibus” (by a bus).
target_language_example: O meu cachorro foi atropelado por um carro.
native_language_example: My dog was hit by a car.

meaning: was able to; managed to (was capable of doing).
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "ser capaz de" + infinitive. Used to talk about a specific completed moment of ability/possibility: "Ele não foi capaz de abrir a caixa" = he couldn’t manage to open it. Often implies success/failure in doing something, and can sound a bit more emotional or emphatic than plain "pôde" (could).
target_language_example: Ela foi capaz de terminar o trabalho antes do prazo.
native_language_example: She was able to finish the work before the deadline.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) + passive voice: "foi" (was) + "construída" (built). Used to talk about when something got built. It agrees with the noun: "foi construída" (feminine singular, e.g., casa/igreja/ponte); masculine is "foi construído" (e.g., prédio); plural is "foram construídos/construídas".
target_language_example: A escola foi construída em 1998.
native_language_example: The school was built in 1998.

additional_notes: Past passive form: foi (was) + construído (built). Used when the focus is on the building/result, and the person/company who built it is unknown or not mentioned. Agree in gender/number with the thing built: masculine singular “foi construído”; feminine singular “foi construída”; plural “foram construídos/construídas”.
target_language_example: Você pode me dizer em que ano este edifício foi construído?
native_language_example: Can you tell me what year this building was built?

additional_notes: Forma passiva (pretérito perfeito) de "criar" no sentido de educar/criar uma criança (“to raise/bring up”). Usa-se muito para falar de criação e contexto de infância (família, religião, lugar). Concorda com o gênero e número: "ele foi criado", "ela foi criada", "eles foram criados", "elas foram criadas".
target_language_example: Ele foi criado nos Estados Unidos, mas sua língua nativa é o japonês.
native_language_example: He was raised in the United States, but his native language is Japanese.

additional_notes: Past (pretérito perfeito) passive form of demitir: “(someone) was fired.” Used to say a person lost their job because the employer ended the contract. It agrees with the person’s gender/number: foi demitido (he/one man), foi demitida (she/one woman), foram demitidos/demitidas (they).
target_language_example: Ele foi demitido por faltar no trabalho.
native_language_example: He was fired for missing work.

additional_notes: Past, passive-voice form: "foi" (was) + past participle "destruída" (destroyed). It agrees with a feminine noun (e.g., "a cidade", "a ponte"). For a masculine subject you use "foi destruído"; for plural: "foram destruídas/destruídos". Often followed by "por" or "pela" to say who/what caused it.
target_language_example: A casa foi destruída pelo incêndio.
native_language_example: The house was destroyed by the fire.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) in the passive voice: "foi" (was) + "destruído" (destroyed). Used when the focus is on what happened to something, not on who did it. It agrees with the noun: masculine singular "foi destruído"; feminine singular "foi destruída"; plural "foram destruídos/destruídas".
target_language_example: O computador foi destruído na enchente.
native_language_example: The computer was destroyed in the flood.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of **ser**: **foi** = “was.” Used to talk about something that was difficult in the past, often followed by an infinitive (**Foi difícil estudar...** = “It was hard to study...”) or with a noun (**O exame foi difícil** = “The exam was difficult”). Common in tag questions: **Foi difícil, não foi?** = “It was hard, wasn’t it?”
target_language_example: Foi difícil terminar o trabalho a tempo.
native_language_example: It was hard to finish the work on time.

additional_notes: Passive voice in the past: (someone/something) “was found,” often by someone unspecified. Used for locating missing people/objects (“foi encontrado”), discovering something (“um meteorito foi encontrado”), or in news/police contexts (“foi encontrado com...” = “was found with...” indicating possession at the time). Feminine form: “foi encontrada”; plural: “foram encontrados/encontradas.”
target_language_example: O documento foi encontrado no carro.
native_language_example: The document was found in the car.

additional_notes: Past passive form: "foi" (was) + "feito" (made/done). Used to say something was made/produced (often with "em" or "no/na" for place: "feito no Japão") or that work/actions were done ("Muito trabalho foi feito"). With people it can mean 'was made into' or 'was taken' in a certain state, e.g. "foi feito prisioneiro" = 'was taken prisoner' / 'was made a prisoner'. For plural, use "foram feitos/feitas".
target_language_example: O bolo foi feito ontem à noite.
native_language_example: The cake was made last night.

additional_notes: Passive form of ferir (“to injure/wound”): ser (in the past: foi) + ferido (past participle). Common in news, accidents, and conflicts. Often followed by details like how/when (durante..., no...) or where on the body (na perna, no braço).
target_language_example: Ele foi ferido durante a briga, mas já está melhor.
native_language_example: He was injured during the fight, but he’s better now.

additional_notes: Past tense of “ser” (foi = was) + “fácil” (easy). Often used impersonal to comment on a situation: “Aquilo foi fácil.” You can add “para + person” to say it was easy for someone: “Foi fácil para eles…”. Common in the negative: “Não foi fácil.”
target_language_example: O teste foi fácil.
native_language_example: The test was easy.

additional_notes: Used to react to or describe a past experience or event. "Foi" is the past tense of "ser" (to be) for "it/he/she," and "incrível" means amazing/incredible. You can swap in a noun: "O filme foi incrível" (The movie was amazing).
target_language_example: A viagem foi incrível!
native_language_example: The trip was amazing!

meaning: "that’s what" / "that was what" (emphasizing what happened/was said/was meant).
additional_notes: Used to highlight or clarify the specific thing that happened, was said, or was meant. Very common with verbs like acontecer (to happen), dizer (to say), querer dizer (to mean), imaginar (to imagine). In negative form: "Não foi isso que..." = "That’s not what...". Often followed by a verb clause: "Foi isso que eu vi" (That’s what I saw).
target_language_example: Foi isso que eu ouvi ontem à noite.
native_language_example: That’s what I heard last night.

additional_notes: Very common, informal apology used alone (“Foi mal!”) or before/after what you’re apologizing for (“Foi mal ter…” / “Verdade, foi mal.”). It can also be literal in other contexts meaning “went badly / did badly,” especially with “em/no/na”: “Ele foi mal no teste” = “He did badly on the test.”
target_language_example: Foi mal, eu esqueci de te responder.
native_language_example: Sorry, I forgot to reply to you.

additional_notes: Past passive form: "ser" (foi) + past participle (morto). Often followed by the agent with "por" ("by"), e.g. "foi morto por um tiro" = "was killed by a gunshot". "Morto" comes from "morrer" (to die), but "foi morto" usually implies someone/something caused the death (killed).
target_language_example: O rei foi morto durante a guerra.
native_language_example: The king was killed during the war.

additional_notes: Uses the past tense of **ser** (*foi* = “was”) + **muito** (“very”) to intensify an adjective: **foi muito + adjective** (e.g., *foi muito simples* = “it was very simple”). Often used to describe how something/someone was in the past.
target_language_example: A viagem foi muito boa.
native_language_example: The trip was very good.

additional_notes: Used to say you really enjoyed something in the past (a meeting, event, concert, experience). Very common as a standalone comment (“Foi muito bom!”). It can be followed by an infinitive to say what was good: “Foi muito bom te ver” (“It was great to see you”).
target_language_example: O jantar foi muito bom, obrigado.
native_language_example: Dinner was very good, thank you.

meaning: 'it was very difficult' / 'that was very hard'.
additional_notes: Uses the past tense of "ser" (foi = "was"). You can use it to comment on a situation in the past, often followed by an infinitive: "Foi muito difícil + verb" (e.g., "foi muito difícil dizer..."). It can refer to something specific just mentioned ("That was very difficult") or to an event in general ("It was very difficult").
target_language_example: Foi muito difícil encontrar um apartamento barato.
native_language_example: It was very difficult to find a cheap apartment.

additional_notes: Past of "ser" ("to be") + masculine singular definite article "o" ("the"). Used to identify or emphasize who/what did something, often in cleft sentences like "foi o Tom quem..." = "it was Tom who...". Changes with gender/number: "foi o" (masc. sing.), "foi a" (fem. sing.), "foram os" (masc. pl.), "foram as" (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Foi o João quem me ligou ontem.
native_language_example: It was João who called me yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something was first in a sequence or the first person to do something. Uses the past tense of ser (foi = “was”). It changes for gender/number: foi a primeira (feminine), foram os primeiros / foram as primeiras (plural). Often followed by a noun or role: “foi o primeiro presidente” = “was the first president.”
target_language_example: Rajendra Prasad foi o primeiro presidente da Índia.
native_language_example: Rajendra Prasad was the first president of India.

additional_notes: Used to say someone did an action after everyone else. Structure: “[Name] foi o último a + infinitive” (e.g., chegar, entrar, sair). With a female subject, it becomes “foi a última a”. With plural subjects, “foram os/as últimos/as a”.
target_language_example: Tom foi o último a chegar aqui.
native_language_example: Tom was the last to arrive here.

additional_notes: Used to state that a single (male) person was the only one to do something. It is typically followed by a verb clause: “foi o único que + verb”. The phrase inflects for number and gender when needed (e.g., “foi a única que” for a female subject; “foram os únicos que / foram as únicas que” for plural).
target_language_example: O Tom foi o único que me ajudou.
native_language_example: Tom was the only one who helped me.

additional_notes: Past (preterite) passive form: ser (foi) + past participle (pego). Often used when someone is caught by someone else (e.g., by the police) or caught doing something. The participle changes for gender/number: foi pego (masc. sg.), foi pega (fem. sg.), foram pegos/pegas (plural).
target_language_example: O ladrão foi pego pela polícia.
native_language_example: The thief was caught by the police.

meaning: "that’s why" / "that’s the reason (why)" (referring to a past reason).
additional_notes: Used to introduce an explanation or the cause of something that already happened. It often points back to something mentioned before. You can change the tense/person: "é por isso que" (that’s why, in general/present), "era por isso que" (that was why), etc.
target_language_example: Eu estava doente; foi por isso que não fui ao trabalho.
native_language_example: I was sick; that’s why I didn’t go to work.

additional_notes: Past (pretérito perfeito) of the passive form of prender (“to arrest”). Used when the subject is the person arrested: Ele foi preso. You can add where/when (na Argélia, na noite passada) or the reason with por + infinitive: Foi preso por oferecer dinheiro à polícia.
target_language_example: Ele foi preso por dirigir bêbado.
native_language_example: He was arrested for driving drunk.

additional_notes:
Past passive form: 
- foi = “was” (past of ser)
- roubada = “stolen” (agrees with a feminine singular thing: bolsa, bicicleta, carteira).
Use it to report theft: “X foi roubada.” For masculine nouns: “foi roubado” (e.g., Meu celular foi roubado).
target_language_example: Minha mochila foi roubada no metrô.
native_language_example: My backpack was stolen on the subway.

additional_notes: Past (perfect) passive with "ser": "X foi roubado" = “X was stolen.” You can use it for objects (car, phone) and also for places/people in the sense of a robbery (e.g., "O banco foi roubado" = “The bank was robbed”; "Ele foi roubado" = “He got robbed”). Feminine/plural changes: "foi roubada" (fem. singular), "foram roubados/roubadas" (plural).
target_language_example: Meu celular foi roubado no metrô.
native_language_example: My phone was stolen on the subway.

additional_notes: Past of "ser" (to be) in the 3rd person singular (ele/ela/você; also used for "it"): "foi" = "was". "um" is the masculine form of "a/an"; before a feminine noun, use "foi uma" (e.g., "Foi uma situação engraçada"). Often used to describe what something/someone was: "Ontem foi um bom dia" = "Yesterday was a good day."
target_language_example: O filme foi um sucesso.
native_language_example: The movie was a success.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened unintentionally. "foi" is the past of "ser" (to be), so this is a common explanation after a mistake or mishap. It can also be used as a question: "Foi um acidente?" = "Was it an accident?"
target_language_example: Desculpa, foi um acidente.
native_language_example: Sorry, it was an accident.

meaning: "It was a disaster." (something went very badly).
additional_notes: Used to describe a situation, event, attempt, or relationship that turned out very poorly. It often refers to something finished (past). You can intensify it with "total": "foi um desastre total" = "it was a total disaster." You can also swap in other subjects: "A festa foi um desastre" (The party was a disaster), "Isto foi um desastre" (This was a disaster).
target_language_example: O encontro foi um desastre, mas pelo menos a comida estava boa.
native_language_example: The date was a disaster, but at least the food was good.

meaning: “it was a day …” (used to describe how the day was).
additional_notes: Commonly followed by an adjective or description: "Foi um dia bom/ruim/cansativo/estressante". Often used with "Hoje" to mean "Today was a … day". You can also add intensifiers like "muito" (very) and "bem" (really/quite) before the adjective.
target_language_example: Hoje foi um dia muito bom.
native_language_example: Today was a very good day.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of **ser**: **foi** = “was.” Used to say that an action, decision, or situation turned out badly: **X foi um erro**. You can intensify with adjectives: **foi um erro grave/imperdoável** (“a serious/unforgivable mistake”). Said about a person (**Você foi um erro**) is very harsh/insulting.
target_language_example: Sair sem avisar foi um erro.
native_language_example: Leaving without letting anyone know was a mistake.

additional_notes: Used to say an event, performance, project, surgery, party, film, etc. went well or achieved the desired result. It’s the past tense of "ser" (foi = was). You can also negate it: "não foi um sucesso" (wasn’t a success). Often appears as "X foi um sucesso" (The X was a success).
target_language_example: A apresentação foi um sucesso, e o público aplaudiu muito.
native_language_example: The presentation was a success, and the audience applauded a lot.

additional_notes: Used to describe/identify something in the past: “It/that/this was a …”. It’s “foi” (past of ser) + “uma” because the noun that follows is feminine (uma surpresa, uma escolha, uma noite). For masculine nouns you use “foi um” (e.g., foi um erro).
target_language_example: Foi uma decisão difícil.
native_language_example: It was a difficult decision.

meaning: "it was an experience" (something you went through).
additional_notes: Used to describe how an event felt or what it was like, often followed by an adjective (e.g., "muito legal", "doida") or a clause explaining the situation. "Foi" is the past tense of "ser" (to be), so this refers to a completed event.
target_language_example: Foi uma experiência incrível conhecer o Rio pela primeira vez.
native_language_example: It was an amazing experience to visit Rio for the first time.

meaning: “it was a great …” / “it was a big …” (used before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to评价 something in the past: “Foi uma grande honra/perda/invenção.” Here, “uma” + “grande” agrees with a feminine singular noun. With a masculine noun, you typically say “foi um grande …” (e.g., “foi um grande erro”). “Grande” can mean “great” (importance/quality) or “big” (size), depending on context.
target_language_example: Foi uma grande surpresa ver você aqui.
native_language_example: It was a big/great surprise to see you here.

meaning: “it was a night…” (talking about how a night was).
additional_notes: Used to describe a past night, usually followed by an adjective or description: “Foi uma noite maravilhosa/escura/quente.” You can also use it on its own (“Foi uma noite.”) to imply “It was quite a night” (often with emotional emphasis). Literal translation is possible, but in English you often add “It was” + description.
target_language_example: Foi uma noite longa, mas muito divertida.
native_language_example: It was a long night, but very fun.

meaning: 'it was you who…' (emphasizes that you did it).
additional_notes: Used to point out or confirm who did something, often in questions. It’s a cleft sentence: **foi** (was) + **você** (you) + **que** (who/that) + verb. You can change the person: **foi ele/ela que…** (it was he/she who…), **fui eu que…** (it was I who…).
target_language_example: Foi você que falou com o gerente ontem?
native_language_example: Was it you who spoke with the manager yesterday?

meaning: "it was you who…" (emphasizes that YOU did it).
additional_notes: This is a cleft structure used for emphasis/contrast, often in questions or accusations. It highlights the subject: Foi você quem fez isso? = “Was it you who did this?” You can change the tense/person: foi ele quem… (“it was he who…”), era você quem… (“it was you who…” / “you used to be the one who…”). In Brazilian Portuguese, “você quem” is common; in more formal writing you may also see “você que”.
target_language_example: Foi você quem me ajudou ontem?
native_language_example: Was it you who helped me yesterday?

additional_notes: Used to talk about going somewhere in the past: **nós fomos** (preterite of *ir*, “to go”) + **ao** (= *a* + *o*, “to the” for a masculine singular place). Common with places and events: *ao parque, ao jogo, ao colégio*. For other forms: **fomos à** (feminine singular), **fomos aos** (masculine plural), **fomos às** (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Ontem, fomos ao cinema depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: Yesterday, we went to the movie theater after work.

additional_notes: Common everyday term for something you wear in or over your ears to listen to audio. Often used with the verbs pôr/colocar (“to put on”) and usar (“to use”). You may also hear just fone in casual speech when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Você pode tirar o fone de ouvido, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you take off your headphones, please?

meaning: “outside the box”; (also literally) “out of the box.”
additional_notes: Often used with the verb pensar: pensar fora da caixa = to think creatively / in an unconventional way. It can also be used literally to mean something is physically outside a box/container; in casual speech it may be used humorously in other “out of the box” senses.
target_language_example: Precisamos de uma solução nova — vamos pensar fora da caixa.
native_language_example: We need a new solution—let’s think outside the box.

meaning: outside the city; out of town.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is not in the city (often away traveling) or that something happens beyond the city limits. Common with verbs like estar (to be), morar/viver (to live), and passar (to spend time): “Ele está fora da cidade” = “He’s out of town.”
target_language_example: Desculpa, não posso ir hoje — estou fora da cidade.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go today — I’m out of town.

additional_notes: Used to indicate leaving this place. Common in commands like "Sai fora daqui!" or the more informal/slangy "Cai fora daqui!" (= “Get out of here!”). It can also be used more neutrally with verbs like "empurrar" (to push) or "tirar" (to remove) someone "para fora daqui".
target_language_example: Vamos embora — eu quero ir para fora daqui agora.
native_language_example: Let’s go — I want to get out of here now.

additional_notes: Used to say something/someone is not inside a place or is beyond a limit (e.g., fora de lá = out of there; fora de alcance = out of reach; fora de nossa jurisdição = outside our jurisdiction). It also appears in set phrases like "fora de brincadeira" meaning "seriously / no kidding".
target_language_example: O restaurante fica fora de mão, mas a comida é ótima.
native_language_example: The restaurant is out of the way, but the food is great.

meaning: out of the house; away from home.
additional_notes: Used for being physically outside your home (e.g., leaving someone/something outside) or being away from home for a period of time. Common with verbs like ficar/passar (“to stay/spend time”) and with activities like jantar/comer (“to have dinner/eat out”).
target_language_example: Hoje vou trabalhar fora de casa.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to work away from home.

additional_notes: Used to say a situation, things, or a person is no longer being managed or restrained and is getting worse/too extreme. Common with verbs like "estar" and "ficar" ("está/está ficando fora de controle"). Can also be said directly to someone as a reprimand: "Você está fora de controle!"
target_language_example: A festa ficou fora de controle depois da meia-noite.
native_language_example: The party got out of control after midnight.

additional_notes: Used to show that something/someone is not inside a place, not within a limit (e.g., “fora do estádio”, “fora do meu raio de visão”), or excluded from something (“fora do assunto”). It’s the contracted form of “fora de + o”. With other nouns you’ll see: “fora da” (de + a), “fora dos” (de + os), “fora das” (de + as). Often used in commands like “Fora do meu caminho!” (“Out of my way!”).
target_language_example: O gato ficou fora do quarto a noite toda.
native_language_example: The cat stayed out of the room all night.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that is not normal/typical. Very common in the pattern “nada fora do comum” (“nothing unusual”), often in reports or when reassuring someone that everything is normal.
target_language_example: Foi um dia tranquilo, nada fora do comum.
native_language_example: It was a quiet day, nothing out of the ordinary.

additional_notes: Used with plural subjects (eles/elas, people) to say someone left a place. It’s the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "ir embora" (to go away/leave). You can often add "já" (already): "já foram embora" = "they’ve already left."
target_language_example: Quando chegamos, eles já foram embora.
native_language_example: When we arrived, they had already left.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of **ir** + **para**, used to say someone went to a destination/place. **Foram** agrees with **eles/elas** (they) or **vocês** (you all). In everyday speech, **para** is often shortened to **pra**: *foram pra casa*.
target_language_example: Depois do trabalho, eles foram para o restaurante.
native_language_example: After work, they went to the restaurant.

additional_notes: Past tense of the passive voice: ser (foram = “were”) + morto(s) (“killed”). Use it when the subject is the victim: Eles foram mortos. The form changes for gender/number: foram mortos (masc. plural/mixed), foram mortas (fem. plural), foi morto/foi morta (singular). Often used in news or reports.
target_language_example: Muitos soldados foram mortos aqui.
native_language_example: Many soldiers were killed here.

additional_notes: Used in everyday and especially scientific/sci‑fi contexts to refer to any kind of living entity (human, animal, microbe, or even an alien/AI). Often appears with an article: "uma forma de vida" (a life form) or in plural: "formas de vida" (life forms).
target_language_example: Não importa o que diga, você não tem provas de que é uma forma de vida!
native_language_example: No matter what you say, you have no proof that it is a life form!

meaning: willpower; self-control to keep doing something even when it’s hard.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "ter" (to have): "ter força de vontade" = to have willpower. Often modified with intensifiers like "muita" (a lot of) or "suficiente" (enough), and it can be used when encouraging, doubting, or praising someone’s discipline and persistence.
target_language_example: Para parar de fumar, você vai precisar de muita força de vontade.
native_language_example: To quit smoking, you’re going to need a lot of willpower.

additional_notes: "Fosse" is the imperfect subjunctive form of "ir" in the expression "ir embora" (to leave/go away). It commonly appears after verbs like "pedir" (to ask) and "querer" (to want), and after "como se" (as if): e.g., "pediu que ela fosse embora" = "asked her to leave".
target_language_example: Ela queria que eu fosse embora mais cedo.
native_language_example: She wanted me to leave earlier.

additional_notes: Used especially after verbs of belief/opinion (e.g., *achar, pensar*) and after *como se* (“as if”) to talk about something that’s uncertain, hypothetical, or just someone’s impression. The subject usually comes before it: *Achei que ele fosse um…* / *Como se fosse um…*.
target_language_example: Ela falou comigo como se fosse um especialista.
native_language_example: She spoke to me as if she were a specialist.

additional_notes: Used to list the two languages someone speaks/knows ("falar"), or to say they are spoken in a place (often with "ser falado": "são falados"). You can swap in other languages: "português e espanhol", etc.
target_language_example: Na minha escola, muita gente fala francês e inglês.
native_language_example: At my school, a lot of people speak French and English.

additional_notes: A common food item. Usually refers to chicken pieces that have been fried; you’ll often hear it in restaurants or when talking about what someone likes to eat.
target_language_example: Vou pedir frango frito no restaurante.
native_language_example: I’m going to order fried chicken at the restaurant.

meaning: 'in front of' / 'facing'; also 'compared to' or 'in the face of'.
additional_notes: Used mainly (1) for physical position: "O carro está frente a casa." (= in front of the house), and (2) in more formal/abstract contexts meaning "when faced with" or "given": "Frente a uma crise...". It can also mean "compared to": "Frente a outras opções...". Very commonly appears as "frente à" when followed by a feminine singular noun with the definite article (a + a = à), but "frente a" may appear when the article is absent.
target_language_example: Frente a este prédio, há uma praça pequena.
native_language_example: In front of this building, there is a small square.

additional_notes: Used mainly in writing and more formal speech. It can mean a physical position ("in front of") or a situation/challenge ("faced with"). The form "à" (with the accent) is used when "a" + "a" combine (e.g., "frente à escola" = "in front of the school"). You may also see "frente a" without the accent in some contexts.
target_language_example: Ficamos em silêncio frente à notícia.
native_language_example: We stayed silent in the face of the news.

meaning: seafood (food from the sea, especially shellfish).
additional_notes: Often used in the plural as "frutos do mar" to refer to seafood in general (common on menus, e.g., "arroz de frutos do mar"). In the singular, "fruto do mar" can refer to one item/piece of seafood, or it may be used as a category name in some contexts. It typically includes shrimp, clams, mussels, and other shellfish.
target_language_example: Este prato leva fruto do mar.
native_language_example: This dish contains seafood.

additional_notes: Common menu/restaurant term for food that comes from the sea (often especially shrimp, crab, mussels, etc.). Used with verbs like comer (to eat) and pedir (to order). Often treated as a mass noun: Comer frutos do mar / Pedir frutos do mar.
target_language_example: Hoje vamos pedir frutos do mar no restaurante.
native_language_example: Today we’re going to order seafood at the restaurant.

additional_notes: Past (pretérito perfeito) of **ir** (“to go”) + **lá** (“there,” usually meaning a place not close to the speaker). Used to say you went to a place at least once in the past; often appears with time words like **uma vez** (once) or **novamente** (again).
target_language_example: Eu fui lá ontem com meus amigos.
native_language_example: I went there yesterday with my friends.

meaning: 'I went to' / 'I went toward' (past of ir + para).
additional_notes: Used to say you went to a destination in the past. 'Fui' is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of 'ir' for 'eu' (I), and 'para' usually means 'to' (often with the idea of heading toward a place). Common with cities, countries, events, etc.: 'Fui para casa' (I went home), 'Fui para o trabalho' (I went to work).
target_language_example: Ontem, eu fui para a praia com meus amigos.
native_language_example: Yesterday, I went to the beach with my friends.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "ir" (to go): "eu fui" = "I went." Used to say you got into bed, usually to sleep or to rest. You can add a time connector like "depois de" (after) or "assim que" (as soon as): "Fui para a cama depois de comer."
target_language_example: Eu estava muito cansado, então fui para a cama cedo.
native_language_example: I was very tired, so I went to bed early.

meaning: "It was me who…" / "I was the one who…" (emphasizing that *I* did it).
additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize the subject (“me”) in the past, often to claim responsibility or deny it (with “não fui eu que…”). It’s a common Portuguese emphasis structure: [ser] + [subject] + que + [verb]. You can change the tense/person, e.g., “foi ele que…”, “fomos nós que…”.
target_language_example: Fui eu que paguei a conta.
native_language_example: It was me who paid the bill.

meaning: "It was I who…" / "I was the one who…" (emphasis: I did it).
additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that YOU were the person who did an action. Literally it’s the past of “ser” (fui = I was) + “eu” (I) + “quem” (who), followed by a verb describing what you did. Common in confessions, clarifications, or defending yourself: “Fui eu quem fez isso” = “I’m the one who did that.”
target_language_example: Fui eu quem ligou para você ontem à noite.
native_language_example: It was me who called you last night.

additional_notes: “Um” is short for “one” of something that’s understood from context—most often “um cigarro” (a cigarette) or, in informal contexts, “um baseado” (a joint). It’s a casual way to say you’re going to smoke one.
target_language_example: Vou ali fora fumar um e já volto.
native_language_example: I'm going outside to smoke one and I'll be right back.

meaning: rock bottom; the lowest point (in a bad situation).
additional_notes: An idiomatic expression used to say someone has reached (or is close to reaching) the worst moment of a crisis—emotionally, financially, etc. Often used with verbs like “chegar ao fundo do poço” (to hit rock bottom) or “ir/levando para o fundo do poço” (to drag/take someone down toward rock bottom). Literally it means “the bottom of a well,” but it’s usually meant figuratively.
target_language_example: Depois que perdi o emprego, achei que tinha chegado ao fundo do poço.
native_language_example: After I lost my job, I thought I had hit rock bottom.

additional_notes: Used to specify the US sport (NFL-style) and distinguish it from "futebol" (soccer) in Portuguese. Often appears with verbs like "jogar" (to play) and "assistir/ver" (to watch).
target_language_example: Eu gosto de assistir futebol americano aos domingos.
native_language_example: I like to watch American football on Sundays.

additional_notes: Refers to the vacation period in summer, especially the school break. Commonly used with possessives (minhas/suas/nossas férias de verão) and with prepositions like depois de (“after”) and nas próximas (“during the next”).
target_language_example: Nas férias de verão, a gente costuma viajar e descansar.
native_language_example: During summer vacation, we usually travel and rest.

meaning: to make a living; to earn one’s livelihood.
additional_notes: Used to talk about earning enough money to support yourself (often by working). It’s common with verbs like "trabalhar" (to work) and can be followed by "com" + an activity: "ganhar a vida com música" (make a living from music).
target_language_example: Ele trabalha duro para ganhar a vida.
native_language_example: He works hard to make a living.

additional_notes: Used to talk about getting money through work, business, investments, etc. In many contexts it’s closer to “earn money” than “win money,” even though ganhar can also mean “to win.” Often appears as an infinitive phrase (e.g., Para ganhar dinheiro..., um jeito de ganhar dinheiro).
target_language_example: Ela quer ganhar dinheiro trabalhando online.
native_language_example: She wants to make money working online.

meaning: 'the cat is' (talking about where the cat is or what condition it’s in).
additional_notes: "Gato" means “cat,” and "está" is the verb "estar" (he/she/it is). Use "estar" for location and temporary states/conditions: "O gato está na cozinha" (location), "O gato está acima do peso" (condition), "O gato está olhando" / "está se escondendo" (actions in progress).
target_language_example: O gato está dormindo no sofá.
native_language_example: The cat is sleeping on the couch.

additional_notes: Informal Brazilian Portuguese expression. Often used with "ser" to describe someone as friendly or kind: "Ela é gente boa." It can also be used as a way to address a group, similar to “folks/guys”: "Gente boa, por favor!" (like “Folks, please!”). Despite containing "gente" (“people”), it can describe one person ("Ele é gente boa") or many ("Tem muita gente boa...").
target_language_example: O João é gente boa, sempre ajuda todo mundo.
native_language_example: João is a nice guy; he always helps everyone.

meaning: a really nice person; good people (often with a sense of being classy/respectable).
additional_notes: Common in Brazilian Portuguese. You can use it to compliment someone’s character (friendly, decent, trustworthy), and sometimes also their manners or social class (“refined”). It can refer to one person (“Ela é gente fina”) or people in general. Often intensified with “muito” or “demais” (e.g., “gente fina demais”).
target_language_example: O João é gente fina; sempre ajuda todo mundo.
native_language_example: João is a really nice guy; he always helps everyone.

meaning: “likes the” / “enjoys the” (talking about a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: In Portuguese, the verb is gostar de (“to like”). When it’s followed by a feminine singular noun with the article a (“the”), de + a contracts to da. So gosta da = “(he/she) likes the …”. Example: gosta da professora (“likes the teacher”). For masculine singular, it’s gosta do (de + o).
target_language_example: Ela gosta da música brasileira.
native_language_example: She likes Brazilian music.

additional_notes: 3rd-person singular form of gostar de. It means 'he/she likes' and is also used for 'you like' with você, o senhor, or a senhora. Portuguese uses de after gostar: gosta de música ('likes music'), gosta de dançar ('likes to dance').
target_language_example: Ela gosta de café.
native_language_example: She likes coffee.

meaning: (he/she) likes to do that / likes doing that.
additional_notes: Used with the verb gostar de + infinitive to talk about enjoying an activity. Here, gosta is the 3rd person singular (ele/ela/você). You can change it: eu gosto de fazer isso (I like to do that), nós gostamos de fazer isso (we like to do that), eles gostam de fazer isso (they like to do that). In everyday speech, you may also hear "gosta disso" (likes that) when the context makes the action clear.
target_language_example: Ela gosta de fazer isso nos fins de semana.
native_language_example: She likes to do that on weekends.

additional_notes: From the verb "gostar de" (to like). It’s used for liking a person; depending on context/tone it can be friendly ("He likes me") or romantic ("He’s into me"). In questions, Portuguese often uses rising intonation: "Ele gosta de mim?". You can swap the pronoun: "gosta de você" (likes you), "gostam de nós" (like us).
target_language_example: Acho que ela gosta de mim.
native_language_example: I think she likes me.

additional_notes: Used with the verb gostar de (“to like”), which takes de before what you like. Here, gosta is the 3rd-person singular (ele/ela/você). You can add a style/genre after música: gosta de música country / música clássica. For other persons: eu gosto de música; nós gostamos de música.
target_language_example: Ela gosta de música clássica.
native_language_example: She likes classical music.

additional_notes: Used to say someone enjoys swimming. "gosta" is the present tense of "gostar (de)" (to like), which is usually followed by "de" + an infinitive (here, "nadar"). You can change the subject/person: "Eu gosto de nadar" (I like to swim), "Você gosta de nadar?" (Do you like to swim?).
target_language_example: Você gosta de nadar no mar?
native_language_example: Do you like to swim in the sea?

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **gostar de** (“to like”), which requires **de** before the person/thing liked: **gostar de + alguém/alguma coisa**. In conversation, it can mean liking someone in a friendly way, or (depending on context/tone) having romantic interest. You’ll also hear **gosta de ti** (more common in Portugal).
target_language_example: Acho que ele gosta de você, mas está com vergonha de falar.
native_language_example: I think he likes you, but he’s embarrassed to say it.

additional_notes: From gostar de ('to like'). Here do is the contraction of de + o, and it is used before a masculine singular noun or masculine possessive phrase. In English, the article often is not translated directly: gosta do seu trabalho = 'likes his/her job.'
target_language_example: Ela gosta do café daqui.
native_language_example: She likes the coffee here.

additional_notes: Used to say someone likes something or someone very much. It’s the verb gostar (to like) in the present tense (ele/ela/você gosta) + muito (“a lot”) + de. After de, you can use a noun (de flores), a pronoun (de você), or a verb in the infinitive (de viajar).
target_language_example: Tom gosta muito de música, especialmente jazz.
native_language_example: Tom really likes music, especially jazz.

additional_notes: “Gostam de” is the present-tense form used with “eles/elas/vocês” (they/you all). The verb is “gostar de” and it normally takes “de” before a noun or an infinitive: “gostam de comida” (like food), “gostam de comer” (like eating).
target_language_example: Eles gostam de estudar de manhã.
native_language_example: They like studying in the morning.

meaning: 'we like' / 'we enjoy' (followed by a verb or a noun).
additional_notes: From the verb "gostar de" (to like). It’s usually followed by "de" + an infinitive verb (e.g., "gostamos de viajar" = we like traveling/to travel) or "de" + a noun (e.g., "gostamos de música" = we like music).
target_language_example: Gostamos de cozinhar em casa.
native_language_example: We like cooking at home.

additional_notes: Used with de before the person, thing, or action: gostar de alguém, gostar de algo, gostar de fazer algo. In English, this de is usually not translated.
target_language_example: Tom costumava gostar de Mary.
native_language_example: Tom used to like Mary.

meaning: to like that; to enjoy that.
additional_notes: "Gostar" means "to like" and normally takes the preposition "de": "gostar de" + a noun/pronoun. "Disso" = "de" + "isso" ("of that"), so "gostar disso" is a very common way to say "like that" when referring to something previously mentioned. You can also say "gostar disso" to predict someone’s reaction: "Ele vai gostar disso" (He’ll like that).
target_language_example: Acho que você vai gostar disso.
native_language_example: I think you’ll like that.

additional_notes: A polite or more formal way to express a desire, request, or preference. It is often followed by an infinitive verb, and it is softer than saying quero ('I want').
target_language_example: Gostaria de reservar uma mesa para dois.
native_language_example: I would like to reserve a table for two.

additional_notes: Used to politely express willingness or desire to help. It can appear with or without the subject “eu” (“Eu gostaria de ajudar…” / “Gostaria de ajudar…”). Often followed by a person or group you want to help: “gostaria de ajudar você/ele/ela”, “gostaria de ajudar meus amigos”, “gostaria de ajudar toda a sua família”.
target_language_example: Olá, eu gostaria de ajudar no que for preciso.
native_language_example: Hi, I would like to help with whatever is needed.

additional_notes: A polite way to talk about what you want to learn (more formal/softer than “quero aprender”). Common in questions and preferences: “Você gostaria de aprender…?” = “Would you like to learn…?” You can add a language or a skill after it (e.g., “português”, “a cozinhar”).
target_language_example: Eu gostaria de aprender português este ano.
native_language_example: I would like to learn Portuguese this year.

additional_notes: A polite, formal way to ask to talk to someone (in person or on the phone). Often followed by a name or role: "... com o gerente" (the manager). You can add "por favor" to be extra polite.
target_language_example: Olá, gostaria de falar com a responsável, por favor.
native_language_example: Hi, I would like to speak to the person in charge, please.

meaning: "I would like to be able to".
additional_notes: Used to express a wish or desire to have the ability/opportunity to do something. It’s often followed by an infinitive verb: “gostaria de poder + verb” (e.g., “gostaria de poder ir” = “I’d like to be able to go”). Polite and common in requests or expressing regret about limitations.
target_language_example: Eu gostaria de poder ajudar mais.
native_language_example: I would like to be able to help more.

meaning: “I/you/he/she would like to know” (polite way to ask for information).
additional_notes: Uses the conditional form of gostar (“would like”), so it sounds more polite/less direct than “quero saber” (“I want to know”). Very common in questions and requests: “Gostaria de saber se…” = “I’d like to know whether/if…”. You can also use it with “mais” (“more”) or an infinitive to express a wish to learn a skill: “Gostaria de saber tocar violão” (“I’d like to be able to play guitar”).
target_language_example: Gostaria de saber quanto custa e como posso pagar.
native_language_example: I'd like to know how much it costs and how I can pay.

meaning: “I’d like to know if …” (polite way to ask whether something is true).
additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect yes/no question. It’s a polite, slightly formal way to ask for information (often when making a request or checking something). You’ll typically follow it with a full clause: “gostaria de saber se + [subject] + [verb] …”.
target_language_example: Gostaria de saber se você pode me ligar mais tarde.
native_language_example: I’d like to know if you can call me later.

meaning: 'I would like to be' / 'would like to be'.
additional_notes: "Gostaria" is the conditional form of "gostar" and is a polite, softer way to say what you want. "Gostaria de ser" is followed by a noun/adjective/phrase describing what someone wants to become or what they’d like to be like. It can also be used in questions with other subjects (e.g., "Quem gostaria de ser...?" = "Who would like to be...?").
target_language_example: Eu gostaria de ser médico(a) um dia.
native_language_example: I would like to be a doctor one day.

additional_notes: A polite way to order or request something. Used when the item is masculine (um); for feminine use "gostaria de uma". Often followed by what you want: "Gostaria de um café." It can also stand alone when the context is clear (meaning “one, please”).
target_language_example: Gostaria de um café, por favor.
native_language_example: I would like a coffee, please.

additional_notes: Used to express a polite desire or preference about what someone should do or what you want to happen. It is typically followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., “Gostaria que você viesse” = “I’d like you to come”). Often translates as “I would like you to…” / “I’d like (it) if…”.
target_language_example: Gostaria que você falasse mais devagar.
native_language_example: I’d like you to speak more slowly.

additional_notes: "Gostariam" is the conditional of "gostar" (to like). With "de" + infinitive, it means “would like to (do something)” (e.g., "gostariam de ir"). With "de" + noun, it means “would like (some)” (e.g., "gostariam de mais torta"). Often used in polite questions, especially with "os senhores/as senhoras".
target_language_example: Vocês gostariam de ver o cardápio?
native_language_example: Would you like to see the menu?

additional_notes: This is the imperfect past of gostar de (“to like”), used for a past liking that was ongoing, habitual, or true for a period of time (not just a one-time moment). It’s commonly followed by a noun or a verb in the infinitive: gostava de poesia; gostava de nadar. Contrast: gostei de = “I liked (it)” as a completed event.
target_language_example: Quando era criança, eu gostava de desenhar.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I used to like drawing.

meaning: '(that someone) likes' / '(that someone) enjoys' (present subjunctive of gostar de).
additional_notes: Used after triggers like "que" (e.g., "Espero que...") to express a wish, hope, doubt, or uncertainty about someone liking something. The verb is "gostar de" and it normally takes "de" before a noun or an infinitive: "goste de Tom" (like Tom), "goste de assistir" (enjoy watching).
target_language_example: Espero que você goste de morar aqui.
native_language_example: I hope you like living here.

additional_notes: “Gostei de” is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of “gostar de” (“to like/enjoy”). Use it to say you liked someone/something or enjoyed doing something: “Gostei de você” = “I liked you” (can be friendly or romantic depending on context), and “Gostei de + infinitive” = “I enjoyed doing …” (e.g., “Gostei de conversar”). It takes “de” before the thing/activity you liked.
target_language_example: Gostei de passar o dia com vocês.
native_language_example: I enjoyed spending the day with you all.

additional_notes: "gosto de" is the 1st-person singular present of "gostar de" (to like). It’s followed by a noun or an infinitive verb: "Gosto de café" (I like coffee), "Gosto de estudar" (I like studying). To say you don’t like something: "Não gosto de...".
target_language_example: Gosto de música brasileira.
native_language_example: I like Brazilian music.

additional_notes: Used to express liking/affection toward someone. With "gostar de" (to like), you normally use "de" before the person/thing you like: "Eu gosto de você". To make it negative: "Eu não gosto de você" (I don't like you). It can also be used romantically depending on tone/context, but it’s often less intense than "eu te amo" (I love you).
target_language_example: Eu gosto de você, mas quero ir devagar.
native_language_example: I like you, but I want to take it slow.

meaning: “I like that one / I like that.”
additional_notes: "Gosto" means "I like" (from the verb gostar). "Dessa" is a contraction of "de" + "essa" (“of that/that one”), and it refers to something feminine or to an idea/situation you’re pointing to (e.g., resposta, confiança, rocha, casa). For masculine nouns, you usually say "gosto desse" (de + esse). Often used as a short, stand-alone reaction: "Gosto dessa!" = “I like that!”
target_language_example: Gosto dessa ideia; vamos fazer assim.
native_language_example: I like that idea; let’s do it that way.

additional_notes: Used to say you like something that’s close in space/time or just being pointed out. It’s the present tense of "gostar de" + "deste" (= de + este). "Deste" is masculine singular; for feminine use "desta" (gosto desta casa), for plural use "destes/destas". You can drop "eu": "Gosto deste livro."
target_language_example: Gosto deste café, mas não gosto deste chá.
native_language_example: I like this coffee, but I don’t like this tea.

meaning: “I like your …” (used before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: From the verb **gostar de** (“to like”) + **do** = **de + o** (“of the”) + **seu** (“your”). It’s used when what you like is **masculine singular**: **gosto do seu site / gato / senso de humor / traje**. For feminine singular, you’d say **gosto da sua …** (e.g., **gosto da sua ideia**).
target_language_example: Gosto do seu carro.
native_language_example: I like your car.

additional_notes: Used to compare preferences. Often comes with a comparison: "Gosto mais de X do que de Y" or "Gosto mais de X que de Y" (= I like X more than Y). When comparing activities, you can use an infinitive: "Gosto mais de viajar...". Note: "Eu não gosto mais de você" usually means "I don't like you anymore" (no longer), which is different from the comparative meaning.
target_language_example: Hoje eu gosto mais de café do que de chá.
native_language_example: Today I like coffee more than tea.

additional_notes: Used to express strong liking. "Gosto" = “I like,” "muito" = “a lot,” and "do" is the contraction of "de + o" used before a masculine singular noun (or something referred to as "o"). For feminine singular, use "gosto muito da"; for plural, "gosto muito dos/das". Often used with people, things, places, or someone’s qualities (e.g., humor, work).
target_language_example: Gosto muito do seu trabalho.
native_language_example: I really like your work.

additional_notes: From the verb **gostar de** (to like). In the past tense, **gostou** means 'liked' or 'did you like?' depending on context. **da** is the contraction of **de + a** ('of the'/'from the'), used before a **feminine singular** noun (e.g., *a comida*, *a festa*). With masculine singular you typically use **do** (*gostou do filme?*).
target_language_example: Ela gostou da música.
native_language_example: She liked the song.

additional_notes: "Gostou" is the past (pretérito perfeito) of "gostar" (to like). It’s usually followed by "de" (to like *something*), so you often see contractions: "do" = "de" + "o" (masculine singular: o show, o carro, o vinho, o desenho). With feminine nouns, use "da" (de + a): "gostou da música". For plurals: "dos" (de + os), "das" (de + as). You can also use it with pronouns/clauses: "gostou disso", "gostou do que eu fiz".
target_language_example: Você gostou do filme ontem?
native_language_example: Did you like the movie yesterday?

meaning: "much" / "a big deal" (often used with "não" to mean "not much" / "not a big deal").
additional_notes: Common in negative phrases: "não sei grande coisa" = "I don’t know much"; "não é grande coisa" = "it’s nothing special / it’s not a big deal". It can also be used sarcastically on its own (like English "Big deal.") to downplay something.
target_language_example: Não foi grande coisa, mas já ajudou bastante.
native_language_example: It wasn’t a big deal, but it already helped a lot.

meaning: “thanks to; because of” (crediting someone/something as the reason).
additional_notes: Used to say that something happened due to someone/something, often with a positive tone (giving credit): “Graças a você, consegui…” = “Thanks to you, I managed to…”. It can also be neutral (“because of”), depending on context. It’s followed by a noun or pronoun: graças a você/ele/ela/vocês/isso.
target_language_example: Graças ao seu apoio, terminei o projeto a tempo.
native_language_example: Thanks to your support, I finished the project on time.

additional_notes: Used to express relief or gratitude that something good happened or that a problem is over. Very common in everyday speech; can be religious literally, but is often just an idiomatic way to say “fortunately.” It can appear as a standalone exclamation (Graças a Deus!) or to comment on a situation (Graças a Deus, eles chegaram. / Você está melhor, graças a Deus.)
target_language_example: Graças a Deus, o exame deu normal.
native_language_example: Thank goodness, the test came back normal.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the historical form of Greek spoken/written in antiquity (as opposed to modern Greek). Often appears in language-learning or history contexts, and can be used after verbs like falar/estudar (e.g., “falar/estudar grego antigo”).
target_language_example: Ela estuda grego antigo na universidade.
native_language_example: She studies Ancient Greek at the university.

additional_notes: A formal title used for an important ruler or aristocrat, often in historical or fictional contexts. It’s commonly used with an article ("o grão-príncipe") and can be used directly to refer to the person holding that title.
target_language_example: O grão-príncipe vai receber os visitantes hoje.
native_language_example: The grand prince will receive the visitors today.

additional_notes: A common noun meaning the object you use to protect yourself from rain. Plural: guarda-chuvas. Often used with comprar (to buy), perder (to lose), precisar de (to need), and in price questions like Quanto custa este guarda-chuva?
target_language_example: Está chovendo; vou pegar meu guarda-chuva.
native_language_example: It’s raining; I’m going to grab my umbrella.

additional_notes: Common noun for an umbrella. It’s often used in the plural (guarda-chuvas), and the singular is usually written the same way: um guarda-chuvas. Gender: masculine (o guarda-chuvas).
target_language_example: Leva um guarda-chuvas porque vai chover.
native_language_example: Take an umbrella because it’s going to rain.

additional_notes: A noun for a person hired to protect someone (a VIP, celebrity, politician, etc.). Often used with the verb “ter” (to have): “Ele tem um guarda-costas.” It’s commonly written with a hyphen; plural: “guarda-costas” (unchanged).
target_language_example: A cantora chegou com dois guarda-costas.
native_language_example: The singer arrived with two bodyguards.

additional_notes: Usually means a piece of furniture for storing clothes (a wardrobe/armoire), and in many contexts it also matches English “closet.” It can also be used more abstractly to mean someone’s collection of clothes (like “wardrobe”). Commonly used with articles: "um/o guarda-roupa".
target_language_example: Vou arrumar o guarda-roupa hoje.
native_language_example: I’m going to tidy up the wardrobe/closet today.

additional_notes: Used for a chemical irritant that makes your eyes burn and tear up, commonly mentioned in contexts like police actions, protests, crowd control, or gas spreading in a room. Often appears with verbs like "jogar" (to throw/use) and with "bombas de gás lacrimogêneo" (tear gas canisters/bombs).
target_language_example: Havia muito gás lacrimogêneo na rua, então fomos embora.
native_language_example: There was a lot of tear gas in the street, so we left.

meaning: to have to; must (followed by an infinitive).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive: "haver de + infinitive" (e.g., "haver de fazer", "haver de ver", "haver de chegar"). It often sounds more formal/literary than "ter de" and can express obligation/necessity or something expected to happen (sometimes close to an emphatic "will/shall"). In normal speech it is usually conjugated (eu hei de, tu hás de, ele/ela há de, nós havemos de, vocês/eles hão de), but the dictionary/citation form is "haver de".
target_language_example: Eu vou haver de falar com o chefe amanhã.
native_language_example: I will have to talk to the boss tomorrow.

meaning: 'there was a' / 'there used to be a'.
additional_notes: Uses the verb **haver** in the imperfect past to say that something existed or was present in the past. It’s very common for descriptions and background information ("There used to be...", "There was..."), and it’s **impersonal** (you don’t say who did it). In everyday speech, many people also use **tinha um** with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Havia um café aqui perto, mas fechou no ano passado.
native_language_example: There was a café near here, but it closed last year.

meaning: "there was a" / "there used to be a" (in the past).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "haver" to indicate existence in the past (an impersonal form like English "there was"). "Uma" is the feminine form of "a/an", so it’s followed by a feminine noun (e.g., "uma razão"). In everyday spoken Portuguese, people often use "tinha uma" with a similar meaning, but "havia uma" is more neutral/formal.
target_language_example: Naquela rua, havia uma padaria muito boa.
native_language_example: On that street, there was a really good bakery.

meaning: the Northern Hemisphere (the half of Earth north of the equator).
additional_notes: Used in geography and when talking about seasons. In the hemisfério norte, seasons are opposite of the Southern Hemisphere (e.g., winter is typically Dec–Mar). Often appears with the preposition “no” (= em + o): “no hemisfério norte”.
target_language_example: Muitos países da Europa ficam no hemisfério norte.
native_language_example: Many countries in Europe are in the Northern Hemisphere.

additional_notes: Refers to the half of the Earth that is south of the Equator (below it on most maps). Common in geography and when talking about seasons, which are opposite to those in the Northern Hemisphere (e.g., summer is around December–March). Often used with the preposition “no” (= em + o): “no hemisfério sul”.
target_language_example: Muitos países do hemisfério sul têm o Natal no verão.
native_language_example: Many countries in the Southern Hemisphere have Christmas in the summer.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a country’s official patriotic song, often played at ceremonies, sporting events, and official occasions. Usually appears with a possessive or a country name (e.g., “o hino nacional do Brasil”).
target_language_example: Antes do jogo, todos cantaram o hino nacional.
native_language_example: Before the game, everyone sang the national anthem.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened earlier today during the morning. Often answers “when?” and can go at the beginning or end of the sentence: Hoje de manhã, eu fui ao mercado. / Eu fui ao mercado hoje de manhã.
target_language_example: Hoje de manhã eu tomei café e saí cedo.
native_language_example: This morning I had coffee and left early.

additional_notes: Used to contrast the present with the past (“back then” vs. “now”). Often placed at the beginning of the sentence (“Hoje em dia, ...”), but it can also appear mid-sentence (“... hoje em dia ...”).
target_language_example: Hoje em dia, muita gente trabalha de casa.
native_language_example: Nowadays, a lot of people work from home.

additional_notes: Used before a specific time expression, very often with "à" + a feminine time phrase (e.g., "à tarde", "à noite", "à uma"), or before a time with "às" (plural) like "hoje às 3". By itself, "hoje à" sounds incomplete—you normally need to finish the phrase (e.g., "hoje à noite").
target_language_example: A gente se vê hoje à noite.
native_language_example: We’ll see each other tonight.
