additional_notes: Means “tonight” (during the evening/night of today). Commonly used to talk about plans or expectations for later today. You can also say “esta noite” for “tonight”; in everyday speech they’re often interchangeable, though “hoje à noite” emphasizes “today at night.”
target_language_example: Vamos jantar hoje à noite?
native_language_example: Are we having dinner tonight?

additional_notes: Used to say something happens later today during the afternoon. "à tarde" = "in the afternoon"; adding "hoje" specifies that it’s today. Common in questions and plans (e.g., what you’ll do, when you arrive, weather).
target_language_example: Vamos nos ver hoje à tarde.
native_language_example: We’re going to see each other this afternoon.

meaning: “today is the …” (used before a masculine noun/date).
additional_notes: Common pattern to say what today is: an event, holiday, or a specific day. Use with masculine nouns (o dia, o feriado). With feminine nouns, use “hoje é a …” (a festa, a data). For days of the week you usually say “Hoje é (segunda-feira)” (no article).
target_language_example: Hoje é o aniversário do meu pai.
native_language_example: Today is my dad’s birthday.

additional_notes: Literally “man of the caves.” Used for a prehistoric caveman, or as an insult/joke about someone who seems outdated, unsophisticated, or behaves in a crude way. Often used with "ser" (to be) or comparisons like "como um homem das cavernas" (like a caveman).
target_language_example: Ele age como um homem das cavernas quando fica com raiva.
native_language_example: He acts like a caveman when he gets angry.

meaning: businessman; a man who works in business (often a company owner or executive).
additional_notes: Used to describe a man involved in business, especially someone seen as professional or successful in commerce/management. Feminine: "mulher de negócios". Plural: "homens de negócios". Also commonly expressed as "empresário" (businessperson/entrepreneur).
target_language_example: Ele é um homem de negócios muito respeitado na cidade.
native_language_example: He is a very respected businessman in the city.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a description of a man using a relative clause. Very common in phrases like “o homem que…” (“the man who/that…”). In Portuguese, “que” often corresponds to English “who/that” when referring back to a person just mentioned.
target_language_example: Conheci o homem que mora ao lado.
native_language_example: I met the man who lives next door.

additional_notes: Used to say that the right moment has arrived to do something (often followed by an infinitive verb): "hora de + infinitive" (e.g., "hora de ir" = "time to go"). Very common in set phrases like "(não) é hora de..." = "it’s (not) the time to..." or "está na hora de..." = "it’s time to...". Can also be followed by a noun: "hora de almoço" = "lunch time".
target_language_example: Está na hora de dormir.
native_language_example: It’s time to sleep.

additional_notes: Used to talk about working beyond your normal scheduled hours, often implying extra pay: fazer hora extra = “to work overtime.” It’s usually treated as feminine in the singular (a hora extra / fiz hora extra) and can be plural (horas extras).
target_language_example: Hoje vou ter que fazer hora extra para terminar o relatório.
native_language_example: Today I’ll have to work overtime to finish the report.

meaning: “hours you …” — used in questions about how many hours you spend/do something.
additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed expression by itself; it’s most commonly seen in the pattern **Quantas horas você + verb…?** meaning **“How many hours do you …?”** (asking about duration). Example: **Quantas horas você dorme?** = “How many hours do you sleep?”
target_language_example: Quantas horas você trabalha por dia?
native_language_example: How many hours do you work per day?

meaning: 'there is something that…' / 'is there something that…?'.
additional_notes: Used to introduce important information or a question about something specific. Usually followed by a clause with a verb: “há algo que + (subject) + precise saber/fazer/proteger…”. In questions, Portuguese often relies on intonation rather than changing the word order: “Há algo que você quer me dizer?” = “Is there something you want to tell me?”.
target_language_example: Há algo que eu quero te dizer antes de você ir embora.
native_language_example: There’s something I want to tell you before you leave.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "haver" (há) to ask if something exists/there is something: "Há algum cinema por perto?" = "Is there any movie theater nearby?". "Algum" changes to match the noun: algum (m. sing.), alguma (f. sing.), alguns (m. pl.), algumas (f. pl.). In time expressions, "há algum tempo" means "for some time / for a while" (literally "there is some time").
target_language_example: Há alguma farmácia aberta por aqui?
native_language_example: Is there any pharmacy open around here?

meaning: a few days ago; for a few days (depending on context).
additional_notes: Uses "há" (from "haver") to talk about time relative to now. With past actions/events, it means "a few days ago" (e.g., "Ele ficou doente há alguns dias"). With a continuing situation plus a duration, it means "for a few days" (e.g., "Ele está lá há alguns dias" = he has been there for a few days).
target_language_example: Comecei a trabalhar aqui há alguns dias.
native_language_example: I started working here a few days ago.

meaning: for years; years ago (i.e., for many years).
additional_notes: Used with "há" (from "haver") to express how long something has been happening or how long ago something started: "há + time period" = "for" / "since" (e.g., "há anos" = "for years"). Often corresponds to English present perfect: "Não jogo xadrez há anos" = "I haven't played chess in years."
target_language_example: Não vejo a Ana há anos.
native_language_example: I haven't seen Ana in years.

meaning: "five years ago" / "for five years" (depending on context).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "haver" (há) to express time distance from the present. With a completed past event, it means "five years ago" (Ela morreu há cinco anos.). With an action/state that started in the past and continues now, it means "for five years" (Está fechado há cinco anos.; Está fazendo caminhadas há cinco anos.). In English you often choose between "ago" vs "for"; in Portuguese "há" can cover both.
target_language_example: Moro aqui há cinco anos.
native_language_example: I’ve lived here for five years.

additional_notes: Used with forms like “O que há de errado?” (“What’s wrong?”) or “Há algo de errado.” (“There’s something wrong.”). Here “há” is from the verb “haver” meaning “there is/are,” and “de errado” means “wrong” in the sense of “wrong with it/this.” Common in questions and to express concern or a problem.
target_language_example: O que há de errado com o computador?
native_language_example: What’s wrong with the computer?

meaning: “ten years ago” / “for ten years” (with a time ago expression).
additional_notes: Uses the verb haver (há) to express time distance from now. With a past event, it means “ten years ago” (Aconteceu há dez anos.). With an action/state that started in the past and continues to now (often with present tense), it means “for ten years” (Moro aqui há dez anos.).
target_language_example: Trabalho aqui há dez anos.
native_language_example: I’ve worked here for ten years.

meaning: two years ago; for two years (ago).
additional_notes: Uses "há" (from "haver") to talk about time elapsed up to now. With past events: "...há dois anos" = "two years ago" (e.g., he quit two years ago). With actions/states that started in the past and continue: "(só) ... há dois anos" = "for (only) two years" (e.g., he has been studying for two years). Often appears at the end of the sentence. You can also see it with "desde" ("desde há dois anos"), meaning "for the past two years"/"since two years ago".
target_language_example: Moro nesta cidade há dois anos.
native_language_example: I’ve lived in this city for two years.

meaning: two days ago; for two days (up to now).
additional_notes: Uses "há" (from the verb "haver") to talk about time elapsed. With a completed past event, it means "two days ago" (e.g., "Ele chegou há dois dias"). With something continuing until now, it means "for two days" / "for the past two days" (often with a negative or ongoing situation: "Não tem... há dois dias", "Procuro vocês há dois dias"). Common alternatives: "faz dois dias" (same idea) and "dois dias atrás" (usually "two days ago" only).
target_language_example: Estou esperando uma resposta há dois dias.
native_language_example: I’ve been waiting for an answer for two days.

additional_notes: Used to say that many of something exist or are present. "há" (from "haver") is an impersonal verb meaning "there is/are" and doesn’t change with the noun; "muitas" agrees with a feminine plural noun (e.g., casas, estantes, lojas, ilhas). For masculine plural, use "há muitos".
target_language_example: Aqui há muitas pessoas todos os dias.
native_language_example: There are many people here every day.

additional_notes: Uses **há** (from **haver**) to say that people exist/are present somewhere (“there is/there are”). Very common to describe how crowded a place is: **Há muitas pessoas no parque.** You can make it a question with intonation or a question mark: **Há muitas pessoas na sala de espera?**
target_language_example: Hoje há muitas pessoas na praia.
native_language_example: Today there are many people at the beach.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a long time in the past. Commonly means “a long time ago” when referring to a past event/time point (often with past tense): "Vi esse filme há muito tempo." It can also mean “for a long time” depending on context. Uses "há" (from "haver") to mean “there is/are” in the sense of “ago” (like "faz" in "faz muito tempo").
target_language_example: Não te vejo há muito tempo.
native_language_example: I haven't seen you in a long time.

additional_notes: Used to say that many of something exist. It is normally followed by a plural noun, like há muitos parques ('there are many parks'). Here há is the existential form meaning 'there is/are'.
target_language_example: Há muitos turistas aqui no verão.
native_language_example: There are many tourists here in the summer.

additional_notes: Used with **há** + a time period to say how long ago something happened (time elapsed up to now). It commonly goes at the end of the clause: *Cheguei aqui há muitos anos.* (I arrived here many years ago.)
target_language_example: Eu moro nesta cidade há muitos anos.
native_language_example: I’ve lived in this city for many years.

meaning: a short time ago; just now.
additional_notes: Used to refer to something that happened recently. It often appears with the past (e.g., "saiu há pouco" = "he/she left a little while ago"). You can also hear "ainda há pouco" to emphasize "just a moment ago."
target_language_example: Ele ligou há pouco e disse que já está a caminho.
native_language_example: He called a little while ago and said he’s already on the way.

additional_notes: Used to ask about a duration from the past up to now ("for how long?" / "since when?"). Common in greetings when you haven’t seen someone in a while: "Há quanto tempo!" = "Long time no see!". Often followed by the present tense (e.g., "Há quanto tempo você mora aqui?") or by "que" ("Há quanto tempo que...") with little change in meaning.
target_language_example: Há quanto tempo você estuda português?
native_language_example: How long have you been studying Portuguese?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the length of time an action or situation has been happening up to now. It’s typically followed by a verb (often in the present, like “você mora”, “você conhece”, or with “estar” + gerund: “você está aprendendo/trabalhando”). Related forms: “há quanto tempo” can also be used without “você” (e.g., talking about someone else), and answers often use “há…” (“Há dois anos.” = “For two years.”).
target_language_example: Há quanto tempo você trabalha aqui?
native_language_example: How long have you worked here?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the duration of an ongoing action or state that started in the past and continues now. Very commonly followed by a verb in the gerund (e.g., "está nadando", "está viajando") or by an adjective/participle describing a state (e.g., "está ocupada", "está sentada"). The phrase "há quanto tempo" literally refers to time elapsed ("for how much time").
target_language_example: Há quanto tempo você está estudando português?
native_language_example: How long have you been studying Portuguese?

additional_notes: Used to ask about duration up to the present. It’s typically followed by a place or situation: "Há quanto tempo você está em Boston?" (= how long have you been in Boston?). Often answered with "Há..." or "Faz...": "Há dois anos." / "Faz dois anos."
target_language_example: Há quanto tempo você está aqui?
native_language_example: How long have you been here?

meaning: for so long; such a long time (ago/for).
additional_notes: Used with "há" (from "haver") to talk about time. It often means a duration up to now: "Moro aqui há tanto tempo" = "I’ve lived here for so long." With an event that happened in the past, it can mean "so long ago": "Não saio há tanto tempo" = "I haven’t gone out in such a long time."
target_language_example: Não te vejo há tanto tempo!
native_language_example: I haven’t seen you in so long!

meaning: a long time ago; for a long time (now).
additional_notes: Common with "há" (from the verb *haver*) to express how long it has been since something happened, or that something has been true for a long time: *há tempos não...* = “I haven’t ... in a long time”, *está assim há tempos* = “it’s been like this for a long time.” It often corresponds to English “for ages” / “in a long time.”
target_language_example: Não vejo a Ana há tempos.
native_language_example: I haven’t seen Ana in a long time.

meaning: three years ago; for three years (in the past).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "haver" (há) to talk about time. With a completed past action, it usually means "three years ago" (e.g., "Fui lá há três anos" = I went there three years ago). With the imperfect to describe an ongoing situation in the past, it can mean "for three years" / "had been ... for three years" (e.g., "Eu morava lá há três anos" = I had been living there for three years).
target_language_example: Comecei a trabalhar aqui há três anos.
native_language_example: I started working here three years ago.

meaning: "three days ago" / "for three days" (depending on context).
additional_notes: Uses "há" (from "haver") to express time relative to now. With a completed past event (e.g., "chegou"), it means "three days ago." With an action/state that started in the past and continues to now (often with "estar"), it means "for three days" (="has been ... for three days").
target_language_example: Estou esperando há três dias.
native_language_example: I’ve been waiting for three days.

meaning: three months ago; for three months (with duration up to now).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "haver" (há) to talk about time. With a completed past action, it means "... ago" (Fui promovido há três meses = I was promoted three months ago). With an action/state that started in the past and continues now, it means "for ..." (Tom está na Austrália há três meses = Tom has been in Australia for three months). You can also hear the structure "Há três meses que..." meaning "It’s been three months since..." / "For three months, ...". Note: "há" is invariable here (always "há", not changing with person).
target_language_example: Moro aqui há três meses.
native_language_example: I’ve lived here for three months.

meaning: three weeks ago; for three weeks (up to now).
additional_notes: Uses "há" (from the verb "haver") to express elapsed time. With past events, it means "three weeks ago" (Eu o vi há três semanas.). With actions/states that started in the past and continue now, it means "for three weeks" (Estamos aqui há três semanas.). It’s common to place the time phrase at the beginning or end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Moro aqui há três semanas.
native_language_example: I’ve lived here for three weeks.

additional_notes: Used to say that something exists or is present. Here, há is the existential form meaning "there is/there are," and um is the masculine singular indefinite article ("a/an" or "one"). Before a feminine noun, you would use há uma instead.
target_language_example: Há um café perto daqui.
native_language_example: There's a café near here.

meaning: a year ago; for a year (up to now).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "haver" (há) to express elapsed time. With past events, it means "a year ago" (Aconteceu há um ano.). With actions/states that continue into the present, it means "for a year" (Eles estão no Brasil há um ano. = they’ve been in Brazil for a year). Many speakers also say "há um ano atrás", but "há um ano" already contains the idea of "ago".
target_language_example: Moro aqui há um ano.
native_language_example: I’ve lived here for a year.

meaning: "there is/there’s a" (referring to a singular feminine noun).
additional_notes: Uses the verb haver (impersonal) to state that something exists or is present. Very common in more formal or neutral writing/speech. It’s followed by a feminine singular noun (uma + noun), e.g., “há uma dúvida”, “há uma chance”. Often interchangeable with “existe uma” or “tem uma” (more informal in some regions).
target_language_example: Há uma possibilidade de chuva amanhã.
native_language_example: There’s a chance of rain tomorrow.

meaning: an hour ago; for an hour (depending on context).
additional_notes: Uses the verb haver (há) to express elapsed time. With a completed past action, it usually means “an hour ago” (e.g., Ele partiu há uma hora.). With an action/state that continues up to now, it means “for an hour” (e.g., Estou procurando há uma hora.). Many speakers add “atrás” (há uma hora atrás), but “há uma hora” already includes the idea of “ago,” so “atrás” is redundant.
target_language_example: Estou esperando há uma hora.
native_language_example: I've been waiting for an hour.

meaning: one week ago; for a week (up to now).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "haver" (há) to express time distance from now. With past events, it means "a week ago" (Ele ganhou o prêmio há uma semana). With actions/states that started in the past and continue to the present, it means "for a week" (Eu estou aqui há uma semana). In Brazil you may hear "há uma semana atrás"; it’s common but redundant because "há" already means "ago."
target_language_example: Estou estudando português há uma semana.
native_language_example: I've been studying Portuguese for a week.

additional_notes: Formed with the imperfect of ir (ia) + infinitive (querer). Common in hypotheticals, conditionals, and rhetorical questions to mean what someone would want in a situation: “Quem ia querer...?” = “Who would want...?”. In negatives: “não ia querer” = “wouldn’t want.”
target_language_example: Quem ia querer trabalhar até tão tarde?
native_language_example: Who would want to work until so late?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a language that is not your native language or not commonly spoken where you live. You’ll also often hear the equivalent phrase "língua estrangeira" (same meaning). Note: "estrangeiro" means "foreign"; it can look like English "stranger" but it’s not the same idea.
target_language_example: Estou aprendendo um idioma estrangeiro para o trabalho.
native_language_example: I’m learning a foreign language for work.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ir (often in the past perfect: tinha ido embora) to say someone had already left by the time something else happened. In exclamations/conditionals like "Se tivesse ido embora!", it expresses regret: "If only (I/he) had left!"
target_language_example: Quando liguei, ela já tinha ido embora.
native_language_example: When I called, she had already left.

additional_notes: Used to compare people/things/actions. It commonly comes before a noun or pronoun: “igual a você” (like you), “igual à sua” (the same as yours). It can also appear in patterns like “igual a antes” (same as before) and “fazer igual a…” (to do like…). In writing, you may see the contraction with the article: “igual ao/à/ aos/às”.
target_language_example: Este vestido é igual ao da foto.
native_language_example: This dress is the same as the one in the photo.

additional_notes: Used to express a guess or assumption (often a polite, less direct way to state what you think is true). It’s commonly followed by the subjunctive in Portuguese: “Imagino que ele esteja…”, “Imagino que seja…”. You can also add words like “logo”: “Logo, imagino que…” = “So/I guess that…”.
target_language_example: Imagino que você esteja cansado hoje.
native_language_example: I imagine you’re tired today.

meaning: to stop him/it; to prevent him/it (from doing something).
additional_notes: "Impedi-lo" = "impedir" (to prevent/stop) + "-lo" (object pronoun meaning "him" or "it"). It’s used after an infinitive (impedir) and can also appear as "impedi-lo de + infinitive" (to prevent him/it from doing something): "Tentei impedi-lo de sair". In everyday speech, many people also say "impedir ele" (informal), but "impedi-lo" is the standard form.
target_language_example: Eu não consegui impedi-lo de entrar.
native_language_example: I couldn’t stop him from coming in.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you think seems true (often with uncertainty). Very common in the expressions **ter a impressão de que** (“to have the impression that / to feel like”) and **dar a impressão de que** (“to give the impression that / to seem like”). Usually followed by a full clause: *Tenho a impressão de que…*
target_language_example: Tenho a impressão de que ele não entendeu a pergunta.
native_language_example: I have the impression that he didn’t understand the question.

meaning: fingerprint; biometric print used for identification.
additional_notes: Most commonly means a fingerprint found on an object (e.g., by the police) or used to unlock/verify identity. Here, “digital” comes from “dedo” (finger), not “digital” (electronics). You may also hear “impressão digital da mão” for a hand/fingerprint scan.
target_language_example: O celular desbloqueia com a impressão digital.
native_language_example: The phone unlocks with a fingerprint.

additional_notes: Used to say someone can’t do something (often physically or emotionally). It’s usually followed by an infinitive (incapaz de + verb). The adjective agrees with the person: incapaz (m./f. singular), incapazes (plural).
target_language_example: Ela ficou incapaz de falar.
native_language_example: She was unable to speak.

additional_notes: This is the verb **incomodar** (“to bother, disturb, inconvenience”) with the object pronoun **-lo** (“him/you” in formal address) attached to the end. It’s common in polite apologies and requests: **Desculpe/Perdão por incomodá-lo** (“Sorry to bother you”). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people often use **incomodar você** instead of **incomodá-lo**.
target_language_example: Desculpe incomodá-lo, mas preciso de ajuda.
native_language_example: Sorry to bother you, but I need help.

additional_notes: Often used with the verb ir (to go), especially in the structure “vai indo bem” to mean something is progressing well/turning out fine. It can suggest things are generally okay, sometimes with a modest or gradual tone (not necessarily “perfect”).
target_language_example: O projeto está indo bem até agora.
native_language_example: The project is going well so far.

additional_notes: Often used with a form of “estar” (e.g., “estou”) to say you’re in the process of leaving, usually right now: “Estou indo embora.” It’s a very common, natural way to say you’re heading out.
target_language_example: Desculpa, estou indo embora porque já está tarde.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm leaving because it's already late.

additional_notes: Used to talk about computer systems/technology that can learn, recognize patterns, and make decisions. Often appears after prepositions like “sobre” (about) or in phrases like “tecnologia de ponta” (cutting-edge technology) related to AI.
target_language_example: A inteligência artificial está mudando a forma como trabalhamos.
native_language_example: Artificial intelligence is changing the way we work.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an illness caused by eating contaminated food. Common with verbs like “ter” (to have) and “estar com” (to be suffering from): “Estou com intoxicação alimentar.” Also used with “morrer de” (to die from) in serious contexts.
target_language_example: Acho que estou com intoxicação alimentar depois de comer no restaurante.
native_language_example: I think I have food poisoning after eating at the restaurant.

additional_notes: **invés de** is widely treated as a misspelling/variant of the standard **em vez de** (“instead of,” used before a noun or an infinitive: *em vez de + coisa / verbo*). You may also see **ao invés de**; in more careful usage it can mean “the opposite of,” but in everyday Portuguese many people use it like *em vez de*. In formal writing, prefer **em vez de**.
target_language_example: Invés de sair, vou ficar em casa.
native_language_example: Instead of going out, I’m going to stay home.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re going to wash yourself (often a shower). It commonly appears as a near-future plan with the verb "ir" (to go) + infinitive: "Eu vou ir tomar banho" / more commonly "Eu vou tomar banho". In Brazilian Portuguese, "tomar banho" is very common for “take a shower.”
target_language_example: Eu vou ir tomar banho agora.
native_language_example: I'm going to go take a shower now.

additional_notes: Used for movement toward a destination, such as a place, event, or appointment. It often contracts with the definite article: ir ao, ir à, ir aos, ir às. With many city names, there is no article: ir a Paris.
target_language_example: Ela quer ir a Lisboa no verão.
native_language_example: She wants to go to Lisbon in the summer.

additional_notes: Used to talk about going to an unspecified destination. Common after verbs like querer (“to want”) or ter que (“to have to”). The verb "ir" typically takes the preposition "a" before a destination in standard usage (ir a + lugar).
target_language_example: Você tem que ir a algum lugar.
native_language_example: You have to go somewhere.

meaning: to go on foot; to walk (somewhere).
additional_notes: Used to say you’re going somewhere by walking, not by car/bus/etc. Often followed by a destination with “a/à/ao”: “ir a pé ao trabalho” (walk to work), “ir a pé à escola” (walk to school).
target_language_example: Vamos ir a pé ao restaurante.
native_language_example: Let’s walk to the restaurant.

additional_notes: Used for physically going to a bank (the financial institution), often to do things like withdraw money (sacar dinheiro), deposit money, or speak with a bank employee. Note that “banco” can also mean “bench,” but in “ir ao banco” it typically means the bank in financial contexts.
target_language_example: Eu preciso ir ao banco para sacar dinheiro.
native_language_example: I need to go to the bank to withdraw money.

meaning: to go to the bathroom (to use the toilet).
additional_notes: Common, polite way to say you need to use the restroom. Often used with precisar/ter de: "Eu preciso/tenho de ir ao banheiro." In Brazil you may also hear "ir ao toalete" or "ir ao banheiro"; in more formal settings you can say "ir ao banheiro, por favor?" or "Posso ir ao banheiro?" (May I go to the bathroom?).
target_language_example: Com licença, posso ir ao banheiro?
native_language_example: Excuse me, may I go to the bathroom?

additional_notes: Used when someone needs medical care or needs to be checked by a doctor. Often appears with advice/urgency words like "deveria" (should) or "imediatamente" (immediately). Can also be used in obligation contexts with "ter que" (to have to). In negative sentences, "não" makes it "not go / can't go" (e.g., "não pode ir ao hospital").
target_language_example: Acho que você deveria ir ao hospital.
native_language_example: I think you should go to the hospital.

meaning: to go to the doctor (for an appointment/checkup).
additional_notes: Used when you need medical care or a checkup. Common with obligation/advice: "tenho de" (I have to), "preciso" (I need to), "deveria" (should). It can refer to visiting a general doctor; for a specific specialist you can say "ir ao dentista" (dentist), "ir ao cardiologista" (cardiologist), etc.
target_language_example: Tenho de ir ao médico hoje.
native_language_example: I have to go to the doctor today.

meaning: to go after; to chase/pursue; to go get (something); to seek (information/help/opportunities).
additional_notes: Commonly used as "ir atrás de + noun/pronoun": "ir atrás de algo/alguém" can be literal (to run after someone) or figurative (to seek/try to obtain something, like information, a job, help). In many contexts it’s closer to "go get" or "track down" than a literal "go behind."
target_language_example: Posso ir atrás de comida?
native_language_example: Can I go get some food?

additional_notes: Used to talk about going to a specific place that’s understood from context or mentioned earlier. "Até" adds the idea of going as far as that place (often like “all the way there”). Common with transport: "ir até lá de carro/a pé/ônibus".
target_language_example: Acho melhor a gente ir até lá amanhã cedo.
native_language_example: I think it’s better for us to go there tomorrow early.

additional_notes: Used to say you will accompany someone. It often appears with verbs like "gostar de" (eu gostaria de ir com você = I’d like to go with you), "poder" (eu posso/poderia ir com você = I can/could go with you), and in negatives (não posso ir com você = I can’t go with you). In Brazil, "você" is common; in Portugal, you’ll often hear "ir contigo" instead.
target_language_example: Eu gostaria de ir com você.
native_language_example: I’d like to go with you.

meaning: go to sleep / go to bed (to sleep)
additional_notes: Used to say you’re going to go to sleep (often implying going to bed now). Common in questions and with obligations: “Posso ir dormir agora?” (Can I go to sleep now?), “Tenho que ir dormir” (I have to go to sleep). Often alternates with “vou dormir” depending on structure, but “ir dormir” is the exact infinitive phrase.
target_language_example: Tenho que ir dormir agora.
native_language_example: I have to go to sleep now.

meaning: to go ahead; to move forward; to carry on.
additional_notes: Used to say you will continue with a plan or action, often despite doubts or obstacles. It can also mean physically moving forward, but very commonly means “to proceed” ("Let’s go ahead"). Often followed by "com" + noun (e.g., "ir em frente com o plano").
target_language_example: Pode ir em frente — eu te encontro lá.
native_language_example: Go ahead—I’ll meet you there.

additional_notes: A very common neutral expression for leaving a place. It is often translated simply as "to leave," though a more literal sense is "to go away."
target_language_example: Acho que você deveria ir embora.
native_language_example: I think you should leave.

meaning: to leave here; to go away from here.
additional_notes: "Ir embora" means "to leave/go away"; adding "daqui" makes it specifically "from here/this place". Often used when you want to get out of a place (sometimes urgently: "agora" = "now"). You can soften it with "podia" (could) or make it stronger with "tem que/precisa" (have to/need to).
target_language_example: Vamos ir embora daqui antes que fique tarde.
native_language_example: Let’s leave here before it gets late.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to increase speed (e.g., a driver, a person walking, or even a machine/vehicle you control). Often appears in questions like “Dá pra ir mais rápido?” (Can you go faster?) or “Você não pode ir mais rápido?” (Can’t you go faster?).
target_language_example: Você consegue ir mais rápido, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you go faster, please?

additional_notes: Used to talk about going somewhere to swim (a pool, the beach, a lake, etc.). It often follows verbs like querer (to want) and poder (can/may): “Quero ir nadar”, “Posso ir nadar?”. You can add a time expression (hoje à tarde) or company (com vocês).
target_language_example: Vamos ir nadar na piscina amanhã de manhã.
native_language_example: Let's go swimming in the pool tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used for the act of going to bed (getting into bed to sleep), often with time words like "cedo" (early) or "tarde" (late), or in fixed phrases like "Está na hora de ir para a cama" (It’s time to go to bed). Depending on context, it can also imply going to bed with someone (sexual/romantic sense), e.g., "ir para a cama com alguém".
target_language_example: Hoje eu vou ir para a cama cedo porque estou cansado.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to go to bed early because I’m tired.

additional_notes: Used with a destination ("para" = "to/toward"). Often implies going there as part of your routine (classes), not just visiting the building. You can change the subject and tense: "eu vou", "ele vai", "preciso ir", "quero ir".
target_language_example: Eu quero ir para a escola.
native_language_example: I want to go to school.

additional_notes: A common way to say returning home. In Portuguese, casa often appears without an article in expressions about home, so ir para casa means 'go home' rather than specifically 'go to the house'.
target_language_example: Depois do trabalho, vou ir para casa.
native_language_example: After work, I'm going to go home.

additional_notes: A common, everyday phrase meaning to leave and head home at this moment. It’s flexible: you can add different subjects/auxiliaries in front (e.g., "eu quero", "você pode", "ele deve") and keep the core phrase unchanged. "Agora" emphasizes immediacy and is usually placed at the end, as here.
target_language_example: Você deveria ir para casa agora.
native_language_example: You should go home now.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "ir" (to go) + an activity verb in the infinitive. You can talk about plans or invitations: "Quero ir pescar" (I want to go fishing), "Vamos ir pescar" (Let’s go fishing), "Quer ir pescar comigo?" (Do you want to go fishing with me?).
target_language_example: No fim de semana, vamos ir pescar no lago.
native_language_example: On the weekend, let’s go fishing at the lake.

additional_notes: Common in everyday speech. "pra" is an informal contraction of "para a" (to the), so "ir pra casa" = "ir para casa". Used to say you’re leaving/returning to your home; can also be used in requests ("deixa eu ir pra casa").
target_language_example: Já está tarde; vou ir pra casa agora.
native_language_example: It’s already late; I’m going to go home now.

meaning: to be arrested; to go to jail.
additional_notes: Commonly used to mean someone ends up under arrest or imprisoned. Often appears with a future idea (e.g., "vai preso") or after "se" to warn about consequences ("Se fizer isso, vai preso").
target_language_example: Se você dirigir bêbado, pode ir preso.
native_language_example: If you drive drunk, you could go to jail.

additional_notes: Used to express going to a destination. Here, à is the contraction of the preposition a + the feminine singular definite article a, so it is used before feminine singular nouns that take the article, e.g. ir à loja ('to go to the store'). With place names, usage depends on whether the place normally takes an article in Portuguese.
target_language_example: Deixem-me ir à loja.
native_language_example: Let me go to the store.

additional_notes: Used to talk about attending school (physically going there), often as part of a routine or obligation. In Portuguese, "à" = "a" + "a" (to + the) before a feminine singular noun like "escola". You can conjugate the verb as needed: "vou à escola" (I go/I’m going), "fui à escola" (I went), "preciso ir à escola" (I need to go).
target_language_example: Tudo o que Tom tem que fazer amanhã é ir à escola.
native_language_example: All Tom has to do tomorrow is go to school.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "ir" (to go) + the preposition "a" (to) + the definite article "a" (the) before "festa". Because "a" + "a" contracts to "à", you say "ir à festa" (not *ir a a festa*). You can swap in other feminine places similarly: "ir à escola" (go to school). With masculine nouns, "a" + "o" = "ao": "ir ao cinema" (go to the cinema).
target_language_example: Eu quero ir à festa.
native_language_example: I want to go to the party.

additional_notes: A vulgar insult used to tell someone off or dismiss them angrily. Most often used in the imperative: “vai à merda” (to one person, informal) or “vão à merda” (to several people). With someone you’d address as “você/o senhor/a senhora”, you may hear “vá à merda” (still extremely offensive). Avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Ele mandou-me ir à merda e eu fui-me embora.
native_language_example: He told me to fuck off and I left.

additional_notes: Used to talk about going to the beach as an activity or plan. It’s literally “to go to the beach” (ir = to go; à = to + a, feminine singular; praia = beach). You can change the subject (eu/você/vocês/ela) and add time words like hoje (today), amanhã (tomorrow), etc.
target_language_example: No verão, a gente gosta de ir à praia no fim de semana.
native_language_example: In the summer, we like to go to the beach on the weekend.

additional_notes: Used for going out (or setting out) to buy things, especially groceries or items in stores. Often used with a time expression: “Vou ir às compras amanhã” (I’m going to go shopping tomorrow).
target_language_example: Eu vou ir às compras depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: I'm going to go shopping after work.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of ir (iria = "would go") + infinitive (acontecer = "to happen") to talk about something that was expected/predicted to happen, often from a past point of view (e.g., "I knew it would happen"). Common with verbs like saber (to know), achar (to think), sentir (to feel), ouvir dizer (to hear say).
target_language_example: Eu não imaginava que isso iria acontecer tão cedo.
native_language_example: I didn’t imagine that was going to happen so soon.

meaning: “would want to” (would be likely to want).
additional_notes: Uses the conditional of ir (iria) + infinitive (querer) to talk about a hypothetical/conditional desire: what someone would want in a given situation. Very common in questions like “Por que eu iria querer…?” (“Why would I want to…?”), often implying doubt or “what reason would I have?”
target_language_example: Eu não sei por que ela iria querer trocar de emprego agora.
native_language_example: I don’t know why she would want to change jobs now.

meaning: younger sister (the youngest sister, or a sister younger than you).
additional_notes: Used to describe a sister who is younger than someone else (often the speaker). It can mean “my younger sister” (minha irmã mais nova) or “his/her younger sister” (sua irmã mais nova). More generally, it can also mean “the younger/youngest sister” among sisters. The phrase is straightforward: irmã = sister, mais nova = younger (literally “more new/younger”).
target_language_example: Vou buscar minha irmã mais nova na escola.
native_language_example: I’m going to pick up my younger sister at school.

meaning: older sister (a female sibling who is older).
additional_notes: Used to specify that your sister is older than you or older than another sister. Often appears with possessives: "a minha irmã mais velha" (my older sister), "a irmã mais velha dela" (her older sister).
target_language_example: A minha irmã mais velha mora em Lisboa.
native_language_example: My older sister lives in Lisbon.

additional_notes: On its own, “irmão mais” sounds incomplete in standard Portuguese. Normally you say “irmão mais velho” (older brother) or “irmão mais novo” (younger brother). “Mais” means “more/most” and is typically followed by an adjective like “velho” or “novo.”
target_language_example: O meu irmão mais velho mora em Lisboa.
native_language_example: My older brother lives in Lisbon.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male sibling who is younger than someone else (often the speaker or another person mentioned). You can also say "meu/minha/seu/sua irmão mais novo" (“my/your younger brother”). Literally “brother more new/younger.”
target_language_example: Meu irmão mais novo tem dez anos.
native_language_example: My younger brother is ten years old.

meaning: "..., isn’t it?" / "..., right?" (tag question asking for agreement or confirmation).
additional_notes: Used at the end of a clause to confirm or seek agreement. In many contexts Portuguese speakers more commonly say just "não é?"; adding "isso" points back to what was just mentioned ("that/this"). Punctuation with a comma is common in writing: "..., isso, não é?"
target_language_example: Você não tem ideia do que seja isso, não é?
native_language_example: You have no idea what that is, do you?

meaning: 'that/it, please' (polite way to refer to something and ask).
additional_notes: Used when you’re politely asking someone to do something with a specific thing or topic you’re indicating (a document, an object, an idea, etc.). Very common in requests with verbs like corrigir (correct), revisar (review), explicar (explain), ajudar a levar (help carry). In speech it often sounds like one unit: "isso, por favor".
target_language_example: Pode olhar isso, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you look at this/that, please?

additional_notes: Used to say that something occurs (often unexpectedly) or to reassure someone that a mistake/problem is normal. Very common with adverbs like às vezes (sometimes) and mesmo (really/indeed): “Às vezes isso acontece.”
target_language_example: Não se preocupe — isso acontece com todo mundo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry—it happens to everyone.

additional_notes: Literally “that/this happen.” Uses the infinitive acontecer (“to happen”) with isso (“that/this”) as the subject. Common after verbs like deixar (to let), ver (to see), evitar (to avoid), impedir (to prevent): “deixar isso acontecer” = “to let that happen,” “ver isso acontecer” = “to see that happen.”
target_language_example: Não podemos deixar isso acontecer.
native_language_example: We can’t let that happen.

additional_notes: Used to say that an event really occurred, often referring back to something just mentioned ("isso" = “that”). In questions, it’s a way to confirm or show surprise: “Did that really happen?”
target_language_example: Não acredito que isso aconteceu ontem.
native_language_example: I can’t believe that happened yesterday.

additional_notes: Often used to add urgency or immediacy: *isso* = “that/it” (referring to something already known from context) and *agora* = “now.” Common in requests and commands: *Faça isso agora.* / *Para com isso agora!* Word order can vary depending on what’s emphasized (e.g., *agora* can also come earlier: *Agora, faça isso!*).
target_language_example: Não consigo fazer isso agora; posso fazer mais tarde.
native_language_example: I can’t do that right now; I can do it later.

additional_notes: Very common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese. It can point to something (often with a gesture): "Deixa isso aí" = “Leave that there.” It can also be an approving/exclamatory reaction meaning “That’s it!”/“Exactly!” The tone can be neutral or slightly dismissive depending on context (like “just that thing there”).
target_language_example: É isso aí, vamos embora!
native_language_example: That’s it, let’s go!

additional_notes: Used when you want to repeat an action, experience, or look at something one more time. Common with verbs like ver (to see), fazer (to do), sentir (to feel), and olhar (to look). Word order is fixed: isso (that/it) + de novo (again).
target_language_example: Vamos fazer isso de novo amanhã?
native_language_example: Shall we do that again tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to say (often accusingly or to confirm) that someone did something intentionally rather than by accident. Very common with verbs like "fazer" (to do/make): "fez isso de propósito" = "did that on purpose." You can also use just "de propósito" after the verb: "Ele fez de propósito."
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu não fiz isso de propósito.
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t do that on purpose.

additional_notes: Used with **dever + ser** to express (1) a **guess/deduction** (“must be”) or (2) what is **supposed to be the case** (“should be”). The exact meaning depends on context: *Isso deve ser Cracóvia* = “That must be Kraków” (deduction); *Isso deve ser removido* = “That should/must be removed” (requirement).
target_language_example: Pelo barulho lá fora, isso deve ser o entregador.
native_language_example: From the noise outside, that must be the delivery person.

additional_notes: Used to comment on something that just happened or something mentioned earlier. "foi" is the past (preterite) of "ser" (to be), so it often introduces an evaluation: "isso foi" + adjective/noun (e.g., "isso foi nojento", "isso foi um desperdício"). It can also start an explanation: "isso foi o que..." = "that was what...".
target_language_example: Isso foi a melhor parte da viagem.
native_language_example: That was the best part of the trip.

additional_notes: Used to say that something causes an emotional state. It’s often followed by an adjective describing how you feel (e.g., furioso/a, triste, nervoso/a, feliz). You can swap the object pronoun: isso te deixa (makes you), isso o/a deixa (makes him/her), isso nos deixa (makes us).
target_language_example: Isso me deixa muito feliz.
native_language_example: That makes me very happy.

additional_notes: Used to confirm something is correct or to strongly agree with what someone just said. It can be said alone ("Isso mesmo!") or with "sim" for emphasis ("Sim, isso mesmo."). With "é" ("É isso mesmo..."), it often means “Is that really what…?” or “That’s exactly what…,” depending on the context (e.g., "É isso mesmo que eu quero!" = “That’s exactly what I want!”).
target_language_example: —Você quer sair agora? —Isso mesmo.
native_language_example: —You want to leave now? —That’s right.

additional_notes: Used to say that something (isso = “that/this”) is not something else. It’s commonly followed by an adjective or noun ("isso não é importante" = “that isn’t important”, "isso não é problema meu" = “that isn’t my problem”), or by a clause with "o que" ("isso não é o que eu quis dizer" = “that isn’t what I meant”). Literally “that/this is not.”
target_language_example: Isso não é a resposta certa.
native_language_example: That isn't the right answer.

additional_notes: Used to downplay something (an effort, problem, or amount), often meaning “that’s nothing compared to…” (comparado com…). It can also reassure someone after thanks/apologies, similar to “don’t mention it.”
target_language_example: Não se preocupe, isso não é nada.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s no big deal.

meaning: 'that/it for me' (i.e., for my benefit; on my behalf; to/for me).
additional_notes: Commonly used when asking someone to do/get/take something for you: "Faça/pegue/levar isso para mim" = "Do/get/take that for me." It can also introduce a personal opinion: "Isso, para mim, ..." = "To me, ... / In my opinion, ..." In writing, commas are often used in the opinion sense ("Isso, para mim, parece estranho").
target_language_example: Você pode guardar isso para mim por um instante?
native_language_example: Can you hold onto that for me for a moment?

additional_notes: Used to give an impression or opinion based on what you see/know. Very common before an adjective or noun phrase (e.g., bom, improvável, muito caro, uma má ideia). You can also change the subject: “Isso” = that, “Ele/Ela” = he/she, “Isso aqui” = this.
target_language_example: Isso parece ser perigoso.
native_language_example: That seems to be dangerous.

additional_notes: Used to say something is possible, or to guess/speculate about what something is like (often followed by an adjective or noun: "isso pode ser difícil" = "that could be hard", "isso pode ser verdade" = "that might be true"). In questions ("Isso pode ser...?"), it expresses surprise or doubt: "Can that be...?".
target_language_example: Isso pode ser uma boa ideia.
native_language_example: That could be a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an imaginary or possible situation/result (often like English “that would be…”). It’s the conditional of the verb “ser” (to be): “seria” = “would be.” Common for giving opinions politely or imagining outcomes: “Isso seria bom/legal/rude.”
target_language_example: Isso seria ótimo, mas não tenho tempo hoje.
native_language_example: That would be great, but I don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used to explain the conclusion or implication of what was just said. Very common in conversation; often followed by a complete clause. You can also say “Isso quer dizer que …” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Se você não tem febre, isso significa que pode voltar ao trabalho?
native_language_example: If you don’t have a fever, does that mean you can go back to work?

additional_notes: A common way to refer to something already mentioned or obvious from context. It is often used to comment on or evaluate a situation: for example, saying something is interesting, normal, or unacceptable.
target_language_example: Isso é exatamente o que eu queria.
native_language_example: That's exactly what I wanted.

additional_notes: Used to say something is good, correct, or satisfactory. Often reacts to what was just said or done (like “that’s good!”). Can also be followed by more info: “Isso é bom inglês” (“That’s good English”) or “Isso é bom o bastante para você?” (“Is that good enough for you?”). With “não é?” it works like a tag question: “That’s good, isn’t it?”
target_language_example: Terminamos mais cedo — isso é bom!
native_language_example: We finished early — that’s good!

meaning: 'That/this is very…' (used to intensify an adjective).
additional_notes: Used to comment on something and emphasize a quality: "isso" = "that/this", "é" = "is", "muito" = "very/a lot". Usually followed by an adjective (complicado, estranho, fácil, injusto), but you can also add a noun phrase like "Isso é muito trabalho" (That’s a lot of work).
target_language_example: Isso é muito caro para o meu orçamento.
native_language_example: That’s very expensive for my budget.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or emphasize the specific thing being referred to or identified. Often followed by a clause (e.g., "isso é o que eu acho") or used as a pointed question: "E isso é o quê, exatamente?". In speech and writing, you may also see variants like "isso é o que eu quero" and the more formal-sounding "isto é o que…".
target_language_example: Isso é o que eu quero dizer.
native_language_example: That’s what I mean.

additional_notes: Used to say there is nothing more beyond what follows. It’s commonly followed by a verb clause: “Isso é tudo o que eu sei” (That’s all I know), “Isso é tudo o que importa” (That’s all that matters). In English you often omit “that”: “That’s all I know.”
target_language_example: Isso é tudo o que precisamos por hoje.
native_language_example: That’s all we need for today.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is the only thing you have/need/know/say, etc. It’s typically followed by a verb clause: "Isso é tudo que eu sei" (That’s all I know). In more careful/standard Portuguese, you may also see "isso é tudo o que" with the extra "o".
target_language_example: Isso é tudo que eu posso fazer hoje.
native_language_example: That's all I can do today.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize an adjective about something: "isso" (this/that) + "é" (is) + "tão" (so). It’s usually followed by an adjective (e.g., chato, engraçado, errado, estranho, legal, relaxante, relevante). You can add "mas" before it to mean "but this/that is so..."
target_language_example: Isso é tão difícil!
native_language_example: This is so hard!

additional_notes: Used to point something out and identify it. Followed by a masculine singular noun (um = “a/an” for masculine). With feminine nouns, you usually say “isso é uma …”.
target_language_example: Isso é um problema sério.
native_language_example: This is a serious problem.

meaning: 'that is a...' / 'this is a...' (introducing a noun).
additional_notes: Used to identify or describe something with a feminine noun: "Isso é uma + [noun]". With masculine nouns, use "isso é um". "Isso" often means "that" (something already mentioned), but it can also point to something near you like "this" depending on context.
target_language_example: Isso é uma boa ideia.
native_language_example: That’s a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to say that something (isto = “this”) is not a certain thing or does not have a certain quality. Very common in simple statements and in corrections/contradictions: “Isto não é verdade!” You can also add intensifiers like “assim tão” to mean “not (all) that”: “Isto não é assim tão fácil.”
target_language_example: Desculpe, mas isto não é o que eu pedi.
native_language_example: Sorry, but this isn’t what I ordered.

additional_notes: Used to deny or correct what something is (or how it should be understood). Because it ends in “uma”, it must be followed by a feminine singular noun (uma brincadeira, uma derrota, uma mesa, uma opinião). For masculine nouns, use “isto não é um …”.
target_language_example: Isto não é uma piada, é sério.
native_language_example: This is not a joke, it’s serious.

additional_notes: A literal combination of isto ("this") and é ("is"). Used to identify or describe a thing, situation, or idea. Isto is a neutral demonstrative, so it often refers to "this thing" or "this situation" rather than a specifically masculine or feminine noun.
target_language_example: Isto é muito importante.
native_language_example: This is very important.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or identify something: “isto” = “this”, “é” = “is”, “um” = “a/an” (used before masculine singular nouns). Before feminine singular nouns, you usually use “isto é uma …”.
target_language_example: Isto é um bom lugar para começar.
native_language_example: This is a good place to start.

additional_notes: Used to identify or point something out. "Isto" = "this" (neutral), "é" = "is", and "uma" is the feminine form of "a/an" (use before feminine nouns like "catedral", "gaivota", "lei", "nota"). With masculine nouns, use "isto é um".
target_language_example: Isto é uma escola.
native_language_example: This is a school.

additional_notes: Used to refer to early childhood education, before primary/elementary school. In Brazil it commonly corresponds to preschool/early years of educação infantil; in Portugal it’s often called (o) jardim de infância and is similar to preschool/kindergarten. You can say “no jardim de infância” (at/in the kindergarten) and “professor(a) de jardim de infância” (kindergarten teacher).
target_language_example: Minha filha vai começar no jardim de infância no ano que vem.
native_language_example: My daughter is going to start kindergarten/preschool next year.

additional_notes: A common, neutral term for “zoo.” Often used with the verb ir/ir ao (to go to): “Fui ao jardim zoológico.” In Brazil, “zoológico” is also very common by itself; in Portugal you may also hear “zoo.”
target_language_example: Vamos ao jardim zoológico no domingo?
native_language_example: Shall we go to the zoo on Sunday?

additional_notes: From the verb "jogar" (to play, for games/sports) + "futebol" (soccer/football). In Brazil, "futebol" usually means soccer. "Joga" is the 3rd-person singular present (ele/ela/você): "Ele joga futebol", "Você joga futebol?". With other subjects: "Eu jogo futebol", "Nós jogamos futebol". Often followed by "com" to say who you play with ("joga futebol com amigos") and time expressions like "Há quanto tempo você joga futebol?" / "Faz quanto tempo que você joga futebol?".
target_language_example: Ele joga futebol muito bem.
native_language_example: He plays soccer very well.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **jogar** (“to play”) + the sport **golfe** (“golf”). The form **joga** is present tense for **ele/ela/você** (“he/she/you”). Other common forms: **eu jogo golfe** (I play golf), **você joga golfe?** (Do you play golf?), **eles jogam golfe** (They play golf).
target_language_example: Meu chefe joga golfe depois do trabalho às sextas-feiras.
native_language_example: My boss plays golf after work on Fridays.

additional_notes: From the verb "jogar" (to play, for sports/games) + "tênis" (tennis). "Joga" is the 3rd-person singular present (ele/ela/você). Common in questions about ability, place, or time: "joga tênis bem?" (plays tennis well?), "onde joga tênis?" (where do you play tennis?), "quando é que joga tênis?" (when does he/she play tennis?). For other subjects: "eu jogo tênis", "nós jogamos tênis", "eles jogam tênis".
target_language_example: Quando é que ele joga tênis?
native_language_example: When does he play tennis?

additional_notes: From the verb "jogar" (to play) + "xadrez" (chess). Used to talk about someone playing chess. You can change the subject and verb form: "Eu jogo xadrez" (I play chess), "Você joga xadrez?" (Do you play chess?), "Nós jogamos xadrez" (We play chess).
target_language_example: Você joga xadrez nos fins de semana?
native_language_example: Do you play chess on weekends?

additional_notes: Common way to specify a person who plays the sport futebol (soccer). In Brazil, futebol usually means soccer, so this typically refers to a soccer player; when talking about American football, people usually say jogador de futebol americano.
target_language_example: Ele quer ser jogador de futebol quando crescer.
native_language_example: He wants to be a soccer player when he grows up.

additional_notes: "Jogando" is the gerund of "jogar" (to play), used like English “playing.” "Jogando futebol" often describes what someone is doing right now (with "estar": "estão jogando futebol") or how/when something happened: "Feri meu joelho jogando futebol" (“I hurt my knee playing soccer”).
target_language_example: Eu me machuquei jogando futebol ontem.
native_language_example: I got hurt playing soccer yesterday.

additional_notes: "Jogando" is the gerund of "jogar" (to play), used to talk about an action in progress or as an explanation of how/when something happened. Common patterns: "estar jogando tênis" = "to be playing tennis (right now)"; "machucou... jogando tênis" = "got hurt while playing tennis"; "passou a tarde... jogando tênis" = "spent the whole afternoon playing tennis".
target_language_example: Estou jogando tênis agora.
native_language_example: I’m playing tennis right now.

additional_notes: "Jogar" is the verb used for playing games/sports; "jogando" is the gerund (-ing form) often used with "estar" to talk about what someone is doing right now ("estou/está/estamos... jogando xadrez"). It can also be used after another verb to mean "by playing" or "playing" as an activity (e.g., "nos divertimos jogando xadrez").
target_language_example: Estou jogando xadrez com um amigo agora.
native_language_example: I'm playing chess with a friend right now.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "jogar" (to play) + the sport name. You can conjugate "jogar" depending on the subject (eu jogo, ele joga, nós jogamos) and keep "beisebol" the same. Often used after verbs like "gostar de" (to like) and "ir" (to go) to say you like to play or you’re going to play.
target_language_example: A gente vai jogar beisebol no parque hoje.
native_language_example: We’re going to play baseball in the park today.

meaning: to play soccer; also, to cooperate / go along (with something).
additional_notes: Most commonly used for playing soccer/football in Brazil: "jogar bola" = to play soccer. In some contexts it’s also figurative, meaning to cooperate, agree, or be helpful (similar to English “play ball”).
target_language_example: Vamos jogar bola no parque depois da aula.
native_language_example: Let’s play soccer in the park after class.

additional_notes: Usually means getting rid of something (often because you think it has no value): “Vou jogar fora isso.” In sports contexts, it can also mean “to play away” (as the visiting team), often with “de casa”: “jogar fora de casa” or “jogar fora do país”.
target_language_example: Isso ainda está muito bom para jogar fora.
native_language_example: This is still too good to throw away.

additional_notes: Means playing the sport of soccer (called futebol in Portuguese). Uses the verb "jogar" (to play, in the sense of playing a sport/game) + "futebol". Common with "vai/vou" (going to) for plans: "vou jogar futebol" = "I’m going to play soccer."
target_language_example: A gente vai jogar futebol no parque no sábado.
native_language_example: We’re going to play soccer in the park on Saturday.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "jogar" (to play) + the sport "golfe" (golf). You can conjugate "jogar" to talk about different times: "eu jogo golfe" (I play), "vou jogar golfe" (I’m going to play), "queria/gostaria de jogar golfe" (I’d like to play).
target_language_example: A gente pode jogar golfe depois do almoço?
native_language_example: Can we play golf after lunch?

additional_notes: Used for the sport tennis. Common patterns: "gostar de jogar tênis" (to like playing tennis), "aprender a jogar tênis" (to learn to play tennis), and "saber jogar tênis" (to know how to play tennis). Often followed by time expressions like "nos fins de semana" (on weekends) or "esta tarde" (this afternoon).
target_language_example: A gente pode jogar tênis amanhã de manhã.
native_language_example: We can play tennis tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "jogar" (to play) + the game name "xadrez" (chess). Common in questions and with "saber" (to know how to): "Você sabe jogar xadrez?" = "Do you know how to play chess?" Also appears with "ensinar a" (to teach to): "ensinar a jogar xadrez" = "teach (someone) to play chess."
target_language_example: Eu aprendi a jogar xadrez na escola.
native_language_example: I learned to play chess at school.

additional_notes: Used mainly to indicate physical proximity (someone/something is right beside another). It can also be used more generally to mean “with/alongside” someone (e.g., being with a person for support). Often interchangeable with "ao lado de" in many contexts.
target_language_example: Posso ficar sentado junto a você?
native_language_example: Can I sit next to you?

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is accompanying or included with someone/something else. Often answers “with whom?” or “with what?” (e.g., junto com você/vocês/a gente). You can also use it for things that “come with” something (included as part of it).
target_language_example: Vou levar meu irmão junto com a gente.
native_language_example: I’m going to bring my brother along with us.

meaning: to swear to God; to swear (that something is true).
additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that you’re telling the truth or making a serious promise. It can sound intense and may feel religious to some people (similar to “I swear to God” / “I swear on God” in English). Common inflected forms include “juro por Deus” and “jurou por Deus”.
target_language_example: Ele chegou a jurar por Deus que não sabia de nada.
native_language_example: He even went so far as to swear to God that he didn’t know anything.

meaning: “I swear (that) …” (used to insist something is true or promise something).
additional_notes: Used for emphasis to convince someone (“I really mean it”) or to make a strong promise. Often said as a quick reply: “Juro que não!” = “I swear I didn’t / No, I swear!” In Portuguese, it commonly introduces a full clause after que (“that”), but English often drops “that.”
target_language_example: Juro que eu não fiz isso.
native_language_example: I swear I didn’t do that.

additional_notes: Used to say something should stop or that a situation has gone too far. You can say it alone (Já basta!) or after an order (Pare, já basta!). It can also introduce a reason meaning “it’s already enough that…” (Já basta o nome dele ser Hector.).
target_language_example: Chega de discussão — já basta!
native_language_example: Enough arguing — that’s enough!

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to stop what they’re doing or saying, often with impatience or firmness. Very common in speech. It can also appear as “já chega de + infinitive” (“enough of + doing something”): “Já chega de brincar” = “Enough playing around.” In a question, it can mean “Is that enough?” (“Você acha que já chega?”).
target_language_example: Já chega de discutir; vamos embora.
native_language_example: Enough arguing; let’s go.

additional_notes: Used with **já** (“already”) + **comeu** (past of *comer*, “to eat”) to say someone has eaten before/earlier, or to ask if they’ve eaten yet. In questions like **Você já comeu?**, it often means “Have you eaten yet?” (whether the action has happened up to now).
target_language_example: Você já comeu hoje?
native_language_example: Have you eaten today yet?

additional_notes: Used to repeat something you’ve said before, often with emphasis or impatience (like “I told you already!”). It can appear alone (“Já disse.”) or followed by what you said: “Já disse para te calar!” (“I already told you to shut up!”). Common in commands: “Pare, já disse!” (“Stop, I said!”).
target_language_example: Já disse que não vou.
native_language_example: I already said I’m not going.

additional_notes: Used to say something is overdue or should have happened sooner. Often said on its own as an exclamation ("Já era hora!") and can sound mildly impatient or relieved. It’s also common in the structure "já era hora de + infinitive" ("já era hora de vocês serem apresentados").
target_language_example: Já era hora de você me ligar!
native_language_example: It’s about time you called me!

meaning: “I’m already…” / “I am now…” (with emphasis that the state has already started).
additional_notes: Used with a following adjective, noun phrase, or expression to say you’ve already reached a certain state or condition (often sooner than expected). Common patterns: “já estou + com + noun” (Já estou com saudade. = I already miss it/you.), “já estou + adjective/participle” (Já estou familiarizado… = I’m already familiar…), and informal “já estou + ferrado” (= I’m already screwed).
target_language_example: Calma, já estou pronto.
native_language_example: Relax, I’m already ready.

additional_notes: Literally 'already is'. Já usually comes before the verb in Portuguese. This exact form uses está (from estar), so it commonly appears with ele/ela/você and with adjectives or states: já está melhor, já está irritado, já está atrasado.
target_language_example: O ônibus já está cheio.
native_language_example: The bus is already full.

additional_notes: Used to report that someone (often an unspecified group: “they”) has already told a man/boy to do (or not do) something. Structure: **Já falaram para o + [male name/noun] + infinitive**. For a woman/girl, use **já falaram para a**. In this context, **falar para** often means **to tell/instruct**, not just “to talk.”
target_language_example: Já falaram para o Pedro esperar aqui.
native_language_example: They've already told Pedro to wait here.

meaning: "has already done that/this" (referring to something someone has done before now).
additional_notes: Used to say that an action is already completed. "já" = already; "fez" is the past of "fazer" (to do/make); "isso" = that/this (a general “it/that thing”). Often appears in questions like "Será que ele já fez isso?" (“Has he done that yet/already?”).
target_language_example: Você já fez isso alguma vez?
native_language_example: Have you ever done that?

meaning: “it’s already over/gone”; often “that was …” (in the past).
additional_notes: Literally “already went/was,” but it’s commonly used to say something is finished or no longer relevant (“já foi!” = “it’s done/it’s gone”), or to comment on something as a past situation (“já foi loucura…” = “it was crazy…”).
target_language_example: Relaxa, já foi—agora é seguir em frente.
native_language_example: Relax, it’s over—now we move on.

additional_notes: Used with **passar** to say something has already gone by or occurred: time elapsed (**Já passou um mês.**), someone/something came by (**O carteiro já passou?**), an experience happened (**Ele já passou por isso.**), or a bad moment is over (**O pior já passou. / Tá tudo bem, já passou.**). In replies like **Já passou, obrigada**, it can mean “No thanks, I’m fine / I’ve already had it / it’s already taken care of,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Não se preocupa, já passou.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s over.

additional_notes: Used to explain the reason for something, often similar to “since” or “seeing that” in English. It can come at the beginning of the sentence or in the middle after a comma: “Já que está com febre, fique em casa.” / “Fique em casa, já que está com febre.” It can sometimes overlap with “now that” when the reason is a new situation, but the main idea is cause/reason.
target_language_example: Já que você terminou cedo, podemos sair agora.
native_language_example: Since you finished early, we can leave now.

additional_notes: *Já* means “already,” and *se* is used with many common Portuguese verbs (reflexive/pronominal verbs), like *se perguntar* (to ask oneself), *se sentir* (to feel), *se espalhar* (to spread), *se ir embora / se foram* (to leave/go away), *se esquecer* (to forget), *se acostumar* (to get used to), *se adaptar* (to adapt). In these cases, *já se* often translates naturally as “already” + the verb in English (you usually don’t translate *se* as a separate word).
target_language_example: Você já se acostumou ao novo trabalho?
native_language_example: Have you already gotten used to the new job?

additional_notes: Literally “already (eu) know.” Used when you already know something (“I know already”), or when you suddenly realize/figure something out (“I know!” / “Got it!”). In repetition (“Eu sei, já sei!”) it can sound a bit impatient, like “I know, I know!”
target_language_example: Já sei o que a gente vai fazer amanhã.
native_language_example: I know what we’re going to do tomorrow.

meaning: “I already told you.” / “I’ve already told you.”
additional_notes: Used when reminding someone of something you said before (sometimes with an impatient or firm tone). Literally “already” (já) + “to you” (te) + “I said/told” (disse). Often followed by a clause: “Já te disse que…” (I already told you that…).
target_language_example: Já te disse que não vou hoje.
native_language_example: I already told you that I’m not going today.

additional_notes: Formed by **já** (“already/ever”) + **teve** (past of **ter**, “to have”). Used to say something happened before now (**already had**) or, especially in questions, to ask if something happened at any time up to now (**ever had**). Often translates as “has had” in English, with **já** adding emphasis (already/ever).
target_language_example: Você já teve um chefe assim?
native_language_example: Have you ever had a boss like that?

additional_notes: Used with a past participle to form the past perfect (pluperfect) in Portuguese: "já tinha" + participle. It says something was already completed before another past event/time (e.g., "Eu já tinha saído" = I had already left). "Já" can sometimes be omitted, but it’s very common when emphasizing "already".
target_language_example: Quando você chegou, eu já tinha terminado o trabalho.
native_language_example: When you arrived, I had already finished the work.

additional_notes: Common in questions. Often implies checking or reviewing something (“Have you looked at it?”), especially with extra phrases like “com calma” (carefully). You can add an object after it: “Já viu isso?” (Have you seen this?), “Já viu o e-mail?” (Have you seen the email?).
target_language_example: Já viu o e-mail que eu te mandei?
native_language_example: Have you seen the email I sent you?

additional_notes: Used when you’re leaving briefly and expect to return soon. Often said on its own ("Já volto.") or with "Eu" for emphasis ("Eu já volto!"). Similar to "Volto já". Very common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Espera um minuto, já volto.
native_language_example: Wait a minute, I’ll be right back.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re about to go/do something very soon. Common as a quick response when someone calls you or is waiting (like “Coming!” / “Be right there!”). Depending on context it can mean you’re going to someone (“I’m coming”) or that you’re leaving/heading somewhere soon (“I’ll go in a moment”). Literally it’s “already” (já) + “I go” (vou), but in English you usually translate it with “coming/going (right) away,” not “already I go.”
target_language_example: Espera só um minuto — já vou!
native_language_example: Wait just a minute—I’m coming!

meaning: “it’s already …” / “it’s now …” (used to say something has reached a point or time).
additional_notes: Used with a noun/adjective/time expression to emphasize that a situation/time has already arrived or is already true: “já é tarde” (it’s already late), “já é hora” (it’s time already), “já é demais / o suficiente” (that’s already too much / enough), “isso já é passado” (that’s already in the past). It often adds a sense of “we’re past the point” or “by now.”
target_language_example: Vamos embora; já é tarde demais.
native_language_example: Let’s go; it’s already too late.

meaning: side by side; next to each other.
additional_notes: Used to say two or more people or things are positioned next to each other (standing, sitting, lying, placing objects). It can also mean acting or fighting together, in close cooperation ("lutar lado a lado").
target_language_example: Vamos sentar lado a lado para conversar melhor.
native_language_example: Let's sit side by side to talk better.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the exterior of something (a building, a room, a container, etc.). Common in phrases like “do lado de fora” (= outside) and contrasts with “do lado de dentro” (= inside).
target_language_example: Pode esperar do lado de fora, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you wait outside, please?

additional_notes: A noun for a weapon/tool that shoots flames. Often used with articles like “um/uma lança-chamas” or in commands (e.g., “Acionar lança-chamas!”). It’s written with a hyphen; plural is usually “lança-chamas” (unchanged).
target_language_example: Eles encontraram um lança-chamas velho no depósito.
native_language_example: They found an old flamethrower in the storage room.

additional_notes: A legal term for hiding the illegal origin of money by moving it through businesses/bank accounts so it appears legitimate. Common in news/crime contexts and with verbs like “fazer” (to do/commit) and “ser acusado de” (to be accused of).
target_language_example: A polícia investigou o caso de lavagem de dinheiro.
native_language_example: The police investigated the money laundering case.

meaning: to wash the dishes (to do the dishes).
additional_notes: A very common household chore phrase. It means washing plates, glasses, cutlery, etc., usually after a meal. You’ll often hear it with verbs like "deixar" (let), "terminar" (finish), or "ter de" (have to): "Deixe-me lavar a louça"; "Já terminou de lavar a louça?". In Brazil, "lavar a louça" is the most common way to say this (also similar to English "do the dishes").
target_language_example: Depois do jantar, eu vou lavar a louça.
native_language_example: After dinner, I'm going to wash the dishes.

additional_notes: A very common everyday phrase, often used as an instruction (e.g., before eating, after using the bathroom). It can appear with verbs like "precisar" (need to), "ir" (go), or as an invitation/command ("Venham lavar as mãos").
target_language_example: Preciso lavar as mãos antes de comer.
native_language_example: I need to wash my hands before eating.

additional_notes: Used with "no/na" or "em seu/seu" to mean "on the deathbed" / "on his/her deathbed"—i.e., during the final moments or period before death. Often appears in phrases like "em seu leito de morte" (on his/her deathbed) and can also refer to someone staying by a dying person: "ficar ao leito de morte de alguém".
target_language_example: Ela fez as pazes com a família em seu leito de morte.
native_language_example: She made peace with her family on her deathbed.

additional_notes: Form of the reflexive verb "lembrar-se" (“to remember”). It’s often used in questions without explicitly saying "você": "Lembra-se de…?" = “Do you remember …?” It normally takes "de" before what’s remembered: "lembra-se de Tom", "lembra-se deles". In everyday Brazilian Portuguese you’ll also commonly hear "Você se lembra…?".
target_language_example: Lembra-se do meu nome?
native_language_example: Do you remember my name?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone remembers a specific thing/person/event. It comes from the verb "lembrar" (to remember). In full form you’ll often see "(você) lembra do..." or "você lembra de..."; "do" = "de" + "o" (of the). With feminine nouns it becomes "da" ("de" + "a").
target_language_example: Você lembra do nome dele?
native_language_example: Do you remember his name?

additional_notes: Imperative form of "lembrar-se" used with "você" (polite/neutral). Common patterns: "Lembre-se de + noun/infinitive" (Lembre-se de tudo.), "Lembre-se que + clause" (Lembre-se que o tempo é dinheiro.), or alone as a reminder ("E lembre-se," ...).
target_language_example: Lembre-se de trancar a porta antes de sair.
native_language_example: Remember to lock the door before leaving.

meaning: “remember” (to more than one person); “remember to…” / “keep in mind.”
additional_notes: Imperative (command/request) form of the verb lembrar-se, used when addressing a group (vocês). It’s a reflexive verb, so it often appears with -se. Common patterns: “Lembrem-se de + noun/pronoun” (Lembrem-se de mim = Remember me) and “Lembrem-se (de) que + clause” (Lembrem-se que aqui mando eu = Remember that I’m in charge here). Often used to emphasize an important reminder, sometimes followed by a comma: “Lembrem-se, crianças, …”
target_language_example: Lembrem-se de trazer os documentos amanhã.
native_language_example: Remember to bring the documents tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with reflexive pronoun “-me” and the preposition “de” to introduce what you remember. It’s commonly followed by a noun (lembro-me de uma pessoa/um lugar) or by an infinitive, often in the past (lembro-me de ter visto…, “I remember having seen…”). In speech, many people also say “eu lembro de …” (without “-me”), especially in Brazil.
target_language_example: Lembro-me de ter deixado as chaves na mesa.
native_language_example: I remember leaving the keys on the table.

additional_notes: Uses the gerund "lendo" (from "ler", to read) to describe an action in progress.
