additional_notes: Used before a noun or adjective to give information about your wife. You can say “Minha esposa é …” or “A minha esposa é …”; both mean “My wife is …”. After it, you can add a profession (often without an article: “Minha esposa é advogada”) or an adjective/nationality (“Minha esposa é polonesa”).
target_language_example: Minha esposa é professora e muito paciente.
native_language_example: My wife is a teacher and very patient.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your relatives as a group. "Minha" is the feminine form of "my" because "família" is feminine; with masculine nouns you use "meu" (e.g., "meu irmão" = my brother).
target_language_example: Vou passar o fim de semana com minha família.
native_language_example: I’m going to spend the weekend with my family.

additional_notes: Literally “my (female) child.” Used to identify your daughter ("Esta é minha filha") or as an affectionate way to address a girl/young woman (similar to “my dear”). In questions it can be rhetorical or show disbelief: “Acha que é minha filha?” (“Do you think she’s my daughter?”).
target_language_example: Minha filha está na escola agora.
native_language_example: My daughter is at school now.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase: minha means "my" with a feminine singular noun, and irmã means "sister."
target_language_example: Minha irmã mora no Brasil.
native_language_example: My sister lives in Brazil.

additional_notes: Used to introduce information about your sister (job, age, personality, etc.). Portuguese usually omits the subject pronoun “ela” here; you can just say “Minha irmã é …”. After “é”, use a noun/adjective (“secretária”, “minha melhor amiga”) or an age comparison (“… anos mais velha/mais nova que eu”).
target_language_example: Minha irmã é muito simpática.
native_language_example: My sister is very nice.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the homework you have to do for school. It’s often said with the verb “fazer” (to do): “fazer a lição de casa” = “to do homework.” You can also say “me ajudar com a (minha) lição de casa” = “help me with (my) homework.” In Brazil, “lição de casa” is very common; you may also hear “dever de casa” in some regions.
target_language_example: Vou fazer minha lição de casa depois do jantar.
native_language_example: I'm going to do my homework after dinner.

additional_notes: Used by a female speaker to refer to her closest friend who is a woman/girl. Grammar: "minha" agrees with the feminine noun "amiga" (so it’s "minha melhor amiga" but "meu melhor amigo" for a male best friend). You can also use it for male speakers; the gender here describes the friend, not the speaker.
target_language_example: Vou viajar com a minha melhor amiga no fim de semana.
native_language_example: I’m going to travel with my best (female) friend this weekend.

additional_notes: Means the speaker’s mind/thoughts (what you’re thinking or remembering). Often used with verbs like estar em (to be in), manter ... ocupada (to keep ... busy), or ler (to read someone’s mind). You’ll also see the equivalent form “a minha mente” (with the article) and the contraction “na minha mente” (= em + a).
target_language_example: Essa música ficou na minha mente o dia inteiro.
native_language_example: That song stayed in my head all day.

additional_notes: In everyday Portuguese, "mulher" can mean "wife" when it’s used with a possessive ("minha/sua/nossa mulher"). Without a possessive, "mulher" usually means "woman". You may also hear "a minha mulher" (with the article) or just "minha mulher" (especially common in Brazil).
target_language_example: Vou jantar com minha mulher hoje à noite.
native_language_example: I'm having dinner with my wife tonight.

additional_notes: A possessive phrase used to refer to the speaker's mother. minha means 'my' and agrees with the feminine noun mãe. In English, 'my mother' is more neutral/formal, while 'my mom' is a common natural translation in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Vou visitar minha mãe amanhã.
native_language_example: I'm going to visit my mother tomorrow.

meaning: “my mother (to) me …” (my mom + “me” before a verb).
additional_notes: Used to say your mother does something to/for you, with the object pronoun “me” (= me) placed before the verb: “Minha mãe me ajuda” (My mother helps me), “Minha mãe me ensinou…” (My mother taught me…). In Portuguese, pronouns like “me/te/o/a/nos” often come before the verb, unlike English where “me” usually comes after the verb.
target_language_example: Minha mãe me ligou ontem à noite.
native_language_example: My mother called me last night.

additional_notes: Used to state that your mother has passed away. In Portuguese, "morrer" means "to die." You may also hear variations like "a minha mãe morreu" (with the article "a") and common time expressions: "minha mãe morreu há quatro anos" (my mother died four years ago), "minha mãe morreu quando eu era criança" (when I was a child), "minha mãe morreu de tuberculose" (died of tuberculosis).
target_language_example: Sinto muita falta dela desde que minha mãe morreu.
native_language_example: I miss her a lot since my mother died.

additional_notes: Used to describe or identify your mother. It’s the possessive “minha” (my) + “mãe” (mother) + the verb “é” (is, from ser). Follow it with an adjective (minha mãe é bonita), a noun/profession (minha mãe é enfermeira), or a phrase (minha mãe é a primeira a levantar). In Portuguese, “mãe” takes a feminine adjective: bonita, bela, etc.
target_language_example: Minha mãe é muito trabalhadora.
native_language_example: My mother is very hardworking.

additional_notes: "Namorada" is a girlfriend (someone you’re dating). Use "minha" because "namorada" is feminine. The masculine version is "meu namorado" (my boyfriend). It’s common in both Brazil and Portugal.
target_language_example: Vou ao cinema com minha namorada hoje.
native_language_example: I'm going to the movies with my girlfriend today.

additional_notes: Used to state your personal view, often with the verb "ser" ("Minha opinião é...") or after asking for someone’s view ("Se querem minha opinião..." = "If you want my opinion..."). "Opinião" is feminine, so it goes with "minha"; in more formal writing you may also see "a minha opinião".
target_language_example: Na minha opinião, isso não faz sentido.
native_language_example: In my opinion, that doesn’t make sense.

additional_notes: Used when you give your promise (Dou-lhe minha palavra), when you keep/break your promise (manter/quebrar minha palavra), or to emphasize sincerity/strong belief (Por minha palavra, ... = “I swear / honestly ...”). It can also mean “my version/testimony” in a disagreement (É a minha palavra contra a sua = “It’s my word against yours.”).
target_language_example: Eu dou a minha palavra de que vou pagar amanhã.
native_language_example: I give you my word that I’ll pay tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your own leg (or sometimes the lower part of your body). In Portuguese, the possessive can appear with or without the definite article: “a minha perna” and “minha perna” both mean “my leg.” Common in injury/health contexts with verbs like machucar (to hurt/injure), quebrar (to break), and morder (to bite).
target_language_example: Minha perna está doendo muito.
native_language_example: My leg hurts a lot.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a female cousin. It’s the feminine form of the possessive + noun: minha (my) + prima (female cousin). For a male cousin, say “meu primo.”
target_language_example: Minha prima mora em Lisboa.
native_language_example: My (female) cousin lives in Lisbon.

meaning: 'my own' (emphasizing that it belongs to me or is chosen/done by me).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine noun (because própria is feminine): minha própria casa/verdade/escolha. It adds emphasis, like “my very own” or “of my own,” and often highlights independence or personal responsibility/choice. For masculine nouns, you’d say meu próprio (e.g., meu próprio carro).
target_language_example: Preciso de um tempo só para mim, para seguir a minha própria vida.
native_language_example: I need some time just for myself, to live my own life.

meaning: "my aunt" (your mother’s or father’s sister; also used for an aunt by marriage).
additional_notes: Used to talk about your aunt. In Portuguese, family terms often appear with a possessive (minha/meu, sua/seu, etc.) and may be preceded by the definite article: "a minha tia" and "minha tia" both mean "my aunt" (the article is common in Brazil). If you mean an older woman who isn’t a relative, Portuguese may use "tia" informally in some contexts, but "minha tia" normally implies a real family relationship.
target_language_example: Vou visitar minha tia no fim de semana.
native_language_example: I’m going to visit my aunt this weekend.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your aunt (your mother’s or father’s sister, or your uncle’s wife). In Portuguese you can include the definite article: “a minha tia” = “my aunt” (often sounds more natural/emphatic in European Portuguese; common in Brazilian Portuguese too). Without the article, “minha tia” is also correct, especially when speaking generally. "Tia" can also be used informally to address an older woman, but here it’s the literal family meaning.
target_language_example: Minha tia mora em Lisboa.
native_language_example: My aunt lives in Lisbon.

additional_notes: A literal phrase used to talk about your life, experiences, or situation. Minha agrees with the feminine noun vida. In some contexts, minha vida can also be used affectionately to address someone, but in these examples it is literal.
target_language_example: Minha vida mudou muito este ano.
native_language_example: My life changed a lot this year.

additional_notes: Plural feminine: use when the group is all women/girls (or you’re referring to a feminine group). It can be a warm form of address in thanks (e.g., “Obrigado, minhas amigas!”). As a possessive, it can appear with or without an article depending on the sentence: “Eu gosto das minhas amigas” (I like my friends) vs. “Minhas amigas foram...” (My friends went...).
target_language_example: Vou sair com minhas amigas hoje à noite.
native_language_example: I'm going out with my (female) friends tonight.

additional_notes: "Minhas" is the feminine plural form of "my" and agrees with "chaves" (keys). Often used when talking about house/apartment or car keys. You may also hear "as minhas chaves" (“my keys,” with the definite article).
target_language_example: Você viu minhas chaves em algum lugar?
native_language_example: Have you seen my keys anywhere?

meaning: “my things / my stuff” (my belongings or personal matters).
additional_notes: Usually refers to your personal belongings (clothes, items, documents, etc.). In some contexts it can also mean your personal business/affairs (e.g., problems to deal with or tasks to sort out: “resolver minhas coisas” = “take care of my things”). Often said as “minhas coisas” or “as minhas coisas” for emphasis.
target_language_example: Preciso passar em casa para pegar minhas coisas.
native_language_example: I need to stop by home to get my things.

meaning: “my back” (my back area; often used when talking about back pain).
additional_notes: Literally “my backs,” but Portuguese uses the plural (as in English “my back” is singular). Common with verbs like doer/estar doendo (“to hurt”) and expressions like “estão me matando” (“are killing me,” meaning they hurt a lot). Can also be used for actions involving your back, like “coçar” (“to scratch”).
target_language_example: Depois de carregar a mala, minhas costas começaram a doer.
native_language_example: After carrying the suitcase, my back started to hurt.

additional_notes: Used to talk about luggage that belongs to the speaker. "Minhas" is the feminine plural form of "my" and agrees with "malas" (bags/suitcases). You may also hear it without "as" ("minhas malas") or with it ("as minhas malas").
target_language_example: Vou deixar minhas malas no quarto e já volto.
native_language_example: I'll leave my bags in the room and be right back.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your own hands, literally (washing, sweating, full) or figuratively to emphasize personal responsibility or direct involvement (e.g., "with my own hands"). In European Portuguese you often hear/see "as minhas mãos"; in Brazilian Portuguese both "minhas mãos" and "as minhas mãos" are common.
target_language_example: Eu fiz isso com as minhas mãos.
native_language_example: I did this with my own hands.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase used to talk about your legs (pain, size, tiredness, etc.). Often appears with body-related verbs like doer (to hurt): “Minhas pernas doem.” In “Minhas pernas estão me matando,” it’s an exaggeration meaning “My legs are killing me” (very tired/sore).
target_language_example: Depois da caminhada, minhas pernas doem muito.
native_language_example: After the walk, my legs hurt a lot.

additional_notes: Used to talk about clothing that belongs to the speaker. You may also see the more common form with the article: “as minhas roupas” (“my clothes”). Often appears with verbs like gostar de (to like), roubar (to steal), estar (to be), or lavar/torcer (to wash/wring).
target_language_example: Preciso lavar minhas roupas hoje.
native_language_example: I need to wash my clothes today.

additional_notes: Refers to coins from a long time ago, often used in contexts like collecting (colecionar) or archaeology/history (found in tombs, etc.). In everyday Portuguese, it can mean simply “old coins,” but it often suggests coins with historical or collectible value.
target_language_example: Ele coleciona moedas antigas desde criança.
native_language_example: He has collected old/antique coins since he was a child.

additional_notes: Used for a sauce made from tomatoes, especially for pasta and cooking. You may also hear "lata de molho de tomate" (a can of tomato sauce) and "fazer ... do zero" (make it from scratch).
target_language_example: Vou fazer pizza com molho de tomate.
native_language_example: I'm going to make pizza with tomato sauce.

meaning: “pile of shit” (very offensive insult) or “this fucking mess”.
additional_notes: Strong profanity. Used either (1) to insult someone directly (“You piece of shit!”) or (2) to complain about a bad situation/thing (“this mess / this shitty situation”). In speech it often appears with articles/demonstratives: “um/esse/este monte de merda”. Avoid in polite contexts.
target_language_example: Eu não aguento mais esse monte de merda.
native_language_example: I can’t take this fucking mess anymore.

additional_notes: From the verb *morar* (“to live/reside”) + *aqui* (“here”). Common in questions like *Há quanto tempo você mora aqui?* (“How long have you lived here?”). In Brazilian Portuguese, *você mora aqui?* means “Do you live here?” (about someone’s residence).
target_language_example: Você mora aqui ou está só de passagem?
native_language_example: Do you live here, or are you just passing through?

additional_notes: From the verb “morar” (to live/reside) + “em” (in/at). Used to say where someone lives (city, country, neighborhood) or sometimes the type of place (e.g., “em um apartamento”). Often followed by a place name or by “um/uma” + noun.
target_language_example: Ele mora em Lisboa, mas trabalha no Porto.
native_language_example: He lives in Lisbon, but works in Porto.

additional_notes: "mora" is from the verb "morar" (to live/reside). "na" = "em" + "a" and usually means "in the" for feminine singular places (na casa, na cidade) and for many countries/regions (na Alemanha, na Austrália). With masculine singular, you often use "no" (no Brasil).
target_language_example: Minha irmã mora na cidade vizinha.
native_language_example: My sister lives in the neighboring city.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone lives. "mora" is the 3rd-person singular of "morar" (to live/reside). "no" is a contraction of "em + o" = "in/on/at the" (masculine singular). For feminine singular, use "mora na" (em + a). For plural, "mora nos / mora nas".
target_language_example: Ele mora no centro da cidade.
native_language_example: He lives in the city center.

additional_notes: Used with a place to say where people live. "Moram" is the present tense (they/you all live) of "morar" + "em" (in). Often followed by a city/country: "moram em Berlim", "moram no Brasil" (em + o = no), "moram na Alemanha" (em + a = na).
target_language_example: Meus pais moram em São Paulo.
native_language_example: My parents live in São Paulo.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone lives, usually with a city, country, neighborhood, or house/apartment. The preposition em often contracts with articles: no, na, nos, nas (for example, morar no Brasil, morar na cidade).
target_language_example: Ela quer morar em Lisboa.
native_language_example: She wants to live in Lisbon.

meaning: "used to live in" / "was living in" (past, ongoing/habitual).
additional_notes: "Morava" is the imperfect past of "morar" (to live/reside). Use it for past situations that were ongoing, repeated, or background information (often with "quando" = "when"). It commonly contrasts with "morei em" (simple past: lived in, completed period). It’s followed by a place: "morava em Boston", "morava em Singapura".
target_language_example: Naquela época, eu morava em Lisboa e trabalhava no centro.
native_language_example: Back then, I used to live in Lisbon and I worked downtown.

meaning: “I live in” (used to say where you live).
additional_notes: “Moro” is the present tense of the verb “morar” (to live/reside) for “eu” (I). It’s followed by “em” + a place (city, country, neighborhood), often with a contraction: em + o = no (moro no Brasil), em + a = na (moro na Itália), em + um/uma = num/numa (moro numa cidade pequena).
target_language_example: Moro em Lisboa, mas trabalho em Cascais.
native_language_example: I live in Lisbon, but I work in Cascais.

additional_notes: Literal meaning is “dying of hunger,” but it’s commonly used as an exaggeration to mean you’re extremely hungry. Often used with estar: “Estou morrendo de fome.”
target_language_example: Depois da caminhada, eu estava morrendo de fome.
native_language_example: After the hike, I was starving.

meaning: to starve; to die of hunger.
additional_notes: Often used both literally (having no food, starving) and hyperbolically to mean being extremely hungry or very poor/without money. The structure is common in Portuguese: "morrer de" + noun can mean being overwhelmed by something (e.g., "morrer de medo" = to be terrified).
target_language_example: Se eu não comer agora, vou morrer de fome.
native_language_example: If I don’t eat now, I’m going to starve.

additional_notes: Used to say the cause of death. In Portuguese, morrer de + [disease/cause] = “to die of/from [disease/cause]”. You can also specify the type/location: “câncer no pulmão” = “lung cancer.”
target_language_example: Minha avó morreu de câncer há cinco anos.
native_language_example: My grandmother died of cancer five years ago.

additional_notes: Literally “dead from hunger.” Used to emphasize that someone is extremely hungry: Estou morto de fome! In some contexts it can also be used as an insult meaning someone is very poor/a nobody (e.g., Um morto de fome), depending on tone.
target_language_example: Depois da viagem, eu estava morto de fome e fui direto comer.
native_language_example: After the trip, I was starving and went straight to eat.

additional_notes: Imperative form of "mostrar" (to show) + the object pronoun "me" (me). Used to ask someone to show you something: "Mostre-me o seu passaporte". In Brazil, it’s also very common to place the pronoun after the verb: "Mostre-me" = "Mostra-me" (informal) and "Me mostre" (especially in casual speech).
target_language_example: Mostre-me onde fica o banheiro, por favor.
native_language_example: Show me where the bathroom is, please.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what the reason leads to, often followed by a noun (e.g., pânico, preocupação) or an infinitive verb (e.g., pedir). Common in negatives like “não há motivo para…” / “não tenho motivo para…” meaning “there’s no reason to…”.
target_language_example: Não há motivo para você se desculpar.
native_language_example: There's no reason for you to apologize.

additional_notes: A common term in news and science for long-term changes in Earth’s climate (especially global warming and its effects). Usually used with the definite article: “a mudança climática”. You may also see the plural when talking about different effects or aspects: “mudanças climáticas”.
target_language_example: Precisamos agir agora para reduzir os impactos da mudança climática.
native_language_example: We need to act now to reduce the impacts of climate change.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to mean changing something: mudar de ideia/opinião = “change your mind,” mudar de canal = “switch channels,” mudar de roupa = “change clothes.” Often implies changing from one option to another.
target_language_example: Você pode mudar de ideia depois, não tem problema.
native_language_example: You can change your mind later, no problem.

additional_notes: Used when you want to stop talking about the current topic and start talking about something else. Common in conversations (sometimes to avoid an uncomfortable topic). Often used with "vamos" (let’s) or "podemos" (can we) + "por favor" (please).
target_language_example: Podemos mudar de assunto? Isso me deixa desconfortável.
native_language_example: Can we change the subject? This makes me uncomfortable.

additional_notes: Used when someone changes their opinion, plan, or decision. Very common after new information, reflection, or persuasion. It can be used on its own (Ele pode mudar de ideia.) or after verbs like fazer (to make someone) and convencer (to convince someone) to highlight what caused the change.
target_language_example: Isso me fez mudar de ideia.
native_language_example: That made me change my mind.

additional_notes: Past tense (3rd person singular) of "mudar de ideia" (to change one’s mind). Used when someone decides differently than before. The subject can be explicit ("Tom mudou de ideia") or implied by context. Related forms: "mudei de ideia" (I changed my mind), "mudamos de ideia" (we changed our minds), "mudou de ideia?" (Did you change your mind?).
target_language_example: Eu ia sair, mas ele mudou de ideia.
native_language_example: I was going to go out, but he changed his mind.

additional_notes: Means “many things” or “a lot going on,” often used in a general/vague way when you don’t want to list items. You can use it as the subject (“Muita coisa mudou...”) or as an object (“Eu perdi muita coisa”). In speech, it’s common in the pattern “tem muita coisa + gerund” to mean “there’s a lot + happening/going on” (e.g., “Tem muita coisa rolando”). Can also soften/minimize: “Não é muita coisa” = “It’s not much.”
target_language_example: Eu tenho muita coisa pra fazer hoje.
native_language_example: I have a lot to do today.

meaning: a lot of people; many people.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a large number of people in general (often like English “lots of people”). It’s very common in everyday speech and can be the subject of a sentence: “Muita gente + verb (singular)”.
target_language_example: Hoje tem muita gente no shopping.
native_language_example: There are a lot of people at the mall today.

meaning: a lot of luck; very lucky.
additional_notes: Used to say someone has had good luck, or (often with "não") that they haven’t had much luck. Common with the verb "ter": "ter muita sorte" (to have a lot of luck).
target_language_example: Você tem muita sorte de ter amigos tão bons.
native_language_example: You’re very lucky to have such good friends.

additional_notes: Used to say there is a large quantity of water (available, used, drunk, etc.). “Muita” agrees with the feminine noun “água” (so it’s “muita,” not “muito”). Often used when talking about drinking water (“água potável”), water supply, or water consumption.
target_language_example: Hoje eu preciso beber muita água.
native_language_example: Today I need to drink a lot of water.

additional_notes: Means an unspecified, general set of things. It’s the feminine plural form: "muitas" agrees with "coisas" (feminine plural). Often used as a subject or object to talk broadly about events, information, preferences, etc. (e.g., "muitas coisas aconteceram" = "many things happened").
target_language_example: Eu tenho muitas coisas para fazer hoje.
native_language_example: I have many things to do today.

additional_notes: Commonly used with the verb "tirar" ("tirar fotos" = "to take photos"). "Muitas" agrees with the feminine plural noun "fotos". In negatives, "não... muitas" means "not many".
target_language_example: A gente tirou muitas fotos na praia.
native_language_example: We took a lot of pictures at the beach.

additional_notes: Used to say that there are a lot of different languages, or that someone learns/speaks several languages. Feminine plural: muita (f.) → muitas; língua → línguas. Often used with verbs like aprender (to learn), falar (to speak), and ensinar (to teach).
target_language_example: Ela fala muitas línguas, mas quer aprender mais uma.
native_language_example: She speaks many languages, but she wants to learn one more.

additional_notes: Means a large number of people. Used as a noun phrase; it can be the subject ("Muitas pessoas decidiram...") or object of a sentence. Commonly appears after existential expressions like "havia" (there was/were): "Havia muitas pessoas...".
target_language_example: Hoje, há muitas pessoas no parque.
native_language_example: Today, there are many people in the park.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens frequently or repeatedly. It can go at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis ("Muitas vezes, ...") or right before the verb ("ele muitas vezes chega...").
target_language_example: Muitas vezes eu esqueço minhas chaves.
native_language_example: I often forget my keys.

additional_notes: Used when you want to emphasize something strongly (“muito” = a lot/very much) and then introduce a contrast with “mas” (= but). Very common in apologies and explanations: “Lamento muito, mas…” (“I’m very sorry, but…”). You can intensify it with repetition: “muito, mas muito mesmo” = “a lot—really a lot.”
target_language_example: Eu queria ajudar muito, mas não posso agora.
native_language_example: I really wanted to help, but I can’t right now.

additional_notes: Repetition of "muito" is used to intensify what comes next (an adjective/adverb) or to emphasize thanks/feelings. In writing it often appears with a comma ("muito, muito"), but in speech it’s just repeating the word for emphasis.
target_language_example: Estou muito, muito feliz por você!
native_language_example: I’m very, very happy for you!

additional_notes: Used to say that someone does something well to a high degree, or that someone feels well. Common after verbs like falar, conhecer, ouvir, dançar, and sentir-se.
target_language_example: Ela cozinha muito bem.
native_language_example: She cooks very well.

additional_notes: Used to describe a feminine noun (or a person referred to with a feminine word): e.g., memória, ideia, comida. With masculine nouns, use “muito bom”. Often comes after the noun: “uma memória muito boa”.
target_language_example: A comida daqui é muito boa.
native_language_example: The food here is very good.

additional_notes: A common way to say that something is of high quality or that someone does something well. It can describe things, situations, or people's abilities. The adjective changes with gender and number: muito boa, muito bons, muito boas.
target_language_example: Este restaurante é muito bom.
native_language_example: This restaurant is very good.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has strong ability/skill in a specific activity or task already mentioned or understood from context. Typically used with “ser” (to be) or “ficar” (to become/get): “Eu sou/era…”, “Ele é/foi…”, “Ele ficou…”. Note agreement: with a feminine subject, it becomes “muito boa nisso” (e.g., “Ela é muito boa nisso”).
target_language_example: Eu era muito bom nisso.
native_language_example: I was very good at it.

additional_notes: Used to compliment a woman/girl or to describe a feminine noun (e.g., cidade, lua, letra). “Muito” intensifies the adjective. Change “bonita” to “bonito” with masculine nouns/people (e.g., “um lugar muito bonito”, “ele está muito bonito”).
target_language_example: Essa foto ficou muito bonita.
native_language_example: That photo turned out very beautiful.

additional_notes: Used to intensify the adjective bonito (“beautiful/pretty”) with muito (“very/a lot”). Bonito changes to match what it describes: muito bonita (feminine), muito bonitos/bonitas (plural). Often comes after the noun (um nome muito bonito), but can also be used on its own as a comment: Eu acho muito bonito. / Isso é muito bonito.
target_language_example: Ela tem um sotaque muito bonito.
native_language_example: She has a very beautiful accent.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re extremely tired. Agree it with the person: muito cansado (male) / muito cansada (female). Common with estar: Estou muito cansado/cansada. You can also use it in guesses or advice: Você deve estar muito cansado/cansada (“You must be very tired”).
target_language_example: Estou muito cansado, mas bem.
native_language_example: I’m very tired, but fine.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize the price/cost of something. Often said as an exclamation ("Isso é muito caro!") and can also be used with "não" to soften/negate it ("não é muito caro" = "it’s not very expensive").
target_language_example: Esse celular é muito caro para mim.
native_language_example: This phone is too expensive for me.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that something is hard (an activity, exam, book, situation, etc.). It can come after the verb ("é muito difícil") or before an infinitive ("é muito difícil de ler" = "it’s very hard to read").
target_language_example: Aprender a dirigir numa cidade grande pode ser muito difícil.
native_language_example: Learning to drive in a big city can be very difficult.

additional_notes: Used to describe an activity or experience as being a lot of fun. Common with verbs like "ser" and "foi" (was), or after verbs of opinion like "achar" (to think/find): "Achei muito divertido" = "I found it very fun." You can also use it with an infinitive to talk about an activity in general: "É muito divertido + verb".
target_language_example: Foi muito divertido assistir ao jogo com você.
native_language_example: It was very fun to watch the game with you.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is very amusing. It can be sincere (a compliment) or, depending on tone/context, sarcastic like “yeah, very funny.” Often refers either to a person (Ele é muito engraçado.) or to a comment/joke (O que você disse foi muito engraçado.). Note: when modifying a feminine noun, it becomes "muito engraçada" (e.g., "Essa piada foi muito engraçada"), but the base term is "muito engraçado."
target_language_example: O meu irmão é muito engraçado.
native_language_example: My brother is very funny.

additional_notes: Used to describe a person, thing, sound, behavior, or situation that feels unusual, odd, or suspicious. Often placed after the noun it describes (e.g., 'um som muito estranho'), and it can also follow linking verbs like 'ser' or 'estar' (e.g., 'foi muito estranho', 'está muito estranho').
target_language_example: Esse lugar está muito estranho hoje.
native_language_example: This place is really weird today.

additional_notes: Used to intensify the feeling of being happy (muito = “very/a lot”). Often appears with ser/estar/ficar (e.g., estou/ficaria muito feliz) and is common in polite phrases like “I’d be very happy to…” (ficaria muito feliz de/por…).
target_language_example: Eu ficaria muito feliz em ajudar.
native_language_example: I’d be very happy to help.

additional_notes: Used to describe a group of people (or “we”) being very happy. It’s plural, so it matches plural subjects like “todos”, “eles/elas”, or “nós”. Singular is “muito feliz”.
target_language_example: Estamos muito felizes com a notícia.
native_language_example: We’re very happy about the news.

additional_notes: Used for physical strength (a strong person), strong taste/alcohol/coffee, strong natural forces (current/wind), or intense experiences/feelings (nausea, a movie that’s too intense). With "pra" it often means "too intense/strong for (someone)" (e.g., "muito forte pra ele").
target_language_example: Esse perfume é muito forte; vou usar menos.
native_language_example: This perfume is very strong; I’m going to use less.

meaning: "very kind" / "very nice" (about a person or something they did).
additional_notes: Used to praise someone's kindness or politeness. Common pattern: "É muito gentil de sua parte + infinitive" = "It’s very kind of you to..." (also: "da sua parte"). In Brazil you’ll also hear "muito legal" in more casual situations.
target_language_example: Foi muito gentil da sua parte me ajudar com as malas.
native_language_example: It was very kind of you to help me with the bags.

additional_notes: Used to describe size or extent. Often appears with “não é muito grande” (“it’s not very big”). With people (e.g., “Você é muito grande”), it can mean physically big/tall/large; depending on context, it may sound a bit direct, so speakers might soften it (e.g., “bem alto/a” = “quite tall”).
target_language_example: O apartamento é muito grande para mim.
native_language_example: The apartment is very big for me.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize the importance of something. "Muito" means "very" and typically comes right before the adjective: "muito importante", "muito bom", "muito difícil".
target_language_example: Isso é muito importante para mim.
native_language_example: This is very important to me.

additional_notes: Used to strongly compliment someone’s intelligence. It typically comes after the verb (e.g., "é muito inteligente") or after a noun (e.g., "um homem muito inteligente"). "Muito" intensifies the adjective "inteligente."
target_language_example: Ela é muito inteligente e aprende rápido.
native_language_example: She’s very smart and learns quickly.

additional_notes: Used to express strong interest or that you found something engaging. Common with verbs like achar (“to think/find”): “Achei muito interessante…”. Word order is flexible: “Isso é muito interessante” / “Isso foi muito interessante” / “Muito interessante foi…”. You can add emphasis with “mesmo” (“really/indeed”): “Foi muito interessante mesmo.”
target_language_example: Achei a conversa muito interessante.
native_language_example: I found the conversation very interesting.

additional_notes: Common, informal-friendly way to say you like something or someone. Used for people, objects, events, and experiences (e.g., "Foi muito legal" = "It was really cool"). In speech it can stand alone as a reaction: "Muito legal!".
target_language_example: O show foi muito legal!
native_language_example: The show was really cool!

additional_notes: Used to say something is at a great distance (physically or in travel time). Often appears with verbs like estar/morar/ir/vir: "Estou muito longe", "Moro muito longe", "Veio de muito longe?". Common with "de" to show distance from a place: "muito longe do centro". In questions about whether a trip is reasonable: "É muito longe pra ir caminhando?" (= Is it too far to walk?).
target_language_example: A praia fica muito longe daqui.
native_language_example: The beach is very far from here.

meaning: 'really crazy' / 'totally crazy' (about a person or idea).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone seems crazy, reckless, or out of their mind. Often expresses surprise, criticism, or disbelief (e.g., 'You’d have to be crazy to do that'). In some contexts it can be playful between friends, but it can also sound insulting depending on tone.
target_language_example: Você tem que ser muito louco pra pular daí!
native_language_example: You’d have to be really crazy to jump from there!

additional_notes: Used to emphasize a comparison or an increase in quantity/degree. Common in sentences with comparisons ("X ... muito mais do que Y" = "X ... much more than Y") and after verbs to mean you need/expect a greater amount ("preciso aprender muito mais" = "I need to learn much more").
target_language_example: Hoje eu entendo muito mais do que antes.
native_language_example: Today I understand much more than before.

additional_notes: Used to compare quantities, degree, value, etc. Pattern: **(subject) + verb + muito mais do que + (comparison)**. Often pairs with **antes** (“before”) for time comparisons (e.g., “more than before”), or with a person/thing (e.g., “more than him/that”).
target_language_example: Esta casa custa muito mais do que eu esperava.
native_language_example: This house costs much more than I expected.

meaning: very sick / very unwell; (also) very badly.
additional_notes: Most commonly used with verbs like "sentir-se" (to feel) to say you feel very unwell: "Estou me sentindo muito mal". It can also describe how someone looks ("Você parece muito mal" = you look very unwell) or how something was done ("fiz muito mal" = I did very badly).
target_language_example: Estou muito mal hoje; acho que vou ficar em casa.
native_language_example: I’m very unwell today; I think I’ll stay home.

additional_notes: Used to compare improvement or a higher quality/skill. Common with verbs like sentir-se (to feel): “sinto-me muito melhor” = “I feel much better.” Also used in comparisons with do que/que (“than”): “muito melhor do que/que…” = “much better than…”.
target_language_example: Depois de descansar, estou muito melhor.
native_language_example: After resting, I’m much better.

meaning: 'much less' / 'let alone' (used to make a negative statement even stronger).
additional_notes: Used after a negative statement or a prohibition to say that a second action is even more unacceptable or unlikely than the first. Common pattern: “não..., e muito menos...” (“don’t..., and much less/let alone...”). It can also be used in exclamations/commands for emphasis.
target_language_example: Eu não tenho tempo para sair hoje, muito menos para viajar.
native_language_example: I don’t have time to go out today, let alone to travel.

meaning: "Thank you very much" (said by a woman).
additional_notes: Use as a strong, polite way to thank someone. Women typically say “obrigada” and men say “obrigado” (so: “muito obrigado”). Often followed by “por ...” (e.g., “por tudo” = “for everything”) or used alone when addressing someone (e.g., “Muito obrigada, senhora.”).
target_language_example: Muito obrigada pela ajuda!
native_language_example: Thank you very much for the help!

additional_notes: A polite, common way to thank someone. You can add what you’re thanking them for with por/pelo/pela (e.g., “muito obrigado pelo presente”). “Obrigado” is typically used by men; women often say “muito obrigada.” You’ll also hear it with “antecipadamente” (“in advance”).
target_language_example: Muito obrigado pela sua ajuda!
native_language_example: Thank you very much for your help!

additional_notes: Used to thank someone for a specific thing or action. It’s followed by **por** + a noun (“por sua ajuda”) or **por** + an infinitive (“por organizar…”). You can also use **por ter + past participle** to mean “for having …” (“por ter vindo”). **Obrigado** agrees with the speaker: **muito obrigado** (male / mixed), **muito obrigada** (female).
target_language_example: Muito obrigado por me ajudar com isso.
native_language_example: Thank you very much for helping me with this.

additional_notes: Used to say a female person is very busy. "Ocupada" agrees with a feminine subject (ela, você, a minha mãe). For a man, use "muito ocupado". Often used with "estar" to describe a temporary state: "Ela está/estava muito ocupada".
target_language_example: Hoje não posso falar; estou muito ocupada.
native_language_example: I can't talk today; I'm very busy.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "estar" to talk about a temporary state (being busy right now/these days). "Ocupado" agrees with the person: "ocupado" (male or mixed group), "ocupada" (female). Can also be used to make a polite assumption: "Você deve estar muito ocupado" (You must be very busy).
target_language_example: Desculpa, hoje estou muito ocupado, mas posso falar amanhã.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm very busy today, but I can talk tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone/something is dangerous. It can describe a person (Eu sou muito perigoso.), an animal (um animal muito perigoso), or a situation/thing (Isto é muito perigoso.). Agree "perigoso" with what it describes: "muito perigosa" (feminine), "muito perigosos/perigosas" (plural).
target_language_example: Não entre aí — é muito perigoso.
native_language_example: Don’t go in there — it’s very dangerous.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is bad (a thing, situation, day, dream, news, etc.). It can stand alone as a short reaction ("Muito ruim.") and can be intensified further with repetition or words like "mesmo" ("Muito ruim mesmo" = "Really bad").
target_language_example: O serviço aqui é muito ruim.
native_language_example: The service here is very bad.

additional_notes: Used to intensify speed. With verbs, it usually means “very quickly” (Ele está aprendendo muito rápido). With actions like driving/swimming, it can also mean “very fast” (Dirijo muito rápido / Nado muito rápido). Word order is typically muito + rápido right after the verb.
target_language_example: Não fale muito rápido, por favor.
native_language_example: Don’t speak too fast, please.

additional_notes: Used to intensify the adjective "triste" (sad). It can describe a person’s emotional state ("Eu fiquei muito triste") or something that makes you sad ("Isso me deixa muito triste"). With "ficar", it often means "to become/get" sad; with "estar/ser", it describes someone as sad ("O Tom é/está muito triste").
target_language_example: Fiquei muito triste quando ouvi a notícia.
native_language_example: I was very sad when I heard the news.

additional_notes: Used as a warning or emphasis to act carefully. Common with verbs like ter (have), tomar (take), and especially in the imperative: Tenha muito cuidado. You can also say Com muito cuidado (“with great care”) when describing how to do something.
target_language_example: Tenha muito cuidado ao atravessar a rua.
native_language_example: Be very careful when crossing the street.

additional_notes: Means “a large amount of money.” Very common with negatives like “não tenho muito dinheiro” (“I don’t have much money”). In positive sentences, English usually prefers “a lot of money” (Portuguese still uses “muito dinheiro”).
target_language_example: Não preciso de muito dinheiro para ser feliz.
native_language_example: I don't need a lot of money to be happy.

additional_notes: Used as a polite set phrase when meeting someone (often said alone: “Muito prazer!”). It can also appear as “com muito prazer” to mean you’re happy to do something (“with pleasure / gladly”). You may hear gender/number agreement in a longer form: “Muito prazer em conhecê-lo/conhecê-la” (“Nice to meet you”).
target_language_example: —Pode me ajudar? —Sim, com muito prazer.
native_language_example: —Can you help me? —Yes, with pleasure.

additional_notes: A common, straightforward expression. After verbs like passar or gastar, it means spending a lot of time doing something. With faz or já faz, it often means 'for a long time' or 'a long time ago'. Tempo stays singular in this expression.
target_language_example: Faz muito tempo que não vejo você.
native_language_example: I haven't seen you in a long time.

meaning: 'a long time to' / 'plenty of time to'.
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to talk about how much time something takes or how much time someone has to do something. Often appears with verbs like "levar" (to take): "levou muito tempo para + infinitive" = "it took a long time to...". It can also mean "plenty of time to" depending on context (having enough time).
target_language_example: Demorei muito tempo para entender essa parte.
native_language_example: It took me a long time to understand that part.

meaning: “a lot of work” / “a lot of trouble (for someone)”
additional_notes: Most commonly means “a lot of work” (often with verbs like fazer/ter/precisar de: "Muito trabalho precisa ser feito"). With "dar muito trabalho a alguém", it means “to cause someone a lot of trouble/effort” (e.g., a task, situation, or person is hard to deal with).
target_language_example: Esse projeto deu muito trabalho, mas valeu a pena.
native_language_example: That project was a lot of work, but it was worth it.

additional_notes: Used to say there are many tasks still pending. The pattern is common and flexible: (ter) muito trabalho a fazer = “(to) have a lot of work to do.” You can change the verb tense (tenho/tinha/tive/teremos) or add time words (hoje, amanhã, antes de...).
target_language_example: Ainda temos muito trabalho a fazer antes da reunião.
native_language_example: We still have a lot of work to do before the meeting.

additional_notes:
Used to talk about a long period of time. Common with time expressions like:
- "há muitos anos" = many years ago / for many years (depending on context)
- "durante/por muitos anos" = for many years
- "muitos e muitos anos" = many, many years (emphasis)
- "Passaram-se muitos anos" = Many years have passed.
target_language_example: Não nos vemos há muitos anos.
native_language_example: We haven't seen each other in many years.

additional_notes: Used to say someone made lots of mistakes. Often appears with the verb "cometer" (to make/commit): "cometer muitos erros". You can add what kind of mistakes with "erros de ..." (e.g., "erros de ortografia" = spelling mistakes).
target_language_example: No começo, eu cometi muitos erros, mas aprendi com eles.
native_language_example: At the beginning, I made many mistakes, but I learned from them.

additional_notes: "Muitos" agrees in gender and number with the noun. With "livros" (masculine plural), it becomes "muitos". Used to talk about a large quantity of books, often after verbs like comprar (to buy) and ler (to read).
target_language_example: Ela tem muitos livros em casa.
native_language_example: She has many books at home.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something has a large number of difficulties or issues. Often followed by a topic or cause: “muitos problemas econômicos” (many economic problems), “muitos problemas com...” (a lot of trouble with...).
target_language_example: Estamos tendo muitos problemas com a internet hoje.
native_language_example: We’re having lots of problems with the internet today.

additional_notes: A fixed phrase used to refer to the non-combatant/civilian group in a community, especially in urgent or dangerous situations (e.g., evacuation orders, “women and children first”). Often appears as a subject or object: “as mulheres e crianças” (the women and children).
target_language_example: Em caso de emergência, levem as mulheres e crianças para um lugar seguro.
native_language_example: In an emergency, take the women and children to a safe place.

meaning: the real world (as opposed to a fantasy/online world).
additional_notes: Used to contrast everyday life and practical responsibilities with something imaginary, idealized, virtual, or fictional. Common in phrases like "Bem-vindo(a) ao mundo real!" (Welcome to the real world!) or "No mundo real..." (In the real world...). Gender/number changes in greetings: bem-vindo (m), bem-vinda (f), bem-vindos (mixed/plural), bem-vindas (all-female).
target_language_example: Depois da faculdade, tive que encarar o mundo real.
native_language_example: After college, I had to face the real world.

additional_notes: Used for the machine you sew fabric/clothes with. Often appears with verbs like "comprar" (to buy), "usar" (to use), and with possessives ("minha/sua máquina de costura").
target_language_example: Preciso consertar a minha máquina de costura antes de fazer a bainha.
native_language_example: I need to fix my sewing machine before hemming it.

additional_notes: A noun phrase meaning the machine used to type text (especially before computers). Often used with articles/possessives: "uma/a máquina de escrever", "minha/sua máquina de escrever". It’s a standard, literal phrase: máquina (machine) + de (of/to) + escrever (to write/type).
target_language_example: Ela encontrou uma velha máquina de escrever no sótão.
native_language_example: She found an old typewriter in the attic.

meaning: washing machine; also used in compounds like “máquina de lavar louça” (dishwasher).
additional_notes: Literally “washing machine” (máquina = machine, lavar = to wash). By itself, “máquina de lavar” usually means a clothes washing machine; to be specific you can say “máquina de lavar roupa”. For a dishwasher, people typically say “máquina de lavar louça” (also “lava-louças” in Brazil).
target_language_example: A máquina de lavar está quebrada, então vou lavar a roupa à mão.
native_language_example: The washing machine is broken, so I’m going to wash the clothes by hand.

additional_notes: A literal phrase meaning a (usually fictional) machine that lets you travel through time. Used in everyday speech mostly in science fiction contexts or hypotheticals ("If you had a time machine...").
target_language_example: Se eu tivesse uma máquina do tempo, eu voltaria para 2010.
native_language_example: If I had a time machine, I’d go back to 2010.

additional_notes: Used for protective equipment worn over the face to filter toxic gases, smoke, or chemicals. Common in safety, military, or emergency contexts. Plural: "máscaras de gás".
target_language_example: Em caso de fumaça, coloque a máscara de gás e siga as instruções.
native_language_example: In case of smoke, put on the gas mask and follow the instructions.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your mother’s current state, location, or what she’s doing right now. Common patterns: **a mãe está a + infinitive** = “mom is (doing) …” (ongoing action); **a mãe está ocupada** = “mom is busy” (temporary state); **está para + infinitive** = “is about to …”.
target_language_example: A mãe está no trabalho agora.
native_language_example: Mom is at work now.

additional_notes: Used to specify which hand (right vs. left), especially in instructions (e.g., “Erga a mão direita.”). Often appears with possessives: “a minha mão direita” (my right hand), “a sua mão direita” (your right hand), “na mão direita” (in/on the right hand).
target_language_example: Escrevo com a mão direita, mas seguro o telefone com a esquerda.
native_language_example: I write with my right hand, but I hold the phone with my left.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the left hand as a body part, often with a possessive: “minha/sua/a mão esquerda” (my/your/the left hand). Common in instructions and descriptions (e.g., levantar a mão esquerda = raise the left hand).
target_language_example: Escrevo com a mão esquerda, mas como com a direita.
native_language_example: I write with my left hand, but I eat with my right.

additional_notes: A fixed command telling someone to raise their hands (often in police/robbery/action contexts). You may also hear it as "Mãos para o alto!" or "Com as mãos ao alto!". In writing, it’s often followed by an exclamation mark.
target_language_example: Mãos ao alto! Isto é um assalto!
native_language_example: Hands up! This is a robbery!

additional_notes: Used to say something happened in the previous month. It’s common with or without the article: "mês passado" or "o mês passado". With "desde" (since), it marks the starting point: "desde o mês passado" = "since last month."
target_language_example: A gente se mudou para cá mês passado.
native_language_example: We moved here last month.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that will happen in the month after the current one. Often used with the future tense (e.g., “vai”, “irá”, “vai ter”) or with a future time reference.
target_language_example: A reunião é mês que vem.
native_language_example: The meeting is next month.

additional_notes: A common genre label. Used with verbs like gostar de (to like), ouvir/escutar (to listen to), and adorar (to love). Often appears without an article: Gosto de música clássica. You can also add an article when speaking more generally: A música clássica é linda.
target_language_example: Ela costuma ouvir música clássica enquanto estuda.
native_language_example: She usually listens to classical music while she studies.

additional_notes: Refers to popular music as a genre. It’s usually used with the verb gostar de (“to like”) and can take an adjective or origin after it (e.g., música pop russa = Russian pop music).
target_language_example: Eu não curto muito música pop, prefiro rock.
native_language_example: I’m not really into pop music; I prefer rock.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like ver/assistir (to watch/see) and estar/aparecer (to be/appear) to talk about something being shown or broadcast on television. It’s the contraction of em + a (“in/on the”) + TV.
target_language_example: Hoje vai passar um jogo na TV.
native_language_example: A game is going to be on TV today.

additional_notes: Used to say where something happens. "na" = "em" + "a" (in/at + the), so it’s used with feminine singular places/nouns like "a biblioteca".
target_language_example: Vou estudar na biblioteca depois da aula.
native_language_example: I'm going to study at the library after class.

meaning: in/on the mouth; at the mouth/entrance (of a place).
additional_notes: Literally, it’s the contraction of "em" + "a" → "na" + "boca" (mouth). Common with actions involving the mouth: "beijar na boca" (kiss on the lips), "colocar ... na boca" (put ... in your mouth), "levar um soco na boca" (get punched in the mouth). It can also mean the entrance/opening of something, like "na boca do túnel" (at the mouth of the tunnel).
target_language_example: Ele colocou o remédio na boca e engoliu com água.
native_language_example: He put the medicine in his mouth and swallowed it with water.

additional_notes: Used literally for something physically resting or falling on your head (e.g., a hat, a raindrop). It’s also used figuratively to mean “in your mind/inside your head,” referring to thoughts, feelings, or panic happening internally. Often appears in expressions like “Mãos na cabeça!” (“Hands on your head!”).
target_language_example: Fiquei com essa ideia na cabeça o dia todo.
native_language_example: I had that idea in my head all day.

additional_notes: Used mainly in Brazilian Portuguese with verbs like estar/ficar (to be), ir (to go), and mandar/prender (to send/arrest): “Ele está na cadeia.” Although cadeia literally means “chain,” in everyday speech it commonly means “jail/prison.” You can also say “na prisão” (more neutral/formal).
target_language_example: Se continuar assim, vai acabar na cadeia.
native_language_example: If you keep going like that, you’ll end up in jail.

meaning: on the chair; in the chair.
additional_notes: "Na" is a contraction of "em" + "a" (= "in/on" + "the" feminine). "Cadeira" means "chair" (also "seat"). Use it for someone/something sitting/lying on a chair (often translated as "on the chair"), and also when someone is tied/held to a chair (often translated as "in the chair").
target_language_example: O casaco está na cadeira.
native_language_example: The coat is on the chair.

additional_notes: "Na" = "em" + "a" (in + the, feminine). Used to say something is inside a box/container. For a masculine container you'd use "no" (e.g., "no saco" = in the bag).
target_language_example: Deixei as chaves na caixa.
native_language_example: I left the keys in the box.

additional_notes: Means “in the bed” or more generally “in bed,” depending on context. With verbs like "estar/ficar" it usually means being/staying in bed (often resting or sick): "O Tom está/precisa ficar na cama." With verbs like "pôr/colocar" it can mean putting someone to bed: "Ela põe os meninos na cama."
target_language_example: Estou doente, então vou ficar na cama hoje.
native_language_example: I’m sick, so I’m going to stay in bed today.

additional_notes: "na" is a contraction of "em" + "a" (= "in/at" + "the" feminine). Use "na casa" for location: someone/something is inside the house or at that house. It can be followed by an owner: "na casa dos meus pais" = "at my parents’ house" / "in my parents’ house" (context decides).
target_language_example: Tem alguém na casa?
native_language_example: Is there anyone in the house?

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located or happens in an urban area. "Na" is the contraction of "em" + "a" (feminine), because "cidade" is feminine: "em a cidade" → "na cidade". Often contrasted with "no campo" (in the countryside).
target_language_example: Eu moro na cidade, mas trabalho no campo.
native_language_example: I live in the city, but I work in the countryside.

additional_notes: Used to say where something is happening or where someone/something is located. It’s the contraction of "em" + "a" + "cozinha" (feminine), so you say "na" with feminine places/rooms like "na cozinha", "na sala".
target_language_example: Estou na cozinha preparando o jantar.
native_language_example: I’m in the kitchen preparing dinner.

additional_notes: “na” = “em” + “a” (in/at + the, feminine). Use “na escola” for being at school in general (studying/working there) or physically inside the school building; context decides. With “escola” meaning the institution, English often prefers “at school.”
target_language_example: Ela está na escola agora.
native_language_example: She is at school right now.

additional_notes: Contraction of "em + a" → "na". Most commonly refers to a train/metro/bus station. Used for location ("We’re at the station") or drop-off/pick-up ("Leave me at the station").
target_language_example: Vou te encontrar na estação às seis.
native_language_example: I’ll meet you at the station at six.

meaning: on the road; on a roadway; (by extension) traveling/in transit.
additional_notes: Used literally to talk about being on a road or something happening there (e.g., ice/salt on the road). It can also mean being on a journey/route to a destination: “Estou na estrada para Berlim” = “I’m on the road to Berlin / I’m traveling to Berlin.” In some contexts, phrases like “jogar alguém na estrada” can imply throwing someone out/abandoning them (leaving them with nowhere to go).
target_language_example: Estamos na estrada há três horas.
native_language_example: We’ve been on the road for three hours.

additional_notes: "Na" = "em + a" (in/at + the). Used to talk about being a university student or being physically at the university, often in past-time stories: "quando eu estava na faculdade" = "when I was in college." In Brazil, "faculdade" commonly refers to higher education (college/university).
target_language_example: Eu estudava muito na faculdade, mas também saía com os amigos.
native_language_example: I studied a lot in college, but I also went out with friends.

additional_notes: "Na" is the contraction of "em" + "a" and means "in/on/at the" for feminine singular places/events. Use it to say you were at a party or that something happened there: "na festa" (at the party).
target_language_example: A gente se viu na festa ontem à noite.
native_language_example: We saw each other at the party last night.

meaning: in the line/queue; waiting in line.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like "ficar/estar/esperar" (to stay/be/wait) to say someone is standing in a queue, often for service or their turn: "na fila aguardando a vez". You can also hear commands like "Entre na fila" (“Get in line”).
target_language_example: A gente ficou na fila para comprar ingressos.
native_language_example: We waited in line to buy tickets.

additional_notes: "na" = "em" (in) + "a" (the, feminine). Used to say someone/something is located in the forest or something happens there. "Floresta" is feminine, so you say "na floresta" (not *no*).
target_language_example: Vamos caminhar na floresta amanhã.
native_language_example: We’re going to hike in the forest tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about position (physical location) or order. For location: "O carro está na frente" = the car is in front. For moving/letting someone proceed: "Vá na frente" = go ahead / go in front (you can also say it to invite someone to enter or proceed first).
target_language_example: Pode ir na frente, eu te encontro lá.
native_language_example: You can go ahead, I’ll meet you there.

meaning: 'in front of' (in front of a feminine noun/place/thing).
additional_notes: Used to indicate a location directly in front of something. It’s composed of "na" (em + a) + "frente" + "da" (de + a). With masculine nouns you’ll usually see "na frente do" (de + o), e.g., "na frente do restaurante".
target_language_example: Normalmente há táxis na frente da estação de trem.
native_language_example: There are usually taxis in front of the train station.

additional_notes: Used to indicate position (physically in front of something/someone) or advantage in a sequence/competition (being ahead). Very common with contractions when followed by an article: na frente do (de + o), na frente da (de + a), na frente dos/das; but the base form is na frente de.
target_language_example: Ele estacionou o carro na frente de casa.
native_language_example: He parked the car in front of the house.

meaning: 'in front of' (in the space ahead of).
additional_notes: Used to indicate position directly ahead of a person/object/place, often with verbs like ficar (to stay), sentar (to sit), and estar (to be). It can also be used for doing something facing an object (e.g., na frente do espelho/televisor/computador). Before a feminine noun, it changes to "na frente da" (e.g., na frente da casa).
target_language_example: O carro está estacionado na frente do prédio.
native_language_example: The car is parked in front of the building.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is located inside the garage. Common with verbs like pôr/colocar (to put), ter (to have), estar (to be), and precisar de (to need). "Na" is the contraction of "em" + "a" (in + the), because "garagem" is usually feminine: "a garagem".
target_language_example: Deixe as bicicletas na garagem, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the bikes in the garage, please.

additional_notes: “na” = “em + a” (in + the, feminine singular). “Geladeira” means “refrigerator/fridge.” Used to talk about where food/drinks are stored (location).
target_language_example: Tem suco na geladeira?
native_language_example: Is there juice in the fridge?

additional_notes: Often means punctuality: "chegar na hora" = "to arrive on time". It can also mean "exactly at the moment" or "just in time", especially with emphasis like "bem na hora" ("right at that moment / just in time").
target_language_example: Cheguei na hora certa para a reunião.
native_language_example: I arrived on time for the meeting.

meaning: at the right time; on time (when it matters).
additional_notes: Used to say something happened at the ideal/matching moment (often with “lugar certo” = “right place”). It can mean arriving exactly when expected (“Chegou na hora certa!”) or finding/doing something early enough for a good result (“descoberto na hora certa”).
target_language_example: Se você me ligar na hora certa, eu posso te buscar na estação.
native_language_example: If you call me at the right time, I can pick you up at the station.

meaning: when it’s time to (do something); at the time of (doing something).
additional_notes: Often used with a verb in the infinitive to say it’s time to do something: "(Já) está na hora de + infinitive" = "It’s (already) time to + verb". It can also mean "at the moment of" doing something (e.g., presenting, leaving). In set phrases like "na hora de dormir" it means "at bedtime".
target_language_example: Já está na hora de ir embora.
native_language_example: It’s already time to leave.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is inside a church building or attending an event/service there. It’s the contraction of "em" + "a" → "na" (feminine singular), used with places: "na igreja", "na escola".
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar na igreja depois da missa.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at the church after Mass.

meaning: in line; (figuratively) behaving / under control; (also) next in line (e.g., to the throne).
additional_notes: Often used with verbs like ficar/estar (“to stay/be”) meaning “to behave, follow the rules, stay under control”: Fica na linha! It’s also used for succession/order: na linha do trono = “in line to the throne.” With pôr/colocar alguém na linha, it means “to put someone in their place / make someone behave.”
target_language_example: Se você quiser continuar aqui, vai ter que ficar na linha.
native_language_example: If you want to stay here, you’ll have to behave.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something is included in a list (guest list, waiting list, to-do list, etc.). Often used with the verb "estar": "estar na lista" = "to be on the list". You can specify which list: "na lista de espera" (on the waiting list), "na lista de convidados" (on the guest list).
target_language_example: Desculpe, mas seu nome não está na lista.
native_language_example: Sorry, but your name isn’t on the list.

meaning: in the shop/store; at the shop/store.
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens inside a store or that someone is at the store. It’s the contraction of "em" + "a" + "loja" (feminine), so it means "in/at the store". Often used with verbs like comprar (to buy), vender (to sell), entrar (to enter/go into), esquecer (to forget/leave behind), and ir (to go).
target_language_example: Deixei meu guarda-chuva na loja.
native_language_example: I left my umbrella at the store.

additional_notes: “na” is a contraction of “em” + “a” (= “in/on the”). Use “na mesa” for something physically on a table (food, objects, a tip left there). In some contexts it can refer more broadly to being on a table/bed used for a purpose, e.g. “na mesa de operação” = “on the operating table.”
target_language_example: Deixa os documentos na mesa, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the documents on the table, please.

meaning: "in the same" (feminine singular), used before a feminine noun like foto, aula, rua.
additional_notes: It’s the contraction of "em" + "a" + "mesma". Use it when something/someone is in the same place/group/thing as someone else: "na mesma foto" (in the same photo), "na mesma aula" (in the same class), "na mesma rua" (on the same street). For masculine singular, you’ll usually see "no mesmo" (ex.: "no mesmo lugar").
target_language_example: A gente trabalha na mesma empresa.
native_language_example: We work at the same company.

additional_notes: A very common combination meaning em + a + minha. It is used before a feminine singular noun: na minha cidade, na minha casa, na minha bolsa. Depending on the noun and context, it can mean in, on, or at my. Compare with no meu for masculine singular nouns.
target_language_example: Deixei o celular na minha bolsa.
native_language_example: I left my phone in my bag.

additional_notes: Used both literally (hearing/seeing something in your mind) and figuratively to say something is only in your imagination or is psychological: "Está tudo na minha cabeça" = “It’s all in my head.” Also common when talking about thoughts, worries, or an internal voice.
target_language_example: Acho que eu só criei isso na minha cabeça.
native_language_example: I think I just made that up in my head.

meaning: "in my face" (right in front of me, or directly/insultingly to me).
additional_notes: Literally “on/in my face.” Used both for something happening physically right in front of you and for rude/direct actions toward you (e.g., laughing at you, hanging up on you: “desligar na minha cara”). You can change the possessive: na sua cara (in your face), na cara dele/dela (in his/her face).
target_language_example: Ele riu na minha cara quando eu contei a novidade.
native_language_example: He laughed in my face when I told the news.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is located or staying at your home. Often appears with verbs like ficar (to stay), dormir (to sleep), estar (to be), and with “há” to say there is/are something at your house. It’s the contraction of “em” + “a” (“na”) + “minha casa” (“my house”).
target_language_example: Hoje vamos jantar na minha casa.
native_language_example: Today we're going to have dinner at my house.

meaning: in front of me (ahead of me).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is positioned or moving ahead of you. Common with verbs like andar (to walk), correr (to run), sentar-se (to sit), ficar/estar (to be), passar (to pass). You can change the possessive to match the person: na sua frente (in front of you), na frente dele/dela (in front of him/her), na nossa frente (in front of us).
target_language_example: Não fique na minha frente; eu não consigo ver.
native_language_example: Don’t stand in front of me; I can’t see.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located on your desk/table, or to request that something be placed there (often meaning “on my desk” in work contexts). In a workplace, it can also imply “on my desk (ready for me to review),” as in getting a report delivered to you.
target_language_example: Deixe o contrato na minha mesa, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the contract on my desk, please.

additional_notes: Used to give a personal viewpoint or judgment. It can appear at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence. Often used with "sincera" to mean "my honest opinion" ("na minha opinião sincera").
target_language_example: Na minha opinião, esse restaurante é o melhor do bairro.
native_language_example: In my opinion, this restaurant is the best in the neighborhood.

meaning: in my life (ever / in my lifetime).
additional_notes: Often used to emphasize that something has never happened before (or is happening for the first time) in your whole life: "nunca... na minha vida" = "never in my life." You may also see stronger versions like "na minha vida toda" (in my whole life). It can also mean "in my personal life" in a broader sense (things that matter or happen to me).
target_language_example: Eu nunca pensei nisso na minha vida.
native_language_example: I never thought about that in my life.

meaning: in the hand; (also) to let someone down.
additional_notes: Most commonly means something is physically being held: "com X na mão" = "with X in (your) hand". In expressions like "deixar (alguém) na mão", it means "to let (someone) down / abandon them" (not literal).
target_language_example: Estou com o passaporte na mão, pronto para sair.
native_language_example: I have my passport in hand, ready to leave.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened during the previous night. Often follows the verb: "Cheguei em casa na noite passada". Also commonly appears as "ontem à noite" (same meaning).
target_language_example: Eu fiquei em casa na noite passada porque estava cansado.
native_language_example: I stayed home last night because I was tired.

additional_notes: Contraction of "em" + "a" + "nossa". Used with feminine singular nouns: "na nossa missão" (in our mission), "na nossa cidade" (in our city), "na nossa empresa" (at our company). With movement words like "direção", it can mean "toward us/our direction" ("na nossa direção").
target_language_example: Eles chegaram na nossa casa cedo.
native_language_example: They arrived at our house early.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located/placed on a wall (e.g., a map, picture, painting). It’s the contraction of "em" + "a" (= "na") + "parede". Often appears after verbs like "estar" (to be) or "olhar/veja" (to look/see): "está na parede", "olhe na parede".
target_language_example: A foto está na parede da sala.
native_language_example: The photo is on the living room wall.

meaning: in the pool; at the swimming pool.
additional_notes: "Na" is the contraction of "em" + "a" and means "in/on/at the" (feminine singular). Use "na piscina" for being inside the pool (swimming) or located at the pool area, depending on context. Common with verbs like "nadar" (to swim), "estar" (to be), "cair" (to fall), "entrar" (to enter), and "ficar" (to stay).
target_language_example: As crianças estão brincando na piscina.
native_language_example: The kids are playing in the pool.

meaning: at/on the door; at the doorway/entrance.
additional_notes: Literally "em + a porta" → "na porta". Used for location (someone is standing/waiting at the door) and with common verbs like bater na porta (to knock on the door) and deixar/colocar algo na porta (to leave/put something at the door or in the door/lock area, depending on context). Often implies the entrance area rather than a specific point.
target_language_example: Tem alguém na porta; vou atender.
native_language_example: There’s someone at the door; I’ll answer it.

additional_notes: "Na" is the contraction of "em" (in/at/on) + "a" (the, feminine), so it literally means "in/at/on the beach." It’s used to say where someone is or where something happens: "estar/ficar na praia" (to be/stay at the beach), "passar o dia na praia" (to spend the day at the beach). In English you usually say "at the beach" or "on the beach" depending on context.
target_language_example: Vamos ficar na praia até o pôr do sol.
native_language_example: We’re going to stay at the beach until sunset.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened on the first occasion you did something (often followed by “que” + a verb: “na primeira vez que…”). It can also mean “on the first try” when correcting/referencing a previous attempt: “Você tinha razão na primeira vez” (= you were right the first time).
target_language_example: Eu acertei na primeira vez que tentei.
native_language_example: I got it right the first time I tried.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is incarcerated or serving time. It’s the contraction of "em" + "a" (feminine singular) → "na", so you’ll also see "na cadeia" (more colloquial) and "no presídio" (in a prison facility).
target_language_example: Ele ficou na prisão por roubo.
native_language_example: He was in prison for theft.

additional_notes: Contraction of "em" + "a" = "na". Often appears with verbs like "passar": "passar na prova" = "to pass the exam/test" (get a passing grade). "Prova" usually means an exam/test (not "proof" in the mathematical/legal sense).
target_language_example: Eu estou nervoso(a) para a prova, mas acho que vou passar na prova.
native_language_example: I’m nervous about the test, but I think I’ll pass the exam.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an event happening on the Monday of next week. It’s a common way to schedule plans or appointments. Often appears with the future tense (será, voltará) or with modal verbs (pode, poderei, precisa/tem que).
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar na próxima segunda-feira às 9h.
native_language_example: We’re going to meet next Monday at 9 a.m.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen during the week after the current one. It’s a common time expression: “na” = “em + a” (“in the”), “próxima” agrees with “semana” (feminine). You can also hear “semana que vem” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Podemos conversar na próxima semana?
native_language_example: Can we talk next week?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a future occasion when something will happen again. Often follows a verb (e.g., "vou fazer melhor na próxima vez") or can introduce a more specific time with "na próxima vez que..." (“the next time that...”).
target_language_example: Na próxima vez, vou chegar mais cedo.
native_language_example: Next time, I’ll arrive earlier.

additional_notes: Contraction of "em" + "a" = "na". Used to say something happened or someone was present during a specific meeting. Often followed by details: "na reunião do nosso povo" (in our people’s meeting) or "na reunião na casa da Mickey" (at the meeting at Mickey’s house).
target_language_example: Vou falar disso na reunião de amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m going to talk about that at tomorrow’s meeting.

meaning: in/on the street; out on the street (homeless).
additional_notes: Literally “in the street.” Used for being physically in the street/public space (walking, meeting, playing), and also in the expression “acabar/ficar na rua” meaning to end up homeless or without a place to live. It can also be used with street names (e.g., “na Rua Park” = “on Park Street”).
target_language_example: Não brinque na rua, porque passam muitos carros.
native_language_example: Don’t play in the street, because a lot of cars go by.

additional_notes: "na" is a contraction of "em" (in/on/at) + "a" (the, feminine singular). "sala" often means "room" in general, but very commonly refers to the living room ("a sala" = the living room) depending on context.
target_language_example: O controle remoto está na sala.
native_language_example: The remote control is in the living room.

additional_notes: "Na" is the contraction of "em" (in) + "a" (the, feminine singular). "Sala de aula" literally means “classroom” (a room for lessons). Used to say someone/something is physically inside the classroom; often appears in rules or instructions (e.g., "Não se pode fumar na sala de aula" = “You can’t smoke in the classroom”).
target_language_example: Por favor, falem baixo na sala de aula.
native_language_example: Please speak quietly in the classroom.

additional_notes: "na" = "em" + "a" (in + the), used with feminine singular places like "a sala". "Sala de estar" is the common word for a home’s living room/sitting room. Often used with verbs like colocar (put), ficar/estar (be/stay), conversar (talk), dormir (sleep), escrever (write).
target_language_example: Deixa as chaves na sala de estar, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the keys in the living room, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening on Monday. It’s very common to say the day name without "feira" in Brazil: "segunda" = "segunda-feira" (Monday). "na" = "em" + "a" (in/on the). You can also use this pattern with other weekdays: "na terça", "na quarta", etc.
target_language_example: A reunião é na segunda, às nove.
native_language_example: The meeting is on Monday, at nine.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens on a specific Monday. It’s the contraction of “em” + “a” → “na” + “segunda-feira” (“Monday”). You’ll often hear similar forms: “na terça(-feira)” (on Tuesday), “na quarta(-feira)” (on Wednesday), etc.
target_language_example: A reunião é na segunda-feira de manhã.
native_language_example: The meeting is on Monday morning.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened during the previous week (the week before this one). Often answers “when?” questions and can go at the end or beginning of the sentence.
target_language_example: A gente se viu na semana passada.
native_language_example: We saw each other last week.
