additional_notes: Used to talk about something planned or expected for the week after the current one. Often comes after the verb (e.g., "podemos nos encontrar na semana que vem") but can also be placed at the beginning for emphasis: "Na semana que vem, ...".
target_language_example: Vou começar o curso na semana que vem.
native_language_example: I’m going to start the course next week.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens on a specific Friday. It’s the contraction of "em" + "a" → "na" + "sexta-feira" (Friday). You can also add time words like "na sexta-feira passada" (last Friday) or "na sexta-feira que vem" (next Friday).
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar na sexta-feira.
native_language_example: We’re going to meet on Friday.

additional_notes: Contraction of "em" + "a sua" (= "in/on the your"). Used with feminine singular nouns: "na sua perna" (on your leg), "na sua casa" (at/in your house), "na sua sala" (in your classroom). With masculine singular you usually use "no seu"; feminine plural "nas suas"; masculine plural "nos seus".
target_language_example: Você pode deixar o casaco na sua cadeira?
native_language_example: Can you leave the coat on your chair?

meaning: at your house; in your home.
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located at the listener’s home (physical place). Common with verbs like deixar (to leave), estar (to be), ter (to have), and also to talk about things happening there. Note: in Brazil, people often use “na sua casa” even when using “você”; with “tu” you might also hear “na tua casa”.
target_language_example: Esqueci minha carteira na sua casa.
native_language_example: I forgot my wallet at your house.

additional_notes: Means something is being shown/broadcast on television, or appears on TV. Often used with verbs like ver/assistir (to watch), passar (to be on), anunciar (to advertise), and aparecer (to appear).
target_language_example: Hoje vai passar um filme bom na televisão.
native_language_example: A good movie is going to be on TV today.

meaning: at the university; in university (at college).
additional_notes: "Na" is a contraction of "em" + "a" and usually means "in/at the" (feminine singular). Use "na universidade" for being at the campus/institution, studying there, or working there (a job at a university). In English you might say "at the university" or just "in college/university" depending on context.
target_language_example: Ela trabalha na universidade e estuda à noite.
native_language_example: She works at the university and studies at night.

meaning: on the porch / on the balcony (outside area attached to a building).
additional_notes: "Na" = "em" + "a" (in/on the), used before a feminine singular noun like "varanda". "Varanda" can mean a porch/veranda (often at the front/side of a house) or a balcony (outside platform of an apartment). Which one it is depends on the building and context.
target_language_example: Vamos tomar café na varanda.
native_language_example: Let’s have coffee on the porch/balcony.

additional_notes: Used to correct or clarify information, often introducing a surprising/contrasting fact (similar to “actually” or “in fact” in English). It can appear at the beginning of the sentence ("Na verdade, ...") or as a parenthetical (", na verdade, ...").
target_language_example: Eu achei que era perto, mas, na verdade, é bem longe.
native_language_example: I thought it was nearby, but actually it’s quite far.

additional_notes: Literally 'in the life' (em + a vida). Often used to talk about life in general: 'momentos na vida' = 'moments in life'. With a possessive or name it means 'in someone’s life': 'na vida dele' = 'in his life'. With negatives it can mean 'ever': 'nunca na vida' = 'never ever'. It also appears in expressions like 'se meter na vida dos outros' = 'to meddle in other people’s business'.
target_language_example: Eu nunca vi isso na vida.
native_language_example: I’ve never seen that in my life.

meaning: in the water; into the water.
additional_notes: “Na” = “em” + “a” (in/on + the, feminine singular). With water it usually means being in the water (“flutuar na água”) or moving into it (“pular/mergulhar na água”). It can also be used for putting something into the water (“botar o barco na água”).
target_language_example: As crianças estão brincando na água.
native_language_example: The kids are playing in the water.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific time period in the past being talked about in the conversation/story. Often appears at the end of the sentence. You can use it for recent past (“at the time”) or more distant past (“back then”), depending on context.
target_language_example: Eu morava em Lisboa na época, mas depois me mudei.
native_language_example: I lived in Lisbon at the time, but then I moved.

meaning: 'in/on the last …' (referring to the most recent or final one).
additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun because it’s a contraction of "em" + "a" ("na") + "última". Common with time expressions (na última semana = last week; na última quarta = last Wednesday) and with items in a sequence/position (na última prateleira = on the last shelf). The noun is often stated right after, and can sometimes be understood from context.
target_language_example: Na última reunião, decidimos mudar o plano.
native_language_example: At the last meeting, we decided to change the plan.

additional_notes: Literally, it means something happening to someone’s face (e.g., bater na cara = hit in the face; cuspir na cara = spit in the face). In very common informal speech, especially with verbs like “estar/ficar”, it can mean that something was obvious: “Estava na cara” = “It was obvious / You could tell.” You may also hear it as a reaction question: “Na cara?” = “In the face?/Right in their face?” depending on context.
target_language_example: Eu sabia que ia dar errado — estava na cara.
native_language_example: I knew it would go wrong — it was obvious.

additional_notes: Used to indicate position or location. Very common as **na frente de + person/thing** (“in front of ...”): *na frente da Rosa*, *na frente do carro*. It can also be used on its own to mean “up front / ahead” when the reference is clear: *Ele está na frente.*
target_language_example: O banheiro fica na frente do elevador.
native_language_example: The bathroom is in front of the elevator.

additional_notes: Used to indicate physical position (someone/something is in front of another) and, sometimes, being ahead of someone (e.g., in a line or race). It is typically followed by a noun or pronoun: na frente de casa (in front of the house), na frente de mim (in front of me). In everyday Portuguese you will often see contractions when the next word has an article: de + a = da, de + o = do (e.g., na frente da escola / do carro).
target_language_example: O ônibus parou na frente de um hotel.
native_language_example: The bus stopped in front of a hotel.

meaning: “at the time” / “at (that) moment”; also “right away” or “it’s time (to…)”.
additional_notes: Common uses: (1) **Tá/Está na hora de + infinitive** = “It’s time to …” (often implying you should do it now). (2) **Na hora de + noun** = “at the time of … / when …” (e.g., *na hora do almoço*). (3) Alone as a reply, **Na hora!** = “Right away!/Sure!”
target_language_example: Tá na hora de ir embora.
native_language_example: It’s time to leave.

additional_notes: Common way to say something is located/placed on a table. It’s the contraction of "em" + "a" → "na" (feminine singular), used with "mesa". In questions like "Comida na mesa?", it’s an informal shortened way of asking if there’s food on the table / if food is served.
target_language_example: Deixa o celular na mesa, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the phone on the table, please.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your personal viewpoint, often at the start of a sentence (followed by a comma). You can change the possessive to match the speaker: na sua opinião (in your opinion), na opinião dele/dela (in his/her opinion), na nossa opinião (in our opinion).
target_language_example: Na minha opinião, devemos conversar com calma antes de decidir.
native_language_example: In my opinion, we should talk calmly before deciding.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened the previous night (the night before today). Often placed at the beginning or end of the sentence: “Na noite passada, …” / “… na noite passada.”
target_language_example: Na noite passada, eu dormi muito cedo.
native_language_example: Last night, I went to sleep very early.

meaning: in the capacity of; as (in an official role).
additional_notes: Used in formal or legal/administrative contexts to state someone’s role or position when doing something. It commonly introduces a title or function: “na qualidade de diretor(a)”, “na qualidade de representante”, “na qualidade de testemunha”.
target_language_example: Assino este documento na qualidade de representante da empresa.
native_language_example: I’m signing this document in my capacity as the company’s representative.

additional_notes: Used to contrast appearance/expectation with what is true (“in reality”), or as a correction/clarification at the start of a sentence (“actually…”). It can refer to someone’s perspective (“Na realidade de quem?” = “Whose reality?”).
target_language_example: Na realidade, eu não tenho tempo hoje.
native_language_example: Actually, I don’t have time today.

meaning: 'in the room' / 'into the room' (depending on the verb).
additional_notes: "Na" = "em" (in/on/at) + "a" (the, feminine). "Sala" commonly means "room" (e.g., living room, meeting room), and in "sala de aula" it means "classroom." With verbs of motion like "entrar" (to enter), it often translates as "into the room"; with location verbs like "estar" or "haver", it’s "in the room."
target_language_example: Ele ficou na sala esperando o médico.
native_language_example: He stayed in the room waiting for the doctor.

additional_notes: Used to correct, clarify, or emphasize what you’re saying (often like English “actually” at the start of a sentence). It can introduce a surprising detail, a correction, or a more precise statement.
target_language_example: Na verdade, eu não moro aqui; só trabalho aqui.
native_language_example: Actually, I don’t live here; I just work here.

additional_notes: Used to correct, clarify, or add a more accurate point—often contrasting with what was just said or assumed. Very common as a sentence opener: “Na verdade, eu…” + verb (e.g., “não sei”, “queria”, “esperava”). You can also drop “eu” if the subject is clear: “Na verdade, não sou.”
target_language_example: Na verdade, eu pensei que você já soubesse.
native_language_example: Actually, I thought you already knew.

additional_notes: Used to correct someone, contradict an assumption, or give a more accurate answer. It can stand alone as a full reply ("Na verdade, não.") or introduce a longer explanation ("Na verdade, não... porque..."). Often adds a polite-but-firm tone: "not really" / "not exactly."
target_language_example: —Você já terminou? —Na verdade, não. Ainda falta uma parte.
native_language_example: —Are you finished already? —Actually, no. There's still a part left.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific past period or situation being talked about. Often sets the background for a story or explanation and can appear at the start of a sentence ("Na época,") or after the subject. Usually refers to the past, but can also mean 'during that period' when the time frame is already known.
target_language_example: Na época, eu morava com meus pais e estudava à noite.
native_language_example: At the time, I lived with my parents and studied at night.

additional_notes: Used to say there’s no risk or downside, so you might as well try (often after “ter”: “não tenho nada a perder” = “I have nothing to lose”). You can also see the longer pattern “não há nada a perder” (“there’s nothing to lose”).
target_language_example: Vamos tentar—não temos nada a perder.
native_language_example: Let’s try— we have nothing to lose.

additional_notes: Common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese. Used to say two things are not connected (“Nada a ver uma coisa com a outra!”) or that someone has no involvement/relationship with someone or something (“não tem nada a ver com ela” = “has nothing to do with her”). Often appears as “não tem nada a ver (com...)”.
target_language_example: Isso não tem nada a ver com o que eu falei.
native_language_example: That has nothing to do with what I said.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the only thing involved (often with a negative tone or complaint). It commonly follows a negative verb: “não … nada além de …” = “doesn’t … anything except …”. Can also be used as a standalone phrase: “Nada além de …” = “Nothing but …”.
target_language_example: Este relatório não é nada além de uma cópia do anterior.
native_language_example: This report is nothing but a copy of the previous one.

additional_notes: Used to minimize or downplay something by saying it’s only that thing and not anything else. It often carries a dismissive or critical tone, especially about a person (e.g., "nothing but a fool"). Structure: "não é/foi/era" + "nada além de" + noun; also common with "não ter" ("não tem nada além de...") meaning someone has/knows/thinks of nothing else.
target_language_example: O problema foi nada além de um mal-entendido.
native_language_example: The problem was nothing more than a misunderstanding.

additional_notes: Used to forbid or reject something, often like a strong instruction: “Nada de + infinitive” = “No + -ing” (Nada de brigar. = “No fighting.”). With a noun, it means “No/none of …” (Nada de soldados aqui! = “No soldiers here!”).
target_language_example: Nada de celular na mesa durante o jantar.
native_language_example: No phones on the table during dinner.

meaning: “none of that” / “nothing of that” (i.e., not any of it).
additional_notes: Used to refer back to something already mentioned or understood from context. Common with negatives to emphasize absence or rejection (e.g., “não tem nada disso” = “doesn’t have any of that”). Can also express disapproval: “Não estou gostando nada disso” = “I’m not liking this at all / any of this.”
target_language_example: Eu não quero nada disso agora.
native_language_example: I don’t want any of that right now.

additional_notes: Used to say that zero things in a group apply, usually followed by a verb clause: "Nada do que + [subject] + [verb]...". Common with verbs like "disse" (said), "fiz" (did), "entendi" (understood). In "Não entendi nada do que ele disse", it means "I didn’t understand any of what he said."
target_language_example: Nada do que você prometeu aconteceu.
native_language_example: None of what you promised happened.

additional_notes: Used as a reaction to something that turned out better than expected, or to give mild praise. Often said alone ("Nada mau.") or with "não é" ("Não é nada mau" = "It’s not bad"). "Hein?" can add a teasing/expectant tone (like "huh?").
target_language_example: Esse restaurante novo? Nada mau!
native_language_example: That new restaurant? Not bad!

meaning: in that house (over there / that specific house).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific house that’s already known from context or being pointed out (often not the one near the speaker). "Naquela" is a contraction of "em" + "aquela" (= "in that"). It can be used for location (where someone lives) or where something happened.
target_language_example: Eu nunca entrei naquela casa.
native_language_example: I’ve never gone into that house.

meaning: “that night” (a specific night, usually already mentioned).
additional_notes: Uses the contraction em + aquela → naquela (“in/on that”). Common when referring back to a particular night in a story or conversation: Naquela noite... You can also ask about it: Onde você estava naquela noite?
target_language_example: Naquela noite, a cidade estava muito silenciosa.
native_language_example: That night, the city was very quiet.

meaning: back then; at that time (in the past).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific period in the past that both speakers can identify from context. Often contrasts with the present ("naquela época... hoje"). Similar to "naquele tempo".
target_language_example: Naquela época, eu morava com meus pais.
native_language_example: Back then, I lived with my parents.

meaning: "on that day" / "that day" (referring to a specific day in the past or previously mentioned).
additional_notes: Used to point to a particular day that the speaker and listener can identify from context (often a past event). It’s the contraction of "em aquele" → "naquele" ("on/in that" + masculine singular), plus "dia". Common with past-tense narration: "aconteceu naquele dia", "choveu naquele dia".
target_language_example: Eu nunca vou esquecer o que aconteceu naquele dia.
native_language_example: I’ll never forget what happened that day.

meaning: “at that moment” / “at that time” (a specific moment in the past).
additional_notes: Refers to a particular point in time already known from context, usually in a story or past situation. It often contrasts with another time (before/after). Also appears at the start of a sentence for emphasis: “Naquele momento, ...”.
target_language_example: Naquele momento, eu não entendi o que estava acontecendo.
native_language_example: At that moment, I didn’t understand what was happening.

meaning: on the back; on someone’s back.
additional_notes: Commonly used for location: carrying/wearing something on your back ("uma mochila nas costas"). It can also be figurative with "carregar" to mean having a heavy burden/responsibility ("carregar o mundo nas costas"). With "bem" it can mean right in the back (e.g., being hit/injured there).
target_language_example: Estou com dor nas costas hoje.
native_language_example: My back hurts today.

additional_notes: "Nas" = "em" + "as" (in + the, feminine plural). Used to say that something is located or happens in the mountains. Often contrasted with being in the city or at the beach.
target_language_example: Vamos caminhar nas montanhas no fim de semana.
native_language_example: We’re going hiking in the mountains this weekend.

meaning: in the hands of (under the control/responsibility of).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is controlled by, decided by, or dependent on someone/something. Very common with religious expressions like “nas mãos de Deus” (“in God’s hands”). It can also describe being at someone’s mercy or being mistreated by them: “sofreu nas mãos de…” (“suffered at the hands of…”).
target_language_example: Agora a decisão está nas mãos de Deus.
native_language_example: Now the decision is in God’s hands.

meaning: in the streets; out on the streets.
additional_notes: Used to talk about things happening in public spaces (streets/roads), often with a sense of being out in the city or out in public. It can refer to people being physically on the streets (e.g., "My cousins are in the streets of Belfast"), events happening there ("There was fighting in the streets"), or more generally to what’s happening in everyday city life ("the real Berlin is in the streets"). Formed from "em" + "as" → "nas" + "ruas" (plural of "rua").
target_language_example: Tem muita gente nas ruas hoje à noite.
native_language_example: There are a lot of people in the streets tonight.

additional_notes: Commonly used with the verb "ver" (to see/watch) or "ao" + infinitive ("Ao nascer do sol..." = "At sunrise..."). You can also say "O nascer do sol" (the sunrise) as a noun phrase.
target_language_example: Vamos sair ao nascer do sol para evitar o calor.
native_language_example: Let’s leave at sunrise to avoid the heat.

additional_notes: Past tense (ele/ela/você) of **nascer** (“to be born”) + **em** (“in/on”). Use **nasceu em** with places (cities, countries) and also with dates (e.g., **nasceu em 10 de agosto**). It can also be used more literally for something that “sprang up/grew” somewhere (e.g., a flower was born/appeared).
target_language_example: Ela nasceu em 1998, no Brasil.
native_language_example: She was born in 1998, in Brazil.

additional_notes: A common term for a vehicle that travels in space. Often used in science, space missions, and sci‑fi contexts. Plural: "naves espaciais". You can also say "a espaçonave" as a synonym.
target_language_example: A nave espacial entrou em órbita da Terra.
native_language_example: The spacecraft entered Earth orbit.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a perceived need/necessity to do something (often followed by an infinitive verb): "necessidade de + [verb]". Common in negative questions like "Você não sentiu a necessidade de...?" meaning "Didn’t you feel the need to...?".
target_language_example: Eu não sinto necessidade de explicar tudo.
native_language_example: I don’t feel the need to explain everything.

additional_notes: Used for strong emphasis that something is very far from being true, sufficient, comparable, or correct. Often appears with "não": "não é nem de longe..." (= "it’s nowhere near..."). It can also be used alone as a short reply: "Nem de longe." (= "Not even close.").
target_language_example: Ele nem de longe é o melhor candidato para o cargo.
native_language_example: He’s nowhere near the best candidate for the job.

additional_notes: Used for emphasis to say that something is true even in an extreme or unlikely case (or that someone/thing is included despite expectations). Often comes before a noun/pronoun (Nem mesmo o presidente.) or before a verb (Eu nem mesmo sei...). Similar in meaning to “nem sequer” (more formal).
target_language_example: Eu não tenho nem mesmo tempo para almoçar hoje.
native_language_example: I don’t even have time to eat lunch today.

additional_notes: Used to say something is not true in every case or doesn’t happen every time. It often softens a statement and can be followed by a verb (e.g., "Nem sempre é fácil...").
target_language_example: Nem sempre eu concordo com ele, mas tento entender o ponto de vista dele.
native_language_example: I don’t always agree with him, but I try to understand his point of view.

meaning: 'not even' (emphasizes that something didn’t happen at all).
additional_notes: Used to stress surprise or emphasis: something is true to an extreme degree (e.g., someone didn’t do the most basic/expected thing). Often comes right before the verb: "Nem sequer pensei...". It can also come before what is being emphasized: "nem sequer sabem" / "nem sequer subiu".
target_language_example: Eu nem sequer tive tempo de almoçar.
native_language_example: I didn’t even have time to eat lunch.

additional_notes: Used to say that a statement is true for some, but not for every member of a feminine plural group. It’s followed by a feminine plural noun (e.g., pessoas, crianças, leis). For masculine, you’d say “nem todos os”. Often used to soften generalizations.
target_language_example: Nem todas as pessoas gostam de café.
native_language_example: Not everyone likes coffee.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true for some people, but not for all. Often followed by a verb: "Nem todo mundo gosta..." (= Not everyone likes...). Similar meaning: "não é todo mundo que...".
target_language_example: Nem todo mundo quer sair hoje.
native_language_example: Not everyone wants to go out today.

additional_notes: Used to say a generalization is not true for every member of a group. It’s typically followed by a masculine plural noun (e.g., nem todos os alunos). For feminine plural nouns, use "nem todas as" (nem todas as pessoas...). Often translates as “Not all…” or “Not everyone…”.
target_language_example: Nem todos os brasileiros falam inglês.
native_language_example: Not all Brazilians speak English.

additional_notes: Used with a negative (usually “não”) to emphasize that something is zero or not in the slightest: “não … nem um pouco” = “not at all.” It can modify adjectives (“não é nem um pouco normal”) or verbs (“não gosto … nem um pouco”). Often placed at the end of the clause for emphasis.
target_language_example: Eu não estou nem um pouco cansado hoje.
native_language_example: I’m not tired at all today.

meaning: not caring at all; “I couldn’t care less”.
additional_notes: Very common in informal Brazilian Portuguese, usually in the pattern “(não) estar nem aí (para/com) …” or “não tô nem aí” to show indifference or lack of concern. You can add what you don’t care about with “pra/para” (e.g., “não tô nem aí pra isso”).
target_language_example: Não tô nem aí pro que eles vão dizer.
native_language_example: I couldn’t care less about what they’re going to say.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something does not happen or is not true in the most extreme/least likely case. Often comes before the word it highlights: "nem mesmo eu" (not even me), "nem mesmo assim" (not even so / even then not). Similar to "nem" on its own, but "mesmo" adds extra emphasis.
target_language_example: Nem mesmo eu entendi a explicação.
native_language_example: Not even I understood the explanation.

meaning: No way! / Not a chance! / Don’t even think about it.
additional_notes: Common, emphatic way to refuse or strongly reject an idea or request. Often used alone as an exclamation ("Nem pensar!") or followed by "em" + infinitive ("Nem pensar em sair agora." = “Don’t even think about leaving now.”).
target_language_example: —Você vai contar pra ele? —Nem pensar!
native_language_example: —Are you going to tell him? —No way!

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something did not happen or is not true—not even in the smallest degree. It often appears in negative sentences to strengthen the negation, and it can come before a verb phrase or a noun/pronoun (e.g., "nem sequer um minuto").
target_language_example: Eu nem sequer tive tempo de almoçar.
native_language_example: I didn't even have time to have lunch.

meaning: none of us; not one of us.
additional_notes: Used to say that zero people in the group (“we/us”) do, want, or know something. It’s often followed by a verb in the 3rd person singular: “Nenhum de nós quer…”. Feminine form: “nenhuma de nós” (none of us women).
target_language_example: Nenhum de nós tem tempo hoje.
native_language_example: None of us have time today.

additional_notes: Used to say that not one person/thing from a specific group applies (often referring back to a group already mentioned). It can also be used alone as a short answer/question: “Nenhum deles.” / “Nenhum deles?”
target_language_example: Eu perguntei pelos documentos, mas nenhum deles estava disponível.
native_language_example: I asked for the documents, but none of them were available.

meaning: in that house (often: in this house of yours).
additional_notes: “Nessa” is the contraction of “em” + “essa” (= “in/on/at that”). It commonly refers to a place near the listener, or a house that has already been mentioned in the conversation: “nessa casa” = “in/at that house / in your house.”
target_language_example: O que tem nessa casa?
native_language_example: What’s in that house?

additional_notes: Used to say something is located or happening within a specific zone or neighborhood. "Nessa" = "em + essa" (in that/this), and it often refers to an area already mentioned or understood from context.
target_language_example: Não tem sinal de celular nessa área.
native_language_example: There’s no cell phone signal in this area.

additional_notes: Used to respond to a situation or condition that was just mentioned, and then state what follows from it (a consequence, decision, advice, etc.). Often appears at the start of a sentence, sometimes with a comma: “Nesse caso, …”.
target_language_example: —Não posso ir hoje. —Nesse caso, vamos amanhã.
native_language_example: —I can’t go today. —In that case, let’s go tomorrow.

meaning: at that moment; right now (at this moment).
additional_notes: Means “in that moment/at that time” or “right now,” depending on context. It often refers to the current situation (“nesse momento”) but can also point to a specific time in the past when the surrounding sentence is in the past tense. Related forms: “neste momento” = at this moment (more immediate/explicit ‘this’).
target_language_example: Desculpa, não posso falar nesse momento.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't talk right now.

meaning: in this house; in our household (here).
additional_notes: "Nesta" is a contraction of "em" + "esta" (in + this). Used to refer to a specific house/building (“in this house”) or more broadly to the family/home as an institution (“in this household / in our family”), often when talking about rules, values, or what is (or isn’t) done there.
target_language_example: Aqui, nesta casa, a gente janta junto todo dia.
native_language_example: Here, in this household, we eat dinner together every day.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something located or happening in the city where you are (or the city being discussed). It’s the contraction of "em" + "esta" + "cidade"; with a masculine noun you’d use "neste" (e.g., "neste bairro" = "in this neighborhood").
target_language_example: Tem um bom restaurante nesta cidade.
native_language_example: There’s a good restaurant in this city.

meaning: in this area; around here (in this field).
additional_notes: Literally "in this area" ("nesta" = "em" + "esta"). It can refer to a physical location/neighborhood (restaurants, hospitals, post office) or to an area of work/study/experience ("nesta área" = "in this field").
target_language_example: Não conheço muitos bons cafés nesta área.
native_language_example: I don’t know many good cafés around here.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the weekend closest to now (the coming weekend, or the one that just happened depending on context). It’s a contraction of "em" + "este" ("in" + "this"), so it often answers “when?” (Quando?).
target_language_example: Vamos viajar neste fim de semana.
native_language_example: We’re going to travel this weekend.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what is happening at the present time. Common with the present tense to describe an action in progress or a situation that is currently true. It can also be used alone as a short answer meaning “Right now.”
target_language_example: Não posso falar neste momento.
native_language_example: I can’t talk right now.

additional_notes: Literally “em + este mundo” (“in this world”). Used for both the physical world and more general/figurative statements about life and society (common in sayings like “Nada é grátis neste mundo.”). Often appears in negative statements: “Não há/existe neste mundo…” = “There is/are no … in this world.”
target_language_example: Não há neste mundo ninguém perfeito.
native_language_example: There is no one perfect in this world.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the country you’re currently in, or the country being discussed. It’s a contraction of "em" + "este" → "neste" ("in this"). You can also change it for gender/number: "nesta cidade" (in this city), "neste lugar" (in this place), "nestes países" (in these countries).
target_language_example: É difícil encontrar emprego neste país.
native_language_example: It’s hard to find a job in this country.

additional_notes: Used to talk about plans or situations happening during the summer of the current year/timeframe. It's the contraction of "em" + "este" + "verão". Also common: "no verão" = "in (the) summer" (more general), and "nesse verão" = "that summer" (often referring to a different/previously mentioned summer).
target_language_example: Vamos viajar neste verão.
native_language_example: We're going to travel this summer.

meaning: "no one would say" / "no one would guess".
additional_notes: Used to express surprise that something isn’t obvious, often meaning “you wouldn’t think so” or “you’d never guess.” It’s the conditional of dizer (diria = “would say”). Commonly followed by a clause with que: “Ninguém diria que…”.
target_language_example: Ninguém diria que ele tem 60 anos.
native_language_example: No one would guess he’s 60 years old.

meaning: 'nobody likes' (followed by a noun or a verb in the infinitive).
additional_notes: Used to say that no one likes something in general, or that no one likes a particular person. After "de", you can use a noun ("más notícias") or an infinitive verb ("perder", "ser enganado"). It can sound like a general statement or complaint depending on context.
target_language_example: Ninguém gosta de esperar na fila.
native_language_example: Nobody likes waiting in line.

additional_notes: Used when you mean that no other person (besides the one(s) already mentioned/understood) does something or is present. Often followed by a verb ("Ninguém mais faz...") or by a location/limit ("Ninguém mais na sala/no mundo..."). Sometimes it implies “anymore” in context (e.g., “Ninguém mais faz isso” = “No one does that anymore”).
target_language_example: Depois que ela saiu, ninguém mais falou nada.
native_language_example: After she left, nobody else said anything.

meaning: "nobody" / "no one" + "me" (as the object): "no one (does something) to me".
additional_notes: Used when the subject is nobody (ninguém) and "me" is an unstressed object pronoun meaning "to me" or "me". Very common before verbs: "Ninguém me ouviu" (Nobody heard me), "Ninguém me respeita" (Nobody respects me). In Brazil it can also be phrased with the pronoun after the verb in more formal writing: "Ninguém ouviu-me" (less common in everyday speech).
target_language_example: Ninguém me ajudou quando eu precisei.
native_language_example: No one helped me when I needed it.

meaning: "no one deserves (it/that)"; often "this is unacceptable/too much".
additional_notes: Literally "no one deserves" (ninguém = nobody, merece = deserves). Commonly used as a strong complaint or expression of indignation about a situation: "Ninguém merece isso!" ≈ "Nobody should have to put up with this!" It can also be used more literally to say someone doesn’t deserve something (positive or negative), including in political contexts (e.g., "Ninguém merece o meu voto" = "No one deserves my vote"). Often followed by isso/assim or a verb in the infinitive (e.g., morrer).
target_language_example: Esse calor no ônibus… ninguém merece!
native_language_example: This heat on the bus… nobody should have to deal with that!

additional_notes: Used to say that it’s impossible for anyone to do something. Often followed by an infinitive verb: "ninguém pode + verbo" (e.g., ajudar, viajar). In European Portuguese you may also see "ninguém pode" with "o/a" in between in some contexts, but the core meaning stays the same.
target_language_example: Ninguém pode entrar aqui sem autorização.
native_language_example: No one can enter here without authorization.

additional_notes: Used to say that no person wants to do something. Common patterns: (1) "ninguém quer" + infinitive (e.g., "ninguém quer falar", "ninguém quer ser..."); (2) "ninguém quer que" + subjunctive to express wanting someone else to do/be something (e.g., "ninguém quer que você seja..."). It can also take object pronouns: "ninguém quer te ouvir" (nobody wants to hear you).
target_language_example: Hoje ninguém quer sair de casa.
native_language_example: Today nobody wants to leave the house.

additional_notes: Used to say that there is no person who knows something. Often followed by a clause or information: "ninguém sabe a verdade" (the truth), "ninguém sabe ao certo" (for sure / exactly), "ninguém sabe que..." (that...), "ninguém sabe onde/aonde..." (where...).
target_language_example: Ninguém sabe quando ele vai voltar.
native_language_example: Nobody knows when he's going to come back.

meaning: “no one is going to / will …” (negative about the future).
additional_notes: Used to say that nobody will do something in the future. Often followed by an infinitive verb: “Ninguém vai + infinitive” (e.g., acreditar, falar, notar, saber). “Vai” is from “ir” and works like English “going to” for future plans/predictions. You can also use it to reassure (“Ninguém vai mexer com você” = “No one will mess with you”) or to warn (“Ninguém vai acreditar em você” = “No one will believe you”).
target_language_example: Não se preocupe: ninguém vai descobrir.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: no one is going to find out.

additional_notes: A common expression used to remind someone (or yourself) that everyone makes mistakes. Often said to soften criticism, apologize, or accept an imperfection. You may hear it with an interjection like “Bom,” or “Bem,” at the start.
target_language_example: Desculpa o atraso — ninguém é perfeito.
native_language_example: Sorry I’m late — nobody is perfect.

meaning: at the airport; in the airport.
additional_notes: "No" is the contraction of "em" (in/at) + "o" (the), so "no aeroporto" = "in/at the airport" (a specific airport). Common with verbs like esperar (to wait), deixar (to drop off/leave), chegar (to arrive), buscar (to pick up), trabalhar (to work). With "chegar" you’ll often see both "chegar ao aeroporto" and "chegar no aeroporto" in everyday Brazilian Portuguese.
target_language_example: Vou te encontrar no aeroporto amanhã de manhã.
native_language_example: I’ll meet you at the airport tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is on a higher floor (often in a house or small building). Common in directions and contrasts with "no andar de baixo" (downstairs).
target_language_example: O banheiro fica no andar de cima, perto dos quartos.
native_language_example: The bathroom is upstairs, near the bedrooms.

additional_notes: Common way to talk about something planned or expected for the following year. Often used with future plans: "vou... no ano que vem" (I’m going to... next year). Literal structure: "no" (in the) + "ano" (year) + "que vem" (that comes).
target_language_example: A gente vai viajar no ano que vem.
native_language_example: We’re going to travel next year.

additional_notes: Used literally for something present in the air (a smell, a feeling, “tension in the air”), and also in a figurative/poetic sense (“love is in the air”). In TV/radio/streaming contexts, means “on air / being broadcast.” Common related phrasing: estar no ar = to be on air; pôr/colocar no ar = to put on air, to air/broadcast.
target_language_example: A entrevista está no ar às oito.
native_language_example: The interview is on the air at eight.

additional_notes: Literally "in the wardrobe/cupboard." Use it to say something is stored inside an armário (a closet/wardrobe for clothes, or a kitchen cupboard/cabinet). In some contexts it can also mean being shut/locked inside a closet (e.g., someone hidden or confined there). It can also appear figuratively like English "in the closet" (hiding one’s sexuality), depending on context.
target_language_example: Os copos estão no armário da cozinha.
native_language_example: The glasses are in the kitchen cupboard.

additional_notes: "No" is the contraction of "em + o" and often means "in/on" depending on the context. Use "no avião" to talk about being aboard the aircraft or doing something while traveling by plane (e.g., reading, seeing someone, already being there).
target_language_example: Vou dormir no avião para chegar descansado.
native_language_example: I’m going to sleep on the plane so I arrive rested.

meaning: in/at the bank; in/on the seat/bench.
additional_notes: "No" = "em + o" (in/at the). "Banco" can mean (1) a financial bank (money, loans, account), or (2) a seat/bench (like a car seat: "no banco de trás" = in the back seat; "no banco do passageiro" = in the passenger seat). The context usually makes it clear which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Vou deixar o dinheiro no banco antes de viajar.
native_language_example: I’m going to leave the money in the bank before traveling.

additional_notes: “No” is a contraction of “em + o” and means “in the” (masculine singular). Use “no banheiro” to say someone/something is located inside the bathroom. With verbs of movement (e.g., “entrar”), it can refer to going into the bathroom.
target_language_example: Deixa a toalha no banheiro, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the towel in the bathroom, please.

additional_notes: "No" is the contraction of "em" + "o" ("in/at" + "the"). Used for being at a bar, meeting someone there, waiting there, etc. Similar contractions: "na" = em + a (in/at the [fem.]), "nos" = em + os, "nas" = em + as.
target_language_example: A gente se encontra no bar às oito.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at the bar at eight.

additional_notes: Used to say something is inside a pocket (usually of clothing or a bag). Very common after verbs like colocar/pôr (to put), guardar (to keep), and ter (to have). It’s a contraction of em + o → no.
target_language_example: Estou com o celular no bolso.
native_language_example: I have my phone in my pocket.

additional_notes: Common way to say what you eat or do at breakfast. It’s the contraction of "em + o" → "no" + "café da manhã". Often used with verbs like "comer", "beber", "tomar" (have/drink), and "fazer" (have breakfast).
target_language_example: Eu tomo café no café da manhã.
native_language_example: I drink coffee at breakfast.

meaning: on the way; on the path/road; sometimes: in the way.
additional_notes: Used for being along a route or during a trip (often with "de" or "para": "no caminho de casa" = on the way home; "no caminho para" = on the way to). It can also mean being on/within a path or area ("Eles estão no caminho"), and with adjectives it forms common phrases like "no caminho errado" (on the wrong way/path). Depending on context, it may imply blocking someone’s way (similar to "in the way").
target_language_example: Estou no caminho para o trabalho.
native_language_example: I’m on the way to work.

meaning: in the countryside; in a field.
additional_notes: Used with places to mean being located in or going to a rural area (“the countryside”) or an open field. Often contrasts with “na cidade” (in the city).
target_language_example: No fim de semana, vamos caminhar no campo.
native_language_example: On the weekend, we’re going for a walk in the countryside.

additional_notes: "no" = "em" + "o" (in/on + the), so "no carro" usually means "in the car." With verbs of movement like "entrar" (to get in), it can correspond to English "into the car" (Portuguese often still uses "em/no" where English uses "into").
target_language_example: Deixa a mochila no carro, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the backpack in the car, please.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located in the central area of a city. It’s the contraction of "em + o" → "no" (literally, "in the center of the city"). Often used with places like shops, offices, monuments, restaurants, etc.
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar no centro da cidade às seis.
native_language_example: Let’s meet downtown at six.

additional_notes: Used to say something/someone is located on the floor/ground. Often used after verbs like cair (to fall), colocar (to put), deixar (to leave), derramar (to spill), or deitar (to lie down). It’s a contraction of em + o chão → no chão.
target_language_example: Deixei minhas chaves no chão.
native_language_example: I left my keys on the floor.

additional_notes: Used to say something is (or happens) on the ground/floor, then continues the sentence with another action using e (“and”). no = em + o (“in/on the” + masculine). chão usually means “ground” or “floor” depending on context.
target_language_example: Deixei o celular no chão e ele quebrou.
native_language_example: I left my phone on the floor and it broke.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has authority or is leading/managing a situation (a team, a place, a vehicle/ship, etc.). Often with the verb “estar/ficar”: “Quem está no comando?” = “Who’s in charge?” “Não estamos no comando do navio” = “We’re not in control of the ship.”
target_language_example: Ela ficou no comando enquanto o gerente viajava.
native_language_example: She was in charge while the manager was traveling.

meaning: at the beginning; in the beginning; at first.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the early stage of something ("at the beginning of...") or to your initial impression/reaction ("at first..."). Often appears as "no começo de + noun" (no começo do outono = at the beginning of autumn) or as a sentence opener (No começo, achei que... = At first, I thought...).
target_language_example: No começo do filme, eu não entendi nada.
native_language_example: At the beginning of the movie, I didn’t understand anything.

meaning: in the hallway / in the corridor.
additional_notes: "No" = "em" + "o" ("in the" + masculine singular). Used to say something is happening/located in the corridor of a building. In fixed expressions like "no corredor da morte", it means "on death row" (literally, "in the death corridor").
target_language_example: Ele está esperando no corredor.
native_language_example: He’s waiting in the hallway.

additional_notes: Literally "in the sky/heaven" ("no" = "em" + "o"). Most commonly it means "in the sky" (things you see above you: clouds, stars, planes). In some contexts—especially religious or poetic—it can mean "in heaven".
target_language_example: Hoje tem muitas estrelas no céu.
native_language_example: There are lots of stars in the sky today.

additional_notes: Contraction of "em" + "o" → "no" ("in the" + masculine singular noun). Used to indicate location or where something happens. You can also specify which desert: "no deserto do Saara" (in the Sahara Desert).
target_language_example: Ele se perdeu no deserto durante a noite.
native_language_example: He got lost in the desert during the night.

meaning: "on the day when" (the day that something happened).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause that specifies what happened on that particular day. Often followed by a verb in the past: "no dia em que eu fui", "no dia em que ele se aposentou". You can also use it to set the scene for a story: "Tudo começou no dia em que...".
target_language_example: Conheci a Ana no dia em que cheguei a Lisboa.
native_language_example: I met Ana on the day I arrived in Lisbon.

meaning: the next day; the following day.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the day after a referenced day/event in the past or future. Often appears at the start of a sentence as a time marker: “No dia seguinte, …”.
target_language_example: No dia seguinte, a gente conversou com mais calma.
native_language_example: The next day, we talked more calmly.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens on a Sunday. "no" = "em" + "o" (on + the), so it literally means "on the Sunday". You’ll often hear it with time expressions like "no domingo passado" (last Sunday) or "no domingo à tarde" (on Sunday afternoon).
target_language_example: Vamos almoçar no domingo.
native_language_example: Let’s have lunch on Sunday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about being in or during the period of Brazilian high school (ensino médio), usually grades 10–12. Literally it’s "in the middle education" (no = em + o), but it corresponds to English "in/during high school." Also used with "estar" to say someone is currently in high school.
target_language_example: A gente se conheceu no ensino médio.
native_language_example: We met in high school.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast with what was just said (often at the start of a sentence, but it can also appear mid-sentence). It’s fairly formal/neutral and common in writing; in speech you might also hear "mas" or "porém" depending on the context.
target_language_example: Eu queria ir, no entanto estava muito cansado.
native_language_example: I wanted to go; however, I was very tired.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or exception to what was just said. It can come at the beginning of a sentence (often followed by a comma) or in the middle after a pause: "..., no entanto, ...".
target_language_example: Queria sair, mas estava chovendo; no entanto, fui mesmo assim.
native_language_example: I wanted to go out, but it was raining; however, I went anyway.

additional_notes: "No" is the contraction of "em + o" and commonly translates as "in" or "at". "No escritório" is used for location (being in the office) and can also mean calling someone at their office/workplace number.
target_language_example: Hoje eu vou trabalhar no escritório.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to work at the office.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is in a place without light (literal darkness). It can also be used figuratively to mean "not knowing" or "being uninformed" (e.g., "Estou no escuro" = "I’m in the dark").
target_language_example: Fiquei no escuro porque ninguém me contou o que aconteceu.
native_language_example: I was kept in the dark because nobody told me what happened.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like olhar (to look), ver (to see), and se olhar (to look at oneself) to say someone is looking/seeing themselves reflected in a mirror. It’s a contraction of em + o → no.
target_language_example: Olhe no espelho antes de sair.
native_language_example: Look in the mirror before you leave.

additional_notes: Used to say something is physically located in the stomach or affects digestion. It also appears in the idiom “borboletas no estômago” (“butterflies in your stomach”), meaning nervous excitement.
target_language_example: Estou com dor no estômago desde ontem.
native_language_example: I’ve had a stomachache since yesterday.

meaning: 'in the exam' / 'on the exam' (during the test).
additional_notes: Contraction of "em" + "o" = "no". Often used to talk about what happens during a test (e.g., cheating) or performance/results related to the test (e.g., passing).
target_language_example: Ela tirou uma boa nota no exame.
native_language_example: She got a good grade on the exam.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is outside their home country. Very common with verbs like viver (to live), morar (to live), trabalhar (to work), estudar (to study), viajar (to travel), estar (to be). It can refer generally to “foreign countries” rather than one specific place.
target_language_example: Ela mora no exterior desde 2020.
native_language_example: She has been living abroad since 2020.

additional_notes: Used for the end of a time period or sequence: "no fim do ano" (at the end of the year), "no fim de outubro" (at the end of October). It can also mean the final result/outcome: "no fim, tudo deu certo" (in the end, everything worked out). Common fixed expressions include "no fim das contas" (when all is said and done) and "no fim da linha" (at the end of the line; with no more options).
target_language_example: No fim, a gente encontrou a solução.
native_language_example: In the end, we found the solution.

meaning: "in the end" / "after all" (when everything is considered).
additional_notes: Used to sum up a final conclusion or outcome after thinking things through, weighing facts, or seeing what actually happened. Common in speech and writing, often set off by commas: “E, no fim das contas, …”. It’s close to “afinal” in meaning, and can also imply “when all is said and done.”
target_language_example: No fim das contas, a gente acabou ficando em casa.
native_language_example: In the end, we ended up staying at home.

additional_notes: Used for either (1) a conclusion/outcome: "No final, ..." = "In the end, ...", or (2) a physical position at the far end of something: "no final deste corredor" (at the end of this hallway), "no final da fila" (at the end of the line). Often followed by de + noun (no final de…).
target_language_example: No final do filme, ela decide ir embora.
native_language_example: At the end of the movie, she decides to leave.

additional_notes: Used to say something is inside the oven (usually cooking/baking or being kept warm). Often used with verbs like estar (to be), pôr/colocar (to put), and assar (to bake/roast).
target_language_example: O bolo já está no forno.
native_language_example: The cake is already in the oven.

additional_notes: Used in two common ways: (1) physical location: “at the back”/“in the back” of a room, bus, etc. (no fundo da sala / do ônibus). (2) figurative meaning: “deep down,” “when it comes down to it,” often to express someone’s true feelings or the real situation (Mas, no fundo, eu te respeitava).
target_language_example: No fundo, eu sabia que ele tinha razão.
native_language_example: Deep down, I knew he was right.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what will happen at a later time. It can mean the distant future or simply “from now on” depending on context.
target_language_example: No futuro, quero morar perto do mar.
native_language_example: In the future, I want to live near the sea.

additional_notes: Used to summarize a situation or make a general statement (not about every single case). Common at the start of a sentence: “No geral, …”. Also appears as “falando no geral” (“generally speaking”).
target_language_example: No geral, o curso foi bom, mas algumas aulas foram difíceis.
native_language_example: Overall, the course was good, but some classes were difficult.

additional_notes: Means "in/at the hospital." It’s the contraction of "em" + "o" → "no" ("in the"). Use it both for being hospitalized (as a patient) and for being there (e.g., visiting someone).
target_language_example: Ele está no hospital desde ontem.
native_language_example: He has been in the hospital since yesterday.

additional_notes: Contraction of "em" + "o" → "no". Used to say someone/something is located at the hotel or that an action happened there. With hotel names, you can also say "no + name": "no hotel Hilton".
target_language_example: Vou te encontrar no hotel às oito.
native_language_example: I'll meet you at the hotel at eight.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens during winter in general. It's the contraction of "em" + "o" → "no" + "inverno". Often contrasts with other seasons: "no verão" (in summer), "na primavera" (in spring), "no outono" (in autumn/fall).
target_language_example: No inverno, escurece mais cedo.
native_language_example: In winter, it gets dark earlier.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the start of a period of time or event (e.g., no início da partida = “at the start of the match”). With a time expression, it can mean the early part of that time (no início da tarde = “in the early afternoon”). It can also mean “at first” when contrasting with what happened later.
target_language_example: No início, eu não entendi, mas depois ficou claro.
native_language_example: At first, I didn’t understand, but later it became clear.

additional_notes: "No" = "em" + "o" (in + the), so it means "in the" with a masculine singular noun. "Jardim" usually means a garden (plants/flowers), and in some contexts can refer to the yard/outdoor area around a house. Very common with actions or things located there: trabalhar/cavar/deixar/ver/encontrar no jardim. In "no jardim do teto", it means "in/on the rooftop garden" (a garden area on the roof).
target_language_example: As crianças estão brincando no jardim.
native_language_example: The kids are playing in the garden.

meaning: in the newspaper; on/at the newspaper (as a workplace).
additional_notes: "No" = "em" + "o" (in/on/at the). With "jornal" it often means (1) in the newspaper as published content: "Está no jornal" = "It’s in the paper"; (2) at the newspaper office / for the newspaper as an organization: "Trabalhar no jornal" = "to work at/for the newspaper." Context makes it clear which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Saiu no jornal que a escola vai fechar.
native_language_example: It was in the newspaper that the school is going to close.

meaning: in the lake; on the lake.
additional_notes: Contraction of "em" + "o" → "no". Used to say something is located in/inside the lake (e.g., fish, birds, boats) or happening there. Often translates as "in the lake"; with boats it can also be "on the lake" in English.
target_language_example: Tem muitos peixes no lago.
native_language_example: There are many fish in the lake.

meaning: in (its/the) place; in place of; in someone’s shoes.
additional_notes: Often literal: put something back where it belongs ("colocar ... no lugar"). It can also be figurative ("colocar a cabeça no lugar" = get your head straight). With "de" it means substitution: "no lugar de" = instead of/in place of. Common set phrases: "no lugar errado" = in the wrong place; "no lugar deles" = in their shoes.
target_language_example: Depois do jantar, coloque os pratos no lugar.
native_language_example: After dinner, put the plates back in their place.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is in an inappropriate or incorrect place for the situation. Very often appears in the fixed expression "no lugar errado, na hora errada" (“in the wrong place at the wrong time”). It can also be used to tell someone they came to the wrong place (e.g., looking for something you don’t have).
target_language_example: Desculpe, você está no lugar errado para fazer essa reclamação.
native_language_example: Sorry, you’re in the wrong place to make that complaint.

additional_notes: Contraction of "em + o" → "no" + "mar". Use it for location (being in the sea) or destination/movement (throwing/falling into the sea), depending on the verb and context.
target_language_example: Eles nadaram no mar a manhã toda.
native_language_example: They swam in the sea all morning.

meaning: in the middle of; halfway through; in the midst of.
additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun after da (= de + a): no meio da avenida (in the middle of the avenue), no meio da discussão (in the middle of the discussion), no meio da tarde (mid-afternoon). With a masculine noun, it becomes no meio do (de + o). It can refer to a physical place (in the middle of a street), a situation/event (in the middle of a battle/discussion), or a time period (mid-afternoon).
target_language_example: Ele me ligou no meio da reunião.
native_language_example: He called me in the middle of the meeting.

meaning: in the middle of the road.
additional_notes: Used to say something is located halfway across the road (often in the center). Common with things like holes, lines/markings, objects, or people. Literally: “in the middle of the road.”
target_language_example: Não pare no meio da estrada.
native_language_example: Don’t stop in the middle of the road.

meaning: in the middle of the night.
additional_notes: Used for something that happens very late at night, often unexpectedly, while people are asleep. Common with verbs like acordar (to wake up), ouvir (to hear), ligar (to call), and vir (to come). It can also be used to complain about being disturbed: “no meio da noite?!”
target_language_example: Eu acordei no meio da noite com um barulho estranho.
native_language_example: I woke up in the middle of the night because of a strange noise.

meaning: in the middle of the street/road.
additional_notes: Used to say something (a car, bus, person, etc.) is stopped or located right in the center of the roadway, often blocking traffic. Common with verbs like estacionar (to park) and parar (to stop).
target_language_example: Não pare no meio da rua.
native_language_example: Don’t stop in the middle of the street.

meaning: in the middle of (during; in the center of).
additional_notes: Used to say something happened halfway through an activity/event (“no meio do concerto”) or right in the center of a place (“no meio do cruzamento / do deserto / do mato”). It’s the contraction of “em” + “o” → “no” + “meio” + “de” + “o” → “do”. With a feminine noun, use “no meio da” (e.g., “no meio da rua”).
target_language_example: O celular descarregou no meio do filme.
native_language_example: The phone died in the middle of the movie.

meaning: “at the market” or “on the market / available for sale.”
additional_notes: "No" = "em" + "o" (“in/at the”). Most often it means a physical place (a market, marketplace, or grocery market): "comprar no mercado" = to buy at the market. In business/product contexts, it can mean something is available for purchase: "estar no mercado" / "chegar ao mercado" = to be on the market / to come onto the market.
target_language_example: Esse produto já está no mercado?
native_language_example: Is this product already on the market?

additional_notes: Means “in the same (place/thing/time)” and is used before a masculine singular noun. It’s a contraction of em + o + mesmo (“in” + “the” + “same”). Common variants: na mesma (feminine singular), nos mesmos (masculine plural), nas mesmas (feminine plural). Often used to say people are in the same group/place/vehicle or that something hasn’t changed (e.g., no mesmo lugar = in the same place).
target_language_example: Ainda estamos no mesmo hotel.
native_language_example: We’re still in the same hotel.

additional_notes: Used to say two people/things are in (or were in) the same neighborhood. Often appears with verbs like morar (to live) and crescer (to grow up). Structure: no = em + o (“in the”), mesmo = “same”, bairro = “neighborhood.” You can change it for gender/number: na mesma rua (on the same street), no mesmo lugar (in the same place), nos mesmos bairros (in the same neighborhoods).
target_language_example: A gente mora no mesmo bairro, mas quase nunca se encontra.
native_language_example: We live in the same neighborhood, but we almost never run into each other.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to mean something like in, on, or at my, depending on context. no is a contraction of em + o. With a feminine noun, Portuguese uses na minha instead.
target_language_example: Deixei as chaves no meu carro.
native_language_example: I left the keys in my car.

additional_notes: "No" is the contraction of "em" (in/on/at) + "o" (the), so "no meu carro" literally means "in the my car" → natural English: "in my car". Used to say someone/something is inside your car, or something was left there (e.g., "deixou ... no meu carro" = "left ... in my car").
target_language_example: Você deixou sua mochila no meu carro?
native_language_example: Did you leave your backpack in my car?

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located in your office, or to tell someone to come/wait/meet there. It's made from "em" (in) + "o" (the) → "no", plus "meu" (my) and "escritório" (office). You can change the owner: "no seu escritório" (in your office), "no nosso escritório" (in our office).
target_language_example: Vou estar no meu escritório às três; pode passar lá.
native_language_example: I’ll be in my office at three; you can stop by.

meaning: in my place; if you were me (in my situation).
additional_notes: Used either literally for someone being in your physical spot/seat (“in my place”), or figuratively to ask what someone would do if they were in your situation (“if you were in my shoes”). It changes with the possessive: no seu lugar (in your place), no lugar dele/dela (in his/her place), etc.
target_language_example: O que você faria no meu lugar?
native_language_example: What would you do in my place?

additional_notes: Used to talk about what is (or was) typical in the country you come from. It’s the contraction of "em" + "o" (no) + "meu" + "país". You can swap "meu" for other possessives: "no seu país" (in your country), "no nosso país" (in our country).
target_language_example: No meu país, as pessoas jantam mais cedo.
native_language_example: In my country, people eat dinner earlier.

meaning: in my room / in my bedroom.
additional_notes: “No” = “em + o” (“in the”). With “meu quarto” it usually means “in my room” (often your bedroom at home). It’s used to say where someone is, goes, stays, sleeps, or where something is located. If you mean “to my room,” you’ll often hear “para o meu quarto” (or “pro meu quarto” in informal speech).
target_language_example: Vou ficar no meu quarto hoje à noite.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay in my room tonight.

additional_notes: Often used to talk about the current situation or what is true/available now: No momento, não temos nenhuma evidência. It can also appear as part of the longer expression "no momento (em) que..." meaning "the moment (that) ... / as soon as ...": Me apaixonei por ela no momento em que a conheci.
target_language_example: No momento, não posso falar; estou em uma reunião.
native_language_example: At the moment, I can’t talk; I’m in a meeting.

additional_notes: Means “in the world” (global sense), often used for comparisons and superlatives: “o melhor no mundo” = “the best in the world.” It can also mean “in the world of … / in the field of …” when followed by a noun: “no mundo da ciência” = “in the world of science.” Literally “in + the + world” ("em" + "o" → "no").
target_language_example: Este é o melhor café no mundo.
native_language_example: This is the best coffee in the world.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens or is true across the whole world. Often follows a noun it describes: "conhecido no mundo inteiro" (known worldwide), "falado no mundo inteiro" (spoken worldwide).
target_language_example: Essa notícia se espalhou no mundo inteiro em poucas horas.
native_language_example: That news spread worldwide in just a few hours.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens or is true everywhere in the world. Often goes with verbs like "ser visto" (to be seen), "ser conhecido" (to be known), and "ser popular" (to be popular). In a more personal/hyperbolic sense, it can mean “in the whole world” (e.g., "meu melhor amigo no mundo todo").
target_language_example: Essa marca é famosa no mundo todo.
native_language_example: That brand is famous all over the world.

additional_notes: Used to set an upper limit on a quantity, time, price, etc. Common in estimates: “Uma semana, no máximo dez dias” (“A week, at most ten days”). It can also mean doing something at full power/maximum setting, especially with machines: “motores no máximo” (“engines at full throttle / at maximum”).
target_language_example: A reunião vai durar uma hora, no máximo.
native_language_example: The meeting will last an hour, at most.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened during the previous calendar month. Often comes at the end of the sentence, but it can also be moved to the beginning for emphasis (e.g., "No mês passado, ...").
target_language_example: No mês passado, eu viajei para São Paulo.
native_language_example: Last month, I traveled to São Paulo.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening in the month after the current one. Common with future tenses and plans: “vou…”, “vai…”, “irá…”, “estará…”, “terá…”. Similar to “na semana que vem” (next week) and “no ano que vem” (next year).
target_language_example: Vamos viajar no mês que vem.
native_language_example: We’re going to travel next month.

additional_notes: Used to talk about things that happen or are true during the autumn season. It’s a contraction of "em" + "o" → "no" ("in the" + "autumn"). You can also place it at the start of the sentence: "No outono, ...".
target_language_example: No outono, eu gosto de caminhar no parque.
native_language_example: In the fall, I like to walk in the park.

additional_notes: "No" = "em + o" (in/on + the). Used to say someone or something is physically on the stage during a performance, presentation, or event.
target_language_example: Ela vai estar no palco às oito horas.
native_language_example: She’ll be on stage at eight o’clock.

meaning: on the paper; on paper (in theory).
additional_notes: “No” is the contraction of “em + o” (“in/on the”). So “no papel” can mean physically on a sheet of paper (writing/drawing), and it’s also used figuratively like English “on paper” = in theory, as an idea/plan (“Parece bom no papel.”).
target_language_example: No papel, o plano é perfeito, mas na prática é difícil.
native_language_example: On paper, the plan is perfect, but in practice it’s hard.

additional_notes: "no" is a contraction of "em" (in/at) + "o" (the). Use it to say someone/something is located in the park or doing an activity there. With a feminine noun, it becomes "na" (em + a), e.g., "na praça" (in/at the square).
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar no parque depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at the park after work.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened earlier in time, or to contrast past behavior/habits with the present. Often placed at the start of a sentence (“No passado, ...”) for emphasis, but it can also come later (“... no passado”).
target_language_example: No passado, eu morava em São Paulo, mas agora moro no Rio.
native_language_example: In the past, I lived in São Paulo, but now I live in Rio.

meaning: just right; ready (at the ideal point/time).
additional_notes: Used a lot in cooking to mean food is at the ideal doneness/consistency (e.g., onions, pasta, sauce). It can also mean someone or something is exactly at the right moment/condition (“right on time”, “perfect timing”). In more formal contexts it can appear in the structure “no ponto em que…”, meaning “in the respect/point that…”.
target_language_example: O molho já está no ponto; pode desligar o fogo.
native_language_example: The sauce is just right now; you can turn off the heat.

additional_notes: Contraction of "em" + "o" → "no" (= "in the"). Used to say something/someone is located in or happening in the basement of a house/building. Without a specific "the," you may also see "num porão" (= "in a basement").
target_language_example: As bicicletas estão guardadas no porão.
native_language_example: The bikes are stored in the basement.

meaning: in the building; into the building.
additional_notes: "No" is the contraction of "em + o" and usually means "in/at the". With verbs of movement like "entrar" (to enter), it often translates as "into the building" (direction). With location/state, it means "in the building".
target_language_example: Ele está no prédio agora.
native_language_example: He is in the building now.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something planned, expected, or scheduled to happen in the year after the current one. Often used with future or intention expressions like "pretender" (to intend), "ter de" (to have to), or "vão" (they are going to).
target_language_example: Vamos viajar no próximo ano.
native_language_example: We’re going to travel next year.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the weekend immediately coming after now. It’s literally “in/on the next weekend”: "no" = "em + o" (in/on + the), "próximo" agrees with "fim de semana". Often used with future plans: "Vou... no próximo fim de semana" / "Você pode... no próximo fim de semana?".
target_language_example: A gente pode se encontrar no próximo fim de semana?
native_language_example: Can we meet next weekend?

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen during the month after the current one. Often appears with future expressions like "vou" (I’m going), "irei" (I will go), or "estarei" (I will be).
target_language_example: Vou começar um curso de português no próximo mês.
native_language_example: I’m going to start a Portuguese course next month.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the summer of the next year/coming summer relative to now. Very common for future plans: ir/viajar/fazer algo no próximo verão. In Portuguese you normally include the preposition + article: "no" (= em + o) before seasons in this kind of time expression.
target_language_example: Vamos viajar no próximo verão.
native_language_example: We're going to travel next summer.

additional_notes: "No" = "em" (in/on) + "o" (the). Used for writing or putting something on a board. With teaching contexts, "o quadro" usually means the classroom board (blackboard/whiteboard). In other contexts, it can mean another kind of board, e.g., "quadro de avisos" = notice board/bulletin board.
target_language_example: Escreve a data no quadro, por favor.
native_language_example: Write the date on the board, please.

additional_notes: Means “in the (bed)room,” referring to location. It’s the contraction of "em" (in) + "o" (the) → "no". "Quarto" can mean "bedroom," and in some contexts (like a hotel) it can also mean "room."
target_language_example: Deixei meu celular no quarto.
native_language_example: I left my phone in the room.

additional_notes: "no" = "em + o" (in the), and "dela" means "of her" (her). Used to say where something happens or where someone is (location).
target_language_example: Deixa o presente no quarto dela, por favor.
native_language_example: Leave the gift in her room, please.

meaning: in his room / in his bedroom.
additional_notes: "no" = "em + o" (in the). "quarto" is a room; in many everyday contexts it means "bedroom". "dele" means "his" (of him) and is often used to make possession clear (e.g., to avoid confusion with "seu"). You can swap the owner: "no quarto dela" (in her room), "no meu quarto" (in my room), "no quarto do Tom" (in Tom’s room).
target_language_example: Ele está no quarto dele estudando.
native_language_example: He’s in his room studying.

additional_notes: “No” is the contraction of “em + o” (= “in/on”). “No que” is used before a clause introduced by “que”, especially after verbs that take the preposition “em” (e.g., acreditar em, pensar em, confiar em). It often translates as “in what” or more naturally “about what / about the thing that …”, depending on the verb.
target_language_example: Pense no que eu disse.
native_language_example: Think about what I said.

meaning: in the backyard / in the yard.
additional_notes: "No" is the contraction of "em + o" (= "in the"). "Quintal" is the yard area of a house (often the backyard in Brazil). Used to say something is located or happening in that outdoor space: trees, animals, activities, etc.
target_language_example: As crianças estão brincando no quintal.
native_language_example: The kids are playing in the backyard.

additional_notes: "No" = "em" + "o" (in/at + the). Used to say where something happens or where someone is (location), and often implies being inside the restaurant. Common with verbs like chegar (arrive), estar/ficar (be/stay), comer (eat), trabalhar (work), reservar (reserve).
target_language_example: A gente se encontra no restaurante às 8.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at the restaurant at 8.

meaning: in the river / into the river (also: on the river).
additional_notes: Contraction of "em + o" → "no" + "rio". Use it for being or doing something in the river (Eu nadei no rio.) and also for movement into the river with verbs like "mergulhar" (to dive) or "jogar" (to throw) (Ele mergulhou no rio.; Joguei-a no rio.). For clear direction, Portuguese may also use "para o rio" (to the river).
target_language_example: No verão, a gente nada no rio quase todo dia.
native_language_example: In the summer, we swim in the river almost every day.

additional_notes: Used to say that an expression, emotion, or a physical feature is visible on someone’s face. Very common with nouns like expressão, sorriso, medo, lágrimas. It contracts de+o → do (e.g., no rosto dele = on his face; no rosto dela = on her face).
target_language_example: Ela tinha um olhar de surpresa no rosto.
native_language_example: She had a look of surprise on her face.

additional_notes: Contraction of em + o + seu, used before a masculine singular noun. Usually corresponds to 'in', 'on', or 'at' + a possessive in English. Portuguese often uses the article before possessives, unlike English, and seu can mean 'your' or sometimes 'his/her/their' depending on context.
target_language_example: Deixei o livro no seu quarto.
native_language_example: I left the book in your room.

meaning: in your place; instead of you; if I were you.
additional_notes: Used to talk about replacing someone/something ("go in your place", "plant another in its place") or to give advice from someone’s perspective ("if I were in your place" = "if I were you"). In "Ponha-se no seu lugar", it can mean "put yourself in your place" (know your place) or "put yourself in their shoes," depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: Se eu estivesse no seu lugar, eu falaria com ela hoje.
native_language_example: If I were you, I’d talk to her today.

meaning: in your room / in his (or her) room.
additional_notes: "no" is the contraction of "em" + "o" (= “in the”). "seu/sua" can mean “your” (formal) or “his/her/its” depending on context, so "no seu quarto" may refer to the listener’s room or someone else’s room.
target_language_example: Pode deixar suas coisas no seu quarto.
native_language_example: You can leave your things in your room.

additional_notes: "no" is the contraction of "em" + "o" and usually means "in/on the" for masculine singular places/objects. With furniture like "sofá", it’s typically translated as "on the sofa" (sitting/lying/sleeping there). In casual speech you may also hear "sentei no sofá" meaning "I sat on the sofa."
target_language_example: Depois do trabalho, gosto de ficar no sofá e assistir TV.
native_language_example: After work, I like to stay on the sofa and watch TV.

additional_notes: Used mainly with verbs like "cair no sono" (to fall asleep) and "pegar no sono" (to manage to fall asleep). "Cair" suggests dozing off (often quickly), while "pegar" emphasizes finally getting to sleep, sometimes after having trouble.
target_language_example: Depois do almoço, eu caí no sono no sofá.
native_language_example: After lunch, I fell asleep on the couch.

additional_notes: "No" is the contraction of "em + o" and is used for masculine singular places: "no supermercado" = "in/at the supermarket". Common with verbs like "fazer compras" (to shop/buy groceries), "procurar" (to look for someone), "esbarrar com" (to bump into/run into), and "trabalhar" (to work).
target_language_example: Vou passar no supermercado depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: I’m going to stop by the supermarket after work.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening on a Saturday (a specific one or Saturdays in general, depending on context). It’s the contraction of "em" + "o" → "no" + "sábado." Can also be used in suggestions/plans: "Que tal no sábado?" = "How about on Saturday?"
target_language_example: Posso te encontrar no sábado de manhã.
native_language_example: Can I meet you on Saturday morning?

meaning: in the attic / up in the attic.
additional_notes: "No" = "em + o" (in the). "Sótão" is the attic: the space under the roof, above the main rooms. Often used for storage, hiding, noises, or a small workspace ("uma oficina no sótão").
target_language_example: Guardamos as malas no sótão.
native_language_example: We keep the suitcases in the attic.

meaning: on the phone; on the telephone.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is currently talking on the phone, or that something happened by phone (e.g., falar no telefone = to talk on the phone). It’s very common in everyday speech; in Brazilian Portuguese you’ll also hear “ao telefone” and “pelo telefone” depending on the context.
target_language_example: Desculpa, não posso falar agora — estou no telefone.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t talk right now — I’m on the phone.

additional_notes: "No" is a contraction of "em" + "o" ("in/on" + "the"), so it often means "on the" with places/surfaces. "Telhado" is the roof of a building/house. Depending on context, English will usually use "on the roof" (e.g., a cat, a person, something sitting on top).
