target_language_example: Tem uma bola no telhado da garagem.
native_language_example: There’s a ball on the roof of the garage.

additional_notes: Used to say where something is located in a building. Common with verbs like estar/ficar/morar (location) and with movement like sair do elevador (getting off the elevator). Literally: em + o = no (“in/on the”) + terceiro andar (“third floor”).
target_language_example: A sala de reuniões fica no terceiro andar.
native_language_example: The meeting room is on the third floor.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened during an exam or regarding your performance/results on it (e.g., “fui bem no teste” = “I did well on the test”; “passei/não passei no teste” = “I passed/didn’t pass the test”). It’s the contraction of “em + o” → “no” (“in/on the”).
target_language_example: Tirei uma nota boa no teste de matemática.
native_language_example: I got a good grade on the math test.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is at their job/place of work. Very common with verbs like estar/ficar (to be/stay), ligar (to call), passar tempo (to spend time), and conhecer alguém (to meet someone) to describe what happens while working or in the workplace.
target_language_example: Não posso falar agora; estou no trabalho.
native_language_example: I can't talk right now; I'm at work.

meaning: on the train; in the train (car).
additional_notes: "No" = "em" + "o" (in/on the + masculine singular). Used to say you are traveling by train or located inside the train. Often contrasts with "na estação" (at the station) and pairs with verbs like "embarcar" (to board) and "conversar" (to talk).
target_language_example: Eu vou ler um livro no trem.
native_language_example: I'm going to read a book on the train.

meaning: in the red (losing money); also: on a red light.
additional_notes: Most commonly used about finances: estar/ficar no vermelho = to be in debt or operating at a loss. With traffic lights, it appears in the expression passar no vermelho = to run a red light (to go through when the light is red).
target_language_example: Este mês eu fiquei no vermelho.
native_language_example: This month I ended up in the red.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens during the summer season. It’s the contraction of "em" + "o" (in + the): "no". Often placed at the start of the sentence to set the time frame: "No verão, ...".
target_language_example: No verão, a gente vai à praia quase todo fim de semana.
native_language_example: In the summer, we go to the beach almost every weekend.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened during the previous summer. Literally “in the past summer” (no = em + o). You can also hear: “no último verão”.
target_language_example: No verão passado, eu trabalhei em um café perto da praia.
native_language_example: Last summer, I worked at a café near the beach.

additional_notes: Used literally for where your hands are ("as mãos no volante") and figuratively to mean someone is driving/in control ("dormiu no volante" = fell asleep while driving). "Volante" here means a car’s steering wheel (not “flyer/leaflet”).
target_language_example: Quem está no volante agora?
native_language_example: Who’s driving right now?

meaning: on the bus; in the bus.
additional_notes: Contraction of "em" + "o" → "no" (meaning "in/on the"). Used to say where someone/something is or where something happened while riding the bus. You can also use it in time/sequence contexts (e.g., "no ônibus, eu li" = "on the bus, I read").
target_language_example: Eu esqueci minha mochila no ônibus.
native_language_example: I forgot my backpack on the bus.

meaning: "in the last" / "in the final" (used before a time period, event, or item).
additional_notes:
Contraction of "em" + "o" (= "no") + "último". It’s used with a noun: 
- time periods: "no último verão" (last summer), "no último outono" (last fall/autumn), "no último Natal" (last Christmas)
- events/moments: "no último momento" (at the last moment)
- items in a sequence: "no último ônibus" (on the last bus).
Note: "último" can look like English "ultimate", but it usually just means "last/final" in order or time.
target_language_example: Cheguei no último minuto.
native_language_example: I arrived at the last minute.

meaning: at the last minute; at the very last moment.
additional_notes: Used when something happens very late, just before a deadline or before it’s too late (often implying little time left and sometimes stress or urgency). It can describe doing something (finished the project), changing plans (canceled), arriving right before something ends (before the store closes), or even losing your ability to speak right at the end (“Faltaram-me palavras no último minuto.” = “I was lost for words at the last minute”).
target_language_example: Consegui enviar o formulário no último minuto.
native_language_example: I managed to submit the form at the last minute.

additional_notes: Very informal, colloquial spelling/pronunciation of “nós vamos ver” (or just “vamos ver”). Used to say you’re not sure yet, to postpone a decision, or to suggest waiting to see what happens.
target_language_example: Calma, no vamo ver o que acontece amanhã.
native_language_example: Relax, we’ll see what happens tomorrow.

additional_notes: Means the previous night (the night before today). Often used without an article in Brazilian Portuguese: "noite passada" = "last night" (you may also hear "a noite passada" in some contexts).
target_language_example: Eu não dormi bem noite passada.
native_language_example: I didn’t sleep well last night.

additional_notes: Common on forms and official documents, often paired with “apelido” (surname/last name), especially in Portugal. It can also be used in grammar to mean a “proper noun/name” (e.g., Maria, Lisboa).
target_language_example: Qual é o seu nome próprio?
native_language_example: What is your first name?

additional_notes: Used as an adjective or noun: um autor norte-americano (a North American author), uma empresa norte-americana (a North American/U.S. company). In many contexts it specifically means “from the United States,” though it can literally mean “from North America” depending on context.
target_language_example: Este romance foi escrito por um autor norte-americano.
native_language_example: This novel was written by a North American/U.S. author.

additional_notes: An adjective and noun used for people or things from North America. In everyday Portuguese, it’s very commonly used to mean “American (from the United States)”, especially to avoid ambiguity with “americano” (which can mean anyone from the Americas). Feminine form: norte-americana. Plural: norte-americanos / norte-americanas.
target_language_example: Ele é norte-americano e mora em São Paulo.
native_language_example: He’s American (from the U.S.) and lives in São Paulo.

additional_notes: “Nos” is the contraction of “em + os” (“in/on the”). With people, it often means being held or embraced (“nos braços dele/dela” = “in his/her arms”). It can also mean physically located on the arms (e.g., marks, scars, massage) depending on context.
target_language_example: O bebê adormeceu nos braços da mãe.
native_language_example: The baby fell asleep in the mother’s arms.

additional_notes: Means that something happens during weekends in general (habitually/typically). Literally “in the ends of the week,” and often used when talking about how busy a place gets or whether someone works on weekends.
target_language_example: O shopping fica lotado nos finais de semana.
native_language_example: The mall gets crowded on weekends.

additional_notes: Literally “in the ends of the week.” Used to talk about what you usually do on Saturdays and Sundays. Very common with habitual expressions like sempre (always), geralmente (usually), and with verbs like gostar de (to like to), ir (to go), jogar (to play).
target_language_example: Nos fins de semana, eu costumo dormir até mais tarde.
native_language_example: On weekends, I usually sleep in.

meaning: in the back; at the back (in the rear area).
additional_notes: Used for location: the back of a room, classroom, bus, theater, etc. Can also mean in a back area of a place/building (e.g., the backyard or back part of a store). Often answers “where?” (onde?).
target_language_example: O banheiro fica nos fundos do restaurante.
native_language_example: The bathroom is in the back of the restaurant.

additional_notes: “Nos” is the contraction of “em + os” (“in + the”). Used to say something was published/mentioned/reported in print news (often contrasted with TV/online news).
target_language_example: O acidente saiu nos jornais hoje de manhã.
native_language_example: The accident was in the newspapers this morning.

additional_notes: Literal phrase meaning “in my eyes” (i.e., inside my eyes). Common with verbs like olhar (to look) and acreditar (to believe): “Olhe nos meus olhos” = “Look into my eyes.” It can also be used in a physical sense (something happening in your eyes), e.g., “coceira nos meus olhos” = “itching in my eyes.”
target_language_example: Olhe nos meus olhos e diga a verdade.
native_language_example: Look into my eyes and tell the truth.

additional_notes: Contraction of "em" + "os" + "olhos" → "nos olhos". Common in expressions like "olhar nos olhos" (“to look someone in the eyes”), indicating direct eye contact. It can also refer to something visible in someone’s eyes (e.g., tears, truth) or sensations located in the eyes (e.g., pain).
target_language_example: Ela me olhava nos olhos e eu não conseguia mentir.
native_language_example: She looked me in the eyes and I couldn’t lie.

additional_notes: Literally “help us.” **nos** is the object pronoun “us.” With an infinitive like **ajudar**, Brazilian Portuguese commonly uses **nos ajudar**; you may also see the more formal/European-style **ajudar-nos**. With a conjugated verb, **nos** usually comes before it: **Ele nos ajudou** (“He helped us”).
target_language_example: Você pode nos ajudar com isso?
native_language_example: Can you help us with this?

additional_notes: From the verb casar-se (“to get married”), in the nós form of the past (pretérito perfeito): nós nos casamos. The pronoun nos shows it’s reflexive/reciprocal (“we married each other”). Often used with time expressions: há/tem um ano (“a year ago”), há três anos (“three years ago”). In speech it’s common to just say “A gente se casou” or even “A gente casou” (more informal).
target_language_example: Nós nos casamos no ano passado.
native_language_example: We got married last year.

additional_notes: From the reflexive verb **conhecer-se** (“to know/meet each other”). **Nos** refers to “each other” (not usually “ourselves” here). It’s used both for already being acquainted (**Nós já nos conhecemos.**) and for talking about the first time you met (**Onde nos conhecemos? / como nos conhecemos?**). It can also be used jokingly/figuratively: **Eu e o dinheiro não nos conhecemos** = “Money and I don’t mix / I’m not familiar with money,” meaning “I’m poor.”
target_language_example: Acho que nos conhecemos no trabalho.
native_language_example: I think we met at work.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said to a group that includes the speaker. **nos** = “to us” (object pronoun), **disse** is the past tense of *dizer* (“to say/tell”), and **que** introduces the information being reported (“that…”).
target_language_example: O professor nos disse que a prova vai ser na sexta-feira.
native_language_example: The teacher told us that the test will be on Friday.

additional_notes: From the verb **encontrar-se** (“to meet/see each other”), with **nos** = “each other/us” and **encontramos** = “we meet/met.” Often used to talk about meeting again (**Nos encontramos de novo.**), where you met (**Onde nos encontramos?**), or to suggest meeting up (**Que tal nos encontramos…?** = “How about we meet…?”). In invitations, it can also mean “let’s meet” depending on context.
target_language_example: Nos encontramos às oito na estação de metrô.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at eight at the subway station.

additional_notes: Used to talk about meeting each other (making plans). Literally it’s “to find/meet us,” but in everyday use it often means “for us to meet” (= each other). Common in questions about time/place: “Onde devemos nos encontrar?” (“Where should we meet?”). You may also see “a gente se encontrar” or “nos encontrarmos” with the same idea.
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar às 18h na estação.
native_language_example: Let’s meet at 6 p.m. at the station.

additional_notes: Common casual goodbye meaning you expect to meet again. Often followed by a time or place: "Nos vemos amanhã" (see you tomorrow), "Nos vemos em Veneza" (see you in Venice). In Brazil you may also hear the shorter form "até mais" or "a gente se vê" with the same idea.
target_language_example: Então tá, nos vemos na sexta-feira!
native_language_example: Alright then, see you on Friday!

additional_notes: Means “see us,” with the object pronoun “nos” (“us”) before the verb “ver” (“to see”). In more formal/written Portuguese you may also see it as "ver-nos" (same meaning).
target_language_example: Você pode nos ver amanhã?
native_language_example: Can you see us tomorrow?

additional_notes: From the verb *ver* (“to see”) in the future tense: *veremos* = “we will see”. With *nos* (“each other/us”), it’s most often used to talk about meeting again in the future, including as a goodbye: *Nos veremos logo* (“We’ll see each other soon”). It can also refer more generally to not seeing someone for a while: *Não nos veremos por um tempo* (“We won’t see each other for a while”).
target_language_example: Ok, então nos veremos amanhã.
native_language_example: Ok, then we’ll see each other tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to react strongly to something you notice or experience. “Nossa” is an interjection (like “wow/oh my”), and “que” introduces what you’re reacting to: often + noun (“que calor”, “que susto”) or + adjective (“que incrível”). Very common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese; punctuation (comma/exclamation) can vary.
target_language_example: Nossa, que lugar bonito!
native_language_example: Wow, what a beautiful place!

additional_notes: Used to talk about help provided by you and others (a group). Often appears with prepositions like “pela nossa ajuda” (for our help/for the help we gave), “da nossa ajuda” (of/from our help), and with verbs like “precisar de” (to need) and “recusar” (to refuse).
target_language_example: Obrigado pela nossa ajuda, vocês foram incríveis.
native_language_example: Thanks for our help; you were amazing.

additional_notes: “Nossa” means “our” and agrees with a feminine singular noun, like “casa.” In Portuguese, “casa” can mean both the physical house and the idea of “home,” so “nossa casa” can be used literally (where we live) or more loosely (a place that feels like home, e.g., a bus or workplace). You may also see it inside the idiom “a nossa casa caiu” (very informal), meaning “we’re in trouble / we got caught.”
target_language_example: Vamos voltar para nossa casa depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: Let’s go back to our home after work.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the city or town that the speaker and others (often the listener) belong to or live in. It’s the feminine singular form of “nosso/nossa” (our). Often appears as “na nossa cidade” = “in our city.”
target_language_example: Na nossa cidade, o transporte público é barato.
native_language_example: In our city, public transportation is cheap.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a group you’re part of (sports team, work team, project group, etc.). It can appear with the article (“a nossa equipe”) or without it (“nossa equipe”); both mean “our team,” and using the article can sound a bit more specific/emphatic.
target_language_example: Nossa equipe está pronta para começar.
native_language_example: Our team is ready to start.

additional_notes: Means a school that belongs to or is associated with “us” (a group that includes the speaker). It’s the feminine singular possessive phrase: nossa (our) + escola (school). You’ll also see it without the article (nossa escola) or with it (a nossa escola); both mean “our school.”
target_language_example: A nossa escola fica perto do parque.
native_language_example: Our school is near the park.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive pronoun "nossa" (our) with a feminine singular noun like "família". You’ll often see it with the definite article: "a nossa família" (= "our family"), especially when referring to a specific family. Without the article ("nossa família"), it can sound a bit more general (e.g., describing who is included).
target_language_example: No domingo, vamos almoçar com a nossa família.
native_language_example: On Sunday, we’re going to have lunch with our family.

additional_notes: Means a daughter who belongs to “us” (the speakers). Often used with the article: **a nossa filha** (“our daughter”), but the article is sometimes omitted, especially in exclamations or after the verb **ser** (“to be”): **Gloria é nossa filha!**
target_language_example: A nossa filha está na escola agora.
native_language_example: Our daughter is at school now.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a teacher who is female. "Nossa" agrees with feminine singular nouns like "professora"; for a male teacher you’d say "nosso professor". Can take a subject area after it (e.g., "nossa professora de alemão" = "our German teacher"). You’ll also see it with the article: "a nossa professora" = "our teacher".
target_language_example: A nossa professora de português está doente hoje.
native_language_example: Our Portuguese teacher is sick today.

meaning: “Our Lady” (the Virgin Mary); also an exclamation like “Oh my God!”
additional_notes: Literally “our lady.” Capitalized (Nossa Senhora) it often refers to the Virgin Mary, common in Catholic contexts and place/saint names (e.g., Nossa Senhora de Fátima). In everyday speech, “Nossa senhora!” is also used as a strong reaction (surprise, shock, frustration), similar to “Oh my God!” or “Good grief!” You may also hear shortened forms like “Nossa!” or “Minha Nossa Senhora!”
target_language_example: Nossa senhora! Que susto você me deu!
native_language_example: Oh my God! You really scared me!

additional_notes: Plural of "nossa vida". Used to talk about the lives of a group that includes the speaker (“we/us”), e.g., family, friends, or a whole group. The possessive "nossas" agrees with the feminine plural noun "vidas" (so you say "nossas vidas," not "nossos vidas"). Often appears in expressions like "salvar nossas vidas" (save our lives) or "mudar nossas vidas" (change our lives).
target_language_example: A pandemia mudou nossas vidas.
native_language_example: The pandemic changed our lives.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "nosso" (“our”) with a masculine singular noun: "clube". It agrees with the thing owned: nosso clube (m. sg.), nossa casa (f. sg.), nossos amigos (m. pl.), nossas ideias (f. pl.). Often used when inviting someone or talking about a group you belong to.
target_language_example: Você quer conhecer nosso clube?
native_language_example: Do you want to meet/see our club?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the country you and the listener(s) belong to (often your own nation). You may also hear "o nosso país" (with the article) or "em nosso país" (without the article); both are common. The possessive agrees with what is owned: país (masculine singular) → nosso.
target_language_example: Precisamos cuidar melhor do nosso país.
native_language_example: We need to take better care of our country.

additional_notes: "Nosso" means "our" (used before a masculine singular noun like "plano"). Often used to talk about a shared idea/strategy: e.g., making, changing, explaining, or following a plan. In Brazilian Portuguese you may also hear "o nosso plano" (with the article) or "plano nosso" in some contexts, but the basic meaning stays the same.
target_language_example: Vamos seguir nosso plano amanhã.
native_language_example: Let's follow our plan tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a teacher/professor shared by the speaker and others (e.g., classmates): nosso/nossa = "our" + professor/professora = "teacher/professor." In Portuguese, the possessive agrees with the thing owned (professor = masculine; professora = feminine). You may also hear "o nosso professor" ("our teacher") with the article, especially when referring to a specific person.
target_language_example: O nosso professor explicou a lição de novo.
native_language_example: Our teacher explained the lesson again.

meaning: "our team" (a group of people on the same sports team or working group).
additional_notes: "Nosso" agrees with the noun it describes. Use "nosso time" with masculine singular "time" (team). Common in sports and also in workplaces/projects to mean "our team". Note: Portuguese "time" means "team" (not "time" as in hours/minutes).
target_language_example: Você vai torcer pelo nosso time hoje?
native_language_example: Are you going to cheer for our team today?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the work or duties shared by a group, team, company, etc. Often appears with verbs like fazer (to do) or continuar (to continue). You can also say o nosso trabalho with the article o for emphasis or when talking about a specific job/task.
target_language_example: Vamos terminar nosso trabalho antes de ir embora.
native_language_example: Let’s finish our work before leaving.

additional_notes: "Nossos" means "our" (masculine plural). "Amigos" is "friends" (masculine plural or mixed-gender group). For an all-female group, you can say "nossas amigas". Often used with the article too: "os nossos amigos" = "our friends".
target_language_example: Hoje vamos jantar com nossos amigos.
native_language_example: Today we're having dinner with our friends.

additional_notes: "Nossos" is the masculine plural form of "nosso" (“our”). It agrees with masculine plural nouns like "clientes" (which can mean customers or clients). Often used in business/service contexts to refer to the people a company serves.
target_language_example: Precisamos ouvir melhor nossos clientes.
native_language_example: We need to listen to our customers better.

meaning: “our children” / “our sons” (masculine plural; can include boys and girls).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the speaker’s children together with someone else’s (e.g., a couple’s kids). In Portuguese, the masculine plural (filhos) is also the default for a mixed group of boys and girls; for only daughters you can say “nossas filhas”. Often appears with the definite article: “os nossos filhos” (“our children”).
target_language_example: Precisamos conversar sobre nossos filhos e a escola.
native_language_example: We need to talk about our children and the school.

meaning: a new era; (often) the New Age.
additional_notes: In general text, you’ll usually see it as **nova era** (“a new era,” a new period or phase). With capitals (**Nova Era**), it can refer to the **New Age** movement/style (music, spirituality, etc.). You may also see **uma nova era** (“a new era”).
target_language_example: Depois da eleição, o país entrou numa nova era.
native_language_example: After the election, the country entered a new era.

additional_notes: Literally “new world.” Often written as “Novo Mundo” (capitalized) when referring to the Americas in a historical/geographical sense (as opposed to the “Old World,” Europe/Africa/Asia). It can also be used more generally to mean a new era or a radically different world/context.
target_language_example: Os europeus chamavam as Américas de Novo Mundo.
native_language_example: Europeans called the Americas the New World.

additional_notes: Literally “new” (novo) + “world” (mundo). Used for discovering something completely new (a place, experience, or way of life). In some contexts it can also refer to the “New World” (the Americas) in a historical/cultural sense.
target_language_example: Viajar sozinho me fez descobrir um novo mundo.
native_language_example: Traveling alone made me discover a whole new world.

meaning: “in a place” / “at a place” (in some place).
additional_notes: Contraction of **em um lugar** (“in/at a place”). Used to say where something happens or where someone is, often meaning “somewhere” or “in a certain place.” In speech it’s very common; in writing you may also see **em um lugar**.
target_language_example: A gente se encontrou num lugar bem tranquilo.
native_language_example: We met in a very quiet place.

meaning: "in the blink of an eye"; very quickly.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happens very fast, or that time seems to pass quickly. Common in both everyday speech and writing. Often appears with verbs like "fazer" (do), "acontecer" (happen), "passar" (pass), or "rastrear" (track).
target_language_example: Eu volto num piscar de olhos.
native_language_example: I'll be back in the blink of an eye.

additional_notes: "Num" is the contraction of "em um" (= "in a"). So "num restaurante" is used to say where something happened (e.g., eating, dining). You’ll also see: "num restaurante chinês" (in a Chinese restaurant), "num restaurante chique" (in a fancy restaurant).
target_language_example: A gente se encontrou num restaurante perto daqui.
native_language_example: We met in a restaurant near here.

additional_notes: Informal expression (common in Brazil). Used to say someone is relaxed/at ease (“estar/ficar numa boa”) or to reassure/agree: “Numa boa!” = “It’s fine / no worries.” Can also be used when addressing someone: “Numa boa, (cara/bro)…” meaning “Easy / chill / take it easy.” Literally it’s “in a good (one/way),” but it functions like “all good.”
target_language_example: Pode falar comigo numa boa; eu entendi.
native_language_example: You can talk to me спокойно / no worries; I understood.

additional_notes: Used to suggest that something might still happen, even if it seems unlikely now. Often said as advice or as a reminder to stay open-minded. You may also hear the variation "nunca digas nunca" (more common in Portugal) or "nunca diga nunca" (more formal/polite).
target_language_example: Eu achei que nunca ia viajar sozinho, mas nunca dizer nunca.
native_language_example: I thought I’d never travel alone, but never say never.

meaning: “was never” / “has never been” (in a place or situation).
additional_notes: Uses the verb estar in the past (esteve = “was”), with nunca to say someone has never been somewhere or never been in a certain state/situation. Often followed by em/na/no (“in/to” a place): nunca esteve na Rússia = “has never been to Russia.” In questions it can express surprise: Você nunca esteve…? = “Have you never…?”
target_language_example: Ela nunca esteve em Portugal.
native_language_example: She has never been to Portugal.

additional_notes:
"Nunca" means "never" and "foi" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "ser" (to be) or "ir" (to go). So it can mean either "never was" (ser) or "never went" (ir), depending on the context: 
- "Ele nunca foi pai..." = "He was never a father..." 
- "Nunca foi caçar...?" = "Have you never gone hunting...?" (often translated as "has never" in English when talking about someone’s life up to now). 
You may also see it at the end for emphasis: "...e nunca foi" = "...and never has been."
target_language_example: Ela nunca foi famosa, mas sempre foi talentosa.
native_language_example: She was never famous, but she was always talented.

additional_notes: Used to say something will not happen again from now on. Often appears with the subjunctive after verbs like "temer" (to fear): "temer que ... nunca mais voltasse" = fear that someone would never come back again. Common with promises/vows: "jurar nunca mais...".
target_language_example: Depois do acidente, ele disse que nunca mais ia dirigir bêbado.
native_language_example: After the accident, he said he would never drive drunk again.

additional_notes: Used to say something never happens to you or someone never does something to/for you. It’s usually followed by a verb: “nunca me ajuda” = “he never helps me”. In Portuguese, with negation words like “nunca”, the object pronoun normally comes before the verb (nunca me + verb).
target_language_example: Ela nunca me liga quando precisa de mim.
native_language_example: She never calls me when she needs me.

additional_notes: Uses the past tense of querer (quis) with nunca to say someone did not want something at any time in the past. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., nunca quis morar/trabalhar) or a noun (nunca quis isso).
target_language_example: Eu nunca quis te deixar triste.
native_language_example: I never wanted to make you sad.

additional_notes: Used when the verb takes the reflexive pronoun "se" (e.g., esquecer-se = "to forget", interessar-se = "to become interested", preocupar-se = "to worry"). The "se" can change to match the subject (nunca me, nunca te, nunca nos, etc.): "Eu nunca me esqueço" (I never forget), "Ele nunca se preocupou" (He never worried). It often appears with commands: "Nunca se esqueça..." (Don’t ever forget...).
target_language_example: Nunca se preocupe com isso.
native_language_example: Don’t ever worry about that.

additional_notes: Used to say something is uncertain or unpredictable (often implying it’s wise to be prepared). It’s an impersonal expression: "se" makes it like “one never knows / you never know.” You’ll often see it followed by "quando" (when), "se" (if), or "o que" (what).
target_language_example: Leva um guarda-chuva — nunca se sabe.
native_language_example: Bring an umbrella—you never know.

additional_notes: "nunca teve" is the negative past of "ter" (to have), meaning someone did not have something at any time in the past. It’s commonly followed by a noun ("nunca teve sorte" = never had luck) or by "a chance/oportunidade" (never had the chance/opportunity).
target_language_example: Ela nunca teve tempo para viajar.
native_language_example: She never had time to travel.

additional_notes: Uses the past perfect ("tinha visto") with "nunca" to say that up to that point in the past, something had not happened yet. Often used with "antes" (before) or with details like "tão" (so) to emphasize a first-time experience (e.g., "nunca tinha visto o mar", "nunca tinha visto ela tão brava").
target_language_example: Eu nunca tinha visto neve antes de viajar para o Canadá.
native_language_example: I had never seen snow before traveling to Canada.

additional_notes: "Nunca" = never, "tive" is the past of "ter" (to have). Commonly used to say you never had something or never experienced something in your life so far. Often followed by a noun (nunca tive dinheiro) or by "que" + verb (nunca tive que estudar = I never had to study).
target_language_example: Nunca tive vontade de morar fora.
native_language_example: I've never wanted to live abroad.

additional_notes: Used to say something will not happen at any time in the future. It’s made of "nunca" (never) + "vai" (3rd person singular of "ir" — goes / is going to), so it’s commonly followed by a verb in the infinitive: "nunca vai desistir" (will never give up), "nunca vai esquecer" (will never forget). Note: with "eu" you normally use "nunca vou" (1st person singular), not "nunca vai".
target_language_example: Fadil nunca vai desistir.
native_language_example: Fadil will never give up.

meaning: “No, I don’t …” / “No, I didn’t …” (a strong, explicit denial).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to answer someone and clearly contradict or refuse what was suggested. It often appears before a verb (e.g., “Não, eu não sei.”). In everyday speech, people may shorten it to just “Não.” or “Não, não …”.
target_language_example: Não, eu não posso ir hoje.
native_language_example: No, I can't go today.

meaning: “no, but …” (a negative answer followed by a contrast or additional point).
additional_notes: Used when you answer “no” and then add something that qualifies it, explains it, or shifts to a related positive/important detail. Common in conversation and can sound more polite/nuanced than a plain “não.”
target_language_example: Não, mas posso tentar ajudar.
native_language_example: No, but I can try to help.

additional_notes: Repetition of “não” for emphasis. Often used to correct someone (“not that / not you”), to urgently stop someone (“don’t!”), or to strongly deny something (“no, I’m not”). In speech there’s usually a pause between the two “não”s (like a quick interruption: “No—no…”).
target_language_example: Não, não é isso que eu quis dizer.
native_language_example: No, that’s not what I meant.

additional_notes: Used to deny or correct what someone just said or suggested. Often followed by an adjective or noun (e.g., “Não, não é besteira.” = “No, it’s not nonsense.”). With “isso”, it means “that”/“that’s it” (“Não, não é isso.” = “No, that’s not it.”). Repetition can add emphasis, as in “Não é não” (“No means no.”).
target_language_example: Não, não é verdade.
native_language_example: No, it isn’t true.

additional_notes: Used with the direct object pronoun **a** (“her” / “it” for a feminine noun). **Não** triggers pronoun placement **before** the verb in Portuguese (proclisis): *não a machuque* = “don’t hurt her.” In English, you usually place “her/it” after the verb (“don’t hurt her”), so this doesn’t translate word-for-word as “not her.”
target_language_example: Por favor, não a acorde agora.
native_language_example: Please don’t wake her up now.

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion, often suggesting you already believe the answer (a leading question). From achar (“to think / to find”). Usually followed by a verb clause: “Não acha que devia parar?” = “Don’t you think you should stop?” You’ll also hear it as “Você não acha que…?” and commonly with a tag like “não?” at the end to seek agreement.
target_language_example: Não acha que está na hora de ir embora?
native_language_example: Don’t you think it’s time to go home?

meaning: "I don’t think it is" / "I don’t think that it’s..."
additional_notes: Used to politely express disagreement or doubt. It uses the verb "achar" (to think) in the 1st person (acho) + "que" + the subjunctive "seja" (from "ser"), which is common after expressions of opinion in the negative ("não acho que..."). Often followed by an adjective or noun phrase: "não acho que seja normal/isso/hora de...".
target_language_example: Não acho que seja uma boa ideia sair agora.
native_language_example: I don’t think it’s a good idea to go out now.

additional_notes: Used to express surprise, disbelief, shock, or frustration about what follows. It’s commonly followed by a full clause (often with the subjunctive in more formal Portuguese, e.g., “Não acredito que ele faça isso”, but in everyday speech you may also hear indicative forms). You can also omit “que” when the sentence continues directly: “Não acredito!”
target_language_example: Não acredito que você fez isso de novo.
native_language_example: I can’t believe you did that again.

meaning: “It’s no use / there’s no point / it won’t help.”
additional_notes: Used to say that an action or effort is useless or won’t change the outcome. Very common with an infinitive: “Não adianta + infinitive” (e.g., não adianta falar, não adianta esperar). It can also be said alone (“Não adianta.”) meaning “It won’t do any good.”
target_language_example: Não adianta discutir agora; vamos resolver isso amanhã.
native_language_example: There’s no point arguing now; we’ll sort this out tomorrow.

meaning: “I can’t take it anymore / I can’t stand it anymore.”
additional_notes: Used to express that you’ve reached your limit with a situation or ongoing annoyance (often frustration, stress, fatigue, or impatience). Commonly followed by what you can’t handle: “não aguento mais + [infinitive]” (não aguento mais morar aqui) or “não aguento mais isso/isto” (I can’t take this anymore).
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu não aguento mais esse barulho.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t take this noise anymore.

additional_notes: Common in casual speech as a reaction to unexpected news—similar to “No kidding?” or “You don’t say!” It can also imply “I’m serious / don’t mess around,” depending on tone and context. Often said alone, and you may hear it as a question: “Não brinca?”
target_language_example: —Passei no exame de primeira. —Não brinca!
native_language_example: —I passed the exam on the first try. —No way!

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t know a person/thing, aren’t familiar with a topic, or don’t recognize/know some information. It’s the negative of “conheço” (“I know / I’m familiar with / I recognize”), from the verb “conhecer”. Often followed by a direct object: “não conheço você / seu pai / o número / muita coisa sobre futebol”. On its own (“Não conheço.”) it means “I don’t know (them/it).”
target_language_example: Desculpe, não conheço essa palavra.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don't know that word.

additional_notes: From the verb "conseguir" (to be able to/manage to), in the 3rd-person singular present tense (ele/ela/você consegue). Used to say someone is unable to do something or fails to do it (often despite trying). Commonly followed by an infinitive: "não consegue ler/abrir/manter/lidar". In Brazilian Portuguese, it’s very common with "você" (formal or neutral in most contexts): "Você não consegue...". Can also appear alone after context: "Ele tenta, mas não consegue."
target_language_example: Ela não consegue ler o que está escrito.
native_language_example: She can’t read what’s written.

additional_notes: Form of the verb "conseguir" (to manage to, to be able to) in the present tense, 3rd person plural: "eles/elas/vocês não conseguem". Often followed by an infinitive: "não conseguem enxergar" (can’t see), "não conseguem escutar" (can’t hear/listen).
target_language_example: Eles não conseguem entender a pergunta.
native_language_example: They can’t understand the question.

additional_notes: Used to say you were unable to do something in a specific past situation. It’s the negative of "consegui" (I managed to) and is commonly followed by an infinitive: "não consegui + verb" (e.g., "não consegui dormir"). With "não consegui" you’re typically emphasizing failure to succeed rather than refusal.
target_language_example: Desculpa, não consegui terminar o trabalho a tempo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I couldn't finish the work on time.

additional_notes: Imperfect past of conseguir (eu/ele/ela/você não conseguia): describes an ongoing difficulty/inability in the past, or repeated failures (“I couldn’t manage to…”). Often followed by an infinitive: não conseguia dormir/abrir/respirar (“couldn’t sleep/open/breathe”). With “mais”, it means “couldn’t anymore” (não conseguia mais…).
target_language_example: Eu não conseguia entender o que ele dizia.
native_language_example: I couldn’t understand what he was saying.

additional_notes: First-person singular of conseguir, used to say that you are unable to do something. It is often followed by an infinitive, as in não consigo ouvir ('I can't hear') or não consigo encontrar ('I can't find').
target_language_example: Desculpa, não consigo ir hoje.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't go today.

meaning: I don’t think (that)… / I don’t believe (that)…
additional_notes: Used to express doubt or disbelief about what follows. It’s commonly followed by the subjunctive (e.g., “não creio que seja”, “não creio que tenhamos”), especially when you’re not stating something as a fact. In speech, it can sound a bit more formal than “não acho que”.
target_language_example: Não creio que ele venha hoje.
native_language_example: I don’t think he’s coming today.

meaning: “it doesn’t cost anything” / “it won’t hurt (to do it)” (it’s no trouble).
additional_notes: Used to encourage someone to do something small or easy, meaning it requires little effort, time, or inconvenience (and sometimes literally no money). Often followed by an infinitive: “Não custa nada + verb” (e.g., “Não custa nada ouvir”). Can also be said alone to reassure: “Não custa nada, certo?”
target_language_example: Não custa nada mandar uma mensagem para avisar.
native_language_example: It won’t hurt to send a message to let them know.

meaning: “it must not be / it shouldn’t be / it’s probably not.”
additional_notes: Form of "dever" (must/should) + "ser" (to be). Used to express prohibition or recommendation ("mustn’t/shouldn’t be"), or a guess/expectation ("it’s probably not / it shouldn’t be"). Often appears in instructions and advice (e.g., "não deve ser consumida") or to say something is unlikely ("não deve ser difícil").
target_language_example: Não deve ser verdade; ninguém confirmou ainda.
native_language_example: It’s probably not true; nobody has confirmed it yet.

additional_notes: Used to say something is not advisable, not appropriate, or not expected/allowed. It’s the negative of “devia” (from “dever”, to have to/ought to). With an infinitive it often means “shouldn’t + verb” (Não devia fazer isso.); with “ter + past participle” it often means “shouldn’t have + done” (Não devia ter dito isso.).
target_language_example: Você não devia ter falado comigo desse jeito.
native_language_example: You shouldn’t have talked to me like that.

meaning: "I/you/he/she/it/we/they shouldn’t have" (regret about a past action).
additional_notes: Used to say a past action was a mistake or shouldn’t have happened. It’s the negative of "devia ter" and is followed by a past participle: "não devia ter + (acordado/contado/ido...)". The subject is often understood from context (eu/ele/você, etc.). You can also use it to criticize or blame someone: "Você não devia ter feito isso."
target_language_example: Eu não devia ter dito aquilo na reunião.
native_language_example: I shouldn’t have said that in the meeting.

additional_notes: Negative command using the present subjunctive of "dizer" (to say/tell). Used to tell someone not to say something ("Não diga isso" = don’t say that) or not to reveal information ("Não diga onde você está" = don’t tell where you are). You can add the person you’re telling: "Não diga nada a ela" (don’t tell her anything).
target_language_example: Por favor, não diga isso para ninguém.
native_language_example: Please don’t tell anyone that.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to keep quiet or keep a secret about something. It can be a firm request (“Don’t say anything!”) or a polite one when combined with “por favor.” In speech you’ll also hear the informal variant “não fala nada.”
target_language_example: Eu te conto depois, mas por enquanto não diga nada.
native_language_example: I’ll tell you later, but for now don’t say anything.

additional_notes: Commonly used to say someone stayed silent or didn’t mention something. Uses past tense of **dizer** (“to say”): **disse** = “said.” The subject is often implied by context (e.g., **Eu não disse nada** = “I didn’t say anything”). You can add details with **sobre** (“about”) or a relative clause: **não disse nada que…** (“didn’t say anything that…”).
target_language_example: Eu perguntei, mas ele não disse nada.
native_language_example: I asked, but he didn’t say anything.

additional_notes: Used to say something can’t be done or isn’t feasible, often with an infinitive verb: “Não dá para + verb” (e.g., não dá para entender = you can’t understand / it’s not possible to understand). It can refer to practical impossibility, difficulty, or a general limitation (sometimes implying “there’s no way to”). In speech it’s often shortened to “não dá pra”.
target_language_example: Hoje não dá para sair mais cedo.
native_language_example: Today it’s not possible to leave earlier.

meaning: "you can't" / "it's not possible to" (often: "it doesn't work to").
additional_notes: Very common in spoken Portuguese. Used to say something isn’t possible or feasible in the situation (because of rules, lack of time, conditions, etc.). It can be followed by an infinitive: "não dá pra usar" (you can’t use), "não dá pra saber" (there’s no way to know). You can also add a person: "não dá pra eu ver" (I can’t see). Similar to "não é possível" but more conversational.
target_language_example: Agora não dá pra entrar; a loja já fechou.
native_language_example: You can’t go in now; the store is already closed.

additional_notes: Used to say someone doesn’t understand something ("Ele não entende") or as a question/tag to check if the listener understands ("Não entende isso?"). Portuguese often drops the subject, so "Não entende" can mean "he/she doesn’t understand" or (in context) "you don’t understand".
target_language_example: Eu já expliquei duas vezes, mas você não entende.
native_language_example: I’ve explained it twice, but you don’t understand.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t understand something (a point, an explanation, a situation). Often followed by what you don’t understand: “não entendo isso” (I don’t understand that), “não entendo a base disso” (I don’t understand the basis of that). You can also use it alone as a response when you’re confused.
target_language_example: Desculpa, não entendo o que você quer dizer.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t understand what you mean.

additional_notes: "Não era" is "não" (not) + "era" (was/were), the imperfect past of "ser" (to be). It describes what something/someone was like in the past (often a state, description, or background): "A opinião dele não era importante" = "His opinion wasn’t important." With "não era para...", it often means "it wasn’t meant/supposed to...": "Não era para a gente estar aqui" = "We weren’t supposed to be here."
target_language_example: Eu não era muito feliz naquela época.
native_language_example: I wasn’t very happy at that time.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past of estar (estava) to say someone/something was not in a place at a certain time (physically absent). Often used to correct assumptions or explain you didn’t witness something: “Eu não estava lá quando aconteceu.”
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu não estava lá na hora, então não vi nada.
native_language_example: Sorry, I wasn’t there at the time, so I didn’t see anything.

additional_notes: Used to negate the verb "estar" in the 1st person singular present: "(eu) não estou". Common with a gerund to deny an action in progress ("não estou mentindo" = "I'm not lying") and with adjectives to describe a temporary state ("não estou bem" = "I'm not well").
target_language_example: Desculpa, não estou pronto agora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I'm not ready right now.

additional_notes: Used when something isn’t operating properly (a device, an app, a pen, a piece of code, etc.). It’s the negative present continuous of “estar funcionando” (“to be working/running”), so it often implies a current problem right now. You can specify what isn’t working: “O celular não está funcionando.”
target_language_example: O Wi‑Fi não está funcionando aqui.
native_language_example: The Wi‑Fi isn’t working here.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is not in a state/place/situation anymore. It’s the present of “estar” (temporary state/location) + “mais” meaning “anymore/no longer”. Often followed by a place (“em casa”) or adjective/condition (“em perigo”, “no controle”).
target_language_example: Ela não está mais doente.
native_language_example: She is no longer sick.

meaning: "is not / isn't" (often: "isn't here" or "isn't in/at [a place]").
additional_notes: Used with "estar" (temporary state/location) to say someone/something is not in a place or not in a certain condition. Often followed by a location: "não está no quarto" (isn't in the room), "não está aqui" (isn't here). It can also appear in tag questions: "Seu marido não está?" (Your husband isn't here/around, is he?). In expressions like "não está nem aí", it means someone doesn't care ("he couldn't care less").
target_language_example: Ela não está em casa agora.
native_language_example: She isn't at home right now.

additional_notes: Used to say that a person, animal, or object is not in this place. It’s the negative of “está aqui” (“is here”). Often used alone as a short answer (“Não está aqui.”). The subject can be implied from context or stated explicitly (e.g., “Ele não está aqui.” / “O meu livro não está aqui.”).
target_language_example: Desculpe, a gerente não está aqui agora.
native_language_example: Sorry, the manager isn’t here right now.

additional_notes: Used to say that something does not exist or is not available/present. Often followed by a noun ("não existe cura") or used with "nada" for emphasis ("não existe nada"). Can also be used for words: "Essa palavra não existe" = "That word doesn't exist."
target_language_example: Aqui não existe transporte público à noite.
native_language_example: There is no public transportation here at night.

additional_notes: From "não" (not) + "fala" (speaks/talks). Often used with an implied subject: "(ele/ela) não fala" = “he/she doesn’t speak.” It can also be an instruction in the informal "tu" form: "Não fala assim!" = “Don’t talk like that!” (more formal: "Não fale assim!"). Meaning can be “speak” (languages) or “talk” (in general), depending on context.
target_language_example: Ele não fala português muito bem, mas entende.
native_language_example: He doesn’t speak Portuguese very well, but he understands.

additional_notes: Negative command using the você form (formal or neutral). Often used to stop someone from speaking, from speaking loudly (Não fale alto), from speaking in a certain way (Não fale assim), or from bringing up a topic (Não fale sobre isso / Não fale em nome de...). With tu, you’d usually say: Não fales.
target_language_example: Por favor, não fale agora; estou ao telefone.
native_language_example: Please don’t talk right now; I’m on the phone.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to stop speaking in that tone or manner (often because it’s rude, disrespectful, or hurtful). It can be followed by “com…” to say who you shouldn’t talk to that way: “Não fale assim com sua mãe / comigo / ela.” More formal/polite: “Não fale assim, por favor.”
target_language_example: Por favor, não fale assim comigo.
native_language_example: Please don’t talk to me like that.

additional_notes: A common combination of não + faz (from fazer). It usually means 'he/she/it doesn't do/make' or 'you don't do/make' with você. Portuguese uses fazer for both 'do' and 'make', so the exact translation depends on context, as in não faz nada ('doesn't do anything') or não faz sentido ('doesn't make sense').
target_language_example: Isso não faz sentido.
native_language_example: That doesn't make sense.

additional_notes: Used to say something is not important or doesn’t change the outcome. Often followed by "para mim" (to me) and/or an "se..." clause: "Não faz diferença para mim se..." = "I don’t mind whether..." It can sound neutral or slightly dismissive depending on tone/context.
target_language_example: Não faz diferença para mim se a reunião é hoje ou amanhã.
native_language_example: It doesn’t matter to me whether the meeting is today or tomorrow.

meaning: "It doesn't make sense." / "That makes no sense."
additional_notes: Used to say something is illogical, confusing, or not reasonable. Common with a subject like "Isso"/"Esse"/"O que você está a dizer" (What you’re saying), or alone as a full reply: "Não faz sentido." You can add emphasis with "simplesmente" (simply) or "nenhum" (at all): "não faz sentido nenhum."
target_language_example: Desculpa, essa explicação não faz sentido para mim.
native_language_example: Sorry, that explanation doesn’t make sense to me.

meaning: “not to do that / not do it.”
additional_notes: Infinitive phrase used to express refraining from a specific action (“isso” = “that/it”). Common after verbs like avisar, pedir, decidir, prometer, recomendar, and especially after “para”: “para não fazer isso” = “so as not to do that.” Often contrasts with a prior idea or temptation (e.g., thinking about doing something, then deciding “não fazer isso”).
target_language_example: Eu tinha sido avisado para não fazer isso.
native_language_example: I had been warned not to do that.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone not to do an action. It’s the negative imperative with "fazer" (to do/make) for "você". Often followed by a verb object or noun: "Não faça barulho" (don’t make noise), "Não faça nada" (don’t do anything).
target_language_example: Por favor, não faça isso aqui.
native_language_example: Please don’t do that here.

additional_notes: Negative command using the você form (faça = imperative/subjunctive of fazer). Used to stop someone from doing something, or to reassure them not to worry about it (like in the example: “It’s fine, don’t do that”).
target_language_example: Não faça isso, por favor.
native_language_example: Don’t do that, please.

additional_notes: Past tense (ele/ela/você): "não" (not) + "fez" (did) + "nada" (anything). Common for saying someone took no action. In the pattern "não fez nada senão + infinitive", it means "did nothing but + verb" (e.g., "did nothing but cry").
target_language_example: Eu liguei para ele, mas ele não fez nada para ajudar.
native_language_example: I called him, but he didn’t do anything to help.

additional_notes: Used to deny responsibility or blame for something. Often said emphatically on its own ("Não fui eu!") or to clarify/insist ("Só para deixar claro, não fui eu"). Literally "not was I" (past tense of "ser": fui).
target_language_example: Eu juro que não fui eu!
native_language_example: I swear it wasn’t me!

meaning: “doesn’t like” (to like something / to like doing something).
additional_notes: Used with the verb gostar: eu gosto de… (I like…), ele/ela/você gosta de… (he/she/you like…), and in the negative: não gosta de… (doesn’t like…). It’s followed by a noun (não gosta de queijo) or an infinitive verb (não gosta de falar).
target_language_example: Ela não gosta de acordar cedo.
native_language_example: She doesn’t like waking up early.

additional_notes: Form of the verb gostar used with a plural subject (eles/elas/vocês). It’s followed by de + noun/verb: não gostam de mim (don’t like me), não gostam de esperar (don’t like waiting). With a singular subject, you’d say não gosta de (he/she/you don’t like).
target_language_example: Meus amigos não gostam de café.
native_language_example: My friends don’t like coffee.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t like something. It’s the negative of “gosto de” (I like). After “de”, Portuguese commonly uses a verb in the infinitive (e.g., “não gosto de ficar…”) or a noun (“não gosto de café”). You can change the person: “não gosta de” (he/she/you formal doesn’t like), “não gostamos de” (we don’t like).
target_language_example: Não gosto de acordar cedo.
native_language_example: I don't like waking up early.

additional_notes: Future tense of "haver" used impersonally to mean "there is/are" in the future. It’s common in predictions, warnings, and rules about what will be available or possible. Usually followed by a noun ("não haverá tempo") or "mais" ("não haverá mais nada").
target_language_example: Se você não estudar, não haverá tempo para aprender tudo depois.
native_language_example: If you don’t study, there won’t be time to learn everything later.

additional_notes: Used to say that no person was present somewhere in the past. Literally “there wasn’t nobody,” but in Portuguese double negatives are normal and still mean a single negative in English. Often followed by a place (aqui, lá dentro, em casa) and sometimes by a description like acordado (“awake”).
target_language_example: Quando cheguei, não havia ninguém na sala.
native_language_example: When I arrived, there was nobody in the living room.

additional_notes: Used to say that something does not exist, is not present, or is unavailable. It is the negative of existential há ('there is/there are'). In this use, há does not change for singular or plural nouns: não há livro = 'there isn't a book'; não há livros = 'there aren't any books'.
target_language_example: Não há café em casa.
native_language_example: There isn't any coffee at home.

additional_notes: Used to say there is no possible way to do something (often because it can’t be done, or there’s no solution). It’s common before an infinitive: “Não há como + verb”. Similar in meaning to “não tem como” (more informal).
target_language_example: Desculpa, não há como resolver isso hoje.
native_language_example: Sorry, there’s no way to fix this today.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **haver** (“to exist/there is/are”) to say something doesn’t exist anymore or isn’t available/possible anymore. Often followed by a noun (**não há mais ninguém** = “there’s nobody left”) or by **o que + infinitive** (**não há mais o que falar** = “there’s nothing more to say”).
target_language_example: Desculpe, não há mais ingressos para hoje.
native_language_example: Sorry, there are no more tickets for today.

additional_notes: Used to say that nothing exists/is happening/is available in a situation. It uses the existential verb phrase “há” (= “there is/there are”, from haver): “não há nada” = “there isn’t anything / there’s nothing”. Common patterns: “não há nada para + infinitive” (there’s nothing to + verb): “Não há nada para explicar.” = “There’s nothing to explain.” Also in the fixed expression “não há nada como…” meaning “there’s nothing like…”: “Não há nada como uma caminhada.”
target_language_example: Não há nada para comer na geladeira.
native_language_example: There’s nothing to eat in the fridge.

additional_notes: Used to say there isn’t anything that needs to be done (often followed by an infinitive: fazer, explicar, cancelar, etc.). Very common with reflexive verbs too: “Não há nada para se preocupar” = “There’s nothing to worry about.” You can change tense/person as needed (e.g., “não havia nada para…”, “não terá nada para…”).
target_language_example: Não há nada para fazer agora.
native_language_example: There’s nothing to do right now.

meaning: "there is nothing that…" / "there’s nothing … (that one can do)".
additional_notes: Used to say that no thing exists that meets a condition, or that there’s no possible action/solution. It’s often followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., possa/possamos/possam/se possa). In negative forms like “Não há nada que eu não…”, it can emphasize “there’s nothing I wouldn’t…” (i.e., I would do anything).
target_language_example: Não há nada que eu possa dizer agora para mudar isso.
native_language_example: There’s nothing I can say right now to change that.

additional_notes: Used with the verb phrase "há" (from "haver") to say something does not exist or is not present. "Nenhum" agrees with the noun: "nenhum" (masc. singular) / "nenhuma" (fem. singular). Often followed by a noun: "Não há nenhum problema."
target_language_example: Não há nenhuma vaga disponível hoje.
native_language_example: There aren't any openings available today.

meaning: “there isn’t any” / “there are no” (before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to say something does not exist or is not present. It’s formed with **há** (from **haver**, meaning “there is/are”) + **não**. **Nenhuma** agrees with a feminine noun (e.g., *nenhuma dúvida*, *nenhuma regra*). With masculine nouns you’d use **não há nenhum**.
target_language_example: Não há nenhuma solução para isso agora.
native_language_example: There isn’t any solution for that right now.

additional_notes: Used to say that nobody is present or exists in a place/situation. It uses "há" (from the verb "haver" = "there is/are"). Often followed by a location or description: "não há ninguém aqui/lá" (there’s no one here/there), "não há ninguém na casa" (there’s no one in the house). In general statements it can mean “nobody/no one” in a broader sense (e.g., “no one is indispensable”).
target_language_example: Não há ninguém esperando por você.
native_language_example: There isn't anyone waiting for you.

additional_notes:
Used to say that something is not important or doesn’t change the situation. Very common:
- Standalone: “Não importa.” = “It doesn’t matter.” / “Never mind.”
- With question words to mean “no matter …”: “não importa como/quanto/quem/onde/quando …” = “no matter how/much/who/where/when …”
Often followed by “se” in the same sense: “Não importa se…” = “It doesn’t matter if…”.
target_language_example: Não importa onde você vá, leve um documento com foto.
native_language_example: No matter where you go, bring a photo ID.

additional_notes: Used to say something does not change even if the situation or action is different. It’s commonly followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., faça, fizer): “Não importa o que você faça…”
target_language_example: Não importa o que aconteça, eu vou te ajudar.
native_language_example: No matter what happens, I’ll help you.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize determination or that something will stay true regardless of future events. It often introduces a promise/decision (e.g., “I won’t change my mind, no matter what happens”). It can appear at the beginning or end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Vou ficar com você, não importa o que aconteça.
native_language_example: I’ll stay with you, no matter what happens.

additional_notes: Used to say something is irrelevant or unimportant. Often appears as a full sentence (“Não interessa!”) to dismiss a detail or stop a line of questioning; depending on tone, it can sound abrupt (similar to “Never mind” or “That’s none of your concern”).
target_language_example: O preço não interessa; eu só quero que funcione bem.
native_language_example: The price doesn’t matter; I just want it to work well.

additional_notes: Used before a verb: não makes the sentence negative, and me means “me” or sometimes “to me,” depending on the verb. After negatives like não, Portuguese normally puts me before the verb.
target_language_example: Eles não me viram.
native_language_example: They didn't see me.

meaning: "Don’t tell me…" (often expressing disbelief or sarcasm).
additional_notes: Literally “don’t tell me.” Very commonly used before a clause with “que” to show you don’t believe what you just heard, or you’re being ironic: “Não me diga que…”. In questions it can sound like “You didn’t really…/Seriously…?” Depending on tone, it can be neutral (“Don’t tell me (the news)”) or sarcastic (“Yeah, right”).
target_language_example: Não me diga que você esqueceu de novo!
native_language_example: Don’t tell me you forgot again!

meaning: “Don’t tell me (that)…” (expresses surprise, disbelief, or suspicion).
additional_notes: Used before a clause introduced by que, often rhetorically. It can show disbelief (“Surely not…”), suspicion/accusation (“Don’t tell me you did X”), or surprised realization (“Don’t tell me it’s you!”). Tone depends on context and can sound skeptical or dramatic.
target_language_example: Não me diga que você esqueceu o passaporte!
native_language_example: Don’t tell me you forgot your passport!

additional_notes: Used to warn or complain about something you don’t want to be forced into doing. It uses the negative imperative/subjunctive of "fazer" with "você" ("faça"). Very often followed by an infinitive: "Não me faça rir" (don’t make me laugh), "Não me faça pedir" (don’t make me ask). Can also be followed by a noun/pronoun for “don’t do anything to me”: "Não me faça nada."
target_language_example: Não me faça esperar muito, por favor.
native_language_example: Don’t make me wait too long, please.

additional_notes: Often used to say something doesn’t bother you or you have no preference. You can also use it to show indifference: "Não me importo mais" = "I don’t care anymore." Common pattern: "não me importo de" + infinitive (e.g., "não me importo de esperar" = "I don’t mind waiting").
target_language_example: Não me importo de esperar um pouco.
native_language_example: I don't mind waiting a bit.

additional_notes: Used to say something doesn’t matter to you or doesn’t concern you. Often followed by a clause with “como” (how) or “se” (whether/if): “Não me interessa como…” = “I don’t care how…”, “Não me interessa se…” = “I don’t care whether…”. Can sound firm or dismissive depending on tone.
target_language_example: Não me interessa o motivo; só quero uma solução.
native_language_example: I don’t care about the reason; I just want a solution.

additional_notes: Used to say you can’t recall something. Often followed by "de" + noun/infinitive: "Não me lembro de nada" (I don’t remember anything), "Não me lembro de ver isso" (I don’t remember seeing that). In casual speech, people also say "não lembro" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Desculpa, não me lembro do seu nome.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t remember your name.

additional_notes: A strong command using the negative imperative of tocar (to touch): não + me (me) + toque (touch, you [formal]/you [informal in some regions]). Often used when someone is being intrusive or aggressive. You can add details like com + body part/object (Não me toque com a mão.) or de novo (Don’t touch me again.). The phrase itself is neutral, but it’s frequently said in angry or confrontational situations.
target_language_example: Por favor, não me toque.
native_language_example: Please, don’t touch me.

additional_notes: Used when the verb action is negated and the object is “us” (nos). With a conjugated verb, “nos” usually comes before the verb: “não nos deixa” = “doesn’t let us.” With an infinitive, “nos” can attach to it: “para não nos preocupar” = “so as not to worry us / so we don’t worry.”
target_language_example: Eles não nos disseram a verdade.
native_language_example: They didn’t tell us the truth.

additional_notes: Usually combines não with the unstressed direct-object pronoun o, so before a verb it means 'not ... him/it': não o vejo = 'I don't see him/it'. In patterns like não o são, o refers back to a previously mentioned idea or quality, meaning something like 'not so' or 'not that'.
target_language_example: Desculpa, não o conheço.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don't know him.

meaning: “you can’t enter” / “no entry” / “not allowed to come in.”
additional_notes: Used to say that entering is not permitted. Often appears on signs or as a firm instruction. The subject “you” (or “one”) is implied; a more explicit version is “Você não pode entrar.”
target_language_example: Desculpe, aqui não pode entrar sem autorização.
native_language_example: Sorry, you can’t enter here without permission.

meaning: "You can't do that" / "you can't do this."
additional_notes: Used to tell someone something is not allowed or not acceptable. It can mean either (1) prohibition/permission (“You’re not allowed to do that”) or (2) strong protest/complaint (“You can’t do that to me!”). In speech it often implies “you (singular)” from context: (Você) não pode fazer isso. For “you (plural),” use: Não podem fazer isso.
target_language_example: Você não pode fazer isso aqui.
native_language_example: You can't do that here.

meaning: "you can't stay" / "you can't keep (doing that)"; sometimes "you can't become/end up".
additional_notes: Used to forbid or warn someone about an action or situation. With places (aí, fora), it often means “can’t stay / can’t remain” (Não pode ficar aí pra sempre. = You can’t stay there forever.). With a repeated action, it can mean “can’t keep (doing that)” (não pode ficar se arriscando = you can’t keep taking risks). With adjectives, ficar can mean “to become/get” (ficar gripado = to get the flu). In expressions like “não pode ficar pior”, it means “it can’t get any worse.”
target_language_example: Você não pode ficar acordado até tão tarde todos os dias.
native_language_example: You can’t stay up that late every day.

additional_notes: Used to say something is not possible or not allowed to exist/happen. Common in rules, strong statements, and general truths. Often followed by a noun (e.g., erros, atrasos) or an abstract idea (e.g., progresso).
target_language_example: Não pode haver confusão durante a prova.
native_language_example: There can’t be any confusion during the test.

meaning: “can’t be” / “cannot be” (it isn’t possible; it must not be).
additional_notes: Used to say something is impossible or not allowed, or that something cannot have a certain quality. Very common with nouns/adjectives: “não pode ser verdade” (“it can’t be true”), “não pode ser aqui” (“it can’t be here”). In rules/instructions it can mean “must not be” (e.g., “não pode ser bebida” = “must not be drunk / isn’t drinkable”).
target_language_example: Desculpe, não pode ser aqui.
native_language_example: Sorry, it can’t be here.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is not allowed to have something (a rule/prohibition) or that it’s impossible to have something. Often followed by a noun or by "as duas" ("both"). In speech you may also hear "não dá pra ter" with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Aqui não pode ter animais no apartamento.
native_language_example: You can't have pets in the apartment here.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is not possible or not allowed. "Podem" is the present tense of "poder" for "eles/elas" (they) and also "vocês" (you all). Often followed by an infinitive: "não podem + verbo" (e.g., "não podem entrar" = they can’t come in).
target_language_example: Vocês não podem entrar aqui sem ingresso.
native_language_example: You can’t come in here without a ticket.

additional_notes: Used with a plural subject (eles/elas/these things) to say something is not possible or not allowed. Very common in the passive with a past participle: “não podem ser + visto(s)/vista(s), lido(s)/lida(s), separado(s)/separada(s)” = “cannot be seen/read/separated.”
target_language_example: Esses documentos não podem ser assinados hoje.
native_language_example: Those documents cannot be signed today.

additional_notes: "Não podemos" is the negative form of "podemos" (from the verb "poder" = "to be able to / can"), used when the subject is "we" (nós). It’s often followed by an infinitive: "não podemos ficar" = "we can’t stay". In questions, it can mean "can’t we...?": "Não podemos ficar em paz?" = "Can’t we have some peace?"
target_language_example: Não podemos falar agora; estamos atrasados.
native_language_example: We can't talk now; we're late.

meaning: "we can't let / we can't allow"; also "we can't help but" (when followed by "de" + infinitive).
additional_notes: Used to say something must not be allowed to happen: "Não podemos deixar isso acontecer" = "We can't let that happen." If it’s followed by "de" + infinitive ("não podemos deixar de + verb"), it means you can’t avoid doing it / you inevitably do it: "Não podemos deixar de admirar" = "We can't help but admire."
target_language_example: Não podemos deixar o medo nos parar.
native_language_example: We can't let fear stop us.

meaning: “couldn’t / wasn’t able to” (past or conditional of poder).
additional_notes: Used with verbs to say someone was unable/wasn’t allowed to do something in the past: “Eu não podia falar.” It can also express a hypothetical/conditional idea (“couldn’t” in the sense of “it wouldn’t be possible”): “Não podia tomar um táxi...?” In set phrases it can intensify meaning: “Não podia estar mais feliz” = “I couldn’t be happier,” and “Não podia ter me acontecido coisa melhor” = “Nothing better could have happened to me.”
target_language_example: Ontem eu não podia sair mais cedo.
native_language_example: Yesterday I couldn’t leave earlier.

additional_notes: Literally combines não + posso ('I can'). The subject eu ('I') is usually omitted in Portuguese, so não posso normally means 'I can't' or 'I cannot.' It can express inability, impossibility, or sometimes refusal depending on context.
target_language_example: Desculpa, não posso ir hoje.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't go today.

additional_notes: Used with **deixar + object** to mean “not leave behind/abandon” or “not leave (it) there.” Used with **deixar que + verb (usually subjunctive)** to mean “not allow/let,” as in *Não posso deixar que faça isso* (“I can’t let you/him do that”).
target_language_example: Não posso deixar você aqui sozinho.
native_language_example: I can’t leave you here alone.

additional_notes: Used to refuse or be unable to give information. Often followed by what you can’t say (e.g., não posso dizer quem/onde/quando) or by nada (nothing). Can also be a complete sentence when you don’t want to explain further.
target_language_example: Desculpa, não posso dizer agora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t say right now.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re unable (or not allowed) to go somewhere. Often followed by a destination with "para" (e.g., "não posso ir para o hospital") or by a description of how you would go (e.g., "não posso ir desse jeito" = "I can’t go like this / this way").
target_language_example: Desculpa, não posso ir hoje.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't go today.

additional_notes: Commonly used to express inability or refusal. Often followed by an infinitive ("Não posso ir" = "I can't go"), but it can also be used alone as a complete answer/exclamation ("Não posso!" = "I can't!" / "I can't do that!"). In speech it can sometimes imply "I can't/won't" depending on context.
target_language_example: Desculpa, hoje eu não posso sair.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't go out today.

additional_notes: From precisar ('to need'). With de + noun, it means someone does not need something: não precisa de ajuda = 'doesn't need help'. With an infinitive, it means 'don't/doesn't need to' do something: não precisa chorar = 'don't need to cry'. Often used without a subject to mean 'you don't need to' or 'no need to'.
target_language_example: Não precisa esperar por mim.
native_language_example: You don't need to wait for me.

additional_notes: Used with the verb precisar + de + noun/pronoun to say something isn’t necessary: Não precisa de dinheiro. In conversation it can also be a polite offer/suggestion when talking to someone: Não precisa de ajuda? Note that precisar means “to need,” not “to be precise” (false friend with English “precise”).
target_language_example: Você não precisa de pressa.
native_language_example: You don’t need to rush.

meaning: "You don’t need to worry." / "No need to worry."
additional_notes: Used to reassure someone that something is fine or taken care of. It can be said as a full sentence on its own. Often appears as “não precisa se preocupar com isso” (“you don’t need to worry about that”).
target_language_example: Não precisa se preocupar, eu resolvo isso amanhã.
native_language_example: You don’t need to worry, I’ll take care of that tomorrow.

meaning: “I don’t need” (followed by a noun or infinitive).
additional_notes: Used to say you don’t need something. “Preciso de” means “I need” and it normally takes “de” before a noun/pronoun: preciso de dinheiro, não preciso de você. With verbs, Portuguese often uses “precisar de + infinitive”: Não preciso de ir (often shortened in speech to “Não preciso ir”). You can change the person: não precisa de (you/he/she doesn’t need), não precisamos de (we don’t need).
target_language_example: Não preciso de ajuda agora.
native_language_example: I don’t need help right now.

additional_notes: Used to say you were unable to do something in the past. It’s the pretérito perfeito (simple past) of the verb poder (“to be able to”): eu pude = “I was able to”, eu não pude = “I couldn’t”. Often followed by an infinitive: “não pude dormir” (“I couldn’t sleep”). In the common pattern “não pude deixar de + infinitive”, it means “I couldn’t help (doing something)” (e.g., “não pude deixar de chorar” = “I couldn’t help crying”).
target_language_example: Desculpa, não pude ir ontem porque estava doente.
native_language_example: Sorry, I couldn’t go yesterday because I was sick.

additional_notes: "Não quer" is the negation of the verb "querer" (to want) in the present tense. It can mean "he/she doesn’t want" (Ele/Ela não quer…) or "you don’t want" when speaking to someone as "você" (common in Brazil): e.g., "Você não quer...?" In questions, "Não quer…?" is often used to offer or invite someone (similar to "Don’t you want…?" / "Would you like…?").
target_language_example: Você não quer tomar um café comigo?
native_language_example: Would you like to have a coffee with me?

meaning: to not want to know; to not care (about something); to want nothing to do with something/someone.
additional_notes: Literally “to not want to know,” but very often used idiomatically to mean you don’t care, you’re not interested, or you don’t want to deal with something. Common patterns: “não querer saber de + noun” = “to not care about / to want nothing to do with …”; it can also imply refusing to listen (“não querer saber” = “not wanting to hear it”).
target_language_example: Hoje eu vou não querer saber de problemas.
native_language_example: Today I'm not going to want to deal with problems.

meaning: didn’t want to / wasn’t willing to.
additional_notes: Imperfect past of querer (“to want”) with negation: não + queria. It often implies an ongoing feeling in the past (“I/they didn’t want to”) rather than a single moment (“I refused”). The subject is often understood from context: eu não queria (I), ele/ela não queria (he/she), a gente não queria (we), etc.
target_language_example: Eu não queria sair, mas acabei indo.
native_language_example: I didn’t want to go out, but I ended up going.

additional_notes: Used to say that you do not want something or do not want to do something. It is the 1st-person singular form of querer, so the subject 'I' is built into quero. It can be followed by a noun or by another verb in the infinitive.
target_language_example: Não quero sair hoje.
native_language_example: I don't want to go out today.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t want to go somewhere or do something that involves going. Often followed by an infinitive to show what you don’t want to go do (e.g., “não quero ir dormir” = “I don’t want to go to sleep”) or by a destination with “para” (e.g., “não quero ir para casa” = “I don’t want to go home”).
target_language_example: Desculpa, hoje não quero ir ao cinema.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t want to go to the movies today.

meaning: "I don’t want (it) anymore" / "I don’t want to anymore."
additional_notes: Used to say you’re done with something and don’t want it to continue. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., ver, sentir, ter que aguentar) or a noun. Stronger than just "não quero" because it adds the idea of "any longer / anymore."
target_language_example: Não quero mais discutir sobre isso.
native_language_example: I don’t want to argue about this anymore.

additional_notes: Used to express what you don’t want to happen or what you don’t want someone to do. It’s typically followed by a verb in the subjunctive: e.g., "Não quero que você vá" (I don’t want you to go), "Não quero que eles falem" (I don’t want them to talk). You can add the person after "que" (eu/ele/ela/você/nós/eles) if needed.
target_language_example: Não quero que você se atrase.
native_language_example: I don’t want you to be late.

meaning: "I don’t want to know" / "I don’t care" (I want nothing to do with it).
