target_language_example: O cachorro está com medo porque tem muito barulho.
native_language_example: The dog is scared because there’s a lot of noise.

meaning: to take the dog for a walk.
additional_notes: Common everyday phrase. You can change the tense: "Levo" (I take), "Levei" (I took), "estou levando" (I’m taking). In Portuguese you usually say "levar ... para passear" (literally “to take ... to stroll/walk”).
target_language_example: Hoje eu vou levar o cachorro para passear depois do jantar.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to take the dog for a walk after dinner.

additional_notes: "O" is the masculine singular definite article (“the”), so "o café" usually means “the coffee” (a specific coffee you’re talking about). In everyday speech it can also refer to coffee in general or a cup of coffee, depending on context (e.g., ordering, serving, stirring).
target_language_example: Você quer o café com açúcar ou sem?
native_language_example: Do you want the coffee with sugar or without?

additional_notes: Common, everyday term for the morning meal. Often used with verbs like tomar (to have) and preparar (to prepare): “tomar o café da manhã”, “preparar o café da manhã”.
target_language_example: Eu tomo o café da manhã às sete.
native_language_example: I have breakfast at seven.

additional_notes: Used for a physical route or direction (“show someone the way”), and also figuratively for a process or route to an outcome (“the path to success”). Often appears with “para” to mean “the way/path to …” (e.g., “o caminho para o aeroporto”).
target_language_example: Pode dizer-me o caminho para a estação?
native_language_example: Can you tell me the way to the station?

meaning: "the way to" / "the path/route to" (a place or destination).
additional_notes: Used to ask for directions or describe the route to somewhere. It’s often followed by a place ("o caminho para a estação") or by an action with an infinitive ("o caminho para chegar lá" = "the way to get there"). In questions, you’ll commonly hear: "Você pode me dizer o caminho para...?"
target_language_example: Qual é o caminho para o centro?
native_language_example: What’s the way to downtown?

additional_notes: Masculine singular noun with the definite article o (“the”). Often used for vehicles that carry loads (delivery truck, moving truck) and in set phrases like o caminhão do lixo (“the garbage truck”). Plural: os caminhões.
target_language_example: O caminhão do lixo passa aqui toda segunda-feira.
native_language_example: The garbage truck comes by here every Monday.

meaning: 'the captain' (a leader in a team, ship, aircraft, or the military/police).
additional_notes: "Capitão" is a masculine noun; the definite article "o" means "the". Used as a rank/title (often capitalized with a name: "o capitão McGan") or as a role ("o capitão do time" = the team captain). Feminine form: "a capitã".
target_language_example: Quem é o capitão do time hoje?
native_language_example: Who is the team captain today?

additional_notes: Informal way to refer to a man/person: “the guy” / “that guy.” Very common in speech. In phrases like “Você é o cara!”, it means “You’re the man!” (a compliment). Although “cara” literally means “face,” this slang meaning isn’t a literal translation.
target_language_example: Não fala assim com o cara.
native_language_example: Don’t talk to the guy like that.

additional_notes: Uses the informal noun “cara” (“guy/dude”) + “que” (“who/that”) to introduce a relative clause describing the man. Common in casual speech; in more neutral/formal contexts you might say “o homem que …” (“the man who …”).
target_language_example: O cara que trabalha aqui mora perto do metrô.
native_language_example: The guy who works here lives near the subway.

meaning: a very vulgar way to strongly reject/deny something (like “the fuck” / “my ass”).
additional_notes: Literally means “the penis” (very offensive). In Brazilian Portuguese it’s commonly used after a word/phrase to contradict it with anger or emphasis: “X é o caralho!” ≈ “X, my ass!” / “No fucking way.” Not appropriate in polite conversation; use only if you understand the social risk.
target_language_example: "Calma" é o caralho — para de me provocar.
native_language_example: “Calm down,” my ass — stop provoking me.

additional_notes: Refers to a specific car. The article o means "the" for a singular masculine noun; compare um carro for "a car."
target_language_example: Eu deixei o carro na garagem.
native_language_example: I left the car in the garage.

additional_notes: Literally “the car of him.” In Portuguese, possession is often shown with "de" + pronoun: "dele" (his), "dela" (hers), "deles" (theirs, masculine/mixed), "delas" (theirs, feminine). This is a clear alternative to "o seu carro", which can sometimes be ambiguous (his/her/your).
target_language_example: O carro dele está na garagem.
native_language_example: His car is in the garage.

additional_notes: A masculine noun meaning an outer layer of clothing. Often used with verbs like pôr/colocar (to put on), tirar (to take off), and usar (to wear). In Brazil, casaco can be a coat or a heavier jacket; in Portugal, it can also mean a jacket.
target_language_example: Está frio—pega o casaco.
native_language_example: It’s cold—grab your coat.

additional_notes: "Casamento" can mean the event (a wedding) or the institution/state (marriage). It’s masculine, so it usually appears as "o casamento". Common patterns: "o casamento de vocês" (your wedding / your marriage), "convidar para o casamento" (invite to the wedding), "falar sobre o casamento" (talk about one’s marriage).
target_language_example: Eles vão celebrar o casamento no sábado.
native_language_example: They’re going to celebrate the wedding on Saturday.

additional_notes: Used for a particular situation or fact pattern ("Espero que esse não seja o caso" = "I hope that’s not the case"), and also for an official matter—especially a police/legal investigation ("resolver o caso" = "solve the case"). Often followed by "de" to specify which one: "o caso de Esteban" (Esteban’s case).
target_language_example: Não sabemos ainda quem fez isso, mas vamos resolver o caso.
native_language_example: We still don’t know who did it, but we’re going to solve the case.

additional_notes: Refers to a castle (a large fortified building/palace). Often used with locations or names: "o castelo de X" ("X's castle" / "the castle of X"). Common in stories/fantasy contexts (e.g., "o castelo de Howl").
target_language_example: Eles moram perto do castelo.
native_language_example: They live near the castle.

additional_notes: Refers to a male horse in the singular. The article “o” means “the” (masculine singular). For “a horse” (unspecified), use “um cavalo.” The feminine form is “a égua” (mare).
target_language_example: O cavalo está no campo.
native_language_example: The horse is in the field.

additional_notes: Common Brazilian Portuguese term for a mobile phone. Uses the masculine definite article: o (singular) / os (plural). Often followed by a possessive: o meu celular (my phone), o celular dela (her phone). In Portugal, you’ll often hear o telemóvel instead.
target_language_example: Você tirou o celular da mesa.
native_language_example: You took the cellphone off the table.

additional_notes: Commonly used with the verb "sentir": "sentir o cheiro (de ...)" = "to smell / to notice the smell (of ...)". It can be positive or negative depending on the adjective: "cheiro horrível" (horrible smell), "cheiro incrível" (amazing smell). Also used alone as a question: "Está sentindo o cheiro?" = "Do you smell it?"
target_language_example: Sinto o cheiro de café fresco.
native_language_example: I smell fresh coffee.

meaning: 'the smell/scent of' (followed by a noun or clause).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a specific smell. Common with verbs like sentir (to smell) and with liking/disliking: amar/detestat o cheiro de... Can be followed by a noun (o cheiro de fumaça) or by something happening (o cheiro de algo queimando).
target_language_example: Senti o cheiro de café assim que entrei na cozinha.
native_language_example: I smelled coffee as soon as I walked into the kitchen.

meaning: "the smell of (the)" (for a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a smell/scent coming from something. "do" is a contraction of "de + o" (= "of the"). It’s used before masculine singular nouns (o café, o ar, o inverno). For other forms: "o cheiro da" (feminine singular), "o cheiro dos" (masculine plural), "o cheiro das" (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Gosto do cheiro do pão saindo do forno.
native_language_example: I like the smell of bread coming out of the oven.

additional_notes: Used for the surface you walk on. Indoors it usually means “the floor” (e.g., the floor is clean). Outdoors it often means “the ground” (e.g., the ground is covered with snow). In expressions like “olhar para o chão,” it means “look down at the floor/ground.”
target_language_example: Deixei as chaves no chão da cozinha.
native_language_example: I left the keys on the kitchen floor.

meaning: the climate; the weather; the mood/atmosphere.
additional_notes: Usually refers to weather conditions in a place (“Como é o clima?” / “O clima está bom.”). It can also mean the general atmosphere or mood of a situation or group (“O clima deles não é sombrio?”). Common patterns: “Como é o clima em…?” (What’s the weather/climate like in…?), “O clima está…” (The weather is…), “O clima mudou” (The weather changed).
target_language_example: O clima hoje está quente e úmido.
native_language_example: The weather today is hot and humid.

additional_notes: A common noun for a computer. Uses the masculine singular definite article "o" (= "the"). Plural: "os computadores". Often used for desktop or laptop computers (for a laptop you may also hear "o notebook" in Brazil).
target_language_example: Preciso usar o computador para enviar um e-mail.
native_language_example: I need to use the computer to send an email.

additional_notes: Used for a formal legal document that sets the terms of an agreement (e.g., work contract, rental contract, license agreement). Common verbs: assinar o contrato (to sign the contract), ler o contrato (to read the contract), concordar em assinar o contrato (to agree to sign the contract).
target_language_example: Antes de assinar o contrato, vou ler tudo com calma.
native_language_example: Before signing the contract, I’m going to read everything carefully.

meaning: the heart (organ); also: the heart (feelings, love, courage).
additional_notes: Used literally for the physical heart (health, medical contexts) and figuratively for emotions, sincerity, compassion, or inner will (e.g., “de todo o coração” = “with all my heart”; “falar com o coração” = “speak from the heart”). Also appears in phrases contrasting emotion vs. reason (e.g., “O coração diz..., mas o bom senso diz...”).
target_language_example: Amo-te de todo o coração.
native_language_example: I love you with all my heart.

additional_notes: Usually means a person’s physical body. In crime/medical contexts, it can also mean “the body” = a dead body/corpse (e.g., “o corpo da vítima”). With the article “o”, it refers to a specific body already known in the conversation.
target_language_example: O corpo do paciente está muito cansado hoje.
native_language_example: The patient’s body is very tired today.

meaning: the guilty person; the person to blame (the culprit).
additional_notes: Used to identify the person responsible for a wrongdoing or problem. Often appears in crime/investigation contexts ("catch the culprit") or when blaming someone ("You’re to blame"). Feminine form: "a culpada". Common patterns: "o culpado foi pego" (the culprit was caught), "culpado de" + noun (guilty/responsible for: "culpado do acidente").
target_language_example: A polícia ainda está procurando o culpado.
native_language_example: The police are still looking for the culprit.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how expensive it is to live in a place (prices for housing, food, transportation, etc.). Often used with verbs like "aumentar" (increase) and adjectives like "alto" (high).
target_language_example: O custo de vida aqui é mais baixo do que em Lisboa.
native_language_example: The cost of living here is lower than in Lisbon.

additional_notes: "O" is the masculine singular definite article (“the”). "Cão" means “dog” (often a bit more formal than "cachorro"). Use it to refer to a specific dog already known in the context.
target_language_example: O cão está no jardim.
native_language_example: The dog is in the garden.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “the sky” (what you see above you). It can also mean “heaven” in religious/spiritual contexts; usually the context makes it clear. Often used with weather/color descriptions: “o céu está azul”, “o céu escureceu”.
target_language_example: Hoje o céu está limpo e bem azul.
native_language_example: Today the sky is clear and very blue.

meaning: “the sky is …” (describing the sky’s current condition/color).
additional_notes: Used to describe how the sky looks at the moment. Often followed by an adjective like a color (azul, negro, vermelho) or weather-related descriptions (nublado, limpo, claro). It’s a normal present-tense statement: “o céu” (the sky) + “está” (is, temporary state).
target_language_example: À noite, o céu está cheio de estrelas.
native_language_example: At night, the sky is full of stars.

meaning: the finger (also: the toe, depending on context).
additional_notes: Most often means a finger on the hand. In some contexts, especially with feet, “dedo” can also mean a toe (e.g., “o dedo do pé”). Common expressions: “apontar o dedo (para alguém)” = to point a finger at someone / to blame someone. In very informal Brazilian Portuguese, “largar o dedo” can mean to let loose/attack (e.g., start shooting or hitting), depending on context.
target_language_example: Cortei o dedo e preciso de um curativo.
native_language_example: I cut my finger and I need a bandage.

additional_notes: Refers to the course of events thought to be decided by forces beyond a person’s control. Common in philosophical or dramatic statements (e.g., accepting what happens: “É o destino”). It can also mean a “destination” (place you’re going), but in these examples it’s clearly “fate/destiny.”
target_language_example: Às vezes, temos de aceitar o destino.
native_language_example: Sometimes we have to accept fate.

additional_notes: Common way to say “homework” in Brazilian Portuguese. Often used with the verb fazer: fazer o dever de casa (to do the homework). You can also hear lição de casa with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Preciso terminar o dever de casa antes do jantar.
native_language_example: I need to finish my homework before dinner.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific day on which something happened. Very common in stories and memories. Often followed by a verb in the past: “o dia em que cheguei” (the day I arrived). It can also be used after “desde” to mean “since the day when…”.
target_language_example: Lembro-me do dia em que nos conhecemos.
native_language_example: I remember the day we met.

additional_notes: Used to say something lasted for the entire day. Often follows the verb: "Choveu o dia inteiro" (It rained all day), "Dormi o dia inteiro" (I slept all day). You can also use it with "ficar" to mean staying/remaining somewhere all day: "Fiquei em casa o dia inteiro".
target_language_example: Fiquei no trabalho o dia inteiro.
native_language_example: I stayed at work all day.

additional_notes: Means you did something continuously or for most of the day. Common word order is also "todo o dia" with the same meaning. It can adapt to other time periods with agreement: "a noite toda" (all night), "a semana toda" (all week).
target_language_example: Eu estudei português o dia todo.
native_language_example: I studied Portuguese all day.

additional_notes: Refers to the devil in a religious or supernatural sense, but it’s also common in idioms and exaggerations. For example, “o diabo tá solto” means “all hell is breaking loose / the devil is loose” (chaos, trouble). It can also be used in sayings to blame “the devil” for bad feelings or behavior.
target_language_example: Parece que o diabo tá solto hoje: só deu confusão.
native_language_example: It feels like all hell is breaking loose today: it’s been nothing but trouble.

additional_notes: Refers to a specific amount of money already mentioned or understood from context. The article o means "the," so this phrase is used when talking about particular money, not money in general.
target_language_example: Onde está o dinheiro?
native_language_example: Where is the money?

meaning: "the money that" (introduces a clause describing the money).
additional_notes: Used when you want to specify which money you mean by adding extra information after que (a relative clause). Very common with verbs like dever (to owe), dar (to give), roubar (to steal), gastar (to spend), and precisar (to need). You can change the article to match context: o dinheiro que (the money that), um dinheiro que (some money that).
target_language_example: Ainda não recebi o dinheiro que você me prometeu.
native_language_example: I still haven’t received the money that you promised me.

meaning: the director; the principal/head (of a school/organization).
additional_notes: Usually refers to a person in charge: the director of a film (movie director) or the head/principal of a school, company, or establishment. Often followed by “de/da/do” to say what they direct (e.g., “o diretor do filme”, “o diretor deste estabelecimento”).
target_language_example: Fale com o diretor da escola amanhã.
native_language_example: Talk to the school principal tomorrow.

meaning: the owner; the person in charge.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the (male) owner of something (a house, account, business, etc.). For a woman, use "a dona". Common pattern: "o dono de + [thing]" (e.g., o dono da casa / o dono da conta). Can also mean "the boss" or "the one running the place" depending on context.
target_language_example: Preciso falar com o dono do restaurante.
native_language_example: I need to talk to the owner of the restaurant.

meaning: the address (street address; also email address).
additional_notes: Used to refer to where someone lives/where a place is located (street + number, etc.). It can also mean an email address; context usually makes it clear (e.g., "endereço de e-mail"). Often used with "qual é" (Qual é o endereço?) and with "de" to specify whose/which address (o endereço dela, o endereço do hotel).
target_language_example: Qual é o endereço do restaurante?
native_language_example: What’s the restaurant’s address?

additional_notes: "Endereço" means "address" (postal address; it can also mean a website address/URL depending on context). "Dele" means "of him / his" and is often used instead of "seu" to avoid ambiguity (since "seu" can mean "his", "her", "your", etc.).
target_language_example: Você tem o endereço dele?
native_language_example: Do you have his address?

meaning: the forest spirit (a supernatural being connected to the forest).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a mythical/supernatural entity that represents or protects the forest. It’s a specific character/title in stories; you can also say just “espírito da floresta” without “o” depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Dizem que o espírito da floresta protege quem respeita a natureza.
native_language_example: They say the forest spirit protects those who respect nature.

additional_notes: Refers to the army (military land forces). Often used with verbs like entrar para (to join), voltar para (to return to), ir para / ir com (to go to/with, e.g., to serve with the army), and falar sobre (to talk about).
target_language_example: Meu irmão entrou para o exército no ano passado.
native_language_example: My brother joined the army last year.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause as a fact or piece of information, often to emphasize it (sometimes contrasting with what someone thinks, feels, or considers). Common with verbs like considerar, negar, esconder, and expressions like é óbvio. Often followed by a full sentence (subject + verb).
target_language_example: O fato de que você chegou cedo me surpreendeu.
native_language_example: The fact that you arrived early surprised me.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a key point or reality (often as a correction, conclusion, or emphasis), similar to “the truth is…” or “bottom line…”. It’s followed by a clause (usually with "que"), and is neutral in formality.
target_language_example: O fato é que não temos tempo suficiente.
native_language_example: The fact is that we don’t have enough time.

additional_notes: Refers to a male child/offspring. Often used with context to mean “her/his/their son” (e.g., "a mãe e o filho" = "the mother and the son"). In Portuguese, possession is sometimes clear from context even without "meu/minha" (my), "dele/dela" (his/her), etc.
target_language_example: Ela foi ao parque com o filho.
native_language_example: She went to the park with her son.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male child belonging to a specific man. It’s a common way to show possession with a noun + “dele” (of him). Contrast: “o filho dela” = her son; “o filho deles” = their son.
target_language_example: O filho dele mora em São Paulo.
native_language_example: His son lives in São Paulo.

additional_notes: Means “the movie/film” (a specific movie known from context). It’s made of the definite article “o” (“the”, masculine singular) + “filme” (“movie/film”). Common with verbs like ver (to watch/see): “ver o filme” = “to watch the movie.”
target_language_example: A gente vai ver o filme hoje à noite.
native_language_example: We’re going to watch the movie tonight.

additional_notes: Means Saturday + Sunday. Often used with prepositions like: no fim de semana (on the weekend), no fim de semana passado (last weekend), no próximo fim de semana (next weekend), passar o fim de semana (to spend the weekend). You can also use it on its own as a topic-starter: “E o fim de semana?” = “How was the weekend?/What about the weekend?”
target_language_example: Vamos viajar no fim de semana.
native_language_example: We’re going to travel on the weekend.

meaning: “the end of the world”; (figuratively) “it’s not a big deal / it’s not the end of the world.”
additional_notes: Often used to reassure someone that a problem or mistake isn’t so serious: “Não é o fim do mundo.” You can also use it more literally for apocalyptic talk, and humorously to mean “that can wait / not urgent” (e.g., “O fim do mundo terá de esperar.”).
target_language_example: Calma — perder o autocarro não é o fim do mundo.
native_language_example: Relax—missing the bus isn’t the end of the world.

additional_notes: Means “fire” (a flame or burning). Common with verbs like apagar o fogo (put out the fire) and o fogo saiu de controle (the fire got out of control). Can also be used more generally for the human ability to use fire.
target_language_example: Cuidado: o fogo está muito alto.
native_language_example: Careful: the fire is very high (burning strongly).

additional_notes: A masculine singular noun phrase used to talk about what will happen later (in someone’s life, in the world, etc.). Common with "de" to say whose/what future it is: "o futuro de alguém" (someone’s future), "o futuro da humanidade" (humanity’s future). Also used in general statements like "O futuro é incerto" (The future is uncertain).
target_language_example: Não se preocupe com o futuro; vamos resolver isso juntos.
native_language_example: Don’t worry about the future; we’ll sort this out together.

additional_notes: Masculine singular: o = “the”, garoto = “boy/kid”. Common in Brazil for a boy or young male (similar to “kid” in English). For a girl, use “a garota”.
target_language_example: O garoto está brincando no parque.
native_language_example: The boy is playing in the park.

additional_notes: "O" is the masculine singular definite article (“the”). "O gato" can refer to a specific cat (“the cat”) or to cats in general depending on context. It can also be used figuratively in some expressions, but the basic meaning is literally “the cat.”
target_language_example: O gato está dormindo no sofá.
native_language_example: The cat is sleeping on the couch.

meaning: 'the cat is' (using estar: a temporary state or location).
additional_notes: "O gato" means "the cat." "Está" is the present tense of "estar" and is used for temporary conditions (safe, sick, tired, etc.) and for location/position (on/under the chair). In Portuguese, "estar" often contrasts with "ser" (more permanent characteristics).
target_language_example: O gato está dormindo no sofá.
native_language_example: The cat is sleeping on the couch.

additional_notes: Used for the person in charge (e.g., in a store, restaurant, hotel, or office). You’ll often hear it in customer-service situations: “Quero falar com o gerente” (“I want to speak to the manager”). Feminine form: “a gerente” (the manager, female) in common usage; you may also see “a gerenta” in some contexts.
target_language_example: Desculpe, posso falar com o gerente, por favor?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I speak to the manager, please?

additional_notes: Usually refers to the national government as an institution (“the government”). In some contexts it can mean the rule/administration of a country or city (“the governance of Gondor”). The noun is masculine, so it commonly appears with the definite article: o governo.
target_language_example: O governo anunciou novas medidas de segurança.
native_language_example: The government announced new security measures.

additional_notes: A common everyday noun. Literally “rain-guard” (guarda + chuva). Often used with verbs like deixar (leave), esquecer (forget), pegar (pick up/take), and usar (use). Plural: os guarda-chuvas.
target_language_example: Está chovendo; vou pegar o guarda-chuva.
native_language_example: It’s raining; I’m going to grab the umbrella.

additional_notes: Used for a specific adult male person. The article o is the masculine singular form of 'the'.
target_language_example: O homem está esperando lá fora.
native_language_example: The man is waiting outside.

meaning: "the man who" (a man + a relative clause).
additional_notes: Used to identify a specific man by adding more information after que (“who/that”). Very common pattern: o homem que + verb (e.g., o homem que me ajudou = “the man who helped me”). In Portuguese, que can mean “who” or “that” depending on context.
target_language_example: A polícia prendeu o homem que roubou o carro.
native_language_example: The police arrested the man who stole the car.

additional_notes: Used in statements describing (1) a specific man, or (2) people/mankind in general. In Portuguese, "o" ("the") can be used generically, so "O homem é..." often means "Man is..." (humans in general), especially in philosophical or general truths.
target_language_example: O homem é capaz de mudar.
native_language_example: Man is capable of change.

additional_notes: A masculine noun, so it uses the definite article "o" (“the”): "o hospital". Used for the place where people go for medical treatment or emergencies; common with verbs like "ir para o hospital" (to go to the hospital) and "ficar perto" (to be near).
target_language_example: Ela foi ao hospital depois do acidente.
native_language_example: She went to the hospital after the accident.

additional_notes: "Hotel" is a masculine noun, so it uses the definite article "o" (the). Used when talking about a specific hotel (one already known from context): "Onde está o hotel?" = "Where is the hotel?" You’ll also see it in descriptions of location ("O hotel é aqui em frente" = "The hotel is right in front of us") and price ("O hotel custa..." = "The hotel costs...").
target_language_example: O hotel fica perto da praia.
native_language_example: The hotel is near the beach.

additional_notes: Usually refers to “hell” in a religious/moral sense, often contrasted with "o céu" (heaven). It can also be used figuratively to mean extreme suffering or a very hard experience ("Você não sabe o inferno que vai enfrentar"). In insults like "Vai/Vá para o inferno!" it means “Go to hell!” and is quite rude/hostile.
target_language_example: Você não sabe o inferno que vai enfrentar.
native_language_example: You don’t know the hell you’re going to face.

meaning: “the enemy” (an opponent, especially in war or conflict).
additional_notes: Uses the masculine singular definite article “o” (“the”). Often refers to an opposing army/country (“o inimigo”) but can also be used more generally for an opponent (e.g., in games: “o inimigo final” = “the final boss”). Plural: “os inimigos” (“the enemies”).
target_language_example: Precisamos entender o inimigo antes de atacar.
native_language_example: We need to understand the enemy before attacking.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male person’s brother. The possessive pronoun "dele" means "of him / his" and usually comes after the noun (common in Brazilian Portuguese). It can be used on its own ("o irmão dele") or after another subject ("Tom e o irmão dele"). For "her brother," say "o irmão dela."
target_language_example: Eu conheci o irmão dele ontem.
native_language_example: I met his brother yesterday.

additional_notes: Refers to dinner/the evening meal. In Portuguese it’s commonly used with the definite article (o) when talking about the meal in general or a specific dinner (e.g., after dinner = "após o jantar").
target_language_example: Vamos sair depois do jantar.
native_language_example: We’re going out after dinner.

additional_notes: Used for a game in general (board games, video games, etc.) and very commonly for a sports match/event. In sports contexts, it often appears with scheduling words like foi (was/on), será (will be), and adiado (postponed), and it can be specified with de + sport: o jogo de beisebol (the baseball game).
target_language_example: O jogo começa às oito, mas pode ser adiado se chover.
native_language_example: The game starts at eight, but it may be postponed if it rains.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a (printed or digital) newspaper: ler o jornal = “to read the newspaper.” In some contexts, especially with TV, it can mean a news broadcast/program: assistir o jornal da noite = “to watch the evening news.” Gender: masculine (o).
target_language_example: Eu compro o jornal todo dia de manhã.
native_language_example: I buy the newspaper every morning.

additional_notes: Uses the definite article "o" (“the”) with "ladrão" (“thief”). Often appears with verbs like "fugir" (to run away/escape), "pegar" (to grab/take), and "prender" (to arrest). Feminine form: "a ladra" (“the female thief”).
target_language_example: O ladrão roubou meu celular no metrô.
native_language_example: The thief stole my phone on the subway.

additional_notes: Refers to a specific book. "o" is the masculine singular definite article, so this phrase is used when the book is known, identified, or specified by context.
target_language_example: Não encontro o livro na mochila.
native_language_example: I can't find the book in the backpack.

meaning: “the book that/which …” (introduces a description of a specific book).
additional_notes: Used to start a relative clause with que (“that/which”) to identify or describe which book you mean: o livro que eu comprei (“the book that I bought”), o livro que está na mesa (“the book that is on the table”). In Portuguese, que is very common here (often where English might use “that,” “which,” or nothing).
target_language_example: Você viu o livro que eu deixei na cadeira?
native_language_example: Did you see the book that I left on the chair?

additional_notes: Used for household waste in general. Common with verbs like colocar/tirar (to put out/take out) and with places like a lixeira (trash can). Can also be used figuratively for something worthless ("to throw/send to the trash").
target_language_example: Você pode tirar o lixo hoje à noite?
native_language_example: Can you take out the trash tonight?

additional_notes: Used with masculine singular nouns to mean the largest in size/amount (o maior peixe, o maior tempo) or the most important/serious (o maior problema). Often corresponds to English “the biggest/longest/most important,” depending on the noun. Feminine form: “a maior.”
target_language_example: Esse foi o maior desafio da minha vida.
native_language_example: That was the biggest challenge of my life.

meaning: as fast/quickly as possible; as soon as possible.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize urgency. It commonly follows a verb (e.g., "corra...", "chegar...", "ir...") and means doing something with maximum speed or without delay. You may also hear the shorter "o mais rápido que puder" (as fast as you can).
target_language_example: Por favor, me responda o mais rápido possível.
native_language_example: Please reply to me as soon as possible.

additional_notes: Used to talk about evil or harm in a general/abstract sense, often contrasted with "o bem" (good). It can refer to evil as a force ("o mal") or to the bad part/cause of something depending on context.
target_language_example: Não responda com o mal; responda com o bem.
native_language_example: Don’t respond with evil; respond with good.

additional_notes: Masculine noun used with the definite article: o mar (“the sea”). Common with verbs like ir para o mar (“go to the sea”) and descriptions of the sea’s condition: o mar está calmo/bravo (“the sea is calm/rough”). Often appears in comparisons and poetic language (azul como o mar, olhos como o mar).
target_language_example: Hoje vamos à praia para ver o mar.
native_language_example: Today we’re going to the beach to see the sea.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a man’s spouse. Often appears with possession: "o marido da Maria" (Maria’s husband), "meu/o seu marido" (my/your husband).
target_language_example: O marido dela trabalha aqui perto.
native_language_example: Her husband works nearby.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific woman’s husband. It’s made of the definite article + noun + possessive: "o" (the) + "marido" (husband) + "dela" (of her). "Dela" agrees with the owner (a woman), not with "marido". Contrast: "o marido dele" = his husband; "o marido dela" can also mean "the husband of her" in the sense of "her husband."
target_language_example: O marido dela trabalha no hospital.
native_language_example: Her husband works at the hospital.

additional_notes: Used to talk about unpleasant weather conditions (rain, storms, cold, etc.) and their effects (delays, canceling plans, feeling unwell). Often appears as the cause of something: "por causa do mau tempo" (because of the bad weather).
target_language_example: Cancelamos a viagem por causa do mau tempo.
native_language_example: We canceled the trip because of the bad weather.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the top or most excellent person, thing, or option. It can come before a masculine singular noun (o melhor aluno = the best student) or stand alone when the noun is understood. Melhor is the irregular comparative/superlative form of bom (“good”). The form changes with gender and number: a melhor, os melhores, as melhores.
target_language_example: Este é o melhor restaurante do bairro.
native_language_example: This is the best restaurant in the neighborhood.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the best option/thing/person in a general sense. Common in set phrases like “fazer o melhor (possível)” = “to do your best (possible)” and “merecer o melhor” = “to deserve the best.” Can also stand alone as an answer meaning “the best, of course.”
target_language_example: Eu quero o melhor para você.
native_language_example: I want the best for you.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like "dar" (to give): "dar o melhor de si" = to do your best / give it your all. "Si" is a reflexive pronoun meaning "oneself," so it can refer to different people depending on context (eu/você/ele/ela/eles).
target_language_example: Mesmo cansada, ela deu o melhor de si na prova.
native_language_example: Even tired, she did her best on the test.

additional_notes: Means “the boy” (definite: a specific boy). In Portuguese, you normally include the article with nouns (“o” = “the” for masculine singular). Often used to refer to a child/young boy; it can also be used more generally like “kid,” depending on context.
target_language_example: O menino está com fome.
native_language_example: The boy is hungry.

additional_notes: Used to say two things/people/situations are identical or equal in some way. It often appears in comparisons with "que" (e.g., "o mesmo ... que eu" = "the same ... as me"). It agrees in gender/number with the noun: "o mesmo" (masc. sing.), "a mesma" (fem. sing.), "os mesmos" (masc. pl.), "as mesmas" (fem. pl.). It can also mean "that same" when identifying someone/something: "É o mesmo X?" = "Is it the same X?".
target_language_example: Você quer o mesmo de sempre?
native_language_example: Do you want the same as always?

additional_notes: Used to say someone repeats an identical mistake, often with verbs like "cometer" (to make/commit) and "repetir" (to repeat). "Mesmo" agrees with the noun: "o mesmo erro" (masc. singular), "a mesma coisa" (fem. singular), "os mesmos erros" (masc. plural), "as mesmas ideias" (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Não quero cometer o mesmo erro de novo.
native_language_example: I don’t want to make the same mistake again.

additional_notes: Here it means that something is identical to what was mentioned before. It is common after verbs like fazer, pensar, and ser: fazer o mesmo = do the same, pensar o mesmo = think the same, não ser o mesmo = not be the same anymore. The form changes with gender and number: a mesma, os mesmos, as mesmas.
target_language_example: Eu faria o mesmo no seu lugar.
native_language_example: I would do the same in your place.

additional_notes: Used to say that one thing has the same meaning/effect/value as another. Common pattern: “X é o mesmo que Y” (X is the same as Y). Often followed by an infinitive verb phrase or a noun phrase.
target_language_example: Esperar demais é o mesmo que perder tempo.
native_language_example: Waiting too long is the same as wasting time.

additional_notes: Used to refer to someone with great skill or authority (e.g., a master of a craft, a mentor, or a respected teacher). It can also be a title before a name (e.g., "o mestre João"). Feminine form: "a mestra".
target_language_example: O mestre explicou a lição com calma.
native_language_example: The teacher/master explained the lesson calmly.

additional_notes: Possessive form used with masculine singular nouns. In the examples, it means "my" before a noun: "o meu cão" = "my dog." On its own, "o meu" can also mean "mine." The article "o" is especially common in European Portuguese; in Brazilian Portuguese, people often just say "meu" before the noun.
target_language_example: O meu carro está na garagem.
native_language_example: My car is in the garage.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male friend; for a female friend, say "a minha amiga". In Portuguese, the possessive usually comes after the article: "o meu" (masc. sing.), "a minha" (fem. sing.), "os meus" (masc. pl.), "as minhas" (fem. pl.). Depending on context, "o meu amigo" can also mean “my boyfriend,” but that’s not always implied.
target_language_example: O meu amigo mora aqui perto.
native_language_example: My friend lives nearby.

additional_notes: Means “my grandfather” (male). Often used as a noun phrase with a possessive: o meu avô (my grandfather). In European Portuguese you may also hear just “o avô” or “o meu avô”; in Brazilian Portuguese “meu avô” is also very common (without “o”).
target_language_example: O meu avô mora perto daqui.
native_language_example: My grandfather lives near here.

additional_notes: Portuguese often uses the definite article with possessives: "o meu cabelo" (literally "the my hair"). In everyday speech, the article is sometimes dropped: "meu cabelo". "Cabelo" is usually singular when talking about hair in general; you may also hear the plural "meus cabelos" in some contexts (e.g., talking about individual hairs or as a stylistic choice).
target_language_example: Preciso lavar o meu cabelo hoje.
native_language_example: I need to wash my hair today.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your own dog: "o" = "the" (masculine), "meu" = "my" (masculine), "cachorro" = "dog/puppy". In Brazil, "cachorro" is the common word for "dog"; in Portugal, people more often say "cão" (and "cachorro" can mean "puppy"). For a female dog, say "a minha cachorra".
target_language_example: Onde está o meu cachorro?
native_language_example: Where is my dog?

meaning: "my car" (the car that belongs to me).
additional_notes: Uses the masculine singular definite article "o" + possessive "meu" + noun "carro". Common in European Portuguese; in Brazilian Portuguese you’ll often hear just "meu carro" without the article. The possessive changes with gender/number (e.g., "a minha casa", "os meus carros").
target_language_example: Não consigo encontrar o meu carro no estacionamento.
native_language_example: I can't find my car in the parking lot.

additional_notes: Literally "the my cell phone." In Portuguese it’s common to use the definite article (o/a) before possessives: "o meu", "a minha". "Celular" is common in Brazil; in Portugal you’ll often hear "telemóvel". You can use it as a subject or object: "O meu celular..." / "Eu perdi o meu celular."
target_language_example: Você viu o meu celular?
native_language_example: Have you seen my cell phone?

meaning: 'my computer' (the computer that belongs to me).
additional_notes: Uses the masculine singular definite article + possessive: "o" + "meu" + noun. Often used when talking about your specific computer (especially in everyday conversation). In Portuguese, possessives are commonly used with the definite article ("o meu", "a minha"), though it may be omitted in some contexts.
target_language_example: Vou usar o meu computador para estudar hoje.
native_language_example: I'm going to use my computer to study today.

additional_notes: Literally “my heart” (o = “the”, meu = “my”, coração = “heart”). Common in emotional/romantic phrases: tocar o meu coração (“touch my heart”), partir o meu coração (“break my heart”), o meu coração pertence a você (“my heart belongs to you”). In everyday Portuguese you can also just say “meu coração” without the article “o.”
target_language_example: Obrigada por me apoiar — você tocou o meu coração.
native_language_example: Thank you for supporting me — you touched my heart.

additional_notes: Used to talk about money that belongs to you, often when asking where it is, demanding it back, or saying where you’ll invest/bet it (e.g., “colocar o meu dinheiro” = “put my money on…”). It can sound forceful in commands like “Devolva o meu dinheiro!”; for politeness you can add “por favor”. In Brazil, it’s very common to drop the article and just say “meu dinheiro”.
target_language_example: Eu quero o meu dinheiro de volta.
native_language_example: I want my money back.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your (male) child. In Portuguese, family members are often said with the definite article: "o meu filho" (my son), "a minha filha" (my daughter). "Meu filho" without "o" is also possible, especially in more direct or affectionate speech.
target_language_example: O meu filho está a estudar para os exames.
native_language_example: My son is studying for the exams.

additional_notes: A possessive noun phrase: o (the) + meu (my) + gato (cat). Often appears as “o meu gato” or more commonly in everyday speech “meu gato” (dropping the article). Changes with the cat’s gender/number: “a minha gata” (my female cat), “os meus gatos” (my cats), “as minhas gatas” (my female cats).
target_language_example: O meu gato dorme no sofá.
native_language_example: My cat sleeps on the couch.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an umbrella that belongs to the speaker. Often appears with verbs like "deixar" (leave), "fechar" (close), "tomar" (take), and "devolver" (return). "Guarda-chuva" literally means something like "rain-guard" (guarda + chuva).
target_language_example: Você viu o meu guarda-chuva?
native_language_example: Have you seen my umbrella?

additional_notes: A common way to say “my brother,” using the masculine singular definite article (o) + possessive (meu) + noun (irmão). In everyday speech, people also often drop the article: “meu irmão.” For a female sibling, use “a minha irmã” (“my sister”).
target_language_example: O meu irmão mora comigo.
native_language_example: My brother lives with me.

meaning: “my book” (the book that belongs to me).
additional_notes: Uses the definite article (o = “the”) plus the possessive (meu = “my”). In Portuguese, possessives are often used with an article: “o meu livro” / “o meu carro”. You may also hear “meu livro” without the article, especially in Brazil. Meus (plural) = “my” for masculine plural: “os meus livros” (“my books”).
target_language_example: Desculpe, você viu o meu livro?
native_language_example: Sorry, have you seen my book?

additional_notes: Used to refer to your own husband. It’s made of the definite article (o = “the”), the possessive (meu = “my”), and the noun (marido = “husband”). In everyday Portuguese you may also hear just “meu marido” without the article, especially in Brazil.
target_language_example: O meu marido trabalha aqui.
native_language_example: My husband works here.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your closest friend who is male. For a female best friend, say “a minha melhor amiga”. In European Portuguese you often include the article (“o/a”) before “meu/minha”, especially in careful speech; in Brazilian Portuguese it’s common to drop it (“meu melhor amigo”).
target_language_example: O meu melhor amigo mora perto de mim.
native_language_example: My best friend lives near me.

additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like dar (to give), fazer (to do), and tentar (to try): dar/fazer/tentar o meu melhor = to do/try my best. It means making your best effort, not necessarily being the best overall.
target_language_example: Prometo que vou dar o meu melhor no trabalho.
native_language_example: I promise I’ll do my best at work.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your own name, often when saying what it is, correcting spelling, or talking about someone remembering/calling it. In Portuguese it’s common to use the definite article with possessives: o meu nome, a minha casa, etc. Often shortened in speech to “meu nome” (without the article).
target_language_example: O meu nome é Ana, prazer em conhecer você.
native_language_example: My name is Ana, nice to meet you.

additional_notes: Used to introduce yourself and say your name. Often followed directly by a name: "O meu nome é Ana." In everyday speech, you’ll also hear the shorter "Meu nome é..." or simply "Eu sou..." (I’m...).
target_language_example: Olá, o meu nome é Daniel.
native_language_example: Hi, my name is Daniel.

additional_notes: Often refers to your phone number in everyday conversation: "Tens o meu número?" / "Quem te passou o meu número?". It can also mean another personal number depending on context (e.g., ID number, room number), but "número de telefone" is the clearest if you want to specify. Note the masculine article: "o".
target_language_example: Podes guardar o meu número no teu telemóvel?
native_language_example: Can you save my number in your phone?

additional_notes: Means “my father/dad.” In Portuguese it’s very common to use the definite article with possessives: “o meu pai” (literally “the my father”), where English usually just says “my father.” You can also hear “meu pai” without the article, especially in some regions and in more direct/addressing contexts.
target_language_example: O meu pai trabalha muito.
native_language_example: My dad works a lot.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your own passport. "o" is "the" (masculine singular) and "meu" means "my". In Brazilian Portuguese, people often also say "meu passaporte" without the article in some contexts.
target_language_example: Preciso do meu passaporte para fazer o check-in.
native_language_example: I need my passport to check in.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the speaker’s own country. It’s made of the masculine singular definite article "o" (the), the possessive "meu" (my), and "país" (country). The possessive changes with the noun: "o meu país" (my country), "a minha cidade" (my city).
target_language_example: Tenho saudades do meu país.
native_language_example: I miss my country.

meaning: “my own” (my personal; belonging to me, not shared).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is yours personally/independently (often something you own, create, or do yourself), like a business, restaurant, place, or way of doing things. It agrees with the noun: o meu próprio restaurante (masc. singular), a minha própria casa (fem. singular), os meus próprios planos (masc. plural), as minhas próprias ideias (fem. plural). Often implies independence: not someone else’s and not shared.
target_language_example: Agora eu tenho o meu próprio restaurante.
native_language_example: Now I have my own restaurant.

additional_notes: Means “my room,” often referring to your bedroom at home. It’s made of the definite article o (“the”) + possessive meu (“my”) + quarto (“room/bedroom”). In everyday Portuguese you can also just say “meu quarto” without the article, especially in some contexts or dialects.
target_language_example: Vou arrumar o meu quarto antes de sair.
native_language_example: I’m going to tidy my room before leaving.

additional_notes: Uses the masculine singular definite article “o” + possessive “meu” + noun. In everyday speech, “relógio” often means a wristwatch; if you mean a wall/desk clock, you can also say “relógio de parede” (wall clock).
target_language_example: Não encontro o meu relógio desde ontem.
native_language_example: I haven’t been able to find my watch since yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a male sibling of one of your parents (or sometimes a close family friend). "o" is the masculine singular definite article (“the”), and "meu" agrees with the noun: "o meu tio" (my uncle). You can also hear it without the article: "meu tio".
target_language_example: O meu tio mora em Lisboa, mas trabalha no Porto.
native_language_example: My uncle lives in Lisbon, but works in Porto.

additional_notes: Means the speaker’s work/job. Often used with verbs like fazer (to do) or terminar (to finish): fazer o meu trabalho = do my job/work; terminar o meu trabalho = finish my work. You may also hear variations like no meu trabalho (“at my job”), do meu trabalho (“from/about my job”), and a minha profissão (“my profession,” more formal).
target_language_example: Desculpa, não posso sair agora — tenho que terminar o meu trabalho.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go out now—I have to finish my work.

additional_notes: Masculine noun: o motor (plural: os motores). Used for engines/motors in cars, motorcycles, boats, and machines. Common with the verb ligar/desligar (to start/turn off) and with adjectives like barulhento (noisy).
target_language_example: O motor do carro não está funcionando.
native_language_example: The car’s engine isn’t working.

meaning: the driver (person who drives a vehicle).
additional_notes: Used for the driver of a bus, taxi, car, etc. Gender varies: o motorista (male) / a motorista (female). Common with "de" to specify the vehicle: "motorista de ônibus" (bus driver), "motorista de táxi" (taxi driver).
target_language_example: O motorista do táxi pode me deixar aqui, por favor?
native_language_example: Can the taxi driver drop me off here, please?

additional_notes: Usually refers to the world in a literal or general sense. Depending on context, it can also mean humanity, society, or the public more broadly. In idiomatic uses like carregar o mundo nas costas, it suggests a very heavy burden.
target_language_example: Ela sonha em conhecer o mundo.
native_language_example: She dreams of seeing the world.

meaning: the whole world; the entire world.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize totality: all parts of the world or everyone/everything in the world. Often follows the noun it modifies (mundo + inteiro).
target_language_example: A notícia correu o mundo inteiro em poucas horas.
native_language_example: The news spread around the whole world in a few hours.

additional_notes: Used to start a statement about how the world is in general. It’s typically followed by an adjective ("cruel", "injusto") or a noun phrase/metaphor ("como um livro"). Don’t confuse with "todo mundo" (= “everyone”).
target_language_example: O mundo é pequeno, e a gente acaba se encontrando de novo.
native_language_example: The world is small, and we end up running into each other again.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs to mean doing something as much as possible: “tirar o máximo (de algo)” (get the most out of something), “economizar o máximo (de dinheiro)” (save as much money as possible), “aprender/desfrutar/esforçar-se o máximo (possível)” (learn/enjoy/try your hardest as much as possible). With “ser/estar/achar (algo/alguém) o máximo”, it’s a casual way to say something/someone is really great. “Se achar o máximo” means to act like you’re the best / be full of yourself.
target_language_example: Aproveite o máximo a viagem!
native_language_example: Enjoy the trip as much as possible!

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific (male) doctor. The feminine form is "a médica". Often followed by "de" to show whose doctor it is: "o médico dele/dela" = "his/her doctor".
target_language_example: O médico vai chegar em dez minutos.
native_language_example: The doctor will arrive in ten minutes.

additional_notes:
Common body-part noun. Often used with verbs like: 
- "sangrar" (O nariz dele está sangrando. = His nose is bleeding.)
- "partir/quebrar" (Parti/Quebrei o nariz. = I broke my nose.)
- "tocar" (tocar o nariz = touch the nose). 
Gender: masculine (o).
target_language_example: Estou com o nariz entupido.
native_language_example: My nose is stuffy.

meaning: “the ship” (a large boat, usually for transporting people or cargo).
additional_notes: A masculine noun: navio. Use "o" for "the" (and "um navio" for "a ship"). Common in travel and sea contexts; can also appear in fixed expressions like "abandonar o navio" (“abandon ship”).
target_language_example: O navio chega amanhã de manhã.
native_language_example: The ship arrives tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or state the name of something/someone that is feminine in Portuguese. It’s the contraction of “de + a” → “da” (“of the”). For a masculine noun, you usually use “o nome do” (de + o → do). Often appears in questions: “Qual é o nome da…?”
target_language_example: Qual é o nome da rua onde você mora?
native_language_example: What’s the name of the street where you live?

meaning: “the name of” (used to specify the name assigned to someone/something, or to refer to the name belonging to someone/something).
additional_notes: Common in: (1) asking/listing names: “Diga o nome de três tipos de pão.” (2) with “dar” to mean “to name/call”: “Deram a ela o nome de Alice.” (3) in set expressions like “associar o nome de X a Y” (“associate the name of X with Y”). Note the contraction with articles is also frequent (e.g., “o nome do…” = “the name of the…”), but the base multi-word term is “o nome de”.
target_language_example: Deram a ela o nome de Alice por causa de sua tia.
native_language_example: They gave her the name Alice because of her aunt.

additional_notes: Used to identify or ask about a female person’s name. It’s made of the definite article + noun + pronoun: o (the) + nome (name) + dela (of her). In questions, you’ll often see: "Qual é o nome dela?"
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu esqueci o nome dela.
native_language_example: Sorry, I forgot her name.

additional_notes: Used to ask or talk about a male person's name. "dele" means "of him / his" and refers back to someone already mentioned or understood from context. For a female person, use "o nome dela" (her name).
target_language_example: Eu não sei o nome dele, mas reconheço o rosto.
native_language_example: I don't know his name, but I recognize his face.

additional_notes: Used to identify a male person’s name. "dele" means "his" (literally “of him”). It can also be used more generally to talk about someone’s name/reputation: "O nome dele é conhecido..." = "His name is known...". For a female person: "O nome dela é" (her name is).
target_language_example: Oi! O nome dele é Carlos.
native_language_example: Hi! His name is Carlos.

additional_notes: Used to introduce who/what something is called. It’s a set phrase made from "o nome" (the name) + "do" (= de + o, “of the”). It agrees with masculine singular nouns; with feminine singular use "o nome da" (de + a), and with plural use "o nome dos / o nome das".
target_language_example: Você sabe o nome do professor?
native_language_example: Do you know the teacher’s name?

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun: o nosso destino = our destiny. Portuguese often uses the definite article before possessives, unlike English. It can also stand alone to mean 'ours' when the noun is omitted.
target_language_example: Este carro é o nosso.
native_language_example: This car is ours.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the speaker’s (and often the listener’s) country, emphasizing shared identity or belonging. Common in patriotic, political, or news contexts. Agreement changes with gender/number (e.g., “a nossa nação” = our nation; “os nossos valores” = our values).
target_language_example: Precisamos cuidar melhor do nosso país.
native_language_example: We need to take better care of our country.

additional_notes: Uses the definite article + possessive: "o" (the) + "nosso" (our) + "professor". In Portuguese you often say "o nosso..." where English usually just says "our...". Refers to a specific teacher known to the speaker and listener. Feminine form: "a nossa professora".
target_language_example: O nosso professor vai chegar atrasado hoje.
native_language_example: Our teacher is going to arrive late today.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to talk about how many there are, often in statistics or formal writing. It can also appear in the structure “O número de X é de Y” = “The number of X is Y.” The verb often agrees with “número” (singular): “O número de estudantes está caindo…”.
target_language_example: O número de pessoas na fila é de vinte.
native_language_example: The number of people in the line is twenty.

meaning: the ocean (a very large body of salt water).
additional_notes: Masculine noun: *o oceano* (plural *os oceanos*). Often followed by a specific name: *o oceano Atlântico*, *o oceano Pacífico*. Common with expressions like *vista para o oceano* (“ocean view”).
target_language_example: Vamos caminhar na praia e ver o oceano ao pôr do sol.
native_language_example: Let’s walk on the beach and see the ocean at sunset.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the remaining person or thing after one has already been mentioned. It can stand alone like a pronoun, as in "one is red and the other is white." This is the masculine singular form; compare "a outra" for feminine.
target_language_example: Eu gostei deste filme, mas o outro era melhor.
native_language_example: I liked this movie, but the other one was better.

additional_notes: `o` is the masculine singular definite article. `o pai` can mean either 'the father' in a general sense or 'dad/her father/his father' depending on context. In Portuguese, especially in Brazil, family members are often used with the definite article: `o pai dela` = 'her father'. For directly calling your father, `pai!` without `o` is more common.
target_language_example: O pai dela mora em Lisboa.
native_language_example: Her father lives in Lisbon.

additional_notes: Uses the definite article (o = “the”) and the possessive pronoun dela (“of her” / “hers”). It refers to the father of a female person already clear from context. Often used instead of “seu pai” to avoid ambiguity (since seu can mean “his/her/your”).
target_language_example: O pai dela trabalha aqui.
native_language_example: Her father works here.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male person’s father. "dele" means "of him / his" and agrees with the person who owns the father (not with "pai"). For a woman, use "o pai dela" (her father). You may also see "o pai do João" (João’s father).
target_language_example: Eu não conheço o pai dele, mas conheço a mãe dele.
native_language_example: I don't know his father, but I know his mother.

additional_notes: "Papai" is an affectionate way to refer to one’s father; with the article "o" it means “the dad/daddy,” often used when talking about him (especially to children).
target_language_example: O papai está chegando!
native_language_example: Dad is arriving!

meaning: 'the paper' (material/sheet) or 'the role/part' (in a play, job, or situation).
additional_notes: Most commonly means paper as a material or a sheet/document: "Corte o papel" (cut the paper), "Você leu o papel?" (did you read the document/paper?). It can also mean a role or part someone plays: "Faz o papel de Hamlet" (plays Hamlet) and "conseguiu o papel" (got the role). Context usually makes it clear.
target_language_example: Ele conseguiu o papel principal no filme.
native_language_example: He got the lead role in the movie.

additional_notes: Used to talk about earlier times or previous events in someone’s life or in history. Often appears with verbs like esquecer (to forget), lembrar (to remember), falar sobre (to talk about), and temer (to fear).
target_language_example: Não quero viver preso ao passado.
native_language_example: I don’t want to live stuck in the past.

additional_notes: Definite article + noun: "o" = "the" (masculine singular) + "peixe" = "fish". Used when talking about a specific fish (or fish as a specific item/meal) that’s known from context.
target_language_example: O peixe está pronto para comer.
native_language_example: The fish is ready to eat.

additional_notes: Uses the masculine singular article “o” with the superlative “pior” to refer to the worst situation, outcome, or part of something. Common in fixed expressions like “o pior está por vir” (the worst is yet to come) and “o pior já passou” (the worst is over), and in contrasts like “o melhor / o pior”.
target_language_example: Achei que ia ser difícil, mas o pior já passou.
native_language_example: I thought it was going to be hard, but the worst is over.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an idea/strategy for what you’re going to do: "Qual é o plano?" = "What’s the plan?". "Plano" can also mean a "plan" in the sense of a subscription/tariff (e.g., phone or health plan: "o plano de saúde"), and in film it can mean a "shot" ("um plano"). Gender: masculine (o).
target_language_example: Qual é o plano para amanhã?
native_language_example: What’s the plan for tomorrow?

additional_notes: Refers to power in different senses depending on context: (1) physical or mental strength/capability ("o poder da minha mente"), (2) an enemy’s might (often military or magical in stories), (3) economic or political power, and (4) the general idea of having control or influence ("buscam o poder"). It’s the masculine singular noun; the plural is "os poderes".
target_language_example: São pessoas que buscam o poder.
native_language_example: They are people who seek power.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a capability or effect that someone or something has. It’s often followed by an infinitive (o poder de + verb): "o poder de mudar" = "the power to change". It can also be followed by a noun: "o poder de uma bomba" = "the power of a bomb".
target_language_example: A leitura tem o poder de mudar a nossa forma de pensar.
native_language_example: Reading has the power to change the way we think.

additional_notes: Masculine singular form used with the definite article o (“the”). Refers to one specific police officer (known from context) or can be used generically (“the officer”). Feminine: a policial. Plural: os policiais / as policiais.
target_language_example: O policial pediu meus documentos.
native_language_example: The police officer asked for my ID.

additional_notes: Used as a noun meaning “the reason” or “the explanation,” often after verbs like saber/entender/explicar/descobrir. It’s commonly followed by "de" ("o porquê de..." = “the reason for.../why...”), or it can stand alone: "Você quer saber o porquê?". Note the accent: "porquê" (with ê) when it’s a noun with an article (o/um) or when it stands alone as “the why.”
target_language_example: Ninguém sabe o porquê de tanta pressa.
native_language_example: Nobody knows the reason for such a rush.

meaning: the gate (a large door/entrance, often for a yard or building).
additional_notes: Refers to a gate you pass through (e.g., at a house, garden, school, or entrance). In commands like "Para o portão!", it can mean "Go/Head to the gate!" or "Stop at the gate!" depending on context. Feminine: "a porta" = (regular) door; "o portão" is typically bigger.
target_language_example: Encontra-me no portão principal às oito.
native_language_example: Meet me at the main gate at eight.

meaning: the people; the population (as a group).
additional_notes: Refers to people as a collective (a community, the general public, or a nation’s citizens). Often used in political or historical contexts (e.g., voting, fighting, protesting). Singular in form but can mean many people; plural is “os povos” (peoples/nations).
target_language_example: O povo quer mudanças.
native_language_example: The people want change.

meaning: “the president” (a leader of a country, organization, or committee).
additional_notes: Used with the masculine singular definite article o (“the”). It can refer to the head of a country (“o presidente do Brasil”) or the chair/leader of a group (“o presidente do comitê”). Feminine form: a presidenta / a presidente (varies by preference and context).
target_language_example: O presidente do comitê vai falar primeiro.
native_language_example: The committee president will speak first.

additional_notes: Means the cost of something. Often used with “de” to say what something’s price is: “o preço da entrada” (the ticket price/admission price). You can ask with: “Qual é o preço (de...)?” (What’s the price of...?).
target_language_example: O preço do café aumentou este mês.
native_language_example: The price of coffee went up this month.

additional_notes: Masculine singular form. It can be used before a noun, as in o primeiro prêmio ('the first prize'), or on its own to mean 'the first one'. The feminine form is a primeira.
target_language_example: O primeiro da lista já chegou.
native_language_example: The first one on the list has already arrived.

meaning: the first step; making the first move (to start something).
additional_notes: Used both literally (the first step in a process) and figuratively (taking the initiative to begin, e.g., in a relationship, a conversation, or solving a problem). Often appears in phrases like "dar o primeiro passo" (to take/make the first step/move).
target_language_example: Se você quiser resolver isso, precisa dar o primeiro passo hoje.
native_language_example: If you want to solve this, you need to take the first step today.

additional_notes: Refers to a specific problem or issue. Note that problema ends in -a but is masculine, so it takes o, not a.
target_language_example: O problema é que estou sem tempo.
native_language_example: The problem is that I don't have time.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the main difficulty or bad news before explaining it. Very common in spoken and written Portuguese. Often followed by a full clause: “O problema é que + [subject] + [verb] …”. You can also omit “que” in some cases, but “o problema é que” is the most natural for beginners.
target_language_example: Eu queria ir, mas o problema é que estou sem tempo hoje.
native_language_example: I wanted to go, but the problem is that I don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Means a male teacher/professor. In everyday school contexts, Portuguese often uses "professor" for "teacher" (not only university professors). The article changes with gender/number: "o professor" (male), "a professora" (female), "os professores" (male/mixed plural), "as professoras" (female plural).
target_language_example: O professor vai explicar a lição de novo.
native_language_example: The teacher is going to explain the lesson again.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the next person or thing in order/sequence. Common in questions like "Quem é o próximo?" (= "Who’s next?"). It agrees with gender/number: o próximo (masc. sing.), a próxima (fem. sing.), os próximos / as próximas (plural).
target_language_example: Você é o próximo da fila.
native_language_example: You’re next in line.

meaning: as soon as possible; as quickly as you can.
additional_notes: Used to say you want something done with maximum urgency (earlier rather than later). Common after verbs like "vir" (come), "ir" (go), "sair" (leave), and "voltar" (return): "Venha o quanto antes" = "Come as soon as possible."
target_language_example: Por favor, me ligue o quanto antes.
native_language_example: Please call me as soon as possible.

additional_notes: Used to ask about or state the degree/amount of something: (1) in questions after another element like "E..." ("And how much/how ...?"); (2) with verbs like "pegar" to mean "as much as" ("Peguem o quanto quiserem" = "Take as much as you want"); (3) in reported speech to express degree, often with adjectives ("disse ... o quanto ela é gorda" = "said how fat she is").
target_language_example: Você sabe o quanto eu gosto de você?
native_language_example: Do you know how much I like you?

meaning: “as much as you want” / “as long as you want.”
additional_notes: Used to emphasize freedom or permission to do something without a limit. It typically follows a verb (often in the imperative or after “poder”): “Estude o quanto quiser” = “Study as much as you want.” Here, “o quanto” means “how much/how long,” and “quiser” is the subjunctive of “querer” used after expressions of permission/indefinite amount. Often interchangeable with “quanto quiser” in casual speech.
target_language_example: Pode ficar aqui o quanto quiser.
native_language_example: You can stay here as long as you want.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a bedroom, especially in a house or hotel context (e.g., “o quarto de hóspedes” = “the guest room”). It can also mean “room” in general, but for non-bedroom rooms Portuguese often uses more specific words like “a sala” (living room) or “a cozinha” (kitchen).
target_language_example: Vou arrumar o quarto antes de sair.
native_language_example: I’m going to tidy the room before leaving.

additional_notes: very common in direct and indirect questions, and also to refer to a thing or action: O que você quer? = 'What do you want?' / Eu sei o que aconteceu. = 'I know what happened.' Here, o is not the usual masculine article 'the'; together o que functions as a set expression.
target_language_example: Não entendi o que você disse.
native_language_example: I didn't understand what you said.

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion. Often appears by itself ("O que acha?") or followed by "de" + noun/idea ("O que acha de…?"). With a specific thing, you can also say "O que acha deste/dessa/daquele…?" (= “What do you think of this/that…?”). In other contexts, "o que acha" can mean “what (someone) thinks,” as in "o que acha certo" (“what you think is right”).
target_language_example: O que acha de irmos mais cedo?
native_language_example: What do you think about us going earlier?

additional_notes: Used with the verb achar (“to think/to find”) to ask for someone’s opinion or guess about something: o que acha que vai acontecer? (“what do you think will happen?”). In questions like O que acha que está fazendo? it often sounds like a reprimand/challenge (“What do you think you’re doing?”). You’ll also see variations for politeness or formality: O que você acha que…? / O que o senhor(a) acha que…?
target_language_example: O que acha que vai acontecer se a gente atrasar?
native_language_example: What do you think will happen if we’re late?

meaning: “What did you think (of it)?” / “How did you like it?”
additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion after an experience. It’s the past tense of achar (“to think/find”), usually referring to something you just tried/visited/met. Commonly followed by de + noun/pronoun: o que achou da comida? (of the food), do Texas? (of Texas), dele? (of him). In the present you’ll often hear: o que acha…? (“What do you think…?”).
target_language_example: E aí, o que achou do filme?
native_language_example: So, what did you think of the movie?

additional_notes: Used to talk about events or outcomes. Often appears in the pattern "É o que acontece..." = "That’s what happens..." (a general result), or as a question "O que acontece?" = "What’s happening?".
target_language_example: É o que acontece quando você não estuda.
native_language_example: That’s what happens when you don’t study.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an event or situation, often after verbs like ver, saber, contar, and entender. Here, o que means "what" or "that which," so the whole phrase works like a clause: "what happened."
target_language_example: Ninguém sabe o que aconteceu ontem.
native_language_example: No one knows what happened yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to ask about someone/something’s situation or fate (often when you haven’t seen them/it in a while or something seems wrong). It’s followed by a masculine noun or name with the article “o” (e.g., o Marcus). For feminine nouns/names, use “o que aconteceu com a…?” (e.g., a Maria). In speech and informal writing, you’ll also see “O que aconteceu com…” without the article when it’s clear from context.
target_language_example: O que aconteceu com o seu celular?
native_language_example: What happened to your phone?

meaning: “what should we do” / “what are we supposed to do”.
additional_notes:
Used to ask for advice or the next step to take. It can be followed by:
- “a respeito disso” = about that/that situation
- “com …” = with … / about … (what to do with something/someone)
- “se …” = if … (what to do in a condition)
Verb: “devemos” is the “we” form of “dever” (should/ought to).
target_language_example: Não sei o que devemos fazer agora.
native_language_example: I don’t know what we should do now.

additional_notes: Used to ask for advice or instructions about the right next action. "devo" is from "dever" (should/ought to) + "fazer" (to do). You can add context after it, e.g., "O que devo fazer em seguida?" (next), "...com isso?" (with this), "...se eu encontrar um?" (if I find one).
target_language_example: Estou perdido. O que devo fazer agora?
native_language_example: I’m lost. What should I do now?

meaning: "what the hell" / "what on earth" (strong surprise, anger, or confusion).
additional_notes: Used in questions to intensify "o que" (“what”). It can sound rude or aggressive depending on tone and context, so it’s common in informal speech and arguments. Similar intensity: "que diabos". Milder options: "o que aconteceu?", "o que foi?", "o que está acontecendo?".
target_language_example: O que diabos você está fazendo aqui?
native_language_example: What the hell are you doing here?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the content of something someone said or something written (like a sign): "O que diz aquela placa?" = "What does that sign say?" It also appears in common expressions like "não sabe o que diz" (he doesn’t know what he’s saying) and in warnings: "Tome cuidado com o que diz!" (watch what you say). The subject is often understood from context; you can also specify it: "O que diz sobre ele?" = "What does it say about him?"
target_language_example: Desculpe, eu não entendi: o que diz a mensagem?
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t understand: what does the message say?

additional_notes: Used to refer to what others say, often as hearsay, public opinion, or a common saying. Usually implies an unspecified group (“they/people”), and can sound skeptical or neutral depending on tone. Common in expressions like “É o que dizem” (“That’s what they say”).
target_language_example: Não acredito em tudo o que dizem na internet.
native_language_example: I don’t believe everything people say on the internet.

additional_notes: Combination of "o que" (what) + "ela" (she). Used in questions ("O que ela faz aqui?" = "What is she doing here?") and in statements/indirect speech to introduce information about something she wants, knows, said, did, etc. Often followed by a verb: "o que ela quer", "o que ela disse", "o que ela fez".
target_language_example: Não entendi o que ela disse.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what she said.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the content of something a woman/girl said. Very common after verbs like entender (to understand), ouvir (to hear), saber (to know), and ficar claro (to be clear): e.g., "Você entendeu o que ela disse?". It’s literally "the what she said" (o que = what/that which; ela disse = she said).
target_language_example: Eu não ouvi o que ela disse.
native_language_example: I didn’t hear what she said.

additional_notes: A common clause fragment meaning "what he...", usually followed by a verb: for example, "o que ele disse" = "what he said" and "o que ele acha" = "what he thinks." It is not an idiom; it is simply "o que" + "ele."
target_language_example: Eu não sei o que ele quer.
native_language_example: I don't know what he wants.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the content of something a man (ele = he) said. Often appears after verbs like entender (to understand), ouvir (to hear), repetir (to repeat), and achar (to think). You can swap ele for other subjects: o que ela disse (what she said), o que você disse (what you said).
target_language_example: Eu não acredito no que ele disse.
native_language_example: I can't believe what he said.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the content of what a man says. Often appears in sentences like “Faça o que ele diz” (“Do what he says”) or as a standalone question: “O que ele diz?” (“What is he saying?”).
target_language_example: Eu não entendi o que ele diz.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what he says / what he’s saying.

meaning: "what is he doing" / "what he is doing."
additional_notes: Used to ask about a man’s current action (a direct question), or inside another sentence to refer to his actions (an embedded question/statement). The present continuous in Portuguese is commonly formed with "estar" + gerund ("está fazendo" = "is doing"). Context words often appear with it, like "agora" (now) or "lá" (there). It can also refer more generally to what he is doing in life/work/politics depending on context.
target_language_example: Você sabe o que ele está fazendo neste momento?
native_language_example: Do you know what he’s doing right now?

meaning: "what he does" (what his job is / what he’s doing).
