additional_notes: Used to ask about a man’s occupation or actions, depending on context. Often appears inside a longer sentence ("Eu não sei ... o que ele faz") or as a standalone question ("O que ele faz?"). In questions, the subject can come after the verb too: "O que é que ele faz?" / "O que faz ele?".
target_language_example: Você sabe o que ele faz da vida?
native_language_example: Do you know what he does for a living?

additional_notes: Used to refer to an action done by a specific man (“he”). Often introduces a clause as the subject of the sentence (“O que ele fez foi…” = “What he did was…”). In questions, it asks about his action (“O que ele fez?” = “What did he do?”).
target_language_example: Eu não consigo esquecer o que ele fez.
native_language_example: I can’t forget what he did.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the thing a man/boy wants. It can be a statement (Ele está fazendo o que ele quer. = “He’s doing what he wants.”) or a direct question (O que ele quer? = “What does he want?”). In conversation, people often drop the subject for a more natural sound: “o que quer?” / “o que você quer?”.
target_language_example: Eu não sei o que ele quer de verdade.
native_language_example: I don’t know what he really wants.

additional_notes: Used to refer to something done, said, known, or thought by a group of people (eles = “they”). Common in questions (e.g., “O que eles sabem?” = “What do they know?”) and in sentences where it means “what(ever) they…” (e.g., “comer o que eles me dão” = “eat what they give me”).
target_language_example: Eu vou perguntar o que eles decidiram.
native_language_example: I’m going to ask what they decided.

meaning: "what it/that used to be"; or "what it was" (in indirect questions).
additional_notes: Common in two patterns: (1) "não é mais o que era" = “it’s not what it used to be anymore” (often about quality, power, status, etc.). (2) In indirect questions after verbs like perguntar/perguntar-se/saber/dizer: "perguntei-lhe o que era" = “I asked him what it was.” It can also refer back to a whole idea: "..., o que era uma mentira" = “..., which was a lie.”
target_language_example: Este restaurante não é mais o que era.
native_language_example: This restaurant isn’t what it used to be anymore.

additional_notes: Used to ask what you and other people ("we") are doing, often to question the plan, what you’re doing in a place ("aqui" = here), what you’re doing wrong ("de errado" = wrong), or why you’re standing still ("parados" = stopped/standing around). Can also be used inside a longer sentence to refer to the action you’re doing now (e.g., "...o que estamos fazendo agora" = what we’re doing now).
target_language_example: O que estamos fazendo aqui tão cedo?
native_language_example: What are we doing here so early?

meaning: what was happening / what was going on.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a situation or event that was in progress in the past. Very common after verbs like ver (to see), perceber (to notice/realize), contar (to tell), and perguntar (to ask): "Ele viu/percebeu o que estava acontecendo". In questions, you’ll often hear the shorter form "O que está acontecendo?" (What’s happening?) for the present.
target_language_example: Eu não entendi o que estava acontecendo na reunião.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what was happening in the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to an activity already in progress in the past. Often appears after verbs like parar (to stop), terminar (to finish), continuar (to continue), or saber (to know), and can refer to the subject (ele/ela) or another person from context.
target_language_example: Ela continuou o que estava fazendo quando eu cheguei.
native_language_example: She continued what she was doing when I arrived.

additional_notes: Literally “what I am doing.” Used either as a direct question (often expressing confusion, doubt, or frustration) or inside a longer sentence after verbs like “não sei” (I don’t know) or “me pergunto” (I wonder). You can add “aqui” (here) or “de errado” (wrong) to specify: “O que estou fazendo aqui?” (What am I doing here?) / “O que estou fazendo de errado?” (What am I doing wrong?).
target_language_example: Às vezes eu paro e penso: o que estou fazendo com a minha vida?
native_language_example: Sometimes I stop and think: what am I doing with my life?

additional_notes: Used to ask what is happening right now (often because something seems strange or unexpected). Very common in conversation. You can add a place/person for emphasis: “O que está acontecendo aqui?” (“What’s going on here?”). Also used inside a longer sentence: “Você sabe o que está acontecendo?” (“Do you know what’s happening?”).
target_language_example: Ei, o que está acontecendo aqui?
native_language_example: Hey, what’s going on here?

additional_notes: Used to ask what someone is doing right now. It can sound neutral or, depending on tone/context, like you’re questioning or scolding someone (“What are you doing?!”). Often expanded with extra words: “o que está fazendo agora?” (…now?), “o que está fazendo aí?” (…there/over there?). In casual speech, people also say “o que você está fazendo?” or shorten it to “o que tá fazendo?”.
target_language_example: Ei, o que está fazendo aqui tão tarde?
native_language_example: Hey, what are you doing here so late?

additional_notes: Used to ask why someone is in a place, often expressing surprise, suspicion, or curiosity. You can add a name before or after it (“Paulo, o que está fazendo aqui?” / “O que está fazendo aqui, Paulo?”). Very common in conversation; “tá fazendo aqui” is a more informal contraction of “está fazendo aqui.”
target_language_example: Paulo, o que está fazendo aqui?
native_language_example: Paulo, what are you doing here?

additional_notes: Used to ask what is happening now, often because something seems wrong, surprising, or confusing. Common with a place ("aqui", "lá") or with "com" + person/group: "O que está havendo com você?" = "What’s going on with you?" Similar to "O que está acontecendo?"
target_language_example: Ei, o que está havendo aqui?
native_language_example: Hey, what’s going on here?

meaning: “what are you (plural) doing?” / “what they are doing.”
additional_notes: Built from: o que (“what”) + estão (present of estar for “you all/they”) + fazendo (gerund of fazer, “doing”). It can be a direct question (often with a question mark): “O que estão fazendo aqui?” = “What are you (all) doing here?” It can also be used inside a longer sentence as an embedded question/statement: “Eu sei o que estão fazendo.” = “I know what they’re doing.” The subject is usually “you all” (vocês) or “they” (eles/elas), depending on context.
target_language_example: Não entendo o que estão fazendo com esse computador.
native_language_example: I don’t understand what they’re doing with that computer.

meaning: "What should I do?" / "What am I supposed to do?"
additional_notes: Used to ask for advice or instructions. You can add details with "com" (what to do with something), "por" (what to do for someone), or "se" (what to do if something happens). In conversation, people often shorten it to "O que devo fazer?"
target_language_example: Não sei o que eu devo fazer agora.
native_language_example: I don’t know what I should do now.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the content of what the speaker says. Very common after verbs like escutar/ouvir (“listen”), entender (“understand”), acreditar (“believe”), and fazer (“do”): e.g., “Escute o que eu digo” = “Listen to what I’m saying.” In commands it can sound firm (like “Do what I say”). Often appears with tudo (“everything”): tudo o que eu digo = “everything I say.”
target_language_example: Por favor, preste atenção no que eu digo.
native_language_example: Please pay attention to what I’m saying.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to your own words (something you said earlier). Often appears after verbs like entender (to understand), esquecer (to forget), lembrar (to remember), repetir (to repeat). Can also be used as a question: "O que eu disse?" = "What did I say?"
target_language_example: Repete o que eu disse, por favor.
native_language_example: Repeat what I said, please.

meaning: "What do I do?" / "What should I do?"
additional_notes: Often used as a question asking for advice or what action to take next ("So what do I do?", "What do I do until then?"). It can also be used more literally to ask what to do with something/someone: "O que eu faço com você?" = "What am I going to do with you?". In statements, it can mean "what I do" as the subject: "O que eu faço é problema meu." = "What I do is my problem."
target_language_example: Eu estou perdido—o que eu faço agora?
native_language_example: I’m lost—what do I do now?

additional_notes: Used to talk about an action you performed, often introducing an explanation or asking someone to notice it. It can be a direct question/statement ("Você viu o que eu fiz?"), or part of a longer sentence ("O que eu fiz foi errado" / "Espero que o que eu fiz tenha ajudado").
target_language_example: Vou te contar o que eu fiz depois da aula.
native_language_example: I’ll tell you what I did after class.

meaning: “What can I do?” / “What can I do to…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask what actions are possible or advisable, often offering help or asking for guidance (e.g., “...para ajudar” = “to help”, “...para me proteger” = “to protect myself”, “...por vocês” = “for you”). It can be a full question by itself (“O que eu posso fazer?”) or followed by a purpose with para + infinitive.
target_language_example: Não sei como resolver isso — o que eu posso fazer?
native_language_example: I don’t know how to solve this—what can I do?

additional_notes: Often used after "o que" (= “what/that which”) to refer to something specific you wanted or intended. It’s very common in an emphatic structure: "O que eu queria era..." (“What I wanted was...”), and it can also be followed by another verb to clarify the intention: "o que eu queria dizer" (“what I meant to say”), "o que eu queria beber" (“what I wanted to drink”).
target_language_example: O que eu queria era só descansar um pouco.
native_language_example: What I wanted was just to rest a little.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize your real desire/intention, often introducing a noun or an infinitive phrase (e.g., "amor", "sair daqui"). Very common in spoken Portuguese to clarify or contrast with other possibilities (similar to “What I really want is…”).
target_language_example: O que eu quero é descansar um pouco.
native_language_example: What I want is to rest a little.

meaning: 'what will we do?' / 'what are we going to do?'.
additional_notes: Used to ask about the next step or plan for 'us' (we), often when there’s uncertainty or a problem. Common add-ons: "O que faremos agora?" (What will we do now?) and "O que faremos sobre isso?" (What will we do about that?). From "o que" (what) + "faremos" (we will do, future of fazer).
target_language_example: O que faremos depois do almoço?
native_language_example: What will we do after lunch?

additional_notes:
Literally "what (you/he/she/it) does" (o que + fazer). Very common as a question:
- To ask what someone is doing, often when you see them somewhere unexpected: "O que faz aí/aqui?" = "What are you doing there/here?"
- In more general/abstract questions, it means "What makes...": "O que faz de nós humanos?" = "What makes us human?"
By itself ("O que faz?"), it usually means "What are you doing?" and can sound a bit abrupt depending on tone; you can soften with "Desculpe" or "O que você está fazendo?" (Brazil) / "O que estás a fazer?" (Portugal).
target_language_example: Ei, o que faz aqui tão cedo?
native_language_example: Hey, what are you doing here so early?

additional_notes: Uses the verb **fazer** (“to do”) with the subject **(você)** implied: **O que (você) faz aqui?** It commonly expresses surprise, suspicion, or disapproval about someone being in a place. In Brazilian Portuguese, **O que você está fazendo aqui?** is also very common and often sounds more natural/neutral in everyday speech.
target_language_example: O que faz aqui a esta hora?
native_language_example: What are you doing here at this hour?

additional_notes: Used either (1) in statements to mean “what we do” (e.g., with a verb like "é": "A vida é o que fazemos dela." = “Life is what we make of it.”), or (2) as a question meaning “What do we do (now/next)?” Often followed by a time word like "agora" or by "com" to ask what to do with something: "O que fazemos com ...?"
target_language_example: Então, o que fazemos agora?
native_language_example: So, what do we do now?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the right action, a decision, or instructions. Common after verbs like saber, decidir, discutir, and dizer, as in não sei o que fazer ('I don't know what to do') or ninguém me diz o que fazer ('nobody tells me what to do').
target_language_example: Ainda não sei o que fazer amanhã.
native_language_example: I still don't know what to do tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used in two very common ways: (1) as “what (someone) did” in statements like "Vi o que fez" (“I saw what you did”); (2) in questions with fazer meaning “to make/cause,” often followed by a person + infinitive: "O que fez o Tom parar?" (“What made Tom stop?”). It can also appear with "fazer com" meaning “do with”: "O que fez com ele?" (“What did you do with him?”).
target_language_example: Não entendi o que fez você mudar de ideia.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what made you change your mind.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your own past action(s). Often appears after verbs like dizer/contar/saber (e.g., "Eu sei o que fiz") or with prepositions like "com" ("não estou satisfeito com o que fiz"). "Fiz" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "fazer" meaning "I did / I made."
target_language_example: Não acredito no que fiz ontem.
native_language_example: I can't believe what I did yesterday.

additional_notes: Used mostly in questions to add emphasis or insistence, similar to “what on earth…?” but not necessarily rude. It combines: o que (“what”) + foi (past of ser, “was”) + que (linking “that”). It can also appear in a relative structure like “seja o que foi que…” = “whatever it was that…”. In everyday speech, people often shorten it to “o que que…?” or just “o que…?”.
target_language_example: O que foi que você disse agora?
native_language_example: What was it that you just said?

additional_notes: A very common conversational question. Although it literally looks like "what was it?", it is often used to ask why someone called you, what the matter is, or what happened. Depending on tone and context, it can also feel like "what's wrong?".
target_language_example: Você me chamou? O que foi?
native_language_example: Did you call me? What is it?

additional_notes: Used to ask about an event or problem, often with "com" + a person/thing: "O que houve com a Dani?" = "What happened to Dani?" You can also use it with a time word like "ontem" (yesterday) or as a statement: "Já sabemos o que houve" = "We already know what happened."
target_language_example: Ei, o que houve com você?
native_language_example: Hey, what happened to you?

additional_notes: Used to ask about an event or change affecting a person/thing (often when something seems wrong, surprising, or you’re looking for an update). It’s the past of haver (“houve” = “there was/there happened”), so it typically refers to something that already happened.
target_language_example: O que houve com o seu celular? Ele não está ligando.
native_language_example: What happened to your phone? It won’t turn on.

o que há de errado com

target_language_multi_word_term: o que há de errado com
meaning: "what's wrong with" (asking what the problem is).
additional_notes: Used to ask what is wrong with someone or something. It’s followed by a noun or pronoun: "O que há de errado com ele?" / "...com esta foto?". You can also use "O que há de errado?" on its own (“What’s wrong?”).
target_language_example: O que há de errado com este computador?
native_language_example: What's wrong with this computer?

additional_notes: Used to highlight what is truly important in a situation. Often appears in structures like “(É) o que importa” (“That’s what matters”) and “Tudo o que importa é…” (“All that matters is…”).
target_language_example: No fim das contas, é o que importa.
native_language_example: At the end of the day, that’s what matters.

additional_notes: Used to ask for the meaning or interpretation of something (“isso” = “that/this” in context). Often appears as a direct question: “O que isso significa?” or inside a longer sentence: “Você pode me dizer o que isso significa?” It can also mean “what does this mean for…?” as in “O que isso significa para o Tom?”
target_language_example: Desculpe, não entendi—o que isso significa?
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t understand—what does that mean?

o que isso tem a ver com

target_language_multi_word_term: o que isso tem a ver com
meaning: “What does that have to do with…?” / “What’s that got to do with…?”
additional_notes: Used to question the relevance or connection between something that was mentioned and another topic/person. Very common in conversation. You can swap **isso** (“that/this”) for **isto** (more formal) and change the following noun/pronoun as needed: **O que isso tem a ver com você?**
target_language_example: O que isso tem a ver com a nossa conversa?
native_language_example: What does that have to do with our conversation?

additional_notes: Used when **lhe** refers to the person affected/concerned (an indirect object), common in questions and statements: *O que lhe aconteceu?* (“What happened to you/him/her?”). **Lhe** can mean **to him / to her / to you (formal)** depending on context. You’ll often see it before the verb: *O que lhe falta é...* (“What you lack is...”), or in rhetorical questions: *O que lhe interessa...?* (“What business is it of yours...?/Why do you care...?”).
target_language_example: O que lhe disseram sobre a reunião?
native_language_example: What did they tell you/him/her about the meeting?

additional_notes: Used to ask for additional information or an additional action beyond what’s already been mentioned. Common in questions ("O que mais você pode...?") and also in statements like "o que mais você precisa fazer" (= "what else you need to do").
target_language_example: O que mais você quer saber?
native_language_example: What else do you want to know?

meaning: “What else did you…?” / “What more did you…?” (asking for additional things or information).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question to ask for extra items, actions, details, or information beyond what was already mentioned. The verb comes after it: “O que mais você fez/viu/quer/precisa…?”. Often translates naturally as “What else…?” rather than literally “What more you…”.
target_language_example: O que mais você quer saber?
native_language_example: What else do you want to know?

additional_notes:
A common question used to ask about plans, next steps, or how to deal with a problem. Often followed by:
- "com" + noun/pronoun: "O que nós vamos fazer com isso?" (What are we going to do with this?)
- "hoje/amanhã" etc.: "O que nós vamos fazer hoje?" (What are we going to do today?)
- "sobre" + person/thing: "O que nós vamos fazer sobre o Tom?" (What are we going to do about Tom?)
"nós" can be replaced by "a gente" in informal speech: "O que a gente vai fazer?"
target_language_example: O que nós vamos fazer depois do almoço?
native_language_example: What are we going to do after lunch?

additional_notes: Usually not a fixed expression by itself: it is o que ('what/that which') followed by o, the masculine singular article before the next noun or some male names. In English, o may translate as 'the' (o que o padre disse = 'what the priest said') or be omitted before names (o que o Tom fez = 'what Tom did'). At the start of a sentence, it can also introduce a question, like O que o Tom fez? = 'What did Tom do?'
target_language_example: Não entendi o que o professor disse.
native_language_example: I didn't understand what the teacher said.

meaning: "what the doctor …" (used to start a question).
additional_notes: Used before a verb to ask about the doctor’s opinion or actions. It’s typically followed by a verb like "acha" (thinks), "está fazendo" (is doing), or "falou" (said): "O que o médico acha…?" = "What does the doctor think…?". Often, "o que" can be shortened to "que" in casual speech ("Que o médico falou?") but "O que" is the safest standard form.
target_language_example: O que o médico disse sobre o exame?
native_language_example: What did the doctor say about the test?

additional_notes: Used to ask a question directly to a man you’re addressing politely (e.g., an older man, a customer, or someone you don’t know well). In Brazilian Portuguese, "o senhor" is a very formal way to say "you" (instead of "você"). Common in questions like "O que o senhor quer?" (“What would you like?”).
target_language_example: O que o senhor deseja?
native_language_example: What would you like?

meaning: "what ... you" / "what ... him" (formal, with "o" as a direct object pronoun).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question: "O que" = "what". The "o" is a direct object pronoun meaning "you" (when addressing someone as "o senhor") or "him" (referring to a man). It commonly appears with verbs like afligir (bother), preocupar (worry), impedir (prevent), trazer (bring): e.g., "O que o preocupa?" = "What worries you?" / "What worries him?". In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people often avoid this form and say "O que te..." or "O que está te..." instead.
target_language_example: O que o incomoda tanto?
native_language_example: What bothers you so much?

additional_notes: Used to ask about possible actions or solutions. Often followed by “para + infinitive” (purpose): “O que podemos fazer para ajudar?” (= What can we do to help?). It can also be used with “por você” meaning “for you” (what we can do to help you).
target_language_example: O que podemos fazer agora para resolver isso?
native_language_example: What can we do now to solve this?

meaning: 'what can I do' / 'what can I do (to help)?'
additional_notes: Used to ask what actions are possible or appropriate in a situation, often when offering help or looking for a solution. Very common pattern: “O que posso fazer para + verb” (e.g., para ajudar, para te convencer). Pronouns can change: “para lhe ajudar” (more formal), “para te ajudar” (informal). You may also see different prepositions depending on meaning: “pela vida dele” (“for his life / on his behalf”) or “sem os meus amigos” (“without my friends”).
target_language_example: O que posso fazer para melhorar o meu português?
native_language_example: What can I do to improve my Portuguese?

meaning: 'what do you want…?' / 'what would you like…?'.
additional_notes: Uses "quer" (from *querer*, 'to want') with an implied subject, usually **você**: "O que quer comer?" = "O que (você) quer comer?" Common in questions before an infinitive (comer, fazer, beber). You may also hear "O que você quer…?" (more explicit).
target_language_example: O que quer fazer hoje?
native_language_example: What do you want to do today?

additional_notes: Used to ask for clarification about the meaning or intention of something. Often appears as a question ("O que quer dizer?"), and you can add "com ..." to specify what exactly you’re asking about: "O que quer dizer com 'muito tempo'?". In statements, it can also mean 'to mean' in the sense of intention: "Entendo o que quer dizer" = 'I understand what you mean.'
target_language_example: Desculpa, o que quer dizer com isso?
native_language_example: Sorry, what do you mean by that?

additional_notes: A common way to ask someone what they’d like to do (now, later, tomorrow, etc.). Often used on its own as a question, or followed by a time phrase (agora, amanhã, depois do almoço). You may also hear the more direct/colloquial version “O que você quer fazer?”; in Portugal it’s very common to drop “você” like this.
target_language_example: O que quer fazer no fim de semana?
native_language_example: What do you want to do this weekend?

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unknown or unimportant thing/action: “whatever it is/was,” “whatever you say/do,” “anything that…”. It’s often followed by the subjunctive: o que quer que seja (whatever it is), o que quer que diga/faça (whatever you say/do). You can also see the shortened form "o que quer que" without an explicit verb when the verb is understood from context (e.g., O que quer que te diga? = Whatever can I tell you?).
target_language_example: O que quer que você faça, avise-me antes.
native_language_example: Whatever you do, let me know first.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the thing(s) someone wants. Often appears in phrases like "fazer o que querem" (to do what they want). "Querem" is the 3rd person plural of "querer" (they want).
target_language_example: As crianças sempre pedem o que querem.
native_language_example: The kids always ask for what they want.

additional_notes: Literally “the thing that we want.” Used to introduce or refer back to a specific desired thing/goal (“O que queremos é…”) or to mean “whatever we want” after verbs like fazer/ter (“Fazemos/temos o que queremos”). Often contrasts desire vs. reality: “Não é o que queremos, mas…”.
target_language_example: O que queremos agora é descansar.
native_language_example: What we want now is to rest.

additional_notes: Often used after verbs like conseguir (to get/achieve), encontrar (to find), comer (to eat), dizer (to tell) to refer to the desired thing. Queria is the imperfect of querer (to want), so it commonly describes an ongoing desire in the past or what someone wanted at that time. The subject is often understood from context (e.g., ele/ela queria; você queria).
target_language_example: Finalmente encontrei o que queria.
native_language_example: I finally found what I wanted.

meaning: "whatever you want" (to do/eat/read/etc.), addressed to more than one person.
additional_notes: Uses the plural (vocês) form: quiserem = "(you all) want". It often expresses permission or indifference: "do/read/eat whatever you want". With an imperative or permission phrase (podem/tem permissão), it can sound friendly or dismissive depending on tone.
target_language_example: Podem escolher o que quiserem para o jantar.
native_language_example: You can choose whatever you want for dinner.

additional_notes: Used to ask what someone knows about a topic. This form omits the explicit subject ("você"), which is common in Portuguese; it still typically addresses "you" based on context. You can add the subject for clarity or emphasis, especially in Brazilian Portuguese: “O que você sabe sobre …?”. Conjugate the verb to match other persons: “O que eles sabem sobre …?” = “What do they know about …?”
target_language_example: O que sabe sobre esse lugar?
native_language_example: What do you know about that place?

additional_notes: Common in questions when you’re guessing or wondering about something, often without expecting a definite answer. It can sound softer/more thoughtful than simply "O que...?". The "será" here is from "ser" and helps express uncertainty (similar to "could it be that...").
target_language_example: O que será que ela quis dizer com isso?
native_language_example: I wonder what she meant by that.

additional_notes: Used to ask for the meaning of a word, phrase, sentence, paragraph, or situation. Often followed by what you’re asking about: “O que significa esta palavra/frase/isso?” You can also embed it in a longer question: “Você pode me dizer o que significa …?”
target_language_example: Desculpe, o que significa “saudade”?
native_language_example: Sorry, what does “saudade” mean?

meaning: “what … you” (used to start a question about what causes/affects you).
additional_notes: Used at the beginning of questions. "o que" = “what”; "te" is the unstressed object pronoun “you” (to you). It often appears with verbs like "faz" (makes), "impediu" (prevented), "mantém" (keeps), etc., to mean “what makes you…?”, “what stopped you…?”, “what keeps you…?” The verb that follows determines the exact meaning.
target_language_example: O que te deixou tão feliz hoje?
native_language_example: What made you so happy today?

additional_notes: Literally "what does it have?" (o que = what; tem = has). Very common as a standalone question meaning "what’s wrong? / what’s the matter?" (often like "What’s up?"). It can also be used more literally, especially in riddles: "O que tem X?" = "What has X?". With "de" + adjective/noun, it often means "what’s so … about it?" / "what’s … about it?": e.g., "O que tem de engraçado?" = "What’s so funny (about it)?" and "O que tem de novo?" = "What’s new?".
target_language_example: Você está quieto hoje—o que tem?
native_language_example: You’re quiet today—what’s wrong?

additional_notes: Used to report/explain an earlier event (past perfect: tinha acontecido) from the point of view of another moment in the past (e.g., he told her what had happened). Very common after verbs like contar (to tell), explicar (to explain), and saber (to know).
target_language_example: Eu expliquei para ela o que tinha acontecido antes da reunião.
native_language_example: I explained to her what had happened before the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to start a question or an embedded question addressed to someone you use **tu** with. It’s typically followed by a verb: **O que tu disseste?** (“What did you say?”). In many varieties you’ll also hear **O que é que tu…** with the same meaning. Common in informal speech and in regions/contexts where **tu** is used.
target_language_example: O que tu queres comer hoje?
native_language_example: What do you want to eat today?

meaning: “what is going to happen” / “what will happen.”
additional_notes: Used to ask or talk about a future event or outcome. Very common with "Eu não sei..." (“I don’t know...”) and with "com" + a person/thing to mean “what will happen to (someone/something)?” You can also add a time (e.g., "às onze horas") to ask what will happen at that time.
target_language_example: Ninguém sabe o que vai acontecer depois da reunião.
native_language_example: Nobody knows what will happen after the meeting.

additional_notes: A common question using **ir + infinitive** (**vai fazer**) to ask about someone’s plans or what action they will take. You can add details after it: **agora** (now), **amanhã** (tomorrow), **no verão** (in the summer), **a respeito de...** (about/regarding...), **com...** (with...), **então** (then/so). Often the subject **você** is implied: **(Você) o que vai fazer?**
target_language_example: E se chover, o que vai fazer?
native_language_example: And if it rains, what are you going to do?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the next plan/decision for a group (“we”). Often followed by a time word (agora, depois) or by phrases like a respeito disso (“about that”), com… (“with…”), para… (“in order to…” / “for…”). In writing it may appear as “O que vamos fazer?”; in speech it can sound like “Que vamos fazer?” or “O que a gente vai fazer?” (more informal).
target_language_example: O que vamos fazer se chover?
native_language_example: What are we going to do if it rains?

additional_notes: Used at the start of a question addressed to você. It is followed by a verb, so the exact English translation depends on the tense: for example, o que você quer? = what do you want? and o que você está fazendo? = what are you doing?
target_language_example: O que você quer comer hoje?
native_language_example: What do you want to eat today?

meaning: "What do you think of…?" / "What’s your opinion about…?"
additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s opinion about a thing/topic. It’s the start of a question and is followed by a noun (often with the contraction "do" = "de" + "o"). With feminine nouns you’ll usually see "da" (de + a): "O que você acha da comida?" You can also ask about a plural noun with "dos/das": "O que você acha dos filmes?"
target_language_example: O que você acha do meu plano?
native_language_example: What do you think of my plan?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion/guess about a situation or what should be done. Often followed by a full clause: “o que você acha que aconteceu / devemos fazer / está aqui”. In questions it commonly starts the sentence, and you can make it more formal by using “o que o senhor/a senhora acha que…”.
target_language_example: O que você acha que vai acontecer amanhã?
native_language_example: What do you think is going to happen tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to ask what someone ate in the past. Often followed by a time expression (hoje de manhã, ontem à noite) or by a meal (no café da manhã, no jantar). In speech, Brazilians often shorten it to "O que você comeu?" or "O que cê comeu?".
target_language_example: O que você comeu no almoço?
native_language_example: What did you eat for lunch?

additional_notes: Used to refer to someone’s previous words. Common in questions ("O que você disse?" = "What did you say?") and in statements ("Acredito que o que você disse é verdade" = "I believe what you said is true"). Adding "mesmo" can mean "again" or "exactly" ("O que você disse mesmo?" = "What did you say again/What exactly did you say?").
target_language_example: Eu não entendi o que você disse.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what you said.

meaning: “What do you say?” (asking for someone’s opinion/response).
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone thinks or how they respond to a suggestion or situation. Depending on tone, it can also sound like “What did you say?” / “Come again?” in a conversational way.
target_language_example: Vamos jantar fora hoje. O que você diz?
native_language_example: Let’s have dinner out today. What do you say?

additional_notes: Used to ask about an action in progress at a specific time in the past (past continuous). Often followed by a time reference (agora, na semana passada) or by a clause with quando (“when…”). In speech, you’ll also hear the shorter forms “O que você tava fazendo…?” and (more informal) “O que cê tava fazendo…?”.
target_language_example: O que você estava fazendo ontem à noite?
native_language_example: What were you doing last night?

additional_notes: A very common question using the present continuous (estar + gerund). It can be neutral (“What are you doing right now?”) or sound surprised/angry depending on tone (like “What do you think you’re doing?”). Often followed by extra info: “...aqui?” (here), “...comigo?” (to/with me), “...em casa tão cedo?” (at home so early). In Portuguese, you may also hear the informal version “o que você tá fazendo?” or “o que cê tá fazendo?”.
target_language_example: Ei, o que você está fazendo aí na minha cadeira?
native_language_example: Hey, what are you doing there in my chair?

meaning: “what would you do if …” (asking a hypothetical question).
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone would do in an imagined situation. Follow it with a clause in the subjunctive (e.g., “se ganhasse”, “se fosse”, “se visse”). You can change “você” to “vocês” (plural) or use a more formal/less direct “o que o senhor / a senhora faria se …”.
target_language_example: O que você faria se perdesse o seu passaporte no exterior?
native_language_example: What would you do if you lost your passport abroad?

meaning: "what do you do?" / "what are you doing?" (what you do).
additional_notes: Literally “what you do.” Used in questions to ask about someone’s job/routine/plans (“O que você faz da vida?” = “What do you do for a living?”) or about what someone does with something (“O que você faz com isso...?” = “What you do with this/that...?”). Meaning depends on context and time: it can be general (“What do you do?”) or right now (“What are you doing?”).
target_language_example: O que você faz nos fins de semana?
native_language_example: What do you do on weekends?

additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s actions or to refer back to them (often with an emotional tone, depending on context). You’ll also see it with other subject pronouns: “o que eu fiz?” (what did I do?), “o que ele fez?” (what did he do?). In questions, it can be said with a stronger tone like “What have you done?!”
target_language_example: Eu ainda não acredito no que você fez.
native_language_example: I still can’t believe what you did.

additional_notes: Used to ask what someone did with an object/person (often implying it’s missing or you disapprove). Very common when you can’t find something: “O que você fez com as minhas chaves?” You can swap pronouns: “O que você fez com o teu…?” (more informal in Brazil) / “O que você fez com o seu…?”
target_language_example: O que você fez com a minha carteira? Eu não encontro em lugar nenhum.
native_language_example: What did you do with my wallet? I can’t find it anywhere.

meaning: "what you told me" / "what did you tell me?"
additional_notes: Used to refer to information someone told you. It can be part of a longer sentence (e.g., "Diga a ele o que você me disse" = "Tell him what you told me") or a standalone question with rising intonation ("O que você me disse?" = "What did you tell me?"). You can swap "você" for another subject: "o que ele/ela me disse" (what he/she told me).
target_language_example: Não conte para ninguém o que você me disse.
native_language_example: Don't tell anyone what you told me.

meaning: “what you can do” / “what can you do?”
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s options, ability, or possible actions. It can be a statement (“I know what you can do”) or a question (“What can you do now?”). Commonly followed by complements like “agora” (now), “para ajudar” (to help), or “por ele/ela” (for him/her).
target_language_example: Não sei o que você pode fazer para resolver isso.
native_language_example: I don’t know what you can do to solve this.

additional_notes: Used both as a direct question ("O que você quer?" = "What do you want?") and inside a longer sentence ("Eu tenho o que você quer" = "I have what you want"). In everyday speech you may also hear "O que cê quer?" (more casual).
target_language_example: Eu não sei o que você quer.
native_language_example: I don't know what you want.

meaning: “what do you mean?” / “what are you trying to say?”
additional_notes: Used to ask for clarification about someone’s words or intentions. Very common in conversation. You’ll also see it with complements: “O que você quer dizer com isso?” = “What do you mean by that?” and “O que você quer dizer ao/para o Tom?” = “What do you want to say to Tom?”. In more informal speech, “você” is often reduced to “cê”: “O que cê quer dizer?”
target_language_example: Desculpa, o que você quer dizer com “mais tarde” exatamente?
native_language_example: Sorry, what do you mean by “later,” exactly?

additional_notes: Common question to ask about someone’s plan or intention. Often followed by a preposition phrase like "a respeito (de)..." (about/regarding), "com isso" (with that), or a time expression like "no próximo verão" (next summer). In Brazil, "você" is widely used; in Portugal you may hear "o que tu queres fazer" or "o que você quer fazer" depending on formality and region.
target_language_example: O que você quer fazer hoje à noite?
native_language_example: What do you want to do tonight?

additional_notes: Uses the past imperfect (queria) and can mean either (1) a description: “what you wanted” (often after phrases like “isso foi…” / “era…”) or (2) a polite/softened question: “What did you want?” / “What were you wanting?” (often implying “how can I help?”). In questions it’s common to add an object or infinitive: “O que você queria me perguntar?” (= “What did you want to ask me?”).
target_language_example: Desculpa a demora — o que você queria comigo?
native_language_example: Sorry for the delay—what did you want with me?

additional_notes: Used to give someone freedom of choice. It literally means “what you want” and can follow verbs like dizer (say), ler (read), pegar (take), comer (eat), fazer (do): “Você pode [verb] o que você quiser” = “You can [verb] whatever you want.” You may also hear the more informal version “o que você quiser” with “você” reduced to “cê”: “o que cê quiser.”
target_language_example: Escolha o que você quiser no cardápio.
native_language_example: Choose whatever you want from the menu.

additional_notes: Used to ask what information someone has about a topic, person, place, etc. It’s a direct question; you can change “você” to be more formal or informal: “o que o senhor/a senhora sabe sobre …?” (formal) or “o que você sabe sobre …?” / “o que tu sabes sobre …?” depending on region. In speech, it’s often shortened to “O que você sabe sobre isso?” (“…about that/this?”).
target_language_example: O que você sabe sobre esse assunto?
native_language_example: What do you know about this topic?

additional_notes: Used to ask what someone has (possesses) or, by itself ("O que você tem?"), what’s the matter/what’s wrong. Very commonly followed by an infinitive or a preposition to form set questions: "O que você tem a dizer…?" (What do you have to say…?), "O que você tem contra…?" (What do you have against…?), "O que você tem em mente?" (What do you have in mind?). In speech, "você" is often shortened to "cê": "O que cê tem?"
target_language_example: O que você tem a dizer sobre isso?
native_language_example: What do you have to say about that?

additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s plans or intended action. Often followed by a time word (agora = now, amanhã = tomorrow, antes do almoço = before lunch) or a context phrase (aqui = here, com isso = with that/about that). In Brazil, this uses “você” (you) and the near-future form “vai fazer” (literally “is going to do”).
target_language_example: O que você vai fazer depois do trabalho?
native_language_example: What are you going to do after work?

additional_notes: Used to start a question addressed to more than one person. It’s usually followed by a verb: "O que vocês fazem...?" (What do you all do...?). In Brazil, "vocês" is the common plural for “you”; depending on context it can feel like “you all / you guys,” but it’s not necessarily informal.
target_language_example: O que vocês querem comer hoje?
native_language_example: What do you all want to eat today?

additional_notes: Used to ask about or refer to an action done by a group of people. "O que" = "what"; "vocês" is the common Brazilian Portuguese plural "you" (used for friends, strangers, and most situations); "fizeram" is the past of "fazer" (to do/make). Depending on context, it can mean a simple past action ("did") or a past action relevant now ("have done").
target_language_example: Eu não entendi o que vocês fizeram aqui.
native_language_example: I didn't understand what you all did here.

additional_notes: A direct question to a group of people. "vocês" = "you" (plural), common in Brazil. Used to ask what they want in general (O que vocês querem?), what they want to drink (…beber?), or what they want from someone (…de mim?). In "Eu tenho o que vocês querem", it means "what you want" (not a question).
target_language_example: O que vocês querem fazer hoje?
native_language_example: What do you (all) want to do today?

meaning: “what am I going to do?” / “what will I do?”
additional_notes: Used when you’re unsure about what to do next, or asking (sometimes rhetorically) what action you should take. Often appears inside a longer sentence (e.g., “I’ll see what I’m going to do”). You can add details after it, like location (“aí” = there) or who/what it involves (“com você” = with you / about you, depending on context).
target_language_example: Não sei o que vou fazer amanhã.
native_language_example: I don’t know what I’m going to do tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to ask for a definition, identity, or explanation: "O que é isto?" = "What is this?" It can also introduce an embedded question after another verb: "Já sei o que é" = "I already know what it is"; "Precisamos descobrir o que é" = "We need to find out what it is." Often you’ll hear the emphatic form "o que é que…?" with the same meaning in everyday speech.
target_language_example: O que é que isso quer dizer?
native_language_example: What does that mean?

additional_notes: Used to talk about what is morally correct or the proper choice. Often appears in contrasts like “o que é certo… mas…” (“what’s right… but…”) or in advice (“Escolha o que é certo”). The “certo” here means “right/correct,” not “certain.”
target_language_example: Às vezes é difícil fazer o que é certo.
native_language_example: Sometimes it’s hard to do the right thing.

additional_notes: A very common question used to ask what something is. "isso" usually refers to something near the listener or something already mentioned (while "isto" is more like 'this' near the speaker), but in everyday speech many people use "isso" even when pointing at something close. Often said with a person’s name or a term of address (e.g., "meu filho") to get their attention.
target_language_example: O que é isso na sua mão?
native_language_example: What is that in your hand?

additional_notes: A common question used to ask for identification or an explanation of something you’re seeing or being shown. Often said with surprise or concern depending on tone. You’ll also hear the simpler version "O que é isso?" (same meaning).
target_language_example: Desculpe, o que é isto?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what is this?

meaning: "what is the...?" (asking for a definition/explanation of a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to ask what something is or what it means. It’s followed by a masculine singular noun with the definite article: "o" (= "the"). For feminine nouns use "O que é a..."; for plural use "O que são os/as...?".
target_language_example: O que é o Wi‑Fi?
native_language_example: What is Wi‑Fi?

additional_notes: Very common question opener meaning “what…?”. It adds emphasis but usually doesn’t change the basic meaning compared to just “o que”. Often used before a verb: “O que é que você quer?” = “What do you want?” (same as “O que você quer?”). In everyday speech it’s frequently reduced to “que é que” after another word: “Então, que é que eu faço agora?”
target_language_example: O que é que vocês estão fazendo aqui?
native_language_example: What are you doing here?

additional_notes: Common in Brazilian Portuguese in casual speech, often when reacting to someone’s tone or interruption. It can sound challenging or defensive depending on intonation, especially when followed by a name or nickname (e.g., “O que é que foi, meu irmão?”).
target_language_example: Ei, o que é que foi? Por que você está bravo?
native_language_example: Hey, what is it? Why are you mad?

meaning: “What is a…?” (asking for a definition of a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to ask what something is (a definition/explanation). You typically follow it with a noun: “O que é um OVNI?”. For feminine nouns, use “O que é uma…?”; for plural, “O que são…?”.
target_language_example: O que é um vulcão?
native_language_example: What is a volcano?

additional_notes: Used before an adjective or adverb to express degree: o quão chateado (how upset), o quão bem (how well), o quão longe (how far). Common after verbs like saber, ver, sentir, imaginar, or in questions. Often corresponds to English “how” in sentences like “I know how uncomfortable you are.”
target_language_example: Você não imagina o quão difícil foi.
native_language_example: You can’t imagine how difficult it was.

additional_notes: Used as a stressed or emphatic form of what, often at the end of a question or by itself. It can express surprise, confusion, or challenge. In Portuguese, quê takes an accent when it is stressed at the end of the phrase or stands alone; compare o que in the middle of a sentence.
target_language_example: Você disse o quê?
native_language_example: What did you say?

additional_notes: "Rapaz" means a boy or young man. With "o" it’s definite: "the". It can also refer generally to “the guy/young man” you’re talking about. Feminine: "a rapariga" (more common in Portugal; in Brazil it can mean “prostitute,” so Brazilians often use "a menina" or "a garota").
target_language_example: Quem é o rapaz que está esperando lá fora?
native_language_example: Who is the young man who is waiting outside?

additional_notes: Refers to a male monarch. "O" is the masculine singular definite article ("the"). Often used with "de" + place/name to mean "the king of ..." (e.g., "o rei de Gondor").
target_language_example: O rei mora no castelo.
native_language_example: The king lives in the castle.

additional_notes: Used for a formal written document that summarizes information, results, or an investigation (e.g., for school, work, or a court). Often used with verbs like escrever (to write), terminar (to finish), entregar (to hand in/submit), and mandar/enviar (to send). Gender: masculine; plural: os relatórios.
target_language_example: Preciso terminar o relatório hoje e entregar amanhã.
native_language_example: I need to finish the report today and hand it in tomorrow.

additional_notes: Definite form (masculine singular): **o** + **restaurante**. Used to refer to a specific restaurant known from context (one you mentioned before, or the one you’re talking about). Common with location and description: **O restaurante fica...** (The restaurant is located...), **O restaurante estava...** (The restaurant was...).
target_language_example: O restaurante fica perto do hotel.
native_language_example: The restaurant is near the hotel.

additional_notes: Used to refer to what remains after a part has been taken/mentioned. Very common in the pattern "o resto de + noun" ("the rest of ..."): "o resto dos seus irmãos" = "the rest of your brothers". It can also be used on its own to mean leftover things, money, food, etc.: "venho buscar o resto" = "I’ll come back to pick up the rest."
target_language_example: Eu já comi metade; você pode ficar com o resto.
native_language_example: I already ate half; you can have the rest.

additional_notes: Used to talk about everything that happens from now until someone dies. Often appears with prepositions like "pelo resto da vida" (for the rest of my life) or "no resto da vida" (in the rest of my life). You can specify the person with "da minha/sua/nossa vida" (of my/your/our life). In casual speech you may hear "pro resto da vida" (for the rest of life).
target_language_example: Vou guardar esse segredo pelo resto da vida.
native_language_example: I’ll keep this secret for the rest of my life.

meaning: the rest of (the remaining part of).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to refer to what remains: “o resto do bolo” (the remaining cake). For feminine singular nouns, use “o resto da” (e.g., “o resto da comida”). Often appears after mentioning part of something and then referring to what’s left.
target_language_example: Vou guardar o resto do pão para amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m going to save the rest of the bread for tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with masculine singular definite article o. In Portuguese, many river names take the article: o rio Amazonas, o rio Nilo. You can also use it generically: sobre o rio (“over/across the river”), atravessar o rio (“to cross the river”).
target_language_example: Vamos caminhar perto do rio amanhã.
native_language_example: Let’s walk near the river tomorrow.

meaning: the risk of; the chance of (something bad happening).
additional_notes: Commonly used in the pattern **correr o risco de + infinitive** (“to run the risk of / risk doing”), e.g., *correr o risco de desabar* (“risk collapsing”). You can also use it as a noun phrase: **O risco de + infinitive/noun** (“The risk of …”), e.g., *O risco de morrer…* (“The risk of dying…”).
target_language_example: Não quero correr o risco de perder o voo.
native_language_example: I don’t want to risk missing the flight.

additional_notes: Commonly used with a possessive or “de + person” to specify whose face (e.g., “o rosto dele/dela”, “o rosto da mulher”). Often appears in descriptions (shape, features) and in phrases like “ver o rosto” (see someone’s face) or “descrever o rosto” (describe someone’s face).
target_language_example: Eu reconheci o rosto dela imediatamente.
native_language_example: I recognized her face immediately.

meaning: the radio (device; also radio as a medium).
additional_notes: Used with the masculine definite article o. Common verbs: ligar o rádio (turn on the radio), ouvir/escutar o rádio (listen to the radio), consertar o rádio (fix the radio). It can refer either to the physical device or to radio broadcasts, depending on context.
target_language_example: Ela ouve o rádio de manhã.
native_language_example: She listens to the radio in the morning.

additional_notes: A common food item/seasoning. Often used at the table with "a pimenta" (pepper), especially in the phrase "o sal e a pimenta" (salt and pepper).
target_language_example: Pode me passar o sal, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you pass me the salt, please?

additional_notes: Basic noun meaning “blood.” Used literally (e.g., in medical or injury contexts) and in figurative expressions about guilt or responsibility (e.g., “com o sangue nas mãos” = “with blood on one’s hands”). Note that Portuguese often omits the article in some contexts (“Tem sangue no chão”), but it can also appear as “o sangue” depending on phrasing.
target_language_example: Tom limpou o sangue da espada.
native_language_example: Tom wiped the blood off the sword.

additional_notes: Used to talk about information that should be kept hidden. Common with verbs like contar (reveal/tell), manter/guardar (keep), and saber (know). Often appears as “manter/guardar o segredo” = “to keep the secret.”
target_language_example: Eu prometo guardar o segredo.
native_language_example: I promise to keep the secret.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to indicate the item in position #2 in an order or sequence: "o segundo homicídio" (the second murder), "o segundo botão" (the second button). Ordinals in Portuguese agree in gender and number with the noun (e.g., "o segundo" for masculine singular, "a segunda" for feminine singular). Note: without an article, "segundo" can also mean "according to" (e.g., "Segundo ele..."), but that’s a different use.
target_language_example: O segundo quarto fica no fim do corredor.
native_language_example: The second room is at the end of the hallway.

additional_notes: A polite, formal way to address or refer to a man. When used directly to someone, it takes third-person verb forms in Portuguese (for example, O senhor está...? ). Before a surname, it usually means "Mr." as in O senhor Smith. The feminine form is a senhora.
target_language_example: O senhor precisa de ajuda?
native_language_example: Do you need help, sir?

additional_notes: Used to address an adult man politely (often a stranger, customer, or older man). It combines the formal form of address “o senhor” (“sir”) with “está” (3rd person singular of “estar”), so in Portuguese you say it like “he is,” but it means “you are” in a formal way. Often followed by a verb in the gerund (e.g., está vendo) or an adjective (e.g., está perdido).
target_language_example: O senhor está com pressa?
native_language_example: Are you in a hurry, sir?

meaning: “Have you already…?, sir” / “Have you… yet?, sir”.
additional_notes: Used to address a man politely/formally (“o senhor” = “sir/you”). It’s followed by a verb in the 3rd person singular (e.g., “o senhor já pediu?”). “já” often means “already” or (in questions) “yet”.
target_language_example: O senhor já tomou o seu remédio?
native_language_example: Have you taken your medicine yet, sir?

additional_notes: “O senhor” is a polite, formal way to address a man (like “sir”), commonly used in Brazil. With “não”, it forms a negative statement (“O senhor não falou.” = “You didn’t speak.”) or a negative question (“O senhor não acha…?” = “Don’t you think…?”). You may also hear a second “não” at the end for emphasis in Brazilian Portuguese (“…não”), which doesn’t change the meaning.
target_language_example: O senhor não quer sentar aqui?
native_language_example: Don’t you want to sit here, sir?

meaning: "do you want...?" (polite/formal, said to a man).
additional_notes: Used when addressing a man respectfully (e.g., a customer, older man, or someone you don’t know well). It literally means “the gentleman wants,” but in service contexts it often functions like a polite “Would you like...?” You can add an object or a clause: “O senhor quer café?” / “O senhor quer que eu ajude...?”.
target_language_example: O senhor quer pagar com cartão ou dinheiro?
native_language_example: Would you like to pay with card or cash?

meaning: formal way to say “do you have…?” (to a man).
additional_notes: Used when speaking politely to an adult man (customer/service situations, formal conversations). Literally it’s “the sir has,” but it functions as “you have” in English. Often followed by a noun or quantity (e.g., bagagem, uma ligação, quantos/quantas).
target_language_example: O senhor tem reserva?
native_language_example: Do you have a reservation, sir?

additional_notes: Used with the verb **ser** to speak politely/formally to an adult man (like “sir”). Common with strangers, older people, or in respectful situations. In conversation it often pairs with titles/names (e.g., **O senhor é o Sr. João?**). It can also be used alone as a prompt meaning “Are you…?” (**O senhor é?**).
target_language_example: Com licença, o senhor é o motorista do ônibus?
native_language_example: Excuse me, are you the bus driver?

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to mean "your," as in o seu currículo = "your résumé." The article o is often used with possessives in Portuguese, even though English normally does not use "the" here. Depending on context, seu can also mean "his," "her," or "their," so it can be ambiguous.
target_language_example: Eu gostei do seu carro.
native_language_example: I liked your car.

meaning: "your friend" (male friend; or friend when you don’t specify gender).
additional_notes: "o" is "the" (masculine singular), "seu" means "your" (also can mean "his/her" in some contexts), and "amigo" is "friend" (male). Used when talking about someone the listener knows. To refer to a female friend, use "a sua amiga". In Brazil, "seu" can sound more formal; many people also say "o teu amigo" (depending on region) or "o amigo dele/dela" to avoid ambiguity.
target_language_example: Eu gostei muito de conhecer o seu amigo ontem.
native_language_example: I really liked meeting your friend yesterday.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive “seu/sua” with the article (“o/a”) to mean someone’s hair. Often used when addressing someone politely (e.g., with “você” or in customer service). If you mean “your (plural) hair” (to more than one person), you would also use “o cabelo de vocês.”
target_language_example: Adorei o seu cabelo; ficou muito bonito!
native_language_example: I loved your hair; it looks really nice!

additional_notes: Uses the possessive "seu/sua" (= your / his / her / their, depending on context). Here it’s with the masculine singular noun "cachorro" (dog), so: "o seu cachorro". In Brazil, "cachorro" is common for "dog" in general; in more formal contexts you may also hear "cão". In speech, people often just say "seu cachorro" without the article "o".
target_language_example: O seu cachorro está bem?
native_language_example: Is your dog okay?

additional_notes: "o" = "the" and "seu" = "your" (masculine singular). In Brazil, "seu/sua" is commonly used with "você" to mean "your". You can also say "seu carro" without "o"; adding "o" often sounds more specific ("your car" / "that car of yours").
target_language_example: Onde você estacionou o seu carro?
native_language_example: Where did you park your car?

additional_notes: Uses the possessive “seu/sua” with the article (“o/a”) to mean “your.” Common in polite speech and in Brazil, often with “você”: “o seu casaco.” In Portugal, people often say “o teu casaco” (informal singular) instead. “Casaco” can mean a coat or a jacket depending on context.
target_language_example: Posso pegar o seu casaco para você?
native_language_example: Can I take your coat/jacket for you?

additional_notes: Means “your cell phone” when speaking to one person using the formal/neutral “você”. With “celular” you’ll often use verbs like estar (Onde está...?), dar (Você me dá...?) and emprestar (Você me empresta...?) when asking where it is, to have it, or to borrow it. In Brazil, “celular” is the most common word; in Portugal you’ll often hear “telemóvel”.
target_language_example: Posso usar o seu celular por um minuto?
native_language_example: Can I use your cell phone for a minute?

additional_notes: Means money that belongs to the person you’re talking to. "Seu/sua" agrees with the thing owned: "dinheiro" is masculine, so it’s "o seu dinheiro". In Brazil, "seu" can sometimes also mean "his/her/their" depending on context, but with "você" it commonly means "your". Often used with verbs like "esconder" (hide), "esquecer" (forget), "roubar" (steal), and "receber" (receive).
target_language_example: Pode guardar o seu dinheiro; eu pago hoje.
native_language_example: You can put your money away; I’ll pay today.

additional_notes: Used to refer to someone’s son/child when speaking to them. "Seu/sua" can mean “your” (formal singular) or “his/her/its” depending on context; with "o" + masculine noun "filho" it’s “your/his/her son.” For “your child” in a gender-neutral way, people often say "seu filho" (if the child is a boy) or "sua filha" (if a girl), or use "seu/sua filho(a)" in writing.
target_language_example: Como está o seu filho?
native_language_example: How is your son?

additional_notes: Uses the possessive "seu/sua" to mean "your" (formal singular "you" = você). "Guarda-chuva" is masculine, so it takes "o" and "seu". Common in questions about finding/bringing/borrowing an umbrella (e.g., "Já encontrou o seu guarda-chuva?").
target_language_example: Não esqueça o seu guarda-chuva; vai chover.
native_language_example: Don’t forget your umbrella; it’s going to rain.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive "seu" with the masculine singular noun "irmão". Common in polite conversation (especially with "você"), and can also mean "his/her/its brother" depending on context; to avoid confusion, people may say "o irmão dele/dela" (his/her brother).
target_language_example: Você pode me apresentar ao seu irmão?
native_language_example: Can you introduce me to your brother?

additional_notes: Used to refer to something that belongs to the person you’re speaking to (or “your” in a polite/formal tone). In Brazilian Portuguese, everyday speech often uses “o seu livro” even when meaning “your book,” though “o teu livro” is common in Portugal and some contexts. Word-by-word: o (the) + seu (your) + livro (book).
target_language_example: Posso pegar o seu livro por um minuto?
native_language_example: Can I take your book for a minute?

meaning: your husband / her husband (depending on context).
additional_notes: "Seu/sua" can mean "your" (formal) or "his/her/its" depending on context and region. In Brazil, "o seu marido" is often understood as "your husband" when speaking to someone; in Portugal and for clarity, people often say "o teu marido" (your, informal) or "o marido dela" (her husband). "Marido" means "husband"; the feminine is "mulher" (wife).
target_language_example: O seu marido vem buscar você mais tarde?
native_language_example: Is your husband coming to pick you up later?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like fazer (“to do”) or tentar (“to try”) to encourage someone or describe that they’re putting in maximum effort. You can also change the possessive: o meu melhor (my best), o nosso melhor (our best), etc.
target_language_example: Faça o seu melhor!
native_language_example: Do your best!

additional_notes: Means “your name,” usually in a more formal/polite register. With você, Portuguese commonly uses seu/sua to mean “your.” Note: seu/sua can also mean “his/her/their” depending on context, but in these examples it’s “your.”
target_language_example: Qual é o seu nome?
native_language_example: What is your name?

meaning: “your new” (masculine singular), as in “your new [noun]” (“o seu novo + noun”).
additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: o seu novo carro (your new car), o seu novo chefe (your new boss). The article o and adjective novo must match the noun’s gender/number. Note: seu/sua/seus/suas can mean “your,” but also sometimes “his/her/their” depending on context; many speakers use dele/dela to clarify.
target_language_example: Você já conheceu o seu novo professor?
native_language_example: Have you met your new teacher yet?

additional_notes: Means “your father” when speaking to someone using você (more formal/polite). Note: seu/sua can also mean “his/her/its” depending on context, so sometimes o seu pai can be ambiguous without more information.
target_language_example: O seu pai mora aqui perto?
native_language_example: Does your father live nearby?

additional_notes: "Seu/sua" can mean "your" (formal) or "his/her/its" depending on context. With "o" + "país" it’s "the" + "country"; Portuguese often uses the article before possessives ("o seu"). If you need to be extra clear, you can say "o país dele/dela" (his/her country) or "o seu país" vs. "o teu país" (your country, informal in Portugal).
target_language_example: Qual é o seu país?
native_language_example: What is your country?

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something belongs specifically to the person you’re talking to, or is theirs to do/make/choose (not someone else’s, not shared). It agrees with the noun: o seu próprio país/caminho/restaurante/quarto (masc. singular), a sua própria casa (fem. singular), os seus próprios amigos / as suas próprias ideias (plural). Often used after the possessive: seu/sua + próprio/a.
target_language_example: Siga o seu próprio caminho e deixe as pessoas falarem.
native_language_example: Follow your own path and let people talk.

additional_notes: Literally “your room.” Often used when telling someone to clean/tidy their room (arrumar/limpar o seu quarto). It can also mean “his/her room” depending on context, because “seu/sua” can refer to you (formal) or to someone else; to be clearer, people may say “o quarto dele/dela” (his/her room).
target_language_example: Você já arrumou o seu quarto hoje?
native_language_example: Have you tidied your room today?

additional_notes: Used to refer to someone’s work or occupation. "Seu/sua" is a formal “your” (often used with você) and can also mean “his/her/their” depending on context; when you want to be extra clear, you can say "o trabalho dele/dela". You’ll also see the informal equivalent "o teu trabalho" (your, familiar).
target_language_example: Obrigado pelo seu trabalho — ajudou muito a equipe.
native_language_example: Thank you for your work — it really helped the team.

meaning: "yours" / "your" (masculine singular; also used as "yours" meaning "your one").
additional_notes: "O seu" refers to something that belongs to the person you’re talking to (or to "you" in a formal sense). It agrees with the thing possessed, not with the owner: use "o seu" for a masculine singular noun (e.g., "o seu relógio" = "your watch"). It can stand alone when the noun is understood: "O meu é vermelho, e o seu?" = "Mine is red, and yours?" Also common after comparison/prepositions: "como o seu" (like yours), "sobre o seu" (on top of yours). For feminine singular, you’d use "a sua"; plural: "os seus / as suas".
target_language_example: Posso usar o seu por um minuto?
native_language_example: Can I use yours for a minute?

additional_notes: Usually refers to a larger structure that controls how things work (e.g., government, rules, bureaucracy, the way society is organized). It can also mean a specific system/mechanism (like a computer system), depending on context. Masculine singular: o sistema.
target_language_example: Às vezes parece que o sistema não ajuda quem precisa.
native_language_example: Sometimes it feels like the system doesn’t help those who need it.

additional_notes: Means the Sun (the star), and also appears in common expressions about sunrise and sunset: “o sol nasce” (the sun rises) and “o sol põe-se” (the sun sets). It can also be used figuratively to mean the brightest/most important person in an area (e.g., “o sol da literatura russa” = ‘the sun of Russian literature’).
target_language_example: Hoje o sol está muito forte.
native_language_example: Today the sun is very strong (very bright/hot).

meaning: the sound; the audio/volume (of a device).
additional_notes: Means “sound” in general (noise, sound of a voice, etc.). In everyday speech it’s also used for the audio/volume on a device, especially with verbs like “aumentar/baixar o som” (turn the volume up/down).
target_language_example: Você pode baixar o som, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you turn the volume down, please?

additional_notes: Means “enough (of it/that)”—the amount needed or desired. Often used after verbs: “Tenho o suficiente.” (“I have enough.”). You may also see “suficiente” without the article (e.g., “é suficiente” = “it’s enough / it’s sufficient”).
target_language_example: Já temos o suficiente para hoje.
native_language_example: We already have enough for today.

additional_notes: Used after an adjective or adverb to say the degree is enough for something to happen or be possible. Common pattern: [adjective/adverb] + o suficiente para + infinitive (e.g., "gentil o suficiente para ajudar", "rápido o suficiente para chegar"). With weather/conditions, it can mean "enough for" an activity ("vento suficiente para velejar").
target_language_example: Você fala português bem o suficiente para viajar sozinho.
native_language_example: You speak Portuguese well enough to travel alone.

additional_notes: Refers to a phone in general (mobile or landline) depending on context. In sentence 1, “atender o telefone” means “to answer the phone.” In sentence 2, “telefone público” means “public phone/payphone.”
target_language_example: Você pode atender o telefone, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you answer the phone, please?

meaning: “the phone rang” (the phone made a ringing sound).
additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of tocar meaning “to ring” when talking about a phone: o telefone tocou = it rang (and stopped). Often used with time clauses: assim que… (“as soon as…”), enquanto… (“while…”). You may also hear: o telefone está tocando (“the phone is ringing” right now).
target_language_example: Eu estava dormindo quando o telefone tocou.
native_language_example: I was sleeping when the phone rang.

additional_notes: Used to describe the current weather conditions. Commonly followed by an adjective: limpo (clear), chuvoso (rainy), ensolarado (sunny), quente (hot), frio (cold), nublado (cloudy).
target_language_example: Hoje, o tempo está nublado e frio.
native_language_example: Today, the weather is cloudy and cold.

meaning: all the time; the whole time.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens continuously or very often ("all the time"), or throughout an entire period/event ("the whole time"). It often comes at the end of the sentence: "... o tempo inteiro."
target_language_example: Eu pensei nisso o tempo inteiro.
native_language_example: I thought about it the whole time.

meaning: "the time that" / "as long as" (the amount of time needed or available).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration or an amount of time. Common in phrases like "o tempo que precisar" / "o tempo que quiser" (= as long as you need / want) and "o tempo que resta" (= the time that remains). It’s followed by a verb clause describing the need, desire, or remaining time.
target_language_example: Você pode ficar aqui o tempo que quiser.
native_language_example: You can stay here as long as you want.

additional_notes: Means something happens continuously or during an entire period. Often used at the end of the sentence for emphasis (e.g., "... o tempo todo"). Commonly follows verbs like estar/ficar/seguir: "Eu estava certa o tempo todo" = "I was right the whole time."
target_language_example: Ele reclamou o tempo todo durante a viagem.
native_language_example: He complained the whole time during the trip.

additional_notes: Used as a common saying/exclamation, often with "Como o tempo voa!" to express surprise that time has gone by fast. You can also extend it with comparisons like "O tempo voa como uma flecha" (time flies like an arrow).
target_language_example: Já faz um ano desde que nos mudamos—o tempo voa!
native_language_example: It’s already been a year since we moved—time flies!

additional_notes: possessive form used with a masculine singular noun, especially with tu. In Portuguese, the article often appears before the possessive, so o teu carro means 'your car,' not literally 'the your car.' Common in European Portuguese; compare a tua for feminine nouns.
target_language_example: Onde está o teu casaco?
native_language_example: Where is your coat?

meaning: "your dad" / "your father" (to one person, informal singular).
additional_notes: Uses the informal singular possessive "teu" (= your) and the masculine article "o". Common when speaking to a friend, child, or someone you address as "tu"; in many situations (and in Brazil) "o seu pai" is more common/formal/polite. You can also say "teu pai" without the article in some contexts.
target_language_example: O teu pai trabalha aqui?
native_language_example: Does your dad work here?

additional_notes: Used for a specific piece of work, task, or job. Depending on context, trabalho can mean work in general, a job, or an assignment. In expressions like ir para o trabalho / até o trabalho, it can also refer to one's workplace.
target_language_example: Preciso terminar o trabalho hoje.
native_language_example: I need to finish the work today.

additional_notes: Used to say what a group of men (or a mixed group) is responsible for doing. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., comprar, conectar, cortar). You can swap the possessive to match the person/number: o meu trabalho é (my job is), o trabalho dela é (her job is), o trabalho deles/delas é (their job is).
target_language_example: O trabalho deles é limpar as salas todos os dias.
native_language_example: Their job is to clean the rooms every day.

additional_notes: Literally “the train” (o = “the”, trem = “train”). Commonly used when talking about train schedules/arrivals. In some regions of Brazil (especially Minas Gerais), “trem” can also mean “thing/stuff,” but in this sentence it clearly means an actual train.
target_language_example: O trem sai às oito.
native_language_example: The train leaves at eight.

meaning: "the train was" (used to describe the train’s state/condition).
additional_notes: "O trem" = "the train" and "estava" is the imperfect past of "estar" ("was"). It’s commonly followed by an adjective or phrase: "estava atrasado" (was late), "estava pronto" (was ready), or "estava para + infinitive" (was about to + verb).
target_language_example: O trem estava lotado quando eu entrei.
native_language_example: The train was crowded when I got on.

additional_notes: Portuguese often uses the article + adjective to talk about a person as a noun. So o velho can mean an old man, or “the older one” (male) in context. Depending on the country and situation, it can also be used informally to refer to someone close (like “the old man” in English), but it can sound rude if used about a stranger.
target_language_example: O velho mora aqui desde 1980.
native_language_example: The old man has lived here since 1980.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: "o" = "the" (masculine singular) + "vento" = "wind". Used to talk about the wind blowing, its strength, and whether it is favorable ("a seu favor" = in your favor).
target_language_example: Hoje o vento está forte, então leve um casaco.
native_language_example: Today the wind is strong, so bring a jacket.

additional_notes: Refers to the summer season. Often used with verbs like chegar (to arrive): "O verão chegou" (Summer has arrived). You can also use it to talk about plans or duration: "para o verão" (for the summer), "o verão inteiro" (the whole summer), "passar o verão" (to spend the summer).
target_language_example: No verão, faz muito calor aqui.
native_language_example: In the summer, it’s very hot here.

additional_notes: Means “the bus” (definite article + noun). Common in Brazilian Portuguese; in Portugal, “bus” is usually “o autocarro”. Often used with travel verbs like “pegar” (to take/catch), “perder” (to miss), “esperar” (to wait for), and with “ponto de ônibus” (bus stop).
target_language_example: Eu pego o ônibus para o trabalho todos os dias.
native_language_example: I take the bus to work every day.

additional_notes: Means the last or final one. It is masculine singular, so it can come before a masculine noun (as in o último desejo) or stand alone when the noun is understood. Common related forms are a última, os últimos, and as últimas.
target_language_example: Eu comi o último biscoito.
native_language_example: I ate the last cookie.

meaning: “the last train” (the final train service of the day).
additional_notes: Used when talking about catching or missing the final train available on a route/day. Common with verbs like apanhar/pegar (to catch) and perder (to miss).
target_language_example: Se a gente perder o último trem, vamos ter que voltar de táxi.
native_language_example: If we miss the last train, we'll have to go back by taxi.

additional_notes: Masculine singular form of único. It agrees with the noun it describes and can be used before a noun (o único jeito = the only way) or by itself to mean "the only one." Common related forms are a única, os únicos, and as únicas.
target_language_example: Ele é o único que entende isso.
native_language_example: He is the only one who understands that.

additional_notes: "o" is a direct-object pronoun meaning “him” (it can also mean “it,” depending on context). In Portuguese, object pronouns often come before the verb: "Você o ama?" = “Do you love him?”
target_language_example: Eu sei que ela o ama de verdade.
native_language_example: I know she really loves him.

additional_notes: “o” is an object pronoun meaning “him” (or sometimes “it”), placed before the verb. “amava” is the imperfect past of “amar”, used for an ongoing feeling in the past, a repeated action, or background description. Very common in reported speech after “disse que…” (said that…).
target_language_example: Eu percebi que o amava há muito tempo.
native_language_example: I realized that I had loved him for a long time.

additional_notes: "o" is an object pronoun meaning "him" or "it" (for a masculine person/thing). "o conhece" is most common after the verb in questions/negatives in Brazilian Portuguese (proclisis), e.g. "Você o conhece?" = "Do you know him?" In many everyday conversations, especially in Brazil, people often replace "o" with "ele": "Você conhece ele?" (very common, but more informal/less formal).
target_language_example: Você o conhece?
native_language_example: Do you know him?
