additional_notes: “O” is a direct object pronoun meaning “him” (or “it” for masculine nouns). It often appears before the verb in European Portuguese (and in more formal/written Brazilian Portuguese): “(Eu) o conheço” = “I know him.” In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, it’s very common to say “Eu conheço ele” instead.
target_language_example: Não se preocupe — eu o conheço há anos.
native_language_example: Don’t worry—I’ve known him for years.

meaning: “left him/it” or “let him/it (do something),” depending on context.
additional_notes: “o” is an object pronoun meaning “him” or “it.” With the verb “deixar,” it can mean (1) “to leave someone” (including breaking up): “Ela o deixou” = “She left him,” or (2) “to allow/let”: “não o deixou ir” = “didn’t let him go.” In negative sentences, “não” comes before the pronoun + verb: “não o deixou …”.
target_language_example: Ela não o deixou entrar na sala.
native_language_example: She didn’t let him enter the room.

additional_notes: "o" is an object pronoun meaning "him" or "it" (and sometimes "you" if referring to "você"). With "fez" (past of "fazer"), it often means either (1) "made him/you do something" + infinitive: "Ela o fez limpar..." = "She made him clean..."; or (2) "did it": "Ele o fez sozinho" = "He did it alone." You can also see it in questions: "Quem o fez?" = "Who did it?"
target_language_example: O que o fez mudar de ideia?
native_language_example: What made you change your mind?

additional_notes: "o" is an object pronoun meaning “him/it” (referring to a previously mentioned masculine person/thing). "matou" is the past tense of "matar" (to kill). In Brazilian Portuguese, object pronouns like "o" are often placed before the verb ("o matou"), but after certain endings you may also see forms like "matou-o" in more formal writing.
target_language_example: A polícia disse que ele o matou ontem à noite.
native_language_example: The police said he killed him last night.

additional_notes: Used mainly in formal or written Portuguese to refer back to a noun (like “which/whom”). It changes for gender and number: o qual (m. sg.), a qual (f. sg.), os quais (m. pl.), as quais (f. pl.). Very common after prepositions: com o qual (with whom/which), para a qual (for which), em relação à qual (in relation to which). In everyday speech, people often prefer que or quem instead.
target_language_example: O relatório, o qual foi aprovado ontem, será enviado hoje.
native_language_example: The report, which was approved yesterday, will be sent today.

additional_notes: "O" is a direct-object pronoun meaning "him" (or "it" for a masculine noun). "Vi" is the past (preterite) of "ver" (to see): "eu vi" = "I saw". In Portuguese, object pronouns often come before the verb: "eu o vi" = "I saw him/it" (common in writing and formal speech). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people often say "eu vi ele" instead of "eu o vi".
target_language_example: Eu o vi ontem no supermercado.
native_language_example: I saw him yesterday at the supermarket.

meaning: “saw him / saw it” (as in “(someone) saw him/it”).
additional_notes: “O” is an unstressed direct object pronoun meaning “him/it/you (formal),” depending on context. “Viu” is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of “ver” for ele/ela/você (“(he/she/you) saw”). Together, “o viu” commonly appears after a subject like “ela” or “você”: “Ela o viu” = “She saw him/it.” In some varieties of spoken Brazilian Portuguese, speakers may instead say “viu ele”/“viu isso,” but “o viu” is standard in writing and careful speech.
target_language_example: Ela nunca o viu.
native_language_example: She never saw him/it.

meaning: “work of” / “the doing of” (caused or made by).
additional_notes: Used to attribute authorship or responsibility. Common with an indefinite article: “obra de um/uma …” = “the work/doing of a …”. It can describe creative works (“obra de ficção” = “a work of fiction”) or blame/credit for an action (“foi obra de alguém” = “it was done/caused by someone”).
target_language_example: O estrago foi obra de um erro simples.
native_language_example: The damage was caused by a simple mistake.

meaning: a work of art; an artwork.
additional_notes: Used for pieces of art like paintings, sculptures, drawings, etc. It can also be used figuratively for something very well made or impressive (e.g., a garden, a dish, a design). Often used with the verb ser: “X é uma obra de arte.”
target_language_example: Esse bolo ficou uma obra de arte!
native_language_example: That cake turned out to be a work of art!

meaning: “thank you for the …” (said by a woman).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for a specific thing that follows, typically a feminine singular noun: pela + [feminine singular noun] (pela = por + a). If the speaker is male, use “obrigado pela”. For masculine singular nouns, use “pelo” (e.g., “obrigada pelo convite”).
target_language_example: Obrigada pela mensagem e pelo apoio.
native_language_example: Thank you for the message and for the support.

meaning: “Thank you for the …” (said by a woman).
additional_notes: Use **obrigada** if the speaker is female; a male speaker says **obrigado pelo**. **Pelo** = **por + o** (“for the”), so it’s followed by a masculine singular noun (e.g., *conselho*, *favor*, *presente*) or a shortened idea like *pelo outro dia* (“for the other day / for the other day we spent together”). For feminine nouns, use **obrigada pela** (*por + a*).
target_language_example: Obrigada pelo presente!
native_language_example: Thank you for the gift!

additional_notes: Used to thank someone for a specific action or reason. Follow it with an infinitive verb (e.g., "obrigada por ajudar") or a noun/phrase (e.g., "obrigada por hoje"). A man says "obrigado por".
target_language_example: Obrigada por esperar por mim.
native_language_example: Thank you for waiting for me.

meaning: 'thank you for (verb)-ing me / doing (something) for me'.
additional_notes: Used by a woman speaker (obrigada). It’s followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., acompanhar, contar, dedicar, salvar) and then the object pronoun me (“me”). You can also say obrigado por me... if the speaker is a man. In everyday speech, you may also hear obrigada por + infinitive without me when it’s clear who benefits.
target_language_example: Obrigada por me ajudar com a mala.
native_language_example: Thank you for helping me with the suitcase.

meaning: “thank you for the …” (used before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for something specific: Obrigado/a pela + feminine noun (pela = por + a). Change to “obrigado” (male speaker) or “obrigada” (female speaker). With a masculine noun, use “obrigado/a pelo …” (pelo = por + o).
target_language_example: Obrigado pela ajuda!
native_language_example: Thank you for the help!

additional_notes: Used to thank someone for a specific thing/event, followed by a masculine singular noun: "pelo" = "por" + "o" (for + the). With feminine singular nouns, use "obrigado pela"; with plural, "obrigado pelos/pelas". Women typically say "obrigada" instead of "obrigado" (agreement with the speaker).
target_language_example: Obrigado pelo seu tempo e pela ajuda.
native_language_example: Thanks for your time and for the help.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone for an action or thing. It is usually followed by a noun or an infinitive/verb phrase: obrigado por ajudares / obrigado por me ajudar. A female speaker typically says obrigada por instead of obrigado por.
target_language_example: Obrigado por vir hoje.
native_language_example: Thank you for coming today.

meaning: "Thanks for" (followed by a verb about what someone did for me).
additional_notes: Used to thank someone for an action: "Obrigado/a por me" + infinitive (e.g., avisar, ajudar, explicar). "Me" means “me” and is the object of the next verb (“for warning me / helping me”). You can also use other pronouns: "por te", "por nos", "por o/a". Note: "obrigado" is typically said by men and "obrigada" by women.
target_language_example: Obrigado por me ajudar com isto.
native_language_example: Thanks for helping me with this.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone for coming/attending. You can add where/when: “Obrigado por vir ao nosso cinema” (…to our cinema), “Obrigado por vir no seu dia de folga” (…on your day off). Also works with “por” + other verbs: “Obrigado por ajudar” (thanks for helping). Gender agreement: men usually say “obrigado”, women “obrigada”.
target_language_example: Obrigado por vir à reunião hoje.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming to the meeting today.

additional_notes: Used for age with "ter" (e.g., "Ela tem oito anos" = "She is eight"). It can also express a duration of time ("em oito anos" = "in eight years" / "for the first time in eight years"; "há oito anos" = "eight years ago"). With comparisons: "oito anos mais velho" = "eight years older". For ongoing duration in the past up to now, beginners will often hear "há oito anos" or "faz oito anos" (more natural than "por oito anos" in many cases).
target_language_example: Moro aqui há oito anos.
native_language_example: I've lived here for eight years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a daily amount of time spent doing something (work, sleep, etc.). Structure: number + "horas" + "por dia" (= per day / a day). You can swap the number: "seis horas por dia", "dez horas por dia".
target_language_example: Eles trabalham oito horas por dia.
native_language_example: They work eight hours a day.

additional_notes: Used to draw someone’s attention to something you’re pointing at ("Olha lá o poste!") or as a warning/caution (similar to "Watch out!"). Often said on its own: "Olha lá!" It’s very common in spoken Portuguese; "olha" is the "you" command form of "olhar" (to look), and "lá" means "there".
target_language_example: Olha lá, cuidado com o degrau!
native_language_example: Watch out, careful with the step!

meaning: "Look" / "just look"; also "listen/hey" to get someone’s attention.
additional_notes: Very common in speech. Used to point something out ("Olha só aquilo!" = "Just look at that!") or to introduce what you’re about to say ("Olha só, ..." ≈ "Look/Listen, ..."). Often conveys surprise, emphasis, or mild frustration depending on tone. Informal; the literal idea is "look" + "only/just."
target_language_example: Olha só, eu já expliquei isso duas vezes.
native_language_example: Look, I’ve already explained this twice.

additional_notes: "Olhando" is the gerund of "olhar" (to look). "Olhando para" is used to say someone is directing their eyes/attention toward a person or thing. It often corresponds to English "looking at" (sometimes "staring at" depending on context). Common pattern: "estar + olhando para" (was/were looking at), and the object comes after "para" (e.g., "olhando para ela", "olhando para as patas").
target_language_example: Por que você está olhando para mim?
native_language_example: Why are you looking at me?

additional_notes: Used for directing your eyes toward someone, something, or a direction. Often followed by a person, object, or place: olhar para mim, olhar para a janela, olhar para trás.
target_language_example: Você pode olhar para mim por um instante?
native_language_example: Can you look at me for a moment?

additional_notes: Imperative (command) form of the verb "olhar" + "para". Used to tell someone to direct their eyes/attention to something: "Olhe para o relógio" (Look at the clock). Often corresponds to English "look at"; it can also mean "look toward" depending on context.
target_language_example: Olhe para mim, por favor.
native_language_example: Look at me, please.

additional_notes: Imperative form of the verb olhar (“to look”), using the polite/neutral command (você). Often used to get someone’s attention or to make them focus on you. In informal situations with friends/family you may also hear: “olha pra mim” (tu) or “olha para mim”.
target_language_example: Por favor, olhe para mim quando eu estiver falando.
native_language_example: Please, look at me when I’m speaking.

additional_notes: Imperative (a command/request) using the formal/neutral verb form (você). Often used to get someone’s attention or to insist they focus on you. “Pra” is a very common spoken contraction of “para” (more formal: “Olhe para mim.”).
target_language_example: Olhe pra mim quando eu estiver falando.
native_language_example: Look at me when I’m talking.

additional_notes: Most commonly used in the expression “a olho nu” = “with the naked eye” (i.e., without binoculars, a microscope, a telescope, etc.). Often used in science/tech contexts: “visível a olho nu” = “visible to the naked eye.”
target_language_example: A Lua pode ser vista a olho nu em noites claras.
native_language_example: The Moon can be seen with the naked eye on clear nights.

meaning: a black eye (bruising around the eye).
additional_notes: Used with the verb “estar” (temporary state): “Estou com um olho roxo” = “I have a black eye.” Often appears with “com” to indicate someone is currently affected. Literally “purple eye,” referring to the bruise color.
target_language_example: Ela apareceu no trabalho com um olho roxo.
native_language_example: She showed up at work with a black eye.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s eye color. Usually appears after the verb "ter" (to have): "ter olhos azuis" = "to have blue eyes." "Olhos" is plural, so the adjective agrees: "azuis" (plural).
target_language_example: Eu tenho olhos azuis, e minha irmã tem olhos castanhos.
native_language_example: I have blue eyes, and my sister has brown eyes.

meaning: “looked at” / “looked to(ward)” (past tense of olhar para).
additional_notes: Used with a direct object to say someone directed their gaze toward something/someone: olhou para + noun/pronoun (e.g., olhou para o céu, olhou para ela). It’s the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of olhar para. You can add details like direction (olhou para cima) or attitude (olhou para alguém com expectativa).
target_language_example: Ele olhou para mim e sorriu.
native_language_example: He looked at me and smiled.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of "olhar para" = “to look at,” with "mim" = “me.” Used for a completed action in the past. You can swap the pronoun: "olhou para você" (looked at you), "olhou para ele/ela" (looked at him/her).
target_language_example: Quando eu entrei, ele olhou para mim e sorriu.
native_language_example: When I came in, he looked at me and smiled.

additional_notes: Used to ask about or refer to a female person’s location. Often appears inside a longer question or statement (e.g., “Você sabe onde ela está?” = “Do you know where she is?”). You can swap the pronoun: “onde ele está” (where he is), “onde você está” (where you are), “onde estão” (where they are).
target_language_example: Eu não sei onde ela está agora.
native_language_example: I don’t know where she is right now.

additional_notes: Used to ask or state someone’s location. It often appears in indirect questions after verbs like saber (to know), achar (to think), dizer (to say/tell), or perguntar (to ask): “Eu não sei onde ele está.” In a direct question, it can stand alone: “Onde ele está agora?” Note: in expressions like “onde ele está com a cabeça”, it’s idiomatic and means “what’s he thinking?” rather than physical location.
target_language_example: Você sabe onde ele está?
native_language_example: Do you know where he is?

additional_notes: Used in direct questions (“Onde ele mora?”) and in indirect questions after verbs like saber (to know), descobrir (to find out), or perguntar (to ask): “Não sei onde ele mora.” Word order stays the same in indirect questions (no inversion like in English). You can swap ele (he) for other subjects: onde ela mora (where she lives), onde você mora (where you live).
target_language_example: Você sabe onde ele mora?
native_language_example: Do you know where he lives?

additional_notes: Used to ask or report someone’s location. Common in direct questions ("Onde eles estão?") and indirect questions/statements after verbs like saber/perguntar ("Não sei onde eles estão"). Often the subject pronoun can be omitted: "onde estão?".
target_language_example: Não sei onde eles estão agora.
native_language_example: I don't know where they are right now.

additional_notes: Used to ask about or point out the current location or situation. Often appears inside a longer sentence (e.g., after verbs like saber (to know), ver (to see), olhar (to look), or as part of a statement like Ninguém deveria saber onde estamos = Nobody should know where we are). In questions, it can imply being lost or checking your position: Você sabe onde estamos?
target_language_example: Acho que estamos perdidos — você sabe onde estamos?
native_language_example: I think we’re lost—do you know where we are?

additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s location in the past. "Onde" = "where" and "estava" is the imperfect past of "estar" (to be/to be located). Often followed by a person/subject (e.g., "Onde estava a Cecília?") or a time reference (e.g., "na hora do..." = "at the time of...").
target_language_example: Onde estava você ontem à noite?
native_language_example: Where were you last night?

additional_notes: Literally “where is going.” The subject is often omitted when it’s understood from context, so it can address a person (“Where are you going?”) or ask about something’s destination (“Where is it going?” e.g., a train). You can add the subject for clarity: “Onde você está indo?” (you), “Onde está indo o trem?” (the train).
target_language_example: Davus, onde está indo?
native_language_example: Davus, where are you going?

additional_notes: Used to ask or say where someone or something is. It can appear in direct questions (Onde está o livro?) or indirect ones (Sei onde está). With você, Portuguese still uses está because você takes third-person singular verbs.
target_language_example: Onde está o banheiro?
native_language_example: Where is the bathroom?

additional_notes: Used to ask where someone or something is when the noun is feminine singular (a). For masculine singular, use "onde está o". Often followed by a name or object: "Onde está a Laurie?", "Onde está a impressora?".
target_language_example: Onde está a minha mochila?
native_language_example: Where is my backpack?

additional_notes: Used to ask where a specific masculine singular noun is. The noun usually comes right after this phrase: for example, "onde está o livro?" = "where is the book?". For feminine nouns, use "onde está a" instead.
target_language_example: Onde está o banheiro?
native_language_example: Where is the bathroom?

meaning: “where is my …?” (asking where something you own is).
additional_notes: Used to ask the location of a masculine noun that belongs to you. Structure: “Onde está o meu + [masculine noun]?” For feminine nouns, use “Onde está a minha + [feminine noun]?” You can also use the plural: “Onde estão os meus…?” / “Onde estão as minhas…?”
target_language_example: Onde está o meu passaporte?
native_language_example: Where is my passport?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the location of something or someone. "Onde" = "where" and "estão" is the plural form of "estar" (to be), so it’s used with plural nouns (or polite "you" referring to plural things). For a single item/person, use "onde está?"
target_language_example: Onde estão os banheiros?
native_language_example: Where are the bathrooms?

meaning: “where are the…?” (asking where several feminine plural things are).
additional_notes: Used to ask for the location of multiple items that take the feminine plural article “as” (e.g., bolachas, colheres, tesouras). For masculine plural nouns, use “Onde estão os…?”. Often followed by the noun: “Onde estão as chaves?”
target_language_example: Onde estão as chaves?
native_language_example: Where are the keys?

meaning: “where are the…?” (asking the location of plural masculine things/people).
additional_notes: Used to ask where specific items or people are. "Onde" = where, "estão" = are, "os" = the (plural masculine). For plural feminine nouns, use "onde estão as" (e.g., "Onde estão as chaves?"). You can also add "meus"/"seus" etc.: "Onde estão os meus filhos?"
target_language_example: Onde estão os banheiros?
native_language_example: Where are the bathrooms?

meaning: “where is the…?” (asking for the location of a feminine noun/place).
additional_notes: Used to ask where something is located. It’s typically followed by a place or building name that is feminine (often with article “a”), e.g., a delegacia, a clínica, a estação, a lavanderia, a piscina. With masculine nouns you’ll usually hear “onde fica o…?” (o banco, o banheiro).
target_language_example: Com licença, onde fica a farmácia mais próxima?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the nearest pharmacy?

meaning: “where is the…?” (asking where a place is located).
additional_notes: Used to ask for the location of a specific place. It’s the start of a question and is followed by a masculine noun (o banco, o consulado, o zoológico). For feminine nouns, use “onde fica a…?” (e.g., onde fica a estação?). You can also use it inside another sentence after “sabe/pode me dizer…” (e.g., “Você sabe onde fica o…?”).
target_language_example: Com licença, onde fica o metrô mais próximo?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the nearest subway station?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the place/store where you can purchase something. Often followed directly by the item (e.g., "Onde posso comprar café?") or by "um/uma" + noun. You can also add "aqui" for "around here" ("Onde posso comprar café aqui?").
target_language_example: Onde posso comprar um cartão SIM?
native_language_example: Where can I buy a SIM card?

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indefinite place: the exact location doesn’t matter or isn’t known. Often followed by the subjunctive (e.g., "onde quer que você vá"). It can appear mid-sentence ("...onde quer que seja") or at the beginning ("Onde quer que...").
target_language_example: Onde quer que você esteja, eu vou te encontrar.
native_language_example: Wherever you are, I’ll find you.

additional_notes: Used to express curiosity or uncertainty about a place. It’s common in spoken Portuguese and often introduces a question you don’t really expect an immediate factual answer to. Structure: onde (“where”) + será (future of ser, here meaning “could it be…”) + que (adds emphasis).
target_language_example: Onde será que deixei minhas chaves?
native_language_example: I wonder where I left my keys.

additional_notes: Used to ask where someone does something or where they put/went somewhere. The verb that comes after você shows the tense, so English often needs do/did even though Portuguese does not.
target_language_example: Onde você mora agora?
native_language_example: Where do you live now?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s opinion/guess about a place or destination. It’s often followed by a full clause (e.g., onde você acha que ele está indo?). In everyday speech, “que” may be dropped: “Onde você acha que ele foi?” / “Onde você acha que ele foi?”.
target_language_example: Onde você acha que fica a estação de metrô mais perto?
native_language_example: Where do you think the nearest subway station is?

additional_notes: Used to ask the place (or source) where someone learned a skill. Follow it with an infinitive verb: “Onde você aprendeu a + [verb]?” In speech you may also hear “Onde você aprendeu a…?” with the rest understood from context.
target_language_example: Onde você aprendeu a dirigir?
native_language_example: Where did you learn to drive?

additional_notes: Used to ask where someone purchased something. Often followed by the item (e.g., “Onde você comprou essa camiseta?”). You can change “você” to “tu” (Onde tu compraste...?) depending on region, and the tense is past (comprou = you bought).
target_language_example: Onde você comprou esse vestido?
native_language_example: Where did you buy that dress?

meaning: “Where did you get (it)?” / “Where did you manage to get (it)?”
additional_notes: Used to ask about the source or origin of something someone has (money, objects, a tan, information, etc.). Often followed by a noun (“Onde você conseguiu esse dinheiro?”) or used alone when the context is clear (“Onde você conseguiu?”). In Portugal you may also hear “Onde conseguiste…?” (informal singular) or “Onde conseguiu…?” (more formal).
target_language_example: Onde você conseguiu esse casaco?
native_language_example: Where did you get that coat?

additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s past location (often because they were missing/late or you expected them). In Brazil it’s common in casual speech; you can make it more polite/neutral by adding “(a)”: “Onde você estava?” → “Onde você estava, por favor?” or “Onde o senhor/a senhora estava?” (more formal).
target_language_example: Onde você estava ontem à noite?
native_language_example: Where were you last night?

additional_notes: A question asking where someone was (their location) during a past period of time. Often implies surprise, concern, or that the person was expected earlier. You can add a time expression: onde você esteve hoje? (today), ontem à tarde? (yesterday afternoon), a tarde inteira? (all afternoon), esse tempo todo? (all this time). Uses esteve (past of estar); for more formal address you may hear: Onde o senhor/a senhora esteve?
target_language_example: Onde você esteve esse tempo todo? Eu estava preocupado.
native_language_example: Where have you been all this time? I was worried.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s location (“Onde você está?” = “Where are you?”) or inside a larger sentence to refer to a place (“Ele sabe onde você está.” = “He knows where you are.”). In everyday speech, people often drop “você”: “Onde está?” (more neutral) or use “você” for clarity/emphasis.
target_language_example: Não sei onde você está agora.
native_language_example: I don’t know where you are right now.

additional_notes: Uses onde (“where”) + você (“you”) + mora (from morar, “to live”). It can be a direct question (Onde você mora?) or used inside a longer sentence meaning “where you live” (Eu sei onde você mora.). In Brazil, você is common; in Portugal you may hear Onde moras? (informal) or Onde é que mora?
target_language_example: Onde você mora atualmente?
native_language_example: Where do you live currently?

meaning: “Where are you going?” / “Where do you go?”
additional_notes: Used to ask about someone’s destination (right now or in general, depending on context). In Brazilian Portuguese it’s very common to also say “Pra onde você vai?” (“To where are you going?”) for emphasis on destination. “Onde você vai?” can sound like “Where are you headed?” or “Where are you going?”
target_language_example: Ei, onde você vai agora?
native_language_example: Hey, where are you going now?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the location of a group (“you all”). It often introduces a full clause: Onde vocês moram? (Where do you live?). In Brazil, people often use “vocês” for plural “you” in most situations (even informal). In Portugal, “vocês” exists but may sound less formal than “os senhores / as senhoras” in some contexts.
target_language_example: Onde vocês estão agora?
native_language_example: Where are you all right now?

additional_notes: Common way to form a “where” question in Portuguese. It’s often interchangeable with just “onde” (e.g., “Onde você mora?”), but “onde é que…” is a bit more emphatic/colloquial in tone. Word order stays like a normal statement after it: “Onde é que você mora?” = “Where do you live?” (literally “Where is it that you live?”).
target_language_example: Onde é que a gente compra bilhetes?
native_language_example: Where do we buy tickets?

additional_notes: Used to say something happened during the night/evening of the previous day. Very common in storytelling and past events. Often comes at the end of the sentence (e.g., "Eu vi isso ontem à noite").
target_language_example: Eu cheguei em casa tarde ontem à noite.
native_language_example: I got home late last night.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened the night before today. It’s a common time expression in the past, often placed at the end of the sentence. You may also hear just “ontem” (yesterday) when the exact time isn’t important.
target_language_example: Cheguei em casa tarde ontem à noite.
native_language_example: I got home late last night.

additional_notes: Time expression meaning the night/evening of yesterday. Very common for talking about what happened the previous night. Usually goes at the end of the sentence, but it can also come at the beginning for emphasis.
target_language_example: A gente chegou tarde em casa ontem à noite.
native_language_example: We got home late last night.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened in the afternoon of the previous day. Very common in everyday narration and storytelling. You can also vary it similarly: "ontem de manhã" (yesterday morning), "ontem à noite" (last night).
target_language_example: Eu te liguei ontem à tarde, mas você não atendeu.
native_language_example: I called you yesterday afternoon, but you didn’t answer.

additional_notes: Plural masculine noun phrase: “os” = “the” (plural), “lobos” = “wolves” (plural of “lobo”). Can refer to actual wolves or be used as a team/mascot name depending on context.
target_language_example: Os lobos vivem em matilhas.
native_language_example: Wolves live in packs.

additional_notes: Plural of "o alemão" (a German man / German person). Used to refer to Germans as a group; depending on context it can mean German soldiers/authorities (especially in war or occupation contexts). Often used with verbs in the plural: "Os alemães estão..."
target_language_example: Os alemães chegaram cedo para a reunião.
native_language_example: The Germans arrived early for the meeting.

additional_notes: Plural of "o aluno". Used for a group of students; in Portuguese, the masculine plural ("os alunos") can refer to a group of only males or a mixed-gender group. For an all-female group, you can also say "as alunas".
target_language_example: Os alunos estão na sala de aula.
native_language_example: The students are in the classroom.

additional_notes: Plural, masculine form used to refer to Americans as a group. Singular: "o americano" (a male American / an American person), feminine: "a americana"; plural feminine: "as americanas". In many contexts it specifically means people from the United States.
target_language_example: Os americanos gostam muito de esportes.
native_language_example: Americans like sports a lot.

additional_notes: Definite plural form of "amigo" (male friends, or a mixed-gender group). Used for friends in general or a specific known group ("the friends"). For an all-female group, use "as amigas"; as a general idea without "the," you’ll often see "amigos" without the article.
target_language_example: Vou sair com os amigos hoje à noite.
native_language_example: I’m going out with (the) friends tonight.

additional_notes: Plural definite form: "os" = "the" (masculine plural) + "animais" = "animals." Used when talking about specific animals or animals in general as a group (e.g., animals in nature, animals being blamed).
target_language_example: As crianças adoram observar os animais no zoológico.
native_language_example: The children love to watch the animals at the zoo.

additional_notes: Plural masculine with the definite article: "os" = "the" + "bandidos" (criminals/robbers). Used for a group of criminals, and sometimes more loosely for “the bad guys” (in a story, movie, etc.). Singular: "o bandido".
target_language_example: A polícia prendeu os bandidos depois do assalto.
native_language_example: The police arrested the criminals after the robbery.

additional_notes: Plural of “o braço” (arm). In Portuguese, body parts are often used with the definite article (o/a/os/as) where English uses a possessive: “Levante os braços” = “Raise your arms.” Common in commands (“Levante os braços!”) and set phrases like “com os braços cruzados” (“with [his/her] arms crossed”).
target_language_example: Ela ficou com os braços cruzados durante a reunião.
native_language_example: She stood with her arms crossed during the meeting.

additional_notes: Plural in Portuguese when talking about head hair in general (like “my hair”, “her hair”), even though English usually uses the singular “hair”. Often used with possessives or with a person implied by context (e.g., “cortou-me os cabelos” = “cut my hair”).
target_language_example: Vou lavar os cabelos antes de sair.
native_language_example: I'm going to wash my hair before going out.

meaning: 'the dogs' (usually pet dogs; can also mean puppies in some contexts).
additional_notes: Plural definite noun phrase: "os" = "the" (masculine plural) + "cachorros" = "dogs". Often used for household dogs, but depending on context "cachorro" can also refer to a puppy/young dog. Common with verbs like "dar comida" (to feed), "querer entrar" (to want to come in), etc.
target_language_example: Os cachorros estão no quintal.
native_language_example: The dogs are in the backyard.

additional_notes: Common in Brazilian Portuguese in casual speech. Refers to a group of men or, more generally, a group of people (similar to “the guys” in English). Note: literally “the faces,” but it’s used to mean “guys,” so the meaning isn’t literal.
target_language_example: Os caras chegaram cedo.
native_language_example: The guys arrived early.

additional_notes: "Os" is the masculine plural definite article (“the”), used with masculine plural nouns like "carros" (carro = car). Commonly used to talk about cars in general or specific cars already known in context.
target_language_example: Os carros estão estacionados na rua.
native_language_example: The cars are parked on the street.

additional_notes: Plural definite form of "cavalo" (horse). Used when talking about specific horses or horses in general (as a species/group), depending on context.
target_language_example: Os cavalos estão no campo.
native_language_example: The horses are in the field.

additional_notes: Plural definite noun phrase: "os" = "the" (masculine plural) + "cientistas" = "scientists". Used to refer to scientists in general or a specific known group, depending on context.
target_language_example: Os cientistas estão estudando uma nova vacina.
native_language_example: The scientists are studying a new vaccine.

additional_notes: Plural masculine form of "o cliente". Used for people who buy something or use a service (e.g., in a store, restaurant, hotel, office). It can also refer to clients in a professional relationship (lawyer, therapist, etc.).
target_language_example: Os clientes querem falar com o gerente.
native_language_example: The customers want to speak with the manager.

additional_notes: Masculine plural definite article + noun: "os" = "the" (plural), "cães" = "dogs". Used to refer to specific dogs already known from context. Singular: "o cão" (the dog).
target_language_example: Os cães estão no quintal.
native_language_example: The dogs are in the yard.

additional_notes: “Dado” can mean either “data/a piece of information” or “a die” (singular of dice). Context usually makes it clear: with verbs like *rolar* or *jogar* → “dice” (*rolar/jogar os dados* = to roll the dice); with verbs like *checar* or *analisar* → “data” (*checar os dados* = to check the data).
target_language_example: Preciso analisar os dados antes da reunião.
native_language_example: I need to analyze the data before the meeting.

additional_notes: Usually refers to fingers: Abra os dedos (“Open your fingers/spread your fingers”), com os dedos (“with your fingers”), cortar os dedos (“cut your fingers”), lamber os dedos (“lick your fingers”). To specify toes, Portuguese often says dedos do pé (“toes”), as in os dedos do pé. In the idiom cruzar os dedos, it means “cross your fingers” (for luck).
target_language_example: Estou com tinta nos dedos.
native_language_example: I have paint on my fingers.

additional_notes: Plural of "o dente" (tooth). Commonly used with hygiene verbs like "escovar" (to brush): "escovar os dentes" = "to brush your teeth." With "perder", it means to lose teeth (e.g., from age or a dental problem).
target_language_example: Eu escovo os dentes antes de dormir.
native_language_example: I brush my teeth before going to sleep.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase with the definite article (o detalhe → os detalhes). Used when asking for more information or the specific points of a plan/story. Common with verbs like dar (give), pedir (ask for), dizer/explicar (tell/explain), and deixar de lado (set aside/ignore).
target_language_example: Pode me passar os detalhes do voo?
native_language_example: Can you give me the flight details?

additional_notes: Plural of “o documento.” Common for paperwork like forms, contracts, IDs, or other official papers. You’ll often see it with verbs like assinar (to sign), enviar (to send), deixar (to leave), trazer (to bring).
target_language_example: Você trouxe os documentos para a reunião?
native_language_example: Did you bring the documents for the meeting?

additional_notes: Means “the two” / “both (of them).” Uses the masculine plural article (os), so it’s used for two males or a mixed-gender pair. For two females, use “as duas.” It can refer to people (“Os dois são da Austrália.”) or things (“quebrou os dois braços” = broke both arms).
target_language_example: Os dois querem ir comigo.
native_language_example: Both of them want to go with me.

additional_notes: “Os” is the masculine plural form of “the” in Portuguese, used before plural masculine nouns (like “elefantes”). You’ll often see it in general statements about a whole group/species (e.g., facts about elephants). Singular: “o elefante” = “the elephant.”
target_language_example: Os elefantes vivem em grupos.
native_language_example: Elephants live in groups.

meaning: 'the students' (male students or a mixed group).
additional_notes: Definite plural with the article "os" + plural noun "estudantes". It’s used for a specific group of students; use "estudantes" without the article for a general idea (e.g., "Estudantes precisam de descanso" = "Students need rest"). Feminine form: "as estudantes" (all-female group).
target_language_example: Os estudantes chegaram cedo para a prova.
native_language_example: The students arrived early for the test.

additional_notes: Plural of "o fato". Used to refer to true information or the real details of a situation. Often appears after verbs like "conhecer" (to know) or "precisar de" (to need).
target_language_example: Antes de decidir, quero ouvir os fatos.
native_language_example: Before deciding, I want to hear the facts.

additional_notes: Plural definite form of "o filho" (son/child). Often used to mean "the kids/children" in general (especially when gender isn’t important), or specifically "the sons" depending on context. Possession is commonly shown with "de": "os filhos deles" (their children), "os filhos do Sully" (Sully’s children).
target_language_example: Os filhos da Ana estudam aqui.
native_language_example: Ana’s children study here.

additional_notes: Plural masculine form used to refer to French people as a group. Singular: "o francês" (a French man / the French language, depending on context); feminine: "a francesa"; plural feminine: "as francesas". Often used with general statements (e.g., habits, history) or to refer to a specific group of French people in a situation.
target_language_example: Os franceses falam francês.
native_language_example: The French speak French.

meaning: "the boys" / "the guys" (male kids or young men).
additional_notes: Plural masculine noun phrase: "os" = "the" and "garotos" = "boys/guys". Often used for a group of male children or teenagers, and sometimes informally for young men (similar to "the guys").
target_language_example: Os garotos estão brincando no parque.
native_language_example: The boys are playing in the park.

additional_notes: Definite article + plural noun. Used to talk about cats in general (“Cats …”) or about specific cats known from context. Singular: “o gato” (the cat). Feminine plural: “as gatas” (the female cats).
target_language_example: Os gatos dormem muito durante o dia.
native_language_example: Cats sleep a lot during the day.

meaning: “the cats are” / “cats are” (plural, present tense of *ser*).
additional_notes: Used with **ser** to describe what cats are like in general or to state a general fact: **os gatos são + adjective/noun**. It can also appear in the proverb **De noite, todos os gatos são cinza** (“At night, all cats are grey”), meaning differences are less noticeable in the dark.
target_language_example: Os gatos são muito curiosos.
native_language_example: Cats are very curious.

additional_notes: "os" is the plural masculine definite article (“the”), used here with "homens" (men). It can refer to specific men (“the men”) or to men as a group in general, often in comparisons like "as mulheres... os homens...".
target_language_example: Os homens da minha família gostam de futebol.
native_language_example: The men in my family like soccer.

additional_notes: Plural form with the masculine plural article “os”, used for mixed-gender groups or people in general. Often used when contrasting humans with animals, gods, aliens, or robots. Singular: “o humano” (the human) or more commonly “o ser humano” (the human being).
target_language_example: Os humanos precisam de água e comida para sobreviver.
native_language_example: Humans need water and food to survive.

additional_notes: Plural, masculine form of “inglês” used to talk about English people as a group. It can refer specifically to people from England, but in everyday speech it’s also often used broadly for “the British,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Os ingleses gostam muito de chá.
native_language_example: The English really like tea.

additional_notes: Definite plural: os + japonês. Used to talk about Japanese people in general, or a specific group already known in context. For an all-female group you can also see “as japonesas.”
target_language_example: Os japoneses gostam muito de comida japonesa.
native_language_example: Japanese people really like Japanese food.

additional_notes: Plural of "o jovem" (a young person). Used with "os" to talk about young people as a group in general (e.g., "popular among young people"). In speech, "Cadê os jovens?" is a casual way to ask where they are.
target_language_example: Esse evento é voltado para os jovens.
native_language_example: This event is aimed at young people.

additional_notes: Masculine plural definite article + noun. Used to talk about specific books that are already known from context (e.g., a set of textbooks, library books, or books on a shelf). Singular: "o livro"; indefinite plural: "uns livros" (some books).
target_language_example: Eu coloquei os livros na mochila.
native_language_example: I put the books in the backpack.

additional_notes: Plural definite form: "os" = "the" (masculine plural) + "macacos" = "monkeys". Used when talking about monkeys in general or specific monkeys already known in the context. Note: "macaco(s)" can also be used as a racist insult in some contexts—avoid using it to refer to people.
target_language_example: Os macacos estão no zoológico.
native_language_example: The monkeys are at the zoo.

meaning: “the best” (plural masculine; can also be mixed-gender).
additional_notes: Used for more than one person/thing. It’s the plural of “o melhor” (“the best”). Often appears with “de/do mundo” (“in/of the world”), or in comparisons like “entre os melhores” (“among the best”). With a noun: “os melhores sanduíches” = “the best sandwiches.”
target_language_example: Quais são os melhores restaurantes aqui perto?
native_language_example: Which are the best restaurants near here?

additional_notes: Definite plural of menino (“boy”). Used to refer to a specific group of boys (already known from context). In Brazilian Portuguese it can also be a casual way to refer to a group of male kids/guys (“the guys”), depending on context.
target_language_example: Os meninos estão brincando no parque.
native_language_example: The boys are playing in the park.

additional_notes: Means a group of male friends or a mixed group (men and women). It’s the plural of "o meu amigo". Often used after prepositions like "com" (with), "sem" (without), and "para" (for/to). In Brazilian Portuguese you may also hear "meus amigos" without "os" depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Hoje vou sair com os meus amigos depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: Today I’m going out with my friends after work.

additional_notes: Literally “the my parents.” In Portuguese, possessives are often used with the definite article (o/a/os/as), especially in European Portuguese, but it’s also common in Brazilian Portuguese. Use it to talk about your mother and father together. The verb may agree in plural: “Os meus pais moram...” (“My parents live...” ).
target_language_example: Hoje vou jantar com os meus pais.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to have dinner with my parents.

additional_notes: Used to talk about shoes that belong to the speaker. Includes the masculine plural definite article + possessive: os (the, plural) + meus (my, masculine plural) + sapatos (shoes). For feminine plural items, you’d use “as minhas …” (e.g., as minhas botas).
target_language_example: Não encontro os meus sapatos.
native_language_example: I can’t find my shoes.

additional_notes: Plural masculine noun phrase used to refer to dead people as a group (often in spooky, religious, or historical contexts). Singular: "o morto" (the dead person). You may also hear "os defuntos" (the deceased) as a more formal/softer option.
target_language_example: Dizem que os mortos descansam em paz.
native_language_example: They say the dead rest in peace.

additional_notes: Plural definite form of "médico" (doctor). Used for a specific group of doctors already known from context (e.g., the doctors treating someone). For an all-female group, you can also hear "as médicas"; as a mixed or general group, "os médicos" is common.
target_language_example: Os médicos pediram mais exames.
native_language_example: The doctors asked for more tests.

additional_notes: Masculine plural noun with the definite article (“os” = “the”). Used for ships/large boats in contexts like arriving at a port, loading cargo, or giving orders.
target_language_example: Os navios vão partir ao amanhecer.
native_language_example: The ships are going to leave at dawn.

additional_notes: Plural masculine form of "o nosso". Used to mean "our" before a masculine plural noun (e.g., "os nossos vizinhos") or on its own as a pronoun meaning "ours" (e.g., "os nossos" = "our people/our things" from context). Feminine plural is "as nossas".
target_language_example: Os nossos amigos chegam amanhã.
native_language_example: Our friends arrive tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to refer to children belonging to “us” (the speaker plus another person or group). You can also say “nossos filhos” without “os” in many sentences (especially after a preposition like “para nossos filhos”). “Filhos” can mean children in general (not only sons), depending on context.
target_language_example: Vamos pensar no futuro dos nossos filhos.
native_language_example: Let’s think about our children’s future.

additional_notes: Used to refer to numerical values, digits, or figures in general. Common in contexts like learning numerals ("os números romanos" = "Roman numerals") and identifying numbers on documents (e.g., the numbers on a check). It can also mean statistics/figures depending on context (e.g., sales numbers).
target_language_example: Podes ler os números no recibo?
native_language_example: Can you read the numbers on the receipt?

additional_notes: Literally “the eyes” (plural). Used for real eyes (Abre os olhos. / Tom cobriu os olhos.) and in many common expressions. In Portuguese, body parts are often said with the definite article (os), where English may use no article or a possessive (“my/your”). Common idioms: “custa os olhos da cara” = “it costs an arm and a leg” (very expensive); “abrir os olhos” can also mean “to wake up / to become alert”; “fechar os olhos” can mean “to close your eyes” or “to ignore something.”
target_language_example: Ele abriu os olhos quando ouviu o barulho.
native_language_example: He opened his eyes when he heard the noise.

additional_notes: A common way to express possession with body parts in Portuguese: definite article + noun + possessive phrase. Here, "dela" = "de" + "ela" (“of her”), and it usually refers to a specific person (not “hers” in general). You can change the owner: "os olhos dele" (his eyes), "os olhos da Maria" (Maria’s eyes). The article agrees with the noun: "os olhos" (plural), but "o olho" (one eye).
target_language_example: Eu não conseguia parar de olhar para os olhos dela.
native_language_example: I couldn’t stop looking at her eyes.

additional_notes: Literally “the eyes of him.” Used to talk about a man’s eyes (color, being open/closed, adapting to darkness, etc.). In expressions like “tirar os olhos dele,” it means “take your eyes off him” (stop looking at him).
target_language_example: Eu reparei nos olhos dele imediatamente.
native_language_example: I noticed his eyes right away.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the remaining people or things in a group already mentioned or understood from context. It often appears with numbers (os outros três = the other three) or with a noun implied (os outros andares = the other floors). Feminine plural is "as outras"; singular: "o outro" / "a outra".
target_language_example: Eu já falei com dois; agora vou falar com os outros.
native_language_example: I've already talked to two; now I'll talk to the others.

additional_notes: Means “the others” (the remaining ones in a group) or “other people” in general. It’s plural and usually refers to people, but it can also refer to things depending on context (e.g., “do que os outros” = “than the others”). Often appears after a verb like ajudar/ouvir/dizer and after comparisons like “mais … do que os outros” (more … than the others).
target_language_example: Não ligue para o que os outros dizem.
native_language_example: Don’t worry about what other people say.

additional_notes: Plural definite form of "o ovo" (egg). Used when talking about eggs as specific items (e.g., in a store, on a tray) or as a general category in context. Often appears in shopping/food situations and in fixed expressions like "quebrar os ovos" (to break the eggs).
target_language_example: Preciso de comprar os ovos para o bolo.
native_language_example: I need to buy the eggs for the cake.

additional_notes: Plural of “o pai” (the father). Often used to mean both parents together (mother and father). Don’t confuse with “o país” (the country) — note the accent: país.
target_language_example: Os pais da Ana trabalham muito.
native_language_example: Ana’s parents work a lot.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a male person's parents. "os" = "the" (plural), "pais" = "parents", "dele" = "of him/his". Often contrasts with "os pais dela" (her parents).
target_language_example: Os pais dele moram perto daqui.
native_language_example: His parents live near here.

additional_notes: Definite article + plural noun: **os** = “the” (masculine plural) and **peixes** = “fish” (plural of *peixe*). Used when talking about specific fish in general or a known group (e.g., the fish in a tank/river).
target_language_example: Os peixes estão no aquário.
native_language_example: The fish are in the aquarium.

additional_notes: Plural of "o pneu" (tire). Common in everyday contexts (car/bike tires) and in racing, where it can mean managing tire wear (e.g., "poupar os pneus" = to save/preserve the tires).
target_language_example: Antes de viajar, vou calibrar os pneus.
native_language_example: Before traveling, I’m going to inflate the tires.

additional_notes: Uses the adjective "pobres" as a noun with the definite article "os" to talk about poor people as a group. Often used in general statements or when referring to people in need (e.g., ajudar os pobres = help the poor).
target_language_example: O governo prometeu mais apoio para os pobres.
native_language_example: The government promised more support for the poor.

additional_notes: Plural definite form: "os" = "the" (masculine plural) + "policiais" = "police officers". In Portuguese, "policiais" is the plural of "policial" and can refer to officers in general or to the police who are present in a situation.
target_language_example: Os policiais chegaram rápido.
native_language_example: The police officers arrived quickly.

additional_notes: Plural of "o prato". It can mean physical plates (tableware) or, in some contexts, the dishes/food being served (e.g., "os pratos típicos" = typical dishes). Often used with kitchen verbs like "pôr" (to put/place), "trazer" (to bring), "lavar" (to wash), "quebrar" (to break).
target_language_example: Depois do jantar, eu lavo os pratos.
native_language_example: After dinner, I wash the dishes.

additional_notes: Plural of "o preço". Used when talking about prices in general (e.g., in shops, rent, the economy). Often appears with verbs like "subir" (to go up) and "cair" (to go down).
target_language_example: Os preços no supermercado estão muito altos.
native_language_example: Prices at the supermarket are very high.

meaning: "the first ones" / "the first" (plural, masculine or mixed group).
additional_notes: Used to refer to the people or things that come before all others in order or time. Common in expressions like "durante os primeiros dias" (“during the first days”) or "ser os primeiros" (“to be the first”). For an all-female group, use "as primeiras"; singular is "o primeiro" / "a primeira".
target_language_example: Chegámos cedo e fomos os primeiros a entrar.
native_language_example: We arrived early and were the first to go in.

additional_notes: Plural of "o problema" ("problem"). Often used with "de" to say whose problems they are: "os problemas do Egito" (Egypt’s problems), "os problemas dos outros" (other people’s problems). Can refer to practical difficulties (work, a test) or personal/family troubles.
target_language_example: Vamos conversar sobre os problemas e encontrar uma solução.
native_language_example: Let’s talk about the problems and find a solution.

additional_notes: Definite plural noun phrase: "os" = "the" (masculine plural) + "professores" = "teachers". Used to talk about a specific group of teachers (e.g., at a school). Singular: "o professor" (male teacher / teacher, masculine). Feminine forms: "a professora" (female teacher), plural "as professoras" (female teachers) or mixed group can also use "os professores".
target_language_example: Os professores estão na sala dos professores.
native_language_example: The teachers are in the teachers' lounge.

additional_notes: Definite plural: "os" = "the" (masculine plural) + "pássaros" = birds. Used for literal birds ("Os pássaros voam") and in the phrase "os pássaros e as abelhas" (“the birds and the bees,” i.e., talking about sex/reproduction, often with children).
target_language_example: De manhã, eu gosto de ouvir os pássaros cantando.
native_language_example: In the morning, I like to hear the birds singing.

meaning: "the feet"; in expressions like "pôr/meter os pés", "set foot" (go/enter a place).
additional_notes: Literal meaning is body parts: "Levante os pés dela" = "Lift her feet." In the common idioms "pôr os pés" and "meter os pés", it means going somewhere/entering a place, often used with "nunca" to mean you’ll never go back: "nunca mais meter os pés" = "never set foot (there) again."
target_language_example: Eu nunca mais vou meter os pés naquele bar.
native_language_example: I’m never going to set foot in that bar again.

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase with the definite article (os = “the” for masculine plural). Common for exam/test results, medical results, research results, election results, or the outcome of a process. Often used after verbs like saber/receber/ver/enviar (to know/receive/see/send the results).
target_language_example: Já saíram os resultados do exame?
native_language_example: Are the exam results out already?

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase: "os" (the, masculine plural) + "romanos" (Romans). Used to talk about the people of Rome, especially in historical contexts. Can also appear in the proverb "Quando em Roma, faça como os romanos" (“When in Rome, do as the Romans do”).
target_language_example: Os romanos construíram muitas estradas.
native_language_example: The Romans built many roads.

additional_notes: Definite plural noun phrase: "os" = "the" + "russos" = "Russians" (masculine plural; can refer to a mixed group). Often used to mean the Russian people, the Russian government, or Russian forces depending on context.
target_language_example: Os russos chegaram ontem à cidade.
native_language_example: The Russians arrived in the city yesterday.

additional_notes: Definite plural: used when talking about a specific pair of shoes or shoes in general. Often appears with verbs like tirar (to take off): tirar os sapatos = to take off your shoes.
target_language_example: Por favor, tire os sapatos antes de entrar.
native_language_example: Please take off your shoes before coming in.

additional_notes: Polite/formal way to address two or more men, often in customer service or formal situations. In European Portuguese it’s also commonly used as a formal plural “you” (instead of "vocês"). Usually takes 3rd-person plural verbs (e.g., "os senhores desejam", "os senhores estão"). Feminine equivalent: "as senhoras".
target_language_example: Os senhores precisam de ajuda?
native_language_example: Do you (gentlemen) need help?

additional_notes: Used to address two or more men (or a mixed group, in some contexts) in a polite/formal way, like “you gentlemen / you sirs.” It’s the present tense of “estar” with the subject “os senhores.” Common in formal speech, customer service, or when speaking respectfully. In Brazil, people often use “vocês estão” instead; “os senhores estão” sounds more formal. In Portugal, you may also see “Os senhores estão a + infinitive” for “you are (doing) …”.
target_language_example: Os senhores estão prontos para começar?
native_language_example: Are you gentlemen ready to start?

meaning: human beings; humans (people as a species).
additional_notes: Used in a general, scientific, or formal way to talk about people as a whole (not specific individuals). Often appears in statements comparing humans to animals or nature. Singular: "o ser humano".
target_language_example: Os seres humanos precisam de água para sobreviver.
native_language_example: Human beings need water to survive.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun: os seus irmãos (“his/her/your/their brothers”), os seus filmes (“…films”). In Portuguese, seu/sua/seus/suas can mean “your” (often formal) or “his/her/their” depending on context, so speakers may use dele/dela/deles/delas to avoid ambiguity (e.g., os talentos dele = “his talents”).
target_language_example: Ela vai trazer os seus documentos amanhã.
native_language_example: She will bring her documents tomorrow.

meaning: your friends (plural, masculine or mixed group).
additional_notes: Means “your friends.” It uses the possessive "seus" (your), which can also mean “his/her/their” depending on context, so speakers may use "os amigos dele/dela" to be extra clear. "Os" and "amigos" agree in gender/number: for an all-female group, say "as suas amigas".
target_language_example: Você vai sair com os seus amigos hoje?
native_language_example: Are you going out with your friends today?

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s children in a polite or more formal way. Literally “the your children” (os = “the” for plural masculine/mixed groups; seus = “your”; filhos = “children/sons”). Often used when addressing someone with “você”. For only daughters, you can say “as suas filhas”.
target_language_example: Os seus filhos vão à escola hoje?
native_language_example: Are your children going to school today?

meaning: “your eyes” (formal or plural) / “his/her/their eyes” (depending on context).
additional_notes: Literally “the your eyes.” In Portuguese, the possessive (seus/suas) can refer to “your” (especially formal ‘you’) or to “his/her/their,” so context usually makes it clear. Common with verbs like fechar (to close): “Feche os seus olhos.”
target_language_example: Por favor, feche os seus olhos por um momento.
native_language_example: Please close your eyes for a moment.

additional_notes: Uses "seus" (plural) to agree with "pais". In Brazilian Portuguese, "seus" often refers to the person you’re talking to, especially in more formal speech or when using "você(s)"; in everyday conversation many people also say "os teus pais" (more informal/closer) depending on region. Can also mean "his/her/their parents" if the context is talking about someone else.
target_language_example: Os seus pais moram aqui perto?
native_language_example: Do your parents live nearby?

additional_notes: Definite plural form: "os" = "the" (masculine plural) + "soldados" = "soldiers". Use it when referring to a specific group of soldiers. Singular: "o soldado" (the soldier).
target_language_example: Os soldados chegaram cedo ao quartel.
native_language_example: The soldiers arrived early at the barracks.

meaning: "yours" (masculine plural), or "your" + a masculine plural noun.
additional_notes: "Os" is the masculine plural definite article (“the”), and "teus" is the masculine plural form of the possessive "teu" (“your”). It’s used with masculine plural nouns: "os teus olhos" = “your eyes”, "os teus pais" = “your parents”. It can also stand alone to mean “yours” when the noun is understood: "Os teus são maiores" = “Yours are bigger.” (In Brazil, "os seus" is often used instead; in Portugal, "os teus" is common in informal contexts.)
target_language_example: Os teus amigos vêm hoje?
native_language_example: Are your friends coming today?

additional_notes: Plural noun phrase. Used to talk about the people who live nearby (e.g., next door or in the same building). Often comes up when discussing noise/being quiet: "os vizinhos!" can be a warning like "(Careful,) the neighbors!"
target_language_example: Não faça barulho; os vizinhos estão dormindo.
native_language_example: Don’t make noise; the neighbors are sleeping.

additional_notes: Used with the plural article "os" because in Portuguese "óculos" is normally plural even when referring to one pair. You can specify the type: "óculos de leitura" (reading glasses), "óculos de sol" (sunglasses). Possession is often shown with "de": "os óculos dele/dela" (his/her glasses).
target_language_example: Você fica melhor sem os óculos.
native_language_example: You look better without glasses.

additional_notes: Used to be vague or give an approximate example, often at the end of a suggestion, list, or question. It can soften what you say and imply “something similar” without being exact. Also common in a slightly annoyed/skeptical question (e.g., “Are you crazy or something?”).
target_language_example: A gente pode ir ao cinema, ou algo assim.
native_language_example: We can go to the movies, or something like that.

additional_notes: Used to present two possibilities: something happens or it doesn't. It often appears after a verb or adjective, especially with se, to mean “whether ... or not,” and in direct questions it can sound insistent: “are you going to ... or not?”
target_language_example: Ainda não sei se vou ou não.
native_language_example: I still don't know whether I'm going or not.

meaning: "or what?" (a tag added to a question for emphasis; often rhetorical).
additional_notes: Used at the end of a question to add pressure, impatience, or challenge (similar to “...or what?” / “...or what, exactly?”). It can sound confrontational depending on tone. It’s also common as a standalone reaction: “Ou o quê?” = “Or what?”
target_language_example: Você vai me ajudar, ou o quê?
native_language_example: Are you going to help me, or what?

additional_notes: Used to clarify, restate, or explain what was just said (like English “that is” or “in other words”). Often followed by a comma: “Ou seja, …”. Don’t confuse it with the pattern “seja … ou seja …” meaning “whether … or …” (literally “be it … or be it …”).
target_language_example: Ele não vem hoje; ou seja, a reunião vai ser amanhã.
native_language_example: He’s not coming today; in other words, the meeting will be tomorrow.

additional_notes: Means “another thing / something else.” Often used when changing topic or suggesting an alternative. With "qualquer" ("outra coisa qualquer"), it means “anything else / something else, whatever.” "Outra" agrees with the noun: feminine singular "outra coisa"; masculine would be "outro + noun" (e.g., "outro assunto" = another topic).
target_language_example: Se você não quiser isso, podemos escolher outra coisa.
native_language_example: If you don't want that, we can choose something else.

additional_notes: Used to contrast with what was just mentioned (“that’s a different situation”) or to drop/park a topic (“But that’s another story”). Often appears as “isso é outra história” or “mas isso é outra história.” Can also be used literally to mean “another (different) story,” especially with an adjective (e.g., “uma outra história mentirosa”).
target_language_example: Eu até posso ajudar, mas pagar tudo sozinho já é outra história.
native_language_example: I can help, but paying for everything alone is another matter.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a different person from the one already mentioned or expected. Often appears with "por" after verbs like "esperar" ("esperar por outra pessoa" = to wait for someone else). You may also see "uma outra pessoa" to emphasize "a different person".
target_language_example: Desculpe, eu achei que você fosse outra pessoa.
native_language_example: Sorry, I thought you were someone else.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens one more time, or repeatedly. Common after the verb: "tentar outra vez" (try again), "fazer ... outra vez" (do ... again), "voltar outra vez" (return again). Often interchangeable with "de novo" in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Pode repetir outra vez, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you repeat again, please?

additional_notes: Used to refer to additional items, tasks, or topics besides the ones already mentioned. Very common in expressions like “entre outras coisas” (“among other things”) and “ter outras coisas para fazer” (“to have other things to do”). In Portuguese it often implies “more things” or “different things” that remain.
target_language_example: Desculpa, não posso sair agora — tenho outras coisas para resolver.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go out now—I have other things to take care of.

additional_notes: Used to talk about people different from the ones already mentioned, or people in general besides yourself/your group. Often appears with the definite article: "as outras pessoas" = "the other people" (a specific group), while without the article it can be more general.
target_language_example: Não compare sua vida com a das outras pessoas.
native_language_example: Don’t compare your life with other people’s.

meaning: “the other day” (recently; on a different day, not today).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a recent past day that isn’t specified (“the other day”). With "no outro dia" it can mean “that other day / the day before” depending on context (often a past occasion you both remember). Also used at the start of a sentence as a time marker: "Outro dia, ..." = “The other day, ...”.
target_language_example: Outro dia, eu te vi no mercado, mas você estava com pressa.
native_language_example: The other day, I saw you at the market, but you were in a hurry.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an alternative method, option, or solution. Often appears with "de" ("de outro jeito" = "in another way") or in questions/negatives like "Não há outro jeito" ("There’s no other way"). You may also hear "um outro jeito" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Não há outro jeito de resolver isso.
native_language_example: There’s no other way to solve this.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a different location than the current/mentioned one. Often appears with prepositions: em outro lugar (“in another place”), para outro lugar (“to another place”), de outro lugar (“from another place”), or with nenhum: em nenhum outro lugar (“nowhere else”).
target_language_example: A gente pode comer em outro lugar.
native_language_example: We can eat somewhere else.

additional_notes: Often used literally (a different world/place) or figuratively to mean a different reality, perspective, or a better possible society. You may also see it with an article: "um outro mundo" / "outro mundo" (both commonly translate as “another world”).
target_language_example: Às vezes parece que eles vivem em outro mundo.
native_language_example: Sometimes it seems like they live in another world.

additional_notes: "Ouvi-lo" = "ouvir" (to hear / to listen to) + "-lo" (him, as a direct-object pronoun). It’s used when "him" comes after the verb (common in European Portuguese and more formal in Brazilian Portuguese). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, many people would say "ouvir ele" instead. In context it can mean simply hearing a sound ("I can hardly hear him") or listening to what someone says ("Why should I listen to him?").
target_language_example: Não consigo ouvi-lo bem por causa do barulho.
native_language_example: I can’t hear him well because of the noise.

meaning: "I heard (that)..." / "I’ve heard (that)..." (a rumor or second-hand information).
additional_notes: Used to introduce information you heard from someone else (not something you know for sure). Often implies hearsay/gossip. You can change the tense/person: "ouço dizer que" (I hear people say that), "ouvi dizer que" (I heard), "tenho ouvido dizer que" (I’ve been hearing).
target_language_example: Ouvi dizer que vai chover amanhã.
native_language_example: I heard that it’s going to rain tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to introduce information you heard from someone else (a rumor, news, or secondhand info). It’s a neutral, common way to start a conversation about what you’ve heard. You can swap the subject: “ouvi dizer que ele/ela…”, “ouvi dizer que vocês…”.
target_language_example: Ouvi dizer que você vai se mudar no mês que vem.
native_language_example: I heard that you’re going to move next month.

additional_notes:
Used to say you heard something mentioned or you’re aware of someone/something. Very common with:
- "ouvi falar de..." = "I’ve heard of/about..." (e.g., a person, place, thing)
- "ouvi falar que..." = "I heard that..." (introduces information/rumor)
In negative form, it often means you haven’t heard from someone: "Nunca mais ouvi falar dela" = "I never heard from her again."
target_language_example: Eu já ouvi falar desse restaurante, mas nunca fui.
native_language_example: I’ve heard of that restaurant, but I’ve never been.

additional_notes: Uses the gerund ("ouvindo") to describe an action in progress, often with "estar": "estou/estava ouvindo música" = "I am/was listening to music." You can add a genre after "música" (e.g., "música country").
target_language_example: Estou ouvindo música agora.
native_language_example: I’m listening to music right now.

meaning: to have heard of; to hear about.
additional_notes: Usually used with “de” + noun/person/thing: “ouvir falar de algo/alguém” = to have heard of something/someone (often without knowing details). It can also be used with “sobre” (about), but “ouvir falar de” is the most common pattern.
target_language_example: Você já chegou a ouvir falar desse restaurante?
native_language_example: Have you ever heard of that restaurant?

additional_notes: Imperative (command/request) of the verb ouvir (“to listen/hear”) + object pronoun me (“me”). Used to get someone’s attention before giving instructions or asking them to take you seriously. You can soften it with por favor (“please”).
target_language_example: Ouça-me um minuto, eu posso explicar.
native_language_example: Listen to me for a minute, I can explain.

meaning: the black sheep (the odd one out / the one considered a disgrace in a family or group).
additional_notes: Used mainly with "ser" (e.g., "Ele é a ovelha negra da família") to describe someone seen as very different from the rest, or as the one who brings shame or trouble. It can be joking or judgmental depending on tone. Usually appears with a group: "da família", "do grupo", "da turma".
target_language_example: Desde que largou a faculdade, dizem que ele virou a ovelha negra da família.
native_language_example: Since he dropped out of college, they say he became the black sheep of the family.

additional_notes: A common breakfast dish. It’s the plural of “ovo mexido” and can be followed by ingredients with “com” (e.g., “ovos mexidos com queijo”). Often used with “quer?” to offer or ask what someone wants to eat.
target_language_example: Eu quero ovos mexidos com queijo, por favor.
native_language_example: I want scrambled eggs with cheese, please.

meaning: to pay the bill (in a restaurant/bar) or pay the check.
additional_notes: Used when paying what you owe after eating/drinking somewhere (the "conta" is the bill/check). Common with verbs like "pedir" (to ask for) and "dividir" (to split): "Podemos pedir a conta?" / "Vamos dividir a conta?"
target_language_example: Desculpe, você pode trazer a conta? Eu vou pagar a conta.
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you bring the bill? I’m going to pay the bill.

additional_notes: Used for paying regular expenses like utilities, rent, credit card bills, etc. You can add a possessive to say whose bills: pagar as contas dela/dele/minhas/nossas. Often refers to the responsibility of covering household or personal expenses.
target_language_example: Preciso pagar as contas antes do fim do mês.
native_language_example: I need to pay the bills before the end of the month.

additional_notes: Used for paying rent on a home/apartment. You can add time expressions like "este mês" (this month) or "hoje" (today). In Brazil, "aluguel" is common; in some places you may also hear "renda" (especially in Portugal).
target_language_example: Tenho que pagar o aluguel hoje.
native_language_example: I have to pay the rent today.

meaning: “to pay for it/that” (pay the cost) or “to pay for it” (suffer consequences).
additional_notes: Often used literally about money: “pagar por isso” = “pay for it/that.” It can also be used figuratively as a warning or threat meaning someone will face consequences: “Você vai pagar por isso!” (“You’ll pay for this!”). Context and tone make the meaning clear.
target_language_example: Se você mentir, vai pagar por isso.
native_language_example: If you lie, you’ll pay for it.

additional_notes: Simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "pagar" (to pay) + "a conta" (the bill). Used for restaurant checks and also for household/utility bills. You can specify whose bill with "a conta dele/dela" (his/her bill) or what kind with "a conta de eletricidade / de energia elétrica" (the electricity bill).
target_language_example: Tom pagou a conta e deixou o restaurante.
native_language_example: Tom paid the bill and left the restaurant.

additional_notes: Most commonly refers to the Christian prayer “pai Nosso” (often said as “pai Nosso que estais no céu…”). It can also be used to refer to the prayer as a whole (e.g., “rezar um pai Nosso” = to say an Our Father). Often written capitalized as “Pai Nosso” and sometimes hyphenated as “Pai-Nosso,” depending on style.
target_language_example: Antes de dormir, a gente reza um pai Nosso.
native_language_example: Before going to sleep, we say an Our Father.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize an exact, literal translation or repetition with no changes. Common with verbs like "traduzir" (to translate) and "repetir" (to repeat).
target_language_example: Ele anotou minhas instruções palavra por palavra.
native_language_example: He wrote down my instructions word for word.

additional_notes: Common everyday item; also appears in the expression "um rolo de papel higiênico" (“a roll of toilet paper”). You may hear it shortened informally to "papel" when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Tem papel higiênico no banheiro?
native_language_example: Is there toilet paper in the bathroom?

additional_notes: Used to dismiss what someone is saying as not true, not serious, or just talk with no substance. Common in Brazilian Portuguese. You can say it as a full reaction ("Papo furado!") or in phrases like "Chega de papo furado" ("Enough with the nonsense") and "Corta o papo furado" ("Cut the bullshit"). Often sounds blunt and can be rude depending on tone/context.
target_language_example: Para com esse papo furado e vai estudar.
native_language_example: Stop that nonsense and go study.

additional_notes: Used to talk about two shoes as one set. Very common with purchases and shopping: "comprar um par de sapatos" (to buy a pair of shoes).
target_language_example: Preciso de um par de sapatos confortáveis para o trabalho.
native_language_example: I need a comfortable pair of shoes for work.

additional_notes: Combination of para ("for/to") + the feminine singular article a ("the"). Used before feminine singular nouns. Before women's names, the article may be optional or regional, and it usually isn't translated in English. In informal speech and writing, para a is often shortened to pra.
target_language_example: Comprei um presente para a professora.
native_language_example: I bought a present for the teacher.

meaning: to jail; to prison (go/put someone in jail).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like "ir" (to go) or "mandar" (to send) to mean being sent to jail/prison. "Cadeia" is an everyday word for jail/prison; in insults like "Vai para a cadeia!" it’s a harsh, angry command.
target_language_example: Se você fizer isso de novo, vai para a cadeia.
native_language_example: If you do that again, you’re going to jail.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of motion (especially "ir") to say someone is going to bed (to sleep/rest): "ir para a cama" = "to go to bed". Often used with routines: "antes de ir para a cama" (before going to bed).
target_language_example: Estou com sono, vou para a cama agora.
native_language_example: I’m sleepy; I’m going to bed now.

additional_notes: Used to say someone goes to bed early. Often appears with verbs like “ir” (to go) or “vou” (I’m going): “Vou para a cama cedo.” You can also shorten it to “para a cama” (“to bed”).
target_language_example: Hoje vou para a cama cedo porque estou cansado.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to bed early because I’m tired.

additional_notes: Used to indicate direction or movement toward the right side. Common with verbs like virar (turn), ir/vá (go), olhar (look), and contar (count): “da esquerda para a direita” = “from left to right.” In some contexts (especially European Portuguese), you may also hear/see “à direita” for “on the right.”
target_language_example: Siga em frente e vire para a direita no próximo cruzamento.
native_language_example: Go straight and turn right at the next intersection.
