native_language_example: That's why I arrived early.

additional_notes: Used to explain a reason or justify what was said or happened. Often comes after (or with) emphasis like "é (exatamente) por isso que…" = "that’s (exactly) why…". In speech, it can also be used on its own: "Por isso." = "That’s why / for that reason."
target_language_example: Eu não tinha dinheiro, por isso que não fui ao cinema.
native_language_example: I didn’t have money, so that’s why I didn’t go to the movies.

additional_notes: Used with **por** to indicate what something is paid/exchanged for ("I paid X for this"), what someone is responsible for ("responsible for this"), or the cause/reason ("because of this" / "this is why..."). In everyday writing/speech you’ll very often see **por isso** instead (especially meaning “because of that / that’s why / therefore”); **por isto** is more literal and points to “this” specific thing/situation.
target_language_example: Desculpa por isto; eu não queria causar problemas.
native_language_example: Sorry for this; I didn’t mean to cause problems.

meaning: “no matter how much / even though” (despite efforts).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast: despite doing something a lot, trying hard, or for a long time, the result still doesn’t happen. Often followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., "tente", "tentasse", "tenha tentado"). Common pattern: "Por mais que + (eu/você/ele...) + verb, ...".
target_language_example: Por mais que eu explique, ele não entende.
native_language_example: No matter how much I explain, he doesn’t understand.

additional_notes: Used to talk about duration. Often appears in comparisons ("por mais tempo do que..." = "for longer than...") and in negatives to mean "any longer" ("não posso ficar aqui por mais tempo" = "I can't stay here any longer").
target_language_example: Não quero esperar por mais tempo.
native_language_example: I don’t want to wait any longer.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “for me” (often like “for my sake”): Faça isso por mim. It also appears in fixed patterns like perguntar por mim (“ask about me”), esperar por mim (“wait for me”), ficar feliz por mim (“be happy for me”), and falar por mim (“speak for me”). In the sense “as far as I’m concerned,” it gives your personal opinion: Por mim, tudo bem. (“I’m fine with it.”).
target_language_example: Por mim, podemos sair mais cedo.
native_language_example: As far as I’m concerned, we can leave earlier.

meaning: because of me; due to my actions (my fault).
additional_notes: Used to say that something happened as a result of you, often implying responsibility or blame. Common with verbs like "ser"/"estar" (to be), "morrer" (to die), "acontecer" (to happen), "destruir" (to destroy). Variations: "por sua causa" (because of you), "por causa dele/dela" (because of him/her).
target_language_example: Ele perdeu o voo por minha causa.
native_language_example: He missed the flight because of me.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a long duration. It can refer to the past ("I lived... for a long time"), the future ("you won’t see... for a long time"), or a general/lasting effect ("will be remembered for a long time").
target_language_example: Não falo com ele por muito tempo.
native_language_example: I haven’t spoken to him for a long time.

additional_notes: Used to express a duration of time that something lasted in the past, present, or future. Often comes after the verb it describes: "morei lá por muitos anos" (I lived there for many years).
target_language_example: Eu trabalhei aqui por muitos anos.
native_language_example: I worked here for many years.

additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens or how much you get/pay in one month (rate or frequency). Often after a number or quantity: "três vezes por mês" (three times per month), "mil peças por mês" (a thousand pieces per month), "R$ 2.000 por mês" (R$2,000 a month).
target_language_example: Eu pago 50 reais por mês pela internet.
native_language_example: I pay 50 reais a month for internet.

meaning: "for nothing" / "for no reason"; also used in negatives as "not for anything (in the world)".
additional_notes: Common uses: (1) with a negative to emphasize refusal: "não ... por nada" / "por nada nesse mundo" = “not for anything (in the world)”. (2) to mean “without any reason/cause”: "chorar por nada" = “cry over nothing”. (3) to mean “in vain/for nothing”: "esperar ... por nada" = “wait for nothing”. In other contexts (especially replies to thanks), "Por nada" can also mean “You’re welcome.”
target_language_example: Eu não troco minha família por nada.
native_language_example: I wouldn’t trade my family for anything.

meaning: for now; for the time being.
additional_notes: Used to say something is temporary or limited to the present moment, often implying it may change later. It can appear at the start of a sentence ("Por ora, ...") or after what it modifies ("... por ora"). Common with verbs like "ficar" or "ser" to mean "for now I’ll stay..." / "that’s enough for now".
target_language_example: Por ora, vamos esperar aqui e ver o que acontece.
native_language_example: For now, let’s wait here and see what happens.

additional_notes: Used to contrast with what was just said, often after a positive/negative point ("but, on the other hand..."). It can also introduce another perspective or a different point to consider. Common in both writing and speech, typically followed by a comma: "Por outro lado, ..."
target_language_example: Gosto deste apartamento; por outro lado, é um pouco longe do trabalho.
native_language_example: I like this apartment; on the other hand, it's a bit far from work.

additional_notes: Used to ask if something is close to your current location (often with "aqui": "aqui por perto"). It can also mean someone is "around" or "present" (sometimes with the nuance of being available or involved), as in "nunca estava por perto" = "was never around."
target_language_example: Tem algum supermercado por perto?
native_language_example: Is there a supermarket nearby?

meaning: barely; by a narrow margin; almost.
additional_notes: Common in near-miss situations: "Foi por pouco" = "That was close." With "por pouco não + verb", it means something almost happened but didn’t: "Por pouco não caí" = "I almost fell." It can also mean "for little (money/effort)": "Não trabalho por pouco" = "I don’t work for little pay."
target_language_example: Por pouco não perdi o ônibus.
native_language_example: I almost missed the bus.

additional_notes: Used to ask about duration (how long something will last) or to refer to an unknown/unspecified length of time. Often appears in questions: “Por quanto tempo…?” = “For how long…?” In statements it can mean “for how long (still/anymore)”: “Não sei por quanto tempo (ainda)” = “I don’t know for how much longer.”
target_language_example: Por quanto tempo você vai ficar aqui?
native_language_example: How long are you going to stay here?

meaning: "for how long" (asking about the duration of time you).
additional_notes: Used to ask about the length/duration of an action or stay. It’s a question phrase; the verb comes after it (e.g., "por quanto tempo você ficou...?"). You can change "você" to "ele/ela" or "vocês" depending on who you’re asking about.
target_language_example: Por quanto tempo você vai ficar aqui?
native_language_example: How long are you going to stay here?

additional_notes: used to ask the reason for something, in both direct questions and indirect questions. As two words, por que is typically followed by a verb or clause. Compare with porque, which usually means "because."
target_language_example: Não entendo por que ela está chateada.
native_language_example: I don't understand why she is upset.

meaning: “why the…?” / “why is the…?” (used before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason. It’s the question form: por que = “why”, followed by a = “the” (feminine singular). Common with nouns like a bruxa (the witch), a fumaça (the smoke), a casa (the house). Note: por que (two words) = “why”; porque (one word) = “because,” which learners often mix up.
target_language_example: Por que a porta está aberta?
native_language_example: Why is the door open?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone for their reason/opinion about something. Common in conversation and interviews. Often followed by a complete clause (e.g., "por que acha que eles fizeram isso?"). You can adjust formality/person: "por que você acha que..." (more explicit), "por que acham que..." (you all/they), "por que o senhor/a senhora acha que..." (formal).
target_language_example: Por que acha que ela não veio hoje?
native_language_example: Why do you think she didn't come today?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason/motivation for a hypothetical action by an unspecified person (alguém = “someone”). Common in questions like “Por que alguém faria/iria querer…?” (“Why would someone do/want to do…?”).
target_language_example: Por que alguém diria uma coisa dessas?
native_language_example: Why would someone say something like that?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason behind people’s actions or behavior. Often followed by a verb in the present tense (e.g., "mentem", "dizem", "são"). In questions, it’s typically written as "por que" (two words).
target_language_example: Por que as pessoas falam tão alto aqui?
native_language_example: Why do people talk so loudly here?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason/justification for doing something. It’s formed by the question phrase "por que" (why) + "devo" (I should / I must), from the verb "dever". It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb: "Por que devo esperar?" (Why should I wait?). In indirect questions, Portuguese often uses "por que" or the combined form "por quê" depending on position, but in this direct question pattern you’ll usually see "Por que devo...".
target_language_example: Por que devo aceitar isso?
native_language_example: Why should I accept this?

meaning: "why on earth?" / "why the hell?" (angry or emphatic “why?”).
additional_notes: Used in questions to add strong emotion (annoyance, disbelief, impatience). It’s more intense than plain "por que" and can sound rude, so avoid it in formal/polite situations. Often followed by a verb: "Por que diabos você fez isso?"
target_language_example: Por que diabos você está gritando comigo?
native_language_example: Why the hell are you yelling at me?

meaning: "why she" / "why is she" (asking for the reason).
additional_notes: Used in questions and indirect questions. In direct questions, it often comes at the beginning: "Por que ela..." (= "Why is she...?"). In indirect questions, it follows a verb like perguntar/saber: "Perguntei ... por que ela..." (= "I asked ... why she...").
target_language_example: Não sei por que ela saiu tão cedo.
native_language_example: I don't know why she left so early.

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason for something involving “he” (ele). It can start a direct question (Por que ele…?) or appear inside an indirect question (perguntei por que ele…). Note: when “por que” comes at the end of a question, it’s usually written “por quê” (e.g., Ele saiu por quê?).
target_language_example: Você sabe por que ele não veio hoje?
native_language_example: Do you know why he didn’t come today?

meaning: "why they" / "why did they" (asking for a reason, with "they").
additional_notes: Used at the start of a direct question (Por que eles...?) or inside an indirect question after verbs like perguntar-se (Eu me pergunto por que eles...). In direct questions it often translates as "Why did they...?" in English; in indirect questions it’s "why they..." (no inversion in Portuguese).
target_language_example: Eu não entendo por que eles fizeram isso.
native_language_example: I don’t understand why they did that.

additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason or explanation about something happening now. "Por que" = "why" and "estamos" = "we are" (present tense of "estar"), so it’s typically followed by a verb in the -ndo form (gerund) like "fazendo", "indo", "rindo": "Por que estamos fazendo isso?"
target_language_example: Por que estamos esperando aqui?
native_language_example: Why are we waiting here?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason something is in a certain state or someone is doing something. Often followed by an adjective/participle (e.g., "vazio" = empty, "dobrada" = folded) or a verb in the -ndo form (e.g., "sorrindo" = smiling). "está" is from "estar" and can refer to "it" (a thing/situation) or "you" (formal "você").
target_language_example: Por que está tão silencioso aqui?
native_language_example: Why is it so quiet here?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for someone’s actions. Often said with an implied subject “você”: “Por que (você) está fazendo isso?”. You can add who it affects with phrases like “comigo” (to me) or add emphasis with “de novo” (again) or “sozinha” (alone/by yourself).
target_language_example: Por que está fazendo isso comigo?
native_language_example: Why are you doing this to me?

meaning: “Why is it so…?” / “Why are you so…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for a situation or someone’s state. Follow it with an adjective (e.g., preocupado, triste) or a description of the environment (e.g., escuro aqui, quieto). In everyday writing you’ll also see the question written as “Por que está tão…?” or “Por que tá tão…?” (more informal).
target_language_example: Por que está tão barulhento lá fora?
native_language_example: Why is it so noisy outside?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason something is happening. **Por que** = “why” in direct questions, and **estão** is the present tense of *estar* for **eles/elas/vocês** (“they/you all are”). In speech, **vocês** is often the implied subject even if it isn’t written.
target_language_example: Por que estão tão quietos hoje?
native_language_example: Why are you all so quiet today?

additional_notes:
Often used at the start of a question when you’re asking the reason for your own action or situation: “Por que eu + verb…?” (e.g., Por que eu confiei…? = Why did I trust…?).

Be careful with spelling:
- **por que** (two words) is used in questions (“why?”) and can also mean **“for which / through which”** after a noun (as in *o caminho por que eu passo* = “the path that I go through”).
- **porque** (one word) usually means **“because.”**
target_language_example: Por que eu disse isso?
native_language_example: Why did I say that?

additional_notes: Used to question the reason or motivation for doing something. It’s often followed by a verb in the infinitive (e.g., ajudar, confiar, ficar, dar). You can change the subject pronoun: "por que você deveria..." (why should you...), "por que a gente deveria..." (why should we...).
target_language_example: Por que eu deveria aceitar essa proposta?
native_language_example: Why should I accept this offer?

additional_notes: Used at the start or in the middle of a question to ask the reason for a situation or fact previously mentioned ("this/that"). Often followed by a verb: "por que isso acontece?" = "why does this happen?". Note: "por que" (two words) is used in questions; "porque" (one word) means "because" in answers.
target_language_example: Você sabe por que isso não funciona?
native_language_example: Do you know why this doesn't work?

additional_notes: Used at the start of a question: **por que** = “why”. **me** is an object pronoun (“me”), used before the verb in Portuguese (e.g., *Por que me procurou?* = “Why did you look for me?”). Note the spelling: **por que** (two words) is used in questions; **porque** (one word) usually means “because.”
target_language_example: Por que me chamou tão tarde?
native_language_example: Why did you call me so late?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason something did not happen, is not true, or is not being done. Depending on the verb, it can correspond to English patterns like 'why don't...?', 'why didn't...?', 'why isn't...?', or simply 'why not?' on its own.
target_language_example: Por que não fazemos isso amanhã?
native_language_example: Why don't we do that tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to suggest or question an action: “Why don’t you bring/buy/kill her/it?” Here, **a** is a direct-object pronoun meaning **“her”** or **“it”** (for a feminine noun). It normally comes **before** the verb after **não** (e.g., *não a trouxe*, *não a compra*).
target_language_example: Por que não a chama para jantar?
native_language_example: Why don’t you call her for dinner?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason. Here, por que means "why" in a question, and o is the masculine singular article "the." Before a masculine noun, it can be translated literally as "why the ..."; before some male names in Brazilian Portuguese, o is often used but usually not translated into English.
target_language_example: Por que o ônibus está atrasado?
native_language_example: Why is the bus late?

additional_notes: Used to ask a “why” question politely/formally to a man. It’s made of **por que** (“why”) + **o senhor** (“you”, formal). Verbs usually go in the **3rd person singular**: *Por que o senhor está…?* / *Por que o senhor achou…?*
target_language_example: Por que o senhor não me avisou antes?
native_language_example: Why didn’t you tell me earlier, sir?

additional_notes: Used to speculate about a reason, often rhetorically. Common in conversation when you don't really expect a direct answer (similar to saying "I wonder why" or "How come?"). It’s typically followed by a clause: "Por que será que...".
target_language_example: Por que será que ele ainda não chegou?
native_language_example: I wonder why he still hasn't arrived.

meaning: "I wonder why..." / "why could it be that...?"
additional_notes: Used to ask a rhetorical or speculative "why" question, often expressing curiosity, doubt, or irony. Common in spoken Portuguese. The verb "será" (future of "ser") adds the sense of guessing/wondering rather than asking for a direct explanation.
target_language_example: Por que será que ele nunca responde às mensagens?
native_language_example: I wonder why he never replies to messages.

additional_notes: Used to start a question asking the reason for something that applies to everyone. In these questions, "por que" = "why". "Todo mundo" means "everyone" (common in speech; a bit more informal than "todos"). It’s usually followed by a verb: "Por que todo mundo está..." (Why is everyone...?).
target_language_example: Por que todo mundo fala disso o tempo todo?
native_language_example: Why does everyone talk about that all the time?

meaning: "why you...?" (used to ask why someone did/does something).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question with the pronoun "tu" (you, informal/singular). It’s followed by a verb: "Por que tu foste...?" / "Por que tu gostas...?" In Brazil, many speakers more often say "Por que você..."; with "tu", the verb is typically in the "tu" form (e.g., "tu foste", "tu gostas").
target_language_example: Por que tu não me ligaste ontem?
native_language_example: Why didn’t you call me yesterday?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for something involving você (“you”). The exact English translation depends on the verb tense that follows: por que você mora...? = “why do you live...?”, por que você foi...? = “why did you go...?” or “why were you...?” It also appears in indirect questions: perguntar por que você quer... = “ask why you want...”.
target_language_example: Por que você está sorrindo?
native_language_example: Why are you smiling?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s reasoning or opinion before a clause. In questions, it’s written as two words: “por que”. Often followed by a full sentence (e.g., “Por que você acha que ele fez isso?”).
target_language_example: Por que você acha que ela está chateada?
native_language_example: Why do you think she’s upset?

additional_notes: Used to ask why someone is in a certain state or doing something right now. It is often followed by an adjective (like nervoso) or by estar + gerund to ask about an ongoing action.
target_language_example: Por que você está tão quieto hoje?
native_language_example: Why are you so quiet today?

por que você está fazendo isso

target_language_multi_word_term: por que você está fazendo isso
additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for someone’s actions. Commonly followed by “com + person/pronoun” to mean “to/with (someone)”: com ela (to/with her), com eles (to/with them), comigo (to/with me). In questions, it’s typically written “por que” (two words).
target_language_example: Por que você está fazendo isso comigo?
native_language_example: Why are you doing this to me?

meaning: "Why are you ...ing me?" (asking why someone is doing something to you).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question. It’s a common pattern: "Por que você está me" + verb (gerund), e.g., "contando" (telling), "olhando" (looking at), "seguindo" (following), "tratando" (treating). "Você está" is like "you are" (often used for actions happening now), and "me" means "me" as the object.
target_language_example: Por que você está me ignorando?
native_language_example: Why are you ignoring me?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for someone’s current state or behavior. It’s normally followed by an adjective (e.g., chateado, nervoso, quieto). In speech, você is often shortened to "cê": "Por que cê tá tão...?".
target_language_example: Por que você está tão preocupado com isso?
native_language_example: Why are you so worried about that?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason behind someone’s action. Often appears as a question ("Por que você fez isso?") but can also be part of a statement ("Sabemos por que você fez isso" = “We know why you did that”). In Brazil, “você” is common; in Portugal you may hear “Por que fizeste isso?” / “Por que fez isso?”.
target_language_example: Por que você fez isso ontem?
native_language_example: Why did you do that yesterday?

meaning: "why did you/why do you ... me" (asking the reason someone did/does something to you).
additional_notes: Used to start a direct question: por que = why; você = you; me = me (object pronoun). You normally add a verb right after: "Por que você me acordou?" (Why did you wake me up?). In questions, "por que" is commonly written as two words. Word order is usually: Por que + você + me + verb.
target_language_example: Por que você me ajudou ontem?
native_language_example: Why did you help me yesterday?

meaning: "why don’t you…?" / "why didn’t you…?" (a suggestion or asking for a reason).
additional_notes: Used to (1) suggest an action: “Por que você não vem comigo?” = “Why don’t you come with me?”, or (2) ask why something didn’t happen in the past: “Por que você não me contou?” = “Why didn’t you tell me?”. The verb form after it shows whether it’s present (não vem) or past (não veio). Can sound neutral or accusatory depending on tone/context.
target_language_example: Por que você não me ajuda com isso?
native_language_example: Why don’t you help me with this?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for someone’s desire/decision. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb: “Por que você quer + verb” (e.g., estudar, morar, ir). In questions, it’s usually written “por que” (two words). “Você” is common in Brazilian Portuguese; with “tu,” you’d often say “Por que tu quer…” (or in some regions “Por que tu queres…”).
target_language_example: Por que você quer trocar de emprego?
native_language_example: Why do you want to change jobs?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for a repeated or habitual action by the person you’re talking to. Structure: por que (why) + você (you) + sempre (always) + verb. In writing, question form is usually "Por que" (two words) at the start of a question. Often sounds annoyed or complaining depending on tone/context.
target_language_example: Por que você sempre chega atrasado?
native_language_example: Why do you always arrive late?

meaning: “why did you come?” / “why have you come?”
additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for someone’s arrival. Often followed by a place (“ao Japão”, “à Coreia”, “para a Malásia”) or by a time-related detail (“tão cedo” = “so early”). In casual speech, people may also say “Por que você veio aqui?” (“Why did you come here?”).
target_language_example: Por que você veio tão cedo hoje?
native_language_example: Why did you come so early today?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for someone having a strong quality or behaving in a certain way. You usually follow it with an adjective (feio = ugly, malvado = mean/evil, pessimista = pessimistic). In writing, the question form here is typically “por que” (two words).
target_language_example: Por que você é tão nervoso hoje?
native_language_example: Why are you so nervous today?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason, addressing more than one person. In questions, it’s usually written as two words: **por que** (“why”). **Vocês** means “you” plural in Brazilian Portuguese (often used in both formal and informal situations). The verb form that follows is typically 3rd-person plural (e.g., **vocês disseram**, **vocês fugiram**).
target_language_example: Por que vocês chegaram tão tarde?
native_language_example: Why did you all arrive so late?

additional_notes: Used to begin a question asking the reason for what a group of people is doing or how they are. "Vocês" is "you" plural (common in Brazil). After "estão" you typically add a verb in the -ndo form (gerund) for an action happening now (e.g., "fazendo", "esperando") or an adjective/state (e.g., "tristes", "nervosos"). Often written without an accent as "por que" in questions; "por quê" can appear at the end of a question.
target_language_example: Por que vocês estão esperando aqui?
native_language_example: Why are you all waiting here?

additional_notes: Very common in speech to emphasize a 'why' question; often interchangeable with just "por que". It’s typically followed by the verb (e.g., "Por que é que você está...?"). Also appears as "por que é que" or "porque é que" depending on spelling preference/region.
target_language_example: Por que é que você não me contou antes?
native_language_example: Why didn’t you tell me earlier?

additional_notes:
Used to ask for a reason (“why?”). In standard Portuguese spelling, **por quê** (with the circumflex) is used when it appears **at the end of a question** or **by itself**, usually before punctuation: *Você fez isso por quê?* / *Por quê?*.
Before a verb inside the question, you normally write **por que** (no accent): *Por que você não vai embora?* (Many people mix these up in informal writing.)
target_language_example: Você está triste por quê?
native_language_example: Why are you sad?

additional_notes: Used to suggest an idea, challenge a reluctance, or ask why something wasn’t done. Often followed by a verb to make a proposal: "Por quê não + verbo?" (“Why don’t you/we…?”). Spelling varies in standard usage: many style guides prefer "por que" in the middle of a sentence ("Por que não vamos?") and reserve "por quê" for the end of a question ("Por quê?"). In informal writing, "por quê não" is also commonly seen mid-sentence.
target_language_example: Então por quê não escreve?
native_language_example: So why don’t you write?

additional_notes: Used to ask why someone does something: “Por que você + verbo…?”. In standard spelling, this is usually written without the circumflex (ê) when it appears at the beginning or in the middle of a question: “Por que você continua…?”. “Por quê” (with ê) is typically used when it comes at the end of a question or when it stands alone: “Você fez isso por quê?” / “Por quê?”. So “por quê você” is nonstandard in careful writing, but it may appear in informal contexts or by analogy with the end-of-sentence form.
target_language_example: Por quê você continua a me incomodar?
native_language_example: Why do you keep bothering me?

additional_notes: Used to express frequency or an amount within one week. Common with numbers and time/quantity words: "X dias/horas/vezes por semana" (X days/hours/times per week).
target_language_example: Eu treino duas vezes por semana.
native_language_example: I work out twice a week.

meaning: by yourself; on your own; by itself.
additional_notes: Used to say someone does something independently ("Decida/Pense por si mesmo" = don’t rely on others), or that something happens without outside help ("resolveu-se por si mesmo" = it solved itself). It agrees with the subject: por si mesmo (he/you masc.), por si mesma (she/you fem.), por si mesmos/mesmas (they). Often interchangeable with "sozinho(a)" in the “by yourself” sense.
target_language_example: Ele preferiu fazer o trabalho por si mesmo.
native_language_example: He preferred to do the work by himself.

additional_notes: Used to insert an additional comment that wasn’t the main point. It can come at the beginning of a sentence (Por sinal, ...) or after what you just said (..., por sinal), often like a quick aside: giving extra info, adding a correction, or changing topic slightly. Neutral in tone (common in speech and writing).
target_language_example: Por sinal, você já falou com a Ana?
native_language_example: By the way, have you already talked to Ana?

additional_notes: Used to say something happened thanks to good luck (often at the start of a sentence, like an adverb: "Por sorte, ..."). It can also mean "as luck would have it" when introducing a lucky circumstance.
target_language_example: Por sorte, eu tinha uma cópia de segurança.
native_language_example: Luckily, I had a backup.

meaning: because of you; due to you (your fault/credit).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone is the reason something happened. Depending on context and tone, it can be negative (blame: “It’s your fault”) or positive (credit: “Thanks to you”). You can also change it for formality/person: por sua causa (you – formal/singular), por tua causa (you – informal/singular, common in Portugal), por causa dele/dela (because of him/her), por nossa causa (because of us), etc.
target_language_example: Eu consegui este emprego por sua causa.
native_language_example: I got this job because of you.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like agradecer/obrigado to give the reason for thanks. Grammar: por + infinitivo composto (terem vindo = “to have come”), referring to a completed action. Terem is plural to match “you (all)/they”; for one person you’d say por ter vindo.
target_language_example: Obrigado por terem vindo hoje.
native_language_example: Thank you for coming today.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun (por toda a + noun) to talk about something being spread everywhere in a place ("all over the house") or happening/lasting during an entire period ("throughout my life"). With masculine singular: "por todo o"; feminine plural: "por todas as"; masculine plural: "por todos os".
target_language_example: Temos lojas por toda a cidade.
native_language_example: We have stores all over the city.

additional_notes: Used to say something is in many places, spread around, or easy to find in any location. Very common with verbs like estar/haver/ter (Está/Há/Tem ... por toda parte) and with procurar (procurar ... por toda parte = to search everywhere).
target_language_example: Depois da festa, tinha lixo por toda parte.
native_language_example: After the party, there was trash everywhere.

additional_notes: Used to say something is spread out in many places, often in a messy or overwhelming way. Common with verbs like "haver/ter" (there is/are) and "estar" (to be). You’ll also hear the variation "por todos os lados" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Depois da festa, havia lixo por todo lado.
native_language_example: After the party, there was trash everywhere.

meaning: behind; from behind; (figuratively) behind/involved in something.
additional_notes: Used for physical position or movement: "por trás" = behind/in the back (often contrasting with "na frente" = in front). It can also mean "from behind" (e.g., someone grabs you from behind). With "de" + noun/pronoun, it’s very common: "por trás do altar" (behind the altar), "por trás disso" (behind that). Figuratively, it can mean the hidden cause or the person responsible: "algo por trás desse assunto" (something behind this matter), "quem está por trás" (who’s behind it).
target_language_example: Quem está por trás disso tudo?
native_language_example: Who is behind all of this?

additional_notes: Used to express the duration of an action or state. Common with the past ("morei..."), with "estar" + state ("estive..."), and with ongoing actions in the present perfect continuous ("venho estudando...", "tem estudado..."). You can swap the number: "por dois anos", "por cinco anos", etc.
target_language_example: Trabalhei nessa empresa por três anos.
native_language_example: I worked at that company for three years.

additional_notes: "Por" + a time period expresses duration (how long something lasts): ficar, esperar, viajar, viver de algo, etc. It answers "Por quanto tempo?" (For how long?).
target_language_example: Vamos viajar por três dias e depois voltar.
native_language_example: We’re going to travel for three days and then come back.

additional_notes: Used to say how long something lasts or how long someone waits/does something. Common pattern: "por + [amount of time]" (por duas horas, por cinco minutos, por um ano).
target_language_example: Fiquei no aeroporto por três horas.
native_language_example: I stayed at the airport for three hours.

additional_notes: Used to say how long something lasts. With verbs like ficar/estar/ter (in some situations), it indicates duration in time. You can swap in other time periods: por dois dias, por uma semana, por seis meses.
target_language_example: Vou ficar aqui por três meses.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay here for three months.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression: it is por + um. The meaning depends on context. It often means by a before the agent in passive sentences (foi destruída por um robô = was destroyed by a robot), and for a in cases like duration, exchange, or searching (por um breve período = for a brief period; trocar por um mais barato = exchange for a cheaper one). It also appears in the common phrase por um fio, meaning hanging by a thread / in a very fragile situation.
target_language_example: O livro foi escrito por um jornalista famoso.
native_language_example: The book was written by a famous journalist.

meaning: for a good while; for quite some time.
additional_notes: Used to say something lasts (or has been happening) for a fairly long period. Often follows the verb (e.g., esperar, ficar, ajudar). It can refer to time in the past up to now ("has been... for quite some time") or a stretch of time in the past ("stayed... for a good while").
target_language_example: A gente não se viu por um bom tempo.
native_language_example: We didn’t see each other for quite some time.

meaning: for a moment; for a brief instant.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens or is needed for a very short time. Common with verbs like hesitar (to hesitate), esperar (to wait), falar (to talk), and usar (to use). In requests, it can sound polite and minimizing: “...por um instante?” = “...for a moment?”.
target_language_example: Espere aqui por um instante, por favor.
native_language_example: Wait here for a moment, please.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a long duration. It can refer to the past ("for a long time"), or—depending on context—to the future ("for a long time"). Often interchangeable with "por muito tempo" in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Não te vejo por um longo tempo.
native_language_example: I haven't seen you for a long time.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to do something briefly (wait, come here, listen, talk). In everyday speech it often just means “a moment/briefly,” not exactly 60 seconds.
target_language_example: Espere aqui por um minuto, por favor.
native_language_example: Wait here for a minute, please.

meaning: for a moment; for a short time.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens briefly or temporarily. Common with actions/states like waiting, being quiet, staying, holding/caring for something, etc. It can also be used as a quick apology/interrupting phrase meaning “sorry, just a moment.”
target_language_example: Espere por um momento, por favor.
native_language_example: Wait for a moment, please.

meaning: for a second; for a moment.
additional_notes: Used to ask someone to pause briefly, calm down, or to say something lasted only a very short time. It can also introduce a brief thought or impression: “Por um segundo, achei que...” = “For a moment, I thought...”.
target_language_example: Espera por um segundo, já vou aí.
native_language_example: Wait a second, I’m coming right there.

meaning: for a while; for some time.
additional_notes: Used to say something lasts for a limited period (often temporary), like staying somewhere, resting, or continuing an activity. Very common after verbs (ficar, continuar, descansar).
target_language_example: Vou esperar aqui por um tempo.
native_language_example: I’ll wait here for a while.

additional_notes: Used with "por" to express duration (how long something lasted). Common with actions like studying, waiting, working, or with a time-limited permission/service. You can swap the number: "por duas horas" (for two hours).
target_language_example: Vou ficar aqui por uma hora.
native_language_example: I’m going to stay here for one hour.

meaning: for a week; for one week (duration).
additional_notes: Uses "por" to express how long something lasts (a period of time). Often used with actions/states like staying, renting, being away, missing school, or being in the hospital. You can also replace the time unit: "por um dia", "por um mês", etc.
target_language_example: Vou ficar em Lisboa por uma semana.
native_language_example: I'm going to stay in Lisbon for a week.

meaning: 'at a time' (one at a time / per turn).
additional_notes: Used to say something should happen separately, not all together. Very common with quantities and actions: "uma pergunta por vez" (one question at a time), "um por vez" (one at a time). Often follows the noun/action it limits.
target_language_example: Calma—vamos entrar por vez.
native_language_example: Easy—let’s go in one at a time.

additional_notes: Used to give an approximate time or estimate. Common with clock times (por volta de sete horas), ages (por volta de sessenta anos), and quantities (por volta de sete mil). Similar to "cerca de" and "aproximadamente".
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar por volta de cinco e meia.
native_language_example: Let’s meet around 5:30.

additional_notes: Used to question the reason for not doing something. As a direct question it often means “why not?” (suggesting something is a good idea). With a past verb, it commonly means “why didn’t you…?” or “why not + verb…?” It can also be used as a suggestion: “Porque não fazemos isso?” = “Why don’t we do that?”
target_language_example: Porque não vem comigo?
native_language_example: Why don’t you come with me?

additional_notes: Very common way to form a “why” question in European Portuguese. It often comes at the start of a question: “Porque é que…?” You can also use it inside a longer sentence after verbs like “saber” (to know) or “explicar” (to explain): “Queres saber porque é que…?” In Brazilian Portuguese, it’s more common to simply say “Por que…?” or “Por que que…?”
target_language_example: Porque é que estás tão cansado?
native_language_example: Why are you so tired?

additional_notes: Used to introduce an explanation that involves a male person (“he”). Often follows a main clause: "... porque ele ..." (= "... because he ..."). It can also start a sentence as a standalone explanation: "Porque ele..." (= "Because he..."). Note: "porque" (because) is different from "por que" (why/for what reason).
target_language_example: Não vou com você porque ele já está lá.
native_language_example: I’m not going with you because he’s already there.

additional_notes: Used to introduce your reason/explanation from your point of view, usually followed by a verb: “porque eu estava…”, “porque eu tenho…”. It can also appear as a short answer to “Por quê?” (“Why?”): “Porque eu te amo.”
target_language_example: Eu não fui à festa porque eu estava muito cansado.
native_language_example: I didn’t go to the party because I was very tired.

additional_notes: Most often, porque não introduces a reason in a negative clause: porque = “because” + não = “not” (e.g., “because I didn’t see it”). In questions, you may also see it with the meaning “why not?”, but this is typically written as **por que não?** (two words) in standard spelling. In real-life texts/messages, people sometimes write **porque não** even when they mean “why not?”.
target_language_example: Fiquei em casa porque não estava me sentindo bem.
native_language_example: I stayed home because I wasn’t feeling well.

meaning: a vulgar intensifier before a noun: “fucking / damn / shitty”.
additional_notes: Used to show anger, annoyance, emphasis, or contempt about the thing that follows (porra de + noun). It’s very offensive/vulgar in most situations; avoid in polite company. You may also see related forms like “essa porra de...” (“this fucking...”) or “na porra de [place]” (“in fucking [place]”).
target_language_example: Não aguento essa porra de trânsito.
native_language_example: I can’t stand this fucking traffic.

additional_notes: A very strong, vulgar way to emphasize “nothing at all,” often used with negatives: “não + verb + porra nenhuma” (e.g., não vejo porra nenhuma = I can’t see a damn thing). It can also be a standalone answer meaning “Nothing.” Avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Eu não entendi porra nenhuma do que ele falou.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand a damn thing he said.

meaning: the back door; the rear entrance.
additional_notes: Used for the door at the back of a house/building (often a less visible or secondary entrance). In directions or commands, you may hear it with a preposition: “Pela porta dos fundos!” = “Through the back door!” / “Use the back entrance!”
target_language_example: A entrega é pela porta dos fundos.
native_language_example: Deliveries are through the back door.

additional_notes: A compartment built into the dashboard of a car (usually in front of the passenger seat) used to store small items like documents, maps, or gloves. Often used with the verb abrir (“to open”) or olhar/procurar (“to look/search”) and commonly appears with the article: o porta-luvas.
target_language_example: Deixa os documentos do carro no porta-luvas.
native_language_example: Keep the car documents in the glove compartment.

additional_notes: Used mainly in Brazilian Portuguese for the storage compartment of a car. It’s written with a hyphen and often stays the same in the singular: "o porta-malas". Plural is usually "os porta-malas". In European Portuguese, you often hear "bagageira" instead.
target_language_example: Coloque as compras no porta-malas, por favor.
native_language_example: Put the groceries in the trunk, please.

meaning: “can do / be able to do” (subjunctive: “may be able to do”).
additional_notes: “Possa” is the present subjunctive of “poder” (to be able to / can). It’s commonly used after expressions like “que” (that), “talvez” (maybe), “duvido que” (I doubt that), and in sentences about possibility, doubt, or uncertainty: “algo que eu possa fazer” = “something I can do.”
target_language_example: Não sei se eu possa fazer isso hoje.
native_language_example: I don’t know if I can do that today.

additional_notes: Used to offer help (often as a question: "Posso ajudar?" / "Posso ajudar com alguma coisa?") or to say you’re able/willing to help ("Eu posso ajudar, se você quiser."). The verb is "ajudar" = "to help"; "posso" is the "I can" form of "poder".
target_language_example: Boa tarde! Posso ajudar com alguma coisa?
native_language_example: Good afternoon! Can I help with anything?

additional_notes: Used to offer help politely. “Posso” = “can I / may I” and “ajudá-la” = “help her / help you (formal, feminine)”. The “-la” refers to a female person and is common in more formal or written Portuguese; in everyday Brazilian Portuguese many people instead say “Posso te ajudar?” or “Posso ajudar você?”. You can add what you’re helping with: “a + infinitive” (posso ajudá-la a encontrar…) or “em algo” (with something).
target_language_example: Boa tarde, posso ajudá-la com alguma coisa?
native_language_example: Good afternoon, can I help you with anything?

meaning: “I can help you” / “Can I help you?” (formal “you,” masculine).
additional_notes: Used to offer help or ask how you can help someone. “Posso” = “I can,” “ajudar” = “to help,” and “-lo” means “him/you (formal)” as an object pronoun; in practice it often means “you” when addressing someone with você/o senhor. For a woman, you may hear “posso ajudá-la.”
target_language_example: Posso ajudá-lo com as malas?
native_language_example: Can I help you with the bags?

additional_notes: Used when offering help to more than one person, or as a polite/formal way to address someone (depending on region and context). Literally “I can help you (them)” where posso = “I can” and ajudá-los = “help you (plural)” (help + -los “you/them” masc. plural). Common in customer service: “Em que posso ajudá-los?” = “How can I help you?” You can add what you’re helping with: “a encontrar algo” (to find something), “com seus casacos” (with your coats), “em algo” (with something).
target_language_example: Olá! Posso ajudá-los a escolher um tamanho?
native_language_example: Hi! Can I help you choose a size?

meaning: “Can I eat …?” or “I can’t eat …” (ability/permission to eat).
additional_notes: From the verb “poder” (to be able to / may) + “comer” (to eat). Use it as a question to ask permission (“Posso comer isto?” = Can I eat this?) or to say you’re unable/not allowed to eat something (“Não posso comer isso” = I can’t eat that). Often used with food items (isto/isso, esta/este + noun) or with “um pouco” (a little).
target_language_example: Desculpe, não posso comer carne.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t eat meat.

meaning: "Can I leave (something) ...?" / "Can I let (someone do something)?"
additional_notes: With an object (e.g., a bag, bike), it usually means leaving something somewhere: "Posso deixar a minha bagagem aqui?" = "Can I leave my luggage here?". With "que" + verb, it means allowing/letting something happen: "Não posso deixar que vá" = "I can't let you/him/her go."
target_language_example: Posso deixar o meu casaco aqui por um momento?
native_language_example: Can I leave my coat here for a moment?

additional_notes: Literally “(I) can say.” It’s the verb poder (posso = “I can”) + infinitive dizer (“to say/tell”). Often used either as a question to ask permission (“posso dizer...?” = “can I tell/say...?”) or as a statement of what you’re able/allowed to say (“só posso dizer...” = “all I can say...” / “I can only say...”). The subject “eu” (I) is usually omitted because it’s clear from posso.
target_language_example: Posso dizer a verdade agora?
native_language_example: Can I tell the truth now?

meaning: “Can I talk to you?” / “May I speak with you?”
additional_notes: A polite, very common way to ask to speak with someone. You can add details like time (por um minuto/por um segundo = “for a minute/for a second”), privacy (a sós/em particular = “in private”), place (lá fora = “outside”), language (em inglês = “in English”), or topic (sobre X = “about X”). Often used to start a request that feels a bit serious or personal.
target_language_example: Oi, posso falar com você em particular por um minuto?
native_language_example: Hi, can I talk to you in private for a minute?

meaning: "Can I do that?" / "I can do that."
additional_notes: From the verb phrase "poder" (to be able to / can) + "fazer" (to do/make) + "isso" (that/this). It can be a statement about ability/permission ("I can do that") or a question asking permission/possibility ("Can I do that?"). In speech, you’ll often hear the question with rising intonation: "Posso fazer isso?" You can add "também" (too) or "com você(s)" (with you [pl.]) depending on the situation.
target_language_example: Posso fazer isso agora ou é melhor esperar?
native_language_example: Can I do that now, or is it better to wait?

additional_notes: A polite, common way to ask permission before asking something. You can add an adjective after "pergunta" (e.g., "uma pergunta rápida" = a quick question, "uma pergunta idiota" = a stupid/silly question) and you can add who you’re asking with "para você" or "a ela". Often used by itself: "Posso fazer uma pergunta?"
target_language_example: Com licença, posso fazer uma pergunta rápida?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I ask a quick question?

meaning: “can I stay?” / “can I remain?” (also: “can I keep…?” with *ficar com*).
additional_notes: *Posso* = “I can / may I”, *ficar* = “to stay/remain.” Often used to ask permission: *Posso ficar aqui até…?* (“Can I stay here until…?”). With **ficar com + noun/pronoun**, it commonly means “to keep” or “to hold on to”: *Posso ficar com isto?* (“Can I keep this?”). With **ficar com + person**, it can mean “to stay with (someone)”: *Posso ficar com você por um tempo?* (“Can I stay with you for a while?”).
target_language_example: Posso ficar aqui mais um pouco?
native_language_example: Can I stay here a little longer?

meaning: Can I stay here? / I can stay here.
additional_notes: Used to ask permission or to say you are able/allowed to remain in this place. Often followed by a time expression ("até segunda-feira" = until Monday, "por um tempo" = for a while, "essa semana" = this week) or a reason/purpose ("para comer alguma coisa" = to eat something). Negative: "(eu) não posso ficar aqui" = I can’t / I’m not allowed to stay here.
target_language_example: Posso ficar aqui até amanhã?
native_language_example: Can I stay here until tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to ask for permission or possibility to go somewhere or go with someone. It’s the 1st-person singular present of the verb phrase “poder” (to be able to / can) + “ir” (to go). Often followed by “a” + place (posso ir ao cinema?) or “com” + person (posso ir com você/vocês?). In Brazil you may also hear “posso ir em/na…” with places (posso ir na sua casa?).
target_language_example: Posso ir com vocês depois do trabalho?
native_language_example: Can I go with you (all) after work?

additional_notes: "Posso" is the 1st-person singular of "poder" (can/may). "Lhe" is an object pronoun meaning "to you" (formal) or "to him/her" depending on context; in these examples it’s a polite "to you". Common in customer-service/polite requests: "Em que posso lhe ajudar?" (How can I help you?), "Posso lhe pedir...?" (Can I ask you...?).
target_language_example: Posso lhe mostrar o caminho.
native_language_example: Can I show you the way?

additional_notes: Used to ask for permission to take/get something. Very common with "emprestado/emprestada" to mean "borrow": "posso pegar (isso) emprestado/a?" = "can I borrow (that)?" Without "emprestado", it often means simply "take" or "pick up". In "posso pegar isso de volta?", "pegar ... de volta" means "get/take ... back".
target_language_example: Posso pegar seu livro emprestado por um dia?
native_language_example: Can I borrow your book for one day?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask permission to ask a question. Often followed by a question word (o quê/por quê/quanto/qual) or by “sobre” + topic (“Posso perguntar sobre isso?”). You can also add “te” or “lhe” to specify the person being asked (e.g., “Posso perguntar-lhe…?” is more formal).
target_language_example: Com licença, posso perguntar onde fica o banheiro?
native_language_example: Excuse me, may I ask where the bathroom is?

additional_notes: Common start of a question with the verb "poder" ("I can / may I") + the object pronoun "te" ("you"). It’s usually followed by another verb: "Posso te ajudar?" = "Can I help you?". Using "te" is informal/colloquial (often replaced by "lhe" in more formal Portuguese).
target_language_example: Posso te ajudar?
native_language_example: Can I help you?

meaning: “Can I call you?” / “May I give you a call?”
additional_notes: Used to ask permission to phone someone. Very common in everyday conversation; you can add a time like “mais tarde” (later), “amanhã” (tomorrow), or “uma hora dessas” (one of these days/sometime). “Te” = “you” (informal, singular), so with more formal “you” you’d say “Posso ligar para você?” or “Posso te ligar?” depending on region.
target_language_example: Posso te ligar mais tarde, depois do trabalho?
native_language_example: Can I call you later, after work?

additional_notes: Used to ask for permission to use something. "posso" = "can I / may I" (from *poder*), and "usar" = "to use". Very common with objects or tools (telefone, computador, banheiro, etc.). You can add politeness with "Por favor": "Posso usar seu computador, por favor?"
target_language_example: Posso usar esta cadeira?
native_language_example: Can I use this chair?

additional_notes: Common way to ask permission or possibility: "posso" (I can / may I) + "ver" (to see). With things like documents or objects (passaporte), it usually means "see"; with TV/movies it often means "watch". Often used as a polite question: "Posso ver...?" = "May I see...?"
target_language_example: Posso ver o menu, por favor?
native_language_example: Can I see the menu, please?

meaning: "Can I see him/it?" or "May I see you?" (formal).
additional_notes: Used to ask for permission or possibility of seeing someone/something. "vê-lo" = "ver" (to see) + the object pronoun "-lo" attached with a hyphen. "-lo" usually means "him" or "it", and can also mean "you" in formal address (replacing "o senhor/a senhora"). Common in questions like "Posso vê-lo?" and "Quando posso vê-lo?"
target_language_example: Posso vê-lo agora ou só amanhã?
native_language_example: Can I see him now, or only tomorrow?

additional_notes: Common way to refer to a place where you buy fuel for a car. Often used with directions/distances: “Tem um posto de gasolina a um quilômetro à frente.” You may also hear “posto” alone when the context is clear, or “posto de combustível” as a more general term (fuel station).
target_language_example: Vamos parar no posto de gasolina para abastecer.
native_language_example: Let’s stop at the gas station to fill up.

additional_notes: Used to say that only a small number of people do something or exist in a place. It’s the feminine plural form of “pouco” because “pessoas” is feminine. Often contrasted with “muitas pessoas” (many people).
target_language_example: Poucas pessoas entendem essa regra no começo.
native_language_example: Few people understand that rule at first.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a slow, step-by-step change or progress over time (improvement, realizing something, something disappearing). It often matches “gradually/over time” in English and can appear at the beginning or end of the sentence for emphasis.
target_language_example: Pouco a pouco, estou aprendendo a falar português.
native_language_example: Little by little, I’m learning to speak Portuguese.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t have enough money right now (e.g., you’re low on cash). Often appears with "estar com" (to have on you/available) or "ter" (to have).
target_language_example: Estou com pouco dinheiro hoje, então vou comer em casa.
native_language_example: I don’t have much money today, so I’m going to eat at home.

meaning: a short time; not much time.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a brief duration. Often appears with "por" (for) to mean "for a short time" ("por pouco tempo"), or with "em" (in) to mean "in a short time" / "quickly" ("em pouco tempo"). Can be intensified as "muito pouco tempo" (very little time).
target_language_example: Vou precisar de pouco tempo para terminar isso.
native_language_example: I’ll need only a short time to finish this.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or indicate an additional small amount, distance, time, or degree. Often appears as "um pouco mais" (= a little more) or with "só" for emphasis: "só um pouco mais" (= just a little more). In requests like "por um pouco mais?", it can mean paying a slightly higher price: "for a little more (money)?".
target_language_example: Espera um pouco mais, por favor.
native_language_example: Wait a little longer, please.

additional_notes: Used to ask for a small increase in volume (especially with speaking/sound: “Fala um pouco mais alto”) or for something to be positioned slightly higher (“Coloca um pouco mais alto”). Often implies “a little more than it is now.”
target_language_example: Pode falar um pouco mais alto, por favor?
native_language_example: Could you speak a little louder, please?

additional_notes: Used before a number/amount to say it’s slightly above that value (time, money, distance, age, etc.). Often appears as: "há pouco mais de" = "a little more than (ago)" and "um pouco mais de" = "a little more than".
target_language_example: O filme dura pouco mais de duas horas.
native_language_example: The movie lasts a little more than two hours.

meaning: a few days; not many days.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a short amount of time measured in days. Often appears with em (“in/within”): em poucos dias = “in a few days / within a few days”, and with há (“ago”): há poucos dias = “a few days ago”. It can also be used before a noun phrase: poucos dias de água = “only a few days’ worth of water.”
target_language_example: Volto em poucos dias.
native_language_example: I’ll be back in a few days.

additional_notes: Very informal and profane. Used mainly in Brazil to intensify an adjective or statement (often after the adjective): "bonito pra caralho" = “beautiful as fuck / extremely beautiful.” It can also intensify actions/amounts: "relaxar pra caralho" = “relax a ton.” Not appropriate for polite or professional situations.
target_language_example: Esse filme é bom pra caralho.
native_language_example: This movie is good as fuck / really, really good.

additional_notes: Very common in Brazilian Portuguese conversation. Used after adjectives or verbs to strongly intensify them: “legal pra caramba” = “really cool,” “gosto… pra caramba” = “I like… a lot.” It’s informal and can sound a bit crude depending on the context; avoid in formal situations. Variant: “pra caralho” is stronger/more vulgar.
target_language_example: Eu tô cansado pra caramba hoje.
native_language_example: I’m really tired today.

additional_notes: "Pra" is a very common spoken/written contraction of "para a" (feminine singular). "Pra casa" is used after verbs of going/coming/returning/taking someone to indicate destination (going/coming back home). In more formal writing, you may see "para casa".
target_language_example: Depois do trabalho, eu vou pra casa.
native_language_example: After work, I’m going home.

additional_notes: “Pra” is an informal contraction of “para”. “Pra cima” is commonly used to indicate direction (look/move upward) and in set commands like “mãos pra cima” (“hands up”). In more formal Portuguese, you may see “para cima”.
target_language_example: As crianças apontaram pra cima quando viram o avião.
native_language_example: The kids pointed up when they saw the airplane.

additional_notes: Colloquial form of "para cá". Common with motion verbs like "vir" (to come) and "trazer" (to bring): "vem pra cá" = "come here". Often contrasts with "pra lá" (over there).
target_language_example: Vem pra cá um minuto, por favor.
native_language_example: Come here for a minute, please.

meaning: "to him" or "for him" (often "at him" after verbs like "look").
additional_notes: "Pra" is a very common spoken/written contraction of "para" (more informal). Meaning depends on the verb: with "olhar" it often means "at" (Olhe pra ele! = Look at him!).
target_language_example: Eu vou dar isso pra ele amanhã.
native_language_example: I'm going to give this to him tomorrow.

meaning: "for us" / "to us"; also "for us to …" (before an infinitive).
additional_notes: "Pra" is the informal spoken contraction of "para". "A gente" is very commonly used to mean "we/us" in Brazilian Portuguese (even though it literally means "the people"). You’ll see "pra gente" used both with a verb ("mentir pra gente" = "lie to us") and to introduce an action ("pra gente conversar" = "for us to talk").
target_language_example: Você pode explicar isso pra gente?
native_language_example: Can you explain that to us?

meaning: 'over there' / 'to there' (colloquial for “para lá”); also in “deixar pra lá” = 'let it go' / 'forget it'.
additional_notes: “Pra” is an informal spoken contraction of “para”. Use “pra lá” to point to a place/direction: “O barco tá pra lá” (It’s over there), “Vou pra lá” (I’m going there), “Entra pra lá” (Go in/over there). Very common fixed expression: “deixar pra lá” = stop worrying about it, drop the subject.
target_language_example: Vamos deixar pra lá e conversar depois.
native_language_example: Let’s let it go and talk later.

additional_notes: "Pra" is an informal contraction of "para" (to/for). "Pra onde" is used to ask or say the destination or direction someone is going. In more formal writing, you may see "para onde".
target_language_example: Você sabe pra onde ele foi?
native_language_example: Do you know where he went (to)?

additional_notes: Common spoken form of "para trás". Used for: (1) movement/direction: "Vá pra trás" = go back/step back; (2) going backwards/declining: "andar pra trás" = go backwards, get worse; (3) leaving something behind: "deixar (algo) pra trás" = leave (something) behind; (4) physical position, often in commands: "mãos pra trás" = hands behind your back.
target_language_example: O policial disse: "Mãos pra trás!"
native_language_example: The police officer said, "Hands behind your back!"

additional_notes: Colloquial form of “para valer”. Used to say something is genuine/serious (not a joke, not just practice or pretending), or that it will really happen and have real consequences. Often used with games, fights, threats, promises, or decisions: “jogar pra valer” = play seriously/for real.
target_language_example: Agora é pra valer: vamos assinar o contrato hoje.
native_language_example: Now it’s for real: we’re going to sign the contract today.

meaning: to see; to watch; to find out (“to see if / wait and see”).
additional_notes:
“Pra” is a very common spoken (informal) contraction of “para”. Often used as:
- “pra ver se ...” = “to see if ...” (checking/trying to find out)
- “espera pra ver ...” = “wait and see ...”
It can also mean “to see/watch” in a literal sense: “não há nada pra ver” = “there’s nothing to see.”
target_language_example: Fica aqui pra ver o final do filme.
native_language_example: Stay here to watch the end of the movie.

additional_notes: Common spoken form of "para você" ("pra" = informal contraction of "para"). Used to show who something is intended for/benefits ("for you"), or the direction/recipient of something ("to you"), depending on the verb and context.
target_language_example: Tenho uma surpresa pra você.
native_language_example: I have a surprise for you.

meaning: “a pleasure to…” / “nice to…” (meet, see, do something).
additional_notes: Literally “pleasure in.” Commonly used in polite greetings: “Prazer em conhecer” (Nice to meet you), “Prazer em conhecê-la/conhecê-lo” (Nice to meet you, to a woman/man), and “Prazer em vê-lo de novo” (Nice to see you again). It can also mean “to be glad to” in offers: “Terei prazer em…” (I’d be happy to / I’d be glad to…). After “em” you typically use an infinitive verb: conhecer, ver, ajudar, ensinar, etc.
target_language_example: Prazer em ajudar; terei prazer em explicar tudo.
native_language_example: Happy to help; I’ll be glad to explain everything.

additional_notes: Used when meeting someone for the first time (or when being introduced). In standard Portuguese, this is a clipped form of “prazer em conhecer” + object pronoun; in Brazil you’ll very commonly hear “Prazer em conhecer você.” In European Portuguese and in more formal contexts you may also see “Prazer em conhecê-lo / conhecê-la” (nice to meet you, with masculine/feminine object). A very common shorter option is simply “Prazer!”
target_language_example: Oi, eu sou a Ana. Prazer em conhecê.
native_language_example: Hi, I'm Ana. Nice to meet you.

additional_notes: Form of the verb phrase "precisar de" = "to need". "precisa de" is used mainly with nouns ("precisa de dinheiro" = needs money) and can also be followed by an infinitive ("precisa de trabalhar" = needs to work). "precisa" here is the present tense for ele/ela/você (he/she/you formal). In the negative: "não precisa de" = doesn’t need.
target_language_example: Você precisa de ajuda?
native_language_example: Do you need help?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "precisar de" + noun to say someone needs something. It’s often followed by a time word like "agora" (now). You can change the subject: "Eu preciso de ajuda" (I need help), "Você precisa de ajuda?" (Do you need help?).
target_language_example: Você precisa de ajuda com isso?
native_language_example: Do you need help with that?

additional_notes: Used with the verb precisar de (“to need”) plus mais (“more”). It’s usually followed by a noun: precisa de mais água/sal (“needs more water/salt”). Sometimes the noun is implied from context: Ninguém precisa de mais. Note: precisa looks like English “precise,” but here it means “(he/she/it) needs.”
target_language_example: Este projeto precisa de mais tempo.
native_language_example: This project needs more time.

additional_notes: From the verb "precisar de" (to need). It’s used to say someone needs your help, presence, or something you can provide. Often appears in questions like "Você precisa de mim?" (Do you need me?). In Portuguese, "precisar" typically takes "de" before the thing/person needed: "precisa de + noun/pronoun".
target_language_example: E para que precisa de mim?
native_language_example: And what do you need me for?

additional_notes: Used with the verb precisar de (“to need”) + the preposition de + the masculine singular indefinite article um. The thing needed comes right after: precisa de um casaco (“needs a coat”). With você/ele/ela it’s precisa; with eu it’s preciso; with nós it’s precisamos. For feminine nouns, use precisa de uma (e.g., precisa de uma ajuda).
target_language_example: Ele precisa de um médico agora.
native_language_example: He needs a doctor now.

additional_notes: From the verb "precisar" (“to need”). It’s followed by "de" + a noun: "precisa de uma" + feminine singular noun (e.g., "uma mão", "uma pintura"). With a masculine noun you use "precisa de um" ("Ele precisa de um carro"). In speech/writing you may also see "precisa de" without an article in some cases (e.g., "precisa de ajuda").
target_language_example: Ela precisa de uma ajuda com a tarefa.
native_language_example: She needs some help with the homework.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone needs to speak with a specific person (often because it’s important or necessary). Common structure: "[Person] precisa falar com [person/role]". "Precisa" is from "precisar" (to need), and "falar com" means "to talk to".
target_language_example: Você precisa falar com o gerente antes de assinar.
native_language_example: You need to talk to the manager before you sign.

meaning: (he/she/you—formal) needs to do that/this; has to do that/this.
additional_notes: Used to express necessity or obligation. "precisa" is the present tense of "precisar" (to need), and "fazer isso" means "to do that/this". "Isso" usually refers to something already mentioned ("that"), but can also mean "this" depending on context. You can change the subject: "Eu preciso fazer isso" (I need to do this), "Eles precisam fazer isso" (They need to do this). In questions it often expresses checking or doubt, e.g., "Você acha que Tom precisa fazer isso?"
target_language_example: Você acha que Tom precisa fazer isso?
native_language_example: Do you think Tom needs to do that?

meaning: 'need(s) to go' / 'have to go (somewhere)' / sometimes 'have to leave'.
additional_notes: Forma com o verbo "precisar" + infinitivo "ir". Usado para dizer que alguém tem necessidade/obrigação de ir a algum lugar ou sair. Pode ser afirmação ("Ele precisa ir...") ou pergunta ("Precisa ir...?" = "Do you need to go...?"). Frequentemente vem com destino: "a/ao/à" (mais padrão) ou "pra" (informal, muito comum na fala).
target_language_example: Tom diz que precisa ir a Boston depois de amanhã.
native_language_example: Tom says he needs to go to Boston the day after tomorrow.

additional_notes:
Used to say something is necessary/required. Very common in the present tense of precisar + infinitive ser: 
- with an adjective/noun: "Precisa ser prudente" = "(He) needs to be careful/prudent."
- with a passive infinitive: "precisa ser consertado" = "needs to be fixed/repaired".
The subject can be stated ("O Tom precisa ser...") or left implied ("Precisa ser da cor certa.").
target_language_example: Isso precisa ser feito hoje.
native_language_example: This needs to be done today.

additional_notes: "Precisam" is the 3rd person plural of "precisar" (eles/elas/vocês precisam). It is usually followed by "de" + a noun or pronoun: "precisam de amor", "precisam de você". In questions, it can be used alone as "Precisam de...?" (= Do you/they need ...?).
target_language_example: Vocês precisam de ajuda?
native_language_example: Do you need help?

meaning: “need to be / have to be” (for “they” or “you all”).
additional_notes: Used to say that multiple things or people require a state or an action. Often followed by an adjective (e.g., “menores”) or by a past participle to express something that must be done (e.g., “precisam ser feitas / lavadas” = “need to be done/washed”). This is the present tense, 3rd person plural of “precisar” + “ser”.
target_language_example: Os relatórios precisam ser enviados hoje.
native_language_example: The reports need to be sent today.

additional_notes: Used to say that a conversation is necessary, often about something important or possibly serious. You can add a topic with "sobre" (e.g., "precisamos conversar sobre isso"). In direct situations, it can also imply “we need to talk (about a problem).”
target_language_example: Precisamos conversar sobre o que aconteceu ontem.
native_language_example: We need to talk about what happened yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to say that “we” (the speaker and others) need something. It’s followed by "de" + a noun or pronoun: "precisamos de água" (we need water), "precisamos de você" (we need you). In Portuguese, you typically keep the "de" even though English doesn’t say “need of.” Not related to English “precise” (a common confusion).
target_language_example: Precisamos de ajuda agora.
native_language_example: We need help now.

additional_notes: Used to say that a group ("we") needs a larger quantity or number of something. Typically followed by a noun: "precisamos de mais + (noun)" (e.g., "precisamos de mais tempo"). You can change the subject: "preciso de mais" (I need more), "você precisa de mais" (you need more), "eles precisam de mais" (they need more).
target_language_example: Precisamos de mais cadeiras para a reunião.
native_language_example: We need more chairs for the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to say you (we) need something: precisar de + noun. Use “um” with masculine singular nouns (um contrato, um tradutor). For feminine singular, use “precisamos de uma …” (uma sala). In many situations you can also say “precisamos de + [noun]” without the article, especially with general/abstract things (e.g., “precisamos de tempo”).
target_language_example: Precisamos de um médico agora.
native_language_example: We need a doctor now.

additional_notes: Used to say that you/your group needs something. "Precisamos" = "we need"; "de" is required after "precisar"; "uma" is the feminine form of "a" (use "um" for masculine nouns: "precisamos de um carro"). Often followed by a noun or noun phrase: "precisamos de uma escada/mesa/senha".
target_language_example: Precisamos de uma resposta até amanhã.
native_language_example: We need an answer by tomorrow.

meaning: “we need to do” / “we have to do.”
additional_notes: From precisar (to need) + fazer (to do/make). It’s the present tense “we” form: “we need to do …”. Portuguese often drops the subject pronoun, so it can imply “we” without saying nós. Commonly followed by an object or an action: “Precisamos fazer isso hoje” (We need to do this today).
target_language_example: Precisamos fazer isso agora.
native_language_example: We need to do this now.

additional_notes: From the verb "precisar" (to need). Used with "de" before a noun or an infinitive: "precisando de ajuda" (needing help), "precisando de dormir" (needing to sleep). Very common in questions to offer help or check if someone needs something: "Você está precisando de...?"
target_language_example: Estou precisando de um pouco de tempo para terminar isso.
native_language_example: I need a little time to finish this.

meaning: "needed" / "was in need of" (imperfect past of "precisar de").
additional_notes: Used to say someone needed something in the past or as an ongoing situation in the past. It’s often followed by a noun or quantity (e.g., mais tempo, uma, um pouco mais de dinheiro). You can also use it in a polite/soft way to explain why something happened: "Eu precisava de..." = "I needed...".
target_language_example: Eu precisava de ajuda ontem, mas ninguém atendeu o telefone.
native_language_example: I needed help yesterday, but no one answered the phone.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or state that you need assistance. It comes from "precisar de" (to need) + "ajuda" (help). You can add details with "com" to say what you need help with (e.g., "Preciso de ajuda com..."), or add a place like "aqui" (here). You can also change the subject: "Você precisa de ajuda?" (Do you need help?), "Ele/Ela precisa de ajuda" (He/She needs help).
target_language_example: Desculpe, preciso de ajuda para encontrar este endereço.
native_language_example: Sorry, I need help finding this address.

additional_notes: Used to say you need a greater quantity of something. It’s often followed by a noun: "Preciso de mais água." You can also add a number or amount: "Preciso de mais dois minutos." (Literally "I need of more" in Portuguese, but the natural English translation is "I need more").
target_language_example: Desculpe, não consigo terminar hoje; preciso de mais tempo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t finish today; I need more time.

additional_notes: Used when the speaker needs one masculine singular thing: preciso de + noun. um can also mean “one,” and with some abstract or mass nouns it can sound like “some/a bit of” (for example, um tempo, um dinheiro). With feminine nouns, use uma instead.
target_language_example: Preciso de um táxi para o aeroporto.
native_language_example: I need a taxi to the airport.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine noun to say you need something: preciso de uma + noun (e.g., uma bolsa, uma mudança). For masculine nouns, use “preciso de um”. You can drop “eu” because it’s often implied: “Preciso de uma…”.
target_language_example: Preciso de uma ajuda com isso.
native_language_example: I need some help with this.

additional_notes: Used to say you need someone (their help, presence, or support). Often followed by a time/place: “Preciso de você agora/aqui/na garagem.” In negatives: “Não preciso de você” = “I don’t need you.”
target_language_example: Desculpa, mas preciso de você comigo hoje.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I need you with me today.

additional_notes: Used to say you must leave or go somewhere (because of a need, obligation, or urgency). Often followed by a destination or purpose: "preciso ir ao/à..." (to the...), "preciso ir para..." (to...), or an infinitive for purpose: "preciso ir trabalhar" (I need to go work). In everyday speech, "para" is often shortened to "pra" (e.g., "preciso ir pra casa").
target_language_example: Desculpa, eu preciso ir agora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I need to go now.

additional_notes: Used to ask or insist that someone does something. After "preciso que você", Portuguese normally uses the present subjunctive: "preciso que você continue/ajude/me dê/pare/quebre". It can sound direct; to soften it, add "por favor" or use "eu queria que você...".
target_language_example: Preciso que você chegue cedo amanhã, por favor.
native_language_example: I need you to arrive early tomorrow, please.

additional_notes: Used to say you require information, often before you can decide or act. Typically followed by a question word or clause: "preciso saber se..." (I need to know if...), "preciso saber que..." (I need to know that...), or a direct object like "preciso saber seu nome" (I need to know your name). "Preciso" is from the verb "precisar" (to need), and the subject "eu" (I) is usually implied.
target_language_example: Preciso saber a que horas você chega.
native_language_example: I need to know what time you arrive.

additional_notes: Used when you stop breathing for a short moment (e.g., underwater, during a medical exam, or from surprise/anxiety). You may also hear the variant “segurar a respiração” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Antes de mergulhar, vou prender a respiração.
native_language_example: Before I dive, I'm going to hold my breath.

additional_notes: Imperative form of the reflexive verb preparar-se (to prepare oneself). Often used to warn or set expectations about what’s coming next (e.g., prepare-se para o pior, para uma surpresa), or to tell someone to get ready to do something (prepare-se para partir). In writing, the hyphen connects the verb to the object pronoun: prepare-se.
target_language_example: Prepare-se para a reunião de amanhã.
native_language_example: Get ready for tomorrow’s meeting.

meaning: “Get ready for / prepare yourselves for …” (plural command).
additional_notes: Imperative used to tell a group (vocês) to get ready for something. It can be followed by a noun (“para a batalha”, “para uma cena forte”) or by an infinitive to express an action (“para abandonar o navio”). Singular form: “prepare-se para …”.
target_language_example: Preparem-se para a prova amanhã.
native_language_example: Get ready for the test tomorrow.

additional_notes: Common medical term for the pressure of blood in the arteries. Often used with estar + adjective: “A pressão sanguínea está alta/baixa.” In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people also say “pressão” by itself to mean blood pressure (e.g., “Medi a pressão”).
target_language_example: Vou verificar sua pressão sanguínea agora.
native_language_example: I’m going to check your blood pressure now.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase “prestar atenção (a/em/no/na…)” = “to pay attention (to…)”. “Presta atenção!” is an (informal) command to one person (tu). In Brazil you’ll also hear “Preste atenção!” (more formal/neutral) and “Prestem atenção!” (to a group). Common with: “prestar atenção ao professor” (to the teacher) and “prestar atenção no/em…” (common in Brazil).
target_language_example: Presta atenção no que eu estou dizendo.
native_language_example: Pay attention to what I’m saying.
