additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "estar" to describe what someone is doing right now: "estou/ele está prestando atenção". It’s also common with "prestar atenção em" or "prestar atenção a" (to pay attention to someone/something). Negative form: "não estava prestando atenção" (wasn’t paying attention).
target_language_example: Você está prestando atenção no que eu estou dizendo?
native_language_example: Are you paying attention to what I’m saying?

meaning: “pay attention” / “pay attention to …” (formal or polite command).
additional_notes: This is the imperative form (você) of **prestar atenção** (“to pay attention”). It’s common with **por favor** to sound more polite. Use **preste atenção a + person/thing** (often **preste atenção nele/nela** = “pay attention to him/her”).
target_language_example: Preste atenção ao que o professor está dizendo.
native_language_example: Pay attention to what the teacher is saying.

additional_notes: Imperative form used to address a group (you all). Often used alone as a warning or to get people to focus. It’s commonly followed by a preposition: **prestar atenção a** alguém/algo (“pay attention to someone/something”); in Brazil you may also hear **prestar atenção em/no/na** with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Pessoal, prestem atenção ao que o professor está dizendo.
native_language_example: Guys, pay attention to what the teacher is saying.

additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive (prestes a + infinitive) to say something is on the verge of happening: "estou/está/estamos/estão prestes a ...". It can describe imminent actions ("prestes a falar") or situations about to change ("prestes a aumentar", "prestes a desmoronar"). Agree "prestes" with the subject: "presto" (masc. singular), "presta" (fem. singular), "prestos" (masc. plural), "prestas" (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Estou prestes a sair, mas posso te ligar depois.
native_language_example: I'm about to leave, but I can call you later.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an assumption or inference, often based on incomplete information. It’s the 1st-person singular present of the verb "presumir" + "que". Frequently followed by the subjunctive (e.g., "esteja"), especially when expressing uncertainty.
target_language_example: Presumo que ele já tenha chegado.
native_language_example: I assume he has already arrived.

meaning: black and white; in black-and-white (not in color).
additional_notes: Used for photos/TV/printing (“em preto e branco” = in black and white). It can also be used figuratively to mean something is seen in a very simple, either/or way (“ver as coisas em preto e branco”).
target_language_example: Eu prefiro fotos em preto e branco.
native_language_example: I prefer black-and-white photos.

additional_notes: Used to talk about predicted weather (temperature, rain, wind, etc.), often for today or the next few days. Common in phrases like “a previsão do tempo para hoje” (today’s forecast) or “ver/consultar a previsão do tempo” (to check the forecast).
target_language_example: Vou ver a previsão do tempo para amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m going to check the weather forecast for tomorrow.

meaning: first class (top category/service, e.g., on a plane/train).
additional_notes: Used for the highest/most expensive class of travel or service (opposed to "classe econômica"). It can also be used more generally to mean "top-notch" or "premium" (e.g., "primeira classe em conforto").
target_language_example: Vamos de primeira classe ou econômica?
native_language_example: Are we going first class or economy?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the initial opinion or feeling you have about someone or something when you first meet/see/experience it. Common with the verb "causar" (to make/cause) as in "causar uma boa primeira impressão" (to make a good first impression). Often followed by "de" to say what it was about: "primeira impressão de Boston". You’ll also see possessives like "a tua/sua primeira impressão" (your first impression—informal/formal).
target_language_example: A minha primeira impressão do professor foi muito boa.
native_language_example: My first impression of the teacher was very good.

meaning: "first person" (either first in order, or the grammatical point of view: I/we).
additional_notes: Often used as a noun phrase meaning "the first person" to do something: "a primeira pessoa a + infinitive" (the first person to...). It can also refer to narration/grammar: "na primeira pessoa" = in the first-person point of view (using "eu"/"nós").
target_language_example: Ela foi a primeira pessoa a me ajudar.
native_language_example: She was the first person to help me.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the first occurrence of an experience or event (often with "a" or "pela" before it: "a primeira vez", "pela primeira vez"). Common pattern: "É/Esta é a sua primeira vez + (aqui/em...)" = "Is this your first time (here/in...)?" Also appears in the saying "Há uma primeira vez para tudo" = "There’s a first time for everything."
target_language_example: É a primeira vez que eu venho a Portugal.
native_language_example: It’s the first time I’ve come to Portugal.

additional_notes: Used as a title for the head of government in many countries. Often preceded by the definite article ("o primeiro-ministro", "do primeiro-ministro") and can also be used directly as a form of address ("Primeiro-ministro, por favor..."). The feminine form is "primeira-ministra".
target_language_example: O primeiro-ministro falou na televisão ontem à noite.
native_language_example: The prime minister spoke on TV last night.

additional_notes: Used in the pattern "ser o/a primeiro/a a + infinitive" to say someone is the first person to do something. It agrees with the person’s gender/number: "o primeiro a", "a primeira a", "os primeiros a", "as primeiras a". Common with past/future forms of "ser" (e.g., "foi", "vai ser").
target_language_example: Ele foi o primeiro a chegar.
native_language_example: He was the first to arrive.

additional_notes: Used to refer to someone’s personal name (not their family name). Often contrasted with “sobrenome” (last name/surname). “Chamar pelo primeiro nome” means addressing someone by their first name, which can suggest a more informal/friendly relationship.
target_language_example: Pode me chamar pelo meu primeiro nome: Ana.
native_language_example: You can call me by my first name: Ana.

additional_notes: Used for basic emergency help given right away after an injury/illness, before professional medical care arrives. Common in phrases like “curso de primeiros socorros” (first-aid course) and “kit de primeiros socorros” (first-aid kit). Often used with verbs like “precisar de” (to need) and “dar” (to give).
target_language_example: Você sabe fazer primeiros socorros?
native_language_example: Do you know first aid?

additional_notes: Used in legal/crime contexts to mean a prison sentence that lasts for the rest of someone’s life. Common with verbs like “ser condenado a” / “ser sentenciado a” (to be sentenced to) and “apanhar” (informal: to get/receive a sentence).
target_language_example: Ele foi condenado à prisão perpétua por homicídio.
native_language_example: He was sentenced to life in prison for murder.

additional_notes: Used with an object (person/thing) you want to find: "procurando por alguém" / "procurando por alguma coisa". In Brazilian Portuguese, "procurar" often appears without "por" ("Estou procurando você"), but both are common. Not the same as English "procuring" (obtaining).
target_language_example: Estou procurando por meu celular.
native_language_example: I'm looking for my cell phone.

additional_notes: Used for someone who teaches the French language (at school, a course, etc.). In Brazilian Portuguese, "professor" is used for teachers in general; "de francês" specifies the subject. For a woman, you’ll often hear "professora de francês". You can also say "meu/minha professor(a) de francês" (my French teacher).
target_language_example: Eu quero me tornar professor de francês.
native_language_example: I want to become a French teacher.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a teacher who teaches the English language. In Portuguese, "professor" can mean a school teacher (not necessarily a university professor). You can change the possessive/article to match who you're talking about and the teacher’s gender: "meu professor de inglês" / "minha professora de inglês".
target_language_example: Meu professor de inglês é muito paciente.
native_language_example: My English teacher is very patient.

additional_notes: Feminine form of "pronto para" (used when talking about a woman or a feminine noun). It’s followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., "pronta para partir" = ready to leave) or by a noun (e.g., "pronta para a guerra" = ready for war). For addressing someone directly, you may also see "Está pronta para...?" (Are you ready to...?) or the command form "Esteja pronta para..." (Be ready to...).
target_language_example: Acho que estou pronta para começar.
native_language_example: I think I’m ready to start.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is prepared for something (often followed by a noun) or prepared to do something (often followed by an infinitive verb). It agrees with the person/thing: pronto (m. sg.), pronta (f. sg.), prontos (m. pl.), prontas (f. pl.). Note: English "pronto" usually means "quickly", but Portuguese "pronto" commonly means "ready" (or "done" in other contexts).
target_language_example: Você está pronto para sair agora?
native_language_example: Are you ready to leave now?

additional_notes: Used with the plural adjective "prontos" (feminine: "prontas") plus "para". Use it before an infinitive verb: "prontos para fazer" (ready to do), or before a noun: "prontos para a festa" (ready for the party). Often appears with "estar": "estamos/eles estão prontos para...".
target_language_example: Estamos prontos para sair agora.
native_language_example: We’re ready to leave now.

additional_notes: Infinitive + object pronoun. “proteger” = to protect, and “-la” = “her” (direct object). In Portuguese, object pronouns are often attached to the end of the verb with a hyphen. The accent in “protegê-” marks a stressed vowel when the pronoun is attached (compare: “proteger” vs. “protegê-la”).
target_language_example: Vou protegê-la a qualquer custo.
native_language_example: I’ll protect her at any cost.

additional_notes: Infinitive verb + object pronoun: proteger (“to protect”) + -lo (“him/it”). The pronoun attaches with a hyphen, and the verb gets an accent shift: proteger → protegê- before -lo/-la/-los/-las. Common after infinitives (and some other forms).
target_language_example: Vou protegê-lo a qualquer custo.
native_language_example: I’m going to protect him at any cost.

additional_notes: Used for the lotion/cream/spray you put on your skin to protect it from the sun. Very common with the verb passar/colocar (to apply/put on): "passar protetor solar" = to put on sunscreen. You can also say "um protetor solar" to mean a (bottle of) sunscreen.
target_language_example: Não esquece de passar protetor solar na praia.
native_language_example: Don’t forget to put on sunscreen at the beach.

meaning: A very strong swear word meaning something like “holy shit!” / “for fuck’s sake!” (shock, anger, frustration).
additional_notes: Very informal and offensive Brazilian Portuguese profanity. Often used as a standalone exclamation, or at the start of a sentence to show strong emotion (surprise, disbelief, annoyance). Can also be said with a rising intonation (“Puta que pariu?”) to express disbelief. Avoid in polite/company or professional settings.
target_language_example: Puta que pariu, eu esqueci minha carteira em casa!
native_language_example: Holy shit, I forgot my wallet at home!

meaning: “Holy shit!” / “Fuck!” (a very vulgar exclamation of shock, anger, or frustration).
additional_notes: Very strong profanity in Brazilian Portuguese, often used alone or before a name/command (“Puta merda, Mike.” / “Puta merda, atira!”). Not appropriate in polite conversation; use milder options like “Nossa!”, “Meu Deus!”, or “Caramba!”.
target_language_example: Puta merda, eu esqueci minha carteira!
native_language_example: Holy shit, I forgot my wallet!

additional_notes: A metal tool used to pry things open (doors, crates, boxes) or to force entry (“arrombar”). Literally means “goat’s foot,” but it refers to the tool, not an animal.
target_language_example: Ele usou um pé de cabra para abrir a janela.
native_language_example: He used a crowbar to open the window.

meaning: a nuisance; an annoying person/thing (a pain).
additional_notes: Informal, very common in Brazilian Portuguese. Used to describe someone or something that keeps bothering you, is irritating, or makes things difficult (similar to "chato" or "um saco"). Often said with verbs like "ser" (Ele é um pé no saco) or "ficar" (Isso fica um pé no saco).
target_language_example: Ele é um pé no saco, fica me ligando toda hora.
native_language_example: He’s such a pain; he keeps calling me all the time.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the time of day when the sun goes down. Often appears with verbs like ver/assistir (to watch/see) and can also refer to the sunset itself (the colors in the sky).
target_language_example: Vamos ver o pôr do sol na praia.
native_language_example: Let’s watch the sunset at the beach.

additional_notes: Noun meaning the time/scene when the sun goes down. Often used on its own as an exclamation/comment (e.g., “Pôr-do-sol, hein?” = “What a sunset, huh?”). Can also be used in phrases like “ao pôr-do-sol” (“at sunset”) and “ver o pôr-do-sol” (“to watch the sunset”).
target_language_example: Vamos ver o pôr-do-sol na praia.
native_language_example: Let’s watch the sunset at the beach.

additional_notes: Literally “the setting of the sun.” Used to talk about the time of day when the sun goes down, or the sunset view itself. Common with verbs like ver/assistir (to watch), admirar (to admire), and with locations: na praia (at the beach), no topo (at the top).
target_language_example: Vamos ver o pôr do sol na praia.
native_language_example: Let’s watch the sunset at the beach.

additional_notes: Used for the board in a classroom where the teacher writes (traditionally with chalk). It’s commonly used with prepositions like “no quadro-negro” (on the blackboard) and verbs like “escrever” (to write), “ler” (to read), and “comparar” (to compare).
target_language_example: O professor escreveu a lição no quadro-negro.
native_language_example: The teacher wrote the lesson on the blackboard.

additional_notes: Used to ask about multiple feminine plural items: "Quais são as alternativas?" = "Which are the alternatives?" Often followed by a feminine plural noun (as alternativas, as chances, as fontes). For masculine plural, use "quais são os"; for singular, "qual é a" (fem.) / "qual é o" (masc.).
target_language_example: Quais são as opções mais baratas?
native_language_example: Which are the cheapest options?

meaning: 'which are the' (asking about plural masculine items).
additional_notes: Used to ask for a list/selection of items: “Which are the …?” It agrees with plural masculine nouns (os limites, os pilares). For plural feminine, use “quais são as”. In speech it often introduces a noun: “Quais são os seus planos?”
target_language_example: Quais são os seus objetivos para este ano?
native_language_example: What are your goals for this year?

additional_notes: Used to ask what’s wrong or what the issue is, often when someone seems upset or something unexpected is happening. It can sound more confrontational depending on tone (like “What’s your problem?”). You’ll also hear the fuller form "Qual é o problema?" and the more common contraction "Qual o problema?" (for "Qual é o").
target_language_example: Ei, qual o problema? Você está bem?
native_language_example: Hey, what's the problem? Are you okay?

additional_notes: Used when there are exactly two options and you’re asking someone to choose between them. It commonly refers back to two previously mentioned items/people. You can also inflect it for grammatical gender/number depending on the noun: e.g., “qual das duas” (two feminine items). Often used alone as a short question (“Qual dos dois?”) or followed by a noun (“Qual dos dois livros...”).
target_language_example: Eu tenho dois livros: qual dos dois você quer?
native_language_example: I have two books: which of the two do you want?

meaning: “what was…?” / “which one was…?”; colloquially, “what happened?” / “what’s up?”
additional_notes: Literally “which/what was,” using the past tense of ser (foi). Common in questions about a past impression, answer, word, etc. In casual speech, “Qual foi?” (often repeated: “Qual foi, qual foi?”) can mean “What happened?” or “What’s your problem?” depending on tone.
target_language_example: Você se lembra qual foi a sua primeira impressão da cidade?
native_language_example: Do you remember what your first impression of the city was?

meaning: “what was the…?” / “which was the…?” (asking about a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to ask about something in the past, especially for facts, reasons, results, or impressions. It agrees with a feminine noun that follows (e.g., causa, resposta, impressão). For a masculine noun, use “qual foi o…?”; for plural, “quais foram os/as…?”.
target_language_example: Qual foi a sua resposta?
native_language_example: What was your answer?

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser to ask for identification or to choose between options. In Brazilian Portuguese, qual é? can also be said informally by itself to mean something like 'come on?' or 'what's up?' depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Qual é o seu nome?
native_language_example: What is your name?

additional_notes: Used to ask for identification or a specific piece of information before a feminine singular noun ("a" = "the"). Often used in questions like definitions, conclusions, relationships, or characteristics. For masculine nouns, use "qual é o". For plural nouns, use "quais são as/os".
target_language_example: Qual é a melhor opção para hoje?
native_language_example: What is the best option for today?

meaning: “what is the distance” / “how far is it”.
additional_notes: Used to ask how far one place is from another, or how far it is to reach a destination. Common patterns: **Qual é a distância até...** (to/until...), **Qual é a distância de X a Y / de X para Y** (from X to Y), and **Qual é a distância entre X e Y** (between X and Y). It can also ask about a distance someone usually covers (e.g., running).
target_language_example: Qual é a distância daqui até a estação de metrô?
native_language_example: How far is it from here to the subway station?

meaning: “which one is yours?” / “what is your …?” (addressing someone formally).
additional_notes: Used to ask about something that belongs to the person you’re speaking to, or to ask which item is theirs. It’s the feminine form because it refers to a feminine noun (e.g., banda, caneta, carteira). For masculine nouns, use “Qual é o seu…?”; in informal speech with friends you’ll often hear “Qual é a tua…?”. Often followed by a noun: “Qual é a sua banda favorita?”
target_language_example: Qual é a sua senha do Wi‑Fi?
native_language_example: What’s your Wi‑Fi password?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the identity, choice, or specific value of a masculine singular noun. In English it often translates as both "what is the" and "which is the," depending on context. Before a feminine noun, use "qual é a".
target_language_example: Qual é o seu nome?
native_language_example: What is your name?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the name of a person, place, street, thing, etc. It’s often followed by "de" + noun/pronoun (e.g., "Qual é o nome da rua?", "Qual é o nome dela?"). In speech you may also hear the shorter "Qual o nome...?".
target_language_example: Desculpe, qual é o nome do restaurante?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what’s the name of the restaurant?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a specific number tied to someone or something (phone number, room number, ID/reference number, etc.). Often followed by “de” + noun (“Qual é o número do quarto?”) or “dela/dele” (“Qual é o número dela?”). In Brazilian Portuguese you’ll also hear “Qual é o número?” on its own when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Com licença, qual é o número do pedido?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what is the order number?

additional_notes: A common question to ask what is wrong or why something is an issue. It can be neutral (“What’s the issue?”) or sound confrontational depending on tone (like “So what’s the problem?”). Often used on its own as a complete question. Literally: “which is the problem?”.
target_language_example: Qual é o problema com este computador?
native_language_example: What’s wrong with this computer?

additional_notes: Used to ask about something that belongs to or relates to the person you’re talking to, usually followed by a noun: “Qual é o seu problema?” = “What is your problem?” The possessive “seu” agrees with what is owned (seu/sua/seus/suas), not with the owner: “Qual é a sua idade?” (your age), “Quais são os seus planos?” (your plans). For plural, you’ll often hear “quais são os seus/as suas…”.
target_language_example: Qual é o seu endereço?
native_language_example: What is your address?

additional_notes: Common, polite way to ask someone’s name (formal/polite “seu”). You can add words after it for more detail: “nome todo” = full name; “nome real” = real name. In informal speech with friends, you’ll often hear “Qual é o teu nome?” (Portugal) or “Qual é o seu nome?” / “Como você se chama?” (Brazil).
target_language_example: Desculpe, qual é o seu nome?
native_language_example: Sorry, what is your name?

meaning: “what size is it?” / “how big is it?”
additional_notes: Used to ask for the size or dimensions of something. Often followed by "de" or "do/da" + the thing: "Qual é o tamanho deste vestido?" (clothing size) or "Qual é o tamanho da memória...?" (amount/capacity). In some contexts it refers to length/area/overall size rather than a specific measurement unit.
target_language_example: Qual é o tamanho do seu sapato?
native_language_example: What size is your shoe?

additional_notes:
Often means “anything” in the sense of “no matter what” or “whatever”: 
- Pode comer qualquer coisa. = You can eat anything.
- Eu farei qualquer coisa, menos isso. = I’ll do anything but that.
It can also mean “something / anything” when you don’t know or don’t want to specify what: Não sei dizer qualquer coisa. = I can’t say anything.
In casual speech it can be used like “If anything / if you need anything”: Qualquer coisa, você me liga. = If anything, call me (i.e., if you need something or if something comes up).
target_language_example: Qualquer coisa, me manda uma mensagem.
native_language_example: If anything, send me a message.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause describing an unspecified thing (followed by a verb): qualquer coisa que + verb. Often refers to actions or tasks ("anything you do", "whatever you want"). You’ll often see it with the subjunctive when the action is uncertain or general (e.g., "qualquer coisa que eu faça").
target_language_example: Eu topo qualquer coisa que você sugerir.
native_language_example: I’m up for anything you suggest.

additional_notes: Often appears as **de qualquer forma**, meaning **'anyway'** or **'in any case'**. It’s used to say that something remains true regardless of the details or circumstances.
target_language_example: De qualquer forma, eu vou amanhã.
native_language_example: Anyway, I'm going tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to mean an unspecified location (it doesn’t matter which). Often appears with "em" ("em qualquer lugar" = "anywhere") or as a standalone option ("Qualquer lugar está bom" = "Anywhere is fine"). You can also use it to exclude a place: "Qualquer lugar, menos aqui" = "Anywhere but here."
target_language_example: Podemos nos encontrar em qualquer lugar perto da estação.
native_language_example: We can meet anywhere near the station.

additional_notes: Used to refer to any other person/thing in the same set, often implying “no different from the rest” (como qualquer outro) or in comparisons (melhor/pior do que qualquer outro). It agrees with the noun it refers to: qualquer outra (feminine) / quaisquer outros(as) (plural).
target_language_example: Sou um homem como qualquer outro.
native_language_example: I’m a man like any other.

additional_notes: Means “any person” / “anyone at all,” often with an idea of “no matter who.” It can be used as a short answer by itself (e.g., “Qualquer um!” = “Anyone!” / “Either one!”). Feminine form: “qualquer uma” (anyone/any one [female/one item]). In plural: “quaisquer” (less common in everyday speech).
target_language_example: Pode entrar qualquer um aqui?
native_language_example: Can anyone come in here?

additional_notes: Used to say that it’s possible for any person (no special skill/permission required), or that anyone is capable of doing something. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., fazer, ler, cometer). You can also hear it with feminine agreement: “qualquer uma pode” (“any woman can” / “anyone can,” referring to a woman).
target_language_example: Com um pouco de prática, qualquer um pode aprender português.
native_language_example: With a little practice, anyone can learn Portuguese.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition or description of a person. It’s followed by a verb (often in the subjunctive when talking about an unknown/unspecified person): "Qualquer um que queira/venha/consiga...". Can also appear in threats or strong statements, like "Mato qualquer um que..." (= I’ll kill anyone who...).
target_language_example: Qualquer um que souber a resposta pode falar.
native_language_example: Anyone who knows the answer can speak.

quando foi a última vez que você

target_language_multi_word_term: quando foi a última vez que você
additional_notes: Used to ask about the most recent time someone did something. It’s followed by a verb in the past (often the simple past): "Quando foi a última vez que você + [verb]...?" You can change "você" to another subject: "ele/ela", "vocês", "a gente", etc.
target_language_example: Quando foi a última vez que você foi ao cinema?
native_language_example: When was the last time you went to the movies?

additional_notes: A common combination used to ask about the time of an action or event involving the person being addressed. It can appear in direct questions ("Quando você volta?") or inside a longer sentence ("Não sei quando você chega."). In Brazilian Portuguese, você is the usual singular "you."
target_language_example: Não sei quando você vai chegar.
native_language_example: I don't know when you'll arrive.

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time someone began doing an action. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., aprender, fazer, ganhar, tocar, usar). In conversation, it’s often completed with a verb phrase: "Quando você começou a estudar português?"
target_language_example: Quando você começou a trabalhar aqui?
native_language_example: When did you start working here?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time or date someone bought something. It’s a question form: quando (“when”) + você (“you”) + comprou (past tense of comprar, “bought”). Often followed by the item (e.g., esses óculos, esta chave de fenda, este guarda-chuva).
target_language_example: Quando você comprou esse celular?
native_language_example: When did you buy that cellphone?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time or moment when someone will do something. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., chegar, falar, partir, se mudar) and can express impatience or emphasis with words like “finalmente” (“finally”). In questions, the verb often stays in the “vai” (present) form to talk about the near future, similar to English “are you going to…”.
target_language_example: Quando você vai terminar o trabalho?
native_language_example: When are you going to finish the work?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time/date or occasion of an action involving “you all” (vocês). Common in questions about schedules, plans, or past events; the verb tense changes depending on whether you mean past, present, or future.
target_language_example: Quando vocês chegam amanhã?
native_language_example: When are you (all) arriving tomorrow?

meaning: 'when' (used to ask about the time something happens).
additional_notes: Very common question pattern. It’s often equivalent to just “quando”, but adds emphasis and sounds more conversational in European Portuguese. In Brazilian Portuguese it exists too, though questions more often use “quando” (sometimes with “é que” for emphasis). Word order: “Quando é que + verb…?”
target_language_example: Quando é que vocês chegam?
native_language_example: When do you arrive?

meaning: "when I got home / when I arrived home."
additional_notes: Used to set the time of another action or situation in the past. It’s a time clause with "quando" (when) + "cheguei" (I arrived, past tense of "chegar") + "em casa" (at home). Often appears at the start or end of the sentence; if it comes first, it’s usually followed by a comma.
target_language_example: Quando cheguei em casa, já era tarde demais para ligar.
native_language_example: When I got home, it was already too late to call.

meaning: “when you grow up” / “when I grow up.”
additional_notes: Used mainly when talking to or about children, to ask or say what someone wants to be in the future. It can also be used figuratively to mean “when you’re more mature/older” (e.g., “You’ll understand when you grow up.”). Often appears without an explicit subject; context tells whether it means “you” or “I.”
target_language_example: Quando crescer, quero ser médica.
native_language_example: When I grow up, I want to be a doctor.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a time clause with a female subject (“ela” = “she”). It can refer to the past (“when she arrived”), the future (“when she feels ready”), or a planned time (“for when she wakes up”). In Portuguese, the verb tense in the clause after “quando” depends on whether it’s a real past event or a future/uncertain event.
target_language_example: Eu te aviso quando ela chegar.
native_language_example: I’ll let you know when she arrives.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a time clause about a male person (“he”). In Portuguese, you often don’t need to repeat the subject pronoun, so you’ll also commonly see just “quando” + verb (e.g., “quando chegar”). Word order can vary: “Quando ele era mais novo, …” or “… quando ele era mais novo.”
target_language_example: Quando ele chegar, me liga.
native_language_example: When he arrives, call me.

meaning: when I was a child / as a child.
additional_notes: Used to talk about things you did, liked, or experienced in your childhood. The subject is often understood from context, but it can change: eu... quando era criança (when I was a child), ele... quando era criança (when he was a child). Literally it’s “when (someone) was a child,” and it commonly goes at the end or beginning of the sentence.
target_language_example: Quando era criança, eu brincava na rua todos os dias.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I played in the street every day.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a period earlier in someone’s life. The verb phrase uses the imperfect (era), commonly paired with habitual actions or ongoing states in the past (e.g., costumava…, jogava…, sabia…). You can adjust the subject/number: quando eu era jovem, quando ele/ela era jovem, quando éramos jovens, etc.
target_language_example: Eu jogava muito basebol quando era jovem.
native_language_example: I played a lot of baseball when I was young.

additional_notes: Used with the future subjunctive of "estar" (eu estiver, você/ele/ela estiver, nós estivermos, vocês/eles/elas estiverem). After time words like "quando" (when), Portuguese commonly uses the future subjunctive to talk about a future situation/condition: "Quando estiver pronto(a)..." = "When (he/she) is ready..." Often followed by an adjective or expression of state: "com raiva" (angry), "pronto(a)" (ready), "prest(es) a" (about to).
target_language_example: Quando estiver em casa, eu te mando uma mensagem.
native_language_example: When I'm home, I'll send you a message.

additional_notes: Introduces a time clause with the speaker as the subject. It can refer to the past, present, or future depending on the verb that follows. In natural Portuguese, the pronoun eu is sometimes omitted when it is already clear from context.
target_language_example: Eu fico feliz quando eu te vejo.
native_language_example: I feel happy when I see you.

meaning: when I was a child / when I was little.
additional_notes: Used to talk about things that happened regularly or at a specific time in the past during your childhood. Often followed by actions in the past (e.g., "eu ia", "meus pais compravam", "minha mãe morreu").
target_language_example: Quando eu era criança, eu brincava na rua todos os dias.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I played outside every day.

meaning: “when I was (… years old)” / “when I used to have” (past).
additional_notes: Most commonly used with an age: "quando eu tinha dez anos" = "when I was ten (years old)." Here, "tinha" is the imperfect past of "ter" (to have), used to describe a past state or ongoing situation. It can also be used more generally to mean "when I had" something in the past (e.g., "quando eu tinha tempo" = "when I had time"), but with ages it’s especially common.
target_language_example: Quando eu tinha vinte anos, eu morava em Lisboa.
native_language_example: When I was twenty years old, I lived in Lisbon.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the moment an action happened in the past, often alongside an ongoing/background action (commonly with imperfect: "eu estava..." / "eu fazia..."). Word order can vary: "Quando o telefone tocou, ..." or "... quando o telefone tocou."
target_language_example: Eu estava tomando banho quando o telefone tocou.
native_language_example: I was taking a shower when the phone rang.

additional_notes: Used to give someone freedom to choose the time to do something. Very common after phrases like "pode" (you can) or "você pode" (you can/you may): "pode ir quando quiser" = "you can go whenever you want."
target_language_example: Você pode me ligar quando quiser.
native_language_example: You can call me whenever you want.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of "ter" ("tinha") to talk about age in the past. The subject is often omitted when it’s clear from context; you can also say "quando eu tinha treze anos" (when I was 13) or add emphasis with "de idade".
target_language_example: Quando tinha treze anos, eu morava com os meus avós.
native_language_example: When I was thirteen, I lived with my grandparents.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a time clause with “you” as the subject. For future events in Portuguese, this clause often uses the future subjunctive: “quando você chegar...” = “when you arrive...”. It can refer to the past, present, or future depending on the context.
target_language_example: Quando você tiver tempo, me liga.
native_language_example: When you have time, call me.

meaning: 'how many people' (asking for the number of people).
additional_notes: Used to ask about a quantity of people. It agrees with the feminine plural noun "pessoas": "quantas". Often followed by a verb like "tem" (there are), "moram" (live), "estão" (are), "vieram" (came). In casual Brazilian Portuguese you may hear "Quantas pessoas tem...?"; in more formal/standard phrasing: "Quantas pessoas há...?" or "Quantas pessoas existem...?"
target_language_example: Quantas pessoas vão vir para a festa?
native_language_example: How many people are going to come to the party?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a number of people. It’s typically followed by a verb: “Quantas pessoas você convidou?” (How many people did you invite?). Because *pessoas* is feminine plural, you use **quantas** (not *quantos*). In writing, a question mark is used, and in speech the intonation rises at the end.
target_language_example: Quantas pessoas você conhece aqui?
native_language_example: How many people do you know here?

additional_notes: Used to ask about frequency or number of occurrences. Often followed by a time period: "quantas vezes por dia/semana/mês" (how many times per day/week/month). By itself ("Quantas vezes?") it can mean “How many times?” or “How often?” depending on context.
target_language_example: Quantas vezes por semana você vai à academia?
native_language_example: How many times a week do you go to the gym?

meaning: “How many times have you…?” / “How often have you…?”
additional_notes:
Used to ask about the number of times something happened. 
- "Quantas" (feminine plural) agrees with "vezes" (times). 
- With "você", Portuguese uses third-person singular verb forms: "Quantas vezes você fez…?" (not *"você fiz"*). 
- Often followed by a verb in the past (fez, faltou, assistiu) or present (faz, falta, assiste) depending on the meaning.
- Note: if you mean "you all" (plural), use "Quantas vezes vocês…" with a plural verb (e.g., "vocês mentiram").
target_language_example: Quantas vezes você já veio aqui?
native_language_example: How many times have you come here? / How often have you been here?

additional_notes: Used before a noun to talk about how much or how many there is/are (quantidade de + noun). With countable nouns it often means “number of” (quantidade de idiomas = number of languages). With uncountable nouns it means “amount of” (quantidade de estresse/sangue/remédio = amount of stress/blood/medicine). Often appears with comparatives (maior/menor quantidade de = a greater/smaller amount/quantity of; a mesma quantidade de = the same amount of).
target_language_example: Preciso de uma grande quantidade de água para cozinhar isso.
native_language_example: I need a large amount of water to cook this.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic you’re talking about, often to contrast it with something else. Common patterns: "Quanto a + noun/pronoun" (Quanto a isso… / Quanto a ti…) and "(não) concordar com alguém quanto a + algo" = "(not) agree with someone about something".
target_language_example: Quanto ao preço, podemos negociar amanhã.
native_language_example: As for the price, we can negotiate tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or refer back to a specific topic/issue (“as for that…”). Common after feelings/opinions like “estar nervoso/curioso quanto a isso” and with doubts/complaints: “ter dúvidas/reclamações quanto a isso”. It can also mean “what to do about that” in questions: “O que vamos fazer quanto a isso?”.
target_language_example: Não se preocupe quanto a isso; eu resolvo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry about that; I’ll take care of it.

additional_notes: Used to ask the price of something. You can say it by itself ("Quanto custa?") or add the item after it ("Quanto custa esse guarda-chuva?"). Often also heard as "Quanto é?" (more casual) or "Quanto custa isso?" (= "How much is that?").
target_language_example: Com licença, quanto custa esta camiseta?
native_language_example: Excuse me, how much does this T-shirt cost?

additional_notes: Used to ask the price of something you’re pointing to or choosing. "Este" is masculine (chapéu, computador, guarda-chuva, negócio, relógio, roteiro). For feminine nouns, use "Quanto custa esta...?" (e.g., "Quanto custa esta blusa?"). You can also hear "Quanto é este...?" in shops, with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Quanto custa este bilhete de ônibus?
native_language_example: How much does this bus ticket cost?

additional_notes: Used in the comparative pattern “quanto mais..., (tanto) mais/menos...” meaning “the more..., the more/less...”. Often followed by a verb: “quanto mais ele trabalha, mais ele ganha” (“the more he works, the more he earns”). You can also use it with adjectives/adverbs: “quanto mais curioso..., melhor” (“the more curious..., the better”).
target_language_example: Quanto mais cedo sairmos, melhor.
native_language_example: The earlier we leave, the better.

additional_notes: Used at the beginning of questions asking about an amount (money, quantity, time, etc.) related to the person addressed: "Quanto você cobra...?" (How much do you charge...?), "Quanto você tem?" (How much do you have?). Often followed by a verb like cobrar (to charge), gastar (to spend), querer (to want). If a noun is stated, "quanto" can change to match it (e.g., "quantos anos..." = how many years).
target_language_example: Quanto você paga de aluguel por mês?
native_language_example: How much do you pay in rent per month?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the amount of money someone has, wants, or that will be spent. It often appears at the start of a question: “Quanto dinheiro…?” In everyday speech, people also commonly say “Quanto é?” or “Quanto custa?” when asking the price of something.
target_language_example: Quanto dinheiro eu preciso para a viagem?
native_language_example: How much money do I need for the trip?

additional_notes: Used to ask about an amount of money. It’s usually followed by a verb: "Quanto dinheiro você ganha/gastou/tem?". You’ll often see "De quanto dinheiro você precisa?" = "How much money do you need?" (the "de" is common with verbs like "precisar" in this kind of question). In Portuguese the subject "você" can come right after "quanto dinheiro".
target_language_example: Quanto dinheiro você tem agora?
native_language_example: How much money do you have now?

additional_notes: Used to ask about duration or the amount of time something takes. In expressions like faz quanto tempo que...?, it asks how much time has passed since something happened: 'how long ago...?'
target_language_example: Quanto tempo você vai ficar aqui?
native_language_example: How long are you going to stay here?

meaning: "how long will (it)" / "how much time will (it)" (usually before a verb like demorar/levar).
additional_notes: Used to ask about duration or time needed. It’s most common as the start of a longer question, e.g. “Quanto tempo vai demorar?” (How long will it take?) or “Quanto tempo vai levar?” (How long will it take?). You can also add a subject: “Quanto tempo vai o filme?” (How long is the movie?).
target_language_example: Quanto tempo vai demorar para chegar lá?
native_language_example: How long will it take to get there?

additional_notes: Used to ask about duration/time spent doing something. It’s commonly followed by a verb in the past ("Quanto tempo você esperou?" = how long did you wait?) or with "faz" + time + "que" for “how long has it been since...” ("Faz quanto tempo que você...?"). In everyday speech, people may omit "que" after "faz": "Faz quanto tempo você...".
target_language_example: Quanto tempo você ficou aqui ontem?
native_language_example: How long did you stay here yesterday?

additional_notes: Used after words like tão/tanto/tanta/tantos (“so/as much/many”) to compare with the listener: tão + adjective + quanto você (“as [adjective] as you”), tanto/tanta + noun or time/amount + quanto você (“as much/many/long as you”). In full form it’s “do que você” in some contexts, but with tão/tanto the common pattern is “tão/tanto ... quanto você”.
target_language_example: Eu não sou tão alto quanto você.
native_language_example: I'm not as tall as you.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s age (people, animals, etc.). Literally “how many years.” It often appears with the verb ter: “Quantos anos você tem?” = “How old are you?” You can also add a person/thing as the subject: “Quantos anos tem o seu gato?”
target_language_example: Desculpa perguntar, mas quantos anos você tem?
native_language_example: Sorry to ask, but how old are you?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s age (a person) or how old something/someone is (a pet, etc.). It literally means “how many years does (he/she/it) have,” and it’s often followed by a noun: “Quantos anos tem o seu filho?” In everyday speech you may also hear “Quantos anos você tem?” (How old are you?) or “Quantos anos ele/ela tem?” (How old is he/she?).
target_language_example: Quantos anos tem a sua mãe?
native_language_example: How old is your mother?

additional_notes: Used to ask a group how many people (among “you all”) fit a condition. Use **quantos** for masculine/mixed groups and **quantas de vocês** for an all-female group. Often followed by a verb: *Quantos de vocês vão?*
target_language_example: Quantos de vocês têm tempo agora?
native_language_example: How many of you have time now?

additional_notes: Used as a number in counting, giving quantities, ages, and in math. In Brazil it’s usually pronounced like “quarenta i cinco”; in Portugal you may hear clearer separation between words.
target_language_example: O ônibus chega em quarenta e cinco minutos.
native_language_example: The bus arrives in forty-five minutes.

additional_notes: Name of the weekday between terça-feira (Tuesday) and quinta-feira (Thursday). Often used with days of the week: Hoje é quarta-feira. / Na quarta-feira (on Wednesday). You can add time expressions like de manhã (in the morning), à tarde (in the afternoon), à noite (at night).
target_language_example: Na quarta-feira, tenho aula de português.
native_language_example: On Wednesday, I have Portuguese class.

additional_notes: Used to say someone very nearly died (often from an accident, illness, or dangerous situation). It’s in the past: *morreu* = “died” (he/she/you died), with *quase* = “almost.” You can add the cause with *de* (e.g., *quase morreu de medo* = “almost died of fear”).
target_language_example: Tom quase morreu naquele acidente.
native_language_example: Tom almost died in that accident.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens very rarely (but not zero times). It can come before the verb ("quase nunca faço") or after the subject ("eu quase nunca faço"). Often interchangeable with "raramente" (rarely).
target_language_example: Eu quase nunca como fast food.
native_language_example: I almost never eat fast food.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens most of the time, but not 100%. Often placed before the verb ("Ele quase sempre chega cedo") or at the end of the sentence ("Ele chega cedo quase sempre"). It can also be said alone as a short answer: "Quase sempre."
target_language_example: Eu quase sempre vou a pé para o trabalho.
native_language_example: I almost always walk to work.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens very frequently, but not literally every single day. Common in spoken Portuguese and can go before or after the verb (e.g., "Eu quase todo dia me levanto às seis" / "Eu me levanto às seis quase todo dia"). You may also hear "quase todos os dias" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Eu tomo café aqui quase todo dia.
native_language_example: I have coffee here almost every day.

meaning: almost every day; nearly every day.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens regularly, but not literally every single day. It’s a common time expression and usually comes at the end of the sentence, though it can also be placed earlier for emphasis.
target_language_example: Eu estudo português quase todos os dias.
native_language_example: I study Portuguese almost every day.

meaning: four years; (when talking about age) four years old.
additional_notes: Used to talk about duration ("por quatro anos" = for four years; "há quatro anos" = four years ago) or age ("tinha quatro anos" = was four years old). In Portuguese, age is usually expressed with the verb "ter" (Tenho 4 anos = I’m 4).
target_language_example: Morei aqui por quatro anos.
native_language_example: I lived here for four years.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration ("for four days" / "it took four days"), a point in time relative to something else ("four days later/after"), or frequency ("four days a week"). Often appears with prepositions like "por" (for), "em" (in), "depois" (after/later), and "por semana" (per week).
target_language_example: Vou ficar em Lisboa por quatro dias.
native_language_example: I'm going to stay in Lisbon for four days.

additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency/number of occurrences ("quatro vezes na semana" = four times a week), comparisons ("quatro vezes mais" = four times more/as much), or multiplication in math ("quatro vezes seis" = four times six). You’ll also hear the shorter form "quatro por" in math ("quatro por seis").
target_language_example: Eu vou ao ginásio quatro vezes por semana.
native_language_example: I go to the gym four times a week.

additional_notes: Used as an exclamation to react positively to news or a situation (“Que bom!”). It can also introduce a clause with the subjunctive to mean “It’s great that…”, e.g., “Que bom estarmos juntos” (“It’s great that we’re together”). Often said when you’re happy to see someone: “Que bom te ver!”
target_language_example: Que bom que você conseguiu!
native_language_example: That’s great that you managed to do it!

additional_notes: Used to express happiness, relief, or approval about something that happened or is true. It’s often followed by a full clause (que bom que + [subject] + verb): “Que bom que você veio” = “I’m glad you came.” In English you might also say “Good thing (that)…”, depending on context.
target_language_example: Que bom que você chegou a tempo.
native_language_example: I’m glad you arrived on time.

additional_notes: Used mainly to express a strong reaction (admiration, surprise, annoyance, etc.). It’s commonly followed by an adjective: "Que coisa linda!" = "What a beautiful thing!" You can also use it more literally to mean "what thing?", but in everyday speech it often sounds like an exclamation.
target_language_example: Que coisa estranha!
native_language_example: What a strange thing!

meaning: "what the hell" / "what the heck" (strong surprise, anger, or impatience).
additional_notes: Used as an exclamation in questions or statements to add emphasis: "Que diabo é isso?" = "What the hell is this?" It can sound rude or aggressive, so avoid it in formal situations or with strangers. Similar in tone to "que raio" (milder) or "que inferno" (also strong).
target_language_example: Que diabo você está fazendo aqui?
native_language_example: What the hell are you doing here?

additional_notes: Used to add strong emphasis to a question, showing surprise, annoyance, impatience, or anger. It can sound rude/impolite, so avoid it in formal situations or with people you don’t know well. Often appears as “que diabos...?” (“What the hell...?”) and also in “de que diabos...?” (“what the hell about / what the hell are you talking about?”). A common variant is “que diabo...?” (singular).
target_language_example: Que diabos está acontecendo aqui?
native_language_example: What the hell is going on here?

additional_notes: Informal and mildly rude. Used as an exclamation on its own ("Que droga!") or in patterns like "Que droga de + noun" to mean "What a crappy + noun" (e.g., "Que droga de música!"). Even though "droga" literally means "drug," in this expression it means "crap/awful thing," not an actual drug.
target_language_example: Que droga! Esqueci minha carteira em casa.
native_language_example: Damn! I forgot my wallet at home.

additional_notes: Common, polite way to ask for the current time. You can add "agora" (now) or specify a place: "Que horas são agora em Londres?" In European Portuguese you’ll also often hear "Que horas são?"; in Brazilian Portuguese it’s very common to say "Que horas são?" or "Que horas são agora?"
target_language_example: Com licença, que horas são?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what time is it?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s age or the age of something. Common patterns: **Que idade tem ...?** (most common in Brazil) and **Que idade é/ são ...?** (also used, especially with children: *Que idade são seus filhos?*). With **com**, it means **"at what age"**: **Com que idade ...?** = “At what age...?/When (how old) did ...?” It can also be used humorously about objects: *Que idade tem esse guarda-chuva?*
target_language_example: Que idade você tem?
native_language_example: How old are you?

additional_notes: A strong, rude exclamation used to show anger, frustration, or disgust (“Damn it!” / “What the fuck?”). It can also be used before a noun to mean “what a shitty …” (e.g., “Que merda de televisão é essa?” = “What a shitty TV is that?”). Avoid in polite or formal situations.
target_language_example: Que merda! Eu perdi o ônibus de novo.
native_language_example: For fuck’s sake! I missed the bus again.

meaning: "What the hell is this?" / "What is this shit?" (very rude).
additional_notes: A strong, vulgar way to show shock, anger, or disbelief about something happening or something you see. Often said as a standalone question, sometimes with "hein?" for emphasis. Use only with close friends or in very informal settings; it can easily offend.
target_language_example: Que merda é essa que você fez com o meu carro?
native_language_example: What the hell did you do to my car?

meaning: “what the fuck” (a very vulgar way to show anger, shock, or disbelief).
additional_notes: Very strong profanity in Brazilian Portuguese. Used alone (“Que porra?”) or in questions (“Que porra está acontecendo?”) to express outrage/confusion. Often appears as “que porra de + noun” (“Que porra de ideia?” = “What the fuck kind of idea is that?”) and can sound aggressive or confrontational. Avoid in polite situations; use milder options like “Que diabos...?”, “O que está acontecendo?”
target_language_example: Que porra você está falando?
native_language_example: What the fuck are you talking about?

meaning: “What the f*** is that/this?” (a very rude, shocked/angry “what is that?”).
additional_notes: Very vulgar Brazilian Portuguese. Used to show strong surprise, anger, or disbelief. It’s common with vocatives like “cara” or “mano” (“dude/bro”). Avoid in polite company; safer alternatives: “O que é isso?” (neutral) or “Que é isso?” / “O que está acontecendo?” (“What’s going on?”).
target_language_example: Que porra é essa? Você mexeu nas minhas coisas?
native_language_example: What the f*** is this? Did you mess with my stuff?

additional_notes: Used to make a suggestion, invite someone, or propose an option. It’s often followed by a noun (Que tal cereal? = How about cereal?) or by a verb in the infinitive (Que tal fazermos uma pausa? = How about taking a break?). You can also use it before a clause with a conjugated verb, especially in invitations (Que tal vocês irem conosco...?).
target_language_example: Que tal irmos ao cinema hoje à noite?
native_language_example: How about going to the movies tonight?

meaning: 'How about...?' / 'What do you think of...?' (to make a suggestion).
additional_notes: Used to propose an idea or invite someone to do something. Common patterns: **Que tal + infinitive?** (Que tal irmos ao cinema? = How about going to the movies?) and **Que tal + noun?** (Que tal uma cerveja? = How about a beer?). It can be friendly or sarcastic depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Que tal a gente sair para jantar hoje à noite?
native_language_example: How about we go out for dinner tonight?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the category or characteristics of something. Often followed by a noun: "Que tipo de carro?" = "What kind of car?" It can also be used in indirect questions after verbs like "perguntar" (to ask): "Ele perguntou que tipo de...".
target_language_example: Que tipo de filme você gosta?
native_language_example: What kind of movies do you like?

additional_notes: Used after a noun as a relative clause meaning “that I know” (from conhecer). Very common in superlatives and expressions like “the best/only/tallest … that I know”: “o melhor X que conheço”, “a única pessoa que conheço”.
target_language_example: Você é a única pessoa aqui que conheço.
native_language_example: You’re the only person here that I know.

meaning: “that (someone) was looking for” / “that you/he/she was looking for.”
additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify which thing you mean (a relative clause): **[noun] + que estava procurando** = “the [noun] (that) (someone) was looking for.” Often used when someone finally finds the correct item. You can make the subject explicit by adding a pronoun before **estava** (e.g., **que eu estava procurando**, **que você estava procurando**), but the base term here omits it.
target_language_example: Eu encontrei o livro que estava procurando.
native_language_example: I found the book I was looking for.

additional_notes: Used to ask what is happening, often when something seems wrong or unexpected. Most commonly appears as a question like "O que está havendo?" or with a place/situation: "Que está havendo aqui?". Similar in meaning to "O que está acontecendo?".
target_language_example: O que está havendo aqui?
native_language_example: What’s going on here?

additional_notes: "que" + "eu" is very common in relative clauses, meaning “that I / which I …” (referring back to a person/thing already mentioned): "a mulher que eu amei" = “the woman that I loved.” It can also refer to time expressions: "no momento que eu a conheci" = “the moment (when) I met her,” and "a hora que eu quiser" = “the time (that/when) I want.” Often English can drop “that,” but Portuguese usually keeps "que."
target_language_example: Este é o livro que eu estou lendo agora.
native_language_example: This is the book (that) I’m reading now.

meaning: 'that I know' / 'that I’ve ever met' (from my experience).
additional_notes: Used after a noun phrase—often with superlatives or comparisons—to limit it to your personal experience: "the best/biggest/fastest ... that I know." It refers to people or things you are familiar with (people you’ve met, things you’ve seen, etc.).
target_language_example: Ele é o professor mais paciente que eu conheço.
native_language_example: He is the most patient teacher I know.

additional_notes: Used with **que** to introduce a relative clause describing something: **o que eu fiz** = “what I did”; **o sanduíche que eu fiz** = “the sandwich (that) I made.” **fiz** is the simple past (preterite) of **fazer** (“to do/make”), and the meaning can be “did” or “made” depending on context.
target_language_example: Este é o desenho que eu fiz ontem.
native_language_example: This is the drawing that I made yesterday.

additional_notes: Used after a noun with a superlative (e.g., mais lindo/a, pior, maior) to emphasize it’s the most/least you’ve seen in your life so far. Literally “that I already saw,” but in this structure it usually translates as “I’ve ever seen.” You can swap the subject: que você já viu (“that you’ve ever seen”), que a gente já viu (“that we’ve ever seen”).
target_language_example: Esse é o melhor restaurante que eu já vi.
native_language_example: This is the best restaurant I’ve ever seen.

additional_notes: Used with the relative pronoun "que" (“that/who/which”) + the verb "fazer" ("faz" = "(he/she/it) does/makes") to describe a person/thing: "o estudante que faz muitas perguntas" = “the student who asks many questions.” It can also mean “that causes/results in”: "É isto que faz o nosso trabalho ser duro" = “This is what makes our work hard.” In the expression "o tempo que faz", it refers to the weather: “the weather it is/that it’s making.”
target_language_example: Ela é a pessoa que faz tudo acontecer.
native_language_example: She’s the person who makes everything happen.

additional_notes: Used in relative clauses to refer back to an action you did in the past. Common patterns: **o que fiz** (“what I did”), **pelo que fiz** (“for what I did”), **foi o que fiz** (“that’s what I did”), and **fui eu que fiz** (“it was me who did it”). **Fiz** is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of **fazer** (“to do/make”) for **eu** (“I”).
target_language_example: Desculpa pelo que fiz ontem.
native_language_example: Sorry for what I did yesterday.

additional_notes: Used in questions to add emphasis or express surprise/insistence, similar to “what was it that…?” / “so what…?” It’s very common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese. It’s often followed by a verb: “Que foi que aconteceu?” = “What (exactly) happened?”
target_language_example: Que foi que você disse agora?
native_language_example: What is it that you just said?

additional_notes: Very common in Brazilian Portuguese in casual speech, often used when reacting to someone calling you, staring at you, or seeming upset. Depending on tone, it can sound neutral (“Yes?”) or annoyed/confrontational (“What?”). You’ll also hear it with a name or a follow-up question: “Que foi, João?” / “Que foi, não gostou?”
target_language_example: Ei, que foi? Você está bravo comigo?
native_language_example: Hey, what is it? Are you mad at me?

additional_notes: "Que" introduces a relative clause (“that/which/who”). "Lhe" is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to you” (formal) or “to him/her.” Together, "que lhe" often means “that I told/sent to you/him/her” or “who wants to talk to you/him/her,” with "lhe" referring back to the person receiving something (information, a message, a package, etc.).
target_language_example: Você viu o e-mail que lhe enviei ontem?
native_language_example: Did you see the email I sent you yesterday?

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. It is usually just que ('that/who/which') + me ('me' or 'to me'). It often introduces a clause connected to the speaker, as in a pessoa que me telefonou ('the person who called me'). With some verbs, me is better understood as 'to me', such as telefonar, restar, and ser possível.
target_language_example: Foi a melhor coisa que me aconteceu.
native_language_example: It was the best thing that happened to me.

additional_notes: Used to add extra information about someone you just mentioned (a relative clause). It comes after a person (“uma filha”, “um irmão”, “uma tia”) and before a place. In Portuguese you don’t need “who/that” separately—“que” does that job here, and “mora em” = “lives in”.
target_language_example: Ela tem um amigo que mora em Lisboa.
native_language_example: She has a friend who lives in Lisbon.

meaning: 'that/who/which ... not' (used to negate a relative clause).
additional_notes: Used after a noun or pronoun to introduce a relative clause with negation: "homens que não..." = "men who don’t..."; "um amor que não..." = "a love that didn’t...". It often corresponds to English "who/that/which + don’t/doesn’t/didn’t". In speech, "Eu que não..." can be an emphatic refusal meaning "No way I’m going to... / Not me."
target_language_example: Conheço gente que não gosta de café.
native_language_example: I know people who don’t like coffee.

additional_notes: "Que" introduces a relative clause ("that/who/which"). The "o" is an unstressed direct object pronoun placed before the verb, meaning "him" or "it" (and sometimes "you" in formal address). Common in sentences like "o homem que o atacou" = "the man who attacked him"; "foi X que o trouxe" = "it was X who brought him/it."
target_language_example: Ela encontrou o menino que o ajudou ontem.
native_language_example: She found the boy who helped him yesterday.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. que usually means 'who', 'that', 'which', or 'what', and se belongs to the following verb. In this pattern, se often marks a pronominal/reflexive verb (que se perderam = who got lost) or an impersonal/passive meaning (para que se usa isto? = what is this used for?).
target_language_example: Não sei para que se usa esta ferramenta.
native_language_example: I don't know what this tool is used for.

additional_notes: Used after a person/thing to introduce its name: “uma tia que se chama Hana” = “an aunt who is called Hana.” Very common with people, but can also be used for things/places. Similar meaning to “que se chama” = “called/named”; you may also hear “chamado/chamada” as a shorter alternative.
target_language_example: Eu tenho um amigo que se chama Pedro.
native_language_example: I have a friend who is called Pedro.

meaning: "How about...?" / "What do you think of...?" (suggesting or asking for an opinion).
additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion about something (“Que tal a liberdade?”) or to make a suggestion/offer (“Que tal uma cerveja?”). It’s very common in conversation and is often followed by a noun or pronoun (que tal esse/essa?) or by an infinitive in other contexts (e.g., “Que tal irmos?” = “How about we go?”).
target_language_example: Que tal um café depois do trabalho?
native_language_example: How about a coffee after work?

additional_notes: Very common, conversational way to make a suggestion or propose an idea: "Que tal + [noun/verb]?" = "How about…?" (Que tal uma praia? = How about a beach trip?). It can also ask for an opinion, especially about something that already happened: "Que tal você achou + [thing/event]?" = "What did you think of…?" Similar to "E aí, que tal?" = "So, how was it?".
target_language_example: Que tal a gente sair para jantar hoje?
native_language_example: How about we go out for dinner today?

additional_notes: "Que" introduces a relative clause ("that/which...") and "te" is the unstressed object pronoun meaning "you" (someone does something to you, for you, tells you, gives you, etc.). Very common in European Portuguese, especially in relative clauses: "o livro que te emprestei" = "the book that I lent you". Note: mixing "você" with "te" (as in the examples) happens in real speech, but in more formal/standard usage you often see "o livro que lhe emprestei" with "você".
target_language_example: Foi a melhor dica que te deram este ano.
native_language_example: It was the best tip they gave you this year.

additional_notes: Often used literally as que + tem = "that/which has," especially after a noun: uma casa que tem seis cômodos = "a house that has six rooms." In questions, it also appears in common patterns like que tem de errado...? ("what's wrong with...?") and que tem a ver...? ("what does ... have to do with ...?").
target_language_example: Ela usa um celular que tem uma câmera boa.
native_language_example: She uses a phone that has a good camera.

additional_notes: Often used after a time word to mean "next," as in "sábado que vem" or "semestre que vem." More literally, it can also mean "that comes" or "is coming" in other sentences.
target_language_example: Na semana que vem, vou viajar.
native_language_example: Next week, I'm going to travel.

additional_notes: Used after words like “o que” (what), “isso” (that), “aquilo/naquilo” (that/ in that) to refer back to someone’s words: “o que você disse” = “what you said”, “foi isso que você disse?” = “is that what you said?”. Often “que” can be translated as “that” (and in English it’s sometimes omitted).
target_language_example: Não entendi o que você disse.
native_language_example: I didn’t understand what you said.

meaning: "what did you do with" / "what have you done with".
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone did with an object (where they put it, how they used it, what happened to it). Very commonly preceded by "O que": "O que você fez com...". You may also hear "Que é que você fez com..." for extra emphasis. In Brazil, "você" is common; in Portugal, you'd often use "tu": "que tu fizeste com...".
target_language_example: O que você fez com a minha chave?
native_language_example: What did you do with my key?

meaning: “that you gave me” / “which you gave me”.
additional_notes: Used to add a describing clause after a noun, specifying the thing (person/object/info) that the other person gave you. Common in phrases like “o/a(s) [noun] que você me deu…”. In everyday speech you may also hear “que você deu pra mim” (more informal).
target_language_example: O livro que você me deu foi muito útil.
native_language_example: The book that you gave me was very useful.

meaning: "What do you mean?" / "What are you trying to say?"
additional_notes: Used to ask for clarification about what someone just said. Literally it’s “what do you want to say,” but in everyday use it functions like “what do you mean?”. Often appears as a question: “O que você quer dizer (com isso)?” (“What do you mean by that?”).
target_language_example: O que você quer dizer com isso?
native_language_example: What do you mean by that?

meaning: "what are you going to do" / "what you are going to do."
additional_notes: Uses the near-future construction "ir" (vou/vai) + infinitive (fazer) to talk about plans or intentions. Often appears in questions like "O que você vai fazer?" (What are you going to do?). Without "o" it can still be understood in conversation, but the most standard form is "O que você vai fazer?" In a statement or embedded question, it can mean "what you are going to do": "Não sei o que você vai fazer" (I don’t know what you’re going to do). "Você" is common in Brazil; in Portugal you may hear "o que vais fazer?"
target_language_example: O que você vai fazer hoje à noite?
native_language_example: What are you going to do tonight?

additional_notes: Used to ask about someone/something’s whereabouts or fate, often with a sense of concern or that it hasn’t been seen in a while: "Que é de você?" (What’s become of you?/Where have you been?), "Que é de João?" (What happened to João?/Where is João?). It’s a set expression and can sound a bit old-fashioned or literary in some contexts.
target_language_example: Que é de você? Faz tempo que eu não te vejo.
native_language_example: What’s become of you? I haven’t seen you in a long time.

additional_notes: Used to ask what something is: “(O) que é isso?” = “What is this/that?” The “o” is often dropped in speech (“Que é isso?”). It can also be an exclamation showing surprise, disapproval, or shock (similar to “What is this?” / “What the heck is this?” depending on tone). Related question: “Para que é isso?” / “Pra que é isso?” = “What is this for?”
target_language_example: Que é isso na sua mão?
native_language_example: What's that in your hand?

additional_notes: used to form direct questions, often with a slightly more explicit or emphatic feel than just que. In everyday speech, it is often interchangeable with o que or simple que, depending on the variety of Portuguese and the sentence.
target_language_example: Que é que você quer comer?
native_language_example: What do you want to eat?

meaning: “what do you…?” (a common way to ask a question directly).
additional_notes: Used to form questions in Brazilian Portuguese, especially in speech: "Que é que você + verb...?" It adds emphasis/clarity, similar to "What is it that you…?" Often shortened in conversation to "que que você..." or replaced with "o que você..."; all mean essentially "what do you…?".
target_language_example: Que é que você quer fazer hoje à noite?
native_language_example: What do you want to do tonight?

additional_notes: Used when introducing a subordinate clause (usually after verbs like pedir/ordenar/deixar/permitir/implorar) and the verb in that clause has the object pronoun “a” attached before it, meaning “her” or “it” (for a feminine thing/person). It often corresponds to English “(someone) asked/ordered/allowed (someone) to … her/it” or “that … her/it,” depending on the structure.
target_language_example: Ele pediu que a chamassem imediatamente.
native_language_example: He asked them to call her immediately.

additional_notes: Most often, this is "que" + the feminine singular definite article "a" (="the"). It commonly appears when "que" introduces a clause and the next noun is feminine: "acredito que a Terra..." ("I believe that the Earth..."). After "até", it can mean "until the": "até que a chaleira..." ("until the kettle...").
target_language_example: Ela disse que a reunião é amanhã.
native_language_example: She said that the meeting is tomorrow.

additional_notes: “A gente” is a very common, informal way to mean “we/us” (literally “the people”). With “mais/menos … que a gente” it means “than us.” After verbs like “preferir”, “querer”, “pedir”, etc., “que a gente + verb” means “that we + verb” (often with the verb in the subjunctive: “que a gente vá”, “que a gente faça”).
target_language_example: Você quer que a gente espere aqui?
native_language_example: Do you want us to wait here?

additional_notes: Used with "que" to introduce a clause where the subject is "alguém" (someone). Very common after expressions like "preciso que..." (I need (someone) to...), "espero que..." (I hope that...), and in purpose phrases like "para que alguém..." (so that someone...). Often triggers the subjunctive in the verb that follows (e.g., "que alguém venha/ajude/encontre").
target_language_example: É importante que alguém me responda hoje.
native_language_example: It’s important that someone answers me today.

meaning: “that things …” (introduces a clause about how things are/were/will be).
additional_notes: Used after many verbs and expressions to introduce what you think, want, know, or pretend about the situation: e.g., "achar/querer/esperar/gostar que as coisas...". Often followed by the subjunctive when expressing a wish, preference, or possibility ("Queria que as coisas fossem diferentes"), and by the indicative when stating a fact ("Não tinha ideia que as coisas estavam tão ruins").
target_language_example: Espero que as coisas melhorem logo.
native_language_example: I hope things get better soon.

meaning: “that people …” / “for people to …” (introduces what people do).
additional_notes: Used after verbs/expressions like esperar (to hope), preocupar-se (to worry), gostar (to like), não é de admirar (it’s no wonder), cansado de (tired of), conseguir (to manage) to introduce a clause about what people do. It often triggers the subjunctive in the verb that follows (e.g., gostem, usem, fiquem, bebam, façam).
target_language_example: É importante que as pessoas respeitem as regras.
native_language_example: It’s important that people respect the rules.

additional_notes: Usually introduces a clause about a female subject, often after verbs like dizer, achar, querer, and esperar. In structures like era ... que ela ..., it helps add emphasis and may not be translated word-for-word in English. At the start of a sentence, especially with the subjunctive, it can express a wish: que ela volte logo = may she come back soon.
target_language_example: Espero que ela chegue cedo.
native_language_example: I hope she arrives early.

additional_notes: A common clause combination: que introduces a new clause, and ele means "he." It often translates as "that he," though English often drops "that" (for example, "I think he knows"). In some sentences, it may also appear inside larger expressions, so the exact English wording can vary.
target_language_example: Eu acho que ele já saiu.
native_language_example: I think that he already left.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like "conseguir", "fazer com que", "permitir", "querer" to introduce what someone wanted/caused/allowed him to do. "fizesse" is the imperfect subjunctive of "fazer" and often corresponds to English "would do" or "to do" depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Ela pediu que ele fizesse isso mais tarde.
native_language_example: She asked him to do that later.

meaning: "that he doesn't / that he didn't / that he isn't" (introduces a negative clause about him).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a subordinate clause after verbs like "say," "notice," "hope," or "know." Structure: "que" = "that," "ele" = "he," and "não" negates the verb that follows (e.g., "que ele não foi" = "that he didn't go," "que ele não está" = "that he isn't").
target_language_example: Eu sei que ele não vem hoje.
native_language_example: I know he’s not coming today.

additional_notes: Commonly used after expressions like "acredito/creio que..." to introduce a clause about him. "seja" is the present subjunctive of "ser" (to be) and often reflects opinion, uncertainty, or a subjective judgment. In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, many speakers also say "que ele é" (indicative) in similar contexts, but "que ele seja" is more formal/careful or more clearly subjective.
target_language_example: Não acho que ele seja culpado.
native_language_example: I don't think he's guilty.

meaning: “that they” (introduces a clause where “they” is the subject).
additional_notes: Used with **que** to connect a main clause to a following clause with the subject **eles** (“they”). Common after expressions like **é óbvio que...** (“it’s obvious that...”), **tenho medo que...** (“I’m afraid that...”), **acho que...** (“I think that...”), etc. In questions, it can appear after **do que** (“of what / about what”).
target_language_example: Acho que eles não vêm hoje.
native_language_example: I think they’re not coming today.

meaning: “that was / that it was” (introduces what someone said, thought, or believed).
additional_notes: Used to start a subordinate clause after verbs and expressions like dizer (to say), achar/pensar (to think), acreditar (to believe), ter a impressão/ilusão (to have the impression/illusion), convencer (to convince), etc. Here, era is the imperfect of ser (“was”), often used for descriptions or ongoing states in the past: “I said that I was…”, “He believed that it was…”.
target_language_example: Ela achava que era tarde demais.
native_language_example: She thought it was too late.

meaning: 'that (someone/something) was' (past form of “to be,” often in reported speech).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like dizer (to say), contar (to tell), sonhar (to dream), etc., to introduce a clause describing a past state or ongoing situation. Often translates as “that I/he/she was …” or “that I/he/she was (doing) …”. Note: “que” = “that”; “estava” is the imperfect past of “estar” (temporary state/location/ongoing action).
target_language_example: Ele me contou que estava doente ontem.
native_language_example: He told me that he was sick yesterday.

additional_notes: A very common combination that introduces a clause where eu is the subject. After verbs like querer, pedir, or esperar, it often corresponds to English "that I" or more naturally "for me to"/"me to". It is often followed by the subjunctive in these contexts, as in "quer que eu atenda" = "wants me to answer."
target_language_example: Ela pediu que eu esperasse aqui.
native_language_example: She asked me to wait here.

meaning: 'that I was' (introduces a clause about what you were).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like saber/dizer/falar/sonhar to introduce reported speech, indirect questions, or imagined situations. Here, "era" is the imperfect of "ser" (to be), often used for background descriptions, ongoing past states, or unreal/imagined contexts (e.g., dreams: "Sonhei que eu era..."). In speech you’ll often hear the shorter form "que eu era" instead of repeating a full sentence.
target_language_example: Eu não sabia que eu era tão alto na foto.
native_language_example: I didn’t know that I looked so tall in the photo.

meaning: 'that I (myself)…' (introduces a clause, often before a reflexive verb).
