additional_notes: Used to introduce a subordinate clause after verbs/expressions like "permitir", "pedir", "deixar", etc. "Eu" = "I" and "me" is a reflexive/object pronoun meaning "myself/me" (common with reflexive verbs like "me apresentar" = "introduce myself", "me formar" = "graduate", "me aposentar" = "retire"). Word order is typically "que eu me + verb".
target_language_example: Você pode esperar um minuto para que eu me arrume?
native_language_example: Can you wait a minute so I can get ready?

meaning: that i don't / that i haven't
additional_notes: Common in sentences like “Faz X tempo que eu não…” (= “It’s been X time since I last…”). Also appears in the set phrase “Não que eu não…” to correct a possible misunderstanding (= “Not that I don’t…”). In more formal/emphatic uses it can introduce a negative wish/command in the subjunctive (often with an implied “Espero/Deus queira”): “Que eu não receba queixas…” ≈ “May I not receive complaints… / I hope I don’t receive complaints…”. It can also be used as an exclamation to express regret: “Que eu não tivesse feito aquilo!” ≈ “If only I hadn’t done that!”
target_language_example: Faz uma semana que eu não falo com ela.
native_language_example: It’s been a week since I last talked to her.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like esperar (to expect/hope) and other expressions that trigger the subjunctive, especially in questions: Você espera que eu pague? = “Do you expect me to pay?” It often carries a tone of surprise or objection, depending on context.
target_language_example: Você quer que eu pague agora?
native_language_example: Do you want me to pay now?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause with the verb in the present subjunctive ("seja" from "ser" = to be). Very common after expressions like "querer" (to want), "precisar" (to need), "esperar" (to hope/expect), and after "crer/achar" (to believe/think), often implying uncertainty, desire, or someone else’s opinion. Often corresponds to English "(that) I be" or more naturally "(that) I am" depending on context.
target_language_example: Você acha que eu seja a pessoa certa para o trabalho?
native_language_example: Do you think I’m the right person for the job?

additional_notes: `fosse` is the imperfect subjunctive of `ser` or `ir`, so the meaning depends on context. It often appears after verbs of wanting, telling, advising, or asking, especially in reported instructions or wishes.
target_language_example: Eu queria que fosse mais fácil.
native_language_example: I wanted it to be easier.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect subjunctive of **ser** (*fosse*) after **que**. Common after verbs of wanting/wishing/opinion (e.g., *querer, gostar, preferir*): *Queria que fosse…* = “I wanted it to be…” / “I wish it were…”. Also appears with conjunctions like **mesmo que** (“even if”) and **até que** (“until”), expressing something hypothetical, desired, or not yet real.
target_language_example: Eu queria que fosse mais fácil.
native_language_example: I wanted it to be easier. / I wish it were easier.

additional_notes: Used with the imperfect of ir (ia) after que (“that”) to report what someone was going to do, or what felt like was about to happen. Common in reported speech (Ele disse que ia...) and with feelings/perceptions (Senti que ia...). Often followed by an infinitive: que ia + verb.
target_language_example: Eu achei que ia chover, então levei um guarda-chuva.
native_language_example: I thought it was going to rain, so I brought an umbrella.

additional_notes: Usually not a fixed expression, but simply que + isso. In many sentences, que introduces a clause ('that') and isso means 'that/it'. After comparatives, as in melhor que isso, it means 'than that'. As a standalone exclamation, Que isso! can also mean 'come on!' or 'no way!' in Brazilian Portuguese.
target_language_example: Eu não sabia que isso era possível.
native_language_example: I didn't know that was possible.

additional_notes: Often used as a short reply to contradict or dismiss what someone just said (similar to “yeah right” or “not a chance”). Common in casual speech, and you may hear it with vocatives like “cara”. Note: in other contexts, "que nada" can also be literal—"que" + "nada" = “that nothing,” as in "Espero que nada tenha acontecido" (“I hope nothing happened”).
target_language_example: —Você ficou com medo? —Que nada!
native_language_example: —Were you scared? —No way!

meaning: like / just like; (in “tão... que nem...”) “so... that (I) can’t even...”.
additional_notes: Very common in informal Brazilian Portuguese. It can introduce a comparison (“like/just like”): “que nem daquela vez...” = “like that time...”. It can also appear after “tão” to intensify: “tão + adjective + que nem + verb” = “so + adjective + that (I) can’t even + verb”. Often interchangeable with “como” (like) or “que” in these patterns, but “que nem” sounds more casual.
target_language_example: Ele ficou branco, que nem um fantasma.
native_language_example: He turned white, like a ghost.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause where the subject is “nobody/no one,” often after expressions like “tão ... que” (so ... that), “achar que” (to think that), “dizer que” (to say that), and with “para que” / “com medo de que” / “com receio de que.” After “para que” and often after fear/concern expressions, Portuguese commonly uses the subjunctive: “para que ninguém visse” (so that nobody would see), “com medo de que ninguém aparecesse” (afraid that nobody would show up).
target_language_example: Fechei a porta para que ninguém entrasse.
native_language_example: I closed the door so that nobody would come in.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a negative clause after another verb, often after verbs like dizer, saber, achar, or fingir. In English, it is often translated as 'that ... not', but the most natural English wording may be 'that he/she didn’t...' or 'not to...' depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Ela disse que não podia ir.
native_language_example: She said that she couldn't go.

additional_notes: Usually just the conjunction que followed by the masculine singular article o. It often introduces a clause: que o professor disse = 'that the teacher said'. Before some male names, Portuguese may use o (for example, o Tom), but English normally does not translate it, so que o Tom... is usually just 'that Tom...'.
target_language_example: Acho que o professor tem razão.
native_language_example: I think the teacher is right.

additional_notes:
Used to compare something with “yours,” usually after a comparative or equality expression: 
- **mais/menos ... que o seu** = “more/less ... than yours” (often with an implied noun: *mais bonito que o seu (carro)*).
- **o mesmo ... que o seu** = “the same ... as yours.”
**o seu** is the possessive pronoun “yours” (masculine singular); you may also see **a sua / os seus / as suas** depending on the thing owned.
target_language_example: Meu computador é mais novo que o seu.
native_language_example: My computer is newer than yours.

additional_notes: Used when a clause introduced by **que** (“that”) contains the object pronoun **o** (“him/it”). In Portuguese, object pronouns often come **before** the verb after words like **que** (this is called *proclisis*): **prometeu que o encontraria** = “promised that she would find/meet him.” **O** can refer to a male person (“him”) or to a thing/idea (“it”), depending on context.
target_language_example: Ela disse que o viu ontem.
native_language_example: She said she saw him yesterday.

additional_notes: Used in two very common ways: (1) in comparisons, after "mais/menos ... que" to mean "than the" + a masculine plural noun: "mais velhos que os nossos" (= older than ours). (2) after verbs like "achar", "descobrir", "dizer" to introduce a clause meaning "that the...": "descobriu que os ladrões..." (= found out that the thieves...). "os" is the masculine plural form of "the"; for feminine plural you’d use "que as".
target_language_example: Eu descobri que os vizinhos já chegaram.
native_language_example: I found out that the neighbors have already arrived.

additional_notes: An insult or emphatic way to say you don’t care, you give up on something, or you reject someone/something. Often used alone (“Que se dane!”) or with a noun (“Que se dane o trabalho.” = “Screw the job.”). Very informal and offensive in many situations; avoid in polite company.
target_language_example: Se eles não gostaram, que se dane — eu fiz o meu melhor.
native_language_example: If they didn’t like it, screw it—I did my best.

additional_notes: A strong, offensive way to show contempt, anger, or that you don’t care anymore. Often used alone (“Que se foda!”) or followed by a person/thing: “Que se foda esse trabalho” = “Fuck this job.” It’s not appropriate in polite conversation.
target_language_example: Perdi o ônibus — que se foda, vou a pé.
native_language_example: I missed the bus—fuck it, I’ll walk.

additional_notes: Uses seja, the present subjunctive of ser. It's common after verbs and expressions of desire, need, or importance, like quero que seja..., preciso que seja..., and é essencial que seja.... On its own, Que seja. can mean "so be it" or "fine then."
target_language_example: Quero que seja simples.
native_language_example: I want it to be simple.

meaning: “that yes” → “yes / that it is / that it will.”
additional_notes: Used after a verb (often with a preceding conjunction like “que”) to confirm something: “I’m afraid so” (Eu temo que sim), “I would have said yes” (Eu teria dito que sim). Commonly contrasts with “que não” (“that no / no”). In English you often just say “yes/so,” but Portuguese keeps “que” in these structures.
target_language_example: Achas que vai chover? Acho que sim.
native_language_example: Do you think it’s going to rain? I think so.

meaning: 'that only' / 'that just' (introduces a clause with a restriction).
additional_notes: Used after verbs or adjectives to add the idea of “only/just” in the following clause: e.g., “acreditar que só…” = “believe that only/just…”. It often emphasizes surprise or limitation. In many cases you can translate it as “that only” or “that just,” but in natural English you may reorder it (e.g., “It’s hard to believe only three months have passed.”).
target_language_example: Achei estranho que só ele soubesse a resposta.
native_language_example: I found it strange that only he knew the answer.

meaning: 'that everyone' / 'that we all' (introduces a clause about everyone).
additional_notes: Used when **que** introduces a subordinate clause and **todos** means **everyone** (or **all of us/them** depending on context). Common in structures like **para que todos...** (“so that everyone...”) or after results/opinions: **tão... que todos...** (“so... that everyone...”), **Você disse que todos...** (“You said that we all...”).
target_language_example: Fale mais alto, para que todos entendam.
native_language_example: Speak louder so that everyone understands.

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression, but a very common combination of que + tu. It introduces a clause about what 'you' do, think, feel, etc., as in acho que tu sabes. In comparisons, it can also appear inside a longer structure like do que tu ('than you'). Tu is the singular 'you' used especially in Portugal and in some regions of Brazil; many Brazilians more often use você instead.
target_language_example: Eu sei que tu estás cansado.
native_language_example: I know that you're tired.

additional_notes: A common combination of que + você. It often introduces a clause after verbs like dizer, acreditar, saber, or temer: que você... = 'that you...'. After comparatives, que can mean 'than': mais alto que você = 'taller than you'.
target_language_example: Eu sei que você está certo.
native_language_example: I know that you are right.

meaning: "that you do this/that" (subjunctive: expressing what someone wants/asks/insists/hopes you will do).
additional_notes: Used after verbs/expressions that trigger the present subjunctive, especially wishes, requests, recommendations, insistence, or expectations (e.g., querer que…, esperar que…, insistir que…). Here, faça is the subjunctive form of fazer (to do/make) for você. In English it often sounds like “(I want you to) do it,” but Portuguese commonly keeps the explicit “que…”.
target_language_example: O médico pediu que você faça isso com cuidado.
native_language_example: The doctor asked you to do this carefully.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a negative clause about “you” after another verb (e.g., know, say, remember, be afraid, make sure): “(verb) + que você não + (verb) …”. The tense comes from the following verb: e.g., “que você não vem/vinha/venha/viu”.
target_language_example: Eu espero que você não se esqueça.
native_language_example: I hope you don’t forget.

meaning: 'that you be happy' / 'may you be happy.'
additional_notes: Uses the present subjunctive (seja, from ser) after que to express a wish, hope, or desire—often after verbs like esperar (to hope), querer (to want), desejar (to wish). It can also be said on its own as a heartfelt wish, like “May you be happy.”
target_language_example: Desejo muito que você seja feliz com essa decisão.
native_language_example: I really hope you’re happy with that decision.

additional_notes: Used when **que** introduces a clause referring to **vocês** (“you” plural). It can mean **“that you…”** in statements (e.g., *Eu sabia que vocês…* = “I knew that you…”) or **“what you…”** in questions (often with *o que é que vocês…* = “what do you…?”). In Brazil, **vocês** is the most common plural “you” (and can also be used as a formal singular in some contexts).
target_language_example: Acho que vocês já entenderam.
native_language_example: I think you (plural) have already understood.

meaning: to beat someone up; to smash someone’s face (threat/insult).
additional_notes: Very informal and aggressive. In these examples it’s used as a threat of physical violence (often said as “Vou quebrar a sua cara” / “Vou te quebrar a cara”). In other contexts, it can also mean “to be proven wrong / to fail” (e.g., “Eu quebrei a cara”), but that’s not the meaning in the sentences given.
target_language_example: Se ele continuar me provocando, vou quebrar a cara dele.
native_language_example: If he keeps provoking me, I’m going to beat him up.

additional_notes: "Quebrou" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "quebrar" (to break). The subject can be a person, a name, or something (e.g., "O vento quebrou a janela" = The wind broke the window). Often followed by details like "de propósito" (on purpose) or "por acidente" (by accident).
target_language_example: Ele quebrou a janela jogando a bola dentro de casa.
native_language_example: He broke the window by throwing the ball inside the house.

additional_notes: Past tense of "quebrar" (to break). In Portuguese, it’s common to use the definite article with body parts ("o braço") instead of a possessive ("meu/seu braço"), when it’s clear whose arm it is. You can specify sides: "o braço direito" (right arm) / "o braço esquerdo" (left arm).
target_language_example: Ele quebrou o braço andando de bicicleta.
native_language_example: He broke his arm while riding a bike.

additional_notes: Used to express a strong wish or regret about something that isn’t true or didn’t happen. It’s typically followed by the subjunctive (often the imperfect subjunctive: "Quem dera eu tivesse…", "Quem dera pudéssemos…"). You may also see it with "que" ("Quem dera que eu pudesse").
target_language_example: Quem dera eu pudesse viajar mais este ano.
native_language_example: If only I could travel more this year.

additional_notes: Used as a rhetorical question to show that something turned out unexpectedly. Very common in the pattern "Quem diria que..." (= "Who would have thought that..."). In other contexts, "a quem diria" can also literally mean "to whom (I) would tell/say (it)"—but the standalone phrase "Quem diria?" is usually the surprised reaction.
target_language_example: Quem diria que ele ia chegar cedo hoje?
native_language_example: Who would have thought he’d arrive early today?

meaning: “who said that…?” (often used to challenge or doubt a claim).
additional_notes: Used to ask who made a statement, and very commonly as a rhetorical question meaning “says who?”/“who told you that?” It can challenge an assumption (Quem disse que seria fácil?) or question someone’s authority/permission (Quem disse que você podia dormir?). Literally: quem = who, disse = said, que = that.
target_language_example: Quem disse que você não pode tentar de novo?
native_language_example: Who said you can’t try again?

meaning: "who was" (asking about someone’s identity in the past).
additional_notes: Used in direct questions (Quem era ela? = Who was she?) and indirect questions (Não sei quem era. = I don’t know who it was). "Era" is the imperfect past of "ser" and often sets background or refers to a past situation/person being talked about.
target_language_example: Você sabe quem era aquele homem?
native_language_example: Do you know who that man was?

additional_notes: Used in questions to ask which person is the writer/author of something (a poem, text, book, etc.). “Quem” = “who” and “escreveu” is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of “escrever” (“to write”), meaning the writing is seen as completed.
target_language_example: Você lembra quem escreveu este livro?
native_language_example: Do you remember who wrote this book?

additional_notes: Used to ask about a person’s identity: "quem" = "who" + "está" (from "estar") = "is". Very often followed by a verb in the gerund (-ando/-endo/-indo) to mean "who is (doing something)": "Quem está seguindo você?" = "Who is following you?" It can also be followed by a noun or phrase: "Quem está no comando?" = "Who is in charge?"
target_language_example: Quem está falando comigo agora?
native_language_example: Who is talking to me right now?

additional_notes: Used to talk about your identity (literally “who I am”). Often appears after verbs like saber (“to know”), adivinhar (“to guess”), and querer saber (“to want to know”): "Eu sei quem eu sou" (I know who I am). Can also be used in a playful/guessing context: "Adivinhem quem eu sou" (Guess who I am).
target_language_example: Às vezes, levo tempo para lembrar quem eu sou.
native_language_example: Sometimes it takes me time to remember who I am.

additional_notes: Used to ask or state the identity of the person responsible for an action. Often appears inside a longer sentence after verbs like saber (to know) or descobrir (to find out): “Eu sei quem fez isso” (“I know who did it”). You may also see the emphatic structure “Foi [person] quem fez isso” (“It was [person] who did it”).
target_language_example: Você sabe quem fez isso?
native_language_example: Do you know who did this?

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize the question about the person responsible for an action. Common in spoken Portuguese; it often sounds a bit more insistent or surprised than just “Quem…?”. It can be used with different tenses depending on context, but the fixed pattern “Quem foi que + verb” is very frequent.
target_language_example: Quem foi que te contou isso?
native_language_example: Who was it that told you that?

meaning: "if only…" / "I wish…" (expresses a strong wish or regret).
additional_notes: Used to express something you really want to be true, often about something unlikely or impossible. It’s typically followed by the subjunctive (e.g., "Quem me dera que ele tivesse vindo"), but it can also appear with an infinitive ("Quem me dera saber…") or even alone ("Quem me dera!" = "If only! / I wish!"). It’s not a literal "who" question; it’s a fixed expression.
target_language_example: Quem me dera poder viajar mais este ano.
native_language_example: If only I could travel more this year.

additional_notes: Used to ask which person is willing to do something, often to invite volunteers (e.g., in a group). It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb: “Quem quer + verb” (Quem quer cortar…? Quem quer responder…?). You can also add “que” in some contexts (“Quem é que quer…?”), but “Quem quer…?” is very common.
target_language_example: Quem quer ir comigo ao mercado?
native_language_example: Who wants to go with me to the market?

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unknown or irrelevant person (“anyone who”). It often introduces a clause and can be followed by the subjunctive, especially in set phrases like “quem quer que seja” (“whoever it is”). Common in more formal or emphatic statements.
target_language_example: Quem quer que tenha deixado a porta aberta, por favor feche.
native_language_example: Whoever left the door open, please close it.

additional_notes: Often used as a standalone question or comment meaning “Who knows?” (expressing uncertainty). It can also introduce a clause meaning “whoever knows”: e.g., “Quem sabe o segredo...” = “Whoever knows the secret...”. In some contexts it works like “maybe/perhaps,” especially when suggesting a possibility: “Quem sabe amanhã.”
target_language_example: Quem sabe a gente se vê amanhã.
native_language_example: Maybe we’ll see each other tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used as a literal question about identity (often in games or introductions: “Guess who I am”). It’s also very common as a rhetorical phrase meaning “it’s not really my place / I’m not in a position” (e.g., “Quem sou eu para reclamar?” = “Who am I to complain?”). In reflective or philosophical contexts it can express questioning one’s identity.
target_language_example: Quem sou eu para te dizer o que fazer?
native_language_example: Who am I to tell you what to do?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the identity of more than one person ("Who are you (all)?") or to ask which people belong to a group ("Who are the responsible people?"). It’s the plural form: "quem é" is singular (who is). Often followed by a plural subject (vocês, eles/elas, as pessoas...).
target_language_example: Quem são eles na história?
native_language_example: Who are they in the story?

additional_notes: Used at the start of questions to ask who did something to you (or for you). "Quem" = "who" and "te" is an unstressed object pronoun meaning "you" (singular). It often translates as “who [verb] you?” / “who [verb] to you?”, e.g. "Quem te disse isso?" = "Who told you that?" In many contexts, using "te" feels more informal/familiar than "lhe" or "a você".
target_language_example: Quem te ajudou com isso?
native_language_example: Who helped you with that?

additional_notes: Used to ask who gave someone some information. Literally “who (to) you told” (quem = who, te = to you, contou = told). Often followed by what was said (isso/a história/as notícias/que…). You can also swap the object: “Quem contou isso pra você?”
target_language_example: Quem te contou que eu estava aqui?
native_language_example: Who told you that I was here?

additional_notes: Used to express a strong wish, often about something unlikely or impossible. It’s commonly followed by an infinitive (e.g., "Quem te dera saber!") or by a verb in the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., "Quem te dera fosses…"). More common with other pronouns too: "Quem me dera" = "If only I…". Somewhat literary/old-fashioned, but still understood.
target_language_example: Quem te dera poder vir conosco!
native_language_example: If only you could come with us!

additional_notes: Used to ask who the person was that gave something to you. It’s typically followed by the thing given (isso/estas flores/esse colar). You’ll also see it with both informal and more formal possessives: teu/te (more informal) and seu/te (can be more formal, but can also be ambiguous: “your” or “his/her”).
target_language_example: Quem te deu esse presente?
native_language_example: Who gave you that gift?

additional_notes: Used to ask who was the person that taught someone (often a skill, language, song, etc.). "Quem" = who, "te" = you (informal singular object), "ensinou" = taught (past tense). You can add the thing learned after it: "Quem te ensinou francês?"
target_language_example: Quem te ensinou a cozinhar assim?
native_language_example: Who taught you to cook like that?

additional_notes: Used to ask who will do something. Very commonly followed by an infinitive: "quem vai + verb" (from the near-future structure "ir + infinitive"), e.g., "Quem vai cuidar?" = "Who’s going to take care of it?".
target_language_example: Quem vai levar as crianças para a escola?
native_language_example: Who’s going to take the kids to school?

additional_notes: Used when asking about a person connected to “you” (the listener), often in questions: “Quem você viu?” = “Who did you see?” It can also appear after prepositions: “a/para/de/em com quem você…?” = “to/for/from/in with whom did you…?” In more formal Portuguese, you may see “Quem você…” replaced by “Quem é que você…” or “A quem você…” depending on the preposition.
target_language_example: Quem você encontrou ontem?
native_language_example: Who did you run into yesterday?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion/guess about a person. Often followed by a verb phrase: "Quem você acha que vai..." (who do you think is going to...), "Quem você acha que pode..." (who do you think can...). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, "você" is often pronounced "cê" ("Quem cê acha que...").
target_language_example: Quem você acha que vai chegar primeiro?
native_language_example: Who do you think is going to arrive first?

additional_notes: Used to identify a person or talk about someone’s identity. Often appears after verbs like saber (“to know”), ver (“to see”), or descobrir (“to find out”). In more formal Portuguese, you may also see “quem você é” replaced by “quem você é você” is not used; or by “quem é você?” in questions. It can be a statement (“Eu sei quem você é.”) or part of a question (“Você sabe quem eu sou?”).
target_language_example: Eu sei quem você é, mas você não sabe quem eu sou.
native_language_example: I know who you are, but you don’t know who I am.

additional_notes: Used to ask or identify who a person is. It can appear in direct questions ("Quem é Tom?") or inside a larger sentence ("sabemos quem é o ladrão" = "we know who the thief is"). The longer pattern "quem é que..." is also common and means the same thing, with extra emphasis.
target_language_example: Quem é aquela mulher?
native_language_example: Who is that woman?

meaning: “who is the…?” (used before a feminine noun/title).
additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s identity or which person fits a description. It’s followed by a feminine word (e.g., a pessoa, a deusa, a Madame, a Charlotte). For masculine nouns, use “quem é o…?”. You can also use “quem é?” alone when the noun is understood from context.
target_language_example: Quem é a professora nova?
native_language_example: Who is the new (female) teacher?

additional_notes: Used to ask who someone is, referring to a feminine person with "essa" (often someone nearby or just mentioned). In real speech it’s usually followed by a noun (e.g., "quem é essa menina/mulher/garota?") or a name ("quem é essa Ana?"). For a masculine person, use "quem é esse?"; for plural, "quem são essas/esses?".
target_language_example: Quem é essa mulher que está falando com você?
native_language_example: Who is that woman who’s talking to you?

meaning: “who is that?” (referring to a male person).
additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s identity. In Brazilian Portuguese, "esse" = “that (one) near you / the one you just mentioned,” and it agrees with a masculine noun/person. It can be neutral ("Quem é esse homem?") or insulting depending on the next word (e.g., "babaca", "idiota", "palhaço"). For a woman, use "Quem é essa...?"; plural: "Quem são esses/essas...?".
target_language_example: Quem é esse cara que está falando com você?
native_language_example: Who is that guy who’s talking to you?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s identity: “quem” (who) + “é” (is) + “o” (the, masculine). It’s commonly followed by a title or noun (e.g., o autor, o próximo). With some names—especially in European Portuguese—you may also hear the article: “Quem é o Tom?”. For feminine nouns/names, use “quem é a …?”.
target_language_example: Quem é o responsável por isto?
native_language_example: Who’s responsible for this?

additional_notes: Used to add emphasis in a question, often suggesting surprise, suspicion, or insistence. Very common in spoken Portuguese. It’s interchangeable in many cases with plain “Quem…?”, just more emphatic. The verb after it is usually in the 3rd person (e.g., “Quem é que fez isso?”).
target_language_example: Quem é que disse isso?
native_language_example: Who said that?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s identity. It can be neutral/polite with “Desculpe” (Sorry/Excuse me), but can also sound challenging or suspicious depending on tone (e.g., “Ei, quem é você?”). You can also use it rhetorically to question someone’s authority (“Então quem é você?”).
target_language_example: Com licença, quem é você?
native_language_example: Excuse me, who are you?

meaning: “Do you want something?” / “Do you need anything?”
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone wants or needs anything. Often said directly to the person as a polite offer (e.g., a waiter, receptionist, or colleague). You can also extend it: “Quer alguma coisa para beber/comer/fazer?”
target_language_example: Você quer alguma coisa para beber?
native_language_example: Do you want something to drink?

additional_notes: Used to say someone wants to learn a skill or how to do an action. Structure: "[ele/ela/você] quer aprender a + infinitive verb". (E.g., "quer aprender a tocar", "quer aprender a fazer"). You can change the person/number: "eu quero aprender a...", "você quer aprender a...", "eles querem aprender a...".
target_language_example: Tom quer aprender a tocar violão.
native_language_example: Tom wants to learn to play the guitar.

additional_notes: Formed by "quer" (from "querer", to want) + the infinitive "comer" (to eat). Used to say someone/animal wants to eat something, or to ask what someone would like to eat (often implied: now/for a meal). You can also use it without an object when it’s understood from context.
target_language_example: Você quer comer alguma coisa agora?
native_language_example: Do you want to eat something now?

meaning: “wants to buy” (also used as “would you like to buy?”).
additional_notes: Formed by **quer** (from *querer*, “to want”) + **comprar** (“to buy”). It can describe someone’s intention (*Ele quer comprar...* = “He wants to buy...”) or be used to ask politely, especially with a question mark and intonation (*Quer comprar isto?* = “Do you want to buy this?”). With formal address: **O senhor / A senhora quer comprar...**.
target_language_example: Você quer comprar um café para viagem?
native_language_example: Do you want to buy a coffee to go?

meaning: "(it) means" / "that means"; also "I mean" (to clarify or correct yourself).
additional_notes: Often used in two main ways: (1) to express meaning or implication: "Isso quer dizer que..." = "That means that..." (as in "Quer dizer que ele enterrou..."), and (2) as a spoken filler to clarify, rephrase, add emphasis, or introduce a question: "Quer dizer, ..." = "I mean, ..." (common in conversation).
target_language_example: Isso quer dizer que a gente vai ter que sair mais cedo.
native_language_example: That means we’ll have to leave earlier.

additional_notes: Used to explain the consequence or interpretation of something, or to ask for confirmation. It can appear mid-sentence ("Isso quer dizer que...") or as a question at the start ("Quer dizer que..."). In speech it often implies: “So you’re saying that…?”
target_language_example: Então quer dizer que a reunião foi cancelada?
native_language_example: So does that mean the meeting was canceled?

meaning: 'wants to talk to you' / 'wants to speak with you.'
additional_notes: Uses the verb querer (quer = 'wants') + falar com ('to talk/speak with') + você ('you'). Common when relaying a message (e.g., 'X said they want to talk to you') or when someone is asking to speak directly, sometimes more formally/seriously depending on context. You can add an adverb like pessoalmente ('in person') or agora ('now').
target_language_example: O chefe quer falar com você agora.
native_language_example: The boss wants to talk to you now.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone wants to speak with you/me. It’s built from "quer" (wants, from *querer*) + "falar" (to talk) + "comigo" (with me). Change "quer" to match the subject: "eu quero falar com você" (I want to talk to you), "você quer falar comigo?" (Do you want to talk to me?), "eles querem falar comigo" (They want to talk to me). In polite requests, you can add "por favor" and a follow-up action (e.g., "me ligue" = call me).
target_language_example: Você quer falar comigo agora ou mais tarde?
native_language_example: Do you want to talk to me now or later?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "querer" (to want) + infinitive "ficar" (to stay/remain) + "aqui" (here). Often appears as a question: "(Você) quer ficar aqui?" = "Do you want to stay here?" In casual speech, "você" is often shortened to "cê" and can be omitted entirely.
target_language_example: Você quer ficar aqui ou prefere ir embora?
native_language_example: Do you want to stay here or would you rather leave?

additional_notes: From querer + ir. It commonly means "he/she wants to go," but with an implied você it can also mean "you want to go" or, in a question, "do you want to go?".
target_language_example: Ela quer ir ao cinema hoje.
native_language_example: She wants to go to the movies today.

meaning: “(Do you) want to see me?” / “(Someone) wants to see me.”
additional_notes: From **querer** (“to want”) + **me ver** (“to see me”). In questions, Portuguese often drops **você**: **Quer me ver?** = “Do you want to see me?” It can also be followed by a complement to mean “want to see me (doing/being) …”: **Quer me ver trabalhando?** (“Do you want to see me working?”) or **Quer me ver morto?** (“Do you want to see me dead?”).
target_language_example: Você quer me ver agora ou mais tarde?
native_language_example: Do you want to see me now or later?

additional_notes: Used to ask what someone wants to hear (information, an answer, news, a song, etc.). Often appears in questions like “O que você quer ouvir?” (“What do you want to hear?”). You can also replace “você” with “tu” in some regions (“O que tu quer/queres ouvir?”).
target_language_example: Você quer ouvir a verdade ou prefere uma versão curta?
native_language_example: Do you want to hear the truth, or would you prefer a short version?

meaning: "(someone) wants us to…" / "Do you want us to…?"
additional_notes: Used to say what someone wants "us" to do. It’s built from "quer" (wants), "que" (that), and "a gente" (we/us). "A gente" is very common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese and usually takes a 3rd-person singular verb (a gente vai, a gente faz). With a question mark, it often means "Do you want us to…?"; without it, it usually means "(He/She/You) wants us to…".
target_language_example: Você quer que a gente te ajude agora ou depois?
native_language_example: Do you want us to help you now or later?

additional_notes: Used with a following verb to say what someone wants the speaker to do: "quer que eu + verb". In a direct question, "Quer que eu...?" usually means "Do you want me to...?". Grammatically, it uses querer + que + the subjunctive.
target_language_example: Quer que eu abra a janela?
native_language_example: Do you want me to open the window?

additional_notes: Used to politely offer or ask if someone wants you to do something. It’s formed by: quer (“(you) want”) + que (“that”) + eu (“I”) + lhe (“to you / for you”, polite; often used with o senhor / a senhora). Common with a verb in the subjunctive after it: "Quer que eu lhe mostre... / traga... / conte...?" In everyday speech, people may also say "Quer que eu te..." (informal, to a friend) or drop "lhe" when it’s clear.
target_language_example: Quer que eu lhe ajude com as malas?
native_language_example: Would you like me to help you with the bags?

meaning: “(Do you) want me to (do something) for you?” / “(He/she) wants me to (do something) to/for you.”
additional_notes: Built from: quer (“wants”) + que (“that”) + eu (“I”) + te (“you” informal object pronoun). It introduces a request/offer or reported request: "Quer que eu te ajude?" = “Do you want me to help you?” The verb after this is usually in the present subjunctive (e.g., dê, ajude, beije).
target_language_example: Quer que eu te ligue mais tarde?
native_language_example: Do you want me to call you later?

meaning: "wants you to" (someone wants you to do something).
additional_notes: Used after a subject (ele/ela/seu pai/Tom, etc.) to say that person wants *you* to do an action: "[Person] quer que você + (verb)". In Brazilian Portuguese, the verb after "que você" is often in the present subjunctive (e.g., "chegue", "lave", "jogue").
target_language_example: Minha mãe quer que você venha jantar com a gente.
native_language_example: My mom wants you to come have dinner with us.

additional_notes: Literally 'wants to know.' Depending on the subject, it can also mean 'do you want to know?' In spoken Portuguese, quer saber? can be used like 'you know what?', se quer saber means 'if you want to know / honestly', and só quer saber de... means 'only cares about...' or 'is only interested in...'
target_language_example: Ela quer saber quando o filme começa.
native_language_example: She wants to know when the movie starts.

meaning: “Do you want to know how…?” / “Do you want to know how (someone) did something?”
additional_notes: Used to introduce an explanation or story that comes next. In questions, "Quer saber como...?" is a very common way to say “Want to know how…?” or “Do you want to know how…?”. It can also appear in statements with another subject: "(Ele/Ela) quer saber como..." = “He/She wants to know how…”. Often followed by a full clause: "quer saber como eu fiz" (“do you want to know how I did it?”).
target_language_example: Quer saber como eu aprendi português tão rápido?
native_language_example: Do you want to know how I learned Portuguese so fast?

additional_notes: Used with a 3rd-person subject to say what someone wants to be or become. It commonly appears before professions, roles, or adjectives: quer ser advogado, quer ser famoso. The dictionary form is querer ser.
target_language_example: Ela quer ser médica quando crescer.
native_language_example: She wants to be a doctor when she grows up.

meaning: “(he/she/you) wants to be a …” (with a masculine noun).
additional_notes: From **querer** (“to want”) + **ser** (“to be”) + **um** (“a/an”, masculine). It’s commonly used to talk about someone’s career goal or what they want to become: **Ele quer ser um médico.** If the noun is feminine, use **quer ser uma**: **Ela quer ser uma médica.** In Portuguese you can omit the subject when it’s clear from context, as in the examples.
target_language_example: Quando crescer, ele quer ser um piloto.
native_language_example: When he grows up, he wants to be a pilot.

additional_notes: From "querer" (to want) + "te" (you, informal singular object) + "ver" (to see). The subject is often implied by context (e.g., "Ele quer te ver" = He wants to see you). You can change the conjugation: "eu quero te ver" (I want to see you), "ela quer te ver" (she wants to see you). In many places you may also hear "quer ver você".
target_language_example: Ele quer te ver hoje à tarde.
native_language_example: He wants to see you this afternoon.

additional_notes: From **querer** (to want) + **ver** (to see). Used with an object that can come after it (**quer ver as minhas traduções**) or as a pronoun (**te quer ver** = wants to see you; also **me quer ver**, **o/a quer ver**). It can also be a question: **Quer ver...?** = Do you want to see...?.
target_language_example: Você quer ver o meu currículo agora?
native_language_example: Do you want to see my résumé now?

meaning: “(Do you/he/she) want to come?” / “wants to come.”
additional_notes: Formed by **quer** (from *querer*, “to want”) + **vir** (“to come”). Used to invite someone (**Quer vir?** = “Do you want to come?”) or to say someone has the intention to come (**Ele quer vir** = “He wants to come”). Often followed by a destination with **para** (“to”): **quer vir para a festa**. With **para dentro**, it means “come inside.” In polite speech you’ll also hear **Você quer vir...?**.
target_language_example: Você quer vir comigo ao mercado?
native_language_example: Do you want to come with me to the market?

meaning: "(they/you all) want to know"; sometimes "(they) don’t care" (with "de").
additional_notes: Form of "querer" (to want) + "saber" (to know) for "eles/elas/vocês". It can be a real question ("Vocês querem saber?") or used to introduce information/opinion: "Se querem saber..." = "If you want to know...". With "de" ("não querem saber de...") it often means "they’re not interested in / they don’t care about...".
target_language_example: Se querem saber, eu prefiro ficar em casa hoje.
native_language_example: If you want to know, I’d rather stay home today.

additional_notes: Most often used to talk about the meaning of words, signs, sentences, or actions. The exact infinitive phrase querer dizer often appears after another verb, such as pode or vai. In many everyday contexts, a conjugated form like quer dizer means 'means' or 'does ... mean?'. Literally, it can also mean 'to want to say'.
target_language_example: É difícil saber o que "saudade" pode querer dizer.
native_language_example: It's hard to know what "saudade" can mean.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of querer (queria) to sound polite/soft, often like “I/you wanted to talk to me?” or “Did you want to talk to me?” It can refer to a present intention (“Were you wanting to talk to me?”) or a past one, depending on context. Word order can change with the subject: “Você queria falar comigo?” / “Ele queria falar comigo.”
target_language_example: Você queria falar comigo agora ou mais tarde?
native_language_example: Did you want to talk to me now or later?

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of "querer" (queria = I/he/she wanted), often implying a desire in the past, something someone used to want, or a softer/more tentative way to express wanting than "quero". "Fazer isso" = "do that/this"; in context, "isso" usually means “that” (something already mentioned). Person changes: eu queria, você/ele/ela queria, nós queríamos, eles/elas queriam.
target_language_example: Eu queria fazer isso ontem, mas não tive tempo.
native_language_example: I wanted to do that yesterday, but I didn’t have time.

meaning: 'I wish I could' / 'I wanted to be able to.'
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of querer (queria) + infinitive (poder) to express a wish, desire, or regret about being able to do something. Very common for polite, softer statements, often closer to 'I wish I could...' than a literal past 'I wanted...' depending on context. Usually followed by another infinitive: queria poder ajudar, falar, pensar, ir, etc.
target_language_example: Queria poder ir com vocês, mas tenho que trabalhar.
native_language_example: I wish I could go with you, but I have to work.

additional_notes: Used to say what someone wanted to happen, usually involving another person’s action. It’s "queria" ("wanted" in the imperfect/past) + "que" ("that"). In Portuguese it’s commonly followed by a verb in the subjunctive: "queria que ela parasse" = "I wanted her to stop". The subject is often omitted when it’s clear: "Queria que ela..." can mean "I wanted her...".
target_language_example: Eu queria que você viesse mais cedo.
native_language_example: I wanted you to come earlier.

meaning: “I wanted him to…” / “I wished he would…”
additional_notes: Used to express what you wanted (or didn’t want) a man (“ele” = he) to do or to be. It’s built with **queria** (imperfect of *querer*, often meaning “I wanted/I would like”), + **que** + **subjunctive** (e.g., *queria que ele estivesse…*, *queria que ele dissesse…*, *queria que ele tivesse ido…*). For “her,” use **queria que ela…**.
target_language_example: Eu queria que ele me ligasse hoje.
native_language_example: I wanted him to call me today.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone wanted you to do. It’s built with the imperfect of querer (queria = “(he/she) wanted”) + que + eu + a verb in the imperfect subjunctive (e.g., fosse, aprendesse, beijasse). Common pattern: “[Person] queria que eu + (subjunctive verb) …”.
target_language_example: Ela queria que eu chegasse mais cedo.
native_language_example: She wanted me to arrive earlier.

meaning: “I wanted you to …” / “I’d like you to …”
additional_notes: Used to express a wish or desire about what someone else should do or how they should be. It’s normally followed by a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., queria que você fosse, fizesse, estivesse). Often sounds like a polite/soft way to ask for something in conversation.
target_language_example: Queria que você me ajudasse com isso.
native_language_example: I wanted you to help me with that.

meaning: “I/they/he/she wanted to know” (often: “I was wondering / I’d like to know”).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of querer (queria) + saber (to know) to express a desire to know something, often in a polite/soft way. Very common before indirect questions: “Queria saber se…” (I was wondering if…), “Queria saber como/quem/o que…” (I wanted to know how/who/what…). The subject can be omitted in Portuguese (“Queria saber…” usually means “I wanted to know…”).
target_language_example: Queria saber se você pode me ajudar.
native_language_example: I was wondering if you can help me.

meaning: "I wanted to know if…" / "I was wondering if…"
additional_notes: Polite way to ask for information or confirmation. Literally uses the imperfect tense (queria = I wanted), which softens the request in Portuguese; often used in messages, emails, and customer-service situations. Usually followed by a verb clause introduced by se (“if/whether”).
target_language_example: Queria saber se você pode me ajudar com isso.
native_language_example: I was wondering if you can help me with that.

additional_notes: From the verb querer (“to want”) in the imperfect past (queria), followed by ser (“to be”). Often used to talk about past desires, goals, or plans (not necessarily achieved). In polite conversation, queria can also sound softer than quero (“I want”), closer to “I’d like…”.
target_language_example: Quando eu era criança, eu queria ser astronauta.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I wanted to be an astronaut.

additional_notes: "Queria" is the imperfect of "querer" and often sounds softer/more polite than "quero" ("I want"). It’s used for wishes, desires, or polite requests in the present or in the past. With "ter" it means wanting to possess something or wanting to be sure of something (e.g., "queria ter certeza" = "wanted to be sure").
target_language_example: Eu queria ter mais tempo para estudar.
native_language_example: I wanted to have more time to study.

meaning: 'I wanted to see' / 'I just wanted to check'.
additional_notes: Literally 'wanted to see' (queria = 'wanted' + ver = 'to see'). Very common to soften what you’re asking or saying: "Eu só queria ver se..." often means "I just wanted to see/check if...". It can also mean wanting to meet/see someone ("queria ver ela" = "wanted to see her") or wanting to look at/inspect something ("ver o que havia..." = "see what was inside...").
target_language_example: Eu queria ver se ainda dava tempo de chegar hoje.
native_language_example: I wanted to see if there was still time to arrive today.

additional_notes: Used to express desire/intention to eat. It’s formed by the verb querer (“to want”) + comer (“to eat”). You can add what you want to eat (quero comer morangos), how much (quero comer um pouco de bolo), or where (quero comer naquele restaurante).
target_language_example: Estou com fome; quero comer agora.
native_language_example: I’m hungry; I want to eat now.

additional_notes: Used to say you intend/want to purchase something. Common pattern: "quero comprar" + item (e.g., "quero comprar pão"). "Quero" is the 1st-person singular form of "querer" (to want); for other people you’ll hear: "você quer comprar" (you want to buy), "ele/ela quer comprar" (he/she wants to buy), "queremos comprar" (we want to buy).
target_language_example: Quero comprar um presente para minha mãe.
native_language_example: I want to buy a gift for my mom.

additional_notes: Used to say you want to go somewhere or leave. You can add a destination with "a/ao/à" (e.g., "quero ir ao mercado", "quero ir à praia") or just use it alone to mean "I want to go/leave." The verb changes with the subject: "eu quero ir", "você quer ir", "nós queremos ir".
target_language_example: Quero ir embora agora.
native_language_example: I want to leave now.

meaning: "I want to go to the…" (to a feminine place).
additional_notes: Used to say you want to go somewhere. It’s followed by a feminine singular noun (because of "a" = "the" feminine), e.g. "quero ir para a praia" (the beach), "quero ir para a escola" (school). With masculine nouns you use "para o" ("quero ir para o parque"). In informal speech, "para a" is often shortened to "pra" ("quero ir pra praia").
target_language_example: Quero ir para a praia amanhã.
native_language_example: I want to go to the beach tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express that you want someone else to do something or be in a certain state. It is normally followed by a verb in the subjunctive: quero que ele venha. If the subject is the same as the speaker, Portuguese usually uses quero + infinitive instead: quero sair.
target_language_example: Quero que você venha cedo amanhã.
native_language_example: I want you to come early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express what you want someone/something (masculine: "o") to do. After "quero que", Portuguese normally uses the subjunctive: "quero que o Tom fique" (I want Tom to stay). In English you often translate it as "I want [someone] to..." rather than "I want that...". "o" is the masculine singular "the" and appears before a masculine noun (o carro) and sometimes before names/titles in some varieties/usages.
target_language_example: Quero que o professor explique de novo.
native_language_example: I want the teacher to explain again.

additional_notes: Used to say that the speaker wants the other person to do something. It is normally followed by a verb in the subjunctive: quero que você + subjunctive verb.
target_language_example: Quero que você chegue cedo amanhã.
native_language_example: I want you to arrive early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to express what the speaker wants a group of people ("vocês" = you all) to do. It is followed by a verb in the subjunctive (usem, parem, fiquem, saibam, se sentem, sejam, vão), often giving an instruction, request, or strong desire.
target_language_example: Quero que vocês me ajudem com isso.
native_language_example: I want you all to help me with this.

meaning: "I want to know" / "I’d like to know."
additional_notes: Used to ask for information or express curiosity/interest. Often followed by a clause or question (e.g., "Quero saber a que horas..." = "I want to know what time...") or by "mais" + "sobre" to mean "I want to know more about...". It’s neutral and common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Quero saber se você vai amanhã.
native_language_example: I want to know if you’re going tomorrow.

meaning: "I want to be" / "I want to become".
additional_notes: Used to talk about what you want to be in the future (a job, role, identity): "Quero ser médico." It can also be used more broadly to express wanting to be in a certain state or situation: "Quero ser dispensado" = "I want to be excused/exempt". The verb changes with the subject (e.g., "eu quero ser", "você quer ser", "ele quer ser").
target_language_example: Quando eu crescer, quero ser engenheiro.
native_language_example: When I grow up, I want to be an engineer.

meaning: “I want to see you.” (often: “I want you to come see me / I need to see you.”)
additional_notes: Used to say you want to meet someone in person or see them (sometimes urgently, like an order/request: “Come see me now”). “Te” is an informal object pronoun (= “you”); in more formal speech you might hear “quero ver você.” Tone depends on context: it can be affectionate (“I miss you”) or confrontational (“I don’t want to see you again”).
target_language_example: Quero te ver hoje à noite para conversarmos.
native_language_example: I want to see you tonight so we can talk.

additional_notes: A literal combination of quero + ver. It is used to say that you want to see something or someone; with people, it can also mean "I want to see/meet" that person.
target_language_example: Quero ver o filme hoje à noite.
native_language_example: I want to see the movie tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say you want to see a female person. It’s formed by "quero" (I want) + "ver" (to see) with the object pronoun "-la" (her) attached to the infinitive: "vê-la". You may also see "quero ver ela" in casual speech, but "quero vê-la" is more standard.
target_language_example: Quero vê-la hoje à tarde.
native_language_example: I want to see her this afternoon.

additional_notes: Day of the week. Often used with dates or time expressions like “desde quinta-feira” (since Thursday), “toda quinta-feira” (every Thursday), and “na quinta-feira” (on Thursday). In Brazilian Portuguese it’s common to shorten it informally to “quinta” when the context is clear.
target_language_example: A reunião é na quinta-feira à tarde.
native_language_example: The meeting is on Thursday afternoon.

meaning: "fifteen years" (an age or a period of 15 years).
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s age (Tenho quinze anos. = I’m fifteen) or about time that has passed (Faz/Se passaram quinze anos… = It’s been fifteen years…). In Brazil, "festa de quinze anos" refers to a girl’s 15th birthday celebration (similar to a quinceañera).
target_language_example: Quando eu tinha quinze anos, eu morava no Rio.
native_language_example: When I was fifteen, I lived in Rio.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (how long something takes or lasts) or a time interval. Common patterns: "esperar quinze minutos" (to wait 15 minutes), "levar quinze minutos" (to take 15 minutes), "passaram quinze minutos?" (have 15 minutes passed?), "de quinze em quinze minutos" (every 15 minutes), and "quinze minutos de caminhada" (a 15-minute walk).
target_language_example: A reunião vai durar quinze minutos.
native_language_example: The meeting will last fifteen minutes.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the cause or justification for something. Often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., “razão para mudar” = “reason to change”) or a noun/pronoun (e.g., “razão para isso” = “reason for that”). Common in phrases like “não tem razão para…” (there’s no reason to…) and “qual é a razão para…?” (what’s the reason for…?).
target_language_example: Não há razão para ter medo.
native_language_example: There’s no reason to be afraid.

additional_notes: Used to express worry or concern about what follows. It’s relatively formal. It often introduces a clause with the subjunctive in Portuguese (e.g., "Receio que esteja chovendo" = “I’m afraid it’s raining”), though you may also see the indicative in some contexts.
target_language_example: Receio que não possamos ir hoje.
native_language_example: I’m afraid we can’t go today.

additional_notes: Used to talk about materials or sources from nature that people use (e.g., water, forests, oil, minerals). Common in environmental, economic, and geography contexts. Plural: "recursos naturais".
target_language_example: A água é um recurso natural essencial.
native_language_example: Water is an essential natural resource.

additional_notes: Refers to materials and sources found in nature that people use, like water, forests, minerals, oil, and gas. Often used in discussions about a country’s wealth, development, or environmental issues (e.g., protecting or wasting natural resources).
target_language_example: Precisamos proteger nossos recursos naturais para o futuro.
native_language_example: We need to protect our natural resources for the future.

additional_notes: Used for online platforms/apps where people create profiles, connect with others, and share posts/messages (e.g., Facebook, Instagram). Often appears with verbs like "ter/criar uma conta" (to have/create an account) and "em alguma rede social" (on any social network).
target_language_example: Eu não tenho conta em nenhuma rede social.
native_language_example: I don't have an account on any social network.

meaning: reluctant to do that/this; unwilling to do it.
additional_notes: Used to say someone doesn’t want to do something, often because they’re hesitant, unsure, or don’t feel comfortable. Common with the structure “relutante em + verb (infinitive)”: “relutante em falar”, “relutante em aceitar”. You can also say “estar relutante” (to be reluctant) or “ficar relutante” (to become reluctant).
target_language_example: Eu estava relutante em fazer isso sozinho.
native_language_example: I was reluctant to do that alone.

additional_notes: Used when talking about finding a solution to a specific problem already mentioned or understood in context. In conversation, you can swap in another demonstrative: “resolver este problema” (this problem—near the speaker) or “resolver aquele problema” (that problem—over there/previously mentioned).
target_language_example: Precisamos resolver esse problema hoje.
native_language_example: We need to solve this problem today.

additional_notes: Used when talking about finding a solution to a specific issue or difficulty. In everyday speech, you’ll also hear it with different demonstratives ("resolver esse problema" / "resolver aquele problema") or without them ("resolver o problema"). "Resolver" is a very common verb for solving problems, issues, questions, or situations.
target_language_example: Vamos trabalhar juntos para resolver este problema hoje.
native_language_example: Let’s work together to solve this problem today.

additional_notes: Common with verbs like "tentar" (try) or phrases like "com facilidade" (easily). In everyday speech it can mean either finding the solution (solve) or taking action so the issue goes away (fix).
target_language_example: Vamos resolver o problema juntos.
native_language_example: Let’s solve the problem together.

additional_notes: Imperative form (a command/request) using the formal/neutral "você" form of the verb respirar. Common when calming someone down, preparing for something stressful, or before an exercise (e.g., breathing, meditation). Often used alone or with softeners like "por favor" or "tá?".
target_language_example: Antes da apresentação, respire fundo e vá com calma.
native_language_example: Before the presentation, take a deep breath and take it easy.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition “a” before the person/thing you answer or respond to: “responder a uma pergunta” (answer a question), “responder a alguém” (answer someone). In some contexts, “responder a (um adulto/uma autoridade)” can mean “talk back” (respond in a rude/defiant way).
target_language_example: O meu filho é capaz de responder a qualquer pergunta.
native_language_example: My son is able to answer any question.

meaning: to be responsible for; to answer for.
additional_notes: Used to express responsibility/accountability for a person, task, area, or for consequences (often in administrative/work or legal contexts). Example meanings: "Ela responde por finanças" (she’s in charge of finances); "Ele vai responder pelo crime" (he will answer for the crime). Note: in legal contexts it commonly appears as "responder por" + a crime/offense; in other contexts it can mean being in charge of something.
target_language_example: Eu vou responder por este projeto na empresa.
native_language_example: I’m going to be responsible for this project at the company.

additional_notes: Used when you reply to a specific question. In Portuguese you say “responder a” (to answer) + “a pergunta” (the question). The “a + a” becomes “à” (with the accent) before a feminine singular noun like “pergunta”. You can also say “responder a uma pergunta” = “answer a question.”
target_language_example: Desculpe, não sei responder à pergunta agora.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t answer the question right now.

additional_notes: Common English loanword in Portuguese, used mainly to name the music style. Often appears after verbs like "gostar de" (to like): "Você gosta de rock and roll?" You can add adjectives like "clássico" (classic): "rock and roll clássico".
target_language_example: Meu pai gosta de rock and roll clássico.
native_language_example: My dad likes classic rock and roll.

meaning: Ferris wheel (the big wheel ride at a fair/amusement park).
additional_notes: A feminine noun: a roda-gigante. It’s commonly used with locations like “na roda-gigante” (“on/in the Ferris wheel”). The hyphen is standard in Portuguese.
target_language_example: Vamos dar uma volta na roda-gigante depois do jantar.
native_language_example: Let’s go for a ride on the Ferris wheel after dinner.

additional_notes: Common Portuguese term for what you wear to swim (at the beach or pool). Often used as a general category (swimwear) and can refer to a one-piece swimsuit, bikini, swim trunks, etc., depending on context.
target_language_example: Esqueci minha roupa de banho no hotel.
native_language_example: I forgot my swimsuit at the hotel.

additional_notes: Used with **saber** + infinitive to express a learned skill/ability: **sabe dirigir** = “knows how to drive / can drive.” Common in questions: **Você sabe dirigir?** It can be followed by the vehicle: **dirigir um carro / caminhão**. Note: **sabe dirigir** is 3rd person singular (ele/ela/você).
target_language_example: O meu irmão sabe dirigir um carro.
native_language_example: My brother can drive a car.

meaning: “(he/she/you) can speak French” / “knows how to speak French.”
additional_notes: Uses the verb "saber" + infinitive ("falar") to express knowing how to do a skill. "Sabe" is the present tense form for "você/ele/ela" (and also for "o senhor/a senhora" in formal address). Other common forms: "eu sei falar francês" (I can speak French), "nós sabemos falar francês" (we can). In questions it often means “Can you speak French?” ("Você sabe falar francês?") or “Does anyone speak French?” ("Alguém sabe falar francês?").
target_language_example: Você tem certeza de que o Tom sabe falar francês?
native_language_example: Are you sure Tom can speak French?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "saber" + infinitive to talk about an acquired skill/ability. It can mean ordinary reading ("sabe ler e escrever") or reading/understanding something like lips or body language ("sabe ler os movimentos dos lábios" = can interpret/understand). You can change the subject: "eu sei ler", "você sabe ler", "eles sabem ler".
target_language_example: Você sabe ler em português?
native_language_example: Can you read in Portuguese?

meaning: "(he/she) can swim" / "(he/she) knows how to swim."
additional_notes: "Saber" + infinitive expresses an ability/learned skill: "saber nadar" = to know how to swim. It changes with the subject: "eu sei nadar", "você sabe nadar", "ele/ela sabe nadar", "nós sabemos nadar". For questions, you can use "Você sabe nadar?" (= Can you swim?).
target_language_example: Você sabe nadar?
native_language_example: Can you swim?

meaning: "(he/she) knows how to play" (a musical instrument).
additional_notes: Used with a person as the subject + "saber" (to know how to) + "tocar" (to play) + an instrument. You can change the verb to match the subject: "eu sei tocar", "você sabe tocar", "eles sabem tocar". Often followed by the instrument without an article: "sabe tocar flauta/violão/piano".
target_language_example: Você sabe tocar violão?
native_language_example: Do you know how to play the guitar?

additional_notes: From the verb "saber" (to know, as a fact) + "a resposta" (the answer). Used to say someone knows the answer to a question: "sabe a resposta para essa pergunta". With "você", it means "you know"; with "ele/ela", it means "he/she knows". You can also negate it: "não sabe a resposta" (doesn’t know the answer).
target_language_example: Você sabe a resposta?
native_language_example: Do you know the answer?

additional_notes: Used with "você" implied (or stated) to ask about someone’s knowledge of a method or the way something is done: "Sabe como se faz?" = "Do you know how it’s done?" It can also introduce a clause in statements: "Você sabe como pode demorar" = "You know how long it can take." Often followed by verbs like "fazer" (to do/make), "chamar" (to call), or by a full clause.
target_language_example: Sabe como chegar lá de ônibus?
native_language_example: Do you know how to get there by bus?

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say someone knows how to do something: “sabe como fazer / dizer / chegar…”. “Sabe” is the present tense of “saber” (to know). It can also appear in questions: “Você sabe como…?” (Do you know how…?).
target_language_example: Ela sabe como chegar lá sem GPS.
native_language_example: She knows how to get there without GPS.

additional_notes: "Sabe" is the (present tense) 'you/he/she knows' form of "saber". "Disso" means 'of that/about that' (de + isso). Used to say someone is aware of a fact or piece of information, or to ask if someone knows it. Polite question uses "O senhor/A senhora sabe disso?"
target_language_example: Você sabe disso, né?
native_language_example: You know that, right?

additional_notes: Used to say someone has a lot of knowledge about a topic or person. It’s the verb saber (to know facts/information) in the 3rd-person singular present (ele/ela/você sabe) + muito (a lot) + sobre (about). You can change the subject: eu sei muito sobre…, nós sabemos muito sobre…, eles sabem muito sobre….
target_language_example: Ela sabe muito sobre moda atual.
native_language_example: She knows a lot about current fashion.

meaning: “do you know what … is?” / “you know what … is.”
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone knows what something is (often followed by a noun or “isto/isso”: “Sabe o que é isto?”). It can also be used on its own (“Sabe o que é?”) when the thing is understood from context. With a name or pronoun instead of “você” (e.g., “Tom sabe o que é”), it means “Tom knows what it is.”
target_language_example: Você sabe o que é saudade?
native_language_example: Do you know what saudade is?

additional_notes: Used to say someone knows the location of a person/thing, or as a question meaning “Do you know where … is?”. “Sabe” is from *saber* (to know), and “está” is from *estar* (to be/located). Often you’ll add the subject or object: “Você sabe onde está o médico?” / “Ele sabe onde está o celular.”
target_language_example: Você sabe onde está a estação?
native_language_example: Do you know where the station is?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause that is known or (in a question) asked about. Often appears with an explicit subject ("ela sabe que…", "todo mundo sabe que…") or with the subject omitted in conversation, meaning "(você) sabe que…". In writing, a question mark makes it a direct question: "Você sabe que…?" = "Do you know that…?"
target_language_example: Você sabe que eu não posso ir hoje?
native_language_example: Do you know that I can’t go today?

additional_notes: Used to report knowledge about a male person ("ele" = "he"). In questions, the subject can be left out: "Como sabe que ele está lá?" often means "How do you/he know he is there?" Context tells who "sabe" refers to.
target_language_example: Ela sabe que ele está em casa.
native_language_example: She knows that he is at home.

additional_notes: Used to ask or state whether someone knows a person’s identity. Often appears inside a larger sentence: “Você sabe quem é ele/ela?” (Do you know who he/she is?) or “Todo mundo sabe quem é X.” (Everyone knows who X is). You can change the subject: “você sabe…”, “ele/ela sabe…”, “vocês sabem…”.
target_language_example: Você sabe quem é o novo professor?
native_language_example: Do you know who the new teacher is?

meaning: "(they) can speak French" / "(they) know how to speak French."
additional_notes: "Sabem" is the 3rd-person plural of "saber" (to know), used to talk about knowing how to do something. The pattern is "saber" + infinitive verb: "saber falar" = "to be able to speak". Here it’s in the plural (“they”): "Eles/Elas sabem falar francês." In questions, you can keep the same order: "Eles sabem falar francês?"
target_language_example: Vocês sabem falar francês?
native_language_example: Can you (all) speak French?

additional_notes: "Sabem" is the present tense (3rd person plural) of "saber" (to know). It’s used before an embedded question with "o que" (“what”), like in "Eles sabem o que fazer" (“They know what to do”). Often followed by a verb in the infinitive ("o que fazer") or by a full clause ("o que está acontecendo").
target_language_example: Vocês sabem o que precisam fazer agora?
native_language_example: Do you (plural) know what you need to do now?

additional_notes: Present tense of **saber** (to know) in the **3rd person plural** (**eles/elas sabem** = they know; **vocês sabem** = you all know) + **que** (“that”) to introduce a clause. Often the subject is omitted because it’s understood from context.
target_language_example: Vocês sabem que a reunião começa às nove?
native_language_example: Do you all know that the meeting starts at nine?

additional_notes: Used to introduce something the speaker believes is known or accepted as true (often by a group). In questions like "Como sabemos que...?", it means "How do we know that...?". "Sabemos" is present tense of "saber" (to know).
target_language_example: Sabemos que isso é importante, mas precisamos de mais tempo.
native_language_example: We know that this is important, but we need more time.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a reason/background fact, often like an English '-ing' clause: "... , sabendo que ..." = "..., knowing that ...". Very common after verbs like "ficar" in "ficar sabendo que" ("to find out/learn that").
target_language_example: Eu não fui à festa, sabendo que você não ia.
native_language_example: I didn’t go to the party, knowing that you weren’t going to.

meaning: to know the truth; to find out the truth.
additional_notes: Used when someone wants or needs the true facts about a situation. Often appears with verbs like querer (to want), precisar (to need), merecer (to deserve), ter direito de (to have the right to), and ter que (to have to). You can also use descobrir a verdade for “to discover/find out the truth.”
target_language_example: Eu preciso saber a verdade antes de tomar uma decisão.
native_language_example: I need to know the truth before making a decision.

additional_notes: A compositional phrase meaning "to know how" to do something. In real usage, the verb is often conjugated (for example, sabe como, sabem como), but the dictionary form is saber como. It can also introduce an indirect question, especially after verbs like querer: quero saber como... = "I want to know how...".
target_language_example: O Tom parecia saber como fazer isso.
native_language_example: Tom seemed to know how to do that.

additional_notes: Used when referring back to something already mentioned or understood from context. "disso" = "de" + "isso" (roughly “about that / of that”), so "saber disso" often means “to know about it/that (fact, situation, detail)”. Common in phrases like "precisar saber disso" (need to know about that) and "não tinha como saber disso" (there was no way to know that).
target_language_example: Você precisa saber disso antes de decidir.
native_language_example: You need to know that before deciding.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t know something or that it’s impossible to be sure. Often appears as "Sei lá" (“I don’t know / who knows”) in casual conversation, sometimes to show indifference or lack of interest.
target_language_example: —Onde é que ele mora? —Saber lá; nunca me disse.
native_language_example: —Where does he live? —Who knows; he never told me.

additional_notes: Used when someone wants information or an explanation about a past event. With "quero" it often expresses insistence or concern: "Quero saber o que aconteceu" (“I want to know what happened”). In questions you’ll often hear: "Você sabe o que aconteceu?" (“Do you know what happened?”).
target_language_example: Eu preciso saber o que aconteceu ontem à noite.
native_language_example: I need to know what happened last night.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect yes/no question: you want to find out whether something is true or will happen. Very common after verbs like “querer/gostar de” (to want/would like): “quero/gostaria de saber se…”. In English it often becomes “to know if” or “to know whether”.
target_language_example: Preciso saber se você vai amanhã.
native_language_example: I need to know if you’re going tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has (or wants) complete knowledge about a topic/person/thing. Very common with verbs like querer/precisar/parecer + saber tudo sobre. The preposition “sobre” means “about” here, and it’s followed by a noun or pronoun: sobre você/isto/este banheiro.
target_language_example: Eu quero saber tudo sobre o seu trabalho.
native_language_example: I want to know everything about your job.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a question or statement about some specific information (often followed by a verb, e.g., “é”, “fazer”, “disse”). In speech it can be a real question (“Do you know what Tom said?”) or a reminder/assumption (“You already know what to do.”). Usually followed by a clause starting with a verb: “sabes o que é…?”, “sabes o que fazer?”, “sabes o que aconteceu?”
target_language_example: Sabes o que aconteceu aqui ontem à noite?
native_language_example: Do you know what happened here last night?

meaning: "(He/She/I) knew how to speak French" / "could speak French" (in the past).
additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of "saber" (sabia) + infinitive to talk about an ability/skill someone had (often as background information or something you discovered/assumed). In the present you’d say "sei falar francês". You can swap "francês" for another language: "sabia falar inglês/espanhol".
target_language_example: Quando eu era criança, eu sabia falar francês, mas esqueci quase tudo.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I could speak French, but I forgot almost everything.

additional_notes: Used with the imperfect of "saber" (sabia) + "disso" (“of that/that”) to say someone already had that knowledge. Often contrasts with new information or surprise, and can be turned into a question: "Você sabia disso?" = “Did you know that?” (implies “before now”).
target_language_example: Eu não sabia disso até agora.
native_language_example: I didn’t know that until now.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect past of **saber** (*sabia*) to talk about what someone knew in a situation in the past. It’s often used after a negative word: **não sabia o que fazer** = “didn’t know what to do.” You can change the subject: **eu sabia**, **você sabia**, **nós sabíamos**, **eles sabiam**. Common extensions: **sabia o que fazer a seguir** (“knew what to do next”).
target_language_example: Eu sabia o que fazer, mas estava com medo.
native_language_example: I knew what to do, but I was scared.

additional_notes: "sabia" is the imperfect past of "saber" (to know), so it often sets background information in the past (what someone already knew). It changes with the subject: eu sabia que (I knew that), ele/ela sabia que (he/she knew that), você sabia que (you knew that).
target_language_example: Eu sabia que você ia chegar cedo.
native_language_example: I knew that you were going to arrive early.

meaning: “knew that the …” (said about a woman/thing, since it’s followed by “a”).
additional_notes: Used in the imperfect past of saber (“to know”): “(ele/ela) sabia” = “he/she knew.” “Que” introduces a clause (“that …”), and “a” is the feminine singular definite article (“the”) that usually comes right before a feminine noun/name with a title (e.g., a Maria). Often followed by verbs like estava (was), tinha (had), ia (was going to), etc.
target_language_example: Eu sabia que a professora estava doente.
native_language_example: I knew that the teacher was sick.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something someone already knew about a woman/girl (“ela”). Often appears as “eu sabia que ela…”, and it can also be shortened by dropping the subject pronoun when it’s clear from context: “Sabia que ela…”. In questions, it becomes “Você sabia que ela…?” (“Did you know that she…?”). Verb tense agrees with the speaker/subject (sabia = past/imperfect of saber).
target_language_example: Eu sabia que ela não ia voltar tão cedo.
native_language_example: I knew that she wasn’t going to come back that soon.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect of **saber** (**sabia**) to describe past knowledge/background information. **que** = “that,” and **eu estava** (“I was”) is often followed by an adjective or a condition: *cansado(a)* (tired), *com sede* (thirsty), *deprimido(a)* (depressed), *pronto(a)* (ready). The ending changes with the subject: *eu sabia* (I knew), *ele/ela sabia* (he/she knew).
target_language_example: Ela sabia que eu estava nervoso antes da entrevista.
native_language_example: She knew that I was nervous before the interview.

additional_notes: Used to report knowledge about a specific masculine noun that follows (o = “the” for a masculine singular noun). “Sabia” is the imperfect past of saber (“to know”), and it often appears in statements like “Ele/Ela sabia que o …” or can be said without the subject when it’s understood from context.
target_language_example: Eu sabia que o voo ia atrasar.
native_language_example: I knew that the flight was going to be delayed.

additional_notes: Used for camping or sleeping somewhere without a bed. "Saco" = bag/sack and "dormir" = to sleep, so it literally means a bag to sleep in. Common with verbs like "emprestar" (to lend) and "caber" (to fit).
target_language_example: Você trouxe seu saco de dormir para o acampamento?
native_language_example: Did you bring your sleeping bag for the camping trip?

additional_notes: A direct command telling one person to leave. Grammatically it’s the imperative for **tu** ("sai"), but in Brazil it’s also commonly used in informal speech even when addressing **você**. A more formal/polite version is **saia daqui**. Often sounds rude/angry depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Sai daqui agora, por favor.
native_language_example: Get out of here now, please.

additional_notes: An informal, often aggressive way to tell someone to leave. Literally "go out" (sair + fora), but used like English "get out!" / "get lost!". "Sai" is the imperative form of "sair" (commonly used when addressing someone as "você" in everyday Brazilian Portuguese). It can be followed by complements like "daqui" (from here) or "com isso/esse..." (take that/that thing with you).
target_language_example: Sai fora daqui agora!
