additional_notes: Often used with the verb phrase "dar uma volta" (= to go for a short walk/drive/ride; to take a lap). In sports/racing, "uma volta" is one lap; "uma volta atrás" means one lap behind.
target_language_example: Vamos dar uma volta no quarteirão?
native_language_example: Shall we take a quick walk/drive around the block?

additional_notes: Used to order or talk about a single serving of coffee. "Uma" = "a/one" (feminine), "xícara" = "cup" (common in Brazil), and "de café" = "of coffee". In polite requests you’ll often hear it with "Gostaria de..." (I’d like...) or "Quer que eu lhe traga...?" (Do you want me to bring you...?).
target_language_example: Vou tomar uma xícara de café depois do almoço.
native_language_example: I'm going to have a cup of coffee after lunch.

additional_notes: Used when ordering or asking for tea in a café/restaurant or at home. "Xícara" is the small cup typically used for tea or coffee. You can add details like "sem açúcar" (without sugar) or "com açúcar" (with sugar).
target_language_example: Posso tomar uma xícara de chá depois do jantar.
native_language_example: I can have a cup of tea after dinner.

additional_notes: “Uma” means “a/an” (feminine singular). “Árvore” is feminine: uma árvore, a árvore. Plural: “árvores” (uma árvore / duas árvores). Very common for describing places in nature (e.g., under a tree: “sob/debaixo de uma árvore”).
target_language_example: Há uma árvore grande no meu quintal.
native_language_example: There’s a big tree in my backyard.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to praise it (e.g., uma ótima noite = a great night; uma ótima pergunta = a great question). It’s short for “uma ótima + [noun]”. The masculine form is “um ótimo + [noun]”.
target_language_example: Você fez uma ótima escolha.
native_language_example: You made a great choice.

additional_notes: Used to praise or agree with a suggestion or plan. Often appears with verbs like achar (“to think/find”) or ser (“to be”): “Acho que é uma ótima ideia.” / “Foi uma ótima ideia.” You can intensify with “mesmo” (“really”): “É mesmo uma ótima ideia.”
target_language_example: Vamos sair mais cedo — é uma ótima ideia!
native_language_example: Let’s leave earlier — it’s a great idea!

additional_notes: Used to pick one item/person out of a group of feminine plural nouns: uma das crianças/estações/janelas/pessoas/respostas. It’s the feminine form; for masculine plural use “um dos” (e.g., um dos meninos). Often followed by a noun with “as” (plural feminine): “uma das + [plural feminine noun]”.
target_language_example: Uma das minhas amigas mora no Porto.
native_language_example: One of my (female) friends lives in Porto.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a duration of 60 minutes (e.g., "uma hora e meia" = one and a half hours; "atraso de uma hora" = a one-hour delay; "uma hora atrás" = one hour ago; "uma hora depois" = one hour later). In some contexts, especially with the future ("uma hora ele vai aparecer"), it can mean "eventually / at some point" rather than a literal hour.
target_language_example: Espera mais um pouco: uma hora ele chega.
native_language_example: Wait a bit longer: he’ll arrive eventually.

additional_notes: Uses the feminine plural indefinite article "umas" (= "some/a few") with "coisas" (= "things"). Very common for talking vaguely about tasks, topics, or items when you don’t want to (or can’t) be specific: "Preciso resolver umas coisas" = "I need to take care of a few things." It can also refer to things someone says: "Você fala umas coisas!" (often meaning "You say such things!" / "The things you say!").
target_language_example: Vou passar no mercado e comprar umas coisas pra jantar.
native_language_example: I’m going to stop by the market and buy a few things for dinner.

additional_notes: Uses the plural of the indefinite article (uns/umas) to mean an imprecise small number. Very common with time expressions, especially with “por”: “por uns dias” = “for a few days.” With “mais,” it means “a few more days.”
target_language_example: Vou ficar em casa por uns dias.
native_language_example: I'm going to stay home for a few days.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a reciprocal action between two or more people/animals (they do the action to each other). It agrees in gender/number with the group: masculine plural uns aos outros (mixed/all-male), feminine plural umas às outras (all-female). Often used with plural subjects.
target_language_example: Eles se ajudam uns aos outros todos os dias.
native_language_example: They help each other every day.

additional_notes: Used to give permission or state that someone is allowed/able to use the dictionary. It often appears with forms of "poder" (can/may): "Você pode usar este dicionário." The verb "usar" = to use; "este" = this (near the speaker); "dicionário" = dictionary. "senhoras/senhores" are polite/formal forms of address; "tu" (informal singular) and "você" (common singular); "vocês" (plural). "vós/podeis" are very formal/old-fashioned in most modern Portuguese, but still taught in some materials and used in some regions/contexts.
target_language_example: Você pode usar este dicionário na aula.
native_language_example: You can use this dictionary in class.

meaning: to use the bathroom; to go to the bathroom (to pee/poop).
additional_notes: A common polite way to say you need to pee/poop. Often used when asking permission or looking for a restroom: “Posso usar o banheiro?” / “Onde posso usar o banheiro?”. Also appears as “preciso usar o banheiro” or (more common in Portugal) “preciso de usar o banheiro”.
target_language_example: Com licença, posso usar o banheiro?
native_language_example: Excuse me, may I use the bathroom?

additional_notes: "Usá-lo" is "usar" (to use) with the object pronoun "o" (it/him) attached using a hyphen. The verb takes an accent (usá-) when the pronoun is attached. It usually refers to an object already mentioned (e.g., a coat, a tool, a chance/strategy) and can be used with different tenses: "pretendo usá-lo" (I intend to use it), "pode usá-lo" (you can use it).
target_language_example: Se você quiser, pode usá-lo agora.
native_language_example: If you want, you can use it now.

meaning: "will end" / "is going to end"; sometimes "will turn out (in the end)".
additional_notes: From "vai" (is going) + "acabar" (to end). Used to talk about something ending in the future ("Quando vai acabar?") or how something will turn out: "não vai acabar bem" = it won’t end well. In "vai acabar por + infinitive", it means "will end up + -ing" (after some process): "vai acabar por descobrir" = will end up finding out.
target_language_example: Se você continuar assim, isso vai acabar mal.
native_language_example: If you keep going like this, this is going to end badly.

additional_notes: Formed with ir (vai) + infinitive (chegar) to talk about a future arrival, often in the near future. Used with places (vai chegar aqui/em casa/em Lisboa) and with time expressions (logo, antes das três). In questions, it asks when someone will arrive.
target_language_example: O ônibus vai chegar em dez minutos.
native_language_example: The bus will arrive in ten minutes.

additional_notes: Used to talk about rain in the near future. It’s the verb *ir* (vai) + infinitive (*chover*), a very common way in Portuguese to express the future (“going to” + verb). Often used with time words like *hoje*, *esta noite*, *amanhã*, *mais tarde*.
target_language_example: Acho que vai chover, então vou levar um guarda-chuva.
native_language_example: I think it’s going to rain, so I’m going to take an umbrella.

meaning: "are you going to eat?" / "will you eat?" (also "go eat" in some contexts).
additional_notes: Literally from "vai" (you go/you’re going to) + "comer" (to eat). Used in questions like "Vai comer aqui?" = "Are you going to eat here?". Be careful: in insults like "Vai comer a sua mãe!" it’s a very vulgar, offensive expression and should be avoided.
target_language_example: Você vai comer aqui ou vai pedir para viagem?
native_language_example: Are you going to eat here or order it to go?

meaning: "is going to start" / "will start" (it’s about to begin).
additional_notes: Uses **ir (vai) + infinitive (começar)** to talk about the near future or something that’s about to happen. It can also be said alone to mean “Here we go again” / “It’s starting,” depending on tone and context (often when someone expects trouble or repetition). You can add **a + verb** after *começar* to say what will start happening: *vai começar a nevar* = “it’s going to start snowing.”
target_language_example: O filme vai começar em cinco minutos.
native_language_example: The movie is going to start in five minutes.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a planned or expected purchase in the near future. It’s the verb "ir" (vai, 3rd-person singular / also used in questions without an explicit subject) + infinitive "comprar". Can be a statement (Ele vai comprar...) or a question (Vai comprar...?).
target_language_example: Você realmente vai comprar aquele carro?
native_language_example: Are you really going to buy that car?

meaning: “will be able to / will manage to” (will succeed in doing something).
additional_notes: Uses the near-future form with **ir**: **vai + infinitive**. **Conseguir** often means “to be able to” or “to manage to (do something)”. Very common with negation: **não vai conseguir** = “won’t be able to / won’t manage to”.
target_language_example: Acho que ela vai conseguir terminar hoje.
native_language_example: I think she’ll be able to finish today.

additional_notes: Form of the verb phrase **vai + infinitive** (near-future): **vai** (it will/it’s going to) + **custar** (to cost). Common in questions about price: **Quanto vai custar?** (“How much will it cost?”). You can add what will cost: **Isso vai custar uma fortuna** (“That’s going to cost a fortune”).
target_language_example: Quanto vai custar o ingresso?
native_language_example: How much will the ticket cost?

additional_notes: Used to express confidence or reassure someone that a plan/situation will succeed. Literally “will give right,” but in practice it means things will go well. Often appears with a subject like “tudo/isso” (everything/that): “tudo vai dar certo.” Can also be used skeptically as a question: “Vai dar certo como?” (“How is that going to work out?”).
target_language_example: Calma, vai dar certo.
native_language_example: Relax, it’ll work out.

meaning: “it’s going to take (a while)” / “it will take time.”
additional_notes: Used to say something will take time. Commonly followed by a time expression: “vai demorar um tempo” (it’ll take a while), “vai demorar bastante” (it’ll take quite a long time), “vai demorar muito?” (will it take long?). You can change the subject/person: “vou demorar” (I’ll take a while), “vai demorar” (you/it will), “vamos demorar” (we’ll).
target_language_example: Desculpa, acho que vai demorar mais uns 10 minutos.
native_language_example: Sorry, I think it’s going to take about 10 more minutes.

additional_notes: Formed with **ir (vai)** + infinitive **dormir** to talk about a planned/expected action in the near future. **Vai** is used with **você/ele/ela** (e.g., *Onde vai dormir hoje?* = asking where someone will sleep/spend the night).
target_language_example: Você vai dormir aqui hoje?
native_language_example: Are you going to sleep here today?

additional_notes: Used with a time expression to say the expected duration of something (e.g., “vai durar 14 dias”, “vai durar uns dois dias”). Very common in questions with “Quanto tempo…?”: “Quanto tempo vai durar…?” = “How long will it last…?”. Also used for things like courses, quarantines, batteries, food, events, etc.
target_language_example: Você acha que a reunião vai durar muito?
native_language_example: Do you think the meeting will last long?

meaning: “(you/he/she) will understand.” Also, said alone: “go figure / who knows.”
additional_notes: Literally it’s the verb *entender* (to understand) in the near-future with *vai* (“is going to”): *vai entender* = “will understand / is going to understand.” It can refer to you, him, her, or someone else—context (or a subject like *você/ele/seu pai*) makes it clear. In casual speech you may hear nonstandard forms like *tu vai entender* (standard: *tu vais entender*). Said by itself (*Vai entender.*), it often expresses puzzlement or resignation, like “Go figure.”
target_language_example: Calma — você vai entender depois.
native_language_example: Relax — you’ll understand later.

meaning: “will be here” / “is going to be here” (future presence).
additional_notes: Uses the common future construction "ir" in the present (vai) + infinitive (estar) + location (aqui) to talk about a near, planned, or expected future situation. Frequently appears with a time expression (e.g., "amanhã", "em breve", "a semana toda") or with a clause like "quando eu voltar". Subject can be a name or noun (e.g., "Tom vai estar aqui") or implied from context.
target_language_example: Você acha que Tom vai estar aqui amanhã?
native_language_example: Do you think Tom will be here tomorrow?

additional_notes: Common near-future form of ficar for a singular subject: 'he/she/it is going to ...'. With a place, it usually means 'stay'; with an adjective, it often means 'be' or 'become'. Before a gerund, it can mean 'keep doing' something.
target_language_example: Ela vai ficar aqui até amanhã.
native_language_example: She is going to stay here until tomorrow.

meaning: “will stay here” / “is going to stay here.”
additional_notes: Uses the near-future construction (ir + infinitive): vai (is going to) + ficar (to stay) + aqui (here). Typically refers to someone staying (for a while) in a place. You can change the subject: eu vou ficar aqui (I’ll stay here), eles vão ficar aqui (they’ll stay here).
target_language_example: O Tom vai ficar aqui por alguns dias.
native_language_example: Tom is going to stay here for a few days.

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone that a situation or a person will turn out okay. Often appears as “tudo vai ficar bem” (“everything will be fine”). It can also be a question (“Vai ficar bem?” = “Will it be okay?”). Literally “will stay/become well,” but in everyday English it’s usually “will be fine.”
target_language_example: Calma, vai ficar bem.
native_language_example: Calm down, it’ll be okay.

additional_notes: Used to say that something will work or succeed (a plan, idea, device, method). Often appears in questions (Acha que vai funcionar? = “Do you think it’ll work?”) and can also mean “it will operate” (e.g., a machine). It’s the verb funcionar (“to work/function”) with vai (“is going to”), from ir (“to go”) used for the near future.
target_language_example: Não se preocupe: vai funcionar.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: it’ll work.

additional_notes: Literally “is going to take/carry,” but in threats it often means “you’re going to get (hit/punished).” It’s commonly followed by what the person will “get”: e.g., “vai levar uma surra” (you’re gonna get a beating), “vai levar um soco” (you’re gonna take a punch).
target_language_example: Se continuar falando assim, vai levar um soco.
native_language_example: If you keep talking like that, you’re gonna get punched.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive: vai me + verb. It means a third-person singular subject (he, she, it, you formal, or a named person) is going to do that action to me. For example, "vai me ajudar" = "will help me."
target_language_example: Ele vai me ligar mais tarde.
native_language_example: He’s going to call me later.

meaning: “will help me” / “are you going to help me?”
additional_notes: Literally “(you/he/she) will help me.” In questions, Portuguese often drops the subject, so “Vai me ajudar?” usually means “Are you going to help me?” (you). With a name or “ele/ela,” it means “(he/she) will help me.” You can also hear “vai ajudar-me” (more formal/European Portuguese style).
target_language_example: Você vai me ajudar a carregar essas caixas?
native_language_example: Are you going to help me carry these boxes?

meaning: “are you going to let me…?” / “are you going to leave me…?”
additional_notes: From "vai" (you are going to) + "me" (me) + "deixar" (to let/allow; to leave). It’s used when asking or stating what someone will allow you to do (deixar + infinitive: "deixar entrar/sair/ir embora/saber") or where they will leave you ("deixar aqui"). Often carries impatience or insistence depending on tone.
target_language_example: Você vai me deixar falar um minuto?
native_language_example: Are you going to let me speak for a minute?

meaning: "(he/she/it) is going to kill me" / "will kill me" (often: "will be furious with me").
additional_notes: Literally means someone is going to kill you. In everyday conversation it’s very often an exaggeration meaning someone (like your mom, boss, partner) will be really angry with you for something you did. Grammatically: "vai" (is going to) + "me" (me) + "matar" (kill). You can change the subject: "Minha mãe vai me matar" (My mom will kill me).
target_language_example: Se eu chegar tarde, minha mãe vai me matar.
native_language_example: If I get home late, my mom is going to kill me.

additional_notes: Uses the near-future construction ir (vai) + infinitive (morrer). Often means something is expected to happen (sometimes soon), but it can also just mean "will" in general depending on context. Negative: "não vai morrer" = "isn't going to die / won't die."
target_language_example: Se ele não for ao médico, vai morrer.
native_language_example: If he doesn't go to the doctor, he's going to die.

additional_notes: Formed with **ir (vai) + infinitive (mudar)** to talk about the near future or a strong prediction: *Isso vai mudar.* Depending on context, it can sound like a promise, warning, or complaint. In questions it often means “Are you going to change…?” In the expression **mudar o disco**, it means “change the subject/stop repeating the same thing.”
target_language_example: Eu acho que isso vai mudar em breve.
native_language_example: I think this is going to change soon.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb to form the near future: **vai + nos + infinitive**. Here, **vai** (from *ir*) means “is going to,” and **nos** is the object pronoun “us” (the people receiving the action). Example pattern: *Ele vai nos ajudar* = “He’s going to help us.”
target_language_example: Ela vai nos ajudar amanhã.
native_language_example: She’s going to help us tomorrow.

additional_notes: Formed by **ir (vai)** + **infinitive (pagar)** to express a near-future action (“is going to pay”). Common for paying money or covering a cost (a bill, fees), and also in **pagar por + [something]** meaning “to pay for” (sometimes “to pay for it / face consequences”).
target_language_example: Ele vai pagar tudo.
native_language_example: He’s going to pay for everything.

meaning: “will pass” / “is going to spend (time)” (depending on context).
additional_notes: From **ir + infinitive** (“going to” future): **vai passar** = “is going to pass / will pass.” Common uses: (1) something ends or goes away: **Vai passar.** = “It’ll pass.” (reassurance). (2) **passar** can mean “spend (time)”: **Onde você vai passar as férias?** = “Where are you going to spend your vacation?” Special pattern: **não vai passar de + noun** = “won’t be more than / won’t amount to”: **Não vai passar de um discurso.** = “It won’t be more than a speech.”
target_language_example: Calma, vai passar.
native_language_example: Calm down, it’ll pass.

meaning: “will get/take/grab” (also “will catch,” “will pick up,” or “will work/hold,” depending on context).
additional_notes:
“Vai pegar” is the near-future form (ir + infinitive) of “pegar” with “você/ele/ela” implied or stated. The exact translation depends heavily on context:
- get/take/grab something: “Ele vai pegar a maleta.” = “He’s going to grab/get the suitcase.”
- pick someone up (give them a ride): “Quem vai pegar você?” = “Who’s going to pick you up?”
- catch / start working / hold (often colloquial): “Então vai pegar.” = “Then it’ll catch / it’ll work.”
Related common set phrases you may see:
- “pegar mal” = “to look bad / be a bad look” (e.g., “vai pegar mal”).
- “pegar de volta” = “to get back / retrieve.”
target_language_example: Quem vai pegar você às oito?
native_language_example: Who’s going to pick you up at eight?

additional_notes: Future form of precisar (“to need”). Often followed by de + noun (vai precisar de ajuda = will need help; vai precisar de uma chave = will need a key) or by an infinitive (vai precisar sair cedo = will need to leave early). The subject can be stated (O Tom vai precisar...) or omitted when understood (Vai precisar de dinheiro...).
target_language_example: Você vai precisar de mais tempo para terminar.
native_language_example: You’re going to need more time to finish.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone will need something in the future. It’s the verb phrase "vai" (is going to) + "precisar" (to need) + "de" (of). The thing that’s needed comes after "de": "vai precisar de dinheiro" (will need money). You can repeat "de" before each item in a list: "de dinheiro e de alguém" (money and someone).
target_language_example: Você vai precisar de ajuda para terminar isso.
native_language_example: You’re going to need help to finish this.

additional_notes: Formed by the verb "ir" (vai = he/she/you/it goes) + "querer" (to want). It’s commonly used to talk about what someone will want in the future, and very often as advice/warning meaning “you’re going to want to…” or “you won’t want to…”. In many contexts, "vai querer" can address "você" (you) without saying it explicitly.
target_language_example: Você vai querer reservar com antecedência.
native_language_example: You’re going to want to book in advance.

additional_notes: Most literally it’s the future of "saber" (to know): "Ninguém vai saber" = "Nobody will know." As a standalone comment (often with a comma: "Vai saber, ..."), it’s a common, informal way to mean "Who knows" / "Hard to say," usually when you don’t have enough information.
target_language_example: Vai saber se ele vai aparecer hoje.
native_language_example: Who knows if he’ll show up today.

meaning: is going to leave / go out
additional_notes: Common future construction: ir (vai) + infinitive (sair) = “to be going to leave/go out.” Depending on context, sair can also mean “to come out” (e.g., a stain comes out, results come out) and in sports/racing “to start/come out” in a position: sair na frente = “to start out in front.”
target_language_example: Não se preocupe, já vai sair.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it will come out soon / it’s going to come out soon.

meaning: "you will regret it" / "(he/she) will regret it."
additional_notes: Used as a warning or threat that someone will feel sorry later for what they did (or didn’t do). Often followed by "de" + noun/verb (vai se arrepender de suas brincadeiras) or "por" + infinitive/past idea (vai se arrepender por não ter...). The subject can be implied (Você vai se arrepender) or explicit (Tom vai se arrepender disso).
target_language_example: Se você fizer isso, vai se arrepender.
native_language_example: If you do that, you’ll regret it.

additional_notes: Used with an explicit subject (ele/ela/você/nome) to talk about a planned or expected marriage in the near or known future. It’s the verb phrase "ir" (to be going to) + "se casar" (to get married). You can add a time expression like "daqui a três meses" (in three months) or "na segunda" (on Monday).
target_language_example: A minha irmã vai se casar no ano que vem.
native_language_example: My sister is going to get married next year.

meaning: “Go fuck yourself.” (very offensive insult; also used like “fuck you”).
additional_notes: Extremely vulgar Brazilian Portuguese profanity. Used to insult someone directly (“Vai se foder!”), to tell them to get lost, or to express aggressive anger. It can also be said about a situation/person in general (“Então vai se foder!” = “then fuck it/fuck them”), but it’s still very harsh. Avoid in polite conversation; using it can start fights. Variations: “Vai tomar no cu” is similar in strength; plural “vão se foder” (to a group).
target_language_example: Se você continuar me provocando, vai se foder.
native_language_example: If you keep provoking me, go fuck yourself.

meaning: “You’re going to hurt yourself / get hurt.”
additional_notes: Used as a warning that someone is likely to get injured if they keep doing something. From the reflexive verb “machucar-se” (to hurt oneself). “Vai” (from “ir”) is often used to talk about a near/imminent future (“is going to”). It can refer to “you” (implied “você”) or, with a subject, to someone else: “Tom vai se machucar.”
target_language_example: Cuidado com isso — você vai se machucar.
native_language_example: Careful with that—you’re going to hurt yourself.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the future with ir + infinitive. This exact form, vai ser, is used with singular subjects like ele, ela, você, isso, or a singular name. It can describe states or qualities (Isto vai ser bom) and also passive constructions (vai ser demitido = is going to be fired).
target_language_example: A reunião vai ser amanhã.
native_language_example: The meeting is going to be tomorrow.

meaning: "it’s going to be difficult" / "it will be hard."
additional_notes: Common way to predict that something in the future will be hard. Uses near-future: "vai ser" (it’s going to be / it will be) + "difícil" (difficult). You can also use other subjects: "Vai ser difícil convencer..." = "It’ll be hard to convince..."
target_language_example: Sem ajuda, vai ser difícil terminar hoje.
native_language_example: Without help, it’s going to be hard to finish today.

meaning: “it’s going to be / it will be” (future of “ser,” using “ir” + infinitive).
additional_notes: Used to talk about what something will be like, what will happen, or where/when something will take place. Common in questions: “O que vai ser?” can mean “What will it be?” or (at a bar/restaurant) “What will you have?”; “Onde vai ser?” = “Where will it be (held)?” Often followed by a time expression: “Vai ser hoje/amanhã.”
target_language_example: A festa vai ser na casa da Ana.
native_language_example: The party is going to be at Ana’s house.

meaning: “is going to” + “you” (object), as in “is going to [verb] you”.
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to talk about what someone/something will do to you soon: **vai te + infinitive**. Here **vai** = “is going to” (from *ir*), and **te** = “you” as an object pronoun (informal singular). Common with verbs like *fazer* (make), *levar* (take/bring), *ensinar* (teach), *custar* (cost), *deixar* (leave/make).
target_language_example: Isso vai te ajudar muito.
native_language_example: That’s going to help you a lot.

additional_notes: Formed by "vai" (3rd person singular of "ir" used as a near-future auxiliary) + the infinitive "tentar" (to try/attempt). It can refer to "he/she" (ele/ela) or the polite "you" (você) depending on context: "Você vai tentar?" (Are you going to try?) / "Ele vai tentar." (He will try.). Plural: "vão tentar".
target_language_example: Você vai tentar dormir de novo?
native_language_example: Are you going to try to sleep again?

additional_notes: Common future with the verb "ter" (to have), using "ir" in the present: "vai ter" = "is going to have" (he/she/it/you formal is going to have). With weather/feelings, Portuguese often uses "ter" where English uses "be": "não vai ter frio" = "he won’t be cold" (literally, “won’t have cold”). In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, "vai ter" is also used impersonally to mean "there will be" (similar to "vai haver"): "vai ter uma boa família" = "there will be a good family" / "you’ll have a good family" depending on context. Note: "vai ter de" means "will have to" (obligation), as in "vai ter de ajudar".
target_language_example: Amanhã vai ter reunião às 9.
native_language_example: Tomorrow there will be a meeting at 9.

meaning: 'will have to' / 'is going to have to' (must).
additional_notes: Used to say someone will be obligated/forced to do something in the future. It’s the near-future of "ter que" (to have to): "vai" (is going) + "ter que" (have to). Changes with the subject: "vou ter que" (I’ll have to), "você vai ter que", "ele/ela vai ter que", "vamos ter que", "vão ter que" (they’ll have to). Common in strong statements like "Vai ter que me matar!" meaning "You’ll have to kill me (first)!"
target_language_example: Se você quiser terminar hoje, vai ter que trabalhar mais rápido.
native_language_example: If you want to finish today, you’ll have to work faster.

additional_notes: Extremely offensive and obscene in Brazilian Portuguese. Used to tell someone off aggressively, similar to “fuck off”/“go to hell,” but more vulgar. Commonly shouted in anger; often appears with intensifiers like “porra.” Avoid in polite situations and with strangers.
target_language_example: Vai tomar no cu!
native_language_example: Go fuck yourself!

additional_notes: Literally “(he/she/it) will see” or “go see,” from the verb *ver* (to see). In context it often means (1) future: “will see” (sometimes as a warning or promise: “you’ll see!”), or (2) an instruction: “go see / go check (with someone)” as in “Vai ver com ele!” (“Go check with him!”).
target_language_example: Vai ver com a recepção se o quarto já está pronto.
native_language_example: Go check with reception to see if the room is ready yet.

additional_notes: "vai voltar" is the near-future form (ir + infinitive) meaning someone is going to return. It changes with the subject: eu vou voltar, você vai voltar, nós vamos voltar, etc. Often used with time phrases like "às cinco" (at five) or "mais cedo ou mais tarde" (sooner or later).
target_language_example: Eu acho que ele vai voltar amanhã.
native_language_example: I think he’ll come back tomorrow.

additional_notes: From the verb "ir" (to go): "vai" is the present tense for ele/ela/você. "ao" = "a" (to) + "o" (the), used with masculine singular places like "cinema". Often used with frequency words like "sempre" (always), "frequentemente" (often), "raramente" (rarely), and time expressions (e.g., "sexta-feira à noite").
target_language_example: Você vai ao cinema hoje?
native_language_example: Are you going to the movies today?

meaning: "(you/he/she) is leaving" / "(you/he/she) goes away"; also "go away!" (imperative, informal).
additional_notes: Formed from ir (“to go”) + embora (“away”), functioning as the common expression ir embora (“to leave/go away”). In "vai embora", "vai" is 3rd-person singular present (ele/ela/você) and can describe a current/future departure ("O Tom vai embora no próximo verão") or be used as an imperative meaning “Go away!” depending on context and intonation. Often refers to leaving a place or situation.
target_language_example: A que horas você vai embora?
native_language_example: What time are you leaving?

additional_notes: Literally means “go there” (ir + lá). In conversation it’s very common as: (1) a simple statement about going to a place ("Ele vai lá todos os dias."); (2) an instruction/encouragement telling someone to go/do it ("Vai lá!" = “Go on!” / “Go ahead!”), sometimes with a challenging tone ("Vai lá, você não é esperto?"). Often used informally, and it can be followed by a destination: "vai lá pra frente" (go up/front).
target_language_example: Vai lá e pergunta pra ela.
native_language_example: Go ahead and ask her.

additional_notes: "Vai" is the present tense of *ir* (to go) for "he/she/it" (and also "you" in Brazil with *você*). "Para" means "to" in the sense of destination: *vai para Boston* = goes/is going to Boston. It’s very common for travel plans and schedules (buses, flights, people). It can also be used figuratively to mean heading toward a result: *vai para a morte certa* (heading to certain death).
target_language_example: Este trem vai para o centro?
native_language_example: Does this train go to downtown?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "ir" in the present tense: "vai" = "(he/she/you formal) goes". "para" means "to/toward". "a" is the feminine singular definite article "the", so it’s used before feminine destinations (e.g., "a academia", "a escola"). With masculine destinations you often see "vai para o" ("o" = "the"). It can also be used for scheduled movement (e.g., a ship/train) or travel for a purpose ("a negócios").
target_language_example: Ela vai para a escola de ônibus.
native_language_example: She goes to school by bus.

additional_notes: "Vai" is the present tense of "ir" (to go) for ele/ela/você. Use it to ask or say how someone gets to school, often with transport: "de ônibus" (by bus), "de carro" (by car), "a pé" (on foot). You can swap the subject: "Eu vou para a escola" (I go to school), "Você vai para a escola?" (Do you go to school?).
target_language_example: Ela vai para a escola a pé todos os dias.
native_language_example: She goes to school on foot every day.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **ir** (“to go”) + **para** (“to/toward”) + **casa** (“home”). **Vai** can mean “he/she goes,” “you go” (informal *tu*), or an imperative “Go home!” Context and tone clarify which one. Often appears as **ir para casa** (to go home) or in other forms like **vou/vamos/vão para casa**.
target_language_example: Está tarde; vai para casa.
native_language_example: It’s late; go home.

additional_notes: Informal spoken Brazilian Portuguese. Used before a clause to suggest a possibility, often when explaining a precaution or plan: 'what if...', 'maybe...', sometimes 'just in case'. It is not a literal use of vai ('goes').
target_language_example: Vou sair mais cedo, vai que tem trânsito.
native_language_example: I'll leave earlier, in case there's traffic.

additional_notes: From the verb ir (to go): ele vai à escola = he goes to school; ela vai à escola = she goes to school. The "à" is a contraction of "a" (to) + "a" (the, feminine), so it literally means "to the school". Often used with frequency (cinco dias por semana) or with how someone gets there (a pé/caminhando, de ônibus, de trem).
target_language_example: Ela vai à escola a pé todos os dias.
native_language_example: She goes to school on foot every day.

additional_notes: Used to say something is worth the effort, time, cost, or risk. Very common in statements and questions: “Vale a pena ver/ir/fazer…?” (“Is it worth watching/going/doing…?”). Often followed by an infinitive verb (ver, ir, fazer) or by a clause with “ser” (vale a pena ser lembrado). Literal idea: “it’s worth the trouble/effort (pena).”
target_language_example: Não sei se vale a pena comprar agora.
native_language_example: I don’t know if it’s worth buying it now.

additional_notes: Used to say that reading something is worthwhile (worth the time/effort). It can refer to a book, article, story, etc. Often followed by what to read: “Vale a pena ler este/esse livro.” You can also add frequency: “mais de uma vez” (more than once), “duas vezes” (twice).
target_language_example: Vale a pena ler este artigo antes da prova.
native_language_example: It’s worth reading this article before the exam.

additional_notes: Used to say something is (or isn’t) worth the effort, time, cost, or trouble. Very common with an infinitive: “vale a pena + verb” (Vale a pena visitar… = It’s worth visiting…). You can also use it about bigger things: “A vida vale a pena” = Life is worth living. Negative: “não vale a pena” (it’s not worth it).
target_language_example: Não vale a pena discutir agora; vamos falar depois.
native_language_example: It’s not worth arguing now; let’s talk later.

meaning: to be worth it (worth the effort/time).
additional_notes: Used to say something is worthwhile or not worthwhile. Common patterns: “Vale a pena + infinitive” (Vale a pena tentar. = It’s worth trying.) and “Valeu a pena” (past: It was worth it). Negative: “Não vale a pena.”
target_language_example: Acho que vai valer a pena visitar esse museu.
native_language_example: I think it’s going to be worth visiting that museum.

meaning: “It was worth it.” / “It was worth the effort.”
additional_notes: Used to say that something was worth doing despite the time, cost, or effort. It’s the past (valeu) of “valer a pena” (“to be worth it”). You can use it alone as a full sentence (Valeu a pena.) or followed by an infinitive: “Valeu a pena esperar” (“It was worth waiting”). It’s also common as a question: “Valeu a pena?” (“Was it worth it?”).
target_language_example: A viagem foi longa, mas valeu a pena.
native_language_example: The trip was long, but it was worth it.

additional_notes: Literally “we go drink” (vamos + infinitive), commonly used as a suggestion/invitation: “Let’s have a drink.” Can also mean a near-future plan (“We’re going to drink…”). Often followed by what you’ll drink (cerveja, vinho) or used in toasts: “Vamos beber à/por…” = “Let’s drink to…” / “Cheers to…”.
target_language_example: Depois do trabalho, vamos beber alguma coisa?
native_language_example: After work, shall we go have a drink?

additional_notes: Often used to suggest or invite someone to eat (like English “let’s eat”). Literally it’s “we go eat,” using "vamos" (from "ir", to go) to mean “let’s …” or “we’re going to …,” depending on context and tone.
target_language_example: Estou com fome — vamos comer!
native_language_example: I'm hungry — let's eat!

additional_notes: Used to signal that you’re ready to begin an activity, meeting, class, event, etc. Often followed by what you’re starting (“vamos começar a festa” = let’s start the party), where you’re starting from (“vamos começar do início” = let’s start from the beginning), or with “por” to mean “start with” someone/something (“vamos começar por Rohan” = let’s start with Rohan).
target_language_example: Tudo pronto? Então vamos começar!
native_language_example: All set? Then let’s start!

additional_notes: Used to suggest or invite a group (including the speaker) to enter a place or get into something (e.g., a bus, a building). It can also literally mean "we are going to enter" depending on context, but very often it functions like an English "let's..." prompt.
target_language_example: Está frio aqui fora; vamos entrar.
native_language_example: It’s cold out here; let’s go inside.

additional_notes: Used to suggest pausing and waiting before doing something (like “let’s wait a moment”). It’s formed by **vamos + infinitive** (“let’s + verb”), and it often sounds like a group decision or suggestion. Commonly followed by **por + someone/something**: *vamos esperar por você* (“we’ll wait for you”).
target_language_example: Vamos esperar um pouco antes de sair.
native_language_example: Let's wait a bit before leaving.

additional_notes: From **vamos** (we go/let’s) + **fazer** (to do/to make). In conversation it often works like an invitation or decision: **Vamos fazer isso?** = “Shall we do it?” It can also state a plan/future: **Nós vamos fazer** = “We’re going to do.” You may also see it with **o que**: **O que vamos fazer?** = “What are we going to do?”
target_language_example: Vamos fazer isso hoje à noite.
native_language_example: Let’s do it tonight.

meaning: “let’s do this” / “we’re going to do this.”
additional_notes: Literally “we go/let’s” (vamos) + “to do” (fazer) + “this” (isso). It can be a suggestion/encouragement (“Let’s do this!”) or a statement about a plan (“We’re going to do this.”). Often followed by words like “juntos” (together) or used as a question: “Vamos fazer isso?” = “Shall we do this?”
target_language_example: Ok, vamos fazer isso agora.
native_language_example: Ok, let’s do this now.

additional_notes: Used to propose doing something together. It’s typically followed by a noun: “Vamos fazer um brinde” (a toast), “Vamos fazer um selfie” (a selfie), “Vamos fazer um time” (a team). In everyday speech, it can sound like “vamo fazer um…”.
target_language_example: Vamos fazer um café e conversar?
native_language_example: Let’s have a coffee and talk?

meaning: "let’s stay" / "we’re going to stay"; also "let’s/we’re going to become" (a state).
additional_notes: Comes from "vamos" (let’s/we’re going to) + "ficar" (to stay/remain/become). Use it to suggest staying somewhere or continuing in a condition: "Vamos ficar aqui" (Let’s stay here). With an adjective it often means "become": "Vamos ficar felizes" (We’ll be happy). With a gerund it can mean "keep (doing)": "Vamos ficar esperando" (Let’s keep waiting).
target_language_example: Vamos ficar em casa hoje.
native_language_example: Let’s stay home today.

additional_notes: From **vamos** (“let’s / we go”) + **jogar** (“to play”). Often used to suggest starting a game or sport (**Vamos jogar!** = “Let’s play!”). Depending on context, it can also mean a plan for the near future (**Vamos jogar tênis amanhã.** = “We’re going to play tennis tomorrow.”). Typically followed by the game/sport: **vamos jogar futebol / Scrabble / uma partida de tênis**.
target_language_example: Vamos jogar futebol depois da aula.
native_language_example: Let’s play soccer after class.

additional_notes: Used before a reflexive verb to mean “let’s …” (inclusive ‘we’). The verb is usually in the infinitive after it: “vamos nos mudar” (let’s move), “vamos nos sentar” (let’s sit down), “vamos nos vestir” (let’s get dressed). Here, “nos” is the object/reflexive pronoun (“us/ourselves”), so it commonly appears with verbs like mudar-se, sentar-se, vestir-se, etc.
target_language_example: Vamos nos preparar e sair cedo.
native_language_example: Let’s get ready and leave early.

additional_notes: Used to suggest doing something together: vamos (let’s) + pegar (get/grab/take/catch). The exact meaning depends on what comes after it: pegar o ônibus = take the bus; pegar os remos = grab the oars; pegar o peixe = catch the fish. By itself ("Vamos pegar!"), it can mean “Let’s go get it!” or “Let’s do it!” depending on context.
target_language_example: Vamos pegar o próximo ônibus.
native_language_example: Let’s take the next bus.

additional_notes: Used to suggest an attempt as a group (“let’s”) or to state intention (“we’ll try”). Often followed by an infinitive ("vamos tentar fazer...") or by “de novo/novamente” (“again”). It can be a question (“Vamos tentar?”) to propose trying something.
target_language_example: Está difícil, mas vamos tentar mais uma vez.
native_language_example: It’s hard, but let’s try one more time.

meaning: "we’re going to have to" / "we’ll have to" (expresses necessity).
additional_notes: Used to say that something is necessary or unavoidable, usually in the near future. It’s the verb phrase "ter que" (to have to) with "vamos" (we’re going to). You can change the subject: "vou ter que" (I’ll have to), "vai ter que" (he/she/you will have to), "vamos ter que" (we’ll have to), etc.
target_language_example: Se chover, vamos ter que cancelar o passeio.
native_language_example: If it rains, we’ll have to cancel the outing.

additional_notes: Used (1) to suggest going to look at something or check something together (“Let’s see the photos/material/eclipses”), and (2) to express uncertainty or to wait and find out (“We’ll see, OK?”). In challenges/threats it can sound like “Let’s see (how you’re going to…)”.
target_language_example: Vamos ver se dá tempo de chegar antes das oito.
native_language_example: Let’s see if we have time to get there before eight.

additional_notes: Used to introduce checking or finding out information (often right now or next). It’s commonly followed by a verb ("vamos ver o que ele faz") or by "vai dar" to mean "let’s see how it goes" ("vamos ver o que dá").
target_language_example: Vamos ver o que acontece se a gente sair mais cedo.
native_language_example: Let’s see what happens if we leave earlier.

additional_notes: Used to check, test, or find out what happens next (often expressing uncertainty). Common before a clause with a verb: “Vamos ver se entendi” (“Let’s see if I understood”), “Vamos ver se é verdade” (“Let’s see if it’s true”).
target_language_example: Vamos ver se ele chega a tempo.
native_language_example: Let’s see if he arrives on time.

additional_notes: A repeated, urging use of "vamos" to push someone to move faster or get going. Often said when you’re impatient or encouraging someone (like "come on, come on!"). Can also be used as a general prompt to start doing something.
target_language_example: Vamos, vamos — estamos atrasados!
native_language_example: Come on, come on — we’re late!

meaning: “let’s go to the movies” / “we go to the movie theater.”
additional_notes: "Vamos" can mean either (1) an invitation/suggestion: “Let’s go…”, often with an exclamation (Vamos ao cinema!), or (2) present tense “we go” when talking about a habit (Nós/Meu amigo e eu vamos ao cinema...). "Ao" = "a" + "o" (“to the”), and "cinema" here means the movie theater.
target_language_example: Vamos ao cinema hoje à noite?
native_language_example: Shall we go to the movies tonight?

additional_notes: Used to suggest leaving or moving on. It can be an exclamation (“Vamos embora!” = “Let’s get out of here!”), a prompt (“Pronto, vamos embora.” = “Alright, let’s go.”), or a question (“Vamos embora?” = “Shall we go?”). Literally it’s “we go away,” but in everyday Portuguese it functions like an English “let’s…”.
target_language_example: Está tarde — vamos embora!
native_language_example: It’s late — let’s go!

additional_notes: A very common expression used to encourage, urge, or push someone to act. Depending on context, it can mean "come on" or "let's go / let's do it."
target_language_example: Vamos lá, você consegue.
native_language_example: Come on, you can do it.

additional_notes: Form of ir (to go) in the present tense. With a subject like “nós”, it means “we go/are going home” (Nós vamos para casa.). Without a subject, it’s often used as an invitation or suggestion: “Let’s go home!” (Vamos para casa!).
target_language_example: Está ficando tarde; vamos para casa.
native_language_example: It’s getting late; let’s go home.

additional_notes: “Veio” is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of *vir* (“to come”) for ele/ela/você. It often appears in questions (*Você veio aqui?*) or with time words like *hoje*, *cedo*, *de novo*, *nunca*. You can change the place word: *veio aí* (“came there/over to you”), *veio lá* (“came there/over there”).
target_language_example: Você veio aqui ontem à noite?
native_language_example: Did you come here last night?

additional_notes: From the verb **vir** (to come) in the past: **veio** = “came” (3rd person singular). **me ver** means “to see me,” and in everyday Portuguese it often implies “to visit me.” You can swap the pronoun: **veio te ver** (came to see you), **veio nos ver** (came to see us). Common with time expressions: **um dia desses** (one of these days / recently), **só no dia seguinte** (only the next day).
target_language_example: Ele veio me ver depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: He came to see me after work.

additional_notes: Used to say someone came/traveled to a (masculine) place or destination in the past. *Veio* is the 3rd-person singular simple past (pretérito perfeito) of *vir* (“to come”): “he/she/you (formal) came”. *Para o* = “to the” before a masculine singular noun (e.g., *para o Brasil*). For feminine places, use *veio para a* (e.g., *veio para a França*). Often followed by time expressions (*há três anos*, *quando criança*) or purpose (*para estudar*).
target_language_example: Ele veio para o Brasil no ano passado para trabalhar.
native_language_example: He came to Brazil last year to work.

additional_notes: Used to talk about friends you’ve known for a long time (not necessarily elderly). Often appears with the verb “ser” (to be) or in comparisons like “como velhos amigos” (like old friends).
target_language_example: Depois de tantos anos, nós ainda somos velhos amigos.
native_language_example: After so many years, we’re still old friends.

additional_notes: From the verb vir (“to come”) + aqui (“here”). In statements/questions, vem is the 3rd-person singular present (“ele/ela vem aqui…”). In requests/commands, vem aqui is an informal imperative meaning “come here” (often said to someone you’re on tu terms with; with você, you’ll often hear “vem aqui” as well in everyday Brazilian Portuguese, or more formally “venha aqui”).
target_language_example: Vem aqui um minutinho, preciso falar com você.
native_language_example: Come here for a sec, I need to talk to you.

additional_notes: Imperative of "vir" (to come) + "cá" (here). Commonly used to call someone over; often said with a person’s name and an exclamation. It can also introduce something you’re about to say, like “come here / listen” (e.g., "Vem cá, preciso falar com você.").
target_language_example: Vem cá, por favor, eu preciso te mostrar uma coisa.
native_language_example: Come here, please, I need to show you something.

additional_notes: Used when someone puts their house/property up for sale or decides to sell it. Often appears with future or intention verbs like "vai" (is going to), "quer" (wants to), "decidiu" (decided to), "está pensando em" (is thinking about), or "tentou" (tried). You can also specify ownership: "vender a casa dele/dela" (sell his/her house).
target_language_example: Eles vão vender a casa no próximo mês.
native_language_example: They’re going to sell the house next month.

meaning: to sell it (referring to a feminine thing).
additional_notes: This is the infinitive verb “vender” (to sell) + the direct-object pronoun “a” (her/it, feminine), attached with a hyphen. The accent (ê) is added for pronunciation when “-la” is attached. It’s used when “it” refers to a feminine noun (e.g., a casa, a ideia). You’ll often see this after modal verbs or expressions like “devo/tenho de/quero/poderia” + infinitive.
target_language_example: Eu não quero vendê-la ainda.
native_language_example: I don't want to sell it yet.

additional_notes: Means “come here.” It’s often used as a direct command. Grammatically, it’s the formal imperative (você) of vir (“to come”), and it also appears after requests with que (e.g., “peço que venha aqui” = “I ask you to come here”). Informal equivalent: “vem aqui” (tu) or “venham aqui” (plural).
target_language_example: Venha aqui, por favor.
native_language_example: Come here, please.

additional_notes: An imperative (command/request) meaning “come along with me.” Often used with time words (agora) or destinations (para Boston). Can also be used to invite someone to accompany you for a purpose (para que possamos...).
target_language_example: Venha comigo até a estação, por favor.
native_language_example: Come with me to the station, please.

additional_notes: Used to call someone (or a pet) to come closer to you. It’s the formal/neutral command form (imperative) of "vir" (to come), often used with a name or a form of address (e.g., "Sofia", "garoto"). Depending on tone, it can sound friendly (calling a child/pet) or a bit firm (calling someone over to talk).
target_language_example: Venha cá um momento, por favor.
native_language_example: Come here for a moment, please.

additional_notes: An invitation/request using the formal command form of "vir" ("venha"), commonly used with "você" (or as a polite imperative). "Me" = "me" (to me), "ver" = "see". Often followed by a time or place (e.g., "amanhã", "na minha sala"). With "tu", you’d usually say "vem me ver".
target_language_example: Se precisar de ajuda, venha me ver depois da aula.
native_language_example: If you need help, come see me after class.

meaning: 'to see the' (with a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: "Ver" means "to see." "A" is the feminine singular definite article (“the”), used before many feminine nouns and female people’s names/titles (e.g., "ver a sua mãe" = “to see your mother,” "ao ver a Mary" = “upon seeing Mary”). It’s simply verb + article, so it changes with gender/number: "ver o" (masc.), "ver as" (fem. plural), "ver os" (masc. plural).
target_language_example: Espero ver a professora amanhã.
native_language_example: I hope to see the teacher tomorrow.

meaning: to see stars (to feel dizzy, stunned, or dazed, often after a hit or bump).
additional_notes: Used both literally (seeing stars in the sky) and idiomatically for the sensation of dizziness or being stunned, especially after hitting your head or getting hit. In the idiomatic sense it commonly appears after impacts: “Bati a cabeça e comecei a ver estrelas.”
target_language_example: Bati a cabeça na porta e comecei a ver estrelas por um segundo.
native_language_example: I hit my head on the door and started to see stars for a second.

additional_notes: Compositional phrase: ver means "to see," and o is the masculine singular word for "the." It is used before masculine nouns (ver o menu = "see the menu"). In some varieties of Portuguese, o can also appear before a man's name, so ver o Tom can mean "see Tom." In patterns like ver o Tom fazer isso, it means "see Tom do that."
target_language_example: Quero ver o filme amanhã.
native_language_example: I want to see the movie tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say you will check/try to find out something: "Vou ver se..." (I’ll see if...). It’s also common when confirming understanding: "deixa eu ver se entendi" (let me see if I understood). Often followed by a clause starting with a verb (e.g., "ver se ele tem tempo").
target_language_example: Deixa eu ver se consigo te ajudar amanhã.
native_language_example: Let me see if I can help you tomorrow.

meaning: "just look" / "you'll see" (used to call attention or introduce something).
additional_notes: Common in spoken Portuguese to draw someone’s attention or emphasize what you’re about to show/say (similar to “look” or “just wait and see”). Often appears as an infinitive phrase ("ver só") especially in informal prompts or captions; in Portugal you may also hear the conjugated imperative "vê só".
target_language_example: Espera um pouco e vais ver só como ficou bonito depois da reforma.
native_language_example: Wait a bit and you’ll see just how nice it turned out after the renovation.

additional_notes: Used with "ver" (to see/watch) + "um filme" (a movie). Very common with "ir" to mean going to watch a movie: "ir ver um filme" = "to go watch a movie" (often at the cinema, but it can also be at home depending on context). You can also drop "ir" when you simply mean watching: "Quer ver um filme?" = "Do you want to watch a movie?"
target_language_example: Vamos ver um filme em casa hoje?
native_language_example: Shall we watch a movie at home today?

additional_notes: Used to introduce an honest or important clarification, often contrasting with what was expected. Commonly followed by a full sentence: “A verdade é que…” or without the article: “Verdade é que…”.
target_language_example: A verdade é que eu não tenho tempo hoje.
native_language_example: The truth is I don’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that a love is real and authentic (often in romantic, poetic, or fairy-tale contexts). You can also say "o meu verdadeiro amor" (my true love) or "o verdadeiro amor" (true love).
target_language_example: Ele acredita que ela é o seu verdadeiro amor.
native_language_example: He believes she is his true love.

additional_notes: A simple noun phrase: vestido (dress) + azul (blue). Used to describe or identify a specific dress by its color. In Portuguese, color adjectives usually come after the noun (vestido azul). With a specific dress, you’ll often see an article or demonstrative: o/um/este vestido azul.
target_language_example: Você viu o vestido azul na vitrine?
native_language_example: Did you see the blue dress in the shop window?

meaning: to be fully committed (to a team, company, or cause).
additional_notes: Common idiom in sports and at work, implying loyalty and involvement beyond the minimum—"to give it your all" for that group. Often used with a specific group: "vestir a camisa do time" / "vestir a camisa da empresa". Literally it means "to wear the shirt," but the usual meaning is figurative.
target_language_example: Ela vai vestir a camisa da empresa e sempre ajudar quando alguém precisa.
native_language_example: She’s going to be fully committed to the company and always help when someone needs it.

meaning: “times a day” (how many times something happens each day).
additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency, especially with a number: "uma vez ao dia" (once a day), "duas vezes ao dia" (twice a day), "três vezes ao dia" (three times a day). Common in routines and instructions (e.g., medicine directions).
target_language_example: Tome este remédio duas vezes ao dia.
native_language_example: Take this medicine twice a day.

additional_notes: Past tense of **ver** (“to see”) + the direct-object pronoun **o** (“him/it”), attached with a hyphen (enclisis). Common in European Portuguese and in formal/written Brazilian Portuguese. In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, people often say **“vi ele”** for “I saw him.” Used with another verb to mean you saw someone **doing** something: **Vi-o atravessando** (“I saw him crossing”) or **Vi-o atravessar** (“I saw him cross”).
target_language_example: Vi-o na estação ontem.
native_language_example: I saw him at the station yesterday.

additional_notes: "Vi" is the simple past (preterite) of **ver** (to see) for **eu**: *eu vi* = *I saw*. It’s often followed by **o** (= *the*, masculine singular) before a noun: *vi o Tom*, *vi o carro*. You can also use it before infinitive/gerund-like structures to describe what you saw happening: *Vi o Tom chegando* (I saw Tom arriving).
target_language_example: Ontem vi o professor no mercado.
native_language_example: Yesterday I saw the teacher at the market.

additional_notes: Used to talk about traveling to the past or the future (often in science fiction). Usually appears with the verb “fazer” (to do/make) or “ser” (to be): “A viagem no tempo é…” = “Time travel is…”.
target_language_example: Se a viagem no tempo existisse, eu voltaria para 2010.
native_language_example: If time travel existed, I would go back to 2010.

meaning: viceroy; a ruler/governor representing a king.
additional_notes: A formal title. Refers to an official appointed to govern a territory or lead in the name of a monarch (or emperor). Used as a form of address before a name ("Vice-rei Zhou") or on its own ("Vice-rei!"). Plural: "vice-reis".
target_language_example: O vice-rei chegou ao palácio para falar com os oficiais.
native_language_example: The viceroy arrived at the palace to speak with the officials.

meaning: social life (your social activities and relationships).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like "ter" (to have) and adjectives like "ativa", "agitada", "boa", "pouca" to talk about how much you go out, meet people, and socialize. You can also use it more broadly for the social side of life (e.g., "para a vida social" = "for social life").
target_language_example: Desde que comecei a trabalhar de noite, tenho pouca vida social.
native_language_example: Since I started working nights, I have little social life.

additional_notes: In Brazilian Portuguese you’ll often see both spellings: "video game" (two words) and "videogame" (one word). It commonly appears with the verb "jogar" (to play): "jogar video game". You can also use "jogo" for a specific game (e.g., "um jogo de videogame").
target_language_example: Eu gosto de jogar video game com meus amigos.
native_language_example: I like to play video games with my friends.

additional_notes: Past tense (pretérito perfeito) of **vir** (to come): **eu vim** = "I came." **aqui** = "here." Often followed by **pra/para + infinitive** to say the purpose: **Vim aqui pra falar com você** (I came here to talk to you).
target_language_example: Vim aqui pra te ajudar.
native_language_example: I came here to help you.

additional_notes: Used to refer to wine made from light-colored grapes (or with minimal skin contact). Often contrasted with "vinho tinto" (red wine). You may also see "vinho branco seco" = "dry white wine".
target_language_example: Para o jantar, vou comprar vinho branco.
native_language_example: For dinner, I’m going to buy white wine.

additional_notes: Used to talk about or order red wine (as opposed to vinho branco, “white wine”). Common with preferences (prefiro…) and when ordering: “Um copo de vinho tinto, por favor.”
target_language_example: Você tem vinho tinto da casa?
native_language_example: Do you have house red wine?

meaning: “twenty years” (age or a period of time).
additional_notes: Used to state someone’s age (often with “ter”: “Ela tem vinte anos (de idade)”) or to describe a duration (“por vinte anos” = “for twenty years”). In comparisons, it can mean “in twenty years” / “in the last twenty years” depending on context (e.g., “o mais frio em vinte anos”).
target_language_example: Faz vinte anos que eu moro aqui.
native_language_example: I’ve lived here for twenty years.

additional_notes: Used as a number on its own (e.g., answering a question, reading out a number) and very commonly in dates: "vinte e dois de fevereiro" = "February 22". In Portuguese, dates are often said as "[day number] de [month]"; you may also see "dia vinte e dois" (“the 22nd day”).
target_language_example: A reunião é no dia vinte e dois de março.
native_language_example: The meeting is on March 22.

additional_notes: Used to say the number 26. Common in dates (day of the month) like “vinte e seis de outubro” and when counting items (e.g., states, people, years). In Portuguese, numbers from 21 to 99 typically use “e” (“and”) between tens and units: “vinte e seis” = 20 + 6.
target_language_example: Tenho vinte e seis anos.
native_language_example: I am twenty-six years old.

additional_notes: Used to say the number 27 in dates ("dia vinte e sete"), in math, and when answering with just the number. Spelled with "e" (“and”) between tens and units: "vinte e sete".
target_language_example: Tenho vinte e sete anos.
native_language_example: I’m twenty-seven years old.

additional_notes: Used as a number: for dates ("vinte e três de outubro" = October 23rd), to answer "which number?"/"what time/price/etc.?" depending on context, or as a countdown/starting cue ("Vinte e três, vamos!" = "Twenty-three, let’s go!"). In dates, Portuguese often says the day number + "de" + month.
target_language_example: Meu número da sorte é vinte e três.
native_language_example: My lucky number is twenty-three.

additional_notes: Used to count, give ages/amounts (e.g., "vinte e um anos"), say dates ("vinte e um de outubro" = October 21st), and in larger numbers like "cento e vinte e um" (121). It can also refer to "vinte e um" as a game (similar to blackjack/21). In some contexts it can be an exclamation meaning "Twenty-one!" (e.g., calling out a number).
target_language_example: Tenho vinte e um anos.
native_language_example: I’m twenty-one years old.

additional_notes: Used for coming to the place where the speaker is, or the place being referred to as 'here'. It's literal: vir = 'to come' and aqui = 'here'. Compare with ir, which means 'to go'.
target_language_example: Você pode vir aqui um minuto?
native_language_example: Can you come here for a minute?

additional_notes: Used when the speaker is referring to their current location (or another specific place understood from context). "Até" adds the idea of coming all the way to here (sometimes implying effort/distance). Often appears with questions about time or reasons: "O que o impediu de vir até aqui?" / "Quanto tempo leva para vir até aqui?".
target_language_example: Você pode vir até aqui amanhã de manhã?
native_language_example: Can you come here tomorrow morning?

additional_notes: Used to invite or ask someone to accompany you somewhere. With a destination, it’s often followed by "a" + the place/event (e.g., "vir comigo ao show"). Common in questions: "Quer vir comigo?" / "Você vai vir comigo?"
target_language_example: Você quer vir comigo ao cinema hoje?
native_language_example: Do you want to come with me to the movies today?

additional_notes: Used to invite or ask if someone will join your group and come along. "Vir" is "to come" (toward the speaker), and "conosco" means "with us". Often used as a question ("Você vai vir conosco?") or as a suggestion/invitation ("Você pode vir conosco.").
target_language_example: Se você quiser, pode vir conosco até o centro.
native_language_example: If you want, you can come with us to downtown.

meaning: "to come to my house" / "to come over to my place."
additional_notes: Used to invite someone to your home or ask when they can come. It’s built from vir (to come) + a/à (to) + minha casa (my house). Often appears in questions with different forms of address (você, tu, o senhor/a senhora, os senhores) depending on formality and number.
target_language_example: Você pode vir à minha casa amanhã à tarde?
native_language_example: Can you come to my house tomorrow afternoon?

meaning: a mixed-breed dog; a mutt/stray (also used as an insult).
additional_notes: Most commonly refers to a mixed-breed dog (often a street dog). In insults, it can be like calling someone a “mangy mutt/mongrel” (very rude), especially when combined with profanity (e.g., “de merda”). Spelling often appears with a hyphen: “vira-lata”.
target_language_example: A gente adotou um cachorro vira-lata do abrigo.
native_language_example: We adopted a mixed-breed dog (a mutt) from the shelter.

additional_notes: Imperative form of "virar-se" (usually addressing "você"). Used as a command to change your body direction: "vire-se de costas" (turn your back), "vire-se para cá" (turn this way). In other contexts, "vire-se" can also mean "manage by yourself / figure it out," but in these examples it’s physical turning.
target_language_example: Vire-se para a direita, por favor.
native_language_example: Turn to the right, please.

additional_notes: Common direction instruction. "Vire" is the formal command form (used with você) of the verb virar (to turn), and it can be used by GPS, signs, or when giving someone directions. Often followed by a place like "na próxima esquina" (at the next corner).
target_language_example: Siga em frente e vire à direita no semáforo.
native_language_example: Go straight ahead and turn right at the traffic light.

meaning: to visit (a place) / to go and see (someone).
additional_notes: "Visitar" means "to visit." It often appears with "a" before a feminine noun ("visitar a mãe", "visitar a Austrália", "visitar a Dinamarca"). With a masculine noun it’s "visitar o" (e.g., "visitar o Brasil"). You can use it for visiting people (often at a specific location like a hospital or prison) or visiting places (countries, cities, etc.).
target_language_example: Quero visitar a minha avó amanhã.
native_language_example: I want to visit my grandma tomorrow.

meaning: to visit her (or: to visit it, referring to a feminine noun).
additional_notes: This is the verb "visitar" (to visit) + the object pronoun "-la" (her/it). The accent in "visitá-" shows the stress when the pronoun is attached. Common after infinitives (e.g., "vou", "quero", "gostaria de", "posso" + infinitive): "Vou visitá-la" = "I'm going to visit her."
target_language_example: Quero visitá-la amanhã.
native_language_example: I want to visit her tomorrow.

meaning: to visit him (to go see him).
additional_notes: "Visitá-lo" = "visitar" (to visit) + "-lo" (him). It’s used when the verb is in the infinitive or ends in -r/-s/-z; the final consonant drops and an accent is added: visitar + o → visitá-lo. Also possible: "visitar ele" (common in speech, often considered less formal).
target_language_example: Vou visitá-lo no hospital hoje à tarde.
native_language_example: I'm going to visit him at the hospital this afternoon.

additional_notes: Used when talking about nutrition and health, especially in foods and drinks (e.g., oranges, tangerines, orange juice). Common with phrases like "fonte de" (source of), "rica em" (rich in), and "conter" (to contain). Often written with a capital letter: "vitamina C".
target_language_example: O kiwi também é rico em vitamina C.
native_language_example: Kiwi is also rich in vitamin C.

additional_notes: Used when talking about the nutrient vitamin D, often connected to sunlight as a natural source ("luz do sol" / "o sol") or to needing more of it.
target_language_example: No inverno, muita gente toma suplementos de vitamina D.
native_language_example: In winter, many people take vitamin D supplements.

meaning: "Did you see (that)?" / "See?" (used to call attention or show surprise/confirmation).
additional_notes:
Common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese. Often rhetorical: 
- "Viu só?" = "See?" / "Did you see that?" (seeking agreement or emphasizing a point).
- "Viu só que + adjective?" = "Did you see how + adjective?" (e.g., que bonito/bonita = how beautiful).
You can also use it as an exclamation: "Viu só!" = "Well, would you look at that!"
target_language_example: Viu só? Eu te disse que ia dar certo.
native_language_example: See? I told you it would work out.

additional_notes: Past tense of ver (“to see”): viu = “saw” (also the formal ‘you’/você form). Used literally for seeing a ghost, and can also be used humorously to suggest someone looks shocked, pale, or frightened (“as if they saw a ghost”). You can change the subject: Eu vi um fantasma (I saw a ghost), Você viu um fantasma? (Did you see a ghost?).
target_language_example: Ele ficou pálido, parecia que viu um fantasma.
native_language_example: He turned pale; it looked like he’d seen a ghost.

meaning: 'lives in' / 'lives at' (is based in a place).
additional_notes: From the verb **viver** (to live): **(ele/ela/você) vive** + **em** + place. Used to say where someone lives/resides. For longer-term residence, it can be similar to **mora em** (“lives in”), and **vive em** can sometimes emphasize someone’s way of life or general living situation depending on context.
target_language_example: Ela vive em Lisboa há três anos.
native_language_example: She has lived in Lisbon for three years.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "viver" (to live) in the 3rd person plural present tense: "eles/elas vivem" = "they live". "na" is the contraction of "em" (in) + "a" (the, feminine), so it’s used before feminine places ("na Alemanha", "na China") and some fixed expressions ("na mesma casa/rua"). For masculine places, you usually use "no" ("vivem no Brasil").
target_language_example: Meus avós vivem na cidade.
native_language_example: My grandparents live in the city.

additional_notes: Used to talk about living/residing in a place (city, country, neighborhood, etc.). It’s followed by a location: "viver em Paris", "viver em Boston". Often interchangeable with "morar em" in everyday Brazilian Portuguese.
target_language_example: Eu quero viver em Portugal no futuro.
native_language_example: I want to live in Portugal in the future.

additional_notes: Used to say you manage (or imagine you can’t manage) life without someone/something. It’s often followed by a noun (viver sem ela, viver sem sexo) or an infinitive can appear with context (e.g., viver sem reclamar = live without complaining).
target_language_example: Eu não consigo viver sem café.
native_language_example: I can’t live without coffee.

additional_notes: "Você" means "you". "A" is an object pronoun meaning "her" or "it" (referring to a feminine noun). It’s used when the direct object is already known from context: "Você a esconde" = "You hide it/her." In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, many speakers often replace "a" with "ela" ("Você esconde ela"), but in more formal writing you’ll see "a" like in the examples.
target_language_example: Você a viu ontem?
native_language_example: Did you see her/it yesterday?

additional_notes: Used to say that you are acquainted with a woman or know who she is. The "a" is a feminine direct-object pronoun meaning "her" (referring to a female person previously mentioned). In Brazilian Portuguese it’s common to place this pronoun before the verb ("você a conhece"); you may also see "você conhece ela" in informal speech.
target_language_example: Você a conhece desde a faculdade?
native_language_example: Do you know her since college?

meaning: “you just (did something)” / “you’ve just (done something)” (very recent past).
additional_notes: Used to say something happened moments ago. Structure: “você acabou de” + infinitive (chegar, comer, fazer, chamar, se levantar, se preparar, ser baleado). Often used in surprised or accusatory questions: “Você acabou de…?” In speech, it can shorten to “cê acabou de…”.
target_language_example: Você acabou de desligar o telefone?
native_language_example: Did you just hang up the phone?

additional_notes: A common way to ask for someone's opinion or guess, usually followed by a full clause. Literally it is like "you think that," but in questions English usually says "do you think."
target_language_example: Você acha que vai chover hoje?
native_language_example: Do you think it's going to rain today?

meaning: "do you think she…?" / "do you believe she…?"
additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion or guess about what a woman is doing, feels, wants, or will do. It’s built from: você (you) + achar (to think/feel/consider) + que (that) + ela (she). In questions, it often introduces another clause: “Você acha que ela vai…?”, “Você acha que ela gosta…?”
target_language_example: Você acha que ela vai ligar hoje?
native_language_example: Do you think she’s going to call today?

meaning: “do you think that this…?” / “you think that this…”
additional_notes: Used to introduce what someone thinks or believes about a situation, often followed by a verb phrase: “você acha que isso vai…?”, “você acha que isso é…?”. In questions, it usually means “Do you think this…?”. In statements (with “eu sei que…” etc.), it means “you think that this…”.
target_language_example: Você acha que isso é uma boa ideia?
native_language_example: Do you think this is a good idea?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion or guess. Literally “you think that the…”. The final word **o** is the masculine singular article (“the”) and changes depending on what follows: **a** (feminine), **os/as** (plural). Often followed by a name or noun: *Você acha que o Tom…?* = “Do you think Tom…?”
target_language_example: Você acha que o ônibus vai demorar?
native_language_example: Do you think the bus will take long?

additional_notes: Used to ask about someone's belief or trust in something. With ideas, religions, and supernatural things it means believing they exist (Deus, destino, milagres). With people, it often means trusting or having confidence in them: "Você acredita em nós?" = "Do you believe in us?" (Do you trust we can do it?).
target_language_example: Você acredita em vida após a morte?
native_language_example: Do you believe in life after death?

additional_notes: A common combination of você ('you', singular) + ainda ('still/yet'). It often starts a question about whether a situation continues to be true. In English, the full translation usually depends on the verb that follows, such as 'do you still...?' or 'are you still...?'.
target_language_example: Você ainda mora em Lisboa?
native_language_example: Do you still live in Lisbon?

meaning: “are you still …?” / “you’re still …” (asking if a state/condition continues).
additional_notes: Used with a verb/adjective or expression to check whether something is continuing. Common with emotions or states: "assustado" (scared), "brava" (mad), "tonto" (dizzy), "por perto" (around), "tendo problemas" (having trouble). "Você" is the informal/common "you" in Brazil (often used in most situations), and "ainda" means "still/yet".
target_language_example: Você ainda está cansado depois da viagem?
native_language_example: Are you still tired after the trip?

additional_notes: Used to ask or say that someone continues to live in the same place as before. Often followed by “em/na/no” (in/at) + a place (Você ainda mora nos Estados Unidos?), “com” (with) + people you live with (Você ainda mora com os seus pais?), or “por aqui” (around here/in this area).
target_language_example: Você ainda mora neste bairro ou já se mudou?
native_language_example: Do you still live in this neighborhood, or have you moved?

additional_notes: "Você" means "you" (common in Brazil). "Comprou" is the past tense of "comprar" (to buy). This phrase can be used as a statement ("you bought...") or a question ("did you buy...?") depending on intonation and punctuation.
target_language_example: Você comprou o ingresso online?
native_language_example: Did you buy the ticket online?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone is familiar with a person, place, or thing (including “a way/method” to do something). It comes from the verb “conhecer” (to know/be acquainted with). Often contrasts with “você sabe”, which is more about knowing a fact or knowing how to do something.
target_language_example: Você conhece um bom restaurante por aqui?
native_language_example: Do you know a good restaurant around here?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone knows a person with a certain skill, job, or connection (often when looking for a recommendation). After "alguém que", Portuguese often uses the subjunctive when the person is unknown or hypothetical (e.g., "Conhece alguém que fale japonês?"); the indicative can also appear when the person is known/specific in context.
target_language_example: Você conhece alguém que possa me ajudar com isso?
native_language_example: Do you know anyone who can help me with this?

meaning: “do you know/are you familiar with (the) …?” (to know a person or to be familiar with something).
additional_notes: Used to ask or state whether someone knows a male person (“o Tom”, “o padre…”) or is familiar with a masculine thing/place/site (“o site…”). For feminine nouns, use “você conhece a…”. For plural, “você conhece os/as…”. Often implies personal acquaintance with people and general familiarity with things.
target_language_example: Você conhece o restaurante aqui perto?
native_language_example: Do you know the restaurant nearby?

additional_notes: From conseguir. It is used to talk about being able to do something or managing to do it. In questions like "Você consegue...?", it often means "Can you...?".
target_language_example: Você consegue abrir a porta?
native_language_example: Can you open the door?

meaning: “can you see…?” / “are you able to see…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone is able to see something (often because it’s small, far away, or unclear). Very common in questions: “Você consegue ver…?” In everyday speech, “Você pode ver…?” is also common and often interchangeable; “conseguir” can imply a bit of difficulty (“manage to”).
target_language_example: Você consegue ver o nome na placa?
native_language_example: Can you see the name on the sign?

additional_notes: From the verb **conseguir** (to get/obtain; to manage to do). **Você conseguiu?** can mean either “Did you get it?” (obtain something) or “Did you manage to do it?” (succeed). Used for congratulations or encouragement: **Você conseguiu!** = “You did it!”
target_language_example: Você conseguiu terminar o trabalho a tempo?
native_language_example: Did you manage to finish the work on time?
