target_language_example: Você é a responsável por isso.
native_language_example: You are the one responsible for this.

meaning: “You are very … / You’re too …” (before an adjective).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective to comment on someone’s qualities or behavior: Você é muito + adjective (pequeno, apertado, mentiroso, rígido, etc.). Often sounds critical depending on the adjective and tone. For “very” with nouns, Portuguese usually uses “você é muito + noun” (e.g., “Você é muito paciente.”).
target_language_example: Você é muito impaciente comigo.
native_language_example: You’re very impatient with me.

additional_notes: Used to identify someone: “you are the …” or, as a question, “are you the …?”. The article agrees with the person/thing: você é o (masc. singular), você é a (fem. singular), você é os/as (plural). In questions, Portuguese often relies on intonation (no word order change): “Você é o João?” = “Are you João?”
target_language_example: Você é o novo gerente?
native_language_example: Are you the new manager?

meaning: “you are so …” (used to intensify an adjective).
additional_notes: Used before an adjective to emphasize a quality: Você é tão gentil. Often shows strong emotion and is common with exclamations (e.g., Que chato! Você é tão irritante!). In comparisons it can appear as “tão … quanto” (“as … as”): Você é tão alto quanto ele. Note: “você” is common in Brazil; in Portugal you may hear “tu és tão …”.
target_language_example: Você é tão engraçado!
native_language_example: You’re so funny!

additional_notes: Used before a singular masculine noun to identify or describe someone or something. In a question, the same words can mean "are you a ...?" depending on intonation or a question mark. For feminine nouns, use "você é uma" instead.
target_language_example: Você é um bom amigo.
native_language_example: You are a good friend.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **ser** to identify someone as male (“a man”) or to describe someone with **um homem + adjective** (e.g., “a patient man”). **Você** is commonly used for “you” in Brazil (often neutral/polite). In European Portuguese, **tu** is more common in informal situations. Can also be a question: **Você é um homem?** (“Are you a man?”).
target_language_example: Você é um homem gentil.
native_language_example: You are a kind man.

meaning: “you are a person …” (used to describe what someone is like).
additional_notes: Common pattern for describing someone with an adjective or noun: “Você é uma pessoa + adjective/noun.” It can be a compliment (maravilhosa) or neutral description (religiosa). Often followed by an adjective like decente, gentil, simpática, etc. In speech it may sound like “cê é uma pessoa…”.
target_language_example: Você é uma pessoa muito gentil.
native_language_example: You are a very kind person.

additional_notes: Used to ask for the opinion/guess of a group (2+ people). Literally "you (plural) think that". In Brazil, "vocês" is the normal plural "you"; in Portugal it can sound more informal (often "vocês" with 3rd-person plural verbs, as here: "acham"). You can also use it for predictions: "Vocês acham que vai chover?"
target_language_example: Vocês acham que vale a pena tentar de novo?
native_language_example: Do you all think it’s worth trying again?

additional_notes: Used with the plural “you” (vocês) plus “still” (ainda) and the verb “to be” (estão). It’s commonly used to ask if a situation continues: “Vocês ainda estão com pressa?” (still in a hurry), “confusos?” (still confused), “em casa?” (still at home). You can follow it with an adjective (confusos), a prepositional phrase (em casa), or “com + noun” (com pressa).
target_language_example: Vocês ainda estão prontos para sair?
native_language_example: Are you still ready to go out?

additional_notes: Used when speaking to two or more people. "Vocês" = "you all" (common in Brazil); "compraram" is the simple past (pretérito perfeito) of "comprar" for "vocês". Often used in questions about what/where/when/why someone bought something.
target_language_example: Vocês compraram tudo o que precisavam?
native_language_example: Did you all buy everything you needed?

additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people (vocês = “you” plural in Brazil) whether they know someone/something or are familiar with a place, language, etc. It’s the present tense of conhecer (“to know/be acquainted with”). Common patterns: “Vocês conhecem + [person]?” (Do you know [person]?), “Vocês conhecem + [place/thing]?” (Are you familiar with [place/thing]?), “Vocês conhecem alguém que…?” (Do you know anyone who…?). Often contrasts with saber, which is more about knowing facts or knowing how to do something.
target_language_example: Vocês conhecem um bom restaurante por aqui?
native_language_example: Do you know a good restaurant around here?

additional_notes: From the verb "conseguir" (to be able to, to manage to). Used with "vocês" (you, plural) to ask whether a group is able to do something or to say they are able to do it. It can also be used as encouragement, like "You can do it!"
target_language_example: Vocês conseguem me ajudar com isso?
native_language_example: Can you all help me with this?

additional_notes: "Vocês" is "you" (plural) in Brazilian Portuguese. "Devem" is the present tense of "dever" for "vocês" and can express advice/expectation ("should/are supposed to") or a stronger obligation ("must"). In some contexts it can also express a logical guess ("you must have...", "you probably...") as in "Vocês devem ter vindo...". For questions, intonation and context show whether it’s obligation or expectation ("Vocês devem trabalhar aos domingos?" = "Do you have to work on Sundays?").
target_language_example: Vocês devem chegar cedo amanhã.
native_language_example: You (all) should arrive early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to give advice, make a recommendation, or say what is expected for a group (“vocês” = you plural). It’s the conditional of “dever” and often sounds like a polite suggestion, but depending on context can also be a strong criticism (e.g., “Vocês deveriam ter visto” = “You should have seen (it)”). Common patterns: “vocês deveriam + infinitive” (Vocês deveriam ir) and “vocês deveriam ter + past participle” (Vocês deveriam ter visto).
target_language_example: Vocês deveriam falar com o professor antes da prova.
native_language_example: You (all) should talk to the teacher before the test.

additional_notes: Used to address two people together. It’s formed from "vocês" (you, plural—common in Brazil) + "dois" (two, masculine default). When speaking to two women, you may also hear "vocês duas".
target_language_example: Eu preciso falar com vocês dois depois da aula.
native_language_example: I need to talk to you two after class.

additional_notes: Used when speaking to two people at once (common in Brazil). "vocês" = "you" (plural), "dois" = "two" (can also be "duas" for two females), and "estão" is the verb "estar" for "you (plural) are," often followed by an adjective ("estão bem") or "com" + noun to talk about a state/feeling ("estão com fome").
target_language_example: Vocês dois estão prontos para sair?
native_language_example: Are you two ready to leave?

meaning: “you (plural) were / you (plural) were being” (imperfect past of *estar*).
additional_notes: Used with **vocês** to talk about an ongoing state, feeling, or action in the past (“you all were … / you guys were …”). Common patterns: **vocês estavam + adjective** (Vocês estavam assustadas. = You were scared.), **vocês estavam com + noun** (Vocês estavam com ciúmes? = Were you jealous?), **vocês estavam + verb (gerund)** (Vocês estavam tentando fugir? = Were you trying to escape?). In Brazil, **vocês** is the usual plural “you”; the verb stays in **3rd-person plural** (estavam).
target_language_example: Vocês estavam esperando há muito tempo?
native_language_example: Were you all waiting for a long time?

additional_notes: Used with "vocês" (you plural) to talk to more than one person. "estão" is the present tense of "estar" (to be, for temporary states/conditions, location, or ongoing situations), so it often appears with adjectives ("bem", "cansados") or with a verb in the -ndo form to mean "are [doing]" ("estão tentando" = "are trying"). In Brazil, "vocês" is the everyday plural "you"; in Portugal, "vocês" can sound more informal or emphatic (often "vocês" + 3rd-person plural verb).
target_language_example: Vocês estão prontos para sair?
native_language_example: Are you all ready to leave?

additional_notes: Used when addressing more than one person (vocês) and describing an action in progress (estão + -ndo). Very common in questions like “Com quem vocês estão falando?” (Who are you talking to?) and “Do que vocês estão falando?” (What are you talking about?). Often followed by de (“about”) or com (“with/to”).
target_language_example: Eu não entendi—do que vocês estão falando?
native_language_example: I didn’t understand—what are you talking about?

additional_notes: Used when talking to more than one person. In Brazil, "vocês" is the most common way to say "you" (plural) in everyday speech and it uses 3rd-person plural verb forms like "falam". Often followed by a language or topic: "Vocês falam inglês?"
target_language_example: Vocês falam português em casa?
native_language_example: Do you speak Portuguese at home?

additional_notes: "Vocês" is an informal/neutral way to say “you all” in Brazilian Portuguese (it uses 3rd‑person plural verb forms). "Fizeram" is the past (pretérito perfeito) of "fazer". It can mean “did” (actions: Vocês fizeram reserva? = Did you book/reserve?) or “made” (made peace: Vocês fizeram as pazes? = Did you make up?). Often used to talk about something completed in the past.
target_language_example: Obrigado! Vocês fizeram um ótimo trabalho.
native_language_example: Thank you! You did a great job.

additional_notes: Used with vocês (“you all”) + gostar (“to like”) and usually followed by de + a verb in the infinitive (gostam de trabalhar = like working) or a noun/thing (gostam de queijo = like cheese). Common in questions (Vocês gostam de…?) and statements (Vocês gostam de…). In European Portuguese, the plural “you” is often vocês too, but the verb form may vary by region/register.
target_language_example: Vocês gostam de viajar nas férias?
native_language_example: Do you all like to travel on vacation?

additional_notes: Polite way to ask a group of people what they would like to do or have. Use it before a verb in the infinitive (e.g., "vocês gostariam de entrar?") or before a noun (e.g., "vocês gostariam de café?"). In Brazil, many speakers often use "vocês gostariam de" even when addressing one person, but it’s still grammatically plural.
target_language_example: Vocês gostariam de pedir sobremesa?
native_language_example: Would you like to order dessert?

additional_notes: Used when talking to a group (vocês = “you all”) and asking if something has happened already or by now (já = “already / yet”). In questions, English often uses “yet” (“Have you chosen yet?”) even though Portuguese uses já.
target_language_example: Vocês já terminaram o trabalho?
native_language_example: Have you all finished the work yet?

additional_notes: Used to say that a group of people lacks something (an object, permission, proof, etc.) or to ask if a place/group doesn’t have something available (often meaning “Don’t you have…?”). Uses the verb ter (to have) in the present tense: vocês têm = you (plural) have; vocês não têm = you (plural) don’t have. In Brazil, many people use “vocês” with 3rd-person plural verb forms like “têm” in most situations; in Portugal, “vocês” is also used but can sound more informal in some contexts compared to “vós” (rare) or “os senhores/as senhoras” (formal).
target_language_example: Vocês não têm tempo hoje?
native_language_example: Don’t you (all) have time today?

additional_notes: Used to make a polite request to a group of people: vocês (“you all”) + poderiam (conditional of poder, “could”). Often followed by por favor. Can also introduce a suggestion/request in a softer way than "vocês podem".
target_language_example: Vocês poderiam falar mais devagar, por favor?
native_language_example: Could you all speak more slowly, please?

additional_notes: Used when speaking to two or more people (“vocês”) to say they need to do something or that something is necessary. Follow it with an infinitive (precisam dormir, precisam parar) or with “de” + a noun/amount (precisam de ajuda, de quantas fotografias precisam?). More formal/plural alternatives include “os senhores/as senhoras precisam”.
target_language_example: Vocês precisam de ajuda agora?
native_language_example: Do you (all) need help now?

additional_notes: “Vocês” means “you” (plural). In Brazilian Portuguese it’s the normal way to say “you all/you guys”; in European Portuguese, “vocês” is common but can sound more informal depending on context. “Querem” is the present tense (plural) of “querer” (to want). Often used to ask what someone wants, make invitations, or check if someone wants you to do something (e.g., “vocês querem que eu…?” = “do you want me to…?”).
target_language_example: Vocês querem comer agora ou mais tarde?
native_language_example: Do you (all) want to eat now or later?

additional_notes: Uses vocês (“you” plural, common in Brazil) + sabem (present tense of saber, “to know” facts/information). Often starts a question to ask a group for information: “Vocês sabem onde…?”, “Vocês sabem se…?”. In Portugal, people may use “vocês” in some contexts, but “vocês sabem” is especially common in Brazilian Portuguese.
target_language_example: Vocês sabem que horas começa a reunião?
native_language_example: Do you all know what time the meeting starts?

additional_notes: Used with the subject pronoun "vocês" (you all) + the verb "ser" in the present tense ("são"). It describes what a group is like/what they are (identity, characteristics, origin): "Vocês são rápidos" (You’re fast). Often used in questions like "De onde vocês são?" (Where are you from?). In most of Brazil, "vocês" is the normal plural "you" in both informal and polite situations.
target_language_example: Vocês são meus amigos.
native_language_example: You all are my friends.

additional_notes: "Vocês" is the common plural form of "you" in Brazil. "Têm" is the present tense of "ter" (to have). It’s used both in statements ("vocês têm um plano") and in questions ("vocês têm um plano melhor?") to ask if someone has something available, knows something, or has an option/plan.
target_language_example: Vocês têm Wi‑Fi aqui?
native_language_example: Do you (all) have Wi‑Fi here?

additional_notes: Used to say that a group of people is required or strongly expected to do something. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., deixar, encontrar, ajudar, voltar). In speech, many speakers also say “vocês têm que” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Vocês têm de esperar aqui.
native_language_example: You all have to wait here.

additional_notes: Used to say an obligation or strong necessity for a group you’re talking to. It’s followed by a verb in the infinitive (e.g., estudar, fazer, reagir). In questions, it can mean 'Do you (all) have to...?'
target_language_example: Vocês têm que chegar cedo amanhã.
native_language_example: You all have to arrive early tomorrow.

additional_notes: "Vocês" is the common way to say "you" (plural) in Brazilian Portuguese. "Viram" is the past tense of "ver" (to see) for "vocês/eles/elas" and can be used in a question (often with rising intonation) or a statement. It’s used to ask if a group saw something, or to check that they noticed what happened (e.g., "Vocês viram?" = "Did you see that?").
target_language_example: Vocês viram onde eu deixei minhas chaves?
native_language_example: Did you (all) see where I left my keys?

additional_notes: Uses "vocês" (you all) + the verb "ir" (to go) in the present ("vão"). Very common to talk about near future plans: "Vocês vão + infinitive" (e.g., "vocês vão nadar?"). Depending on context, it can also mean simple future (“will”), especially in questions. Common with "votar" (to vote), "se divorciar" (to get divorced).
target_language_example: Vocês vão sair hoje à noite?
native_language_example: Are you (all) going out tonight?

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (voltar a + verb) to say you do something again or resume doing it. Example: "quero voltar a dormir" = "I want to sleep again / go back to sleep". In the negative, it can mean "not ... anymore": "não voltou a falar" = "he/she never spoke again".
target_language_example: Depois do almoço, vou voltar a trabalhar.
native_language_example: After lunch, I’m going to go back to work.

meaning: to go back to work; to return to working.
additional_notes: Used when resuming work after a break, time off, illness, or a pause in an activity. Common with "ter de/ter que" (have to) and "precisar" (need to): "Tenho de voltar ao trabalho". "Vamos voltar ao trabalho" can mean getting back to work right now.
target_language_example: Depois do almoço, vou voltar ao trabalho.
native_language_example: After lunch, I’m going back to work.

additional_notes: Used to say someone goes back to their home (after being out). It often implies returning from somewhere else (work, a trip, a friend’s place, etc.). In everyday speech you may also hear "voltar pra casa" (pra = para).
target_language_example: Depois do trabalho, vou voltar para casa cedo.
native_language_example: After work, I’m going to go back home early.

meaning: Go back home; return home. (imperative: “come back home”)
additional_notes: Uses the verb voltar (“to return”) + para casa (“home”). "Volte" is the você-form imperative (also the present subjunctive used after requests/wishes: "Espero que... volte"). Often followed by a time limit: "Volte para casa antes de...".
target_language_example: Por favor, volte para casa agora.
native_language_example: Please come back home now.

additional_notes: A polite, friendly phrase said to customers or guests when they leave (often after "Obrigado/a"). "Volte" is the imperative (command) form of "voltar" (to return/come back), used here as a courteous invitation.
target_language_example: Foi um prazer ajudar. Volte sempre!
native_language_example: It was a pleasure to help. Come back anytime!

meaning: (he/she/you formal) went back home; returned home.
additional_notes: Past tense of "voltar" (to return/go back) + "para casa" (home). Used when someone returns to their house/home base. Often matches English "went home" or "came home" depending on context (where the speaker is). The subject can be "você" (formal you) or a third person ("ele/ela").
target_language_example: Depois do trabalho, ele voltou para casa de ônibus.
native_language_example: After work, he went back home by bus.

additional_notes: Used to express a desire/urge or someone’s will. Common patterns: (1) "ter vontade de" + infinitive/noun = "to want to / to have the urge to"; (2) "estar/ficar com vontade de" + infinitive/noun = "to feel like"; (3) "dar vontade de" + infinitive = "to make you feel like" (often a spontaneous urge). It can also mean "the will of" someone (e.g., "a vontade de Sauron" = "Sauron’s will").
target_language_example: Estou com vontade de comer alguma coisa.
native_language_example: I feel like eating something.

meaning: “Your Highness” (a formal way to address royalty).
additional_notes: Used when speaking directly to or referring to a prince/princess or other high-ranking royal. Very formal and respectful; common in historical contexts, ceremonies, or fiction. Often capitalized (Vossa Alteza) and can be used alone as an address (e.g., “Vossa Alteza!”).
target_language_example: Com licença, vossa Alteza, posso falar um momento?
native_language_example: Excuse me, Your Highness, may I speak for a moment?

meaning: “Your Majesty.” (a very formal way to address a king/queen).
additional_notes: Used when speaking directly to a monarch, usually with verbs in the 3rd person (e.g., “Vossa Majestade diz…”). Written with a capital letter in formal contexts. In modern everyday Portuguese it’s rare outside historical fiction, ceremonies, or very formal protocol. Often shortened to “Majestade” when addressing the person (“Majestade,”).
target_language_example: Vossa Majestade gostaria de entrar agora?
native_language_example: Would Your Majesty like to come in now?

meaning: “I’ll go get (it/them),” “I’m going to fetch,” or “I’m going to look for.”
additional_notes: From **ir** (vou = “I’m going”) + **buscar** (“to get/fetch/look for”). Often used as a quick standalone reply meaning “I’ll go get it.” With an object it usually means “go pick up/get” (Vou buscar o carro. = “I’ll go get the car.”). With something abstract like **abrigo**, it can mean “go look for/seek” (Vou buscar abrigo. = “I’ll look for shelter.”).
target_language_example: Vou buscar meu irmão na escola.
native_language_example: I’m going to pick up my brother at school.

additional_notes:
Used with different meanings depending on what comes after:
- leave something somewhere: “Vou deixar o café aqui.” (I’ll leave the coffee here.)
- leave something blank/undone: “Vou deixar em branco.” (I’ll leave it blank.)
- leave something with someone: “Vou deixar com você.” (I’ll leave it with you.)
- drop someone off somewhere: “Vou deixar vocês na fronteira…” (I’ll drop you off at the border…)
It’s “vou” (I’m going) + “deixar” (to leave/let), and often implies a near-future decision.
target_language_example: Vou deixar minha mochila aqui por um minuto.
native_language_example: I’m going to leave my backpack here for a minute.

additional_notes: Formed with **ir (vou) + infinitive (dizer)** to talk about what you’re about to say (near future) or what you intend to say. Often used to introduce a statement: **Vou dizer uma coisa...** (“I’ll tell you something / I’m going to say something...”). Can be followed by what you’ll say: **vou dizer o meu nome** (“I’ll say my name”).
target_language_example: Vou dizer a verdade: não sei.
native_language_example: I’m going to tell the truth: I don’t know.

additional_notes: Uses the near-future construction "ir" (to go) + infinitive: "vou" (I’m going to) + "entrar" (to enter/go in). Often followed by a place with "em/no/na" (e.g., "vou entrar no hospital" = I’m going into the hospital).
target_language_example: Espera aí, que eu já vou entrar.
native_language_example: Wait there, I’m about to go in.

meaning: "I’m going to do/make" (near-future plan or intention).
additional_notes: "Vou" is the present tense of "ir" (to go) used with an infinitive to talk about the near future: "vou" + "fazer". "Fazer" can mean "to do" (an action/task: "fazer isso", "fazer nada") or "to make" (create/prepare something: "fazer chá", "fazer uma construção"). You can also use it in questions like "Como vou fazer isso?" (How am I going to do that?) and "Que vou fazer?" (What am I going to do?).
target_language_example: Vou fazer isso amanhã.
native_language_example: I’m going to do that tomorrow.

additional_notes: Uses **ir (vou)** + infinitive (**fazer**) to talk about an intention or something you expect to do (often in the near future). **isso** usually means “that/this” (a general thing already known from context). In questions like **Como vou fazer isso?**, it means “How am I going to do this?”
target_language_example: Tá bem, vou fazer isso hoje.
native_language_example: Okay, I’m going to do it today.

meaning: “I’m going to stay” or “I’m going to become / get (a certain state).”
additional_notes: Literally "I go to stay" (ir + infinitive), used to talk about a decision or near-future plan. With a place/context, it often means "to stay" (not leave): "Acho que vou ficar" = "I think I’ll stay." With an adjective or feeling, it often means "to become/get": "vou ficar nervoso" = "I’m going to get nervous." It can also be used in set expressions like "ficar de dedos cruzados" (to keep one’s fingers crossed).
target_language_example: Está tarde, então vou ficar em casa.
native_language_example: It’s late, so I’m going to stay home.

meaning: "I'll take it" / "I'll take them" (often: "I'll buy it/them").
additional_notes: Literally “I’m going to take.” Very common in shops or restaurants to tell the seller you’ve decided to take an item (i.e., purchase it). You can add the object after it: “vou levar um”, “vou levar esses”, “vou levar dois”.
target_language_example: Gostei deste. Vou levar.
native_language_example: I like this one. I’ll take it.

additional_notes: "Vou" is the 1st-person singular of **ir** (to go) used to form the near future: **vou + verb (infinitive)** = "I’m going to + verb". **Lhe** is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to you" (often polite/formal) or "to him/her" depending on context. It commonly appears between **vou** and the main verb: **vou lhe dizer / vou lhe mostrar / vou lhe escrever**.
target_language_example: Vou lhe ligar mais tarde.
native_language_example: I’m going to call you later.

meaning: “I’m going to …” (with “me” for a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Used with the near-future structure **ir (vou) + reflexive pronoun (me) + infinitive**. It often means you’ll do something to/for yourself: **vou me trocar** (I’m going to change [clothes]), **vou me abaixar** (I’m going to bend down), **vou me casar** (I’m going to get married), **vou me especializar** (I’m going to specialize), **vou me redimir** (I’m going to redeem/make it up). Often translates naturally as just “I’m going to + verb,” but Portuguese keeps **me** because the verb is reflexive.
target_language_example: Vou me preparar para a entrevista.
native_language_example: I’m going to get ready for the interview.

additional_notes: Uses **ir (vou) + infinitive** to express near-future or expected outcome (“I’m going to…”). It can be **literal** (serious danger: “Without medical care, I’m going to die”) or **exaggerated** in everyday speech to show strong emotion (fear, embarrassment, exhaustion, laughter). You can change the subject: **ele vai morrer** (he’s going to die), **a gente vai morrer** (we’re going to die), **eles vão morrer** (they’re going to die).
target_language_example: Se eu não comer logo, vou morrer de fome.
native_language_example: If I don’t eat soon, I’m going to die of hunger.

additional_notes: "Vou pegar" is "vou" (I’m going to) + "pegar" (to get/pick up/take/grab). It’s very common when you mean you’ll go get something ("Vou pegar mais água") or pick someone up ("vou pegar as crianças na escola"). In some contexts it can also mean "I’ll take it" (e.g., taking something for someone: "Vou pegar para o senhor") or "I’ll get you!" as a warning/threat ("Vou pegar vocês!"). By itself ("Vou pegar."), it often means "I’ll get it" (e.g., the phone/door, or the thing you just mentioned).
target_language_example: Espera aí, vou pegar meu casaco e já volto.
native_language_example: Wait a second, I’m going to get my coat and I’ll be right back.

additional_notes: First-person singular of the near-future (ir + infinitive): vou (I’m going) + pensar (to think). Very often used with “em” or “nisso” to mean “think about”: “vou pensar em algo” (I’ll think about something), “vou pensar nisso” (I’ll think about it). It can also mean “I’ll consider it” when responding to a suggestion or request.
target_language_example: Obrigado pela ideia — vou pensar nisso.
native_language_example: Thanks for the idea — I’ll think about it.

additional_notes: From **ir** (to go) + **sair** (to leave/go out). Used to say you’re about to leave a place or go out somewhere soon. It can also mean going out socially (e.g., **vou sair hoje**, **vou sair com a Jo** = “I’m going out with Jo”). With a time expression: **vou sair dentro de uma hora** = “I’m leaving in an hour.” With a place/direction: **vou sair ali** = “I’m just stepping out (right over there).”
target_language_example: Já vou sair, mas te ligo mais tarde.
native_language_example: I’m about to leave, but I’ll call you later.

additional_notes: Used before another verb to talk about a near-future action affecting "you." The main action comes in the following infinitive: vou te ajudar, vou te dizer, vou te pegar. Very common in Brazilian Portuguese.
target_language_example: Vou te ligar mais tarde.
native_language_example: I'll call you later.

meaning: “I’m going to give you…” / “I’ll give you…”
additional_notes: Used to promise or announce that you will give/provide something to someone soon. It’s "vou" (I’m going to) + "te" (to you, informal singular) + "dar" (to give). Very common with objects like comida (food), informações like a hora e o lugar (the time and place), presentes (gifts), or help/services like uma carona (a ride). In more formal situations, you’ll often hear "vou lhe dar" instead of "vou te dar".
target_language_example: Calma—vou te dar os detalhes mais tarde.
native_language_example: Relax—I’ll give you the details later.

meaning: "I’m going to kill you." (a threat; often said in anger).
additional_notes: Literally “I will kill you” (vou = I’m going to / I will, te = you, matar = to kill). In real life it’s a very serious, aggressive phrase and can be taken as a threat. In some contexts it can be used hyperbolically/jokingly (like “I’m gonna kill you!”), but it’s still very harsh—beginners should generally avoid using it.
target_language_example: Se você encostar no meu filho de novo, vou te matar.
native_language_example: If you touch my son again, I’m going to kill you.

additional_notes: Used when the speaker is about to show something to the listener. It’s the near-future form with ir + infinitive: vou (I’m going) + te (to you) + mostrar (to show). In many contexts, English “I’ll show you” is a natural translation. The object can come after: “Vou te mostrar algumas fotos / onde fica / como é.”
target_language_example: Espera um segundo — vou te mostrar no mapa.
native_language_example: Wait a second—I’m going to show you on the map.

additional_notes: Used to say you will make an effort to do something. It’s the verb "tentar" (to try) with "vou" (I’m going/I will), and it’s commonly followed by an infinitive: "vou tentar falar" (I’ll try to talk), "vou tentar chegar" (I’ll try to arrive). You can also use it alone as a quick response meaning “I’ll try!”.
target_language_example: Vou tentar terminar isso hoje.
native_language_example: I’ll try to finish this today.

meaning: “I’m going to have to” / “I’ll have to” (I must; I’m obliged to).
additional_notes: Used to say you will be forced or required to do something. It’s the near-future of “ter que” (to have to): eu vou ter que…, often followed by an infinitive (fazer, ir, limpar). You can change the subject: "você vai ter que...", "a gente vai ter que...", "eles vão ter que...". Common in speech; in writing you may also see "terei que" (I will have to).
target_language_example: Desculpa, vou ter que sair mais cedo hoje.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m going to have to leave early today.

additional_notes: "Vou" is the present tense of "ir" (to go) used to talk about the near future (“I’m going to…”), and "voltar" means “to return/go back.” Often followed by "para" or informal "pra" + a place: "vou voltar para/pra + lugar".
target_language_example: Já é tarde, então vou voltar para casa.
native_language_example: It’s already late, so I’m going back home.

meaning: “I’m going to the movies / I go to the cinema.”
additional_notes: From **ir** (“to go”): **vou** = “I go / I’m going” (present tense). **ao** = **a + o** (“to the”), and **cinema** here means the movie theater/cinema. In the examples it’s often used with frequency expressions like **quase nunca** (almost never), **raramente** (rarely), **com frequência** (often), **de vez em quando** (from time to time), **uma vez por mês** (once a month).
target_language_example: Hoje vou ao cinema com uns amigos.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to the movies with some friends.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re leaving (often right now). It’s the present tense of ir (“to go”) with embora (“away”), and can sound like a quick goodbye: Vou embora! You can add time info: vou embora hoje à noite (“I’m leaving tonight”).
target_language_example: Desculpa, está tarde — vou embora.
native_language_example: Sorry, it’s late—I’m leaving.

additional_notes: Used to say you are going to a (usually feminine) place. It’s made of: vou (I go / I’m going) + para (to) + a (the, feminine). For masculine places, you typically use “vou para o …” (e.g., vou para o trabalho). It can refer to the near future (“I’m going now/soon”) or a habitual action depending on context.
target_language_example: Depois do almoço, vou para a praia.
native_language_example: After lunch, I’m going to the beach.

additional_notes: Used to say you are going to your home (or to the place you consider ‘home’) now or later. It’s the present tense of the verb *ir* (“to go”) with *eu* implied: *Eu vou para casa*. Often used on its own as a complete sentence (e.g., when leaving). You can add time (*às quatro*, *agora*) or purpose (*vou para casa ver...* = “I’m going home to see...”).
target_language_example: Estou cansado(a); vou para casa agora.
native_language_example: I’m tired; I’m going home now.

meaning: “I go to school” / “I’m going to school.”
additional_notes: Uses the verb **ir** (to go) in the present tense: **vou** = “I go / I’m going.” **à** is a contraction of **a + a** meaning “to the” (feminine), used because **escola** is feminine: **a escola**. Often refers to going to school as part of a routine, but it can also mean you’re on your way there right now (context makes it clear).
target_language_example: Hoje vou à escola mais cedo.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to school earlier.

additional_notes: Imperative form of "ir" + "buscar" (usually used with "você", or as a polite/formal command). Used to tell someone to fetch/retrieve something (often followed by an object: "vá buscar o carro"). Depending on tone and context, it can sound like a sharp order.
target_language_example: Por favor, vá buscar o documento na recepção.
native_language_example: Please go get the document at reception.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to continue or start doing something, often as permission (“Go ahead.”) or encouragement. It can also sound challenging/defiant depending on tone, like “Go ahead, I dare you!” (as in the third example).
target_language_example: Se você quiser perguntar, vá em frente.
native_language_example: If you want to ask, go ahead.

additional_notes: "Vá" is the formal command form of "ir" (to go), used with "você". "Embora" here means "away" (as in leaving a place). Common in requests or orders: "Por favor, vá embora" (Please go away/leave), "Vá embora daqui" (Go away from here), and in the subjunctive after verbs like "esperar/querer/preferir": "Espero que ele vá embora" (I hope he leaves). For an informal command to one person, you’ll often hear "vai embora".
target_language_example: Por favor, vá embora agora; está tarde.
native_language_example: Please leave now; it’s late.

meaning: “go there” (command); also “come on!/all right” (encouraging or reluctant agreement).
additional_notes: Literal use: imperative/subjunctive of ir (“to go”) + lá (“there”), telling someone to go somewhere (“Vá lá de novo.”). Idiomatic use (often with an exclamation): used to encourage someone or to signal reluctant acceptance, like “Come on!” / “All right then.”
target_language_example: Vá lá, tenta mais uma vez!
native_language_example: Come on, try one more time!

additional_notes: Imperative (command) form of the verb ir: "vá" = "go" (formal você / also used after certain expressions with que). Used with "para" + destination/place: "Vá para Boston" (Go to Boston), "Vá para a cama" (Go to bed). With pronouns: "vá para o seu quarto" (your room, more formal) vs. "vá para o teu quarto" (your room, more informal/Portugal and some regions). Can also be used as an insult: "Vá para o inferno!" (Go to hell!).
target_language_example: Por favor, vá para casa agora.
native_language_example: Please, go home now.

additional_notes: Used mainly as an instruction/command in the você form (imperative/subjunctive of ir: vá). It can also appear after expressions like “não sei se…” meaning “I don’t know whether (someone) should go home.” For a more informal command with tu, you’ll often hear “vai para casa.”
target_language_example: Por favor, vá para casa e descanse.
native_language_example: Please go home and rest.

additional_notes: Extremely offensive and aggressive. Literally “go (and) fuck yourself.” Uses the command form “vá” (from ir: to go) + “se” (yourself) + “foder” (to fuck). Commonly said in anger, often with insults like “cara” or swear words like “porra.” Avoid in polite/company settings; in some contexts it can also be used as a harsh “fuck off.”
target_language_example: Se você continuar me tratando assim, vá se foder.
native_language_example: If you keep treating me like this, go fuck yourself.

additional_notes: "Várias" means "several" or "many" (a plural feminine form of "vário"), agreeing with "línguas" (languages). Common in contexts like speaking, learning, or translating into multiple languages.
target_language_example: O site está disponível em várias línguas.
native_language_example: The website is available in several languages.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens repeatedly. It often comes at the end of the sentence (e.g., "Já expliquei várias vezes"). You may also hear it emphasized as "várias e várias vezes" = "over and over again / many, many times."
target_language_example: Eu já tentei ligar para você várias vezes.
native_language_example: I’ve already tried to call you several times.

additional_notes: Used to say someone studies, speaks, or works with more than one language (often implying many, but not necessarily). Common with verbs like falar (to speak), estudar (to study), aprender (to learn), and entender (to understand).
target_language_example: Ela fala vários idiomas, mas quer aprender mais um.
native_language_example: She speaks several languages, but she wants to learn one more.

additional_notes: Formed with the verb "ir" (vão = "they/you all go") + an infinitive (fazer = "to do/make") to talk about a planned or near-future action. "Vão" can mean either "they" or "you all" depending on context.
target_language_example: Eles vão fazer o jantar hoje.
native_language_example: They’re going to make dinner today.

meaning: “are going to stay” / “will stay”; also “are going to become” / “will become.”
additional_notes: "Vão" (they/you plural) + infinitive "ficar" is a common way to talk about the future. With places or duration, it usually means "to stay" (e.g., stay in a house/country). With adjectives, it often means "to become/turn" (e.g., ficar bem = be/turn out fine; ficar grande = become big/too big).
target_language_example: Vocês vão ficar aqui hoje?
native_language_example: Are you (plural) going to stay here today?

meaning: “they’re going to … us” / “they will … us” (3rd person plural + “us”).
additional_notes: Used with a verb to say that “they” (some other people) are going to do something to “us”: e.g., vão nos pegar (“they’re going to catch us”). In Brazilian Portuguese, the object pronoun often comes before the main verb in this kind of structure (vão nos + verb).
target_language_example: Se a polícia chegar, vão nos prender.
native_language_example: If the police arrive, they’re going to arrest us.

additional_notes: "Ir embora" means to leave/go away. "Vão" is the present tense for "vocês" (you all) or "eles/elas" (they), so "vão embora" can mean either "you all leave" (a command) or "they leave" (a statement). Often followed by "daqui" = "from here".
target_language_example: Por favor, vão embora daqui agora.
native_language_example: Please leave here now.

additional_notes: "Vão" is the present tense of "ir" for "eles/elas" (they) or "vocês" (you all). It’s commonly followed by "para" to indicate destination (going to a place). Often used with a place word like "lá" (there) or a specific location.
target_language_example: Eles vão para o trabalho agora.
native_language_example: They’re going to work now.

additional_notes: "Vê-las" = "ver" (to see) + "-las" (them, referring to a feminine plural noun like "as flores" = the flowers). The accent in "vê" marks the stressed vowel in this verb form. It’s used when the object pronoun comes after the verb (common with infinitives, e.g., "para vê-las", "preciso vê-las"). For masculine plural "them," use "vê-los".
target_language_example: Quero vê-las de perto.
native_language_example: I want to see them up close.

additional_notes: Ver + the object pronoun "o" (him/it) attached with a hyphen. It’s common after an infinitive (e.g., "quero vê-lo") and in some commands. "vê" is "ver" with an accent added when pronouns like -lo are attached.
target_language_example: Preciso vê-lo hoje.
native_language_example: I need to see him today.

meaning: to see him again (also used as “to see you again,” formal).
additional_notes: "Vê-lo" is "ver" (to see) + "o" (him/it) attached with a hyphen (common with object pronouns). In polite/formal speech, "o" can mean "you" (male) when addressing someone as "o senhor" implicitly, so "É bom vê-lo de novo" can mean "It’s good to see you again" (formal). "Deixa-me" is informal; "Deixe-me" is more formal/polite.
target_language_example: Foi um prazer vê-lo de novo.
native_language_example: It was a pleasure to see you again.

additional_notes: This is the verb "ver" (to see) + the direct object pronoun "os" (them), attached with a hyphen. The accent (vê-) marks the stressed vowel when the pronoun is attached. Common in more formal/written Portuguese and after infinitives (e.g., "quero vê-los" = "I want to see them"). Use it mainly for groups that are masculine or mixed gender; for an all-female group, use "vê-las".
target_language_example: Quero vê-los amanhã à tarde.
native_language_example: I want to see them tomorrow afternoon.

additional_notes: Common in Brazil for a video game in general, and also used to mean a video game console depending on context (e.g., “um vídeo game novo” can be a new console). Often written as “videogame” as well. Plural: “videogames” or “vídeo games”.
target_language_example: Ele ganhou um vídeo game no aniversário.
native_language_example: He got a video game for his birthday.

additional_notes: Used in chess when the king is in check and has no legal move to escape; the game ends immediately. You can say it as an exclamation (“Xeque-mate!”) or use it with verbs like “dar”/“fazer” (“dar xeque-mate em/ao rei”, “dar xeque-mate no adversário”).
target_language_example: Com essa jogada, eu dou xeque-mate.
native_language_example: With that move, I checkmate.

additional_notes: Used to count how many cups of coffee someone drank or usually drinks. You’ll often see it with numbers (duas/três xícaras de café) and common verbs like tomar or beber.
target_language_example: Sempre tomo duas xícaras de café de manhã.
native_language_example: I always have two cups of coffee in the morning.

additional_notes: Informal and derogatory. Used to belittle someone as unimportant, with no status or influence (similar to “a nobody” / “a nobody from nowhere”). Often used with articles like “um/uma zé-ninguém” and can be used in the plural (“uns/umas zé-ninguém”).
target_language_example: Ele me tratou como se eu fosse um zé-ninguém.
native_language_example: He treated me like I was a nobody.

additional_notes: Used for things that happen during nighttime. With a specific day like "hoje" it often means "tonight" ("hoje à noite"). Without a specific day it usually means "at night" in general. Common pattern: "de dia" (during the day) vs. "à noite" (at night).
target_language_example: A gente se fala à noite, depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: We’ll talk tonight, after work.

meaning: on the edge/verge of; close to (often an extreme situation).
additional_notes: Used with nouns to show something is about to happen or someone is near a limit: à beira da extinção (on the verge of extinction), à beira do suicídio (close to suicide), à beira de um colapso (near a breakdown), à beira das lágrimas (about to cry). It can also be literal for a physical edge, often with places: à beira do mar (by/on the seashore), à beira de um penhasco (on the edge of a cliff). Usually appears as: estar/ficar/viver à beira de/da/do/das/dos + noun.
target_language_example: Depois de tantas noites sem dormir, eu estava à beira de desistir.
native_language_example: After so many sleepless nights, I was on the verge of giving up.

additional_notes: Indicates motion/direction toward the library. It’s the contraction of "a" (to) + "a" (the, feminine singular) → "à". Used with verbs of going/returning like "ir", "voltar", "levar".
target_language_example: Eu vou à biblioteca depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: I'm going to the library after work.

meaning: on the right; to the right (side).
additional_notes: Used to indicate direction or location. Common in giving directions: “É à direita” = “It’s on the right.” With “de” it specifies position relative to something: “à direita de X” = “to the right of X.”
target_language_example: Vire à direita no próximo cruzamento.
native_language_example: Turn right at the next intersection.

meaning: at a distance; from far away.
additional_notes: Used to say something is far away or seen from far away (e.g., “ver à distância”). It can also mean keeping someone/something away: “manter (alguém/algo) à distância” = “to keep (someone/something) at bay / at a distance.”
target_language_example: Dá para ver o castelo à distância.
native_language_example: You can see the castle from far away.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (ir, voltar, chegar, levar, etc.) to indicate going to school. "à" is a contraction of "a" (to) + "a" (the, feminine), because "escola" is feminine: "a + a escola" → "à escola".
target_language_example: Eu vou à escola todos os dias.
native_language_example: I go to school every day.

additional_notes: Commonly used with the verb "estar": "estar à espera" = "to be waiting". Often followed by "de" + noun/infinitive to say what/whom you’re waiting for: "à espera de o conhecer" = "waiting to meet him"; "à espera que" + verb is also used to mean "expecting that" (e.g., expecting that something will happen).
target_language_example: Estou à espera do autocarro.
native_language_example: I'm waiting for the bus.

additional_notes: Used to indicate position or direction. Common in directions and navigation (often contrasted with “à direita” = on/to the right). You can use it after verbs like “virar” (to turn) and “ficar” (to be/located): “Vire à esquerda” (Turn left), “Fica à esquerda” (It’s on the left).
target_language_example: O banco fica à esquerda do supermercado.
native_language_example: The bank is to the left of the supermarket.

additional_notes: "À" = "a" (to) + "a" (the), used with feminine singular places like "a estação". Often used with transport contexts: "ir à estação" (go to the station), "voltar à estação" (return to the station). If you name the station, you can say "à Estação X"; with "de trem" it’s "à estação de trem" (to the train station).
target_language_example: Vamos pegar um táxi até à estação.
native_language_example: Let’s take a taxi to the station.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (like ir, voltar, chegar) to mean going to a specific party/event. It’s the contraction of "a" + "a" (feminine singular) = "à".
target_language_example: Você vai à festa amanhã?
native_language_example: Are you going to the party tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to say something is done against someone’s will or using physical/authoritative coercion. Common with verbs like levar/trazer (to take/bring), obrigar (to force), and in passive ideas like construído à força (“built by force”). In “Vamos à força”, it means “we’ll go even if we’re forced / even if we don’t want to.”
target_language_example: Eles o tiraram de lá à força.
native_language_example: They dragged him out of there by force.

additional_notes: Used for position or direction: "lá/ali à frente" = "up there ahead"; "a X metros/quilômetros à frente" = "X meters/kilometers ahead." With "de": "à frente de" = "in front of" / "ahead of" (also in the sense of leading: "ficar à frente" = "to be in the lead"). "Mais à frente" can mean "further ahead" or "later on" depending on context.
target_language_example: O restaurante fica logo à frente do hotel.
native_language_example: The restaurant is right in front of the hotel.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (ir, voltar, vir) to mean going to a church building/service. It’s the contraction of "a" (to) + "a" (the) → "à" + "igreja" (church). Often appears in routines: "ir à igreja" (to go to church).
target_language_example: Eu vou à igreja no domingo.
native_language_example: I go to church on Sunday.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (ir, voltar, correr, levar) to mean going to a store. It’s the contraction of "a" (to) + "a" (the) + "loja" (shop/store) → "à loja". Contrast: "na loja" = in/at the store (location), and "da loja" = from the store.
target_language_example: Vou à loja comprar pão.
native_language_example: I’m going to the store to buy bread.

meaning: to the light; in the light (of). Also used in “dar à luz” = to give birth.
additional_notes: In the common expression **dar à luz** (often in the gerund: **dando à luz**), it means “to give birth” (literally “to bring to the light”). With **do sol** it means **sunlight**: **à luz do sol** = “in the sunlight / in the light of the sun.” In more formal contexts, **à luz de** can mean “in light of” (considering something).
target_language_example: Ela deu à luz ontem à noite.
native_language_example: She gave birth last night.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a reason or context that affects a decision, opinion, or conclusion. Common in formal or written Portuguese (news, reports, emails). Typically followed by a noun phrase (e.g., à luz de novos dados, à luz de fatos, à luz de evidências) or a more specific framing like "à luz do/da" (a contracted variant with a definite article).
target_language_example: À luz de novos dados, vamos mudar o plano.
native_language_example: In light of new data, we're going to change the plan.

additional_notes: Used to show two things happening or changing in parallel over time: as one thing increases/decreases or progresses, another also changes. Common with gradual processes (ageing, weather getting colder, seasons approaching). Often followed by the present tense for general truths ("À medida que ficamos velhos...") or by past forms to describe a change in progress in the past ("À medida que o clima foi esfriando...").
target_language_example: À medida que você pratica, fica mais confiante.
native_language_example: As you practice, you get more confident.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens at exactly 12:00 a.m. It often answers “when?” and can come after the verb (Chegamos… à meia-noite) or at the end of the sentence. Note: “meia-noite” is feminine, so it uses “à” (= a + a).
target_language_example: O filme começa à meia-noite.
native_language_example: The movie starts at midnight.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is at a table (often for eating, meeting, or being seated). Common with verbs like "estar" (to be) and "sentar" (to sit). The "à" is the contraction of "a" + "a" (= "to/at the" + feminine "the").
target_language_example: Todos estão à mesa para o jantar.
native_language_example: Everyone is at the table for dinner.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (especially **vir** “to come” and **ir** “to go”) to say someone is going/coming to where you live. **à** is the contraction of **a + a** (“to + the”), and it’s common to say **à minha casa** (to my house) rather than *para minha casa* in many everyday situations.
target_language_example: Você pode vir à minha casa amanhã?
native_language_example: Can you come to my house tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used after certain verbs to indicate an outcome that ends in death. Very common in set phrases like “condenado/sentenciado à morte” (“sentenced/condemned to death”) and “levar (alguém) à morte” (“to lead (someone) to death”). Also appears in “até à morte” (“until death”).
target_language_example: Ele foi condenado à morte, mas a sentença foi anulada.
native_language_example: He was sentenced to death, but the sentence was overturned.

additional_notes: Common with past participles to mean something is done manually: "pintado à mão" (hand-painted), "escrito à mão" (handwritten). With "estar" it means "to be at hand/within reach" (nearby, ready to use). You may also see "à mão de" meaning "in the hand/possession of" someone. Fixed phrase: "à mão armada" = "at gunpoint" / "in an armed robbery".
target_language_example: Prefiro escrever à mão, é mais fácil para mim.
native_language_example: I prefer to write by hand; it’s easier for me.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens during the night or evening period, often as a general time expression: de dia e à noite = during the day and at night.
target_language_example: Nós quase sempre jantamos à noite.
native_language_example: We almost always have dinner at night.

meaning: aside; apart; separately; in a different category.
additional_notes: Used to set something off from the main topic or group. Common patterns: (1) “Brincadeiras à parte, …” = “Joking aside, …” (now speaking seriously). (2) “um/uma X à parte” = “a special case / a world of its own” (something unique or different from the rest). (3) At the start of a sentence, “À parte (isso/aquele detalhe) …” can mean “Aside from that / apart from that …”.
target_language_example: À parte isso, eu concordo com você.
native_language_example: Aside from that, I agree with you.

additional_notes: This is the contraction of the preposition + article: "a" + "a partida" → "à partida". It often appears after the verb "assistir a" (to watch/attend): "assistir à partida" = "to watch the match". Note: "partida" can also mean "departure" in other contexts, but in these examples it means a sports match.
target_language_example: A gente vai assistir à partida hoje à noite.
native_language_example: We’re going to watch the match tonight.

additional_notes: Contraction of "a" (to) + "a" (the) = "à" (feminine singular). Used after verbs that take "a" to show who something is directed to, e.g. "contar à polícia" (tell the police), "entregar à polícia" (hand over to the police), "oferecer dinheiro à polícia" (offer money to the police).
target_language_example: Vou ligar à polícia agora.
native_language_example: I'm going to call the police now.

meaning: at the door; at the doorway.
additional_notes: Often used with verbs like "bater" (to knock): "bater à porta" = "to knock on the door." It can also mean someone is waiting/standing at the door: "Há alguém à porta" (There’s someone at the door). In some contexts English uses "on the door" (knocking), but Portuguese uses "à" (at/to the).
target_language_example: Tem uma encomenda à porta para você.
native_language_example: There’s a package at the door for you.

additional_notes: Used after verbs of movement like ir/voltar/chegar to indicate going to a place. It’s the contraction of "a" (to) + "a" (the, feminine) + "praia" (beach) = "à praia". Often used with "ir": "ir à praia" (to go to the beach).
target_language_example: Vamos à praia depois do almoço.
native_language_example: We’re going to the beach after lunch.

meaning: at first sight; at first glance.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a first/immediate impression, either from seeing someone/something for the first time or from considering an idea briefly. Often appears at the start of a sentence: “À primeira vista, ...”. Common with “amor”/“apaixonar-se”: “amor à primeira vista” (love at first sight).
target_language_example: À primeira vista, eu achei que seria fácil, mas me enganei.
native_language_example: At first glance, I thought it would be easy, but I was wrong.

additional_notes: Used with the verb estar (most common: "Estou à procura de...") to say you’re searching for someone or something. It’s slightly more formal than "procurar" or "estar procurando" and is often followed by a noun or person ("à procura de uma pasta", "à procura de uma pessoa").
target_language_example: Estamos à procura de um hotel perto do centro.
native_language_example: We’re looking for a hotel near downtown.

additional_notes: Means “to the meeting,” usually after verbs of movement/attendance like ir (to go), chegar (to arrive), and comparecer (to attend). The accent in “à” is the crase: a + a (the preposition “a” + the feminine article “a”) before the feminine noun “reunião.” Note: “reunião” looks like English “reunion,” but in Portuguese it commonly just means a (work) meeting.
target_language_example: Vou chegar cedo à reunião para falar com o gerente.
native_language_example: I’m going to arrive early to the meeting to talk to the manager.

meaning: to (someone’s) health; for health (as an effect).
additional_notes: Used with adjectives like essencial/perigoso/prejudicial and verbs like fazer bem/mal to say something is beneficial or harmful to health. Grammatically it’s “a + a saúde” → “à saúde” (to the health), often translated as “to your/their health” or “for your/their health” depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Comer mais verduras faz bem à saúde.
native_language_example: Eating more vegetables is good for your health.

meaning: to your mother; to his/her mother.
additional_notes: Means motion/direction toward someone’s mother (often after verbs like "ligar" (to call), "devolver" (to return), "perguntar" (to ask)). "à" is the contraction of "a" (to) + "a" (the, feminine). "sua" can mean "your" (often more formal) or "his/her" depending on context—Portuguese sometimes uses "a mãe dele/dela" to be clearer.
target_language_example: Vou entregar isso à sua mãe amanhã.
native_language_example: I’ll deliver this to your mother tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say when something happens during the afternoon (after midday). Often used with days of the week: "segunda-feira à tarde" (Monday afternoon), "sexta-feira à tarde" (Friday afternoon).
target_language_example: Vamos nos encontrar à tarde, depois do almoço.
native_language_example: Let’s meet in the afternoon, after lunch.

meaning: for nothing; in vain; without reason.
additional_notes: Used to say something happened without a good reason or purpose ("não foi à toa" = "it wasn’t for nothing"). It can also describe doing something aimlessly/with nothing to do ("ficar à toa" = "to be idle").
target_language_example: Eu não chorei à toa; aconteceu uma coisa séria.
native_language_example: I didn’t cry for nothing; something serious happened.

meaning: for sale; on sale (available to buy).
additional_notes: Used to say something is being sold or is available to purchase. Often after the verb “estar/ficar” (e.g., “está à venda”). Can also follow “colocar/pôr” to mean “to put up for sale” (“colocar à venda”). In sentence 5, it’s used figuratively: “put me up for sale / sell me,” meaning treating someone like a commodity.
target_language_example: O apartamento está à venda desde o mês passado.
native_language_example: The apartment has been for sale since last month.

meaning: in sight; (payment) in cash / paid in full upfront.
additional_notes: Most commonly means “in sight / visible” (often with “não estar à vista” = “not in sight”). In shopping/payment contexts, “pagar à vista” means paying immediately in one lump sum (often cash), as opposed to paying in installments (“a prazo”, “parcelado”).
target_language_example: Não vejo ninguém à vista, então vamos embora.
native_language_example: I don’t see anyone in sight, so let’s leave.

additional_notes: Used in two very common ways: (1) to encourage someone to do something freely/without restriction (often like “feel free”): "Comam/Bebam/Fiquem à vontade!" = help yourself / make yourself comfortable. (2) With "sentir-se/ficar" to mean being comfortable or at ease in a place or with someone: "Sinto-me/Estou à vontade."
target_language_example: Pode perguntar à vontade.
native_language_example: You can ask as much as you like / Feel free to ask.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. It’s formed by **a + as** ("at" + "the" [hour]) → **às** for most clock times: **às cinco**, **às seis**, etc. With **one o’clock**, Portuguese uses **à uma** (singular). You can add parts of the day: **às cinco da tarde** (at 5 p.m.), **às cinco da manhã** (at 5 a.m.), or minutes: **às cinco e meia** (at 5:30).
target_language_example: Nos encontramos às cinco em frente ao café.
native_language_example: We’ll meet at five in front of the café.

additional_notes: Used mainly with the verb "ir" (or "ir a") to mean "to go shopping": "ir às compras". Literally means "to the purchases/buying" and refers to going out to buy things (often for groceries, errands, etc.).
target_language_example: Vamos às compras depois do trabalho.
native_language_example: Let’s go shopping after work.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. It’s "às" (a + as) because hours are feminine plural: às uma (at 1:00), às duas (at 2:00), etc. You can add a time-of-day phrase like "às nove da manhã" (at 9 a.m.) or "às nove da noite" (at 9 p.m.).
target_language_example: A reunião começa às nove.
native_language_example: The meeting starts at nine.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. "Às" is the contraction of "a" + "as" and is used with most clock times (às duas, às oito). With 1 o’clock you usually say "à uma" (singular). You can add parts of the day: "às oito da manhã" (at 8 a.m.), "às oito da noite" (at 8 p.m.).
target_language_example: A reunião é às oito.
native_language_example: The meeting is at eight.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something quickly because they don’t have time (often implying stress, urgency, or not doing it carefully). Common with verbs like sair (leave), voltar (return), entrar (get in), almoçar (have lunch), and ser levado (be taken) in urgent situations.
target_language_example: Saímos às pressas quando começou a chover.
native_language_example: We left in a hurry when it started to rain.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. It’s the contraction of “a” + “as” (at + the, for hours): a(s) + as → às. Often followed by “horas,” but you can omit it when the context is clear.
target_language_example: A reunião começa às seis.
native_language_example: The meeting starts at six.

additional_notes: Used to say the time something happens. It’s the contraction of "a" + "as" (= "at the" for clock times): "às" is used with plural hours (às duas, às sete). With 1 o’clock you usually use "à uma" (singular). You can also add "horas": "às sete horas".
target_language_example: A aula começa às sete.
native_language_example: Class starts at seven.

meaning: “to your” (feminine plural), usually before a noun.
additional_notes: Contraction of "a" + "as" + "suas". Used mainly with verbs that take the preposition "a" (e.g., "dizer adeus a" = to say goodbye to; "voltar a" = to return to; "prestar atenção a" = to pay attention to). Can also appear in set phrases like "às suas ordens" (at your service / yes, sir/ma’am). The following noun is feminine plural: "às suas amigas" (to your (female) friends), "às suas posições" (to your positions).
target_language_example: Voltem às suas cadeiras, por favor.
native_language_example: Go back to your seats, please.

additional_notes: A common adverb for something that happens on some occasions but not regularly. It can appear at the beginning, middle, or end of a sentence.
target_language_example: Às vezes eu vou a pé para o trabalho.
native_language_example: Sometimes I walk to work.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens occasionally (not always). In Portuguese, you can replace "ele" with other subjects: "às vezes eu" (sometimes I), "às vezes ela" (sometimes she), "às vezes a gente" (sometimes we), etc. Often appears in patterns like "Às vezes..., às vezes..." to show alternation.
target_language_example: Às vezes ele prefere ficar em casa.
native_language_example: Sometimes he prefers to stay at home.

additional_notes: A polite, common way to ask for water, especially in cafés/restaurants. You can use it alone (“Água, por favor.”) or with a quantity like “um copo de água” (a glass of water) or “uma garrafa de água” (a bottle of water). Word order is flexible: “Um copo de água, por favor.” / “Por favor, um copo de água.”
target_language_example: Para mim, uma garrafa de água, por favor.
native_language_example: For me, a bottle of water, please.

additional_notes: A sea animal that can sting (often said as “ser queimado por uma água-viva” = “to be stung by a jellyfish”). It’s usually written with a hyphen: “água-viva”. Plural: “águas-vivas”.
target_language_example: Fui queimado por uma água-viva.
native_language_example: I was stung by a jellyfish.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or describe water that is not hot/warm. Adjective agreement: "fria" is feminine to match "água" (feminine), so you say "água fria" (not *"água frio"). Common in restaurants and cafés when specifying temperature.
target_language_example: Pode me trazer um copo de água fria, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you bring me a glass of cold water, please?

additional_notes: Literally “water from the faucet.” Used when talking about drinking water that comes from the sink tap (as opposed to bottled water). You can also specify the location: “água da torneira da cozinha” = “kitchen tap water.”
target_language_example: Aqui, a água da torneira é potável.
native_language_example: Here, the tap water is drinkable.

additional_notes: Literal phrase meaning water that is cold (temperature). Common in cooking instructions (e.g., cover something with cold water), for bathing (banho com água fria), and when ordering a drink (“Uma água fria, por favor” = a cold bottle/glass of water). In some contexts it can be used figuratively as “a cold shower”/“a bucket of cold water” to mean something unpleasant or discouraging.
target_language_example: Pode me trazer uma água fria, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you bring me a cold water, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask for or talk about bottled mineral water in shops, restaurants, hotels, etc. Very common with "com gás" (sparkling) or "sem gás" (still). You can also say "uma garrafa de água mineral" (a bottle of mineral water).
target_language_example: Pode trazer uma água mineral sem gás, por favor?
native_language_example: Can you bring a still mineral water, please?

additional_notes: Used to refer to water that is safe for human consumption (not contaminated). Common in practical contexts like travel, emergencies, infrastructure, and public services. Often contrasted with "água não potável" (non-drinkable water).
target_language_example: Precisamos de água potável.
native_language_example: We need drinking water.

additional_notes: Used for water at a high temperature, especially for bathing, washing, or cleaning. Common in phrases like “Não há água quente” (There’s no hot water).
target_language_example: Preciso de água quente para tomar banho.
native_language_example: I need hot water to take a shower.

additional_notes: Used for the decorated tree people put up for Christmas. Usually feminine: "a árvore de Natal"; plural: "árvores de Natal". Can refer to a real (pine) tree or an artificial one.
target_language_example: Vamos montar a árvore de Natal hoje à noite.
native_language_example: Let's set up the Christmas tree tonight.

additional_notes: A very common combination of é ("is") + a (the feminine singular article). It is used to identify or define something with a feminine singular noun, as in "é a Torre Eiffel". In some varieties of Portuguese, a can also appear before women's names, so "é a Karin" can mean "it's Karin".
target_language_example: A vencedora é a Maria.
native_language_example: The winner is Maria.

meaning: "is the capital of" (used before a feminine country/region name).
additional_notes: Used to state that a city is the capital of a place. It agrees with feminine nouns: "da" = "de" + "a" (“of the” feminine). With masculine names, use "é a capital do" (do = de + o): "Lisboa é a capital do Portugal" (rare/unnatural because people usually say "a capital de Portugal"). Most commonly you’ll also hear "é a capital de" + country name (without article): "Madri é a capital de Espanha".
target_language_example: Brasília é a capital da República Federativa do Brasil.
native_language_example: Brasília is the capital of the Federative Republic of Brazil.

additional_notes: Used to state the capital city of a place. It agrees with the gender/number of the place that follows: use "do" (= de + o) with masculine singular places (do Brasil), and "da" (= de + a) with feminine singular places (da França). With plural names, use "dos/das". Often appears in questions like "Que cidade é a capital do... ?"
target_language_example: Lisboa é a capital do Portugal.
native_language_example: Lisbon is the capital of Portugal.

meaning: "is the key" (the most important thing for achieving something).
additional_notes: Used in the pattern “X é a chave para Y” to say that X is essential to reach/achieve Y. It can be literal (an actual key) but is very often metaphorical (“the key to success”).
target_language_example: A prática diária é a chave para melhorar o português.
native_language_example: Daily practice is the key to improving Portuguese.

meaning: “is the most … (thing)” (used to say something is the most + adjective).
additional_notes: Used with superlatives: é a coisa mais + adjective (encantadora, preciosa, linda, forte) + (de/da/do) + noun, or followed by a clause: “que temos/que existe”. Very common, informal-neutral way to emphasize that something is the most important/beautiful/etc. You can also use it with masculine adjectives (e.g., “é a coisa mais importante”).
target_language_example: Este lugar é a coisa mais bonita da cidade.
native_language_example: This place is the most beautiful thing in the city.

meaning: “is the language” (used to identify what a language is).
additional_notes: Used in statements to say that a certain language is someone’s native language or is the language with a certain characteristic. Often followed by extra information (e.g., “com mais falantes…”, “mãe dela”). You can swap in another subject: “Português é a língua oficial de Angola.”
target_language_example: Português é a língua oficial do Brasil.
native_language_example: Portuguese is the official language of Brazil.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the best among others. Portuguese adjectives agree with the noun: use "é o melhor" with masculine nouns (e.g., "O café é o melhor"), and "é a melhor" with feminine nouns (e.g., "A seleção é a melhor"). Often followed by a noun: "é a melhor opção" (it’s the best option).
target_language_example: Para mim, esta é a melhor solução.
native_language_example: For me, this is the best solution.

meaning: “is mine” (referring to something feminine); or “is my …” before a feminine noun.
additional_notes: Used with the verb “ser” to identify possession/relationship or to state that something is your favorite, your first time, etc. It agrees with a feminine noun: “a minha” (feminine singular). For masculine you’d say “é o meu”. Often followed by a noun: “É a minha caneca” = “It’s my mug.” It can also stand alone if the noun is understood: “Aquela caneca? É a minha.” = “That mug? It’s mine.”
target_language_example: Essa mochila é a minha.
native_language_example: That backpack is mine.

meaning: “is the most … woman” (superlative: the woman who is the most …).
additional_notes: Used to form the superlative about a woman: “(someone) é a mulher mais + adjective + (de/do/da...)” (“the most … in the world”) or “é a mulher mais + adjective + que...” (“the most … that/who…”). The adjective agrees in gender: “gentil/rica/alta/quieta”. You can swap “mulher” for another noun: “é o homem mais…”, “é a pessoa mais…”.
target_language_example: Ela é a mulher mais inteligente da turma.
native_language_example: She is the smartest woman in the class.

meaning: “is ours” / “it’s our …” (referring to a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns to identify something as belonging to “us” (our/ours), often in contrast to others: “Aquela é a nossa vizinha.” With a noun, it means “it’s our + noun” (e.g., “É a nossa família!”). Without a noun, it can mean “it’s ours,” as long as the thing being talked about is feminine.
target_language_example: Não se preocupe — é a nossa responsabilidade.
native_language_example: Don’t worry — it’s our responsibility.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is the most (superlative) in a group or compared to others. Structure: [Name] + é a pessoa mais + adjective + (de/do/da + group) or + que + verb (e.g., que conheço = “that I know”). Adjective agrees with pessoa (feminine): mais baixa, mais gorda, mais preguiçosa, etc.
target_language_example: Ela é a pessoa mais simpática da turma.
native_language_example: She is the nicest person in the class.

additional_notes: Used to say or ask whether something is happening for the first time. Very common with the present tense in Portuguese (e.g., "É a primeira vez que estou aqui"), where English often uses the present perfect ("it’s the first time I’ve been here"). You can adapt it for formality: "a senhora / o senhor" (formal), "você" (neutral), "vocês" (plural).
target_language_example: É a primeira vez que eu venho a este restaurante.
native_language_example: It’s the first time I’ve come to this restaurant.

additional_notes: Often used literally in explanations/definitions ("X é a vida..."). It can also be said on its own as a common expression meaning acceptance or resignation about a situation (similar to “that’s life”).
target_language_example: Perdemos o ônibus, mas é a vida.
native_language_example: We missed the bus, but that’s life.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the only option/thing/person. It’s the feminine form, agreeing with a feminine noun that follows or is implied (e.g., a única coisa, a única lei, a única maneira, a única família). For masculine nouns, use “é o único” (e.g., é o único caminho). Often followed by a noun: “É a única maneira…”.
target_language_example: Para mim, esta é a única solução.
native_language_example: For me, this is the only solution.

additional_notes: Used with ser (é) + alérgico/alérgica + a + the allergen (food, medicine, dust, etc.). Use alérgico for males and alérgica for females: Ela é alérgica a leite. To ask a question, you can use intonation or add a question mark: Você é alérgico a…?
target_language_example: Tom é alérgico a amendoim.
native_language_example: Tom is allergic to peanuts.

additional_notes: Used to downplay or limit something (“nothing more than…”). Often followed by a noun or phrase: “é apenas um porco” = “it’s just a pig”, “é apenas emocional” = “it’s just emotional”, “é apenas meio período” = “it’s only part-time”. You can also say “apenas” without “é” depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Calma, é apenas uma pergunta.
native_language_example: Relax, it’s just a question.

meaning: “it’s just a / it’s only a” (to downplay or say something is nothing more than that).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to minimize or define something as nothing more than what follows. It agrees with the noun: é apenas um (masc. singular), é apenas uma (fem. singular), são apenas uns/umas (plural). Often translated as “just/only” in English.
target_language_example: Não se preocupe, é apenas um teste.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, it’s just a test.

meaning: "that's how" / "this is how" (introduces the way something is or is done).
additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to explain a manner, method, or typical situation. Often followed by a verb clause: “É assim que + [subject] + [verb] …” (e.g., “É assim que fazemos…”). Can also introduce a general statement: “É assim que a vida é…” (“That’s what life is like…”).
target_language_example: É assim que se aprende português: praticando todos os dias.
native_language_example: This is how you learn Portuguese: by practicing every day.

meaning: "is quite / pretty" (used to emphasize an adjective).
additional_notes: Used with an adjective to mean “quite/rather/pretty” (a moderate-to-strong emphasis): é bastante estressante/improvável/inesperado. Note that "bastante" can also mean "enough" in other contexts (e.g., "Já é bastante!" = "That’s enough!").
target_language_example: O trabalho é bastante difícil, mas eu gosto.
native_language_example: The job is quite difficult, but I like it.

additional_notes: Used to intensify an adjective or description: é bem antigo = “is quite/very old.” With comparatives, bem often means “much” or “far,” as in é bem mais jovem = “is much younger.” In other contexts, bem can also mean “well,” but in these examples it works as an intensifier.
target_language_example: O filme é bem interessante.
native_language_example: The movie is quite interesting.

additional_notes: A very common phrase meaning that something is good, nice, useful, or satisfactory. It is made of é ("is") + bom ("good"). It can also describe a person's skill in some contexts, especially with com, as in é bom com números ("is good with numbers").
target_language_example: Esse restaurante é bom.
native_language_example: That restaurant is good.

additional_notes: Used with "ser" to talk about ability/skill in a subject or activity. It’s followed by a noun or a verb (often in the infinitive): "Ele é bom em biologia" / "Ele é bom em cantar". Agree "bom/boa" with the person: "Ele é bom", "Ela é boa"; plural: "Eles são bons", "Elas são boas".
target_language_example: Ele é bom em biologia, mas não é muito bom em física.
native_language_example: He’s good at biology, but he’s not very good at physics.

additional_notes: Often followed by the subjunctive ("é bom que + verb"), to express recommendation/approval: "É bom que ele vá" = "It’s good that he goes / He should go." In some contexts, especially with "você", it can sound like a warning or threat: "É bom que você chegue cedo" = "You’d better arrive early." It can also introduce something worth mentioning: "É bom que se diga..." = "It’s worth saying..."
target_language_example: É bom que você me avise antes de chegar.
native_language_example: You’d better let me know before you arrive.

meaning: 'is beautiful/pretty' (said about a female person or feminine noun).
additional_notes: Uses the verb "ser" (é = "is") + the feminine adjective "bonita". Agree it with the noun: masculine "é bonito"; plural "são bonitas/bonitos". In questions, Portuguese often keeps the same order and uses a question mark/intonation: "Ela é bonita?"
target_language_example: A sua irmã é bonita.
native_language_example: Your sister is beautiful.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (é = “is”) to describe something/someone as beautiful/nice. Bonito changes to match what you’re describing: bonito (masc. sing.), bonita (fem. sing.), bonitos (masc. pl.), bonitas (fem. pl.). When talking about a person, it can mean “good-looking / handsome” (masc.) or “pretty” (fem.).
