target_language_example: O lugar é bonito, mas é longe.
native_language_example: The place is beautiful, but it’s far.

additional_notes: Used to state someone’s nationality: “(he/she/it) is Canadian.” You can swap the subject: “Eu sou canadense” (I am Canadian), “Você é canadense?” (Are you Canadian?), “O Tom é canadense.” (Tom is Canadian). Note: “canadense” stays the same for men and women (no -o/-a change).
target_language_example: Você é canadense?
native_language_example: Are you Canadian?

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (to be) to state someone’s marital status. Often followed by "com" + a person to say who someone is married to: "Ele é casado com a Ana." For a woman, you usually say "é casada". For the plural: "são casados/casadas".
target_language_example: Ele é casado com a minha irmã.
native_language_example: He is married to my sister.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that what follows is obvious, certain, or expected. Often translates as “of course” in conversation, and as “clearly/evidently” in more formal writing. Tone depends on context: it can be neutral, reassuring, enthusiastic, or sarcastic/irritated (especially with insults or strong emotion).
target_language_example: É claro que eu vou te ajudar.
native_language_example: Of course I’m going to help you.

meaning: “is like a…” (used to make a comparison).
additional_notes: Used to compare someone or something to a noun: X é como um/uma Y (“X is like a Y”). Choose um (masculine noun) or uma (feminine noun). Often expresses similarity, not identity.
target_language_example: Este livro é como um guia para mim.
native_language_example: This book is like a guide for me.

meaning: "it’s like a" (used to make a comparison).
additional_notes: Used to compare something to something else, usually to explain an idea with an analogy. Often followed by a noun: "É como uma montanha" (It’s like a mountain). In everyday speech you’ll also hear "é como" without the article, depending on what comes next.
target_language_example: Aprender português é como uma aventura.
native_language_example: Learning Portuguese is like an adventure.

meaning: "it’s as if" / "it’s like" (introducing an unreal or hypothetical comparison).
additional_notes: Used to compare reality to an imagined situation: “It’s as if…”. It’s typically followed by the subjunctive in Portuguese (e.g., fosse, tivesse), often expressing something that seems true but isn’t certain or is contrary to fact. Can also be used for emphasis or dramatic effect.
target_language_example: É como se eu não existisse para eles.
native_language_example: It’s as if I don’t exist to them.

additional_notes: Used to contrast two situations or to signal an exception/changed condition. Often implies “that’s another matter/then it changes things,” as in: “If you don’t love me, then it’s different.” You can also hear it with an implied subject: “Mas aí é diferente.” (= “But then it’s different.”)
target_language_example: Se for só por hoje, tudo bem; mas se for sempre, aí é diferente.
native_language_example: If it’s just for today, that’s fine; but if it’s always, then it’s different.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is hard, challenging, or not easy. é is the present form of ser ("to be"). In some contexts, difícil can also describe a bad or serious situation, not just something mentally hard.
target_language_example: No começo, é difícil entender tudo.
native_language_example: At first, it's hard to understand everything.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb to say something is difficult to do: "é difícil de + verb" (e.g., "é difícil de resolver"). Often you’ll also see "é difícil" without "de" ("É difícil resolver este problema"), and both are common. In some cases Portuguese adds "se" before the verb ("difícil de se viver"), especially when talking about living somewhere or general actions.
target_language_example: Este texto é difícil de entender.
native_language_example: This text is hard to understand.

additional_notes: Used to point back to a specific thing or topic just mentioned. Common in emphatic expressions like “É disso que estou falando!” (“That’s what I’m talking about!”). Often followed by a verb phrase (e.g., estou falando, temos medo). “disso” = “of that/about that” (de + isso).
target_language_example: É disso que eu preciso agora.
native_language_example: That’s what I need right now.

additional_notes: Used with "é" (it is) + adjective to say an activity or situation is fun. Common patterns: "É divertido + infinitive" (É divertido jogar...) and "É divertido + estar com + person" (É divertido estar com a Jane). With a person, "Você é divertido" means "You’re fun".
target_language_example: É divertido aprender português com amigos.
native_language_example: It’s fun to learn Portuguese with friends.

additional_notes: Used to identify or point to something with the demonstrative pronoun/adjective "essa" (feminine). It agrees with a feminine noun (e.g., "pergunta"), and can be used in questions with inversion: "É essa a sua opinião?" = "Is that your opinion?" (more literally, "Is that the opinion of yours?"). For masculine, you’ll often see "é esse"; for a neutral idea/situation, "é isso" is common.
target_language_example: É essa a resposta que você quer?
native_language_example: Is that the answer you want?

additional_notes: A very common combination of é + esse, often used in questions after a noun to ask what something is: Que livro é esse? = 'What book is that?' In English, it may sometimes sound more natural as 'is this' depending on the situation. Esse usually refers to something near the listener or something already mentioned.
target_language_example: Que barulho é esse?
native_language_example: What noise is that?

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize an adjective after the verb “ser” (é = “is”). Common pattern: “X é extremamente + adjective” (e.g., importante, chato, suspeito, teimoso). It’s fairly formal; in casual speech you might also hear “é muito” (“is very”).
target_language_example: O filme é extremamente longo.
native_language_example: The movie is extremely long.

meaning: "is made of" (what something is made from).
additional_notes: Used to describe the material or components something is made from. It agrees with the subject: é feito de (masc. singular), é feita de (fem. singular), são feitos de (masc. plural), são feitas de (fem. plural). Often used with materials (pedra, papel, ouro) and with parts/components (átomos).
target_language_example: A mesa é feita de madeira.
native_language_example: The table is made of wood.

additional_notes: Used to say what something is made from. Very common with materials (madeira, ouro, papel) and ingredients (trigo, suco de uva). You can also use it with feminine/plural subjects: “é feita de” (fem. singular), “são feitos/as de” (plural).
target_language_example: Este brinquedo é feito de madeira.
native_language_example: This toy is made of wood.

additional_notes: Used to say something is easy. Common patterns: (1) “É fácil + infinitive”: “É fácil se perder.” = “It’s easy to get lost.” (2) “É fácil para + person + infinitive”: “É fácil para mim ler este livro.” = “It’s easy for me to read this book.” You can also use it as a contrast: “não o que é fácil” = “not what is easy.”
target_language_example: É fácil aprender português com prática diária.
native_language_example: It’s easy to learn Portuguese with daily practice.

additional_notes: Used to describe size (physical dimensions) or sometimes importance/status ("a great person/thing"). It can also be used in the sense of "grown-up/old enough" (e.g., "você é grande o suficiente..." = "you’re old/big enough..."). For plural, use "são grandes".
target_language_example: Essa cidade é grande.
native_language_example: That city is big.

additional_notes: Used to say something is excessive. In Portuguese, "demais" often comes after the adjective: "grande demais" = "too big" (also works with other adjectives, e.g., "caro demais" = "too expensive"). It can refer to physical size or to degree/intensity (e.g., a risk, a problem).
target_language_example: Essa mochila é grande demais para mim.
native_language_example: That backpack is too big for me.

additional_notes: Used to say that the moment to do something has arrived. It’s often followed by an infinitive verb: "É hora de comer" (to eat), "É hora de dormir" (to sleep). You can add "agora" for emphasis: "Agora é hora de...".
target_language_example: É hora de ir embora.
native_language_example: It’s time to leave.

additional_notes: Used to state equality, especially in math, measurements, and conversions. The pattern is: [X] é igual a [Y]. In speech it’s often shortened to "igual a" in equations (e.g., "cinco mais três, igual a oito").
target_language_example: Dois mais dois é igual a quatro.
native_language_example: Two plus two is equal to four.

additional_notes: Used to say that something matters or has significance. Often followed by "para" to show who/what it matters to (e.g., "é importante para mim" = "it’s important to me"). You can also form a question with it: "Para quem isso é importante?" = "Who is this important to?".
target_language_example: É importante chegar cedo.
native_language_example: It’s important to arrive early.

additional_notes: Used with **é** ("is") + **impossível** ("impossible") to state that something can’t happen or can’t be done. Often followed by an infinitive: **É impossível + verbo** (e.g., *É impossível entender tudo* = "It’s impossible to understand everything"). It can also be used in questions: *É impossível…?* = "Is it impossible…?"
target_language_example: É impossível chegar a tempo sem um carro.
native_language_example: It’s impossible to arrive on time without a car.

additional_notes: Used to express strong positive surprise, admiration, or enthusiasm about something. Often appears as a stand-alone exclamation ("É incrível!") or with a subject ("Este livro é incrível"). You can also change the tense/person: "foi incrível" (it was amazing), "será incrível" (it will be amazing).
target_language_example: A vista daqui é incrível!
native_language_example: The view from here is amazing!

additional_notes: Used with the verb *ser* + adjective to state that someone is innocent (often meaning “not guilty” when someone is accused). You can emphasize it with words like *para mim* (“to me/in my opinion”) or *só* (“just/only”), as in *Para mim, ele é inocente!*
target_language_example: Eu sei que ele é inocente.
native_language_example: I know he’s innocent.

additional_notes: Common spoken expression used to confirm, agree, or wrap something up. It can mean you’ve found the right thing (“That’s the one”), you agree with someone (“Exactly”), or you’re emphasizing a conclusion (“That’s it, done”). Often said on its own as a short reply.
target_language_example: —Então a senha é 4321? —É isso aí!
native_language_example: —So the password is 4321? —That's right!

meaning: “Is that what…?” / “Is that the thing that…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask for confirmation or clarification about something (often with surprise or doubt). It’s typically followed by a clause: “É isso o que você quer?” = “Is that what you want?” In everyday speech, people very often shorten it to “É isso que …?” (same meaning).
target_language_example: É isso o que você quis dizer?
native_language_example: Is that what you meant?

additional_notes: Used to point to or identify something: “that’s what …”. Very common before a verb clause (é isso que + verb) to mean “that’s what (someone) …”. In questions, it often means “is that what …?”
target_language_example: É isso que eu estava procurando.
native_language_example: That's what I was looking for.

additional_notes: Used to say someone isn’t old enough to do something, understand something, or have something. Pattern: (person) + é + jovem demais + para + infinitive (e.g., viajar, entender, ser) or + noun phrase (e.g., este trabalho). Often used with “ainda” (“still”): “ainda é jovem demais para…”.
target_language_example: Ela é jovem demais para dirigir.
native_language_example: She is too young to drive.

additional_notes: Used to say something is fair or deserved (often in discussions about rules, treatment, or decisions). It can also describe a person as fair (e.g., “Tom é justo.”). In questions, it often expresses disagreement or asking for confirmation: “É justo isso?” = “Is that fair?”
target_language_example: Não é justo eu pagar tudo sozinho.
native_language_example: It’s not fair for me to pay everything alone.

additional_notes: In Brazilian Portuguese, **legal** is very commonly used to mean “cool/nice/awesome,” describing a person, thing, or situation: *Ele é legal* = “He’s nice.” It can also mean “legal/lawful” in more formal contexts, but in everyday conversation it often means “cool,” so it can be a false friend for English speakers.
target_language_example: O seu plano é legal, mas acho caro.
native_language_example: Your plan is cool, but I think it’s expensive.

meaning: “is beautiful” (said about a woman/girl or a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "ser" (é = "is") + the adjective "linda". "Linda" agrees with feminine subjects (A Mary, esta parte, você when addressing a woman). For masculine subjects, use "é lindo"; for plural, "são lindas/lindos".
target_language_example: A sua filha é linda.
native_language_example: Your daughter is beautiful.

additional_notes: Used to say something (or an experience) is beautiful. Often refers to masculine singular nouns (e.g., “O apartamento é lindo.”). For feminine singular use “é linda” (e.g., “A casa é linda”); plural: “são lindos/lindas”. You can also use it with an infinitive to talk about an action/experience: “É lindo ver...” = “It’s beautiful to see...”.
target_language_example: É lindo ver o pôr do sol aqui.
native_language_example: It’s beautiful to watch the sunset here.

additional_notes: Used with "ser" + "maior" + "do que" to compare size, amount, number, age, importance, etc. It agrees with the thing being compared: "é maior" (singular), "são maiores" (plural). Common variants: "mais ... do que" (more ... than) and "menor do que" (smaller/less than).
target_language_example: Este problema é maior do que parece.
native_language_example: This problem is bigger than it seems.

meaning: 'is bigger/larger than' (can also mean 'is older than').
additional_notes: Used to compare two things or people. With sizes/quantities it means “bigger/larger than”; with people (especially in age contexts) it can mean “older than.” Often used with demonstratives like “esta... que aquela” (“this... than that”) or pronouns like “eu/você.”
target_language_example: Meu quarto é maior que o seu.
native_language_example: My room is bigger than yours.

additional_notes: Used to form comparisons with adjectives/adverbs: **X é mais + adjective + (do) que Y** (“X is more … than Y”). Often appears with **do que** or **que**. In the negative **não é mais**, it can mean “is no longer” (e.g., *Você não é mais bem-vindo aqui.* = “You’re no longer welcome here.”).
target_language_example: Este caminho é mais rápido do que o outro.
native_language_example: This route is faster than the other.

additional_notes: Used to compare strength, ability, or overall power. Structure: [subject] + é + mais forte + do que + [comparison]. It can be literal (physical strength) or figurative (a team/opponent is stronger). In phrases like “É mais forte do que parece!”, it means something is stronger/more intense than it appears.
target_language_example: Este remédio é mais forte do que o outro.
native_language_example: This medicine is stronger than the other one.

additional_notes: Used to compare difficulty: **é mais fácil + infinitive** (“it’s easier to…”). It often appears with **do que** to compare two actions/things (“easier than…”): *É mais fácil atacar… do que…*. You may also see **mais fácil que** in informal speech, but **mais fácil do que** is generally preferred for comparisons.
target_language_example: É mais fácil aprender com prática do que só com teoria.
native_language_example: It’s easier to learn with practice than only with theory.

additional_notes: Used with the verb “ser” + “mais velho” + “que” to compare age: “X é mais velho que Y”. “Velho” agrees with the subject’s gender/number (e.g., “ela é mais velha que...”; “eles são mais velhos que...”). With “qualquer um/uma”, it can mean “older than anyone”: “é mais velho que qualquer um daqui”.
target_language_example: Tom é mais velho que Mary.
native_language_example: Tom is older than Mary.

additional_notes: Used to soften a statement or express that something is true only to a degree (often before an adjective): "é meio estranho/complicado/embaraçoso". In speech it’s very common as a hedge, similar to "kind of" in English. The word "meio" literally means "half/middle," but here it works like an adverb meaning "somewhat."
target_language_example: Esse assunto é meio delicado.
native_language_example: This topic is kind of delicate.

additional_notes: Used to compare two things/people. Structure: [something] é melhor do que [something else]. “Melhor” agrees in number only when used as an adjective before a noun (e.g., melhores), but in this pattern it usually stays “melhor”. Often appears with possessives: “o meu é melhor do que o seu” = “mine is better than yours.”
target_language_example: A comida aqui é melhor do que a de lá.
native_language_example: The food here is better than the food there.

meaning: "It’s better not to…" (advice/warning to avoid doing something).
additional_notes: Used to suggest that doing something is a bad idea or could cause problems. It’s often followed by an infinitive verb: “É melhor não + verb” (e.g., “É melhor não falar”). It can also be used alone when the action is understood from context.
target_language_example: É melhor não sair agora; está chovendo muito.
native_language_example: It’s better not to go out now; it’s raining a lot.

additional_notes: Used to compare two people/things/ideas. It agrees with the thing being described: é (he/she/it is), são (they are). You can also say “é melhor do que” (often interchangeable with “é melhor que” in everyday Portuguese).
target_language_example: Dormir cedo é melhor que ficar acordado até tarde.
native_language_example: Going to bed early is better than staying up late.

additional_notes: Used to give strong advice or a warning about what someone should do. It’s often followed by an infinitive verb: “É melhor você + verbo” (e.g., aprender, aproveitar, tomar). You can also hear “É melhor você não + verbo” for negative advice (“You’d better not…”).
target_language_example: É melhor você sair agora, porque vai chover.
native_language_example: You’d better leave now, because it’s going to rain.

additional_notes: Used to add emphasis or confirmation to what you’re saying: "Ele é mesmo..." = “He really is...”. It can also be used in yes/no questions to express surprise or to double-check information: "Ela é mesmo neta...?" = “Is she really the granddaughter…?”. In context it can mean “right there/actually there” when talking about location: "É mesmo ali" = “It’s really right there / it’s exactly there.”
target_language_example: Ele é mesmo muito gentil.
native_language_example: He really is very kind.

additional_notes: Used to show possession. Before a masculine singular noun, it means 'is my' (e.g. é meu amigo = 'he is my friend'). On its own, it can mean 'is mine'. The feminine form is é minha, and the plural forms are são meus / são minhas.
target_language_example: Este livro é meu.
native_language_example: This book is mine.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone is your (male) friend. “É” is the 3rd-person singular of “ser” (to be), used for identity/relationship. For a female friend, you’d say “é minha amiga.” Plural: “são meus amigos / são minhas amigas.”
target_language_example: Tom é meu amigo.
native_language_example: Tom is my friend.

additional_notes: Used to identify someone as your son. Often appears with a subject before it (e.g., “Este menino é meu filho.” = “This boy is my son.”). Portuguese often drops the subject when it’s clear from context: “É meu filho.” = “It’s my son.”
target_language_example: Aquele rapaz é meu filho.
native_language_example: That young man is my son.

additional_notes: Used to identify someone as your brother. The subject is often implied (ele/aquele/isso), or it can refer back to someone already mentioned ("É meu irmão."). You can also use it when introducing someone: "Este é meu irmão."
target_language_example: Prazer, este é meu irmão, o Pedro.
native_language_example: Nice to meet you, this is my brother, Pedro.

additional_notes: Used to say something belongs to you: "X é meu." For feminine nouns, use "é minha" (e.g., "A bolsa é minha"). You can also use it as a question: "Isso é meu?" = "Is this mine?"
target_language_example: Esse celular é meu.
native_language_example: This phone is mine.

additional_notes: Used to state ownership or responsibility for a feminine noun (explicit or implied). It agrees with the gender of the thing owned: "é minha" (feminine), "é meu" (masculine). Common with words like "cor" (f.), "obrigação" (f.), "culpa" (f.), etc. You can also include the noun: "A casa é minha" (The house is mine).
target_language_example: Essa mochila é minha.
native_language_example: That backpack is mine.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is your friend; "amiga" is feminine (for a male friend, use "é meu amigo"). Often appears with a subject before it (e.g., "A Maria é minha amiga"), but the subject can be omitted when it’s obvious ("É minha amiga!"). "minha" agrees with the gender of the noun (amiga/amigo), not the speaker.
target_language_example: A Ana é minha amiga.
native_language_example: Ana is my friend.

additional_notes: Used to identify someone as your daughter (often in response to a question or to clarify who someone is). Portuguese can omit the subject pronoun, so this can stand alone as a full sentence: “É minha filha.” You can also add emphasis with “sim”: “Sim, é minha filha.”
target_language_example: Aquela garota ali é minha filha.
native_language_example: That girl over there is my daughter.

additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns (e.g., caneta, bolsa, casa, grana, luta). Often appears in ownership statements like “X é minha” (“X is mine”) or in the negative “não é minha” (“it isn’t mine”). Can also be said emphatically to claim something (“A praça é minha!”). For masculine nouns, you’d say “é meu”.
target_language_example: Esse livro não é meu, mas essa cadeira é minha.
native_language_example: That book isn’t mine, but this chair is mine.

additional_notes: Literal use: describes texture/consistency (food, materials): “A batata é mole.” Figurative/colloquial use: “é mole” = something is easy; “Não é mole” = “It’s not easy.” As a question (“É mole?”) it can mean “Is it easy?” and can also sound like a skeptical “You think it’s that easy?” depending on tone/context.
target_language_example: Esse exercício é mole.
native_language_example: This exercise is easy.

additional_notes: Commonly used before an adjective or adverb to intensify it: é muito bom = 'is very good'. Here, é is the third-person singular of ser ('is').
target_language_example: Ela é muito inteligente.
native_language_example: She is very intelligent.

meaning: “it’s too high” / “it’s very high” / “it’s very loud” / “he’s very tall.”
additional_notes: "Alto" changes meaning depending on what you’re describing: for people it usually means "tall" (Ele é muito alto. = He’s very tall). For sounds/volume it means "loud" (O som é muito alto. = The sound is very loud). For abstract things like price, level, or risk it means "high" (O risco é muito alto. = The risk is very high). In this phrase, "é" can refer to a thing (it’s), or to a person when the subject is understood (he’s/she’s).
target_language_example: Esse preço é muito alto.
native_language_example: That price is very high.

additional_notes: Used to describe something feminine (or referred to with a feminine noun like comida, ideia) as very good. With masculine nouns, use “é muito bom”. For plural, use “são muito bons/boas”. You can add “mesmo” or “realmente” for extra emphasis.
target_language_example: A sobremesa é muito boa.
native_language_example: The dessert is very good.

additional_notes: Literally “is very good.” Used to describe someone/something as very good (“Tom é muito bom.”). With **para + infinitive**, it means “is very good at (doing something)” (“Ele é muito bom para mudar de assunto.”). You can also use it impersonally as **É muito bom + infinitive** to mean “It’s really nice/good to …” (“É muito bom vê-la.”).
target_language_example: É muito bom ter você aqui.
native_language_example: It’s really nice to have you here.

meaning: "is very beautiful" (said about a feminine noun/person).
additional_notes: Used to describe something/someone feminine as very beautiful. It’s the verb ser (é = “is”) + intensifier muito (“very”) + feminine adjective bonita (“beautiful”). For masculine nouns, you say: é muito bonito. For plural feminine: são muito bonitas; plural masculine/mixed: são muito bonitos.
target_language_example: A cidade à noite é muito bonita.
native_language_example: The city at night is very beautiful.

meaning: “it is very beautiful / it’s very nice.”
additional_notes: Used to compliment something you can see or are talking about (a place, object, clothing, etc.). Often said with emphasis or an exclamation (“É muito bonito!”). You can change the subject (e.g., “O jardim é muito bonito.”) and the adjective for gender/number (bonito/bonita/bonitos/bonitas).
target_language_example: Esse pomar é muito bonito!
native_language_example: That orchard is very beautiful!

additional_notes: Used to complain or comment that something costs a lot. "é" = "it is"; "muito" intensifies ("very/really"); "caro" = "expensive". You can specify the thing before it (e.g., "Este vinho é muito caro") or just say it alone ("É muito caro!"). For feminine nouns, change to "é muito cara" (e.g., "A casa é muito cara").
target_language_example: Desculpe, para mim é muito caro.
native_language_example: Sorry, for me it’s very expensive.

additional_notes: Used to describe something as being very hard or challenging. You can add a subject before it (e.g., "Russo é muito difícil") or use it by itself as a full sentence ("É muito difícil...") followed by an infinitive ("de aprender", "impressionar").
target_language_example: É muito difícil encontrar um bom apartamento aqui.
native_language_example: It’s very difficult to find a good apartment here.

additional_notes: Used to say an activity is very enjoyable. Often followed by an infinitive verb phrase (e.g., “É muito divertido jogar...” = “It’s very fun to play...”) or used after a gerund/infinitive as the subject (“Jogar tênis é muito divertido.” = “Playing tennis is very fun.”).
target_language_example: Aprender português é muito divertido!
native_language_example: Learning Portuguese is very fun!

additional_notes: Used to describe someone as intelligent or clever. "Esperto" can be a genuine compliment (“smart”), but depending on tone/context it can also imply someone is “sly” or “crafty” (good at getting what they want). You can change the subject and agreement: "Ela é muito esperta" (she is very smart), "Você é muito esperto" (you are very smart), "Eu sou muito esperto" (I am very smart).
target_language_example: Sabe, Carl, esse cara é muito esperto.
native_language_example: You know, Carl, that guy is very smart.

additional_notes: Used to say something has a lot of strength, power, or intensity. With drinks it often means high alcohol content (strong). With a person it can mean physically strong. With movies/scenes/experiences it can mean intense, shocking, or not suitable for someone (“too much for them”), often followed by “pra/para” + person (e.g., “pra ele/ela”).
target_language_example: Essa cena é muito forte pra crianças.
native_language_example: That scene is too intense for children.

additional_notes: Used to say something is very easy to do or understand. Often followed by an infinitive with “de” to mean “easy to …”: “É muito fácil de ler” (“It’s very easy to read”). You can replace “muito” with another intensifier (e.g., “bem”) or remove it: “É fácil.”
target_language_example: Para mim, é muito fácil aprender essas palavras.
native_language_example: For me, it’s very easy to learn these words.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone as kind (Tom é muito gentil) or as a polite way to thank someone for an action, often in the pattern "É muito gentil da/de sua parte + [infinitive]" (e.g., "É muito gentil da sua parte me emprestar..."). In Brazil, "da sua parte" is common; "de sua parte" is also used, often sounding a bit more formal.
target_language_example: É muito gentil da sua parte me ajudar com as malas.
native_language_example: That’s very kind of you to help me with the bags.

meaning: 'is very big/large' (or 'it's too big/large,' depending on context).
additional_notes: Used to describe the size of something. Often followed by "para + infinitive" to mean "too ... to ..." (e.g., "É muito grande para..." = "It’s too big to..."). Also commonly appears with a subject: "X é muito grande" = "X is very big."
target_language_example: Essa mala é muito grande para levar no avião.
native_language_example: That suitcase is too big to take on the plane.

additional_notes: Used to stress that something matters a lot. Common in explanations and instructions, often followed by an infinitive: “É muito importante + verb” (e.g., “É muito importante assinar…” = “It’s very important to sign…”). You can also use it with “para” to show who/what it’s important to: “X é muito importante para Y” = “X is very important to Y.”
target_language_example: É muito importante chegar cedo amanhã.
native_language_example: It’s very important to arrive early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to describe something you find interesting. It often follows the thing you’re talking about (subject + é muito interessante). You can change it to match the subject: é (it/he/she is), são (they are). You can also adjust intensity: é interessante (interesting), é bem interessante (quite interesting), é muito interessante (very interesting).
target_language_example: A aula de hoje é muito interessante.
native_language_example: Today’s class is very interesting.

additional_notes: Used to say someone doesn’t have the right age (or isn’t mature enough) to do something: **ser + muito jovem + para + infinitive** (é muito jovem para dirigir) or **ser + muito jovem + para + noun/pronoun** (é muito jovem para isso). You can change the person/tense: *sou/era/foi muito jovem para...*
target_language_example: Tom é muito jovem para dirigir um carro.
native_language_example: Tom is too young to drive a car.

additional_notes: Used to say something (or someone) is very nice, cool, or fun. “Legal” here means “cool/nice” (not “legal” as in lawful). You can use it about objects (Um relógio é muito legal.) or people (Ele é muito legal.). Often said with a positive, friendly tone; “não?” at the end means “right?/isn’t it?”.
target_language_example: Esse filme é muito legal!
native_language_example: That movie is really cool!

additional_notes: Used to describe a feminine noun (e.g., a vila, a caixa, a possibilidade). For masculine nouns, you say “é muito pequeno” (e.g., “O apartamento é muito pequeno.”). It can refer to physical size (“The box is very small”) or to something abstract like a chance/possibility (“The possibility is very small”).
target_language_example: A chance de chover hoje é muito pequena.
native_language_example: The chance of rain today is very small.

additional_notes: Used to warn or emphasize that a situation, action, place, or person is very dangerous. Common patterns: "É muito perigoso + infinitive" (É muito perigoso nadar aqui. = It’s very dangerous to swim here.) and "X é muito perigoso" (Tom é muito perigoso. = Tom is very dangerous.). Often said on its own as a warning: "É muito perigoso!".
target_language_example: É muito perigoso atravessar a rua aqui.
native_language_example: It’s very dangerous to cross the street here.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is very useful. Often followed by “para + [person/thing]” to mean “for (someone/something)”: “É muito útil para mim” = “It’s very useful for me.” You can also use it with different subjects: “Este site é muito útil.”
target_language_example: Este aplicativo é muito útil para estudar português.
native_language_example: This app is very useful for studying Portuguese.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is needed/required. Common patterns: (1) “é necessário + infinitive”: “É necessário reduzir os custos.” (It’s necessary to reduce costs.) (2) “é necessário que + subjunctive”: “É necessário que você faça isso agora.” (It’s necessary that you do this now / You need to do this now.) You can also use it alone as a short reply: “É necessário.” (It’s necessary.)
target_language_example: É necessário estudar um pouco todos os dias.
native_language_example: It’s necessary to study a little every day.

additional_notes: Used to say something is usual, expected, or not strange. Often followed by a clause with “que”: “É normal que…” = “It’s normal that… / It’s normal for…” (i.e., it’s expected). You can also use it as a question: “Isso é normal?” = “Is that normal?”
target_language_example: É normal ficar nervoso antes de uma entrevista.
native_language_example: It’s normal to feel nervous before an interview.

additional_notes: Combines é, the third-person singular of ser ('is'), with o, the singular masculine form of 'the'. It is used before singular masculine nouns or adjectives used as nouns, as in identification, description, or emphasis.
target_language_example: Hoje é o último dia.
native_language_example: Today is the last day.

meaning: 'he's the guy' / 'that's the guy' (often: 'he's the man' = really good/cool).
additional_notes: Uses the informal noun "cara" (= guy/dude) to identify someone: "Tom é o cara com barba" (Tom is the guy with a beard) or "É o cara da loja?" (Is he the guy from the store?). Depending on context/intonation, it can also be praise meaning "he's the man" / "he's awesome."
target_language_example: Ele é o cara que conserta celulares aqui.
native_language_example: He's the guy who fixes cell phones here.

additional_notes: Used to say someone owns something (é o dono da empresa/loja/casa) or is the person in charge. Often followed by "de" or "da/do" + the thing owned. Feminine form: "é a dona".
target_language_example: Ele é o dono da empresa.
native_language_example: He is the owner of the company.

additional_notes: Used to identify or define a specific man by adding a relative clause with que (“who/that”). Word order can change for emphasis (e.g., “Feliz é o homem que…” = “Happy is the man who…”). In everyday speech you’ll also hear “Ele é o homem que…”.
target_language_example: Ele é o homem que resolveu o problema.
native_language_example: He’s the man who solved the problem.

additional_notes: Used to say something is the largest in size/amount/importance within a group or category. It uses the superlative idea with **maior** (“bigger/greater”). It agrees with the noun: **é a maior** (feminine), **são os maiores / as maiores** (plural). Often followed by **do/da** + place/group: *do mundo* (“in the world”), *do país* (“in the country”).
target_language_example: Este shopping é o maior da cidade.
native_language_example: This mall is the biggest in the city.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something is the top choice or the highest quality in a group. It’s the verb “é” (is) + “o melhor” (the best, masculine singular). For feminine nouns you’ll often see “é a melhor” (e.g., “Ela é a melhor médica daqui.”).
target_language_example: Para mim, este restaurante é o melhor da cidade.
native_language_example: For me, this restaurant is the best in the city.

additional_notes: Combines é ("is") with o meu ("my/mine"). It is used before a masculine singular noun, like é o meu chefe = "he is my boss." Portuguese often uses the article o before possessives, even though English does not.
target_language_example: Este é o meu amigo João.
native_language_example: This is my friend João.

additional_notes: Means “is our” when referring to a masculine singular noun. Portuguese often uses the article with possessives: “o nosso + [noun]” = “our + [noun]” (e.g., “o nosso rei” = “our king”). Variations: “é a nossa” (feminine singular), “são os nossos / são as nossas” (plural).
target_language_example: Este carro é o nosso favorito.
native_language_example: This car is our favorite.

additional_notes: Used to say that something/someone comes before all others in order, ranking, or time. Often followed by a noun ("é o primeiro dia" = "it’s the first day"), or by "de" + plural to mean “the first of …” ("é o primeiro de todos" = "it’s the first of all"). With an infinitive, you often use "a/em" ("não é o primeiro a cometer" = "you’re not the first to make").
target_language_example: Este é o primeiro dia do curso.
native_language_example: This is the first day of the course.

additional_notes: Used to identify, define, or emphasize something: "X é o que..." = "X is what...". It often introduces what matters, what someone says, or what something/someone really is, as in "é o que importa" or "é o que dizem".
target_language_example: Isso é o que eu queria ouvir.
native_language_example: That's what I wanted to hear.

meaning: "It is what it is." (accepting a situation you can’t change)
additional_notes: Used to show acceptance or resignation: things are the way they are, and there’s not much you can do about it. Common in casual conversation after something disappointing or unavoidable.
target_language_example: Queria que fosse diferente, mas é o que é.
native_language_example: I wanted it to be different, but it is what it is.

additional_notes: Used to state that something/someone is in 2nd position in a sequence, ranking, size, or hierarchy. It must agree with the noun: "é o segundo" (masc. singular), "é a segunda" (fem. singular), "são os segundos" (masc. plural), "são as segundas" (fem. plural). Common patterns include: "é o segundo + [noun]" ("Hoje é o segundo dia do mês"), "é o segundo + [adjective]" ("é o segundo maior"), and "é o segundo + em/na/na linha de..." (position/hierarchy).
target_language_example: Hoje é o segundo dia do mês.
native_language_example: Today is the second day of the month.

additional_notes: Used to say something is last in a sequence (time, order, ranking, etc.). It agrees with the thing/person: é o último (masc. singular), é a última (fem. singular), são os últimos (masc. plural/mixed), são as últimas (fem. plural). You can also use it on its own to mean “(he/she) is last,” as in “Tom é o último.”
target_language_example: Este é o último ônibus para o centro.
native_language_example: This is the last bus to downtown.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something is the single one in a group or situation. If no noun follows, it means "the only one." The form changes to match gender and number: é a única, são os únicos, são as únicas. Although único looks like English "unique," in this pattern it usually means "only."
target_language_example: Ele é o único que sabe a resposta.
native_language_example: He is the only one who knows the answer.

additional_notes: Used to say that only one person or thing (the subject) has a certain quality or performs a certain action. Typically followed by a verb phrase (e.g., “é o único que sabe…”, “é o único que está…”). Masculine singular form; for a female subject, it becomes “é a única que”.
target_language_example: Tom é o único que sabe disso.
native_language_example: Tom is the only one who knows that.

additional_notes: Used to describe something’s size with the verb "ser" (é = "is") + adjective. "pequeno" agrees with what it describes: "é pequeno" (masc. singular), "é pequena" (fem. singular), "são pequenos/pequenas" (plural). Often followed by "demais" to mean "too" (e.g., "é pequeno demais" = "it’s too small").
target_language_example: Esse quarto é pequeno, mas confortável.
native_language_example: That room is small, but comfortable.

additional_notes: Used to describe something (or someone) as ideal or without flaws. It’s the verb ser (é = “is”) + the adjective perfeito (“perfect”) in the masculine form; for feminine nouns use “é perfeita” (e.g., A casa é perfeita). Often used as a strong compliment.
target_language_example: Para mim, este plano é perfeito.
native_language_example: For me, this plan is perfect.

additional_notes: Used with "ser" (é) to say something is dangerous. Very common pattern: "É perigoso + infinitive" (e.g., "É perigoso nadar aqui" = "It’s dangerous to swim here"). You can also use it with a noun/pronoun: "Isto é perigoso" ("This is dangerous").
target_language_example: É perigoso andar sozinho à noite.
native_language_example: It’s dangerous to walk alone at night.

additional_notes: Used to say that something can happen or can be done. Often followed by an infinitive: "É possível viajar..." (= "It’s possible to travel..."). In questions, the same phrase is used with rising intonation: "É possível...?"
target_language_example: É possível pagar com cartão?
native_language_example: Is it possible to pay by card?

additional_notes: Used to express possibility or uncertainty. It’s very commonly followed by the subjunctive (e.g., "É possível que ele chegue tarde" = "It’s possible that he arrives late"). In questions it can also sound like surprise or disbelief ("Como é possível que...?" = "How is it possible that...?").
target_language_example: É possível que eu chegue um pouco atrasado.
native_language_example: It’s possible that I’ll arrive a little late.

additional_notes: Impersonal expression meaning “it’s necessary/required.” Common patterns: **é preciso + infinitive** (É preciso observar as regras. = It’s necessary to follow the rules) and **é preciso que + subjunctive** (É preciso que vocês me escutem. = You need to listen to me). In fixed phrases like **nem é preciso dizer que...**, it means “it goes without saying that…”. Note: **preciso** can also mean “accurate/precise,” so don’t confuse it with English “precise” here.
target_language_example: É preciso estudar um pouco todos os dias.
native_language_example: You need to study a little every day.

additional_notes: Used on signs and in rules to say an action is not permitted. It’s the verb ser (é = “is”) + the adjective proibido (“forbidden”). Often followed by an infinitive: É proibido + entrar / fumar / fazer fotos. You may also see agreement with a noun: É proibida a entrada. (“Entry is forbidden.”)
target_language_example: Aqui é proibido fumar.
native_language_example: Smoking is not allowed here.

additional_notes: Used on signs or in rules to say that smoking is not allowed. Word order can vary (e.g., “Aqui é proibido fumar” or “É proibido fumar aqui”). You can replace “fumar” with another activity: “É proibido estacionar” (Parking is prohibited).
target_language_example: Neste prédio, é proibido fumar em todas as áreas comuns.
native_language_example: In this building, smoking is prohibited in all common areas.

meaning: "it’s likely/probable that" (introduces something that is likely to happen or be true).
additional_notes: Used to express probability or a reasonable guess. Very often followed by the subjunctive: "É provável que ele chegue tarde". You can also use it in the middle of a sentence: "O Tom é provável que ainda esteja...".
target_language_example: É provável que a gente chegue depois das oito.
native_language_example: We’ll probably arrive after eight.

additional_notes: Most often appears as part of the structure “X é que você…” meaning “the important/only thing is that you…” or “my opinion is that you…”. It can also be used to introduce an explanation/excuse: “É que você…” = “It’s just that you…”. In questions, “por que é que você…?” adds emphasis, like “why is it that you…?” (often just “why do you…?” in natural English).
target_language_example: O problema é que você não me avisou.
native_language_example: The problem is that you didn’t let me know.

additional_notes: Form of the verb "ser" ("é" = "is") + the adjective "real". Often used to confirm whether something is true/exists ("Então, é real?") or to state that something is genuine ("É real."). Note: "real" can also be a noun meaning Brazil’s currency ("o real"), but in this phrase it’s the adjective "real".
target_language_example: Isso é real ou é só boato?
native_language_example: Is this real, or is it just a rumor?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "ser" ("é" = "is") to emphasize that something is true or to express surprise/doubt, especially in questions ("Ele é realmente...?" = "Is he really/actually...?"). Often translates naturally as "really" or "actually" in English depending on context.
target_language_example: Isso é realmente importante para mim.
native_language_example: That’s really important to me.

meaning: “is rich” (has a lot of money); also “is rich in” (has a lot of something).
additional_notes: Used with the verb ser: (ele/ela/você) é rico/é rica; (eles/elas/vocês) são ricos/são ricas. It can mean financially wealthy (Meu irmão é rico.) or, with em + noun, “rich in” in a broader sense (O Japão não é rico em recursos naturais.).
target_language_example: Para mim não faz diferença se você é rico ou pobre.
native_language_example: It doesn’t matter to me whether you are rich or poor.

additional_notes: Used to say something is of poor quality or negative. Common pattern: "X é ruim" (X is bad) and "X é ruim para Y" (X is bad for Y). Often appears in the negative to soften criticism: "não é ruim" = "not bad" / "pretty good" depending on context.
target_language_example: Dormir pouco é ruim para a saúde.
native_language_example: Sleeping too little is bad for your health.

additional_notes: Used to say a place/situation is safe, or as a yes/no question: “É seguro?” = “Is it safe?” Often followed by a location with “aqui/lá/fora de…” (here/there/outside of…). Negative: “Não é seguro” = “It’s not safe.” Note: “seguro” can also mean “insurance” as a noun, but in “é seguro” it means “safe.”
target_language_example: É seguro andar aqui à noite?
native_language_example: Is it safe to walk here at night?

additional_notes: Used to say that something belongs to someone. Here, seu means "yours" and agrees with the thing owned: é seu (masculine singular), é sua (feminine singular), são seus / são suas (plural). In context, seu can also sometimes mean his, her, or their, so the situation usually makes it clear.
target_language_example: Esse livro é seu.
native_language_example: That book is yours.

meaning: “it’s yours” (feminine form, referring to something feminine like “a bola”, “a escolha”).
additional_notes: Used to say that something belongs to “you” (informal singular: você/tu, depending on the region) and the thing owned is feminine. Often appears as “A/Esta/Essa + noun (feminine) + é sua.” Also used in set phrases like “A escolha é sua” (“The choice is yours”). For masculine nouns, use “é seu” (e.g., “O livro é seu”).
target_language_example: Esta chave é sua?
native_language_example: Is this key yours?

additional_notes: Used to say something is only one thing, or to make it seem simple or limited. In the pattern é só + infinitive, it often means 'you just need to...' or 'all you have to do is...'.
target_language_example: É só esperar mais cinco minutos.
native_language_example: You just need to wait five more minutes.

additional_notes: Used to downplay or minimize something (“nothing serious, just a…”). It’s made of "é" (it is) + "só" (only/just) + an indefinite article. It changes with gender/number: "é só uma" (fem.), "são só uns/umas" (plural).
target_language_example: Calma, é só um erro pequeno.
native_language_example: Relax, it’s just a small mistake.

meaning: “It’s just a …” (referring to a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to minimize or downplay something (“only/just one”, “nothing more than”). It’s followed by a feminine noun: é só uma fase, é só uma meia. With masculine nouns, use “é só um …”.
target_language_example: Calma, é só uma pergunta.
native_language_example: Relax, it’s just a question.

additional_notes: Used to say that there's no longer enough time to do something or that the opportunity has passed. Often followed by "para" + infinitive: "É tarde demais para pedir desculpas." You can add emphasis with "já": "Já é tarde demais."
target_language_example: Desculpa, mas é tarde demais para mudar de ideia.
native_language_example: Sorry, but it's too late to change your mind.

additional_notes: Used to blame someone or something for a situation. It’s normally followed by who/what is to blame, most often with "de" ("É tudo culpa de..."), or contracted forms like "do/da" ("de + o/a"): "É tudo culpa do roteirista." You can also use a possessive: "É tudo culpa sua!" (It’s all your fault!).
target_language_example: Perdemos o voo; é tudo culpa do trânsito.
native_language_example: We missed the flight; it’s all the traffic’s fault.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser ("to be") to mean "it is all/everything". Very common before a noun phrase to emphasize that something is entirely/just that thing: "É tudo influência do Arthur" = "It’s all Arthur’s influence"; "É tudo por sua causa" = "It’s all because of you". Can also mean "it’s all I have left" ("é tudo que me resta").
target_language_example: Não se preocupe; é tudo parte do plano.
native_language_example: Don’t worry; it’s all part of the plan.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize degree with an adjective/adverb: "é tão + adjective" = "is so + adjective". Often appears in comparisons as "tão ... quanto" ("as ... as"): "é tão belo quanto" = "is as beautiful as". Can also be followed by "a ponto de" to mean "so ... that": "é tão poderoso a ponto de..." = "is so powerful that...".
target_language_example: Este filme é tão bom que eu quero ver de novo.
native_language_example: This movie is so good that I want to watch it again.

additional_notes:
Used to emphasize how good/nice something or someone is. It can mean:
- "He/She is so nice" (often with a person + "com"): "Ele é tão bom comigo." (= so good to me).
- "So good at" a skill (with "em"): "Ela é tão boa em xadrez." 
- "It feels so good" (often with "quando" + a situation): "É tão bom quando..." 
Agreement: "bom" changes with gender/number (bom/boa/bons/boas).
target_language_example: É tão bom quando você chega cedo.
native_language_example: It’s so good when you arrive early.

additional_notes: Used to compare difficulty or emphasize how hard something is. Often followed by "como" to make a comparison: "não é tão difícil como..." = "it’s not as difficult as...". In questions, it can express surprise or challenge: "É tão difícil...?" = "Is it really that hard...?"
target_language_example: Aprender a pronúncia no começo é tão difícil, mas depois fica mais fácil.
native_language_example: Learning pronunciation at the beginning is so difficult, but later it gets easier.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize how fun/funny something is. "Tão" = "so" (degree/intensity). "Divertido" can mean "fun" (an enjoyable activity) or "funny" (makes you laugh), depending on context. Often appears with "(não) ... assim" to soften or contrast: "não é tão divertido assim" = "it’s not *that* fun/funny."
target_language_example: Viajar com amigos é tão divertido!
native_language_example: Traveling with friends is so fun!

additional_notes: Used to emphasize importance. Often followed by comparisons with quanto/como (“as … as”): é tão importante quanto/como…. With assim (“é tão importante assim?”), it often expresses doubt or surprise (“Is it really that important?”). You can also add para mim/para ele (“to me/to him”) to show who it matters to.
target_language_example: Isso é tão importante para mim quanto a minha família.
native_language_example: This is as important to me as my family.

additional_notes: Used to identify or describe someone or something before a singular masculine noun. It combines é ('is') with um ('a' / 'one'). For feminine nouns, Portuguese uses é uma.
target_language_example: Meu irmão é um professor excelente.
native_language_example: My brother is an excellent teacher.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is (or is considered) a friend. Often follows a name or pronoun (e.g., “O Tom é um amigo.”). You can add possessives like “um amigo nosso” (a friend of ours) or expand it: “um amigo da família” (a family friend), “um amigo de um amigo” (a friend of a friend).
target_language_example: Ele é um amigo de verdade.
native_language_example: He’s a true friend.

additional_notes: Used to identify something as an animal. Structure: "é" (it is) + "um" (a) + "animal" (animal). With a specific animal noun: "A raposa é um animal selvagem" (“The fox is a wild animal”). You can add adjectives after "animal" (e.g., "fiel" loyal, "perigoso" dangerous, "forte" strong).
target_language_example: Esse bicho é um animal noturno.
native_language_example: That creature is a nocturnal animal.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (é) to state that someone is an artist (profession/identity). The phrase agrees with the subject: for a woman, you’d typically say “é uma artista.” It can be expanded with adjectives (e.g., brilhante, maravilhoso) or a relative clause describing the type of art.
target_language_example: O meu filho é um artista que pinta quadros.
native_language_example: My son is an artist who paints pictures.

additional_notes: Used to state someone’s profession/identity: "[Name] é um ator." The verb "é" is from "ser" (to be) and is used for roles/professions. For a woman, say "é uma atriz".
target_language_example: Ele é um ator famoso no Brasil.
native_language_example: He is a famous actor in Brazil.

meaning: "is a beautiful" / "is a fine" (used before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with a noun to describe it positively. It must agree with the noun: masculine singular é um belo (país), feminine singular é uma bela (cidade), masculine plural são uns belos, feminine plural são umas belas. Depending on context, belo can mean "beautiful" or more generally "fine/great" (e.g., a fine example/design).
target_language_example: Lisboa é um belo lugar para visitar.
native_language_example: Lisbon is a beautiful place to visit.

meaning: 'he is a good man' (a good person, especially male).
additional_notes: Used to describe a man's character positively (kind, decent, trustworthy). Often said about someone even if you’re not close to them ("Ele não é meu amigo, mas..."). For women, you’d say "é uma boa mulher"; for a general (gender-neutral) version, "é uma boa pessoa". The literal structure is "é" (is) + "um" (a) + "bom" (good) + "homem" (man).
target_language_example: Ele comete erros, mas no fundo é um bom homem.
native_language_example: He makes mistakes, but deep down he's a good man.

meaning: "is a guy" / "is a (certain kind of) person" (about a man).
additional_notes: Used with adjectives to describe a man: "Ele/Tom é um cara + adjective". "Cara" is informal and common in everyday Brazilian Portuguese; in more formal contexts you can use "homem" or "rapaz" (depending on age). In some contexts, "cara" can be more general like "person," but it most often refers to a male.
target_language_example: Ele é um cara muito legal.
native_language_example: He’s a really nice guy.

additional_notes: Often used with an adjective to classify someone/something: "é um caso clássico" (a classic case), "é um caso raro" (a rare case). In set phrases it can be more idiomatic, e.g. "é um caso perdido" = "he/she is a lost cause" (someone who probably won’t change or improve).
target_language_example: Isso é um caso típico de falta de comunicação.
native_language_example: That’s a typical case of lack of communication.

meaning: “is a citizen” (a national of a country).
additional_notes: Used to state someone’s citizenship/nationality. Often followed by a nationality adjective (italiano, australiano, canadense, estadunidense) or by “de/do/da + country” (cidadão do Brasil / cidadão de Portugal). In questions you’ll hear: “Você é um cidadão de que país?” Can also take descriptive adjectives like “leal” (e.g., “um cidadão leal”). Feminine form: “é uma cidadã”.
target_language_example: Mario é um cidadão italiano.
native_language_example: Mario is an Italian citizen.

additional_notes: An insult used to call someone a coward. With the verb "ser" (to be): "Você é um covarde" = "You’re a coward"; "Ele é um covarde" = "He’s a coward"; "É um covarde!" can be said without naming the subject (it’s understood from context). Feminine form: "é uma covarde" (for a woman).
target_language_example: Ele é um covarde e não quer admitir.
native_language_example: He’s a coward and doesn’t want to admit it.

additional_notes: Used to say that an action is against the law, or (more loosely/hyperbolically) that something is morally outrageous or unacceptable. Common pattern: “Em [place], é um crime + infinitive” (In [place], it’s a crime to + verb).
target_language_example: Aqui, é um crime dirigir sem carteira de motorista.
native_language_example: Here, it’s a crime to drive without a driver’s license.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something belongs to a group (often followed by a superlative like “mais + adjective”: “é um dos mais famosos” = “is one of the most famous”). Agreement changes with gender/number: “é um dos …” (masc. plural), “é uma das …” (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Lisboa é um dos destinos mais populares de Portugal.
native_language_example: Lisbon is one of the most popular destinations in Portugal.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser (é) to identify someone as a student. Refers to a male student (um estudante). For a female student, you typically say é uma estudante. It can be followed by a qualifier like universitário (“university/college”). In the negative, you typically say não é um estudante (“is not a student”).
target_language_example: Tom é um estudante universitário.
native_language_example: Tom is a university student.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone or something as outstanding in a role or category. It’s followed by a masculine singular noun (often a profession/role): “Ele é um excelente professor.” For feminine, change only the article (and the noun if it has gender): “Ela é uma excelente professora.” For plural: “Eles/Elas são excelentes …”. “Excelente” itself doesn’t change for gender, only for number (excelentes).
target_language_example: Tom é um excelente advogado.
native_language_example: Tom is an excellent lawyer.

meaning: is a great ... / is a big ...
additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun to describe someone or something as great/important (often) or big/large (sometimes). It typically appears as "é um grande + noun" (masc.). For feminine nouns, use "é uma grande + noun". Note: placing "grande" before the noun often suggests greatness/importance ("um grande homem" = a great man), while after the noun it more often suggests physical size ("um homem grande" = a big/tall man).
target_language_example: Ele é um grande homem.
native_language_example: He is a great man.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "ser" to describe someone as exceptionally intelligent or gifted. It can be sincere praise, or sometimes ironic depending on tone and context. Agreement: for a woman you can say "é uma gênia" (also common to hear "é um gênio" even for women in casual speech).
target_language_example: Você é um gênio por ter resolvido isso tão rápido.
native_language_example: You're a genius for solving that so fast.

meaning: "(he) is a hero." / "is a hero." (with an implied subject, depending on context)
additional_notes: Used to say that someone (male) is a hero. "é" is the present tense of "ser" (to be) for ele/ela/você. For "I am a hero," say "sou um herói"; for a female hero, say "é uma heroína". You can intensify with "de verdade" (a real/true hero) or specify with adjectives like "nacional" (national).
target_language_example: Ele acha que é um herói.
native_language_example: He thinks he is a hero.

additional_notes: Used with the verb ser ("to be") + um homem ("a man"). It can be literal (an adult male: "Ele é um homem") or used to emphasize character/qualities with an adjective or complement (e.g., "é um homem honesto", "é um homem em quem se pode confiar"). For a woman, you’d say "é uma mulher".
target_language_example: Ele é um homem de palavra.
native_language_example: He is a man of his word.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **ser** to insult someone’s character/intelligence. It’s rude/offensive in most situations—use with care. **Idiota** agrees in gender/number: **é um idiota** (he/it is an idiot), **é uma idiota** (she/it is an idiot), **são idiotas** (they are idiots).
target_language_example: Não acredito que ele fez isso — é um idiota.
native_language_example: I can’t believe he did that — he’s an idiot.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to say that something is a place, often followed by an adjective or description: “X é um lugar incrível/famoso/bonito.” You can also add “de + noun” to describe the type of place: “um lugar de classe” (“a classy place”).
target_language_example: Este bairro é um lugar tranquilo para morar.
native_language_example: This neighborhood is a peaceful place to live.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "ser" (é = "is") to identify someone as a boy. "Um" means "a". Often followed by adjectives or descriptions (e.g., "É um menino tímido" = "He’s a shy boy"). In Portuguese, the subject pronoun (ele = he) is often omitted when it’s clear from context.
target_language_example: Ele é um menino muito inteligente.
native_language_example: He is a very smart boy.

additional_notes: Used to say (often strongly) that a man lies or can’t be trusted. Feminine: "é uma mentirosa". Plural: "são mentirosos/mentirosas". Often used after a name or pronoun: "Ele é um mentiroso."
target_language_example: Não acredite nele — ele é um mentiroso.
native_language_example: Don’t believe him—he’s a liar.

meaning: "it’s a miracle" (something surprising or hard to believe).
additional_notes: Used both literally (a miracle) and as an exaggeration meaning “it’s amazing” or “I can’t believe it happened.” Very common pattern: “É um milagre que + subjunctive” to say it’s surprising that something is true (e.g., “É um milagre que ele esteja vivo.”).
target_language_example: É um milagre que você tenha chegado a tempo.
native_language_example: It’s a miracle you made it on time.

additional_notes: Used to say that something (often a word like Tom, Brigitte, etc.) is a name, sometimes adding extra information: nationality/origin ("é um nome francês"), a description ("é um nome legal" = a cool/nice name), or details like spelling/length ("é um nome de três letras" = a three-letter name).
target_language_example: Sofia é um nome muito comum no Brasil.
native_language_example: Sofia is a very common name in Brazil.

additional_notes: Used to state that something (a place/territory) is a country. Often followed by more information with adjectives or clauses: “é um país independente/desenvolvido/grande…”. Note the structure: [Place] + é + um país. In plural: “são países”.
target_language_example: Portugal é um país pequeno, mas muito bonito.
native_language_example: Portugal is a small country, but very beautiful.

meaning: “It’s a pleasure” (nice to meet you / glad to).
additional_notes: Used as a polite, formal-friendly phrase to show pleasure or appreciation about meeting someone or doing something. Often followed by an infinitive: “É um prazer + verb” (e.g., “É um prazer estar aqui.”). With “conhecer” it means “Nice to meet you”: “É um prazer conhecê-lo(a).” You can intensify it with words like “imenso” (“É um prazer imenso...”).
target_language_example: É um prazer ajudar você hoje.
native_language_example: It’s a pleasure to help you today.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is (or might be) an issue. Often followed by an adjective (e.g., grave) or a type of problem (e.g., médico). In questions ("É um problema?"), it means "Is it a problem?"
target_language_example: Chegar um pouco atrasado é um problema?
native_language_example: Is arriving a little late a problem?

additional_notes: Used both literally (talking about dreams) and figuratively to say something feels unbelievably good, perfect, or hard to believe. Often said on its own as an exclamation: “É um sonho!”
target_language_example: Viajar para Portugal é um sonho para mim.
native_language_example: Traveling to Portugal is a dream for me.

additional_notes: Used to classify or describe something by category. It’s often followed by a noun (e.g., “uma flor”, “um animal”). You can adjust for gender/number: “é uma espécie de” (similar), “são um tipo de” (they are a kind of).
target_language_example: Isso é um tipo de comida típica daqui.
native_language_example: That’s a kind of food that’s typical from here.

additional_notes: Used to describe something as a job, task, or piece of work, often with an adjective: é um trabalho difícil (it’s a difficult job), pesado (hard work), enfadonho (boring), excelente (excellent work). You can also use it in questions: É um trabalho pesado? (“Is it hard work?”). In some contexts, it can imply effort rather than employment.
target_language_example: Arrumar a casa é um trabalho cansativo, mas necessário.
native_language_example: Cleaning the house is tiring work, but necessary.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to emphasize that someone or something strongly fits that description (often meaning “a real,” “a true,” “a genuine”). Agree it with the noun: é um verdadeiro (masc. singular), é uma verdadeira (fem. singular), são verdadeiros / são verdadeiras (plural). Common in compliments (um verdadeiro cavalheiro) or criticism (um verdadeiro covarde).
target_language_example: Tom é um verdadeiro líder.
native_language_example: Tom is a true leader.

meaning: "is a great/excellent" (talking about a masculine singular person/thing).
additional_notes: Used to praise someone/something: subject + "é" (is) + "um" (a) + "ótimo" (great/excellent). It agrees with gender/number: "é uma ótima" (feminine), "são ótimos/ótimas" (plural). Without the article, "é ótimo" often means "it’s great" (about a situation/idea).
target_language_example: Ele é um ótimo professor.
native_language_example: He is a great teacher.

meaning: "is one of my …" (one of my favorites / one of my own; one of the ones in my group).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something belongs to your set/group (often followed by a plural noun like "poetas", "pratos", "pacientes") or that it’s among your favorites when combined with "favoritos". Agreement changes with gender/number of the implied plural noun: masculine plural "é um dos meus" (e.g., "autores"), feminine plural "é uma das minhas" (e.g., "músicas"). Common pattern: "X é um dos meus + [plural noun] (+ favoritos)".
target_language_example: Frango assado é um dos meus pratos favoritos.
native_language_example: Roast chicken is one of my favorite dishes.

additional_notes: used before a feminine singular noun to identify or classify someone or something. At the start of a sentence, it often corresponds to 'it's a/an' in English.
target_language_example: Lisboa é uma cidade muito bonita.
native_language_example: Lisbon is a very beautiful city.

meaning: "is an art" (something takes skill, creativity, or practice).
additional_notes: Used literally to say something is a form of art (e.g., literature, poetry), and also figuratively to mean it’s not an exact science and requires judgment, sensitivity, or practice. Common pattern: "X é uma arte".
target_language_example: Cozinhar bem é uma arte.
native_language_example: Cooking well is an art.

additional_notes: Used to describe something or someone feminine: “É uma bela casa” (a beautiful house) or “Ela é uma bela mulher” (a beautiful woman). It typically comes right before a feminine noun (bela mulher, bela garota, bela casa). For masculine nouns, use “é um belo” (e.g., “É um belo dia”).
target_language_example: Ela é uma bela artista.
native_language_example: She is a beautiful artist.

additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns: é uma boa ideia/câmera/matéria (“it’s a good idea/camera/subject”). On its own, “É uma boa!” can mean “That’s a good idea/option!” Feminine form: uma boa (masculine would be “um bom”).
target_language_example: É uma boa ideia sair mais cedo.
native_language_example: It’s a good idea to leave earlier.

meaning: "it’s a good idea" / "that’s a good idea."
additional_notes: Used to say that a plan or suggestion is sensible or recommended. Often used in questions to ask for advice or someone’s opinion: "É uma boa ideia...?" (= Is it a good idea to...?). You can add "acho que" to soften it: "Acho que é uma boa ideia" (= I think it’s a good idea).
target_language_example: Acho que é uma boa ideia reservar com antecedência.
native_language_example: I think it’s a good idea to book in advance.

meaning: 'is a city' (used to describe a place).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "ser" ("é" = "is") to identify something as a city or to describe it: "X é uma cidade + adjective" (e.g., grande, segura, bonita). "Uma" agrees with the feminine noun "cidade". The plural is "são cidades".
target_language_example: Lisboa é uma cidade muito interessante.
native_language_example: Lisbon is a very interesting city.

meaning: "it’s something"; used to describe or emphasize a fact/quality (often with an adjective).
additional_notes: Very common with an adjective: "é uma coisa séria/maravilhosa/boa" = "it’s a serious/wonderful/good thing." Can also introduce a contrast: "X é uma coisa, Y é outra" = "X is one thing, Y is another." Sometimes used for emphasis in casual speech: "É uma coisa de louco" = "It’s crazy/insane."
target_language_example: Aprender português é uma coisa difícil, mas vale a pena.
native_language_example: Learning Portuguese is something difficult, but it’s worth it.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone as a child (often to explain behavior: "But he’s a child"). With names you can say "O/A [nome] é uma criança...". For age you typically use "tem" ("Ele tem 7 anos" = He is 7), not "é 7".
target_language_example: Ela é uma criança muito educada.
native_language_example: She is a very well-mannered child.

meaning: “is one of the” (referring to a feminine singular item).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something belongs to a group: “X é uma das + plural noun/superlative.” For masculine singular, use “é um dos” (e.g., “Ele é um dos melhores”).
target_language_example: Esta praia é uma das mais bonitas da região.
native_language_example: This beach is one of the most beautiful in the region.

meaning: "is a way of" / "is a form of."
additional_notes: Used to define or describe something by classifying it as a type of thing or as one method/means of doing something. Common in explanations and definitions. It’s followed by a noun ("uma forma de governo") or by an infinitive verb ("uma forma de ajudar").
target_language_example: Trabalhar em equipe é uma forma de aprender mais rápido.
native_language_example: Working as a team is a way to learn faster.

additional_notes: Used to identify someone as a girl. "Garota" often means “girl/young woman,” and can also be used more generally like “a girl” (similar to English). In Portuguese you can drop the subject when it’s clear from context, so "É uma garota" can mean “She’s a girl.”
target_language_example: Ela é uma garota muito inteligente.
native_language_example: She’s a very smart girl.

meaning: “is a great / big (one)” (used to emphasize size, importance, or intensity).
additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns: é uma grande + noun (e.g., nação, ameaça, ilha, capital, parte, honra). Often means “great” in the sense of “important/remarkable” (uma grande honra, uma grande nação) or “big/large” in the sense of physical size (uma grande ilha). With abstract nouns it commonly means “a major” (uma grande ameaça = a major threat). For masculine nouns, use “é um grande …” (e.g., é um grande problema).
target_language_example: Esta é uma grande oportunidade para nós.
native_language_example: This is a great opportunity for us.

additional_notes: Used to say that something (often the name of a language) is a language, and it’s commonly followed by an adjective: “O francês é uma língua interessante.” You can also specify which language it is: “O francês é uma língua românica.” (Note: when naming languages in Portuguese, they’re often not capitalized: “o francês”, “o italiano”.)
target_language_example: O português é uma língua muito falada no Brasil.
native_language_example: Portuguese is a language widely spoken in Brazil.

additional_notes: Used to identify or describe someone as a girl. "É" can mean "he is," "she is," or "it is" depending on context, and "uma" is the feminine singular "a." You can add adjectives after "menina" (e.g., "é uma menina tímida" = "she is a shy girl").
target_language_example: Ela é uma menina muito inteligente.
native_language_example: She is a very smart girl.

additional_notes: A crude, offensive way to say something is very bad, awful, or disappointing. Used with a subject before it (e.g., "Isso é uma merda" = "This is crap"). Not appropriate in polite conversation; prefer "é ruim" (it’s bad) or "é horrível" (it’s awful).
target_language_example: Esse filme é uma merda.
native_language_example: This movie sucks.

additional_notes: "É" is the 3rd person singular of "ser" (to be), used for identity/definition. It’s often followed by an adjective or description: "É uma mulher bonita/moderna". You can also use it to emphasize someone’s status or identity: "Ela é uma mulher" (She is a woman). For men, the parallel phrase is "é um homem".
target_language_example: Ela é uma mulher forte e inteligente.
native_language_example: She is a strong and intelligent woman.

meaning: "is a very" (used to describe someone with an adjective).
additional_notes: Used with a following adjective to describe someone’s personality or characteristics: "[Name] é uma pessoa muito + adjective". You can also say "Ele/Ela é muito + adjective" (more direct) or "Ele/Ela é uma pessoa muito + adjective" (a bit more descriptive). The word "pessoa" is feminine, so adjectives may appear in feminine form (e.g., "uma pessoa muito simpática") even when talking about a man; in everyday speech you may also hear masculine agreement with male people.
target_language_example: O João é uma pessoa muito calma.
native_language_example: João is a very calm person.

additional_notes: Used to say something is a joke (a funny story), or to question it. In context and with tone, it can also express disbelief or annoyance, like "You’ve got to be kidding" or "This is ridiculous." Often appears as a statement ("É uma piada!") or a question ("É uma piada?").
target_language_example: Você está falando sério ou é uma piada?
native_language_example: Are you serious or is it a joke?

meaning: "it's a matter of" / "it's a question of".
additional_notes: Used to say what something mainly depends on or comes down to (often followed by a noun like confiança, prioridades, gosto, tempo). Can express importance or urgency depending on context (e.g., “uma questão de segundos” = “a matter of seconds”).
target_language_example: Não é sorte; é uma questão de prática.
native_language_example: It’s not luck; it’s a matter of practice.

additional_notes: Used to praise something described by a feminine noun. Structure: "[subject] é uma ótima + noun" (e.g., cidade, pergunta, religião, piloto). It’s the feminine singular form: uma ótima. For masculine nouns, you’d use "um ótimo" (e.g., "é um ótimo livro").
target_language_example: Ela é uma ótima professora.
native_language_example: She is a great teacher.

additional_notes: Used to confirm that something is true or correct. It can stand alone as a full response ("É verdade.") or come after a subject or clause, as in "isso é verdade" or "nada disso é verdade".
target_language_example: É verdade, mas ainda não entendo.
native_language_example: That's true, but I still don't understand.

additional_notes: Used to ask for confirmation or to state that something is true. In questions it often means “is it true that…?” (with rising intonation or a question mark). In statements it means “it’s true that…”. You can also hear the shorter form “é verdade?” = “is that true?”
target_language_example: É verdade que você mora aqui desde criança?
native_language_example: Is it true that you’ve lived here since you were a child?

additional_notes: Used to ask for confirmation about something you heard or suspect. It’s a neutral-to-slightly-challenging way to check a fact. In real speech, you’ll also hear: “É verdade que…?” (without “você”) or “É verdade?” when the rest is understood.
target_language_example: É verdade que você vai se mudar no mês que vem?
native_language_example: Is it true that you’re going to move next month?

additional_notes: Used to ask for confirmation about something you heard or suspect. "Vocês" is the plural "you" (common in Brazil), and the verb that follows is typically in the plural: "vocês fizeram", "vocês foram", etc. You can also use it as a statement: "É verdade que vocês vão embora amanhã."
target_language_example: É verdade que vocês vão viajar amanhã?
native_language_example: Is it true that you’re going to travel tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to introduce something you consider clear or evident. Often followed by a full clause (subject + verb): “É óbvio que + [sentence]”. It can sound a bit blunt or emphatic depending on tone/context; in more polite speech you can soften it with “Acho que…” or “Parece que…”.
target_language_example: É óbvio que ela não vai chegar a tempo.
native_language_example: It’s obvious that she won’t arrive on time.

meaning: “Yeah, but …” (agreeing/acknowledging, then adding a contrast or objection).
additional_notes: Common conversational filler, especially in spoken Brazilian Portuguese. “É” here works like “yeah/right/true,” not literally “it is.” Often used to soften disagreement or to pivot to a different point.
target_language_example: É, mas eu não posso ir hoje.
native_language_example: Yeah, but I can’t go today.

meaning: “Yeah, I…” / “Well, I…” (a casual way to start a reply).
additional_notes: Used in conversation as a filler/lead-in before saying what you think or confirming something. It often sounds like you’re agreeing, admitting, or acknowledging (“Yeah, I know / I agree / I did”). Very common in spoken Brazilian Portuguese; you’ll also hear it as “É, eu…” with a pause.
target_language_example: É, eu acho que você tem razão.
native_language_example: Yeah, I think you’re right.

meaning: time of year; season (period in the year).
additional_notes: Used to refer to a particular period of the calendar year, often linked to weather, holidays, tourism, or typical activities. Very common with demonstratives like “esta/nessa época do ano” (this/that time of year). Not the same as “estação do ano” (the four seasons: primavera, verão, outono, inverno), though it can overlap in meaning.
target_language_example: Nesta época do ano, as praias ficam cheias.
native_language_example: At this time of year, the beaches get crowded.

additional_notes: Used for glasses that protect your eyes from the sun. In Portuguese it’s usually plural (óculos), even when referring to one pair, so you say: "Meus óculos de sol" (my sunglasses) and "Os óculos de sol" (the sunglasses). You may also hear the shorter "óculos escuros" (dark glasses).
target_language_example: Esqueci meus óculos de sol no carro.
native_language_example: I forgot my sunglasses in the car.

additional_notes: Refers to glasses with dark/tinted lenses, usually to protect from sunlight or to hide your eyes. Often used with verbs like usar/estar usando (to wear), pôr (to put on), and tirar (to take off). You’ll also hear simply óculos when the context makes it clear.
target_language_example: Está muito sol—vou pôr meus óculos escuros.
native_language_example: It’s very sunny—I’m going to put on my sunglasses.

additional_notes: Refers to the bus used to take children/students to and from school. You’ll often see it with verbs like pegar (to take/catch), esperar (to wait for), and dirigir (to drive): pegar/esperar o ônibus escolar; dirigir um ônibus escolar.
target_language_example: As crianças pegaram o ônibus escolar às sete da manhã.
native_language_example: The children took the school bus at seven in the morning.

additional_notes: Used when it’s the final opportunity to do something before it becomes impossible or the moment passes. Often said with urgency or as a warning (“Essa é a sua última chance!”). You’ll commonly see it with "uma" or "a" (uma última chance / a sua última chance) and followed by "de" + infinitive ("última chance de fazer...").
target_language_example: Você tem uma última chance de me dizer a verdade.
native_language_example: You have one last chance to tell me the truth.

additional_notes: Used to express surprise because someone is very unexpected in a situation. Often followed by context: “...aqui”, “...para me ajudar”, “...no trabalho”, etc. You can also hear variations like “a última pessoa que eu esperava ver”.
target_language_example: Você é a última pessoa que eu esperava encontrar aqui.
native_language_example: You’re the last person I expected to run into here.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s most recent past occurrence of an action. It’s typically followed by a verb phrase (often in the past): “a última vez que você + [verb]”. Very common in questions starting with “Quando foi a última vez que você…?” (“When was the last time you…?”).
target_language_example: Quando foi a última vez que você foi ao médico?
native_language_example: When was the last time you went to the doctor?

additional_notes: Used to say it’s the final day of an activity, period, job, school, etc. Often followed by "de"/"da"/"do" to specify what it’s the last day of: "o último dia de aula" (the last day of class), "o último dia da sua vida" (the last day of your life).
target_language_example: Amanhã é o meu último dia no trabalho.
native_language_example: Tomorrow is my last day at work.
